Kyrgyzstan to build new oil refinery

Kyrgyzstan to build new oil refinery
Kyrgyzstan is set to build a new oil refinery in Kochkor Ata with an annual capacity of 450,000 tons of petroleum products. President Sadyr Zhaparov announced this at a meeting with local officials and residents of Nooken and Mailuu-Suu during his working visit to the Jalal-Abad region, Qazinform News Agency learned from Kabar.
According to Zhaparov, the facility is expected to reach full operational capacity by the end of this year, creating approximately 300 jobs.
The president also addressed efforts to restore the Mailuu-Suu Electric Lamp Plant.
"The enterprise has been receiving support since 2022, and the establishment of the Mailuu-Suu Industrial Park is intended to help attract investment, launch new production facilities, and introduce modern technologies," Sadyr Zhaparov stated
Earlier, it was reported that Batumi Sea Port handled 6.25 million tons of cargo from January to September 2026, marking a 13% increase year on year, with growth recorded across all major cargo categories. The port is operated by a subsidiary of Kazakhstan’s oil pipeline company KazTransOil.

Zelensky accuses Trump of ‘totally false’ statements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
23:58:43 UTC
08:58:43 KST

Zelensky accuses Trump of ‘totally false’ statements
President Donald Trump made “totally false” statements when he blamed rising US diesel prices on Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, Vladimir Zelensky has claimed, accusing the American leader of “deflecting the focus away from Iran.”
Zelensky’s remarks came amid a growing spat with Trump, who has repeatedly accused Kiev of exacerbating the global energy crisis with continued attacks on Russian oil infrastructure.
Russia has historically been the world’s second-largest exporter of diesel fuel, behind only the United States, accounting for roughly 10% of global exports. Disruptions to Russian supplies have tightened the global market, driving up prices even in countries that do not directly import Russian fuel, including the US.
“The volume of diesel exports is so negligible from Russia that it has zero impact on prices in the US. That is totally false information,” the Ukrainian leader claimed during an appearance on Steven Bartlett’s The Diary of a CEO podcast on Thursday.
If Trump cares so much about US energy prices, then “why do American companies export energy?” Zelensky wondered rhetorically. “Well, because how can the president of the United States ban private sector exports?... It sells and money comes in.”
Zelensky accused Trump of unfairly “deflecting the focus away from Iran” and lamented that “everything gets shifted onto us and I’m made the target as the leader of our country.”
According to Zelensky, “the root of the problem” lies in the Strait of Hormuz, where crude exports and other maritime traffic have dwindled to a trickle following the start of the US-Israeli military campaign against Iran in February.
Earlier this month, Zelensky similarly hit out at what he described as a “weak decision” by the Trump administration after Washington temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel exports to ease the global fuel crisis.
Moscow agreed to immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to American and global markets, followed by 500,000 tons in November, another million tons shortly thereafter, and potentially another 3 million tons, depending on refinery capacity.
Washington struck the deal with Moscow after Zelensky had repeatedly ignored Trump’s requests to stop strikes on Russian refineries. “We said, you can do whatever you want to Russia, don’t hit the refineries, because that’s a world problem that’s caused,” the US president recounted earlier this month.
“And what does he do? He goes and hits the diesel fuel,” Trump lamented, accusing Zelensky of wanting to “make problems for the world.”
Trump also said he found it more difficult to deal with Zelensky than with Russian President Vladimir Putin, suggesting that Ukraine should get a new leader who would not obstruct Washington’s mediation efforts.
Rising fuel prices have become an increasingly pressing domestic issue for Trump ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. US diesel prices surged to record highs above $6.50 per gallon in September, with prices in California exceeding $8 in some areas.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said last week that Zelensky was directly challenging Trump by refusing to accept a deal aimed at easing the global diesel shortage.
In recent months, Ukraine has ramped up long-range strikes on targets inside Russia, including civilian and energy infrastructure, amid continued setbacks at the front. Moscow has denounced the attacks as acts of terrorism and responded with strikes on Ukrainian military-related facilities.

Arab nations condemn deadly funeral attack at church in Jordan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
23:57:40 UTC
08:57:40 KST

Rania R.a. Abushamala
24 October 2026•Update: 24 October 2026
Officials, institutions, and factions from 11 Arab countries condemned Friday’s terror attack on mourners attending a funeral at a church in southern Jordan, expressing solidarity with the kingdom and rejecting attempts to sow division.
Condemnations came from Lebanon, Syria, Iraq, Palestine, Egypt, the United Arab Emirates, Oman, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and Bahrain, as well as the Arab League and the Arab Interior Ministers Council.
The attack killed seven people and injured 27, according to Jordan’s Public Security Directorate.
Arab League Secretary-General Nabil Fahmy denounced attacks on places of worship as “an unacceptable terrorist act and a crime condemned by every standard,” pledging support for Jordan’s measures to protect its security and stability.
He urged national unity against attempts to spread discord, division, and chaos.
The Arab Interior Ministers Council expressed “full solidarity” with Jordan and confidence in its security agencies’ ability to apprehend the perpetrators. 
Lebanon, Syria, Iraq, Palestine
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said the attack violated the sanctity of places of worship, the deceased, and mourners.
“Terrorism has neither a religion nor a homeland,” he said, warning that it seeks to undermine coexistence and sow discord.
The Syrian Foreign Ministry expressed support for Jordan’s security, stability, and national unity.
Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein conveyed Baghdad’s solidarity in a call with his Jordanian counterpart Ayman Safadi.
The Palestinian presidency said targeting innocent people and places of worship is a crime that cannot be justified under any pretext, stressing that the attack will not undermine Jordanians’ unity.
Palestinian Vice President Hussein al-Sheikh, Hamas, and Palestine’s Higher Presidential Committee for Church Affairs also condemned the attack.
The committee urged Palestinian churches to ring their bells at 9 pm Friday and urged Muslims and Christians to join a solidarity gathering Sunday at 11 am in Bethlehem’s Manger Square. 
Egypt, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Oman, Kuwait, Qatar, and Bahrain
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi pledged support for Jordan against “all forms of violence and terrorism.” The Foreign Ministry and Al-Azhar Grand Imam Ahmed al-Tayeb also condemned the attack.
Saudi Arabia and the UAE rejected terrorism aimed at undermining Jordan’s security, while Oman condemned violence against places of worship and the terrorizing of civilians.
Kuwait and Qatar backed Jordan’s measures to preserve its security and stability. Bahrain also expressed support for efforts to pursue the perpetrators and bring them to justice.
Jordanian authorities said unidentified gunmen opened fire on St. George Greek Orthodox Church in Hamoud, Karak. Citing an unnamed source, public broadcaster Al-Mamlaka TV reported that two assailants stepped out of a vehicle and opened fire during a funeral.
Interior Minister Mazin Al Farrayeh said security agencies are working around the clock to find the attackers, stressing that it is too “early to discuss the perpetrators and their affiliations.”
King Abdullah II pledged the harshest punishment for those responsible.

Senators plan to block Trump’s nominees over Ukraine satellite network restrictions — NYT

Unknown Publisher

23:44:17 UTC
08:44:17 KST

NEW YORK, October 24. /TASS/. Senators from the Republican and Democratic parties have warned the White House that they will block the confirmation of US President Donald Trump’s government nominees unless the administration guarantees the restoration of Ukraine’s access to satellite communications, The New York Times (NYT) reported citing sources.
It is noted that disagreements between the senators and the administration may escalate after the November 3 midterm elections, when Republicans will likely try to secure the confirmation of dozens of Trump’s nominees to various positions before the new Congress begins its work.
Earlier, American Congresswoman Anna Paulina Luna (a Republican from Florida) called on Democratic lawmakers to stop advocating for the continuation of the Ukrainian conflict and to support Trump’s efforts to resolve it.
The American leader said on Thursday that Ukraine’s access to Starshield military·grade satellite communications was restored. He was commenting on media reports saying he had asked SpaceX CEO Elon Musk to lift restrictions on the use of Starshield in Ukraine. However, former adviser to the Ukrainian Defense Minister Sergey Sternenko later said that the restrictions are partially still in place.

Snow leopard conservation efforts in SW China's Xizang
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
07:39:03 CST
08:39:03 KST

Staff members of the Nainang ecological and cultural protection center walk on the way to collect the infrared cameras in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, Oct. 22, 2026.
Snow leopards are under China's highest national-level protection and are listed as vulnerable by the International Union for Conservation of Nature. World Snow Leopard Day falls on October 23 annually.
Nainang Valley, which is only 38 kilometers away from the urban area of Lhasa in a straight line, is a rare stable habitat for snow leopards located in the suburb of a city in Xizang.
The Nainang ecological and cultural protection center in Doilungdeqen District was established in May 2023. To date, 40 snow leopards have been identified and named within the 200-square-kilometer monitoring area of Nainang Valley. (Xinhua/Jigme Dorje)

Cuban FM denounces Trump's new military threat
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
07:38:44 CST
08:38:44 KST

HAVANA, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez Friday denounced a new threat of military intervention against the Caribbean nation by U.S. President Donald Trump.
In a post on X, Rodriguez rejected "any threat regarding U.S. ambitions toward Cuba" in response to remarks by Trump, who said Friday that U.S. ships "will pass" Cuba on their way back from Iran.
"They'll raise up their hands. And then we're going to send (Secretary of State) Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal," Trump said at a campaign rally in Fort Myers, in the southern U.S. state of Florida. He said one of the ships would stop about 50 yards (about 46 meters) off the coast.
"On our shores there are beautiful beaches, but also diente de perro (a jagged coastal coral formation), inhospitable to those who arrive with hostile aims and a thirst for domination," Rodriguez wrote.
Rodriguez, Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel and other officials have denounced U.S. threats of military intervention, which have escalated since early 2026, and have defended the island's sovereignty and its right to self-defense.
In May, Trump said in Florida that the United States would be taking over Cuba "almost immediately." ■

Brazil's electoral court seeks explanations from Meta, X ahead of runoff
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
07:38:36 CST
08:38:36 KST

BRASILIA, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Brazil's Superior Electoral Court (TSE) has asked social media companies Meta and X to provide, within 24 hours, technical explanations of their use of artificial intelligence, the distribution of political content, the publication of electoral ads and the removal of posts ahead of the presidential runoff on Sunday, Oct. 25.
The decision, announced Friday, was made Thursday night by the court's inspector general Ricardo Villas Boas Cueva, who set a daily fine of 500,000 reais (about 100,000 U.S. dollars) for each company in case of unjustified noncompliance.
The measure responds to an electoral investigation brought by a political coalition supporting incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who is seeking reelection against opposition candidate Flavio Bolsonaro.
With the runoff approaching, Cueva demanded that the companies explain the criteria for content distribution and any differences in treatment between the candidates competing for the presidency.
United Nations experts sent a letter to Meta earlier this week seeking an explanation of alleged unequal treatment of the presidential candidates in Brazil. ■

Trump modifies scope of 50-pct tariffs on Canadian products
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
07:38:12 CST
08:38:12 KST

NEW YORK, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- U.S. President Donald Trump on Friday signed a proclamation modifying the scope of 50-percent additional tariffs on certain Canadian products, removing some goods from the tariff list and adding others, with the changes set to take effect on Oct. 30.
According to the proclamation posted on the White House website, products including plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment, and certain packing crates and boxes imported into the United States from Canada will no longer be subject to the additional 50-percent ad valorem duty.
Instead, certain valves, carpets, waste products and other items imported into the United States shall be subject to the additional 50-percent ad valorem duty.
The changes will apply to goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn from warehouses for consumption, on or after Oct. 30, according to the proclamation.
"The modification in this proclamation will offset the burden or disadvantage on U.S. commerce, is consistent with the public interests and the interests of the United States, is required by the public interests, and will better serve the public interest," the proclamation states. It describes the duties as a response to what it calls Canada's "discrimination or unreasonable and unequal imposition" on U.S. auto and auto parts exports.
Trump imposed 50-percent tariffs on about 20 billion U.S. dollars worth of Canadian goods on Aug. 22, prompting Canada to retaliate with tariffs on an equivalent value of U.S. imports, which took effect on Sept. 8. ■

Chabad rabbi arrested on suspicion of murder after fatal Costco collision in California
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
23:27:59 UTC
08:27:59 KST

A Chabad rabbi in Southern California has been arrested on suspicion of murder after a 28-year-old man was fatally struck by a vehicle in the parking lot of a Costco store near Los Angeles.
The suspect, Rabbi Abba Bryski, 35, of Agoura Hills, is the son of Rabbi Moshe Bryski, a prominent Chabad leader in Southern California and a well-known figure in the Los Angeles Jewish community.
The incident occurred Tuesday evening near the gas pumps of a Costco location in Camarillo, northwest of Los Angeles. According to the Ventura County Sheriff's Office, deputies were dispatched to the scene after receiving a report that a pedestrian had been struck by a vehicle.
When deputies arrived, witnesses directed them to Bryski, identifying him as the driver involved in the collision. Officers located him sitting inside his vehicle in the parking lot, detained him and subsequently placed him under arrest.
The victim, a 28-year-old resident of Modesto, California, was taken to a nearby hospital in critical condition, where he was later pronounced dead. Authorities have not released his identity.
Bryski was booked into the Ventura County Jail on suspicion of murder. He also faces an allegation of resisting or obstructing a law enforcement officer. His bail was set at $3 million.
Investigators have not revealed whether the collision was deliberate
The circumstances surrounding the fatal incident remain unclear. Investigators have not disclosed what happened in the moments before the collision, whether an altercation occurred between Bryski and the victim, or whether the vehicle strike was intentional.
Authorities have also not explained what evidence led them to investigate the death as a homicide rather than a fatal traffic accident.
Under California law, a murder conviction does not necessarily require proof that a defendant specifically intended to kill. In some circumstances, conduct carried out with knowledge of a serious danger to human life and conscious disregard for that danger can support a murder charge. Ordinary driving negligence, however, is not sufficient on its own.
The investigation is being led by the Ventura County Sheriff's Office Major Crimes Bureau, which has appealed to the public and potential witnesses for information that could help establish the circumstances of the incident. The county medical examiner is responsible for determining the cause and manner of death.
Son of a prominent Chabad leader
Bryski's father, Rabbi Moshe Bryski, is a leading figure in the Chabad-Lubavitch movement in Southern California and oversees the organization's activities in the Conejo Valley region.
He serves as executive director of Chabad of the Conejo and dean of the Conejo Jewish Academy, a Jewish educational institution in Agoura Hills. Over several decades, he has played a central role in establishing Jewish educational programs, synagogues and community institutions throughout the area.
His influence extends beyond the local community. He was previously named among the region's 25 most influential figures by a local weekly publication and was selected to deliver the keynote address at Chabad's international gathering of emissaries, one of the movement's most prominent annual events.
Authorities have not disclosed a possible motive in the case, and investigators have yet to establish publicly what led to the fatal encounter in the Costco parking lot.

US lawmakers demand answers from Elon Musk over Ukraine Starlink restrictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
23:25:08 UTC
08:25:08 KST

U.S. Representative Gregory Meeks and Senator Peter Welch led four other lawmakers on Oct. 23 in demanding that Elon Musk answer questions about Ukrainian Starlink disruptions.
In a public letter, Democratic Senators and Representatives listed five questions concerning Starlink restrictions impacting Ukrainian forces, addressed to Musk.
"As a publicly traded company, SpaceX has a legal obligation to disclose to shareholders and the public material events that could affect your business model," the lawmakers wrote in the letter. "The revelation that you personally wielded control over a foreign country’s military communications would require disclosure of elevated risks for corporate governance, geopolitical exposure, and potential adverse actions by foreign governments."
The lawmakers gave Musk until October 31 to answer their questions.
The demand comes as Ukrainian forces continue to experience severe problems operating Starlink military systems. 
Since mid-October, Starshield, the militarized version of Elon Musk's satellite internet system, Starlink, has been operating at limited capacity. With speed limit caps, Kyiv's ability to defend from deadly Russian jet-powered drones and coordinate strikes against Russian targets is hindered.
"Just last month, more than 300 Ukrainian civilians were killed and 2,000 injured by Russian drone and missile strikes," the lawmakers wrote in their letter. "Ukraine has built an innovative network of drone systems to defend against the thousands of strikes launched each month by Russia. However, these life-saving systems often depend on Starlink’s military version, Starshield, for accurate communication and transmission of targeting data."
Despite Ukrainian and U.S. officials apparently engaging in discussions to resolve the disruptions, nobody has publicly taken credit — or blame — for making or implementing the decision. However, the Trump administration officials continue pointing fingers firmly at SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Oct. 23 that Trump had ordered SpaceX CEO Elon Musk on Oct. 21 to lift the restrictions, saying the president was "frustrated the system's speeds remained capped at around 160 kilometers (100 miles) an hour."
Trump said he had not spoken to Musk about the issue but might do so if the problems persisted.
"I have not spoken to him," Trump said. "I might have to, but I have not... I've heard it's fixed. If it's not, I will speak to him.... If there's a problem, I will get it straightened out."
On Oct. 23, President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that issues with Starlink continued to plague Ukrainian forces. 
"The speed restrictions for Starlink and Starshield are still in effect," Zelensky said. "The speed has not been restored. And the supply of interceptor missiles to protect against Russian ballistic missiles is still delayed."
On Oct. 23, U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal, also a Democrat, announced that he is opening a probe into the Starlink disruption. Blumenthal's investigation asks the Pentagon to clarify who ordered the restrictions and to provide information on the U.S. military's own reliance on Starlink.

This is the fancy new F-16 Ukraine could get. It’s not what its pilots need most.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
23:23:00 UTC
08:23:00 KST

- Ukraine's air force has discussed the F-16 Block 70/72 with US manufacturer Lockheed Martin, which then gave President Zelenskyy a model of one
- The Block 70/72 is smarter and tougher than Ukraine's ex-European F-16 Block 15 Mid Life Updates, but that doesn't mean the newer model is a major priority
- The Ukrainian air force needs munitions more than it needs new airframes
When Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met a Lockheed Martin team led by Orlando Sanchez Jr., head of its aeronautics division, in Kyiv on 19 October, the talk was of Patriot interceptors and of repairing the Ukrainian air force's small but growing fleet of ex-European F-16 fighters inside the country. Lockheed designed the F-16 and still builds it.
But the Lockheed officials may have had other things on their minds. They gave Zelenskyy a scale model of a new and improved F-16 variant in Ukrainian livery, according to a photo posted by the MilitaryNewsUA account.
In late September, Ukraine's air force commander, Lt. Gen. Anatolii Kryvonozhko, and Lockheed discussed a possible move to newer F-16s. Now we have a clearer idea what those F-16s might look like—and what they might be capable of. The model Lockheed officials gave to Zelenskyy appears to be based on the Block 70/72 version of the classic supersonic fighter that Lockheed manufactures at its factory in Greenville, South Carolina.
It's a world-class jet. But a pricey batch of factory-fresh Block 70/72s isn't actually at the top of the Ukrainian air force's wish list. Not as long as the air force's existing warplanes lack munitions.
The Block 70/72 boasts a better radar, more fuel capacity, and a tougher airframe compared to older F-16 models, which have been flying since the late 1970s. The F-16 is still one of the most numerous fighter types in US Air Force service. Surplus 1980s-vintage F-16s from Denmark and the Netherlands make up the bulk of the Ukrainian air force's front-line fleet. Norway's six are still being refurbished, and Belgium's are coming.
Whether Ukraine ever gets new F-16s is anyone's guess. Kyiv would need to pay around $100 million per copy, or find an ally to finance the purchase. Either could be a heavy lift. And to be sure, Ukraine has options as it rebuilds its battered air force. Sweden is donating 16 older Saab Gripens, the first due early next year, and Kyiv plans to buy 20 newer ones. Kyiv has negotiated to buy 16 Dassault Rafales from France, which may not arrive until 2028. Belgium has promised as many as 53 older F-16s, the last of them perhaps not until 2029.
Welcome jets
But new Block 70/72 F-16s would be welcome. The Block 70/72 builds on what already makes the F-16 great: its agility, flexibility, reliability, excellent electronic warfare systems, and compatibility with a wide array of munitions.
Trending Now
Where the Block 15 Mid Life Update F-16s Ukraine currently flies have the older analog AN/APG-66(V2) radar, the Block 70/72 has a digital APG-83 active electronically scanned array radar. It can also carry overwing conformal fuel tanks for extra range.
Perhaps most exciting for the Ukrainian air force, a newly made Block 70/72 is good for 12,000 hours of flight: enough for about 30 years at 400 flying hours a year. An aging Block 15 has a structural life of about 8,000 hours, and Ukraine's jets fly hard. Zelenskyy has said about half of them spend long stretches abroad for repairs, many at Sabena Aerospace Engineering in Belgium, a process that can take months.
Newer F-16s require less maintenance. They can fly and fight more often. In that sense, 50 Block 70/72s are worth more than 50 Block 15s.
But the availability of airframes isn't the biggest problem in the 107th Aviation Wing, the Ukrainian air force's sole F-16 unit. The wing is desperately low on air-to-air missiles. Its pilots often resort to gunning down Russian drones and cruise missiles with the F-16's built-in 20-mm cannon—a risky tactic given how close a fighter must get to its target to make use of its gun.
While a few billion dollars' worth of fresh F-16s could keep the 107th Aviation Wing in fighting shape for decades to come, fresh airframes aren't actually the most urgent priority. Given a choice between getting new F-16s or getting substantial supplies of missiles for its old F-16s, the wing would surely opt for the latter.
Belgium’s 10 F-16s bring Ukraine’s promised fleet to about 100 jets. Fewer than 40 are flying, as Russia’s jet drones run them ragged

Said Amori, Rania Abushamala
24 October 2026•Update: 24 October 2026
 Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Friday that Israel must prepare for the end of US military assistance worth tens of billions of dollars, calling the prospect “only a matter of time.”
Speaking just days before hard-fought elections, Netanyahu told Israel’s business broadcaster Channel 10 that he had ordered preparations for potential economic and banking sanctions, including exploring alternative financial technologies.
“If you think we're going to continue receiving what I secured twice, and that's tens of billions of dollars in American aid for the defense budget, prepare yourselves and get used to the fact that it won't happen, because America has changed,” he said, apparently referring to growing opposition in the US to such aid in light of Israel’s genocide in Gaza and mistreatment of the Palestinians.
“This is over, and it will end. It is only a matter of time.”
Netanyahu gave no date for an end to the assistance and announced no formal US decision, instead calling for preparations for a possible future halt.
On potential sanctions, he said Israel must develop alternative economic and financial mechanisms.
“You have to understand that there could be sanctions, including banking sanctions. You need to prepare an economy that can get around them,” he said.
Asked whether blockchain technology could offer an alternative for dealing with economic sanctions, Netanyahu replied: “Yes, that's one of the ways. And I've already asked for a plan to be prepared.” 
Opposition pushes to replace Netanyahu’s government
Opposition Democrats party leader Yair Golan criticized Netanyahu’s remarks on US social media company X, accusing him of being detached from reality.
He argued that preventing economic sanctions requires combating “Jewish terrorism” that damages Israel’s international standing, preserving strategic alliances, and replacing the government in next week’s election.
Golan called for a new government “without Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir and Deri,” referring to National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Shas party leader Aryeh Deri.
The remarks came four days before Israel’s Tuesday parliamentary elections, amid debate about relations with Western allies and the potential consequences of economic sanctions.
Under a pact signed with Washington in 2016, Israel receives $38 billion in military assistance over a 10-year period set to end in 2028.
Netanyahu has previously called for reducing Israel’s dependence on US military aid and strengthening its domestic defense industry.

Andy Bloke appears vaguely normal on Gogglebox – but Kemi dodged a bullet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
23:16:33 UTC
08:16:33 KST

On nights like this a man can feel like he’s slipped through the looking-glass. I’m sitting on the sofa watching the TV, poised to make some gags about the prime minister and the mayor of Liverpool, who are themselves sitting on a sofa at No 10, poised to make some gags about what they are watching on TV.
Life doesn’t get more meta. The saving grace is that this episode of Gogglebox is a charity special for Stand Up to Cancer. Andy Burnham has requested that any journalist writing about the programme makes a donation to SU2C. I’m happy to oblige. Cancer is costing me a great deal more than money.
Meet Andy Bloke and his best mate, Steve Bloke. Two career politicians who still manage to look and sound vaguely normal. Not totally normal, mind. In real life, Steve Bloke would have said to Andy Bloke: “This is a total shithole you’re living in.” And Andy Bloke would have replied: “I know. It’s been a complete tip since Boris was here. You can’t get rid of the stains.”
You can’t deny that Andy Bloke and Steve Bloke are naturals at this. Not so bland that you want to turn off, a genuine connection with one another and a sense of fun that can’t be faked. Kemi Badenoch is reportedly annoyed she wasn’t invited on the programme.
The reality is that she’s dodged a bullet. Kemi just doesn’t have the woman of the people shtick. It’s something you’ve either got or you haven’t and she really doesn’t. If you let her on Gogglebox the only laugh you would get from her would be if she was livestreaming an execution from the US.
Mind you, it’s a slow burn. At first Andy and Steve look like they are feeling their way into the programme. But then so do the other celebs, Joe Lycett and his aunties, Stanley Tucci and his wife, Felicity, and Paul Whitehouse and Lenny Rush. The bantz feels a bit contrived and Andy Bloke – a Cambridge English grad – fails to recognise a photo of Margaret Atwood.
If Steve Bloke had been more on the ball, he’d have taken the piss mercilessly. But Andy and Steve are nothing if not a team. They’ve got each other’s backs and bond over filling in the blanks on members of the royal household in Only Connect.
“The king will be pleased with me at our next weekly meeting,” says Andy Bloke. He probably will be. I suspect Camilla will have made Charles watch this. The Man of the People meets the King of the People.
Halfway through, we get a reminder that this isn’t all about the laughs. There is the story of Callum who died at the age of 16 from brain cancer. Then the story of a woman whose mother died of pancreatic cancer when she was 11, was diagnosed with cervical cancer shortly after her child was born and whose husband died of bowel cancer a week after diagnosis. Sometimes shit really does happen to good people. All the celebs were fighting back tears. Andy was no exception.
“I’d like to see Match of the Day,” says Paul Whitehouse. “Why? To hear how crap Spurs are?” Lenny joked. Careful, Lenny, careful. We might be past the watershed but it’s still way too early for gags about Spurs.
But some football would have been nice. Andy Bloke and Steve Bloke would have been in their element. You could have made an entire programme of the pair of them pissing themselves laughing as Manchester United were beaten 4-1 by Como in the Champions League. It might even have earned a Bafta nomination.
For some reason, Andy Bloke and Steve Bloke were excluded from watching an X-rated natural history about some young birds that haven’t yet learned to fly and are so dim that they literally just stand there as tortoises eat them alive. Well, not all. One bird managed to hop on top of a tortoise shell. Though not before the tortoise had taken a chunk out of a wing. A happy ending of sorts. The celebs couldn’t quite believe they were being forced to watch such ultra-violence.
Normal service was resumed with a mercifully brief excerpt from Strictly Come Dancing. Brief because none of the real celebs had any idea who the celebrity contestants were. Andy Bloke admitted he still had PTSD from watching Ed Balls crashing around the dancefloor. Steve Bloke wisely helped himself to another beer. Maybe this was the way they used to do business when Andy Bloke was also a mayor.
We ended on an upbeat note. The Celebrity Traitors. Steve Bloke had no idea what was going on so Andy Bloke tried to fill him in as they cracked up over some crisps, pork scratchings and Skips. Me neither. I guess that was one were you had to be in the room.
“You should be quite good at this,” Andy Bloke said, encouragingly. “You can generally spot the wrong ’un in the room.” I guess that depends on how often you’ve been in the same room as Michael Gove.
Claudia Winkleman was announcing that the murder would be done in plain sight by boring a Faithful to death. Steve Bloke had the solution. Just make them watch the proceedings in the House of Commons. Boom boom.
Neither Steve nor Andy Bloke had much to say about Ross Kemp’s worrying levels of paranoia or Jerry Hall’s complete charisma bypass. How do you bore someone who is already boring? That could have been a question for Only Connect. Maybe we had come full circle. Or perhaps their gags about Rupert Murdoch got cut in the editing suite.

UN, October 24. /TASS/. The West’s patronage has deprived the Ukrainian regime’s mindset of criticism on the issue of nuclear safety and the Zaporozhye nuclear power station, Alexander Repkin, Russia’s Deputy Permanent Representative to the UN, said.
"Unconditional protectionism from the West has normalized the absence of any critical line in Kiev’s mindset. How the Cambridge Analytica scandal still haunts Mark Zuckerberg
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
23:13:03 UTC
08:13:03 KST

How the Cambridge Analytica scandal still haunts Mark Zuckerberg
‘Cambridge Analytica’ is by now a byword for the social media Wild West of 2016, when regulations were non-existent and unscrupulous brokers sold personal user data to advertisers and political operatives. RT explores the scandal that Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg still can’t dodge.
On October 22, Meta was ordered by a New Mexico judge to pay $25 billion in civil penalties over the collection of personal data from 44 million Facebook users by Cambridge Analytica more than a decade earlier.
The judge concluded that Meta’s misconduct warranted a penalty exceeding $219 billion under state law, but reduced the amount to $25 billion, making it one of the largest fines ever imposed on an American corporation.
Meta, operating at the time as Facebook, knowingly and systematically deceived users about how it managed their personal data and allowed its harvesting by third-party companies like Cambridge Analytica. The jury also found Meta’s senior executive team knew of, and lied about, deceiving users about how it planned to investigate data-harvesting companies after the Cambridge Analytica scandal became public.
To understand how Meta ended up owing an eighth of its annual revenue in just one judgment, it’s necessary to go back to 2013, when Cambridge Analytica emerged from Britain’s shadowy private intelligence sector.
What was Cambridge Analytica?
Cambridge Analytica was founded in 2013 as a subsidiary of SCL Group, a London-based private intelligence firm that has provided data analytics and “behavioural analysis” services to the British Defense Ministry and Foreign Office.
Cambridge Analytica CEO and SCL Group Director Alexander Nix has admitted under oath that his companies worked with American and British intelligence agencies, provided psychological warfare training to several Western militaries, employed multiple staff with security clearances in the UK and US, and hired former Israeli spies.
SCL Group’s work for NATO, Israel, Ukraine, and other governments and militaries was extensive, and Cambridge Analytica drew on its parent company’s experience in military psyops to become one of the world’s most effective election influence operations, according to whistleblower Christopher Wylie. On the other hand, SCL insists that its military and political wings were separate entities. Whichever account is true, Cambridge Analytica had been hired by political candidates in 200 elections by 2018, according to company documents. These included parliamentary elections in the Czech Republic, India, and Italy, the Brexit referendum in the UK, and most infamously, the 2016 presidential election in the US.
What did Cambridge Analytica do in 2016?
Cambridge Analytica was paid nearly $6 million by then-candidate Donald Trump’s campaign in the runup to the 2016 election. The company used its unprecedented access to Facebook user data to identify persuadable voters and potential donors, select effective markets for television ads, and target certain Hillary Clinton supporters for “deterrence” – adverts discouraging them from going to the polls on election day.
How did this become a scandal?
Cambridge Analytica did not break any laws to obtain this data. It was scraped from tens of millions of Facebook users who had, unbeknownst to themselves, given a third-party Facebook quiz application access to their messages, their profile data, and that of their friends.
Cambridge Analytica hired a Cambridge University professor, Aleksandr Kogan, to develop a personality quiz app, named ‘This is Your Digital Life’. Between 250,000 and 270,000 American Facebook users took the quiz in 2015, and by accessing their data, but crucially, under Facebook terms, accessing the data of all of their friends on the platform, Cambridge Analytica was able to compile detailed psychological profiles on roughly 87 million users.
Cambridge Analytica employee Christopher Wylie revealed the workings of the scheme to The Observer in 2018, telling the British newspaper that “we exploited Facebook to harvest millions of people’s profiles, and built models to exploit what we knew about them and target their inner demons. That was the basis the entire company was built on.”
Was Cambridge Analytica the only data-scraper doing this?
“Facebook never cared,” Kogan told NBC News in 2018, explaining that “tens of thousands” of developers created apps like his quiz, and sold user data to companies like Cambridge Analytica. Among the developers were CubeYou, which used a “one-click personality test” app to gather information for commercial use, and LocalBlox, which scraped data from 48 million users, which it then sold to marketers.
AggregateIQ, Global Science Research, and Eunoia Technologies all used data gleaned by Kogan for political ends. However, long before these companies existed, Blue State Digital, an American political consultancy, surreptitiously harvested Facebook data, including friends’ data, for use by Barack Obama’s 2012 campaign.
Cambridge Analytica, however, had its work for the Trump campaign exposed at the height of the ‘Russiagate’ hoax, at a time when Democrats and liberal media outlets were convinced that Russia intervened in the election on behalf of Trump. Cambridge Analytica’s data-scraping dovetailed neatly into a narrative of “Facebook bots” and “Russian military hackers” working with the Trump campaign, and the company became a whipping boy for an industry that transcended partisan lines.

US Special Counsel Robert Mueller and the Senate Intelligence Committee eventually investigated claims that Cambridge Analytica helped the Russian government target political ads at American voters, but both determined that these claims were untrue, and neither investigation found any proof of “collusion” between the Trump campaign and the Kremlin.
Has Facebook been punished?
At the time that the information was collected, Facebook had stopped allowing third-party apps to access friends’ data. However, a loophole allowed apps active on the platform before this change to continue harvesting information through 2015. Within days of Wylie’s revelations hitting the headlines, SCL Group and Cambridge Analytica were suspended from Facebook. Two months later, both companies ceased operations, leaving Facebook to handle the fallout.
Facebook initially went into damage control mode, insisting that “People knowingly provided their information” to Kogan’s app, and that “everyone involved gave their consent.”
However, the US Federal Trade Commission determined that Facebook made its privacy settings deliberately opaque, spreading them out over 20 separate screens and opting users into sharing data with third-parties by default. Facebook settled with the FTC for $5 billion in 2019, setting the stage for a series of similar payouts in the following years.
In 2018, Zuckerberg told lawmakers on Capitol Hill that Facebook was aware that user data had been transferred from Kogan to Cambridge Analytica (this transfer was in breach of its policies) since 2015, but opted not to inform users. He said that Facebook asked Cambridge Analytica to delete the data, but never followed up and made sure the company did. “We considered it a closed case,” he told Congress.
The following year, the US Securities and Exchange Commission accused Facebook of misleading investors by presenting “the risk of misuse of user data as merely hypothetical,” when it knew since 2015 that “a third-party developer had actually misused Facebook user data.” Facebook settled the case with the SEC for $100 million.
In 2022, Meta settled a $725 million class-action lawsuit brought by a group of Facebook users, who alleged that the company violated privacy and consumer protection laws by misrepresenting its data-sharing laws and failing to protect their personal information.
Meta attempted to shut down further legal action over the Cambridge Analytica scandal this August, when it reached an $18 billion settlement with 51 attorneys general across US states, territories, and the District of Columbia. Although the cases concerned the addictive design of Meta’s platforms and their effect on children’s mental health, the settlement included a clause resolving a multistate investigation into Facebook’s sharing of user data with third parties “whether known or unknown,” including Cambridge Analytica.
Even if participating states were to discover new facts about the data sharing, they have now waived their right to sue Meta. New Mexico was one of two states that was not party to this agreement, hence the $25 billion penalty.
Did Cambridge Analytica get Trump elected?
Ten years after the fact, it remains unclear how prominent a role Cambridge Analytica played in Trump’s victory over Clinton. The Trump campaign’s use of Facebook and X (then called Twitter) is widely cited as instrumental in his win, but the campaign’s digital director, Brad Parscale, has since said that he stopped using the company’s data several months before election day, considering it inaccurate.
What about Brexit?
Cambridge Analytica worked with Nigel Farage’s Leave.EU organization in late 2015 and early 2016, and carried out some preliminary data analysis for the campaign. However, the data was never used, and the UK Information Commissioner’s (ICO) office concluded in 2020 that the company had no impact on the referendum. As in the US, the ICO found no links between Cambridge Analytica and Russia, and no evidence that Russia interfered in the vote.
Is Zuckerberg in the clear?
The $25 billion judgement handed down on October 22 may be the largest fine ever imposed on Meta, but it does not mark the end of Zuckerberg’s legal woes. In addition to a Washington DC lawsuit holding him personally responsible for the Cambridge Analytica debacle, Zuckerberg’s company is being sued by investors in California over Facebook’s alleged efforts to conceal the misuse of user data by the company.

Typhoon Champi hits Taiwan, killing one and injuring 350

Typhoon Champi hits Taiwan, killing one and injuring 350
Authorities warn of ‘destructive winds’ and urge residents to shelter as the storm passes the island’s northeast.
Typhoon Champi has struck Taiwan, killing one person and injuring at least 350 others, as authorities warned of “destructive winds” and instructed people to stay indoors.
The storm swept past the island’s northeast on Friday, toppling trees, shutting shops and schools, cutting power to thousands of households, and forcing more than 4,300 people to evacuate from their homes.
Champi is heading towards China and Japan, forcing the cancellation of hundreds of flights in the region.
“From tonight through tomorrow morning conditions will be very windy and stormy everywhere,” Central Weather Administration (CWA) forecaster Lin Ping-yu said in a briefing. “Please try to stay indoors.”
Champi was briefly a super typhoon with winds of nearly 300 kilometres per hour (186 miles per hour) but has since weakened. The US Joint Typhoon Warning Center reported maximum winds of 185km/h (115mph).
Worse is still expected to come on Saturday. Champi could drop up to 900mm (35 inches) of rain between Thursday and Saturday, with the northeast hit hardest, the CWA said. More than 400mm fell in Yilan County on Friday.
CWA forecaster Lu Kuo-chen said the typhoon could slow near the island’s northeastern tip, prolonging its impact.
About 8,400 households in Japan’s Okinawa islands were without power on Friday afternoon, according to the Okinawa Electric Power Company. Champi is forecast to hover near Okinawa and then China’s eastern coast before turning northeast towards mainland Japan.
Champi is the latest storm in a Pacific season supercharged by El Nino.
The United Nations said on Wednesday that El Nino, a natural cycle that warms the tropical Pacific, is heading off the charts.
“The current El Nino event could be unprecedented in strength. Literally off the monitoring charts that we have used for the past four decades,” said Celeste Saulo, secretary-general of the World Meteorological Organization.
It is expected to peak in December, with its impact lasting into 2027 and beyond.

North Korea has opened up bridges to Russia and China – in which direction will it go?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
23:10:16 UTC
08:10:16 KST

For more than a decade, local Chinese residents pilloried it as nothing more than an empty bridge that led to a North Korean vegetable patch on the other side.
Fast forward 12 years and dozens of trucks are now traversing the bridge linking China to North Korea, boosting trade for the reclusive regime. But it has also triggered concern that it could intensify a struggle for influence over the North between Beijing and the region’s other major power, Russia.
The New Yalu River Bridge connects the north-eastern Chinese city of Dandong with Sinuiju in North Korea and has four lanes and stretches 3km (1.9 miles) across the Yalu river. It is expected to ease congestion on the ageing Friendship Bridge nearby.
It opened on 15 October, about a month after another major crossing – this time between North Korea and Russia. The first road bridge across their short shared border, named the Yakov Novichenko Bridge, reportedly made Chinese officials uneasy, coming on top of signs from the North Korean leader Kim Jong-un that he is prioritising ties with Moscow.
“China’s interest in buttressing its influence in North Korea is certainly reinforced by the diversifying North Korea-Russia relationship — ties that China tolerates but watches closely as they add complexity to its relationship with its provocative neighbour,” says Carla Freeman, director of the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies’ Foreign Policy Institute.
Since late 2024, the North Korean leader has sent ammunition and as many as 16,000 troops to support Vladimir Putin’s war in Ukraine, and has held two summits with the Russian president in the past three years. In 2024, the leaders signed a mutual defence pact that includes a clause requiring the countries to come to each other’s aid if attacked.
In return for arms and combat soldiers, Pyongyang is getting hard currency, real-time battlefield experience for its troops, weapons technology and the opportunity to extend political and economic cooperation beyond its traditional ally China.
North Korea stands to benefit from increased trade but for China, the bridge could be of more geopolitical value than economic given how little trade China does with its neighbour compared with its other partners.
However, the insular regime in Pyongyang is thought to be reluctant to increase its economic dependence on China, by far its biggest trading partner and aid donor, and may still resent Beijing’s previous support for UN sanctions targeting the North’s nuclear weapons programme.
In the past two years, however, Russian and Chinese support for UN sanctions has collapsed. “The main restriction on trade with North Korea is not the infrastructure but international sanctions,” says Justin Hastings, a professor of international relations and comparative politics at Sydney University. “However, because China’s enforcement of UN sanctions has become desultory and Russia has actively repudiated their enforcement, North Korea is in a position to benefit from increased trade and weapons help (at least from Russia).”
The North’s “open” border with China contrasts dramatically with the one it shares with South Korea. In 2024, the North said it would sever all rail and road links with its neighbour, months after Kim said he would abandon the goal of peaceful reunification and declared South Korea his country’s “principal enemy”.
But Fyodor Tertitskiy, a North Korea expert at Korea University in Seoul, believes neither China nor Russia can influence North Korea in any meaningful way, citing Kim’s refusal to surrender his nuclear weapons or moderate his iron grip on power – two changes that would be welcomed in Moscow and Beijing.
“Both countries understand that Kim Jong-un would rather accept a complete breakdown in relationships than submit,” he says. “So I doubt we are seeing a straightforward struggle for influence. Kim is trying to play the two against each other, but China and Russia are not rivals like the Soviet Union and China were in the 1970s.”
Kim is more likely to turn to China improve his country’s struggling economy, while Beijing is eager to revive its role as the North’s biggest influence, according to Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul.
“After expanding military cooperation with Russia … Kim Jong-un is leveraging his windfall from Moscow for additional gains from Beijing. China may seek to recover lost influence by increasing trade and people-to-people exchanges, but the Kim regime prizes autonomy and wants to limit foreign ideological and cultural influences.”
The South Korean government said last year that at least 17 active road and rail links connect North Korea and China along their 1,400 km-long border.
Tertitskiy is “not particularly optimistic” that the increased contact the bridges will bring means improvements to the lives of ordinary North Koreans or lead to a more western-style economy. “I think it will make reform even less likely. Why pursue reforms and take risks when you can just get what you need from abroad?”
Analysts say the expected rise in trade across the Yalu bridge is likely to be modest at first. But it could become a bellwether for the state of Sino-North Korean ties, says Easley.
“China remains economically indispensable to North Korea in ways that Russia cannot replace,” he says, adding, “In that sense, the bridge may offer an inadvertent window into bilateral relations if flows are visibly interrupted in the future.”

US quietly moves diplomats and families across Middle East as fears of wider war grow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
23:04:54 UTC
08:04:54 KST

The United States is quietly relocating some diplomats and their family members from posts across the Middle East amid growing concerns that the escalating conflict involving Iran-backed Houthi rebels could spread across the region, CNN reported, citing multiple sources familiar with the moves.
The State Department this week ordered non-emergency personnel and all family members to leave Saudi Arabia, citing the recent escalation in Houthi attacks. At the same time, Washington has been making less-publicized staffing adjustments at embassies in Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and Lebanon.
Unlike the formal departure order issued for Saudi Arabia, the changes at those six embassies have not been publicly announced. The State Department maintains that their operational designations remain unchanged and that they continue to operate under "restricted operations" status, which allows staffing adjustments without a formal change in embassy status.
The moves come as Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia intensify, prompting repeated State Department warnings that the hostilities "have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area."
Tensions have also risen following President Donald Trump's suggestions that the United States could resume military strikes against Iran after the November midterm elections. Israel, meanwhile, has reportedly pressed Washington to take military action sooner, although those efforts have so far been unsuccessful, according to sources familiar with the discussions.
Diplomats describe chaotic departures and mounting frustration
For many American diplomatic families, the latest relocation instructions have brought back painful memories of the earlier stages of the war with Iran. Some had only recently returned to their overseas assignments after being evacuated earlier this year, forcing them to find temporary housing and arrange schooling for their children.
Now, those families face another round of upheaval, with some reporting that the financial assistance available to them is less generous than during their previous departures.
"To say it has been chaotic is an understatement," one U.S. diplomat said, explaining that the assistance offered so far does not cover the full cost of relocating an entire family.
Nikki Gamer, spokesperson for the American Foreign Service Association (AFSA), which represents U.S. foreign service officers, said the repeated disruptions were taking a significant toll.
"This echoes the chaos families experienced earlier this year. Some had barely settled back in before being told to leave again," Gamer said. "They are understandably upset, confused, and angry."
Not every embassy had permitted children to return following the earlier evacuations, although most had allowed spouses to rejoin personnel stationed abroad. Now, even those family members who recently returned are being told to leave again.
One source in the Jordanian capital described the atmosphere as eerily familiar. "There’s a very Groundhog Day vibe," the source said, referring to personnel being asked to leave Amman once more.
Families uncertain whether Washington will cover relocation costs
The latest departures have also prompted complaints about poor coordination between State Department headquarters in Washington and diplomatic personnel serving abroad.
One person familiar with the arrangements described communication between officials in Washington and embassies overseas as "just as much of a shit show" as during the early stages of the Iran war.
Some personnel have expressed concern that the department may not provide their families with daily living allowances, commonly known as per diem, to cover accommodation and other expenses after returning to the United States.
The source said several embassies had not held the planning meetings or staff briefings that would normally precede such departures, leaving employees and their families uncertain about the next steps.
"A lot of people are hearing about it through the news instead of their leadership at post," the source added.
AFSA has also raised concerns about the handling of the process, describing reports "of bureaucratic ping-pong."
In a statement Thursday, the association criticized the lack of clarity surrounding financial assistance for families being asked to leave their posts for a second time.
"Families that had barely returned to their posts and re-enrolled their children in school are being told to prepare to evacuate again without being advised as to what level of financial support they can count on," the association said.
According to Gamer, the uncertainty is particularly acute at embassies where no formal change in operating status has been announced.
"families outside Saudi Arabia have told AFSA they are being directed to leave without confirmed housing assistance or per diem."
She said families had been told that the uncertainty surrounding their benefits was linked to the fact that their embassies remained under the existing restricted-operations designation.
For diplomatic households suddenly forced to relocate, such allowances can be essential to securing temporary accommodation, especially when the employee must remain behind to carry out critical embassy duties.
"Families deserve to know how they will pay for a place to live before they board a plane," Gamer said.

Ukraine now fights two enemies. One is America
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
23:02:16 UTC
08:02:16 KST

On 18 October, President Zelenskyy accused Donald Trump of trying to pressure Ukraine into capitulating to Russia.
Asked by NBC whether Ukraine could win the war without the US, he answered: "Without United States support it's very difficult. But if United States will support Putin, it's historic mistake and big tragedy.... If the United States officially will take the side of Russia, if these two countries will be together, of course we will not prevail and we will not be able to stand."
He said Ukraine hopes Trump will be on its side, or at least "in the middle," and that he will "change his decisions" on Russia, as "it's all mistakes, it will not help us, and it will not help United States." In an interview with NBC's Meet the Press, when asked whether Trump is still an ally of Ukraine, Zelenskyy said: "I hope so." Not a definitive yes, but a weak maybe.
As diplomacy goes, statements do not come much stronger than this. What triggered them?
Probably the sum of all things. We all remember Trump and Vance humiliating Zelenskyy in the White House on 28 February 2025. Trump told the Ukrainian President that he was "gambling with" a third world war. Zelenskyy was told to come back "when he is ready for peace". Most will also remember that the USA enacted the decision to halt its aid to Ukraine across two separate, sweeping actions taken during the first months of the second Trump administration in early 2025. Presently, it is only delivering military aid decided by former President Biden.
Some might have forgotten that Trump called Zelenskyy a "dictator without elections," suggested Ukraine started the war, and pushed a "peace plan" whose original 28-point draft gave Russia terms more favorable than what Moscow sought at the 2022 Istanbul talks.
After 640 days in office, Trump's disdain for Ukraine and admiration for Russia seem to grow by the day, and his kakistocracy—government by the least qualified—keeps undermining Ukraine's defense. In less than two weeks:
- 9 October: the administration imposed new sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC), an institution crucial for holding Putin and the Kremlin accountable for their atrocities in Ukraine.
- The same day, Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports, effectively helping fund Russia's wars.
- 10 October: Trump said of the elected president of a country fighting off Russia's full-scale invasion: "It's time for Ukraine to get a new president."
- 11 October: Trump declared on Truth Social an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine that bound only Ukraine. Zelenskyy said it was "news to him."
- 14 October: SpaceX restricted Starshield, the classified, military-grade version of Starlink; Reuters reported on 15 October that the order came from the White House, undermining Ukraine's ability to defend itself against Russian jet-powered drones and strike Russian forces in occupied territory.
- 15 October: the US suspended critical intelligence sharing for three days, Zelenskyy said on 18 October, leaving Ukraine without warnings of Russian ballistic missile launches against its citizens and energy infrastructure.
- 16 October: two days before they were due to take effect, Trump waived the sanctions, restrictions and tariffs on Russia required by the Graham Act, calling it in the US national interest, and put nearly all of the congressional sanctions package on hold.
- 18 October: the administration reportedly proposed that Europe resume buying Russian gas to help "entice Russia to end the war in Ukraine." Europe balked.
- 19 October: it emerged that the US is delaying Patriots procured by allies under NATO's Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), leaving Ukraine short of defenses against Russian ballistic missiles. Ukrainian officials say the shipment is stalled because Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has not signed the transfer documents on his desk.
- 19 October: Trump said that "Xi Jinping has been very fair on Ukraine. He hasn't been very much involved. Same with Russia. They haven't been nearly what they could've been," ignoring that Russia is waging an unjust, unprovoked and genocidal war against Ukraine.
- The same day, Trump claimed Zelenskyy targets Russian refineries knowing the attacks are seriously hurting world diesel markets, including in the US, and that he "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did."
- Talking to reporters outside the White House, Trump said Zelenskyy should get someone else to negotiate on Ukraine's behalf, and that he is willing to meet Putin and Xi to discuss the war, without the Ukrainian president. Kyiv fears Washington might decide Ukraine's future without it.
- 20 October: Vice President JD Vance said Ukraine should not join NATO and should stop striking Russian energy. He refused to call Ukraine a US "ally," downgrading it to a "partner": "We don't have a formal alliance... they're not in NATO... we're going to work together on some things, but also we're going to be opposite on some things, too."
- 21 October: after four and a half years of genocidal full-scale war and amid persistent Russian air strikes on Ukrainians, US special envoy Steve Witkoff praised Putin as a "humanitarian," echoing Trump's claim that Russia had restrained itself.
- The same day, Trump said the end of the war is closer than ever. He may step up efforts to coerce Ukraine into a deal by the end of 2026, The Atlantic reports, with Ukraine's prospects shaped by the US midterms and possible Trump-Putin-Xi talks in November.
Less than two weeks, summarized.
This is how Trump's administration talks about, and acts towards, the victim of an unjustified, unprovoked and horrendous war. Trump's USA (TUSA) is siding with autocracy against democracy and the rules-based world order. It talks about America's former allies in a similar manner: derogatory and disrespectful. None of the above is the word or deed of an ally.
When one chooses to see the world as it is, Zelenskyy's statements become both necessary and important. This is not only about Ukraine's self-respect and survival. Once we acknowledge the realities—that Europe is in an undeclared war with Russia at a moment when the USA has chosen to become a strategic adversary—we stand better prepared to defend ourselves: to accept that our present security system does not work and new solutions are urgently needed, and that diplomacy alone does not work and military force is essential to protect freedom, democracy and international law.
More than a year ago, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned that Europe is "not at war, but no longer at peace either" with Russia. Other heads of state have echoed him. NATO has since shifted from a peacetime alliance to one focused on urgent wartime readiness. Unfortunately, the process started years too late.
By seeing the world as it is, European leaders might reach the long-overdue conclusion that Russia's wars in Ukraine and Europe can only be stopped by a demonstration of strength: an alliance willing and capable of using military force to stop Russia. The alliance Russia fears isn't NATO. It's a coalition that will actually fight.
European courage and action are urgently needed. Ukraine is exposed to a two-front war, defending itself against both Russia and TUSA, and their attacks are increasing in scale and scope. Both Moscow and Washington want to end the war this year and are ramping up their assaults on Ukraine accordingly.
Irrespective of one's view of Ukraine, it is commonly understood that it is stopping Russia from advancing and increasing its border with NATO and the EU. Ukraine is defending European values and principles, ensuring the rest of us can continue living in something resembling peace. The consequences of its defeat would be truly devastating.
There can be no European strategic autonomy without Ukraine. There can be no European security and stability without Ukraine. Europe can never become a Great Power without Ukraine. And neither Russia nor the USA want Europe to achieve any of the above.
It is time to act according to the present-day realities and face down Europe's two strategic adversaries. In the worst case, Ukraine's destiny might be decided in November already.

MINSK, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Belarus plans to increase the share of electric public transport to 25 percent of its ground public passenger fleet by the end of 2029, Belarusian Industry Minister Andrei Kuznetsov said Friday.
Belarus currently has about 7,900 units of public transport vehicles, including 6,101 buses, 198 electric buses, 1,354 trolleybuses and 247 trams, which indicates that ground public transport is widely used across Belarus, Kuznetsov said at a meeting on the development of domestic passenger transport production.
