====================================================================================================

American Jews fly to West Bank to help Palestinian olive harvesters amid settler attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
22:43:43 UTC
07:43:43 KST

The thud of a body hitting the ground startled the group. "Oh, Jerry, what happened?" the volunteers called out in English as they rushed toward an elderly man sprawled across a black plastic sheet, trying to assess the damage after falling from a ladder.
"I'm fine," he groaned, also in English, before getting to his feet with a smile and some help from his companions. "An accident while picking olives. That's a first for me." Satisfied that he was unharmed, the others picked up their small plastic rakes and returned to work.
The scene unfolded in a modest olive grove of just a few dozen trees in Jalud, a Palestinian village near Nablus in the northern West Bank. The village is surrounded by 13 Israeli settlement outposts. Its residents own approximately 23,000 dunams, or 5,700 acres, of agricultural land, most of it planted with olive trees. But fear of attacks by violent settlers prevents them from reaching much of it.
"Because of the fear, we only harvest the olives inside the village, between the houses," said Riyad Haj Mohammed Abu Amr, head of the village council. "Even inside the village, we're not safe. Just yesterday, settlers came and threw stones at our elementary school. The children were terrified and crying. You can't imagine how frightening it was."
Standing in the grove, less than 100 meters from the school building, with nearby settlement outposts visible in the distance, Rabbi Toba Spitzer described the fear she and her fellow volunteers experienced when they first arrived.
"It was our second day picking olives," said Spitzer, 63, who leads Congregation Dorshei Tzedek in Newton, Massachusetts, outside Boston. "We had only arrived in Israel on Friday, and before Shabbat our families back home started sending worried messages asking whether we were all right."
The concern followed the attack on Heidi Levine, a photographer working for The Washington Post, who was beaten by Israeli settlers while covering the Palestinian olive harvest. Footage of the assault circulated widely across American news outlets.
"Our families thought that if someone could attack a Washington Post photographer who had come to document Palestinians harvesting olives, who knew what might have happened to us?" Spitzer said. "We weren't there to take photographs. We had actually come to harvest. We reassured them that we hadn't gone into the fields yet and wouldn't begin until Sunday."
The following day, around noon, the group heard screams from the village.
"People were shouting, 'The settlers are attacking the school,' and we didn't know what to do. We were in the middle of our work and, of course, we were very frightened. We know that if settlers come into the village and see us, they won't spare us."
Then she offered a dose of humor.
"They say we're anarchists who came here to provoke people. Look at me. I'm 63. Another woman in our group, Sue, is 82, and Jo is 80. We're very, very frightening. I wouldn't advise anyone to cross our path," she laughed. "I'm joking, of course. Heaven forbid someone takes that seriously."
Hundreds of Jews travel to the West Bank to help Palestinian farmers
Every day during the current olive harvest, Israeli volunteers travel to Palestinian communities to help residents pick their crops. Their presence does not necessarily prevent violent settler attacks, and sometimes the volunteers themselves become targets. Still, for farmers who are afraid to enter their fields alone, even a small sense of security can make a difference.
The Israeli human rights organization Yesh Din documented 640 incidents of violence involving settlers and soldiers against Palestinian residents during the first 24 days of the harvest, an average of 26.7 incidents a day, across 189 West Bank communities. Of those, 316 were directly connected to the olive harvest, averaging 13.2 incidents daily.
Against that backdrop, it is hardly surprising that many Palestinian farmers are reluctant to harvest their trees without accompaniment.
Alongside the Israelis are several hundred volunteers from abroad, most of them Jews from communities in the United States and Britain. Like Spitzer, many say they could no longer remain at home watching the disturbing images emerging from the West Bank.
Their motivation goes beyond the basic humanitarian desire to help people in distress. For many, including committed Zionists, it reflects a profound concern about Israel's future and the direction in which the country is heading.
Under the olive trees, with the possibility of another settler attack never far from their minds, the volunteers explained why they felt compelled to come now, just days before Israel's October 27 election. Its outcome, they believe, will affect not only Jews living in Israel but Jewish communities around the world.
Newton, where Spitzer lives, is a prosperous Boston suburb known for its expensive homes, strong schools, parks and gardens. For its residents, there is little obvious reason to leave the comfort of their surroundings to spend days harvesting olives in one of the West Bank's most volatile areas.
"It's a place with many different Jewish communities," Spitzer explained. "Our congregation, for example, has 270 households. These are people for whom Israel is a meaningful part of their Jewish identity. Israel matters to them in the deepest, most fundamental way. We have family and friends here."
"Our community follows the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. We understand the fears of Israelis living here. Those fears aren't imaginary. They are real and justified. But we also care about human rights, whoever the person may be."
She said the images emerging from the West Bank convinced the group that they needed to witness the situation firsthand.
"This is the first time any of us has harvested olives in a Palestinian village in the West Bank. After just two days here, I can tell you that I don't think American Jews understand the scale of settler violence, how widespread it is, how it happens every day and how severe it has become."
"And it's not just American Jews who don't understand what's happening. I think most Israelis don't know what's going on here either, barely an hour from Tel Aviv."
‘We're here for the soul of the Jewish people’
Some members of the group asked that the location of their accommodation in Israel not be published. Others agreed to speak only if their names were withheld. Their concern was not about criticism from their communities back home, but about possible action by Israeli authorities.
Since the beginning of 2026, Israel has deported 54 foreign nationals, many of them Jews, who came to participate in solidarity activities with Palestinians in the West Bank. The authorities have also halted the immigration processes of two young people following their participation in protective-presence activities in Palestinian communities.
Spitzer, however, refuses to be intimidated.
"I would be deeply saddened if they decided to deport me or take away my right to visit Israel in the future because of this activity," she said. "What we're doing here isn't against the Israeli establishment. It's not against anyone or anything. It's an act of human solidarity. We're here for the soul of the Jewish people."
She pointed to the case of Lila Stillman-Utterback, the daughter of her friend Danielle, who was detained and had her passport confiscated before being deported.
"She was banned from entering Israel for 10 years. She grew up in America loving Israel. She came here to promote coexistence, to show Palestinians that there is also a Judaism that brings goodness into the world, that cares about basic human rights. She paid a heavy price for it."
By lunchtime, the volunteers had settled beneath the olive trees in Jalud to eat. One of them agreed to speak on the condition that only his first name be published.
"The reason is simple. I want to be able to return to Israel in the near future," he said. "My wife has relatives here, and I have friends here. We're both retired, and we love visiting Israel."
His name is Mitchell. At 78, he is a retired philosophy professor from a major university in Massachusetts, and he is deeply troubled by what he sees happening in Israel.
"We didn't have to come here," he said. "But when you see the horrors taking place here, you can't just sit at home and do nothing, even when you live across the ocean."
"I care about Israel. I care about the Jewish people. I'm part of that people. That's why I came here and not to Sudan, where terrible things are also happening."
What frightens him most, he said, is the damage Israel may be inflicting on itself.
"I'm very afraid because it seems you've set a mechanism of self-destruction in motion without understanding the disastrous consequences it could bring."
"How do you think what's happening here looks in the United States? It's shameful, truly shameful. American media outlets can't understand how something like this can happen, how the Israeli military and government allow masked Jewish extremists to attack women and elderly people with clubs, burn Palestinian homes and property, without being arrested or anyone trying to stop them."
He said the violence and the response of the authorities were beginning to shape how Americans viewed Israel.
"In mainstream American media, they ask, 'How can this happen?' And commentators answer, 'Because this is the policy of the Israeli government.'"
"That makes me deeply anxious about Israel's future. You're approaching a crucial election. But it's not crucial only for Israelis. It's crucial for me as an American Jew, too."
"If the outcome is that the same government remains in power, more and more Americans will ask whether Israel is truly an ally of the United States, whether we share the same values and whether maintaining such strong ties with Israel is really in America's interest."
His concern, he stressed, goes far beyond politics.
"Israel is an idea. Every Jew in the world has a meaningful and profound connection to this place."
When helping farmers is treated as a provocation
As the school day ended in Jalud, children ran into the olive grove and wandered among the elderly volunteers.
"They're not used to seeing Jews coming here to help us," one village resident said. "There have been four attacks on our village in the past week alone."
One of the most striking aspects of the situation is the way humanitarian activities of this kind are increasingly portrayed as provocations intended to disturb public order.
Against the backdrop of violence by extremist settlers, the foreign Jews and Israelis helping Palestinian farmers are sometimes treated as anarchists and lawbreakers who should be detained and removed. It represents a profound reversal of how acts of solidarity are understood.
The only Israeli lawmaker encountered in the fields on Tuesday was Gilad Kariv of the Democrats, an opposition party.
While fellow Knesset member Zvi Sukkot has visited Palestinian villages under military and parliamentary security escort, including during incidents in which he smashed memorials, Kariv was moving around the West Bank alone, without protection.
"Two days ago, I informed the Knesset Guard that I intended to visit Sinjil and Suwaya to see how the olive harvest was going," Kariv said.
"A few hours later, my contacts in those villages called and begged me not to come. One of them told me, 'The army came to us and said that if an Israeli Knesset member visits, we won't allow you to harvest anymore.'"
"So today, I went into the area without informing anyone."
Anton Goodman, acting CEO of Rabbis for Human Rights, said his organization was in contact with Jewish communities around the world and repeatedly encountered the same questions.
"People ask us, 'What's happened to you over there? Have you lost your minds? What kind of Judaism is this?'"
"What they see in the photographs and videos are Jews wearing ritual fringes, sidelocks and large skullcaps doing terrible things. On Shabbat and religious holidays, they're driving vehicles, filming on their phones, burning homes and attacking people with clubs. They're imposing terror based on an ideology of Jewish supremacy."
Goodman said these images were prompting a growing number of Diaspora Jews to take action.
"We're seeing an awakening among Jews abroad who simply cannot bear to watch these scenes any longer and stand aside. They're willing to buy plane tickets with their own money, come here and put themselves at risk to help Palestinians."
Kariv described the volunteers' work as a Jewish and Zionist act reflecting deep concern for Israel, its future and its character.
"I hope more and more Israelis and Jews from around the world join activities like these," he said.
He also promised that if an alternative government emerged from the coming election, it would do everything possible to stop violence by Jewish extremists.
‘Iran isn't Israel's greatest danger’
The visit ended beneath Spitzer's olive tree. We held the ladder as she stood above us, working a small plastic rake through the branches to knock the olives loose.
After several days in the West Bank, she said, her understanding of the threats facing Israel had changed.
"I've come to realize that Iran isn't Israel's greatest danger," she said. "It's the brutal violence of settlers against Palestinians in the West Bank. That's the greatest danger facing Israel today."
"If you don't put an end to it, if you don't make a determined effort to stop it through real action, Israel will become internationally isolated. It will turn into a Jewish ghetto."
Dozens detained during olive harvest, including US congressional candidate
The following day, Wednesday, Israeli security forces detained 42 American and Canadian Jews who had joined 28 Israeli activists from Rabbis for Human Rights to harvest olives in Nahalin, a Palestinian village south of Bethlehem.
The official explanation was that the group had entered agricultural land for harvesting without prior coordination or authorization from the IDF.
The volunteers were taken by bus to a police station in the Israeli settlement of Beitar Illit. Among those detained was Brad Lander, the Democratic nominee for New York's 10th Congressional District in the U.S. midterm elections scheduled for early November.
After a lengthy day at the police station, the 28 Israeli activists were barred from entering the West Bank for periods ranging from 15 to 30 days.
Thirty-eight foreign nationals, most of them Americans, were released without conditions. Four Americans were questioned on suspicion of supporting a terrorist organization before being released under orders prohibiting them from entering the West Bank for 15 days.
For the activists, the incident underscored the risks of an effort they regard as a basic expression of Jewish solidarity and a moral obligation toward Palestinian farmers.
"What happened in Nahalin was simply madness," Goodman said. "We are determined to continue showing solidarity with Palestinian farmers throughout the olive harvest."

Kenya announces second Ebola death, says ‘no evidence’ of community spread
Kenya has announced its second Ebola death, as the virus outbreak spreads from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) to several parts of Africa.
The Kenyan Ministry of Health said on Friday that the latest death was that of a 65-year-old woman who had developed symptoms during quarantine and was a close relative of a Kenyan man who died of Ebola earlier this month.
The ministry added that Kenya currently has seven Ebola cases receiving treatment at two isolation facilities.
All the cases are within “one cluster, with no evidence of community spread”, it added.
Kenya’s first Ebola case was identified this month in a man who travelled from DRC to Kenya and died at a Nairobi hospital on October 5.
Since then, Kenyan authorities have traced 135 contacts, all of whom were placed in quarantine, with nine cases confirmed, including the two patients who died.
African outbreak
The DRC declared its 17th Ebola outbreak in May and has since reported more than 9,000 cases and more than 4,600 deaths. The deadly disease has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past 50 years.
The current outbreak has now been reported in four countries across eastern, central and western Africa, giving it the widest geographic spread of any Ebola outbreak on the continent to date.
On Tuesday, Nigeria became the fourth African country to report an Ebola case. Nigerian Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate said on Friday that an analysis showed the case was closely related to the virus detected in the index case in Kenya.
Uganda announced on Saturday that travellers with a history of travel to DRC would not be permitted to transit through the East African nation.
Uganda had recorded 20 people infected, almost all of whom had travelled from DRC, and two deaths before being declared Ebola-free in August.

Macron brands Paris suburb shooting France’s first ‘racist terrorist attack’

Macron brands Paris suburb shooting France’s first ‘racist terrorist attack’
French President Emmanuel Macron has described a deadly shooting near Paris as the country’s first “racist terrorist attack,” appearing to overlook decades of Islamist terrorism, including the deliberate murders of Jewish civilians and children.
A gunman opened fire from a car in Trappes and neighboring La Verriere on Friday morning, killing 26-year-old aspiring MMA fighter Pengo Bossio Wangi and injuring five others, including a 12-year-old girl who was shot eight times. Other victims reportedly included a woman wearing a headscarf, a man of North African origin and two school cleaners of African origin.
The suspect, identified as 39-year-old Kevin T., was arrested after a shooting spree lasting approximately 15 minutes. Police recovered a submachine gun from his vehicle and discovered three gas cylinders wired to a timer in his apartment. He reportedly had 13 previous criminal-record entries but was not on a terrorism watchlist.
Visiting Trappes on Friday evening, Macron declared the shooting a historic “turning point” for France.
“This is the first time there has been a terrorist act aimed at killing our compatriots and our children for the colour of their skin or what their religion is thought to be,” he claimed. Macron also alleged that the suspect deliberately spared certain people because of their skin color, citing statements allegedly made after his arrest.
The French leader’s sweeping claim sparked criticism online, with commentators pointing to previous Islamist terrorist attacks that specifically targeted people because of their religion.
In March 2012, Islamist gunman Mohamed Merah murdered a rabbi and three Jewish children at a school in Toulouse, having previously killed three French soldiers.
In January 2015, ISIS-linked terrorist Amedy Coulibaly attacked the Hyper Cacher kosher supermarket in Paris, deliberately targeting Jewish shoppers and killing four hostages. Later that year, ISIS terrorists massacred 130 people in coordinated attacks across Paris and Saint-Denis, including 90 concertgoers at the Bataclan music venue.
Following the backlash, the Elysee sought to clarify Macron’s remarks, telling TF1 that he had specifically meant the first racist terrorist attack motivated by skin color, despite his explicit reference to religion.
The shooting comes amid nationwide unrest that has fueled a bitter political dispute over immigration and security. US President Donald Trump has blamed uncontrolled immigration and radical groups for the violence, while Macron has accused the ultra-left of orchestrating riots and denounced anti-immigration rhetoric portraying France as overrun by Islamists.
The Trappes shooting has also intensified political tensions ahead of next year’s presidential election. Communist presidential candidate Fabien Roussel accused the far right of spreading “racist hatred,” while National Rally leader Marine Le Pen condemned the shooting and its “abject motive of racism.”
France’s anti-terrorism prosecutors have opened an investigation into suspected terrorist murder with a racist motive. The suspect’s precise ideological affiliations remain under investigation.

Final Israel election polls put Eisenkot's Yashar ahead of Likud, but neither bloc wins a majority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
22:29:16 UTC
07:29:16 KST

Israel's final television election polls have delivered a clear but politically complicated verdict: former military chief Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party is ahead of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud, yet neither the opposition nor Netanyahu's allies are projected to secure the 61 seats needed to form a government.
The three surveys, published Friday by Kan 11, Channel 12 and Channel 13 ahead of Tuesday's October 27 election, give the bloc seeking to replace Netanyahu a lead of between two and six seats. With about 7.3 million Israelis eligible to vote, the results point to another potentially difficult round of coalition negotiations, and possibly even another election if no governing majority emerges.
All three networks project Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc winning exactly 50 seats in the 120-member Knesset, while the opposition's so-called change bloc receives between 52 and 56 seats. The Arab parties, which are not counted as part of either bloc, are projected to win between 14 and 16 seats.
How the political blocs are divided
Kan 11 projects 52 seats for the opposition bloc and 50 for Netanyahu's allies. The Arab parties receive another 14 seats, while the Reservists-Economic Party, led by Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha, wins four seats that are not assigned to either major bloc.
Channel 12 gives the opposition its strongest showing, with 56 seats compared with 50 for Netanyahu's bloc. The Arab parties receive 14 seats.
Channel 13 predicts a narrower opposition advantage of 54 seats to 50, with the Arab parties winning 16 seats.
The figures highlight the central challenge facing both camps. While the opposition leads in all three surveys, it remains short of a majority without additional parliamentary support. The Arab parties could therefore become pivotal, although their projected strength does not automatically translate into support for an opposition-led government.
Eisenkot, a former IDF chief of staff, emerges as the leader of the largest party in all three polls. Yashar wins 22 seats in the Kan 11 survey, 23 in Channel 12 and 22 in Channel 13.
Likud follows with 20, 21 and 19 seats, respectively, while former prime minister Naftali Bennett's B'Yachad, or Together, comes third with 14, 15 and 14 seats.
The electoral threshold could decide the outcome
Beyond the rivalry between Eisenkot and Netanyahu, one of the biggest uncertainties concerns smaller parties struggling to cross Israel's 3.25% electoral threshold, the minimum share of valid votes required to enter the Knesset.
Former IDF general Ofer Winter's People of Israel party, known in Hebrew as Amcha Yisrael, falls below the threshold in all three surveys. It receives 2.9% in Kan 11's poll, 2.5% in Channel 12's and 3.1% in Channel 13's, coming closest to entering parliament in the latter survey.
The joint Reservists-Economic Party, headed by former minister Yoaz Hendel and economist Yaron Zelekha, faces a similarly uncertain future. While Kan 11 projects it winning four seats, Channel 12 puts its support at just 2.4% and Channel 13 at 3.0%, both below the threshold.
The Haredi Public party, led by Moti Leitner and seeking support among ultra-Orthodox voters, also remains well below the cutoff, receiving between 0.5% and 1.3% across the three polls.
The consequences could be substantial. Votes cast for parties that fail to cross the threshold do not translate into parliamentary representation. Depending on which parties fall short, the resulting redistribution of seats among those that qualify could alter the balance between the rival political camps.
The poll of polls: Eisenkot leads with 22 seats
A combined picture based on the three television polls places Eisenkot's Yashar first with 22 seats, followed by Netanyahu's Likud with 20 and Bennett's B'Yachad with 15.
The Democrats, led by Yair Golan, and the Arab-majority Joint List, headed by Yousef Jabareen, each receive nine seats in the published composite.
Three parties receive eight seats apiece: Avigdor Liberman's Yisrael Beytenu, Itamar Ben Gvir's Otzma Yehudit and United Torah Judaism, led by Yaakov Asher.
Aryeh Deri's Shas and Bezalel Smotrich's Religious Zionism-Zehut alliance each receive seven seats, while Ra'am, the Arab party led by Mansour Abbas, receives six.
Winter's People of Israel and Hendel and Zelekha's Reservists-Economic Party both fall below the threshold in the overall assessment, although the latter retains a residual average of approximately one seat because it crosses the threshold in one of the three surveys. That statistical remainder does not mean the party is projected to enter parliament.
The complete results from the three television polls
Kan 11 poll
Yashar: 22 seats; Likud: 20; B'Yachad: 14; Joint List: 9; Democrats: 8; Otzma Yehudit: 8; Yisrael Beytenu: 8; United Torah Judaism: 8; Shas: 7; Religious Zionism-Zehut: 7; Ra'am: 5; Reservists-Economic Party: 4.
Below the electoral threshold: People of Israel, 2.9%; Black Color, 0.8%; Haredi Public, 0.7%.
The survey was conducted by Kantar, headed by Dudi Hasid, among 1,006 respondents, with a reported sampling margin of error of 3 percentage points.
Channel 12 poll
Yashar: 23 seats; Likud: 21; B'Yachad: 15; Democrats: 10; Joint List: 9; Shas: 8; Yisrael Beytenu: 8; Otzma Yehudit: 8; United Torah Judaism: 7; Religious Zionism-Zehut: 6; Ra'am: 5.
Below the electoral threshold: People of Israel, 2.5%; Reservists-Economic Party, 2.4%; Haredi Public, 0.5%.
The survey was conducted by the Midgam polling institute, headed by Mano Geva, in cooperation with iPanel. It included 1,018 respondents and had a reported sampling margin of error of 4.4 percentage points.
Channel 13 poll
Yashar: 22 seats; Likud: 19; B'Yachad: 14; Democrats: 10; Joint List: 9; United Torah Judaism: 8; Yisrael Beytenu: 8; Religious Zionism-Zehut: 8; Otzma Yehudit: 8; Shas: 7; Ra'am: 7.
Below the electoral threshold: People of Israel, 3.1%; Reservists-Economic Party, 3.0%; Haredi Public, 1.3%.
The survey was conducted by HaMadad, headed by Shmuel Rosner and Noah Slepkov, together with Stat-Net, the Midgam Project and Asakria, with additional data from Hive and statistical advice from Professor David Steinberg. It included 1,875 respondents and had a reported sampling margin of error of 2.3 percentage points.
Could Israel face another election?
The final surveys leave considerable uncertainty over Israel's next government, with both political camps facing obstacles to building a workable parliamentary majority.
The outcome could change significantly depending on voter turnout, particularly among supporters of smaller parties, and on how many votes ultimately go to lists that fail to enter parliament.
Last-minute shifts in voter preferences could also reshape the final distribution of seats, while party leaders may find themselves under pressure to reconsider commitments made during the campaign if coalition negotiations reach a deadlock.
For now, the three television polls show Eisenkot's party leading the race, but winning the largest number of seats is not the same as securing the premiership. The decisive question on October 27 will be not only which party finishes first, but which political leader can assemble the 61 lawmakers needed to govern.

US, allies and China vie for influence through Pacific security deals
New mapping tool highlights contrasting approaches, with Beijing expanding policing ties as Washington maintains defence pacts
Strategic competition between China and the US and its allies is intensifying across the Pacific islands, with both sides pursuing a growing range of security agreements to expand their influence, according to an interactive mapping tool released this week by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), a Washington think tank.
The tool details 56 security arrangements among 14 Pacific island countries and the US, Australia, New Zealand, mainland China and Taiwan in a bid to map out linkages in a region that has long seen Beijing and Washington spar for influence, particularly under the administration of former president Joe Biden.
The matrix assigns different weights to treaty-level defence commitments, status of forces agreements, maritime surveillance arrangements, policing cooperation and memorandums of understanding.
The mapping tool classifies them into three categories based on the level and nature of the security ties: “defence treaty ally”, “formal security agreement” without defence guarantees and “non-binding cooperation only”.

Pentagon designates Confucius Institutes in US a national security threat
WASHINGTON – The US Defense Department has designated Chinese-funded cultural centres on university campuses known as Confucius Institutes as a threat to US national security, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Oct 23.

MOSCOW, October 24. /TASS/. Saudi Arabia not to host the international music competition Intervision this year, a source told TASS.
"Due to a combination of circumstances, holding it in Saudi Arabia is not currently possible. According to our information, the competition is proposed to be held in 2027," the source said.
Back in early August, a source in Riyadh told TASS that the organization of the competition in 2026 was in doubt and there was no guarantee that the event would take place.
In May, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov expressed hope that escalation in the Middle East would not undermine the plans to organize the Intervision there. However, Saudi Arabia has not yet publicly announced the music competition and has not provided possible dates and the lineup of participants.
Intervision was a song contest organized by the International Organization of Television and Radio Broadcasting (OIRT), which existed from 1946 to 1993. It was held in the 1960s-1980s, following the same model as "Eurovision," a music award of the European Broadcasting Union, which broke away from OIRT. The contest involved not only socialist countries close to the USSR, but also Austria, Belgium, Spain, Canada, the Netherlands, Portugal, and Finland.
The Intervision was revived in 2025 in Moscow. Russia was represented by Honored Artist of the Russian Federation Yaroslav Dronov (Shaman). More than 20 countries, including all BRICS states, took part.

Barack Obama’s Belfast speech was a shameful, distorted rewrite of Israel's history - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
22:14:01 UTC
07:14:01 KST

Barack Obama has apparently discovered a new historical crime: the Jewish people stole their own homeland.
That, at least, is the impression left by his latest attempt to rewrite Middle Eastern history.
Speaking in Belfast on October 13, the former American president managed to turn the Jewish people’s return to the Land of Israel into a story of persecuted European Jews who sought refuge, took Palestinian land, and provoked an understandable demand to get it back.
Never mind 3,000 years of Jewish history, two Temples in Jerusalem, or centuries of Jewish longing for Zion. In Obama’s telling, the Jews somehow became interlopers in the very land where their national story began.
“The Jewish people, for millennia, were oppressed, discriminated against, killed,” he said. They “understandably sought a refuge” but “took land off people, and they were excessive.” Palestinians, he added, “understandably said, ‘This is injustice, and I want my land back.’”
Former president Obama barely made an effort to explain the Jewish people’s ancient connection to the land
Obama made little effort to explain the Jewish people’s ancient connection to the land. Instead, he presented their return to their ancestral patrimony primarily as an act of injustice.
Let’s start with the most basic fact that Obama chose to downplay: the Jewish people are indigenous to the Land of Israel.
More than 3,000 years ago, the Israelites had already established themselves in the Land. By the 10th century BCE, they had formed a kingdom, developed their own language, and centered their national and religious life on Jerusalem. According to the biblical account, King David made the city his capital, and his son King Solomon built the First Temple there.
That is not a late European invention. It is a starting point of Jewish history.
The archaeological record provides striking evidence. The Tel Dan Stele, a ninth-century BCE stone monument discovered in northern Israel in 1993, contains an ancient Aramaic inscription referring to the “House of David.” It is the earliest known reference to David’s royal dynasty outside the Bible.
Hebrew inscriptions, Israelite seals, and the remains of ancient fortifications and settlements appear throughout the land.
After the Babylonian exile ended in 516 BCE, Jews returned and rebuilt the Temple.
Roman ruins, the Western Wall, coins from the Jewish revolts against Rome, and the Dead Sea Scrolls all attest to the Jewish people’s deep historical roots in the Land of Israel.
Even after the Romans destroyed the Second Temple in 70 CE and suppressed the Bar-Kochba revolt, Jews never severed their connection to the land. Communities persisted in Jerusalem, Hebron, Safed, and Tiberias – the four holy cities. Jewish legal and religious life continued there.
For centuries, Jews prayed facing Jerusalem, invoked Zion in their daily prayers, and ended the Passover Seder with the words “Next year in Jerusalem.” The connection was not a modern recovery of ancient memory. It was never broken.
Nor did Zionism begin as a desperate European response to Hitler. The First Aliyah began in 1882, bringing thousands of Jewish pioneers back to the Land of Israel. And in 1897, Theodor Herzl convened the First Zionist Congress, decades before the Holocaust.
Jewish pioneers purchased land from Arab owners and built farms, towns, and thriving agricultural communities. To reduce this remarkable enterprise to simple theft, as the former president effectively did, is a gross distortion of history.
OBAMA SKIPPED the diplomatic record, too.
In 1917, Britain issued the Balfour Declaration endorsing a Jewish national home. Five years later, the League of Nations Mandate explicitly recognized “the historical connection of the Jewish people with Palestine” and the grounds for “reconstituting their national home” there.
The word “reconstituting” is important. The League of Nations was acknowledging the Jewish people’s preexisting connection to the land, not creating a new one.
Then came November 29, 1947.
The UN voted to partition British Mandatory Palestine into two states, one Jewish and one Arab. Jewish leaders accepted the plan. Arab leaders rejected it.
That refusal was hardly new. In 1937, Britain’s Peel Commission had also proposed partition. Zionist leaders accepted partition as a basis for further negotiations, while Arab leaders rejected it outright. A decade later, another chance for two states met much the same fate.
Violence followed, and when Israel declared independence on May 14, 1948, neighboring Arab armies invaded. The nascent Jewish state fought for its survival.
Israel’s Declaration of Independence even appealed to its Arab inhabitants to help build the new state as equal citizens and extended a hand of peace to neighboring countries. That hardly fits Obama’s account of a nation conceived simply as an instrument of dispossession.
The fact is that there was no sovereign Palestinian state that Israel overthrew in 1948. There was, however, an internationally proposed Arab state that the Arab leadership refused to accept.
Israel also absorbed hundreds of thousands of Jewish refugees driven from Arab lands after 1948. Yet while Israel integrated these refugees into its society, most Arab states refused to grant Palestinian refugees citizenship, leaving generations in a state of uncertainty.
And the rejection did not end in 1948. For nearly two decades, Jordan controlled Judea and Samaria and eastern Jerusalem, while Egypt administered Gaza. Neither established a Palestinian state.
Obama would have his audience believe that Palestinian rejectionism was simply a response to Jewish dispossession. But the historical record clearly tells a very different story.
Obama’s treatment of Palestinian violence
MORE DISTURBING still was Obama’s treatment of Palestinian violence.
Speaking about Hamas’s Oct. 7 massacre, Obama declared that “you could not have designed something that was less likely to produce meaningful change.”
Think about that.
When terrorists murder approximately 1,200 people and kidnap 251, the principal issue is not whether their actions will produce meaningful political change. It is that they committed an act of unimaginable barbarity.
By discussing the massacre in terms of its political effectiveness, Obama risks reducing a moral atrocity to a tactical mistake. Would the slaughter have been any less reprehensible had Hamas managed to advance its political objectives?
Indeed, no political claim, no matter how loudly asserted, confers a license to murder families in their homes or drag hostages into Gaza.
And terrorism did not begin with Israel’s founding, let alone the 1967 war. In 1929, Arab rioters murdered 67 Jews in Hebron, destroying an ancient Jewish community nearly two decades before independence.
WHAT OBAMA did in Belfast was more than distort Israel’s history. He turned the descendants of ancient Israel into trespassers in their own homeland, while treating the massacre of Jews as a failed political strategy.
Obama is, of course, entitled to his own opinions. But he is not entitled to his own version of history.
The Jewish people lived in the Land of Israel long before Barack Obama entered the world stage. And they will still be there long after his shameful revisionism has been forgotten.■
The writer served as deputy communications director under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar attended a flag-raising ceremony outside parliament on Lajos Kossuth Square before laying flowers at memorials and graves, including that of Imre Nagy, the former prime minister executed after the 1956 revolution.
The uprising, which began on 23 October 1956, lasted 15 days before Soviet troops and tanks crushed the revolt, killing up to 3,000 revolutionaries.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen joined the commemorations, addressing Hungarian lawmakers during a special parliamentary session attended by European Council President António Costa. She praised the courage of Hungarians who fought for freedom, democracy, and justice, drawing parallels with the country's recent political transition following Viktor Orbán's departure from power.
Her visit comes as Budapest seeks the release of billions of euros in frozen EU funding, withheld over rule-of-law and corruption concerns. Brussels maintains that further reforms are needed before the funds can be unlocked, a key challenge for Magyar's new government.

In 1956, Moscow agreed to withdraw its troops from Budapest. One week later, it launched a 60,000-soldier operation to crush Hungary’s revolution.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
22:01:04 UTC
07:01:04 KST

In 1956, Moscow agreed to withdraw its troops from Budapest. One week later, it launched a 60,000-soldier operation to crush Hungary’s revolution.
On October 23, 1956, hundreds of thousands of Budapest residents took to the streets to demand political reforms, free elections, and the withdrawal of Soviet troops. Peaceful demonstrations quickly turned into an armed uprising. Within days, Hungary was on the verge of leaving the Soviet bloc. The Soviet leadership initially agreed to make concessions and withdraw troops from the capital, but then reversed course. On November 4, the Soviet army launched a large-scale military operation that crushed the uprising. Thousands of people died, and about 200,000 Hungarians left the country. Western governments condemned Moscow’s actions but stopped short of intervening. Why did Hungarians rise up against the communist regime? What made Khrushchev abandon compromise? Could the United States and Europe have helped the insurgents? And why, 70 years later, do the events of 1956 still provoke political disputes in Hungary? Historian Alexey Uvarov answers these and other questions about the uprising.
What was happening in the world in the fall of 1956?
By the mid-1950s, the Cold War had been underway for almost 10 years. After World War II, Europe split into two camps. The United States played the leading role in Western Europe, while communist regimes under Soviet control took power in Poland, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Romania, Bulgaria, and East Germany. In 1949, the United States and its allies formed NATO; in 1955, the Soviet Union and Eastern European countries established the Warsaw Pact.
The confrontation extended beyond Europe. From 1950 to 1953, the United States and its allies fought in the Korean War against North Korea, which had Soviet and Chinese backing. By then, both superpowers had nuclear weapons and understood that a direct conflict between them could have catastrophic consequences.
Tensions began to ease after Joseph Stalin’s death in 1953. The Korean War ended, and in 1955, the Soviet Union withdrew its troops from Austria, which became a neutral state. That same year, the leaders of the Soviet Union, the United States, Britain, and France met in Geneva for the first time in 10 years. Their rivalry continued, but both sides sought to avoid a direct confrontation.
Soviet policy was changing, too. Stalin’s death set off a power struggle in Moscow that Nikita Khrushchev won. In February 1956, at the 20th Congress of the Soviet Communist Party, he delivered a secret speech condemning Stalin’s cult of personality and mass repression. At the same time, the Soviet leadership began talking about the possibility of national paths to socialism. Across Eastern Europe, this prompted public debate about possible reforms and loosening Moscow’s political control.
Dwight Eisenhower had been president of the United States since January 1953. His administration publicly advocated the “liberation” of Eastern Europe from communist rule, while the Washington-funded broadcaster Radio Free Europe encouraged anti-Soviet sentiment. In practice, however, White House policy was far more cautious. In June 1953, Soviet troops had crushed an uprising in East Germany, and the United States had not intervened. American leaders decided that attempting to liberate Eastern Europe by force could lead to nuclear war. They therefore sought to weaken Soviet influence primarily through peaceful means.
The Suez Crisis erupted as events unfolded in Hungary. In late October 1956, Israel, Britain, and France launched a military operation against Egypt, whose president, Gamal Abdel Nasser, had nationalized the Suez Canal. The United States opposed its own allies’ actions, dividing the Western powers.
The fall of 1956 was a time of contradictions. The Cold War continued, yet the superpowers were seeking to avoid confrontation and had resumed contacts broken off under Stalin. Changes underway in the Soviet Union were raising hopes for reform in Eastern Europe. But no one knew what the limits of those reforms might be or how far Soviet leaders were prepared to go in supporting them.
What was Hungary like in the first half of the 20th century?
Until 1918, Hungary was part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, where it enjoyed considerable autonomy. The Kingdom of Hungary covered a much larger territory than modern Hungary, encompassing present-day Slovakia, Transylvania, and Croatia. After its defeat in World War I in 1918, Austria-Hungary disintegrated. Hungary became independent, and a republic was proclaimed in Budapest, but the new government could not hold on to power. In the spring of 1919, communists led by Béla Kun seized power. They proclaimed the Hungarian Soviet Republic, which lasted a few months. Communist rule brought political terror and ended in defeat by the Romanian army.
After the communists fell, Miklós Horthy, a former admiral in the Austro-Hungarian navy, came to power. In 1920, Hungary became a kingdom again, but without a king. Horthy became regent and effectively ruled the country until 1944. His regime was conservative and authoritarian, though parliament and some political parties continued to exist. The country’s most pressing problem was the aftermath of the 1920 Treaty of Trianon: Hungary lost about two-thirds of its territory, and roughly a third of ethnic Hungarians found themselves outside its new borders.
The desire to recover those territories largely shaped Horthy’s foreign policy. Hungary gradually drew closer to Fascist Italy and Nazi Germany, whose support helped it regain some of the lost lands from 1938 to 1941. The price, however, was participation in World War II on Germany’s side. In 1941, Hungary entered the war against the Soviet Union, and in 1943 its army suffered catastrophic losses on the Eastern Front.
In March 1944, Germany occupied Hungary, fearing that it would pull out of the war. With the active participation of the Hungarian authorities, more than 400,000 Jews were deported to Auschwitz within a few months. That fall, Horthy tried to negotiate an armistice with Germany’s enemies but was removed from power. The Nazis replaced him with Hungarian far-right politicians from the Arrow Cross Party.
In February 1945, after a siege lasting almost two months, the Red Army took Budapest. The city had suffered extensive destruction, and Hungary was once again on the losing side of a world war. Its political future now depended largely on the Soviet Union, whose troops were stationed in the country.
What happened in Hungary between 1945 and 1956? Did it become a copy of the Soviet Union?
Hungary was treated as a defeated ally of Nazi Germany, so its reconstruction and political future depended on the victorious powers. Formally, the Allied Control Commission monitored compliance with the armistice, but Soviet representatives led by Marshal Kliment Voroshilov dominated the commission. Hungary also had to pay reparations, a substantial share of which was to go to the Soviet Union.
Initially, the country retained a multiparty system. Free parliamentary elections were held in November 1945. The Smallholders’ Party won about 57% of the vote, while the communists received just 17%. With Moscow’s support, however, the communists kept their places in the coalition government and retained control of key security agencies. Their leader, Mátyás Rákosi, gradually eliminated political opponents using what he himself called “salami tactics”: Opposition parties were weakened piece by piece as their leaders were accused of conspiring and engaging in activities against the state.
By the end of the 1940s, the communists had established complete control. In 1947, Soviet security services arrested Béla Kovács, a leader of the Smallholders’ Party, and Prime Minister Ferenc Nagy was forced to resign. In 1948, the communists absorbed the Social Democratic Party, and in 1949 a Soviet-style constitution was adopted. Hungary became a people’s republic, with one party holding a virtual monopoly on power.
A harsh dictatorship took shape in the years that followed. Rákosi, who called himself Stalin’s best pupil, established a system of mass repression. Opposition figures, clergy, intellectuals, and even members of the Communist Party itself were arrested. In 1949, former Interior Minister László Rajk was executed on fabricated espionage charges. Cardinal József Mindszenty, the head of Hungary’s Catholic Church, was sentenced to life in prison. Tens of thousands of people were sent to prisons and camps, and many families were forcibly expelled from cities.
At the same time, the authorities tried to restructure the economy along Soviet lines. Industry was nationalized, peasants were forced to join agricultural cooperatives, and resources went primarily toward the rapid expansion of heavy industry. The aim was to turn Hungary into an industrial hub for the Soviet bloc despite its limited raw material reserves. These policies led to falling living standards, shortages of consumer goods, and growing public discontent.
By the early 1950s, Hungary’s political and economic system largely replicated that of the Soviet Union under Stalin. The communist regime lacked broad public support and survived mainly because of the Soviet military presence. After Stalin’s death, the discontent that had built up began to surface more forcefully.
What happened in Hungary between Stalin’s death and the start of the uprising?
In March 1953, Soviet leaders began reassessing their policies in Eastern Europe. Moscow understood that repression and economic hardship were fueling public discontent and decided to move away from Stalin’s approach to foreign policy. In June, Hungary’s leaders were summoned to the Kremlin, where Mátyás Rákosi faced sharp criticism. He was accused of mass repression, excessive industrialization, and ruining agriculture. Moscow demanded that Rákosi hand the prime minister’s post to Imre Nagy while remaining leader of the Communist Party.
Nagy was a longtime party member who had spent many years in the Soviet Union. After World War II, he served as agriculture minister and oversaw a land reform that distributed large estates among peasants. On becoming prime minister in the summer of 1953, Nagy announced a “new course.” The authorities slowed industrialization, eased pressure on peasants, began releasing political prisoners, and gave greater priority to producing consumer goods. There was no talk yet of abandoning socialism or introducing a multiparty system, but the changes were substantial compared with previous policies. The reforms quickly made Nagy popular with the public.
But Rákosi remained party leader and opposed these policies. The outcome of his struggle with Nagy depended largely on who prevailed in Moscow. In early 1955, Khrushchev strengthened his position, while Georgy Malenkov, who supported Nagy, lost his post as head of the Soviet government. This enabled Rákosi to oust his rival from power. In April 1955, Nagy was removed as prime minister and later expelled from the party. Socialist Hungary’s leaders tried to return to their previous policies, but it was too late: Reform-minded writers, journalists, and party officials continued to push for change.
These movements gained momentum after the 20th Congress of the Soviet Communist Party in February 1956, where Khrushchev condemned repression. Rákosi, who regarded himself as a follower of Stalin, became even more vulnerable. Public debate intensified in Budapest, particularly in the Petőfi Circle, a discussion group named after the poet Sándor Petőfi, which drew thousands of participants. In the summer of 1956, the Politburo decided to remove Rákosi but installed his closest associate, Ernő Gerő, as party leader. Most critics of the regime saw this as merely a symbolic concession that fell well short of what was needed.
Tensions continued to mount. On October 6, the authorities allowed a ceremonial reburial of László Rajk, the party official executed in 1949 on fabricated charges. Tens of thousands attended, turning the ceremony into a mass demonstration against the Stalinist past. On October 13, Nagy was readmitted to the party. The leadership, however, still hesitated to undertake serious reforms.
The situation in Hungary was full of contradictions. Moscow had first supported reforms, then allowed them to be rolled back, and then once again advocated change and began de-Stalinization. Yet the people responsible for repression and harsh policies remained in power in Hungary. Hungarians increasingly doubted that the communists could carry out the necessary reforms, and soon they decided to take to the streets.
How and why did the uprising begin?
Events in neighboring Poland provided the spark. In October 1956, Polish communists decided to restore Władysław Gomułka to the party leadership. He had been removed from power and imprisoned under Stalin. Moscow tried to prevent his return: On October 19, Khrushchev and other leaders hurried to Warsaw, and Soviet troops began advancing toward the city. After negotiations, however, the Kremlin accepted the appointment of Gomułka, who promised to preserve the alliance with the Soviet Union. In Hungary, these events raised hopes that similar changes could be achieved at home.
On October 22, students at Budapest’s Polytechnic Institute drew up 16 demands for the authorities. They called for the withdrawal of Soviet troops from Hungary, Nagy’s return as prime minister, free elections, an end to censorship, and accountability for the country’s former leader, Rákosi. The students decided to hold a demonstration the following day in support of Poland’s reforms.
The October 23 demonstration began peacefully but quickly grew into a mass protest. Workers and other Budapest residents joined the students; by evening, hundreds of thousands of people were in the streets. Some demonstrators gathered outside parliament, demanding Nagy’s return, while others toppled an enormous statue of Stalin. Gerő, the Communist Party’s first secretary, went on the radio and accused the protesters of nationalism and hostile actions against the socialist system. His speech only fueled the anger.
Meanwhile, thousands of people gathered outside the state radio building. They demanded that the students be allowed on air to read their 16 demands. The building was guarded by political police, and the demonstrators’ representatives, who had been allowed inside for talks, had still not come back hours later. Rumors spread through the crowd that they had been arrested or even killed. Tensions rose as demonstrators demanded the delegation’s release and tried to enter the building. State security officers used tear gas and then opened fire on the crowd, which included unarmed demonstrators. Some people were killed, and others were wounded.
The authorities then lost control of the situation entirely. Protesters began arming themselves. Hungarian soldiers and police officers who refused to disperse the demonstration gave them some weapons; the protesters obtained others from warehouses and factories. Street fighting broke out around the radio building and continued through the night. Within hours, a peaceful demonstration had become an armed uprising.
How did the Soviet leadership respond? Did Moscow immediately decide to crush the uprising by force?
On the evening of October 23, as protests escalated into armed clashes, the Hungarian authorities asked Moscow for military assistance. Soviet leaders convened an emergency meeting at the Kremlin that night. Most supported sending in troops. Only Anastas Mikoyan opposed the move, believing that force would only deepen the crisis. The other Politburo members did not support him, however, and Soviet tanks entered Budapest on the morning of October 24. At the same time, Nagy was reappointed prime minister of Hungary in the hope that this would calm the protesters.
But sending in troops had the opposite effect: A local protest against the communist leadership became a national uprising against Soviet domination. Street fighting continued, and some Hungarian troops joined the insurgents. On October 25, demonstrators outside parliament came under fire on an even larger scale, and dozens of people were killed. The authorities were rapidly losing control of the country: Revolutionary committees sprang up in cities, and workers’ councils formed in factories.
Soviet leaders again tried to find a political solution to the crisis. On October 28, Hungary’s new prime minister, Nagy, announced a ceasefire, recognized the uprising as a national democratic movement, and promised to disband the political police. Moscow, in turn, agreed to begin withdrawing troops from Budapest.
Records of Soviet leadership meetings from October 28 to 31, 1956, reveal considerable hesitation. On October 28, for example, Soviet Prime Minister Nikolai Bulganin called a full-scale military operation a “reckless venture,” a view supported by Politburo member Lazar Kaganovich. That same day, Khrushchev himself advocated a political solution, saying, “All we’re doing is shooting.” On October 30, Foreign Minister Dmitry Shepilov even suggested that Moscow stop dictating terms to Eastern European countries.
Soviet leaders changed course on October 31. They concluded that concessions had failed to halt the revolution: Communist Party rule in Hungary was rapidly crumbling, and Nagy’s government could no longer guarantee that the country would remain in the Soviet bloc. Meanwhile, the start of the British-French operation against Egypt reinforced Khrushchev’s fear that withdrawing from Budapest would be seen as a sign of weakness. Fear of criticism from the Soviet Communist Party’s conservative wing also played a role, as did confidence that the United States would stop short of military intervention. Khrushchev gave this explanation:
If we leave Hungary, it will encourage the American, British, and French imperialists. They will see it as weakness on our part and press forward. We would be exposing the weakness of our position. Our party would not understand us. We would then be giving them Hungary on top of Egypt. We have no other choice.
Moscow therefore abandoned compromise and decided to restore control over Hungary by force.
How was the uprising crushed? How many people died? And what kind of regime emerged in Hungary?
After deciding to intervene militarily on October 31, the Soviet Union began moving additional troops into Hungary. Dubbed Operation Whirlwind, the operation was led by Marshal Ivan Konev. About 60,000 Soviet troops took part in total. The plan called for seizing Budapest and other major cities simultaneously, disarming the Hungarian army, and taking control of key government institutions.
Meanwhile, Soviet leaders continued to pretend they were willing to negotiate a peaceful settlement. On November 3, Hungarian and Soviet representatives discussed a troop withdrawal. That evening, however, the Hungarian delegation, led by Defense Minister Pál Maléter, was invited to a Soviet military base, where KGB officers arrested its members. At dawn on November 4, the Red Army launched its offensive. Prime Minister Nagy managed to broadcast a radio message announcing the invasion before taking refuge in the Yugoslav embassy. Moscow announced the formation of a new Hungarian government led by János Kádár.
The Hungarian army was unable to mount organized resistance. Soviet troops quickly disarmed most of its units, leaving volunteer groups — mainly young workers and students — to do most of the fighting. Despite the Soviet Union’s overwhelming military superiority, street battles in Budapest continued for several days. The last major pockets of resistance were crushed by mid-November.
About 2,500 to 2,700 Hungarians died in the fighting, and roughly 20,000 more were wounded. A total of 669 Soviet soldiers were killed in action or died of their wounds. Another 51 servicemen were missing, and about 1,500 were wounded. Resistance continued even after the fighting ended: Workers’ councils organized strikes, demanding the restoration of the country’s independence. With Soviet support, Kádár’s new government gradually suppressed these protests.
Military defeat was followed by mass repression. Tens of thousands of people were convicted of taking part in the uprising, and about 230 were executed. More than 200,000 Hungarians left the country. Nagy, who had been promised safe passage from the Yugoslav embassy, was detained and taken to Romania. He was later returned to Hungary, where he was sentenced to death in a trial closed to the public. On June 16, 1958, Nagy was executed along with several associates.
Kádár remained in power for more than 30 years. The early years of his rule brought brutal repression, but the regime gradually softened. A broad amnesty was announced in 1963, and in later years Hungarians gained more economic freedom and greater freedom in their private lives than people in many other Soviet-bloc countries. This system later became known as “goulash communism.” Political power, however, remained in the party’s hands, Soviet troops stayed in the country, and the events of 1956 were officially regarded as a “counterrevolution.”
How did Western countries respond to the uprising? And why didn’t they help the Hungarians?
The uprising caught the United States and its European allies off guard. American intelligence services had not expected a mass armed revolt against the communist regime, even though the Eisenhower administration advocated the “liberation” of Eastern Europe from Soviet domination. The American-funded broadcaster Radio Free Europe also encouraged anti-communist sentiment and called for resistance. Some Hungarians therefore expected the West to come to their aid if they rose up.
But as events in East Germany in 1953 had already shown, the United States had no intention of liberating Soviet-bloc countries by military force. Washington understood that such a confrontation could escalate into nuclear war. When the Hungarian uprising began on October 23, 1956, the White House therefore ruled out direct intervention almost immediately.
Instead, the Americans tried to find a diplomatic solution. Washington hoped that Hungary could become an independent, neutral state, following Austria’s example. Hungary would no longer be under Soviet control but would not join NATO either. On October 27, Secretary of State John Foster Dulles publicly said that Washington did not regard Eastern European states as potential military allies. American leaders hoped this would persuade Moscow to refrain from another military intervention.
The Suez Crisis complicated matters. As the uprising unfolded, Britain and France joined Israel in launching a military operation against Egypt, which the United States sharply condemned. Serious divisions emerged among the Western allies. The main reason Western governments refused to intervene militarily, however, was not the Suez Crisis but their unwillingness to risk a direct war with the Soviet Union.
American policy thus proved contradictory: Washington publicly supported the liberation of Eastern European countries but had no intention of going to war for them. As a result, some Hungarian insurgents waited for Western help that never came.
What form did Western support take, then?
Although Western countries ruled out military intervention, they publicly supported the uprising and condemned Soviet actions. British Foreign Secretary Selwyn Lloyd told Parliament that the British government was following the Hungarians’ struggle for freedom with admiration. French Prime Minister Guy Mollet rejected Soviet accusations that fascists had organized the uprising. West German Chancellor Konrad Adenauer called the Hungarian resistance an example of extraordinary heroism. Mass demonstrations in solidarity with Hungarians took place in European capitals.
The U.N. Security Council began considering the situation in Hungary as early as October 28, and after the renewed Soviet invasion on November 4, Western countries demanded the withdrawal of Soviet troops. Moscow, however, used its veto to block a resolution to that effect. The issue was referred to the U.N. General Assembly, which voted on November 4 to condemn the Soviet intervention and demand a troop withdrawal. In January 1957, a special U.N. committee was established to investigate the events. Its report confirmed that the uprising had been a mass movement against Soviet domination, rather than a Western-organized coup. But General Assembly resolutions were not binding, and the United Nations could not compel Moscow to change its policy.
The largest practical contribution was taking in refugees. After the uprising was crushed, more than 200,000 people — about 2% of the population — left Hungary. As many as 185,000 fled to neighboring neutral Austria, and about 20,000 more to Yugoslavia. Many crossed the border on foot without assistance. This was relatively easy because some of the border barriers between Hungary and Austria had been dismantled in the summer of 1956.
The Austrian authorities set up temporary camps and provided refugees with food, shelter, and medical care. With support from the United Nations, the Red Cross, and other international organizations, refugees began resettling in other countries. The United States, Canada, Britain, West Germany, and other countries took in tens of thousands of Hungarians. In total, about 180,000 refugees later moved from Austria and Yugoslavia to countries around the world.
How were the events of 1956 remembered in Hungary — and how are they remembered today?
After the uprising was crushed, the communist authorities led by Kádár officially called it a “counterrevolution” organized by enemies of socialism. Participants were persecuted, and public discussion of the events was tightly controlled. Over time, the authorities preferred to keep silent about the subject, since memories of the Soviet invasion called the legitimacy of the Moscow-backed regime into question. Nevertheless, the memory of the uprising lived on among emigrants and opposition circles, particularly through the circulation of samizdat — publications distributed outside state censorship — in the 1970s and 1980s.
The situation began to change in the second half of the 1980s, influenced by perestroika in the Soviet Union and reforms in Hungary itself. In 1988, Kádár was removed as party leader. In January 1989, Imre Pozsgay, a leader of Hungary’s Communist Party, publicly called the events of 1956 a popular uprising. A turning point came with the ceremonial reburial of Nagy and his associates on June 16, 1989, which drew about 250,000 people. A young opposition politician, Viktor Orbán, spoke at the ceremony, demanding the withdrawal of Soviet troops and free elections. On October 23, 1989, the anniversary of the uprising’s start, Hungary officially ceased to be a socialist republic.
After the communist regime fell, the 1956 revolution became one of the symbols of Hungary’s new democracy. In 1990, October 23 was declared a national holiday. Gradually, however, political groups developed different interpretations of the uprising’s legacy. Liberal politicians more often emphasized the struggle for democracy and political freedoms, while national conservatives stressed resistance to foreign domination and the defense of national independence. Nagy himself also became a subject of dispute: He had led the revolutionary government and been executed, but he had also risen through the communist movement and initially advocated reforming socialism rather than abolishing it.
Under Orbán, who headed the government from 2010 to 2026, the government’s official commemoration of 1956 increasingly emphasized national independence. Orbán repeatedly compared the Hungarians’ struggle against Moscow in 1956 to Budapest’s contemporary disputes with the European Union. In late 2018, a monument to Nagy was removed from a square near parliament and later installed elsewhere. The decision drew criticism from the opposition.
After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the memory of the uprising became the subject of fresh disputes: Orbán’s opponents pointed to the contradiction between his reverence for those who fought the Soviet invasion and his warm relations with Putin’s Russia. In September 2024, an adviser to Orbán said that if Russia invaded, Hungary should not follow Ukraine’s example of armed resistance, because the 1956 uprising had ended in tragedy. The remark prompted another wave of criticism. Orbán was forced to distance himself publicly from his adviser’s words, calling them a mistake.
The Hungarian uprising was one of the Cold War’s most dramatic events. It showed how sweeping the demands for change inspired by de-Stalinization could become, and how little change Soviet leaders were willing to allow. When Hungary’s place in the Soviet bloc came under threat, Moscow chose military intervention over political compromise. Despite their public support for the Hungarians, Western countries stopped short of a direct confrontation with the Soviet Union, limiting their response to diplomatic protests and aid for refugees.
The uprising was crushed, but its memory survived and, three decades later, played an important role in the fall of the communist regime. Yet the history of 1956 has not become a national symbol everyone agrees on: Politicians still interpret the uprising’s goals and lessons differently. Hungarians continue to debate what freedom, independence, and resistance to outside pressure mean today.

France to deploy 70,000 police officers ahead of protests

France to deploy 70,000 police officers ahead of protests
October 24, 2026
As France braces for new protests on Saturday, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez warned that calls for violence and looting were circulating online and pledged to deploy 70,000 police officers to secure order across the country.
"We will be uncompromising with rioters, looters and all those who commit acts of violence," Nunez told reporters on Friday.
The regular police officers will be reinforced by elite units, mounted police and heavy vehicles, and also equipped with helicopters, water cannon, drones and anti-drone systems, according to the minister.
"We will be extremely vigilant," he added, vowing to "let absolutely nothing pass."
Paris storekeepers prepare for more looting
The apparent show of force comes a week after riots ripped through Paris and other major cities.
While the ongoing political standoff started with students demanding better facilities, more teachers, and other improvements to the country's education system, it has grown into a general outpouring of anger over the cost of living.
Last Saturday, the protests escalated into violent riots, with authorities accusing radical militants and bands of young looters of taking advantage of the protesters' anger to sow chaos.
Police have faced groups of masked looters burning cars and buildings. Thousands of stores were ransacked.
Addressing reporters on Friday, the interior minister said that the unrest was "completely unacceptable" and said the authorities "will do everything in our power" to avoid a repeat of the violence.
Meanwhile, Paris shopkeepers were seen boarding up their windows. The city council called on residents and business owners to remove objects that could be set on fire or used as either projectiles or barricades.
Who will be marching on Saturday?
Nunez also said authorities will maintain curfews in designated areas of the city. This will include restrictions between 11 pm and 6 am in two central Paris squares, according to the local police.
The police approved only one protest march, organized by labor union CGT, on a limited route through Paris on Saturday. The authorities rejected requests by France's biggest student union UNEF and its anti-establishment Yellow Vest movement to hold their own rallies.
However, UNEF pledged to go ahead with its protest regardless, while Yellow Vest supporters were expected to join the official march.
Authorities had banned all protests in France's second largest city, Marseille, before walking the decision back and allowing a union demonstration. Authorities also intend to keep protesters away from the center of Lyon, France's third most populous city.
Students 'not satisfied' after meeting Macron
The government, led by centrist President Emmanuel Macron, sought to differentiate between what they see as legitimate protests and the violent unrest.
Macron himself also dismissed the narrative that Islamist extremists and migrants were driving the violence. He has, however, pointed to far-left groups and accused them of trying to stage a coup.
On Friday, Macron also held his first-ever meeting with representatives of secondary school students. However, the meeting ended with the pupils calling for more protests.
"We are not satisfied," said student representative Nathanael Combary, president of campaign group High School Renewal.
He told reporters that the president had been "attentive" but that the students were still waiting for concrete proposals to be presented at their meeting with the prime minister on Monday.
He urged his fellow students to "continue to mobilize" and maintain a "standoff" with the government.

Pentagon labels Confucius Institutes in US a national security threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
22:00:36 UTC
07:00:36 KST

The US Defense Department has designated Chinese-funded cultural centres on university campuses known as Confucius Institutes as a threat to US national security, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said.
Hegseth, in a video posted on social media on Friday, alleged that Confucius Institutes were operating under disguise at US universities and that the Pentagon had added them to its list of institutions that threaten US national security.
"It turns out that 80 new propaganda cells across 30 universities had popped up using different names and different charters, but with the same mission: to steal intellectual property and to infiltrate the minds of American students," Hegseth said.
Washington has long accused Confucius Institutes of being Chinese propaganda tools and has taken steps to crack down on them.
The Defense Department over the past two months has "systematically dismantled every single one of these organisations," Hegseth said.
US Congress restricted funding to universities that welcome Confucius Institutes, which are funded by Beijing to teach the Chinese language but are accused of presenting only the communist government's worldview.
The Chinese embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
