====================================================================================================

American Catholics reported a greater sense of meaning in life after Pope Leo XIV’s election, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
22:00:05 UTC
07:00:05 KST

The election of Pope Leo XIV in May 2025 was followed by a modest rise in the sense of meaning in life among a sample of practicing Roman Catholics in the United States, according to a study published in The Journal of Positive Psychology. Through the end of the study’s 10-day post-election window, participants reported a stronger sense that their lives had meaning, along with a gradual decline in their search for meaning. The pattern held after the researchers accounted for participants’ religious commitment and their feelings about the new pope sharing their American nationality.
In psychology, meaning in life refers to the subjective judgment that one’s existence is worthwhile, makes sense, and is guided by an overarching purpose. Psychologists break this concept down into three parts: having a motivational goal or purpose, feeling that life is coherent, and believing that one’s life matters. Rather than treating meaning as a single feeling, researchers distinguish between the presence of meaning and the search for meaning. As a 2006 validation study demonstrated, already feeling that one’s life has purpose is distinct from actively looking for something that makes life feel meaningful.
Religion is a major source of this sense of purpose for many people. For example, a 2005 study found that religious people tend to report greater well-being, largely because they feel their lives have purpose and direction. Similarly, a study covered by PsyPost in 2022 indicated that religious individuals tend to experience a stronger sense of meaning largely through feeling that they matter on a grand, cosmic scale.
Most psychological research on religion and meaning has examined steady, long-term beliefs rather than specific religious events. One of the most prominent rituals in the Roman Catholic tradition is the papal conclave, the secluded meeting of cardinals inside the Sistine Chapel to elect a new pope. Filled with symbolic traditions like burning ballots to send black or white smoke from a chimney and the Latin announcement of “Habemus Papam” (“We have a Pope”), the conclave is framed by the Church as a moment of divine guidance.
The research, led by Stefan Stieger of Karl Landsteiner University of Health Sciences in Austria, examined whether living through this major religious transition alters how Catholics experience meaning from day to day. The authors drew on three psychological frameworks to explain how a papal election might affect believers. Under the meaning-making model, the death of a pope may create a temporary spiritual void that disrupts a believer’s worldview, and electing a successor may help restore a sense of order and coherence.
Social identity theory offers a second perspective, suggesting that people derive self-worth from belonging to social groups; losing a leader can threaten that shared identity, whereas choosing a new leader may restore group unity. A third possibility involves emotional contagion, the tendency for feelings to spread rapidly across a crowd or through global media coverage. For instance, a 2024 field study of a public Hindu ritual found that participants who stood close to one another during the ceremony experienced synchronized emotional arousal, showing how collective religious practices can align feelings across a group.
To capture how the 2025 papal transition affected believers in real time, the researchers used an experience sampling method. Instead of asking people to recall their feelings weeks later, this technique prompts participants to answer short smartphone surveys during their normal daily routines, reducing memory biases. Beginning on May 3, 2025, four full days before the conclave started, the team tracked participants across 14 consecutive days covering the pre-conclave, conclave, and post-conclave phases.
The researchers recruited English-speaking United States citizens through the online platform Prolific who identified as practicing Roman Catholics. After excluding 17 individuals who did not identify as Roman Catholic, dropped out early, or provided inconsistent demographic data, the final sample consisted of 117 American Roman Catholics. Participants ranged in age from 19 to 76 years, with an average age of about 45, and were split nearly evenly between men (52.1 percent) and women (47.9 percent).
At the start of the study, participants installed an open-source smartphone app called ESMira and completed a baseline survey. On 1-to-100 scales, the group reported being fairly religious on average (72.7) and relatively balanced between conservative and progressive views in both their theological orientation (46.1) and political views (47.4). They also completed a 10-item questionnaire measuring both their private religious devotion and their involvement in their church community.
Every evening at 8:00 p.m. local time, the app prompted participants to complete an end-of-day survey assessing their current sense of meaning in life. Using a 7-point scale from 1 (absolutely untrue) to 7 (absolutely true), participants rated five statements about the presence of meaning (such as “At this moment, I understand my life’s meaning”) and five statements about the search for meaning (such as “At this moment, I am looking for something that makes my life feel meaningful”). Across the two-week window, the 117 participants completed 1,470 daily questionnaires.
When the cardinals elected Pope Leo XIV, an unexpected factor emerged: the new head of the Catholic Church was also from the United States. To help account for the possibility that any boost in meaning among the American participants was a byproduct of national pride, the researchers added a question to the final survey. Participants rated how much Pope Leo XIV’s American background influenced their feelings toward him on a scale from -4 (much more negative) to +4 (much more positive).
To analyze the daily ratings, the researchers divided the timeline into a four-day pre-conclave baseline, the conclave phase (from the first black smoke signal until the day before the election), and 10 post-conclave days starting with the day of the papal announcement. Using multilevel statistical models, they tracked daily changes within each individual while controlling for age, gender, personal and social religious commitment, and feelings about the pope’s American nationality.
Across the four pre-conclave baseline days, participants averaged 5.16 out of 7 on the presence of meaning and 4.34 out of 7 on the search for meaning. During the conclave itself and on the first day of the post-conclave phase (the day Pope Leo XIV was announced), neither dimension showed a notable shift from baseline, possibly because not all participants had heard the news before completing that first evening survey. Starting the day after the election, however, the presence of meaning rose above the pre-conclave baseline and stayed elevated through the final day of tracking.
On the 7-point scale, daily presence-of-meaning scores increased by 0.14 to 0.20 points above the 5.16 baseline on every day from Day 2 through Day 10, except for Day 8, when a 0.09-point increase was not statistically significant. Standardized effect sizes during this period ranged from 0.09 to 0.14, which the authors describe as small to medium; in raw terms, the increases amounted to roughly 3 to 4 percent of the baseline score.
At the same time, participants reported a gradual decline in their search for meaning, with statistically significant drops on Days 2, 7, 9, and 10. Compared to the 4.34 baseline, search-for-meaning scores fell by 0.23 points on Day 7, 0.34 points on Day 9, and 0.30 points on Day 10, with standardized effect sizes reaching -0.19 on Day 9 and -0.17 on Day 10. This pattern suggests that participants felt more settled in their sense of purpose and less driven to look for missing meaning.
These shifts held after the researchers accounted for age, gender, religious commitment, and feelings about the pope’s nationality. On average, participants viewed the pope’s American nationality positively (averaging 2.03 on the -4 to +4 scale), and those more active in church communities tended to feel warmer about it. However, the analysis adjusted for these factors rather than testing whether the post-election boost was larger or smaller for particular groups, so it cannot show whether less devout Catholics, or those less enthusiastic about an American pope, experienced the same shift.
The authors noted that their findings are compatible with all three psychological frameworks they examined. They suggest that emotional contagion from widespread media coverage may have contributed, and that because media excitement typically fades, the persistence of the effect, with the drop in searching for meaning strongest on Days 9 and 10, points to deeper social identity and meaning-making processes as well. They also acknowledge, however, that emotional contagion can sometimes last several days, so the line between these explanations is not sharp.
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. The study does not appear to have been preregistered. Because it began just four days before the conclave, after the death of Pope Francis had already occurred, there is no way to know what the participants’ sense of meaning looked like before the papal vacancy began. The post-election increase in meaning might represent a genuine rise above their typical everyday levels, or a rebound back to normal after a temporary dip caused by the previous pope’s death.
In addition, the tracking period ended 10 days after the election, leaving open the question of how long the heightened sense of purpose lasted before leveling off. The study also focused solely on Roman Catholics in the United States and had no comparison group tracked over the same days, so it cannot rule out that scores would have drifted for other reasons, such as participants growing accustomed to answering the same questions each evening.
Because the new pope’s American nationality became known at the same moment as his election, the study also cannot fully separate a religious response from a patriotic one. Including people from other religious backgrounds exposed to the same news coverage would help future researchers separate media-driven emotional contagion from the spiritual effects of welcoming a new religious leader.
The study, “The election of Pope Leo XIV and its impact on the meaning of life for Roman Catholic Christians: A longitudinal experience sampling method study in the USA before, during, and after the pope’s election,” was authored by Stefan Stieger, Selina Volsa, and David Willinger.

In Brussels, six tram lines remained affected on Friday evening due to damaged overhead lines, according to public transport operator STIB. On Flemish motorways, traffic jams reached a combined length of about 250 km at their peak during the evening rush hour.
Authorities also closed parks, nature reserves and wooded areas in Brussels until Saturday morning. Residents were advised to avoid trees and unnecessary travel.
The Port of Antwerp-Bruges said vessel arrivals and departures had been suspended, with traffic expected to resume on Saturday morning. Shipping to and from the Port of Ghent was also affected. At Brussels Airport, two inbound flights were diverted to Amsterdam because of strong winds, while other flights were delayed, according to the airport.
The storm brought down trees, damaged rooftops and blocked roads across the country, prompting numerous calls to emergency services. The Brussels fire service said it had completed dozens of storm-related operations by Friday evening, with dozens more pending. Belgium's National Crisis Center said nearly 2.8 million alert messages were sent through the BE-Alert system on Thursday and Friday.
According to the RMI, winds were expected to ease inland later on Friday evening, while strong gusts would persist along the coast. Another storm, Boelo, was forecast to bring fresh rainfall and stronger winds from Saturday evening into Sunday. ■

Feature: More than a sweet -- Türkiye's lokma tradition offers comfort in grief
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-24
05:56:00 CST
06:56:00 KST

ANKARA, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Outside the historic Haci Bayram Mosque in Ankara, the capital of Türkiye, strangers reached for golden pieces of lokma, a traditional fried dough sweet soaked in syrup. For Adnan Kirbas, the treats carried a meaning far beyond their sweetness.
The retired Ankara resident had arranged for the sweets to be distributed to the public to mark the second anniversary of his mother's death. Each serving he handed to a stranger was a small tribute to the mother he still deeply missed.
"This is part of our tradition," Kirbas told Xinhua.
As the pastries passed from hand to hand, strangers became part of a family's act of remembrance. They offered prayers and blessings. Their kind words brought comfort to a son still seeking ways to honor his mother's memory.
Their prayers, Kirbas said, helped ease the grief of those mourning a loved one, reminding them that they did not have to bear their sorrow alone.
Fried dough sweets are enjoyed across the Mediterranean and the Middle East, while charitable food-sharing traditions take different forms across cultures. In Türkiye, this practice takes a distinctive form known as hayir lokmasi, or charity lokma, in which freshly prepared sweets are distributed free of charge to the public to honor deceased loved ones or mark joyful occasions, such as births and personal achievements.
Families typically hire a mobile lokma van, where a specialist prepares and fries batches of yeast-based dough on site, coats the golden pieces in light sugar syrup, and serves them on small disposable plates with toothpicks.
For Ankara shopkeeper Serkan Erdogan, the tradition carries a similar personal significance. The previous week, he had arranged for lokma to be distributed in memory of both his late father and his wife's late father.
Erdogan learned the custom from older generations and hopes his children will carry it on. Yet he worries that younger people are gradually drifting away from such traditions in an increasingly digital age.
"We are trying to pass certain things on to the younger generation, but we have not been very successful," he said.
His concern points to what is at stake beyond lokma itself: a tradition that draws people out of their private lives and encourages them to share with others.
Ismail Kadir Aran, a lokma maker who began learning the family trade at the age of 13, summed it up simply: "People want to share their happiness and their sadness with others. That is why they offer these treats."
The sweets soon disappear. But the remembrance, shared among hundreds of strangers, lingers a little longer. ■

Inside Russia’s School-to-War Pipeline, Where Students Help Build Drones and Ammunition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
21:40:37 UTC
06:40:37 KST

- Category
- Investigations
Inside Russia’s School-to-War Pipeline, Where Students Help Build Drones and Ammunition
Students at no fewer than 40 civilian educational institutions across Russia are helping produce military drones and munition components, according to an investigation by Vot Tak published on October 22.
The outlet noted that 33 universities, 5 colleges and 2 technical schools were involved. Participants include not only future engineers but also lawyers, political scientists, teachers and agronomists.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
One of them, 19-year-old Nikita Kazakevich, studies agricultural machinery repair at a technical college in Nazarovo, Krasnoyarsk region. Outside class, he assembles FPV attack drones that are shipped to the front.
“Then these drones are sent to our army, to Donetsk and Luhansk,” Kazakevich told Vot Tak.
Vot Tak noted that the college has assembled the drones since January 2025 from nine-inch carbon frames delivered to the school. Students install electronics and motors, program the aircraft and test-fly them in the gym. Kazakevich explained that he can build one in about half an hour.
Shipments leave every month, he added, with nine drones sent in September. Students are not paid, but teachers reward participation with good grades and sometimes release them from lessons.
The drone assembly program at the technical college in Nazarovo began when Alexei Yolkin, head of a local veterans' organization, was asked by troops for quadcopters. Alexander Aul, a former director of a local insulation plant, buys the frame kits. According to Kazakevich, local Cossacks also help deliver the finished drones. Vot Tak requested interviews with 18 students involved in such work, and only two agreed.
The practice extends well beyond extracurricular workshops. In March 2023, a bakery in Tambov began producing Bekas suicide drones , and students of a local transport college joined within weeks, according to local media.
Vot Tak wrote that production left the bakery in early 2024, and the business closed in July 2026 amid falling demand. The technology was transferred to India, and the EU sanctioned the producer the same month.
Other students are employed rather than volunteering. Under Rostec's “Wings of Rostec” program, launched in 2020, participants work at partner enterprises from their first year and receive a salary plus stipends. Rostec deputy director general Nikolai Volobuev stated that drones are a priority through 2036.
In August 2026, the Moscow Aviation Institute and Rostec completed their first intake for a drone-design degree, with 17 of 60 state-funded places going to program participants. The Kalashnikov plant in Izhevsk joined the list of partners in 2026.
The People's Front movement acts as an intermediary, Vot Tak found, working with at least 11 civilian institutions. It supplies 3D printers and plastic so students can print tail sections, striker parts and electronic drop mechanisms for VOG-17 grenade rounds. By March 2026, Volga State University of Technology had sent 2,500 sets of VOG-17 parts to the front, the university stated.
Some students go further than assembly. Sergei Berstnev, 25, designed the "Russian Mavic" strike drone while studying at Vladimir State University. Vot Tak established that operators of the 28th motorized rifle regiment used one to destroy a building in the Kherson region. Berstnev, who is listed in the Myrotvorets database, told the outlet that Russian security services monitor his team and warned him against publicity.
Student design bureaus follow a similar pattern. At Pacific National University in Khabarovsk, the PolitechProm bureau builds suicide drones, and its members include students of the university's law institute and its institute of social and political technologies. Vot Tak found comparable bureaus in Korolyov, Tomsk and Ulan-Ude.
Universities often leave frontline use off their websites. In Ulan-Ude, graduates made propellers for the Burya-10 drone system. Buryatia deputy premier Ivan Alkheev confirmed in January 2025 that 21 such complexes had been handed over to the combat zone, with three more being transferred. The university's website still contains no mention of this.
The use of students in weapons production has a precedent at the Alabuga complex in Tatarstan, Russia's largest drone-production site.
Ukraine first struck Alabuga in April 2024, when a drone hit a dormitory at its “Alabuga Polytech” college. Students there, including minors, have been drawn into assembling Geran drones. Russian authorities have also used an international youth festival in Yekaterinburg to promote the college to foreign visitors, promising rapid employment.

Kremlin-seized German company Metro AG transfers 1 billion rubles to Russian military without approval
Almost one month after being placed under the Kremlin's control, German wholesale food retailer Metro AG announced on Oct. 23 that its Russian subsidiary had donated 1 billion rubles (11.1 million euros/ $12.4 million) to support Russian forces without the company's approval.
On Sept. 28, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree placing the Russian subsidiary of Metro AG under the Kremlin's control.
Metro AG responded on Oct. 23, saying it did not approve the donations.
"The decision by Metro Russia to donate to the Russian organization “All-Russia People's Front” was neither coordinated with Metro AG nor authorized or approved by Metro AG," the company said in a press release. "Since Metro Russia was placed under forced temporary administration as of September 28, Metro AG no longer has operational control over Metro Russia and has no influence over its operational decisions."
The Russian-controlled Metro transferred money to Russia's "People's Front. All for Victory!" fund. The funds "will be used to purchase equipment needed by soldiers on the front lines," according to a press release from the Russian company.
Metro AG is one of the world’s largest retailers, specializing in food wholesale and food distribution to restaurants and hotels. Metro AG first entered the Russian market in 2001 and operated 91 wholesale stores, employing around 9,000 employees in the country.
Moscow has seized Russian subsidiaries of Western companies throughout the war.
On Sept. 17, Putin signed a decree confiscating the assets of several international companies, including Nestle and Auchan. Other companies placed under Russian government management include Bati Logistics, FM Logistics, and Le Monlid LLC.
According to Deutsche Welle, other foreign companies taken over by the Kremlin in Russia have been used to donate to the "People's Front" fund.
In 2026, the fund received 1.5 billion rubles from Poland's Can-Pack, 1 billion rubles from the Dutch firm Akzo Nobel, and 600 million rubles from Denmark's Rockwool after all companies were placed under Russian control.

- The White House said the easing covers plywood, paper products, machinery and refrigeration equipment, but new tariffs on carpets, valves and waste products start on Oct 30.
- The move may help Collins in a tight race, while Canada still faces heavy tariff pressure after trade talks failed and tensions rose.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - President Donald Trump’s administration lifted some tariffs on Canadian imports on Oct 23, two weeks ahead of midterm elections, after a vulnerable Republican candidate said she’d lobbied for the change.
The easing of tariffs will apply to products including “plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment,” the White House said in a statement.
The change could help Senator Susan Collins, who faces a strong challenge from a Democrat in the US-Canada border state of Maine, which has been hit hard by Trump’s trade war.
She posted on social media that she had “secured” the exemptions for “products crucial to Maine’s agricultural industries, including blueberry, potato, apple, and seaweed producers.”
Democrats are targeting Collins’ seat in their attempt to win control of Congress from the Republicans in the Nov 3 midterms.
US-Canada trade
The economies of the US and Canada are heavily inter-connected, with roughly 70% of all Canadian exports heading to the US.
Tensions between the North American neighbours have been high since trade talks broke down in August, with Trump imposing a slew of new tariffs in response.
The Oct 23 action lifts tariffs on certain goods, but imposes levies on new ones, including carpets, certain valves and waste products, the White House said. The new measures will take effect on Oct 30.
“The Canadian government takes note of these recent tariff measures adopted by the United States,” Dominic LeBlanc, Ottawa’s minister in charge of US-Canada trade, said in a statement to AFP.
“While evaluating these recent measures, Canada remains ready to work together in a constructive and good-faith manner” with the US, he added.
Collins said many farmers in her state “rely on specialised equipment, packaging materials, and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense.”
Previous Trump levies on autos, steel, aluminium and lumber have hit Canada hard, forcing job losses and stunting growth. Canada has entered a technical recession this year after two consecutive quarters of economic contraction.
Trump’s tariffs enforced after the talks broke down impacted around US$20 billion worth of goods, or 5.5% of Canadian exports to the US, targeting products ranging from hockey sticks to cement.
Since taking power in his second term, Trump has upended the global trade order by imposing wide-ranging tariffs on friend and foe alike, saying that other countries have been taking advantage of the United States.
He has also explicitly tied some threatened tariffs to political or foreign policy objectives. AFP

China unveils space governance paper prioritizing preventing arms race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
21:29:45 UTC
06:29:45 KST

Saadet Gökce
24 October 2026•Update: 24 October 2026
China on Friday unveiled a position paper on strengthening outer space governance, prioritizing efforts to prevent an arms race in space.
"The achievements of outer space exploration should benefit all countries," said the paper, warning that the existing international legal framework for outer space lags behind rapid advances in space science and technology and their widespread applications.
"The risk of an arms race in outer space and the trend of turning outer space into a new theater of conflict have become the gravest threat and challenge to space security," it said. "Strengthening global space governance is an urgent issue for humanity and the shared responsibility of all States."
China advocates that countries take the common values of humanity as their fundamental guide, uphold sovereign equality, abide by international law, practice multilateralism, and pursue a people-centered, action-oriented approach, said the paper.
It also urged a balanced approach to outer space development and security, as well as stability and sustainability, with the aim of building a community with a shared future in space for the benefit of all humanity.
The paper’s release comes after US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink told a defense conference last month that the US Space Force has "on-orbit space control weapons" capable of defending American forces against hostile action.
China urged countries to commit to openness and shared benefit, ensure equitable access to outer space, promote space research and technological innovation, respect all states’ rights and security interests, oppose offensive military policies, and prevent an arms race.
It also called for abiding by the international rule of law, safeguarding common security, greater transparency to reduce misunderstandings, the regulation of commercial space activities, deeper international cooperation, and the UN remaining the main channel for global space governance.
The paper called for equitable, non-discriminatory access to outer space and opposed activities threatening other states' sovereignty, security, and development, adding that the principle of refraining from the threat or use of force in international relations and preventing the threat or use of force against outer space objects should be reaffirmed to avoid armed conflict in outer space.
Separately, China on Friday also launched a remote sensing satellite from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center in north China's Shanxi Province, according to the state-run Xinhua news agency.
It will mainly be used for land survey and estimating crop yields, as well as disaster prevention and relief.

Talks in November
Putin stated that Moscow and Washington had agreed Russia was ready to resume trilateral contacts. He added that he generally agreed with a US point that European security architecture should also be discussed.

"Historical Russia"
In a 21 October Fox News interview, asked about a freeze leaving Ukraine 75% or more of its land, Zelenskyy answered: “Yes, right now, we have to freeze.”
Trump cannot get Putin to halt strikes on Ukraine’s power grid, so he blames Ukraine instead, Zelenskyy says

One-time minnows Tonga and Samoa now star World Cup attractions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
21:22:36 UTC
06:22:36 KST

Fri, 11 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Rabbitohs 10, Knights 20
Once seen as minnows, Tonga and Samoa are now Rugby League World Cup drawcards
At Western Sydney Stadium last week, Toa Samoa had a moment of pure elation, a crushing 78-4 victory over France at the men's Rugby League World Cup.
It was capped off with an extraordinary final play that saw a penalty goal attempt from Stephen Crichton ricochet off the post and bounce.
Benaiah Ioelu then scored a try after the full-time siren had sounded, delivering Samoa's largest-ever victory.
What was more extraordinary was that a game with a kick-off time of 5:45pm on Friday, playing out what was likely and ultimately proved to be a walkover, still drew a crowd of 13,000.
It was a horror slot to play in: a workday, outside school holidays, in a busy part of Sydney where traffic was banking up across the many arterial roads that led to it.
Yet the crowd, largely comprising Western Sydney's large Samoan population, bellowed Ua fa'afetai — a traditional song of thanks and gratitude.
Fiji and the Cook Islands played each other on Sunday in Newcastle; there was a tick over 10,000 in the stands and another 1.7 million watching on television across Australia, outrating several flagship current affairs shows, news bulletins and reality programs.
These are just two examples that show this is a World Cup transformed by Pasifika passion.
The growing strength of Samoa and Tonga's men's teams has been no secret, but now more than ever the iron grip of dominance largely held by Australia on international rugby league, occasionally disrupted by New Zealand, could be under threat.
What has also been clear to those at the grounds or watching from home is that this World Cup in Australia, New Zealand and Papua New Guinea is one where diaspora communities have breathed life into a tournament that has previously lacked the same level of excitement or prestige compared to other international sporting events.
Australia's migration story tracks with this
The shift will be most obvious on November 1, when Samoa and Tonga play each other in Sydney, in a game that was the first to sell out despite being in the third week of the tournament.
Already a series of ex-players and pundits have raised the call to move the game to the larger Stadium Australia to accommodate a crowd beyond the 30,000 that Western Sydney Stadium holds.
The interest should come as no surprise though, as the Pasifika population in Australia has been steadily increasing.
In 2011, 165,000 Australians identified as being from Pasifika communities; by 2021, that number had almost tripled to 415,033.
Data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics shows outer suburban areas of Sydney and Brisbane have burgeoning communities.
Sierra Keung, a senior lecturer in sports leadership and management at Auckland University of Technology, said she was not surprised by the fan turnout.
"The pride for our cultures, for our people, it's more than just a jersey for our Pasifika communities," Dr Keung told ABC Sport.
She cited a distinctive moment on the field that set this explosion in motion.
In 2017, the International Rugby League changed the rules to allow players with cultural ties to multiple nations to play for the country of their choosing.
The most famous change in allegiance was Jason Taumalolo.
That rule change is on full display at this tournament.
Of the listed starting line-up for Tonga's match against Lebanon last night at Western Sydney Stadium, none of the players were born in Tonga, but all have deep familial ties to the island nation.
Tonga beat Lebanon 36-0 to keep its campaign on track.
"This is years in the making, and it's come down to people making bold decisions, like Jason Taumalolo to be the first to say, 'I'm going to go home and represent my people,'" Dr Keung said.
Salesi Foketi is one of a number of Tongan players that chose to represent his familial roots over his country of birth, New Zealand.
"Right from when I was a boy, it was always Tonga," he said.
Winger Jojo Fifita made his debut last weekend for Tonga and it was a moment to acknowledge his forebears.
"Being able to represent my dad's side was something I'd always wanted to do when I was older and I finally got that opportunity," he said.
Extension beyond Pasifika diaspora may be the future
There is another team outside the South Pacific that is relying on heritage and cultural ties as the bind for players to represent it.
Lebanon will face Tonga tonight, and winger Jason Saab has potentially the most unique ties to the country.
His stepfather, whose name he took, is Lebanese, and Saab is now lining up for the Cedars.
Saab told ABC Sport in September of the sincere ties to Lebanese culture through his stepdad Pierre.
"That's the culture that raised me ultimately, that whole community of people. That's kind of where I found my identity to be," he said.
While all players in the Cedars squad were born in Australia, Lebanon coach Michael Cheika, who is also Lebanese Australian, said the small but dedicated rugby league community in Lebanon was driving the entire playing group, especially for those with family in Lebanon where strikes from Israel continued amid a broader conflict in the region.
"With everything that's going on over there … you've got to understand that they may not have enough petrol to get to the games, let alone field markings, fields that are available," he said.
As Samoa and Tonga have brought a genuine competitiveness to the tournament, there are other countries with large populations in Australia, such as Fiji and the Cook Islands, that could also challenge the Kangaroos, who have won 12 world titles, including six of the last seven.
"The talent is just through the roof right now, both men's and women's," Dr Keung said.
"So I'm really excited for this World Cup, but also for future World Cups too, because it's just going to get better and better each time it comes around."
There is no doubt rugby league has cottoned on to its international life blood, and it seems the public is following suit.

Russia, Ukraine agree on ceasefire in embattled town, to hold peace talks next month
Oct 23 - Ukraine and Russia said on Friday they had agreed on a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky, brokered through US first lady Melania Trump, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said peace negotiators would meet next month for new talks.
The two sides said the ceasefire would go into effect on October 27, allowing the delivery of aid and the evacuation of residents through humanitarian corridors.
Amid a US push to organise new talks aimed at ending the 4-1/2-year-old war, Zelenskiy said negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the United States had agreed to technical-level meetings in the first half of November in Abu Dhabi. A US official later said the three countries may hold their next talks in a couple weeks in Abu Dhabi or Switzerland.
Zelenskiy said he hoped a meeting of the countries' leaders would follow.
Previous rounds of talks headed by the United States stalled in February with no significant progress towards ending the bloodiest conflict in Europe since World War Two. Russia continues to demand Ukraine cede all of the eastern Donbas region, including territory Russia has not occupied militarily, while Kyiv rejects any notion of giving up land it currently holds.
The latest peace efforts follow a rift between Washington and Kyiv in recent weeks and a series of moves by US President Donald Trump seen as favouring Russia.
A major source of friction was limitations placed on SpaceX's Starlink communication system that Ukraine uses to protect against incoming attacks. Trump said on Friday that if Ukraine still faced a problem with the system, he would straighten it out and, if necessary, speak about the matter to SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.
Another contentious point was Trump's announcement of a deal to allow Russia to provide diesel for the US and global markets, an agreement denounced by Ukraine and meant to keep prices down as the president's Republicans contest US midterm elections.
On Friday, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said the first three tankers with Russian diesel were on their way to North America.
In the town of Oleshky, occupied by Russian forces since February 2022, residents have reported that they faced a deepening food crisis.
"Both nations agreed to temporarily stop all military action in Oleshky to allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway," the White House said in a statement.
The chief of staff of Russian forces, Valery Gerasimov, said on the Defence Ministry's Telegram channel that Russian troops would halt fire from 4 a.m. local time (0100 GMT) on October 27 to allow for the humanitarian operation to start.
Ukraine's General Staff issued a statement agreeing to observe the ceasefire from the same time and pledging to "do everything possible to help Oleshky's residents." Ukraine says it has already used drones twice to send food into the town.
Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, also said the ceasefire would go into effect on October 27 and told Reuters the operation would involve demining roads to the town, deliveries of food and evacuations of civilians.
MELANIA TRUMP'S DIPLOMATIC EFFORTS
Both sides said Melania Trump played an important role in coordinating the agreement. The first lady has been active in trying to get Ukrainian children seized by Russia during the war returned to their families.
"Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster," she said in a statement.
"Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food and clean water."
Pope Leo had spoken in the past week both to Zelenskiy and to Russian President Vladimir Putin about conditions in Oleshky.
The White House said Oleshky, located across the Dnipro River from the Ukrainian-held city of Kherson, had 1,700 to 2,000 residents remaining, down from 24,000 before the war.
US ENVOYS
Zelenskiy's comments on resuming peace talks followed a meeting with US presidential envoy Steve Witkoff in Norway early this week and a subsequent meeting between Witkoff and Putin in St Petersburg.
Zelenskiy said he spoke on Friday with Witkoff and US envoy Jared Kushner. He said any peace agreement would need strong security guarantees for Ukraine and funding for 10 years to maintain the Ukrainian army.
"The plan is to meet in the first half of November, and as early as possible, of course," Zelenskiy told the Hudson Institute think tank via a video link. He said much would depend on Russia, noting that a similar meeting expected this month had not materialised.
Zelenskiy spoke of the importance of continued diplomatic efforts to reach a ceasefire and end the war, now in its fifth year, adding that Europe should also be involved in the talks.
Ukrainian officials said on Friday that speed restrictions on Starlink systems in Ukraine remained in place, despite Trump's previous statement that the services had been fully restored.
Trump told reporters at the White House on Friday that he had not spoken to Musk about the restrictions but would do so if required.
"If there is a problem, I'll get it straightened out," he said. The caps have been in place since October 13.
Ukraine and Russia also swapped 270 servicemen each in a prisoner exchange on Friday, the Russian Defence Ministry said. Zelenskiy described the swap, the first since August, as a "very important result."
Ukraine's acting prosecutor, Anton Kovalskyi, writing on Telegram, said more than 19,000 Ukrainian civilians, including 762 children, had been killed since Russia launched its full-scale war more than four years ago. REUTERS

At least seven killed in ‘terror attack’ on church funeral in Jordan (VIDEOS)
At least seven people have been killed and some 34 others wounded in a terrorist attack on a Greek Orthodox church in Jordan. The authorities have described the suspects as “extremists” who fled the scene and are still on the loose.
The slaughter unfolded on Friday afternoon in the village of Hmoud in western Karak Governorate, which is home to a sizable Christian community in the majority-Muslim country.
A group of at least three assailants arrived at the local St. George’s Church, where a funeral ceremony was underway. Highly graphic footage shows the suspects repeatedly shooting wounded victims in the head as they lay on the ground, apparently to finish them off.
Jordanian King Abdullah II has vowed to “confront the terrorist act that targeted Karak with the harshest penalties.” The country’s interior minister, Mazen al-Faraya, confirmed during a news conference that the suspects still remain at large, describing the attackers as a “group of extremists” without providing any further detail.
He described the attack as “painful and horrific,” stating it was “unparalleled in the history of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan,” which has rarely seen such levels of violence.
The massacre has prompted a major response from the authorities, with Hmoud flooded by assorted security forces. Tightened security measures have also been implemented in the city of Karak, where the bulk of the wounded were transferred for treatment.
The king visited the victims at a hospital later on Friday to show support, promising to punish the perpetrators. Abdullah could be seen arriving at the facility in a military field uniform, accompanied by a large security detail.

Serbia at a crossroads: What’s at stake and what Moscow can expect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
21:21:17 UTC
06:21:17 KST

Serbia at a crossroads: What’s at stake and what Moscow can expect
Serbia is heading into a snap parliamentary election on October 25 following nearly two years of anti-government protests sparked by a deadly railway station canopy collapse.
Former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic is running for prime minister against a fragmented opposition seeking to capitalize on the protest movement. The result could reshape Serbia’s political landscape and its delicate balancing act between Russia and the EU.
What is Serbia voting for, and why does it matter?
Voters will elect 250 members of the National Assembly, with 126 seats needed for a majority. A total of 18 electoral lists, comprising 2,418 candidates, are contesting the election, including the ruling coalition, student-backed candidates, established opposition parties and representatives of national minorities.
The vote will test whether the protest movement can challenge the ruling coalition at the ballot box.
What led to the snap election?
The crisis began after a concrete canopy at the Novi Sad railway station collapsed on November 1, 2024, killing 16 people. Protesters blamed the disaster on alleged corruption and failures of government oversight.
Demonstrations intensified after students and lecturers involved in a vigil commemorating the disaster at Belgrade’s Faculty of Dramatic Arts on November 22, 2024 blocked traffic, prompting drivers to clash with the crowd; some of the motorists were later identified from photos posted online as Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) officials.
Students began blockading university faculties, demanding the release of documents relating to the station’s renovation, accountability for attacks on protesters, an end to the prosecution of detained demonstrators and increased funding for public universities.
The authorities said the demands had been met, but protesters disputed the claim.
Serbian Prime Minister Milos Vucevic resigned in January 2025 following another attack on students, but the protests continued. A major rally in Belgrade on March 15 attracted an estimated 275,000 to 325,000 people, according to the organization Arhiv javnih skupova.
Parliament elected a government headed by Djuro Macut in April, but the student movement demanded snap elections on May 5.
Vucic has accused foreign organizations and intelligence services of financing the protests, alleging on Thursday that outside actors were seeking to remove him from power.
Serbia was the victim of perhaps Europe’s first ‘color revolution’ in 2000, when the opposition, having received extensive funding and training from the National Democratic Institute (NDI), International Republican Institute (IRI), and USAID, as well as support from George Soros’ Open Society Foundations (operating in 2000 as the Fund for an Open Society – Yugoslavia), brought down the government.
Has Vucic lost power, or is he trying to hold on to it?
Vucic resigned as president on September 27, saying he intended to campaign in the parliamentary election without holding the presidency.
He now heads the ruling coalition’s electoral list and is running for prime minister.
Who is running, and who could form a government?
The ruling camp is led by the ‘Aleksandar Vucic – United Serbia’ coalition, built around the SNS. Its longstanding partner, Ivica Dacic’s Socialist Party of Serbia, is running separately under the ‘Factor of Stability’ banner.
The main challenger is the ‘Student List – Students Are Winning,’ which emerged from the protests and includes lecturers, professionals and public figures.
Marinika Tepic and Zdravko Ponos’s ‘European Serbia’ and Milos Jovanovic’s ‘Authentic Right’ are also running independently. Some opposition groups have backed the students rather than fielding their own candidates.
The latest opinion polls offer conflicting assessments of support for the two main contenders.
An Ipsos survey published on October 22 put Vucic’s coalition at 47.4%, compared with 40% for the Student List and 3.2% for Dacic’s Socialists. The poll surveyed 3,624 respondents between October 20 and 22.

An online survey published by Nacija TV on October 21 showed a much narrower gap, with Vucic’s coalition at 42.9% and the Student List at 42%. The poll surveyed 1,204 respondents between October 16 and 18.
An earlier Faktor Plus survey, published on September 21, put Vucic’s coalition at 48.6% and the Student List at 37.1%, based on 986 respondents interviewed between September 16 and 20.
National minority and smaller parties could become important in coalition negotiations if no major group wins a majority.
What unites the opposition, and what divides it?
The groups challenging Vucic differ on key foreign policy issues, particularly relations with the EU, NATO, and Russia.
The Student List has said it would maintain Serbia’s refusal to impose sanctions on Moscow. Its representative Jovo Bakic has proposed a referendum on EU membership and opposed joining NATO.
European Serbia supports alignment with EU foreign policy, including sanctions against Russia, a position advocated by Tepic.
Jovanovic opposes EU membership and sanctions against Moscow, while Socialist representative Snezana Paunovic supports EU accession but has criticized the bloc’s current policies.
Territorial tensions: Where do the parties stand on Kosovo and Republika Srpska?
Kosovo remains one of Serbia’s most sensitive political issues. The province declared independence in 2008, a move recognized by the US and many of its allies. Belgrade still considers Kosovo part of Serbia, as do Russia and China, and some 90 other countries.
The declaration followed NATO’s 1999 bombing campaign against Yugoslavia, conducted without authorization from the UN Security Council. Belgrade’s relations with the ethnic Albanian-led authorities in Pristina remain tense.
Successive SNS-led governments have refused to recognize the breakaway Kosovo while participating in EU-mediated negotiations with Pristina.
The Student List has also rejected recognizing the so-called Kosovo precedent. In a memorandum published in May, it described Kosovo as an integral part of Serbia and called for a negotiated settlement in accordance with the Serbian Constitution and international law.
Republika Srpska, the Serb-majority constituent entity of Bosnia and Herzegovina, whose autonomy is guaranteed under the 1995 Dayton peace agreement, is another touchstone.
Vucic has maintained close ties with its leadership while supporting Bosnia and Herzegovina’s territorial integrity. Former Republika Srpska President Milorad Dodik has openly backed Vucic’s coalition, urging Serbian citizens living there to vote for it.
The Student List has sought support among Serbian voters in Republika Srpska but has not outlined a comparably detailed policy toward the entity. Some Bosnian Serb opposition politicians have backed the students, while others have refused to take sides.
Belgrade and Brussels: The beatings will continue
Serbia applied to join the EU in 2009 and received candidate status in 2012. Accession negotiations began in 2014, but no new negotiating chapters or clusters have been opened since 2021.
Brussels has made further progress toward EU membership conditional on the normalization of relations with Kosovo and alignment with the bloc’s foreign policy, including sanctions against Russia, as well as other judicial, media, and governmental reforms.
Serbia’s accession process has remained stalled while other candidates have moved forward. In July, eight EU member states opposed advancing talks with Belgrade, while Montenegro, Albania, Ukraine, and Moldova have made progress toward membership.
Vucic has expressed frustration with the slow pace of EU enlargement, warning in July that candidate countries should not expect major breakthroughs in the coming years.
EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos questioned Serbia’s commitment to membership in September, saying the country was at a crossroads and that further progress depended on the political direction chosen by its voters.
Kos has also warned against allowing prospective EU members to develop dependencies on outside powers that could conflict with the bloc’s interests.
“We should not risk our future members building dependencies on others that run counter to our long-term interest,” she said.
The commissioner identified Russia as an adversary in the enlargement process and criticized the influence of US President Donald Trump’s MAGA movement on European politics.
Vucic has maintained that Serbia intends to pursue EU membership while preserving its independent foreign policy.
What makes the ties between Serbia and Russia so strong?
Serbia and Russia share longstanding historical and cultural ties, reinforced by their Orthodox Christian traditions and Slavic heritage.
Relations were further shaped by NATO’s 78-day bombing campaign against Yugoslavia in 1999, which Moscow strongly opposed. Russia has since backed Belgrade’s position on Kosovo at the UN Security Council and refused to recognize the province’s independence.
Under Vucic, Serbia has maintained diplomatic and economic cooperation with Moscow while refusing to join Western sanctions over the Ukraine conflict.
In an interview with Russian journalist Ksenia Sobchak published on Tuesday, Vucic said European leaders regularly pressed him on the issue.
”We are not sitting on two chairs; our only chair is Serbia,” he said.
Do Russia and Serbia have an energy deal?
Energy remains central to the relationship. On September 30, Russia’s Gazprom extended its gas supply agreement with Serbia for another three months, until December 31, on unchanged terms, according to Srbijagas CEO Dusan Bajatovic.
The previous three-year contract expired in May 2025, with the two countries relying on short-term extensions since then.
Following talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in September, Vucic said Serbia was paying around €318 per 1,000 cubic meters of gas, compared with a market price of approximately €868 at the time.
The latest extension secures supplies through the beginning of winter but leaves arrangements for 2027 unresolved.
The future of NIS, which operates Serbia’s only oil refinery, also remains uncertain following US sanctions over its Russian majority ownership. Hungarian oil and gas company MOL has been negotiating the purchase of the Russian stake.
Serbia, however, maintains relations with Kiev and supports Ukraine’s territorial integrity, a position Vucic reaffirmed during an August meeting with Vladimir Zelensky. He has also said he would not object if Serbian ammunition sold to European buyers ultimately reached Ukraine, although he did not confirm direct deliveries to Kiev.
Where would each party take Serbia if they win?
Vucic has emphasized his determination to preserve Serbia’s sovereignty and keep the country out of a war with Russia, which he said he believes the EU is preparing for.
”I do not want Serbia to be part of that war, and I would not allow Serbia to be part of that war,” he said in an interview with TV Prva on Wednesday.
He accused Western governments of seeking to install politicians who would follow their instructions.
”They want to bring in people who will do as they are told, people who will be patted on the back, and everyone will be delighted,” Vucic said.
How could the election affect relations with Moscow?
The next Serbian government will face decisions on future Russian gas supplies, the ownership of NIS, and the country’s military exports.
Russian observers will monitor the election at Serbia’s invitation, according to Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova. The delegation will include representatives of both chambers of the Russian parliament and the Central Election Commission, with Russian officials also participating in international monitoring missions.
Moscow has said it hopes to maintain close ties with Belgrade after the election. Zakharova described the relationship as rooted in “strong fraternal traditions, a shared worldview, and respect for genuine values.”
She added that “continuity in these ties will serve the national interests of both countries and help strengthen peace and stability in the Balkans.”

"And they saw nothing / No future at all / Yet I was free". "They saw nothing, no future at all, but I was free".

Ebola: Kenya announces second death
October 23, 2026
Kenya has recorded a second Ebola death, the Health Ministry said on Friday.
Officials identified the patient as a 65-year-old woman, a close relative of a Kenyan man who died of Ebola earlier this month.
The woman began showing symptoms 10 days ago while in quarantine. She began receiving supportive care at an infectious disease unit in the capital, Nairobi.
"Sadly, she succumbed to the disease early this evening," the ministry said.
Medical personnel "did everything possible to save her life," the ministry said, adding that it had notified her family and would arrange a safe and dignified burial in consultation with relatives.
Seven people continue to receive treatment for the illness in Kenya.
What else do we know about the 2nd Kenyan Ebola death?
Kenya's first Ebola case was announced on October 6. The virus was found in a 40-year-old Kenyan man living in Congo, who travelled to Kenya via Uganda, arriving on October 3.
He tested positive for the disease on October 5 and died on the same day.
Of some 135 who were identified as contacts with the patient, 118 were placed in quarantine, with eight testing positive. They included four health workers and four close family members.
The remaining seven cases are all within "one cluster, with no evidence of community spread", the ministry added.
Nigeria's 1st Ebola case resembles the Kenyan strand
Meanwhile, genomic tests announced by Nigeria's Health Minister have revealed that the Ebola virus found in Kenya's patient zero resembles that found in Nigeria's first case, which was announced earlier this week.
Nigerian health officials detected the infection in the wife of a staff member at Switzerland's embassy in Abuja. She had returned from Uganda on October 3.
On Friday, the Swiss Foreign Ministry denied Ugandan government reports saying the patient had visited the Democratic Republic of Congo, the epicenter of a major Ebola outbreak.
African health authorities are trying to trace the source of the infection. The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention had suggested she may have come into contact with Kenya's first patient at the airport. The two flew from Uganda on the same day.
Nigerian Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate said "the viruses are appearing to be related," and the case "is highly similar to that from Kenya."
The current outbreak flared in the DRC in May, and has since spread to Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria.
The deadly Bundibugyo species has no approved vaccine or specific treatment.
To date, infections have surpassed 9,700 confirmed cases, including 4,690 deaths, as per World Health Organization figures as of October 20.

When a business suddenly collapses, how can customers get money back?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
21:07:49 UTC
06:07:49 KST

Can paying a deposit by credit card help you claw back losses when a company suddenly goes bankrupt?
The spate of caravan companies going bust has led to hundreds of customers losing tens of thousands of dollars in deposits.
From Sunshine Coast based Zone RV last December to Australian Off Road just last month, there is a long list of manufacturers going bust after trading while insolvent.
But buyers being caught up in business insolvencies is not a new issue.
Building companies and tech giant Dick Smith in 2016 have left customers out of pocket, while the collapse of whitegoods company Kleenmaid saw a former director jailed.
When it comes to getting back money you have forked out for a deposit, Deloitte senior liquidator Richard Hughes said there are no guarantees.
"There is no risk-free way of doing anything these days,"
he said.
"You have to be really careful."
And if possible, he warns, do not pay by cash.
Is paying by credit card the answer?
Mr Hughes helped creditors fight over the carcass of Kleenmaid, which collapsed owing $100 million, and says credit card payments can be good insurance.
His forensic examination of the company's books found customers were set to lose $25 million in deposits.
But when he realised half of those had been paid on credit card, he was able to help get $12.5 million back into disillusioned customers' bank accounts.
This was through charge back requests, which is when customers have paid for good or services they did not receive, like a cancelled flight or a brand new caravan.
How does a charge back request work?
The Australian Banking Association describes it this way.
"When someone pays for goods or services by card that they never receive, they can ask their bank to dispute the transaction," a spokesperson said.
"The rules are set and administered by the card schemes, such as Visa and Mastercard — time limits apply, so customers should contact their bank as soon as possible."
The customer's bank lodges the claim through the scheme with the business's bank.
"If the claim succeeds, the money goes back to the customer and is taken from the business's bank," the spokesperson said.
"Payments by cash don't carry charge back rights."
The Office of Fair Trading said financial institutions may be able to assist customers who have paid "by credit card, debit card, or through a secure payment provider such as PayPal".
Will changes to card fees make it hard to pay by credit?
From October 1, the reserve bank banned credit and debit card surcharges across major card networks.
Some customers may be concerned about whether these changes will impact their ability to pay a deposit, and whether companies may stop accepting credit card payments.
But Mr Hughes said he believed businesses would still be happy to take credit card deposits, with card fees most likely added into their quotes.
If a small business insists on only cash, it could be seen as a red flag.
Customers are also encouraged to do a financial health check on the business they are putting their faith in.
It is also important to remember that unlike real estate companies, which are legally bound to hold deposits in a protected trust account, small businesses are not.
How to check if a business is struggling
ASIC says warning signs customers can watch out for include:
- bad reviews
- ongoing losses
- board disputes and director resignations, or loss of management personnel
- suppliers placing the company on cash-on-delivery terms
- a sudden change of name
- movement of a business or its assets to another company
ASIC encourages customers to check whether a company has entered liquidation or external administration through ASIC Connect or ASIC's Published Notices website.
Will creditors get money back?
When a company goes into liquidation, the question every creditor wants answered is simple: am I going to get my money back?
According to ASIC, the data is stark.
In most small to medium-sized corporate insolvencies, 97 per cent of creditors received between 0–11 cents in the dollar.
In the recent cases of collapsed caravan companies, majority of customers have not been able to get their money back, and have seen their savings vanish.
Caravanning Queensland Trade advised any customers who have purchased a product they haven't received to contact the appointed administrator or liquidator as soon as possible, and bring their contract, receipts and proof of payment.
"For anyone considering buying a caravan, Caravanning Queensland recommends a deposit of 10 per cent of the purchase price, with the balance paid when the completed van is ready for inspection and handover," chief executive Jason Plant said.
"We remain committed to promoting responsible business practice, transparency and consumer confidence across the caravan and RV industry."

Peace talks, Zelensky, the EU, ‘political schizophrenia’ and a new Cold War: RT stories that shaped the week

Peace talks, Zelensky, the EU, ‘political schizophrenia’ and a new Cold War: RT stories that shaped the week
Witkoff returns to Russia
US envoy Steve Witkoff arrived in St. Petersburg on Wednesday to present a new set of peace proposals to Russian President Vladimir Putin. As was the case in every round of talks so far, Moscow found little to agree with in the terms put forward by Kiev and its European backers, Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov told reporters afterwards.
Although the key issues of the conflict – territory and Ukraine’s neutrality – remain unresolved, Witkoff and Putin pressed ahead with striking their own deals. Russia released US Air Force veteran Stephen Hubbard, who had been convicted on charges of fighting for Ukraine, Putin confirmed his willingness to hold trilateral talks with Washington and Kiev, and within two days of the meeting, the first tanker of diesel fuel left Russia for the US since the so-called “diesel deal” was struck last week.
That the US would even consider meeting with Putin rubbed the Europeans the wrong way. Speaking after Witkoff met Zelensky in Oslo on Tuesday, EU chief diplomat Kaja Kallas accused US President Donald Trump and his envoys of “trying to push Ukraine into surrender.”
Kallas is in an unenviable position. Trump has proven able and willing to negotiate with Putin above the Europeans’ heads, as he did when he waived sanctions on Russian diesel. Faced with the prospect of being cut out of an eventual peace deal, the EU is reportedly searching for an envoy to represent Brussels’ interests at the negotiating table. As anti-Russia hardliners, Kallas and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen have essentially ruled themselves out; French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz are drowning in domestic turmoil and watching their legitimacy collapse in real time; and the supposed ‘compromise candidate’ trumpeted by EU media, Finnish President Alexander Stubb, is a potentially toxic choice.
EU leaders, Putin remarked on Thursday, suffer from “a kind of political schizophrenia.” The Europeans “now go so far as to constantly speak of a ‘Russian threat’ and even discuss preparations for a war with Russia” against the will of their citizens, he explained. “They will hopefully realize that it is better to live in harmony with Russia – a path that truly serves the interests of their own peoples.”
The only European official present at the St. Petersburg meeting was von der Leyen’s chief of staff, Bjorn Seibert.
Zelensky scorned again
Zelensky signaled his disapproval with the Witkoff-Putin meeting in as clear a manner as possible; firing drones at St. Petersburg and the surrounding Leningrad Region. His own meeting with Witkoff in Oslo didn’t go so well either. The New York Times reported that the US envoy “reproached Zelensky for his sharp responses” to Trump’s recent assertion that Zelensky “doesn’t know what he’s talking about,” and “should have this war settled a long time ago.” Zelensky spent the rest of the week trying to dress up a ceasefire as a new idea that hadn’t been discounted dozens of times already by Moscow.
The deepening rift between Kiev and Washington is one of multiple diplomatic crises facing Zelensky.
South Korea pulled diplomats from the Ukrainian capital over Ukraine’s refusal to apologize for exposing the secret transfer of North Korean POWs to Seoul, a move that the South Koreans warned could endanger the POWs’ relatives in North Korea and undermine stability on the Korean Peninsula.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk slammed the Ukrainian government for allowing the city of Lviv to dedicate 2027 to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) and its leader, Nazi collaborator Roman Shukhevich. Tusk, one of Ukraine’s most loyal sponsors, called the move a “suicidal tactic.” The city, a hotbed of nationalism and neo-Nazism, has since reportedly backtracked.
Ukraine’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) confirmed on Wednesday that it is investigating National Bank of Ukraine chief Andrey Pyshny in a graft probe reportedly aimed at Zelensky’s inner circle. One day earlier, NABU accused Ukraine’s cybersecurity agency of stealing $5 million by purchasing drones at inflated prices.
RT has covered the rampant graft in Kiev extensively in our ‘State of Corruption’ series, which you can read here.
France fails
Just as corruption has come to define Zelensky’s Ukraine, the fiery collapse of the social contract now defines the closing stages of Emmanuel Macron’s presidency in France. After mass protests over rising prices and deteriorating social conditions degenerated into riots last week, almost 3,000 people were arrested this week as violent unrest continued to plague the streets of French cities.
Macron has refused to accept that his migration policies may be to blame for the riots, which Trump claimed are being led by “migrants, jihadists, and communists.” His government has also refused to change course on an austerity budget that will do little to alleviate the protesters’ economic concerns.
Instead, the French president has ordered military personnel into the streets, banned “illegitimate” protests, and imposed localized curfews. Whether he can count on the police to enforce these measures for much longer is unclear: France’s largest police union said on Thursday that it intends to sue the French state for creating the conditions that led to the riots, and leaving officers “betrayed and abandoned” to handle the violence without adequate training or protection.
The EU’s Cold War in the Arctic
The EU updated its Arctic Strategy, insisting the region is “Europe’s Northern Neighborhood” and announced its plan to redraw the map of the northern hemisphere completely. In an ominous document assessed here by RT, the bloc set out plans to build military logistics corridors above the Arctic Circle, develop polar-capable weapons systems, increase surveillance of Russian shipping in the Arctic Ocean, and encourage its member states to hold more military exercises in the frozen north.
The Starlink wars return
The EU and its member states may be Ukraine’s leading backers, but the US provides Zelensky with something that the Europeans don’t have: access to SpaceX’s Starlink satellite constellation. Ukraine depends on Starshield, SpaceX’s military-grade version, to guide its drones, connect to NATO headquarters, and receive real-time updates from Palantir’s battlefield management software.
As long as this dependence exists, the US holds a powerful instrument of leverage over Zelensky. While nobody in SpaceX or the US government has taken responsibility for throttling Ukraine’s access to the network earlier this month, the Wall Street Journal claimed this week that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk – who has condemned Ukraine’s drone strikes on Russian oil refineries – personally ordered that the Ukrainian military’s access to the network be restricted.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied that the government played any role in the slowdown, saying that “it sort of happened” accidentally. However, a turn of phrase by Rubio suggested that the connection problems may have been deliberate, and intended as a warning to Zelensky: “Ukraine,” he said on Wednesday, “would not exist as a sovereign state” without US support.
Moscow is well aware that Kiev uses Starlink to strike civilian targets as well as military ones. Russia’s Investigative Committee confirmed this week that two of the seven drones that struck a female dormitory at a college in Starobelsk in May – killing 21 people – were guided by SpaceX’s network. As long as Kiev continues to use this system, it remains a potential source of escalation between Russia and the US.
What we’re watching
We’re keeping a close eye on three consequential elections over the coming days, starting on Sunday with a presidential election in Brazil and parliamentary elections in Serbia. The showdown between Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Flavio Bolsonaro is an intensely personal battle between two bitter rivals, with the potential to pull another Latin American nation into the orbit of the US and reshape the future of the BRICS group.
RT looked at the candidates, the issues, and the competing accusations of corruption and foul play here, and we’ll be analyzing the results by Sunday night.
In Serbia, former President Aleksandar Vucic is now running for prime minister, in a snap election pitting his ruling coalition against a new political faction put together by the organizers of anti-government protests raging in Serbia since 2024. Vucic’s coalition has a narrow lead, but accusations of foreign interference are flying, and we’ll know by Monday whether Vucic’s gambit paid off.
Few world leaders have been as consequential as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Perennially on the verge of prosecution over multiple corruption scandals and facing mass protests, Netanyahu’s political fortunes changed with Hamas’ October 7 attack on Israel in 2023. Three years later, Netanyahu has managed to achieve almost all of his war aims – leveling Gaza, diminishing Hezbollah in Lebanon, neutering Syria, and leading the US into war with Iran.
However, with the Iran war stalled and Netanyahu offering no plan for a post-conflict Gaza, dissent has returned, and polls suggest that his right-wing coalition will fall up to 10 seats short of the 61 needed to govern. The closing of polls on Tuesday night may signal the start of a lengthy process of political horse-trading, with Netanyahu’s future no clearer than it is now.
For more on these stories as they develop, stick with RT.

Kadena Implements Curfew, Alcohol Restrictions for Junior Troops After Japanese Civilian Dies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:59:50 UTC
05:59:50 KST

The top Air Force commander on the Japanese island of Okinawa has clamped down alcohol and issued a curfew for junior enlisted Airmen and Guardians at Kadena Air Base for the next month. The order came roughly two weeks after a U.S. Marine was arrested for allegedly robbing and murdering a Japanese woman on the island.
Brig. Gen. John B. Gallemore, commander of the 18th Wing at Kadena, issued the Oct. 22 memo, ordering the “Curtailment of Liberty and the Consumption of Alcohol,” according to a memo posted on the popular unofficial Air Force amn/nco/snco Facebook page.
A PACAF spokesperson confirmed the memo’s authenticity. The order went into effect Oct. 22 and will last “throughout the 30-day period of reflection,” concluding on Nov. 8, according to the memo:
- All personnel within the grades of E-1 through E-4 are not to consume alcohol.
- Off-base liberty between 10 p.m. and 5 a.m. local time is curtailed for all personnel within the grades of E-1 through E-4.
- Possession of alcohol is banned in all dormitories within Kadena Air Base, to include dormitory common areas.
During the period, “commanders at all levels are authorized to conduct unannounced, systematic health and welfare inspections of dormitory rooms to ensure compliance of this order,” the memo states.
The memo follows an Oct. 6 memo from United States Forces Japan that ordered similar liberty restrictions and personal conduct training as part of a “period of reflection” following the Marine’s arrest in connection with the alleged murder of an Okinawan woman in Naha.
Japanese police arrested Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, of the III Marine Expeditionary Force, on Oct. 4 for allegedly killing 39-year-old Anna Yagi and stealing her wallet, Marine Corps Times reported.
“Incidents like this demand we pause for reflection,” Benjamin T. Watson, area coordinator for U.S. Forces Japan, wrote in the memo. “These allegations are extremely serious, and we will continue to ensure full cooperation with Japanese authorities throughout the investigation.”
Watson added that serving on Okinawa “comes with responsibility.”
“We live, work, and socialize alongside the people of Okinawa; their home is our home,” Watson wrote. “Every interaction with our neighbors either builds or undermines the trust that is essential to our team. When that trust is damaged, it affects the strength of our alliance and the security of this region.”
The USFJ memo prohibited alcohol consumption for 48 hours from Oct. 7-9 but stopped short of restricting consumption during the 30-day period of reflection. In a statement, PACAF Gallemore’s Oct. 22 memo contains extra restrictions.
“The 18th Wing continually assesses measures to reinforce good order and discipline and maintain positive relationships with our host community,” the PACAF statement read. “As part of the ongoing 30-day period of reflection on Okinawa, Japan, [Gallemore] determined that additional preventive measures were appropriate to reinforce expectations for responsible conduct among service members.”
Periods of reflection and associated restrictions have been used by commanders on Okinawa in the past to reinforce discipline after violent, criminal incidents involving U.S. personnel and Japanese residents. In 2024, USFJ prohibited all American troops in the country from publicly consuming alcohol from 1 a.m. to 5 a.m. every day after a string of alleged sexual assaults. In 2017, the command prohibited all drinking and cut off-base liberty for troops on Okinawa after a fatal car crash involving a drunk Marine. In 2010, then-Brig. Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach—now the Chief of Staff—instituted a brief period of reflection restricting alcohol and off-base liberty at Kadena after a string of alcohol-related arrests. In 2008, commanders imposed the measure to calm an uproar in the surrounding community over allegations that a Marine raped a 14-year-old girl on the island, The Guardian reported.
Kadena is the closest U.S. air base to Taiwan, making it a strategically vital location should China ever launch an invasion.
