stars return to frank lloyd wright’s only built planetarium after twenty years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:55:19 UTC
05:55:19 KST

stars return to frank lloyd wright’s only built planetarium after twenty years
at florida southern college, the restored 1950s-era building reopens with its original circular seating and new digital projection system.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
a dome full of stars returns to florida southern college
Two rings of curved red seating surround a central projector beneath the domed ceiling of Frank Lloyd Wright‘s only built planetarium, which has reopened at Florida Southern College in Lakeland. After more than two decades without regular star shows, the 1950s building has been restored by a team led by Jeff Baker of MCWB Architects. Its original seating has been returned to Wright’s circular arrangement, and a new digital projection system brings the night sky back overhead. The Miller Planetarium welcomed the public again on September 26th, 2026.
The planetarium occupies the southern end of the Polk Science Building, part of the college‘s collection of thirteen Wright-designed structures. Built between 1954 and 1958, its pale concrete walls are patterned with geometric textile blocks, while a white dome rises above the surrounding low-slung buildings. Wright had explored the idea of designing a planetarium for decades before incorporating one into his plans for Florida Southern. Its first show took place in April 1960, a year after the architect’s death.
restoring the original concrete textile blocks
Work began on the exterior in 2021, addressing years of water damage and deterioration in the building’s concrete surfaces. The team at MCWB replaced sections of roofing and repaired failing stucco, while more than 280 hand-cast textile blocks around the planetarium’s perimeter required replacement. These decorative concrete units form part of the architectural language Wright developed across the Florida Southern campus. To reproduce their geometric patterns, the restoration team used contemporary fabrication methods, including 3D printing to develop molds for new blocks designed to match the originals.
The work also revealed some unexpected details behind the facade. During construction, Baker’s team discovered areas of steel framing and open cavities behind the upper walls, where they had anticipated a more typical arrangement of Wright’s concrete blocks. The discovery made it possible to introduce insulation into portions of the building that had previously been left exposed to Florida’s heat. Elsewhere, the architecture posed a different challenge. Wright’s concrete surfaces often serve several structural functions at once, leaving little concealed space for the mechanical systems needed in a contemporary building.
wright’s curved plywood seating returns to its circular layout
Inside the planetarium, the restoration focused on recovering the original spatial arrangement, which had been altered through decades of repairs and technological additions. A computer closet installed during the 1980s had interrupted the circular seating plan. Its removal allowed the architects to return Wright’s original plywood benches to their intended positions, arranged in two concentric rings around the projection equipment. Local craftspeople repaired the surviving seating, retaining its curved forms and colored vinyl upholstery.
The room’s finishes have also been returned to their earlier appearance. Deep-blue wall paint was replaced with a lighter scheme based on the original design, while damaged plaster was repaired. Underfoot, the floor was refinished in Wright’s familiar Cherokee Red, its glossy surface reflecting the curved benches above. The restoration preserves an unusual arrangement for a planetarium, where visitors sit in the round beneath a complete dome. Many newer facilities use forward-facing theater seating, but Wright’s design brings the audience together around the center of the room.
modern projection technology beneath the historic dome
The final phase introduced a COSM digital projection system and Bowen sound system, updating equipment that had prevented the planetarium from operating since 2004. The building had continued to see occasional use after the old projector stopped functioning, though regular astronomical presentations were suspended. With the new technology installed, the restored room can once again host presentations about the solar system and distant planets, along with programs developed for students and visiting school groups.
The reopening also continues a longer preservation effort across Wright’s Florida Southern campus, which was commissioned by college president Ludd Spivey in 1938. Restoration projects have included the Waterdome fountain and the Annie Pfeiffer Chapel, along with the campus’s network of concrete esplanades. At the Miller Planetarium, the latest work returns the building to the educational purpose Wright envisioned. Visitors can now take their seats in the original circular auditorium, with its restored red interior beneath a sky projected across the dome.

Loaded on the day Moscow promised

From a pledge to a partial lift
On 9 October, Trump wrote that Russia would immediately supply over 300,000 tons of diesel “to the American and Global Marketplace.” Another 500,000 tons would follow in November, then 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.”

‘Generation Right’: Israeli youth show strong support for the right

‘Generation Right’: Israeli youth show strong support for the right
Poll shows some three quarters of Jewish first-time voters identify as right or centre-right, higher than the rest of Israeli society.
The first Israeli elections in four years have brought with them a record number of first-time voters – most of whom are keen to make their voices count.
But while youth around the world are leaning to the left, young adults in Israel are heading in the opposite direction, according to recent polls.
The Israeli Central Elections Committee says more than half a million voters were added to the roll since the last elections in 2022. They are aged between 18 and 22 and polls show that 80 percent of them plan to vote in the October 27 legislative election.
Although their political activism and engagement in the public sphere are limited, a survey by the think tank, Israel Democracy Institute (IDI), found that a majority of young Jewish Israelis feel that the ballot box can influence reality and shape their country’s future.
But what does the future they hope for look like?
Around three quarters of Jewish first-time voters polled identified as “right or centre-right”, according to a recent poll for Israel’s Channel 12. That’s significantly higher than the rest of the Israeli population, which has already been shifting to the right for years.
Now the title “Generation Right” is being used to reference Israel’s Jewish youth – though not the Palestinian citizens of Israel.
Mainstreaming far-right views
The first Israeli elections since the October 7, 2023 attack are contentious and polarising – and they will be decisive for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s political survival and his right-wing approach.
Critics of the longest-serving PM in Israel’s history accuse him of supporting “far-right” politicians to stay in power. They say that his handing of key government positions to extreme politicians such as National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich helped empower those camps and make their policies mainstream.
In 2017, Smotrich laid out his position for the future of Israel where the Israelis are the only ones who will have self-determination, whereas Palestinians will have to emigrate, stay without political representation, or be treated as “terrorists” if they refuse either of the two options. In 2022 he secured a portfolio in the defence ministry where he facilitates land grabs and empowers the illegal settlement enterprise in the occupied West Bank.
Indeed, this incitement and view of Palestinians has become more prevalent.
A recent video published by the Israeli satirist Lior Schleien shows a young man saying he would kill Arabs in Israel.
Schleien, a left-wing activist, has been visiting schools and speaking with young people often before their army service. His videos are giving Israelis, and the world, a chance to understand the younger generation.
In the video, Schleien asks the student how he proposes to kill Arabs. The answer: “Give me a knife and I will do it.”
Schleien asks whether October 7 changed his views. “I’ve always been racist,” the young man answers, adding that Arabs shouldn’t be allowed to live in the state of Israel. Even though the young man’s face is slightly covered, shielding his identity, Schleien removed the video after a public backlash.
In another town hall meeting, Schleien addresses the question of whether there are innocent people in Gaza. When asked if Israel is committing a genocide in Gaza, Schleien denies it, only for a female student to ask, “Do you think it should be done?”
Schleien looks unimpressed, but the student assures him that she is asking a serious question. Her friend, next to her, chuckles.
Speaking the language of the youth
At a recent meeting of young supporters of the left-leaning Democrats party in Tel Aviv, 18-year-old Gili told the AFP news agency that she believed Israeli society had abandoned the idea of peace.
She said the scars of October 7 instilled fear among people, making it hard for them to believe peace could ever be achievable.
While the October 7 attack may have accelerated the country’s push to the right and far-right, many say Israeli society has been heading this way for years.
A survey by the Israeli newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth shows more than 16 percent of new voters plan to cast their ballot for far-right parties.
From a large field in southern Israel, 18-year-old Amihai was wearing a shirt with far-right minister Ben-Gvir’s photo. The event he was attending called for the establishment of illegal Israeli settlements on Palestinian territory.
Talking to other young activists from a place overlooking the destroyed parts of the Gaza Strip, Amihai said he plans to vote for Otzma Yehudit, a party led by Ben-Gvir, who himself lives in an illegal settlement in the occupied West Bank.
Although Ben-Gvir did not pass the threshold of the 2020 elections, he was given a central position in the 2022 government of Netanyahu.
In the years since, the minister seems to have learned to speak the language of Israel’s youth. Despite having been convicted of supporting “terror” organisations as well as other criminal offences, Israeli surveys show that a chunk of his potential supporters in this election are first-time voters.
Ben-Gvir has also made sure to use his position to lobby for his “I am not mincing my words” policies.
As a minister, he often visits Israeli jails and detention centres to threaten Palestinian prisoners as well as international activists – all the while making sure that it is caught on camera.
His videos often go viral, a move that has earned him more youth support – and not just from his usual base of settlers, such as the violent “Hilltop Youth”, some of whose members have been sanctioned by the European Union and the United Kingdom.
The IDI survey found that social media and messaging apps such as WhatsApp and Telegram are key sources of information – often exposing young people to political content through their feeds rather than through active searching.
It is a language Ben-Gvir understands.

NASA lays out a packed 14-day schedule for Artemis III
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:51:11 UTC
05:51:11 KST

NASA’s upcoming Artemis III will be the tiebreaker between two potential lunar landers for future crewed missions to the moon’s surface, the space agency’s head Jared Isaacman said on Friday. But both SpaceX and Blue Origin are planning to touch down on the moon in 2028 no matter what.
Only one will take part in Artemis IV, the 2028 mission to return humans to the lunar surface—NASA will wait as long as possible before making a selection.
Artemis program manager Jeremy Parsons said at a press briefing on Friday that both companies “are planning for lunar landing missions in 2028.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Before that, they must get through Artemis III. In that mission, NASA’s Orion crew capsule will attempt to dock with both Blue Origin’s Blue Moon and a version of SpaceX’s Starship. Though no exact launch window was announced, Artemis III is expected to lift off in the summer of 2027, Isaacman said.
Artemis III was previously slated to be a crewed mission to the moon’s surface but was reconfigured earlier this year to instead allow for a complex, two-week-long test run of both landers in orbit.
Artemis III requires several rockets to be in space at once. First, Blue Moon will launch onboard a Blue Origin New Glenn rocket. Once in orbit, tests will be conducted to ensure the lander is in good shape.
Meanwhile NASA’s Orion will already be on the launchpad atop a Space Launch System (SLS) rocket. “We’re going to do everything we can to ensure that that vehicle is ready to go as quickly as we can after that first Blue Origin launch,” Parsons said.
Because the SLS only needs to put Orion into orbit, the rocket has been modified to remove its upper stage.
“When we pivoted to a low-Earth orbit mission, the SLS team quickly came back and said, ‘We don’t need the upper stage for that. Core stage has plenty of performance to drop us in the orbit we need,’” Parsons said.
Three days after Blue Moon launches, Orion will attempt to dock with the spacecraft, after which there will be two days of testing its guidance, navigation and communications systems.
On day six, SpaceX’s Starship will launch, and Orion will detach from Blue Moon, adjust its orbit and attempt a second docking with Starship. The Artemis III crew will not enter Starship during the operation, however, and the test will last just two hours.
“Once Starship operations are complete, Orion and the crew have the remaining days available for additional test objectives before needing to come home,” Parsons said.
Hurdles have to be overcome before any of this can happen: Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket has not launched since one of the spacecraft exploded spectacularly in May. Parsons said the company expects to resume launches in November and that, right now, NASA has no contingency plans to send Blue Moon to space onboard an alternate vehicle.
“Their design for the Artemis III lander test article is in good shape,” he said. “We have gone through design reviews. We’ve been participating with them, and they have parts coming together from across the United States.”
Meanwhile SpaceX is aiming to conduct another test of Starship next month, which will include upgrades to the craft’s Raptor engines. Starship has seen a number of hiccups, including several explosions during test flights. But in its most recent demonstration, the vehicle was able to enter orbit for the first time—a major milestone on the way to being ready for Artemis III.
Artemis III’s optimal flight timeframe is 14 days, but the mission could be expanded to 17 days if necessary. While the attempted dockings with the landers are key, the mission will also involve collecting vital data on the health of the astronauts.
“Every day of this mission is built around specific tests that reduce risk, give us valuable science and allow us to test out our capabilities before we go and undertake the lunar landing,” Parsons said.
And looking ahead, work has already begun on assembling and testing the Orion crew and service modules that will be used on Artemis IV, Parsons added.
“We are hardly in a position to ‘set it and forget it,’” Isaacman quipped at the event, referring to future Artemis missions planning. “We will never stop listening to data and adapt as circumstances require.”

Israel's Foreign Ministry on Friday evening urged Israeli citizens in France to exercise heightened caution and remain vigilant amid fears of renewed violent unrest across the country. The ministry advised Israelis to avoid demonstrations, protests, large gatherings and areas affected by public disturbances, even when protests appear peaceful, warning that they could suddenly escalate into violent confrontations. It also urged travelers to leave areas where clashes occur immediately and safely, and not to gather nearby to watch or film the events. Israelis were advised to prepare for disruptions to public transportation, roadblocks and changes to traffic arrangements, and to check road and transport conditions before setting out.
The ministry also recommended paying attention to movement restrictions and nighttime curfews that have been imposed or may be introduced in certain parts of France, checking the regulations in force at their current location and planned destinations, monitoring local media and official French announcements, and following instructions from police and security forces. Travelers were advised to check security conditions at places they intend to visit and remain prepared for restrictions or changes introduced at short notice.
In an emergency, Israelis can contact the Foreign Ministry's 24-hour Situation Center at +972-2-530-3155, or the emergency hotline of the Israeli Embassy in France at +33-6-59-44-44-61. France's general emergency number is 112.
Preparing for renewed riots: Cultural institutions close to visitors
French authorities are preparing for major demonstrations against the country's economic situation over the weekend, amid fears that the protests could reignite the violent riots that swept through France, particularly Paris, last weekend. As part of the preparations, museums, cultural institutions and luxury stores announced that they would either close completely on Saturday or operate under restrictions.
Among the institutions announcing closures or reduced operations are the Louvre, the Musée d'Orsay, the Grand Palais, the Picasso Museum, the Musée de l'Orangerie, the Art Basel Paris international art fair, luxury retailers Cartier and Louis Vuitton, the National Library of France and affiliated institutions, and the Palace of Versailles.
At Versailles, restrictions will affect the palace and its surrounding estate. According to the palace's updated visitor information, the main building will admit only visitors who already hold tickets, until noon Saturday. The Trianon estate will remain closed throughout the day, while the gardens and park will close at 1 p.m.
On Thursday, French President Emmanuel Macron announced that authorities would prohibit demonstrations organized by groups he described as lacking legitimate authority, referring primarily to far-left organizations that the government accuses of responsibility for last weekend's violence.
Lyon announced restrictions on demonstrations across a broad area of its city center on Saturday. Authorities in Marseille initially announced a sweeping ban as well, but subsequently agreed to allow a union-organized march along an approved route. Protest organizers have challenged restrictions imposed in several cities, arguing that they infringe on the constitutionally protected right to demonstrate.
Among those calling for nationwide demonstrations Saturday are France's national student union, UNEF, and supporters of the Yellow Vest movement, which emerged in 2018 during protests against the cost of living and Macron's economic policies.
With fears that the demonstrations could once again deteriorate into widespread violence, the government has promised a massive police deployment, following the October 17 protests, which descended into chaos as rioters attacked police officers and government buildings and looted hundreds of businesses across France.
Macron's government acknowledged that it had been insufficiently prepared for the scale of the previous demonstrations, which drew hundreds of thousands of people, far exceeding official expectations. This time, authorities say the security response will be considerably stronger.
Military personnel will also assist with public security over the weekend, including soldiers from Operation Sentinelle, France's counterterrorism security mission, which has patrolled French cities since the wave of Islamic State attacks in France and elsewhere in Europe beginning in 2015. The soldiers will be assigned to protect sensitive locations, freeing additional police officers for crowd control and efforts to prevent looting.
Last weekend's riots followed large demonstrations against the rising cost of living and deteriorating conditions in educational institutions. The protests were led in significant part by radical-left groups and included substantial participation from immigrant communities.
Rioters attacked police officers, threw stones at them, assaulted passersby, set fire to garbage bins, vehicles and buildings, and looted or vandalized approximately 3,000 businesses in Paris, Marseille, Lyon, Nice, Nantes, Limoges and other cities.
More than 2,700 people were detained during the unrest, and nearly 1,000 police officers and other security personnel were injured, several seriously. Macron and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu acknowledged failures in intelligence preparations for the riots and said police had found themselves at a disadvantage against the rioters.
On Thursday, authorities in Paris again attempted to prevent demonstrations over fears that they could turn violent, but a court overturned a police ban on one protest. Following the ruling, thousands demonstrated in the capital, although the gathering remained stationary rather than proceeding as a march, as originally planned. No unusual incidents were reported.
One of the signs carried by protesters read: "We don't need tear gas for our future to look bleak."
Meanwhile, Macron convened a special security meeting at the Élysée Palace, where he again accused far-left organizations of orchestrating the violence in an effort to create anarchy in France.
"Last Saturday, we saw political and even seditious acts carried out by organized far-left groups seeking to bring down the Republic," Macron said.
Macron added that the strategy adopted by the authorities for the coming days would be to reject requests to hold demonstrations submitted by individuals or groups without legitimate authority.
"The rules are simple, and I think they're simply a matter of common sense," Macron said. "The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations in the coming days. For those who nevertheless wish to demonstrate, if they are trade unions, the prefects will propose alternative routes."
The president was referring to routes intended to pose less danger to businesses, whose owners fear further looting.
Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin, meanwhile, called for tough measures against those who violate protest bans, including stripping offenders of their voting rights. He also proposed restrictions on social media use by people involved in violence, looting or attacks on police officers.
In recent days, calm has largely returned to Paris and other French cities, partly because of partial curfews imposed in several areas. On Thursday evening, authorities in the capital announced an extension of the nighttime curfew covering Place de la République and the Les Halles district, from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. local time, until Monday morning.
At the same time, the French Culture Ministry confirmed that several of Paris' most important museums, including the Louvre and the Musée d'Orsay, would remain closed on Saturday.
The Grand Palais, Picasso Museum and Musée de l'Orangerie will also be closed. The Culture Ministry instructed institutions under its authority to take all necessary measures to ensure visitor safety, protect staff and preserve works of art.
Organizers of Art Basel Paris, the international art fair, also announced that the event would close for the weekend. Paris City Hall urged residents and visitors to exercise extreme vigilance Saturday because of the risk of further violence by rioters unaffiliated with the broader social protest movement.
Last Saturday's demonstrations brought together high school students, university students, labor unions and supporters of the Yellow Vest movement. The protests followed weeks of student demonstrations that began last month in schools in poorer suburbs north of Paris over teacher shortages and deteriorating educational conditions.
Those demonstrations were also accompanied by numerous violent incidents, and the protest movement has since spread to other European countries, including Belgium.
In France and abroad, some commentators have emphasized the involvement of immigrants and descendants of immigrants from African, Arab and Muslim countries in the demonstrations and violence. Such claims have circulated since the student protests began earlier this month.
U.S. President Donald Trump also suggested that the unrest was evidence of what he described as an attempt by Islam to take over France. Macron rejected that characterization as a "complete lie," instead emphasizing the role he believes far-left organizations played in the riots.
Prime Minister Lecornu and figures on the French right have also accused Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of the far-left France Unbowed party, of helping fuel the violence. They allege that the unrest is being used as a show of political strength ahead of next year's presidential election, in which Mélenchon and far-right leader Marine Le Pen are expected to be prominent figures.

Yemen’s peace process has a structural blind spot: The south’s political future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:47:23 UTC
05:47:23 KST

Yemen’s prolonged conflict is frequently discussed through the familiar language of ceasefires, military de-escalation, humanitarian assistance and negotiations between the principal armed parties. These are important elements of any effort to end the war. Yet they do not fully explain why successive political initiatives have struggled to establish a durable settlement.
The deeper problem is structural:
Yemen’s crisis is not simply a contest over who controls the central government. It is also a dispute over the nature of the state, the distribution of political authority and the future status of its different regions. Among these questions, the Southern Question remains one of the most consequential and least adequately resolved.
A peace process that postpones this question risks producing an agreement that reduces violence temporarily without resolving the political disagreements capable of generating another conflict. The challenge for regional governments and international mediators is therefore not merely to bring the parties back to the negotiating table, but to design a political framework that addresses the underlying causes of instability.
The Limits of a Narrow Peace Process
Yemen’s war has multiple dimensions, involving competing political projects, regional rivalries, institutional fragmentation and a severe economic crisis. Negotiations focused exclusively on the confrontation between the internationally recognised government and the Houthis cannot, by themselves, resolve every dispute shaping the country’s future.
The United Nations’ efforts to promote a negotiated settlement have helped maintain international attention on diplomacy and the need to reduce violence. Nevertheless, the broader question remains: what political order is a settlement intended to establish, and whose aspirations must it accommodate to remain sustainable?
The distinction matters. An agreement can distribute positions within existing institutions without resolving fundamental disagreements about the legitimacy of those institutions or the territorial structure of the state. It can also establish temporary security arrangements while leaving competing political claims untouched.
Such agreements may create valuable space for diplomacy, but they should not be mistaken for a comprehensive settlement.
The Southern Question illustrates this difficulty.
For many southerners, the issue is not limited to representation within a unified state. It concerns historical experience, political identity, governance, the distribution of resources and the right to determine the South’s future status.
Treating these demands as secondary matters to be addressed after a national agreement has been reached risks placing the most difficult questions at the end of a process that may never reach them.
Why the Southern Question Is Fundamentally Political
The unification of the former North Yemen and South Yemen in 1990 created a new political framework, but it did not permanently settle disagreements over power, representation and the character of the state. The 1994 war deepened divisions, while subsequent grievances contributed to the emergence of a broader southern political movement.
These historical developments do not mean that every southern community shares the same political preferences or supports a single representative. Southern Yemen contains diverse political currents, regional interests and social constituencies. Hadramout, Aden, Shabwa, Lahj, Abyan, Al-Mahra and other southern areas have distinct histories and priorities that any credible settlement must take seriously.
Recognising this diversity is essential. The Southern Question should neither be reduced to the position of one political organisation nor dismissed because southern political actors disagree over leadership, strategy or the desired constitutional outcome.
A sustainable process must create meaningful opportunities for southern participation, allow competing perspectives to be expressed peacefully and establish a credible mechanism for determining the region’s future.
The central principle is that political disagreement should be addressed through an agreed and legitimate process, rather than indefinitely deferred or settled through military pressure.
For international mediators, this requires a more explicit approach to the South. Instead of assuming that its future can be determined automatically through a broader Yemeni agreement, negotiations should establish a dedicated political track with clear objectives, representative participation and a defined timetable.
Without such a framework, the Southern Question is likely to remain a source of uncertainty even if other fronts experience de-escalation.
The Constitutional Declaration: Political Significance and Legal Questions
On 2 January 2026, the Southern Transitional Council, led by Aidarous Al-Zubaidi, announced a constitutional declaration associated with a proposed transitional process for the South. The initiative outlined a two-year period intended to facilitate dialogue and prepare for a popular referendum on self-determination.
The announcement brought the question of southern statehood into sharper focus. It also highlighted the distance between the political aspirations advanced by the Southern Transitional Council and the existing international framework, which continues to recognise the Republic of Yemen as a state.
The declaration should therefore be examined on two distinct levels: its political significance and its legal status.
Politically, it represents an attempt to establish a defined pathway for addressing the South’s future rather than leaving the question open-ended. Its proposed referendum also places popular consent at the centre of the debate, an important consideration in any discussion of self-determination.
Legally and diplomatically, however, a unilateral declaration does not automatically create an internationally recognised state or impose an obligation on other governments to recognise it. The Yemeni government rejected the initiative, and the proposal did not receive an announced endorsement from the United Nations when it was introduced.
These distinctions should not obscure the underlying political question. The absence of immediate international recognition does not eliminate the need to address southern aspirations, just as the announcement of a constitutional framework does not, by itself, settle questions of representation, territorial governance, institutional legitimacy or international law.
The appropriate response is serious diplomatic engagement.
Regional governments and international institutions should examine the declaration’s proposed transitional arrangements, the practical conditions required for a referendum, the participation of different southern constituencies and the safeguards needed to ensure that any political process is peaceful, transparent and credible.
They should also clarify what legal and political steps would be required for any future change in the South’s status to gain wider international acceptance.
This approach would neither prejudge the outcome nor dismiss the initiative without examination. Instead, it would create a framework through which a contested political claim could be addressed through diplomacy rather than renewed confrontation.
International Recognition Must Be Part of a Political Strategy
Calls for international recognition of the South’s political aspirations are likely to remain central to the debate. However, recognition should be understood as part of a broader diplomatic process, not as a substitute for one.
Governments considering the South’s future must weigh the principles of self-determination, territorial integrity, regional stability and the peaceful resolution of disputes. They must also consider the extent to which any proposed arrangement reflects the freely expressed preferences of the population concerned and provides credible protections for those who hold different views.
For supporters of southern independence, the objective should be to secure international engagement with a clear and credible pathway towards self-determination, including the possibility of recognising an independent southern state if the necessary political and legal conditions are met.
That requires more than declarations of support. It requires sustained diplomacy, inclusive southern representation, institutional preparation and an agreed process capable of earning domestic and international confidence.
The international community should not allow the absence of consensus over the final outcome to become a permanent justification for avoiding the question itself.
At the same time, no political actor should assume that recognition can be secured solely through unilateral measures or the establishment of institutions without broader political legitimacy. Durable outcomes require processes that can withstand disagreement and accommodate the interests of affected communities.
The task is therefore to establish a credible route from political aspiration to a peaceful and legitimate determination of status.
Hadramout and the Challenge of Southern Representation
Hadramout illustrates why the future of southern Yemen cannot be approached through a narrow focus on competing political leaderships.
Its geographic position, economic resources, social structures and connections with the wider Gulf give it particular significance. Yet its importance is not merely strategic or economic. Hadramout’s people have their own political interests and expectations concerning local governance, security, resource management and representation.
Any settlement concerning the South must take these interests seriously. A process that assumes a single political organisation can automatically speak for every southern community risks reproducing the very problem that negotiations are intended to solve: the exclusion of significant constituencies from decisions about their future.
This does not mean that southern political aspirations should be fragmented into competing local vetoes. Rather, it means that a credible framework must combine a coherent political process with meaningful guarantees for regional participation and local decision-making.
For Hadramout, this includes transparent arrangements for managing public resources, accountable local institutions, reliable public services and a meaningful role in determining the political and economic future of the region.
These considerations are equally important for the wider South. Political legitimacy cannot be established through slogans alone; it must be reflected in the institutions through which people participate, exercise rights and hold authorities accountable.
A Practical Framework for International Engagement
If international mediators want a settlement capable of lasting beyond an initial reduction in fighting, four steps deserve particular attention.
First, establish a dedicated political track for the Southern Question. Its mandate should explicitly address the South’s future status, political representation and the range of constitutional options available. The process should have a clear timetable and should not be indefinitely subordinated to negotiations on other fronts.
Second, develop an inclusive framework for southern participation. Political parties, regional representatives, civil society and other relevant constituencies should have meaningful opportunities to contribute. Participation must be substantive rather than symbolic, and the process should provide safeguards for peaceful political disagreement.
Third, clarify the legal and diplomatic pathway. The constitutional declaration announced by Al-Zubaidi should be subject to serious examination alongside the wider question of self-determination. International actors should identify the procedures, guarantees and political agreements required for a credible process, without presenting contested legal claims as settled facts.
Fourth, connect political negotiations with economic and institutional recovery. Any future arrangement must address public revenue, local governance, security, infrastructure and the provision of essential services. Political legitimacy is difficult to sustain when people experience persistent economic insecurity and weak public institutions.
These steps would not guarantee agreement. They would, however, make the process more realistic by confronting the questions that a sustainable settlement must ultimately answer.
The Cost of Leaving the Question Unresolved
The international community has understandable reasons to prioritise immediate de-escalation in Yemen. Renewed fighting threatens civilian lives, deepens economic hardship and risks destabilising the wider region, including areas of importance to international maritime trade.
But urgency should not be confused with a preference for temporary arrangements over difficult political decisions.
A settlement that leaves the Southern Question unresolved may reduce violence in the short term while preserving the conditions for future confrontation. Conversely, a serious process addressing the South’s political future could help transform a recurring source of conflict into a structured diplomatic negotiation.
This requires regional governments to recognise that stability cannot be measured solely by the absence of active fighting. It must also be assessed by whether political arrangements are sufficiently credible, inclusive and legitimate to withstand future disputes.
The same principle applies to international policy. Maintaining existing diplomatic formulas simply because they are familiar may appear less risky than reconsidering them. Yet if those formulas fail to accommodate the political realities of Yemen, preserving them indefinitely may carry its own substantial risks.
Conclusion: Peace Requires a Political Answer
Yemen does not need another agreement that postpones the most difficult questions until a later stage. It needs a political process that addresses the causes of conflict and establishes a credible framework for determining the country’s future.
The Southern Question must be treated as a central component of that process. The constitutional declaration announced by Aidarous Al-Zubaidi has brought the debate over southern statehood and self-determination into sharper focus, but its announcement alone cannot resolve the political and legal questions surrounding the South’s future.
Those questions require serious international engagement, inclusive participation, a clear timetable and a peaceful process capable of establishing political legitimacy.
For the international community, the objective should not be to impose a predetermined outcome. It should be to ensure that the South’s future is addressed directly, that its people have a credible opportunity to determine their political status and that any resulting arrangement is pursued through a legitimate and peaceful framework.
The test of diplomacy is not whether it can postpone a difficult dispute. It is whether it can create a process capable of resolving it.
Yemen’s peace process will remain incomplete for as long as the political future of the South remains an unanswered question.

South Korea proposes military talks with North Korea to ease tensions along border
South Korea renewed its offer Friday to hold military talks with North Korea to discuss their conflicting views on where the inter-Korean border sits, seeking to ease tensions sparked by last month's land mine blast inside the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), Yonhap reported.
"Different perceptions remain over the Military Demarcation Line (MDL)," Deputy Defense Minister Kim Hong-cheol said in a press briefing, referring to the border separating the two Koreas.

Seoul and Pyongyang have traded sharp rhetoric since South Korea blamed the North for the Sept. 21 mine blast inside the DMZ that injured three South Korean troops. Pyongyang has denied responsibility and vowed to take military actions along the border if needed.
The latest escalation of tensions comes amid Seoul's suspicions that North Korean forces have repeatedly crossed the MDL to carry out border fortification work, such as erecting fences and laying mines, in potential violation of the armistice that halted the 1950-53 Korean War.
Earlier, South Korea voiced concern over North Korea heightening border tensions with threats.

Former BBC Radio 1 DJ Tim Westwood has appeared in a London court on two additional sex offense charges, British media reported on Friday.
The 69-year-old faces a total of 17 charges involving nine women, including allegations of rape and sexual assault. The alleged offenses span more than three decades, from 1983 to 2016.
The two additional charges were announced by London’s Metropolitan Police in September. They concern the alleged indecent assault of a girl aged 16 or 17 in west London in 1991 and the alleged sexual assault of an 18-year-old woman in south London in 2004.
Former Radio 1 DJ Tim Westwood in court charged with two further offences https://t.co/1OAT99G8aq
— ITV News (@itvnews) October 23, 2026
During Friday’s hearing at Westminster Magistrates’ Court, Westwood indicated that he would plead not guilty to both charges, according to court officials cited by British media. He has already pleaded not guilty to the original 15 charges, including four counts of rape.
Among the earlier allegations is the rape of a woman in a hotel in 1996. Westwood is also accused of several indecent assaults on BBC premises during the 1990s, as well as sexual offenses at other locations in London and elsewhere in England.
Westwood was released on conditional bail and is due to appear at Southwark Crown Court on November 12. His trial on the original charges is scheduled to begin on January 25, 2027.
Westwood was one of Britain’s best-known hip-hop DJs, working for BBC Radio 1 and Radio 1Xtra between 1994 and 2013.
In February 2025, the BBC apologized after an independent investigation found evidence of bullying and misogynistic behavior by Westwood. The broadcaster admitted it had been “too deferential to high-profile individuals” and missed opportunities to address complaints about his conduct.
The case comes against the backdrop of a number of sexual abuse scandals involving prominent BBC personalities. Jimmy Savile, a former television and radio presenter, was accused of abusing hundreds of people, many of them children, over several decades. The allegations emerged publicly after his death in 2011, prompting investigations into how the broadcaster had handled complaints.
Other former BBC entertainers, including Stuart Hall and Rolf Harris, were convicted of sexual offenses involving underage girls and served prison sentences. In 2024, former BBC News presenter Huw Edwards received a six-month suspended prison sentence after pleading guilty to offenses involving indecent images of children.
The broadcaster faced further scrutiny in March 2026 when it dismissed prominent radio presenter Scott Mills following allegations about his conduct. The BBC later acknowledged that it had known about a previous police investigation into alleged sexual offenses involving a teenage boy. FCC Democrat warns broadcasters to resist Trump’s media pressure tactics
Democrat Anna Gomez warns broadcasters against yielding to Trump-era FCC’s claims of fake polls and news distortions.
Anna Gomez, the sole Democratic member of the United States Federal Communications Commission (FCC), called on the National Association of Broadcasters (NAB) to ramp up its response to pressure from the administration of US President Donald Trump on major news networks and broadcast television stations in advance of the midterm elections on November 3.
“I would not be doing my job if I did not say plainly that the volume of that response has not yet matched the scale of what your members are facing,” Gomez said in a four-page letter to the industry group’s CEO and President Curtis LeGeyt on Thursday.
Gomez pointed to a recent assertion by Trump-appointed Brenden Carr, who claimed that administration channels could violate their regulatory obligations by airing “entirely fake polls” before the consequential midterm elections, which may determine which political party controls both houses of the US Congress.
“Many journalists and broadcasters have been amplifying or airing these Polls without regard to basic journalistic ethics and without informing the public that those Polls lack a scientific, accurate, or even real basis,” Carr said in a post on the social media platform X.
Al Jazeera reached out to the FCC for clarity on which journalists and broadcasters allegedly aired fake polls and which polls he was referring to, but the agency did not address Al Jazeera’s inquiry.
Seth Stern, the chief of advocacy at the Freedom of the Press Foundation, criticised Carr’s comments.
“Brendan Carr is not the journalism police. And he is just about the least qualified person in the country to lecture the press about journalistic ethics. The tell is that literally every time he attacks the press, it’s because of reporting that was unfavorable to his boss,” Stern said in a statement.
Carr said in his social media post that “Broadcasters are advised to avoid engaging in News Distortions or running Broadcast Hoaxes”.
“This Administration is running a coordinated, government-wide effort to reshape the media into its sanctioned messenger, and the Federal Communications Commission has become one of its most active instruments. That is playing out across several fronts. One of the most brazen efforts involves how this Commission has recently suggested that broadcasters who air polling that does not align with this Administration’s preferred narrative could face an FCC news distortion or broadcast hoax investigation,” Gomez said in her letter.
Gomez added that there is a high barrier for proof of news distortion for it to be actionable, saying that it only applies when a broadcaster “knowingly airs false information about a crime or catastrophe and that broadcast directly causes immediate and substantial harm to public safety or property”.
Gomez added that the agency does not have the authority to act unless there is clear evidence.
“Reporting the results of a poll this Administration happens to dislike does not come close to meeting those standards,” Gomez said.

Time ‘running out’ to reach Yemen’s Taiz amid deepening crisis, UN says

Time ‘running out’ to reach Yemen’s Taiz amid deepening crisis, UN says
More than 800,000 people have been cut off from aid since the Houthis encircled Taiz city in early October.
A mounting humanitarian disaster is gripping Yemen’s Taiz after nearly three weeks of a Houthi siege that has prevented supplies from entering the city, the United Nations has warned.
The Iran-backed Houthis have encircled Taiz since early October, cutting off the road that links it to Aden, which serves as the interim capital of Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
Little fuel, food or other supplies have reached the city since.
“It’s 20 days and counting since Taiz has been cut off,” Jens Laerke, spokesperson for the UN’s humanitarian arm, OCHA, told a news conference in Geneva on Friday. “We are seeing increasingly that the fighting makes it impossible for us to get in and impossible for people to get out.”
Most people depend on water brought in by trucks, the cost of which has tripled, Laerke said. Cooking gas is also “largely unavailable”, threatening community kitchens that provide meals to families.
Altogether, more than 800,000 people in Taiz are cut off from aid, about three-quarters of whom depend on humanitarian assistance, according to the UN World Food Programme (WFP). At least 200,000 are women and children.
While local humanitarian groups have been able to distribute their remaining supplies to keep water pumps and hospitals running, Laerke said, “It comes with a time code: The clock is running out.”
‘Desperate’ for access
Fighting in Taiz province has intensified in recent days, with clashes reported in the Jabal Han highlands and the Dhubab and al-Masrakh districts.
Colonel Majid al-Nuzaili, a spokesperson for the forces of the internationally recognised government, said on Friday that troops had conducted raids and counterattacks in Taiz over the last 24 hours, “neutralising” 620 Houthi fighters and destroying 190 vehicles.
Al Jazeera could not independently verify the figures.
Hospitals in the province are meanwhile reporting critical shortages of fuel, oxygen, medicine and supplies. Forty-two Taiz facilities face “acute” deficits, the World Health Organization spokesman Christian Lindmeier said.
The fighting has also deepened an ongoing hunger crisis. In Taiz alone, UN screenings have found more than 52,000 children to have acute malnutrition; approximately 11,500 are suffering from severe acute malnutrition.
“We’re desperately trying to regain access to Taiz, and we continue to support the broader operations across Yemen,” said Azfar Deen, a WFP regional communications officer for eastern and Southern Africa.
In response to the humanitarian fallout, the European Commission said on Friday that it would release an additional 22.5 million euros ($25.2m) in aid to Yemen, adding to the 87.5 million ($97.9m) previously allocated for 2026.
Yemen has been rocked by conflict since the Houthis seized Sanaa and other provinces in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in 2015 to support the internationally recognised government.
A truce was brokered by the UN in 2022, but it fell apart this July, when the Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi ports.
The ensuing escalation has displaced nearly 260,000 people, the majority in Taiz and Lahij provinces, according to the UN. More than 3,800 people have also fled to neighbouring Djibouti.
At least 1,574 people have been killed and 6,939 others wounded in the conflict since August.

Costa Rica AG says new joint DEA ops will target politicians, businessmen
SAN JOSE, Oct 23 - Costa Rica will deepen cooperation with the US Drug Enforcement Administration to target what the nation's newly re-elected attorney general calls "invisible drug traffickers," including business executives and politicians hiding alleged links to the drug trade behind respectable public profiles.
Attorney General Carlo Diaz, who has repeatedly clashed with the government of President Laura Fernandez, was re-elected by the judiciary on Monday to another four-year term. In an interview with Reuters on Thursday, he said investigators would show no leniency if those implicated held senior positions.
"This second phase (of DEA cooperation) focuses on people we have termed 'invisible drug traffickers,'" Diaz said, after an initial phase of joint missions targeted members of criminal organizations.
"These are business people, sometimes professionals or politicians, who are successful or highly visible. But behind that facade lies a direct link with these kinds of activities."
Diaz also hailed Costa Rica's ability to extradite its own nationals to the US as a watershed in the fight against transnational crime, saying 6 people had been sent and another 25 extradition proceedings were underway.
The DEA's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Costa Rica's government has previously collaborated with the DEA to arrest dozens of drug traffickers, who Costa Rican authorities deem responsible for a surge in homicide rates over recent years in the long-peaceful Central American nation.
Officials have said the region serves as a key corridor shifting narcotics from South America to the US.
Fernandez, a conservative ally of President Donald Trump, has aligned Costa Rica closely with Washington on security, joining the US president’s Shield of the Americas initiative against drug trafficking and organized crime.
POLITICAL DIVISIONS
Diaz said DEA officials had directly expressed concern to him about political and institutional divisions in Costa Rica, which he said were hampering the fight against organized crime. He has repeatedly clashed with Fernandez and her predecessor Rodrigo Chaves, accusing the government of seeking to weaken the judiciary.
Despite backing deeper cooperation with the DEA, Diaz rejected Fernandez's suggestion last month that Costa Rica could benefit from US forces operating on its territory.
"If we focus on providing the resources the security forces need, they could take control of the territory without needing to bring in armed forces from other countries," he said.
Fernandez’s government has built a 5,100-capacity prison modeled on El Salvador’s security crackdown, an approach Diaz has questioned amid his broader clashes with the government. He said the prison could ease overcrowding but would not itself curb organized crime, stressing that Costa Rica’s criminal landscape differs sharply from El Salvador’s.
The homicide rate in Costa Rica, long considered one of the region's safest countries, peaked at 17.2 per 100,000 people in 2023, or 906 killings.
"This is one of the most complex moments in our history," Diaz said. "(The DEA) is well aware of the situation." REUTERS

What’s on Russia’s target list – and why?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:40:41 UTC
05:40:41 KST

What’s on Russia’s target list – and why?
The main theme of the Russia-Ukraine conflict this year has been the so-called ‘war of cities’, characterized by mutual strategic strikes on targets in the rear. In the first half of the year, Kiev had managed to bolster its strike capabilities and even attempted to pressure Moscow into accepting its terms for a ceasefire.
However, by fall, the situation shifted dramatically. Russia began deploying new jet-powered drones, such as Banderol and Geran-4/Geran-5 UAVs, and significantly increased the intensity of its ballistic strikes. Meanwhile, Ukraine has exhausted its stocks of Western-supplied interceptor missiles, and its own domestically produced air defense systems have proven ineffective against high-speed jet-powered UAVs and ballistic missiles.
The Ukrainian propaganda widely published by liberal media outlets portrays Russian attacks as indiscriminate and aimed at civilians. In this article, we strive to demonstrate that this is not the case.
We will examine the specific targets that Russia has struck in Ukraine’s rear, and the rationale behind these attacks. We’ll also take a look at the targets it deliberately avoids, along with measures taken to minimize risks to Ukrainian civilians.
Industrial enterprises
In the early years of the military operation, Russia targeted Ukraine’s defense industry facilities – both old Soviet plants like Yuzhmash in Dnepropetrovsk and new, smaller enterprises focused on drone assembly and munitions production.
In response, Ukraine began relocating and dispersing production to any available industrial facilities or even warehouses. This strategy was openly discussed in Ukrainian propaganda as a crucial element of resilience against Russian assaults.
As Russia increased its striking capabilities, it adopted a broader approach, targeting all industrial facilities based on a straightforward principle: if a facility can be used for drone assembly, it qualifies as a legitimate military target.
Ammunition depots
Soviet military doctrine emphasized storing ammunition in centralized depots far from residential areas. Munitions were kept in shelters designed in such a way that the destruction of one would not affect the others.
One of the largest such depots, the 65th Rocket and Artillery Arsenal in Balakleya, sustained damage from a series of explosions even before the military operation. Control over it was handed from one side to another multiple times. It still contains tens of thousands of tons of expired munitions, which have been repurposed for use in attack drones.
The situation mirrors that of the industrial sector. In order protect ammunition from airstrikes, it is moved out of the isolated weapons depots and hidden in any available facilities. Western missiles are transported from Poland to these locations as well.
The consequences of this approach are dire: an attack leads to the detonation of ammunition, gravely endangering the surrounding residential areas. On August 29, 2026, a strike on a warehouse operated by Fire Point in the village of Milaya resulted in the death of 38 civilians.
Logistics networks
Lacking a proper military supply system, the Ukrainian Armed Forces have relied on civilian infrastructure for military logistics since the ATO in Donbass in 2014-15. A key player in this strategy has been the courier service Novaya Pochta. This approach was touted as innovative – modern, cost-effective, and efficient – and gained traction not only in Ukraine but also in Russia.
However, there are two sides to every coin. From the start of the war, Russia has targeted Novaya Pochta warehouses, and in 2026, it began systematically destroying them. In addition to Novaya Pochta, major retail and marketplace chains like Epicentr and Rozetka also came under fire, followed by other logistics companies in Ukraine.
Russia’s reasoning is straightforward: if Ukraine employs civilian infrastructure for military purposes, then all such facilities become legitimate military targets.
Energy sector
Electricity forms the backbone of any support system. Without it, production halts, communication falters, and supplying the army becomes increasingly difficult. Based on this logic, since 2022, the Russian military has systematically targeted Ukraine’s electricity generation, reducing its capacity from 50-55 GW before the war to just 12-15 GW during the winter of 2025-26.
Simultaneously, energy consumption in Ukraine declined; heavy industry ground to a halt, rolling blackouts were implemented, and some consumers turned to autonomous power sources like generators. Consequently, Ukraine transformed from Europe’s largest electricity exporter to an importer.
At the core of Ukraine’s generation capacity are three nuclear power plants, which, for obvious reasons, remain untouched by Russian attacks. Instead, this fall, Russian forces have focused on electrical networks, targeting distribution substations and transmission lines. For example, one of the two power line crossings over the Dnieper River in Kiev was destroyed, significantly hampering power supplied not only to Kiev, but to the entire territory of eastern Ukraine.
Attacks on Combined Heat and Power (CHP) plants – which generate both electricity and heat – continue as well. The goal isn’t to freeze the residents of Kiev, but to dismantle Ukraine’s unified energy system, breaking it into isolated segments that can be dealt with individually.
Oil and gas industry
Before the war, Ukraine had only one operational oil refinery in Kremenchuk, which had been running at about 15% capacity since 2014. Since 2022, it has faced relentless attacks and has completely ceased operations. Now, Ukraine relies entirely on imported fuel.
Ukrainian gas production facilities across the country and in the Black Sea are regularly attacked. The latest attacks occurred on October 12 in Kharkov Region.
Another target is the underground gas storage facility in Stryi, located in western Ukraine. One of the largest such facilities in the world, it was part of a vast gas transportation system from Russia to Europe and is currently not used for its original purpose. This facility is a challenging target; while drone strikes can damage surface infrastructure (which is relatively easy to repair), even a nuclear explosion might not destroy the storage facility itself.
In the absence of better targets, this summer, Russia specifically targeted gas stations in both frontline areas and Kiev. The goal was to disrupt military logistics. Reports estimate that over 200 gas stations were destroyed nationwide during the summer months.
Data centers
Until this fall, Russia refrained from striking Ukrainian data centers. However, these facilities are as integral to military infrastructure as any other component; they facilitate troop command, communications, and logistics management. They support critical Ukrainian systems like Obereg and Rezerv+ recruitment centers, the electronic procurement platform Prozorro, and the Diia Unified State Web Portal of Electronic Services. Disrupting these systems would undoubtedly undermine Ukraine’s military operations.
In the past month, Russia has targeted various data centers, including Bi-Mobile in Kiev, De Novo Data Center, NewTelco, United DC, as well as Kievstar, Parkovy, and Vodafone telecommunications centers.
Despite these disruptions, the unified digital environment of Ukraine remains largely intact. In response, the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) struck several Yandex data centers in Russia.
In this ‘war of cities’, the fate of data centers and the resilience of communication networks are being monitored particularly closely worldwide, with many countries considering the security of their own networks.
Ports and maritime traffic
Up until this year, Russia had largely turned a blind eye to Ukraine’s maritime trade. Despite intermittent attacks on warehouses, the Black Sea ports in Odessa, Illichevsk, and the Danube ports of Izmail and Reni continued their operations, exporting local grain and metal while importing fuel, heavy machinery, and, of course, weapons.
However, in the spring and summer of this year, Ukrainian naval and aerial drones systematically began targeting Russian maritime traffic in the Black Sea, striking everything from tankers to bulk carriers laden with grain. In retaliation, Russia quickly imposed a complete maritime blockade on Ukraine, implementing it in its most severe form – attacks were directed not only at the ports but also at commercial vessels approaching or leaving them.
From a legal standpoint, all commercial vessels capable of transporting weapons or troops are considered by Russia as legitimate military targets. The same universal logic applies here – if a ship can carry weapons, it is a target.
These strikes have been incredibly painful for Ukraine. Without the ability to export goods over land, the country has effectively lost crucial revenue streams and one of its last remaining sources of budgetary funding. Additionally, there have been disruptions in the supply of transformers, fuel, and, according to certain reports, heavy weaponry – all of which were transported by sea.
According to several experts, this maritime blockade threatens to cost Ukraine up to 10% of its GDP.
Other targets
In addition to the aforementioned categories, Russia is attacking a wide range of military and dual-use targets.
Locomotives: Since the start of the Russia's military operation, over 300 mainline diesel and electric locomotives have been rendered inoperable. With the number of remaining working locomotives decreasing, the transportation capacity of the railways is nearing exhaustion. Both railway depots and trains are being attacked.
Trucks: The AFU takes pride in how they’ve adapted civilian trucks for launching long-range drones. However, this makes any cargo truck a legitimate military target for Russia and has led to the destruction of dozens of such launch platforms, which are tracked through intelligence efforts.
Bridges: Major bridges are undoubtedly attractive strategic targets, but they are also difficult to destroy. There are currently 22 crossings over the Dnieper River, and none have yet been destroyed by long-range strikes. In the past month, there have been multiple attacks on bridges in Kiev, but so far, they continue to operate.
Land border crossings with Poland, Slovakia, Hungary, and Romania are another bottleneck in Ukraine’s transportation logistics. To safeguard the border crossings from ongoing attacks, the authorities have begun relocating them entirely to neighboring territories.
Lastly, there are a few specific targets mentioned in intelligence reports. For example, on July 24, Russian forces bombed a weapons exhibition near Kiev attended by prominent figures from Ukraine’s defense sector.
What targets doesn’t Russia strike?
Russia has refrained from targeting civilian and humanitarian facilities such as residential buildings, hospitals, and schools. Hits on these types of structures are often due to the operation of air defense systems. The structures are sometimes struck by debris from intercepted missiles and drones, or even accidentally struck by interceptor missiles. Russian officials maintain that the strike on the Okhmatdet hospital in Kiev on July 12, 2024, was caused by an interceptor missile launched from the Norwegian-supplied NASAMS system.
Water supply and sewage facilities are not attacked by Russian forces. Throughout the conflict, there have been no recorded strikes on this critical infrastructure. However, during attacks on Kiev and other major cities, water outages frequently occur, indicating that backup generators at vital infrastructure sites are not operational.
As previously noted, Ukrainian nuclear power plants – including the three functional ones and the decommissioned Chernobyl facility – have not been targeted. Nevertheless, in February 2025, a downed drone landed on the sarcophagus of Chernobyl’s Reactor 4.
Observers are particularly surprised by the immunity of the government district in Kiev, leading to jokes about it being the safest place in Ukraine. This could suggest some kind of behind-the-scenes agreements.
Overall, even Ukrainian and Western analysts acknowledge that Russia continually enhances the accuracy of its strikes while improving its management, guidance, and navigation systems. Russia has established a communication network for drones using mesh networks and has developed and implemented the Susanin optical navigation system, which provides 1-meter strike accuracy even in conditions of heavy electronic interference.
If Russia’s ultimate goal were to terrorize the civilian population, there would be no need to develop such complex and expensive systems. It could simply fire indiscriminately at Kiev. But with such an approach, there would’ve been tens of thousands of civilian casualties – one may consider the example of Gaza.
Currently, in Kiev, as well as in other rear cities across Ukraine, estimates indicate that up to 95% of residents disregard air raid warnings and remain above ground during alerts. Moreover, local authorities have eased air raid protocols to keep the city functioning.

A modem from a Russian drone led reporters to its Chinese maker—which invoiced 500 for Russia’s drone plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:38:37 UTC
05:38:37 KST

Undercover reporters ordered 500 drone mesh modems from a Chinese firm, which billed them to Russia’s Alabuga drone plant, investigation by The Insider found. The outlet estimates the firm makes about half the high-power mesh modems that let Russia steer its drones deep into Ukraine. The firm’s director also named US company AMD as the source of a key chip, and AMD says it has not sold to the firm.
Geran drones and Banderol drone-missiles have become Russia’s main weapons against Ukraine’s energy grid. Russia began this winter’s strike campaign against that grid in late September, ISW assessed. Ukrainians’ survival this winter depends largely on how fast the West halts mesh modem sales to Russia, the outlet argued.
What a mesh modem does
A mesh modem links drones into one radio network. Each unit relays data for the others, so if one drone is shot down, traffic reroutes through the rest. Information keeps flowing even if nearly 80% of the drones are downed, Ukrainian defense adviser Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov said in November 2025.
Range is the other half of the threat. One XK F-359 holds a line-of-sight link over 100–300 km, The Insider says. In theory, a couple of relay drones could keep a whole attack on Kyiv connected. Operators can then send new commands in flight and steer around air defenses. Russia’s Gerbera drones, first built as cheap decoys, increasingly carry these modems.
A modem from an upgraded Gerbera
To trace the part, The Insider’s correspondent in Ukraine examined an unmarked mesh modem from an upgraded Gerbera with a vertical tail fin, a version that appeared this summer. The outlet identified it as Xingkai’s XK F-359, the part Ukrainian intelligence and earlier reporting, Euromaidan Press included, had logged as the XK-F358. The Insider calls that label a misidentification.
Next, The Insider and the Nordsint investigative project contacted Xingkai on WeChat, posing as a Russian military supplier based in Alabuga. A company employee who introduced himself as “Jack Jiang” confirmed the firm is the model’s sole maker. The Insider identified him as Jiang Qin, Xingkai’s director and owner.
500 modems, three banks
The reporters then ordered 500 units for delivery to Alabuga, home to the plant that makes most of Russia’s long-range drones. Jiang invoiced 19.5 million yuan, which The Insider put at about $2.87 million. He offered two ways to pay: dollars to Xingkai’s DBS Bank account in Hong Kong, or yuan to his personal Ping An Bank account.
America has sided with Russia against Ukraine. Europe should stop pretending and build a coalition against Russia, China, and even the US
In the chat, the reporters said outright that the end user was a military production facility. Jiang raised no objection, The Insider reported.
Later, after the reporters asked to update the address, Xingkai sent a revised invoice with “Alabuga” spelled in Latin letters. This time, it routed payment to a China Merchants Bank account in the name of a former Xingkai manager. She left a management post at the company in 2025, according to Tesari corporate records cited by The Insider. None of the three banks answered The Insider’s requests for comment.
Jiang also claimed the modem’s programmable chip is made by AMD. Asked for an AMD license, he refused, saying Xingkai buys the chips through a middleman. AMD told The Insider that Xingkai “is not an AMD customer or authorized partner,” and said it had sold the company nothing. AMD added that it bars exports of its products to Russia that violate US export controls and sanctions.

Why is Trump questioning Ilhan Omar’s name?

Why is Trump questioning Ilhan Omar’s name?
A Justice Department filing listed a different name for her, prompting Trump to call for her resignation.
United States President Donald Trump has called for Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar to resign from the US Congress, reviving allegations of identity fraud after a court filing identified the Minnesota politician by an additional name.
The DOJ filing, submitted on Wednesday, refers to Omar as “Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar” – “a/k/a” is an abbreviation for “also known as”.
The document filed by the administration does not establish that Omar committed fraud.
In response to allegations that Ilhan Omar is not her real name, the lawmaker posted on X, “So let’s make it crystal clear. My name has always been Ilhan Omar”.
The controversy follows a federal investigation into Omar’s immigration history and a search of her Washington, DC, home on October 12.
Omar has said she plans to move out of the home, citing safety concerns.
Here is how it all unfolded.
October 12: Federal agents search Omar’s home
Federal agents searched Omar’s Washington, DC, residence under a “judicially authorised search warrant” as part of an ongoing criminal investigation. It reportedly concerns allegations that Omar or her late father provided false information on immigration paperwork when the family fled Somalia and came to the United States in 1995, when she was a child. Omar has denied wrongdoing and described the search as political intimidation.
October 15: Requests to unseal court records
Judicial Watch and The New York Times, alongside 14 other press organisations, filed applications in the US District Court for the District of Columbia seeking access to sealed records related to the search warrant. Judicial Watch said it wanted the warrant, supporting affidavits and an inventory of seized materials made public.
October 21: Justice Department filing identifies Omar by another name
In a motion seeking additional time to respond to the requests for records, the Justice Department referred to the congresswoman as “Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar”.
The filing did not explain the relationship between the names. Instead, prosecutors asked the court to delay their response until after they fully executed the search warrant. The government said it would submit a status report within 30 days of completing the search.
October 22: Name allegations become public, Trump calls for resignation
Fox News Digital cited the court filing and reported that unnamed sources said that Omar’s birth name was Ilhan Nur Said Elmi. The article prompted renewed speculation about her name and longstanding rumours concerning her 2009 marriage to Ahmed Nur Said Elmi. Some have claimed he is Omar’s brother, an allegation she has repeatedly denied.
President Trump publicly escalated his attacks on Omar, calling for her resignation as the name controversy spread. He has presented the alternative name listed in the court filing as evidence of fraud, even though the filing makes no such finding and she has not been charged with any criminal offences.
October 23: Representative Omar responds
A spokesperson for Omar told Al Jazeera in a statement: “The Congresswoman’s name has always been Ilhan Omar. Any indication otherwise is flat out false”.
Omar also rejected the allegations in a post on X, accusing Trump of promoting conspiracy theories through the Justice Department.
“Whenever the news turns bad, this creep reaches for one name: mine. So let’s make it crystal clear. My name has always been Ilhan Omar,” she added, before telling Trump to focus on “what your VP’s real name is”.
Muslim American candidates face attacks over their names
In an interview with MS NOW’s Chris Hayes, Omar argued that the attacks were intended to drive her out of Congress, saying her critics believed someone of her background and faith “shouldn’t be in Congress” or hold a position influencing US law.
“I have a legal right to be a member of Congress, and I am honoured,” she said.
The scrutiny of Omar’s name comes amid a wider wave of attacks on Muslim American politicians, including Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for the US Senate in Michigan.
In an interview with Al Jazeera on Thursday, a Michigan voter questioned why El-Sayed does not use his “real name”, seemingly referring to his full name.
“Abdul’s barely out there. He doesn’t even say his real name. Like, why can’t you share your real name?” the voter said. When asked if she knew the full name of El-Sayed’s Republican opponent Mike Rogers, she said, “Mohamed’s not his middle name”.
El-Sayed, whose full name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, has faced attacks on his Arab heritage and Muslim faith during his Senate campaign. Trump has mocked his name and called him a “jihadist”. Trump also said at a rally that he could call El-Sayed “Mohammed”, adding that he could call him “whatever the hell I want”.
