The new Arab bargain: When Egypt offers to protect Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:33:46 UTC
05:33:46 KST

When Egyptian officials signalled their readiness to support Saudi Arabia against attacks by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis, the announcement was presented as a familiar display of Arab solidarity. Yet beneath the diplomatic rhetoric lies a much more significant story, one that says less about military cooperation and more about the changing balance of power in the Middle East.
The immediate question appears straightforward: What kind of protection can Egypt realistically offer Saudi Arabia?
The more important question is whether Egypt’s offer reveals that the traditional hierarchy of the Arab world has been quietly reversed.
For decades, Egypt occupied a unique position in Arab politics. It was the state that projected military weight, diplomatic influence, and cultural authority across the region. Saudi Arabia possessed financial power, but Cairo was widely regarded as the Arab world’s strategic center of gravity.
Today, however, the relationship between the two countries is increasingly defined by a different reality. Egypt remains demographically and militarily significant, but its economic fragility has created a level of dependence on Gulf stability that would have been almost unimaginable in previous generations.
The offer to help defend Saudi Arabia therefore deserves to be viewed not as a demonstration of Egyptian strength, but as evidence of a broader geopolitical transformation.
Military realities explain why.
Despite possessing one of the Arab world’s largest armed forces, Egypt is neither politically nor economically positioned to undertake a large-scale military intervention in Yemen.
The trauma of Gamal Abdel Nasser’s disastrous Yemen campaign in the 1960s remains deeply embedded in Egyptian strategic thinking. That conflict consumed enormous military resources, cost thousands of lives, and distracted Cairo from more immediate national priorities.
No Egyptian leadership is likely to repeat that experience.
Moreover, Egypt today faces a crowded security agenda closer to home. Instability in Sudan, uncertainty in Libya, tensions in the Red Sea, challenges in Sinai, and concerns surrounding the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam all compete for Cairo’s attention. Under such circumstances, the prospect of deploying large numbers of Egyptian troops into another protracted Yemeni conflict appears highly improbable.
If Egypt contributes militarily, its role will likely be concentrated in the maritime domain: securing sea lanes, protecting Red Sea navigation routes, enhancing intelligence cooperation, and supporting regional deterrence efforts. These are meaningful contributions, but they fall far short of the image invoked by traditional narratives of Arab military intervention.
This is where the deeper story emerges.
The Houthis are not merely threatening Saudi Arabia. They are threatening Egypt’s economic lifeline.
The disruption of shipping through the Bab al-Mandab Strait has severely affected traffic through the Suez Canal, one of Egypt’s most important sources of foreign currency. Every escalation in the Red Sea directly translates into economic pressure on Cairo.
In practical terms, Egypt’s interest in stabilizing the Gulf and confronting threats to regional navigation is not an act of altruism; it is an act of economic self-preservation.
That should not be surprising.
States do not mobilize because of gratitude. They mobilize because of interests.
Yet Middle Eastern political discourse still tends to frame relations between Arab states through the language of fraternity, loyalty, and historical obligation. Such language often obscures what is actually taking place. Egypt’s support for Saudi Arabia is driven not by sentiment but by a recognition that Egyptian prosperity is increasingly linked to Gulf stability.
The irony is striking.
For much of the twentieth century, wealthy Arab states depended upon Egypt as a source of political legitimacy, military expertise, and strategic backing. Today, Egypt’s own economic stability has become intertwined with Gulf investment, Gulf aid, and Gulf confidence.
This is not a temporary fluctuation. It reflects a structural shift in how power operates within the Arab world.
The rise of Gulf sovereign wealth funds, ambitious development strategies, and expanding regional investment networks has altered the traditional equation. Political influence is no longer derived primarily from military manpower or ideological leadership. It increasingly flows from economic resilience, investment capacity, and the ability to shape regional outcomes through finance.
Under this new reality, Saudi Arabia has become not merely an oil producer or regional actor, but one of the principal anchors of economic stability across significant parts of the Arab world.
Seen from this perspective, another apparent contradiction suddenly becomes easier to understand.
While expressing support for Saudi Arabia, Egypt also maintains diplomatic communication with Iran. To some observers, this appears inconsistent. Why would Cairo coordinate with Riyadh while simultaneously engaging Tehran?
The answer lies in the changing nature of Middle Eastern politics.
The region no longer operates according to the rigid bloc politics that defined much of the past decade. Saudi Arabia itself has restored relations with Iran. The United Arab Emirates maintains extensive economic links with Tehran. Across the region, governments increasingly seek to combine deterrence with dialogue rather than choose between them.
Egypt’s communication with Iran therefore reflects a wider regional trend: reducing the risk of escalation while maintaining strategic alignments. Cairo has little interest in becoming a frontline participant in a broader regional confrontation. Its primary objective is stability, particularly in waterways and trade corridors that directly affect its economic survival.
This calculation exposes a larger truth about the contemporary Middle East.
The old question, “Who protects whom?” may no longer make sense.
Saudi Arabia does not require Egyptian divisions stationed on the Yemeni front to guarantee its security. Equally, Egypt cannot sustain its economic stability without a relatively secure Gulf environment. What has emerged instead is a relationship of mutual dependence, in which military capability and economic power reinforce one another.
The traditional image of Egypt as the Arab world’s protector and Saudi Arabia as its financier belongs increasingly to another era.
A new bargain is taking shape.
Egypt remains too important to be ignored. Saudi Arabia remains too influential to be separated from broader Arab stability. Yet neither country occupies the role it once held. The balance has become more symmetrical, more transactional, and arguably more honest.
That is why Egypt’s offer to defend Saudi Arabia matters.
Not because it signals the beginning of a new war, but because it reveals the emergence of a new Arab order. An order in which economics has become as important as armies, investment as influential as ideology, and mutual dependence more decisive than old narratives of leadership.
The real significance of Cairo’s offer is therefore not military at all.
It is historical.
For the first time in modern Arab politics, the region’s traditional center of political gravity is openly acknowledging that its own security and prosperity are inseparable from the stability of the Gulf. And in that admission lies one of the most consequential geopolitical shifts the Arab world has witnessed since the end of the Cold War.
The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Monitor.

Ukraine’s Battlefield Lessons Reshape How Bundeswehr Trains Its Combat Medics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:33:00 UTC
05:33:00 KST

Germany’s armed forces are overhauling the way they train their combat medics, evacuate casualties and protect field hospitals, after closely studying Ukraine’s experience in treating soldiers wounded in a war now dominated by drones.
The changes follow a September visit by Surgeon General Ralf Hoffmann, commander of the Bundeswehr’s Central Medical Service, and a team of specialists to Kyiv and to Dnipro, a city in southeastern Ukraine roughly 60 to 75 miles (100 to 120 kilometers) from the active frontlines.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to a report published Monday, Oct. 19 on the Bundeswehr’s official website, Ukrainian figures reportedly shared with the delegation show that drones now cause roughly 90% of combat injuries among Ukrainian soldiers.
The Ukrainian doctors also told the delegation that about 100,000 military personnel have undergone amputations since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Wounds above the body armor
Ukrainian medics described a front line where close-quarters fighting has become increasingly rare. Surveillance and strike drones cover a zone stretching about 25 kilometers (15 miles) behind the line of contact, making any movement in that area extremely dangerous.
The type of wounds has shifted accordingly.
According to the Bundeswehr’s report, drones that drop grenades or detonate on impact tend to strike soldiers from above and in front, with the blast often hitting areas left exposed by body armor.
Oleshky Evacuation: Russia Announces Kherson Frontline ‘Silence Regime’
Ukrainian doctors reported a high number of severe wounds to the face, neck, arms and hands, saying that eye injuries now make up a large share of upper-body trauma. Protective eyewear, they noted, is rarely worn in Ukrainian military units.
The German delegation concluded that personal protective equipment needs to be reassessed with these new patterns in mind.
Medical facilities moved underground
Due to the constant threat of strikes, Ukraine’s Defense Forces have moved some frontline medical facilities underground.
These include Role 1 facilities, where wounded soldiers are first stabilized, and Role 2 facilities, where surgeons perform emergency operations to save lives before patients are transferred to other medical institutions.
In a war where drones can spot and strike almost anything above ground, a visible aid station has itself become a target.
According to Ukrainian accounts cited in the report, one of the buried medical facilities in the Zaporizhzhia region was hit by 10 glide bombs without a single member of its staff being injured.
The German medical service is now examining how to build and run such treatment facilities, hidden and protected under a persistent drone threat.
Following the trip, Hoffmann announced closer cooperation with the Special Engineer Regiment 164, a specialized unit under the Bundeswehr’s Logistics Command based in Husum, whose heavy equipment could be used to dig in field hospitals quickly and test new procedures.
The threat is no longer theoretical for Germany.
On Wednesday, Oct. 21 Germany’s armed forces raised the Russian sabotage threat to “significant,” the second-highest level on its internal scale, after an explosives-laden drone was found near Wunstorf air base in Lower Saxony mid-September.
Increased hybrid warfare tactics from Moscow prompted Berlin to strengthen its protective measures.
Up to 12 hours between injury and surgery
Because of the dangers a ground evacuation under drone surveillance poses, it can take up to 12 hours before a wounded Ukrainian soldier reaches a medical facility.
According to the report, Ukrainian doctors told the German delegation that these delays are a major reason for the high number of amputations.
A tourniquet applied on the battlefield can quickly stop bleeding and save a soldier’s life, but if surgery does not follow quickly, the limb often cannot be saved.
The long wait has also made the first hours of care far more important, with soldiers and frontline medics now responsible for keeping severely wounded comrades alive for much longer than military medical doctrine traditionally assumed.
To limit long-term damage, Ukraine has moved specialists, including eye surgeons and ear, nose and throat doctors, unusually close to the frontline. Early treatment of facial and eye injuries, which are now common in drone attacks, significantly improves soldiers’ chances of recovery.
Because of this, the Bundeswehr is now testing both ground and aerial drones for medical use.
A first drone sub-unit is being trialed by Medical Regiment 3 in Dornstadt, and Hoffmann said medics will need to learn to operate a range of unmanned systems, potentially including drones that deliver blood supplies.
Ukraine is applying the same approach. On Oct. 16, the government approved a pilot project to deliver medicine, medical devices, blood samples and donor organs between hospitals through drones, aiming to make deliveries significantly faster, particularly to remote areas.
The Health Ministry’s Heart Institute in Kyiv will serve as the first site of the pilot and it already operates three specialized drones capable of flying up to 700 kilometers (435 miles) and landing at hospital sites.
Reshaping German training
The Bundeswehr said it has already substantially reworked its first-aid and medic courses based on lessons from Ukraine.
New programs, including Combat Life Saver, Combat Paramedic and Combat Physician courses, are designed to prepare frontline troops to keep severely wounded comrades alive for longer before professional medical teams can take over.
The courses are being rolled out this year, with the aim of eventually training the entire force.
The German medical service said it has worked closely with Ukraine’s Defense Forces for years and plans to deepen the cooperation, covering surgical care, medical logistics, training, drone use and digitization.

The best books from Meduza’s publishing house, according to the people who work here
In the three years since Meduza launched its publishing house, we’ve published more than 30 books in Russian. Now, when people ask which we recommend, we have to ask a few questions: Fiction or nonfiction? Or perhaps diaries or autofiction? And on what subject? War, history, politics, film, music, parenting? Yes, we have all of that, and we’re very proud of it. Choosing just one is getting harder. But we gave it a try — and asked our colleagues to write a few sentences about their favorite book from Meduza’s publishing house. Save the list or buy the books as gifts for people you love. Every recommendation here comes straight from the heart.
Galina Timchenko, publisher
Anton Dolin, “Plokhiye russkiye” (“Bad Russians”)
Reading books because it’s all “work — deadlines — got to get it done…” really isn’t as much fun as choosing a book yourself. There’s a story we tell in the newsroom about “Bad Russians”: After the first edit, the manuscript grew by 300,000 characters. And yes, it’s an enormous book, but I found “Bad Russians” as gripping as a detective novel. I even rewatched some of the films I thought I remembered down to the last frame. It was a rare weekend when nothing could get me off the couch. Anton’s extraordinary gift for storytelling is matched by his expertise. I think this is his best book, though he’d surely pick a different one (he’s published 15 already).
Ivan Kolpakov, Meduza’s editor-in-chief
Sergei Lebedev, “Belaya dama” (“The Lady of the Mine”)
Meduza’s publishing house has been around for three years now, and this is still one of my favorite books we’ve published — definitely my favorite work of fiction. The blurb opens with “July 2014, Donbas,” so you might immediately form all kinds of ideas about this book. But unless you already know something about it, I’m sure you won’t guess what it’s like. Anyway, I want to declare my love for this book and its author. Thank you, dear Sergei Lebedev. And to anyone who somehow hasn’t heard of it, I recommend buying it right away.
A. Z., publishing editor
Lana Estemirova, “Pozhaluysta, zhivi” (“Please Live”)
“It mattered to me that this book could be read by a housewife in Ohio, a girl in Germany interested in strong women, and people in Russia who know nothing about Chechnya,” Lana Estemirova says of “Please Live.” For me, the way this book speaks to everyone is perhaps its greatest strength. It brings together hazy childhood memories and wartime chronicles; family stories about how her grandfather survived deportation in 1944 and human rights reports on war crimes in the 1990s; and teenage experiences captured in emails and diaries alongside newspaper articles about the rise of authoritarianism in Chechnya in the 2000s.
The book isn’t detailed enough to be called a biography, isn’t objective enough to claim to be a historical study of Chechnya, and is too painfully true to count as autofiction. But somehow, magically, it weaves together the best of all three genres — more than three, really. A documentary account becomes a sweeping novel about growing up, loss, working through grief, and an immense, incredibly powerful maternal love that even death cannot defeat.
Without false modesty, and with enormous gratitude to the translator who worked under a pseudonym, I’ll say that “Please Live” is equally good in English and Russian.
Dmitry Ivanov, publishing editor
Konstantin Gaaze, “Kuda dreyfuyut diktatury?” (“Where Do Dictatorships Drift?”)
Over these three years, I’ve read quite a few books (and even edited some) devoted to the same question: How did we end up here? Why did Russia attack Ukraine, disregarding the views of its own people, the judgment of the international community, and, finally, historical memory? Different authors offered different answers, but perhaps no one has examined the problem as deeply and systematically as Konstantin Gaaze in “Where Do Dictatorships Drift?” His account doesn’t start in the era of Peter the Great or with Ukraine’s Maidan protests. He aims to show that the current outbreak of Russian aggression was neither predetermined by some historical trajectory nor solely a response to the other side’s actions, as Vladimir Putin’s favorite refrain — “we were left with no choice” — would have it.
Konstantin reconstructs the basic logic of autocracy from Herodotus to the present to show that the Kremlin’s stance toward the West developed along the fairly common “besieged fortress” model. Ukraine became the target of the attack through a whole series of steps taken by Vladimir Putin and his inner circle beginning in 2008. Those steps pulled in different directions and were sometimes independent of one another. Readers will learn how an autocrat’s fears prompt his inner circle to peddle threats, where the “Putin majority” came from and what sustains it, why liberal economists and administrators lost their strategic struggle with officials from the security services and law enforcement, and, finally, how the 2008–09 global financial crisis relates to Putin’s conviction that America could no longer tell him what to do. Where do dictatorships drift? Konstantin Gaaze’s answer: often toward a major war, though with whom and on what terms depends on the particular historical circumstances.
Hi, I’m Vladislav Gorin.
I’m the host of Meduza’s daily Russian-language news podcast. This summer, the Russian authorities opened a criminal case against me — not for committing a crime, but for telling the truth about Russia and its war against Ukraine.
Because the Kremlin has branded me a criminal, I can’t go home. I also can’t safely travel to countries like Turkey — even though it’s a NATO member — because I could be arrested and extradited to Russia. I can’t even renew my passport at the consulate anymore.
None of this is going to stop me. I know there are hundreds of thousands of people in Russia who don’t want this war and who still believe in freedom and democracy, and they deserve access to independent journalism. Please support Meduza so I can keep reaching them.
Sonya, publishing manager
Konstantin Zarubin, “Nashe serdtse byotsya za vsekh” (“Our Heart Beats for Everyone”)
Some books create worlds that, for some inexplicable reason, lodge in your head for good. You’ll be standing in the checkout line at the supermarket, lost in thought, and suddenly find yourself somewhere far, far away without even noticing. Konstantin Zarubin’s novel is one of the books I “jump” into like that. A Selecta cappuccino from a coffee machine in the gray corridors of Iceland’s immigration office, a commuter train car baked by the summer sun on the Riga–Saulkrasti line, the summer cottage community of Medvedkovo, and an awkward portrait drawn in crayon from a VKontakte photo — I remember every house, every street, and every name in “Our Heart.”
I’m mesmerized by this broken, complicated world, so indifferent to the people who live in it. Absolutely anything can happen there — bad or good. I think it’s this unpredictability (sometimes quite cruel), with all its “chance” coincidences and encounters, that puts our humanity to the test and makes life what it is.
Quoting a review, Zarubin calls his novel “a decent light read.” I think that’s an understatement. “Our Heart” is certainly written with a light touch and plenty of wit, and it’s a pleasure to read. But I don’t think just “a light read” (even a decent one) can get so deep inside your head.
Natasha, manager of Meduza’s Magaz shop
Zhenya Berezhnaya, ”(Ne) o voyne” (”(Not) About War”)
”(Not) About War” is a book about the very first days of the full-scale war and being forced to leave. At first, you tense up with anxiety as you read the especially difficult passages. Then, page by page, you begin to relax. By the end, the heaviness gives way to hope: Everything will be all right.
And yet the war never goes away. It’s there the whole time, but even in a world like this, there’s still room for a miracle. I think that’s what the book is about.
The writing helps, too. Before the war, Zhenya Berezhnaya wrote fairy tales, and you can hear echoes of that in the novel: It’s a painful autobiographical story told in wonderfully warm, inviting language.
The book’s design deserves a mention of its own: Yellow symbols are scattered across a green background — they could be spiky anti-tank obstacles or little flowers with petals. Just like the book itself, where a miracle grows alongside the war.
I’m not the only one who liked it: The novel was shortlisted for the Dar literary prize.
Olya V., publishing staff member
Maria Alyokhina, “Politicheskaya. Kak vyzhit v iz Rossii” (“Political Girl: Life and Fate in Russia”)
I didn’t think I’d like Maria Alyokhina’s “Political Girl: Life and Fate in Russia.” But I was wrong. This book is a candid, dramatic diary that never slips into melodrama. Alyokhina feels injustice acutely, and even in the most difficult situations, she doesn’t let hurt and fear get the better of her.
“We don’t choose where we’re born. We don’t choose the color or the lettering on our passports. But we do choose how we live,” Maria writes. The book is her account of that choice. Perhaps “A Political Prisoner” will give you hope and strength — so many people are short of both in these dark days.
And — most importantly — Punkʼs not dead!
Alexander Polivanov, deputy editor-in-chief
Ilya Barabanov and Denis Korotkov, “Nash biznes — smert” (“Our Business Is Death”)
I read Ilya Barabanov and Denis Korotkov’s book about the Wagner private military company roughly two years after Yevgeny Prigozhin’s mutiny and his death. I thought I’d give up halfway through — I mean, what could it tell me about Prigozhin that journalists (including Barabanov and Korotkov themselves) hadn’t already reported?
But “Our Business Is Death” is a book you race through; some of the events feel as if you’re learning about them for the first time. Partly because as soon as something drops out of the news, you forget the details, the things that made it distinctive fade, and all that’s left is a few lines on Wikipedia. From where we stand in 2025–26, Prigozhin’s mutiny seems unimaginable, while his methods of managing people and waging war have, sadly, become commonplace.
A. F., news editor
Sergei Lebedev, “The White Lady” (and more!)
Much of today’s Russian-language publishing abroad focuses on political and social commentary and nonfiction, and that makes sense. It’s really great that Meduza’s publishing house also pays such close attention to contemporary fiction and discovers talented Russian-language authors. Konstantin Zarubin and his novel “Our Heart Beats for Everyone” deserve special mention — it’s a gripping cyberpunk utopia that is, horrifyingly, coming true almost to the letter. Or there’s Natalia Krupenina’s moving young adult book “Ya umeyu padat” (“I Know How to Fall”), a healing balm and a lifeline for teenagers (and adults, too!) in difficult times.
But for now, my top pick is “The Lady of the Mine.”
One setting: a mining settlement in the Donbas. Four characters: Zhanna, Valet, the general, and the engineer. Just five chapters: five days in the summer of 2014. Sergei Lebedev’s novel is compact and full of substance, fewer than 200 pages, but its seemingly simple, self-contained plot quickly expands into a tragedy of universal proportions. The author builds his narrative around the real history of this ill-fated Ukrainian region, closely intertwining events from the current war and a past one: Malaysia Airlines Flight MH17, shot down by pro-Kremlin separatists, and a mine pit that the Nazi occupiers used for executions. The historical parallels really are chilling. It takes your breath away, as great literature does.
P.S. If you do prefer commentary and want more facts about this story, I recommend pairing Lebedev’s novel with “Dom na linii ognya” (“A House in the Line of Fire”), journalist Dmitry Durnev’s true account of the contemporary Donbas.
Katya Abramova, head of communications
Sergei Lebedev, “The Lady of the Mine”
Of course I knew about Sergei’s book: We’d discussed it at work meetings, planned the release, promotional materials, and so on. But I wasn’t in a hurry to read it — I just didn’t have the strength to read any more about war and the Holocaust. Then things didn’t go as planned: My colleagues at the publishing house asked me to help sell books at Sergei’s book event at Berlin’s Panda platforma. I agreed, though without much enthusiasm — it was a Saturday evening. And then… I was spellbound! It was an amazing, fascinating, nuanced discussion that gave me strength without leaving me feeling crushed at all. Despite the difficult subject. I went home and had finished the book by Monday. Now I recommend it to everyone.

Zelensky: Russia waging hybrid war against Europe to undermine aid to Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:31:00 UTC

Zelensky: Russia waging hybrid war against Europe to undermine aid to Ukraine
He made these remarks on Friday during an online address at the Hudson Institute in Washington, according to a Ukrinform correspondent on the ground.
“Russia has launched hybrid attacks not only against Ukraine. We’re talking about the former Soviet republics, which are now independent states. And not just them. Drone attacks have already taken place against Romania, Germany, Poland, Moldova, and Bulgaria. And just today, they attacked Romania in the Black Sea. They completely destroyed a ship carrying agricultural products,” Zelensky said.
According to him, Russia will use drones as a tool for hybrid attacks and to exert pressure on Europe, and will also attempt to block the Black Sea and attack ships carrying agricultural products and energy resources.
“I think the Russians’ goal is to exert as much pressure on Europe as possible. They hope this will influence European societies and force Europeans to reconsider how to reduce their support for Ukraine and how to protect themselves,” the President noted.
He added that Moscow is trying to divide the European Union and weaken support for Ukraine by threatening European countries with cyberattacks, hybrid attacks, and drone strikes.
Zelensky also stated that Russia plans to mobilize an additional 300,000 troops. Ukraine will prepare for possible challenges, although it is not yet known what portion of these forces Moscow will use against Ukraine.
The head of state explained that some European countries still do not fully grasp the danger posed by Russia, as they believe that war may threaten Ukraine and Europe’s eastern flank, but not themselves.
“It’s hard to believe that war could come to your home, to your family, until it actually happens. It’s hard to believe that war could come to your country, your city, to your home,” Zelensky said.
He noted that some countries, while supporting Ukraine, are at the same time trying first and foremost to strengthen their own defenses, in particular by acquiring systems to intercept missiles and drones.
However, according to the President, European countries will not be able to effectively defend themselves against Russia on their own if Ukraine fails to hold its defenses.
“If they break through our defensive lines, if our country falls, no one will be able to defend themselves on their own. It is very difficult to defend against a country that is ready for anything, that is ready to kill ordinary people, civilians, using missiles, drones, and any other means,” Zelensky emphasized.
He stressed that Ukraine must become an important component of NATO’s and Europe’s security system.
The president also warned against attempts to reach an agreement with Russia through diplomatic means alone, noting that Moscow will attack if it senses weakness in its opponents and an opportunity to secure the easing of sanctions, the return of funds, or the unfreezing of frozen assets.
“To be secure, we must be strong. Ukraine is an important—even an extremely important—part of this security system,” he emphasized.
As reported by Ukrinform, Zelensky believes that the first step toward genuine diplomacy in relations with Russia should be a ceasefire, after which it will be possible to work substantively on a peace plan.

Iran’s new military doctrine is designed to make victory meaningless
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:30:55 UTC
05:30:55 KST

Iran’s latest military doctrine rests on a dangerous proposition: a country does not have to defeat a superior enemy on the battlefield to deny it a meaningful victory. By threatening broader retaliation, expanding the geography of conflict and exploiting vulnerabilities in regional trade, Tehran is attempting to make the political rewards of military action increasingly difficult to secure.
On Oct. 21, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) announced that Iran’s military doctrine would move beyond retaliatory strikes towards offensive and asymmetric operations.
The declaration reinforced earlier statements by Iranian military officials that the country was shifting away from a predominantly defensive posture.
Although official announcements do not establish how comprehensively this change has been implemented, they reveal the direction in which Tehran wants its adversaries to believe its strategy is moving.
The distinction matters because military superiority and strategic success are not interchangeable. Washington and Israel may destroy military facilities, disrupt command structures and degrade Iran’s weapons production. Yet these achievements cannot, by themselves, guarantee political compliance, regional stability or a durable settlement.
Iran’s objective, therefore, is not necessarily to win a conventional war against the United States. Rather, it is to deny Washington the ability to translate battlefield superiority into a political outcome that Tehran considers unacceptable.
This strategy could raise the costs of another attack, but it could also deepen the insecurity that makes another war possible. The central question is no longer simply who can inflict greater damage. It is whether either side can turn military force into a political settlement that lasts.
What It Means to Win a War
Iran’s strategic predicament is straightforward. Its conventional air power and technological capabilities cannot match those of the United States and Israel. A strategy built around symmetrical warfare would leave Tehran vulnerable to sustained aerial attacks, precision strikes and the systematic destruction of military infrastructure. Its response has consequently relied on a different calculation: if it cannot prevent an adversary from striking, it can make the consequences of that strike more costly and unpredictable.
Missiles, drones, dispersed launch systems and decentralised command structures are central to this approach. Rather than depending exclusively on the survival of major military installations, Iran can seek to preserve enough capacity to retaliate after suffering substantial damage. Its longstanding emphasis on asymmetric warfare also allows it to exploit the difference between the relatively low cost of some offensive systems and the expense of intercepting them.
The strategic logic extends beyond weapons. Iran can threaten military facilities, shipping routes and economic infrastructure across a wider regional theatre.
A conflict that begins with strikes on Iranian territory could therefore create security and economic consequences for states that are not directly involved in the initial attack.
The threat of escalation becomes part of Iran’s deterrent, even before every threatened operation is carried out.
This is a strategy of strategic denial. Its purpose is not necessarily to defeat an opponent in every engagement but to prevent that opponent from achieving its political objectives at an acceptable cost. If Washington seeks to eliminate a military threat, compel Iranian concessions or reshape Tehran’s regional behaviour, the relevant measure of success is not simply the number of targets destroyed. It is whether the intended political outcome follows.
Yet strategic denial should not be confused with victory. A state that survives an attack may still lose military capacity, economic resources and diplomatic leverage. Iran’s ability to impose costs does not automatically give it the ability to dictate the terms of a settlement. Its doctrine may complicate an adversary’s calculations without resolving the underlying imbalance of power.
Beyond Iran’s Borders
The most consequential feature of Iran’s approach is its potential to widen the conflict geographically. Tehran does not need to confine its response to the immediate battlefield if it believes that pressure on regional infrastructure and international commerce can influence an adversary’s decisions. This creates a direct connection between military strategy and the global economy.
The Strait of Hormuz illustrates the problem. The US Energy Information Administration estimated that roughly 20 million barrels of oil per day passed through the strait in 2024, equivalent to about one-fifth of global petroleum liquids consumption. The route is also critical to international liquefied natural gas trade.
Any sustained disruption could increase energy prices, raise shipping and insurance costs, and intensify inflationary pressure across economies far beyond the Middle East.
For Iran, the strategic attraction is clear. A threat to a vital maritime chokepoint can make the consequences of military escalation visible to governments, businesses and consumers around the world. The resulting economic pressure may complicate the calculations of states supporting military action against Tehran. It also forces regional governments to consider whether hosting foreign military forces could expose their own economies to retaliation.
But this leverage has limits. Disrupting the Strait of Hormuz would also damage Iran’s interests, aggravate economic hardship and alienate states that might otherwise favour diplomacy. Other countries could respond by strengthening maritime coalitions, expanding alternative supply arrangements or increasing military pressure on Iran. A tactic designed to internationalise the cost of war could therefore internationalise the opposition to Tehran.
Nor does economic pain necessarily translate into political concessions. Governments may absorb substantial costs if they believe their security or credibility is at stake. The assumption that higher energy prices or disrupted trade will compel Washington to retreat is no more reliable than the assumption that military strikes will automatically force Tehran to comply.
Iran’s widening battlefield is thus both a source of leverage and a mechanism of escalation. It raises the stakes for all parties, but it also increases the number of actors with reasons to intervene. The more regional commerce becomes an instrument of coercion, the harder it becomes to separate military confrontation from the wider economic order.
Why Strategic Denial Is Not the Same as Victory
Iran’s doctrine may be designed to make an adversary’s victory elusive, but it cannot guarantee that Tehran will emerge in a stronger position. The strategy depends on the credibility of its threats, the survival of enough military capability to carry them out and the willingness of its opponents to consider the potential costs before acting. Each condition can change during a conflict.
A sustained campaign could weaken Iran’s missile infrastructure, reduce its stockpiles and disrupt the command systems needed to coordinate retaliation. Regional partners could also become less willing or less capable of supporting Tehran if the costs of confrontation rise. Meanwhile, attacks on neighbouring states or commercial shipping could encourage closer security cooperation between Gulf governments, Washington and other external powers.
There is also a fundamental political problem. A doctrine built around imposing unacceptable costs can deter an adversary, but it can also reinforce the adversary’s belief that Iran must be contained through stronger military pressure.
If every attack is answered by a wider threat and every response produces another escalation, the logic of deterrence risks becoming a cycle of mutual insecurity.
This is where Iran’s strategic calculation becomes especially precarious. Preventing an opponent from claiming victory is a negative objective. It can obstruct an adversary’s plans, but it does not establish a stable political order or secure long-term economic recovery. For Tehran, a meaningful strategic outcome would require more than surviving a confrontation. It would require preserving national security, reducing the risk of renewed war and creating conditions in which economic reconstruction becomes possible.
The same distinction applies to Washington and Israel. Tactical success may weaken Iran’s military capabilities, but it cannot by itself resolve the political disputes that sustain the confrontation. If military action leaves both sides convinced that the other remains an intolerable threat, battlefield gains may simply postpone the next round of conflict.
A more durable outcome requires a credible path from deterrence to diplomacy. Crisis communication channels, arrangements to protect commercial shipping and verifiable agreements on the issues driving confrontation would not eliminate the rivalry. They could, however, reduce the risk that a local incident triggers a broader regional war. Such mechanisms matter precisely because neither side can reliably control every consequence of escalation.
Iran’s new doctrine should therefore be understood not as proof that Tehran can defeat a militarily superior opponent, but as an effort to make the exercise of that superiority politically and economically costly. Its success will depend on whether the threat of retaliation changes adversarial behaviour without provoking a response that leaves Iran more isolated and vulnerable.
Ultimately, the measure of success is not whether an adversary can be prevented from claiming victory. It is whether either side can achieve a political settlement that remains viable after the guns fall silent.
A doctrine that makes victory elusive may deter aggression. Without a credible path to peace, however, it can also make the next war harder to avoid.

The AI-Discovered Bug That Could Have Become a Cybersecurity Disaster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:28:02 UTC
05:28:02 KST

In early August, Sagi Tzadik asked an AI agent to take a security flaw it had found in WordPress and see whether the same weakness could be made to work against Drupal, another popular content management system. Eight hours later, the agent reported that it had failed. Then it added that, in the course of trying, it found a flaw in PHP, the programming language on which both systems—and as much as 70% of the web—depend.
Tzadik, a security researcher at cybersecurity firm Wiz, assumed that the AI had made a mistake. “Models tend to hallucinate,” he tells TIME. But the exploit, which took advantage of a weakness that had gone undetected for more than a decade, worked.
Unbeknownst to Wiz’s team, researchers at another cybersecurity firm, Calif—working with OpenAI—had used AI to find a related flaw. It suggests that once AI reaches a certain capability level, it is a matter of time before some longstanding weaknesses are unearthed. AI companies have been trying to ensure that defenders including Wiz and Calif get there first by giving them early access to new AI models before the equivalent capabilities trickle down to malicious users. This time, it worked.
The episode offers a glimpse into a new phase in cybersecurity in which AI helps defenders find vulnerabilities while giving them less time to fix them. While the bugs’ announcement has prompted alarm of a much-speculated “cyber-apolocalyse”—in which AI discovers world-melting bugs, plunging society into chaos—those who helped discover it are optimistic. “We are fixing vulnerabilities at an unprecedented rate, and this is doing security overall a very good thing,” Tzadik says.
But the details reveal just how close things came to disaster. Word of the vulnerabilities began circulating online two days before the patch’s scheduled release, prompting PHP’s maintainers to bring it forward by a day. Hours later, with the patch still unavailable, Calif mistakenly posted a video showing its exploit at work, and copycat attempts multiplied. Cloudflare counted thousands before the public announcement, tens of thousands within 45 minutes of it, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and eventually millions. Even after the patch was released, many webpages, including those of government agencies and parts of Wikipedia, were taken down as a precaution as security teams scrambled to install the update.
“If it had leaked a month earlier,” before a patch was ready, “this would have been a very different situation,” says Tomer Schwartz, CTO of exposure management and appsec at Wiz.
That a patch was prepared was the result of a loosely organized sprint. After Calif and Wiz sent reports to PHP, the groups joined forces. Researchers from competing companies shared their findings in common channels, with no contracts governing the arrangement. Over the following weeks, the group of roughly 15 people spoke almost daily to trace the vulnerabilities to their common source and devise a fix. The process, Schwartz says, was “just based on trust.”
That process will have to sustain increasing pressure. OpenAI has said that the PHP bugs were among “several significant vulnerabilities we’ve already found and are working to fix,” and predicted that similar discoveries would “increase sharply in the coming months.” As those findings multiply, so will the number of dangerous secrets waiting for fixes. “We have to rethink all of our processes, all of our methods, all of our tech stack … to be able to keep up the pace against attackers,” Schwartz says.
Though defenders are being given a head start, they face a disadvantage of another sort. Attackers only have to succeed once. “But, as defenders, we need to make sure that every single vulnerability is covered,” Schwartz says.
AI is helping defenders find those vulnerabilities first. Previously, testing suspected bugs could take weeks, forcing researchers to prioritize which were most promising. But now AI agents allow researchers to test many ideas at once, Tzadik says. “It’s months of traditional research condensed to, like, days—couple hours to days, really.”
But even with AI, the process is labor intensive. After the agent helped Wiz uncover the PHP vulnerability, it still couldn’t describe how the bug worked, Tzadik says. Its explanations were “just slop.” He and colleagues spent days untangling the cause of a bug and eventually reproducing it.
Cost is another constraint. Joshua Saxe, Meta’s former AI security tech lead, who left in February to co-found Abundance Security says he’s working with an organization that has spent roughly $1 million using Anthropic’s Mythos to identify bugs, adding that more bugs remain.
“As an industry, I think we’re deer in the headlights right now,” Saxe says.
"In the climate that we’re in today, you have to do cybersecurity well. It’s not an option to kind of half-a-- it,” says Adam Meyers, senior vice president of counter adversary operations at CrowdStrike. But even a successful exploit offers further opportunities for defenders to intervene. “Exploits are going to happen, and that’s not the end of the story,” he says. “It’s the beginning of the attack.”

In one of the West's few swing races, a Democrat tries to keep a Trump district

In one of the West’s few swing races, a Democrat tries to keep a Trump district
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Gluesenkamp Perez has modeled an independent streak that has helped her win two elections but disappointed some in her own party.
- Braun has packaged his conservatism as balanced while assuring supporters that he’s rowing in the same direction as the president and party leaders.
LONG BEACH, Wash. — Tourist dollars are drying up in this small town at the edge of the Pacific Ocean. Foot traffic is down. Visitors have less to spend on souvenirs.
And beachgoers now bring packed lunches instead of stopping at Captain Bob’s Chowder Sisters, said Melissa Huddleston, waiting for customers at her sister-in-law’s shop on Sunday.
Huddleston, 60, is depressed about the state of the country, and while she’s planning to vote in the Nov. 3 midterms, she hasn’t decided who she’ll vote for. This swing district, Washington’s 3rd, is home to a tight congressional race that will help determine the balance of power in the U.S. House.
Huddleston doesn’t think anyone in Congress can really do what she wants: Bring decorum back to the national discourse and bring the economy back to life. She isn’t a particular fan of Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, the independent-leaning Democratic incumbent, nor is she persuaded by state Sen. John Braun, the Trump-endorsed Republican challenger.
“I don’t know which one is better,” Huddleston said, shaking her head. “I really don’t.”
As the battle to persuade midterm voters intensifies in the election’s final stretch, its fever pitch is evident in places like this largely rural stretch of southwest Washington — a rare three-time Trump-voting district with a Democratic incumbent.
Republican-aligned groups are pouring money into flipping the district red, considering it one of the GOP’s best chances to gain a House seat in an increasingly unfavorable environment, while Democrats see retaining the district as urgent to their effort to secure control of the chamber.
The contest offers a glimpse into a purple region a time when both parties are testing strategies for winning voter loyalty — not just in the midterms but looking ahead to 2028. And the dynamic in the candidates’ race to capture swing voters reflects the national debate gripping both parties about how moderate to be.
As Democrats debate whether progressives or centrists should chart the party’s path, Gluesenkamp Perez has modeled an independent streak that has helped her win two elections but disappointed some in her own party. And as Republicans grapple with low public support for Trump, Braun has packaged his conservatism as balanced while assuring supporters that he’s rowing in the same direction as the president and party leaders.
Interviews with more than 30 voters across the district revealed a mix of support for the two candidates, largely based on partisan politics, views about Trump and concern with which party controls the House.
“This is a very pivotal time, and this area has a history of being more of a swing [district],” said Mark Maxwell, 46, of Vancouver, Washington, who planned to vote blue. “It’s a chance for our voice to be heard.”
The number of congressional battlegrounds nationwide has shrunk with gerrymandering and political polarization, making the district one of about two dozen races that will decide the House majority. The West’s other highly competitive contests include three in California — those of Republican Rep. David Valadao and Democratic Rep. Adam Gray in the Central Valley and the open seat of retiring Republican Rep. Darrell Issa in the San Diego area.
In southwest Washington, polling has indicated the congressional race may be essentially tied. A late September poll commissioned by Oregon Public Broadcasting had Braun up by one point. A July Emerson College poll showed the same. Earlier this month, election forecaster Cook Political Report moved the race from a toss-up rating to lean-Democrat.
‘Stubborn loyalty’
Across the district last week, left-leaning voters said they were backing Gluesenkamp Perez — some precisely because of her maverick streak.
“She’s voted against the Democrats and I know she’s voted against the Republicans, which is what one would hope,” said Helios Ovando, 69, of Battle Ground, Wash., who decided this year to volunteer for Gluesenkamp Perez’s campaign for the first time. “She’s more about the local scene.”
Ovando has been turned off by what he sees as Republicans’ adherence to the party line; Gluesenkamp Perez’s willingness to “buck the system” gives him more confidence in her integrity, he said.
Gluesenkamp Perez, 38, who ran an auto shop with her husband before being elected to Congress, frames her mission as one built around the practical needs of her district. She argues that Democrats should break the Republican hold on rural districts and talks about reestablishing voters’ confidence that the Democratic Party is “listening to and reflective of working people.”
“When you have people come to Congress with a very stubborn loyalty to their communities, you get better federal policy,” Gluesenkamp Perez said in an interview.
“That’s the value of breaking up the monopolization of politics in rural America,” she added. “It gets you to a better place from a policy lens.”
She points to funding wins and work to mitigate pressures on public schools and housing costs in Congress. On Saturday evening, she talked to a crowd at a brewery about restoring shop class to junior high schools and creating measures that facilitate repairing rather than replacing electronics and appliances.
Gluesenkamp Perez’s independence has also earned her critics. She twice helped House Republicans advance their legislative agenda in September, angering Democratic leaders, and voted to fund the Department of Homeland Security in January. In each case, she said the packages contained secondary measures that aligned with her constituents’ values.
At a “No Kings” protest last weekend in Vancouver, the district’s urban center, several Democratic voters said they weren’t happy with Gluesenkamp Perez but still planned to back her.
“I will vote for her even though I don’t like her policies,” said Carol Rochat, 71, of Vancouver. “We need all the Democrats we can get, at least to get the majority, and then we’ll still work on her to try to be a little bit more progressive.”
‘Win their trust’
Gluesenkamp Perez ran against a hard-right candidate in her first two races, but this time she’s facing a less-polarizing and better-funded opponent in Braun, 59, a business owner and former Navy captain who has represented a slice of the district in the state Legislature for 13 years.
He made his pitch to a group of supporters at Long Beach’s historic train depot, framing his mission as balancing out the state’s Democratic voices in Congress and helping government “get out of the way” of its citizens.
“That’s sort of the American dream,” he said. “Government doesn’t create success for each of us, but we can set the framework for each of us to go out and find whatever success means for us.”
Braun talks about reforming tax and energy policy, funding infrastructure improvements and backing the military. He argues for balancing the federal budget, envisioning doing detailed, line-level work to find cuts that will reduce the national debt.
“He’s in line with my thinking,” said Liz Glenn, 63, of Raymond, Wash., listing Christian values, support for law enforcement and “protecting children” as some of her top concerns. A retired bookkeeper who is concerned about immigration and wants to see the House seat turn red, Glenn said she viewed maintaining a Republican majority as critical.
“It’s the only way to protect our country’s growth,” she said, adding, “Without the Republicans fighting against the perversions of the world, there’s so much non-American value being brought in.”
Braun told supporters that Trump’s endorsement had helped bring in financial support for his campaign. But, like other Republicans across the country, he has tried to appear independent on issues such as the war in Iran, which Braun has said the United States needs a plan to end.
“This district is a very independent district. I think it gives an opportunity to go make your case directly with the voters and win their trust ... regardless of what the national picture is,” Braun said in an interview.
Pattie Gray, 66, who chairs the county Republican Party and watched Braun stump at the train depot, said Braun’s legislative and military experience made her view him as a “natural fit” for the seat.
“We need somebody who’s representing us the way we want to be represented,” Gray said. “He sees what this state needs.”
Gray, who is running for a Pacific County commissioner seat, has been door-knocking for Braun and other local Republican candidates. She’s optimistic about the chances to flip the seat, though it’s not “a shoo-in,” she said.
“We have to work really hard,” Gray said of turning out voters. “We’ve only got a couple more weeks.”
Huddleston, at the chowder shop, didn’t cast a ballot in 2024, unable to stomach supporting either party. She is motivated to vote this time because she wants to back a local Republican sheriff, whose campaign sign hung on the shop door.
But she’s upset with Trump’s brand of political divisiveness and where it has taken the country. She would prefer a Democratic majority in Congress, she said, to see if they can help fix the economy.
That might, Huddleston mused, lead her to support Gluesenkamp Perez when she fills out her ballot. But if so, it won’t be with gusto.
“Our country is horrible now,” Huddleston said. “How can you be enthusiastic about an election?”

Detained migrants no right to bond hearings, US court rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:24:57 UTC
05:24:57 KST

Breadcrumb
Detained migrants have no constitutional right to bond hearings, US court rules
A US appeals court ruled on Friday that President Donald Trump's administration is not required under the US Constitution to give detained immigrants a chance to seek release on bond.
In a 10-7 ruling powered by its conservative majority, the New Orleans-based 5th US Circuit Court of Appeals decided that the Constitution's Fifth Amendment due process protections do not require that immigration detainees receive bond hearings.
"To the extent petitioners seek to vindicate a liberty interest to be free from physical restraint in the most abstract sense, they can do so at any moment by agreeing to leave the country," US Circuit Judge Cory Wilson, a Trump appointee, wrote in the decision.
The ruling, if left to stand, would eliminate a key avenue for detained migrants in the three states under the 5th Circuit's jurisdiction — Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi — to argue for release, especially if the US Supreme Court decides the administration's detention practice complies with immigration law.
The Supreme Court this month agreed to consider the issue, which has divided lower courts. Numerous lawsuits by migrants arguing they were being unlawfully detained have flooded the courts as US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, implemented Trump's mass deportation agenda.
The Supreme Court is considering only whether such hearings are required by statute, not by the Constitution, the issue the 5th Circuit addressed with Friday's decision.
While the 5th Circuit in February had adopted the administration's reading of immigration law as requiring mandatory detention, a 2-1 panel of the court in July held that ICE could not constitutionally detain people for more than 90 days without providing hearings to argue for release on bond.
The decision, which came in lawsuits by two Mexican citizens and one Honduran, carried particular importance because Texas and Louisiana, within the 5th Circuit's jurisdiction, house the nation's largest numbers of immigration detainees.
But the full 5th Circuit agreed to rehear the case, and on Friday reversed course, concluding that detained immigrants are not constitutionally entitled to proceedings in immigration court beyond what Congress provided by statute.
"This ruling opens the door to more people being locked up for no reason, with devastating consequences for them, their loved ones and their community," Ellie Norton, a lawyer for the non-US citizens in the case at the National Immigration Project, said in a statement.
James Percival, the general counsel for the US Department of Homeland Security, in a social media post hailed what he called a "big win in the 5th Circuit on mandatory detention for illegal aliens."
Among the dissenting judges was US Circuit Judge Dana Douglas, an appointee of Democratic President Joe Biden, who wrote that "unchecked, executive authority to arrest and detain, indefinitely, echoes fearfully from history."

Freed US citizen was tortured in Russian jail, former Ukrainian prisoners say
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
21:18:13 BST
05:18:13 KST

Freed US citizen was tortured in Russian jail, former Ukrainian prisoners say
- Published
Ukrainians held alongside freed US prisoner Stephen Hubbard have said they witnessed him being beaten and humiliated by Russian guards during his four-year detention.
Dmytro Khyliuk first met Hubbard at the Novozybkov prison in Bryansk, not far from Russia's border with Ukraine, in September 2022.
"We heard it from the guards. They came during inspections and were asking: in which cell is the American? And then they used obscene words. They threatened him, they mocked him from the first days."
Ihor Shyshko also remembers Hubbard's arrival at the jail and says his nationality marked him out to the officers.
"It attracted such attention because they mocked him, forced him to learn the Russian language, sing the national anthem and repeat the rules of the prison schedule, which he could not read."
Hubbard was captured in April 2022, when Russian soldiers occupied the eastern city of Izyum, where he was living with his Ukrainian partner.
He was accused of serving in Ukraine's armed forces and convicted in a trial in Moscow before being sentenced to six years and 10 months. Shyshko and Khyliuk were held alongside Hubbard as he awaited trial.
Shyshko said he witnessed and heard Hubbard being beaten by prison guards and electrocuted with a stun gun.
"They beat him on the legs, on the back, on the arms," he said. "Of course, they didn't give him food, they didn't give him medical care. They kept him in the cold.
"He was always treated more harshly, because he was an American. They claimed he was a mercenary, and said 'let's beat him'."
Shyshko, a captured Ukrainian soldier, alleges Hubbard was subjected to sexual humiliation and abuse for the entertainment of the prison staff.
Accounts from the two former Ukrainian prisoners corroborate statements made by Hubbard's family that he was tortured in prison.
The 74-year-old was released by the Kremlin after four-and-a-half years, on the day US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg to discuss the war in Ukraine.
Witkoff praised the Russian President as a "humanitarian", despite the ongoing full-scale invasion and daily Russian attacks across Ukraine.
US President Donald Trump said he had asked Putin to free Hubbard during a phone call the week before.
Khyliuk, a journalist, was held in the earliest days of the invasion, when Russian troops advanced towards the capital Kyiv.
He said he knew Hubbard's health was declining over the months they were initially held in nearby cells because he heard his complaints and the guards calling him more often to see the prison doctor.
Khyliuk described broken windows and biting cold, with detainees using time out of their cells to huddle together in the bathroom for warmth.
"It was very difficult conditions in Novozybkov, worse than in the next prison. It was very cold there in winter, terribly cold," he said.
Both men encountered the retired English teacher again at their next prison, Pakino, where Shyshko says Hubbard's condition worsened.
"There was not a single spot on his knees or on his feet without rot," he said.
"Everything was rotten. We all had scabies. It was very, very difficult for him. I even bandaged him once at the medical centre, because the doctor didn't want to do it. He just couldn't do it himself, and I had to help. He was quite weak then and he almost couldn't move."
They detailed a harsh regime and a meagre diet of porridge, bread and potatoes, with a daily routine of beatings and humiliation, being forced to run or hold stress positions.
"There's a handler with a dog, who lets go so it can bite you on the buttocks, on the elbow, or bite your leg. Then these wounds fester very badly," Shyshko said.
Khyliuk claimed that soon after their transfer to Pakino, Hubbard was hidden to conceal his condition from a team of International Red Cross visitors.
"I would like to say that an international humanitarian organisation that receives a lot of funding could do better. They saw only what was shown to them and they were happy with that," he said.
The International Committee of the Red Cross said in a statement that "in any situation where the ICRC has been granted access, we request to see every individual and assess the conditions they are held in. We continue our discussions with parties to the conflict on this issue."
Khyliuk said Hubbard disappeared from the prison in 2024 and he thought he must have been released. Khyliuk was returned to Ukraine in August 2025 in a prisoner exchange.
He likened their treatment to the regime of Soviet leader Joseph Stalin.
"Russian captivity is a torture machine. From the first second of your detention, they do everything to suppress you, to intimidate you. This is torture in all its manifestations, from psychological to physical. Beatings, hunger, cold, lack of any information, lack of the opportunity to communicate even with other prisoners".
Khyliuk said he was pleased to see Hubbard finally released and heading to the US.
"I understand what it is like to be in terrible captivity. Moreover, it was not his war. He ended up in the wrong place and at the wrong time," he said.
But he described the timing as "shameful PR of the US president, who is losing votes in elections to Congress".
Shyshko said he hoped one day their torturers would face justice.
"Evil must be punished, and so it will be. I have hope for that".
