====================================================================================================

Can Serbia’s student protesters stop Aleksandar Vučić from becoming prime minister? The country’s longtime leader has called an early election to extend his hold on power.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:15:13 UTC
05:15:13 KST

Can Serbia’s student protesters stop Aleksandar Vučić from becoming prime minister? The country’s longtime leader has called an early election to extend his hold on power.
Just over a month ago, Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić addressed the nation on television. He lamented the difficult circumstances but said that, despite everything, the country had “managed to preserve stability.” To ensure that Serbia could continue “to develop and maintain its internal unity in the face of external threats,” Vučić announced that he would dissolve parliament and call early elections for October 25, 2026. He resigned shortly afterward. Vučić needs the election to stay in power: His presidential term would have expired soon. But he may not succeed. His main rival is the “Student List — Students Win” movement, which formally emerged a month ago but became known around the world during mass protests across Serbia in 2024. We explain why Vučić called the election now, what the main parties are campaigning on, and who is most likely to win.
Why Serbia’s election matters
Aleksandar Vučić joined the Serbian Radical Party as a young man and became known as an ardent Serbian nationalist. He became prime minister in 2014 and was elected president three years later. With the backing of the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), Vučić built a regime that political scientists abroad describe as authoritarian.
As early as 2019, the U.S. nonprofit Freedom House downgraded Serbia’s status from free to partly free. That same year, the European Parliament said Vučić and the SNS were blocking parliamentary debate on bills they opposed, accusing their critics of betraying the country, and suppressing independent media.
Five years later, Freedom House said the ruling party was undermining political rights and civil liberties and putting pressure on independent media and civil society organizations. In 2024, V-Dem, an independent Swedish research institute that studies democracy worldwide, called Serbia an “electoral autocracy.” This year, the German think tank Bertelsmann Stiftung classified it as a moderate autocracy, citing the concentration of power in Vučić’s hands.
Other indicators also show the problems facing Serbian democracy. Between 2014 and 2026, the country fell from 54th to 104th place in the annual press freedom index compiled by the international organization Reporters Without Borders.
Transparency International ranked Serbia 78th in its Corruption Perceptions Index in 2014 and 116th in 2025. A survey conducted last year by Transparency Serbia found that 22% of respondents considered corruption the country’s biggest problem — the highest share in a quarter century.
All this makes the coming election especially consequential. It will determine whether Serbia continues on the authoritarian course it has followed over the past decade and a half under Vučić and the SNS, or gets a chance to democratize if the Student List, the main opposition group, wins.
How the electoral system works
Serbia is a parliamentary republic. Parliament, officially known as the National Assembly, elects the government and holds it accountable.
The constitution limits the president’s powers: He commands the armed forces, signs laws, and nominates a prime minister for parliament’s approval. He can also dissolve the Assembly — for example, if it fails to approve a government within 90 days. But the president cannot dismiss the government or hold other positions while in office. Vučić disregarded the latter rule: From his first election as president until May 2023, he also led the ruling party.
The Assembly has a single chamber with 250 members. Under the constitution, elections are held every four years, but early elections have effectively become the norm since 2000. Only the 2012 and 2020 elections took place on schedule.
Voters cast ballots for party lists; there are no single-member districts. Parties must clear a 3% threshold to enter parliament, but this requirement does not apply to ethnic minority parties. The current Assembly includes parties representing Hungarians, Bosniaks, Croats, Albanians, and even Russians. If the ruling party or coalition needs a few more votes to secure a parliamentary majority, ethnic minority lawmakers can wield disproportionate influence.
Serbia has seen sustained anti-government protests over the past three years
The previous parliamentary election, held on December 17, 2023, was marred by serious irregularities, including the so-called Bulgarian train ballot-swapping scheme, busing in voters from Republika Srpska, and vote-buying. These practices helped the SNS win nearly 47% of the vote and a parliamentary majority, while the opposition Serbia Against Violence coalition had to settle for 23.7% and 65 seats.
The vote-rigging triggered mass protests, but they had petered out by the end of December 2023. New grievances soon emerged. In July 2024, thousands took to the streets against a project to extract lithium at the Jadar mine in western Serbia. Events in Novi Sad, Serbia’s second-largest city, prompted a far larger response.
On November 1, 2024, a canopy at the city’s railway station collapsed, killing 16 people, including children. The irony was that renovations at the station had been completed just four months before the disaster. Two Chinese state-owned companies had carried out the work under a contract awarded by the Serbian authorities without competitive bidding.
Officials initially denied any responsibility. Pro-government media and Goran Vesić, the construction, transport, and infrastructure minister, repeatedly said that the station canopy had not been part of the renovation. The Transport Ministry refused journalists’ requests for financial documents relating to the work.
All this raised suspicions of corruption and sparked large protests in Novi Sad and other cities. Many students joined and became the protests’ main driving force. The largest demonstration, on March 15, 2025, drew up to 325,000 people — an enormous number in a country with a population of just over 6.5 million. In addition to calling for the release of documents relating to the station’s renovation and for increased spending on higher education, protesters demanded the government’s resignation and early elections.
The government could hardly ignore the protests. Vesić resigned in November 2024 and was behind bars a few weeks later. He and 12 other officials faced charges, but these were later dropped for lack of evidence. Prime Minister Miloš Vučević resigned in January 2025.
Vučić, meanwhile, suggested that unnamed foreign powers were instigating the protests. Pro-government media accused protesters of betraying their country and committing crimes and called for their arrest and lengthy prison sentences.
Police treated demonstrators harshly. Participants in a mass demonstration in Belgrade in March 2025 said a sound cannon had been used against them. During protests in Valjevo in August, police beat 25 demonstrators with batons. In Belgrade, police arrested, beat, and humiliated 15 protesters and threatened women with sexual violence.
Why did Vučić call the election now?
Protesters have been demanding new elections for the past two years, but Vučić did not dissolve parliament to accommodate them. He has his own reasons. His second presidential term was due to expire in May 2027, and Serbia’s constitution bars him from running again. But Vučić does not want to relinquish power.
He is well positioned to hold on to it. He has the backing of the SNS, which has come to dominate Serbian politics over the past decade and a half. The party enjoys substantial political advantages through its access to state institutions and directly or indirectly controls all the country’s major television channels. These advantages helped it secure a decisive victory in the 2023 election. On October 25, it hopes to repeat that success and preserve the current regime.
Under these circumstances, Vučić’s calculation is clear: He wants to move from the presidency to the prime minister’s office. That post would give him considerable powers. Under the constitution, the prime minister determines domestic and foreign policy, can introduce bills in parliament, oversees the state administration, appoints and dismisses ministers, and can even initiate the dissolution of parliament.
The election date is no accident. First, Vučić has sought to deny the students time to build a stronger political organization. Their movement is not even a party, and it has yet to establish an extensive network of local branches to mobilize voters. Second, the election was scheduled for the earliest date legally possible after parliament’s dissolution: 46 days later. That gives the students as little time as possible to campaign, while Vučić and the SNS have been promoting themselves for months.
Serbia will elect a new president in December, and Vučić will try to install a loyalist. One possibility is Ana Brnabić, the Assembly’s speaker and now acting president. She has already proved her loyalty to Vučić: During her years as prime minister, she effectively ceded all real authority to the president. Another candidate is Miloš Vučević, the SNS leader and a close Vučić ally, who ranks second on the party’s electoral list.
The main contenders and their platforms
A total of 18 parties and coalitions, including those representing ethnic minorities, will contest the October 25 election. But the main battle will be between the Aleksandar Vučić — United Serbia coalition and the opposition Student List.
The pro-government camp
The dominant party on the government side is the Serbian Progressive Party, founded in 2008 after a split in the Radical Party. The SNS espouses nationalist, conservative, and populist views, while its economic positions lean toward neoliberalism. With around 800,000 members in 2020 — 13% of Serbia’s population — it is Europe’s largest party by membership. It is running as part of the Aleksandar Vučić — United Serbia coalition, but its partners carry little weight.
The SNS platform rests on several key tenets. These include defending Serbia’s territorial integrity — meaning refusing to recognize Kosovo’s independence — and supporting Serbs living abroad; steady economic development and efforts to combat corruption; social justice; and joining the EU while cooperating with Russia, the United States, and China. There is one problem with the platform published on the party’s official website, however: It dates from 2011 and has not been updated since.
In the current campaign, the ruling party and Vučić are focusing primarily on recent economic successes. Serbia’s GDP has indeed grown steadily in recent years. According to the World Bank, it rose by 3.9% in 2024 and 2% in 2025, while the International Monetary Fund forecasts growth of 3.3% this year. Serbia has also been actively attracting foreign investment, which reached 5.2 billion euros in 2024 and nearly 3.5 billion in 2025. This September, Vučić proudly said Serbia accounted for 62% of all foreign direct investment in the Western Balkans.
To sustain growth, the authorities are banking on large projects that can double as publicity opportunities. Work has recently picked up, for example, on the Belgrade metro, a project first launched in the 1990s. Chinese companies are now involved, and Vučić said with great fanfare that two enormous tunnel-boring machines were due to arrive in the capital in October — just in time for the election. For now, however, the spectacle of their arrival has had to be postponed: Technical problems have left the machines stuck in the Romanian port of Constanța.
But nothing is stopping the ruling party from constantly talking about Expo 2027, the world’s fair that Belgrade will host. Vučić frequently visits the construction site and says the “historic” exhibition is moving the capital and the country as a whole “forward.” The exhibition was also one of the official reasons given for calling the early election: Vučić said the vote needed to be timed so that afterward the country could focus on preparing for Expo.
The authorities also emphasize the need for stability. Serbia went through a turbulent period in the 1990s, and the authorities now use fears of a return to that era to argue that people should vote for the SNS. In their view, the main threat to stability comes, naturally, from the protesting students, who they say receive foreign funding and want to organize a “color revolution” in Serbia.
SNS lawmaker Biljana Pantić said the choice in this election was clear: On one side are the SNS and Vučić, who put “care for citizens, stability, and Serbia’s continued development” first; on the other are those “who have no concrete platform or results and have reduced their politics to hatred, violence, and attacks on everything Aleksandar Vučić does or says.”
The opposition
The students, who form the backbone of the protests, hold a wide range of views, and their ranks include both nationalists and liberals. Nevertheless, they have managed to stay united by avoiding contentious issues such as European integration, relations with Russia, and Kosovo’s independence.
On September 9, 2026, the day parliament was dissolved, they announced the formation of their own political movement, Student List — Students Win. In just a few days, the students collected the required number of voter signatures to run in the election and submitted their candidate list to the Electoral Commission, which unanimously approved their inclusion on the ballot on September 15.
The list contains 250 parliamentary candidates. None are students; instead, they include scholars, university professors, experts, and athletes. At the top is cardiologist Ilija Srdanović, a professor at the University of Novi Sad, although the students stress that they are not looking for “a new leader around whom another personality cult could form.”
The movement’s election platform is called the ”Student Plan” and consists of 11 points grouped into three sections. The first, “Serbia or the Mafia,” calls for stronger efforts to fight corruption, barring from public office officials who have broken the law and have ties to the mafia, and guaranteeing media freedom.
The second section, titled “Knowledge Is Power,” calls for adapting the education system to modern needs, introducing competitive selection for teaching positions, and subsidizing startups and innovation.
The third section, “Serbia Grows With Us,” addresses social and economic issues. Among other things, it proposes providing housing for young families and essential workers, and improving health care by standardizing medication prices nationwide and modernizing hospitals, particularly in rural areas.
The other parties
Among the other contenders, two coalitions — Stability Factor and European Serbia — have a chance of clearing the 3% threshold, according to a poll conducted by Serbian market research agency Factor Plus and published on September 21.
Stability Factor, led by Ivica Dačić, brings together the Socialist Party and partners such as the Social Democrats and the Greens. The coalition presents itself as an alliance of the patriotic left and intends to work with the SNS and Vučić. It is going through a difficult period, however, facing criticism for cooperating with the regime. On August 31, the Socialist Party expelled its vice president, Branko Ružić, for supporting the protesting students. Two members of its main council and several regional party leaders then left in protest.
European Serbia, meanwhile, consists of pro-European parties and has a detailed plan to dismantle the regime built by the SNS within 100 days and begin building a “European Serbia.” The coalition did not join forces with the students but is willing to cooperate with them after the election.
How the campaign unfolded
Although the official campaign began on September 9, Vučić and the SNS effectively started much earlier. The SNS put its own spin on the student movement’s main slogan, “Students Win!” For several months, enormous billboards reading “Serbia Wins!” could be seen across the country.
Government-controlled TV channels heavily promote Vučić. An analysis by the Friedrich Naumann Foundation found that he appeared on various channels 129 times in August — an average of four times a day. He appeared in his capacity as head of state, meaning he did not pay for the airtime.
Vučić has used other methods as well. In September 2026, the government set aside money for one-time payments of 160 to 300 euros to pensioners. Vučić also promised to raise public-sector salaries by 8% and social workers’ salaries by 12% — but only starting in December, after the election.
The students have no such resources, so they have to rely on social media and direct campaigning. They have set up booths in various Serbian cities where people can talk to candidates and learn about their platform. The students are also going door to door, trying to persuade voters to support the Student List.
Meanwhile, opposition supporters face direct pressure and restrictions from the authorities. Universities are firing professors sympathetic to the protesters, while television gives the opposition half as much airtime as pro-government parties and portrays it negatively. CRTA, an independent Serbian election-monitoring organization, says opposition candidates, observers, and activists face surveillance, insults, intimidation, and even physical attacks.
Who will win?
It is difficult to gauge support ahead of the election: Opinion polls vary widely. According to Factor Plus, 48.7% of voters are prepared to vote for the SNS and its coalition partners, and 37.1% for the Student List. European Serbia, at 3.6%, and the Socialist Party-led coalition, at 4.9%, also cleared the 3% threshold in the poll. But opposition politicians accuse the agency of bias and of working for the SNS, whose support it consistently overstates.
On September 30, Đorđe Vukadinović, editor in chief of the independent political science journal Nova srpska politička misao (New Serbian Political Thought), put support for the students at 44.4% and for the pro-government coalition at 41.7%. He did not explain the basis for those estimates. On October 15, political analyst Mirko Dautović suggested that support for the students had risen above 50% over the preceding month, but he too cited no specific poll.
Serbia faces a fierce electoral contest, but observers say tensions could persist afterward. First, there is no guarantee that Vučić would willingly step back if he lost — he could declare the results invalid. But that would risk a repeat of Slobodan Milošević’s fate: In the fall of 2000, he too refused to acknowledge defeat, only to be forced to give in after 10 days of mass protests.
Second, the students are determined and make no secret of the bleak future awaiting Vučić if they win: He will be put on trial. In September, a student-made video appeared online showing Vučić in various settings, followed by a figure mopping a prison floor. The video achieved its aim — it infuriated the Serbian authorities.
Even setting Vučić’s fate aside, a student victory would leave the movement facing the question of what to do next. Once their common opponent is gone, their disagreements over Kosovo, European integration, and relations with Russia and China — which they have set aside for now — will surface. Maintaining a consensus will be very difficult. And winning an election alone will not be enough to eradicate corruption. As the example of 2000 shows, democrats coming to power does not necessarily mean a victory for democracy.
What the election means for Russians living in Serbia
After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Serbia declined to impose sanctions on Russia while also taking in tens of thousands of Russians. By December 2024, the Serbian authorities had issued 67,000 temporary residence permits.
Estimates put the number of Russians in Serbia at 55,000 to 62,000 at the end of 2025, with more than 80% living in Belgrade. Most are young: People ages 24 to 39 account for 55%. And 66% of the Russians who have relocated to Serbia have a university education.
Temporary residence does not, of course, give Russians the right to vote, but Serbian politics is of little interest to them. A survey by the Belgrade Centre for Security Policy found that 72.8% of Russians who had moved to Serbia did not want to take part in political or civic activities. They were far more concerned about their personal safety and economic well-being.
The government’s approach to Russians who have relocated appears unlikely to change if the pro-government coalition wins. The Serbian authorities, for example, have repeatedly said they have no plans to revise the existing visa-free travel agreement with Russia.
If the Student List wins, its policy toward Russian emigrants is impossible to predict at this point: The students have carefully avoided commenting on Russia or on Russians who have moved to Serbia.

Kenya's world marathon champion Peres Jepchirchir has been provisionally suspended after testing positive for the banned blood booster EPO in a sample taken before her Sydney Marathon victory, the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) said on Friday.
The AIU added that the out-of-competition sample collected in Kenya returned an adverse analytical finding for EPO (erythropoietin), which boosts the production of red blood cells.
"I can only say that I feel terrible about what happened and I think it's only right that an athlete who uses the performance enhancing drugs should be disqualified," her agent Gianni Demadonna said in an emailed statement.
The 33-year-old is one of the most decorated women in the sport, having won gold at the Tokyo Games in 2021 and having claimed major marathon victories in New York (2021), Boston (2022), London (2024) and Sydney (2026). She previously held the half marathon world record.
Jepchirchir is the latest in a long string of Kenyan athletes to fall foul of doping rules. More than 140 Kenyan athletes have been sanctioned since the AIU was established in 2017.
"So much of what I see when I'm on a broadcast call I do not believe. I'm not surprised by this," said Olympic 10,000 metres silver medallist and broadcaster Kara Goucher, who was a whistleblower in the Nike Oregon Project case.
"I am, however, sad for all the athletes who finished behind her and were screwed out of a podium."
Jepchirchir dominated the women's race in Sydney in August, pulling clear of the field to finish in 2:18:31, more than 3 minutes ahead of second-placed compatriot Irine Cheptai.
The Sydney Marathon, which was added to the list of world majors beginning in 2025, said it was "extremely disappointed" by the news.
"Our commitment to clean sport is unwavering. Every athlete who lines up in Sydney deserves to race on a level playing field," it said in a statement.
Last year, Kenya's women's marathon world record holder Ruth Chepngetich was banned for three years after admitting anti-doping rule violations involving hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ), a prohibited diuretic, though her world record of 2:09:56 remained on the books because it was set before her positive test.

Massive floods have engulfed four U.S. states: people are being rescued from rooftops, evacuations have been ordered

Massive floods have engulfed four U.S. states: people are being rescued from rooftops, evacuations have been ordered
Kyiv • UNN
Heavy rains have caused massive flooding in Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona, and Utah. Hundreds of households have been evacuated, and there is damage to infrastructure.
Powerful downpours in the western United States caused massive flooding that affected the states of Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona, and Utah. UNN reports this, citing the Associated Press and The Guardian.
Rescuers are evacuating people from flooded homes, including by helicopter, while local authorities report damage to roads, bridges, and other infrastructure.
Details
The most difficult situation developed in the Four Corners region ("Four Corners"), where the borders of four U.S. states meet. As a result of intense rainfall, rivers burst their banks, flooding residential neighborhoods and transportation routes. In particular, in San Juan County, New Mexico, approximately 600 households were ordered to evacuate. In some homes, water levels rose to 1–1.5 meters. The U.S. National Guard was involved in the rescue operations, using helicopters, boats, and specialized equipment. Some residents had to be rescued directly from the roofs of flooded buildings.
Temporary shelters for evacuees were opened in the city of Farmington and nearby communities. At the same time, flooding in Bloomfield forced the suspension of operations at water treatment facilities, creating an additional threat of water contamination.
In Colorado, a state of emergency was declared in 11 counties. Archuleta County and the town of Pagosa Springs were particularly affected, with floodwaters damaging roads, bridges, and utility infrastructure. Because of the disaster, authorities closed certain sections of highways, suspended the operation of municipal institutions, and canceled classes at schools.
In Utah, flooding affected the city of Hurricane. According to local authorities, approximately 130 homes and residential trailers were affected by flooding. Roads, bridges, and power supply facilities were also damaged in the city.
In Arizona, the disaster affected settlements of Native American peoples. In particular, rescuers assisted 30 people in Dennehotso, while evacuations of local residents were carried out in other communities.
In addition, severe storms and tornadoes passed through the region. At least one person was reported injured in Arizona.
Water levels may exceed the historical maximum
According to the U.S. National Weather Service (NWS), on October 23, the level of the San Juan River near Farmington reached approximately four meters. Meteorologists forecast a further rise in water levels to 4.27 meters, which could exceed the historical maximum recorded in 1909.
Experts explain the extensive flooding by prolonged rains, which saturated the soil with moisture and left it unable to absorb additional precipitation.
According to weather forecasts, further downpours are possible in some areas over the weekend of October 24–25, so the threat of additional flooding remains.
The exact number of people affected and the total amount of damage remain unknown. Local authorities continue to assess the consequences of the disaster and conduct rescue operations.

Study traces how an El Niño changed the pollution map
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:02:24 UTC
05:02:24 KST

That atmospheric conditions regulate pollution levels was always known. (File photo)
The winter of 2022-23 was remarkably clean in north India with PM2.5 levels down by up to 30% from the average of the previous three years, while peninsular India was considerably dirtier, with average PM2.5 levels in Mumbai spiking by 45%. The next winter (2023-24), the pattern dramatically reversed: PM2.5 spiralled in the North, while falling sharply in peninsular India.What changed within a span of a year? The big difference, as per a new study, was that 2022-23 was a La Niña year, while El Niño prevailed in the subsequent winter.Coming ahead of India’s peak pollution season, the paper, titled ‘Air quality in flux: The baffling ENSO transition in India’, published in Atmospheric Pollution Research journal Thursday, found that La Niña/El Niño conditions altered atmospheric circulation, PM2.5 transport pathways and weather conditions that determine whether pollution disperses or gets trapped.
Study traces how an El Niño changed the pollution map
That atmospheric conditions regulate pollution levels was always known. What the study shows is how the atmosphere in winters can behave very differently under El Nino and La Nina conditions, determining where pollutants accumulate and where they are carried away even when emissions remain broadly similar. However, the researchers caution that the study does not establish that El Niño invariably worsens air quality in Delhi or north India.
“We are not implying that the 2023-24 El Niño pattern will be repeated this winter. The two years that we studied were unusual and unique,” said atmospheric scientist Gufran Beig, one of the study’s authors. “This year’s El Niño is likely to be the strongest on record.”The study found that during the La Niña winter of 2022-23, stronger winds over north India helped disperse emissions from stubble-burning and local sources. The altered circulation bypassed Delhi and its surroundings and transported these pollutants southwards towards peninsular India. This resulted in substantially higher PM2.5 levels in cities such as Mumbai and Thiruvananthapuram.The following winter, the atmospheric setup changed. Under El Niño, winds over northern India were weaker and passed through areas, including Delhi and Jaipur, rather than carrying pollutants away. The resulting stagnation favoured the accumulation of PM2.5. Jaipur, for instance, recorded an increase of about 50% compared with the 2019-22 average, while Delhi logged a spike of over 10%.Weather conditions also mattered differently in the two years. Rain can remove pollutants from air, while high pressure, weak winds and a shallow boundary layer can trap them close to the ground. In Jaipur, rainfall was more strongly associated with lower PM2.5 during 2022-23, whereas surface pressure became a more important factor during 2023-24, leading to pollution spikes after rain.The researchers also used backward air-mass trajectories to trace where the air reaching cities had travelled from. Jaipur continued to receive air from polluted northern regions during the El Niño winter. Hyderabad, by contrast, received more marine and southern air, helping explain why its pollution pattern moved in the opposite direction.
Overall, the study found substantial year-to-year PM2.5 variations from average levels in 2019-22 — ranging from about a 40% decline to a 70% increase, despite no major changes in emissions or pollution-control policies during the period. The authors underlined that the correlations neither establish direct causation nor can these be extrapolated to other years.For Delhi-NCR, this has an important implication: relatively low local or agricultural emissions do not automatically guarantee cleaner air if large-scale circulation turns stagnant. Conversely, even substantial emissions can have a smaller local impact when strong winds efficiently disperse or divert them.The winter pollution story may begin in Delhi and its neighbourhood, but increasingly, the weather that decides its intensity is being written on a much larger canvas.

Kenya reports second death from Ebola
NAIROBI, Oct 23 - Kenya has recorded a second Ebola death, the health ministry said late on Friday, adding that the 65-year-old woman had developed symptoms during quarantine and was a close relative of a Kenyan man who died of Ebola earlier this month.
The outbreak, which started in the Democratic Republic of Congo, has now been reported in four countries across eastern, central and western Africa, giving it the widest geographic spread of any Ebola outbreak on the continent to date.
Kenya's first Ebola case was identified this month in a man who travelled from Congo to Nairobi and died at a Nairobi hospital on October 5.
Since then, Kenyan authorities have traced 135 contacts, all of whom were placed in quarantine, with nine cases confirmed.
The Ebola victim who died on Friday evening was a direct contact of the index patient, the ministry said.
"This loss brings the number of deaths to two among the nine confirmed cases. The remaining seven patients continue to receive care in the two isolation facilities," the ministry said, adding there was no evidence of community spread in the country.
Late on Monday, the US State Department advised Americans to reconsider travel to Kenya and raised its travel advisory level for the country because of health risks.
On Tuesday, Nigeria became the fourth African country to report an Ebola case, with officials scrambling to work out how and where the patient, who had not travelled to the Democratic Republic of Congo, contracted the disease.
Ebola has infected nearly 10,000 people and killed more than 4,600 in Congo. The disease can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhoea and, in severe cases, internal and external bleeding. Only people with symptoms can transmit the virus.
The rare Ebola species behind the current outbreak has no approved treatment or vaccine. REUTERS

Russia Targets Pro-Ukraine US Candidates With AI-Driven Influence Campaign Ahead of Midterms
Russia has launched a covert online influence campaign aimed at undermining both Democratic and Republican US candidates supportive of Ukraine ahead of the midterm elections, Politico reported on October 21.
Senate Intelligence Committee Vice Chair Mark Warner and House Intelligence Committee ranking member Jim Himes described the findings after receiving a classified US intelligence community report on foreign election interference earlier this week.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“It’s a carnival out there,” Himes told Politico, describing Russian digital operations as designed to generate “a sense of chaos and anarchy.”
According to Himes, the campaign includes efforts to undermine trust in US institutions and cast doubt on the reliability of voting machines. Warner added that Russia is using artificial intelligence tools to spread such narratives faster and target Americans more effectively.
The lawmakers did not identify specific candidates targeted by the campaign. However, they stated that political figures supportive of Ukraine from both major US parties were likely targets of Russian influence efforts.
The US intelligence community has not identified evidence that Russia attempted to hack election infrastructure or political campaign networks, according to the lawmakers.
Politico also pointed to one Russia-linked operation that has already surfaced publicly. Graphika, a company that tracks online influence operations and disinformation, reported that Storm-1516 is a Russian-linked influence network active since 2023. The network produced and distributed deepfake videos on X accusing Texas Senate candidate James Talarico of sexual assault.
X separately announced that it had removed more than 13,000 accounts linked to election-related influence campaigns originating from Russia, Iran, and China. The platform described the campaigns as targeting candidates and public figures across the political spectrum.
Warner noted that Russia has repeatedly conducted influence operations around US elections since 2016. Russian intelligence officers were previously linked to the hacking of the Democratic National Committee and campaign staff accounts during that year’s presidential race.
Politico reported that the classified intelligence assessment also detailed influence attempts linked to China and Iran, although Warner and Himes singled out Russia as conducting particularly significant activity.
A spokesperson for House Intelligence Committee Chair Rick Crawford criticized the disclosure, accusing Warner and Himes of selectively releasing classified information.
Himes stated that the committee is expected to receive another bipartisan classified briefing on election threats next week.
Russia’s latest campaign builds on disinformation tactics already documented across Europe. UNITED24 Media previously reported that the Kremlin-linked Storm-1516 network used fake journalist identities, fabricated articles, and AI-generated videos to target elections and political figures while eroding trust in Western institutions.

When politicians echo white replacement theory, extremist activity rises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:00:05 UTC
05:00:05 KST

When political leaders publicly endorse white replacement conspiracy theories, their rhetoric is linked to measurable increases in real-world extremist activity. A recent analysis published in PLOS One shows that the repetition of these narratives by elected officials corresponds with upticks in white supremacist organizing. The research also highlights how such statements shape local public attention regarding immigration.
White replacement theories are false narratives claiming that a secretive group is orchestrating mass immigration to replace a nation’s native-born population. These ideological tropes have periodically resurfaced across Western countries over the last century. In the United States, these conspiracy theories often suggest that white Christian conservatives are being intentionally reduced to a demographic minority. Historically, these ideas were confined to fringe extremist groups trying to recruit members and justify hostilities.
Over the past decade, variations of these conspiracies have entered mainstream political discourse. Some politicians use explicit language about demographic replacement or foreign invasions. Others employ subtler versions of the narrative, alleging that left-leaning politicians are encouraging illegal immigration simply to secure future voters.
Sociologists Jack Gabriel Risien Wippell and Laura Dugan from The Ohio State University wanted to see if these political statements translate into tangible social consequences. The researchers designed a study to evaluate how political endorsements of these theories relate to both general public interest and extremist mobilization. They hypothesized that signaling from prominent leaders might create a sense of emboldenment among individuals holding prejudiced views. By normalizing hostile language, elites can lower the perceived social risks of collective action and make extreme ideas seem viable.
The researchers compiled a database of public statements made by federal and state legislators, as well as political candidates, between 2021 and 2023. They specifically isolated 25 endorsements of replacement theories that received coverage in major news outlets. To count as an endorsement, a statement had to reference immigration as a deliberate plot to replace a native population. By focusing on media-amplified statements, they ensured they were analyzing rhetoric that actually reached a broad audience.
Wippell and Dugan first conducted a national analysis using weekly data spanning three years. They compared the timing and accumulation of the political endorsements against weekly Google Trends data for the topic of immigration. They also measured national extremist activity using data from the Anti-Defamation League, an open-source database compiled from news reports and government documents. This dataset provided a comprehensive record of white supremacist protests and public demonstrations.
At the national level, the researchers found a positive association between the accumulation of these political statements and subsequent white supremacist events. As media reports of politicians endorsing replacement narratives piled up, the frequency of extremist demonstrations increased across the country. The relationship between the political rhetoric and national Google searches for immigration was not statistically significant.
The research team then shifted their focus to a state-level analysis, evaluating the data on a monthly basis. They linked each political endorsement to the specific state represented by the politician making the claim. For this local analysis, they tracked state-level Google searches for immigration and expanded their extremist activity metrics to include the distribution of white supremacist propaganda.
Within individual states, the associations were distinct and robust. When state representatives endorsed replacement theories, their specific constituencies experienced an increase in both white supremacist events and propaganda distributions. The data indicates that local political environments play a highly influential role in community-level extremist behavior.
The state-level analysis also revealed a shift in general public attention. The accumulation of replacement theory endorsements by local politicians was tied to an increase in Google searches about immigration within their respective states. This suggests that politicians exert a stronger influence on the attention of their immediate constituents than on the broader national discourse.
The researchers note a few limitations regarding how the data captures media exposure. Tracking the exact public reach of a news story is incredibly difficult, as clips and quotes often spread virally through person-to-person communication and unmonitored social networks. The study treats media exposure as a flat metric between statements, which likely underestimates the true societal spread of the rhetoric.
The tools used to measure public attention also come with inherent caveats. Google Trends measures search interest for a topic relative to all other searches, rather than providing absolute search volumes. This means the data reflects proportional shifts in what the public is paying attention to within a limited attention economy.
Finally, the relationship between political statements and public attention might not be a one-way street. Supplementary analyses by the researchers suggest a bidirectional dynamic at the state level. While political endorsements might draw public focus toward immigration, politicians might also be reacting to rising public interest by increasing their use of these narratives.
The study, “Endorsing narratives of white replacement: Elite discourse, public attention, and extremist mobilization,” was authored by Jack Gabriel Risien Wippell and Laura Dugan.

Warhound wants to engineer and clone military superdogs—can they do it?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:58:08 UTC
04:58:08 KST

A new biotechnology start-up wants to use gene-editing technology, cloning and advanced military technology to create a new dog optimized for combat. But does the science to back up its claims exist? And if so, can the company possibly deliver on the idea?
The start-up, called Warhound, is the brainchild of Colossal Biosciences’ Ben Lamm and Anduril Industries’ Palmer Luckey. Warhound intends to clone and genetically modify military service dogs to produce larger, more efficient working dogs for use in conflict zones and policing. Experts say that the science the company proposes is possible—but that it is also prone to error, inefficiencies and a slew of ethical concerns.
Warhound has already biobanked the genetic material from a group of elite service dogs, Lamm says, including breeds such as Belgian Malinois and shepherds. Warhound’s scientists intend to clone the cells of those dogs and edit the cloned embryos to produce new puppies. They’re expecting the first litters in early 2027.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Cloning dogs is not a new science. Research has shown that cloning service dogs produces puppies that have many of the same desirable traits. But the process can be harmful, says Lisa Moses, a veterinarian and bioethicist at Harvard University. The rate of successful live offspring remains low among the cloned dogs, and the process can put the surrogate mother in danger.
“It is by no means a perfect science, and by that, I mean it’s still a fairly inefficient process,” Moses says. “It requires a lot of dogs to have invasive things done to them and to be killed in order to produce one cloned puppy.”
Warhound intends to make several genetic modifications in its cloned embryos to make the dogs healthier, stronger and better workers. First, the company hopes to modify the dogs to reduce the risk of health conditions such as hip disease, vision loss and cancer predisposition—and, eventually, to optimize ideal traits for military dogs.
“The standard is that no dog enters service carrying a genetic marker known to cause a common career-ending condition,” Lamm says. “From there, we are working on edits specifically targeting additional longevity and health, as well as performance factors.”
Both scientists and private companies have genetically edited dogs before, and the research can “accelerate really fast because genomics in dog breeds already has a lot of data,” says Ben Novak, chief scientist at Revive and Restore, who works on wildlife cloning for conservation. Researchers have edited dogs to tweak genes for hip dysplasia, make them hypoallergenic and treat muscle disease, although the long-term health effects of these changes remain unclear.
But optimizing traits at scale and across service dogs could take time—and leave room for unintended consequences, Novak adds.
“It can be hard to figure out exactly what genetic element is creating a trait,” he says, “and some traits can be the combinations of hundreds or thousands of mutations across genes.”
Colossal Biosciences, which has a stake in Warhound and is providing much of the science, is no stranger to genetic engineering: last year the firm cloned and edited a gray wolf to create an animal that was genetically similar to the extinct dire wolf. The process for Warhound will look similar, Lamm says, but with modern dogs.
In its launch announcement, Warhound said it had raised $200 million in funding. Novak says that from a commercial perspective, the concept makes sense.
“For a biotech company, it is certainly a slam dunk idea: guaranteed military contracts, which is the most funded aspect of U.S. government science, with an actual potential to improve a sector of military use that I think everyone can agree is important.”
But from a bioethics standpoint, Moses says, involving man’s best friend in biotechnology can quickly become fraught.
“I’ve had lots of conversations about what Colossal Biosciences is doing and has done. But when you start messing around with dogs, people feel very differently,” Moses says.
Robert Lanza, former chief scientific officer at the Astellas Institute for Regenerative Medicine and a pioneer of cloning research, says the ethics and technique of Warhound’s premise are far from “black or white.”
“I think such goals are definitely achievable from a scientific perspective. But then again, it’s highly unlikely it could be done without many, many failures and defects,” he says.

Greek Parliament approves social media ban for children under 15

Greek Parliament approves social media ban for children under 15
The Parliament of Greece approved a bill on October 23, 2026, banning children under the age of 15 from using social media. The restriction will take effect on January 1, 2027, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The bill was backed only by the ruling New Democracy party, while major opposition parties voted against it or abstained. Parliamentary debates lasted more than 16 hours.
Under the legislation, platforms will be required to introduce reliable age-verification mechanisms. These may include the government applications Kids Wallet and Gov.gr Wallet, or other solutions that comply with national and European legislation. Platforms will receive only confirmation of whether a user has reached the age of 15, without access to their name, date of birth, or other personal data.
Companies that fail to comply with the requirements will face fines of up to 6% of their global annual turnover, in line with the provisions of the European Union’s Digital Services Act (DSA).
Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis announced plans to introduce the ban in April this year. Authorities say the measure is necessary to protect children's mental health, arguing that endless scrolling deprives minors of sleep, concentration and time to socialize with their peers, while platform algorithms are designed to be addictive.
Greece is becoming one of the first European Union countries to introduce such a restriction. Australia previously implemented a similar ban for children under 16. In France, a similar law was rejected by the Constitutional Council. Athens is also calling for a common EU-wide approach to protecting minors in the digital environment.
Initially, the ban will cover platforms such as Instagram, Facebook and TikTok, with the list potentially expanding in the future. Parents will not be able to grant permission for their children to use social media, and existing accounts belonging to children under 15 will not be exempt from the restriction.
Earlier, it was reported that Türkiye had introduced new regulations prohibiting social media platforms from providing services to children under the age of 15.

Cybersecurity experts sound the alarm over a new era of AI-powered hacking
Kyiv • UNN
Experts warn of a massive wave of vulnerabilities that AI is finding and helping to exploit. Millions of attacks targeting PHP vulnerabilities are already being recorded.
Cybersecurity leaders are sounding the alarm after a serious vulnerability was discovered this week. They predict that in the coming months, artificial intelligence (AI) tools will uncover even more fundamental weaknesses in the global internet infrastructure, reports UNN, citing The Guardian.
"I no longer think we will be able to fix all the bugs," Sam Altman said on Thursday evening, joining other industry leaders who have voiced similar concerns. Against the backdrop of events already dubbed "Black October" (during which researchers used AI to identify critical flaws in a programming language used by millions of websites and which may have remained vulnerable for years), technology sector representatives are warning that AI will be used both to find and to exploit vulnerabilities in security systems—and on an unprecedented scale and at incredible speed.
According to Jason Clinton, Anthropic's deputy chief information security officer, a "tsunami of vulnerabilities" is coming. "There simply will not be enough time to patch critical infrastructure," Clinton wrote on the social network X on Thursday evening. Marc Benioff, CEO of Salesforce, agreed, calling the situation a "red alert level of threat."
Matthew Prince, CEO of Cloudflare, said that AI is capable of finding and identifying security gaps in ways and at a speed that will have catastrophic consequences: cybersecurity professionals simply will not be able to respond to these threats in time. "It will feel as though the sky is falling to Earth. It will feel as though there is nothing we can do.
The next two years will be extraordinarily, simply unbelievably, packed with the emergence of new tools that have limitless patience for searching for vulnerabilities across the entire internet," he wrote in a post on the social network X.
Although cybersecurity experts have been warning for several months about a "vulnpocalypse"—a situation in which artificial intelligence makes it significantly easier to identify security flaws—it was during "Black October" that researchers managed to use AI to discover such a fundamental and critical vulnerability, which was announced on October 21.
Serious vulnerabilities were discovered in the PHP programming language, leaving millions of websites built on it potentially vulnerable to hackers for years. According to some experts' estimates, 70% of all websites on the internet were at risk of being hacked.
However, although AI will help identify vulnerabilities at unprecedented speed, technology industry leaders fear that malicious actors will use it just as quickly to exploit these flaws.
Attempts to exploit the PHP vulnerability have already begun.
After information about the vulnerabilities was disclosed, operators of government and private websites in the United States and the United Kingdom temporarily suspended their operation to address the flaws. The U.S. National Security Agency (NSA) issued a warning recommending that administrators of all websites running on PHP install the relevant updates immediately. The NSA noted that malicious actors could try to exploit these vulnerabilities to gain unauthorized access to servers.

"Such an access vector could allow malicious actors to steal confidential data, disrupt services, or penetrate deeper into the network," the warning said.
In a post on the social network X, Prince said that the security company CloudFlare had recorded attempts by thousands of users to exploit PHP vulnerabilities as early as 10 hours before the official announcement.
"Within 45 minutes of the announcement, the number of such attempts had risen to tens of thousands; after two hours, to hundreds of thousands; and now we are talking about millions," he wrote.
In their blog, researchers from Wiz, a platform focused on securing artificial intelligence systems, noted that this was "one of the most serious vulnerabilities ever discovered in PHP, and possibly one of the most dangerous in the history of software."
"These fundamental flaws had existed for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an extraordinarily complex chain of actions—at the limit of what human researchers are even capable of carrying out in practice," they wrote.

The discovery of a Jewish Negro League star forces a rewrite of Jewish baseball history
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:56:07 UTC
04:56:07 KST

For more than a century, Oscar Levis was hiding in plain sight.
He pitched a no-hitter and dominated the Cuban Winter League. He tallied five straight seasons without losing a game against one of the Northeast’s toughest white semiprofessional clubs. He was so dominant that W. Rollo Wilson, the preeminent Black sportswriter of his era, held him up as a benchmark of pitching excellence – the kind of player a younger star would aspire to equal.
For all of that, Oscar Levis does not appear on any official roster of Jewish major leaguers.
The reason is straightforward and ugly: the Negro Leagues – the professional leagues Black players built and played in after being barred from the White major leagues – were not recognized as major leagues until 2020. For decades, that exclusion meant that players like Levis were not considered major leaguers at all.
And there was another reason: Levis was Black, and the prevailing assumption was that Blackness and Jewishness were identities that seldom, if ever, overlapped.
But months of archival research, family testimony, and genealogical detective work have now established what Levis’ contemporaries occasionally hinted at but never fully acknowledged: Oscar Levis was Jewish. The son of a Jewish father from Jamaica whose family roots stretched through the Caribbean back to Portugal, Levis carried a Jewish identity that his world did not know how to fully accommodate – and that baseball history, until now, did not know how to find.
A clue left in the digital margins
In 2018, Gary Ashwill, the foremost authority on Negro League statistics and co-creator of the comprehensive database Seamheads, published an article identifying Oscar Levis as Jamaican by birth – a fact that had itself been hidden for decades, since Levis routinely identified himself as Panamanian, the country where he grew up and learned to pitch. Ashwill noted that Levis’ father was a man named Amos DaCosta Levy, but that beyond the name, he had been unable to learn much more about him.
People reach out with information on webpage
What happened next was the digital equivalent of a message in a bottle. Readers who recognized the Levy name began leaving comments on Ashwill’s webpage. One, who identified himself as Amos Levy’s great-great-nephew, wrote that Amos was Jewish. Another commenter was more specific. “I’ve never heard of [Oscar],” she wrote, “but just wanted to say that Amos DaCosta Levy is one of my ancestors. He was not a black man, he was a white, yes Jewish, man.”
Those comments caught my attention. My previous foray into Jewish baseball history had already produced one meaningful discovery – the posthumous identification of one-game major leaguer Monte Pfeiffer as Jewish. But where Pfeiffer had played a single game, Levis had played and been a star for more than a decade.
The blog comments served as a starting point, not a conclusion. Tracking down their claims took months. I reviewed digitized editions of The Gleaner, Jamaica’s newspaper of record, which confirmed DaCosta Levy’s public prominence – his election to the Legislative Council, his Masonic leadership, his business dealings. Jamaican civil and ecclesiastical records, accessible through genealogical archives, corroborated the synagogue marriage record for DaCosta Levy’s parents. I contacted historians specializing in Caribbean Jewish history, including Stanley Mirvis, whose scholarship on Jamaican Jewry provided crucial context for understanding how Jewish identity operated in that world.
I communicated directly with DaCosta Levy’s descendants, who were able to confirm, from within their own family history, what the blog commenters had suggested. And I called Shaare Shalom Synagogue in Kingston – the historic heart of Jamaica’s Sephardic Jewish community – where staff were able to confirm the existence of records connecting the Levy family to the congregation. The picture that emerged from these independent sources was consistent: DaCosta Levy was a member of Jamaica’s Jewish community, and Levis was his son.
When the evidence pointing to Levis’ Jewish identity began to solidify, I reached out to Rebecca Alpert, a professor of religion at Temple University who had spent years thinking about exactly this kind of story.
Her 2011 book, “Out of Left Field: Jews and Black Baseball,” examined the largely overlooked history of Jewish involvement in the Negro Leagues – and her expertise at the intersection of religion and sports made her the ideal partner for a discovery that sat squarely in both. Together, we reviewed the historical record, stress-tested the evidence and considered what Levis’ story means for our understanding of Jews in baseball – a conversation that only deepened my confidence in what the research had found.
An upbringing at the margins of Jamaica’s Jewish world
DaCosta Levy was born in 1848 in Port St. Mary, Jamaica, to parents whose marriage is recorded in synagogue records. According to family history, DaCosta Levy’s family lineage traced to Portugal, where his ancestors had been mariners – almost certainly Sephardic Jews who scattered across the Atlantic world after the Inquisition. By the late 19th century, DaCosta Levy had built a prosperous mercantile firm, Levy Brothers & Company, that imported goods from the United States and England. He was elected to Jamaica’s Legislative Council for St. Mary’s Parish. He was also a Worshipful Master of the Caledonian Masonic Lodge, helped found Jamaica’s Masonic Benevolence Association, and served as a justice of the peace. A 1919 article in the Kingston Daily Gleaner, written when DaCosta Levy was living in Panama, called him “the oldest foreign Mason on the Isthmus” and praised him for “faithful services.”
Levis’ mother, Theodosia Foreman, was a Black Jamaican woman who worked as a dressmaker. The union between DaCosta Levy and Foreman was not uncommon in the Caribbean Jewish world of the era. Mirvis has explained that relationships between Jewish men and women of color were relatively widespread in Jamaica and throughout the Caribbean, shaped by the power dynamics of the plantation economy. The children of such relationships occupied a complicated place – neither fully inside nor fully outside the Jewish community, a status scholars have described as “peripheral inclusion.” Contemporary observers, including one 20th-century American rabbi, noted that many Black Jamaicans bore Jewish surnames and took pride in their heritage. Levis was among them.
That identity, however, needs to be understood on its own historical terms – rooted in the Caribbean Sephardic world Levis was born into, not the standards prevalent elsewhere. Mirvis has explained that Jamaica’s Jewish community in this period was composed almost entirely of former Portuguese conversos and their descendants, a population that had never developed the same rigidity around matrilineal descent that characterizes Orthodox practice. Within this particular Sephardic tradition, patrilineal descent carried more communal weight than it did elsewhere – a distinction that shaped how men like Oscar were understood by those around them. In the Caribbean context specifically – where relationships between Jewish men and women of color were common, and children of those unions were frequently integrated into Jewish social and economic life, however conditionally – the boundaries of who belonged were porous in ways that defy easy categorization.
Levis appears to have understood himself within this tradition. His family has confirmed that he was proud of his Jewish heritage and aware of it throughout his life, though he rarely foregrounded it publicly – a pattern consistent with Black Jews of the period, who frequently navigated skepticism from both White Jewish communities and the broader Black community. Jewish Baseball News – an independent organization that maintains the definitive roster of Jewish players in professional baseball – applies a deliberately inclusive standard. “We define the term ‘Jewish’ broadly,” the organization states. “If a player has at least one Jewish parent … does not practice another faith, and is content to be identified as a Jew, we include him.” Levis had a Jewish father, was publicly identified as Jewish by contemporaries, and his family confirms he was proud of that heritage throughout his life.
Growing up on the color line
By the time Levis was a young man, his family had relocated to Panama, drawn by the economic opportunities opening up around the canal. It was a decision that shaped him as much as his father’s bloodline.
The US-controlled Panama Canal Zone was a masterclass in racial hierarchy. White American workers received higher wages, better housing, and superior facilities on what the system called the “gold roll.” Black workers – among them the tens of thousands drawn from Jamaica and Barbados to perform the most grueling excavation labor – were paid lower wages, housed in substandard quarters, and segregated at pay windows, hospitals, and schools. Levis, known locally as “Chick Levy,” would have understood the color line intimately before he ever set foot in the United States.
Despite those conditions, it was in Panama that he became a baseball star. He emerged as the premier pitcher on the isthmus, a “popular figure in the baseball world” celebrated for his dominance of the local clubs. Even after his American career took off, Levis returned in 1923 to pitch for a combined Panama–West Indian All-Star team before massive crowds at Balboa Stadium. Two years later, the Panamanian government awarded him a medal for his baseball achievements, and in the 1930s, he was offered – but declined – the opportunity to coach Panama’s national team for the Central American Olympics.
The Cuban stars and a career in the shadows
Levis arrived in New York in 1918. By 1921, Alex Pompez – the Cuban-American entrepreneur who owned the Cuban Stars and would eventually be inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame – had recruited him to join the team. Levis became one of the first non-Cuban international players in the Negro leagues, and one of their most effective pitchers.
What followed was a career of genuine distinction. Levis pitched in the Negro leagues for the Cuban Stars (East) and the Hilldale Daisies across more than a decade, supplementing the short Negro League season with year-round appearances in exhibition games, barnstorming tours and the Cuban Winter League, where he pitched for the Almendares, the Habana Reds and the Marianao Grey Monks. On Oct. 11, 1924, he threw the first no-hitter in Cuban baseball history. He was voted to the All-Eastern Team in 1925 and led the Eastern Colored League in shutouts in 1927. He went five straight seasons without losing a game to a rival club which fielded white players, the Brooklyn Bushwicks. Cuban sports editor Jose Massaguer calculated that Levis pitched in more than 500 games across his career, and Cuban pitching records attributed to him reportedly stood for decades beyond his retirement.
None of that success saved him from the color line that excluded Black players from what was known at the time as Major League Baseball. Ashwill, the statistician, has assessed Levis as a very good pitcher whose talent was more than sufficient for the white majors – a verdict echoed by sportswriter Rollo Wilson, who in 1929 called Levis one of the sharpest and most effective right-handers in the game.
In 2020, Major League Baseball officially recognized the Negro Leagues as major leagues, and in 2024 incorporated their statistics into its historical record. By that accounting, Levis pitched in 102 major league games and accumulated a career WAR (wins above replacement) of 12.9, which ranks eighth all-time among Jewish pitchers: Sandy Koufax (48.9), Max Fried (32.3), Ken Holtzman (27.3), Dave Roberts (23.6), Barney Pelty (19.2), Steve Stone (17.1) and Erskine Mayer (13.5).
Based on his officially recognized statistics alone, Levis had the most successful professional career of any Jewish player in the 1920s.
Hidden in plain sight
What makes Levis’ story even more compelling is that his Jewish identity was not entirely hidden – it surfaced in scattered notices buried in the newspaper record.
In 1926, after Max Rosner – the Jewish immigrant who owned the rival white semi-pro team the Brooklyn Bushwicks – signed Levis’ naturalization papers, a Brooklyn newspaper ran the headline: “Oscal, Cuban Pitcher, Is a Spanish Jew.” The following year, a New York sportswriter named Aloysious Palma made the point plainly. John McGraw, manager of the (baseball) Giants, had recently signed a Jewish infielder named Andy Cohen specifically to attract Jewish fans to the Polo Grounds. Palma wrote that Levis had the talent and ability to pitch for the New York Giants – that he should have been McGraw’s Jewish star. He was the right religion. He had the right arm. He was the wrong color.
A third article, published during his managerial tenure in the 1930s, again noted his Sephardic Jewish heritage. “Oscal Levis, pitcher and manager,” the Brooklyn Times Union reported, was “of Spanish-Jewish extraction.”
Taken together, the three articles form a quiet paper trail – Levis’ Jewish identity was occasionally noted, but never coherently recognized or integrated into the broader baseball record.
He was neither the mainstream white Jewish player typically celebrated in the New York press, nor the Black player whose Jewish identity was fully acknowledged and chronicled in the Black press. He belonged to both worlds, an identity for which mainstream America had no framework.
Harlem, and the life after
When Levis’ playing and managing days ended, he built a second life in Harlem, New York. He and his wife, Lovana, operated Chick’s Bar and Grill on Seventh Avenue – a short walk from the Apollo Theater – for 35 years, making it a mainstay of the neighborhood. He served as chairman of the Harlem Riverside Tavern Owners Association, raising money for hospitals, the YMCA, the Police Athletic League and the Boy Scouts. He organized interracial boxing events at the Golden Gate Arena to keep youth out of trouble. And he was a 33rd-degree Prince Hall Freemason – the highest rank of the Scottish Rite – following directly in the tradition of his father, who had served as Worshipful Master of a Masonic lodge in Jamaica.
But even in retirement, Levis never left the game of baseball. Friends recalled that he loved to “stick his finger in the baseball pie whenever he got a chance.” He returned to Cuba just to sit in the stands “day and night.”
He was also, in his own quiet way, a witness to the great transformation of the sport he had played under the cruelest constraints. As chairman of the Jackie Robinson Day Committee, Levis helped organize the celebration and personally presented the ceiling-shattering Black major leaguer with gifts from fans across the country. New York Amsterdam News reporter George Palmer captured what the day meant to him:
“He claims that one of his biggest thrills was Jackie Robinson Day – when he had the chance to see how the public took to Jackie. He, as a former ball player, knew the hardships and obstacles which Jackie had to overcome to reach the top. To him, Jackie Robinson’s Day was what every colored ball player dreams about – so much so that it was like a dream come true.”
A name that belongs on the list
In 1943, Rollo Wilson wrote a column pushing back against the habit of comparing Black ballplayers to white stars. The “Black Babe Ruth” formulation, he argued, was both lazy and diminishing – to the player being praised and to the tradition being ignored. Black baseball had produced its own immortals, and Wilson listed Oscar Levis among them. To be considered their equal, Wilson wrote, was a standard worth chasing for any young baseball star.
Just as Wilson named Levis among the immortals of Black baseball, this research names him among the greats of Jewish baseball. His inclusion changes the historical record – and adds a dimension to the story of Jewish contributions to the game that has long been hiding in plain sight.
He was one of the finest pitchers of his era. He was Black and he was Jewish. And for a century, baseball didn’t have the categories to say so.
It does now.

Tigray rebels urged to disarm as commander vows to fight Ethiopia’s gov’t
Rebel commander pledged to continue fighting government-allied forces who seized Ethiopia’s Tigray capital.
Residents recount drone strikes in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region
An official in Tigray’s new federally backed administration has urged rebel forces to lay down their weapons in the northern Ethiopian region.
The call on Friday came hours after a rebel commander told his fighters to continue resisting government-backed forces despite losing control of Mekelle, the Tigray region’s capital.
Fighters from the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) were forced to withdraw from Mekelle in early October, after government-allied fighters entered the city to crush a rebel attempt to overthrow Ethiopia’s government.
Ethiopia’s government then installed a six-month caretaker administration in Tigray, promising to restore services, help displaced people return and prepare for elections.
But some fighting has continued, with Mekelle residents reporting a drone strike that killed four people and injured six others as they loaded goats onto a truck on Tuesday. The casualties could not be independently verified.
Redae Halefom Woldeselassie, a senior official in Tigray’s new caretaker administration, said rebel forces were collapsing and urged fighters to lay down their weapons.
“This is not the time for settling scores – I call upon you to return to your homes and continue your civilian lives,” he said in Mekelle.
He dismissed the prospect of the rebels retaking the city, maintaining the conflict served a small clique of leaders and not the people of Tigray.
Hours earlier, Lieutenant General Fisseha Kidanu, who was identified in a television broadcast as commander of the Tigray army, pledged to reverse recent military setbacks, saying Tigray was still at war.
“Local militias across the region – alongside all volunteers joining the resistance – are expected to engage the enemy,” he said Thursday on Tigray Broadcast Media, a new rebel television station. His location was not disclosed.
Fisseha urged attacks on government-held positions despite his opponents’ advantages in drones and heavy weapons. The TPLF has also claimed to have inflicted heavy losses on government forces. The Associated Press could not independently verify those claims.
The government’s allies include the Tigray Peace Force, comprising former members of the TPLF’s armed wing – a division within Tigrayan forces that has complicated the renewed conflict.
Redae said Ethiopian troops and allied forces were conducting joint security operations, including measures to prevent looting. He promised preparations for displaced residents to return but gave no timetable.
Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, speaking Monday to the Ethiopian Broadcasting Corporation, accused the TPLF of forcibly recruiting young people to fight instead of disarming under the terms of the November 2022 Pretoria peace agreement.
The renewed fighting has effectively shattered the agreement, which ended the region’s devastating 2020-2022 war.
That conflict caused an estimated 500,000 civilian deaths through violence, famine and collapsed health services, according to researchers at Ghent University in Belgium.

Northwest India turned drier, south wetter over 70 years, finds IMD study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:54:20 UTC
04:54:20 KST

The findings, published in the IMD’s peer-reviewed journal Mausam.
NEW DELHI: A new IMD study finds that northwest India has turned drier, with its dry climate zone expanding from about a quarter to one-third of the total geographical area, whereas the south peninsula became wetter due to a rise in overall quantitative rainfall over the past seven decades.The findings, published in the IMD’s peer-reviewed journal Mausam, note that the dry zone that once ended in western UP is now extending into the east of the state, with the scientists warning the change could affect paddy cultivation in the north.
‘Hot, dry zone pushed east into UP over past 70 years’
In northwest India, the hot semi-arid zone grew from about a quarter of the region’s area in 1951-1980 to a third in 1991-2020, while the temperate zone shrank from about a quarter to less than a fifth, meaning that an area equal to roughly 7% of the region moved into the drier zone as temperatures rose and rainfall declined, said the study.It said peninsular India, on the other hand, reported shrinking of its hot semi-arid zone from about 30% of the region to 16%, and most of that land moved into the tropical savannah zone, which now covers three-quarters of the peninsula, a change the authors attribute to rising rainfall over southern India.
“Within these broader shifts, Marathwada and west Vidarbha in Maharashtra moved into the hot semi-arid zone, and the tropical monsoon zone extended along the Konkan coast, coastal Karnataka and Kerala,” said the study, conducted by scientists from IMD and Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology.
“When we compared India’s climate map decade by decade from 1951 to 2020, the clearest change was in the north, where the hot, dry zone has pushed east into Uttar Pradesh, and because this is one of the country’s most important farming regions, the timing of sowing and harvesting there needs to be watched closely,” said Ananya Karmakar, the study’s lead author.Since the scientists highlight potential implications for agriculture and the need to track long-term climate shifts, the study could be handy for farm sector policymakers.
Vishwa Mohan is Senior Editor at The Times of India. He writes on environment, climate change, agriculture, water resources and clean energy, tracking policy issues and climate diplomacy. He has been covering Parliament since 2003 to see how politics shaped up domestic policy and India’s position at global platform. Before switching over to explore sustainable development issues, Vishwa had covered internal security and investigative agencies for more than a decade.
