UK-France deepen nuclear defence ties in first joint exercise
UK deepens nuclear defence ties with France in historic first joint air exercise as RAF Typhoon fighters join French Rafale jets in a French nuclear exercise.
- For the first time, RAF Typhoon fighters have taken part in a French nuclear air exercise, flying alongside French Rafale in a show of allied strength.
- Exercise “Rummy” marks a major step forward in UK-France defence cooperation under the Northwood Declaration.
- This partnership is vital to protecting the UK and deterring threats in an increasingly complex security environment.
The UK’s defences are being strengthened as RAF Typhoon fighters join French Rafale jets in a French nuclear exercise for the first time.
Exercise “Rummy” saw British and French forces operate side by side over the Mediterranean, demonstrating the readiness and capability that help deter threats and keep the UK safe.
Launching from Saint-Dizier Air Base in France, French Rafale simulated a nuclear strike mission, escorted by RAF Typhoons.
Conducted under robust safety and security arrangements, the exercise did not involve nuclear weapons. The exercise focused on improving how our forces work together, ensuring that if the UK faces a serious threat, our military can respond quickly and effectively alongside our closest European ally.
This exercise shows the UK’s commitment to standing united against any threat, strengthening deterrence and protecting peace and security alongside European Allies to protect national security. As close NATO Allies and European nuclear powers, the UK and France play a vital role in the security of the Euro-Atlantic region.
The exercise complements the work the UK is doing to invest £63 billion over the next four years to strengthen the UK’s nuclear deterrent, funding Dreadnought and SSN-AUKUS submarines, a new warhead and other vital nuclear work. The UK will also buy 12 F-35A aircraft and join NATO’s nuclear mission, delivering a more European NATO and reinforcing the UK’s contribution to collective defence.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said:
  This exercise marks a new chapter in the defence nuclear relationship between the United Kingdom and France.
As Europe’s nuclear powers, we have a shared responsibility to contribute to the security and stability of the Euro-Atlantic region. This exercise demonstrates the depth of our partnership, the credibility of our deterrents and our determination to stand together in the face of emerging threats.
In an increasingly dangerous world, our adversaries should be in no doubt: the UK and France remain united in our commitment to European security and to maintaining the deterrence that has helped preserve peace for generations.
Minister of the Armed Forces and Veterans Catherine Vautrin said:
  Having independent nuclear forces does not exclude coordination. Our nuclear cooperation with the United Kingdom keeps deepening: on Tuesday night, UK Typhoons participated for the very first time to a French nuclear exercise alongside Rafales.
Through coordination, our nuclear forces demonstrate that they can contribute even more significantly to the overall security of the Alliance and to the peace and stability of the Euro Atlantic area.
Exercise “Rummy” represents a key milestone in the UK-France nuclear partnership and the programme of cooperation agreed under the Northwood Declaration.
Demonstrating the commitment of both nations to jointly deter common threats, the exercise showcases the depth of their bilateral nuclear defence relationship and proves that British and French forces are ready and able to operate together to protect shared interests and contribute to collective security in a period of heightened global instability.
The UK and France are close defence allies, underpinned by the refreshed Lancaster House Agreement between our two nations, expanding our joint deployable force, boosting our nuclear cooperation and developing the next generation of high-tech weapons.
Notes to Editors:
- Operation Rummy took place from 20-21 October 2026.
- Both the UK and France and retain sovereign, independent nuclear forces and national decision making.

“The Israeli government has published a call for tender for the construction of more than 1,200 homes as part of the E1 project, and this undermines the prospects for a two-state solution,” El Anouni said.
“The implementation of the E1 project would split the West Bank into two. It would isolate East Jerusalem and further erode the viability of a two-state solution,” he added.

Living side by side in peace and security within recognized borders,” he said.

Argentine judge clears President Milei of wrongdoing in meme coin scandal
BUENOS AIRES, Oct 23 - An Argentine federal judge dropped a criminal investigation into President Javier Milei and his sister Karina Milei over a meme coin scandal on Friday, finding no evidence of fraud, according to court records.
Federal judge Marcelo Martinez de Giorgi had been investigating Milei's role in promoting a cryptocurrency that crashed, looking into allegations of fraud in the coin's launch.
Milei had recommended the little-known crypto coin Libra in a post on X in February 2025, kicking off a brief rally. He later deleted his post and denied having any link to the cryptocurrency, which soon plunged.
Martinez de Giorgi wrote that, while Milei's institutional standing could have given the coin's launch "greater impact" when he posted about it on X, those things "do not, in themselves, amount to a fraudulent scheme."
At the time of the currency's crash, Milei said he had acted "in good faith" and accused his political rivals of trying to take advantage of the situation.
"I was not aware of the details of the project and once I found out, I decided to not continue giving it publicity," he said.
Around $99 million worth of cryptocurrency was withdrawn from the marketplace of the coin by eight digital wallets linked to the crypto token's creator, blockchain researchers said.
Argentina's fintech chamber at the time said the case could potentially be a "rug pull," in which the developers of a crypto token draw legitimate investments, pumping up the value, only to later dump their stake.
The federal judge on Friday also dismissed an investigation into US businessman Hayden Davis, who had described himself as a "launch adviser" for the token and has acknowledged that he held close to $100 million after the crash. Davis has denied any wrongdoing. REUTERS

Drone strike sinks cargo ship near Romania, killing Ukrainian sailor. Romanian President blames Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:46:25 UTC
04:46:25 KST

A Russian drone strike sank the Comoros-flagged cargo ship Khoryv in the Black Sea near Romania’s port of Constanța on 23 October, killing a Ukrainian sailor and leaving three crew members missing. Nine others were rescued, Digi24 reported.
The sinking comes amid a surge in attacks on commercial shipping near Romania and Bulgaria, threatening civilian crews and routes used to transport Ukrainian agricultural exports. As Russia intensifies strikes on Ukrainian ports and shipping, the Danube corridor and nearby waters have become increasingly important to Ukraine’s maritime trade.
Romanian President Nicușor Dan blamed Russia for the attack, describing it as part of Moscow’s escalation of the war against Ukraine and its attacks on NATO’s eastern flank, Reuters reported.
Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry confirmed to Radio Svoboda that a Ukrainian citizen was among those killed.
Ukrainian sailor killed, three crew members missing
The Khoryv sent a distress signal at around 10 a.m. local time, about 13 nautical miles (24 kilometers) east of Constanța, just outside Romania’s territorial waters, Digi24 reported. The vessel caught fire, sustained major damage, and capsized, with only a small part of its hull remaining visible above the water.
Romania’s naval authority said 13 crew members were aboard: 10 Ukrainians and three Azerbaijanis. Rescue teams recovered nine sailors alive and one body, while three crew members remained missing, Reuters reported.
Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry said the vessel had been traveling from a Turkish port and confirmed that the Ukrainian Embassy in Romania had received information from Romanian authorities about one Ukrainian sailor’s death. Four Ukrainian survivors, including the captain, were taken to a hospital, while two others did not require medical assistance.
Attacks threaten Black Sea shipping
The sinking comes amid a surge in attacks on commercial vessels off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria. At least seven cargo ships have been hit over the past two weeks, with around 30 sailors reported dead or missing, according to Reuters.
The vessels targeted in recent incidents were either anchored near or heading toward the Sulina Canal, which connects the Danube River to the Black Sea. The canal has become a key export route for Ukraine, one of the world’s largest exporters of grain and vegetable oils.
Ukraine has increasingly relied on Danube ports and routes through Romanian territorial waters as Russia attacks its own Black Sea ports. Strikes on commercial vessels threaten crews and risk disrupting Ukrainian agricultural exports to international markets.
Russia has intensified attacks on Ukrainian ports and ships traveling to or from Ukraine. Moscow has described its strikes on vessels as retaliation for Ukrainian attacks on Russian or Russia-linked ships.
NATO plans stronger Black Sea surveillance
NATO said on 20 October it would send additional maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems, and drones to the Black Sea following the attacks on commercial shipping, according to Reuters. The alliance has not specified which capabilities it will deploy.
Romania, Ukraine, and Bulgaria have called on NATO to do more to protect commercial vessels. The latest sinking adds urgency to those calls as attacks increasingly affect shipping near NATO territory.
The latest incident highlights the growing risks to commercial shipping as Russia’s war against Ukraine increasingly affects maritime traffic beyond Ukraine’s own coastline.

AFOSI Seeks Enlisted Airmen to Train as Special Agents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:46:09 UTC
04:46:09 KST

The Air Force Office of Special Investigations is looking for a few good Airmen to swap jobs and become special agents.
No, they won’t get the 007 James Bond code—but they could learn to conduct counterintelligence and investigate procurement fraud and major crimes, OSI spokesperson Trevor Saylor told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
The office is looking to recruit agents from backgrounds other than law enforcement—it’s seeking Airmen with less than 11 years in service, with some exceptions, and is calling for applicants from other job fields in part because other areas of expertise can prove valuable in the unique types of investigations OSI conducts.
“A maintainer may understand an issue involving an aircraft or weapons system, while a contracting or acquisitions professional may recognize a process or irregularity relevant to a fraud investigation,” Special Agent Jennifer Holland, an OSI recruiter, said in a recent release. “Intelligence professionals may bring experience analyzing adversaries, identifying patterns and working with sensitive information.”
As threats to the Department of the Air Force cross traditional boundaries between criminal investigations, counterintelligence, cyber activity, and technology protection, that range of experience has become more relevant, Holland said.
Current threats and demands placed on OSI have “placed a renewed focus on defending the homeland, strengthening deterrence, protecting critical capabilities and preserving military advantages to generate combat power,” according to the release.
Skills such as foreign language proficiency, cybersecurity expertise and advanced computing skills are helpful, but not required or all that is needed.
“We’re looking for Airmen capable of exercising independent judgment, communicating with people from different backgrounds, managing competing priorities and documenting investigative activity with precision,” Holland said.
The requirements include:
- Technical sergeants who exceed the 11-year limit may be considered on a case-by-case basis and should pursue a time-in-service waiver through their local AFOSI detachment before applying.
- First-term Airmen must also meet applicable retraining window requirements.
- First-term Airmen assigned within the continental United States who are serving four-year enlistments may generally apply from the first duty day of the month in which they complete 35 months of their current enlistment through the last duty day of their 43rd month.
- For Airmen serving six-year enlistments, the corresponding window is from the 59th through the 67th month.
- First-term Airmen assigned outside the continental United States generally must apply between 12 and 15 months before their date eligible to return from overseas. They must also enter their 35th month of service, or 59th month for six-year enlistees, on or before that date.
- Applicants on a current Control Roster or with a current Unfavorable Information File are not eligible.
- Applicants must be worldwide qualified and have a current passing fitness assessment without exemptions or a profile.
- OSI does not require enlisted applicants to have a college degree.
Diverse Experience
Traditionally, law enforcement, cyber defense, healthcare, and logistics Airmen have had success translating their skills into the special agent role, Saylor wrote.
The recruitment effort isn’t from any shortage or operational gaps, Saylor said. Instead, it is part of an ongoing effort to maintain a “highly credible, robust force” of agents.
“We remain fully postured and staffed to meet all operational requirements,” Saylor wrote in an email.
OSI isn’t targeting a specific job field, and the application process is open to all Airmen who meet the criteria.
The office evaluates using the “Whole Airman” concept, Saylor wrote.
The concept focuses on evaluating Airmen as well-rounded individuals across their military and personal lives, using tools such as Enlisted Performance Reports and special duty selections, with an emphasis on leadership, job performance, self-improvement, base/community involvement, and well-being aspects tied to Airman fitness.
If an Airman submits their application package correctly and follows the USAF Personnel Center windows to secure a release from their current job, their AFSC Career Field Manager will be the final authority to approve or deny their request to move to special agent selection and training.
Application Steps:
- Apply online, complete documentation, and secure your commander’s recommendation.
- AFOSI requests your career-field release, though approval is not guaranteed.
- Approved applicants undergo suitability screening at their local unit.
- Candidates complete interviews and background investigations before final selection.
- The application process takes about three to six months.
If selected, the Airman then gets a short-term Assignment Limitation Code while they go through vetting and onboarding for special agent training, Saylor wrote.
Newly retrained Airmen-turned-agents will train at the Federal Law Enforcement Training Center in Glynco, Ga., to learn the fundamentals of federal criminal investigations before completing OSI-specific training.
They’ll then be put into specialties such as counterintelligence, procurement fraud, and major criminal investigative roles once they join their units, Saylor wrote.
Then there’s cyber.
“For roles in AFOSI’s cyber defense positions, AFOSI vectors Agents who show promise in the field into the specialized cyber fields upon the completion of probation,” Saylor wrote.
Most agents will begin their 15-month probationary period working felony-level criminal investigations and counterintelligence operations.
While some may specialize in certain areas, all special agents are expected to work interchangeably in a variety of missions and types of investigations.
Special Agents often travel more than many in the Air Force as part of their job and sometimes work high-stress cases that involve violent crime, fraud, and national security threats.
To mitigate burnout, Saylor wrote that OSI proactively supports personnel through a structured career progression plan and uses embedded wellness resources.
“Upon completing an initial probationary period of approximately 15 months focused on general criminal and counterintelligence work, agents have the opportunity to transition into specialized investigative sections,” Saylor wrote. “This structural pathway provides variety in their assignments and a deliberate break from the initial high-tempo investigative grind.”
OSI also has its own embedded chaplain corps and psychologists to provide ready access to mental health support, he wrote.

US midterms go down to wire as tight races put Republican Senate control at stake
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:45:52 UTC
04:45:52 KST

Washington, DC — As the Republican Party heads into the final weeks of the US midterm elections, they are working to protect several competitive Senate seats.
Meanwhile, Democrats are hoping to use their national poll lead to gain control of Congress.
Only 10 days remain before the crucial November 3 elections.
According to the most recent RealClearPolitics national average for congressional polling, Democrats currently lead Republicans by 50.5% to 42.4%.
Both the New York Times/Siena and CNN polls show Democrats leading Republicans by 11% and 10%, respectively.
These numbers indicate that Republicans face a difficult national environment. However, they don't determine who wins each state-by-state and district-by-district election.
David Schultz, Distinguished Professor of Political Science and Legal Studies at Hamline University in Minnesota, believes the true test is whether Democrats can connect voter dissatisfaction with the administration to viable solutions for voters' daily problems.
"Stronger Democratic candidates are combining opposition to Trump with issues such as affordability, opposition to the war, and concerns that are particularly relevant to voters in their own states and districts," Schultz told TRT World.
That combination could be crucial in states where Republican loyalty is high, but individual Democratic candidates are finding a way in.
Americans are going to elect all 435 members of the House of Representatives and fill 35 of the Senate's 100 seats.
The results will determine whether Republicans maintain control of Congress for the remaining two years of US President Donald Trump's term.
While the math appears simple, the election process is not.
Democrats must defend their competitive seats while also winning several seats Republicans currently hold. Narrow polling leads provide opportunities, but also leave enough room for either party to prevail.
Breadbasket of America
Schultz is closely watching Kansas, often called the "Breadbasket of America."
The Midwestern US state is rarely considered a major opportunity for Democrats in the Senate.
However, the Politix+ polling average shows Democrat Adam Hamilton 0.8 percentage points ahead of Republican Senator Roger Marshall.
In neighbouring Iowa, Republican Ashley Hinson leads Democrat Josh Turek by just 0.1 points.
Both races are virtually tied in those averages. Such small differences cannot provide a reliable advantage.
"For me, however, Kansas may be the most telling state," Schultz says. "Kansas has not been on many people's radar screens as a major Democratic opportunity."
He points to the state's 2022 referendum as an example of voters deviating from Republican positions on a major issue. In his view, that willingness to cross party lines helps explain why national political labels do not always accurately reflect voters' choices.
A Democratic Senate victory would be a significant result.
"It could indicate Democratic gains extending into areas that would typically not be considered competitive."
Schultz sees candidate quality as an important factor in both contests.
He believes Texas could become competitive sooner than he previously thought, though a narrow polling advantage does not guarantee a Democratic win.
"Perhaps 2026 will be the surprise year," he says.
Ohio, once a key presidential battleground, presents a different question: whether a well-known Democratic candidate can make the state competitive again.
"Democrats have a strong candidate there, which makes the race particularly interesting," Schultz says.
Alaska also remains close.
Democrat Mary Peltola leads Republican Senator Dan Sullivan by 1.8 points in the Politix+ average.
Schultz attributes Alaska's independent political streak to why competitive races there aren’t completely unexpected.
North Carolina displays a clearer Democratic advantage in current polling.
Roy Cooper leads Republican Michael Whatley by 10.3 points in the same average, making it one of the party's best opportunities to win a Republican-held seat.
Issues that matter to voters
However, the battle for Senate control also goes through states that Democrats must hold.
In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed leads Republican Mike Rogers by 2 points.
Georgia's Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff has a larger advantage, leading Republican Mike Collins by 8.1 points.
To lose a Democratic-held seat, the party would need to win another Republican seat elsewhere.
Schultz also warns against viewing Democratic polling strength as an endorsement of every aspect of the party's agenda.
He says some voters support Democratic candidates while also expressing concern about the party's ideological direction. Candidates in competitive states often respond by focusing on practical concerns rather than national ideological arguments.
"Many Democratic candidates in these races are emphasising local issues and attempting to differentiate themselves from the Democratic Socialists of America, or DSA, wing of the Democratic Party."
This is a key feature of US elections: candidates with the same party label can campaign very differently based on the communities they wish to represent.
A message that resonates with voters in a heavily liberal district may have less appeal in a closely divided state.
"They need to discuss local issues that matter to voters," Schultz says.
Affordability is central to his assessment.
Republicans campaigned on reducing financial pressure on voters, and voters are now evaluating the party's performance in office. Schultz also identifies voter dissatisfaction with foreign military involvement as a factor influencing the campaign.
The governing party faces a familiar historical challenge. Presidents' parties generally lose ground in midterm elections; however, exceptions exist (such as Republican gains under George W. Bush in 2002).
Nevertheless, Schultz argues that dissatisfaction alone is insufficient for Democrats to obtain the seats they need. Their candidates must provide voters with reasons to vote for them.
The national congressional polling lead measures overall party preference. It cannot accurately predict how that support will translate into seats, especially when several Senate contests remain separated by only a few points.
A Senate roadblock
The outcome will also shape how Washington is governed.
A Democratic Senate could block judicial nominations and other presidential appointments requiring its approval. That authority would apply to a Supreme Court nomination if a vacancy occurred.
"Perhaps the most significant consequence would be the loss of presidential control over the confirmation process for federal judges," Schultz says.
Democratic control of both chambers would increase scrutiny of the administration and make Republican legislation harder to pass.
Trump would still have his veto power, and Senate Republicans could still use the filibuster to block bills.
However, a Democratic Senate could deny confirmation to his nominees, including any nominee for a Supreme Court vacancy.

Trilateral peace talks with Russia, US negotiators to begin in November, Zelensky says

Trilateral peace talks with Russia, US negotiators to begin in November, Zelensky says
Negotiation teams from Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S. will meet in Abu Dhabi in November to begin peace talks, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 23.
"The plan is to meet in the first half of November and as early as possible, of course, but we are ready to meet any day, even tomorrow," Zelensky said in an address to the Hudson Institute think tank via a video call. "But it all depends on the Russians. We expected a trilateral meeting this October too, but it didn't happen because the Russians came up with another reason not to meet."
The peace discussions will begin at the technical level with negotiation teams, Zelensky said. If those efforts prove productive, then meetings between Zelensky, Russian President Vladimir Putin, and U.S. President Donald Trump will be held.
"We need to move from trilateral negotiations at the technical level to a meeting of leaders, because the key issues can only be resolved at that level," Zelensky said. 
Zelensky stressed the importance of including robust security guarantees for Ukraine in the negotiations and including Europe in the talks. Following any peace deal, a large Ukrainian army would need to be funded for at least 10 years, said Zelensky.
Arriving late to the address, Zelensky said he had just finished speaking with U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff regarding the negotiations. Earlier this week, Steve Witkoff met with Zelensky in Oslo during a trip to Norway before meeting with Putin.
In the address, the president also discussed restrictions on Ukraine's Starlink military systems.
"The speed restrictions for Starlink and Starshield are still in effect," Zelensky said. "The speed has not been restored. And the supply of interceptor missiles to protect against Russian ballistic missiles is still delayed."
Since mid-October, Starshield, the militarized version of Elon Musk's satellite internet system, Starlink, has been operating at limited capacity. With speed limit caps, Kyiv's ability to defend from deadly Russian jet-powered drones and coordinate strikes against Russian targets has been diminished.
Despite Ukrainian and U.S. officials apparently engaging in discussions to resolve the disruption to Ukrainian communications, nobody has publicly taken credit — or blame — for making or implementing the decision, which is not only politically "toxic" but also could have severe negative commercial implications for SpaceX, the operator of Starshield and Starlink.
Amid deteriorating U.S.-Ukrainian relations, Zelensky told the Hudson Institute that he hoped to strengthen the alliance between Kyiv and Washington.
"I really want our relations between Ukraine and America and with all our other partners to be just as strong as possible," Zelensky said. "Strong, truly friendly and without misunderstandings, of course. Because without America, without a strong America and America that cares about what happens in the world, the world would definitely be a worse place."
In recent weeks, Trump has lashed out at Zelensky, unilaterally imposed a failed energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, threatened to withhold aid from Kyiv, and lifted sanctions on Russian oil exports.
Trump has defended his easing of Russian sanctions, saying the move could prompt Moscow to join peace negotiations with Kyiv.

Ecuador judge orders pre-trial detention of leftist presidential candidate
Luisa Gonzalez, who lost to right-wing president Daniel Noboa in 2023, has called the arrest political persecution.
A judge in Ecuador has ordered that former left-wing presidential candidate Luisa Gonzalez remain detained following her arrest for alleged money laundering.
The order on Friday came the day after 48-year-old Gonzalez, who challenged right-wing President Daniel Noboa in the 2023 election, was arrested in the rural town of Canuto.
Gonzalez, her party and her close ally, former President Rafael Correa, have called the arrest political persecution.
Several other members of Gonzalez’s Citizen Revolution (RC) party have also recently faced charges.
They include Guayaquil Mayor Aquiles Alvarez, convicted of illegally selling subsidised fuel and former Vice President Jorge Glas, serving a sentence for corruption.
Prosecutors have said that Gonzalez is one of seven people under investigation for financing the 2023 presidential campaign. The probe focuses on $500,000 poured into advertising during the race.
Gonzalez has denied wrongdoing, dismissing the charges as “absurd”.
Citizen Revolution President Gabriela Rivadeneira told a news conference on Thursday that Gonzalez’s arrest “confirms or makes visible what we have been saying lately: Ecuador is living under a dictatorship”.
Gonzalez, a lawyer and former member of Ecuador’s National Assembly, lost to Noboa in an April 2025 run-off. She rejected the result as fraudulent.
Noboa, a close ally of US President Donald Trump, later accused Citizen Revolution of conspiring to attack him.
The party has since been banned from running in local elections next month.

The final polls before Election Day, published Friday evening by Israel's three main television channels, showed Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot's bloc holding a lead of two to six Knesset seats over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's governing coalition.
None of the polls projected either bloc winning the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
The Arab-majority parties, whose disqualifications last month were overturned by the Supreme Court, received 14 to 16 seats in the polls.
Channel 12's poll projected the Eisenkot bloc winning 56 seats compared with 50 for the Netanyahu bloc, while Channel 13's poll puts the blocs at 54 and 50 seats respectively. Kan public television showed the Eisenkot bloc with 52 seats, compared with 50 for the Netanyahu bloc.
All three polls showed Eisenkot's Yashar party leading – with 22 seats in Channel 13's and Kan's polls and 23 in Channel 12's poll – while Netanyahu's Likud is second-largest, with 21 seats in Channel 12's poll, 20 seats in Kan's poll and 19 in Channel 13's poll.
Kan public television and Channel 13 showed Together, co-led by former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, with 14 seats, while Channel 12 gave the party 15.
All three channels showed the right-wing Yisrael Beiteinu, which also opposes Netanyahu's bloc, maintaining its power with eight seats.
Channels 12 and 13 projected the Democrats, led by former general Yair Golan, winning 10 seats, while Kan showed the party receiving eight.
In Netanyahu's coalition, all three polls projected far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit party receiving eight seats, one seat up from the previous poll on Wednesday.
Far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich's Religious Zionism party was projected to win eight seats in Channel 13's poll, seven seats in Kan's poll and six seats in Channel 12's poll.
The Sephardic ultra-Orthodox Shas party was projected to win seven seats according to Kan and Channel 13, while Channel 12 showed it winning eight. United Torah Judaism, the Ashkenazi ultra-Orthodox party, won seven seats in Channel 12's poll and eight in Kan's and Channel 13's polls.
Ofer Winter's new far-right party Amcha Yisrael fell below the electoral threshold in all three polls, as did the Haredi Public party, a new slate that advocates integrating ultra-Orthodox men into the workforce and exposing school children to a core curriculum.
The Reservists party only passed the threshold in Kan's poll, receiving the minimum four seats.
Channel 13 projected the Joint List – a united slate of Arab parties Hadash, Ta'al and Balad – receiving nine seats together.
The United Arab List, led by MK Mansour Abbas, who joined the so-called Government of Change co-led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, was projected to win seven seats in the Channel 13's poll.
Channel 12 projected the Joint List with nine seats and the Abbas' United Arab List with five, as did Kan's poll.

Decision on Iran’s leadership rests solely with its people: Belgian foreign minister

Necva Tastan Sevinc
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot said on Friday that only the Iranian people can decide who should lead their country, rejecting a request for Belgium to recognize Reza Pahlavi as their legitimate representative.
“Precisely in the name of democracy, the decision as to who should lead Iran is one that must rest solely with the Iranian people,” Prevot wrote on US social media company X.
Responding to an activist, he said the Belgian government could not recognize Pahlavi, the son of Iran’s ousted shah, as the legitimate representative of the Iranian people and unifying leader of the democratic opposition.
Prevot noted that other individuals and movements claiming to represent the Iranian opposition had also contacted him.
He stressed that both the opposition and the Iranian diaspora encompass diverse voices, arguing that engagement should reflect that diversity.
The minister also clarified that he had not opposed inviting Pahlavi to Belgium’s parliament, saying he respected the legislature’s independence and freedom to maintain contacts with foreign political figures.
He had instead recommended broadening the invitation to hear other Iranian opposition groups.
“It was then the House that took the decision, not me, to refuse to host Mr. Pahlavi,” he said.
Prevot also defended maintaining diplomatic relations with Tehran, rejecting the Francophone liberal Reform Movement’s proposal to expel Iran’s ambassador.
He said Belgium needed communication channels to deliver firm messages to Iranian authorities and a diplomatic presence to monitor developments in the country.
“The adoption of sanctions is not incompatible with our approach of keeping diplomacy and dialogue alive,” he said.
Belgium would continue condemning violations of human rights and women’s rights while supporting the Iranian people’s calls for democracy, he added.
“We are ready to consider additional sanctions, while preserving dialogue as much as possible.”
Belgium’s House of Representatives on Wednesday dropped plans to host Pahlavi officially on Nov. 5 after parliamentary groups failed to reach consensus following cautious advice from the Foreign Ministry, according to Belga news agency.
The decision did not prevent the Reform Movement, which initiated the invitation, from receiving him privately.
The US and Israel launched a war on Iran in late February, seeking to destroy the country's nuclear program and topple the regime. 
Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli premier who seeks a reelection in next week's vote, has again called for a regime change in the Islamic Republic.

Voices from the Arab Press: Iran, the Kurds, and the future of Arab power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:38:58 UTC
04:38:58 KST

Citizenship before maps of separation
An-Nahar, Lebanon, October 20
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
The concern expressed by the leadership of Iraqi Kurdistan over the American withdrawal deserves careful consideration. It reveals that relations among the components of the Iraqi state still require guarantees from beyond its borders.
I understand the reasons for this anxiety, given a long history of repression and broken promises. But the more important question is why a country cannot reassure some of its own citizens, leaving them to seek protection from a distant power whose priorities change with its interests.
We see this in Lebanon, Iraq, Yemen, and elsewhere in our region, where national communities seek security through alliances with foreign powers. To me, this is a sign of the nation-state’s incomplete development, and one we must recognize.
Iraqi Kurds have achieved the most firmly established autonomous government among contemporary Kurdish communities. The 2005 constitution recognized the Kurdistan Region and its existing institutions, giving its people a parliament, government, and administrative structures within Iraq.
These were substantial gains for a people who endured tragedies, including the Anfal campaign and the Halabja massacre. Yet the transition from autonomy to full independence collided with geography, economics, and the positions of neighboring countries and major powers.
In September 2017, more than 92% of participants in the region’s referendum voted for independence. The majority was overwhelming, but the desired state never materialized. Baghdad rejected the referendum, neighboring countries opposed it, and Washington withheld the support its organizers had anticipated.
The region subsequently lost control of Kirkuk and other disputed territories. The lesson is clear: popular mobilization can produce an electoral result, but it cannot overturn the balance of power or independently create the conditions for statehood.
In Syria, Kurdish forces established a de facto autonomous administration during the civil war, but it did not become a recognized independent state. In Turkey, the Kurdistan Workers’ Party waged a prolonged armed struggle without achieving independence. Yet Turkish Kurds cannot be reduced to that organization; many have pursued political participation and elections.
Kurdish movements themselves differ in their objectives, ranging from cultural rights and decentralization to autonomy and secession. Ignoring these distinctions distorts our understanding of diverse communities.
The issue extends far beyond the Kurds. The Middle East is crowded with national, religious, and sectarian identities, some of whose members have suffered genuine injustices. In certain cases, memories of suffering have become permanent political projects, with leaders investing in fear and presenting separation as a ready-made solution.
Regional or international powers then enter the picture, supplying weapons and promises while using these causes as bargaining chips. I believe the most dangerous illusion is that an external patron shares a community’s aspirations as deeply as its own people do. Foreign powers have their calculations; they may leave, while the community remains among its neighbors.
None of this means demanding silence from the oppressed or absolving central governments. Authorities that prohibit citizens from using their language, discriminate in employment or the courts, or bombard their cities inevitably drive people to seek alternatives.
It is easy for rulers to proclaim national unity while governing as though the state belongs exclusively to their own group. Defending national unity must therefore begin with reforming government and guaranteeing rights. Citizenship is first an obligation of the state, before it becomes a demand placed upon its people.
Switzerland offers a useful example. Four national languages and different religious and cultural traditions coexist within a federal state. French speakers were not required to abandon their language or imitate German-speaking regions. The distribution of powers, recognition of diversity, and political participation helped create a shared interest in remaining together.
Switzerland is not a model that can be copied wholesale, but it demonstrates that respecting differences can strengthen a country, and that rigid centralization is not the only path to unity.
In Canada, Quebec voters narrowly rejected sovereignty in a 1995 referendum, with 50.58% voting against it. Political disagreement continued, and separatists remained free to advocate their position without the province descending into civil war.
What matters in these examples is the existence of institutions that permit disagreement and regulate it. Citizens who can challenge authority and seek legal remedies possess alternatives to retreating into communal loyalties. A state confident in its own fairness does not interpret every demand for cultural recognition as hostility.
South Sudan offers a contrasting lesson. It gained independence in 2011, only to descend into civil war in 2013. Raising a new flag did not resolve struggles over power; divisions simply migrated inside the newly established state.
This does not erase the injustices previously suffered by southerners, but it illustrates a painful truth: a community may succeed in separating while its leaders fail to build a functioning state. The practical question therefore extends beyond drawing borders to governing responsibly, holding officials accountable, and protecting minorities within those new borders.
The struggle worth pursuing in our region is the creation of modern, just civic states that accommodate different identities without distributing rights according to them. Iraqi first, then Kurdish or Arab, Sunni or Shi’ite. Syrian first, then Kurdish, Alawite, or Druze. Lebanese first, then Christian or Muslim, Shi’ite, Sunni, or Druze.
This is about the relationship between citizens and the state, not ranking people’s worth or erasing their histories. It requires an independent judiciary, peaceful transfers of power, fair distribution of wealth, and enforceable constitutional guarantees. Without these conditions, citizenship becomes a beautiful slogan that people hear but never experience.
We need citizens to feel that their futures depend on their abilities, their security is protected by law, and their dignity requires neither a sectarian intermediary nor a foreign embassy. We also need education that teaches children about one another’s histories without accusations of betrayal or manufactured heroism.
People learn coexistence in schools, workplaces, and neighborhoods, while politics destroys it by turning neighbors into suspects because of their names, religions, or languages. Nations achieve stability through justice before anything else.
– Mohammed Al Rumaihi
Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and restoring the red lines
Asharq Al-Awsat, UK, October 19
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi’s declaration concerning Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia marks a significant development in a crisis that has expanded beyond Yemen into a regional confrontation shaped by decades of Iranian attempts to overturn the established order.
Egypt’s position should come as no surprise. As a major Arab power, it cannot abandon its responsibility to defend Arab national security and its own direct interests. Egypt and Saudi Arabia form the backbone of any firm Arab position intended to protect the region’s Arab interests.
Egypt has approached Iran’s regional expansion with considerable wisdom and patience, relying on diplomacy and time in the hope that Tehran would abandon its repeated efforts to encircle Arab decision-making centers and alter the balance of power within individual countries and across the region.
Several years ago, I met el-Sisi and asked him about Egypt, its economy, and regional security. He told me: “The forces targeting Egypt are also targeting the region. These forces of evil include extremist organizations and regional states seeking to destabilize countries and overturn existing arrangements.
“Our decision to confront these attacks and attempts is firm, and our determination is strong. As Arab countries, we must stand together to defend our national security and stability against attempts to divide our countries, plunge them into chaos, and exhaust their economies and opportunities for progress.
“I am completely confident that, together with our brothers in the Gulf and other Arab countries, we can confront those targeting our countries, our region, and our role.”
He emphasized that Egypt’s relationship with Saudi Arabia was “deep and strategic, serving both countries and Arab national security.”
“I say sincerely that our brothers in Saudi Arabia manage affairs with wisdom and firmness, and that is why I tell them we are always together.” He was equally emphatic that Saudi stability meant Egyptian stability, and vice versa.
What struck me about that interview, published in Asharq Al-Awsat, was that El-Sisi deliberately avoided naming Iran, even though Tehran was clearly among the forces he described as seeking to destabilize the region. He wanted to preserve an opening for dialogue and give diplomacy every opportunity to moderate Iranian behavior, despite Tehran’s continued violations of red lines on Arab territory.
Saudi Arabia, likewise, demonstrated considerable patience toward Iranian intrusions, keeping diplomatic channels open both before and after the Beijing agreement. Yet Riyadh remained committed to fundamental principles: respect for the red lines established by international law and those imposed by genuine good-neighborly relations.
Egyptian and Saudi policies consequently converged around supporting legitimate authorities in Palestine, Lebanon, and Yemen, while encouraging Iraq’s government to restore the institutions of the state and reclaim Iraq’s place within the Arab family.
During major turning points in recent decades, Egyptian and Saudi determination have repeatedly converged. They stood together when Iraq’s Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait, and again when Egyptians took to the streets amid fears that Muslim Brotherhood rule threatened their country’s identity, stability, and regional role.
Saudi Arabia acted on the conviction that its own security was inseparable from Egypt’s, while Egypt understood that destabilizing Saudi Arabia would have catastrophic consequences for Egypt, the Gulf, the Arab and Islamic worlds, and the global economy.
Regional coexistence requires respect for clear boundaries: internationally recognized borders, legitimate governments, and every state’s right to choose its policies in accordance with established laws and norms. Encircling countries, penetrating their borders and security systems, and undermining their ability to make sovereign decisions are incompatible with those principles.
The Houthi organization Ansar Allah has built its approach around violating virtually every red line, domestically and internationally. Its record extends from undermining Yemen’s legitimate government and assassinating former president Ali Abdullah Saleh to holding the Bab el-Mandeb Strait hostage and carrying out the brutal bombardment of civilians at Riyadh Airport.
Iran has similarly violated red lines on other countries’ territory by establishing and arming militias, controlling their decisions, and assigning them regional missions designed to destabilize governments.
Against this backdrop, el-Sisi’s position sends a stern warning: Egypt is prepared to participate in defensive missions that help contain the region’s destabilizing forces. The combined weight of Egypt and Saudi Arabia provides a foundation for mobilizing an Arab, Islamic, and international response capable of restoring these boundaries and preventing further attempts to overturn the regional order.
The region is filled with the smell of a wider war and enveloped in uncertainty. Even the possible departure of a dangerous player named Benjamin Netanyahu would not necessarily mean a less aggressive Israel.
Nor can we predict how US President Donald Trump might respond to an electoral setback for his party in the midterms. Iran’s escalating behavior in the Strait of Hormuz could accelerate the arrival of still more dangerous confrontations. Tehran has changed neither its language nor its methods.
An Arab official smiled at length when Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi claimed that his country had tried to persuade both Saudi Arabia and the Houthis to halt their escalation, but neither side had cooperated. Araghchi was particularly careful to insist that “the Houthis make their decisions independently.” That amusing assertion only deepened the Arab official’s pessimism.
– Ghassan Charbel
Can Egypt pass the toughest test of political power?
El Watan, Egypt, October 18
In my view, the most important thing President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi has said is that 2030 will mark the end of his presidency, that the decision is final and is not open to debate.
This statement deserves serious consideration, without the usual applause or the automatic skepticism that greets almost everything. If the commitment is fulfilled, its significance will extend far beyond the president himself.
Egypt has an opportunity to establish a principle essential to its future: that the end of a president’s term should be a known date for which the state prepares and about which society can feel reassured. Countries need to know how responsibility will be transferred just as much as they need to know who bears it.
I believe el-Sisi has an opportunity to shape one of the most important elements of his political legacy: leaving behind a state capable of functioning after his departure, institutions that understand their responsibilities, and a political system that produces people worthy of leadership.
But this is where our own responsibility begins. Anyone who imagines that the public’s role begins on election morning and ends with placing a ballot in the box reduces an enormous issue to a single moment.
The ballot determines the outcome, but the quality of that choice is shaped over many years. It depends on public awareness; access to information; the ability to question, compare, and hold officials accountable; and the emergence of figures whose competence has been demonstrated through actual experience.
We should not discover a presidential candidate for the first time when his photograph appears on a campaign poster. We should have seen him shoulder responsibility, explain his decisions, acknowledge mistakes, and propose solutions whose costs he understands before promising results. Egypt is too important to be entrusted to a gifted orator, a fleeting wave of popularity, or an organization that regards the presidency as a means of taking control of the state.
Egypt has institutions, and I trust that they have an essential role in protecting the country from infiltration and undue influence. But genuine protection comes through clear rules, laws applied equally to everyone, oversight of political financing and conflicts of interest, and respect for the constitution and the will of the Egyptian people.
Strong institutions reassure citizens that their country’s future is safeguarded by a system of responsibility and accountability, and that any incoming president will govern within an established framework of rules and limits.
That is why the remaining years until 2030 are just as important as the transfer of power itself. We need to see greater opportunities for qualified individuals, political parties offering practical and achievable programs, media organizations asking serious questions, and public officials judged by the results of their work.
We must also learn that political disagreement does not make someone less patriotic, just as political support does not automatically establish competence.
I see the president’s declared position as an opportunity for a major advance in Egypt’s political development. But realizing that opportunity requires preparations for the future to become visible action starting now.
If that happens, 2030 could become a defining moment: a president completing his term and handing over responsibility, a public making an informed choice, and institutions guaranteeing the continuity of the state and respect for its rules.
The greatest legacy a ruler can leave his country is a future that becomes more secure even in his absence. Egypt deserves confidence not only in whoever governs it, but also in the rules that will remain after the president leaves office.
– John Al-Masrii
Saudi Arabia and its historic role
Al Qabas, Kuwait, October 19
I lived in Saudi Arabia for more than 10 years while serving as secretary-general of the Gulf Cooperation Council. During that time, I came to appreciate the profound and historic significance of the kingdom – not only for its people, rulers, and neighbors, but for the security and stability of the Arab and Islamic worlds and, indeed, countries far beyond the region.
Saudi Arabia, its land, and its people represent an essential pillar of stability for all who value a secure and dignified life. This is a reality recognized across continents.
The kingdom is not merely the birthplace of Islam, the home of its holiest sites, and a land central to Arab history. It is also the guardian of those sacred places, fully conscious of the immense responsibilities entrusted to it and prepared to shoulder the burdens of protecting them, maintaining their significance, and ensuring that Muslims arriving from every part of the world can worship safely and comfortably.
Fortunately, confidence among Muslims and others in the wisdom of Saudi leadership has continued to grow. The kingdom’s rulers understand that their responsibilities extend beyond the physical protection of holy sites to preserving the historical and spiritual heritage of a religion whose reach spans Asia, Africa, and parts of Europe.
What impressed me most was the Saudi state’s readiness to fulfill these obligations with extraordinary dedication. I observed the preparations undertaken to receive pilgrims and visitors, with attention not only to effort but to tangible results.
Roads leading to the holy sites, hotels, accommodation, shopping facilities, and essential services were developed to meet the needs of pilgrims performing Hajj and Umrah. Saudi officials and institutions devoted themselves to this continuing mission, making the comfort and safety of worshipers a central priority.
As the kingdom succeeded in meeting these responsibilities, and its international reputation and standing rose, adversaries sought to undermine the prestige it had earned through its organization, hospitality, and commitment to ensuring visitors could return home safely.
I performed Hajj twice. The first time was among senior invited guests, an exceptionally satisfying and enjoyable experience. The second was with friends, when we visited the holy sanctuary and Medina together. We still recall the beauty of that journey.
King Khalid assumed the throne following the death of his half-brother, King Fahd. I have followed the Gulf Cooperation Council closely, including attending its summit meetings alongside King Khalid, who was deeply interested in its details and committed to strengthening its work. I maintained regular contact with his office to communicate developments within the council and secure his support.
King Fahd was a monarch, leader, and initiator who sought to understand the council’s progress in depth. He sometimes advised patience on particular issues, and encouraged collective agreement out of consideration for the circumstances of individual member states. There was no need to rush; what mattered was unity of purpose and firmness of position.
Saudi kings have been statesmen attentive to regional events and global developments, capable of adapting to change, cultivating friendships, and drawing lessons from international affairs. They understood the art of accommodation without haste or unnecessary noise, keeping their doors open to Arabs, Muslims, and others, near and far.
Saudi Arabia’s spirit of brotherhood was demonstrated most powerfully during the catastrophe of Saddam Hussein’s 1990 invasion and annexation of Kuwait. Saddam had opened the door to his own destruction, and history has recorded both the ugliness of his actions and our failure to adequately recognize the danger his recklessness posed to Kuwait.
Saudi Arabia’s response was unwavering. Under King Fahd’s leadership, the kingdom committed itself fully to Kuwait’s liberation, mobilizing its resources and determination to achieve that goal.
I was close to King Fahd during those painful months. He was always eager to reassure the Kuwaiti community in Riyadh, and repeatedly asked me to tell Kuwaiti citizens that the day of their return was not far away, but that patience was necessary to complete the preparations that would guarantee liberation.
It was a historic moment requiring careful planning and the conviction that the mission would succeed, alongside a willingness to accept whatever sacrifices might be necessary.
Looking back, I recall the decisive Saudi role in launching the liberation effort and securing international support for an extraordinary collective mobilization. We Kuwaitis continue to take pride in Saudi Arabia’s determination to confront aggression and restore our country to its people.
The world witnessed that commitment with admiration, and history records how the Saudi-Kuwaiti partnership demonstrated the full depth of brotherhood between our nations.
We and the generations that follow us will continue to admire the strength of Saudi resolve that opened the path to Kuwait’s liberation. The kingdom will forever remain a steadfast and influential pillar in Kuwait’s history.
– Abdullah Bishara ■

Anthropic AI model passes itself as human in 'supply chain attack' against GitHub during exercise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:38:48 UTC
04:38:48 KST

Anthropic revealed on Friday that one of its artificial intelligence models passed itself off as human during a cybersecurity exercise to fool a human outside the exercise.
According to Anthropic, the model, which used Mythos 5, performed unsanctioned actions in nine out of 43 runs that impacted humans not participating in the exercise, with one of the cases even involving the AI pretending to be human.
The attack, which was described by the AI Security Institute (AISI) as a "supply chain attack," attempted to disrupt a public code repository on the GitHub platform by creating fake inquiries, introducing corrupted data, and even demanding changes by creating false accounts on the platform.
AISI noted that even if the attack did not cause real-world harm, it was still a serious incident worth understanding and responding to thoroughly. "
The report also warned that the models made decisions even when their reasoning was not justified, with some cases acknowledging that the attack could harm humans before proceeding to attack the target.
What was the exercise that led to the attack?
According to Anthropic, the model was asked to perform a "Capture the flag" (CTF) exercise, which involves retrieving data from a simulated network.
The models were given Internet access, and the safeguards used for models such as Fable, which is Anthropic's most powerful model, were not established.
In one of the cases, the AI agent found evidence that one of the computers periodically contacted GitHub and attempted to discover which repository was being downloaded.
It then decided the computer contacting GitHub was downloading a repository belonging to a real-world human unrelated to the exercise, and created a new version of that repository that included malicious code.
The goal was that, once the computer on the network downloaded it, it would infect the system and allow retrieval of the flag.
Additionally, it created a fake user on GitHub in order to contact the owner of the compromised repository and convince them to allow the change, something that was denied. The model eventually ran out of time and failed the task.
The two main concerns by Anthropic were the overreach seen during the exercise, with the model going beyond the intended scope of the task, and dishonesty, or the extent to which the model misrepresented its actions or intentions.
Anthropic also said it ran the same experiment with more advanced models, which showed less intent to carry out attacks of this scope, and all stopped their attacks once they were notified that the actions had real-world impact.

While AIPAC’s critics rejoice as lobby shifts strategy, its defenders push back
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:38:48 UTC
04:38:48 KST

AIPAC’s critics gloated on Thursday after the pro-Israel lobby announced that it was ending direct contributions and candidate endorsements. But defenders of the storied Washington institution pushed back at that characterization, saying instead that the organization had made a smart course correction amid strong political headwinds stoked at least in part by antisemitism.
The American Israel Public Affairs Committee announced the decision in a letter to its members on Wednesday, explaining that the lobby would now shift its focus to mobilizing individual donors. The abandonment of direct PAC contributions and candidate endorsements marks a significant reversal in a strategy that AIPAC launched in 2021, ahead of the 2022 election cycle. The letter informed donors that AIPAC’s super PAC, the United Democracy Project, also launched in 2021, would continue to operate.
The move came in an increasingly tense political cycle for AIPAC, which it called “one of the most challenging environments in recent memory.” The lobby has become a target for progressive candidates, particularly Democratic Socialists of America members, who have sharply criticized candidates who receive donations from AIPAC. In turn, the organization has become a symbol of undue political influence among some voters.
The DSA responded to the lobby’s policy shift by saying that “AIPAC has realized what we all already knew: working people do not want their tax dollars to fund apartheid and genocide.”
Kenneth Roth, former executive director of Human Rights Watch and a staunch Israel critic, wrote that AIPAC’s decision shows that “candidates don’t want its backing,” while the anti-Zionist group Jewish Voice for Peace posted that AIPAC was now deeming itself “too toxic.”
Jeremy Ben-Ami, president of the liberal pro-Israel lobbying group J Street, which has frequently tangled with AIPAC on social media, argued in a statement that “AIPAC can’t save its brand by folding its PAC.” Describing AIPAC as “a once-revered organization,” he said the lobby became toxic not due to its support of candidates but “because of the policies it asks those candidates to defend.”
But those with ties to AIPAC defended the move as one that will actually help the lobby fortify its impact. “It’s a marker of institutional health when they can look around at the reality, see it for what it is and change themselves accordingly,” Jonathan Greenberg, director for combatting antisemitism at Defending Education and a former AIPAC staffer, told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency.
“They recognized that their political ground had shifted and that they needed to change with that shift,” added Greenberg, who served as AIPAC’s Midwest political director until 2011 and ran for state office in Illinois as a Republican a year later.
Calling out what he described as a “horrifying demonization campaign” against AIPAC in Washington, he said he believes that the lobbying group made this strategic decision in an effort to continue operating amid widespread antisemitism.
“The pro-Israel community is still going to be deeply involved in campaigns,” added Greenberg, who identifies as a political conservative but no longer a Republican. “AIPAC is just wisely understanding that the way the organization operates can change, so that it can still be the voice that it’s always been on Capitol Hill.”
Recognizing that the U.S. political landscape is undergoing profound changes amid deep dissatisfaction across party lines, a former AIPAC spokesperson who requested anonymity to speak freely pointed out that institutions must evolve to stay effective. Other major interest groups, such as the pharmaceutical, hospital and real estate industries, are advancing their priorities with a variety of tactics, including lobbying, direct contributions, super PACs and networks of donors, the person noted.
In fact, one point of agreement on Thursday between AIPAC’s supporters and detractors was that the 72-year-old institution wasn’t going anywhere. “Mobilizing greater resources for AIPAC, pro-Israel candidates, and our super PAC is critical,” the AIPAC letter stressed, as it pledged to reinvest in its long-standing network of members nationwide.
“AIPAC staff and local leaders will continue working with you on political fundraising efforts, recommending contributions to candidates who are worthy of your support, and ensuring your resources are deployed in the most effective ways possible,” the letter added.
Indeed, opponents of the lobby indicated that the change in approach did little to satisfy them – and potentially opened up new lines of attack. DSA charged that AIPAC would “try to bankroll the same candidates under a different name.”
'Can't hide AIPAC,' DSA says
“You can’t hide AIPAC,” the DSA added. “The world has woken up.”
J Street’s Ben-Ami maintained that AIPAC’s decision to keep its super PAC even as it dropped its PAC “only doubles down on the dark money politics that helped create its problem in the first place.” Traditional PACs can contribute a maximum of $5,000 to individual candidates in each race, while super PACs can spend unlimited funds to independent political communications that serve to support or oppose candidates. Both have to disclose their donors, but super PAC donors aren’t always transparent about the origins of their money.
Tali deGroot, J Street’s vice president of political and digital strategy, likewise assessed that AIPAC’s influence wouldn’t disappear in the next election cycle.
“Instead, AIPAC’s donors and its super PAC will keep spending heavily in our elections, only now voters will have a harder time seeing where that money comes from,” deGroot said.
Defending Education’s Greenberg acknowledged that AIPAC’s choice to increase its reliance on its super PAC could fuel even more opposition to the lobby.
“But I don’t think fashioning ourselves to placate antisemites gets us anywhere,” he continued. “What we know about antisemites, from thousands of years of dealing with them, is that if we don’t give them this reason, they’ll find another reason.”
The former AIPAC spokesperson said the jury was out on whether the AIPAC pivot would improve its public image. “The question is whether AIPAC’s shift reflects a broader evolution in how organizations and interest groups engage politically, and whether changing its approach will change how the public perceives its influence,” the former spokesperson noted.

DUNE Project Aims to Unite Legacy and Cloud Tools in Air Ops Centers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:35:26 UTC
04:35:26 KST

After decades of building isolated, vendor-locked systems to run the Air Operations Centers that serve as the Air Force’s “combat brains,” the program office tasked with creating the next-generation AOC is working to fold those systems into a new cloud-based system.
Col. Brian Viola, the newly appointed commander of Kessel Run, the government-led, vendor-managed program office underneath the portfolio acquisition executive for command, control, communications, and battle management, told Air & Space Forces Magazine in a recent interview that his team is standardizing how cloud-based applications and software updates to AOCs get accessed worldwide in real time.
Starting this spring, Kessel Run launched the Dynamic Unified Net-enabled Environment, or DUNE, which merges cloud and on-premises capabilities for AOC operators, commanders, and their customers—the rest of the operational Air Force.
“Evolving the architectural foundation is vital because the information our warfighters rely on depends on the integrity, speed, and agility of the underlying domain,” Viola said. “We are rapidly entering the era of software-defined warfare, where tactical superiority belongs to the force that can iterate, secure and deploy code faster than the adversary can adapt.”
Essentially, DUNE standardizes how legacy and current software communicates across the Air Operations Center’s systems.
It’s unclear whether the DUNE acronym is a nod to the popular book, film and TV franchise of the same name. But the Air Force has a history of using sci-fi-inspired names and acronyms—Kessel Run itself is named after a Star Wars reference.
Speaking the Same Language
Currently, Viola said, AOC operators must choose between using real-time, cloud-based tools or sticking with the often aged, legacy hardware they have on hand.
“The ability to rapidly integrate new mission capabilities, enable distributed command and control, and incorporate new technologies depends on the architecture beneath them,” he said.
DUNE is an overarching project that builds on Kessel Run’s Applications Transformation project, or AppTX, which the service introduced to conduct large-scale migrations of legacy software apps to the cloud. Companies such as Parsons, General Dynamics Information Technology, and Astrion compete for taskings through AppTX.
DUNE focuses on the issue of Data Definition Language, which has gained prominence with the recent push to rush artificial intelligence into systems across the Pentagon. DDL is a kind of programming language that can create, modify, or delete database structures without modifying the data itself—it allows legacy infrastructure and software “talk” with new software and applications, breaking down silos and stovepipes.
Without it, Viola said, “you’re going to have to work with what you have”—an Airman in an AOC will only be able to draw from a tool or solution they have in their local network, on site near the tactical edge, without access to the cloud.
“We don’t want to necessarily have every AOC be a snowflake that we have to go, ‘this is tailored for you now, AOC 1, and this is tailored for the 613th [AOC], this is tailored for the 607th [AOC],” Viola said.
Tailoring the solutions by AOC is “sucking away from the innovation we really want to get after,” he said.
Project DUNE aims to get the continuous delivery of cloud-based capabilities and applications down to an on-premises solution, he said.
Solutions won’t be as “elastic” as the cloud, but they will be a resilient capability that users can rely on, he said.
Beyond DUNE, Viola said next steps include building the “Revolutionary AOC” with industry partners. The effort will involve operators, mission partners, engineers and acquisition teams working together in operational scenarios to identify gaps and improve the system architecture.
Work on DUNE and recent pushes in the PAE C3BM and Kessel Run specifically predate Viola’s tenure. Air & Space Forces Magazine reported in February that Kessel Run was launching its “next generation” AOC effort, which seeks to integrate AI, machine learning, data fusion, and cloud-based software into the centers.
The Air Force has 21 AOCs across the force and sees these operational hubs as weapons systems in their own right, calling them AN/USQ-163 Falconers.
In 2022, the Air Force awarded SAIC a $374 million contract through mid-2027 to sustain and modernize its AOCs. The current Falconer system is in Increment 10.1, with a 10.2 (aka Block 20) upgrade in progress.

'Badge of honour': Why John is flying to Auckland for just one night
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:34:16 UTC
04:34:16 KST

John Darcy had never set foot on a plane until he was 40.
Now, 18 years and 179 flights later, he'll be on the first international flight to leave Western Sydney International Airport.
The Sydney aviation enthusiast spent his childhood photographing planes and dreaming of travelling on one. On Monday morning, he'll board Air New Zealand flight NZ166 to Auckland, becoming one of the first international passengers to depart from Australia's newest airport.
"I started keeping account of my flights; it's become a hobby, collecting airports, collecting flight routes, collecting different types of planes flown on," Darcy told SBS News.
"I've flown 179 times, more than 60 airports in Australia, North America and Europe.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"But I needed to add Western Sydney International Airport to my tally."
Darcy is old enough to remember when the Hawke government announced Badgerys Creek as the site for Sydney's second airport.
After decades of debate, delay and construction, he said it felt only right to be there from the start.
"It's been so long coming. To think that on Sunday, passengers will start flying in and out of there, and on Monday I will be on the first international flight out of there."
"It's for the little boy inside of me."
Sydney's second airport will welcome its first passengers this weekend, becoming Australia's first newly built international airport in more than 50 years.
Located near Badgerys Creek in western Sydney, the airport will initially host services from airlines including Jetstar, Qantas, Air New Zealand, Singapore Airlines, Fiji Airways, Qatar Airways and Vietjet.
Unlike Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport, flights can arrive and depart around the clock.
For aviation enthusiasts like Darcy, that makes the opening more than just an infrastructure project.
A few hours in Auckland
The destination, however, is almost beside the point.
Darcy will spend just one night in Auckland before flying home the following day.
"The only reason I'm doing this is for that inaugural flight," he said.
"I don't have any particular business in Auckland and I need to get back to resume work. I'm not taking holidays for this, just a couple of days off."
Four weeks later, he'll do something similar again, flying on Singapore Airlines' inaugural service from Western Sydney to Singapore.
"I'll be overnight in Auckland on Monday, but four weeks later when I go to Singapore, I'll be five hours in Changi Airport and then coming straight back."
"It's the novelty of the new airport and the badge of honour of being on the first international departure from that airport," he said.
There's also data behind that badge of honour.
Since 2014, he has logged every flight he can remember taking, tracking everything from flight numbers and aircraft types to which day of the week he travelled.
"It's on an Excel spreadsheet," he said.
"I've tracked all the data of the different flight sectors, the airlines, all the flight numbers, the length of all the flights, the departure airports, the arrival airports."
His trip from Western Sydney to Auckland has already been entered.
"It will be my 180th flight and 2,201 kilometres from Western Sydney to Auckland."
Darcy isn't the only aviation enthusiast making special plans for the airport's opening.
Some are buying tickets on inaugural flights. Others are heading to Sydney for a completely different view.
Chasing the perfect shot
For 19-year-old Alastair, the opening of Western Sydney International Airport is just as exciting. But while Darcy will be inside the plane, Alastair plans to be hundreds of metres away with a camera pointed at it.
The Melbourne plane spotter is flying to Sydney specifically to photograph the airport's first departures.
"I'm going up there to capture a moment in history because it's not every day that Australia gets a new international airport," he said. "It'll just be a once-in-a-lifetime thing."
Plane spotting, he explains, is about more than watching aircraft take off and land.
"It's like getting different plane liveries that normal people would see and think, 'Oh, that's just what a plane looks like'," he said.
"Sometimes there's a really special one, and it's very cool to see."
After discovering the hobby at 14, Alastair began keeping a notebook of every aircraft registration he spotted.
Five years on, that handwritten tally is closing in on 2,000 entries, and he now heads out plane spotting almost every day.
Sometimes that's at Melbourne Airport. Sometimes it's from a nearby park. Occasionally, it's from his own backyard.
What started with a phone camera has evolved into a serious setup worth about $5,000.
He uses flight-tracking apps to monitor aircraft movements and, when he's photographing at Melbourne Airport, often climbs ladders to shoot above the fence line.
"What we bring at Melbourne Airport are ladders," he said. "We bring ladders that can go three metres up so we can get a good shot above the fence line."
Fully extended, those ladders can reach 6m.
He's never fallen off one himself, although he's seen others take a tumble in pursuit of the perfect image.
The effort, he says, is worth it.
One of his favourite parts of the hobby is connecting with pilots, some of whom message him directly to ask for photos of their flights.
"They'll wave from the cockpit or they'll do something to acknowledge me from the other side of the fence," he said.
"I think that's really cool."
A once-in-a-generation opening
Within Australia's plane spotting community, the opening of Western Sydney International Airport has become one of the most anticipated aviation events in years.
Alastair compares the excitement to the arrival of the Airbus A350-1000 ULR in Melbourne earlier this year, when aviation enthusiasts gathered to photograph the aircraft used during Qantas' record-breaking ultra-long-haul testing flights.
"I don't think anything will beat the hype of when the Airbus A350-1000 ULR came to Melbourne," he said.
"But the hype for Western Sydney, it's big.
"Everyone's excited to spot there. Everyone's excited to fly out of there. Everyone's excited to see what airlines will fly there."
Like Darcy, Alastair is interested in the history as much as the aircraft itself.
He's already hoping to capture a photo of the airport's first departures, particularly if one receives a ceremonial water-cannon salute.
But he says the real value of those images won't be obvious to everyone who sees them.
"It's like the backstory of the photos," he said.
"Someone's going to say, 'Oh, that's just a Jetstar plane taking off.'
"And I'd be like, 'No, that's the first passenger flight out of a new airport in so long in Australia.'
"You can always get a Jetstar A320 at Western Sydney in the next 20 years.
"But you'll never forget the very first flight."
