Why Australia's falling birth rate is everyone's problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:33:47 UTC
04:33:47 KST

This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.
Share your feedback and help us improve this feature. Read more about how we use AI at SBS here.
"I had my baby at 38," says Heer Kaur, an Indian migrant living in Beveridge, north of Melbourne, who had always imagined having a big family.
But the reality of building a life in a new country, establishing a career and raising a child without family support meant rethinking that dream.
Kaur eventually decided to have just one child, weighing her desire for a large family against the financial and practical demands of parenthood.
"As migrants, we have to rebuild everything in the new country. I kept postponing marriage or having children for later. I wanted to be settled first. Be a permanent resident, build a career, have some stability," she tells SBS Punjabi.
"I wanted to have at least two kids. I assumed I would be able to have kids whenever I tried. But that was not the case."
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
SBS News has withheld her real name for privacy reasons.
Kaur says the lack of family support in Australia also meant spending more on childcare.
More money spent on childcare meant having to work longer to earn more, and then less time with my child. Then I had to settle for a quality life for my son, even though it meant him being an only child.
"The compromise comes with guilt as a parent. We work hard to ensure he learns social skills, how to share, and has a network of his own, beyond us."
She says she hopes the family she built was the result of her own choices, not dictated by social and economic circumstances.
Kaur's experience reflects a wider question facing Australia: what happens when the family people want, and the family they can afford, are not the same?
Kaur is not alone in finding herself at this crossroads.
The Treasury's Intergenerational Report (IGR) 2026 puts Australia's total fertility rate at a historic low of 1.48 births per woman, lower than the total fertility rates projected in previous IGRs.
The replacement-level fertility rate — the rate at which a population replaces itself over time without migration — is about 2.1 births per woman.
The report projects that Australia's fertility rate will decline further to 1.34 births per woman by 2065–66.
It identifies delayed childbearing as a key factor contributing to smaller families and lower fertility rates.
Why are Australians delaying having kids?
The IGR identifies establishing a career as one reason people delay parenthood. It also points to access to childcare, the burden of unpaid care, housing security, and workplace flexibility as factors influencing people's decisions about whether to start a family or have more children.
The trend towards later childbearing is not unique to Australia.
In 2023, more than one in three births worldwide were to women aged 30 and over, compared with about one in four in 1990.
However, experts say delayed parenthood is only part of the picture. Financial pressures, changing social expectations and individual circumstances can also shape decisions about family size. The reasons vary, and lower fertility rates do not necessarily mean that everyone wants more children but is unable to have them.
But as Australia's fertility rate falls and its population ages, the implications extend beyond individual families.
The IGR warns that if birth rates and migration fall below baseline expectations, Australia's population would be 1.9 million smaller and the economy 7.4 per cent smaller by 2065–66.
And with deaths projected to outnumber births by the 2060s, migration is expected to play an increasingly important role in sustaining population growth and meeting workforce needs.
Australia's growing reliance on migration
Migrants already make up a large and growing share of the health care and social assistance workforce.
The IGR notes that migration can help moderate population ageing as new migrants are "typically younger than the existing population".
Demographer Liz Allen says Australia's ageing population and below-replacement fertility rate mean the country will rely more on migration to support its workforce and economy.
"Australia is on the way to what's considered super-aged. It essentially means that, in proportion speaking, we have more people aged over 65 than we have young people," she tells SBS Punjabi.
"Currently, we rely on individual income taxpayers to contribute to the economy; with an ageing population and below-replacement-level fertility, we have a shrinking relative working-age population. That means fewer tax dollars coming from that biggest source of taxpayers, individual workers."
At the moment, migrants present the biggest share of population growth in this country. And that's because the local population isn't growing the way it used to.
Allen says migration also brings social and cultural benefits alongside its economic contribution.
The IGR found new migrants are typically younger than the existing population, with a median age of 26 compared with 38 in 2024-25. As a result, migration helps slow population ageing and increases the share of working-age people beyond what would be achieved through natural increase alone.
Do migrants have more children?
Research by the University of Melbourne's demographer Peter McDonald shows that temporary migrants are predominantly young adults aged 20 to 35, many of whom come to Australia to study or establish their careers. While they are included in the population's childbearing age group, they contribute relatively few births.
Allen says migrants can also adopt the fertility patterns of their new country, which "in some cases, means even have lower fertility rates than the local population".
"Upon arrival in Australia, many migrants prioritise work and education, which delays family formation into their late 30s or beyond. This trend mirrors the broader patterns seen in the Australian population," she says.
For Adelaide-based freelance photographer Naina Redhu, moving to Australia meant meeting her partner, Jamie. While she says she is happy with her partner, neither of them wants to have children.
The 46-year-old says she has always been clear that she doesn't want children. Yet the decision has often prompted questions and unsolicited advice, including suggestions that she freeze her eggs as a precaution.
"My ex-husband and I were clear that we did not want children, but later, he did want to have kids some years down the line," she tells SBS Punjabi.
This is a fundamental choice; it narrates what kind of life you are choosing for yourself.
"I think it is selfish to have kids, and we ended up parting ways."
Redhu says not having a child doesn't mean she takes motherhood lightly.
"I believe parenting is a 24X7 commitment for the rest of your life. For someone like me, it would mean putting everything aside and being completely focused on raising the child, and I am not ready for that commitment yet," she says.
"There are so many things that I have to do and still want to do."
The barriers to having children
Allen says Australia should focus less on achieving an ideal number of children and more on removing hurdles that prevent people from having the families they want.
"We need to reach a point where having a much-wanted child, or a second child, is truly possible and not obstructed by barriers that feel insurmountable. Otherwise, the consequences ripple across society," she says.
She warns that smaller families may also have broader social consequences, including greater pressure on individuals to provide care for ageing relatives or fewer family connections to rely on.
Ultimately, having a child is not just a mother's responsibility; it is a societal concern.
"Until we address major challenges including housing affordability, economic security, climate change, and gender equality, Australians may lack the confidence and hope needed to plan for the future."

Iran plans to target Gulf undersea cables if attacked: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:32:00 UTC
04:32:00 KST

Iran has prepared detailed plans to strike undersea communications cables in the Gulf in retaliation for any renewed U.S. or Israeli military attack, two senior Iranian security officials told Reuters, raising concerns over potential disruptions to regional and global connectivity.
Their comments followed warnings by Iranian officials that undersea cables in the region could become targets in any renewed conflict if diplomacy with Washington collapses.
The two Iranian security officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, gave few details and did not say how or where exactly Tehran would carry out such attacks. But one of them said Iran would aim to prevent repairs after any attacks to prolong disruptions to communications, including internet connections.
"If Iran is attacked, there will be no more red lines ... from undersea cables to military bases, including covert ones," one of the officials said.
The official warned Washington not to "play with fire", and said Iran had full access to the undersea cables and could easily destroy them.
Yadollah Javani, the deputy head of political affairs for Iran's Revolutionary Guards (IRGC), said on Wednesday that Iran could target seven major internet cables beneath the Strait of Hormuz if Iranian infrastructure came under attack.
Undersea cables carry around 99% of global internet traffic, according to the International Telecommunication Union, a U.N. agency. But the global impact of such attacks by Iran could be limited as less than 1% of international bandwidth passes through the Strait of Hormuz, said Alan Mauldin, research director at telecommunications research firm TeleGeography.
The strait separates Iran and Oman, linking the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea.
The U.S. Department of State and Iran's Foreign Ministry did not respond to Reuters' requests for comment on the Iranian security officials' remarks. There was no immediate comment from Gulf states.
The plans for possible attacks on undersea cables reflect a conviction in Iran's leadership that a renewed US military campaign would have to be met with a stronger response than before.
Top security official Mohsen Rezaei warned this month that US-linked digital infrastructure across the Gulf, including data centres and AI facilities, could be targeted in a renewed conflict.
Washington's Gulf allies have invested heavily in such infrastructure and they "should hold Washington, not Tehran, responsible for any damage to undersea cables," the second Iranian security official said.
Alex Vatanka, director of the Iran program at the Middle East Institute in Washington, said such threats were intended to deter renewed conflict and put pressure on Washington by making Gulf governments and U.S. companies fear for their investments in the region.
"Tehran wants Gulf states and corporate executives to press (U.S. President Donald) Trump over the risks his policies pose to their investment plans," said Vatanka.
Multiple cable cuts could slow internet services and disrupt financial transactions, e-commerce and cloud computing, analysts said. The impact would depend on how operators rerouted traffic and the capacity available on alternative connections, Mauldin said.
Restoring connections during wartime could be difficult, experts said, and higher insurance costs and delays in obtaining permits to enter territorial waters could further complicate repairs.
The Red Sea could offer a more significant target than the Strait of Hormuz, particularly if Iran had support from its Houthi allies in Yemen, though Tehran has made no public statement indicating it plans to target cables there.
The Red Sea carries data between Europe, East Africa and Asia, with capacity routed through it accounting for about 3% of global international demand and around 10% of traffic travelling between regions, Mauldin said.
Gulf governments have been investing heavily in technology to diversify beyond oil and become global artificial intelligence hubs, deepening ties with U.S. technology firms.
Iranian strikes directly hit two Amazon Web Services facilities in the UAE in March and damaged infrastructure near one of its facilities in Bahrain. The IRGC named U.S. tech companies including Microsoft, Google, Apple and Nvidia as legitimate targets at the height of the war in March.
Land-based connections can provide alternative routes for internet traffic, and Gulf states and U.S. technology companies are investing in additional infrastructure to improve resilience.
Microsoft plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030.

The state will compensate up to 80% of wartime losses to civilian shipping: who will receive the funds and how to apply
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
22:29:33 EEST
04:29:33 KST

The state will compensate up to 80% of wartime losses to civilian shipping: who will receive the funds and how to apply
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine will compensate up to 80% of wartime losses to vessels provided they have valid insurance. Applications must be submitted to the Ministry for Development within 180 days.
The state will compensate up to 80% of certain losses incurred by civil shipping that are not covered by insurers. The relevant decision was adopted by Ukrainian government officials at the beginning of the month.
UNN explains the conditions under which applications for payments may be submitted, and outlines the required documents and the deadlines for submitting them.
The state will compensate up to 80% of war-related losses: what the government’s decision provides
The Cabinet of Ministers approved the procedure for state guarantees by Resolution No. 1248 dated October 7, 2026, which was published on October 15. Its aim is to support maritime transportation amid attacks by the russian federation on ports and vessels.
Insurance for vessels against war risks is becoming more expensive, while insurers do not cover some of the damage. Therefore, the state is offering non-repayable compensation, but it must be supported by documents. Payments depend on the budget.
Who can receive compensation for war-related losses
Owners, operators, and charterers of seagoing vessels and inland-waterway vessels flying the flag of Ukraine or a foreign state may apply for state guarantees. A charterer hires a vessel, while an operator ensures its operation. The application for compensation is submitted by the shipowner. The vessel must transport non-military cargo to or from an open Ukrainian seaport. No vessel traffic ban may be in effect at the respective port. The program does not cover housing, vehicles, or other losses incurred by individuals.
What losses the state will compensate
Under the resolution, claims may be made for damage resulting from the loss of a vessel or its constructive total loss when repair is impractical. Compensation is also provided for the costs of eliminating damage that rendered the vessel unseaworthy, including emergency rescue operations.
In addition, compensation may be provided for the loss of or damage to cargo, damage to third parties resulting from a collision, the removal of wreckage and marking of the accident site, environmental cleanup, and pollution fines. The list also includes damage to the life and health of passengers and crew members, as well as the costs of their repatriation.
An independent assessment is required for the loss of a vessel, its structural damage, and damage to third parties resulting from a collision. It is commissioned by the shipowner, the owner of the damaged property, or a person authorized by them. Loss of cargo and certain actually incurred expenses are confirmed by documents without such an assessment.
Under what conditions can 80% compensation be received
The damage must occur while the vessel is in Ukraine’s territorial sea, within the Temporary Maritime Route, or in the waters of an open Ukrainian port where vessel traffic is permitted. Damage is taken into account from the date Resolution No. 1248 enters into force.
At the time of the incident, the shipowner must have a valid insurance contract or a P&I policy, which generally covers liability to third parties. However, the relevant war risk must be excluded from the insurance coverage, or the coverage must not extend to areas of hostilities, navigation restrictions, or military strikes. Assistance will not be granted without a valid insurance contract or P&I policy.
For losses assessed by an independent specialist, the maximum payment is 80% of the assessed amount. For example, for damage amounting to UAH 10 million, up to UAH 8 million may be paid. The review of the report is ensured by the State Property Fund, while the actual payment depends on the budget.
How to apply for compensation: step-by-step instructions
Step 1. Document the circumstances of the incident. Collect confirmation of the date, location, nature of the attack, and damage to the vessel and cargo.
Step 2. Check the insurance coverage. Determine whether the contract or P&I policy was valid and which specific war risks it does not cover. Prepare a duly certified copy.
Step 3. Determine the amount of the loss. For the types of damage provided for by the resolution, commission an independent assessment; for other losses, collect the cargo documents and confirmation of the actual expenses incurred.
Step 4. Prepare the application. The application letter is drawn up in free form and describes the circumstances and date on which the damage was caused. The document is signed by the shipowner.
Step 5. Submit the package to the Ministry for Development. The documents may be sent by mail to the ministry’s address or submitted electronically. Electronic materials must include scans or photocopies of the originals of paper documents and a qualified electronic signature or an advanced electronic signature based on a qualified certificate. Save the confirmation of submission.
The resolution does not provide for a single application through Diia or a special online form: the documents are addressed directly to the ministry. In the paper version, it is advisable to include a description of the contents.
What documents are required to receive compensation
The following must be submitted to the Ministry for Development:
-  a letter-application signed by the shipowner, describing the event and the date the damage occurred; 
-  a certified copy of the insurance contract or P&I policy;  
-  materials confirming the relevant type of loss.  
The insurance document may be certified by a notary, a consular institution, the insurer — a party to the contract, or the relevant P&I club.
Depending on the nature of the damage, the following may also be required:
-  an appraiser’s report;  
-  cargo documents and evidence of its loss or damage;  
-  documents regarding the costs of removing debris, eliminating pollution, paying fines, health-related damage, and repatriation. 
All documents in a foreign language must be accompanied by a Ukrainian translation whose accuracy has been certified in accordance with legislation on notarial matters. Check that the scans are legible and complete.
How much time is available to submit an application and when the money will be paid
The shipowner must apply to the Ministry for Development no later than 180 calendar days from the date the damage was caused. The period does not depend on the completion of repairs or the assessment.
If the Ministry for Development identifies violations of the requirements for the submitted materials or finds that the applicant does not meet the established conditions, it will notify the applicant in writing of the refusal within 10 working days from the date it receives the documents. The resolution does not specify a clear payment date for positively reviewed applications.
Compensation will be transferred in hryvnias to an account at a bank registered in Ukraine. An important nuance: losses caused in 2026 will be financed from the 2027 state budget, if the relevant funds are provided for in it. Immediate payment is not предусмотрено.
Can compensation be refused, and what should be checked before applying
Refusal is possible if the vessel, route, or applicant does not meet the conditions of the resolution, the procedure for preparing the documents has been violated, or the claimed damage has not been properly confirmed. It is also necessary to check that the insurance is valid and to meet the 180-day deadline.
The program has restrictions concerning vessels whose owners, shipowners, or related persons have the ties to russia and belarus specified in the resolution, as well as concerning persons subject to Ukrainian sanctions. An exception is established for citizens of these states who permanently and lawfully reside in Ukraine. Compensation is also not available to a shipowner who has already received insurance compensation under the mechanism of Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 1140 dated November 2, 2023.
Before applying, one should verify the date and location of the attack, the port’s status, the nature of the cargo, the insurance contract, the documents relating to the losses, and the shipowner’s details. A complete package does not guarantee payment of exactly 80% of the losses. Before applying, one should also clarify with the Ministry for Development the current channels for submitting electronic documents and keep copies of all submitted materials.
A reminder
In June 2026, Ukrainians were allowed to apply for compensation for new categories in the Register of Damages.

Air Force Considering Air-to-Air Role for Bombers amid Fighter Procurement Constraints
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:29:17 UTC
04:29:17 KST

The Air Force’s future strategy for fighting wars could include arming bombers with air-to-air strike capabilities, the service said in a new report to Congress.
The report, titled “Long-Term USAF Fighter Force Structure” and submitted to lawmakers Oct. 16, said that “developing air-to-air capabilities on bombers” is being considered as a way to expand the service’s combat capabilities.
In the report, which was briefed to reporters Oct. 20 and obtained by Air & Space Forces Magazine, the Air Force estimates it will need 1,509 combat-coded aircraft by 2035 to meet the demands of the National Defense Strategy at moderate risk, with about 40 percent of its fighter fleet consisting of F-35A Joint Strike Fighters. That’s up from the 1,288 combat-coded fighters the service has today.
The Air Force is working on ways to procure as many Lockheed Martin F-35As, Boeing F-15EX Eagle IIs, and Boeing F-47 sixth-generation fighters as possible, the report said. However, the report acknowledges that hitting its fighter procurement targets may not be achievable due to “fiscal realities and industrial production limitations.”
Other recapitalization options could include acquiring an entirely new fighter, relying more on semi-autonomous drone fighters known as Collaborative Combat Aircraft—and giving air-to-air roles and capabilities to bombers, the report said.
Air Force fighters have long carried out air-to-ground strikes, but bombers have not traditionally performed air-to-air missions.
However, with the Air Force’s fleet constrained by slow procurement of new fighters and the retirement of aging ones, the service has been looking for new ways to accomplish its missions.
Former Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. David Allvin signaled an openness to the B-21 Raider stealth bomber carrying out a greater role in the service’s air dominance plans in an October 2024 discussion with reporters in Washington.
At the time, the Air Force had put its F-47 program—then called Next-Generation Air Dominance—on hold amid concerns about its potential costs. The Air Force was reviewing its approach to air superiority to try to figure out ways to get the job done, potentially without the plane that would become the F-47.
When asked if the air superiority review could lead to a more prominent role for the B-21, Allvin said “We have not taken that off the table.”
A year later, in September 2025, sources told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the Air Force was studying whether a large flying wing-type stealth aircraft—potentially based on a B-21—armed with dozens of air-to-air missiles could be an element of its future air superiority force.
In its latest report, the Air Force wrote that it is “committed to the full modernization and recapitalization of its legacy fighter fleet, while placing an enormous effort into our newest fighter, the F-47.”
CCAs are also rapidly advancing and likely to at least meet, if not beat, the program’s schedule, the report said. But the Air Force said CCAs aren’t yet ready to change how the service plans for its future fighter fleet, though that day will come.
“There is absolutely a world in which the incorporation of CCAs into the force will mitigate the requirement for the number of fighters,” Lt. Gen. David Tabor, deputy chief of staff for plans and programs, told reporters Oct. 20.
The report also said it will be “essential” to modernize its current cadre of older F-15s and F-16s into a fleet of “advanced fourth-generation capability” jets—planes that do not have stealth capabilities but can still operate in highly contested environments, often with the aid of advanced sensors and electronic warfare weapons.
But it would take more than a decade of investments in the Air Force’s current depot infrastructure to modernize enough jets to increase the Air Force’s aircraft availability, the report said, calling that approach “insufficient, as it perpetuates reliance on a fleet averaging 30+ years in age.”
Aside from upgrading existing fighters, the service could also buy new advanced fourth-gen jets like the F-15EX and, potentially, a new version of Lockheed Martin’s F-16 Fighting Falcon, dubbed the F-16G. Tabor said the service has not yet made any decision on buying new F-16s, “and we’re not in a position where that decision has to be made immediately.”
In its report, the Air Force said it has to pursue a two-track strategy of modernizing existing aircraft to meet immediate operational requirements, while recapitalizing its legacy fighters at the same time.

Emmanuel Macron has condemned racism in French society after a gunman opened fire from a car west of Paris on Friday, killing one person, wounding a 12-year-old girl and injuring four others in what the president called a “racist terrorist attack”.
Macron arrived at the scene of the drive-by shooting in Trappes on Friday night, saying he was deeply saddened by what he called the “premeditated” attack. The 12-year-old girl, who was shot eight times, is being treated in hospital.
“What happened today marks a turning point for our country; what happened today was a terrorist and racist attack,” Macron said.
He said the gunman had targeted people because of the colour of their skin. The president said racism had often become part of the “ambient discourse in France” and created “an atmosphere”.
He said: “Don’t let this terrorist attack divide us.” He called for “respect and unity”, saying many French people would be scared and thinking “this could happen to me”.
Ali Rabeh, the leftwing mayor of Trappes, said the gunman had set out by car on Friday morning “firing at random, wanting to cause a bloodbath” as he drove through the town and neighbouring La Verrière. The mayor called it “objectively a racist attack, probably Islamophobic”.
Rabeh, whose family has Moroccan roots, said: “The people targeted today could just as easily have been my mother, my brothers or my sisters-in-law.
“A 12-year-old girl is between life and death after being targeted by a volley of automatic gunfire in our country. Her crime was probably being of colour,” he added. “It’s probably one of the first attempts at a mass crime of Islamophobia and racism.”
Rabeh said everyone in France had a responsibility to bring “calm and harmony”. He called for a collective condemnation of rhetoric that “ideologically arms those capable of carrying out such acts”.
Anti-terrorism prosecutors are investigating whether the gunman targeted the “real or supposed race, ethnicity, nationality or religion” of the victims.
The 39-year-old suspect, who was stopped by police in his car, was named by France’s anti-terrorism prosecutor as Kevin T. He had driven through the towns of Trappes and La Verrière in Yvelines at about 10.30am on Friday. Over the course of 15 minutes, he repeatedly fired an automatic weapon, first at a petrol station, then a medical centre and a children’s playground.
The French public broadcaster reported that he shot dead a young black man, then targeted a woman wearing a headscarf, before shooting the 12-year-old girl, who was being treated for her eight gunshot wounds at a children’s hospital on Friday night.
The prosecutor said in a statement on Friday night that the medical status of the five wounded victims was not stable.
The man killed was named as Pengo Bossio Wangi in an Instagram post by the mixed martial arts academy of which he was a member. The Atch Academy paid tribute to a man who “set an example” and said that memories of “his smile, his energy, and his generosity will remain etched within our walls and in our hearts”.
Nicolas Dainville, the mayor of La Verrière, told Agence France-Presse that two of the wounded people in his town were cleaners of African origin attending to a school Friday on morning when the shooter got out of his car to open fire.
The prosecutor said that when the suspect was stopped by police in his car he was found with a sten gun – a British submachine gun used in the second world war – as well as teargas grenades.
The man had also booby-trapped his home with gas canisters and electric wires connected to a timer, authorities said, adding that a member of his family was arrested and taken into custody for questioning.
“The investigations are ongoing, but it is clearly a terrorist crime. It is an extremely serious act,” the interior minister, Laurent Nunez, told reporters from Yvelines.
The shooting comes at a moment of particular tension in France. Last Saturday saw one of the most violent days of unrest in years, which left public buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and looted, and at least 2,400 people arrested in cities across the country.
Renewed protests, over teacher shortages and crumbling buildings in high schools as well as the high cost of living, are expected on Saturday.
Marine Le Pen, the leader of the far-right anti-immigration the National Rally party, is polling highly ahead of next spring’s presidential election when Macron steps down.
After the Trappes attack, Fabien Roussel, a Communist candidate, wrote on social media that the far right was responsible for “racist hatred” in France.
Le Pen condemned what she called the “abject motive of racism” of the “barbaric act”.

Beijing’s priority is peaceful coexistence between Iran and neighbors
Unknown

Beijing’s priority is peaceful coexistence between Iran and neighbors
Majid Sharifi, an international affairs analyst, told the Iran newspaper that China’s approach toward Iran is not based on identity ties or ideological alignment. As a result, Beijing does not necessarily view stronger relations with Tehran as entering into confrontation with the United States.
 
China defines its ties with Iran within the broader network of its regional relationships and seeks to maintain balance among them. Therefore, the expansion of Tehran-Beijing relations cannot be explained solely by the intentions of the two sides or by existing opportunities for bilateral cooperation. From this perspective, one of the key prerequisites for deeper economic cooperation and stronger political relations is Iran’s achievement of peaceful coexistence and stable ties with neighboring countries. Such a situation could reduce the complexity of China’s strategic calculations and create more favorable conditions for expanding cooperation.
Kayhan: US not seeking negotiations
Kayhan addressed Trump’s unsuccessful effort to force Iran into submission through negotiations. The newspaper wrote that the confrontation between Iran and the United States spans four dimensions: military, economic resilience, diplomacy, and cognitive-psychological warfare. According to the article, the last of these has become the backbone of Washington’s strategy. It argued that the Trump administration, having failed to achieve its goals in reality, has relied heavily on psychological and influence operations. Recent US military movements, while appearing to signal war preparations, were portrayed as part of a broader strategy aimed at creating the illusion of diplomacy and inducing miscalculations among officials and the public. Referring to the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding and Washington’s repeated violations of its commitments, the paper argued that these experiences demonstrate that the United States is not genuinely interested in real negotiations or meaningful concessions.
Ettelaat: Short but intense
Ettelaat explored the possibility of another military confrontation in the Persian Gulf region. The newspaper argued that the previous round of conflict involving Iran, the United States, and Israel increased energy prices, accelerated global inflation, weakened Middle Eastern security, and placed significant pressure on Pentagon air defense stockpiles. Citing reports from The New York Times, it said that the United States and Israel have prepared plans to resume military operations against Iran after the US midterm elections in early November. According to the article, planning is underway for a short but highly intense operation. Some officials reportedly believe that another large-scale wave of attacks could push Iran’s economy toward crisis and force Tehran to make political concessions. Iranian officials, however, have stated that they are aware of such plans and are developing new targets and tactics in response. Tehran has also warned that any future conflict would not be brief and could extend to infrastructure in the region, including submarine internet cables and major Saudi oil facilities such as Aramco.
Hamshahri: Iran knows how to play the game
Hamshahri argued that the Islamic Republic, through its firm adherence to its principles, has sent a clear message to the White House that it does not trust the United States. According to the article, Trump and Netanyahu openly speak of weakening or destroying Iran, while soaring energy prices have become the main source of pressure on Trump. Rising oil prices have increased diplomatic activity by mediators seeking engagement with Tehran. The paper suggested that Munir’s recent visit was intended to help stabilize oil markets and provide political relief for Trump ahead of elections. Nevertheless, it argued that the united stance of Iran’s political leaders and senior military officials demonstrated that Tehran fully understands regional power politics. As a result, Munir reportedly left without achieving his objectives.
Sazandegi: America’s strategy through psychological warfare
Sazandegi examined remarks attributed to Trump regarding the possibility of Iranian attacks on cities such as Los Angeles and San Diego. The newspaper argued that, if the statements were accurately reported, they could serve several purposes. First, they may be designed to amplify perceptions of an Iranian threat among the American public and justify confrontational policies or potential military action. Second, they could help rally international allies, increase pressure on Iran, and strengthen support for containment policies. Third, the rhetoric may carry domestic electoral benefits, ranging from reducing voter dissatisfaction to boosting Republican candidates. The article also suggested that such statements could indirectly strengthen the political position of Netanyahu and his allies in Israel. According to Sazandegi, the success of this strategy depends on the credibility of the claims, developments on the ground, and public reaction. It concluded that Iran’s most effective response would be fact-based communication, active diplomacy, and efforts to prevent the country from being portrayed internationally as a threat.

China-Russia Defense Cooperation Deepens as Weapons Technology Flows Both Ways
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:14:05 UTC
04:14:05 KST

- Category
- World
China-Russia Defense Cooperation Deepens as Weapons Technology Flows Both Ways
A new report found that Russian defense production is increasingly moving into China, while advanced weapons expertise is flowing in both directions, the Center for Advanced Defense Studies (C4ADS) reported on October 22.
The cooperation between the two countries is deepening despite an increasingly asymmetric relationship.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The report examined Chinese-Russian cooperation around advanced conventional weapons, including industrial supply chains, joint research and development, and academic links between defense-affiliated institutions.
C4ADS identified 314 shipments involving 52 Russian suppliers and 21 Chinese recipients in Russian trade records covering 2010–2025. The transfers involved military dual-use inputs, manufacturing capabilities, intellectual property, and technologies linked to advanced weapons development.
According to the report, Russian private and state-owned companies are increasingly working with Chinese counterparts to meet immediate wartime demand by moving parts of defense production and manufacturing activity into China.
Joint research and development also allows Russian and Chinese defense companies to test existing designs, reduce development costs, and bridge the gap between weapons design and serial production, according to C4ADS.
The relationship remains uneven. Russia contributes Soviet-era engineering and scientific expertise, while China provides greater industrial scale, advanced manufacturing capacity, and a more heavily funded system for turning technological innovation into military applications.
C4ADS noted that cooperation appears strongest when it serves Beijing’s own technological ambitions. China remains more dependent on access to US and Western markets, capital, and technology than on Russia, limiting how far Beijing may be willing to deepen military-industrial cooperation.
The report also found that academic ties could help institutionalize longer-term cooperation. Joint publications involving Chinese defense-industry specialists and Russian defense-linked universities suggest that research networks and personnel exchanges may support future weapons development.
The findings build on the two countries’ “no limits” partnership declared shortly before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Although direct Russian arms exports to China have declined as China’s own defense industry has advanced, C4ADS assessed that deeper industrial, scientific, and technological cooperation has continued and in some areas expanded.
The report comes amid growing evidence that Chinese technology is already feeding into Russian weapons production. Earlier in October, an investigation found that Shenzhen Xingkai Technology was prepared to supply mesh communication modems to Russia’s Alabuga drone factory even after being informed that the equipment was intended for military use.

How EU ships are still able to carry Trump's Russian diesel despite so many sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:13:14 UTC
04:13:14 KST

How EU ships are still able to carry Trump's Russian diesel despite so many sanctions
BRUSSELS, Belgium — When news broke on Oct. 23 that a ship was reportedly carrying a new supply of Russian diesel for U.S. President Donald Trump, one question immediately arose: How, after more than 20 rounds of EU sanctions, could European ships still be involved in facilitating that trade?
Trump's Oct. 9 deal to buy Russian diesel was part of a wider pivot towards Moscow that was met with widespread condemnation by EU leaders. The deal itself might also be illegal under U.S. sanctions policy.
However, media reports circulated on Oct. 23 that a ship called the Agioi Fanendes, which had just left Russia's Baltic Sea port of Primorsk, was carrying 40,000 metric tons to New York, and the ship has been traveling through the Baltic Sea westwards ever since.
Adding to the sense of mystery, ship-tracking website MarineTraffic noted that the Agioi Fanendes updated its status on Oct. 23 from heading to New York to, "for orders" — ship-speak for final destination unconfirmed.
That ship is owned by the Greek company Eastern Mediterranean Maritime, owned by billionaire Thanasis Martinos. It is flying under a Maltese flag. Both countries are part of the EU, so the Agioi Fanendes has to comply with the bloc's 21 sanctions packages imposed on Russia since it launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
"EU law hasn't changed," wrote Ukraine's sanctions chief Vladyslav Vlasiuk on social media.
"An EU-flagged, EU-managed ship may carry Russian diesel only if it was bought at or below the $100 a barrel price cap," Vlasiuk said.
That price refers to the G7 oil price cap, agreed in 2022 to reduce the profits Russia can make from the oil trade while still ensuring the world's energy supply.
A European Commission spokesperson confirmed to the Kyiv Independent Vlasiuk's interpretation of what is legally possible.
"EU operators are only allowed to provide maritime transport and related services for Russian crude oil and petroleum products if these are sold at or below the relevant price caps," they said.
And written guidance prepared by the Commission makes explicit that shipowners also bear some responsibility for ensuring their cargo is compliant with sanctions.
"Shipowners should obtain from their customer an attestation in which the customer confirms the Russian oil cargo transported or to be transported has been purchased at or below the price cap."
When asked to confirm the financial value of Agioi Fanendes' cargo, a spokesperson for Eastern Mediterranean Maritime instead said "kindly be advised that Agioi Fanendes is proceeding for orders as discharging port is not confirmed yet."
They had not yet replied to a follow-up question confirming receipt of the EU-required attestation by the time of publication.
To get to the U.S., the Agioi Fanendes will first have to travel through the Baltic Sea, and if it enters the territorial waters of any EU country on the way — 12 miles from their shoreline, they can also intervene to stop the ship.
The Finnish Border Guard told the Kyiv Independent when the ship was just leaving that country's territorial waters that there was no planned intercept, and no information they could share.
Sweden's coastguard, which has previously boarded several Russian shadow fleet ships, said "we are monitoring the sea traffic in the Baltic Sea 24/7 and keep an updated and thorough situational awareness."
However, they declined to comment on specific ships, adding only that they "keep track of all oil transporting ships."
In the meantime, the Agioi Fanendes has moved via international waters in the center of the Baltic Sea. But in international water, the law of the country whose flag your ship is flying is the one that applies.
"Malta is firmly committed to the rigorous implementation of European Union sanctions and expects full compliance with all applicable restrictive measures," the country's sanctions unit told the Kyiv Independent.
"Vessels flying the Maltese flag are likewise required to comply fully with the sanctions applicable to them," they said.
"We are aware of the reports concerning this particular shipment, and the relevant attestations are being sought from the vessel's owners and operators," the Maltese sanctions unit confirmed.
Only when that attestation is provided that the diesel aboard the Agioi Fanendes complies with the G7 price cap can it legally satisfy the U.S.' thirst for Russian fossil fuels.
With the buyer, seller, and the agreed price of the diesel all unknown, according to the original Reuters article on the Agioi Fanendes, the only possible way to prove that the ship is not in breach of EU sanctions would be for that attestation Malta is waiting for to be provided.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has warned that disruptions to global shipping routes could trigger famine in vulnerable countries, citing Russian attacks on Black Sea shipping as part of the wider threat to international food supplies.
Russia has increasingly targeted civilian shipping in the Black Sea as part of its campaign against Ukraine’s maritime trade, striking cargo vessels, port infrastructure, and ships transporting agricultural goods. The attacks threaten Ukraine’s ability to export grain to global markets, raise risks for international shipping companies, and jeopardize food supplies in countries that rely on Ukrainian agricultural exports.
Speaking ahead of a meeting of foreign ministers in Istanbul on Friday, 23 October, Wadephul said attacks and threats to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, and the Black Sea were disrupting trade in food and fertilizers, DW reported. The impact extends far beyond the conflict zones, threatening countries that depend on imported wheat and agricultural inputs.
Wadephul said fertilizer shortages could threaten basic agricultural production in poorer countries, where access to imported food and farming supplies is already limited. He also pointed to Türkiye, the world’s largest wheat-processing country, as vulnerable to disruptions in the supply of grain.
Russian attacks disrupt Ukraine’s grain exports
Russia has intensified attacks on Ukraine’s Black Sea ports and civilian cargo ships, disrupting a maritime corridor that carries most of the country’s agricultural exports. In July, Russian strikes brought traffic through the corridor close to a standstill during the harvest season, leaving grain with fewer routes to international markets.
The attacks have also hit foreign-flagged vessels carrying or preparing to load Ukrainian grain. On 16 October, Euromaidan Press reported that Russian attacks had sunk merchant ships and damaged others in the Black Sea region, with seafarers missing. The campaign has increased risks for shipping companies and reduced the routes available for Ukrainian exports.
Ukraine is a major supplier of wheat and other agricultural commodities to global markets, including countries in the Middle East and Africa. Disruptions to its exports can tighten global supplies and push prices higher, adding pressure on countries that depend on imported grain.
Wadephul made the remarks ahead of a meeting of foreign ministers in Istanbul, where he said countries must send a signal that they will not accept Iran or Yemen’s Houthi militia holding global trade hostage. He called for an end to indiscriminate attacks on shipping and neighboring countries, warning that prolonged insecurity puts vulnerable populations at greater risk of hunger.
His remarks place Russia’s attacks on Ukrainian shipping within a wider pattern of threats to key maritime trade routes, with consequences for food security far beyond the regions directly affected.

Fatherland Is One of the Most Quietly Surprising Films of the Year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:09:12 UTC
04:09:12 KST

The title of Pawel Pawlikowski’s extraordinary, compact drama Fatherland has a double meaning. In this somewhat fictionalized story of Thomas Mann’s brief 1949 visit to Germany, the Nobel Prize-winning author, after having lived in exile in California for 16 years, is challenged with finding his mooring in a country he can no longer call home; if it’s his fatherland, it long ago turned its back on him and his ideals. But fatherland can also be a state of mind where fathers live, a state both more specific and more elusive than fatherhood. In Pawlikowski’s telling of this portion of Mann’s story, it’s during this trip that Mann learns of the death of his son, Klaus—also a writer, though not as successful as his father—by suicide. If the elder Mann feels any emotion when he hears this news, it’s frozen inside him, a bubble of feeling isolated on its own ice floe. Fatherland, so secure in its rigid borders, is a cold, cold place.
Mann’s freedom from this interior island prison happens in the film’s last five minutes, a wordless reckoning that’s as quietly moving as anything you’ll see at the movies this year. But that moment wouldn’t hold so much power if Pawlikowski—with the help of his cowriter, Hendrik Handloegten—weren’t so skilled at sketching in the feathery details leading up to it. Pawlikowski is also the director of the 2013 Ida, as well 2018’s Cold War, pictures that, like this one, deftly balance postwar Eastern Bloc realities with the truth that all humans strive for connection and belonging. These aren’t dour movies, but serious, lustrous ones, less “political” pictures than movies about people trying to sort out what living really means.
At the beginning of Fatherland, no one—not even the aged Mann, played here in a quietly extraordinary performance by Hanns Zischler—has figured that out. The movie opens with a long-distance phone call: Mann’s semi-estranged son Klaus (August Diehl), living in Cannes and clearly in emotional distress, has reached out to his sister Erika—we’ll later realize it’s Sandra Hüller’s voice we hear on the other end of the line. Erika, an actress, writer, and onetime race-car driver, has become her father’s assistant, and she now urges Klaus to join her and their father on the trip they’re about to undertake, from California to the “new” barely postwar Germany. In the year of Goethe’s 200th birthday, Mann will be accepting two awards, one in Frankfurt, in the West, the other in the East, in Weimar: his justification is that his literary idol was born in one city and died in the other, though it’s obvious that Goethe couldn’t have imagined that chasm that would open between the two within 200 years' time.
Both cities are in transition, and in crisis, though neither wants to admit as much. In Frankfurt, a gray city crumbling at the corners and still finding its footing after the war, though somehow doing its best to pretend all is well, Mann and Erika are greeted by the mayor and hustled off to a press conference. There, the esteemed man himself answers the respectful but probing questions of journalists. Once they learn that he’ll also be traveling to the East, it’s not lost on them that doing so could make him a target at home in the States, where anti-Communist storm clouds have long been gathering. And there are other, more spiritual questions for him to consider. An American journalist, a woman who, it turns out, is an old friend of Erika’s and possibly a former lover (she’s played by Anna Madeley), asks him where he feels his true home is, now that he’s an American citizen. His answer is courtly but honest. He may live in the United States, he says, “but where my Heimat is, my home, is a much more difficult question.” He’s a man between states, both literally and figuratively.
In Weimar, the chief way to welcome a returning hero is apparently to greet him with a somber folk song sung by a choir dressed in dark clothing; at one point, he’s serenaded by a group of children singing the then-newly pened East German national anthem. Mann accepts it all gracefully, but there’s also something a bit quizzical and lost in his expression. He’s jarred by one alarming moment: a wild-eyed man appears at the hotel suite where he and Erika are staying, begging him to reveal in his speech that the nearby former concentration camp Buchenwald is now being used as a detention center for political prisoners. The man is whisked way by officials before he can finish his spiel, though it’s doubtful any of it has swayed Mann at all. In both the East and West, when it’s time to address the audiences who have eagerly gathered to hear his thoughts, he gives heartfelt speeches, anchored in the legacy of Goethe, about the power of art to transform and sustain not just individuals, but whole nations. He seems to truly believe, as he says at one point, that art doesn’t recognize borders—or at least, he truly wants to believe it.
Through all of this, Hüller’s Erika serves her father dutifully. When necessary, she translates his responses to journalists into fluid French; she attends cocktail parties in his honor, even when it means suffering the indignity of running into an oily, traitorous, Nazi-loving ex-husband she’d rather forget forever; she drives her father through the countryside, and though we can’t see her face as she does so, we wonder if this particular task gives her some joy, given her car-racing past. But through it all, because Hüller is such a subtly expressive actor, almost gossamer in the ways she shifts moods, we see the ways in which her resentments toward her father can’t help simmering to the surface. When she learns of her beloved brother’s death, her composure doesn’t crumple visibly—only somehow we know her emotional reserves are folding in and flattening like a house of cards. And when she sees how little this event seems to trouble her father, she can barely go through the motions of helping him on his mission, which, as he seems to envision it, is to save his homeland with his lofty views on art.
How these two find their way back to one another, and to a place of acknowledged and shared grief, is a kind of unspoken miracle that unfolds in last 15 minutes or so of this elegant, remarkably economical movie. Artistically and emotionally, Fatherland accomplishes more in its 82-minute runtime than any two-hour-plus movie released this year. Cinematographer Lukasz Zal, who also shot Ida and Cold War, renders Fatherland in the same satiny black and white, as well as the same serenely squarish, or Academy, aspect ratio. Every frame is spare, elegant, intimate, and the film moves along so gracefully that you’re barely prepared for how exhilarating, and how quietly devastating, its final moment is. At one point, Hüller’s Erika tells her father that Klaus had once said he felt Bach made him feel life was worth living. Her father shrugs that information off, but the final moments of Fatherland—incorporating a serendipitous conjuring, like a specter, of “Jesu, Joy of Man’s Desiring”—bring it back to him. Can a person have more than one Heimat? Or can that place of spiritual belonging shift over time? Perhaps Bach had the answer. Perhaps he put it in a piece of music, for us to find when we most need it, in a church or even in a movie.

Palestinian fighters kill 2 Israeli soldiers in fierce Al-Khalil confrontation
TEHRAN — Two Palestinian fighters from Al-Khalil (Hebron) held off Israeli troops for more than 20 minutes on Friday morning, killing two occupying soldiers before they were martyred at the Farsh al-Hawa checkpoint on the city’s northern edge.
The fighters were Hamouda and Firas al-Jaabah, both 27, from the same family, each married with two children. Shortly after 7:30 a.m., they stepped out of their car at the junction Israel calls “Judea Junction” and opened fire on a Home Front Command unit.
The army named its dead as Staff Sgt. Ron Yonatan Roytman and Sgt. Yuval Shai Svilem and admitted to three lightly wounded, though early Hebrew-media reports counted six wounded. The Israeli military concedes it had no warning.
Hamas called it a “heroic operation” without claiming it. In its statement, the movement described the attack as the living embodiment of a steadfast people’s will and a message that resistance will only grow stronger until the occupation is driven from the land and the holy sites.
It described the operation as the natural, legitimate answer to the occupation’s crimes in the West Bank and al-Quds (Jerusalem) and its continuing war on Gaza.
Hamas also called for total mobilization in every city, village and camp to ignite the ground beneath settlers and invaders. Every Palestinian who bears arms, it said, should aim them at soldiers and settlers.
The al-Qassam Brigades praised the attack, Islamic Jihad’s al-Quds Brigades urged further confrontation, and the PFLP and DFLP welcomed it. Hezbollah saluted Hamouda and Firas and described the operation as a response to Israeli killing, genocide, destruction and desecration of holy sites.
Netanyahu arrived in Al-Khalil (Hebron) with War Minister Israel Katz and announced what the city would get. “We will act to destroy this place,” he said, promising to evacuate the neighborhood, search house to house, and apply the method used in the northern refugee camps, whose destruction displaced thousands in 2025.
Katz put it in these words: “The Jenin refugee camp model arrives in Hebron.” By afternoon, bulldozers were working, and a soldier gave one housing complex five minutes to get out.
Residents told Reuters the homes had no connection to the attackers. Hebron and Halhul sit under cordon, the Ibrahimi Mosque has been shut and its staff expelled, according to the Palestinian Awqaf Ministry, and relatives of the martyrs were arrested.
Involved in the campaign while the elections are close, Netanyahu also floated an operation “on a scale unseen since the Six-Day War,” then trimmed his full West Bank closure to a cordon around two cities.
He accused Israel’s enemies of timing attacks to sway the vote. The territory was due to be sealed for Tuesday’s election anyway.
Bezalel Smotrich ordered demolitions, and he and Itamar Ben-Gvir demanded the Palestinian Authority be dismantled.
Hebron has lived under this logic since 1994, when a settler massacred worshippers at the Ibrahimi Mosque and Israel’s answer was to hand settlers half of it and split the city.
Smotrich moved this year to revoke parts of the Hebron agreements. Palestinian monitors logged 647 settler attacks in September alone.

Russia's attacks on Ukraine's capital, Kyiv, are intensifying. DW asked people on the ground what life is like
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:08:00 UTC
04:08:00 KST

With repeat attacks, Russia has put Kyiv on war's front line
October 23, 2026
Until a few months ago, life was relatively peaceful in Kyiv when compared with the situation near the war's front lines elsewhere in Ukraine. Now, as Russia expands its attacks on the capital, Kyiv has increasingly become a front-line city.
With too few shelters for the 4 million residents of Kyiv, subway stations double as makeshift dormitories. Starting at about 10 every night, people create sleeping areas with mattresses and small tents. Children snuggle up to adults; pets seek comfort from their owners or find a spot among strangers between the cold walls.
"We're alive," Halyna told DW, holding her 5-year-old son, Roman, close. "We've been lucky once again." Most evenings — even when no air-raid siren has sounded — she takes the boy to the nearest subway station. Her apartment is located in the Lukyanivka district, which Russia has systematically targeted over the war's four years and eight months.
'These sick monsters don't care who they kill'
In September, 14-year-old Daniel Umanskyj was doing homework in his room when a Russian drone struck the apartment building in the central district of Pechersk. A neighbor named Vlad happened to be in the hallway with his daughter at the time of the strike. "We were late that day — and this saved our lives," Vlad said. "Daniel's death is a tragedy." He added: "These sick monsters don't care who they kill." Flowers have been planted in front of the damaged apartment building in memory of Daniel.
Russia also targets places where children gather. In early October, a drone struck a school building in southwestern Kyiv. Fortunately, pupils and teachers were already in shelters at the time.
"We've been teaching all the pupils in person because we have a large shelter that can accommodate more than 500 students," Valentyna Chorna, the school's principal, told DW. As there is enough space in the shelter for everyone, students in the first through ninth grades are able to go to school, she said.
Danger at home, at school — everywhere
Whether classes take place depends not only on the decision of the parents and the school administration: It also depends on whether shelters are available and how long the air-raid siren continues to sound. If an alarm sounds in the morning while children are still at home, they may not be able to go to school that day.
"This is an enormous burden for parents," said a colleague from the DW bureau in Kyiv, whose daughter attends school. "You have to go to work — and the child stays home alone."
"Even the walk to school is dangerous because an air-raid alarm can go off at any time," she said. Her daughter attends a school not far from the Antonov aircraft factory. "One day she texted me: ‘You can't imagine what a huge explosion that was!'" she said. "I don't know if something was shot down or if there was a strike somewhere." She added: "Things like that really scare children." And staying home brings its own risks.
In September, a Russian drone struck their building. The apartment itself wasn't damaged, and her daughter was at school that morning, but it was another reminder of just how much survival has become a matter of luck. When an air-raid siren sounds, no one knows who will be spared, she said.
Kyiv's population persists
Russia's attacks have become deadlier in 2026. According to the military administration in Kyiv, 140 people were killed in the capital during the first eight months of the year, compared with 172 for all of 2025. If this trend continues, 2026 could become Kyiv's deadliest year since the start of the Russian invasion in 2022.
Attacks on warehouses have led to shortages in supermarkets on a scale not seen since the early months of the war. At the end of September, emergency power outages resumed in Kyiv. The subway was paralyzed by a Russian attack. Given the strikes on the energy infrastructure, it is unclear how the capital can reliably supply residents with heat, electricity and water during the upcoming winter.
Despite Russia's attempts to render Kyiv uninhabitable, 72% of the city's residents said in September that they are prepared to endure the war for as long as necessary, the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology reported in early October. The authorities are striving to maintain normal life in the city, where the curfew has been shortened and now runs from 1 a.m. to 5 a.m.
Some facilities have even been allowed to continue operating during "yellow" alerts. During "red" alerts, however, people must immediately seek shelter: This could mean ballistic missiles, cruise missiles or massive combined attacks.

Kushner’s hacked iPhone exposed billions in secret Saudi and Emirati money

Kushner’s hacked iPhone exposed billions in secret Saudi and Emirati money
TEHRAN — Dutch military hackers sat inside Jared Kushner’s iPhone in 2018 and watched him log in to a Dubai bank account that had taken in hundreds of millions of dollars, according to a new book by journalist Matthew Cole.
The account was allegedly one of at least two through which Abu Dhabi and Riyadh gave Donald Trump’s son-in-law access to about $2 billion while he steered Middle East policy from the White House.
Cole’s excerpt, published October 22 in Vanity Fair, starts with a GRU operative who specialized in stolen bank data. The Dutch MIVD learned he was headed for Britain, got London’s permission to seize him on arrival, and gave him a choice between working for The Hague and facing espionage charges.
He chose The Hague. In late 2017, he opened a GRU server in Rostov, where the Dutch found screenshots of Kushner’s iPhone X.
The MIVD reverse-engineered the Russian break-in. By early 2018 its team could watch Kushner’s screen whenever he used the phone.
Dutch press reported they spent years inside the Cozy Bear hacking group and fed the Americans warnings. This time the target worked in the White House.
Alpha, Beta and a defense fund
On that screen, Cole writes, was a First Abu Dhabi Bank account that Kushner signed for but did not own.
It belonged to the Watani Al Emarat Foundation, a state-funded Emirati “charity” that Cole says doubled as cover for covert weapons purchases abroad.
Roughly $750 million in cash reportedly entered through Azerbaijan, a channel that Cole says was used to conceal the money’s origins in the Arab monarchies of the Persian Gulf.
The ruling Arab families had initially floated a fund exceeding $10 billion to advance Trump’s foreign policy agenda, before settling on accounts for Kushner. “Jared was looking for shortcuts in his diplomacy,” one source told Cole.
A second account, Beta, allegedly held about $1 billion in Israel’s Central Bank by spring 2018. Netanyahu supposedly demanded notice of any transfer, relayed through Ambassador David Friedman, and much of the money later went to Cyprus.
A third deposit was reportedly earmarked for Israeli assistance to the UAE in countering Iran. Cole says the Dutch probably saw only Alpha.
In return for these financial commitments, Kushner backed Abu Dhabi and Riyadh’s regional demands from inside the White House and helped negotiate a secret defense pact committing Israeli military aid to provide military backing to the UAE.
Four senior Trump officials, among them two national security advisers, a chief of staff and a former CIA director, told Cole they knew of no presidential approval for Kushner to use a foreign government account.
A former Mueller prosecutor told him any promise made in return for the money could break bribery and foreign agent laws. House Oversight Democrats say Kushner must answer before the American people.
A marketplace, and Iran across the table
In 2018, The Intercept reported that Mohammed bin Salman bragged to Mohamed bin Zayed that Kushner was “in his pocket.”
Months after leaving office, Kushner took $2 billion from the Saudi sovereign fund for Affinity Partners, over a screening panel’s finding that its due diligence was “unsatisfactory in all aspects.” Rep. Jamie Raskin has since put Affinity’s assets at $6.16 billion.
Cole’s account paints a stark picture of how Washington, Tel Aviv and the Arab monarchies in the Persian Gulf operate behind closed doors.
Israel wanted “normalization” with the Arab states on its own terms. Mohamed bin Zayed and his Israeli allies wanted the 2015 nuclear deal (JCPOA) blown up. Mohammed bin Salman wanted the crown.
Kushner, an unpaid White House adviser with signing rights on an Emirati account, sat at the center of all three demands. Trump pulled out of the Iran deal in May 2018, in the very months the Dutch say they were watching that account.
On the book’s account, the strategy against Iran and the wider Resistance ran on secret slush funds, dark money and a corruption so routine that one source told Cole the Arab rulers in the Persian Gulf spend a billion or two on such arrangements every year.
The reports in Cole’s book date from Trump’s first term. In the second, the money may no longer need hidden accounts, because it moves through deals in plain view.
A $2 billion Emirati investment was tied to the Trump family’s USD1 stablecoin. Steve Witkoff met Tahnoon Bin Zayed on a yacht off Sardinia, and months later the White House moved to ease AI chip exports to Tahnoon’s G42.
David Sacks, the administration’s AI and crypto czar, received an ethics waiver to join those talks despite earlier fund ties to Persian Gulf investors. Tahnoon is the same man who chaired First Abu Dhabi Bank when, Cole says, the Alpha account was filling up.
What has emerged is a marketplace where Saudi and Emirati money, Israeli strategic interests and a president’s son-in-law met behind closed doors and conspired.
That same son-in-law is now a White House envoy deeply involved in Washington’s regional misadventures, including the war on Iran. Tehran has every reason to ask who he really works for.

Centre bans reuse of single-use medical devices across hospitals; flags recycling of disposables

Govt Flags Recycling Of Disposables In Critical Ops (Generative image)
NEW DELHI: The Centre has directed public and private healthcare facilities across the country to strictly stop reusing medical devices and disposable surgical items meant for one-time use, flagging patient safety risks from the practice, particularly in critical care.In a letter dated Oct 16, the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) said it had come to its notice that some private and corporate hospitals were reusing single-use devices after sterilising them, including items used in cardiology, nephrology, oncology, cardiothoracic and vascular surgery (CTVS), neurosurgery and other clinical services.The DGHS said that reuse could expose patients to cross-infection, device malfunction, reduced performance and other complications. It said the practice could violate provisions of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, the Medical Devices Rules, 2017, the Clinical Establishments Act, 2010, and applicable infection-control and biomedical waste management requirements.
The DGHS said that reuse could expose patients to cross-infection, device malfunction, reduced performance and other complications.
The directive calls on state health authorities and drug controllers to maintain strict vigilance, inspect and monitor healthcare establishments, and take action against violations under applicable laws and regulations.
Devices labelled for single use must be used in accordance with the instructions and recommendations of the original equipment manufacturer.The letter, addressed to health authorities in states and Union Territories, the Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI) and the central govt health scheme (CGHS), also flagged cases in which patients were charged the full cost of devices that had been reused, or the cost was reimbursed by govt authorities.The DGHS said the CGHS had issued an office memorandum on the issue in Nov 2016 for hospitals empanelled under the scheme.Single-use devices reportedly reused in India include cardiac catheters and guidewires used in angiography and angioplasty, dialysis equipment, certain surgical instruments and disposable syringes and needles. Such practices raise concerns about infection risks and patient safety, particularly when patients are not informed.
Welcoming the directive, the Association of Indian Medical Device Industry (AiMeD) said reuse of devices designed and validated for one-time use could put patients at risk. Its forum coordinator, Rajiv Nath, said enforcement should also clarify responsibility when a device is reused contrary to the manufacturer’s instructions.AiMeD called for regular inspections, traceable records of device use and disposal, staff training and action against violations. It also urged govt to ensure that cost does not become a reason for hospitals to reuse disposable devices.The directive places the responsibility for enforcement on state and UT authorities. However, the letter does not specify a new inspection schedule or a separate penalty for hospitals found reusing such devices.

Mobarak puppet festival closes with tributes to Minab children, veteran artists
TEHRAN- The 21st Tehran-Mobarak International Puppet Theater Festival concluded in Tehran with a tribute to the children martyred in Minab and honors for two veteran figures in Iranian puppetry, Adel Bezdoudeh and Homa Jeddikar.
The closing ceremony was held at Tehran’s City Theater Complex on Thursday, bringing together theater artists and cultural officials to mark the end of the five-day festival, which featured performances for children and young adults, adult audiences, and open-air and inclusive theater programs, Mehr reported on Friday.
A central theme of the ceremony was remembrance of the children killed when the Shajareh Tayyebeh school in Minab was struck in a US-Israeli military attack, killing 168 students and other civilians and causing widespread grief in the local community. The festival also introduced a special section titled “Minab’s Imaginative Chronicle,” using puppetry and theatrical expression to commemorate the children, the report added.
Speaking at the ceremony, Poopak Azimpour, secretary of the festival, praised the artists whose performances had brought different emotions and perspectives to audiences across Tehran. She expressed hope that children would always have access to imagination and dreams.
Mehdi Shafiei, deputy culture minister for artistic affairs, described puppetry as an art capable of bringing objects to life and giving form to imagination and hope. He said the art form could communicate ideas that people sometimes struggle to express directly.
Shafiei also highlighted the festival’s international dimension, noting that performances by foreign artists could help foster cultural dialogue. He pointed to a performance by Peter Schumann in memory of the children of Minab as an example of how puppetry could serve as a means of artistic expression and solidarity.
He called for puppet theater to become a more regular part of public cultural life rather than being confined to festival periods. He also emphasized the need to expand public performances for adult audiences and revive student puppet theater festivals, which had previously helped nurture artists and productions.
The ceremony honored Homa Jeddikar for her lifetime contribution to puppet theater, recognizing her longstanding professional work in the field.
Adel Bezdoudeh, another prominent figure in Iranian puppet theater, was also honored for his decades of work. Theater director and playwright Marzieh Boroumand recalled their long professional association, highlighting his contributions as a puppet designer and maker, set designer, director, and instructor. The non-competitive festival also recognized participating artists and directors across its different sections, including performances for children and young adults, adult theater, and open-air and inclusive productions.
The Tehran-Mobarak International Puppet Theater Festival is one of Iran’s established events dedicated to puppetry, bringing together artists and productions that explore the artistic and storytelling possibilities of the form. “Land of Angels” competing in 14th Asian Film Festival Barcelona
TEHRAN – Babak Khajehpasha’s “Land of Angels” has been selected for the official section of the 14th Asian Film Festival Barcelona (AFFBCN), which was launched in Barcelona, Spain, on October 22 and will run until November 1.
The film tells the story of the suffering of children in Gaza and portrays the human consequences of war through the experiences of a woman who struggles to survive while protecting a group of innocent children from the horrors of conflict, ILNA reported.
Amid the bombings and military offensive in Palestine, the story follows the painful and courageous journey of a woman trapped on the front line. As everything collapses around her, the protagonist takes on the dangerous task of surviving the war while trying to protect, feed, and guide a vulnerable group of innocent children, keeping them safe from the horrors of armed conflict. Through her perspective, the feature film becomes a deeply human portrait of the instinct to protect, the loss of childhood innocence, and civilian resilience under extreme conditions.
The film features Arab actors and centers on the lives, dreams, and struggles of children against the backdrop of the war in Palestine. Rather than presenting the conflict solely through political or military events, the film approaches it from the perspective of civilians, particularly children whose lives have been profoundly affected by the violence.
The production was filmed in Tehran over a period of one and a half years. The film’s international screenings began with its participation in the Kazan festival, following its successful national festival run in Iran.
“Land of Angels” received the Grand Prix for Best Feature Film at the 22nd Altyn Minbar Kazan International Film Festival.
Prior to its appearance in Kazan, “Land of Angels” was the most decorated film at Iran’s 44th Fajr International Film Festival, where it received five Crystal Simorgh awards and eight honorary diplomas.
Among its Fajr honors, Khajehpasha received the jury’s special prize for directing, while Syrian actress Sulaf Fawakherji was honored for her performance. The film also received awards for set design, visual effects, and other categories.

Following a solid career in television, he achieved immediate international critical recognition with his debut feature film, “In the Arms of the Tree” (2023), a drama on family fractures that was officially selected to represent Iran at the Academy Awards.
With “The Land of Angels” (2026), Khajehpasha takes on the roles of screenwriter and director to deliver a humanitarian drama focused on civilian victims of contemporary conflicts in the Middle East. It has also been officially selected as Iran’s submission to the 99th Academy Awards in the best international feature film category.
The Asian Film Festival Barcelona is organized by Casa Asia. True to its commitment to promoting contemporary Asian cinema, the festival presents more than one hundred films representing the latest independent, experimental and auteur cinema from across the continent.
The selection brings together works from 25 countries in the Asia-Pacific region, mostly produced between 2025 and 2026.
This edition pays particular attention to emerging film industries in countries such as Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Mongolia, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Cambodia, as well as established industries with a long history at the festival, including Iran, India, China, South Korea, Japan, and the Philippines.
The program also includes films from Hong Kong, Indonesia, Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam, as well as productions from Australia and New Zealand.
According to its director, Menene Gras Balaguer, AFFBCN aims to establish itself as a leading international showcase for Asian cinema and to continue attracting new audiences. “We want more and more viewers to discover the vitality and talent of these film industries and to help ensure that their growing recognition translates into a greater presence in cinemas and at festivals. We are committed to cinema that brings us closer to the cultural diversity of Asia and invites us to understand the world from other perspectives.”
