Strange triangular craft reported in new U.S. government UFO release
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:03:30 UTC
04:03:30 KST

The Pentagon released yet more documents related to unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP) on Friday.
This is the seventh tranche of records released since May, though, unlike previous releases, there are no videos or images included. Instead the latest trove is an assortment of memos and reports of encounters with possible UAP.
The most in-depth account is a report from this year in which multiple federal law enforcement agents in an undisclosed location witnessed a UAP “presenting as a matte black triangular shape of extremely low aspect ratio.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The object reportedly had a 13- to 15-foot wingspan, measured about six to nine feet in length and had a thickness of one to two feet. According to the agents, the craft was steady as it climbed about 200 or 300 feet into the air above a ridgeline over the course of 10 seconds. At that point, it hovered for another 20 seconds before it flew out of sight at fighter-jet-like speeds into a nearby canyon while hugging the low-lying terrain and executing fluid turns.
The craft didn’t make any of the sounds associated with a fighter jet, however, such as roaring engines or whooshes as it flew through the air. Nor did it display any apparent exhaust plumes or other emissions expected from powered flight. It did show up on an agent’s handheld infrared monocular, however, with a uniform thermal signature across the entire body. According to the report, optical views through binoculars revealed “no propulsive apertures, rotating elements, rivets, panels, windows, canopy, cabin structures, and no protrusions or structural features” on the UAP.
Previous releases have been greeted with skepticism by researchers, who have said that much of what’s been included in those releases was previously seen or had context omitted. But Harvard University professor Avi Loeb, who heads the U.S. government’s UAP Science Advisory Council, said in a blog post that the agents’ newly released story raises questions that could be vital to national defense.
“The fundamental question is whether the triangular object was manufactured in a black project of an adversarial nation or an extraterrestrial project with off-world technology,” he wrote, adding that his current goal for the advisory council is to deploy new sensors in the areas where the UAP were observed.
“As we get higher quality data, we will be able to identify the nature of these mysterious objects,” he wrote. “In collecting better clues, we will either help the Pentagon and the Intelligence Community fulfil their mission of protecting the U.S. from adversaries or discover technology of non-human origin. Investing in the related research is a win-win proposition.”
Friday’s release also included several other witness accounts. Among them was a 1957 Air Force report on an incident involving a B-52 bomber making radar contact with a UAP for five to seven minutes over Saudi Arabia and a 1955 report in which a civilian in California recounted seeing a “very bright and orange” object falling straight down.

The Trump administration is considering a ‘heat ray’ weapon for the border—here’s what to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:03:21 UTC
04:03:21 KST

The Pentagon has granted the Department of Homeland Security permission to test a controversial and little-used “heat ray” weapon at the U.S.-Mexico border, prompting questions over how safe it is and how it works.
The weapon is called the Active Denial System, and it is considered a nonlethal weapon: it causes pain but is not supposed to damage tissue. It works using millimeter waves, which—true to their name—have wavelengths between one and 10 millimeters. Millimeter waves are also used in full-body scanners, such as those in airports—but the military weapon puts out its 95-gigahertz waves at a higher intensity for just a few seconds at a time, says Kenneth Foster, a professor emeritus of bioengineering at the University of Pennsylvania.
This energy penetrates about 0.4 mm, the thickness of about four sheets of standard printer paper, of the skin, where it excites water molecules in cells and heats them up. The feeling is reportedly similar to standing in front of a hot oven. “It causes intense pain, but the exposure is not long enough to do damage,” Foster says.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
If the weapon is used at the border, it will mark one of the few uses of this technology ever since its development in the early 2000s, as CNN reported on Wednesday. According to the nonprofit Physicians for Human Rights (PHR), the system was used briefly in Afghanistan in 2010 but has not been employed in warfare since then. Prison officials in Los Angeles considered testing the device for riot control in 2010, yet pushback from civil rights groups and the Federal Communications Commission led to the program being scrapped.
“The weapon is politically toxic,” Foster says.
The system is bulky and temperamental; it doesn’t work well in rain, fog or mist because the moisture attenuates the heating effect on the targeted person. Foster suspects that the system’s cost, expense and bulk have a lot to do with why it hasn’t been used more; other nonlethal methods such as sound cannons are cheaper and more available, he says.
Persistent concerns about the safety of something that sounds suspiciously like a microwave oven are also a barrier. Microwaves, with their longer wavelengths, penetrate farther into skin and can cause more damage. Military testing suggests that exposure to millimeter-wave nonlethal weapons does not cause skin damage. Tests on volunteers in 2005 and 2006 did lead to a handful of people getting skin blisters and rashes, however. An incident in 2007 in which the weapon was set at the incorrect power and pulse duration led to one airman receiving second-degree blistering burns on 8 percent of his body. So it is possible that improper usage could cause injury.
“There is very, very little published on these weapons,” says Rohini Haar, an emergency physician at the University of California, Berkeley, School of Public Health and a medical adviser at PHR. Without published research, she says, there is little information on their safety in general or on potential differences in safety in real-world usage versus experimental or training exercises.
John Erath, Senior Policy Director for the Center for Arms Control and Non-Proliferation, a nonprofit, points out that testing such weapons in human trials for safety is “an ethical dead-end.”
PHR has also documented numerous cases of crowd-control weapons being used against people with no easy way to escape. Indiscriminate use of the system could cause injury not just from the heat itself but also from the reaction of those targeted, says Michael Crowley. He is a senior researcher at the U.K.-based nonprofit Omega Research Foundation, which tracks the use of military and police weapons and human rights abuses.
“Given its silent and invisible nature, the ‘pain ray’ makes avoidance of the weapon difficult, which could prevent people from dispersing safely, lead to panic-driven stampedes and consequent serious injuries,” Crowley says.
“Furthermore, those subsequently injured or crowd members who have existing mobility difficulties, including the elderly and very young, may not be able to leave the area and then be subject to repeated or prolonged exposure of this weapon, potentially leading to further intolerable pain and serious injuries,” he adds.

US designates helium as critical material as Europe faces supply squeeze
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:02:40 UTC
04:02:40 KST

The US has declared helium a critical material as war in the Middle East and export curbs by Russia and China squeeze global supplies of a gas vital to chipmaking, leaving Europe scrambling to secure its share.
The United States designated helium as a critical material on Friday, citing its essential role in semiconductor manufacturing and energy production, as well as growing concerns over disruptions to global supplies.
The move by the US Department of Energy will make additional federal funding available to helium producers and bring the material under closer government monitoring.
Helium is mainly extracted as a byproduct of natural gas processing. The US is the world's largest producer of both natural gas and helium, with Qatar and Russia also among the leading helium producers.
Helium exports from Qatar have been severely disrupted by Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz amid its war with Israel and the US. Iranian strikes on Qatari infrastructure have further affected supplies, while Russia introduced temporary export restrictions in April to protect its domestic market.
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the Trump administration was seeking to reduce dependence on foreign sources of critical materials, boost domestic manufacturing, support American jobs and strengthen economic and national security.
“President Trump is bringing back America’s manufacturing industry, and that means making sure we have the materials needed to build things in America again,” Wright said in a statement.
Europe faces mounting pressure on helium supplies
While the US is seeking to strengthen domestic production, Europe has faced growing difficulties securing helium supplies, compounded by China's decision in July to impose a temporary export ban on the gas.
Although China is not a major helium producer, it has served as a transit hub for Russian supplies reaching Europe, according to a July report by the Financial Times.
The EU banned direct imports of Russian helium in 2024, but some supplies reportedly continued to reach European markets through China.

First tanker carrying Russian diesel to U.S. heads for New York after Trump-Putin deal, set to arrive after midterm elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:01:16 UTC
04:01:16 KST

The first tanker carrying Russian diesel to the United States since January 2022 is already on its way across the Atlantic following an agreement between Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump. The Malta-flagged Agioi Fanendes loaded 40,000 metric tons of diesel at the Baltic port of Primorsk on Oct. 22 and set course for New York, Reuters reported, citing LSEG data. The tanker is expected to arrive Nov. 7, four days after the U.S. congressional midterm elections.
According to data from ship tracking platform Starboard Maritime Intelligence reviewed by The Insider, Agioi Fanendes (IMO 9798375) left the Russian port of Primorsk at 10:58 p.m. GMT on Oct. 22. As of the morning of Oct. 23, the vessel was in the Gulf of Finland between the Finnish and Estonian coasts, traveling west at about 12 knots per hour (23 kilometers per hour). The crew listed New York as its destination, with an estimated arrival date of Nov. 7.
Starboard Maritime Intelligence data showed that after leaving Primorsk, the tanker’s reported draft increased from 7.8 meters to 11 meters, consistent with the vessel having taken on cargo. Agioi Fanendes is 183 meters long and 32 meters wide. Its registered owner is Maltatankers Shipping Ltd., and its operator is Greece-based Eastern Mediterranean Maritime Ltd. The tanker is carrying ultra-low-sulfur diesel.
After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February of 2022, the United States banned imports of Russian energy products, including refined petroleum products. However, on Oct. 9, Trump announced an agreement with Putin under which Russia would supply 4.8 million metric tons of diesel to the U.S. and global markets.
Under the announced plan, Russia was to export the first 300,000 metric tons in October and another 500,000 metric tons in November, to be followed by larger volumes at later stages. The current 40,000-ton shipment amounts to about 13% of the volume initially promised for October.
The open-source intelligence project TankerTrackers later reported that it had identified three tankers carrying Russian diesel to the United States. According to the project, all three vessels loaded at Russian fuel terminals and openly listed U.S. ports as their destinations.
On the same day Trump announced the agreement, the U.S. Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued General License No. 135, authorizing transactions involving the sale, delivery, unloading, and import of Russian diesel, including direct imports into the United States. The authorization is valid through April 7, 2027. In response, Russian authorities lifted restrictions on diesel exports ahead of schedule. The restrictions had been introduced due to domestic fuel shortages following Ukraine’s sustained campaign of strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Speculation regarding Trump’s motivation for striking the deal has focused on the idea that he is hoping Russian supplies will help reduce domestic diesel prices, thereby providing his Republican party with a popularity boost ahead of the upcoming midterm elections. The first tanker, however, is not expected to reach the U.S. coast until after voting concludes on Nov. 3, and the physical arrival of a cargo does not necessarily coincide with the timing of its effect on futures or wholesale market prices.
As previously reported by Reuters, Russian fuel began returning to other traditional markets after the restrictions were lifted. Tankers leaving Primorsk headed to Turkey and Brazil, and deliveries to Morocco also resumed. Overall Russian diesel exports since the start of 2026, however, have fallen 41% year-on-year — to an average of 345,000 barrels a day.
Sanctions expert George Voloshin previously told The Insider that Russia could realistically meet its initial commitments to export 300,000 to 500,000 metric tons, but that increasing deliveries to between 1 million and 3 million metric tons a month was more doubtful. He said Russian oil companies would have to restore damaged refinery capacity and increase exports at the expense of rebuilding strategic fuel reserves at home.
The Trump-Putin agreement has drawn criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and U.S. lawmakers. Zelensky called Washington’s decision “weak,” while a group of Democratic senators described it as a betrayal of Ukraine and a threat to U.S. national security. They argued that renewed U.S. purchases of Russian energy products would provide Moscow with additional revenue to continue its war.

‘Feels like New York after COVID’: Tel Aviv residents alarmed by street disorder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:59:09 UTC
03:59:09 KST

Just six weeks after giving birth to her first child, Noa, 31, a resident of Tel Aviv's Montefiore neighborhood, is already afraid to take her daughter out for an evening stroll. She lives in a luxury building with security guards and pays high maintenance fees, but says even the building's security measures can no longer give her a sense of safety. In the mornings, she encounters discarded syringes in the garden beneath her home, while in the evenings, she says, numerous homeless people roam the neighborhood.
About a month ago, for example, a homeless woman entered Noa's building, knocked on residents' doors and shouted. In another incident, she says, a man carrying a saw attempted to break into apartments.
"We have security guards in the building, and I'm supposed to feel extra protected, but it doesn't feel safe anymore," she says. "I now have a six-week-old baby, and there are lots of small children in the building. It's terribly stressful. I'm not going downstairs in the evening with the stroller and my daughter for a walk. It feels like Harlem here."
For years, homelessness and public drug use have been associated with the area around Tel Aviv's old Central Bus Station and several neighborhoods in the city's south, which have suffered from severe neglect and what residents describe as an inadequate police presence. Now, however, residents of other neighborhoods say they are experiencing similar conditions. From Dizengoff Square to Montefiore, Jaffa's Noga district and the streets surrounding Rothschild Boulevard, residents describe sanitation problems and a growing sense of insecurity.
Noa has lived in Tel Aviv for a decade, but says the past year has been unlike anything she previously experienced.
"I feel things are getting worse," she says. "Rothschild used to be pleasant, but that's really not the case anymore. I would never walk around my neighborhood alone in the evening. I'd ask my husband to accompany me or take the car."
According to Noa, the scenes are not confined to the area immediately surrounding her building.
"Yesterday morning, I went to see a doctor in central Tel Aviv, and on the way I saw an unbelievable number of homeless people and drug addicts," she says. "Near the Gindi mall, people are lying on the ground. It's become a real scourge. It feels like New York after COVID. I don't remember ever experiencing anything like this in any apartment I've lived in around the city."
She also believes the municipality's response is inadequate. "I never see municipal patrol vehicles in my area, and even when we call the municipal hotline, it takes them a long time to arrive."
Her conclusion is bleak. "I feel like I'm getting signs that you can't live in Tel Aviv with children, as if the city is driving us out," she says.
‘You can't describe the smells’
In Jaffa's Noga district, Adi, who has lived in the neighborhood for five years, describes a situation that she says has become particularly difficult over the past year. She believes part of the problem is connected to a homeless shelter in Jaffa that, according to her, operates only during the evening and nighttime hours, leaving those who stay there without a place to go during the day.
"In the morning, they leave the shelter and wander around the neighborhood. That means they have to be somewhere during the day," she explains. "And that somewhere is our stairwells, the Salame light rail station, wherever they manage to sit down. These are human beings, not rats on a construction site. They have nowhere to relieve themselves during the day, so they simply do it in the middle of the street or in the stairwells of the buildings we live in."
In one incident, residents of her building had to call the municipal 106 hotline after a homeless person fell asleep at the entrance and blocked access to the building.
"People have relieved themselves at the entrance to our building. You can't describe the smells," she says. "It's a problem that's getting worse and worse. I've lived here for five years, and over the past year it's become an absolute catastrophe. Even walking from my home to the car, you can see two guys with syringes in their hands, one on the ground and another on a bench. And that's within just two meters."
Adi also describes shouting, harassment of people sitting at cafés and attempted car break-ins, which she says have become part of life in the neighborhood.
"The streets are dirty, they stink, and they're unsafe," she says. "I don't go out alone in the evening anymore."
But rather than simply demanding that homeless people be removed from the neighborhood, Adi emphasizes that any solution must also address their distress. According to her, the municipality has deployed patrol officers who circulate through the area, but their presence does not change the situation. It merely moves people from one location to another.
"If five guys are sitting on Jerusalem Boulevard using drugs, they move to another pedestrian street, and 15 minutes later they'll be moved back to Jerusalem Boulevard, and it goes on and on," she says. "They're playing cat and mouse with them instead of finding a solution. A humane solution for both the residents and the homeless people."
She says her appeals to municipal officials have gone unanswered. "I've approached various people at the municipality, and they simply ignore me. If it's convenient not to deal with something, they don't deal with it. No response. It's insulting. At least respond."
Adi also criticizes the municipality's priorities. "The municipality treats Noga as an upscale neighborhood. If all of Tzahala were full of homeless people, I'd understand the property tax rates and the way we're treated, but this isn't Tzahala. This is Jaffa. Jaffa doesn't get resources from the municipality. Period."
‘The change began after the war’
Longtime residents of central Tel Aviv, particularly around Dizengoff Square, also describe a noticeable change. Yuval Ben Gal, 30, a fitness studio owner who lives on Sirkin Street, says she encountered several unusual incidents near her home over the past week.
"On Saturday morning at 11, I was coming back from walking my dog when I saw a drug addict trying to dismantle an electric bicycle outside the building," she recalls. "The next day, on my way to the bus, I saw homeless people lying everywhere. All my friends are talking about it."
According to Ben Gal, Dizengoff Square itself has also become a focal point for public drug use. "Drug addicts inject themselves there on Friday evenings," she says.
In another incident, she describes a woman standing in the area, shouting and displaying signs offering passersby sexual acts involving herself and a dog in exchange for payment. According to Ben Gal, municipal inspectors arrived and took the dog, although she does not know how the incident was ultimately handled.
Ben Gal says homeless people also regularly sleep outside her studio. To her, the situation represents a significant change from previous years.
"Something has changed over the past year. It was never like this, and I've lived here for seven years," she says.
Naama, who grew up near Dizengoff Square and still lives in the area, describes a similar feeling. She says some of the neighborhood's problems have been familiar to her since childhood, including a location on Bograshov Street that she claims is used for prostitution. But in recent years, she has noticed another shift. "Since the war, there's really been a change. I see more drug addicts at night," she says.
Tel Aviv, it should be noted, is hardly unique in this respect. Homeless people are drawn to major cities such as Tel Aviv and New York primarily because of easier access to essential resources, welfare services and opportunities for survival that are harder to find in smaller communities. Above all, metropolitan areas offer extensive networks of shelters, soup kitchens and aid organizations that provide for basic daily needs.
In addition, high population density and the constant movement of pedestrians and tourists significantly increase opportunities to ask for money or collect bottles and other recyclable items, which can provide an important source of income. Drugs are also more readily accessible.
Major cities also tend to have developed public transportation systems, allowing people to move around without a car. Their busy urban environments provide a degree of anonymity, enabling people experiencing homelessness to blend into the cityscape and avoid some of the stigma and social scrutiny more common in small, close-knit communities.
Responses
The Tel Aviv-Yafo Municipality said: "Personal safety in public spaces and the enforcement of criminal offenses, including drug offenses, are first and foremost the responsibility of the Israel Police. At the same time, the municipality works continuously to reduce public nuisances, increase its presence on the ground and provide assistance to residents and people experiencing homelessness.
"In recent months, a dedicated unit for people living on the streets has been established within the municipal Sela division, in cooperation with the Social Services Administration. The unit conducts proactive patrols, responds to residents' complaints and promotes treatment and rehabilitation services. In 2025, the municipal homeless services unit assisted 1,263 people experiencing homelessness. At the same time, there was an increase of approximately 300% in referrals for involuntary psychiatric evaluations in cases where these were deemed necessary.
"Contrary to the claim that no assistance is available during the daytime, a new day center for homeless people began operating in June at the Gagon shelter in Jaffa, alongside the shelter's regular activities. Regarding residents' complaints, the municipality is working to improve response availability, increase its presence on the ground and provide targeted treatment at locations that generate repeated complaints.
"The municipality will continue working with law enforcement and welfare agencies to reduce public nuisances, strengthen residents' sense of personal safety and expand services for people experiencing homelessness and distress."
According to Tel Aviv-Yafo Municipality figures, 1,825 complaints relating to homelessness were received through the municipal 106 hotline in 2026 from northern Jaffa, Montefiore and the southern part of the Old North.
In the Old North, 941 complaints were recorded, with the main issues including violence involving homeless people and encroachment on public property. An additional 187 complaints concerned drug use and related nuisances, while 653 involved noise and disturbances in public spaces.
In the area around the Noga Theater, 47 service requests have been opened since the beginning of the year. The municipality said all of them had been handled and closed.

Iran calls for end to double standards in IAEA’s implementation of its statute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Iran urges end to double standards in IAEA’s implementation of its statute
TEHRAN — Iran has called on the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) to end the selective and politically motivated implementation of its founding statute, urging the organization to uphold its legal obligations impartially and ensure equal treatment of all member states.
In a statement issued on Friday, October 23, to mark the 70th anniversary of the adoption of the IAEA Statute, Iran’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations and other international organizations in Vienna stressed that the agency’s founding document must be implemented fully and consistently, without discrimination or political interference.
The mission said the anniversary should serve not merely as an occasion for commemoration but as an opportunity to assess the agency’s adherence to its founding principles, restore institutional accountability and renew its commitment to impartiality.
“The Statute is the Agency’s constitution,” the statement said, emphasizing that it must not be invoked selectively or interpreted according to the interests of powerful states.
The IAEA’s full mandate
Iran stressed that the agency’s responsibilities extend beyond nuclear safeguards and verification to include promoting the peaceful use of nuclear energy and advancing international scientific and technical cooperation.
Citing Articles II and III of the Statute, the mission said the IAEA is mandated to expand the contribution of atomic energy to global peace, health and prosperity, support peaceful nuclear research and applications, and ensure that its resources benefit all member states, with particular attention to the needs of developing countries.
The statement warned that an approach focused disproportionately on inspections, at the expense of technical cooperation and peaceful nuclear development, would undermine the agency’s ability to fulfil its mandate in a balanced manner.
Sovereign equality and NPT
The Iranian mission said the principles of sovereign equality and non-discrimination must guide the agency’s dealings with all members, regardless of geopolitical considerations.
It cited Article IV.C, which establishes the sovereign equality of the agency’s members, and Article III.C, which prohibits making assistance conditional on political, economic or military considerations incompatible with the Statute.
As an example of a discriminatory approach, Iran pointed to the scrutiny of its nuclear activities alongside the absence of comprehensive IAEA safeguards covering all nuclear activities of Israel, which is not a party to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT).
The mission said this disparity raised questions about the consistency and credibility of international nuclear non-proliferation efforts, calling for a comprehensive and non-discriminatory verification framework across the Middle East.
It added that regional security could not be built on selective scrutiny and unequal expectations, stressing that all relevant legal obligations must be applied fairly.
Iran also called for the agency to protect the right of all member states to benefit from peaceful nuclear technology and scientific cooperation.
Independence and institutional credibility
Iran further emphasized the importance of safeguarding the IAEA’s independence, professional integrity and confidentiality.
Referring to Article VII.F of the Statute, the mission said the agency’s director general and staff must remain free from external instructions, while sensitive information obtained in the course of their duties must be protected.
It maintained that the agency’s reports, assessments and decisions should be based on verifiable evidence, sound technical analysis and applicable legal obligations rather than political pressure or selective interpretations. Any misuse of confidential information, it added, could undermine trust and compromise nuclear safety and security.
Reaffirming the importance of credible safeguards and professional verification, Iran said it remained committed to engagement within the framework of its applicable legal obligations and its sovereign rights and interests.
However, the mission stressed that meaningful cooperation required good faith, mutual respect, professional integrity and the consistent implementation of legal commitments.
It called on the IAEA, particularly its Board of Governors and director general, to end double standards, resist politicization, protect confidential information, condemn attacks against peaceful nuclear facilities and restore the full implementation of its statutory mandate.
The mission also urged the agency to pursue an effective, balanced and non-discriminatory technical cooperation policy, enabling all member states, especially developing countries, to benefit from nuclear science and technology.
Concluding its statement, Iran said the IAEA’s credibility depended not only on its authority to conduct inspections but also on its impartiality, independence, respect for international law and commitment to the legitimate rights of all members.

New Pentagon materials on UFOs indicate: mysterious &quot;black triangles&quot; were spotted over an important facility in the United States

New Pentagon materials on UFOs indicate: mysterious "black triangles" were spotted over an important facility in the United States
Kyiv • UNN
Two military observers said they saw a black triangular object over a facility in the United States. The Pentagon released a report without video or photos.
Two high-ranking military observers reported that earlier this year they saw a mysterious black triangular object flying at an extremely high speed over an important facility in the western United States. This information is contained in another batch of UFO sighting data released by the Trump administration on Friday, UNN reports, citing The Guardian.
Details
The report submitted to the Department of Defense states that the unidentified object displayed none of the characteristics typical of conventional military aircraft. It disappeared suddenly and silently, literally within a matter of seconds, leaving behind neither exhaust trails nor any other evidence of its existence.
The incident was described by anonymous sources who have "significant operational experience working alongside government agencies." The location of the incident was redacted in the document released on Friday.
According to the observers, the "unidentified anomalous phenomenon" (UAP)—a term that has replaced "UFO" in military, government, and scientific circles—resembled a drone with a delta-shaped wing and a wingspan of between 2.75 and 4.5 meters. They estimated the object's speed at 1,800 miles per hour (approximately 2,900 km/h).
Like hundreds of other reports released by the Pentagon since May—as part of Donald Trump's promise to ensure transparency regarding UFO documents that had remained classified for decades—many details in this material remain vague, uncertain, or completely concealed.
While many previous reports were accompanied by actual photographs or video recordings, the report on "black triangles" contains nine identical images of the same canyon, with small triangular silhouettes crudely superimposed on them—presumably to demonstrate the movement of the object reported by the observers.
"It really looks like nothing more than a black triangular figure superimposed on a landscape image to illustrate the report. I don't think it adds anything substantial to the document itself," said Greg Eghigian, a professor of history and bioethics at Pennsylvania State University and author of the 2024 book "After the Flying Saucers Came: A Global History of the UFO Phenomenon." Following the initial flurry of reports from the Pentagon, they have appeared less frequently in recent months; their volume has also declined significantly since February, when the U.S. president ordered the government to fully disclose the information it possesses about UFOs and the search for extraterrestrial life.
The move came in response to claims made in Congress in 2023 by a former intelligence official. He alleged that successive administrations had concealed relevant data and that the government possessed the wreckage of crashed extraterrestrial spacecraft.
The materials released on Friday contained fewer than 25 text documents—there were no videos or images among them.

“The World Is for Two” – A song of love that transcends time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:54:32 UTC
03:54:32 KST

Author
Tsvetana Toncheva
News
Highlights of Bulgarian musical culture
“The World Is for Two” – A song of love that transcends time
Friday 23 October 2026 20:30
Friday, 23 October 2026, 20:30
Maria Neykova
PHOTO archive
Font size
Maria Neykova was one of the most talented and genuine figures in Bulgarian popular music. A captivating singer and an original composer with a distinctive style, she was also a modest, gentle and sensitive person. In interviews, she described herself as unconventional, said she disliked restrictions and was glad she had never succumbed to the “star syndrome.”
Her career took off on her 23rd birthday, on December 21, 1968, when she made her debut at Bulgaria Hall in Sofia. Three years later, on the same date, Neykova survived a tragic plane crash at Sofia Airport that claimed 30 lives. Among the victims were many talented artists and musicians, including her close friend Pasha Hristova. Maria Neykova sustained severe injuries and spent months recovering. After December 21, 1971, she never celebrated her birthday again. 1972, however, proved to be a highly successful year for her.
Maria Neykova and Pasha Hristova in the New Year’s Eve programme Kozya Pateka (“Goat Path”) at the end of 1971
PHOTO dir.bg
Her original song Good Evening, Good Night (Dobar vecher, leka nosht) received the Special Award of the Union of Bulgarian Composers at the prestigious Golden Orpheus festival, in recognition of “creating a new national style in Bulgarian pop music.”
On October 5 that year, the drama film The Goat Horn (Koziyat Rog) premiered. To this day, it is regarded as one of the greatest achievements of Bulgarian cinema. The film’s music became a defining part of Maria Neykova’s legacy as a composer and performer, most notably through the unforgettable song Dvama (Two of Us). The footage filmed by director Metodi Andonov affected Neykova so deeply that it literally made her ill. Nevertheless, within a week, she managed to sketch out several musical ideas for the film.
Director Metodi Andonov and cinematographer Dimo Kolarov during the filming of The Goat Horn
PHOTO arcnive
The melody of “Varvyat li dvama” (“When Two People Walk Together”) moved Andonov to tears, and he was adamant: this is the music for The Goat Horn. Later, poet Bogomil Gudev wrote the lyrics for the song, which became known as “Dvama”.
Maria Neykova composed another magnificent melody for what many consider “the greatest Bulgarian feature film of all time”, The Goat Horn. Today, the song “Svetat e za dvama” (“The World Is for Two”) holds a special place in the hearts and memories of several generations of Bulgarians, with its deeply human message of believing that separation cannot erase true love. The melody is set to lyrics by the distinguished poet, writer and journalist Dimitar Tochev. Rejected by Metodi Andonov for his legendary film, “Svetat e za dvama” went on to forge its own path, becoming one of the most recognisable Bulgarian pop hits.
“The World Is for Two”- Orlin Goranov
PHOTO personal archive
Almost a decade after recording “Varvyat li dvama”, Maria Neykova wanted another singer to perform her other song inspired by The Goat Horn. Panayot Slavchev, who created the song’s deeply moving arrangement, proposed the young, charismatic Orlin Goranov, whose voice boasts an extraordinary velvety timbre. The combination of the melody, lyrics and the singer’s distinctive voice proved to be a perfect match. Years later, Orlin Goranov recalled in a television interview how the song was recorded at Bulgarian National Radio’s Studio One in just 55 minutes.
Moving and genuine, the song has remained, from the early 1980s to the present day, a symbol of the timeless bond between two people in love, transcending time and distance. One of the most evocative images in the lyrics is that of a spring blossom, where love must be sought. The feeling becomes part of nature itself-it is reborn, takes on new forms and continues to exist even after loss.
“The World Is for Two” captures the idea that life finds its meaning in being shared, and that love leaves traces that time cannot erase. Sometimes, a single song is enough to bring us back to what matters most-the person without whom the world seems different.
Translated by Kostadin Atanasov

IRGC Navy chief: US forces have moved 700 kilometers away from Strait of Hormuz

IRGC Navy chief: US forces have moved 700 kilometers away from Strait of Hormuz
TEHRAN— The commander of the Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy says US forces have moved 600 to 700 kilometers away from the Strait of Hormuz, attributing a retreat from the strategic waterway to the 'sacrifices of Iranian personnel killed in the line of duty.'
Brigadier General Ali Ozmaei made the remarks during visits to the families of Iranian personnel killed in the Ramadan War and in operations related to the Strait of Hormuz. He met the families of martyrs Ghodrat Zarangari, Abbas Eslami, Abdolreza Golzari and Javad Raoufi-Moqaddam at their homes in Bandar Abbas, conveying the message and greetings of Iran’s commander-in-chief.
During the meetings, Ozmaei paid tribute to those killed in the conflict and stressed the importance of continuing their path.
He said the sacrifices of those killed in the Strait of Hormuz had played a decisive role in confronting the United States, describing their actions as a blow to Washington’s regional presence.
‘The US has no place in the Strait of Hormuz’
Referring to the history of foreign powers’ presence in the waterway, Ozmaei said the Strait of Hormuz had once been under the influence of powers including Britain, the United States and Portugal. He argued that the current regional situation was markedly different, asserting that US forces had withdrawn farther from the strait.
“Today, the Americans are not present in the Persian Gulf and have moved 600 to 700 kilometers away from the Strait of Hormuz,” he said, adding that US vessels were no longer visible in the area.
Ozmaei declared that the United States no longer had a place in the strategic waterway, linking Iran’s strengthened position to God's grace and the sacrifices made by those killed in the conflict.
The Strait of Hormuz, which connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and the wider Indian Ocean, is one of the world’s most strategically important maritime passages and a critical route for global energy shipments.
Addressing the families, the IRGC Navy commander expressed respect for their sacrifices and pledged continued support.
He described the families of those killed as a source of pride, saying that serving them would remain a duty for the armed forces.
Ozmaei also reaffirmed his readiness to defend the country, saying he regarded martyrdom in the service of God as his ultimate aspiration.
“If there is a war, we will be there,” he said, asking the families to pray for his martyrdom.
The visits, according to the report, were intended to honor the memory of those killed and reaffirm the IRGC Navy’s commitment to their families and the continuation of their path.

US fines Air France, KLM $425,000 for codeshare violations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:51:46 UTC
03:51:46 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
The US Department of Transportation issued fines totaling $425,000 against Air France and KLM for operating flights under Delta Air Lines' code in prohibited airspace, according to an official statement Friday.
The department announced fines against Société Air France of $105,000 and KLM Royal Dutch Airlines of $320,000 on Friday.
The agency penalized the carriers for operating flights under Delta Air Lines' designator code in airspace restricted by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).
The FAA prohibits flight operations by US operators in foreign-managed airspace where conflict, militant activity, or heightened tensions pose safety risks to civil aviation.
Foreign airlines operating flights with a US carrier's code must abide by these flight bans.
"Under the Trump Administration, if you fly carrying a US code, following our safety rules is not optional," US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said.
Duffy added that authorities will not hesitate to hold any airline accountable for failing to comply with agency regulations.
Both carriers were ordered to cease and desist from future violations.

Brazil election meddling: The stakes could not be higher
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:50:48 UTC
03:50:48 KST

Brazil election meddling: The stakes could not be higher
Cut through the corporate damage-control flimflam – ‘technical’ issues and ‘mistakes’ but no politics, they say – and the Oversight Board of Meta, the parent company of Facebook, WhatsApp, and Instagram, has just had to deny but really admit that its platforms have been caught trying to influence Brazil’s upcoming presidential elections.
In essence, they have favored the challenger and US favorite Flavio Bolsonaro, commonly referred to as ‘Flavio’ in Brazil, and harmed the incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, usually called ‘Lula’.
Meta, to be clear, hasn’t (sort of) fessed up because Mark Zuckerberg’s behemoth has suddenly discovered a conscience. Instead, it was pressure from Brazilian investigative reporting that forced the company’s hand.
Whatever effect the American meddling will have on the election result, one thing is already certain: It has made the contest and the fierce political struggle behind it even more polarized than before. A few days before the decisive and very close final round, Lula and Flavio are trying to have each other excluded from the election; when dealing with a badly divided country, just leave it to Washington to make everything even more vicious.
The crude attack on Brazil’s electoral integrity is anything but a surprise. Historically speaking, it’s the bad old normal rejigged for the social-media age. In Brazil, as throughout Latin America, the US has a long history of brutally intervening in domestic politics, featuring highlights such as a full-blown coup in 1964 and massive subversion by a lawfare-spying-propaganda campaign in the 2010’s.
And those interventions mattered. The 1964 coup removed a mildly leftish-etatist reformer whose real sin, under American eyes, was to take Brazilian sovereignty seriously. Plans for agrarian reform and the nationalization of key companies as well as a foreign policy permitting Brasilia to talk to – oh horror – China, Cuba, and the Soviet Union were enough to cost Joao Goulart his office. Back then, you might say, the nasty role now played by Meta was filled by the US Agency for International Development (USAID), fronting for the CIA and American commercial interests.
Brazil’s post-coup dictatorship was no short intermission either. It ended only in 1985. Washington to Brasilia: Regime change plus two decades of military rule – that’s what you get for not knowing your place in our backyard.
And the lawfare-spying-propaganda campaign of the 2010s – in part disclosed by whistleblower Edward Snowden – targeted and removed two Brazilian presidents. One of them, Lula, even ended up in prison, before his convictions were annulled in 2021.
Yet, while there is a long, sad history of American attacks on Brazilian democracy and sovereignty, the stakes are especially high now, perhaps as high as they have not been since the 1964 coup. For one thing, the choice Brazil’s voters are facing is stark: Flavio Bolsonaro, the favorite not only of the US but Donald Trump personally, stands for the Bolsonaro family empire itching to strike back. His father Jair Bolsonaro is currently doing time for trying to instigate a coup. If his son comes to power, Brazil will face a great, dirty settling of scores and severe danger of sliding into authoritarianism again.
Politically, Lula and Bolsonaro Jr. could not be more different: Lula is on the left; Flavio – like his father – very solidly on the right. More importantly, the rivals represent diametrically opposed ideas of Brazil’s place in the world. Brazil is not only an important G20 member, but Lula belongs to the founding generation of BRICS and is a proponent of the rising multipolar world order in general. He demands reform at the UN, especially its Security Council, and openly challenges the predominance of the US dollar, arguing for alternatives for payments, investments, and reserves.
Lula has also castigated Israel’s genocide in Gaza and compared it with the Nazi Holocaust, for which Israel has declared him persona non grata, while Brazil has joined South Africa at the International Court in accusing Israel of genocide.
On all these issues Flavio Bolsonaro stands for the opposite. Son of an oligarchic clan, his loyalties lie with the US and the rich. Washington’s recently declared ‘Donroe Doctrine’ – a Monroe Doctrine without the charm – does not repel but attracts the Bolsonaros. Like several other Latin American leaders recently, such as Argentina’s Xavier Milei or El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele, they positively crave to be absorbed into Washington’s rapidly hardening system of vassals. Where Lula thinks globally, Flavio thinks in terms of the Western hemisphere – and that hemisphere, he accepts with enthusiasm, belongs to the US.
The only other country cherished with equal fervor by the whole Bolsonaro family is – surprise, surprise – Israel. Go to a Bolsonaro rally and you are likely to see three flags: Brazil’s, that of the US, and of Israel.
And then there is China. Due to its demographic and territorial heft, its location, and its rich agricultural and industrial resources, Brazil is the prime prize in Washington’s dialing up to 11 of its traditional backyard colonialism. Lula has not only been bold enough to openly call it out but to declare that his country will never be a US colony when defying a typically Trumpian tariff attack.
What is worse from Washington’s perspective, he has worked hard to increase Brazil’s resilience by seeking connections beyond Latin America and especially with China. Beijing has been Brasilia’s main economic partner since 2009, with their trade volume reaching a record $171 billion last year. Brazilian exports to China exceed its combined exports to the US and the EU; and Brazil is now at the top of Chinese investment abroad.
The recent American de facto conquest of Venezuela was also a lesson in what Washington likes to do to those in its backyard daring to engage with America’s favorite hate object across the Pacific. But Brazil is no Venezuela; subduing it in one rapid cloak-and-dagger operation is impossible.
Yet the dark arts of interference have worked before. Recall that, in 1964, one of Joao Goulart’s unforgivable sins was to talk to China. By comparison, Lula’s determined policy of deep engagement with Beijing is off the American scale of intolerable rebelliousness. And for a reason: Without breaking Brazil once again, the continental cage the Donroe Doctrine is designed to rebuild sturdier than ever remains, at best, half-finished. And an unsubdued Brazil will always be an example of resistance.
The stakes could not be higher: sovereignty and, most likely, democracy itself for Brazil; strategic imperial triumph or failure for the US.

18:48:48 UTC
03:48:48 KST

Leaders in cybersecurity are sounding the alarm after the discovery of a major vulnerability this week. They are predicting that artificial intelligence tools will expose more fundamental weaknesses in global internet infrastructure in the months to come.
“I no longer think we’re going to be able to patch all bugs,” said Sam Altman on Thursday evening, joining the chorus of executives. In the midst of what’s being called “Black October”, for which researchers used AI to help identify critical flaws in a coding language that is used across millions of websites and may have been unpatched for years, tech executives are warning about the ways AI will be used both to identify and exploit security vulnerabilities at an unprecedented scale and pace.
The next few months will see a “vulnerability tsunami”, according to Jason Clinton, Anthropic’s deputy chief information security officer. “There won’t be enough time to patch critical infrastructure,” Clinton said in a post on X on Thursday evening. Marc Benioff, the Salesforce CEO, agreed and called it a “code red”.
AI is uniquely able to find and identify security flaws in a way and at a pace that will feel catastrophic because the security community will not be able to move quickly enough to address them, said Matthew Prince, the Cloudflare CEO. “It’s going to feel like the sky is falling. It’s going to feel like there’s nothing we can do.
“The next two years are going to be incredibly, incredibly, incredibly fraught with new tools that have infinite patience to go look for vulnerabilities across the Internet,” he wrote in a post on X.
While cybersecurity experts have been warning about a “vulnpocalypse”, or the ability for AI to more easily identify security bugs for months, it wasn’t until “Black October” that researchers were able to use AI to find a flaw as fundamental and critical as the one announced on 21 October.
Massive bugs were found in a programming language called PHP, which may have left the millions of websites that run on it vulnerable to hackers for years. Some experts estimated 70% of all the sites on the internet were at risk of hacking.
However, in the same way AI will be used to aid in identifying security vulnerabilities at an unprecedented pace, tech leaders worry it’ll also be used by malicious actors to exploit those bugs at an unprecedented pace.
Attempts to exploit the PHP vulnerability have already begun.
After the vulnerabilities were announced, government and private websites across the US and UK temporarily took down their sites to patch the bugs. The US National Security Agency (NSA) issued an alert recommending any site that runs on PHP implement the patches immediately. Malicious cyberactors may seek to further exploit these bugs to access servers without authorization, the NSA said.
“Such an access vector could help attackers steal sensitive data, disrupt services or move deeper into a network,” the warning read.
In a post on X, Prince said CloudFlare, a security provider, had seen evidence of thousands of people trying to exploit the PHP flaws in the 10 hours before it was announced.
“That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now,” he wrote.
In a blogpost, researchers at AI security platform Wiz said that this was “among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history”.
“The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve,” they wrote.

Iran will not resume talks until its conditions are met: top security official

Iran will not resume talks until its conditions are met: top security official
TEHRAN — Major General Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, has stressed that Iran will neither resume negotiations nor reopen the Strait of Hormuz until its seven conditions are met, warning that communications cables, regional data centers and artificial intelligence facilities could be targeted if hostilities resume.
In an interview with Mehr News Agency, Rezaei, who represents the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, addressed recent regional developments and Iran’s position, emphasizing that any action against the country would carry a cost.
“If diplomacy can establish this understanding, we prefer diplomacy,” he said. “But if the war continues, Iran has the necessary capabilities to sustain its response.”
Rezaei noted that Iran had not deployed all its capabilities during previous stages of the conflict. The country had introduced additional capabilities in proportion to the intensity of the fighting, he said, adding that Iran was prepared for the next stage.
Prolonged conflict threatens energy stability
Warning of the broader consequences of continued hostilities, Rezaei said the current situation would have far-reaching strategic implications, including prolonged instability in global energy markets.
“Energy markets will not return to calm for the next three years,” he said.
He also argued that the continuation of the conflict had shifted regional dynamics in Iran’s favor, pointing to a rapid reassessment of relations with Tehran by Persian Gulf states.
According to Rezaei, these countries have come to recognize that the US military is unable to protect even its own bases, despite their expectations that Washington would defend their territories.
US regional assets could be targeted
Rezaei warned that the United States maintains valuable assets across the region that could come under attack if a new war breaks out.
“Cables, data centers and artificial intelligence facilities could also be within range if war resumes,” he said, adding that Iran had a broader plan prepared for a renewed confrontation.
His remarks signaled that a potential escalation could extend beyond conventional military targets to include digital and communications infrastructure.
Strait of Hormuz: Security, not revenue, is the priority
Turning to the Strait of Hormuz, Rezaei said the strategic waterway was under Iran’s control and that Tehran was managing it.
“Smuggling exists everywhere in the world, but the Strait of Hormuz is under Iran’s control, and we manage it,” he said.
Command (CENTCOM) of leading these operations and said Emirati military forces were also being used.
Rezaei emphasized that Iran’s management of the strait was a strategic national asset and that the issue went well beyond collecting transit fees.
“The main issue is security,” he said, adding that charges could also be levied to cover security, insurance and environmental costs. However, he stressed that the strategic importance of managing the waterway far exceeded any revenue it might generate.
Seven conditions must be met before talks resume
Rezaei said Iran would not return to the previous diplomatic process but would not abandon diplomacy altogether.
According to Rezaei, Iran has conveyed seven new conditions through mediators. He said the country would not reopen the Strait of Hormuz or return to negotiations until those conditions had been implemented.
He outlined a proposed sequence for a new agreement, saying that its structure would itself contain guarantees for compliance.
“First, the commitments must be implemented. Then Iran will decide to reopen the strait, followed by the resumption of maritime traffic under new arrangements agreed upon with Oman,” he said.
Rezaei stressed that Iran was no longer interested in an agreement whose only safeguard was the other side’s political goodwill.
Iran will not relinquish its leverage prematurely
Rezaei said a path remained open to reopening the Strait of Hormuz and continuing diplomacy if Washington honored its commitments.
“Iran will not first give up the leverage that brought the other side to the negotiating table and then wait to see whether its promises are fulfilled,” he said.

It's been a week that’s seen mass protests hijacked by violent rioters across France. The looting of shops, trashing of public buildings, the burning of Lyon’s Tourist Information and the iconic Limoges City Hall. After the riots, came the curfews, and the contemplation, who did what and why weren’t they stopped. Seditious groups, ultra left anarchists and opportunist criminals said President Macron, with a qualified mea culpa: failures in anticipation and authorities dropped the ball in intelligence gathering. Macron is out of breath, exhausted and disorientated claimed the Presidential Frontrunner Marine Le Pen, the far right leader now polling in an even stronger position for the Presidency. Foreign leaders had a free for all too, President Trump wading in and Israel’s prime minister settled old scores ahead of elections there. But France wasn’t isolated in its protests and unrest, Milan was a mirror image, with demonstrations in Spain, Portugal, Belgium too, An Autumn of Discontent, and more protests to follow this weekend:
It’s been a week of American flattery in the court of Vladimir Putin. St Petersburg’s Constantine Palace was the setting for the toasting of Russia’s President by President Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff, after the release of 74 year old US teacher Stephen Hubbard who’d been held for four years accused by the Kremlin of serving as a mercenary in Ukraine, but widely seen as a pawn of hostage diplomacy. Freshly released, Steve Witkoff told Mr Hubbard that Putin sent his blessings, and then blessed Putin himself calling him a “humanitarian”, just as Russia was launching another mass aerial attack on Kyiv. The hostage deal appeared to be one result of the US lifting sanctions on Russian diesel, and, there was also an apparent commitment by Moscow to renew trilateral peace talks with Kyiv and Washington. Critics allege that the Trump administration has disregarded a just peace over the lure of business deals dangled by the Kremlin, and that Witkoff’s in Wonderland, accused of falling down a rabbit hole of Russian propaganda.
And it’s been an intense and bitter week of final rallies in Israel ahead of the first election since the October 7th attacks and the global fallout that followed. Prime ministerial candidates have been described as shouting rather than debating on issues of responsibility for the wars in Gaza, Lebanon, and Iran to the escalating settler violence in the West Bank, now on the verge of lockdown after an attack today. Voters head to the polls with a government increasingly isolated on the world stage. A last minute endorsement came Benjamin Netanyahu’s way from President Trump, who behind the public warmth is said to have harboured deep private frustration with Israel’s longest serving leader, previously calling him quote “a conman, who everyone’s sick of” according to New York Times insiders Maggie Haberman and Johnathan Swann, though this was dismissed by the US President as untrue. And Netanyahu claimed this week successive US presidents before Trump had tried and failed to get him out of office … for the past three decades.

Russia’s prison service finds no violation of the rights of political prisoner Alexander Kynev, whose leg was broken during his arrest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:46:49 UTC
03:46:49 KST

The Moscow branch of Russia’s Federal Penitentiary Service (FSIN) said it found no violations of the rights of political scientist Alexander Kynev, who was diagnosed with two fractures of his tibia after being detained. The legal rights project Slovo Zashchite (lit. “Word to the Defense”) reported the finding after publishing the agency’s response to an appeal by urbanist Mikhail Popov, who had asked authorities to investigate reports that Kynev was beaten.
In an Oct. 22 letter, FSIN said Kynev’s conditions of detention complied with Russian law and that it had found no threats to his life or health. The agency also said it had found no violations of Kynev’s rights or treatment degrading to his human dignity. The published response, however, says nothing about the circumstances of Kynev’s arrest, during which he says he suffered his injuries.
The FSIN review concerned Kynev’s detention at Moscow’s Pretrial Detention Center No. 1 (SIZO-1), known as Matrosskaya Tishina, even though he had already been transferred on Oct. 14 to another facility, Pretrial Detention Center No. 4 (SIZO-4), known as Medved (lit. “The Bear”). As The Insider previously reported, Kynev was placed in the prison hospital at Matrosskaya Tishina after his detention with two fractures of the tibia.
A source for Slovo Zashchite in the FSIN medical service said the injuries were the result of torture. Kynev’s leg was put in a cast, and his condition was assessed as moderately serious. At the time, it was already reported that the Moscow branch of FSIN had opened an internal review.
On Oct. 22, Kynev told the Moscow City Court personally that he had been injured during his arrest. He said the officers did not identify themselves and that the force they used caused a serious double fracture of his right leg, along with multiple bruises.
Kynev said that he remembered little of what happened after officers forced him to the floor. He also complained that he was not receiving necessary medical care and was having difficulty moving around the detention center.
A medical discharge summary reviewed by the court showed that Kynev was treated in a surgical ward from Sept. 25 through Oct. 8 for a closed fracture. He was discharged in satisfactory condition with a note saying he was able to move with the support of a cane. His lawyers, however, warned that without the necessary medical treatment, he risked being left permanently disabled.
Lawyer Mikhail Biryukov had previously said that materials concerning bodily injuries allegedly inflicted on Kynev during his arrest by unidentified people had been separated into a distinct proceeding. The FSIN response does not indicate what decision was made regarding those materials or whether investigators directly examined the actions of the officers who carried out Kynev’s arrest.
Alexander Kynev was detained on Sept. 25, 2026. Moscow’s Perovo District Court ordered him held in pretrial detention the same day on charges of attempted large-scale drug trafficking. He denies the accusation.
On Oct. 22, the Moscow City Court rejected appeals filed by Kynev’s lawyers and ordered him to remain in custody through Nov. 24 despite his health condition.
Alexander Kynev holds a doctorate-equivalent degree in political science and is an expert on Russian elections and regional politics. He previously taught at the Higher School of Economics in Moscow. He has monitored regional and federal election campaigns, including Russia’s recent State Duma elections in September 2026.
In February, Russia’s Justice Ministry added Kynev to the register of so-called “foreign agents.”
The Nobel Peace Prize-winning human rights organization Memorial has recognized Kynev as a political prisoner.
Russia’s September 2026 State Duma elections ended with a landslide official victory for the ruling United Russia party, which retained a constitutional majority. Independent monitors and statistical analysts, however, reported widespread irregularities, including ballot stuffing, inflation of turnout, voter coercion, and manipulation of vote counts, with reliable estimates putting United Russia’s actual support at around 34% — rather than the official 57.8% declared by the Central Election Commission.
The European Parliament subsequently declared the September vote illegitimate and undemocratic and refused to recognize the newly elected State Duma as Russia’s legitimate legislative body. The resolution passed by 482 votes to 41, with 39 abstentions. Many of the MEPs that voted against it, such as Slovak politician Luboš Blaha, German MEP Petr Bystron, and Czech MEP Ondřej Dostál, have documented ties to Russia and have traveled to Moscow since the start of the full-scale invasion to meet with Kremlin officials.
