Meduza’s sources say prosecution of popular Russian Communist was planned before his election defeat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:40:58 UTC
03:40:58 KST

Moscow’s Basmanny District Court has ordered Oleg Mikhailov, a former State Duma deputy and former head of the Communist Party’s Komi branch, held in pretrial detention. He is charged with justifying terrorism over a post supporting imprisoned political scientist Boris Kagarlitsky and faces up to seven years in prison. Mikhailov built one of the Communist Party’s strongest regional branches, brought together people with different political views, took part in environmental protests, and challenged the republic’s authorities. During his State Duma election campaign, he was also one of the few Communist candidates to campaign for peace. Yet after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began, Mikhailov repeatedly voted for repressive laws.
Warning: This article contains profanity.
Meduza previously reported that the presidential administration was urging the Communist Party’s leadership not to nominate strong regional candidates who had defeated United Russia candidates in single-member districts in the previous election. Among them was Mikhailov, a Communist from the Komi Republic.
The Communist Party partly complied, but its Komi branch leader ran anyway, both in his district and on the federal party list. His original position on the list offered him no prospect of winning a seat.
A Communist Party source told Meduza that the party leadership provided almost no funding for Mikhailov’s district campaign. After his nomination, the source said, Mikhailov and the party began receiving “hints” from the Kremlin: If he did not withdraw, he would face a criminal investigation. Meduza has learned, however, that the authorities planned to launch an investigation regardless, and that the Federal Security Service (FSB) began examining Mikhailov’s social media accounts as early as 2024.
“I told him: Go on vacation after the election, to whatever country you can, and maybe stay a little longer. He agreed to take a vacation, but he ruled out emigrating. He wanted to stay in Russia,” an acquaintance of the former deputy told Meduza, requesting anonymity.
Mikhailov failed to win reelection to the State Duma in September 2026. On October 21, he was detained at Moscow’s Domodedovo Airport as he returned from vacation.
Mikhailov was born in 1987 in Pechora, a district seat in Komi. After studying biology at Syktyvkar State University, he went to graduate school, earned a doctorate, and worked at Komi’s Institute of Biology. He joined the Communist Party in 2007 while still a student and became an activist. At the time, the party’s Komi branch attracted little attention compared with branches in other regions that had prominent local politicians.
“You could’ve called the Komi regional party committee a retirees’ club. They were an opposition group — not very active, but honest,” Pavel Andreyev, founder of the Revolt Center and an acquaintance of Mikhailov’s, told Meduza. “At first, he came across as pretty off-putting — this guy with no sense of fashion, like he’d stepped out of Soviet times. But the older crowd liked that.”
An acquaintance of Mikhailov’s who spoke to Meduza anonymously said he “steadily worked his way up through the party”:
He’d help [the branch leadership] with one thing, lend a hand with another. They promoted him for obvious reasons: He did the things [the branch leadership] didn’t have enough people to do, and [the party leaders] also felt it was time to retire.
And before he knew it, Oleg had become a Syktyvkar city council member, then head of the regional party committee and a member of the regional legislature.
As head of the committee, Mikhailov actively supported protests against the construction of a landfill at Shiyes railway station. The station is in the Arkhangelsk region, practically on the Komi border, and much closer to Syktyvkar than to Arkhangelsk. Mikhailov laid out his position on Shiyes in 2019:
There’s no middle ground on Shiyes: You’re either for it or against it. If you’re for it, you’re an accomplice to the garbage occupiers; if you’re against it, you’re a normal person. There’s no third option.
Another deputy once said to me, “Maybe you should go work in the Arkhangelsk region? It’s their problem, after all.” That tells you something about a deputy who doesn’t understand that administrative and national borders are drawn by people, while nature has no borders. It’s all one ecosystem: Pollution will flow into the Vychegda and Northern Dvina [rivers], then into the White and Barents seas, and we’ll pollute half of Europe.
Speaking to Meduza that same year, Mikhailov called the landfill’s construction “a political issue, rather than an environmental one.” He spoke with considerable emotion in that interview:
The federal government treats Russia’s regions and the people who live in them unfairly. What are we, second-class citizens? Is that why you’re building a dump here? How about we put a dump in your backyard? We’re a region that sends out huge amounts of resources — 151 billion rubles in taxes last year. We send you money, resources, and even our talent. The best of everything goes to Moscow! And we get Moscow’s garbage.
At the time, Mikhailov organized Syktyvkar’s largest protest in several years: The Communists said at least 1,800 people attended. The republic’s authorities authorized the rally at the local “Hyde Park,” a designated protest area, but it turned into a march and continued in the city’s main square.
During the Shiyes protests, the Communist Party’s Komi branch built ties with environmental activists and the Komi national movement. Mikhailov told Meduza that he was half Komi himself and supported compulsory Komi-language instruction in the republic’s schools. It had become voluntary shortly before, in January 2018.
“In places like Vorkuta or Inta, nonindigenous residents openly say, ‘What do we need this language for?’ But if you live here, if you’re staying rather than waiting to move away, then respect the traditions of the local people. If I move to any European country and want to live there, I have to learn the language,” Mikhailov told Meduza indignantly.
In 2019, the Communist Party’s Komi branch actively supported Komi national activists in elections to the interregional civic organization Komi Voityr. For the Communists, that campaign was something of a warm-up for the 2020 elections for the republic’s leader and its State Council. By then, residents saw the Communist Party as the main force for political protest.
Hi, I’m Yulia.
I’m an editor at Meduza, and for almost five years now, I haven’t been sleeping well for one reason: I’m worried about my colleagues in Russia.
I’m often woken up by messages from our freelance reporters inside the country. They sometimes work late at night or early in the morning, and they message me at all hours. I never silence my phone at night in case of an emergency. Every notification jolts me awake. Half-asleep, my first thought is always the same: they’re texting me because the police have come to search their home. In Russia, you can go to prison for working with Meduza. Sometimes I have nightmares about my reporters being interrogated by the FSB. Some of those nightmares have come true.
Meduza’s reporters risk their freedom to tell the world what’s happening inside Russia. They believe their work can help make a better future possible, and they refuse to leave. Please donate so they can keep reporting.
An acquaintance of Mikhailov’s said he had “an ability to build electoral alliances with people of different views.” Previous secretaries of the Communist Party’s regional committee had focused solely on the party and its voters, the acquaintance told Meduza, while Mikhailov worked with “the whole range of civic activists — environmentalists, housing activists, human rights advocates, liberals, and patriots.”
“This guy, who basically never picked fights, hoovered up opposition-minded people and pulled them into his orbit. But the activists didn’t roll over for him. They just understood that Oleg was a reasonable person they could work things out with,” Mikhailov’s acquaintance said.
Opposition to the Kremlin’s appointee, Komi leader Sergey Gaplikov, and his team of “outsiders” was central to the Communists’ 2020 State Council campaign. Gaplikov had had no connection to Komi before his appointment. Mikhailov spoke about him to Meduza in 2019:
Before Gaplikov, the leaders had at least built their careers here. He’s a complete outsider. The State Council meets seven to nine times a year, and the republic’s head shows up exactly once a year, to deliver his report. [During rallies,] people stand on the steps of the republic’s government building, shouting, “Gaplikov must go!” — and he couldn’t care less. The main thing is that everyone who’s more or less politically active understands that these people are just passing through, here for a stint. They’ll leave anyway.
The Communists did well in the republic’s State Council election, winning 14.8% of the vote — nearly twice their share in the previous election, in 2015. Four Communist Party candidates won seats in Komi’s parliament: three through the party list and one in a single-member district. United Russia received 28% of the vote.
Shortly before the election, the republic did get a new leader: Another “outsider,” Vladimir Uiba, replaced Gaplikov. Mikhailov was barred from running for Komi’s top job after the republic’s election commission ruled that he had failed to collect the required endorsements from municipal officials.
Uiba proved a poor choice for the job. The new leader clashed with local residents and with Mikhailov himself. At a State Council meeting in April 2021, Mikhailov told the republic’s head that Uiba had “even run his campaign like a complete coward, picking outright spoiler candidates as his opponents.” Uiba responded by calling Mikhailov a “horse” and threatening to “beat the shit out of” him.
This confrontation only cemented Mikhailov’s position as Komi’s leading opposition politician — and possibly its most popular politician overall. He regularly traveled around the region and met with residents. In the 2021 State Duma election, he won his single-member district, while the Communist Party received 26.9% of the vote in Komi, according to official figures. United Russia had one of its lowest vote shares nationwide in Komi that year: 29.4%, compared with 49% across Russia.
After Mikhailov moved to the federal parliament, libertarian Viktor Vorobyov took over his State Council seat and his position as the party’s caucus leader there.
In the State Duma, Mikhailov did not vote for the 2022 laws recognizing the independence of the self-proclaimed Donetsk and Luhansk people’s republics, or for the law imposing penalties for “discrediting the army.” Nevertheless, the European Union, the United States, and Canada sanctioned him for allegedly supporting the latter law.
Mikhailov did support other measures, including the November 2022 ban on “LGBT propaganda,” the November 2024 ban on adoptions by people in countries that allow “sex changes,” and the July 2025 law allowing the FSB to establish its own pretrial detention centers.
Meanwhile, the Communist Party’s Komi branch continued to oppose Uiba, who remained in office until November 2024 despite his unpopularity. He was replaced by Rostislav Goldstein, the former head of the Jewish Autonomous Region. Goldstein had close ties to Komi: He had run businesses in the republic, served in its State Council, and then represented the region in the federal parliament.
An acquaintance of Mikhailov’s said that, unlike Uiba, Goldstein and his team initially “tried to reach an understanding” with the Communists. “At least an agreement not to fight dirty with each other,” the acquaintance told Meduza. Gradually, however, relations between the republic’s authorities and the Communist Party branch began to deteriorate, he said.
“Goldstein is a pretty tough guy. He also wanted to show the federal leadership that he’d brought everyone to heel in a region known for protest and dealt with the Communist Party problem,” a source close to the presidential administration’s domestic politics team told Meduza.
The confrontation between Goldstein and the republic’s Communists culminated in Mikhailov being barred from the 2025 election for regional leader. As before, the official reason was his alleged failure to collect the required endorsements from municipal officials.
Ahead of the 2026 parliamentary election, Komi’s authorities deliberately worked to keep the “troublesome deputy” out of the State Duma, a political consultant who works with the presidential administration’s domestic politics team told Meduza. To that end, the consultant said, they fielded Stanislav Kochev, who had fought in the war against Ukraine, in the single-member district. “A veteran can’t lose — anything goes to make sure he wins,” the consultant said.
Mikhailov, meanwhile, campaigned on the slogan “For peace,” a rarity among Communist Party candidates. Officially, he lost the State Duma election, but the vote tallies from in-person polling stations where observers were present indicate otherwise. In electronic voting, the United Russia candidate received 2.5 times as many votes as Mikhailov.
An acquaintance of Mikhailov’s said the politician’s arrest could make it harder for the Communist Party’s Komi branch to function and would probably turn it into a typical, largely inactive party branch. “Yeah, he probably could’ve done more. But he could’ve done jack shit, like most politicians,” the acquaintance said of Mikhailov’s work.
The acquaintance still considers Mikhailov one of Komi’s most popular political figures: “His [Telegram] channel is called ‘Voice of the Republic.’ I think that’s how residents see him — as the voice of the people.”

Italy-Mexico: 2026 Awards Presented for Bilateral Economic Ties

Unknown Publisher

The 16th edition of the Italy-Mexico Award, an annual event organized by the Italian Chamber of Commerce to celebrate bilateral economic ties, took place in the Mexican capital. Italian Ambassador Alessandro Modiano noted that Mexico is the second-largest destination for Italian exports on the continent and announced that Italy will participate as the guest of honor at the Guadalajara Book Fair in late November.
                                    
Among the most prominent companies is Eni México, which received the Solidarity Award. UN sounds alarm on besieged Yemen city Taiz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:39:42 UTC
03:39:42 KST

Breadcrumb
UN sounds alarm on besieged Yemen city Taiz
Time is running out to get aid into Taiz, besieged by pro-Iran Houthi fighters who are preventing supplies from reaching Yemen's third-largest city, the United Nations said Friday.
Houthi fighters have encircled Taiz since early October, blocking the road that links it to Aden, interim capital of the Saudi-backed, internationally-recognised government.
"Safe, sustained and unimpeded humanitarian access is urgently needed so that essential supplies and life-saving assistance can reach people in need," said the UN humanitarian agency OCHA.
"It's 20 days and counting since Taiz has been cut off," said OCHA spokesman Jens Laerke.
"We are seeing increasingly that the fighting makes it impossible for us to get in and impossible for people to get out," he told a press conference in Geneva.
Laerke said the dwindling water supply was a growing concern, as most residents depended on water brought in by trucks.
"With the roads closed and the diesel to run the trucks very scarce, water production in the city has fallen by about half," he said.
"The cost of the truck water has roughly tripled. You can imagine what that does to these people who are trapped there."
Laerke said that while local humanitarian groups were distributing their remaining supplies, including fuel to keep water pumps and hospitals running, "it comes with a time code: the clock is running out".
"Cooking gas is another item that is largely unavailable, and the shortage is already threatening community kitchens that provide hot meals to families," he added.
Hospitals struggling: WHO
The Houthis, from Yemen's rugged north, seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, sparking a brutal civil war with a Saudi-led coalition fighting for the government.
The civil war reignited in July, months into the US-Iran conflict that has plunged the Middle East into crisis.
The World Health Organisation said hospitals in Taiz governorate were struggling to maintain life-saving services, faced with critical shortages of fuel, oxygen, medicine and medical supplies.
"With hospital services severely disrupted and stocks running dangerously low, urgent action is needed to sustain life-saving care for thousands of patients," the UN health agency's spokesman Christian Lindmeier said.
"In Taiz city alone, 42 health facilities are reporting acute shortage," he said.
Fuel shortages were threatening oxygen production, emergency transport and vaccine cold chains, he added.
The UN children's agency UNICEF said that in Taiz alone, it had screened more than 168,000 children this year, with over 52,000 found to be acutely malnourished, including more than 11,500 suffering from severe acute malnutrition -- the worst form.
The malnutrition situation "remains extremely concerning", spokesman Ricardo Pires said.

Austria expels Russian Embassy and OSCE diplomats over suspected spying. Vienna remains a Russian spy hub
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:37:33 UTC
03:37:33 KST

Austria has ordered four Russian diplomats to leave the country over suspected espionage, declaring them persona non grata following findings by Austrian security authorities, Austrian media outlet Heute reported on 23 October.
The expulsions come as European countries step up efforts to counter suspected Russian intelligence operations amid Moscow’s war against Ukraine. Three of the diplomats worked at the Russian Embassy in Vienna, while the fourth served in Russia’s delegation to the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), which is headquartered in Vienna.
Austria’s Foreign Ministry said the four had engaged in “activities incompatible with their diplomatic status,” a term usually used for spying, Reuters reported. It did not disclose details of the alleged activities or the intelligence findings behind the decision.
The three embassy diplomats were declared persona non grata under Article 9 of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations. The fourth, who worked on military security and arms control at Russia’s OSCE delegation, was also ordered to leave Austria.
Vienna remains a hub for Russian intelligence
The latest expulsions bring the number of Russian diplomats Austria has expelled since 2020 to 18, according to Reuters. In May 2026, Austria expelled three Russian Embassy employees suspected of using antennas on diplomatic buildings to intercept satellite internet data transmitted by international organizations based in Vienna.
Vienna’s concentration of international organizations, including the OSCE and United Nations agencies, has made it a key location for intelligence activity. A 2024 report by The Wall Street Journal, described Vienna as a major Russian spy hub for operations targeting Western countries, including surveillance of arms supplies to Ukraine.
Russia’s Deputy Foreign Minister Dmitry Lyubinsky said Moscow’s response to the expulsions was unavoidable, according to Russian state news agency TASS, AP reported.

France to deploy 70,000 police officers amid new protests
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
21:34:41 EEST
03:34:41 KST

France to deploy 70,000 police officers amid new protests
Kyiv • UNN
France is preparing around 70,000 police officers for protests against the cost of living. The authorities will deploy elite units, armored vehicles and drones.
On Saturday, France will deploy around 70,000 police officers across the country. The government is seeking to prevent new civil unrest after some of the most violent street clashes in years erupted during protests against the rising cost of living last weekend, UNN reports, citing The Guardian.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said on Friday that the security forces would include elite units usually deployed for counterterrorism operations and hostage rescues. He added that calls for violence by "far-left" groups had appeared on social media.
"This is absolutely not a peaceful, friendly demonstration," Nuñez told reporters after a meeting attended by senior officials and ministers and chaired by President Emmanuel Macron. "Tomorrow we are ready to act with the utmost resolve and will not tolerate any violations."
Macron and his government are trying to bring under control a crisis that caught them off guard — just six months before the presidential election, in which the successor to the incumbent head of state is to be elected. The government acknowledged that on Saturday it had "lost control" of the large-scale unrest.
The largely peaceful demonstrations were exploited by groups of aggressively minded participants, leading to outbreaks of violence and mass looting in Paris, Marseille, Lyon and other cities. In Limoges, the town hall building was set on fire and partially destroyed.
"We will show no leniency toward rioters, looters and anyone who resorts to violence," Nuñez said. He added that, in addition to 10,000 extra police officers, water cannons, armored vehicles, mounted police, helicopters and drones would be deployed to maintain order.
Demonstrations are also expected in a number of other countries this weekend. They are part of a broader Europe-wide wave of discontent caused by the deterioration in the quality of public services, housing affordability problems, cuts in public-sector spending and the sharp rise in the cost of living.
Protests linked to similar demands are scheduled for Saturday in the Italian cities of Milan, Rome and Turin; Vienna, Austria; the Spanish cities of Madrid, Barcelona and others; as well as Lisbon and Porto (Portugal), Dublin (Ireland) and Tirana (Albania). Protests are expected across France on Saturday, although demonstrations have been banned in a number of cities or organizers have been forced to change their planned routes to protect shops and public buildings. In addition, forecast heavy rain and gusty winds could lead to lower turnout.
Protesters are prohibited from entering central Lyon and some other major cities. At the same time, Paris authorities allowed a trade union march to take place but restricted its route to the eastern part of the capital — between the Bastille and Nation squares — in order to avoid the city center.
Applications to hold rallies in Paris submitted by France’s main student union (UNEF) and the "yellow vest" movement (gilets jaunes) were rejected. The latter, whose nationwide protests shook the country in 2018, has scheduled 600 small-scale rallies across France for this Saturday.
UNEF said that its rallies — which emerged against the backdrop of last month’s protests by high school students over a shortage of teachers and the run-down condition of educational institutions — would go ahead anyway. Several prominent cultural institutions in Paris, including the Louvre, said they would be closed on Saturday.
The authorities in Marseille initially also banned all protests, but on Friday announced that a demonstration organized by trade unions would be allowed "as an exception." It will be the only authorized protest in the southern department of Bouches-du-Rhône.

Severe flooding in US west triggers rooftop rescues and evacuation orders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:32:23 UTC
03:32:23 KST

Severe flooding in the Four Corners region on Friday led to water rescues – some from rooftops – and impassable roads, with some residents being told to evacuate low-lying areas of Colorado and New Mexico and others advised to shelter in place until water levels go down.
It followed several busy days of flooding in the region that swamped dozens of homes in Utah. Earlier in the week, tornadoes blew off roofs, knocked trees on to houses and downed power lines in Arizona. At least one person was injured.
An unknown number of people were rescued overnight and continued to be rescued on Friday by New Mexico guard boats, helicopters and amphibious vehicles, Devin Neeley, a San Juan county spokesperson, said.
“We’re picking people off of roofs and pulling people out of houses that have 3 or 4ft (1-1.5 metres) of water in them, and there’s more water coming,” Neeley said.
Skies were clearing but the rivers continued to rise, with forecast crests surpassed, he added.
“This is serious. We’re still sending deputies as I speak to get people out of their homes right now. In fact, our sheriff is damn near going to lose his home today,” Neeley said.
About 600 households were told to evacuate in Farmington, where areas along the San Juan River were closed off, city spokesperson Gina Intoppa said.
“We are kind of all hands on deck,” Intoppa said.
In a Facebook post on Friday morning, Farmington police said: “Agencies have been working through the night and are doing everything they can to respond as quickly as possible.”
Additionally, a flood warning in Rio Chama said: “The current extent of the flooding along the San Juan River in New Mexico has not been observed since before the completion of Navajo dam in 1962.”
On Friday, the National Weather Service issued a flood warning across west central Montezuma county in southwestern Colorado
Farmington is the biggest city in the Four Corners, the only place in the US where four states – Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona and Utah – come together.
National guard members also were deployed to assist with flooding in south-west Colorado. Rising waters prompted mandatory evacuations along four rivers, including the San Juan River through Pagosa Springs. The resort town famous for its riverside hot springs suffered flooding from a similar weather pattern a year ago.
“Please shelter in place, water levels are beginning to recede, but many roads are impassable and unsafe for travel,” the Archuleta county sheriff’s office posted online on Friday.
In nearby Rio Grande county, trailers at a campground were surrounded by high water and trucks were partially submerged in other areas.
Some homes along the Conejos River in the San Juan Mountains experienced up to 7ft of interior flooding, while homes in the South Fork area saw water levels reach 4-5ft, the Colorado Sun reported.
The small mountain town of South Fork reported a missing bridge that extended over Forest Service Road 380, the outlet added.
Meanwhile, the sheriff’s office of Archuleta county warned residents on Friday to shelter in place, saying: “Water levels are beginning to recede but many roads are impassable and unsafe for travel.
“The evacuation check-in center is not currently accessible, if you need an evacuation location the PLPOA Clubhouse at 230 Port Ave, Pagosa Springs CO is open and available,” it added.
Photos posted online by the Colorado Department of transportation showed a road washout near Silverton on Highway 550, where brown floodwaters surged across a large section of the damaged roadway, Colorado Public Radio reported.
Jared Polis, Colorado’s governor, had declared a disaster emergency in 11 counties in response to heavy rain and flooding in the south-west part of the state.
The city of Hurricane in far south-western Utah was cleaning up after declaring a state of emergency on Thursday. Reddish-brown flood water lapped into and about 80 homes in a neighborhood and 50 recreational vehicles in an RV park.
Surreal scenes included a shipping container drifting slowly down a street.
An evacuation order was issued for the Willow Wind RV Park in Hurricane.
Other videos posted online showed people in Hurricane leading horses to safety through murky floodwaters.
“The full extent and severity of the damage, as well as the potential displacement of residents, remain under assessment,” Hurricane officials said, adding that the floods have damaged or affected bridges, culverts, public roads and electrical power boxes.
The flooding was not unexpected, just the latest from two months of heavy rain that ended a summer of drought. While parts of the south-west are rocky with little vegetation and are naturally prone to flash flooding, the recent rains have made flooding everywhere more likely, said Kate Abbott, a National Weather Service meteorologist in Grand Junction, Colorado.
“At this point we’re saturated and can’t take too much more without flooding,” Abbott said. “This is the third or fourth round of this kind of moisture we’ve seen in as many weeks.”
The severe flooding follows weeks of extreme weather across the south-west, including Thursday’s storms in Arizona, which brought golf ball-size hail and tornadoes, and a prolonged heat dome that pushed temperatures across the region into the triple digits.
Meanwhile, California was gripped by an unprecedented heatwave last week, with downtown Los Angeles reaching a record 104F, surpassing the previous high of 101F set in 1953.

Finding community saved a young Magda Szubanski's life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Magda Szubanski tells how finding community saved her young life
When Magda Szubanski's mother held her newborn daughter for the first time in 1961 she looked at baby Magda, her third child, and announced, "This one's for the world".
Sixty-five years on, after a career in comedy, on Australian TV, stage and movie screens, Mrs Szubanski's prophecy has all but come true with her daughter easily described as a national treasure.
While Szubanski is known for embodying the hilariously accident-prone and eternally optimistic Sharon Strzelecki in Kath & Kim, life hasn't always been a barrel of laughs.
In fact, the opposite was the case when, as a young gay person, she felt the intense isolation of growing up in an era when homosexuality was widely stigmatised.
"Realising I was gay was terrifying," Szubanski told Richard Fidler on ABC Conversations.
"I used to pray that I would not be gay."
With a Polish father and a Scottish mother, Szubanski was raised as a practising Catholic, hearing strict messaging condemning homosexuality.
It was a time when homosexuality was criminalised in many Australian states, and being openly gay could lead to being rejected by your family, friends and community.
Szubanski said the "terror" she felt that her secret would be found out was akin to living under Poland's post-war regime.
"Having been to Warsaw and having seen how circumspect people had to be under communism, that's what it felt like being gay," she said.
"You could not let your face betray anything. It was the most horrible feeling."
As a teenager, while she watched her older sister openly sharing anecdotes about her life with their mother, Szubanski withdrew.
"I wouldn't tell anything because I couldn't let anyone go near it because I knew they might find out," she said.
"I became even more isolated, until I eventually told my sister because I felt suicidal.
"I don't mean I started making plans, but I was just so desperate because I knew more and more that this was my truth and that it was going to, at the very least, have to be suppressed for my whole life, which was a form of misery."
At 17, Szubanski found love and support from opening up to her sister, but, as she has written in her latest memoir, coming out to the rest of her family was too uncertain.
"My parents were born in 1924. How would they react? There was simply no knowing," Szubanski wrote.
"In 1978, reactions to homosexuality were unpredictable like Russian roulette. I simply felt I couldn't risk it."
As an emotional distance from the rest of her family grew, things changed for Szubanski when she started university.
She found refuge and belonging through Melbourne University's Women's Room, and the "terrible shame" she felt about her sexuality subsided.
"When I got into that world, I didn't feel that [shame] so much. In fact, that changed completely," Szubanski told Conversations.
"Melbourne Uni saved me. It really actually saved me … I finally felt safe.
"Losing that intense, terrifying sense of isolation was literally a lifesaver."
Fighting for marriage equality
While Szubanski was openly gay among her comedic peers, it wasn't until Australia's same-sex marriage campaign reignited that she came out publicly.
It was Valentine's Day 2012 when she declared live on Channel 10's The Project that she was "absolutely not straight".
"I wouldn't define myself as bisexual either.
"I would say I am like gay, gay, gay, gay, gay, gay, gay, a little bit not gay, gay, gay, gay, gay."
It was a defining moment in Szubanski's advocacy for marriage equality that made national headlines. Szubanski was met with an outpouring of public support.
"And actually, the number of women who told me they felt incredibly relieved when I said that — because that was their experience — was great," she said.
Five years later, Australians voted in support of same-sex marriage.
Once the vote was passed, Szubanski said she felt "joy" as she celebrated the result.
"It was nothing but relief because we were safe. We were safe with the Australian public behind us," she said.
But for Szubanski, marriage equality is about much more than "love and rainbows".
"It's about helping someone to die. That's the thing that we have never felt safe with," she said.
"If you look at what happened to a lot of gay men during the HIV/AIDS epidemic, the way they were treated when their partner died was horrific, just absolutely discounted.
"It's having the right and the capacity to be able to be there at the worst time … caring for the people that you love."
'I knew something was wrong'
If Szubanski's younger years were marked by keeping a significant part of herself hidden, her experience with cancer was almost the opposite.
"I'd been feeling ill for a really long time," she said. "I knew something was really, really wrong."
After receiving a stage-4 mantle cell lymphoma diagnosis in May last year, a rare and aggressive cancer, Szubanski said she immediately turned to her support network.
"I just got on the phone … texting my friends and calling my friends," she said.
"I was just in complete shock for about two weeks.
"I started realising that it was gonna shorten my life expectancy. We don't know by how much, but at that point, before you've reached remission, it could be pretty drastic."
Her diagnosis was accompanied by something else unexpected.
"I felt — from me — this outpouring of love for my family, my friends and the world," Szubanski said.
"I just felt pure love. And I still feel that a lot of the time."
Loading...
Szubanski says she is now in "deep remission" after completing chemotherapy and won't be doing maintenance therapy.
While her body is weak as she continues recovering, Szubanski says she's feeling like herself again.
"I feel strong in spirit, but physically I'm knackered," she said.
"I had dinner with my friends a few weeks ago, and they went, 'You're back. She's back.'"
With treatment behind her, Szubanski explained how her diagnosis has fundamentally shifted her perspective on life.
"It completely changes everything," she said.
"One is the uncertainty — the fear of relapse — because it's known as an incurable, relapsing cancer.
"And then there's the other thing; of not [having] much time for bullshit. 'Cause cancer is a full-time job."

Signs point to renewed major US military ops against Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:28:53 UTC
03:28:53 KST

Breadcrumb
Signs point to renewed major US military ops against Iran
The United States appears to be preparing to resume large-scale strikes against Iran, but there is unlikely to be a military solution for either side in the devastating conflict, experts say.
Washington and Tehran's forces have settled into a pattern of strikes on commercial ships, with the United States seeking to enforce a blockade of Iran's ports and the Islamic republic trying to exert control over the key Strait of Hormuz waterway.
Neither country has engaged in major attacks on land-based targets since early September, but that may soon change.
"I'm banking now on the likelihood of strikes shortly after the midterms," said Suzanne Maloney, director of the foreign policy program at the Brookings Institution, referring to November 3 elections in the United States.
She pointed to potential signs including the movement of additional US military assets and troops to the Middle East, warnings issued to Americans in the region, and a high alert status for Israeli forces.
Additionally, President Donald Trump "came out publicly and said that he wouldn't strike before the midterms," and "it wouldn't seem to help him at the polls to do so," Maloney said.
The US-Israeli war against Iran -- launched in late February -- is largely unpopular in the United States, especially because it has sharply driven up fuel prices, and is likely to be a drag on Trump's Republican Party in the key vote.
"Fundamentally, the situation isn't sustainable in its current state," Maloney said, noting that the US blockade is "creating greater pain for the Iranians," while Washington has a large number of naval assets tied up in enforcing it.
"There has to be some kind of a resolution, either through diplomacy or through military action," she said.
Asked about the Iran on Friday, Trump told journalists that "we could end it very quickly," but said the question is "do we want to finish it off, or... do we just want to let it wither?"
Tom Barrack, the US ambassador to Turkey and special envoy for Syria and Iraq, meanwhile said Friday that there could "absolutely" be a strike this weekend, ahead of Tuesday's Israeli elections.
'Impossible to predict'
Jason Campbell, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, said there have "certainly been recent signs that renewed strikes may be in the offing," or that "the US is expecting strikes carried out by Iran" or their Houthi allies in Yemen.
He noted the planned deployment of the USS Theodore Roosevelt to the Middle East -- which could at least temporarily bring the number of carrier strike groups there to three -- as well as the decision to dispatch another Marine Expeditionary Unit to the region.
Campbell also said Israeli warplanes recently carried out a "show of force" mimicking previous strikes on Iran, and noted that US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel.
However, "timing here is impossible to predict," he said of renewed strikes, while noting that "this is admittedly an expansive set of actions to take if the intent is to simply pressure Iran to the negotiating table."
Campbell said Trump's options are more limited than they were earlier in the conflict, with damage to US bases in the region having made any potential ground operation more difficult.
"At this point, there is no safe place to stage the thousands (in some scenarios tens of thousands) of forces that would be required for such an operation," he said.
Maloney meanwhile said that "most of the conventional military sites (in Iran) have already been heavily degraded" by previous strikes, meaning any new campaign will likely "entail more strikes on civilian infrastructure and targets that impact the Iranian population."
But that -- or any type of military action -- is unlikely to bring about a resolution to the conflict.
"From the start... this has been a war that can't be ended with further escalation on either side," Maloney said.
Campbell agreed, saying: "I do not see how renewed strikes on Iran akin to the first fifty days of the war will move the strategic needle for the Iranian regime."
"They have demonstrated a willingness to absorb a significant amount of physical pain and even some alterations to targeting that includes key mixed or even civilian infrastructure will not significantly change this," he added.

On the morning of Oct. 23, the cargo ship KHORYV (IMO: 8138712) capsized and sank off the coast of Romania, the press service of the country’s Interior Ministry has reported, along with local media. Romanian President Nicușor Dan has placed the blame for the accident on Russia.
At around 10 a.m. local time, the coast guard received a report of a fire on the vessel, which was located approximately 13 nautical miles (roughly 24 km) from the port of Constanța.
The Starboard Maritime Intelligence service map shows several rescue vessels heading toward the ship at the time of the distress signal.
The cargo ship had 13 people on board when the fire broke out. Nine were picked up by another commercial vessel that was in the vicinity (apparently the Norwegian SARTOR). One person was killed, and three are still listed as missing.
The KHORYV was sailing from the Turkish port of Ereğli, also on the Black Sea. Its destination was listed as the Romanian port of Sulina at the mouth of the Danube — the main shipping route that connects the Black Sea with Ukrainian ports on the river. At the end of September, KHORYV had already traveled this route to reach the port of Galați, one of the most important shipment points for exporting Ukrainian grain.
Romanian President Nicușor Dan writes that the vessel was hit by a drone and calls the incident “an example of the tragic consequences of Russia’s aggression against Ukraine.”
In recent weeks, at least six civilian vessels have been attacked off the coast of Romania and neighboring Bulgaria. Against this backdrop, Romania proposed creating a joint command for Black Sea NATO countries to defend against drones. This week, NATO spokesperson Allison Hart said that the alliance will strengthen its grouping of maritime patrol aircraft and drones in the region.

Former FBI officials charged in connection with Hunter Biden laptop probe
Lawyers for two accused officials say Department of Justice seeking to revive scandal before midterm vote.
Two former Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) agents have been charged in connection with a 2020 probe into a laptop belonging to former President Joe Biden’s son, Hunter Biden.
The former officials, Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, were charged with lying to Congress. They made their first court appearance in Washington, DC, on Friday.
Lawyers for the officials accused the Department of Justice of filing the charges to revive the salacious saga just days before the November 3 midterm vote, in which Republicans face an uphill battle against Democrats to maintain control of Congress.
A lawyer for Floris said she “served our nation as a dedicated FBI intelligence officer for nearly 20 years”, while accusing the Justice Department of building its case on hearsay.
“Yet today, the DOJ [Justice Department] has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts,” the statement said.
“It’s no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election.”
Floris and Benavides had overseen the Foreign Intelligence Task Force (FITF) at the FBI when Hunter Biden’s laptop was found. The pair testified to Congress that the unit, which focuses on foreign interference in US elections, was not involved in the laptop investigation.
In a criminal complaint, federal prosecutors alleged the statements contradicted messages sent during the same period.
While launched by Trump during his first term, the FITF was heavily targeted by Republicans under former US President Joe Biden. They charged the unit was politically biased and used to cover up information about Biden’s laptop.
The unit was disbanded when Trump took office for the second time in January 2025.
Scandalous saga
The existence of the laptop became known in October of 2020, just weeks before Biden and Trump faced off in a presidential election.
Its strange origins, having been dropped off at a Delaware computer repair shop and apparently abandoned by Hunter Biden, prompted suspicion. Its contents were first reported on by the New York Post, based on information provided to Trump lawyer Rudy Giuliani.
Several former intelligence officials warned that the laptop had the hallmarks of a Russian disinformation campaign. However, the FBI later seized and verified that the laptop and its contents, including messages related to the younger Biden’s foreign business ties and explicit photos of his drug use, were authentic.
The laptop was later used to back federal gun and tax evasion charges against Hunter Biden, although no wrongdoing related to his business ties or connection with his father was found.
Trump FBI Director Kash Patel has pledged to investigate the agency’s conduct throughout Biden’s presidency. Critics have accused him of flagrant politicalisation.
“Lying to Congress by senior FBI officials strikes at the heart of our system. No one is above the law,” Patel said in a statement posted on X.
The Justice Department has historically sought to avoid public and overt investigative acts in the direct lead-up to an election that involve candidates or that risk influencing an outcome.
But officials in the last two weeks have made a series of bold moves in cases with political undertones, including a search of Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar’s house in an immigration fraud investigation.
The department also unsealed a corruption indictment on Thursday against powerful Democratic Virginia state Senator L Louise Lucas.

Italy is tightening security measures due to the threat of new riots — 500 troops will be sent to Milan

Italy is tightening security following riots at protests against the cost of living. 500 troops will be sent to Milan; a curfew is not planned.
Italy is stepping up security measures and deploying hundreds of troops ahead of new protests following last weekend’s large-scale riots. In Milan, Rome and Turin, there are fears of renewed clashes, looting of shops and street violence. Deutsche Presse-Agentur reports, writes UNN.
Details
Security has been reinforced in several cities due to the risk of new clashes. According to media reports, significant additional security forces are on standby.
Last weekend riots broke out in Milan and other cities following protests against the high cost of living, which had initially proceeded peacefully. On Friday, surveillance and controls were tightened at railway stations in the Lombardy region, where Milan is located, to prevent large numbers of young people from arriving in the city.
According to the newspaper Corriere della Sera, demonstrations will not be allowed in central Milan, and police are preparing for preventive arrests. Joint teams of police officers and military personnel are to conduct patrols.
At present, the Italian authorities are not considering introducing a curfew, as was done in neighboring France.
According to Corriere della Sera, the authorities seek to prevent public life in Milan from coming to a standstill. Shops, museums and metro stations will be closed only if the situation escalates, should circumstances require it.

How a Fake Pollster May Have Hurt Real Candidates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:21:19 UTC
03:21:19 KST

A pollster admitted this week to using fabricated data in its surveys that were picked up by leading publications across the U.S., claiming the stunt was an “experimental project” intended to showcase the “vulnerabilities” of the polling industry. The announcement has shaken trust in polling infrastructure ahead of the midterms, especially as some candidates say their campaigns were directly harmed by the fake numbers.
After election analysis website FiftyPlusOne submitted an inquiry to Wedgewood Polls regarding the authenticity of its data and methodologies, the pollster put out a statement across social media on Tuesday, saying it had been conducting a test to show "how easy is it for an entirely fabricated polling firm to gain traction, be taken seriously, and expose how little scrutinization exists in media and public commentary?" In the statement, which has since been deleted, the group claimed it had been “far too easy” to distribute false data and insisted it "highlights a systemic breakdown in media vetting and data aggregation.”
Wedgewood's polls had been used by multiple national outlets for their midterm reporting, including the New York Times, Newsweek, MS NOW, and POLITICO. The Times, which cited around 15 Wedgewood polls between June and October, has since removed the data from its stories. In an accompanying editor’s note, the publication detailed its checking process for polls and said Wedgewood had answered several of their inquiries prior to the data being published, including questions on the identities of the group’s pollsters, the methods used to draw their samples, and the source of their funding.
TIME's email to Wedgewood Polls bounced back.
In another fraudulent polling operation uncovered in August, a company called Median Strategies fabricated polls for races in Wisconsin, Nevada, and California and similarly called the ploy a “social experiment” in a statement to the Los Angeles Times.
“It's very troubling that we've had two examples of this within a very short period of time during election campaigns, creating a lot of problems for legitimate polling,” says Michael Traugott, a professor emeritus of political science at the University of Michigan, who previously served as president of the American Association for Public Opinion Research (AAPOR).
Here’s what to know about the Wedgewood scandal, and what it says about polling ahead of the pivotal midterm elections.
What do we know about Wedgewood Polls?
The polling group called itself a “fictional entity run by a small group of industry veterans” in its statement. Its X account, which contained many of its polls, no longer exists.
G. Elliot Morris, a pollster and journalist who works at FiftyPlusOne, tells TIME that he and his colleagues had been suspicious about a “crop of new polling firms” that have emerged and released anonymous data. An individual eventually tipped off FiftyPlusOne to Wedgewood's polling, which was “the straw that broke the camel's back for us,” he says.
FiftyPlusOne said in a public statement that Wedgewood “operated as if it were a legitimate polling firm” by collecting money from donors to carry out crowd-funded polls and share its survey data.
The poll analysis group said Wedgewood disclosed two names in connection to the company: Jack Sims and Andrew Prater. According to FiftyPlusOne, Sims had prior experience in the polling industry. SoCal Strategies, another polling firm, this week acknowledged in an email to an NPR affiliate in Michigan that Sims had worked there, but is not currently employed by the company and “has not been for a year.”
“It is not atypical for a pollster to leave an existing firm, form their own, and self-fund some surveys to build reputation; we had no reason at the time to believe this case was any different,” FiftyPlusOne said regarding Sims.
“This event does not help what is a decades-long trend of declining confidence in the polling industry,” Morris added, when asked about Sims’ involvement with Wedgewood. TIME has been unable to reach Sims for comment.
Senate candidate in Michigan says fake polling damaged her campaign
The polling scandal has sparked a flurry of reactions within the politics and government sector, with one former Senate hopeful claiming the numbers circulated by Wedgewood contributed to the collapse of her campaign.
Democratic Michigan state Sen. Mallory McMorrow recalled how a poll from Wedgewood had shown her “plummeting into single digits.”
Wedgewood released polling on June 29 that placed McMorrow as having the support of only 9% of registered voters, leaving her trailing behind Haley Stevens and Abdul El-Sayed. Other polls also showed McMorrow in third place with single digits. A Susquehanna Polling survey conducted June 9 to 14 put McMorrow at 9%, although 49% of Democratic primary voters surveyed were undecided. A July 1 Quantus Insights poll put her at under 8%. McMorrow suspended her campaign on July 5, just one month before the primaries.  
In a statement posted to social media on Oct. 20, McMorrow said donations “dried up” and she was “hounded” with calls to exit the race after the circulation of the “infamous” Wedgewood poll numbers. 
Advising others not to trust the polls, McMorrow said she hoped Democrats are ready to “blow up the system with campaign finance and transparency reforms.”
Jennifer Holdsworth, a Democratic strategist who ran a SuperPAC that supported McMorrow, claimed the fake poll had been “used by several donors to pull back funding at a time we were being outspent by $80 million.”
Amid widespread discussions over fabricated data, Federal Communications Commission (FCC) Chair Brendan Carr said, without naming any specific instance, that there has been a “significant surge” in fake polls and blamed news outlets for “amplifying or airing” them “without regard to basic journalistic ethics.”
Democratic FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez quipped back and shifted the onus onto fraudulent pollsters themselves.
“Pollsters who intentionally mislead the public should answer for it, but broadcasters who report publicly available polling data should never be punished when a poll is wrong,” she said in response to Carr. “FCC rules on news distortion or hoaxes do not apply to a station that reports this data in good faith.”
What impact can polls have on elections?
While documented fake polls are rare, according to experts, polling in general often plays a large role in shaping the narrative of hotly contested races.
Traugott tells TIME that polls can affect voting behavior and support for campaigns “because by and large, the average citizen is interested in backing the winner, and backing means not just votes; it also means financial contributions, contributing time and effort to the campaign, and the like.”
Research has demonstrated what is known as the “bandwagon effect,” in which voters become more likely to vote for candidates or issues that are more favored in polls. A 2023 study from the Journal of Elections, Public Opinion and Parties showed that polls discouraged support for less popular ballot items, or as the paper’s authors put it: “polls demobilize the minority and mobilize the majority.”
It also found that moderate voters, who often represent a crucial demographic of voters and can swing tight elections, were the most impressionable when it comes to being influenced by polling. “Social conformity is strongest among ideological moderates,” the study said.
This effect has been documented going back decades.
A 1996 experiment showed that participants who were shown a fabricated poll ahead of that year’s primary had a “significantly greater tendency” to vote for the candidates favored by the poll.
This phenomenon has similarly been demonstrated in prediction markets, which have been shown to sway voters almost as much as polls. A study released on Oct 20 by policy think-tank the Brennan Center showed that voters were 10% more likely to say that a candidate would win in an election if that person had higher odds of winning based on a prediction market.
Likewise, voters were less likely to believe that a candidate would win if their odds were predicted to be lower. These prediction market odds, the study said, had a similar effect on perceived electability as traditional polls.
Traugott says that generally speaking, voters who identify with a specific party are unlikely to change their vote as a result of polling, but that they might not show up to the polls at all if they see their party’s nominee is disfavored to win.
“It's often the case in the general election that the polls have an influence in terms of turnout,” he says.
Should you trust polls?
Michael Dimock, the president of the Pew Research Center, says that in tight races, of which there are many in the upcoming midterms, “it's very easy for polls to ‘pick the wrong winner.’”
“I do think that people should be very cautious in over-interpreting pre-election polls' ability to project an election outcome, whether it's at a national level, state level, a district level, [or] local level,” he tells TIME.
One of the main reasons for this, Dimock contends, is that even if participants in a survey say who they would vote for, they still might not show up to cast their ballot. He refers to this immeasurable but important factor as “enthusiasm differences.”
“What polls are really bad at capturing is who's going to actually show up and cast a ballot. It's really hard,” Dimock adds. “Human beings are bad at predicting their [own] future behaviors.”

Criminals are recruiting vulnerable people, including children, to damage houses suspected of being HMOs, police in Manchester believe.

Salford council has also taken down roadside banners that had been put up, which read: “IRLAM AND CADISHEAD SAY NO TO MIGRANT HMOs.”

Posts with pictures of the damaged houses have attracted hundreds of comments, many of them praising the attacks and predicting further violence.

Four people have been arrested this week in relation to the attacks. On Monday, a 46-year-old man and a 39-year-old man were arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit criminal damage, and on Wednesday a 33-year-old man was also arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit criminal damage.
Police have also made previous arrests in relation to the spate of criminal damage, including a 13-year-old boy.

PrivatBank has launched an open banking service in its Privat24 app for individual customers and in the web version of Privat24 for Business for individual entrepreneurs, the financial institution's press service reported.
"For individuals, this will change the experience of using financial apps, since all accounts and personal finances will be brought together in one Privat24 app. For individual entrepreneurs, it offers an opportunity to simplify the tracking of operating expenses in Privat24 for Business," said Dmytro Musienko, a member of PrivatBank's management board responsible for retail banking.

As reported, National Bank of Ukraine Resolution No. 80, which provides for authorized third-party service providers to access customer account information only with the customers' consent, took effect on August 1, 2025.
For the following 12 months, the regulator did not impose enforcement measures for violations of requirements concerning continuous access to accounts and the configuration of dedicated interfaces.
PrivatBank is Ukraine's largest bank. According to the National Bank of Ukraine, the financial institution's total assets stood at UAH 983.82 billion as of September 1, 2026, accounting for 22.8% of the banking sector's total assets.

US Announces Russia-Ukraine Ceasefire Deal for Civilian Evacuations in Temporarily Occupied Oleshky
Unknown

2026-10-23
18:17:30 UTC
03:17:30 KST

- Category
- World
US Announces Russia-Ukraine Ceasefire Deal for Civilian Evacuations in Temporarily Occupied Oleshky
UPD: Russian Chief of the General Staff Valery Gerasimov announced on October 23 that Russian forces would introduce a ceasefire in the Kherson sector starting at 4:00 a.m. Moscow time on October 27 to facilitate a humanitarian operation in the temporarily Russian-occupied town of Oleshky. On the Ukrainian side, senior negotiator Davyd Arakhamia confirmed preparations for an operation to unblock Oleshky and establish humanitarian corridors.
US First Lady Melania Trump secured an agreement between Ukraine and Russia for a localized ceasefire in Oleshky, Kherson region, scheduled to begin October 29.
The White House announced the agreement on October 23, stating that both countries had agreed to temporarily suspend military operations in the city to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and civilian evacuations through a designated safe corridor.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
However, Ukraine has not officially confirmed the ceasefire agreement announced by the White House. On October 23, Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets indicated that negotiations with Russia over civilian evacuations from Oleshky were still underway, although they were nearing completion.
"The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster," Melania Trump stated. She emphasized that the remaining residents, predominantly elderly people, urgently need food, clean water, medicine, and medical assistance.
According to the White House, Melania Trump and her representative negotiated directly with Ukrainian and Russian leadership, coordinating the agreement's timing, technical procedures, and implementation. The first lady acted as an "Exclusive Intermediary" between the two sides.
Under the arrangement, civilian representatives from both countries will visit residents in their homes to assess their humanitarian needs. Those wishing to evacuate will receive transportation and assistance in reaching their preferred destinations, whether in Ukrainian-controlled territory or Russia.
Melania Trump also announced that an independent American media organization would accompany the Ukrainian and Russian teams to document the evacuation process and help ensure residents' preferences are respected.
The agreement includes coordination on demining operations, as roads around Oleshky remain contaminated with explosives. The White House did not specify how long the ceasefire would last or how compliance with the temporary suspension of hostilities would be monitored.
Oleshky lies on the temporarily Russian-occupied eastern bank of the Dnipro River, opposite the city of Kherson. Before Russia's full-scale invasion, approximately 24,000 people lived there.
The White House estimates that between 1,700 and 2,000 residents remain, primarily elderly civilians, alongside approximately 50 children. No comprehensive population census has been conducted since 2022.
The city also suffered extensive destruction following the collapse of the Kakhovka Dam in June 2023, when approximately 90% of its territory was flooded, according to the White House.
The ceasefire agreement builds on earlier humanitarian contacts established by Melania Trump's office to reunite Ukrainian children separated from their families during Russia's invasion.
On April 2, 2026, the White House announced arrangements for seven Ukrainian children taken by Russia to return home. On July 30, she facilitated another reunion, helping five children return to their families in the fifth such operation. Her office maintained direct communication with Ukrainian and Russian officials throughout these efforts, establishing channels later used in the Oleshky ceasefire negotiations.
The agreement capped weeks of diplomatic pressure over the humanitarian crisis in the temporarily occupied city. On October 16, Pope Leo XIV urged the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, in a phone call to accept a ceasefire around Oleshky so food and medical aid could reach civilians.
By October 19, Kyiv and Moscow were moving to finalize an evacuation from Oleshky and six nearby settlements, where around 6,000 civilians, including up to 200 children, were believed to remain.

Russia, Ukraine agree to US-brokered, 1 city ceasefire

Russia, Ukraine agree to US-brokered, 1 city ceasefire
October 23, 2026
US first lady Melania Trump helped broker a ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia in the city of Oleshky, the White House announced Friday. The localized truce, according to the White House, is slated to begin on October 29.
What do we know so far about the ceasefire deal in Oleshky?
The Ukrainian city occupied by Russia on the frontline of the war faces a humanitarian crisis and only around 2,000 people still live there. Prior to the war, the city had a population of around 24,000.
Oleshky has been under blockade since 2025 and was first occupied when Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
The city is located in southern Ukraine, just 9 kilometers (around 5.6 miles) from the major city of Kherson.
"Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food and clean water," Melania Trump said in a statement. "The people of Oleshky have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks."
Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, thanked the first lady for securing the deal.
"Under our agreement: first a ceasefire will be put in place; second, humanitarian aid will be delivered to Oleshky; and third, civilians will be allowed to move freely out of Oleshky," Lubinets said in a video message posted on Telegram. "The operation will be carried out gradually and is extremely challenging to implement."
Russia also confirmed the agreement and said it will halt fire earlier than what the White House announced at 0400 local time (0100 GMT) on October 27.
According to the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights, residents in Oleshky say Russian occupying forces prevented them from leaving the city. Oleshky residents also say Russia has used civilians to shield military positions in the city — a war crime under international humanitarian law.
Fresh Ukraine talks expected in Abu Dhabi next month
The ceasefire deal in Oleshky comes as US, Ukrainian and Russian negotiators are expected to meet in Abu Dhabi next month to discuss ending the war.
"The plan is to meet in the first half of November, and as early as possible, of course," Zelenskyy told the US conservative Hudson Institute think tank.
In comments to Russian state news outlet TASS, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov also said preparations are underway for a three-way meeting in mid-November. Russian President Vladimir Putin said security would be a main topic for the Abu Dhabi talks.
"That is the security of both countries, Russia and Ukraine, after there has been a transition to a peace settlement," Peskov said.
The Kremlin spokesperson said Russia only sees the Europeans at the table during a later stage in the talks. European leaders such as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz have said Europe must be involved in future Ukraine peace talks.
"It is clear that the architecture of European security cannot be discussed without other participants," Peskov added.
US President Donald Trump has grown increasingly frustrated at Zelenskyy, and is pressuring him to "make a deal."
Trump has blamed Ukraine for rising diesel prices in the US, as the US-Israeli war against Iran has caused the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and drove up the cost of gas at the pump for American consumers.
Trump has backed a deal to buy diesel from Russia to lower prices at fuel pumps, drawing criticism from Ukraine. The Kremlin said Friday that the first tanker of Russian diesel has set sail for the US despite the backlash from Ukraine.
Ukraine still dealing with Starshield issues as Trump defends Musk
Most recently, there has been controversy that tech billionaire Elon Musk ordered a slowdown of the Starshield military communications system that Ukraine relies on, possibly with the backing of Trump.
Trump has denied that he ordered restrictions on Starlink. He also defended Musk in comments to reporters on Friday and said, "Elon will never do anything wrong."
"You know, whether I called or whether somebody else called, doesn't make any difference," Trump said. "I guess the bottom line, he put it back."
Meanwhile, Zelenskyy and Ukraine said Friday that the system was still being throttled in Ukraine.
"It works, but it's still limited," Zelenskyy told US broadcaster ABC News.
A source in Ukraine's Defense Ministry told AFP news agency and other news outlets that Ukrainians were witnessing "instances of signal loss" when using Starshield.
"There is currently no confirmation that the restrictions have been lifted," the source added.

Nationwide protests against the rising cost of living are expected in Italy and France on Saturday 24 October. Authorities and business owners fear a repeat of what happened on 17 and 18 October, when hundreds of people were involved in violent incidents targeting shops and law enforcement.
Protests are planned in several Italian cities, including Milan, Bologna, Genoa, Turin, Rome and Florence. According to "Mappa della rivolta", a website that collates protest initiatives, more than 30 mobilisations are scheduled, ranging from marches and sit-ins to assemblies and strikes.
The capital will be under tight security for the occasion. Rome's police headquarters has drawn up a security plan to manage both notified demonstrations and spontaneous rallies announced online. In addition to the usual units deployed to handle protests, drones from the State Police's 1st Flight Department and aircraft from the Carabinieri will also be used. In all, around 1,500 officers will be deployed, with checks stretching from city squares to railway stations.
Tactical advice on how to deal with police clashes on social media
Rome's Cybersecurity Centre is also operational, monitoring posts and activities on social media in coordination with Digos, the specialized operational division of the Italian State Police.
The digital dimension is making it harder to manage the protests. On Telegram, TikTok and Instagram, guides on how to prepare for clashes are circulating. Advice ranges from bringing water, painkillers and vinegar to lessen the effects of tear gas, to guidance on what to wear and how to behave if disorder breaks out.
In Milan, there will be around one thousand police officers and Carabinieri, 300 municipal officers and 500 soldiers deployed following the latest government security decree. Here too, drones will be used to monitor the marches. Authorised demonstrations will take place away from the Duomo, while protests are banned in the Garibaldi and Porta Venezia districts.
In Turin, a demonstration is expected that has been organised by activists from the antagonista scene linked to the former Askatasuna social centre, together with members of the 17 October Movement and students. Marches are due to start at 2 p.m. in Piazza Arbarello.
Following the unrest on 17 October, on Friday Digos carried out searches targeting around 100 people, 51 of whom were minors. Operations took place in several cities, including Bari, Bergamo, Florence, Genoa and Verona.
