College-educated people aren’t Big Tech’s biggest fans. They’re its most conflicted, study suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:00:04 UTC
03:00:04 KST

Public opinion toward major technology corporations does not fall neatly along a simple spectrum from support to opposition, according to new research published in Research and Politics. Analyzing survey data from six countries, researchers found that higher levels of education are linked to mixed, conflicted views rather than outright enthusiasm for large tech firms. The study also indicates that political ideology is linked to these attitudes in distinct ways, with left-leaning individuals more likely to be skeptical and highly educated right-leaning individuals increasingly likely to hold ambivalent views.
Big Tech refers to the largest and most dominant companies in the information technology industry, specifically global corporations such as Google, Apple, Meta, Amazon, and Microsoft. Beyond selling consumer products and digital services, these firms control the core infrastructure of modern communication, commerce, and emerging tools like artificial intelligence. Because their platforms influence how citizens find information, participate in public debates, and interact with democratic institutions, governments face growing questions about whether to regulate these companies more strictly or support their continued growth.
Political scientists have spent considerable effort examining how technological shifts affect workers and voters, though less attention has gone toward how the public evaluates the specific corporations driving those changes. For example, a 2022 review noted that workplace automation and digitalization tend to divide the workforce into economic winners who favor the political status quo and routine workers who face job risks and gravitate toward populist politics. Similarly, a study covered by PsyPost in 2022 found that workers facing higher exposure to job automation were more likely to support radical-right parties and report lower satisfaction with democracy.
When turning from workplace technology to the specific corporations behind it, Tobias Tober and colleagues at the University of Konstanz expected education and political ideology to guide public attitudes. In modern knowledge economies, which rely heavily on information and technical expertise rather than manual labor, university-educated individuals usually enjoy stronger job prospects and greater familiarity with digital tools. Prior work, including a 2024 cross-country survey, conducted in part by two of the same researchers, linked how much job risk people perceive from digitalization to how they want governments to respond. Based on these patterns, the authors initially expected highly educated people to view Big Tech companies positively.
Ideology was also expected to play a central role, though in different ways across the political spectrum. Individuals on the political left generally distrust corporate monopolies, wealth inequality, and unchecked private power, which suggests they would view tech giants critically. On the political right, expectations are more complicated because traditional pro-business values favor large corporations, whereas right-wing populist movements often distrust the cultural and social shifts tied to digital capitalism.
To test how these factors work in practice, the researchers commissioned the survey firm Kantar Public to collect data in June and July 2022 across six countries: Germany, Japan, Poland, Spain, Sweden, and the United States. The sample included 3,300 adults aged 18 to 64 in each country, totaling 19,800 respondents. The researchers used quota sampling for age, gender, and education so that the participants reflected the broader national populations of their respective countries.
Participants rated their agreement on a five-point scale with six statements about the societal role of global technology companies like Amazon, Apple, Google, Facebook, and Microsoft. Three statements reflected positive contributions: providing useful services to the public, promoting innovation and economic development, and aiding democracy by offering a digital space for open debate. The other three statements captured negative impacts: undermining the national welfare state by avoiding taxes, weakening labor standards, and becoming so powerful that they threaten democracy.
The researchers then used exploratory factor analysis, a statistical technique that groups related survey answers together to uncover underlying patterns in how people think. Rather than finding a single scale where positive views sit at one end and negative views sit at the other, the analysis pointed to two separate dimensions that barely correlated with each other. Agreeing with positive statements about Big Tech had almost no bearing on whether a person disagreed with negative statements.
Next, the authors applied a grouping method called k-means cluster analysis to see how respondents combined these positive and negative evaluations. The researchers sorted the 19,800 participants into five profiles. The largest group was the neutral cluster (8,140 respondents), consisting of people who neither agreed nor disagreed with most statements, followed by the ambivalent cluster (5,114 respondents), who agreed with both positive and negative statements at the same time.
The remaining participants fell into three smaller categories. Big Tech supporters (3,739 respondents) agreed with the positive statements and rejected the negative ones, while skeptics (2,123 respondents) endorsed the negative statements and rejected the positive ones. Finally, a small dismissive group (685 respondents) disagreed with both positive and negative characterizations of the industry.
To see how education and ideology predicted membership in these five groups, the team ran statistical models that accounted for income and differences between countries, and the results held when they also accounted for technology use at home and at work. Education was divided into three levels based on international standards, ranging from lower secondary schooling up to university degrees. Political ideology was measured on an 11-point scale where respondents placed themselves from far left to far right.
Contrary to the researchers’ initial expectations, higher education was not linked to a large jump in outright support for Big Tech. Moving from the lowest to the highest education level increased the predicted probability of being a supporter by only about 3 percentage points, and the probability of being a skeptic by about 2 percentage points. Instead, the probability of belonging to the ambivalent group rose from 22 percent among less educated respondents to 33 percent among university-educated respondents, while the likelihood of being neutral dropped from 43 percent to 30 percent.
Political ideology also separated respondents in distinct ways, with people in the political center most likely to belong to the neutral group. Moving from the center to the far left increased the predicted probability of being a skeptic by about 10 percentage points. Moving from the center to the far right increased the probability of skepticism by about 6 percentage points, while raising the probability of belonging to the ambivalent group by roughly 10 percentage points. These patterns were broadly similar across the six countries, though with some differences.
When the researchers looked at how education and ideology interacted, they found that ideological divisions were sharpest among university-educated citizens, with declining neutrality on the left translating mainly into higher skepticism. On the right, the pattern ran counter to the researchers’ expectations: there was some evidence that support declined toward the far right among the highly educated, while the probability of holding ambivalent views rose by about 16 percentage points from the political center to the far right. The authors suggest this may reflect a conflict between pro-market beliefs and conservative concerns over how tech platforms influence culture and speech.
The authors also examined whether these five attitude groups aligned with policy preferences regarding government regulation and state financial or political backing for tech firms. Across the full sample, 38 percent of respondents favored stronger regulation of Big Tech, 20 percent opposed it, and 42 percent were undecided. Similarly, 32 percent favored giving the companies more economic and political support, 19 percent opposed doing so, and 49 percent remained undecided.
Breaking these numbers down by group showed that attitude profiles closely tracked policy demands. Skeptics overwhelmingly backed stricter regulation at 82 percent and opposed government support for the industry at 65 percent, while supporters showed little appetite for regulation (23 percent in favor) and leaned toward government backing (40 percent in favor). Ambivalent respondents tended to want both interventions simultaneously, with 72 percent favoring more regulation and 46 percent favoring more government support.
These patterns align with research covered by PsyPost earlier this year, which examined public beliefs regarding the economic and labor impacts of artificial intelligence rather than evaluations of Big Tech companies, and similarly found that political ideology structures technology-related attitudes and regulatory preferences. The heightened skepticism on the left is also broadly in line with a 2023 study covered by PsyPost, which analyzed sentiment in news coverage of artificial intelligence rather than public survey attitudes toward major tech corporations and found that liberal-leaning media outlets expressed more negative sentiment toward artificial intelligence than conservative outlets.
To explain why higher education is linked to ambivalence rather than simple support, the authors propose an explanation drawn from a classic theory of how people form political opinions. In this view, education serves as a rough indicator of political awareness, so highly educated people may encounter more competing arguments about both the benefits and dangers of digital platforms. Rather than settling on a one-sided view, they may absorb both sets of arguments, or experience a clash between their economic preferences and cultural values, though the authors note their account remains incomplete.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. Because the study relies on survey responses collected at a single point in time in 2022, it cannot establish cause-and-effect relationships or track how attitudes might have shifted following recent breakthroughs in generative artificial intelligence. The survey also included only adults aged 18 to 64 and used quota sampling rather than random sampling, so the results may not fully represent older adults or each country’s population as a whole. In addition, educational attainment overlaps with several other characteristics, such as income and digital literacy, making it difficult to isolate the exact reason why university graduates express more mixed views.
The researchers also note that their analysis treats political messages as broadly similar across the six surveyed nations. In reality, political parties and news media frame technology debates differently across the United States, Japan, and Europe, which could create local variations that broad cross-national models only partly capture. Future studies could track how these public attitudes evolve over time in response to shifting political rhetoric and new regulatory laws.
The study, “Big Tech, big risk? How education and ideology shape public attitudes toward Big Tech companies,” was authored by Tobias Tober, Marius R. Busemeyer, and Sebastian Koos.

In the 60s, Weizenbaum tried to show the limitations of AI. No-one listened
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

The Interview: Eliza playwright Tom Holloway on the human story underneath AI
In 1966, German American computer scientist Joseph Weizenbaum, a professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), created a computer program he dubbed ELIZA.
It was a rudimentary version of artificial intelligence, named after Eliza Doolittle, the working-class woman from George Bernard Shaw's Pygmalion who learns how to behave like a "lady".
The program could do little more than repeat back what it was told, phrased as a question. For Weizenbaum, who escaped Nazi Germany 30 years earlier, ELIZA was a way to highlight the limitations of AI.
For some users, including his secretary, it became almost a companion; when she noticed Weizenbaum watching her use ELIZA, she said: "Would you mind leaving the room, please?"
Now, AI pervades our lives; some people use it as a therapist, researcher, confidante. But it has also stirred up complicated legal conversations, as AI companies attempt to override Australia's copyright laws, even as experts like Bill Gates warn of the technology's potentially lethal consequences.
That's not to mention AI's impact on the environment, with Sydney Water warning data centres could use the equivalent of a quarter of the city's current annual drinking water supply within a decade.
As these conversations continue, artists are also grappling with the impacts of AI. For playwright Tom Holloway, that meant going back to the story of Weizenbaum and ELIZA for his new play, also called Eliza, now at Melbourne Theatre Company.
Why did you want to write Eliza?
I can't remember when I first heard the Weizenbaum story. It was like 10, 15 years ago. It might have been a Radiolab podcast or an Adam Curtis doco. But it just hit me.
There was something deeply human about these conversations between a human and this computer program. There was a deep need and loneliness in the original transcripts that had been shared.
The story is more complicated because Weizenbaum was an AI sceptic and created the program to say, look, this thing can seem intelligent, yet it's absolutely not. It's only 400 lines of basic code. He was trying to use this chatbot of ELIZA to highlight that a computer could never understand human intelligence and never really connect with a human, and it was interpreted in exactly the opposite way. Even that seemed deeply human.
The story stayed with me, and then a few years ago, when we all started living in this same world as Weizenbaum's nightmare, it seemed like the story that needed to be told. Because we forget, don't we? We don't know this has been something we've been dealing with for 60 years and much longer too.
Every new technology brings terror and causes disruption before we find ways to work with it.
What I love about stories like Weizenbaum's is that humanity, that sense of the person grappling with the thing they have made, like Mary Shelley's Frankenstein or, more recently, Christopher Nolan's Oppenheimer.
If we remember AI is simply a technology, the tool is incredible, and as long as we double-check everything it tells us, it can give us access to so much that humans have articulated for all time, because it's stolen that from us.
And that's the problem with it. The problem with it is how it's been created, the people behind it, and what it does to the environment. We just need to regulate it and work out how to stop it destroying the environment and free it for us all, reclaim it, because it's built on us.
It can be frustrating as a journalist to hear accusations about writers using "AI voice" or that em dashes are a tell for someone using AI, when AI was trained on our writing.
I had to sign a thing because some of my plays had been discovered to have been illegally used in the training of one of the models!
How did you feel when you found out AI had been trained on your work?
It might have been my first play, Beyond the Neck. It's about how humans and communities survive something as terrible as the Port Arthur massacre. It's this attempt to talk about something very difficult and deeply human.
I wasn't surprised because we already knew [stealing creative work] is what it has done. It continues to be shocking that we allowed that to happen, and not just that, but the levels [AI companies would] go to. There was the story that Anthropic [was] specifically trying to get rare books, feed them into the machines, and then destroy them, so that knowledge wasn't anywhere else.
That's more than just taking what's on the internet. That is specifically trying to control knowledge, and that's awful. That's the stuff that we should be rioting over.
That and how much water it's using…
Obviously, there are worrying things that happen with AI, but that's because of the people giving the prompts and not being clear enough, and there's not enough of a safety net around those things.
The Medicare breach was, from what I've read — as a playwright, I feel quite far out of my element talking about some of this stuff — it was asked to get some health statistics, and it did it by whatever means it needed to. And the Hugging Face thing was quite similar.
It all comes back to the human and human error, and a lack of a safety net built in by us humans. That's why I think regulation is key.
Has your relationship to or understanding of AI changed since you first started writing Eliza?
I've been writing it for about three years, so I think everyone's relationship to it has changed over that time. It's almost like an abusive relationship. Humans are using it every day, and yet we're also terrified of it. Was it earlier this year there were all those speeches given at graduation ceremonies in America where guests were talking about it as a positive thing, and the students all booed?
The thing that writing Eliza has really brought home is it's not the tech that I'm worried about; it's those people [behind it]. And that was a real revelation for Weizenbaum back then too. He said he was shocked at how quickly reasonably minded people were deluded by technology. And that's not just the people using it; that's the people making money from it too and using it to manipulate other people.
Do you use AI?
Yes, I use it, and I have all my settings set up so that it's not allowed to use any of my chats. I delete the chats as soon as they've happened. I donate to environmental charities to make up for it.
Because I think the actual technology can push you intellectually and creatively. If you relinquish those skills to it, there is danger there, and you are only going to get worse work back from it.
But it can stimulate you, push you, and make offers that can help advance the work or creativity you're doing yourself.
If we can free AI, I think there's a future where artists will use it as a tool to create things we can't even imagine now.
Did you use AI to write Eliza?
I used ELIZA to write Eliza.
Weizenbaum got really disillusioned and hid a lot of the original coding and transcripts [for ELIZA] in the MIT archives. And there's this team of some of the biggest cybernetics brains in the world from Stanford and Oxford and other universities, who during COVID went back in and found the lost files. They've been reading drafts and giving me tidbits and facts and helping me.
In writing this play about a technology isolating people, I've grown more connections with more people, and discovered theatre is the right form to tell this story because it becomes a kind of act of protest against that isolation [AI companies] are hell-bent on forcing us all into.
The communal nature of the creative process in theatre, and then with audiences, feels like we're coming together to go, "No, we're what's important in all this."
So, would you like to see artists' copyright be protected?
It's deeply important.
To be an artist, you have to accept risk and discomfort into your daily life, and you do it because you want to try to say something that might help other people.
Whenever I see anyone else putting anything into the world, I think that person has risked so much. There's something very hopeful about the act and very generous about the act that I think needs protecting.
Eliza is at Melbourne Theatre Company until October 31.
This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.

When it comes to new technology, being first can come at a cost
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

analysis
Being first can come at a cost: The case to go slow on AI is growing louder
This columnist recently had the good fortune of a visit to Greece.
Wonderful country. Rich in history. Ethos, pathos and logos by the bucket load. Which they invented of course.
Another discovery the Greeks are sometimes (debatably) credited with — thanks to the story of the Minoans at the Palace of Knossos in Crete in 1700 BCE — is flushing toilets.
The irony, as anyone who has spent time there knows, is that the Greek sewer system can't handle dunny paper because the pipes, at around 50mm, are too small. Aussie residential pipes are double that width.
The result is that everyone is told to put the paper in a nearby bin or risk setting off a hideous plumbing disaster.
During the visit, our algorithm-enabled Instagram feed filled with posts from tourists poking fun at this jolly reality.
Greece's predicament — of being vulnerable to a single foreign visitor's indifference to the basic laws of fluid dynamics — is an imperfect reminder that there can be a curse attached to being first in class.
If you value reliability, safety and flexibility, you might avoid adopting the initial iteration of a technology.
Being first can mean getting lumped with a bad outcome for a long time. Sometimes it's better to let others take the hit and learn from them. Flush out all the problems, so to speak. And put in bigger pipes.
This notion sits near the surface of the federal parliament's ongoing joint select committee inquiry into artificial intelligence, which is looking at both the opportunities and risks of the technology for Australia.
Full-steam ahead or hasten slowly?
The Albanese government has imposed a tight timeline on the committee and is working with the Coalition on a quick outcome.
The committee has until the end of November to report, ahead of the introduction early next year of legislation to set standards for large data centre operators and settle the treatment of intellectual property and artist's rights. It aims to also shape responsible AI usage.
Such is the rush, that Labor and Coalition committee members have already issued a raft of recommendations this month that would require AI companies to submit to safety checks, reserve computing power for local use and provide security agencies with frontier models.
There are good arguments for not dawdling.
AI is expanding at a breathtaking pace around the world and there's a stunning wave of capital on offer.
"If we dither, if we do nothing, then of course that opportunity will sail by our country and our adversaries will be taking advantage of that opportunity at our expense," said committee deputy chair and Liberal Senator Jonno Duniam earlier this month.
According to Treasurer Jim Chalmers, Australia is one of the "world's top ten markets for data centre capacity".
Some $150 billion of AI infrastructure is slated for construction in the country over the next five years. In its submission to the committee, Treasury says global investment by hyperscale cloud computing providers will exceed $1 trillion this year.
So there's logic in ramping up efforts to lure those dollars here.
"We are a digital hub in the Indo-Pacific with the land, energy, skills and capital to make the most of the AI investment boom," Chalmers told a Citi economic conference in Sydney on Friday.
But there are also those who say it's better to hasten slowly.
The committee has been flooded with more than 500 submissions, many of them voicing deep community concern about where AI is headed. And at what cost.
If the federal government thinks it's on a winner by aggressively driving the country towards adoption and investment, it may have a big job ahead convincing voters that there are benefits.
There are many drivers of this scepticism, but one of them is the age-old fear of disruption. And it's always worse when there's a sense of control relinquished or stolen.
"Unlike any technology we've ever dealt with, the business model of AI is to generate mass unemployment," economist Richard Denniss told the committee a few days ago.
His argument is that the eye-wateringly high — if recently wobbly — stock prices of AI giants is "literally based on the assumption that hundreds of millions of people will lose their jobs".
Denniss challenged the committee to think through questions about how the claimed benefits of AI would be shared between Australians and foreign-owned AI firms; and what a wave of data centres means for electricity, water and construction costs, and inflation more broadly.
"Will the government be spending more money to equip public servants with AI tools, or will the government be funding AI rollout through job shedding?"
Loading
The barriers and the backlash
Arguments about AI are complex and rapidly changing, but the speed at which the government is pressing ahead will do little to ease a jittery community if voters feel they've never had a proper say in the matter.
"The only way the Department of Health can spend a billion dollars on AI is if it spends a billion dollars less on humans or if you guys increase their budget by a billion dollars," Denniss told the parliamentarians.
"All that money that Anthropic is betting on is coming from somewhere and that's going to have very real consequences for individuals, for communities, for the economy, for the way Commonwealth budgets are drawn up."
Prominent Egyptian-American economist and investor Mohamed El-Erian, writing alongside two colleagues in a piece published this week by Foreign Affairs, warns of the "narrow but feasible path to collective good" from AI.
El-Erian notes that AI is a major issue in American politics, driven by understandable anxieties.
"AI adoption risks repeating the mistakes of globalisation, which generated large and widely spread economic benefits but led to concentrated losses of jobs, growth, and industry in particular communities," they write.
"Government support in response was insufficient or arrived too late. Although the economy gained overall from free trade, the political bargain failed to give affected workers and communities a credible stake in the gains, even as individuals benefited as consumers from lower prices.
"The result was a backlash that contributed to the protectionism and fragmentation that continue to plague today's politics and society."
In its submission, Treasury is largely upbeat about AI and its potential, but there are jarring caveats.
AI will "increase the scale, speed and sophistication of information weaponisation and radicalisation".
"It is expected to lower barriers to harmful biological and chemical activity and simplify criminal and terrorist activity planning," the submission states.
Furthermore, according to the department, "women and girls currently experience disproportionate harm from AI-facilitated abuse, including deepfakes and targeted harassment".
The flip-side of this argument is that there's a case for governments to have access to AI for security and defence. Denniss stated that the use of AI by intelligence services is largely unrelated to the boom of data centre builds.
"There's plenty of technologies that the military use that I do not have access to.
"But this rush, this sort of generalised assertion that if we don't say yes to everything now, we will miss out is, I would suggest, unprecedented."
Senator David Pocock accused the government this week of being "starstruck" by US AI giants like OpenAI and Anthropic, and he called for a 5 per cent tax on data centre revenue.
"What our communities want to know is what will they do for us," Pocock said in a speech to the National Press Club on Wednesday. "How do data centres benefit us now and over the long term? Where are the protections for communities?
"Why has all this been left so late?"
Jacob Greber is political editor of ABC's 7.30 program.

Airbnb host floats 'dishes and utensils fee' as guest chore ban sparks debate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Airbnb hosts launch online petition against check-out chores ban
It began with three air mattresses on the floor of a San Francisco apartment and two young men looking for a way to make extra money to help pay their rent.
Almost two decades later, Airbnb is a multi-billion-dollar company, with 9 million active listings across more than 220 countries and regions.
The global accommodation giant is embroiled in a dispute over who should wash the dishes, strip the beds and take out the rubbish when guests check out.
This week, Airbnb announced that from November 20, hosts would no longer be allowed to ask guests to complete a check-out chore list, having already paid a cleaning fee.
The changes sparked an outcry among hosts around the world, with online petitions launched against the new rules and some planning a "nationwide host blackout" on November 20, by closing their properties to bookings on that day.
Felicity Stevens leads Airbnb's Sydney host club, a network of about 800 members who rent out some of the world's most expensive properties.
"I don't think it's too much to be able to ask a guest to put the dishwasher on before you leave and to put the rubbish out,"
Ms Stevens said.
She runs a cottage in Sydney's northern beaches that she has been renting out through Airbnb for 14 years.
"We pay a lot for the housekeepers because it's a job that's not a regular nine till five Monday to Friday job," she said.
She is far from alone.
A community centre chat on Airbnb has been flooded with frustrated posts from hosts reacting to the announcement.
"I find it completely unacceptable and utterly disrespectful to us hosts, who bend over backwards to welcome our guests in the best possible way … we are not our guests' servants," Sandy, from France, wrote.
Andrea from New York City said she would put up her prices.
"We could start charging a "dishes and utensil fee" for guests who don't want to use paper plates and plastic utensils," she wrote.
One woman, who owns three listings in Townsville, told the ABC earlier this week she was considering banning the use of her kitchen if guests were unwilling to clean their own dishes.
Ms Stevens said she understood why Airbnb had made the decision and that some hosts had gone "too far" with their check-out demands.
"You're on holiday … you're not there to water the plants, you're not there to be a caretaker," she said.
From home-sharing to a global business
In 2007, Airbnb's founders Brian Chesky and Joe Gebbia were struggling to afford their San Francisco apartment when they came up with an idea to make extra money.
With hotels booked out during a design conference, they offered visitors somewhere to sleep on air mattresses in their living room, with breakfast included.
The concept became Airbed & Breakfast, which officially launched in 2008. A year later, it was renamed Airbnb, and the business began expanding beyond spare rooms to entire apartments, houses and holiday properties.
Last year the company reported annual revenue of US$12.2 billion (A$17.4 billion) and had more than 9 million active listings.
Tourism and consumer behaviour researcher Sara Dolnicar said the platform had gradually moved away from its original home-sharing concept.
"It's slowly assimilated. It became more and more like hotels. And this is almost just the next step of assimilating," Professor Dolnicar said.
She said the growth of the platform had also changed what travellers expected from their accommodation.
"When Airbnb first started, everyone who booked knew, 'Oh, I'm in someone's house, it's not going to be perfect,'" she said.
"Now, as it became more perfect, the expectations also increased alongside that."
In a statement, Airbnb said the changes were designed to make house rules clearer and check-out requests more reasonable, while allowing hosts to continue setting and updating their rules.

Israel's election could be a turning point for the entire Middle East

analysis
Israel's election could be a turning point for the entire Middle East
Even in a region too used to conflict, there is an air of ominous apprehension sitting over the Middle East this weekend.
Sure, regional tensions are competing for our attention – and anxiety – with events in Ukraine, unrest across Europe, the perils of AI and financial market jitters.
But it is the sheer danger of regional instability embedded in Tuesday's elections in Israel – underlined once again this week when Palestinian gunmen targeted a military checkpoint in Hebron – and the ongoing rumblings of renewed war with Iran, that have put people here on edge.
For a bitterly divided Israel, Tuesday's election is seen as an historic turning point for the country.
Benjamin Netanyahu has cast the election as a choice between standing up for Israel or succumbing to international pressure for a Palestinian state (despite the fact no-one in this election is proposing the establishment of a Palestinian state).
His Likud Party's campaign slogan is "Yamin o Palestin", meaning "The Right Wing or Palestine".
But the thing to understand about this election is that it is not a choice between the far right and the left in classical terms. It feels to many Israelis more like a choice between the current state of play continuing, and the possibility of Israel going further to the right if Netanyahu were to stay in power.
For the anti-Netanyahu opposition, he is a threat to the state of Israel as a democracy. The ultra-right parties on which Netanyahu has relied have proposed changes that include allowing parliament to override Supreme Court decisions.
Then there are the territorial ambitions.
The ultranationalist national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has publicly promoted a plan to remove 1.86 million Palestinians – almost 90 per cent of Gaza's population – over the next seven years. He and other far-right parties are calling it "voluntary" emigration, as well as "encouraging" the emigration of Palestinians from the West Bank.
Another far-right leader, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, says Israel should annex the 60 per cent plus of Gaza it already controls, as well as the 20 per cent of Lebanon it currently occupies.
Brutally, the fate of Palestinians is not an issue that features much in the election campaign. But the unanswered question of where these Palestinians are actually supposed to go shows a reckless disregard for the sort of instability such actions would have on the regional neighbours – Egypt, Jordan and Syria – that would be expected to take in millions of people.
But in a world where the idea of "Greater Israel" – documented this week by my ABC colleague Matthew Doran and our digital colleagues – has become mainstream, a more extreme biblical view of greater Israel would eventually include the entire Kingdom of Jordan as well as the Sinai Peninsula, most of Syria, and large swathes of Iraq, so the question of whether such a movement of people might provoke war with more Israeli neighbours, or actually destroy a poorer and less populous country like Jordan, doesn't get much of a mention.
International tensions
There is also a sense of the clock ticking on events that may unfold immediately after the election, whatever the outcome.
Hostilities between Iran and the US for now remain the loud rumbling background noise to the election, and in the region more broadly. There is a regular stream of stories about how Israel and/or the US is planning renewed attacks on Iran, and of Iran announcing it is changing its military posture from a defensive one to an offensive one.
For people living through it, there are the daily reports of the massing and preparation of US and Iranian troops, but also the knowledge that the defensive weapons that largely kept civilian populations safe are now in short supply.
The widespread damage to US bases across the region has seen US troops and assets moved en masse to Jordan.
There has been a change in the nature of attacks that have continued through the technical ceasefire. It is now civilian infrastructure – like Riyadh's airport – that has been targeted, rather than just military installations.
Iran has also threatened to escalate its attacks on countries throughout the region, and to infrastructure like data centres and underwater cables.
In Israel, though, all the attention is on the election. The campaign has been verbally violent, and its messages have often exploited violence.
A pundit on a conservative television channel who is seen as a Netanyahu mouthpiece this week called opposition party leader Gadi Eisenkot "a Moroccan monkey controlled by Ashkenazi elites", a reflection of some of the internal divides and racism in Israeli society.
Law enforcement agencies have been instructed to stop National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir from accompanying demolition operations in the West Bank, amid accusations he is using the images for election campaigning.
A billboard for the more left-wing of the parties running for office was vandalised in recent days with calls for the murder of party leader Yair Golan scrawled across it, according to the newspaper Haaretz.
Among the messages written on the sign was: "Despicable killer of Jews, wanted dead or alive."
Loading
Concerns about Netanyahu
Netanyahu himself is the main issue in the campaign.
Like many really long-serving political leaders, there is a sense that he is campaigning by just pulling the same string, even though it doesn't really work anymore.
Very few polls suggest Netanyahu is going to win.
Most predict a bigger vote for parties standing against Netanyahu's Likud, but not a large enough one to create a majority.
Israelis who want to see Netanyahu gone – because of the corruption allegations against him; because of the security failures before October 7; because they believe he actually represents a threat to Israel remaining a democracy – still talk hopefully of an election boilover.
But whatever the number of seats in Israel's parliament, the Knesset, after Tuesday, Netanyahu is expected to stay on as a caretaker prime minister for the foreseeable future.
That is seen as posing its own risks, both domestically and abroad.
In the short term, the concern is that, at home, Netanyahu and his ultra-right colleagues will accelerate their attempts to change Israel's legal system, and towards full annexation of the West Bank. And abroad, there are fears Netanyahu will renew hostilities with Iran with the aim of establishing wartime conditions that would allow him to stay on in office, irrespective of the election outcome.
All the signs show that Netanyahu is much more driven and steady in his determination to recommence hostilities with Iran than is the US president.
The New York Times reported this week that Israel and the United States came close to striking Iran early this month, but Mr Trump again decided at the last minute to postpone the attack.
Trump has declared there will be no attacks before the US mid-term elections on November 2. Apart from the politics involved in such a call – when the war is deeply, deeply unpopular in the US – it reflects the fact that the American military build-up in the region is not expected to be ready until that time.
The question now has to be whether the sheer desperation and determination of Benjamin Netanyahu means he may be prepared to risk stoking regional conflict on a range of fronts, irrespective of the vacillating decisions of the United States President.
Laura Tingle is reporting from Jerusalem as the ABC's Global Affairs Editor.

Russia’s deputy justice minister defends a new blacklist that effectively imposes ‘civil death’ on dissidents living abroad
Russia’s Justice Ministry has published a registry of people subject to “temporary restrictive measures” on its website.
The list contains 12 names, with Mikhail Khodorkovsky first. It also includes political scientist Yekaterina Schulmann, businessman Yevgeny Chichvarkin, philanthropist Boris Zimin, and several others.
1. Mikhail Khodorkovsky
2. Alexey Nesterenko
3. Anastasia Shevchenko
4. Yekaterina Schulmann
5. Leonid Gozman
6. Yevgeny Chichvarkin
7. Michael Nacke
8. Yelena Kotyonochkina
9. Boris Zimin
10. Vladimir Milov
11. Mark Zakharov
12. Anastasia Burakova
Clicking on a name in the registry opens an entry with personal information — date and place of birth, taxpayer identification number, and pension insurance number — along with the grounds for the restrictions.
Deputy Justice Minister Oleg Sviridenko discussed the registry’s creation in an interview with TASS the previous day. He said the law establishing it — dubbed the “civil death” law on social media — was “neither excessive nor a violation of constitutional rights, but a justified effort to restore the rule of law and justice.”
“I can’t rule out that, as the law is applied, it may need fine-tuning and targeted adjustments to ensure it is fully consistent with the broader legal framework for protecting national sovereignty,” Sviridenko said.
In late July 2026, the State Duma passed a law in both its second and third readings introducing “temporary restrictive measures” against people outside Russia who have been found guilty of an offense in the country and are “evading” an administrative or criminal penalty. Among other provisions, the law called for a registry — effectively a list of “enemies of the people.” The registry began operating in test mode in late August.
Placement on the registry effectively amounts to “civil death.” Restrictions include freezing funds in Russian banks, barring access to online banking, prohibiting sales of real estate and vehicles, banning all transactions conducted under a power of attorney, and denying access to consular services.

Trump administration sues to block possible Democratic win in Alaska
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
17:57:54 UTC
02:57:54 KST

Trump administration sues to block possible Democratic win in Alaska
The Justice Department lawsuit raises concerns the administration may be looking to meddle in some of this midterm cycle’s races.
With just more than a week until the pivotal US midterm elections, the US Department of Justice has filed a lawsuit to block certification of the results in Alaska’s hotly contested Senate race.
In a lawsuit filed on Thursday, the Justice Department argued that an independent candidate with the same name as the state’s incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan, who is currently running for re-election, is purposefully running to mislead voters.
“Given the substantial likelihood that the inclusion of Daniel J Sullivan will confuse or mislead voters looking to cast a vote for Senator Sullivan, and thus distort the will of Alaskan voters, there is a substantial likelihood that a certification of the election will reflect an electoral process that lacked integrity,” the Trump administration’s filing read.
The Justice Department is asking a federal judge to delay certification to allow time for an investigation into “whether votes cast for Daniel J Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan”.
During a visit to Florida on Friday, Trump took credit for the lawsuit after reporters asked about it.
“I’m the one that said ‘do it,'” he told reporters in Fort Myers, Florida.
A Justice Department spokesperson did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
The lawsuit raises concerns among Democrats and voting rights groups that the Trump administration may be looking to meddle in some of the upcoming midterm races as Republicans across the United States struggle to push back a growing wave of Democratic support.
The Justice Department, as of late, has taken several actions against Democratic critics of President Donald Trump that have bolstered those worries, including charging a high-ranking Virginia lawmaker, state Senator L Louise Lucas, in a public corruption case and launching a probe into Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar over allegations of immigration fraud. Both have said the actions are politically motivated.
Trump critics have long expressed worries that the Justice Department could seek to block certification of elections the US president’s party loses.
On Wednesday, as Lucas’s indictment was announced, US Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters his agency would not do so unless extreme circumstances warranted such action.
“It is not DOJ’s intention to – and it’s never our intention to – improperly interfere with elections or the state certification process,” Blanche said.
The Brennan Center for Justice’s senior counsel, Lauren Miller Karalunas, said in a statement that election certification is handled by US states and the federal government has “no role” in it.
“Rest assured, state certification processes were created to meet this moment,” Karalunas said. “Centuries ago, state legislatures recognized that bad actors could use the process to manipulate election outcomes. They built in safeguards specifically designed to stop that from happening.”
The Alaska state Supreme Court in June rejected a previous Republican effort to remove Daniel J Sullivan from the ballot. He will appear without a party designation by his name, while Senator Sullivan will be listed as the Republican candidate.
However, under Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system, voters can select both Sullivans if they are unsure.
Which party controls the US Senate after November 3 could, ultimately, come down to Alaska’s Senate race, where Senator Sullivan is engaged in a challenging re-election fight against former US Democratic Congresswoman Mary Peltola.
Polling of the race has consistently shown a race that is well within the margin of error. A survey conducted by Public Policy Polling earlier this month suggested Peltola had a narrow one-point lead.
The campaign teams for both Sullivans and Peltola did not immediately return requests for comment.

The Foreign Ministers of the Republic of Türkiye, Arab Republic of Egypt, Islamic Republic of Pakistan, and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (R4 Group), met today in İstanbul to discuss regional issues of mutual concern, united in their commitment to contribute to diplomatic efforts and guided by the mutual interest to promote peace and stability in the region and beyond, in line with the principles and purposes of the UN Charter.
The Ministers underscored that the Israeli occupation constitutes the fundamental source of instability in the region and beyond, and that Israeli policies create a deep sense of injustice in global public opinion. They called for the early implementation of the two-state solution in accordance with the relevant UN resolutions. They reiterated their support for the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people, including their inalienable right to self-determination and to establish an independent, sovereign, viable, and contiguous State of Palestine on the basis of the 4 June 1967 lines, with East Jerusalem as its capital, in accordance with relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions in order to achieve comprehensive peace in the Middle East.
The Ministers called for an urgent end to the ongoing Israeli violence, as well as attempts to change the legal and historical status of Jerusalem, and to bring an end to further destruction and humanitarian tragedy in Palestine. They condemned all the previous and current settlement activities in the West Bank and Jerusalem, as well as the settler violence against Palestinians. They underlined the urgent need for uninterrupted flow of humanitarian aid to and reconstruction in Gaza.
Regarding Yemen,the Ministers condemned in the strongest terms the unacceptable escalation by the Houthi militia, which has deepened humanitarian suffering, as well as the continued strikes carried out by the Houthi militia against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, particularly those targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure, and the attacks carried out against commercial shipping in the Red Sea and the Bab Al Mandeb. They expressed their full solidarity with the Government of Yemen and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and called on the Houthi militia to immediately cease all military actions, threats and attacks, and to return to the political process in good faith.
Concerning the military conflict between the US/Israel and Iran as well as around the Strait of Hormuz, the Ministers underlined the urgent need to address this conflict only through dialogue and diplomacy as well as to prevent the targeting of civilians and civilian infrastructures, including vessels. They expressed support for the Islamabad MoU and welcomed continued diplomatic efforts to prevent further escalation and reaffirmed their commitment to a lasting negotiated solution.
The Ministers underscored the vital importance of freedom of navigation, permanent maritime safety and security, and safeguarding navigational rights and freedoms. They noted that disruption of sea lanes threatens the security and prosperity of all, through blocking global supply chains, flows of energy, fertilizer and food, impacting vulnerable populations in the region and beyond, and thus, requires collective efforts by the international community to address these challenges.
The Ministers also rejected any measures or restrictions that impair lawful navigation and called for the swift and full resumption of safe, secure and unimpeded passage through the Strait of Hormuz.
The Ministers agreed to maintain close consultation and coordination on the afore-mentioned matters.

The United Nations and an Israeli human rights group raised alarm Friday over escalating Israeli violence, sweeping closures and the threat of forced Palestinian displacement in the occupied West Bank, as Israel ordered an immediate lockdown of Hebron following a deadly attack on its troops.
U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres expressed deep concern over deteriorating conditions across the occupied territory, where Israeli military operations, illegal settler attacks and restrictions on Palestinian movement have intensified.
"We are extremely alarmed by the intensifying violence that we're seeing in the occupied West Bank," U.N. spokesperson Stephane Dujarric told reporters Friday.
He said Guterres was particularly concerned about widespread Israeli-imposed closures affecting Palestinian communities, warning that the restrictions severely limited freedom of movement, access to essential services and livelihoods.
The U.N. chief also raised concerns over reports of home demolitions and the possible displacement of Palestinian residents in Hebron.
The warnings came as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered the immediate closure of Hebron and instructed security forces to prepare for a full lockdown across the occupied West Bank following a deadly shooting incident.
The Israeli military said two soldiers were killed and three others seriously wounded in a gun battle in Hebron on Friday.
Separately, an Israeli human rights organization called for international pressure to prevent Israeli authorities from forcibly displacing Palestinians in response to the attack.
The organization urged action to stop measures that could uproot Palestinian communities as Israeli authorities considered further restrictions and security operations.
Dujarric said Guterres also condemned the violence resulting from record numbers of attacks by illegal Israeli settlers against Palestinians in 2026.
"He recalls Israel's obligation under international law as the occupying power to protect the Palestinian population from such attacks and to hold perpetrators to account," the spokesperson said.
The U.N. chief called for an immediate end to violence and urged all parties to avoid actions that could further destabilize the occupied territory.
"He calls on all parties to immediately cease all acts of violence, to exercise restraints, and refrain from action that could further inflame tensions," Dujarric said.
Violence across the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, has intensified since Israel launched its war on the Gaza Strip in October 2023.
Israeli military operations and attacks by illegal settlers have involved killings, arrests, home demolitions, the destruction of agricultural land and attacks on Palestinian property.
Palestinian communities have also faced restrictions on access to farmland, the burning of homes, mosques and vehicles, and displacement amid continued expansion of illegal Israeli settlements.
The latest closures have heightened concerns about the humanitarian consequences for Palestinian residents, particularly those already facing restrictions on movement and access to basic services.
Beyond the West Bank, Guterres expressed continued alarm over civilian casualties in the Gaza Strip, including the deaths of children, and severe restrictions on humanitarian assistance.
Dujarric said the U.N. chief was particularly concerned about obstacles to aid deliveries as winter approaches, warning of the growing risks facing vulnerable civilians.
He reiterated the urgent need to protect civilians and ensure humanitarian assistance reaches those in need.
The U.N.'s latest warnings underscore mounting international concern over the humanitarian situation in the occupied Palestinian territories, as Israeli military measures and settler violence continue to place Palestinian communities under increasing pressure.

"Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require," Melania Trump was quoted as saying in the press release.
"Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine."

Civilian cargo ship sinks off coast of Romania after Russian drone strike, authorities say
A civilian cargo ship sank after being struck by a Russian drone near Romania's Black Sea coast on Oct. 23, Romanian authorities reported.
The attack is the latest in a series of brazen Russian strikes on civilian shipping in the Black Sea, part of a broader escalation in Russia's economic warfare against Ukraine this year.
The ship, Khoryv, was sailing from Turkey under the flag of the Comoros and was crewed by Ukrainian and Azerbaijani nationals.
According to Romanian President Nicusor Dan, one person was confirmed dead and three others were missing from the 14-member crew.
Ukraine's Foreign Ministry later confirmed that a Ukrainian crew member on board the Khoryv was killed. Four other Ukrainian nationals, including the ship's captain, were hospitalized, while two Ukrainian crew members did not require medical assistance.
The ministry said the vessel had sunk near the Romanian city of Constanta with 14 crew members on board. According to preliminary information, a drone strike may have caused the sinking.
Ukraine's Embassy in Romania is working to establish the circumstances of the incident, as well as the whereabouts and condition of the rescued Ukrainian nationals, while remaining in contact with Romanian authorities, the ministry said.
"This attack is a new example of the tragic consequences of Russia’s aggression against Ukraine," Dan wrote on social media.
"It is time for Russia to take the peace initiatives proposed by the United States and Europe seriously, accept the ceasefire proposals and end the war."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen condemned the attack, describing it as another Russian escalation in the Black Sea.
"These reckless attacks target innocent lives and openly defy international law," von der Leyen wrote on X.
Romania's Interior Ministry later confirmed that nine crew members had been rescued, publishing a video showing the keel of the overturned ship barely protruding above the water's surface.
In response to a series of attacks on civilian shipping, NATO plans to increase its military presence in the Black Sea by deploying additional maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems, and drones.
The announcement came after NATO's main decision-making body, the North Atlantic Council, met at the alliance's headquarters in Brussels on Oct. 20 to discuss security in the Black Sea.

Ukraine to end automatic 100% mobilization exemptions for critical industries, Prime Minister says
Ukraine's government finalized changes to its military exemption system that will end automatic 100% exemptions for employees in critical industries, including defense manufacturing and energy, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi announced on Oct. 23.
Koretskyi said the changes seek to make the exemption system fairer and prevent abuses.
"The number of workers exempted from mobilization is growing by tens of thousands every month. Meanwhile, those who have been defending the country for five years must have the opportunity to return home from military service. That is why we are making difficult but necessary decisions," Koretskyi said.
Companies working in critical sectors, including defense manufacturing, energy, telecommunications, logistics, and utilities, will retain their critical status. However, the government will review the criteria used to determine which businesses qualify as critical.
Companies will still be able to request higher exemption quotas if needed to maintain operations, while the government is also developing a mechanism that would allow companies to exempt all their employees if they regularly arrange for some of their workers to voluntarily join the military, Koretskyi said.
Those joining the military would know where they would serve and for how long, while keeping their jobs and salaries, Koretskyi said.
"This will give those on the front line confidence that rotations are possible and that others will take their place. Those joining the military will also know that they are serving for a clearly defined period," he said.
Under the new rules, defense industry companies will be able to exempt up to 95% of their eligible employees from mobilization, the Defense Ministry said.
The ministry stressed that exemptions should remain available to employees directly involved in producing weapons and other equipment for Ukraine's military.
"Companies must be able to plan their operations, retain specialists, and increase production," Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said.
The Defense and Economy ministries will work out the conditions for the mechanism with businesses, with the government aiming to approve it by Dec. 1., Korestkyi said.

270 Ukrainian POWs return home in latest swap with Russia
Ukraine and Russia exchanged prisoners of war on Oct. 23, with 270 Ukrainian service members returning home, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced.
The exchange, the first in two months, also saw 270 Russian prisoners of war returned to Russia from Ukrainian captivity.
According to Zelensky, most of the Ukrainians returning home had been captured during the Siege of Mariupol in spring 2022. They included service members from the Ground Forces, Navy, and Air Assault Forces, as well as border guards and fighters from the Azov regiment, which led the city's defense.
Five of the released POWs survived the Olenivka prison massacre in July 2022, when a thermobaric munition was detonated inside a prison barracks housing Ukrainian prisoners of war.
According to Ukraine's Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, a "significant portion" of the released prisoners had been found guilty on sham criminal charges while in Russian captivity.
Seven Ukrainian civilians were also brought back from Russia with the help of Ukrainian authorities on Oct. 23, Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said in a Facebook post. Lubinets added that another seven civilians had traveled to Russia as part of family reunification efforts supported by the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC).
Zelensky, as well as the Coordination Headquarters later said that nine civilians had been released.
Lubinets called the prisoner exchange "historic," saying it brought home the largest number of convicted Ukrainian service members since 2022: 86 convicted soldiers and one person who had been facing criminal prosecution.
Ukraine, international human rights organizations, and the U.N. have described such trials in Russia as war crimes. The Third Geneva Convention grants POWs protected status under international humanitarian law and prohibits prosecuting them solely for their participation in hostilities, subject to the rules governing lawful combatant conduct.
Lubinets added that the exchange marked the return of Azov Regiment service members for the first time "in a long while."
Two of those released had been held in Russian captivity since 2018 and 2020, spending eight and six years in captivity, respectively, Lubinets said.
The youngest released POW was 24, while the oldest was 63, he added.
While intermittent U.S.-mediated "peace talks" between Russia and Ukraine have failed to secure even a partial ceasefire, prisoner exchanges remain one of the few channels of regular cooperation between Moscow and Kyiv.
The latest swap was the 11th reported prisoner exchange of 2026. The previous two exchanges took place in August.

Officials say the building, in Nairobi’s busy Eastleigh area, had no occupation certificate but its ground floor was in use.
Several people are missing and others may be trapped after a multistorey building under construction collapsed in Kenya’s capital, leaving a huge mound of concrete as rescuers dig through the rubble.
The building came down on Friday at about 1pm local time (10:00GMT) on a busy commercial street in Eastleigh, a neighbourhood in Nairobi crowded with thousands of traders and residents.
Nairobi police chief Issa Mohamud said more than 10 upper floors were under construction, and Kenya’s Interior Minister Kipchumba Murkomen said there were 67 workers at the site – one of whom was injured, while the other 66 escaped unharmed.
The basement and ground floor had been rented to an electronics shop, a butchery and a grocery, according to the Associated Press news agency. Those shops were occupied by about 11 people, who are yet to be accounted for, Murkomen told reporters.
“The good news is that from the rescue team, which includes national government, county government and Red Cross, it is reported that they have made contact with some of the survivors who are still trapped inside,” he said.
Al Jazeera’s Catherine Soi, reporting from Nairobi, said the developers and authorities are being asked “to answer now” as people were not supposed to be inside a building under construction.
She said rescue efforts were expected to continue through Friday night and Saturday.
Rescuers used poles stripped from trees and excavators to move concrete bound with steel, as heavy equipment was slow to arrive.
The Kenya Red Cross said two injured people had been rescued and taken to Kenyatta National Hospital, local media outlet The Eastleigh Voice reported.
Mohamud warned of a potential second collapse because the building was leaning on its neighbour.
Local media reported looting immediately after the collapse and police firing tear gas to disperse crowds.
‘Our concern is to save lives’
Joseph Kaula, a plasterer working on the fifth floor of the collapsed building, told AP that he was the last person to walk out.
“The whole area was filled with dust,” he said.
Relatives of those trapped said some had phoned for help immediately after the collapse, but their phones later became unreachable. A tent was set up to report missing relatives.
“Our concern is to save lives,” Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja told reporters.
He said the building had been approved for construction but had no certificate of occupation, so opening shops on the ground floor was illegal.
“This has potentially cost lives,” he told reporters on site.
He said that it was possible “one or two” people had died and that more would be known as time went on.
Mohamud said police had launched a manhunt for the building’s owner.
The National Construction Authority said the project was registered on July 30, 2025, The Eastleigh Voice reported. It was not immediately known whether the building had been inspected before its collapse.
Kenya’s National Building Inspectorate found that 87 percent of buildings audited nationwide last year failed to meet standards or lacked approvals, according to the AFP news agency.
Sakaja said county governments needed stronger enforcement powers, calling lenient penalties a “slap on the wrist”. Police said they would carry out investigations and anyone found negligent would face the law.

Oleshky Evacuation: Russia Announces Kherson Frontline ‘Silence Regime’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
17:49:02 UTC
02:49:02 KST

Chief of the Russian General Staff Valery Gerasimov announced Moscow will halt fire along the Kherson frontline in what it described as a “silence regime” to allow a humanitarian operation in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, starting Oct. 27.
Gerasimov set the announced date two days earlier than the date previously agreed upon with the White House, noting that it would take effect at 4 a.m. Moscow time.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“To ensure the safety of people and the delivery of socially important cargo, engineering reconnaissance will be organized and safe movement of a humanitarian convoy into the settlement of Oleshky in Kherson region will be ensured,” Gerasimov said, according to Interfax-Russia on Friday, Oct. 23.
The operatio to last several days
Asked about the duration of the humanitarian operation, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov declined to provide a specific timeline.
However, according to Russian state-owned media TASS, he said that the operation would “naturally” take “at least several days.”
Kyiv confirms the ceasefire
Although Ukraine has confirmed the White House-brokered arrangement, it has yet to comment on Moscow’s earlier start date.
The Kremlin’s decision to declare a ceasefire raises immediate concerns of possible sabotage among Ukrainian media, given Moscow’s pattern of breaking previous ceasefires, particularly those it declares itself.
Ukraine’s human rights commissioner, Dmytro Lubinets, who led the talks with his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova, earlier confirmed that the ceasefire would take place on Oct. 29.
Air Defenses at Russian Drone Factory Linked to Forced Labor Rival Putin’s Residence
He outlined three key components of the deal. “First, a silence regime will be ensured; second, humanitarian cargo will be delivered to Oleshky; third, free movement of civilians from Oleshky will be ensured,” Lubinets said, according to Ukrainska Pravda.
However, he did not provide additional details on how long each stage would take, nor how much aid would be delivered. No details were given on the evacuation routes either.
Lubinets also urged the public and media to be careful when sharing information about the mission. “The whole world now knows about Oleshky,” he said, promising to keep Ukrainians informed and show the results of the operation.
Davyd Arakhamia, who heads President Volodymyr Zelensky’s Servant of the People party in Ukraine’s parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, said that the operation to unblock Oleshky and its surroundings would begin soon.
He described the agreement as a result of a long process involving many people at different political levels, singling out Pope Leo XIV and Melania Trump for their roles.
At the time of the report, neither Kyiv nor Washington has explained why Moscow announced a start date earlier than the one agreed upon.
How the negotiations unfolded
Oleshky, located in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region on the left bank of the Dnipro River, about 5 km (3 miles) southeast of the city of Kherson, has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Ukrainian officials and European leaders have long been aware of the crisis in Oleshky and have worked for months to secure a safe evacuation and restore food supplies, which have not reached the city since May 26.
Beyond food, the town’s residents barely have any drinking water or medicine.
According to Tetiana Hasanenko, head of the Oleshky City Military Administration, Oleshky’s only pharmacy has also reportedly run out of essential medications months ago, while overall medical care has been significantly complicated due to power cuts and lack of fuel as the city remains isolated.
“Families are starving, surviving on leftover garden vegetables, canned goods, and even snails. Residents say that Russian soldiers have threatened them at gunpoint to seize their food,” Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said.
In a statement on Sept. 16, Lubinets said that the residents had started escaping on foot independently across mined fields and under threat of constant Russian drone attacks, simply because they saw no other way out. At the time, he also said Russia had failed to uphold previously agreed arrangements for a humanitarian mission.
“They see no other way to escape this hell,” Lubinets said, adding that his office had received 176 appeals regarding the humanitarian situation in Oleshky, and had already verified at least 358 people who urgently need assistance to leave safely.
On Monday, Oct. 19, Lubinets confirmed that Kyiv and Moscow were in daily contact over a possible evacuation, noting that the Russian side had taken up all proposals previously submitted by Ukraine.
“I cannot disclose many details, but I will say this: In my view, we have made significant progress,” he said.
Ukrainian authorities estimate that about 6,000 people, including some 200 children, remain across Oleshky and the surrounding settlements.
According to European Parliament Vice President Pina Picierno, who declared a hunger strike on Tuesday, Oct. 20, in protest over the starvation of civilians in Oleshky, roughly 1,700 people remain in the city from a prewar population of 24,000, including 47 children.
However, neither figure could be independently verified, particularly because Russian occupation authorities narrowly restrict access to information from the area.
White House brokers a date
Earlier on Friday, the White House announced that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to temporarily halt military activity in Oleshky to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and prepare civilian evacuations, starting Oct. 29.
It was not specified how long the truce would last or how many people are expected to be evacuated.
According to Washington’s statement, non-military representatives from Ukraine and Russia would visit residents at home to assess their needs.
“The people of Oleshky have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks. It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible,” said US First Lady Melania Trump.
The Associated Press previously reported that neither the Ukrainian nor the Russian government immediately commented.
Vatican reaches out to both countries
Pope Leo XIV held a telephone discussion with Putin on Oct. 16, in what marked the second phone call between the two, following their first conversation on June 4, 2025 that also focused on the war in Ukraine.
The pope had expressed his deep concern about the humanitarian situation in Oleshky, urging the Russian president to agree to an immediate ceasefire and allow the delivery of food and medical assistance to the city.
He also called for a safe evacuation of the civilians.
While the Kremlin backed Vatican’s initiative and agreed to cooperate, it again pinned the blame for the crisis on Ukraine, despite Kyiv’s repeated appeals to Russian authorities and international partners to secure humanitarian access to the town.
The pontiff then spoke to President Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday, Oct. 19, reiterating his earlier request for a humanitarian ceasefire. He expressed hope for a cooperation between Kyiv and Moscow which would allow for the desperately needed food and medical supplies to reach trapped civilians.
“We are working to help our people there. We are preparing decisions,” Zelensky said, confirming the conversation.

Parl panel bats for intercensal surveys, gender-inclusive census town norms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
17:46:40 UTC
02:46:40 KST

NEW DELHI: A parliamentary panel has called for “intercensal surveys” -- surveys between two successive censuses -- in India considering that cities and urban settlements undergo major changes in 10 years, and has also recommended review of the criteria for notifying “census towns” to make it more gender inclusive.At present, to qualify an urban area to be a census town, 75% male main working population must engage in non-agricultural activities. As per Census Commissioner of India, the proportion of female workers engaged in non-agricultural activities is not used as a criteria for classifying ‘census towns’ because female workforce participation fluctuates significantly due to social factors, under-reporting, and the informal nature of the work.The parliamentary standing committee on housing and urban affairs has recommended that this criteria is “based on a male-centric understanding of work and does not adequately reflect the growing participation of women in economic activities”. The panel added, “It also fails to capture the contribution of women engaged in self-employment, informal work, home-based work, service sector activities and other forms of employment that are often undercounted.
”It has highlighted how female labour force participation has been steadily increasing and labour force participation rate for persons aged 15 years and above stood at 34.8% in Aug, 2026. “In this context, continuing with a criterion based exclusively on male main workers would not reflect the changing socio-economic realities of India,” the panel said.The panel, in its report, has referred to a ministry’s suggestion for introduction of periodic intercensal surveys to capture rapid changes in urbanisation and emerging settlement patterns, as well as to address data gaps in the targeting, implementation and monitoring of various schemes and programmes.It has recommended the ministry, in consultation with the Office of Registrar General and Census Commissioner of India (ORGI) and other ministries and departments concerned to examine the feasibility of instituting periodic intercensal surveys for capturing changes in urbanisation, emerging settlement patterns and other relevant urban indicators.
ORGI had informed the panel that its primary mandate is to conduct the census and discharge related statutory functions while adding that proposal for conducting periodic intercensal surveys to capture rapid urban changes is a policy matter which may be examined separately by govt.The committee has also recommended the ministry to engage with states and UTs after the release of Census 2027 data to examine the feasibility of converting eligible census towns into statutory urban local bodies, while maintaining an updated database of their status.

UN condemns 'horrifying toll' of drone attacks in Sudan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
17:45:49 UTC
02:45:49 KST

Breadcrumb
UN condemns 'horrifying toll' of drone attacks in Sudan
The United Nations said Friday drone attacks in Sudan had killed more than 300 people so far in October, accusing both sides of launching such attacks, often on civilian targets.
"The increasing use of drones, already accounting for the majority of conflict-related civilian deaths in Sudan this year, is deeply disturbing and is exacting a horrifying toll," UN rights chief Volker Turk said in a statement.
"Scores of civilians have been killed and vital infrastructure and services on which they depend eviscerated, driving further displacement and deepening the already severe humanitarian crisis."
Aid workers estimate that the war between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which erupted in April 2023, has killed more than 200,000 people.
They say the conflict has forced more than 13 million to flee their homes, creating the world's largest hunger and displacement crisis.
In the first three weeks of October, the UN Human Rights Office said it had documented at least 306 deaths and hundreds of injuries from drone strikes.
The attacks, attributed to both sides in the conflict, hit homes, markets, hospitals, displacement sites, as well as power stations and water sources, it added.
Civilian sites attacked
The office said that a strike on a transport truck Sunday had killed at least 139 people and wounded dozens more in Al-Dibab town in the southwestern RSF-controlled state of West Kordofan.
On Tuesday, AFP gave the death toll as 80.
The UN rights office also highlighted a "particularly disturbing trend" of drone attacks on displacement camps.
Between October 6 and 10, drone strikes on displacement shelters in Ghubeish and El Nuhud in West Kordofan, attributed to the SAF, killed at least 25 civilians, it said.
On October 9 in Abu Shendi in Blue Nile state, a suspected RSF drone struck just outside a displacement camp, near an informal gold mining site.
A person involved in burying the victims told AFP that 26 women and four children had been killed.
Suspected RSF drones hit the Bajaun gold mining area in Gadeer, South Kordofan this month, killing 42 civilians, the rights office said.
"Attacks on gold mining areas are tied to the war economy sustaining the conflict," it said.
Markets are being hit with drones "with alarming regularity", it said, citing three recent strikes that reportedly killed 23 civilians.
Turk called again for both sides to commit to a ceasefire.
"Broader peace efforts must squarely address the continued influx of arms that is fuelling the conflict and press for an end to the transfer of arms that are used in manifest disregard of the international humanitarian law obligations protecting civilians," he said.
