‘Realistic and reassuring’: UK public ‘responding calmly’ to Be Ready campaign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
17:22:18 UTC
02:22:18 KST

When the UK government launched its “Protect and Survive” public information campaign in 1980 on how to stay alive after a nuclear attack, it was met with a combination of scepticism, disbelief and derision.
The advice included how to build a “fallout room” at home, how to whitewash windows to protect from a blast, and how to store a dead body for up to five days.
You might expect this would have prompted widespread panic, but in fact it led to a political backlash, and was later lampooned on TV and in music.
It shows the risks governments take when launching such campaigns, and the fine balance that must be struck between hammering home a practical message without causing panic – or other unintended reactions.
The government’s new Be Ready campaign is advising the public to stock up on three day’s worth of supplies for use during severe weather or cyber-attacks, so help can be directed to the most vulnerable first.
In a concise, two-page document, it suggests people stock bottled water and non-perishable food for three days, a torch with spare batteries, a wind-up FM radio, a first aid kit and a copy of their passport. To stave off panic buying, it advises people to check their cupboards first and build up items gradually on regular shopping trips.
While there is no evidence the advice has triggered mass panic, the public is clearly responding. Jack Brown, who co-owns Sgt Prepper Shop, which stocks emergency food and survival tools, said he received a month’s worth of orders in the first 24 hours of the Be Ready campaign.
“I thought my phone was glitching or being hacked with the number of orders coming in,” he said.
Brown said the advice seemed sensible and proportionate. Three days was the “sweet spot”, he said, with most everyday emergencies like power cuts, a burst water main or flooding sorted within that timeframe.
It is also “realistic, affordable and fits in a cupboard”, he said, adding that asking people to stock up on a month’s worth of supplies would feel overwhelming and most people would do nothing at all.
A wind-up radio was also a sensible suggestion, and ones with a built-in torch and phone-charging USB port make them “one of the most useful bits of kit you can own”, he said.
Dr Sarita Robinson, associate dean for the school of psychology and humanities at the University of Lancashire, said there was little evidence to suggest these kinds of messaging campaigns cause panic.
“There’s this perception that if we tell people the truth we’re somehow going to panic them and it isn’t the case,” she said.
“When we use accurate messaging about emergency situations, the public will engage with that proactively. It’s when we start to hide information and there’s a void of information, that’s when things can go wrong for government.”
She said Be Ready was “realistic, quite low level, and should be reassuring because it’s basically treating the public like the grownups they are”.
Dan Goss, who runs Start Prepping UK, said traffic to his website was up 700% since news of the campaign emerged in August. He said he was glad to see the subject finally being taken seriously and spoken about in “plain language” by the government, and felt the risk of panic was low.
“The level of uptake required for that would be huge – you would need to have an enormous number of people all take the government’s advice very seriously and all jump on it as a priority,” he said.
“We’re definitely in a phase now where we’re seeing lots of more disruption to people’s lives – not necessarily apocalyptic disasters, but things that have a big impact on small areas, so this advice is very much needed.”
Robinson said the campaign showed how the perception of “prepping” has shifted, especially since the Covid-19 pandemic when most people will remember seeing empty supermarket shelves.
“We did a study during Covid that showed people who did mild levels of prepping, such as having food, masks and hand gel in the house a few weeks before the pandemic, had lower anxiety and depression, and less stress,” she said.
“The government really needs to portray that this is just normal, everyday, very common in other countries, and isn’t wearing a tinfoil hat and building a nuclear bunker in your back garden.”

Iran has plans to hit Gulf undersea cables if war resumes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
17:22:07 UTC
02:22:07 KST

Breadcrumb
Iran has detailed plans to hit Gulf undersea cables if war resumes, officials say
Tehran has drawn up detailed plans to target undersea communications cables in the Gulf if the United States and Israel attack Iran again, two senior Iranian security officials told Reuters.
Their comments followed warnings by Iranian officials that undersea cables in the region could become targets in any renewed conflict if diplomacy with Washington collapses.
The two Iranian security officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, gave few details and did not say how or where exactly Tehran would carry out such attacks. But one of them said Iran would aim to prevent repairs after any attacks to prolong disruptions to communications, including internet connections.
"If Iran is attacked, there will be no more red lines ... from undersea cables to military bases, including covert ones," one of the officials said.
The official warned Washington not to "play with fire", and said Iran had full access to the undersea cables and could easily destroy them.
Yadollah Javani, the deputy head of political affairs for Iran's Revolutionary Guards (IRGC), said on Wednesday that Iran could target seven major internet cables beneath the Strait of Hormuz if Iranian infrastructure came under attack.
Undersea cables carry around 99% of global internet traffic, according to the International Telecommunication Union, a UN agency. But the global impact of such attacks by Iran could be limited as less than 1% of international bandwidth passes through the Strait of Hormuz, said Alan Mauldin, research director at telecommunications research firm TeleGeography.
The strait separates Iran and Oman, linking the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea.
The US Department of State and Iran's Foreign Ministry did not respond to Reuters' requests for comment on the Iranian security officials' remarks. There was no immediate comment from Gulf states.
'Stronger response'
The plans for possible attacks on undersea cables reflect a conviction in Iran's leadership that a renewed US military campaign would have to be met with a stronger response than before.
Top security official Mohsen Rezaei warned this month that US-linked digital infrastructure across the Gulf, including data centres and AI facilities, could be targeted in a renewed conflict.
Washington's Gulf allies have invested heavily in such infrastructure and they "should hold Washington, not Tehran, responsible for any damage to undersea cables," the second Iranian security official said.
Alex Vatanka, director of the Iran program at the Middle East Institute in Washington, said such threats were intended to deter renewed conflict and put pressure on Washington by making Gulf governments and US companies fear for their investments in the region.
"Tehran wants Gulf states and corporate executives to press (US President Donald) Trump over the risks his policies pose to their investment plans," said Vatanka.
Multiple cable cuts could slow internet services and disrupt financial transactions, e-commerce and cloud computing, analysts said. The impact would depend on how operators rerouted traffic and the capacity available on alternative connections, Mauldin said.
Restoring connections during wartime could be difficult, experts said, and higher insurance costs and delays in obtaining permits to enter territorial waters could further complicate repairs.
The Red Sea could offer a more significant target than the Strait of Hormuz, particularly if Iran had support from its Houthi allies in Yemen, though Tehran has made no public statement indicating it plans to target cables there.
The Red Sea carries data between Europe, East Africa and Asia, with capacity routed through it accounting for about 3% of global international demand and around 10% of traffic travelling between regions, Mauldin said.
Gulf governments have been investing heavily in technology to diversify beyond oil and become global artificial intelligence hubs, deepening ties with US technology firms.
Iranian strikes directly hit two Amazon Web Services facilities in the UAE in March and damaged infrastructure near one of its facilities in Bahrain. The IRGC named US tech companies including Microsoft, Google, Apple and Nvidia as legitimate targets at the height of the war in March.
Land-based connections can provide alternative routes for internet traffic, and Gulf states and US technology companies are investing in additional infrastructure to improve resilience.
Microsoft plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030.

How Israeli settlers wearing keffiyehs are attacking West Bank olive groves
The olive harvest officially began in the West Bank on October 15, 2026, and it has coincided with an uptick in violence towards Palestinians carried out by both Israeli settlers and soldiers. Meanwhile, the settlers and soldiers have been using social media to promote an aesthetic, Instagram-friendly and nationalistic view of these harvests.
At first glance, it is an Instagram video like any other. There’s rousing music, sunshine, smiles, coffee and three people harvesting olives. But the video's caption situates these charming scenes in a different, much more violent reality: "That took us a good four hours. We are asking you to come and showcase the land of Israel and harvest olives.”
This footage was captured in the occupied West Bank. David Kela, an illegal Israeli settlement, is identified as the scene's location in the post.

The olive harvest officially began on October 15, 2026 and lasts until the end of November. In recent years, however, this period has become synonymous with an uptick in violence towards Palestinians, carried out by the Israeli army and settlers. Because of this, many Palestinians began their harvest two weeks early this year to reduce the risk of violence.
However, the violent reality hasn’t prevented some Israelis from taking to social media to present an image of a pleasant and convivial harvest, often with a message to social media users to come and join them. There are dozens of these posts on social media.

In his caption, he calls on viewers to go and harvest olives "in the nearest orchard, located just behind the gate to your town” and calls on them to “reinforce the Jewish presence on our country’s land”, both nationalistic messages.
To display this content from Instagram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
On October 15, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) counted nearly 200 attacks linked to the olive harvest that resulted in bodily injury or material damage affecting the harvest season.
OCHA also confirmed that the number of attacks affecting the olive harvest carried out by settlers in the West Bank this year has already surpassed the 185 incidents recorded in 2025.
'They banned us from going to our own olive grove'
Omar (not his real name) lives in the Hebron Governorate in the occupied West Bank. The Israeli army has blocked his access to his olive grove since June 16, 2026.
 On Tuesday, June 16, we discovered that a dozen Israeli settlers had come into our olive grove. I inherited this land from my father and my grandfather.
They were hitting the olive trees with bats.
We called the Israeli police, who came to the site, but they didn’t come close enough to make them leave. They just stayed on the main road. Then, the army came and the soldiers went towards the settlers and some left, but not all.
The settlers who remained started to ransack the olive trees. They beat them with bats and specifically targeted the most beautiful trees. The settlers took some of the olives and then stamped on the rest.
Then, they brought over about 200 sheep, led them into the olive orchard and let them graze all over. The settlers stayed there with their sheep from the morning to sunset.
To display this content from , you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
 They banned us from going into our orchard, claiming that this land was now part of a military zone. We don’t know what to do.
Olives are an incredibly important source of income for tens of thousands of Palestinians in the West Bank. According to OCHA, in 2019, more than 10 million olive trees were a source of primary or secondary income for between 80,000 and 100,000 families. In its report "The Elimination Project", the Israeli human rights NGO B’Tselem reported that, on average, the olive sector brought in $170 million per year (more than €151 million) to the economy of the occupied West Bank.
The various restrictions and violence around the 2025 harvest – including designating olive groves as military zones or national parks, acts of violence or intimidation, and military orders preventing Palestinians from harvesting their olives – resulted in the Palestinian economy losing more than $46 million in revenue, or nearly €40 million, according to OCHA.
'The whole system supports settlers'
Yair Dvir is the spokesperson for B’Tselem. He highlighted the close links between settlers and the army as well as a system created to restrict Palestinian access to their land.
 Every year, for decades, we see an uptick in violence during this time of year. But each year, the violence continues to intensify. The violence perpetrated by settlers and soldiers leads to injuries or even deaths.
The violence also includes theft carried out by settlers. There are a number of eyewitness accounts and videos showing settlers stealing olives directly from the trees or waiting for Palestinians to finish their harvest and then just taking their olives from them.

 In many of the cases, we’ve found that the Israeli army is actively participating in these acts: they are there while it is happening and are letting the settlers attack and steal. Often, they even participate in the attacks, arresting Palestinians, firing on them and using tear gas.
One thing that we’ve observed recently – as well as throughout the years, though it is particularly striking now – is that we’ve seen more and more clearing of olive groves, carried out not just by settlers but also by the army.

'We saw settlers wearing keffiyeh come and attack us'
Mohammed (not his real name) is the president of an agricultural committee in a Palestinian village. He spoke to us about the role that olive trees play in Palestinian culture.
 Growing olives is a historic, cultural and religious act for us.
Most of the Palestinians in the West Bank have not been refugees. That means that there are people who have never been separated from their land, who have plots where they gather olives each year and produce their oil. However, suddenly, they are no longer able to do that.
Culturally, the Palestinian keffiyeh (a traditional scarf) often features embroidery that represents olive branches. Women’s traditional dresses, or thobes, also have special patterns that represent olive trees. Olive oil is essential to the food we make.
In the Quran, olive and fig trees – which have a symbiotic relationship and which, historically, were planted together in Palestine – are often jointly mentioned. Olive trees play an integral role in the Quran’s sacred texts.
I don’t think it is possible to explain what these olive trees mean for us. It goes beyond symbolism. Grave stones of martyrs are inscribed with the words: “We die standing up, like Palestine’s olive trees.”
 It’s revolting to see the settlers pretend to be locals and that their relationship with the olive tree is natural when it is them who have literally been destroying and cutting down olive trees for the past decade.
We see our culture being stolen from us. Soon, they are going to try to steal the thobe (traditional garment), too. We even saw colonists wearing keffiyeh come to attack us."
The FRANCE 24 Observers team contacted the Israeli army, who said that in the case of “disturbances affecting the harvest”, they took the “necessary measures for prosecution or, if needed, to disperse those present, all while attempting to avoid any injury”. The army added: “Most instances of friction that occur in the areas where olive harvesting doesn’t require coordination [Editor’s note: Palestinian farmers must obtain so-called prior coordination permits to access land that has been blocked by the army] or where security forces are not present. Most coordinated harvests are taking place as planned.”
OCHA reported that attacks linked to the olive harvest this year have so far resulted in the death of one person and more than 120 people injured. More than 2,500 olive trees or young plants have been damaged or destroyed. Since 2023, at least 100,000 olive trees have been destroyed, ripped out or burned in the occupied West Bank, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Agriculture.

The penalized club is currently preparing an appeal, focusing on
Article 10 of the Code of Sports Justice—the provision cited in
the ruling—which states in its first paragraph: "A club held
responsible for events or circumstances that have affected the
orderly conduct of a match, or that have prevented the match
from taking place as scheduled, shall be penalized with the loss
of the match, recorded as a 0-3 forfeit defeat."
However, paragraph five—which will be the focal point of the
appeal—states: "When events occur during a match that, by their
very nature, cannot be assessed using purely technical criteria,
the sports justice bodies shall determine whether, and to what
extent, such events influenced the proper conduct of the match."
In such cases, the measures that may be taken include awarding a
forfeit loss or ordering a replay of the match deemed to have
been irregular.
                                    
The latter is the outcome requested by Mascarino.

subsequent victory awarded by default, Vigor Pieve's president
had indicated that the club might consider a request to replay
the match; however, they will not be able to do so.
                                    
The decision will rest with the fifth-tier sports justice body,
assuming—as is now certain—that Mascarino files an appeal
against the sports judge's ruling, in the belief that a
different assessment could be reached.
                                    
"We will evaluate whether to pursue criminal action against the
player who made the racist insult, and for our next match, we
will show up with only seven players; one of them will
immediately leave the pitch, triggering a suspension, a forfeit
loss, and a points deduction," Mascarino president Antonello Le

US and Israel are warned against launching fresh strikes on Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
17:18:34 UTC
02:18:34 KST

Foreign ministers at a summit of eight European and Middle Eastern countries have urged the US and Israel not to renews their attacks on Iran, warning a fresh outbreak of fighting would spread conflict and push oil prices even higher.
The development of a new multinational “anti-war bloc” represents a challenge to the increasingly open plans by the US and Israel to relaunch strikes on Iran while talks on Tehran’s nuclear programme remain deadlocked.
The Turkish foreign minister, Hakan Fidan, joint convener of the summit in Istanbul, said: “Military intervention in Iran is not any kind of solution. We agreed that a new military attack would spread the war and the conflict in the region. All the countries around the table do not want the war to spread even more, once again.”
Ministers also demanded an end to the Houthi assaults on Saudi Arabia, and an immediate opening of the strait of Hormuz currently blockaded by Iranian ships and drones.
Jean-Noël Barrot, the French foreign minister, said another war between Iran and the US would be bad for both sides, and only worsen rising oil prices, which have hit their highest level since May. Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, also urged both sides to embrace diplomacy.
The Istanbul meeting, an unprecedented gathering of regional and European leaders initiated by Turkey and Germany, represented a rare chance for European ministers to have any input into the crises afflicting the Middle East, including in Yemen, Palestine and Iran. They have largely been left as bystanders, apart from sending air force protection to Saudi Arabia as it tries to fend off Houthi drone and missile assaults on its airports and energy installations.
The Middle Eastern states were represented by Fidan, Egypt’s Badr Abdelatty, Pakistan’s Ishaq Dar and Saudi Arabia’s Faisal bin Farhan. Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia formed the Mecca defensive security pact in August, a grouping Egypt may join.
The European side was represented by Barrot, Miliband, Germany’s Johann Wadephul and Italy’s Antonio Tajani. The agenda covered the Palestinian issue, including settlement expansion, settler violence and the two-state solution, as well as security in the strait of Hormuz, Yemen and efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war and prevent spillover into the Black Sea.
Wadephul said: “We are united by the impact these deadlocked conflicts are having on the economy and security of our countries and by the will to seek new ways to bring about solutions.”
He made no criticism of the US but accused “the Houthis and Iran of blackmailing world trade and continuing to stranglehold global supplies of energy and fertiliser”.
“We are feeling the effects of the attacks on shipping routes and whether at the petrol pump or the supermarket,” he said. “Elsewhere there is threat of famine.”
Tajani said the aim of the meeting was to work for “de-escalation to guarantee freedom of navigation”.
“I do not believe the problem can be solved from a purely military standpoint,” he added. “If we want to reopen Hormuz, which is vital for our economies, we must promote dialogue and make Iran understand that this attitude cannot continue.”

Speed limits for Starlink, Starshield remain in effect – Zelenskyy
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:18:19 EEST
02:18:19 KST

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that speed limits on SpaceX's Starlink satellite communication terminals and their military version, Starshield, remain in effect, creating problems for the Ukrainian military.
"The speed restrictions on Starlink and Starshield are still in place; speeds have not been restored, and the delivery of interceptors to defend against Russian ballistic missiles is still delayed. We are waiting for the interceptors that have already been agreed upon, but they still haven't arrived. We hope they're already on their way. And this is a real problem for us, since Russian attacks are happening almost daily – Russia is launching massive strikes. That's how the situation looks today," Zelenskyy said during an online meeting at the Hudson Institute on Friday.
According to him, this is happening while Ukraine continues its "fairly successful operations on the front lines" and continues to defend its positions. "The situation has become more complicated, partly due to the policies regarding Starlink and Starshield and the speed restrictions. But our front line is still holding, and we are doing everything possible to ensure our logistics continue to function, and we continue to defend ourselves," the president added.
At the same time, the head of state stated that he "truly wants our relations with America and all our other partners to be as strong as possible, genuinely friendly, and, of course, free of misunderstandings."
"After all, without America – without a strong America that cares about what's happening in the world – the world today would undoubtedly be a worse place. People ask why Ukraine is increasingly opening up and speaking directly to the world. The answer is simple: we want people to understand us-and by that I mean people, societies, nations, as many people as possible. And when people understand what is really happening, political leaders can choose a more decisive course – one that will truly bring us closer to peace. And peace is what we want more than anything else. And I hope that our conversation today will help people in America better understand our position and see what we can achieve through diplomacy," Zelenskyy said.
As previously reported, on the night of October 14, the Ukrainian military noted disruptions in the operation of Starshield terminals – the military version of the Starlink satellite communication system. According to Interfax-Ukraine sources in the Ministry of Defense, the terminals lost connection while moving at speeds exceeding a set threshold, which ranged from approximately 72 to 161 kilometers per hour depending on the equipment. This complicated the operations of interceptor drones and strike UAVs, as well as logistics, reconnaissance, and communications relay. The Ministry of Defense held consultations with the United States, SpaceX, and NATO partners and tested backup communication channels.

Team leaves pitch following racist insult, handed 0-3 forfeit loss
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:18:07 CEST
02:18:07 KST

After a teammate was subjected to
racist insults, the players of an Italian lower-tier team walked
off the pitch but their act of solidarity and protest resulted
in a forfeit loss of 0-3.
                                    
Mascarino, a team competing in the Terza Categoria tier in the
province of Bologna, which faced Vigor Pieve 1925 on Sunday, is
now preparing an appeal.
                                    
The incident occurred in the 41st minute of the second half,
with the score at 0-1. The player responsible for the
discriminatory remarks was immediately sent off, but Mascarino
chose to abandon the match.
                                    
Vigor Pieve filed a complaint, and the sports judge, Carlo Del
Percio, handed down a 10-match suspension to the individual who
made the insult, while also awarding a 0-3 forfeit victory to
Vigor Pieve.
                                    
When contacted, the Bologna branch of the Italian Football
Federation (FIGC) declined to comment.
                                    
The penalized club is currently preparing an appeal, focusing on
Article 10 of the Code of Sports Justice—the provision cited in
the ruling—which states in its first paragraph: "A club held
responsible for events or circumstances that have affected the
orderly conduct of a match, or that have prevented the match
from taking place as scheduled, shall be penalized with the loss
of the match, recorded as a 0-3 forfeit defeat."
However, paragraph five—which will be the focal point of the
appeal—states: "When events occur during a match that, by their
very nature, cannot be assessed using purely technical criteria,
the sports justice bodies shall determine whether, and to what
extent, such events influenced the proper conduct of the match."
In such cases, the measures that may be taken include awarding a
forfeit loss or ordering a replay of the match deemed to have
been irregular.
                                    
The latter is the outcome requested by Mascarino.
                                    
Following the uproar caused by their formal complaint and the
subsequent victory awarded by default, Vigor Pieve's president
had indicated that the club might consider a request to replay
the match; however, they will not be able to do so.
                                    
The decision will rest with the fifth-tier sports justice body,
assuming—as is now certain—that Mascarino files an appeal
against the sports judge's ruling, in the belief that a
different assessment could be reached.
                                    
"We will evaluate whether to pursue criminal action against the
player who made the racist insult, and for our next match, we
will show up with only seven players; one of them will
immediately leave the pitch, triggering a suspension, a forfeit
loss, and a points deduction," Mascarino president Antonello Le
Fosse told Il Resto del Carlino newspaper.

PrivatBank allocates UAH 5 mln to rebuild Strazhesko Institute operating unit
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:17:43 EEST
02:17:43 KST

PrivatBank will allocate UAH 5 million to purchase medical equipment to restore the operating unit of the M.D. Strazhesko Institute of Cardiology, which was destroyed in a Russian attack on October 20, the financial institution's press service reported.
"These UAH 5 million will go toward the urgent purchase of medical equipment so that doctors can return to the operating rooms as soon as possible and continue saving the lives of Ukrainians," said Olesia Zhulinska, head of public relations and communications at PrivatBank.
According to the bank, the institute's sixth floor was severely damaged in the attack, and the operating unit there was completely destroyed.
The funds will be provided through PrivatBank's charitable program, "Urgent Donation: Assistance to Hospitals and Medical Institutions in Ukraine."
This was the second attack on the Strazhesko Institute. In the fall of 2025, departments on the third through fifth floors were damaged. At that time, PrivatBank, together with charitable donations from its customers, allocated UAH 3 million to restore the operation of the operating rooms.
PrivatBank is Ukraine's largest bank. According to the National Bank of Ukraine, the financial institution's total assets stood at UAH 983.82 billion as of September 1, 2026, accounting for 22.8% of the banking sector's total assets. In the first half of the year, the bank allocated UAH 357.88 million to charitable causes.

Ukraine to end automatic 100% mobilization exemptions for critical industries, Prime Minister says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
17:16:32 UTC
02:16:32 KST

Ukraine to end automatic 100% mobilization exemptions for critical industries, Prime Minister says
Ukraine's government finalized changes to its military exemption system that will end automatic 100% exemptions for employees in critical industries, including defense manufacturing and energy, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi announced on Oct. 23.
Koretskyi said the changes seek to make the exemption system fairer and prevent abuses.
"The number of workers exempted from mobilization is growing by tens of thousands every month. Meanwhile, those who have been defending the country for five years must have the opportunity to return home from military service. That is why we are making difficult but necessary decisions," Koretskyi said.
Companies working in critical sectors, including defense manufacturing, energy, telecommunications, logistics, and utilities, will retain their critical status. However, the government will review the criteria used to determine which businesses qualify as critical.
Companies will still be able to request higher exemption quotas if needed to maintain operations, while the government is also developing a mechanism that would allow companies to exempt all their employees if they regularly arrange for some of their workers to voluntarily join the military, Koretskyi said.
Those joining the military would know where they would serve and for how long, while keeping their jobs and salaries, Koretskyi said.
"This will give those on the front line confidence that rotations are possible and that others will take their place. Those joining the military will also know that they are serving for a clearly defined period," he said.
Under the new rules, defense industry companies will be able to exempt up to 95% of their eligible employees from mobilization, the Defense Ministry said.
The ministry stressed that exemptions should remain available to employees directly involved in producing weapons and other equipment for Ukraine's military.
"Companies must be able to plan their operations, retain specialists, and increase production," Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said.
The Defense and Economy ministries will work out the conditions for the mechanism with businesses, with the government aiming to approve it by Dec. 1., Korestkyi said.
The announcement comes amid criticism from lawmakers and businesses concerned that reduced exemption quotas could leave critical industries without enough workers.
The government approved proposed changes on Oct. 13, reportedly including cuts to exemption quotas for defense and energy companies from 100% to 85%, and for utility companies from 75% to 60%.
Three days later, 63 lawmakers submitted a resolution calling on the government to reconsider the changes and consult businesses.
Ukraine faces the challenge of mobilizing more troops while keeping essential industries running amid wartime labor shortages.
The prime minister said some companies had been created specifically to obtain military exemptions, turning the system into a business.
Koretskyi said the changes do not mean mobilization will intensify immediately, but warned that Ukraine must be prepared for possible developments, including increased mobilization in Russia.

Doctors call Moderna, Merck cancer vaccine data a major advancement — despite Wall Street reaction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
17:15:08 UTC
02:15:08 KST

Leaked confidential data. A major stock sell-off.
Beneath the chaos surrounding Moderna and Merck's latest data on their personalized cancer vaccine, oncologists see something else: an important milestone in melanoma treatment.
The companies on Thursday released detailed results from a phase 3 trial on their mRNA-based shot after partial data leaked on social media platforms earlier that day.
The vaccine, known as intismeran autogene, reduced the risk of melanoma recurrence or death by 42% when given alongside Merck's immunotherapy Keytruda, compared with Keytruda alone. The combination also reduced the risk of cancer spreading to distant parts of the body or death by 38%, compared with just the immunotherapy, according to the trial on roughly 1,100 patients whose tumors were removed by surgery.
The stock market's reaction contrasted with the assessment of six melanoma specialists, who told CNBC the results represent a clinically meaningful advance that could eventually become a standard of care for patients who undergo surgery first and have not received immunotherapy before their operation.
"This has the potential to be a major breakthrough in melanoma treatment and also cancer immunotherapy in general that will open the door to greater outcomes for patients," said Dr. Sekwon Jang, a melanoma specialist at Inova Schar Cancer and principal investigator at one of the trial's U.S. sites.
Dr. Janice Mehnert, NYU Langone skin cancer specialist and trial investigator, added that "this is the first time we're seeing that when you add something to immunotherapy, you actually boost the efficacy of the immunotherapy."
The vaccine is not far from potentially entering the market for the first time and reaching melanoma patients. In an interview ahead of the results, Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel said the company is finishing a filing with regulators as it aims to get the drug fully approved next year.
"It's a very, very happy moment for the field, for patients," he said.
Major advance in melanoma
An immunotherapy like Keytruda wakes up the immune system to detect and attack cancer cells. Unlike preventative vaccines, which protect against infections that can cause cancer, Moderna and Merck's treatment acts like a blueprint to train the immune system to recognize and hunt residual cancer cells based on the specific mutations in an individual patient's tumor.
The significance of the phase 3 data extends beyond delaying a recurrence, doctors said. Melanoma can become much more difficult to treat when it returns after surgery and spreads to distant parts of the body, such as the lungs, brain or liver. Patients with advanced disease may require additional treatments, including immunotherapy, radiation or further surgery, and those methods are not guaranteed to work.
Preventing the cancer from returning could spare patients from ever facing the risks and complexities of metastatic disease altogether.
"If we can essentially cure more patients with earlier-stage melanoma and never have to deal with unresectable metastatic disease — that's a wonderful advance," said Dr. Michael Postow, chief of the Melanoma Service at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center and an investigator on the trial.
Ideally, patients in the future may be able to undergo surgery and receive the vaccine and Keytruda without needing further melanoma treatment, Postow told CNBC.
Still, questions remain about whether the combination ultimately helps patients live longer, what the benefit looks like over longer periods of time and which patients benefit most.
The results also leave open where the personalized vaccine would fit into a changing melanoma treatment landscape, some experts said.
The trial tested the vaccine after surgery, alongside Keytruda, rather than against immunotherapy regimens given before surgery. That's an approach increasingly used for eligible patients with resectable melanoma, where the primary tumor can be removed. The data does not show that using the vaccine approach is more or less effective than receiving immunotherapy before surgery.
The medical community will get more clarity after Moderna and Merck present the detailed results at the European Society for Medical Oncology conference on Saturday.
Investors diverged from doctors
Moderna shares fell as much as 25% Thursday, before regaining some ground, after partial data from the trial leaked on social media. The sell-off came despite the positive results, underscoring the gap between the treatment's clinical promise and investor expectations for its commercial potential. Moderna shares are also up nearly 600% this year due to the cancer shot optimism, creating more potential for a Wall Street letdown.
Investors had hoped the vaccine and Keytruda would replicate the results of an earlier phase 2 trial, which showed a roughly 49% reduction in the risk of recurrence or death at five years, RBC Capital Markets analyst Trung Huynh wrote in a note Thursday. Huynh described the phase 3 results as clinically meaningful and likely to support regulatory approval, but said the primary efficacy result landed at the low end of investor expectations.
But there was a key difference in the studies: The phase 3 trial included patients with a broader range of risk profiles, including some at lower risk of recurrence than those enrolled in the earlier phase 2 trial, said Dr. George Ansstas, who leads the melanoma department at Washington University in St. Louis. That may have slightly tempered the results, since patients considered lower risk have less chance of recurrence to begin with.
"It's great data actually. It's overall consistent with what we've proven in the phase 2 trial," said Ansstas, who also worked on the phase 2 trial.
The combination showed little difference from Keytruda alone during the first six months of treatment, the companies said. But a separate analysis of the phase 3 data offered a more encouraging signal about the treatment's effect after the six-month mark. The vaccine and Keytruda reduced the risk of recurrence or death by 58% after that point, compared with Keytruda alone.
The 42% figure comes from the primary analysis, which included patients' outcomes throughout the trial's follow-up period. The median follow-up was about two years at the time of the analysis, so the result reflects the overall treatment effect, not just what happened before or after the six-month mark.
Ansstas said the benefit of the personalized cancer vaccine may take several months to emerge because each shot must be custom-manufactured, a process that can take roughly six weeks, while patients begin Keytruda in the meantime. After vaccination begins, the immune system also needs time and repeated doses to develop a response against tumors.
That timeline could help explain why the group that received the combination regimen saw even greater benefits around six months, Ansstas said. Still, the explanation is a hypothesis rather than proof of when the vaccine's effect begins.
Dr. Hussein Tawbi, a melanoma expert and trial investigator at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, also highlighted the relatively mild side effects associated with the vaccine, including injection-site reactions, as a positive.
Keytruda and other cancer therapies can cause potentially serious immune-related side effects. Detailed safety results released on Saturday should help clarify the trade-offs of adding the vaccine to the immunotherapy regimen.
More work to be done
For Moderna, the stakes extend beyond melanoma. The company is working to build a business beyond its Covid vaccine, while Merck is preparing for the eventual loss of patent protection on Keytruda.
The companies have several hurdles ahead of them, including selling an individualized therapy that takes several weeks to create for a patient at scale.
"I think the downside is that it's super labor-intensive, and you're gonna have to make vaccines for each person, and so you can't just stockpile a million vaccines and then just ship it out when somebody needs it," said Dr. Adil Daud, professor of medicine and melanoma oncologist at the University of California San Francisco, who was the lead investigator on the phase 3 trial. "There is the time and expense, and it's probably going to cost like a lot of money."
Moderna and Merck have not disclosed any details about the manufacturing costs for the vaccine.
He added that most people who walk into the clinic with a tumor that has not been surgically removed may stick to receiving Keytruda before an operation because "that approach is simpler and doesn't put the patient through the delay" of creating the vaccine.
Daud said he expects the vaccine combination to be used primarily in the adjuvant setting, after surgery, rather than replace established immunotherapy regimens given before an operation. For patients who receive immunotherapy before surgery but show little or no response, the vaccine combination could offer another option, he said, though that would likely be for a smaller group of patients.
Moderna and Merck still need to validate the approach in other cancers, including non-small cell lung cancer, bladder cancer and renal cell carcinoma. Success in melanoma does not automatically guarantee that the approach will work in other tumors.
"I can dream of creating a log cabin, but we got some wood chops, and we've just knocked down one tree," Merck Research Laboratories President Dean Li said in an interview ahead of the results. "Knocking one tree does not give you a cabin or a village."
Moderna's Bancel sees a bright future for the vaccine, saying he believes it will eventually be able to help "literally thousands and then tens of thousands and then hundreds of thousands of people across different tumors around the world."

Romania blames Russia for drone strike that sinks cargo ship in Black Sea, killing one sailor and leaving three missing
Unknown

Romania blames Russia for drone strike that sinks cargo ship in Black Sea, killing one sailor and leaving three missing
The Comoros-flagged cargo ship Khoryv sank in the Black Sea off Romania’s coast after a drone attack, Reuters reported. The ship had 13 sailors from Ukraine and Azerbaijan aboard. One crew member was killed, nine were rescued, and three remain missing.
“It is part of Russia’s escalation process in its war in Ukraine,” Romanian President Nicusor Dan said. He told reporters that the ship had sunk after being hit by a drone.
Romania’s naval authority said the Khoryv sent a distress signal 24 kilometers (about 15 miles) from the port of Constanta, just outside Romania’s territorial waters.
At least seven cargo ships have been attacked off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria in the past two weeks, Reuters reported. About 30 sailors have been killed or gone missing.
Most of the ships attacked were near the Sulina Channel, which connects the Danube to the Black Sea. After strikes on Ukraine’s Black Sea ports, the channel became the main export route for Ukrainian grain and vegetable oil, Reuters reported.
Ukraine, Romania, and Bulgaria have called on NATO to do more to protect commercial ships in the Black Sea.

Netanyahu orders blockade of West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Netanyahu orders blockade of West Bank
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered a blockade of the occupied West Bank in the aftermath of a deadly shootout between IDF troops and two suspected Palestinian gunmen at a security checkpoint.
The incident unfolded on Friday in the southern West Bank at the temporary checkpoint at the Judea Junction on Route 35. An AFP photographer who witnessed the shootout reported the two Palestinian suspects armed with a handgun and an automatic rifle exchanged fire with Israeli soldiers. Five Israelis were wounded in the attack, with two servicemen succumbing to their wounds in hospital, while the gunmen were killed on the site of the shootout, which lasted more than 20 minutes, according to a preliminary Israeli military investigation.
The Israeli military described the incident as a thwarted “terror attack” without specifying the intended target of the suspects. Netanyahu vowed a “very extensive” retaliatory operation in the aftermath of the incident, announcing the demolition of the entire neighborhood the attackers come from and displacing its residents, as well as requesting the cancellation of all political meetings on October 23.
“I have instructed the IDF and security forces to immediately blockade the city of Hebron and prepare to completely blockade the entire area of Judea and Samaria from today,” he added, referring to the West Bank by its Israeli name.
Far-right Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir demanded even more severe retaliation, calling for the dissolution of the Ramallah-based Palestinian Authority (PA). No evidence, however, has emerged thus far linking the PA to the incident.
“The Palestinian Authority must be dissolved and demilitarized, and all terrorist infrastructure must be completely wiped out,” Ben-Gvir, known for extremely hostile anti-Palestinian rhetoric and assorted controversial stunts, said.
The deadly shooting comes ahead of the high-stakes legislative election in Israel scheduled for October 27. The upcoming polls are the first voting to take place since the October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel and the ensuing Gaza war. The prolonged conflict has prompted repeated allegations against Netanyahu of deliberately dragging out the hostilities to keep his grip on power. The latest opinion polls put the incumbent PM in a tight race with Gadi Eisenkot, a former head of the IDF, and the prospects of Netanyahu losing his post remain high.

Russia vows ‘inevitable’ retaliation over Austrian diplomat expulsions

“A response will follow inevitably,” Lyubinsky told TASS on Friday. He did not specify what retaliatory measures Moscow could take.
Austria announced the expulsions earlier on Friday, citing findings by its security services. Three of the diplomats were stationed at the Russian Embassy in Vienna, while the fourth worked at Moscow’s delegation to the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), dealing with military security and arms control.
The Austrian Foreign Ministry accused the four of engaging in “activities incompatible with their diplomatic status” and ordered them to leave the country. It did not identify the diplomats or provide details of the alleged violations.
The Russian Embassy rejected the accusations as “outrageous” and unfounded. Responding to Friday’s decision, the mission accused Vienna of blindly following Western anti-Russian policies and described the expulsions as another unfriendly move against Moscow.
Austrian media have sought to link the expulsions to alleged Russian espionage, although Vienna has provided no public evidence to substantiate the claims. According to the magazine Profil, the country’s Defense Ministry circulated a warning to military personnel and reservists in August about supposed Russian intelligence operatives, complete with the names and photographs of 21 individuals.
The warning reportedly prompted a wave of reports about suspicious contacts, though their nature and credibility remain unclear. Profil also claimed that disagreements between Austria’s Defense and Foreign Ministries had delayed the expulsions. None of the allegations have been publicly substantiated, and no evidence directly implicating the four Russian diplomats in espionage has been presented.
Austria has expelled 18 Russian diplomats since 2020. Despite its longstanding military neutrality, Vienna has joined EU sanctions against Moscow and provided political and financial assistance to Ukraine.
Moscow has previously responded to Austrian expulsions with reciprocal measures. In September 2025, Russia declared an Austrian diplomat persona non grata after Vienna expelled a Russian envoy over alleged espionage involving an employee of the Austrian energy company OMV. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said at the time that Moscow would respond to such moves in kind.
The diplomatic standoff escalated again in May, when Austria expelled three Russian Embassy employees over allegations that antennas installed on diplomatic buildings in Vienna were being used to intercept satellite communications. The Russian Embassy dismissed the accusations as “outrageous,” “unjustified” and politically motivated, warning of a harsh response.

The website of the International Burke Institute (IBI), an Israeli pseudo-expert center linked to a Kremlin disinformation campaign, was transformed within hours of the publication of an investigation by The Insider. Political analysis and country rankings were replaced with images of Ilya Gambashidze, the head of a Kremlin-linked disinformation operation, wearing boxer shorts, along with joke advertisements for what were presented as his own branded underwear.
The homepage of ibi.institute began featuring a piece titled “The Boxer Sovereignty Index, 2026 Edition.” Illustrations showed a man with Gambashidze’s face modeling underwear against backdrops of European cities, in a library, and in front of a classroom blackboard.
The International Burke Institute itself was renamed the “Ilya Boxer Institute,” preserving the initials IBI.
From a sovereignty index to a boxer-shorts index
Those behind the changes did more than simply replace photographs. They turned the website into a parody underwear catalog while preserving the pseudo-academic tone of the original institute. Instead of assessing the sovereignty of countries, the IBI now analyzes different types of boxer shorts using the language of policy reports, diplomacy, and official documents. Each model comes with descriptions of its fabric, sizing charts, care instructions, shipping information, and return conditions.
One model, “The Index,” is presented as the benchmark against which the institute intends to compare all others. Its description says the “waistband keeps the garment in place rather than starting a discussion.” Customers are also advised not to use bleach, with the clarification: “The Institute has nothing further to say about bleach.”
“The Field Standard” is described as the control sample used for testing. Its creators say the underwear was deliberately designed without decoration so as not to influence comparison results. Its specifications list 100% cotton, manufacturing in Portugal, and a 35 mm waistband.
Another model, “The Quorum,” is intended for meetings: “The Quorum does not hold a vote. It waits until those present reach agreement,” the description says. The authors add that the institute does not claim the underwear improves decision-making and clarifies that some decisions are simply better made after everyone has left the table.
“The Backchannel” is advertised as close-fitting underwear for travel, long meetings, and situations requiring confidentiality. The description stresses that the underwear has no conspicuous logos or other attention-grabbing details. “Discretion is a form of precision,” the authors explain. The model, they say, is designed not for the beach but for a work schedule.
The range also includes “The Reading Room,” a pair of lounge pants intended for reading and rereading documents: “The Institute has observed that important proposals are usually read twice, while trousers are rarely designed with a second reading in mind.” Customers are advised to empty their pockets before washing. The institute disclaims responsibility for any receipts discovered inside.
Another model, “The Protocol,” is intended for closed-door events and informal meetings. Its description says the underwear should be put on after the tie has come off and there is no longer an audience in the room. “The Institute recommends ‘The Protocol’ for events that end without photographs,” the authors say. The model is also intended “for the transition between a long evening and a short night.”
At the bottom of the page is an advertisement showing Gambashidze seated in a leather armchair with a book. In front of him are three packages of boxer shorts bearing the IBI logo. The slogan reads: “A brief study in relaxation. Make yourself comfortable.”
“Rotten Reliable News”: A reference to the Kremlin-linked RRN network
Every post ends with the signature: “With love, made by RRN.world — Rotten Reliable News.” This is clearly a joke aimed at the Kremlin-linked disinformation operation.
Recent Reliable News, or RRN, is a pro-Kremlin propaganda outlet associated with the Doppelgänger campaign. The network used the rrn.world domain to distribute material promoting narratives favorable to the Kremlin.
How the Kremlin created pseudo-expert centers in Israel
On Oct. 22, The Insider published an investigation into the activities of a Kremlin-linked disinformation operation in Israel — including the creation of the ”International Burke Institute,” which was formally registered as a nonprofit organization in Israel in July 2025.
Internal documents from the Russian Presidential Administration’s Social Design Agency (SDA), reviewed by The Insider showed, that Russian political consultants planned to create organizations abroad that would present themselves as independent research centers, using them to spread narratives favorable to the Kremlin.
The institute also falsely listed the United Nations, UNICEF, UNESCO, the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, and the World Bank as partners. All of those organizations told The Insider they had never worked with IBI.
In August 2026, OpenAI reported that material published by the institute had been created using ChatGPT by operators in Russia. The company blocked accounts linked to the activity.
The Insider identified links between IBI leadership and other organizations that promoted pro-Russian narratives, as well as ties to political activists, rabbis and members of the Knesset.
However, the participation of those politicians and public figures in events with the organizations does not by itself mean they knew of any connection to a Kremlin-linked disinformation campaign.
Ilya Gambashidze heads the Social Design Agency.
His work has been linked to the Doppelgänger campaign, whose operators create fake versions of well-known media websites and circulate fabricated stories disguised as legitimate news.

The US naval blockade of Iran: an illegal act of coercion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
17:09:06 UTC
02:09:06 KST

The US naval blockade of Iran: an illegal act of coercion
TEHRAN - An examination of the legal grounds for the US blockade of Iranian ports, what the UN Charter says, and how international law experts assess the action.
Imagine a country deciding to stop another country’s commercial ships, prevent goods from reaching its ports, and effectively impose its own rules on vessels travelling through international waters. Does military power, combined with claims of national security, give that country the right to do so? If the answer is yes, what would stop any major power from turning the seas into tools of pressure and blockade whenever it has a dispute with another country?
These questions lie at the heart of the US naval blockade of Iran. A naval blockade is not simply a matter of stopping ships. It can disrupt a country’s trade, drive up economic costs, and affect people’s daily lives. For that reason, international law does not give countries unlimited authority to restrict maritime traffic simply because they have military superiority or claim to be acting for security reasons.
Under international law, the US naval blockade of Iran cannot be justified simply by Washington’s announcement or its claims of national security. Given the absence of UN Security Council authorisation and the lack of a valid legal basis for self-defence, the blockade, as part of the use of force against Iran, is illegal. One important distinction must be made, however: even during wartime, rules govern how a naval blockade may be carried out. Possible compliance with some of those rules does not, by itself, make the original use of force lawful.
What does the UN Charter say?
The main legal document relevant to the US action is the United Nations Charter. Article 2(4) prohibits states from threatening or using force against other states. The purpose of this rule is to prevent governments from using their military strength to impose their will on other countries.
The Charter recognises two principal legal grounds for the use of force: authorisation by the UN Security Council and self-defence under the conditions set out in Article 51. A country seeking to justify a military blockade of another country must therefore demonstrate that its actions fall within one of these legal frameworks.
In the case of the blockade of Iran, the United States cannot create its own legal authority simply by declaring a security emergency or seeking to put economic pressure on Iran. If the military action lacks a valid basis under the UN Charter, it cannot become lawful merely because Washington gives it an official name or announces a justification.
What do international law experts say?
One important contribution to the legal debate is an article by Michael Schmitt, a professor and specialist in international law, published by Just Security. In his article, “Iran’s Conditions for Reopening Hormuz: What International Law Requires, Permits, and Forbids,” Schmitt examines the legal basis for the US use of force against Iran.
Schmitt explains that, under the UN Charter, the use of force must generally be based on Security Council authorisation or the right of self-defence in response to an armed attack. According to his analysis, most international law experts believe that the initial US attack was not authorised by the Security Council and did not meet the necessary conditions to qualify as self-defence. He therefore considers the start of US military operations to be inconsistent with the country’s obligations under the UN Charter.
His analysis is directly relevant to the blockade. If the legality of the original use of force is in question, the blockade cannot be treated as an entirely separate action and declared lawful simply by referring to the rules of naval warfare.
Steve Prest, a retired naval officer and analyst at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), raises similar concerns in his article, “The ‘US Blockade’ of Iran: How It Might Function (Or Not!).” He argues that the legality of the US action depends on whether the necessary conditions for using force have been met. Without Security Council authorisation, self-defence is the principal legal justification available to Washington, but Prest points to serious questions about whether that argument can justify the operation.
These analyses highlight the central issue: the question is not merely how the United States stops ships, but on what legal grounds it claims the right to use military force to blockade Iranian ports.
Do the laws of war make the US blockade legal?
The United States may argue that naval blockades are a recognised method of warfare. That claim reflects part of the legal picture, but it does not tell the whole story.
The San Remo Manual on International Law Applicable to Armed Conflicts at Sea, adopted in 1994, sets out restrictions on naval blockades. Under its rules, a blockade must be declared, its limits must be specified, and it must be effectively enforced. It must also respect the rights of neutral states. Rules protecting civilians and ensuring access to essential supplies must be observed as well.
The San Remo Manual is not, in itself, a binding treaty. However, it is a recognised reference for assessing the law governing naval warfare.
The key point is simple: the fact that certain methods of warfare may be lawful does not mean that starting a war or using force is lawful.
A legal analysis published by German broadcaster Tagesschau on 18 July 2026 makes the same distinction. Citing Pierre Thielbörger, a professor of international law at the University of Bochum, the report explains that the legality of resorting to force must be distinguished from the legality of how military operations are conducted. In other words, a particular action may be assessed separately under the rules of naval warfare, but that does not erase the possibility that the war itself was unlawful.
For this reason, citing the rules governing naval blockades does not, on its own, answer the fundamental question: did the United States have the legal right to use force to blockade Iranian ports in the first place?
US sanctions do not give Washington the right to shut down Iran’s trade
Another issue is the attempt to link the naval blockade to US sanctions. Washington may place companies or ships on its sanctions lists, but a decision made by one government does not automatically become international law.
Keri Batsov, a former US Treasury Department official, said: “Iran will not surrender under sanctions; the naval blockade has worn down the US military, and Iran’s low-cost drones have challenged Washington’s expensive weapons.”
Article 92 of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea recognises the principle that ships on the high seas are generally subject to the jurisdiction of their flag state. Article 110 sets out specific circumstances in which foreign ships may be boarded on the high seas.
These provisions make clear that the seizure of ships in international waters requires a legal basis. A vessel’s commercial links to Iran, or its inclusion on a US sanctions list, does not by itself give the United States unlimited authority to seize it.
Mark Nevitt, a legal scholar specialising in military and maritime law, raised concerns about this issue in an article published by Just Security on 1 May 2026. He warns that the United States is grouping several types of maritime operations, each with a different legal basis, under the single label of a “blockade.” He distinguishes a blockade of Iranian ports from the seizure of US-sanctioned ships in different parts of the world, stressing that each operation must have its own clear legal justification.
This distinction is crucial. Even if a limited blockade under certain conditions of armed conflict can be defended on legal grounds, that does not give the United States the authority to stop every ship linked to Iran anywhere in the world.
The human cost of a naval blockade
A naval blockade is not just a military measure directed at ports. Its effects can reach deep into the economy and people’s everyday lives. Restrictions on ships entering and leaving ports can disrupt trade, raise shipping costs, and make essential goods more difficult to obtain.
International humanitarian law contains rules intended to prevent unjustifiable harm to civilians. Using starvation of civilians as a method of warfare is prohibited, and a blockade must not be used as an excuse to disregard people’s essential needs.
Ismail Kowsari, an Iranian parliament member and member of the National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, has called for legal action over US measures against Iran. He said international legal mechanisms lack sufficient power and enforcement guarantees to address violations and hold those responsible to account. This, he said, has allowed some powers to pursue their interests without sufficient regard for the rights of other countries and peoples.
Kowsari said it was necessary to stand firmly against this approach and to drive the United States out of the region so that international law could be implemented in practice. Criticising international judicial institutions for failing to address US violations earlier, he said this should not bring legal efforts to a halt. Iran’s judiciary, he argued, should carefully document US actions and violations against Iran, including the naval blockade, and pursue them through legal channels.
Kowsari also stressed the need to document the humanitarian consequences of sanctions, particularly in the medical and pharmaceutical sectors. He said patients and vulnerable groups depend on essential medicines and medical equipment, and that any disruption to access could have serious consequences. Despite these needs, he added, sanctions can obstruct access to essential supplies while those imposing them continue without sufficient regard for the human impact.
He said the effects of these measures should be recorded accurately through credible documents, evidence, and other supporting material so that they can be pursued before the competent international bodies.
Assessing a blockade therefore requires more than counting the number of ships stopped or measuring the economic pressure it creates. Its impact on civilians must also be examined, including whether essential supplies remain available in practice.
A naval blockade can thus become more than an instrument of military pressure. It can develop into a humanitarian and legal crisis, and governments cannot escape responsibility simply by declaring that their actions serve security objectives.
The UN Charter and the analyses of international law experts show that the blockade of Iran cannot be assessed solely through the technical rules of naval warfare. The fundamental question remains: on what legal basis is the United States using force to blockade Iranian ports?
Michael Schmitt, writing for Just Security, questions the legal basis for the initial US attack. Steve Prest, writing for RUSI, raises serious doubts about whether self-defence can justify the operation. Mark Nevitt, also writing for Just Security, explains why a limited blockade cannot be turned into a blanket licence to seize sanctioned ships around the world. The UN Charter sets out the underlying principle: the use of force must be justified under international law.
The US naval blockade of Iran is therefore illegal in the absence of Security Council authorisation and a valid legal basis for the use of force. The rules of naval warfare cannot, on their own, resolve this fundamental problem. Nor do unilateral US sanctions give Washington unlimited authority to control Iran’s maritime trade.
This is not just about Iran. It is about whether major powers will abide by the rules they accepted as part of the international order established after the Second World War. If military power is allowed to replace the law, naval blockades will no longer be exceptional measures. They could become tools that powerful countries use whenever they want to force another state to submit to their demands.

Iran has detailed plans to strike undersea cables in the Persian Gulf if war resumes - media

Iran has detailed plans to strike undersea cables in the Persian Gulf if war resumes - media
Kyiv • UNN
Iran has developed plans to strike undersea cables in the event of a new attack by the US and Israel. Less than 1% of the world's transmission capacity passes through the Strait of Hormuz.
Tehran has developed detailed plans to attack communications cables in the Persian Gulf in the event that the United States and Israel strike Iran again. Two senior Iranian security officials told Reuters, reports UNN.
Details
The statements followed warnings from other Iranian officials that undersea cables in the region could become targets if the conflict resumes, should diplomatic efforts with Washington fail.
The two Iranian security officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity, provided few details and did not specify exactly how or where Tehran plans to carry out such attacks. However, one of them said Iran would seek to prevent repair work after the attacks in order to prolong disruptions to communications, particularly internet services, as much as possible.
"If Iran is attacked, there will be no more 'red lines' — everything will come under attack, from undersea cables to military bases, including secret ones," one of the officials said.
He warned Washington against "playing with fire" and added that Iran has full access to the undersea cables and could easily destroy them.
Yadollah Javani, deputy head of the political bureau of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), said on Wednesday that Iran could attack seven major internet cables laid beneath the Strait of Hormuz if Iranian infrastructure came under attack.
According to the International Telecommunication Union (a specialized agency of the United Nations), about 99% of the world's internet traffic passes through undersea cables. However, as Alan Mauldin, research director at telecommunications analytics firm TeleGeography, notes, the global consequences of such actions by Iran could be limited, since less than 1% of international network capacity passes through the Strait of Hormuz.
The strait separates Iran from Oman and connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea.
The U.S. State Department and Iran's Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not respond to Reuters' requests for comment on the statements by the Iranian security officials. No comments have been received from the Persian Gulf states either.

Ukraine hires Rothschild to advise on Ukrgasbank and Sense Bank privatization
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:07:45 EEST
02:07:45 KST

Ukraine's Ministry of Finance, state-owned banks Ukrgasbank and Sense Bank, and N.M. Rothschild & Sons Limited, part of the Rothschild & Co group, have signed three-party agreements to provide financial advisory services for preparations to sell the state-owned stakes in the two banks.
"Rothschild & Co was selected following a competitive selection process. Rothschild & Co will provide the services in a consortium with FinPoint, a Ukrainian investment banking company," the Finance Ministry said in a press release on its website on Friday.
Under the agreements, the adviser will provide comprehensive financial advice, including coordinating due diligence on the banks, among other things to determine the initial sale price; preparing information about the banks for potential investors and attracting investors; and assisting in organizing the tender for the sale of the share packages.
"Engaging an international financial adviser is an important step in implementing the strategy to reduce the state's share in the banking sector. Our task is to ensure a transparent, competitive process for selling the state-owned stakes in Ukrgasbank and Sense Bank, attract strategic investors and create conditions for the further development of these institutions," Finance Minister Serhiy Marchenko was quoted as saying in the press release.
The banks will announce further steps in preparations for privatization on their official websites, the press release also said.
As reported, on October 1, 2025, the government adopted a resolution on preparations for the sale of the state-owned stakes in Sense Bank and Ukrgasbank. On October 29, it approved the procedure for engaging an adviser, and on March 31, 2026, it announced a competition to select one. The adviser's compensation will consist of a fixed fee and a success fee of up to 3% of the actual proceeds received by the state budget from the sale of the share packages. The government also established a commission to oversee the sale of state-owned stakes in the banks.
N.M. Rothschild & Sons Limited is a Rothschild & Co group company registered in England and Wales, with its head office in London. It specializes in financial advisory services, corporate finance and mergers and acquisitions (M&A) transactions.
Rothschild & Co previously advised Ukraine on sovereign debt restructuring. Ukrzaliznytsia also hired the group this year to restructure its Eurobonds.
Ukraine has repeatedly undertaken commitments under programs with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to engage an adviser for the privatization of Sense Bank and Ukrgasbank. The first such engagement was planned by the end of September 2024, while the most recent commitment, under the new program, set a deadline of the end of July this year.
According to National Bank of Ukraine data, as of July 1, 2026, Ukrgasbank, with total assets of UAH 228.74 billion, ranked seventh, while Sense Bank, with UAH 157.73 billion in assets, ranked ninth among Ukraine's 59 banks.

The Guardian view on Europe’s protests: the social contract has broken – and young people want solutions | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
17:07:23 UTC
02:07:23 KST

France sneezed, and Europe has again caught the cold. The wave of unrest which began with teenagers at a high school soon drew in hundreds of thousands of people nationwide and then spread across the continent. Protests have filled the streets in Lisbon and Madrid, and have ignited into violence in Milan, Brussels and Tirana as well as in French cities.
French authorities say they are deploying 70,000 officers on Saturday and are allowing only marches organised by unions. They blame hard-left militants as well as opportunistic young perpetrators for last weekend’s destruction and looting, when a minority hijacked largely peaceful protests. But with fuel prices set to rise further over the winter, the demands and participants broadening, and President Macron utterly failing to meet the moment, there is no sign of an end to the wider discontent and no speedy resolution in sight.
Europe is experiencing distinct movements, with distinct causes, demands and actors, which should not be elided. In France, crumbling and overcrowded schools were the touchpaper, with Greek protesters echoing their complaints about educational underfunding this week. In Spain and Portugal, housing is the central issue. German students are angered by the possible reintroduction of compulsory military service. But those involved see the commonalities, with some Italian demonstrators chanting in French.
Underlying all these is the breakdown of the social contract. A generation expect, with reason, to be worse off than their parents. They are understandably angry at inadequate education and job precarity, are struggling to rent places of their own well into their 20s, and are paying for pensions which they don’t believe that they will ever receive themselves, while the climate crisis haunts their futures. They see that governments worried about debt and fearful of the bond markets either cannot or will not offer them solutions. It might be more remarkable if they were happy with their lot, or confident that casting a vote at their next opportunity would fix it.
Meanwhile, increasing inequality means that they watch others grow wealthy, sometimes profiting directly from their misfortune, with flats and houses treated as financial instruments rather than homes.
This unrest also echoes the wave of gen Z protests seen around the world last year – with some of those on the streets in France, Italy and Germany even borrowing emblems used earlier from Morocco to Madagascar. The affordability crisis, heavy-handed security forces and the sense that ordinary people are being left behind while governments have no convincing answers for them were at work in those cases too.
In Europe, far-right parties, egged on by the Trump administration, are seeking to capitalise on the unrest through lies that immigrants and open borders are to blame, and that a strong hand is needed to restore order. Within the next year, four of the biggest states – Spain, France, Poland and Italy – will hold elections, threatening a radical rightwards shift that could fundamentally change the EU. Yet these parties do not have real answers to the questions raised by protesters, and a financial crisis in France might yet highlight Marine Le Pen’s economic weak spot and National Rally’s internal divisions. The future course of the continent is being shaped, for better or worse, on the streets as well as at the ballot box.
