BBC profiles Russian exile who says his surveillance network tracked General Staff officer Fanil Sarvarov before his assassination in Moscow
In December 2025, Lieutenant General Fanil Sarvarov, head of the Russian Armed Forces General Staff’s Operational Training Directorate, was killed in a car bombing in Moscow. A Russian man who left the country in 2022 and now coordinates a network of volunteers tracking Russian military personnel says he helped prepare the killing. His role is detailed in the BBC documentary ”Traitors, Patriots, Spies: Shadowmen Helping Ukraine Inside Russia.”
The film introduces the man as Foma. His face is hidden — viewers see only his silhouette and hear his voice. The filmmakers say that in early 2022, Foma warned Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, the HUR, about Russia’s planned invasion. He then fled Russia, and the Ukrainians helped him settle in Warsaw. He now lives in Poland.
Foma says he coordinates a network of about 30 people operating in Russia, Ukraine, and several European countries. He says he also maintains ties with sources in Russia’s intelligence services. According to the film, years of working among Russia’s elite gave him a unique network of contacts and a steady flow of inside information.
Foma says his network gathers intelligence on where storage depots and headquarters are located, where units are stationed, where generals live, where officers working at those headquarters live, where strategic bomber pilots who attack Ukraine live, and who gives the orders.
The HUR confirmed that it had worked with Foma, the investigative outlet iStories reported.
One scene shows Foma training volunteers to conduct surveillance in Moscow. He tells them not to bring a phone. He also warns that if they are caught, they face terrorism charges and 25 years in prison.
In the film, Foma says he wants Russian soldiers and officers who order the shooting of prisoners and the rape and murder of civilians to think long and hard before giving such orders, to be scared, and to stop. Those who turn into animals and those who kill people, he says, need to be punished.
The next segment covers the December 2024 killing of General Igor Kirillov, head of Russia’s Radiation, Chemical, and Biological Protection Troops. Foma told the BBC that he was not involved in that killing but confirmed that his network passes information about Russian military personnel to Ukraine. He insists the people his volunteers follow are war criminals.
Sarvarov was killed a year after Kirillov. When the BBC filmmaker asked Foma about Sarvarov’s killing, he said: “Keeping track of him took quite an effort. He lived alternately with his mistress and his colleague. Covered his tracks and constantly changed his schedule.” Foma stresses, however, that his group does not take part in the killings themselves.
A man using the same pseudonym has appeared as a military expert on The Breakfast Show’s morning broadcasts since mid-September. Robinson had posted a video in which he told Daily Mail journalists he would find them after they wrote about his alleged role influencing England’s 2024 riots. He told them he had obtained details of where they and their families lived and warned them to abide by “men’s rules”.
Ben Holt, prosecuting, told the jury: “Let’s get real, shall we, and not live in a vigilante world where ‘men’s rules’ apply? Whatever they are. Let’s ground ourselves in a country where there is law and order.”
Summing up the case, Holt said Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, had accepted that sharing images of journalists’ homes and partial photos of their loved ones was intended to exert pressure.
However, he rejected Robinson’s insistence that the journalists on the receiving end of what the prosecution described as “bullyboy and intimidatory” conduct would not have been in fear of violence as a result.
Robinson, 43, is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence in 2024 to two journalists who were working for the Mail, Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber. He denies the charges.
Robinson said in evidence that he had been in “a panic” after the Mail had in effect identified a hotel in Cyprus where he had gone with family and friends and published a photo of his ex-wife, which he said put her at risk.
But Holt said Robinson had never asked for the image to be taken down in calls and messages to the journalists and the Daily Mail’s editor. “Instead, he just threatened people. He acted like a bully,” he said.
Holt repeated the words Robinson had directed at the journalists: “Good for the goose, good for the gander. You are coming for me, I am coming for you.” Holt described this as “straightforward retaliation”.
Such was the concern of the journalists that the police had to be called on a number of occasions, said Holt, who pointed to “unpleasant” comments made by Robinson’s supporters online after some of his posts. Robinson had close to 1 million followers on X at one point, and some of his supporters are “unpredictable”, Holt said.
Alisdair Williamson KC, for the defence, said Robinson’s actions were justified because the “fear for him is real”.
“When you judge whether what he did was reasonable, you might think that he showed some restraint,” he told the jury. “I know what language I might use if people put my family in that position. The fear for him is real.”
Williamson said the journalists did not care about Robinson’s concerns about the article, nor the stress it caused him, adding: “They don’t care to pick up the phone.”
A series of agreed facts that were read out to the court before the closing speeches included a reference to four threat-to-life warning notices that police had given to Robinson in 2018, 2019 and 2024, shortly after the Daily Mail article.
The court also heard that a video had been posted online in August 2024 by a man named Omar Abdirizak in which he said: “Tommy Robinson I got a message for you … we got pirates in every corner. Muslims in every corner,” before making a rifle gesture.
The trial continues.

Fewer people are flying as airfare soars. Here's why airlines aren't worried
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:51:21 UTC
01:51:21 KST

Fewer people are flying this year, but with airfare this high and climbing, airline executives say that's just fine.
The number of people screened at U.S. checkpoints is on track for its first annual decline since 2020. Major U.S. carriers have said capturing higher fares is more important than fully filling their planes or flying record numbers of travelers.
"We're actively prioritizing yield versus load factor and really happy as we see it. It fits right in with the premium investments that we're making," American Airlines Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper said on the company's earnings call Thursday.
American's load factor, a gauge of how full planes are flying, fell to 83.4% in the third quarter from 86% in the same quarter of 2025.
Fares keep climbing
The price of plane tickets has skyrocketed as airlines grapple with a spike in jet fuel prices, their biggest expense after labor, and pass more of those costs on to customers.
Fares in September were up more than 22% from a year earlier, according to the latest inflation read. Fare tracker Hopper said it expects this holiday season to come with the most expensive ticket prices in years.
The average Southwest Airlines fare in the third quarter, for example, was $231.69, up close to $50 from a year earlier. That doesn't include Southwest's new fees, like its extra charges for checked bags or a seat closer to the front of the plane.
The airline's count of revenue passengers, however, fell 3.2% from a year ago, to about 33.5 million people.
Still, both fares and the passenger counts exceeded Southwest's expectations.
"Passenger fares came in about $3 above what our forecast was and the more important thing is that passenger volumes also exceeded our expectations," Southwest CEO Bob Jordan said on an earnings call Thursday.
Since April — when airlines began warning in earnest about profits taking a hit from the spike in jet fuel — through Thursday, about 9.3 million fewer people were screened at airport checkpoints compared with the same period of 2025, according to the Transportation Security Administration. While that's down less than 2% from last year, it follows years of growth.
With jet fuel prices more than double year-ago levels — as seen in U.S. Gulf Coast spot prices going for $4.63 a gallon, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration — airlines have been focused on recovering as much of the fuel spike as possible.
Even despite some drops, airline executives said during their earnings calls that travel demand overall is robust, especially for profitable premium cabins like business class.
And not every carrier is seeing a decline. United Airlines flew 2.4% more passengers in the third quarter than it did a year ago, and said its unit revenue rose by 16%, the biggest increase since the pandemic.
"I've been pleasantly surprised at the industry's ability this year to raise yields and pass through much of the increase in fuel prices," CEO Scott Kirby said on the company's earnings call Wednesday. "So it's possible that airlines will continue to focus on yields at the expense of load factor and that alone could get us to double-digit margins next year."
Profit hit
Most airlines are anticipating that fuel costs will continue to bite, but executives say they're confident in their pricing power.
United, for example, said it expects to pay an average of $4.80 a gallon for fuel in the fourth quarter, up from an average price of $3.90 a gallon in the third.
American, United, Delta Air Lines and Southwest all cut their profit forecasts for 2026 this month when they reported earnings. American is the only one of the four that expects to post a loss this year.
American and others have also reduced growth plans or warned the industry could dial back on its goals for expanding capacity, which could keep fares elevated. Reduced capacity can make bookable seats scarcer, driving up prices even more if demand holds.
The carriers said demand has been particularly strong for premium seats, which command hundreds, if not thousands of dollars, more than coach tickets.
Smaller airlines set to report results in the coming weeks, including Frontier Airlines and Allegiant Air, have traditionally focused on more price-sensitive customers, which could show if those travelers are pulling back at all.
One factor that could also affect air travel is the demise of Spirit Airlines, which went out of business in early May.
"Some of its customers have likely stopped flying," Bank of America said in a research note Thursday.

The operation will be extremely complicated: Lubinets explained how people will be evacuated from Oleshky

The operation will be extremely complicated: Lubinets explained how people will be evacuated from Oleshky
Kyiv • UNN
The parties agreed on a ceasefire, humanitarian aid, and the safe passage of civilians out of Oleshky. The operation will be complex and carried out in stages.
Ukraine and Russia have agreed on a "silence regime" in Oleshky, which will mark the beginning of an operation to rescue Ukrainians trapped in the occupied city. On October 23, Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets spoke about the details, UNN reports.
The operation involves delivering humanitarian aid and ensuring the free movement of civilians and, according to Lubinets, it will not be easy.
Melania Trump joined the talks on rescuing people in Oleshky
As reported by the Ukrainian ombudsman, U.S. First Lady Melania Trump issued a statement on the launch of a humanitarian mission aimed at rescuing people who remain in Oleshky. He confirmed the relevant agreements and expressed gratitude to the American side for taking part in the negotiation process.
"First, I confirm this statement and personally thank Melania Trump and her team for their efforts, leadership, and coordination between the two negotiating groups of Ukraine and the russian federation in reaching agreements," Lubinets said.
He clarified that he personally represented the Ukrainian side during the negotiations. Meanwhile, Yana Lantratova conducted the talks on behalf of the Russian side. According to the ombudsman, the parties managed to reach agreements on organizing a humanitarian mission to assist the civilian population in Oleshky.
Silence regime, humanitarian aid, and civilian movement: what the parties agreed on
Lubinets said that the agreements reached provide for three main areas of the humanitarian mission. First and foremost, the parties agreed to ensure a silence regime necessary for carrying out humanitarian measures.
In addition, humanitarian cargo is planned to be delivered to Oleshky for the civilian population. The third point of the agreements was to ensure the possibility of free movement for people from the settlement.
"Under our agreement, first, a silence regime will be ensured. Second, humanitarian cargo will be delivered to Oleshky. Third, the free movement of the civilian population from Oleshky will be ensured," the ombudsman said.
Lubinets did not specify the exact timelines for implementing each point of the agreements, the volume of humanitarian aid, or the number of people who would be able to make use of the opportunity to leave.
The humanitarian operation will be difficult and will proceed gradually
The Verkhovna Rada Commissioner for Human Rights separately drew attention to the complexity of the upcoming operation. According to him, its implementation will require a phased approach. He also called on the public to treat the dissemination of information about the progress of the humanitarian mission responsibly.
"I ask everyone to be understanding regarding the dissemination of public information about this humanitarian mission. The whole world now knows about Oleshky. The operation will take place gradually; it is extremely difficult to implement," Lubinets emphasized.
He added that, despite the agreements reached, carrying out the humanitarian mission would require further coordination between the parties. The ombudsman has not yet disclosed details regarding specific routes for civilian movement or the organization of aid deliveries.
Lubinets promised to inform Ukrainians about the results of the operation
The Verkhovna Rada Commissioner for Human Rights emphasized that the Ukrainian side continues to make efforts to rescue citizens who remain in Oleshky. According to him, the public will receive information about the progress of the humanitarian mission and its results.
"I will inform Ukrainian society and show the results of this operation. As of today, the Ukrainian side has done and is doing everything to rescue the citizens who are in Oleshky," Lubinets concluded.
Reminder
Earlier, David Arakhamia, head of the parliamentary faction of the political party "Servant of the People" in the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine, reported that an operation to unblock the settlement of Oleshky would begin in the near future.

GRU-linked hackers wiped data at Ukrainian grain company after two-month intrusion, ESET reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:44:07 UTC
01:44:07 KST

Russian hackers destroyed data belonging to a Ukrainian grain logistics company after remaining undetected in its computer systems for two months. To control infected devices, the attackers used previously unknown malware that communicated with a server through the decentralized Yggdrasil network.
Cybersecurity researchers at ESET found that two hacking groups linked to Russian interests were behind the attack. They included Sandworm, which Western intelligence agencies have identified as a unit of Russia’s GRU military intelligence service.
The breach began on July 16, 2025. According to ESET, initial access was obtained by the group UAC-0099, which sent an employee a phishing email containing a malicious attachment.
After the file was opened, a loader called MATCHBOIL and a remote-access tool called MATCHWOK were installed on the computer. The next day, July 17, the hackers deployed another program that had not previously been known to cybersecurity researchers.
The researchers named the new malware “MythicRatatoskr.” It allowed the attackers to execute commands on infected computers, browse files, take screenshots, transfer documents, and redirect network connections.
Unlike conventional malware that communicates with servers using publicly accessible internet addresses, MythicRatatoskr connected to its command-and-control server inside Yggdrasil, an experimental decentralized network in which devices exchange encrypted data without a central coordinating authority.
The setup makes it more difficult to identify a command-and-control server and disrupt the attackers’ infrastructure. ESET said this was the first case it had documented of a state-linked hacking group using Yggdrasil in this way.
Yggdrasil itself, however, is not designed to provide anonymity, as its developers note. Even so, researchers had difficulty determining the server’s physical location.
On Sept. 17, 2025, two months after the initial intrusion, the hackers destroyed data on the company’s systems using the SDelete utility, launched through a mechanism that allows commands to be executed centrally across computers on a corporate network. ESET attributed this part of the operation to Sandworm with high confidence.
Researchers also said with high confidence that UAC-0099 had handed the compromised access over to Sandworm. They were unable, however, to determine which of the two groups operated MythicRatatoskr. The name of the affected company and the extent of the damage have not been disclosed.
ESET had already reported attacks by Sandworm against Ukraine’s grain sector in November 2025. At the time, the company said the group had deployed data-wiping malware against Ukrainian government organizations, energy and logistics companies, and businesses in the grain industry. Researchers said those operations appeared to be intended to weaken the Ukrainian economy.
Sandworm has been linked to Military Unit 74455 of Russia’s Main Intelligence Directorate, better known as the GRU. In 2020, the U.S. Justice Department charged six officers from the unit over a range of cyber operations, including the development of the NotPetya malware, attacks on Ukraine’s power grid, and attacks targeting computer systems used by the 2018 Winter Olympics.
The Insider subsequently identified additional information about members of the hacking group and confirmed that several of those charged were connected to Military Unit 74455.
In May 2026, in an investigation into the training of GRU hackers at Bauman Moscow State Technical University, The Insider identified two more graduates of the university’s military training center who had served in Military Unit 74455: Alexei Kondrashov and Ilya Boikov.

PRESS RELEASE 159
Albares strengthens bilateral relations between Spain and Switzerland with counterpart
- The ministers have signed an agreement on political consultations that consolidates the dialogue between the two countries
The Minister for Foreign Affairs, European Union and Cooperation, José Manuel Albares, met on Friday with his Swiss counterpart, Federal Councillor for Foreign Affairs Ignazio Cassis, with whom he discussed the good bilateral relations between Spain and Switzerland, as well as the main issues on the EU and international agenda. During the meeting, the ministers also signed an agreement to establish a mechanism for regular consultations that will consolidate and expand bilateral political dialogue between the two countries.
Spain and Switzerland enjoy good bilateral relations across all areas. There is a large community of Spanish residents in Switzerland – more than 149,000 – and, in terms of trade and investment, the situation is positive, with tourism being the main item in the balance of services: 2.25 million Swiss citizens visited our country last year.
The potential for bilateral scientific cooperation is particularly noteworthy, with a large number of Spanish researchers and scientists in Switzerland working in sectors such as health, artificial intelligence and quantum technologies.
Politically speaking, the relationship is also strong, and the agreement signed this Friday is proof of this. The aim is to hold annual consultations – and whenever deemed necessary – on thematic and geographical areas of mutual interest.
EU agenda
The ministers also discussed relations between Switzerland and the European Union, and Switzerland’s prospects for closer ties with EU institutions through the so-called ‘Bilaterals III’ package, which is currently under consideration.
This package of agreements governs, amongst other matters, the conditions for Switzerland’s access to the EU’s internal market, as well as the alignment of its legislation with EU regulations and case law. Switzerland’s contribution to European peace and security in the current international geopolitical context was also discussed.
International agenda
Finally, on the international agenda, the ministers discussed security, the Russian aggression against Ukraine, the war in the Middle East and the defence of multilateralism. Switzerland hosts several international organisations and is the depositary and guarantor of the Geneva Conventions on international humanitarian law.
On this last point, both countries reaffirmed their support for the work of the International Criminal Court.

That is why we are making difficult but necessary decisions," Koretsky said on his Telegram channel.
According to him, the first change involves separating a company's criticality from its economic performance.
"Sectors that actually contribute to defense and the economy – such as the defense industry, energy, communications, logistics, housing and communal services, and others – should be designated as critical. Nothing will change for them. At the same time, sectoral and regional criteria for criticality will be updated and monitored for abuse," he said.
The second change is that the maximum level of reservation – particularly for the energy sector and the defense industry – will no longer be 100%.
"Unconditional full exemption is unfair to those who serve and opens the door to abuse. There were companies created specifically to take advantage of the exemption, and it became a business," the prime minister said.
At the same time, Koretsky said the government will not relax the requirements for those who manufacture weapons or maintain critical infrastructure. Specifically, if a company needs to reserve more personnel to ensure uninterrupted operations, it will be able to submit a substantiated request to the Coordination Center.
The third change is that the Ministry of Defense is increasing penalties for evading military service.
"Fourth, we are developing a mechanism for 100% exemption from military service, provided that mobilization obligations are fulfilled. A company will be able to fully reserve its employees if it regularly and voluntarily enlists some of them for military service. It is essential that the individual knows where they are going and for how long. Their job and salary will be preserved," Koretsky said.
He said the Ministry of Defense and the Ministry of Economy will work out the details together with the business community.
"The government's goal is to approve a transparent and effective mechanism by December 1. This will give confidence to those on the front lines: rotation is possible, and others will take their place. And for those who are going to serve, it means they are going for a clearly defined period," the prime minister said.
He said the ultimate goal is to ensure that no one is left searching for anyone on the streets.
"These decisions do not mean that mobilization will be intensified tomorrow. They are needed first and foremost to bring order to the conscription process and root out abuses. At the same time, as a state and a society, we must be prepared for any turn of events, including an intensification of mobilization in Russia. We are waging a war for the survival of the state and our people. These decisions are not easy, but they must be made," the prime minister said.

Netanyahu vows collective punishment after Hebron shooting

2026-10-23

Breadcrumb
Netanyahu vows collective punishment against Palestinian neighbourhood after Hebron shooting
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has vowed to carry out collective punishment against a Palestinian neighbourhood in the city of Hebron after an attack on an Israeli army checkpoint in the occupied West Bank killed two soldiers.
Speaking during a visit to the city with Defence Minister Israel Katz, Netanyahu said: "First of all, we will act to destroy this place, to change it completely."
"But we are going to do something that has not been done until now: We will implement the successful and aggressive model we used in the refugee camps, which are essentially terrorist strongholds," he added, according to the Times of Israel.
Netanyahu's comments refer to Israel's policy of forcibly expelling thousands of Palestinians from several northern West Bank refugee camps, including Jenin, Tulkarm and Nur Shams, that occurred in early 2025, with around 33,000 being expelled.
Laying out the plan for the neighbourhood, Netanyahu said: "We will evacuate the residents, we will go house to house, we will remove the weapons there as well, and all the terrorist infrastructure will be dealt with and destroyed."
He added that the Israeli military would carry out a major operation in the occupied West Bank, the largest since it first occupied the area following the 1967 war when it first took control of the area.
The announcement comes in response to the killing of two Israeli soldiers and wounding three others at an Israeli army checkpoint in the occupied West Bank, with two Palestinian gunmen also killed in the incident.
Israel Katz confirmed Netanyahu's comments, saying "the Jenin refugee camp model arrives in Hebron."
The attack comes days before Israel's Knesset elections that could see the formation of a new government, with polling suggesting that both the pro-Netanyahu and opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot are both under the threshold to form a majority government, with many politicians putting out statements on the incident.
Zizette Darkazally, an Associate Fellow at Chatham House's Middle East and North Africa Programme, told The New Arab that the reactions from Israel's politicians confirm the preexisting positions that they already held.
This includes Bezalel Smotrich, the far-right finance minister who also oversees Israel's military occupation in the West Bank, who announced he had already ordered the destruction of several buildings near the site of the shooting, and approved new farms in the area of Masafer Yatta, where Palestinian residents have long fought against Israeli attempts to destroy Palestinian homes.
Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir also weighed in, again calling for the government to dismantle the Palestinian Authority that governs parts of the West Bank, while opposition politicians Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, and Yair Golan praised the Israeli military's response.
Darkazally said that Netanyahu's announced policies were an attempt to exploit the attack to gain more votes and further his self-proclaimed image as 'Mr Security', but that it's unlikely to change the base of voters between the two blocs.
"I don't think the attack will change votes of the base in any of the two blocs," she said, adding, "most of the 'undecided' at this stage are undecided within the same camp, meaning that they are undecided between parties in the same bloc", Darkazally said.
‘Restrictions on top of restrictions’
Restrictions announced by Netanyahu have immediately come into effect, according to Amir Daoud, Director of Publishing and Documentation at the Colonisation and Wall Resistance Commission, who told The New Arab that the city has been cordoned off, with preparations for wider closures occurring across the West Bank.
Hebron is the largest city in the occupied West Bank, with 250,000 Palestinians calling it home.
Daoud noted that these restrictions come on top of the plethora of restrictions, checkpoints, and barriers that are already in place across the area that impede freedom of movement for its three million Palestinian residents.
"According to the latest figures documented by the Colonisation and Wall Resistance Commission, there were 942 movement obstacles across the West Bank as of September 2026," he said, adding that "these restrictions have transformed Palestinian movement between cities, villages and communities into a process controlled by Israeli military decisions."
Israel's ever-tightening policies in the occupied West Bank have occurred in conjunction with its expansion of settlements and parallel infrastructure allowing them freedom of movement across the territory.
The policy, which rights groups have labelled apartheid, comes alongside an uptick in settler terror attacks against Palestinians that have escalated dramatically since the start of Israel's genocide in Gaza.
Daoud said that the restrictions mean Palestinians will be unable to reach their jobs or get medical treatment, with farmers losing access to land and markets to sell produce. This is set to impact the olive harvest season, already disrupted by widespread settler violence.
Medical Aid for Palestinians warned on Friday that, following announced restrictions and an Israeli military escalation in the occupied West Bank, its staff are reporting increased obstacles to reaching Palestinians in need of care.
The aid group noted that settler attacks in the village of Umm Safa, north of Ramallah, illustrate the risks posed to Palestinians amid the heightened security.
Aseel Baidoun, the group's Deputy Director of Advocacy and Communications in the West Bank, warned that both settler attacks and ministerial threats of collective punishment and forcible displacement meant "the risk of atrocity crimes is acute."
There is also a risk of these measures becoming permanent, adding to the layers of restrictions that already impact life in the occupied West Bank.
"Our concern is that measures initially introduced as temporary security responses frequently become prolonged restrictions or are incorporated into the existing system of military control," Daoud told The New Arab.
“From our perspective, the fundamental issue is the cumulative effect of these measures,” he said, adding, “what we are witnessing is not merely a temporary interruption of movement, but the continued consolidation of a system in which freedom of movement is increasingly treated as an exception rather than a basic right.”

Peace or escalation? The Ukraine conflict enters a critical phase
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:41:59 UTC
01:41:59 KST

Peace or escalation? The Ukraine conflict enters a critical phase
The latest surge in diplomatic activity surrounding the conflict in Ukraine follows a familiar pattern, although each round brings its own peculiarities. This time, US President Donald Trump is particularly angry with Vladimir Zelensky, whom he increasingly blames for the failure to end the war.
Their personal animosity has been evident since their first meeting of Trump’s second term in office, more than 18 months ago. But there’s now an additional factor, and it’s American domestic politics.
With the Republicans facing a difficult election, Trump needs a political success. There is little time for major achievements, but powerful images can still make an impression and stabilizing the fuel market through diplomacy with Moscow offers precisely that opportunity.
Peacemaking in a bloody conflict is an achievement in itself, but voters are generally more concerned about their own finances and Trump understands this, so he appears to have returned to the conviction he held from the outset that Zelensky is more susceptible to pressure than Moscow.
Russia has established the limits of its flexibility and shown little inclination to retreat from them; Washington, meanwhile, failed last year to bring Ukraine and its European backers into line. Indeed, they even briefly managed to persuade Trump that Kiev could fundamentally reverse the military situation, but now the pendulum has swung back.
Zelensky’s repeated refusal to heed Trump’s appeals to stop attacking Russian energy infrastructure has particularly infuriated the American president, and this isn’t simply because Trump dislikes being defied.
He remembers how the Ukrainian leadership sought to assist the Democrats during the 2020 presidential campaign and he appears to be interpreting Kiev’s current behavior in much the same light: as an attempt to help his domestic opponents. Trump rarely forgives such conduct, hence the increasingly harsh rhetoric.
Knowing the president, one might expect this attitude to endure, but it would be a mistake to assume that his hostility towards Zelensky guarantees a successful peace settlement.
A policy favorable to Moscow commands little support within the American establishment, regardless of party affiliation, so opponents will exploit every opportunity to obstruct it.
Western Europe, meanwhile, is determined not to be excluded from negotiations and its governments have continued to resist a settlement they believe would serve Russian interests.
Trump can be pushed in one direction or another, but fundamentally changing his outlook is another matter, because for all his apparent unpredictability, he’s remarkably consistent in his underlying worldview and once he forms an opinion, he rarely abandons it.
These, however, are questions of personality and political psychology, so what of the settlement itself?
The negotiations remain opaque, as genuine diplomacy generally does and their direction can only be inferred from indirect signals.
It’s reasonable to assume that discussions continue within the framework established at Anchorage last summer, given that Russian officials repeatedly refer to certain understandings reached there, whose implementation has stalled because Washington has been unable to persuade its partners to accept them.
Western commentary tends to identify territory as the principal obstacle and there’s some justification for this, as the course of military operations has progressively elevated territorial questions beyond the importance they held at the beginning of the conflict.
Vladimir Putin has consistently warned that rejecting Russia’s proposed settlement terms would mean confronting less favourable conditions later, and that’s precisely what has happened, particularly regarding territory, yet territorial concessions are not the whole story.
The broader principles of European security, both military and political, remain central. They were, after all, the decisive considerations behind Moscow’s decision to use force in 2022.
Indeed, we might suggest that security, understood in its widest sense, has become, or is about to become, the central issue in negotiations, and this is inseparable from the territorial question.
The less confidence there is in durable agreements on mutual guarantees and military restrictions, the greater the incentive to expand buffer zones and diminish an adversary’s capabilities over the longer term, so territory, in other words, becomes a substitute for security arrangements that neither side believes it can trust.
Following the meetings in Oslo and St. Petersburg, American representatives have spoken of substantial progress, while Europeans describe a convergence of positions and the emergence of new ideas.
Moscow acknowledges that fresh proposals have appeared, but makes clear that they remain insufficient.
For now, diplomacy continues along its familiar trajectory, with another expert-level trilateral meeting expected in November to address technical questions, following two previous rounds.
Yet the combination of developments suggests that the military phase of the conflict may be approaching a significant turning point, even if its conclusion remains some distance away.
Yuri Ushakov has expressed hope that the end is approaching and that may be optimistic, but the alternatives are becoming clearer: either serious peace negotiations encompassing the full range of disputed issues, or a transition to a new level of escalation.
The first option requires credible security guarantees and technical arrangements alone will not suffice, so what’s needed is a stable political framework capable of surviving changes in circumstances and leadership.
This is also the context in which the possibility of a trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, China and the United States is being discussed.
The proposed gathering at next month’s APEC summit in Shenzhen has generated considerable speculation, but whether it will happen remains uncertain. Even if it does, there will be no new Yalta and no sweeping grand bargain because the international environment simply does not permit such an outcome.
Nevertheless, a meeting between Vladimir Putin, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump would carry considerable significance.
Within an increasingly complicated international landscape, it would demonstrate the level at which the world’s most consequential decisions are being made, a level commensurate with the scale of the challenges. Perhaps that, in itself, would yield a new perspective.

All Four Moscow Airports Halt Flights Amid Reports of Drones Approaching the Capital
All four of Moscow’s major airports suspended arrivals and departures on October 23 amid reports of a large-scale drone attack, while an evacuation was reported at a government office complex in Moscow City.
Russia's Federal Air Transport Agency, Rosaviatsia, announced the restrictions on its official Telegram channel, identifying Sheremetyevo, Vnukovo, Domodedovo, and Zhukovsky airports.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"The restrictions are necessary to ensure flight safety," the agency stated, without specifying how long the measures would remain in force. The restrictions took effect at 2:05 p.m. Moscow time.
All four airports remained closed to incoming and outgoing flights as of 3:55 p.m., according to the Russian flight-monitoring services. At Sheremetyevo Airport, authorities declared an air raid alert and began evacuating passengers to designated shelters amid the drone threat.
At the same time, Russian Telegram channels reported that fragments of a drone fell on the grounds of Sheremetyevo Airport during the attack.
The airport shutdown coincided with Russian reports of drones approaching Moscow. Mayor Sergei Sobyanin claimed that Russian air defenses had intercepted several drones heading toward the capital, while residents reported hearing explosions in parts of the Moscow metropolitan area.
The disruption also extended beyond Moscow. Kaluga's Grabtsevo Airport, southwest of the Russian capital, suspended flight operations at 12:56 p.m., with restrictions still in place at the latest reported update.
Drone threats have repeatedly disrupted civilian aviation in and around Moscow. On October 22, Russian authorities also suspended operations at all four major airports during another reported drone attack, forcing airlines to adjust schedules and cancel flights.
Meanwhile, Russian outlets reported an evacuation from the IQ-Kvartal tower in the Moscow City business district, citing eyewitnesses. The building houses offices of Russia’s Ministry of Digital Development, Ministry of Economic Development, and Ministry of Industry and Trade.
The disruptions extend a pattern of drone-driven airport shutdowns around the Russian capital, with a similar closure a week earlier during overnight attacks on October 16 that targeted Moscow, the Moscow region, and the Vladimir and Rostov regions.
All four Moscow airports suspended operations at the time, and more than 20 aircraft were diverted to alternative airports. Moscow officials claimed 94 drones heading toward the capital were intercepted overnight, while falling debris in the Rostov region sparked a fire at production and warehouse facilities and injured a man in the Aksay district.
Those strikes came after Russia launched more than 850 Shahed-type drones against Ukraine between the start of October 14 and 9 a.m. on October 15.

Brazil’s right has already changed the balance of power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:41:09 UTC
01:41:09 KST

Brazil’s right has already changed the balance of power
Bolsonaro’s party has strengthened its position in Congress, posing a formidable challenge to another Lula presidency.
In a televised presidential debate in Sao Paulo on October 18, Flavio Bolsonaro brought a number from Brazil’s prisons into an argument over crime. “Seventy-three percent”. The 45-year-old senator claimed that was the share of prisoners who had voted for his opponent, President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, 80. The figure came from polling stations inside detention facilities, where staff and eligible detainees awaiting trial could cast ballots. Convicted prisoners serving final sentences could not vote. Lula paused. “I want 100 percent,” he replied. “Even your father.”
Jair Bolsonaro, the absent father, had spent 28 years in Congress, where he repeatedly praised the 1964 military coup that ushered in more than two decades of dictatorship. He went on to become president, lost re-election to Lula in 2022 and was later convicted of plotting to overturn the result. He is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest. A week after Lula’s inauguration, thousands of Bolsonaro supporters invaded and vandalised the presidential palace, Congress and Supreme Court in Brasilia, claiming without evidence that the election had been stolen.
Back in the studio, Flavio was promising to “redemocratise” Brazil. He demanded respect for the 56 million Brazilians who had voted for him and said he would send Lula into retirement.
On October 4, Brazil held the first round of its presidential election, alongside elections for the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate. Flavio received 56.1 million votes, or 47.03 percent of valid ballots, against Lula’s 53.9 million and 45.16 percent. Since then, Bolsonaro’s lead in the polls has narrowed, with several surveys placing the candidates within the margin of error. The latest readings suggest Lula is gaining ground, although just days before the October 25 run-off, it remains uncertain whether the president can overcome Flavio’s first-round lead.
The October 18 debate had begun with a discussion of armed groups spreading through Brazilian neighbourhoods. Nearly 69 million Brazilians say they perceive the presence of criminal gangs or militias in their neighbourhoods, even as the country’s murder rate falls. Flavio called for treating those organisations as narcoterrorists and for Brazil to join United States President Donald Trump’s Shield of the Americas alongside Javier Milei’s Argentina. He promised 500,000 additional prison places, easier civilian access to firearms and a reduction in the age of criminal responsibility from 18 to 16, and to 14 for certain serious crimes.
For residents of poorer neighbourhoods, Flavio proposed a Ministry of Prosperity, promising vocational training and credit to help families receiving government assistance to start businesses of their own. The word “prosperity” had a history of its own in Brazil’s influential evangelical churches, where sermons sometimes link material advancement to faith and individual endeavour.
Taken together, the promises linked the prospect of safer streets to a particular idea of prosperity, in which government assistance would become a starting point for vocational training, credit and small businesses.
Lula spoke of the social gains of his governments and of restoring democratic institutions after the Bolsonaro years. A former union leader who helped found the centre-left Workers’ Party (PT), he proposed stronger federal coordination of public security. The tougher approach to crime was not confined to Flavio’s campaign. Lula, too, supported lowering the age of criminal responsibility to 16 for certain serious offences.
Two days before the debate, Lula had stood among congressional leaders to celebrate a reform that would gradually bring Brazil’s six-day working week to an end, reducing hours from 44 to 40 without cutting wages. After initially criticising the reform as opportunistic, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro changed his position and voted for it, saying he had listened to workers on the campaign trail.
Lula had other economic gains to highlight. Unemployment in Brazil has fallen from 7.8 percent in 2023 to 5.3 percent this year, while real wages have risen. For many households, however, expensive credit and debt repayments have dampened the impact of any improvements. Flavio has sought to capitalise on the resulting economic frustration, as well as concerns about public security.
If re-elected, Lula would have to address those frustrations while dealing with a Congress reshaped by the October 4 legislative elections. In the 513-seat lower house, Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party (PL) won 121 seats, up from 97. The PT-led bloc moved from 82 to 88, while the largest alliance of traditional centre-right parties lost 18 seats. The sharpest rearrangement had taken place within the right, leaving the parliamentary left’s numbers largely intact.
The right’s gains raise a question about the kind of change the Bolsonaro movement represents. In an October Datafolha survey, 48 percent of Lula’s supporters mentioned social protection, while 41 percent of Flavio’s supporters expressed a desire for change. Yet the PL’s new deputies were hardly political novices. Of the 121 elected, 111 had held office before and 93 had belonged to other parties.
In 2002, the same party had placed Jose Alencar, a conservative textile magnate, next to Lula on the presidential ticket that first brought the former union leader to power. Alencar remained vice president until 2010, though he left the PL in 2005 amid a corruption scandal involving its leadership. Jair Bolsonaro joined only in 2021. The party now housed his family’s ambitions alongside politicians whose careers had begun under very different banners.
In a country where presidents rarely command a parliamentary majority of their own party, politicians of such experience are seldom without work. Governments change, and parties move between coalitions to negotiate cabinet appointments and influence over the funds that reach their constituencies. Established centre-right parties have served administrations of widely differing orientations. Jair Bolsonaro eventually relied on them after campaigning against the political establishment. His movement’s gains had not made those alliances obsolete.
Lula has spent much of his political career constructing governments with former adversaries. His current vice president and running mate, Geraldo Alckmin, once challenged him for the presidency as the candidate of the centre-right opposition. A fourth term would demand more of that experience, with the right holding greater power in Congress. Lula’s successor, Dilma Rousseff, was impeached in 2016 amid a deep recession and the collapse of her governing coalition, circumstances quite different from those Lula faces today.
The new balance of power would be particularly consequential for the Supreme Court. Alexandre de Moraes had overseen the case that sent Jair Bolsonaro to prison. As the Bolsonaro family accused him of political persecution, Lula’s party defended his authority as part of its defence of democracy. But the court has become a major target of the right’s parliamentary ambitions.
Moraes’s name had travelled through the October 4 Senate elections, in which 54 of the chamber’s 81 seats were contested. Candidates allied with the Bolsonaros promised to impeach him and curb the court’s powers. Some wanted its jurisdiction narrowed, while others sought to limit the authority of individual justices to act alone. The collapse of Banco Master, a private bank that had a lucrative contract with the law firm of Moraes’s wife, raised questions about possible conflicts of interest. The firm has denied wrongdoing.
A fourth Lula term would face 28 Liberal Party senators in an 81-seat chamber empowered to approve Supreme Court appointments and remove justices through impeachment. A survey by Folha de S. Paulo identified at least 49 members of the next Senate who had expressed support for impeaching Supreme Court justices in some circumstances. That was five short of the two-thirds required for removal, even before agreement on a particular case. Support for restricting the court’s powers extended beyond the Bolsonaro movement.
Congress’s growing power could also constrain Lula’s ability to deliver the economic and social improvements on which he has based much of his political appeal. Control over public money had been moving towards Congress. In 2025, parliamentary allocations for local projects reached about 47 billion reais ($9.3bn) in committed funds, more than four times their level 11 years earlier. Legislators increasingly choose where that money goes. A president can secure their votes for a particular measure without recovering control over the funds they distribute.
On Wednesday, Lula sent Congress a proposal to make public transport free on weekends and public holidays, allowing some workers who would soon have two days off to travel without paying fares. He suggested using money politicians had set aside for projects in their constituencies. The Speaker of the lower house welcomed the idea. He wanted the money to come from somewhere else.

Ukraine Brings Home 270 People From Russian Captivity, Including 86 Convicted by Russian Courts
Ukraine has brought home 270 people from Russian captivity, including service members from multiple branches of the military and nine civilians, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced on October 23.
Those released include National Guard troops, including Azov fighters, border guards, territorial defense personnel, Navy service members, Ground Forces troops, Air Assault Forces personnel, and members of the State Special Transport Service.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets described the exchange as historic because it returned the largest number of Ukrainian service members who had been convicted by Russian courts. Lubinets stated that the exchange followed several months of negotiations by the working group of Ukraine’s Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, which includes the Ombudsman’s Office.
“We remember every single person and continue searching for everyone,” Zelenskyy wrote.
“I am grateful to our soldiers on the front lines who are replenishing the exchange fund for Ukraine so that we can bring our people home,” he continued.
The exchange comes as hundreds of Ukrainians remain in Russian captivity. In July, Dmytro Lubinets reported that 494 Ukrainian women, including civilians and service members, were still being held by Russia, while Moscow had largely stopped including women in prisoner exchanges.

EDITORIAL: Beware of politicians bearing gifts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:40:18 UTC
01:40:18 KST

The opposition-controlled Legislative Yuan on Wednesday last week passed the third reading of amendments to the Senior Citizens Welfare Act (老人福利法), which would require the central government to fully subsidize National Health Insurance (NHI) premiums for people aged 65 or older if their income falls below the tax filing threshold or is taxed at a rate of less than 20 percent.
Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) lawmakers opposed the measure, and Minister of Health and Welfare Shih Chung-liang (石崇良) warned that it would strain the NHI system’s finances and leave some disadvantaged people with less support. They also raised concerns that the amendment would remove the legal basis for other subsidies not covered by the NHI system, particularly for lower-to-
middle-income seniors who might not qualify for public assistance.
Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) legislators defended the amendment, saying it shifts responsibility for seniors’ premiums to the central government’s social welfare budget, keeping the expense separate from the NHI fund. They argued that the Public Assistance Act (社會救助法) and other provisions already authorize subsidies for medical copayments and expenses, and that moving the premium burden away from local governments would free up money for other assistance.
However, their response does not address the policy’s most glaring flaw — it uses age and a broad tax criterion as a substitute for financial need. The 20 percent tax rate kicks in at NT$1.33 million (US$40,913) in annual net taxable income, meaning about 83 percent of people aged 65 or older would be covered. Shih added that about 30 percent of seniors in the affected tax bracket are still working and insured through their jobs, showing how little the tax threshold has to do with whether someone actually needs help. Healthcare subsidies should be means-tested, not extended to the vast majority of seniors based on age and a broad tax threshold.
Taiwan’s demographic circumstances make the policy particularly difficult to justify. People aged 65 and older make up more than one-fifth of the population, and that proportion is growing. The National Development Council projects that seniors would account for 37 percent of the population in 2045 and 50.4 percent by 2065. Meanwhile, the working-age population is shrinking, and Taiwan’s birthrate remains stubbornly low.
The government might be able to absorb the additional NT$40 billion annual expense in the near term, but how sustainable would that be in five or 10 years as the number of eligible seniors rises and the pool of contributors falls? It already faces mounting pressure to sustain NHI financing and address a litany of issues across the healthcare system, from nursing shortages to overcrowded hospitals and emergency departments. Expanding eligibility so widely without a sustainable funding plan could compound these problems and ultimately undermine the financial foundations of the healthcare system itself.
The policy would also deepen inequities by shifting disproportionate costs onto younger people. Shih said that people aged 65 or older pay an average of NT$9,912 a year in premiums, but use an average of 90,149 NHI points in services — more than nine times what they pay in. Children aged six and younger are the second-highest group of users of healthcare. Of course, these figures reflect the legitimate medical needs of these groups and are not a reason to begrudge them care. However, they also demonstrate the NHI system’s reliance on working-age contributors, who utilize far fewer services despite paying more.
As the labor force contracts over time, broad subsidies would become increasingly difficult to sustain without higher premiums, higher taxes or cuts to other public spending. Many younger adults already support their own children and aging parents, and shifting more of the cost onto a shrinking workforce could undermine the NHI system’s principles of ability to pay and intergenerational mutual assistance, deepening generational inequity.
As mentioned in yesterday’s editorial, “Beware of money-pit legislation,” the amendment’s convenient timing makes it hard to rule out political motivations. Older voters tend to be an important constituency for the pan-blue camp, and local elections are on Nov. 28. The choice of a threshold covering such a large share of seniors suggests that targeting those in genuine need is not the priority. By shifting the financial burden to the DPP-controlled central government, the KMT and the TPP can free up funds for local governments they control while campaigning on a popular promise to seniors.
Those with real financial need deserve assistance in paying for healthcare, but a truly sustainable system should rely on shared responsibility and targeted support — otherwise, future generations would be left footing an ever-growing bill.
The most troubling message coming out of Washington for Taipei is not any single statement but the cumulative effect of a series of signals suggesting that US President Donald Trump is rethinking Taiwan’s strategic value while viewing the US-China relationship through the lens of a transactional great-power bargain. The danger behind Trump’s new softness toward Beijing is a potential US-China bargain that undermines Taiwan’s core interests. During Chinese President Xi Jinping’s (習近平) recent state visit to Washington, Trump and Xi appeared to rewrite the history of World War II. In a Sept. 25 fact sheet on Xi’s visit, the White House said,
The official English name for Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen’s (沈伯洋) campaign is “the Taipei Current.” It comes from the Chinese term yangliu (洋流), a direct translation of which would be “ocean current,” using the last character of Shen’s name, yang (洋, “ocean”). The Chinese term is a reference to the 2018 campaign for Kaohsiung mayor that swept to power a hitherto marginal player within the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT), Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜), now legislative speaker, whose successful campaign then was termed the “Han Wave” (韓流). Shen’s usage of the Chinese term is intentional.
There was a moment, in 2015 or 2016, when Tulum was the coolest town on Earth. On the eve of the MLB World Series, there is a realization that these might be the competition’s last games for a while.
Owners are pushing for a salary cap, which could prompt a lockout starting on Dec. 2 and result in canceled games next year.
“It would be a real bummer to lose a season, that’s for sure,” Tampa Bay Rays ace Drew Rasmussen said on Thursday ahead of the World Series opener against the Milwaukee Brewers. “I think the industry as a whole is in way too good of a place.”
Photo: AP
The World Series is scheduled to start at 8am today, Taiwan time, at American Family Field in Milwaukee, Wisconsin.
For the first since 1991, it is between teams both in the bottom half of payrolls: Milwaukee ranked 19th as of Aug. 31 and Tampa Bay 25th.
The MLB says that a cap is needed to help all teams compete more consistently, but players contend because of the method owners use to define expenses, a cap would lead to management taking a greater share of the sport’s revenue.
“The system that’s being proposed, which is similar to other leagues in terms of revenue-sharing system, not only will help us compete, but more importantly all of the teams with lower payrolls, too, which is something also I think the fans want,” Brewers owner Mark Attanasio said.
MLB’s proposal would cap spending next year at US$245.3 million using figures for luxury tax payrolls, and limit a player to 15 percent of a team’s payroll.
Free agents would be capped at US$265 million over six seasons — far under Juan Soto’s record US$765 million, 15-year deal with the New York Mets.
The players’ association vows never to accept a cap.
“If they’re going to sit there and wave their little magic wand at us saying they’re going to get a salary cap, it’s not going to happen,” Brewers pitcher Trevor Megill said.
Negotiations for a collective bargaining agreement to replace the five-year deal expiring on Dec. 1 could turn into each side trying to outlast the other.
“My thought with it all is keep building on the former generations and build on what they gave us,” said Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski, who is set to throw the first pitch of the World Series. “You don’t want to be the generation to send something backwards. You just keep building on what former generations have given you and hope for the best.”
Attanasio said that the Brewers ranked 11th in non-player baseball operations spending this year and the Rays were ninth.
The owner said that about 250 people report to general manager Matt Arnold.
Milwaukee was ranked 30th and last in market size in MLB and could become the first small-market team to win the title since the 2015 Kansas City Royals.
“We have to keep an eye on the present and one eye on the future in every move that we make. Every trade we have to think about that,” Arnold said. “There are tradeoffs for what you can do to help the team today and what that looks like going forward.”

Military to restructure on tech, firepower: source
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:40:17 UTC
01:40:17 KST

Taiwan is beginning reorganization and restructuring centered on using firepower and technology to reduce the dependence on troop numbers, a source said yesterday.
The next step in the force transformation plan would focus on new artillery, coastal defense, uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) and counter-UAVs, a defense official said on condition of anonymity.
The reorganization followed the establishment of the air force’s 7th Flight Training Wing; the navy’s Littoral Combat Command and the Naval Anti-Submarine Aviation Command; the army’s Uncrewed Systems Training Command; marine security, fires and drone battalions; and the scattering of drone units across services.
Photo: Ritchie B. Tongo, EPA-EFE
For the incoming stage, the armed forces would reorganize and expand artillery following the introduction of the High Mobility Artillery Rocket System and the M109 self-propelled howitzer in the 6th, 8th and 10th army corps, the official said.
The modern artillery platforms require a three-soldier crew per vehicle, down from the nine to 11 soldiers per towed artillery piece, resulting in significant personnel savings, they said.
The surplus personnel would be utilized to form rocket artillery battalions from the nuclei of extant rocket artillery companies, boosting the artillery arm’s mobility and long-range precision-strike capabilities, the source said.
UAV units would be integrated under army corps-level artillery headquarters, as the artillery branch views the role of drones as analogous to guns, they added.
Army UAV battalions are to be equipped with the National Chungshan Institute of Science and Technology’s first-person-view attack drones and reconnaissance drones, as well as the Altius-600M loitering munition, they said, adding that the army is also placing an order for 2,000 Altius-700M anti-armor drones and Altius-600ISR drones.
Artillery headquarters would use reconnaissance drones, attack drones, tube artillery and rocket systems to form a digitized kill chain capable of destroying enemy forces upon detection, the official said.
The Littoral Combat Command is to create a 4th Littoral Combat Group, and dedicated UAV units under each group would operate the vertical take-off and landing drones they are to receive, the source said.
The Air Force Security Guards would be expanded into a brigade-sized unit to defend radar stations, air bases and other key installations against Chinese UAVs and special operations forces, they said, adding that it would be composed of a mix of conscripts and professional soldiers armed with Stinger missiles, Kestrel anti-armor rockets and other weapons.
The air force would establish units to operate Patriot Advanced Capability-3 Missile Segment Enhancement (PAC-3 MSE) interceptors and National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile Systems (NASAMS), contingent on Washington’s approval of a US$14 billion arms package to Taiwan, the official said.
Integrating these weapon systems would result in significant changes to the organization of the Air Force Air Defense and Missile Command, they added.
The military’s restructuring would also enhance counter-UAV tactics and asymmetric weapon handling training for draftees, as infantry battalions of conscripts would furnish a vital part of frontline combat strength, the official said.

US moots curbs on funds to Chinese biotech firms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:40:16 UTC
01:40:16 KST

The administration of US President Donald Trump is seeking to restrict investment in Chinese biotechnology companies, potentially complicating financial ties at a time when US drugmakers are increasingly turning to China for new medicines.
The US Department of the Treasury on Thursday proposed adding biotechnology to a list of sensitive technologies subject to investment limits involving foreign adversaries, citing national security concerns.
The proposed regulations would require US investors to notify Washington about some transactions involving foreign companies developing sensitive technologies and prohibit others entirely.
Photo: AFP
The rules would expand a program targeting investments in areas including artificial intelligence, semiconductors and quantum computing.
The move represents the latest escalation in Washington’s efforts to rein in China’s biotech advances.
Last year, the US Congress passed the Biosecure Act to restrict federal agencies and government-funded companies from using or procuring services from designated Chinese biotech firms, although the restrictions were weaker and narrower than initially proposed.
The US tightening comes as Beijing is also adjusting its own approach.
In a sign of biotechnology’s growing strategic importance, China last week proposed adding several biomedical technologies to its export-control list — although its plan explicitly allows licensing deals for drugs to continue.
Chinese biotechnology companies have become a source of innovation for the pharmaceutical industry. US drugmakers are increasingly turning to China to license promising treatments as they search for new products to replenish their pipelines.
Licensing deals are not expressly prohibited under Washington’s proposed rules, according to Duane Wright, senior healthcare policy analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence.
Wright said that the Treasury Department proposal begins with a “very broad definition” of biotechnology — covering small molecules, biologics, vaccines and cell and gene therapies — but leaves room to narrow the pharmaceutical provisions after stakeholder comments.

ANALYTICAL ENGLISH 解析英語(常春藤)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:40:16 UTC
01:40:16 KST

Food has a way of reinventing itself over time. Some products that were once believed to have medicinal value are now treated as everyday snacks or drinks. Coca-Cola and ketchup are two famous examples.
Coca-Cola is one of the most popular drinks in the world. Today, most people see it as a sweet, bubbly soda often enjoyed with fast food. However, the original recipe of Coca-Cola vastly differs from the drink we know today. It was originally developed and marketed as a medicinal tonic by Dr. John S. Pemberton in the late 1800s.
Pemberton created the drink as a way to help with the severe morphine addiction he developed after getting seriously injured in the Civil War. He made a sweet syrup with ingredients like coca leaves and kola nut, hoping to offer stimulation without the need for alcohol or other drugs. Pemberton marketed the syrup as a cure-all that could be added to soda water. Advertisements claimed that the drink could treat conditions such as headaches, nerve pain, and even a low mood. At the time, such claims seemed believable because carbonated water was thought to have health benefits, while coca leaves were often recommended by doctors as a stimulant.
Photo: Ivy English 照片:常春藤解析英語
As the addictive and harmful effects of cocaine became widely recognized, Coca-Cola removed the cocaine-containing coca extract from the drink after growing public concern. The company later used processed coca leaves without cocaine while continuing to provide a mild stimulating effect through caffeine. With advancements in bottling, carbonated drinks soon became commonplace, and people gradually stopped viewing them mainly as health products. What began as a medicinal concoction was eventually transformed into a sweet and refreshing indulgence enjoyed worldwide today.
食物會隨著時間不斷改變自身定位。有些曾被認為具有藥用價值的產品，如今被視為日常零食或飲品。可口可樂與番茄醬就是兩個著名例子。
可口可樂是世界上最受歡迎的飲料之一。如今，大多數人都將它視為一種常搭配速食享用的帶有氣泡的甜味汽水。然而，可口可樂最初的配方與我們今日所熟知的這款飲料有很大差異。它最初是在1800年代晚期由約翰．彭伯頓醫師開發並作為藥用補品販售。
彭伯頓研發出這款飲料，來幫助改善自己在南北戰爭中受重傷後所產生的嚴重嗎啡成癮問題。他以古柯葉與可樂果等原料製成一種甜味糖漿，希望在不需依賴酒精或其他藥物的情況下，也能提供刺激作用。彭伯頓將這種糖漿作為可加入蘇打水中的萬靈藥來販售。廣告宣稱這款飲料能治療頭痛、神經痛，甚至情緒低落等症狀。在當時，這類說法看似可信，因為碳酸水（編按：蘇打水 soda water為碳酸水carbonated water的一種）被認為具有健康益處，而古柯葉也常被醫師推薦作為興奮劑。
隨著古柯鹼令人上癮且有害的影響逐漸廣為人知，在大眾憂慮日益升高後，可口可樂便將含有古柯鹼的古柯萃取物從飲料中移除。之後，公司改用不含古柯鹼的加工古柯葉，同時繼續透過咖啡因提供輕微的刺激效果。隨著瓶裝技術的進步，碳酸飲料很快變得相當普及，人們也逐漸不再主要將其視為健康產品。這種原本作為藥用調製品的飲料，最終轉變成今日風靡全球、甜而清爽的享受。
What Did You Learn?
Photo: Ivy English 照片: 常春藤解析英語
1-2 請根據選文內容，從文章中選出兩個單詞，分別填入下列句子空格，並視句型結構需要作適當的字形變化，使句子語意完整、語法正確，並符合全文文意。每格限填一個單詞（word）。（填充題）
Coca-Cola was once promoted as a medicinal drink, while tomato-based ketchup was believed to have __1__ health effects. Over time, changing beliefs and marketing strategies brought about a complete __2__ in how people viewed these products.
答案：1. beneficial 2. transformation
Photo: AdobeStock 照片：AdobeStock
Words in Use
1. vastly adv. 非常
Life in the city is vastly different from life in the countryside.
城市生活和鄉村生活非常不同。
2. severe a. 嚴重的
Daniel had a severe headache and went home early.
丹尼爾頭痛得很嚴重，所以提早回家。
3. addiction n. 成癮，上癮
Too much screen time may lead to addiction in some teens.
過多的螢幕時間可能導致一些青少年成癮。
4. injured a. 受傷的
Marcus got injured while playing soccer with his classmates.
馬可斯和同學踢足球時受傷了。
5. syrup n. 糖漿
Doris poured maple syrup over her warm pancakes.
桃樂絲把楓糖漿淋在熱鬆餅上。
Practical Phrases
1. see A as B 將A視為B
= view A as B
= think of A as B
Many people see exercise as an important part of a healthy lifestyle.
許多人將運動視為健康生活的重要一環。
2. differ from. . . 與……不同
This year’s design differs from the previous one in several ways.
今年的設計在好幾個方面都和前一版不同。
3. add A to B 把A加入B
The chef added fresh herbs to the sauce for extra flavor.
主廚在醬料中加入新鮮香草來增添風味。
4. remove A from B 把A從B移除
Jack removed several old files from his computer yesterday.
傑克昨天從電腦裡刪除了幾個舊檔案。

CGA urges Beijing not to use typhoons to assert jurisdiction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:40:15 UTC
01:40:15 KST

The Coast Guard Administration (CGA) yesterday urged China not to exploit typhoons to assert jurisdiction over the Taiwan Strait.
The CGA issued the remarks after it found that China was shadowing eight Japan Coast Guard ships that sheltered in Taiwan proper’s western waters due to Typhoon Champi.
Eight Japan Coast Guard (JCG) vessels sailed southward along the Taiwan Strait median line from 6am on Thursday, reaching waters southwest of Penghu County’s Cimei Island (七美島), outside Taiwan’s contiguous zone, which extends 24 nautical miles (44.4km) from the territorial sea baseline, it said.
Photo copied by Chiu Chun-fu, Taipei Times
As the Japanese ships prepared for the typhoon, they were followed by five China Coast Guard vessels, the CGA said.
Three of the Japanese vessels were large patrol vessels capable of carrying helicopters — the Reimei (PLH-33), the Yashima (PLH-22) and the Ryukyu (PLH-09) — and five were large patrol vessels — the Taketomi (PL-81), the Kabira (PL-83), the Matsushima (PL-74), the Irabu (PL-95) and the Osumi (PL-202), it said.
China had deployed five coast guard vessels, including the 3,000-tonne-class Baita (CCG-2304), the Xiushan (CCG-2305) and CCG-2308, as well as two 5,000-tonne-class Daishan patrol vessels, CCG-2501 and CCG-2502, the CGA said.
The Japanese coast guard was entitled to pass through the international waters of the Strait under international law and maritime humanitarian principles, the CGA said, citing the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.
The China Coast Guard, by tailing foreign government ships in a storm, exploited a natural disaster to unlawfully assert control over the Taiwan Strait as part of Beijing’s campaign to transform it into a Chinese inland sea, contravening maritime freedoms, navigational safety and the rules-based international order, it said.
The CGA is carrying out disaster prevention duties, maintaining all-weather surveillance of the Chinese vessels and remains fully prepared to take actions necessary to defend the freedom of navigation, safety at sea and Taiwan’s national security, it added.
Additional reporting by CNA

What on earth persuades disgraced people like Elizabeth Holmes to let the cameras in?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:40:14 UTC
01:40:14 KST

In You Can See Everything, convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes invites film-makers Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim into her home in a supposed act of “radical transparency.” Holmes is filmed, along with her partner, Billy Evans, and their two young children, in the weeks before starting a prison sentence for defrauding Theranos investors.
“The best way for people to see who she is,” Evans says, “is to give as much access as possible into our daily lives.”
It may also be the best way to market “Theranos 2.0,” which the couple are working on during filming. But the documentary questions whether Holmes is presenting her authentic self or a manufactured persona. Fielder speaks for the audience when he asks Holmes in a tense exchange whether she’s “being real” with him. “I’m always being real,” she says.
Photo: AP
That question of authenticity is at the heart of documentary film-making. You Can See Everything is as much about the ambiguous relationship between film-maker and subject as it is about Holmes herself. There is often a power struggle over narrative control in documentaries, with both sides of the dynamic wanting different outcomes from the final film. Watching You Can See Everything inevitably prompts the question: why would Holmes, days before she heads to jail, invite the scrutiny of a film crew?
Some people, like Holmes, think a documentary will help rebuild their reputation after public disgrace. When Anthony Weiner, who resigned from Congress after tweeting a photo of his bulging groin, tried to stage a professional comeback with a New York mayoral bid, he allowed cameras to film the journey. Only, he had more to hide: when further sex scandals emerged, his campaign went from a story of public redemption to innuendo-laden humiliation. And all the while, the cameras kept rolling. Weiner is a prime example of a subject losing control of the narrative.
Weiner may have wanted a sympathetic portrayal, but he should have known that film-makers always have their own agendas. In the book The Journalist and the Murderer, Janet Malcolm reflects on the relationship between journalists and their subjects.
“The subject becomes a kind of child of the writer, regarding him as a permissive, all-accepting, all-forgiving mother, and expecting the book to be written by her,” she writes. “Of course, the book is written by the strict, all-noticing, unforgiving father.”
The same is surely true of the documentarian.
When Jackie and David Siegel allowed Lauren Greenfield to film their attempt to build a modern-day Versailles in Florida, the director wasn’t giving them free PR. Rather, with The Queen of Versailles, Greenfield was interested in the corrosive effects of extreme wealth. The Siegels agreed to be filmed because they were proud of their success. When their dream collapsed following the 2008 financial crash, The Queen of Versailles turned from a story of Xanadu-like grandeur to one of hubristic overreach. David later sued Lauren — unsuccessfully — for defamation, but he should have known from the beginning: it may have been his story, but it was never his film.
A few years after Versailles, Greenfield made The Kingmaker, about former first lady of the Philippines Imelda Marcos and her attempt to return the family to power. From the beginning of the film, Greenfield said, there was a power struggle over who was telling the story. Marcos, known for her lavish lifestyle during her husband’s brutal rule, understood the power of optics. In a children’s cancer ward, she hands out money to children in a public display of compassion.
“Perception is real,” Marcos says in the film, “and the truth is not.”
Some people agree to projects believing they will have editorial control. Idi Amin gave Barbet Schroeder unprecedented access after the director essentially promised that they would make the film together. But Amin was unhappy with General Idi Amin Dada: A Self Portrait and demanded some footage be cut, rounding up more than 100 French residents in Uganda and holding them hostage until his demands were met. Schroeder agreed. It helps to be as ruthless as Amin if you want final cut.
Documentaries are often about the past, but some of cinema’s most memorable moments show people acting violently in the present, fully aware that they are being filmed. Frederick Wiseman’s austere films show abuse in psychiatric institutions (Titicut Follies) and horrific police violence (Law and Order). Why did people do unspeakable things in front of a camera?
“People basically go about their business,” Wiseman told an interviewer, “and the presence of the camera doesn’t have much, if any effect on their behavior.”
But cameras did have an effect on the subjects of Joshua Oppenheimer’s The Act of Killing, probably the most morally complex example of the film-maker-subject relationship in cinema history. Perpetrators of Indonesia’s mass killings gleefully re-enact their crimes, restaging their violent memories in the style of Hollywood movies. They do not profess their innocence. Rather, they agree to be filmed because they are proud of what they did. They really do want us to see everything.
Perhaps the most interesting case of someone willingly putting themselves under scrutiny is Lance Armstrong. Alex Gibney’s documentary on Armstrong was expected to be a puff piece. When the full extent of Armstrong’s doping was revealed, however, Gibney’s film changed direction, becoming a documentary not on a cyclist’s triumph but on a master manipulator who lied to everyone, including the film-maker. In The Armstrong Lie, Armstrong admits that he “was prepared to say anything” to keep his lie going.
Some people are simply arrogant enough to think they can get away with their lies. But others become so invested in their skewed version of reality that to refuse a documentary crew would be like admitting their deception. So they welcome the cameras, often doing more damage than if they had simply retreated from public view. But unlike Armstrong, Holmes still insists she has done nothing wrong. As she says in You Can See Everything: “I have nothing to hide.”

Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an’s (蔣萬安) recent, surprising suggestion that the airport be converted to an AI park is just the latest variation on an old theme. Replacing Songshan airport with some kind of green or park space

Laid out on bamboo racks by the Keya River (客雅溪), freshly made noodles dried in the wind without compromising their quality or texture. The ideal conditions, it was once said, were 70 percent wind and 30 percent sun. Most producers were concentrated in the Nanshih (南勢) area, which became known as Mifenliao (米粉寮, literally “rice noodle shed”). The round number was easy to remember and the idea caught on, despite there being no scientific evidence for 10,000 steps as a specific threshold for health. “When the research community looked into it, they found that there were health benefits, so it didn’t necessarily get thrown out as pseudoscience,” McNamara says.
