and GQEBERHA, South Africa
Sri Lanka on Thursday trumped Harry Brook’s record double century in their ODI clash, while in South Africa earlier in the day, the hosts set up a Test series decider with a comeback innings victory against Australia.
Sri Lanka pulled off the second-highest successful run chase ever in ODI cricket history to hand England a second successive defeat in the Pakistan tri-series.
Photo: AP
Brook’s 116-ball 202 propelled England to 429-4, but Sri Lanka counterpunched with a chase of 430-8 for an extraordinary two-wicket win.
Needing six runs off Josh Tongue’s final two balls, Janith Liyanage lofted the fast bowler over long-off for a winning six to guide Sri Lanka to their most memorable ODI victory since winning the 1996 Cricket World Cup.
Sri Lanka’s run-chase was second only to South Africa’s chase of 438-9 in a one-wicket win over Australia at Johannesburg in 2006.
“Incredible game of cricket, both teams were exceptional,” Brook said. “Sri Lanka just outplayed us. They played exceptional cricket to knock off 400”-plus.
Brook was the first England batter to score 200 in the ODI format. He reached the milestone from 114 deliveries, breaking the previous mark of 116 set just last month by India’s Shubman Gill. He is the first batter to score 200-plus in an innings and finishing on the losing team.
Avishka Fernando, who hit 97 from 83 balls, and Pavan Rathnayake set up the strong chase with a 166-run third-wicket stand after Sri Lanka lost two wickets inside the first five overs of the reply.
Dasun Shanaka added an electrifying 133 runs with Rathnayake off just 79 balls.
Rathnayake completed his second ODI century, making 130 off 106 balls with 15 fours and three sixes to reduce the target to 107 off 58 balls before holing out to long-on.
Shanaka kept going, smashing the England bowlers for eight sixes and six boundaries as he raced to 97 from 50 deliveries.
Sam Curran took particular punishment, returning figures of 2-103.
England got back in contention in the 44th over when Shanaka’s dismissal left Sri Lanka needing 67 from six overs, but Liyanage smashed three sixes and seven fours in an unbeaten 61 off 27 balls as England’s attack kept leaking boundaries.
With eight needed of the final over, Tongue bowled Wellalage (8) and Eshan Malinga (0) off successive balls, but Asitha Fernando denied a hat trick and gave the strike back to Liyanage to finish off.
“We chased very well. I enjoyed it as captain,” Sri Lanka skipper Kusal Mendis said. “Everyone believed we can do it.”
At St George’s Park in Gqeberha, South Africa won on day 5 of the second Test, despite a lot of time lost to rain.
The morning session on Thursday was a washout, but the hosts dismissed Australia for 295 in their second innings an hour after the tea interval to complete a win by an innings and 31 runs.
After losing the opener in Durban by 214 runs, South Africa tied the series 1-1 and set up a deciding third Test in Cape Town from Tuesday as they chase World Test Championship points.

Real-time sensors monitor trees in storm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:40:12 UTC
01:40:12 KST

The Kaohsiung Mass Rapid Transit Bureau yesterday said that it has used 211 inclinometers to monitor tree stability in green tunnels of the city’s light-rail system during Typhoon Champi.
Kaohsiung’s light rail is known for two green tunnels: Totoro Tunnel, which is between Kaohsiung Museum of Fine Arts Station and Neiwei Arts Center Station and lined with Madagascar almond trees, and Hulk Tunnel, which runs from Heart of Love River Station to the Shu-Te Home-Economics and Commercial High School Station, featuring tall rain trees.
Kaohsiung Deputy Mayor Charles Lin (林欽榮) yesterday inspected the fixation work for the light-rail green channels.
Photo: Wang Jung-hsiang, Taipei Times
He said that the city government has collaborated with the National Center for Research on Earthquake Engineering on introducing technology to monitor the light rail section along Dashun Road.
Tree inclinometers were set up along the green channels to monitor tree stability around the clock, Lin said, helping enhance the city’s disaster response capabilities during the typhoon as any abnormality can be reported in real-time.
The bureau said it has set up typhoon-resistant fixation work for all 453 Madagascar almond trees and rain trees along the light rail.
Different supports such as steel tubes, steel cables, bamboo poles or ropes were applied, depending on the tree species and operating conditions, it said, adding that it had trimmed 42 trees along the light rail following the previous typhoon.
An additional 11 tree inclinometers were set up in the green tunnels prior to Typhoon Champi, the bureau said.
Kaohsiung Rapid Transit Corp general manager Joseph Wang (王亞洲) said that Kaohsiung’s light rail system had a daily ridership of about 40,000 passengers from January to this month.
While the annual ridership reached 13.33 million passengers last year, it is projected to surpass 15 million passengers this year, up by 66 percent compared with the originally estimated 9 million passengers, he said.

China using militia boats to ramp up war readiness
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:40:09 UTC
01:40:09 KST

China is combining militia vessels with coast guard ships to expand “battlefield preparation” around Taiwan and into the western Pacific, the Coast Guard Administration (CGA) said, warning the operations were also putting pressure on Japan and the Philippines.
Responding to a Reuters exclusive this month on the first known sighting of a Chinese militia boat off Taiwan’s Pacific coast in the middle of August, the CGA said it had dispatched a patrol boat to drive away the vessel, which was operating alongside a Chinese coast guard ship and a research vessel.
It confirmed details in the Reuters report, identifying the suspected militia fishing boat as the Minfudingyu 07902, and said it had come as close as about 2.7 nautical miles (5km) outside Taiwan’s restricted waters on Aug. 16.
Photo: Yu Tai-lang, Taipei Times
China has increased such activity since June in overlapping economic waters involving Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines, the agency said, after Tokyo and Manila announced talks on maritime boundary delimitation in their exclusive economic zones (EEZ).
EEZs extend 200 nautical miles from the coast and give a coastal state rights to exploit, conserve and manage natural resources in those waters.
“Such complex gray-zone operations not only increase the maritime surveillance and response burden on Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines, but may also create regional security pressure and affect the existing international maritime order,” the CGA said in a statement.
The Chinese Ministry of National Defense and the Philippine defense and foreign affairs departments did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Japan’s coast guard declined immediate comment.
The CGA said the vessels’ coordinated activity was part of a broader pattern of Chinese “gray zone” operations using law-enforcement, scientific and civilian cover to expand Beijing’s influence at sea while remaining below the threshold of open conflict.
The Chinese operations were aimed at “assisting ‘battlefield preparation,’” the CGA said, adding that Taiwan’s east coast was an important maritime traffic and supply route and that continued Chinese activity there could further increase security pressure on Taiwan.
Taiwanese officials said they believe China is practicing for a possible maritime blockade using overlapping military, paramilitary and civilian assets.
China has repeatedly said its operations off Taiwan’s east coast are “legitimate and lawful,” because they are in Chinese waters, a position Taipei’s government strongly rejects.
The CGA said it had placed the Minfudingyu 07902 on a priority watchlist, assessing the boat showed the “characteristics” of Chinese maritime militia activity and said it would continue tracking the vessel.
Dating back to the 1950s, China’s maritime militia uses fishing vessels with trained, state-supported crews to operate in disputed waters, often alongside coast guard ships around South China Sea flashpoints, helping Beijing assert maritime claims while maintaining a civilian appearance.
The surveillance report reviewed by Reuters was conducted by Taiwan’s Apex Aviation, which used radar screenshots, infrared imagery and automatic-identification system data from a reconnaissance flight to document the cluster of vessels.

Warnings for Chiang’s campaign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:40:05 UTC
01:40:05 KST

In Taipei’s political landscape, Daan (大安), Wenshan (文山), Songshan (松山), Xinyi (信義), Neihu (內湖) and Nangang (南港) districts have long been regarded as Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) strongholds. However, recent polls suggest that Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an’s (蔣萬安) lead in these traditional bastions has narrowed considerably, with his Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) rival, Legislator Puma Shen (沈伯洋), even overtaking him in certain areas. The weakening of these defensive lines reflects a combination of governance performance issues, disconnect with voters, a self-siloing campaign strategy and structural shifts in the electorate.
First is the crisis of municipal performance and deficit of public trust. Food safety incidents in Taipei schools have damaged public confidence in the city government, alongside controversies over tree felling, the “rat plague,” the Taipei Dome incident, severe flooding and issues with the eastern extension of the Taipei Metro’s Tamsui-Xinyi Line.
As Lao Tzu (老子) wrote in the Taoist classic Tao Te Ching (道德經), “governing a great nation is like cooking a small fish” — mishandling a situation can very quickly go awry and lead to a breakdown of trust.
Chiang’s sudden proposal to remove Taipei International Airport (Songshan airport) to build an artificial intelligence park also left many doubting the weight behind such grand promises. Public policy theory warns that proposals without feasibility analyses can fall into the trap of symbolism without substance.
The strategy missteps have alienated voters beyond immediate supporters, and the negative attacks seem to have backfired. Faced with a challenger, Chiang has chosen to avoid open debate and instead retreated to media outlets within his own political echo chamber, appearing like a script-reading machine.
In the “Light and Darkness” (Ming An, 明暗) chapter of the political treatise “Comments of a Recluse” (Qianfu Lun, 潛夫論), the Eastern Han Dynasty scholar Wang Fu (王符) wrote: “Listen to both sides and you will be enlightened; heed only one side and you will be left in the dark.” For Chiang, excessive reliance on home-turf media have undermined dialogue with centrist voters.
Meanwhile, decontextualized smear attacks on his rival have sparked protests from medical professionals and social workers. Issue management theory suggests that baseless attacks can easily lead to those same fear-appeals backfiring on the messenger.
Second is Chiang’s disconnect with grassroots voters. Chiang’s cultivated image as one of the political elite only adds to the impression of him being out of touch, such as when he was gifted a ceremonial stalk of sugarcane during a temple ceremony and subsequently discarded on the roadside, drawing criticism for lacking basic social etiquette. As the military strategy treatise Wei Liaozi (尉繚子), written during the Warring States Period, states: “He who cannot win people’s hearts can never win their strength.” By contrast, Chiang’s opponent has been making soapbox speeches, handing out pamphlets, canvassing night markets and using digital tools to project a more down-to-earth image, highlighting their differences even further.
Finally is the loss of votes from centrist and former third-party candidate supporters.
Strategic management theory suggests that those without a competitive edge are eventually sidelined. Polling data indicate that of the 340,000 votes cast for former independent Taipei mayoral candidate Vivian Huang (黃珊珊) in 2022, as many as 53 percent have shifted to Shen, while only 39 percent favor Chiang. His lead among voters aged 20 to 49 and centrist voters has also fallen sharply, cutting his advantage in traditional strongholds by half. As the Chinese philosopher Mencius (孟子) wrote: “A just cause wins support, while an unjust one loses it.” With younger and more educated voters seeing support for Shen as an embrace of innovation, this structural shift might prove hard to reverse.
The weakening of Chiang’s traditional electoral strongholds reflects a dual crisis in municipal governance and campaign strategy. If the incumbent continues to rely on image management, avoids discussing municipal affairs and retreats into an echo chamber, he must ultimately face the public’s verdict. Only by returning to substantive achievements, engaging directly with public concerns and demonstrating a genuine grassroots commitment can he solve the crisis of trust.
Hsu Chi-hsiang is an immigration professional.

Why everyone wants to meet with Kim Jong-un
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:40:04 UTC
01:40:04 KST

North Korean leader Kim Jong-un might be the world’s most in-demand leader. US President Donald Trump wants to meet him during a visit to Asia next month. So, too, does South Korean President Lee Jae-myung and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. He stood shoulder-to-shoulder with Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) and Russian President Vladimir Putin at a giant military parade in Beijing last year, and has an outstanding invitation to visit Russia.
It is not just the diplomatic isolation that is lifting. With a bridge between North Korea and China officially opening earlier this month, and a new border crossing with Russia launching in last month, Pyongyang has deepened its economic ties with Beijing and Moscow, further blunting the impact of international sanctions.
His involvement in the Ukraine war has given Kim credible alternatives, something North Korean leaders have rarely possessed. The billions of dollars in arms sales and military support to Moscow have markedly improved his economic position and arguably increased his value to Beijing. That means Washington’s most powerful bargaining chip — sanctions relief — is worth far less than it once was.
Kim has plenty of reasons to breathe easier these days. When Trump and Xi met in Washington last month, neither mentioned North Korea’s denuclearization: Beijing has been avoiding the term for some time, while the US used it as recently as May. Still, it is likely not enough to convince Kim that another meeting with Trump is worth his time, particularly given that their last summit in Vietnam in 2019 ended badly.
While the overtures from the US president have been mostly met with silence, the regime has loudly rejected Lee’s call for talks aimed at formally ending the state of war between the two Koreas and halting Pyongyang’s nuclear buildup. It is similarly disparaging about Takaichi’s proposal for a summit with Kim to resolve the issue of North Korea’s abduction of Japanese nationals.
They are not wrong to want contact. Facing a deteriorating security landscape — with North Korea’s expanding nuclear arsenal and rapidly improving conventional capabilities at its center — it is clear that isolation is not going to keep the peace on the peninsula. Yet Kim can afford to be selective about who he grants an audience. As Bloomberg reported, his family-run dictatorship has amassed as much as US$22 billion in foreign revenue from 2022 to last year.
The shift in the balance of power has helped Kim reposition himself on the international stage — not as a pariah, but as a member of a powerful group of anti-Western nations. The relationships he is cultivating are producing immediate and tangible results, Stimson Center senior fellow and a North Korea specialist Jenny Town said. And that means there is no impetus for him to deal with states such as the US or Japan that make what he considers unreasonable demands, she said.
That raises a difficult question for global powers. If the goal of talking to Kim is no longer denuclearization, then what is the strategy? Perhaps the reestablishment of communication channels and risk reduction is a more realistic outcome of any meeting with Pyongyang right now. The nuclear issue could be dealt with at a later date, but that prospect grows weaker with every move Trump makes, from cutting short joint military exercises with South Korea to praising Kim and acknowledging his nuclear arsenal. The priority should be on stabilizing the region and reducing the risk of war, and that means bolstering alliances between the US, South Korea and Japan, not undermining them.
Moscow’s war has been a boon for Kim way beyond the economic benefit. Thousands of North Korean troops have deployed to support Russian operations against Ukraine, along with engineers, mine-clearance personnel and drone operators. Those who return home come with invaluable combat experience and technical knowhow on modern warfare. It is helping Pyongyang upgrade its defense capabilities, and there is mounting evidence of more sophisticated technology transfer.
In the last month alone, North Korea has tested two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles, and fired multiple ballistic missiles off its east coast. However, beyond the showy displays of military might, it is the smaller conflicts that have Korea watchers worried about the prospect of an accidental escalation on the peninsula. The north and south are locked in a dispute over landmine blasts along the border that wounded South Korean soldiers last month. It is a dangerous flashpoint that signals there would be more of these flare-ups.
The problem is that Kim is harder to pressure and stronger than ever — and it is not clear what it would take to draw him back into talks.
Ruth Pollard is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Asia politics and policy. She previously covered South and Southeast Asia on the Bloomberg government team and was Middle East Correspondent for The Sydney Morning Herald. Young Optics expects shipments drop
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:40:04 UTC
01:40:04 KST

Camera lens supplier Young Optics Inc (揚明光學) yesterday said it expects shipments this quarter to decline sequentially due to soft demand, partly because customers’ planned changes to new logistics projection lenses could delay or suspend demand.
Shipments of 3D printing products this quarter are expected to increase slightly as customers begin testing new models, Young Optics said in a statement to the Taiwan Stock Exchange.
Shipments from other product lines are expected to remain flat or decline slightly from last quarter as customers become more cautious about year-end inventory management, the company said.
Photo: Ou Yu-hsing, Taipei Times
Young Optics yesterday posted a second consecutive quarterly decline in net profit of NT$1.22 million (US$37,529) last quarter, slumping 76.25 percent from NT$5.14 million the previous quarter. That represented an improvement from a net loss of NT$10.08 million a year earlier, company data showed.
Earnings per share were NT$0.01, down from NT$0.05 the previous quarter, but up from losses per share of NT$0.09 a year earlier.
Gross margin rose to 16.8 percent last quarter from 16.44 percent in the second quarter, but was down from 17.02 percent a year earlier.
In the third quarter, shipments of smart home products were flat from the previous quarter as continued growth in new models shipments was offset by the phaseout of older low-end lens products, Young Optics said.
Shipments of optical components increased quarter-on-quarter as customers’ new augmented reality (AR) glasses entered mass production, while 3D printing product shipments slowed as customers adjusted inventories of older models and conducted verification of new models, it said.
Automotive product shipments increased slightly as new lidar lens models entered mass production and replaced older models, the company added.
The third-quarter shipment trends largely matched the guidance provided in July.
In the second quarter, automotive products accounted for about 15 to 20 percent of Young Optics’ NT$738.28 million in revenue, while optical components made up 25 to 30 percent, company president Cynthia Chang (張雅容) said at the time.
The share of optical components could rise to about 30 percent this year, supported by volume production of logistics projection lenses and AR glasses, Chang said.
Regarding fiber array unit products, the company said two mechanical transfer ferrule projects are undergoing trial production, while molded glass lens arrays and optical transceiver modules remain in the proof-of-concept verification phase, Young Optics said.
The company is also developing new automotive lidar lens products, Young Optics said.
Increases in manufacturing complexity, particularly in molded glass components, could weigh on gross margin during the initial stage of mass production, it said.
Young Optics has three major customers for applications related to AR glasses, mainly supplying optical engine components, said Wayne Lin (林威嶧), another company president.
One customer focuses primarily on swimming goggles, while the others are leading North American customers for AR glasses, Lin said.
One of the two North American customers is already in mass production, while the other began mass production last year and plans to launch a second-generation product in the second half of this year, he said.

Seoul proposes border talks with North
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:40:03 UTC
01:40:03 KST

South Korea yesterday proposed military talks with North Korea to resolve disagreements about where their border lies and prevent accidental clashes in frontline areas, seeking to ease tensions after recent landmine blasts injured three South Korean soldiers.
It is unclear whether North Korea will agree to talks. North Korean leader Kim Jong-un has taken a hard line toward Seoul and has suspended virtually all dialogue and cooperation with the South over the past few years. Meanwhile, North Korea has been adding mines, barbed wire fences, tactical roads, anti-tank walls and other fortifications to what is already one of the world’s most heavily armed borders.
South Korea’s military has said North Korean soldiers crossed the border’s military demarcation line 50 times this year during fortification work, and that it responded with warning shots and broadcasts.
Photo: Yonhap via AP
Seoul has shown greater urgency to ease tensions after the Sept. 21 mine blasts at the border, which the South’s military concluded were caused by North Korean mines planted south of the military demarcation line.
“Our Ministry of National Defense officially proposes to North Korean authorities that South-North military talks be held to mutually confirm the exact location of the ground military demarcation line between the South and the North, discuss the restoration of military communication lines, and discuss measures to prevent accidental clashes in border areas,” South Korean Deputy Minister for Defense Policy Kim Hong-Cheol said, adding that Seoul was also open to three-way talks involving the UN Command.
The proposal came days after Kim Jong-un’s powerful sister visited front-line areas where North Korean troops are reinforcing the border. During her visit, she renewed a threat to retaliate against any South Korean provocation aimed at the fortification work.
The North planned to activate border loudspeakers for anti-Seoul propaganda broadcasts and has placed unspecified “new counter means” on alert along the border, she said.
She blamed the South for firing warning shots and broadcasting warnings toward North Korean soldiers fortifying the border under what she called a false pretext that they were crossing the demarcation line.
South Korean officials have said North Korea’s recent border activities have highlighted the Koreas’ disagreement over exactly where the military demarcation line lies. The line was drawn up under the 1953 armistice that stopped the fighting of the Korean War, and some decades-old boundary markers have been lost over time.
Kim said leaving the dispute over the military demarcation line unresolved would increase the risk of accidental clashes, because troops from both sides act on their own understanding of the line. “
The recent increase in North Korean activities along the military demarcation line, as well as our warning broadcasts and warning shots, is also related to this situation,” he said.
North Korean army marshal Pak Jong Chon denied that North Korean soldiers were breaching the border during fortification work, saying “our army knows where our borderline is better than any others.”
He accused the South of making “deliberate, premeditated and absurd” claims to shift blame over the rising tensions and threatened an “overwhelming response” to South Korean provocations.

European, Mideast ministers hold talks in Istanbul
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:40:03 UTC
01:40:03 KST

Foreign ministers from eight European and Middle Eastern countries yesterday met in Istanbul in an unprecedented format for talks on the Strait of Hormuz and crises across the Middle East.
Ministers from the UK, France and Germany — the so-called E3 — as well as Italy met counterparts from the newly created R4 group comprising Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt to discuss the Palestinians, developments in Yemen and Hormuz, and ways to end the Russia-Ukraine war, a Turkish Ministry of Foreign Affairs source said.
The talks began at an Istanbul hotel overlooking the Bosphorus after the separate meetings of European top diplomats and regional countries, the source added.
Photo: Reuters
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband’s office said the Istanbul talks would essentially revolve around “the Strait of Hormuz and the situation in Saudi Arabia.”
Miliband “will advocate for a diplomatic solution to the [Hormuz] crisis that restores full navigational rights and freedoms,” it said.
He would also stress “how Iranian tactics are being replicated across the region, with attacks on Saudi Arabia further destabilizing the region and increasing pressure on vital waterways and global chokepoints, such as Bab al-Mandeb and the Suez Canal,” it added.
France confirmed the talks on “the Iranian crisis in its various ramifications,” hailing it as a first “in this format... against a backdrop of extreme instability and uncertainty in the region.”
The meeting aims to “strengthen coordination between Europeans and Middle Eastern countries in the face of crises that we did not choose and that affect us all,” the French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs said.
Turkish Minister of Foreign Affairs Hakan Fidan is hosting the meeting as Turkey steps up efforts to bolster its regional role.
Fidan praised regional cooperation, saying: “Lasting solutions cannot be imposed from outside.”
During the talks, Fidan was expected to stress that regional security requires countries in the region to “assume responsibility” and that Turkey prioritizes cooperation mechanisms based on “regional ownership,” Turkish officials said.
He was also expected to say that “existing disputes should not be allowed to feed one another, conflicts should not be allowed to spread to new areas and regional tensions should not be allowed to turn into broader instability,” they said.
Fidan was expected to call for increased international pressure on Israel over settlement expansion and what Ankara describes as “settler terrorism,” and reiterate Turkey’s support for Saudi Arabia’s security in the face of Houthi attacks and underline the need to safeguard freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandeb.
The Black Sea was also expected to feature prominently, with Fidan highlighting Turkey’s efforts to prevent the Russia-Ukraine war from spilling into the region.

NTU opens chip facilities
to university researchers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:40:02 UTC
01:40:02 KST

National Taiwan University (NTU) has established open semiconductor research facilities that give researchers access to equipment for chip fabrication, development, analysis and testing.
The facilities were established under the National Science and Technology Council’s (NSTC) Taiwan Chip-based Industrial Innovation Program (CBI), allowing researchers from other universities to use the equipment to create an open semiconductor research and development environment.
The NSTC has identified gaps in the resources available for university-led semiconductor research and invested NT$300 million (US$9.2 million) over three years to establish 60 key facilities and pieces of equipment at seven semiconductor research institutes nationwide, CBI convener and National Chi Nan University president Wu Tung-hsing (武東星) said.
Photo: Cheng I-hwa, AFP
NTU contributed NT$100 million toward 11 of the facilities and has made them available to academics, students and researchers through its Web site, Wu said.
The CBI program has helped integrate semiconductor-related resources at universities, while NTU’s participation has helped bring its research capabilities in line with those of leading universities overseas, NTU College of Advanced Technology dean Wu Chih-i (吳志毅) said.
NTU has a cleanroom that has been used by more than 12,000 people over the past three years. Usage increased from 7.5 percent in 2024 to 23.8 percent this year, NTU professor Chen Chien-fu (陳建甫) said.
The university has electron-beam lithography equipment with a resolution of up to 8 nanometers, atomic layer deposition and etching systems, and equipment for measuring nanomaterials and semiconductor devices, Chen said.
The program has also contributed to research published by NTU professors, including a paper published in Nature on July 1 titled “Directly probing the carrier transfer length in 2D-material transistors.”
A team led by Lee Min-hung (李敏鴻) has also developed a hafnium zirconium oxide nanocapacitor that combines energy storage, waste-heat power generation and active chip cooling, providing a potential new approach to energy and thermal management for future chips.
NTU said it has approached Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co, Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing Corp, Etron Technology, Ennostar Corp, Radiant Opto-Electronics Corp, Innolux Corp and Materials Analysis Technology about collaborations based on its research.
The collaborations could be worth a combined NT$84 million, it said.
The university is also working with international partners, including Pennsylvania State University, on cross-border research and training for semiconductor talent, it added.

Gilgeous-Alexander’s 20-point streak comes to end
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:40:01 UTC
01:40:01 KST

Shai Gilgeous-Alexander on Thursday scored just 17 points to snap an NBA-record streak, but the Oklahoma City Thunder knocked off the Denver Nuggets 96-84 at home.
Gilgeous-Alexander had scored 20 or more points in an NBA-record 141 consecutive games. He had not been held below 20 points in the regular season since Oct. 30, 2024.
Gilgeous-Alexander had a chance to extend the streak, but with less than two minutes remaining and Oklahoma City up by 17, Nuggets coach David Adelman emptied his bench following a timeout.
Photo: Alonzo Adams / Imagn Images via Reuters
The reigning two-time NBA Most Valuable Player did not wait for direction from Thunder coach Mark Daigneault, taking his place on the bench to officially end the streak.
Up ti that point, Gilgeous-Alexander had been making a strong push toward keeping the streak alive with 10 fourth-quarter points.
Oklahoma City had not led since going up 3-0 in the opening seconds until Ajay Mitchell’s transition layup with just over two minutes remaining in the third quarter.
In the closing seconds of the third quarter, Gilgeous-Alexander raced up the court after a rebound from Jaylin Williams and drained a three-pointer in transition to put the Thunder up by six.
Gilgeous-Alexander was initially called for a foul on Nikola Jokic’s three-point heave as time expired in the quarter, which would have given Jokic three free throws, but the play was challenged and the foul call was overturned.
Gilgeous-Alexander missed all seven shots he attempted in the first half and did not get on the board at all until sinking a pair of free throws with less than two minutes remaining.
He quickly broke that stretch without a field goal in the third quarter, but it was not until that three-pointer late in the period that he found an offensive rhythm.
It did not matter, though, as the Thunder forced 13 second-half turnovers and turned them into 19 points.
Jalen Williams led Oklahoma City with 21 points, while Chet Holmgren had 12 points and 17 rebounds.
In Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, the 76ers erased a 29-point deficit to stun the Cleveland Cavaliers 114-106 in LeBron James’s first home game since landing in Philly as a free agent.
Tyrese Maxey scored 32 points and Joel Embiid added 24 — including a jump shot with 6 minutes, 54 seconds left to play that gave the Sixers their first lead of the night — one they did not relinquish on the way to an epic comeback.
Former Celtics star Jaylen Brown, the Sixers’ other big off-season acquisition, scored 21 points and pulled down eight rebounds, while four-time NBA champion James added 17 points, 10 rebounds and five assists to help the 76ers author their biggest comeback of the play-by-play era that started in 1996.
It was also the biggest comeback of James’ career. The league’s all-time leading scorer called it a good win — but not a position he wants to be in often.
“You don’t want to rely on that,” he said. “I think it’s great to know [that] deep down we’re not going to have that quit mentality. You never want to look around and say guys gave up, but you don’t want to put yourself in too many of those situations.”
Cleveland, disappointed not to land hometown hero James after he announced he was leaving the Los Angeles Lakers after eight seasons, appeared to be on a mission to show him what he missed.
Donovan Mitchell scored 22 of his 32 points in the first half as the Cavs seized control against a 76ers team struggling to find a rhythm and protect the ball.
Philadelphia center Joel Embiid looked creaky, and James had five of the Sixers’ 15 first-half turnovers — which led to 22 Cavs points and provoked boos from Philly fans whose hopes of a title run have been raised by the arrivals of James and Brown.
The boos turned to raucous cheers as the re-energized 76ers opened the third quarter on an 11-0 run. They cut the lead to single digits on back-to-back baskets from Maxey that pulled them within 80-73.
The Cavs were struggling to regroup. Maxey reduced the deficit to two points with a running finger roll layup with 2 minutes, 33 seconds left in the third before Cleveland reeled off six straight points to take a 90-82 lead into the fourth quarter.
However, the 76ers kept coming. They outscored the Cavaliers 60-37 in the second half, clamping down defensively and giving up just two turnovers.

China orders all-out rescue after quake in Tibet kills 16
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:40:01 UTC
01:40:01 KST

China yesterday ordered an “all-out” rescue effort in a remote area of Tibet after an earthquake killed at least 16 people and injured dozens more, state media reported.
Footage showed rescue workers clambering in the dark through some of the 339 houses that Xinhua said collapsed or were damaged in Thursday evening’s magnitude 7.0 quake.
Seventy-six people were injured, 11 of them seriously, and more than 12,000 residents were evacuated following the quake, Xinhua reported.
Photo: Xinhua via AP
Hundreds of rescue workers and police were deployed, as well as sniffer dogs and equipment, to locate people under the rubble, CCTV said, adding that more than 300 soldiers were also mobilized.
The epicenter was in Baqing County, state media said.
One resident told local media that her family had just gone to bed when her home shook, knocking over objects, and that they “rushed outside without even taking the time to get dressed.”
“My legs were shaking the entire time I was heading downstairs, and by the time I reached the bottom, I was so terrified that I burst into tears,” the woman said.
Residents “are afraid to return to their homes,” she said. “They set up tents along the roadside or spent the night in their cars.”
CCTV also showed emergency personnel with helmets carrying a person and shining flashlights on damaged buildings, some with collapsed roofs.
Tibet is largely inaccessible to foreign journalists and Chinese authorities are the only source of official information.
Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) said the tremor caused “significant casualties” and took place at a “high-altitude location” in cold weather.
We “must go all-out to carry out search-and-rescue operations and do our utmost to treat the injured, so as to minimize casualties,” Xinhua quoted Xi as saying.
In Taiwan, the Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) yesterday expressed condolences to China over the deadly earthquake and urged Taiwanese in the area to stay safe.
The Straits Exchange Foundation was trying to contact Taiwanese in the affected area to check on their safety, the MAC said.
The government’s registration system for Taiwanese traveling to China, Hong Kong and Macau showed that 164 people were in Tibet, the council said, urging Taiwanese to stay safe.
Additional reporting by CNA

Unemployment drops to 3.36 percent: DGBAS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:40:00 UTC
01:40:00 KST

The nation’s unemployment rate fell to 3.36 percent last month, the lowest recorded for the month in 26 years, data released by the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics (DGBAS) showed yesterday.
The rate fell 0.05 percentage points from August as more fresh graduates found jobs, the first decline after rising for three consecutive months since June, the DGBAS said.
The DGBAS attributed the decline to fewer first-time job seekers, as well as a drop in the number of people who left their jobs, down by 3,000 and 2,000 respectively.
Photo: CNA
After seasonal adjustments, the unemployment rate rose 0.01 percentage points from August to 3.33 percent, the data showed.
The number of unemployed people last month fell by 6,000 from August to 405,000, down 2,000 from the same month last year, the agency said.
By age group, people aged 15 to 24 had the highest unemployment rate at 11.59 percent, as most were first-time job seekers adjusting to the workplace, the DGBAS said.
The rate was 5.69 percent among those aged 25 to 29 and 3.40 percent among those aged 30 to 34, while it was below 3 percent among those aged 35 to 64.
From January to last month, the average number of unemployed people was 402,000, down 1,000 from the same period a year earlier, the data showed.
Meanwhile, employment declined to 12.045 million in last year, down 21,000 from August but up 8,000 from a year earlier. The average employment in the first nine months was 12.044 million, up 20,000 from the same period last year, the DGBAS said.
The labor force participation rate was 59.59 percent last month, down 0.1 percentage point from August, but still higher than a year earlier. The average rate for the first nine months was also 59.59 percent, up 0.20 percentage points from the same period last year.

Student protesters seek to unseat Serbia ruling party
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:39:59 UTC
01:39:59 KST

After nearly two years of protests, student activist Masa Perepeliuc believes Serbia’s grassroots movement can end more than 14 years of rule by the governing party in elections tomorrow.
“I am sure we will win, and I am sure that on the 26th, we will wake up in a free Serbia,” the 21-year-old political science student said ahead of the snap vote.
For Perepeliuc and thousands of student activists, the election marks the culmination of a campaign against a government they accuse of deep-rooted corruption.
Photo: AFP
The movement emerged after 16 people were killed when a concrete canopy collapsed at Novi Sad’s newly renovated train station in November 2024.
The tragedy sparked some of Serbia’s largest protests since the fall of former Serbian president Slobodan Milosevic in 2000 and snowballed into a political challenge to former president Aleksandar Vucic and his right-wing populist Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which has held power since 2012.
Most of the 250 candidates on the Student List have never held public office, with many coming from academia and professional circles rather than party politics.
The movement remains largely leaderless, with assemblies based around university faculties voting to select candidates.
Vucic, by contrast, has concentrated power and cultivated an image as an indispensable statesman, walking a diplomatic tightrope between the EU and Russia.
“We are not looking for a new leader around whom another cult of personality will be built,” the students’ Web site states.
Radomir Saicic, a candidate on the student list, said the movement offered an alternative to the “political games” of the past.
“This is a wave of popular discontent, hope and faith in victory that cannot be stopped,” the chemistry professor said.
The students have faced a formidable ruling-party machine backed by dozens of pro-government media outlets, including tabloids that regularly target opponents.
Saicic said activists had been wiretapped, followed, arrested or harassed.
Dozens of protesters have been detained, some accused of plotting to overthrow the constitutional order.
Cars have ploughed into demonstrations several times, while masked men have violently confronted protesters.
Earlier this year, digital rights group SHARE Foundation said the phones of people linked to the movement had been infected with sophisticated spyware, although authorities have denied any knowledge of it.
Vucic, who resigned last month to run for prime minister, has repeatedly called the movement a foreign-backed coup attempt, a claim widely echoed by supportive media.
Serbia lacks reliable independent polling, and surveys have produced widely differing results.
Right-leaning think tank New Serbian Political Thought published a poll this week putting the student list ahead of the SNS by 44.5 percent to 42.7 percent.
However a poll last month by Faktor Plus, seen as close to the authorities, put the SNS ahead at 48.6 percent and the students at 37.1 percent.
Political scientist Dusan Vucicevic nevertheless expects the students to win more than 40 percent of the vote, significantly better than most opposition groups under SNS rule.
He attributed their appeal to occupying the political center and largely sidestepping divisive foreign policy issues, particularly relations with Russia.
Students have organized some of Serbia’s biggest demonstrations in decades, including a rally last year in Belgrade that drew about 300,000 people, an independent count said.
As they marched across the country, residents in smaller towns greeted them with food, flags and fireworks.
“They saw with their own eyes that we were coming, knocking on their doors and passing by, and they came out to greet us,” organizational sciences student Neda Simonovic said.
The movement has promised measures ranging from improved healthcare to more affordable housing, but its central theme remains the fight against corruption.
Saicic said students and experts drafted a 1,200-page governing program, but it has yet to be published.
Critics have questioned the movement’s opposition to sanctions on Russia, while it has not fully clarified its position on Serbia’s bid to join the EU.
Vucicevic warned that even an election victory would leave the students facing immense challenges.
“They will certainly have a great deal of work ahead of them to turn Serbia into a well-governed and democratic state,” he said.

September industrial production rises 19 percent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:39:56 UTC
01:39:56 KST

Industrial production rose more than 19 percent year-on-year last month, driven by the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, marking the 31st consecutive month of growth, the Ministry of Economic Affairs said yesterday.
The industrial production index rose 19.17 percent from a year earlier to 140.76 last month, while the manufacturing subindex, which accounts for more than 90 percent of total production, rose 20.21 percent to 143.31, ministry data showed.
In the third quarter, industrial production rose 21.95 percent year-on-year, with the manufacturing subindex up 23.05 percent, while in the first nine months of the year, industrial production grew 20.53 percent, with the manufacturing subindex up 21.83 percent, the data showed.
Photo: CNA
The export-oriented manufacturing sector continued to benefit from strong global demand for AI applications, high-performance computing devices and cloud services, the ministry said in a statement.
Launches of new consumer electronics by international brands also boosted Taiwan’s information and electronic components industries, while also lifting non-tech manufacturers, the statement said.
Last month, production in the electronic components industry rose 23.62 percent year-on-year, led by 12-inch wafer foundries, integrated circuit (IC) packaging and testing firms, memorychip suppliers, IC designers and IC substrate makers, it said.
Production in the computer, electronic and optical products industry soared 45.92 percent last month from a year earlier as AI development pushed up demand for AI servers, switches, semiconductor inspection equipment and solid-state drives, the statement said.
That marked the 39th straight month of growth, the ministry said.
With semiconductor suppliers installing equipment to expand capacity, production in the machinery industry rose 26.02 percent year-on-year, while base metal production rose 1.39 percent on a recovery in demand, it said.
Bucking the trend, production in the chemical material and fertilizer industry fell 4.29 percent year-on-year due to slower demand and reduced output during annual maintenance, it said.
Production of autos and auto parts rose 2.35 percent year-on-year, driven by higher output of electric passenger cars and all-terrain vehicles, it said.
Looking ahead, the global AI boom and year-end holiday shopping season are expected to continue supporting Taiwan’s industrial production for the rest of the year, although geopolitical tensions and major economies’ trade policies could continue to create uncertainty for the global economy, the ministry said.
Manufacturing production is expected to expand by 20.5 to 24.2 percent year-on-year this month, it added.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:39:55 UTC
01:39:55 KST

Fiercely proud of its culinary traditions, India is increasingly open to foreign influences, with French cooking schools attracting students eager to make their mark on the country’s growing fine-dining sector.
“Ten or 15 years ago, there were far fewer young people dreaming of becoming chefs,” said Aabhas Jain, director of bakery and pastry training at Ecole Ducasse, a French culinary school also operating in India. “But with the rise of social media... today’s students have greater ambitions in this profession.”
In the world’s most populous country, the need for high-end hospitality workers is immense, fueled by economic growth and the rise of a middle class that travels more and increasingly eats at plush establishments.
Photo: AFP
“There are plenty of job opportunities,” said Saurav Chhabra, head of French hotel school Vatel’s Indian campus, which has been based in Gurugram since 2015. “Employers’ expectations are very high, particularly in five-star hotel chains.”
Culinary and pastry courses, once relatively rare in India, have proliferated over the past decade, with foreign private schools helping drive its high-end hospitality sector.
Such is the enthusiasm that France is considering opening vocational schools, notably in Puducherry, the former French colonial port in India’s southeast.
Ecole Ducasse has more than 600 students, most from affluent backgrounds.
Indian chefs who have worked at prestigious restaurants, including overseas, teach their respective specialties: Indian, European, Mediterranean and Asian cuisine, as well as bakery and pastrymaking.
Siddhant Marwah joined the school to acquire “French techniques that represent the quintessence of culinary expertise.”
French and Indian cuisines share techniques such as “braising, blanching and slow cooking in stews,” he said as he put the finishing touches to a gratin dauphinois — a dish of sliced potatoes baked in cream.
While France boasts its beef bourguignon, India is not to be outdone with goat nihari, a meat dish cooked for hours in a spicy broth.
Drawn by the opportunities for travel and meeting people that a career as a chef offers, Marwah dreams of opening his own restaurant in India.
Amitabh Sukhwal has just enrolled at Vatel, whose tuition fees are considerably lower than those at Ecole Ducasse.
The school has about 120 students, many from modest backgrounds.
Sukhwal, who calls himself a “lover of the French language,” plans to go to France in four years to pursue a master’s degree, gain experience abroad and then draw on it to open a hotel in India.
He learned French through interactions with guests at the small hotel run by his parents in Chittorgarh, India, and is now honing his skills at his new school, where French-language classes are compulsory.
After working for many years in India’s luxury hotels, chef Shikha Gupta, who teaches bakery and pastrymaking at Vatel, is pleased to see her classes have “as many men as women.”
“Over the past 10 to 12 years, attitudes have changed and many women have chosen to enter the culinary profession,” Jain said. “We now see near parity, or even a ratio of 60 percent women to 40 percent men.”

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:39:55 UTC
01:39:55 KST

The National Police Agency (NPA) has conducted a body armor wear test, collecting anonymous feedback as part of the evaluation process to award a NT$1.1 billion (US$33.8 million) contract for new tactical vests.
The agency said it expects to place a total order of 55,556 to equip police officers nationwide.
The NPA has increased the maximum allowable per-unit cost of tactical vests from NT$12,000 previously to NT$30,000, following complaints about the quality of standard-issue armor, it said.
Photo copied by Chiu Chun-fu, Taipei Times
The agency said it earlier this year procured 1,000 tactical vests under the old budget constraints and fielded them to patrol officers, who reported that their armor was stiff, uncomfortable and ill-fitting.
In response, NPA Director-General Chang Jung-hsin (張榮興) ordered the agency to open a bid for replacement tactical vests that offer improved wearer comfort, fit and protection, the agency said.
The armor must offer ballistic and anti-stab protection, as patrol officers come in close contact with subjects during traffic stops, random drug or alcohol tests, and incident responses, it said.
More than 10 Taiwanese and other Asian, European, and US manufacturers that expressed interest qualified for the bid, the NPA said.
The agency would give no preference to any domestic or foreign company in the selection process, it said.
As part of the evaluation, 60 police volunteers were gathered earlier this month to wear and grade the body armor examples submitted by the manufacturers, with a focus on ergonomics, fit and comfort, it said.
The volunteers provided anonymized feedback to the NPA’s logistics section, it said, adding that it would also implement changes to regulations to allow body armor to be part of personal equipment instead of a pooled resource for a precinct or beat.

MAGA at the Acropolis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:39:54 UTC
01:39:54 KST

On a visit to Athens, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio extolled ancient Greece as the foundation of Western civilization and drew inspiration for the US today as the leader of the West. Rubio’s speech at the Pnyx, a hill west of the Acropolis where democracy was first practiced, was a bold and eloquent attempt to trace MAGA’s ideological roots back to Athenian democracy, as well as to Christendom, important discoveries and imperial conquests. And it was about “us” and “them” — the West and the rest.
According to Rubio, the values that made the West great and dominant include “fierce individuality and relentless ambition,” “daring exploration and invention,” and an “insatiable curiosity about the world and the principles by which it operates.”
Those are all well and good, but Rubio made no mention of cooperation, solidarity or the common good. Indeed, he and the entire MAGA movement seem to view human interaction as a constant fight in which the best (or the strongest) wins — and the rest are forgotten.
The same logic applies to global affairs. In Rubio’s own words, the US has chosen “the unapologetic pursuit of national power.” If the goal is to save Western civilization and maintain its dominance, international relations become a zero-sum game — except for the transatlantic alliance, which Rubio thinks must be bolstered.
Similarly, there should be no more ceding of sovereignty to “global bureaucracies” — presumably the UN, the EU and the International Criminal Court (ICC), which have all said or done something that angered US President Donald Trump, although Rubio chose not to name them. To match deeds with words, Rubio announced sweeping new sanctions against the ICC only a few days after leaving Athens and following the news that a former ICC judge had won the Nobel Peace Prize. Unsurprisingly, Rubio’s speech made no mention of international law.
Although Rubio’s speech was delivered thousands of miles from the US, it was largely addressed to an American audience — a society deeply divided and hugely unequal. The Acropolis offered a dramatic backdrop for a political leader trying to bolster not only MAGA’s standing, but also his own. However, unlike other Trump administration officials, who have subjected Europeans to insults and threats, Rubio has taken a different tack, emphasizing the shared civilizational inheritance.
In his speech, Rubio encouraged the US and its European allies to embrace thumos, which he translated as “the fire of passion, strength, courage, pride” and, in his telling, the driving force behind the success of ancient Athens.
However, had he read the ancient Greek historian Thucydides’ account of the Peloponnesian War, he might have come across another Greek word: hubris, a source of the internal political decay and imperial overreach that brought down ancient Athens and its democracy.
Instead of looking inward, Rubio and the rest of the Trump administration have focused on Europe. In their view, the continent is in decline and facing the stark prospect of “civilizational erasure,” as described in the National Security Strategy released by the White House last year.
The list of supposed sins is long: Europe has been free-riding on the US for defense (which, alas, is true) and is unable to stand its ground against the big powers, including the US. Europeans are too apologetic about their colonial past and talk too much about minority rights, welfare policies, digital regulation and climate change. They have been “invaded” by immigrants and influenced by “woke” culture. And, most importantly, Europeans have ceded too much of their sovereignty to the EU bureaucracy in Brussels. In short, they represent everything that MAGA holds in contempt.
However, Europe has learned some lessons from the carnage of two world wars about the unrestrained projection of national power. There are few missionaries left on the continent. And European governments have come to understand that there is strength in unity when confronting an increasingly anarchic and highly asymmetric world.
What does Rubio propose instead to Europeans? To simply relegate responsibility to the leader of the West and become obedient followers? And where would that leave non-Western countries? What conclusions are they meant to draw?
The world is not returning to a bipolar order like that during the Cold War. The signs of multipolarity are everywhere. Rubio’s ideologically loaded speech, delivered in a setting evoking the origin of the “West,” would not change that.
Loukas Tsoukalis is president of ELIAMEP, a Greek foreign-policy think tank, and an affiliate professor at the Paris School of International Affairs at Sciences Po.
Copyright: Project Syndicate

Manufacturing sentiment rises to a 55-month high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:39:53 UTC
01:39:53 KST

Business sentiment in the export-oriented manufacturing sector rose to its highest level in 55 months last month, buoyed by the global artificial intelligence (AI) boom, the Taiwan Institute of Economic Research (TIER, 台經院) said yesterday, while warning of potential risks ahead.
The manufacturing sector’s composite index, which gauges business sentiment among local manufacturers, rose 0.50 points from August to 101.39, its highest level since February 2022, data compiled by TIER showed.
The composite index for the service sector fell 3.15 points month-on-month to 92.65, while the index for the construction industry rebounded from a previous decline, rising 2.81 points from August to 110.42, the data showed.
Photo: Lin Chin-hua, Taipei Times
TIER, one of Taiwan’s leading economic think tanks, said that manufacturers continued to benefit from massive global investments in AI infrastructure and inventory buildup by international brands ahead of new product launches, including the iPhone 18 series and iPhone Duo.
A surge in international crude oil prices also pushed up the prices of petrochemical products, while the completion of annual maintenance by some non-tech industries helped boost production, the institute said.
In TIER’s survey last month, 26.8 percent of manufacturing respondents said business conditions had improved that month, up from 19.5 percent in August, while 20.3 percent said conditions had worsened, down from 25.6 percent a month earlier.
However, expectations for the next six months weakened.
In the survey, 24.0 percent of respondents expected business conditions to improve, down 3.1 percentage points from August, while 19.8 percent expected them to deteriorate, up 1.8 percentage points.
Gordon Sun (孫明德), director of TIER’s Economic Forecasting Center, said that despite support from the AI boom and the peak season for consumer electronics, Taiwan’s economy still faced risks, including the possibility of the US Federal Reserve taking a more hawkish stance to curb inflation.
A Fed rate hike would likely strengthen the US dollar against the Taiwan dollar, potentially prompting foreign institutional investors to pull funds out of Taiwan and causing volatility in local financial markets, Sun said.
Military conflicts in the Middle East could push crude oil prices higher and prompt upstream petrochemical suppliers to raise prices, although such increases could weaken demand from downstream buyers, Sun said.
Sun also noted concerns about a possible slowdown in AI development, which have recently weighed on global stock markets.
In the service sector, recent financial market volatility has made businesses more cautious, although the food and beverage industry continued to benefit from rising demand, TIER said.
In construction, easing of selective credit controls in the middle of last month by Taiwan’s central bank supported the property market, but the industry still faces a large inventory of unsold homes, the think tank said.

Taipei faces double aging crisis: data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:39:46 UTC
01:39:46 KST

Taipei is facing a double aging challenge, with nearly one-quarter of its population aged 65 or older and nearly three-quarters of its homes more than 30 years old, government statistics show.
In August, 24.76 percent of Taipei residents were aged 65 or older, the highest proportion among Taiwan’s 22 administrative regions. In the second quarter, 74.47 percent of the city’s homes were more than 30 years old, the second-highest proportion, real-estate professionals said.
A total of 17 of Taiwan’s 22 regions have become super-aged societies, where people aged 65 or older account for at least 20 percent of the population. Only Taoyuan, Taichung, Hsinchu City, Hsinchu County and Lienchiang County are yet to reach that threshold.
Photo: Taipei Times
Colliers International Taiwan head of occupier services Huang Shu-wei (黃舒衛) said that Taipei, one of the areas hardest hit by the double aging problem, must look beyond the age of its housing stock and address associated safety risks.
Policies that prioritize redevelopment benefits while overlooking critical social issues, including public safety and health, are inadequate, Huang said.
The aging of the city’s population is irreversible, and the departure of younger residents is creating a sharp demographic imbalance, he said, adding that current policy measures are producing diminishing returns.
The immediate priority is to move beyond a narrow real estate perspective and coordinate solutions across sectors, Huang said. The government should improve coordination among agencies and integrate measures such as reverse mortgages, senior-care trusts and insurance to turn equity tied up in aging homes into a source of income.
Rental management and housing exchange services could also help create a safer living environment for residents of all ages, he said.
Sinyi Realty research project manager Tseng Ching-te (曾敬德) said that Taipei developed earlier than many other areas and faces a particularly serious problem of older residents living in old buildings.
The government has in the past few years promoted elevator installations in apartment buildings to make access easier for older residents. However, not every building has enough space for an elevator, Tseng said, adding that the government should provide more assistance to affected residents.
Housing Trend Institute chief executive Ho Shih-chang (何世昌) said Taipei’s high housing prices have made it difficult for younger and middle-aged residents to buy homes in the city.
Resale apartments in Taipei average about NT$800,000 (US$24,609) per ping (3.3m2), while presale homes often cost more than NT$1 million per ping, Ho said.
As a result, many younger buyers look to Keelung, New Taipei City and Taoyuan, where transport links allow them to commute to Taipei, Ho said.
This is one factor contributing to the declining proportion of younger and middle-aged residents in the capital, he added.
Meanwhile, the Ministry of the Interior’s Real Estate Information Platform showed that the average age of homes nationwide reached 34.46 years in the second quarter.
Of Taiwan’s 22 regions, only Taoyuan, Hsinchu County and Kinmen had an average housing age of less than 30 years, meaning homes in the other 19 jurisdictions are at least three decades old on average.
The data showed that three areas have average housing ages exceeding 40 years: Yunlin County at 41.31 years, Chiayi County at 41.32 years and Penghu County at 44.33 years.
The figures point to a growing stock of aging homes, raising concerns among real estate professionals that more older adults in Taiwan would find themselves living in increasingly aging properties, critics said.
Huang said that the widespread aging of homes in urban areas reflects two major gaps in housing supply: the lack of mechanisms to phase out aging properties and a shortage of undeveloped land available for construction in metropolitan areas.
These constraints have slowed the supply of new homes, leaving too few newly built properties to replace older buildings and bringing the housing market’s renewal cycle to a near standstill, he said.
He added that older residents and aging homes are increasingly concentrated in prime urban districts, where jobs, healthcare and daily amenities are clustered in established neighborhoods.
Many seniors are reluctant to move after years of living in familiar surroundings, further reinforcing the trend of older people remaining in aging city centers, he said.
The challenges of living in aging homes — including safety risks, costly repairs and limited accessibility — have become widespread concerns among older adults, Ho said.
As a result, more seniors are opting to buy homes in elevator-equipped buildings, while walk-up apartments are gradually falling out of favor. This shift is widening the price gap between apartments without elevators and buildings with elevators in urban areas, a trend that is expected to spread from major metropolitan areas to the rest of Taiwan, he said.

Chinese promoter of surrogacy deported
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:39:46 UTC
01:39:46 KST

A Chinese influencer who promoted surrogacy-related services for same-sex couples has been deported and fined NT$200,000, the Kaohsiung City Government said yesterday.
The influencer posted videos promoting fan meetups in Taiwan and providing information on how to have a child through assisted reproduction, the Kaohsiung Department of Health said.
The man contravened the Medical Care Act (醫療法), which prohibits entities other than medical institutions from advertising medical services, it said.
Photo courtesy of the National Immigration Agency
He was neither a physician nor a licensed medical institution, it added.
Given his large social media following and wide reach, the penalty was increased to NT$200,000 in accordance with the law, it said.
The Assisted Reproduction Act (人工生殖法) stipulates requirements for medical providers, eligible recipients and procedures, while commercial surrogacy is not permitted, it said.
The department urged people seeking fertility services to consult qualified medical institutions and physicians.
The National Immigration Agency ordered the man, who was arrested in Kaohsiung on Thursday, to be deported.
The man had entered Taiwan on a tourist visa, but engaged in activities inconsistent with the purpose of his visit, in violation of regulations governing mainland Chinese visitors, the agency said.
The man, known as “Berlinsun” on social media, has more than 1 million followers on Instagram and Douyin.
Local media said he and his partner live in Malaysia and have talked about their experience of having children through egg donation and surrogacy on social media.

‘Cockroaches,’ Gen Z and Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:39:44 UTC
01:39:44 KST

In Hong Kong in 2019, “cockroach” was an insult directed at people protesting a proposed extradition bill. In India this year, controversial “cockroach” remarks by the country’s chief justice provoked a backlash among young people and inspired the satirical Cockroach Janta Party.
Young activists turned a term of derision into an icon of political defiance.
When young citizens doubt that education, hard work and institutions can deliver a meaningful future, even an insult can become a language of political solidarity for Gen Z.
India and Hong Kong are profoundly different, despite their shared British colonial history. India is the world’s largest democracy. Hong Kong’s 2019 uprising unfolded amid an escalating struggle over Beijing’s authority under the framework of “one country, two systems.”
Yet both situations raise an important question for Taiwan as it approaches its local elections on Nov. 28: What convinces young citizens that democratic institutions still respond to them?
For Hong Kongers, “cockroach” carries a painful memory. During the 2019 anti-extradition movement, the term was used to dehumanize protesters. A citizen has rights and legitimate grievances. A cockroach is a pest to be removed. Once authorities reduce people with grievances to problems to be eliminated, coercion becomes easier to justify in the name of restoring order.
India’s activists turned that logic on its head, recasting an insult meant to diminish them into a source of collective empowerment. A generation raised on memes and social media understands something important about power: Politics involves not only control over institutions and streets, but also contests over words, images and identities.
Taiwan’s democratic transition has shown that civic engagement occurs beyond the voting booth. Its vibrant civil society has made public space and youth participation integral to democratic life. The challenge for democracy is not simply telling citizens to vote, but giving them reason to believe that participation matters.
One striking characteristic of Hong Kong’s 2019 uprising was the prominence of educated young people. They formed human chains, organized strikes, circulated information, created visual symbols and mobilized through decentralized networks. Their frustration was never reducible to economic discontent. Although Hong Kong’s political crisis concerned the erosion of freedom and autonomy, it exposed a generation increasingly uncertain about its future.
For generations, education has sustained a promise of social mobility across Asia: Study hard, earn the right credentials, compete successfully and advancement should follow.
What happens when that bargain falters?
Artificial intelligence is disrupting expectations about employment just as younger generations confront intense competition for professional work.
An unemployed or underemployed graduate does not automatically become an activist. However, something changes when enough educated people view their predicament as structural. Private disappointments can evolve into collective grievances.
The underlying crisis is one of trust. If education no longer provides a reasonable expectation of advancement while established institutions seem unable to respond, young people might question the credibility of the system itself.
Hong Kong’s protesters famously embraced the principle of “be water,” using digital networks to exchange information, coordinate action and challenge official narratives. Young Indians inhabit the same technological world, in which political participation need not begin with joining a party or reading a manifesto. Sometimes, it begins with a joke.
The cockroach metaphor deserves to be taken seriously. Satire can accomplish something that conventional political rhetoric often cannot: It gives strangers an instantly recognizable language of shared experience.
Social media does not manufacture political discontent. It connects people who previously imagined they were suffering alone. They discover others expressing the same anxieties. A joke becomes a meme. A meme turns into an identity. And an identity can travel from smartphones to public squares.
These forms of mobilization challenge established institutions. Horizontal movements might look leaderless and disorganized to officials accustomed to negotiating with recognized representatives, but decentralization can also make them resilient.
The crucial question is why their message resonates.
India is not Hong Kong and a simple analogy would obscure more than it reveals. After 2020, Beijing’s national security measures sharply narrowed the space for political dissent in Hong Kong. Enforcing compliance is not the same as earning trust.
India has its own tradition of Gandhian nonviolent resistance. Taiwan followed its own path from authoritarian rule to democracy. Their histories differ, but they face a common challenge: Do young citizens still believe their voices matter?
As Taiwan enters another electoral season, the answer matters more than which party wins which municipality.
From Beijing’s Tiananmen protests in 1989 to Hong Kong in 2019 and India today, young people living under very different political systems have turned private frustrations into public demands. Their political language has evolved: Hierarchies give way to networks, manifestos compete with memes and satire travels farther than formal speeches. Even an insult can be reclaimed as an identity.
To embrace a name meant to demean you is to deprive it of some of its power. Humiliation becomes humor; humor creates recognition; recognition builds solidarity.
Taiwan need not repeat another society’s history to learn from it. As Taiwanese prepare for another election day, the lesson from India and Hong Kong is not to fear politically assertive youth, but to ask what gives them reason to invest in the society they will inherit. A democracy’s strength lies not only in the freedom to speak and vote, but in the conviction that speaking and voting can make a difference. Perhaps that is the lesson India’s Gen Z “cockroaches,” and Hong Kong before them, offer Taiwan.
Joseph Tse-Hei Lee is a professor of history at Pace University in New York.

Shen’s usage of the Chinese term is intentional.

Gen Z protest movement could oust Serbia’s strongman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:39:44 UTC
01:39:44 KST

History might not be about to repeat itself in Serbia, but it is beginning to rhyme. Just over a quarter of a century ago, Serbian citizens turned out to vote in large numbers to inflict a historic defeat on the then strongman in Belgrade, Slobodan Milosevic, who was seeking re-election as president. He lost despite his extensive control over the media, the judiciary and the security forces. When he was reluctant to leave office, Serbs poured onto the streets in their hundreds of thousands, finally forcing him to go.
Tomorrow, a new generation could have the decisive voice in an equally fateful election, this time for the national parliament. Today’s strongman, Aleksandar Vucic, resigned as president to fight the election with the aim of swapping the locus of power from the presidency to the prime minister’s office.
However, Vucic, who has been in almost total control of Serbia for 14 years, finds himself on the back foot for the first time since he assumed power, just as Milosevic did in 2000. Like his close friend Viktor Orban, who was decisively beaten in elections earlier this year, Vucic has felt compelled to pull out all the stops to halt the opposition electoral coalition, known as the Student List (SL).
Illustration: Louise Ting
Unlike Orban’s Fidesz party, Vucic’s Serbian Progressive party (SNS) is unlikely to be humiliated in tomorrow’s vote. Opinion polls vary widely — some giving the SL a lead of almost 10 percentage points, others suggesting the race is neck and neck.
Pollsters also suggest that the higher the turnout, the greater the chances for the opposition. Some fear that the aftermath could even be violent.
Vucic is throwing the kitchen sink at the campaign to skew the result his way. He has tightened his grip on the media by supporting a change in ownership of what was until recently the most important independent news group, United Media. Last weekend, 10 prominent journalists from its most important outlet, the TV station N1, resigned in protest against senior editorial appointments believed to favor Vucic and the SNS.
N1 had been key in reporting the rapid rise in support for the student protest movement since it emerged spontaneously in November 2024. Students first took to the streets when the canopy over the main rail station in Novi Sad in the north of Serbia collapsed, killing 16 people. The tragedy occurred just months after a Chinese consortium had finished renovating it in what critics claim was a corrupt deal.
At first, Vucic’s response was to wait until the demonstrations petered out, but despite various attempts to coerce the students to retreat from the streets, the protests grew throughout last year and this year.
In March last year, during a 15-minute period of silence to honor the victims of the Novi Sad disaster, protesters alleged that police deployed a sonic weapon, the US-made LRAD 450XL, causing the crowd to disperse in panic. The government denied the use of the weapon and later the interior ministry filed a criminal complaint against one military analyst over his claim that a sonic weapon was probably used.
The demonstrations have showed no sign of letting up in the past two years. The big challenge facing the students was how to channel the undoubted energy they generated through the movement into a coherent political force capable of challenging Vucic.
The old opposition parties were riven by factionalism and lacking dynamic leadership. However, this summer the students announced they had selected candidates to stand in a new formation, including prominent academics, engineers, workers, cultural figures and students. Their straightforward slogan is “Serbia or the mafia.”
Vucic has responded to the challenge by cranking up the nationalist rhetoric in the past few months in order to mobilize the far right. He has welcomed the support of his neighbor, Milorad Dodik, the de facto leader of Republika Srpska, the Serbian entity in Bosnia. Dodik has long been regarded as Vladimir Putin’s main man in the Balkans and has cozied up to US President Donald Trump, whose associates are investing in a gas pipeline with his help.
Vucic, too, has been cultivating support from Moscow. Personal relations between Putin and the Serbian leader have been strained in the past. Vucic has been supplying Ukraine with a significant amount of munitions while playing his complex game of trying to balance friendly relationships with the west and Russia.
However, with the gloves off, the Serbian leader has become less coy. Another sign of how seriously he views the students’ challenge was his decision to allow the nationalist jamboree of a state funeral for the man known as the “Butcher of Bosnia,” convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic, with the aim of bolstering his support among nationalists.
If despite all this the SL emerges victorious at the election, the shock waves would be felt as powerfully across Europe as they were when Orban was defeated.
Above all, it opens the possibility of a swifter integration with the EU, a move that would be welcomed not just in Brussels, but in London as well. Successive British governments are concerned that the Balkans represents the soft underbelly of European defense where Russia can exert significant pressure.
Since Brexit, Britain’s influence here is limited politically, but it has been active in promoting security cooperation across the region, with NATO and the EU.
Student activists and their supporters have been disappointed by an apparent indifference on the part of the EU to their political struggle and a general perception in the outside world that Serbia’s democracy is a lost cause. Tomorrow, they aim to prove them wrong.
Misha Glenny is a former central Europe correspondent for The Guardian and the BBC.
