SK Hynix cancels IPO of Solidigm unit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:39:43 UTC
01:39:43 KST

SK Hynix Inc yesterday scrapped plans for a potential US$10 billion US listing of its Solidigm unit after facing strong opposition from regulators and shareholders, becoming the latest firm to pull an initial public offering (IPO) while growing investor unease over the artificial intelligence (AI) boom rocks markets.
The retreat followed domestic regulatory scrutiny over concerns that Solidigm’s IPO could dilute share value for minority investors and complicate SK Group’s ownership structure. The South Korean chipmaker, which also halted discussions around pre-IPO investment, in a regulatory filing cited “recent capital market conditions.”
Solidigm, one of the world’s largest makers of flash memory critical to storage in data centers, is the latest high-profile firm to suspend or cancel an IPO. It joins data center developers Firmus Grid Ltd and AirTrunk in pulling back at a time fears of an AI bubble are roiling global markets.
Photo: AFP
However, in SK Hynix’s case, the withdrawal was driven largely by regulatory opposition in South Korea.
The controversy over Solidigm had become a test of Seoul’s efforts to improve corporate governance and minority shareholder protections — addressing the country’s chronic equity undervaluation, known as the “Korea discount.”
The decision is “a major positive for [South] Korean corporate governance,” said Ryan Albert, founder and managing member of Terton Capital. “Shareholders, governance groups and the regulator all weighed in, identifying the core conflict of the group keeping control of Solidigm.”
After the announcement, SK Hynix’s shares rose, defying a broad market slide triggered by a rout in US technology stocks. They had plunged about 60 percent from their June peak, battered by worries over slowing memorychip demand exacerbated by dilution fears.
The company in July completed the biggest-ever US listing by a foreign company, raising US$26.5 billion.
Solidigm had already picked banks including Goldman Sachs Group Inc and Morgan Stanley to work on the offering, looking to raise about US$10 billion, people familiar with the matter have said.
It planned to list as soon as next year, in a deal that would have valued the company at as much as US$100 billion, Bloomberg News has reported.
The market value of SK Hynix’s Seoul-listed shares is about US$679 billion, about half of their June peak.
SK Hynix at the time said that Solidigm was reviewing options to improve its business competitiveness. Now, the company sought to reassure investors that the decision to pull the deal does not reflect changes in the unit’s growth prospects or investment needs.
“In light of recent capital market conditions and share price trends, Solidigm determined that it was necessary to reassess whether an IPO would be the most beneficial option for SK Hynix and its existing shareholders at this time,” the company said in a statement.
The reversal follows concerns by South Korean regulators that the planned offering could amount to a duplicate listing.
Fibonacci Asset Management Global chief executive officer Jung In-yun said that the cancelation was positive for SK Hynix shareholders because it would ease concerns about dilution of the parent company’s economic interest in Solidigm, and the valuation discount associated with listing both a parent and its subsidiary.

Clawing back the cost of living
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:39:42 UTC
01:39:42 KST

With one eye on her baby in a pushchair, Minae Kamata operates an arcade machine in a Tokyo suburb, manipulating a claw to grab not a stuffed toy but a pack of toilet paper.
As inflation weighs on Japanese households, huge arcades on the outskirts of major cities are installing claw machines filled with eggs, rice, laundry detergent and other necessities.
The “shop-and-play destinations” merge essential buying with entertainment so that families do not feel a choice between bringing home the basics and treating themselves to a day out.
Photo: AFP
Kamata, a 25-year-old housewife, said she won her prize after only two tries, at 100 yen (US$0.64) per attempt.
“If you’re a bit lucky, it’s the same as buying at a discount,” she said.
Experts say the trend is a response to Japan’s prolonged wave of inflation, with prices having outpaced wage growth for years.
“Spending on food and everyday products has been continuously declining for five years because these have become targets for budget cuts,” said Naoko Kuga, a consumer behaviour specialist at the NLI Research Institute.
So “retailers are trying to make purchasing fun to encourage buying” and ease a sense of guilt, she added.
THE COSTCO MODEL
Claw machines were already booming in Japan before the inflation wave.
The “prize game” market more than doubled in 10 years to reach 417.7 billion yen (US$2.7 billion) in 2024, and now accounts for nearly 70 percent of arcade revenues, according to the Japan Amusement Industry Association.
In recent years, families in search of everyday items have become a larger part of their clientele.
In Kawasaki, on the southern outskirts of Tokyo, hundreds of machines at a venue operated by the specialist chain Benex are filled with bottles of soda, bags of sweets, and detergent.
“When a family spends 10,000 yen on a day of karaoke or bowling, they have fun and that’s it. But at Benex, you go home with toilet paper, bottles and toys,” said Teruaki Tsuchiya, an executive at Tisco, which operates Benex.
“With inflation, parents are choosing the most cost-effective entertainment option.”
The company, which has five locations in Greater Tokyo and claims over one million visitors a year, scrapped its video games and token machines last year to refocus on claw machines.
It says revenue through household product sales has increased 2.6-fold in two years.
Tsuchiya said the model is similar to chains like Costco or Ikea: large stores on the outskirts of cities, where land is cheaper and loyal customers come by car and spend relatively more.
‘TREAT MYSELF A LITTLE’
Japan’s inflation rate has hovered near the central bank’s two-percent target in recent months — a modest figure for many developed economies but a shock for a country used to decades of stagnant or falling prices.
After “two or three hours” on the machines, Chiaki Sugai, a 56-year-old sushi restaurant employee, pushes a huge cart filled with trophies which cost her nearly 8,000 yen.
“Before, I used to buy a lot of snacks at convenience stores, but now I grab them here,” she said.
Forty-nine-year-old Sachiko Iyokawa also appeared satisfied with her winnings: two boxes of premium eggs, cheaper than in supermarkets.
“Normally I’m careful, but here I treat myself a little,” she said.
Large retailers are jumping on the bandwagon.
Aeon Fantasy, an amusements subsidiary of the sprawling Aeon Group, opened its first area dedicated to food and household prizes targeting mothers in October last year.
It now has seven such spaces and plans to open around 60 by 2030.
“At a time when consumers are highly sensitive to cost, we offer an experience that combines fun with the thrill of getting a good deal,” said Yuya Shiozawa, a manager at Aeon Fantasy.
“We see, for example, customers who, after winning vegetables, go to the supermarket next door to buy ingredients to complete their dinner.”
According to Kuga, the trend should outlast the current period of inflation, as brick-and-mortar retailers seek new reasons to attract customers who are increasingly buying household products via Amazon subscriptions.
She predicted that “stores will multiply initiatives to bring customers in, whether with claw machines or in other forms.”
The Han Kuang exercises in August simulated the repelling of attackers from the People’s Republic of China (PRC). One scenario saw the PRC seizing Taipei International Airport (Songshan airport) in a daring helicopter assault. Oct. 19 to Oct 25 For many in Hsinchu, the cold, dry October winds bring uncomfortable weather. But in the past, rice noodle makers waited all year for these winds. Laid out on bamboo racks by the Keya River (客雅溪), freshly made noodles dried in the wind without compromising their quality or texture. The ideal conditions, it was once said, were 70 percent wind and 30 percent sun. Most producers were concentrated in the Nanshih (南勢) area, which became known as Mifenliao (米粉寮, literally “rice noodle shed”). The idea that we need to walk 10,000 steps a day originated not in medical research but in a 1960s marketing campaign for a pedometer, says Jack McNamara, senior lecturer in clinical exercise physiology at the University of East London. The round number was easy to remember and the idea caught on, despite there being no scientific evidence for 10,000 steps as a specific threshold for health. “When the research community looked into it, they found that there were health benefits, so it didn’t necessarily get thrown out as pseudoscience,” McNamara says. A senior officer with the Taipei Military Police unit responsible for guarding the Boai Special District (博愛特區) — home to key government institutions — has been removed pending an investigation into allegations of abuse and a cover-up of a major security incident, the Military Police Command confirmed yesterday.
MORALE BUSTER
Local media reports said Military Police Colonel Tsai Cheng-chien (蔡正建) was the subject of a joint complaint filed with the Presidential Office and the Ministry of National Defense, accusing him of repeatedly using profanity and insulting personnel during gatherings, undermining morale.
Photo: Taipei Times
The complaint also alleged that during the Han Kuang exercises in October last year and August this year, Tsai failed to report cases of personnel going absent without leave (AWOL) or nearly engaging in self-harm after being berated by him.
It added that a corporal who fell and sustained a bone fracture during a base test in May and a sergeant first class who sustained serious injuries after punching a piece of glass after being reprimanded by Tsai were not taken to hospital by ambulance.
The complaint claimed Tsai wanted to prevent the incidents from being recorded and reported to his superiors.
POOR LEADERSHIP?
The Military Police Command said the allegations pointed to possible mismanagement and poor leadership.
The armed forces would not tolerate mistreatment, concealment of reports or abuse of authority, it said, adding that medical assistance and psychological counseling had been arranged for affected personnel.
The case would be investigated swiftly and handled strictly, while ensuring that no one was wrongfully accused or spared, it said.
If misconduct is confirmed, those responsible would face administrative, criminal and disciplinary action, with no one shielded from accountability, it added.

Ministry collaborates on push for green packaging
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:39:41 UTC
01:39:41 KST

The Ministry of Environment has launched 350 green-packaged products in cooperation with major sales channel operators and consumer goods companies, with the aim of increasing the figure to 1,000 products within the next two years.
Products in supermarkets all require packaging, but overpackaging takes a toll on the environment, it said.
The ministry in the past few years has promoted reducing retail packaging, following the EU’s target of reducing packaging by 10 percent per capita by 2035.
Photo: CNA
The ministry has established a strategic alliance with supermarket or hypermarket channels, such as Prosperity Plaza, Uni-Prosperity and Mega PX Mart to promote the reduction of packaging for products such as food and beverages, cleaning supplies, and cosmetics, it said earlier this week.
Ten major consumer goods companies also took part: Kao Corp, Swire Coca-Cola, Lian Hwa Foods Corp, PX Mart Co, Wedison Enterprise Co, Heineken Taiwan Co, Unilever Taiwan, Uni-Prosperity Lifestyle Corp, Taiwan FamilyMart Co and Taiwan Homemakers United Consumers Co-op.
A total of 350 green-packaged products were launched across 61 product categories, the ministry said.
Minister of Environment Peng Chi-ming (彭啟明) said that product consumption would rise in volume as the economy expands.
However, that means that the volume of packaging waste would climb too, he said, adding that the key to waste disposal is upstream waste reduction.
The ministry would continue to encourage companies to create green packaging for their products based on the five green packaging design principles: lightweight, mono-material, regeneration, circulation and substitution, he said.
The goal is to boost the number of green-packaged products to 1,000, he said, adding that they would be incorporated into the ministry’s circular economy mark certification to help environmentally friendly products dominate the market.
The ministry’s Resource Circulation Administration said that Prosperity Plaza has used the “Start from i” sustainability label to help consumers identify plastics-reduction products.
PX Mart has set up a packaging-free shopping section for more than 350 products at its stores, it said.
Combined with lightweight packaging for fresh food and circular produce mesh bags, PX Mart’s packaging reduction effort reduced plastic use by more than 11 tonnes last year, it said.
Taiwan Homemakers United Consumers Co-op has introduced post-consumer recycled plastic packaging ranging from 30 percent to 100 percent for its store-brand products, it said.
To encourage public support for green-packaged products, people who buy such products at Prosperity Plaza stores nationwide before the end of next month can participate in a lucky draw, it said, referring the public to its Web site for detailed information and the list of raffle prizes.

Typhoon Champi shuts down Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:39:40 UTC
01:39:40 KST

Typhoon Champi, which caused widespread damage and injuries, and prompted road closures and evacuations across Taiwan yesterday, is expected to continue to bring heavy rain this morning, with up to 900mm of rain forecast for mountainous areas of New Taipei City, Taoyuan and Yilan County, the Central Weather Administration (CWA) said yesterday.
At one point a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the Pacific this year, Champi was packing gusts of about 191kph near its center as of 8:30pm, the CWA said.
Taipei, New Taipei City, Keelung, Taoyuan, Hsinchu city and county, Taichung; and Yilan, Miaoli, Changhua, Nantou, Yunlin and Lienchiang counties announced a second consecutive typhoon day.
Photo courtesy of the Central Weather Administration
In all other regions today is a regular working day.
At 8pm yesterday, the storm was about 100km east of Yilan, moving north-northeast at 16kph, and had maximum sustained winds of 155kph and a radius of 320km, the CWA said.
The storm’s forecast track showed that it would pass just off northeastern Taiwan late last night, turn north toward the Chinese coast and eventually move into southern Japan.
Photo: Huang Cheng-chia, EPA
CWA forecaster Liu Pei-teng (劉沛滕) said the center making landfall could not be ruled out if it “stalls, loops or wobbles from side to side” on its approach to Taiwan.
“The storm’s wind radius is quite large, among the bigger ones in recent years,” he said. “If the storm slows down, the strong winds will affect Taiwan for longer.”
Cumulative rainfall at the Taipingshan weather station in Yilan County exceeded 500mm as of 7pm yesterday, reaching the extremely torrential rain level, the CWA said.
Photo: CNA
Rainfall at the Cuifeng Lake (翠峰湖) and Cuifeng Forest Road (翠峰林道) stations, which ranked second and third respectively, exceeded 400mm, approaching the same threshold, it said.
The CWA forecast that from Thursday, when Champi began affecting Taiwan, through midnight tonight, cumulative rainfall in New Taipei City, Taoyuan and Yilan could reach 600mm to 900mm.
In low-lying areas, rainfall could reach 500mm to 700mm in New Taipei City and 400mm to 600mm in Yilan, it said.
Photo courtesy of the Banciao District Office via CNA
The rain is expected to begin easing this afternoon, it added.
More than 2,600 people had been evacuated from vulnerable, mountainous areas, the government said, adding that thousands of military personnel are on standby to assist with rescue efforts.
The Central Emergency Operations Center said one person was killed and 350 were injured as of 7:30pm yesterday.
Photo courtesy of the Fifth Theater of Operations
The death occurred in in Pingtung County’s Liouciou Township (琉球), where a man was swept away by storm-driven waves on a beach, it said.
Police received a report at about noon on Thursday that the man had been swept away, it said, adding that rescuers found him without vital signs at about 2pm.
He was pronounced dead at about 5pm after being rushed to a hospital.
Photo: Fang Pin-chao, Taipei Times
The Civil Aviation Administration said that as of yesterday morning, all of Taiwan’s 262 domestic flights and 715 international flights were canceled.
Flights to and from Taiwan have also been canceled or postponed today, and domestic flights and ferry services have also been suspended, airlines and ferry authorities said, urging passengers to check the latest flight information before departing for airports.
Meanwhile, Taiwan Power Co said a total of 77,498 households across Taiwan had experienced power outages as of 2 pm, of which 58,469, or more than 75 percent, had their electricity restored.
Additional reporting by Wu Liang-yi

Beijing targeting family of ‘separatists’: US report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:39:37 UTC
01:39:37 KST

The People’s Republic of China (PRC) could be intensifying suppression of family members of so-called “diehard Taiwanese separatists,” including the father of Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋), in an attempt to sway the upcoming election, a report by a US think tank said on Tuesday.
Beijing is “likely targeting family members of ‘separatists’ to coerce the ‘separatists’ to stop their activities that the PRC views as promoting ‘Taiwanese independence,’” the Institute for the Study of War said in its latest “China and Taiwan Update,” written in collaboration with the American Enterprise Institute.
The paper referenced its sanctioning of VWAY, a company owned by Shen Tu-cheng (沈土城), the father of Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator Puma Shen.
Photo: Dado Ruvic, Reuters
The sanctions, announced on Wednesday last week by China’s Taiwan Affairs Office (TAO), prohibit VWAY from trading with PRC organizations, enterprises or individuals, it said.
Puma Shen was added to the list of about a dozen “diehard separatists” in October 2024, who may face severe punishment — including the death penalty — under 2024 legal interpretations of Beijing’s “Anti-Secession” Law, it said.
Other political figures facing coercive measures from Beijing include the brother of United Microelectronics Corp founder Robert Tsao (曹興誠), who was denied entry to China earlier this month, and the nephew of the Minister of the Interior Liu Shyh-fang (劉世芳), who lost his job in China in April, it said.
Meanwhile, a woman was arrested in California earlier this month for allegedly spying on the son of President William Lai (賴清德) on behalf of China, the report said.
Lai, Puma Shen and Liu are all members of the DPP, which “considers Taiwan and the PRC to be separate countries,” it said.
The article suggested that Beijing was ramping up coercive measures against Puma Shen in the lead-up to the nine-in-one local elections on Nov. 28.
In a poll by Taipei Trust in Democracy Association last month, Puma Shen was trailing his main opponent, Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安), by 1.2 points, but the latest poll by the same group showed him ahead by 17 points.
“Jun Zhengping,” a social media account affiliated with the Chinese military, and the TAO also blasted Taiwanese television host Kevin Tsai (蔡康永) for attending a campaign event for Puma Shen, saying that advocates of “Taiwanese independence” are “betrayers of the Chinese nation” and that there is no room for ambiguity in “matters of principle,” the article said.
Even if these efforts fail to convince Puma Shen to drop out of the race, public targeting could dissuade Taiwanese public figures from associating with the legislator or his views, it added.

Fitness industry booms, gyms hit record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:39:35 UTC
01:39:35 KST

The nation’s fitness industry has grown 45.7 percent over the past five years, with the number of gyms hitting a record high, the latest Ministry of Finance figures show.
Growing health awareness and the rising popularity of exercise has fueled the development of sports facilities, the ministry’s Department of Statistics said in its latest fiscal statistics report that reviewed changes in the number of sports facilities and their sales revenue in Taiwan from 2020 through the end of July.
According to business registration and sales data, the number of sports facilities increased from 2,106 in 2020 to 3,069 last year, while total revenue rose from NT$29.89 billion (US$919.5 million) to NT$42.6 billion, the report said.
Photo: CNA
The figures represent increases of 45.7 percent and 42.5 percent respectively, with fitness centers accounting for the largest share of the growth, it said.
Statistics showed that Taiwan had a record 1,127 fitness centers last year, up 54.8 percent from 2020. The number rose to 1,166 as of the end of July this year, accounting for 36 percent of all sports facilities and making fitness centers the largest category by far, ahead of golf courses and driving ranges, swimming pools and other facilities.
The Department of Statistics attributed the growth to fitness centers’ focus on general physical conditioning and their ability to operate regardless of weather, making them accessible to more people.
The industry has also diversified its services beyond traditional gym equipment, expanding to include group classes and personal training while reaching out to new user segments, it said.
Fitness centers generally recorded year-on-year growth during the period surveyed, with the exception of 2021, when income fell to NT$12.36 billion amid the COVID-19 pandemic, the report said.
Last year, revenue at fitness centers nationwide reached NT$21.25 billion, surpassing NT$20 billion for the first time and marking a 39.7 percent increase from five years earlier, it said.
Revenue continued to rise in the first seven months of this year, reaching NT$11.36 billion, up 12.6 percent from the same period last year, it added.
Regionally, fitness centers were concentrated in Taiwan’s six special municipalities, where commercial activity is more densely clustered, the department said.
The six regions had a combined 840 fitness centers last year, accounting for 74.5 percent of the national total. Taipei had the most, with 181 centers, or 16.1 percent, followed by Taichung with 173, or 15.4 percent.
The concentration was even more pronounced in terms of revenue, the report showed. The six special municipalities accounted for 82 percent of total fitness center revenue nationwide, led by Taipei with NT$4.03 billion. New Taipei City and Taichung ranked second and third respectively.
Comparing figures from 2020 and last year, Taoyuan recorded the fastest growth in the number of fitness centers, with an increase of more than 160 percent, followed by Taichung, where the number rose 71.3 percent, the report showed. Growth in revenue was more consistent across the six special municipalities, ranging from 25.2 percent to 53.3 percent.

Han Ferris wheel leaves Ko Chih-en spinning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:39:31 UTC
01:39:31 KST

Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Kaohsiung mayoral candidate Ko Chih-en (柯志恩) has run into a problem for which she has only herself to blame.
On Saturday last week, Legislative Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜) appeared at her campaign rally in Kaohsiung. While he might have been expected to warm up the crowd and rally some support for Ko, Han instead used his speaking time to make suggestions such as building “a great wall” between Kaohsiung and Tainan, supposedly cutting the two cities off.
He also reiterated a policy proposal to build a “Love Ferris Wheel” from his time as Kaohsiung mayor eight years ago. It was Ko, in the end, who was left to clean up the mess.
At the Double Ten National Day celebrations, Han called for differences to be reconciled and efforts to be united; just seven days later, he started talking about building a wall. Why would a city that is valued precisely because of the air and sea transport links connecting it with the rest of the world suddenly decide to isolate itself from its neighbor?
The next day, Ko attempted to explain that Han was simply emphasizing that Kaohsiung’s self-sufficiency and economic might were enough to bring surrounding areas such as Tainan and Pingtung into the fold, in line with the spirit of 2019’s “Great South” policy agenda.
However, cutting off cities and codevelopment are clearly two very different directions. If we are to buy Ko’s reasoning, Chinese emperor Qin Shi Huang (秦始皇) must have also intended the Great Wall of China to be a collaborative project in nature.
As for the Love Ferris Wheel, Han’s fixation is unusually persistent. He was adamant about it being built during his time in office, and the city government even held investment briefings, looked for a site and discussed construction.
Eight years later, he is still bringing it up on someone else’s campaign trail; the Ferris wheel might only be turning in Han’s mind, and he certainly does not seem to be able to get off. Voters might have come out to hear how Ko would govern Kaohsiung, but they first had to endure a rehash of Han’s old dreams.
Ko said that Han was not actually suggesting that a Ferris wheel should be built, but that commercial districts should develop a distinctive character. Perhaps the city government’s efforts in 2019 were also in pursuit of a metaphor. From Han’s initial insistence to Ko’s abstraction of the issue, a development promise from eight years ago has now become a lesson in spin.
So, the Ferris wheel is metaphorical and great walls promote codevelopment. Is Ko running for mayor, or simply cleaning up after Han? She seems to be managing to not only edit his work, but imbue a deeper meaning into his words with her explanations.
When a candidate invites someone to campaign on their behalf, the hope is that the guest might help persuade voters. However, this was a case of Han making grand pronouncements and Ko dealing with the aftermath; Han’s ramblings had to be explained away before she could even get to her own policies.
For voters, what Han hoped to achieve might not be entirely clear to see, but the mess he left Ko to clean up certainly is.
Chang Shang-yang is a farmer.

Ukraine’s skaters twizzle on amid war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:39:26 UTC
01:39:26 KST

When music suddenly stopped at a Kyiv ice rink and a siren blared out announcing a drone threat, Ukraine’s top young skaters did not miss a beat, and carried on perfecting jumps and honing twizzles.
Two days later, a Russian overnight strike ripped open the venue, leaving a gaping hole in the wall, but no casualties.
Between sleepless nights and incessant air raid sirens, the future Olympic hopefuls have long had to compete not just with their peers, but against wartime odds.
Photo: AFP
However, Yulia Ratnykova, mother of 11-year-old skater Katya, said that even with the severe damage to the rink, they were undeterred.
“Naturally, the girls were very upset — there were even tears,” Ratnykova said, but added: “No one is quitting, training will go on.”
“Every time you head out to a competition in the morning and see all the children, you know the night has gone well,” trainer Oleksandr Tumanovsky said. “If they’re alive, that’s already a success.”
Tumanovsky, a former leading Soviet skater, now wears a jacket emblazoned with Ukraine’s national symbol and keeps a watchful eye on his group of three girls aged nine to 11 practicing to rhythmic music.
At 6:15am, just more than an hour after the end of the overnight curfew, the ice was brimming with a few dozen other children, from toddlers to adolescents, mastering steps, jumps and twirls.
With Kyiv on near-constant alert against Russian strikes, halting workouts with every siren has proved impossible, Tumanovsky said.
At first, the children would run to shelter in a school nearby — but that turned to a “track-and-field” workout instead, he said.
With the parents’ blessing, training continued despite the alerts, but one thing has changed.
“When the blasts get too loud, we turn the music up — so the children don’t get scared,” Tumanovsky said.
Yulia Yermolayeva and her daughter Myroslava moved to Kyiv after fleeing Kharkiv near the Russian border when Moscow invaded.
Myroslava now trains six hours a day, six days a week under Tumanovsky, but sleep is a constant battle.
“There are days when it’s incredibly hard,” the mother said.
At times she has to wake her daughter up and move to a shelter. On more dangerous nights, they sleep in the car in an underground car park, wake up “and head straight to training.”
Myroslava sometimes sleeps in the hallway on an improvised bed of pillows, blankets and duvets.
“It’s obviously not as soft as a regular bed, but it’s fine,” she said.
Ratnykova has a similar arrangement for her daughter Katya, who sleeps on a camping mat and inflatable mattress.
“To be honest, I don’t even remember when she last slept in her own bed,” she said.
Each morning, the parents have to weigh the risks to decide whether to let the girls go skating.
“It’s a bit like being in a forest full of dangers: You have to stay constantly alert to avoid them,” Ratnykova said.
Yermolayeva said the ordeal takes a toll on the children and their performance, adding: “Compared to other children training in better conditions in Europe, we aren’t really competitive — she simply can’t give 100 percent.”
Air alerts are also a permanent fixture at competitions in Ukraine.
“The children have to leave and sit in a shelter for two hours. By the time they come back out, they’re in no state to compete: The right mindset is completely gone,” Yermolayeva said.
Competing abroad has also been hampered by the closure of Ukrainian airspace.
“The journey now takes 24 hours instead of three... The longer the trip, the higher the risk that things won’t go as well as they should,” Tumanovsky said.
After the attack that damaged the rink, the Ukrainian Figure Skating Federation wrote in protest to the International Skating Union, saying: “Ukrainian skaters are being deprived of the most basic conditions necessary to train, compete, and pursue their lives as athletes.”
As his group trained, Tumanovsky said it was “truly terrifying” that children were getting used to the sound of explosions.
“Children should be getting used to completely different kinds of sounds, like the rustling of leaves or the wind blowing, but not the sounds made by those scumbags,” he added.
Work began almost instantly to repair the rink.
“Walls can be rebuilt, and I’m hopeful that by next week we’ll be back on the ice,” said Tumanovsky. “We’re Ukrainians, after all.”

DPP lawmaker calls for changes to security law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:39:22 UTC
01:39:22 KST

Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator Wang Ting-yu (王定宇) yesterday said that he plans to propose amendments to the Anti-Infiltration Act (反滲透法) and the National Security Act (國家安全法) to increase penalties for transnational repression and emerging forms of crime allegedly directed or funded by Beijing.
The law does not adequately cover some acts of cross-border repression carried out at the direction of or with funding from hostile foreign forces, Wang said.
The proposed amendments would target new forms of crime, including laundering money through online donations to streamers and online harassment carried out by public relations firms, he said.
Photo: Taipei Times
The Anti-Infiltration Act focuses on election-related offenses, including voting, elections, recalls and referendums, as well as breaches of social order and laws governing assemblies and marches allegedly committed at the behest of hostile foreign forces, he said.
However, it does not adequately cover newer forms of cross-border repression enabled by technology and online platforms, Wang said.
The planned amendments would establish disclosure requirements for online financial transactions and give authorities the legal power needed to investigate suspected offenses, he said.
They would also stiffen penalties and strengthen investigative powers for threats, cyberbullying and online humiliation carried out by domestic Internet companies or online marketing firms acting under the direction of or receiving funding from the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), Chinese government or Chinese military bodies, he said.
The law as it is either imposes insufficient penalties or fails to account for the effects such activities could have on Taiwan’s domestic affairs, Wang said.
The proposed amendments were nearing the end of the cosigning process and would be submitted soon, he said.
He called on lawmakers across party lines to support the changes to protect the public from harassment, intimidation and threats from hostile foreign forces.
Political parties can compete as fiercely as they like, but the public’s right to hold different political views must be protected, he said.
People can criticize the views of others, but should not attack them at the behest of or in exchange for benefits from the CCP, he said.
Citing alleged surveillance of DPP Legislator Puma Shen (沈伯洋), the party’s Taipei mayoral candidate, including the photographing of a minor child, as well as attacks on political commentator Akio Yaita and comedian Huang Yi-hao (黃逸豪), Wang said acts that appear to constitute ordinary contraventions of the Personal Data Protection Act (個人資料保護法) or the Criminal Code should be assessed differently if they involve authorization or funding from hostile foreign forces.
Wang likened the proposed changes to stipulations of the Organized Crime Prevention Act (組織犯罪防制條例), which allows authorities to target criminal organizations behind individual offenses.
“China can be described as the biggest criminal organization today — the biggest gang as far as Taiwan is concerned,” he said, adding that failing to account for the organizations behind such crimes would undermine deterrence.

How the upcoming U.S. and Israeli elections could lead to the third round of the Iran war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:38:19 UTC
01:38:19 KST

There is little doubt that the United States and Israel are about to renew the war on Iran that they started without provocation, or any real planning, back in February. The question is only about the timing.
In fact, by the time you read this, the war may have resumed in full force. More likely, though, it will be delayed until after the U.S. midterm elections. That will put it after Israel’s elections as well.
Israel may find itself with an entirely new leadership after its upcoming elections on October 27, which, while still seeing Iran as a hated enemy, might have different ideas about how to attack that enemy.
The United States is even more uncertain following the midterm elections on November 3. Donald Trump will remain president and free of electoral concerns, as he will not be allowed to run in the next election. But a Congress hostile to this war can make it harder for him to continue his current course. Conversely, an indecisive Congress unwilling to confront Trump on the war could unleash his worst tendencies.
Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu both have personal interests that the war might serve. Both could seek to undermine their country’s election results, and a war that escalates into a global economic crisis could give them the cover they need.
Iran and the Israeli election
Netanyahu has been pushing hard for a renewed war. In a public phone call with Trump, Netanyahu told him, “We have a job to finish.”
Beyond the bombast, there have been concrete actions. The United States and Israel have been busy drawing up plans for another attack on Iran even if it seems that Netanyahu is not content to wait as long as Trump wants him to.
Trump has repeatedly said that the U.S. would not attack Iran before the midterm elections. Given his history, there is no reason to take Trump at his word. To the contrary, Trump has repeatedly broken such promises, sometimes due to impulsiveness, sometimes because he lied intentionally to try to get Iran to drop its guard. Moreover, Trump has not said that he would continue to block Israel from attacking before the midterms.
But in this case, there is good reason to believe that Trump is telling the truth. Nothing is certain, but the United States is moving a considerable number of troops and a third aircraft carrier to the Gulf. By most accounts, they are slated to arrive in late November.
That works for Trump, but less well for Netanyahu.
For Trump, an escalation against Iran will be useful for months, from the election until the beginning of January, when the new Congress would be seated.
Netanyahu has less time.
The Israeli election will take place next week. Many analyses in the United States have misunderstood how a renewal of war affects Netanyahu’s position.
Had it happened a few weeks before the election, Netanyahu might have been able to postpone the election (which would require approval from 80 of 120 members of the Knesset), or sway some voters toward his camp. Now, with only a few days left, those prospects are very dim.
But an Israeli election is not like an American one where votes are cast, someone wins, and that’s supposed to settle the matter. Israel’s unstable coalition politics mean the real intrigue happens after the votes are counted, as the leaders of the top parties jockey for the right to form a coalition government.
Netanyahu is not going to win this election, according to almost every poll that has been conducted recently and since the beginning of the year. The parties that would join with his Likud coalition simply won’t have enough seats to form a majority unless a real miracle happens.
But the opposition, although in a better position, also doesn’t have a good chance of forming a majority coalition. Their only hope, which is not available to Netanyahu, is support from the parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up around 20% of the population.
But that is complicated. The opposition leader, Gadi Eisenkot, has vowed not to form a government with Arab parties. But he could form a government with less than a majority of seats by getting support from Arab parties outside the governing coalition.
That’s a fraught path in as racist a society as Israel’s. Even the non-nationalist, conservative United Arab List (called Ra’am) would trouble some of Eisenkot’s other coalition partners. And it is hard to imagine parties led by right-wing figures like Avigdor Lieberman or Naftali Bennett agreeing to a coalition that gets any support from the Joint List, which is much more representative of Palestinian national sentiment than Ra’am.
And even with Ra’am’s support outside the coalition, the opposition could still fall short of the 61 votes needed to form a government.
Netanyahu is counting on the opposition’s inability to form a coalition. If that should happen, Netanyahu can try to poach parties or even individual Knesset members from the opposition to reach a majority. That would be difficult, but possible.
Or he could simply ride the impasse to another round of elections, leaving him in charge of a caretaker government, the most likely scenario at present.
In either case, a hot war with Iran is a significant boon to Netanyahu.
Under the threat of Iranian missile attack, Netanyahu can make the case that Israel needs continuity to win the war, to stop Iran’s nuclear program, and all the other accusations Netanyahu will make. If polls don’t show he is gaining ground, he can also propose a national unity government, and a hot war will absolutely bolster that case.
Netanyahu needs the stalemate that comes with the opposition failing to form a government. Yet, if he gets it, and there are no Iranian or Hezbollah missiles raining down on Israel, his failings will only come under even more scrutiny, and he will stand even less chance in the next round of elections. So he needs a war even more than usual.
Netanyahu’s push for an early resumption of the war, against Trump’s preferences, was motivated by several factors.
First, given Trump’s indecisiveness and strong tendency to flip-flop, he wanted to lock in American support for renewing the war. Second, he wanted to refocus the war’s guiding principle on regime change, an idea he has been banging on in recent days but that has largely fallen out of favor in Washington, even among the most hawkish voices.
Finally, Netanyahu knows that the U.S. is planning a quick, impactful strike. He also knows this is almost certainly not going to happen, and he wouldn’t want it to. He wants prolonged engagement to maximize both his own political gains and the chances of stressing Iran to the point of threatening the Islamic Republic’s continued existence. Time is not on his side, as he knows that this may be his last chance to defeat Iran.
So, Netanyahu pushed to rekindle the war earlier this month, knowing that it would almost certainly last until well after Israel’s election.
Iran and the U.S. midterms
Trump is probably sincere about his desire to hold off the attack on Iran until after the midterms, but this is just another indication of how little he grasps the depths of his own failure.
The damage to the Republican chances in the midterms is done, and resuming the war on Iran won’t make things much worse. But, even more than with Netanyahu in Israel, the Republicans are about to take a beating at the ballot box. The only question is how bad it will be.
It is overwhelmingly likely that the Democrats will take back the House of Representatives, and they stand a good chance of taking the Senate as well. For Trump, even though he is not on the ballot, this will be a humiliating loss, and we have already seen how he reacts to such things.
This is where a renewed war on Iran comes in for him. Trump is sure to do all he can to throw the results of the election into doubt, and to stir up suspicions as he did in 2020. With a smaller base of support now than before, and no pandemic, he will need to sow even more chaos than he did then.
A war with Iran will do that for several reasons.
First, the war itself will be intense and will immediately send shock waves through the global economy.
But that will only be the start. Iran has been clear that it is going to respond more forcefully than before and that it will calibrate that response to the intensity of the American and Israeli attack.
Iran has warned that they will target data centers, which they know are important to Trump, as well as underwater fiber networks that are key to the internet. That will cause disruption across many different industries.
And that will be added to Iran’s targeting of Gulf energy infrastructure if the U.S. and Israel target theirs. They could also target civilian infrastructure, including desalination plants, which would devastate the entire region.
None of this will matter to Israel, which will see it as pressure on the Gulf Arab states to join in the war effort. Israel wants to see as much chaos as possible, because that is the road to the regime change in Iran they crave.
But Trump should be concerned about the potential crash of Gulf economies and the massive impact this will have on the entire world.
Crippling Gulf infrastructure will send oil prices soaring much higher than they already are. It will greatly expand the fertilizer-export crisis from the region and could further devastate the liquefied natural gas market. Global inflation could surge, and the measures used to date to keep prices from that kind of massive inflation are unlikely to be sufficient.
Yet the chaos it will cause in the United States might offer Trump an advantage in forestalling the seating of a new Congress, or increasing his opportunities to once again cast doubt on the election results.
These efforts are unlikely to get Trump what he wants. His base is too small, the country is more aware of this potential, and many of the foot soldiers Trump had six years ago now recognize that he betrayed and used them.
But an attack on Iran will succeed in causing global devastation, beginning in Iran itself, and quickly expanding outward.
Israel, too, is much more vulnerable than it was last time around. The protective ring of American installations and support from places like Saudi Arabia and Jordan in intercepting Iranian missiles and drones is severely diminished. Many American bases are gone, and the Americans stationed in the region have few interceptors left.
Israel has managed to save many interceptors of its own, having relied on American missiles against Iran. But even they had to use quite a few to defend against attacks from Lebanon. More to the point, because Iranian missiles will have a much clearer path to Israel than they did before, more missiles will be shot down above Israeli space, meaning more debris will fall on Israel, while more Iranian missiles are likely to get through Israel’s defenses since so many more will get into range.
Perhaps Trump is not thinking about how to use a war to undermine elections in the U.S. Maybe he is tired of losing the war and is desperately grasping at the idea that this time the bloodshed and destruction that have repeatedly failed will work.
That sad fact is the very definition of murderous insanity.

Israeli roadblocks disrupt schools and medical care in West Bank village
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:37:59 UTC
01:37:59 KST

Israeli roadblocks disrupt schools and medical care in West Bank village
Residents of Madama describe being cut off from hospitals, schools, and olive groves as Israeli forces blockade village.
Wail Qut, 42, usually commutes to work in Ramallah, in the occupied West Bank. But for more than two weeks he has been stuck at home in the village of Madama, south of Nablus, due to a tight Israeli siege.
On October 11, the Israeli army blocked the village’s four entrances with earthen barriers, citing “security reasons”. Qut says that the Israeli military has told residents that the restrictions would remain until Palestinian farmers stopped trying to access their land, particularly in the northern part of the village, where an illegal settler outpost is located.
The decision has completely restricted the movement of more than 2,500 residents. On October 20, the army briefly opened the northern entrance for a few hours before closing it once again.
Qut works as a legal consultant for the Jerusalem Legal Aid and Human Rights Center in Ramallah. Three days into the siege, he needed to reach his office in the city to deal with urgent case files.
“The residents managed to clear a rough, unpaved dirt track between Madama and Asira, which I used to reach Ramallah. It was a dangerous gamble, though the area is swarming with settlers, and the path is not even passable for most vehicles,” he told Al Jazeera.
Whenever Palestinian residents attempted to leave Madama via this makeshift route, the Israeli army deployed a drone to monitor them. Soldiers have also attacked the residents and fired sound grenades and tear gas canisters to force them back.
The soldiers have subsequently blocked the dirt track, cutting off the only small opening that had allowed some residents to leave the village. As a result, Qut was forced to spend days away in Ramallah, only returning home once he learned that the northern entrance had been briefly reopened.
“I returned to the village and found settlers everywhere, monitoring the tight siege. Shortly afterwards, the army closed the entrance once again. Some residents who had left were unable to return and had to leave their vehicles outside the village,” he added.
Uprooting trees
The restrictions have coincided with Israeli bulldozing operations that residents say have destroyed agricultural land and uprooted hundreds of olive trees.
Locals in Madama have described the scenes as “horrific”, particularly as they came during the annual olive harvest season, a vital source of income for local farmers already struggling to access their land because of Israeli restrictions.
Al Jazeera has reached out to the Israeli military for comment, but has yet to receive a response.
Rami Nassar, head of the Madama Village Council, told Al Jazeera that the village spans about 340 hectares (840 acres). He said Israel had seized village land in the 1980s for the establishment of the illegal Yitzhar settlement, while another portion was taken in the 1990s to construct a settler-only road – Route 60 – which now restricts residents’ access to their agricultural land.
Last April, Nassar said, Israeli settlers established an illegal pastoral settlement northwest of the village, near the al-Murabbaa checkpoint. Since then, he said, settlers have been siphoning electricity and water from the village’s utility networks and destroying agricultural crops.
Last July, the council leader added, under the protection of the Israeli army, settler bulldozers levelled what he estimated to have been about 57 hectares (140 acres) of land in the northwest of the village, and uprooted hundreds of mature, fruit-bearing olive trees.
During the current olive harvest season, according to Nassar, Israeli soldiers have chased Palestinian farmers away from their fields, while settlers have stolen both harvested olives and farming equipment from those who managed to reach their land.
“The olive harvest season has come to an end for the people of Madama, a season they rely on entirely, especially given their harsh living conditions. Every year, the harvest felt like a celebration; now, all we see is them bulldozing and uprooting our trees,” Nassar said sorrowfully.
The closures have disrupted daily life in Madama, preventing residents from reaching work, schools and hospitals, while blocking the delivery of essential supplies, including cooking gas, Nassar said.
“A few days ago, a resident suffered a heart attack and needed to be taken to a hospital,” he recalled. “As the village doctor, I had to transport him carrying him over earthen berms and navigate through olive groves and steep slopes in a private vehicle travelling between various villages to reach a nearby hospital. It took over two hours to get him there; under normal circumstances, this journey would take no more than 15 minutes.”
The plight of students
The siege has also disrupted schooling across Madama and neighbouring villages, preventing teachers from reaching classrooms.
Samer al-Jamal, director general of education for the southern Nablus district, said that the closure of roads and gates, combined with the restrictions on the movement of educational staff, had deprived thousands of students of their education.
Three schools in Madama, Burin, and Asira were forced to switch to remote learning for three days following the imposition of the blockade. As the closure continued, students and teachers were eventually compelled to cross earthen barriers on foot to reach their schools.
Maryam Rayan, 48, the principal of al-Fayha Kindergarten in Asira, told Al Jazeera that the simple task of ensuring children could arrive at and leave the kindergarten safely was increasingly dangerous, as 35 of the school’s enrolled children live in Madama.
She explained that she lives in the neighbouring village of Burin. The journey from there, passing through Madama to reach Asira, should typically take no more than eight minutes; however, due to the blockade of Madama, the trip now takes more than an hour and a half.
“The kindergarten bus would have to stop near the earthen barrier after we verified that no soldiers or settlers were present, and we would wait for the children to arrive on a local shuttle from within the village. I would then cross the barrier on foot to help them get over it, one by one. It was a tragic scene, but we had no other choice,” she added.
On the return journey, Rayan would again help the children cross the barrier, boarding the shuttle with them to ensure they all reached their homes safely. Afterwards, she would cross the barrier alone to return to the kindergarten bus, which would then take her back to Burin.
“I have been working in education for 25 years, yet I have never encountered circumstances as difficult as those we have lived through due to the blockade of Madama. From the moment I left my home until I returned, I felt tense, fearful, and anxious, all because I am responsible for the lives of 135 children at the kindergarten, while the streets are filled with soldiers or settlers,” she explained.
On Thursday, Israel reopened the northern entrance to Madama, though Palestinians expect it could be closed again at any moment, especially since the other entrances to the village remain shut. And on Friday, Israel began imposing widespread restrictions on movement throughout the West Bank after an attack in Hebron killed two soldiers, with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordering preparations for a complete lockdown and a large-scale operation throughout the occupied territory.
The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said it had identified 925 physical obstacles restricting the movement of Palestinians in the West Bank by December 2025, including 167 earth mounds, which collectively affect the movement of approximately 3.4 million Palestinians.
The agency noted that these obstacles sever connections between villages, towns, and main roads, forcing residents to take longer, alternative routes and limiting their access to workplaces, essential services, and agricultural land.

New York City to phase out Central Park horse-drawn carriages by Jun 1, 2028
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:36:03 UTC
01:36:03 KST

New York City to phase out Central Park horse-drawn carriages by Jun 1, 2028
The New York City Council has approved historic legislation to phase out the city’s horse-drawn carriage industry by June 1, 2028, following decades of concerns about animal welfare and public safety, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The bill, known as Romanch’s Law, was passed after the death of 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan, who was killed this summer after being thrown from a horse-drawn carriage in Central Park.
Horse-drawn carriages have been operating in Central Park since 1858, originally serving as a mode of transportation and evolving into a popular tourist attraction.
The legislation prohibits the issuance or renewal of licenses for carriage horses, carriages, and horse-drawn cab drivers on or after June 1, 2028. It also requires the city to develop a transition plan by April 1, 2027, to support carriage owners, drivers, and other industry workers, including stable employees. The plan will include employment assistance and consider programs to help horse owners rehome their animals and dispose of equipment, as well as provide compensation to carriage owners for their businesses, licenses and equipment.
The law also establishes protections to ensure the humane treatment of horses and prohibits their sale or transfer for slaughter or use in other horse-drawn carriage businesses.
Council Speaker Julie Menin said: "Today, the City Council made history. Our landmark vote to pass Romanch’s Law is a demonstration of this Council’s commitment to animal welfare, public safety, and worker protection."
Earlier, Qazinform reported that a snow leopard named Altai became the first in Kazakhstan's Southern Altai to be fitted with a satellite tracking collar. The satellite collar will allow researchers to track the snow leopard's movements, study its travel routes, and identify key areas of its habitat.

Dozens feared trapped as high-rise collapses in Kenya’s Nairobi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:36:00 UTC
01:36:00 KST

A multistory building collapsed in Kenya’s capital, Nairobi, on Friday, leaving many people feared trapped beneath massive piles of concrete as more than a dozen floors crumbled on top of one another.
The building was under construction when it collapsed at about 1 p.m. along a busy commercial street in Nairobi's Eastleigh area, which is often crowded with thousands of traders and residents.
Nairobi police chief Issa Mohamud said the building had more than 10 upper floors under construction. Rescue operations were complicated, with police firing tear gas at people who had begun looting neighboring shops, as officers sought to clear the area and provide access to emergency response teams.
Joseph Kaula made it out just in time. A plasterer working on the fifth floor, he said he heard screams and spotted other workers rushing outside, shouting that the building was collapsing.
"I was the last person to walk out before it collapsed and the whole area was filled with dust,” Kaula said.
Kaula suspects a few of his colleagues were trapped in the basement.
One injured woman was rescued and hospitalized, and another person who was crying for help had gone silent, the police chief said.
Mohamud also warned of a possible secondary collapse, as the collapsed building was leaning on its neighbor.
There was little in the way of heavy equipment immediately available. Hours later, a group of rescuers in hard hats were using poles stripped from trees to poke at the huge pile of rubble. One excavator began to move concrete bound with steel away. By evening, at least two more back shovels arrived.
Rescuers were hoping to reach into any spaces left in the basement and the ground level, which had been rented out for an electronics shop, a butchery and a grocery while construction continued on the upper floors.
Residents said some of their loved ones who were trapped had made phone calls calling for help immediately after the collapse, but that their phones later became unreachable. A tent was set up where people could report the missing. How many might be inside the wreckage wasn't known.
Building collapses are a recurring problem in Nairobi . County officials responsible for issuing building permits have been accused of failing to conduct adequate inspections to ensure developers comply with safety guidelines and construction standards.
"Investigations will be carried out,” Mohamud said. "We’ll make sure people face the law for any negligence.”
Nairobi Gov. Johnson Sakaja said the building had been approved for construction, but did not have a certificate of occupation, so opening shops on the ground floor was against the law. Kenya's county governments need stronger enforcement powers, he said, arguing that lenient penalties for non-compliance are just a "slap on the wrist” for developers that violate regulations.

Opposition deepfake video sparks outrage in Spain ahead of election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:35:48 UTC
01:35:48 KST

A political ad from Spain’s main opposition party that used a deepfake video of the prime minister’s wife has sparked outrage and set off a wider debate on AI, as the deeply polarised country gears up for general elections next month.
Launched this week across the social media channels of the conservative People’s party (PP), the video used artificial intelligence to manipulate the likenesses of various people linked to Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party and appeared to show them admitting to acts such as soliciting prostitutes and taking kickbacks.
An AI-generated version of Sánchez’s wife, Begoña Gómez, for example, speaks about receiving a university post thanks to her husband’s job, while a deepfake of the former Socialist president José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero speaks about hiding jewellery in a safe. Both lines are nods to ongoing investigations in which Gómez and Zapatero have denied any wrongdoing.
The Socialist party was swift to respond to the video, which by Friday had racked up nearly 2m views. “It’s telling people a colossal lie, and for a party to do it on its official accounts seems intolerable to me,” Óscar López, Spain’s digital transformation minister, told the broadcaster TVE on Friday.
While the video noted at the bottom – in tiny, nearly transparent font – that it had been created with AI, López pointed to the wider risk. “It’s very easy for anyone who isn’t used to AI to confuse that video with reality,” he said. “And call me crazy, but that seems extremely serious to me.”
On Friday, one of those whose likeness was used in the video filed a legal challenge against the PP, calling on the party to immediately take down the campaign advert. In a court complaint, Leire Díez, a former Socialist party member, reportedly accused the PP of defamation and digital identity theft, after the video used her likeness to hint at accusations that she worked to undermine judicial and law enforcement in order to help the Socialists.
A majority of the nine legal experts consulted by the newspaper El País concurred that what the PP had done was not illegal, given that the video was labelled as AI-generated and that the overall tone was one of political satire. “Given the context, everyone knows those people didn’t say those things,” Íñigo Navarro, a former dean of the faculty of law at Madrid’s Comillas Pontifical University, told the paper.
But the legality of the video was just one aspect, said Juan Antonio Lascuraín, a professor of criminal law at the Autonomous University of Madrid. “It’s quite another matter to ask whether it’s appropriate, exemplary or ethically and politically correct.”
Many sought to contextualise the videos within the wider effort – under way by officials across much of the world – to crack down on the impact of disinformation.
“It’s truly regrettable that the official account of a party that claims to want to govern and revitalise democracy is using AI-generated deepfakes in its campaign,” said José Javier Olivas, an associate professor who researches populism, conspiracy theories and AI biases at Spain’s National University for Distance Education.
He pointed to the wider backdrop of the election campaign, in which both mainstream parties have sought to rally voters by stoking emotions and attacking the morality of their rivals, but he said the video was a “red line” in terms of how campaigns normally unfolded.
“You’re using the images of other people, putting words in their mouths that they’re not saying, [and] this qualifies for disinformation,” he said.
The use of AI to generate or enhance political ads has also become a talking point in the US ahead of next month’s midterm elections. A recent report by a research group based at Wesleyan University in Connecticut identified more than 200 such ads, the vast majority of them tied to the Republicans.
“AI is making its way into the 2026 midterms in a big way this year,” said Erika Franklin Fowler, a co-director of the Wesleyan Media Project. “For comparison, we identified less than $50,000 in spending on AI-generated ads in the 2024 cycle. Much of the AI use is not disclosed through any type of disclaimer.”
In Spain, the PP has brushed off criticism. “If there had been malicious intent to make people believe that the characters who appear there are real, then we’d have a problem,” Borja Sémper, of the party, told reporters. “But everyone can see that this is a way of using digital tools to highlight the hypocrisy in which the Socialist party operates.”
Most polls suggest the PP will win the 29 November general election but will need to rely on the support of the far-right Vox party to form a government.

Two ex-FBI officials charged with allegedly lying about Hunter Biden probe: DOJ

Two former senior FBI officials were taken into custody on Friday after being charged with lying to Congress about their roles in investigations into Hunter Biden, top Department of Justice officials announced.
The former officials, 46-year-old Nikki Floris and 56-year-old Bradley Benavides, surrendered on arrest warrants Friday morning, the DOJ said in a press release.
The charges were filed less than two weeks before the midterm election, breaking with longstanding DOJ guidance discouraging actions that could affect upcoming political races.
The announcement also comes amid growing concerns that President Donald Trump — who refused to accept his 2020 election loss and tried repeatedly to overturn those results — is looking for ways to challenge potential Republican midterm losses.
On Thursday, the DOJ filed an unusual lawsuit against Alaska seeking to preemptively challenge the results of that state's Senate race if incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan narrowly loses.
The charges unveiled Friday morning accuse the two ex-FBI agents of lying in 2023 testimony before the House Judiciary Committee about their agency's probe of Hunter Biden, the now-56-year-old son of former President Joe Biden.
The agents were "actively involved" in federal investigations of Hunter Biden, which began in 2019 on tax- and money-laundering-related matters, but said otherwise in separate interviews before the House panel, according to an FBI special agent's affidavit in support of the charges.
"Floris and Benavides allegedly lied to Congress about their roles in the FBI's Hunter Biden investigations, with one claiming they only learned about it from Wikipedia — despite evidence showing their involvement in helping shape the public narrative about Hunter Biden's laptop right before the election," U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro said in an X post.
FBI Director Kash Patel said on X that the charges "stem from an ongoing investigation into the since-dissolved FBI Foreign Influence Task Force."
Floris and Benavides, who both worked on that task force, testified that it "was not involved in the Hunter Biden investigations," Patel wrote. "Documentary evidence, contemporaneous communications, and witness accounts contradict their testimony."
Attorneys for Floris called the charges "nonsense," and accused the Trump administration of deliberately filing them just before the Nov. 3 midterm election in hopes of gaining political advantage.
"Nikki Floris is a patriot. She served our nation as a dedicated FBI intelligence officer for nearly 20 years. Yet today, the DOJ has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts," read a statement from her counsel, including Margaret Donovan, Chris Mattei, Mary Dohrmann and Kyle Freeny.
"It's no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election," they wrote.
"The government's reasons for charging Nikki are as transparent as they are unjust: to push a false narrative for a shot at political points," their statement added. "It's another sad day for the DOJ, but we look forward to Nikki's day in court."

The US administration has filed a lawsuit to block certification of the US state of Alaska's Senate race if Republican Senator Dan Sullivan loses while another candidate with the same name is on the ballot.

The Department of Justice filed a lawsuit on Thursday in federal court in Alaska, asking the court to block the state from certifying a Peltola win if Daniel J. remains on the ballot.
“The United States accordingly brings this lawsuit to protect the integrity of the 2026 Senate election in Alaska,” the lawsuit says, contending that federal law requires states to protect the integrity of federal elections.
The Alaska Supreme Court rejected a previous Republican effort to remove Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot.
He will appear without a party designation next to his name, while the senator will be listed as the Republican incumbent.
Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system will also let voters select both men if they're confused.
Election certification process
Democrats have long feared that the administration will try to block certification of elections that GOP loses.
US Attorney General Todd Blanche said that was unlikely outside of extreme circumstances. “It is not DOJ’s intention to, and it’s never our intention to, improperly interfere with elections or the state certification process,” he told reporters in Virginia before the lawsuit was filed.
Derek Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame, said the lawsuit would likely only kick in if Republicans narrowly lost the Alaska Senate race.
“The statute simply doesn’t let the Department of Justice enjoin certification,” he said. “The lawsuit could well be mooted by a wide Democratic victory or a narrow Republican one, and if not, the court will likely dismiss it next month.”
The US Constitution grants states the power to run their own elections. Elections for federal office like the Senate must comply with standards Congress sets.
Trump has complained about Daniel J. Sullivan’s presence on the ballot, referencing it at a rally in Alaska this month and in repeated social media posts, including one this week in which he called it “CHEATING.”
“We are looking at powerful legal options to remove the fraudulent Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. from the Ballot, and holding the Democrats accountable for their Election Interference, in the pursuit of Justice and Fairness,” the president wrote on Wednesday.

WASHINGTON -- US First Lady Melania Trump has brokered a localized cease-fire between Russia and Ukraine for the Russian-occupied southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky, with Kyiv confirming preparations for an operation to establish humanitarian corridors and evacuate civilians.
The White House said on October 23 that the temporary halt in military action would begin on October 29, allowing humanitarian aid to enter the city and residents to leave through a designated safe passageway.
The announcement credited Melania Trump with working directly with the Russian and Ukrainian leadership to negotiate the arrangement, an unusual diplomatic role for a US first lady.
Humanitarian Operation
David Arakhamia, head of the Ukrainian parliament's Servant of the People faction, confirmed the planned operation in a social media post, thanking Melania Trump and Pope Leo XIV for their roles in the effort.
“An operation to unblock the settlement of Oleshky and its surrounding areas will begin in the near future,” Arakhamia wrote. “Its goal is to establish permanent humanitarian corridors for the safe evacuation of civilians and the delivery of aid.”
He said a cease-fire would be reached soon to facilitate the operation, referring to the announcement by the US first lady.
Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, who led the negotiations on the Ukrainian side, confirmed to RFE/RL the launch of a humanitarian mission to rescue civilians in Oleshky.
He said that Melania Trump's involvement in the process had helped get the effort "moving forward," adding that Kyiv had been trying to resolve the issue since early this year. "The negotiation process itself was, to put it mildly, difficult and protracted," Lubinets said.
He added that "the humanitarian mission itself will be carried out in several stages" and that Kyiv has already begun implementing its part of the agreement.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov welcomed Melania Trump's involvement in coordinating the humanitarian operation in Oleshky, highlighting cooperation between Russian and Ukrainian officials.
“Building upon the agreements reached between Presidents [Vladimir] Putin and [Donald] Trump, and with the direct involvement of Mrs. Trump, extensive work was carried out by Yana Lantratova -- an official appointed by the president of the Russian Federation to address human rights issues -- alongside her counterpart from the Ukrainian side,” Peskov said.
Oleshky Residents Face Dire Conditions
Oleshky lies on the Russian-occupied bank of the Dnipro River, opposite the regional capital of Kherson. Before Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, the city had approximately 24,000 residents.
Melania Trump's office estimates that between 1,700 and 2,000 people remain, including about 50 children. Most are believed to be elderly residents who have been unable or unwilling to leave. There has been no formal demographic count since 2022.
The city has endured years of fighting, displacement, and isolation. The destruction of the nearby Kakhovka Dam in June 2023 compounded the devastation, with an estimated 90 percent of Oleshky's territory flooded.
Residents face severe shortages of food, clean water, electricity and medical care. Melania Trump described the city as a frontline community on the brink of disaster, saying roads were mined and military attacks continued regularly.
Russian authorities do not permit independent media to enter Oleshky, making it difficult to independently establish the full extent of the humanitarian crisis.
Ukrainian officials and volunteers have told RFE/RL that civilians in the city are effectively being held hostage to Russia's military objectives in the occupied south. They argue that their presence complicates Ukrainian military operations against Russian positions in the area.
Evacuations From Oleshky
Melania Trump said civilian representatives from Russia and Ukraine would visit residents in their homes to assess their needs. Those wishing to leave would receive coordinated assistance and transportation to their preferred destinations.
“I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine,” she said.
Her office said the parties had worked on the technical arrangements, including demining, but did not disclose the planned routes, the number of expected evacuees, or the mechanisms for monitoring compliance with the cease-fire.
The first lady said she had also secured an American media organization to accompany and document Russian and Ukrainian teams during the operation, arguing that independent documentation would help ensure families' wishes were respected. Conservative US outlet Newsmax said it would participate.
Melania Trump said the crisis came to her attention during a private discussion at her Fostering the Future Together event in New York during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly.
She said her representative used communications channels established during previous efforts to reunite children separated from their families during the war. According to her office, those efforts have helped reunite 34 children with their families.
President Trump praised the initiative, saying both sides were cooperating with his wife.
“She wants to see babies come back to their families and that's between Russia and Ukraine,” Trump told reporters. He said the cease-fire had been negotiated in a particularly difficult area and described his wife's work as “great.”
Zelenskyy Seeks Security Guarantees
The announcement came as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy addressed the Hudson Institute in Washington, where he called for renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war while warning that any settlement must prevent Russia from attacking Ukraine again.
Zelenskyy said he had spoken shortly before the event with US President Donald Trump's envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, about recent meetings and ways to advance negotiations.
He said a trilateral meeting involving Ukraine, the United States and Russia was being planned for the first half of November, potentially at the technical level, with the longer-term goal of talks between the countries' leaders.
“We need these meetings, and we need diplomacy to move forward,” Zelenskyy said, adding that progress would depend on Russia's willingness to participate.
He said Ukraine was ready to meet at any time but accused Moscow of repeatedly finding reasons to delay negotiations. Zelenskyy also emphasized the need for continued American pressure on Russia and said Europe should be included in the broader discussions.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine would need financial support to maintain a strong army for at least 10 years, alongside reconstruction assistance and access to advanced weapons systems.
He also said Ukraine was still waiting for previously agreed deliveries of interceptors for Patriot air-defense systems, which he described as essential as Russia continued large-scale attacks with drones and missiles.
“The most important thing is not just negotiating,” he said. “We need results.”
Starlink Restrictions Persist
Zelenskyy's comments came as he said restrictions affecting Ukraine's access to Starlink satellite communications remained in place, despite reports that the problem had been resolved.
Asked about the issue outside the White House, Trump said he had not spoken to Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX operates Starlink but might contact him if the restrictions continued.
“I've heard it was fixed, but if it's not, I'll speak to him,” Trump said.
Zelenskyy told the Hudson Institute that limitations affecting Starlink and delays in interceptor deliveries were complicating Ukraine's defense, although he said Ukrainian forces continued to hold their positions and maintain military logistics.
