Israel’s olive harvest attacks demand full UK sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:02:16 UTC
01:02:16 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel’s olive harvest attacks demand full UK sanctions
Some fifteen years ago, I was lucky enough to be in Palestine during the olive harvest season. So much about what I saw on that visit was overwhelmingly sad and infuriating. The ugly infrastructure of apartheid was everywhere—the huge concrete apartheid wall with the looming Israeli sniper towers, checkpoints seemingly at every turn, menacing armed soldiers and hilltops dotted with settlements. But a visit with farmers in a village outside Jenin felt like stepping into an alternate universe, full of joy and beauty.
Multiple generations of Palestinian families all gathered together in varying degrees of work and play. Teenagers, usually glued to their mobile phones, were getting gentle lessons from their elders on the best way to shake the tree branches to loosen the crop. Joyful toddlers waddled around their grandmothers and mothers, who made tea while chatting and preparing the freshest, most delicious bread I’ve ever eaten, filled with fresh cheese and za’atar.
If you could train your eyes on this scene, you could imagine, for a moment, what a free Palestine might look and sound like.
The olive harvest season is not just a time for Palestinians families to gather and celebrate their heritage. It is traditionally the economic lifeblood of Palestine, already under significant pressure because of decades of Israel’s land grabs, not to mention restrictions on exports which benefit Israeli settlers and harm Palestine’s indigenous olive economy under occupation.
The olive harvest used to be a significant part of the economy in the Gaza Strip, where olive trees are now largely a memory of a time past, before endless expanses of rubble dominated the terrain.
A site of existential threat
In recent years, on top of the ordinary hardship of occupation, the olive harvest in the West Bank has increasingly been hit with violence and danger. Gone are the days when the olive groves could offer a glimpse of a possible future life — now they are a site of existential threat and fear.
The UN reported that last week, the official week starting the olive harvest, saw nearly 200 settler attacks across the expanse of the West Bank, with casualties, property damage or both, including damage to 2,500 trees and saplings. This is already more than the 185 comparable incidents recorded during the entire olive harvest season last year in 2025, which was already the worst many could remember.
These settler attacks don’t come out of nowhere. UN human rights experts raised alarm that the Israeli military had issued orders in September for the removal of vegetation, including provisions to uproot olive trees, from approximately 339,000 square metres (84 acres) of Palestinian agricultural land in the West Bank.
In what has now become a predictable pattern, the Israeli military provided a blueprint for settler attacks on the olive harvest through its policies. It is the same military, of course, which provides armed cover for the settlers when they wage their violent attacks.
When Palestinians report that the settlers and the army are working hand in hand, this is what they mean.
News footage from Palestine this week shows this starkly. Farmers work as quickly as possible before the mobs of settlers arrive, armed with clubs or worse. For Palestinian farmers, the thought of bringing family members who aren’t able to work quickly is unimaginable now, because of the looming danger in every minute.
The settler attacks are ruthless and don’t spare any man, woman or child. Mainstream news outlets globally showed videos last weekend of settlers beating and attacking a Washington Post journalist covering the West Bank, as well as European diplomats who had been on an official visit. One journalist who tried to help his colleague reported the difficulty of reaching her. This was not only because of the settlers, but also because the Israeli military was firing tear gas and live ammunition into the area, forcing the Palestinian farmers to flee their own fields.
You don’t need much more information to guess that if that is how white Americans and Europeans are being treated, Palestinians are confronted with violence that is ten times worse.
Weaknesses in the UK government’s response
Here in Britain, Israel’s colonial settlements have had more media exposure in the past few months than possibly ever before, as the British government announced new measures last month to ban the import of settlement goods and some limited sanctions, along with other measures designed to curb the actions of what Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband called “settler terrorists”.
Whilst these measures are certainly a step in the right direction, they don’t go nearly as far as they should. This month’s spike in attacks on Palestinians harvesting their olives shows both the weaknesses of the British sanctions as they are currently formulated, but also the possibilities that could be pushed if the government is serious about tackling settler violence.
The weakness of the British government’s position is that it has rhetoric that is tough on settler violence but treats that phenomenon as its own isolated problem. Understanding the inextricable link between the settler movement, the colonial settlements already established for decades, and Israel’s military occupation itself is key to intervening in the violence.
The settlers couldn’t function as they do without the full-throated support they enjoy from the Israeli military. And despite commitments to curb the flow of arms that enable the occupation, no additional arms exports to Israel have been halted since Miliband’s announcement last month.
The problem goes even further if one understands the link between the settler movement and the Israeli government itself. The British government seems to be still entertaining the fantasy that the settler movement can be isolated and treated separately from the Israeli state.
Of course it is the Israeli state itself which, over decades and across parties, has enacted policy and funded the settlements. Nowadays top Israeli government ministers come directly from the far-right settler movement, but this is a result of decades of normalisation of settlements, rather than the start of it.
Even if you could magically remove the far-right settler movement in isolation, many of Israel’s earliest West Bank settlements are now major hubs of the Israeli agricultural industry. They profit from land grabs from Palestinians, enriching themselves from Palestinian land and water, and dominating the exports of produce abroad, whilst Palestinian olive farmers struggle, and still would even without the violent settler attacks.
In order to really tackle settler violence, the British government must extend its sanctions proposal to be state sanctions on Israel. There is no separating out the settlements from the state, and there is no legitimate trade with a state committing apartheid and genocide.
These sanctions must include, but not be limited to, a full two-way arms embargo on Israel.
Stemming from this, the tasks of the solidarity movement are clear. We must continue to push the British government to strengthen its sanctions on Israel, through lobbying and protesting, but also by exposing the contradictions in what is currently in place.
None of these actions will stop the horror of settler attacks during this olive harvest season. The coming month will be a painful time for Palestinians who are being forced to defend themselves, their families, their livelihoods and their lands.
Whilst political debates within our solidarity movement rage on, certainly we can all agree that we absolutely cannot lose sight of the stakes for Palestinians, and the horrible costs they are paying every day. But this urgency must compel our solidarity forward to push our government to enact full sanctions on Israel now.
Ryvka Barnard is the Deputy Director of the Palestine Solidarity Campaign UK.

Personalized cancer vaccine cuts risk of melanoma recurrence or death by 42% in trial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:01:36 UTC
01:01:36 KST

Aysu Bicer
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
A personalized cancer vaccine administered alongside an immunotherapy drug reduced the risk of death or melanoma recurrence by 42%, according to results from a major clinical trial involving more than 1,000 patients.
The phase three trial found that the combination of the vaccine and Keytruda, an immunotherapy drug widely used in cancer treatment, also reduced the risk of melanoma spreading by 38% over two years compared with treatment with Keytruda alone.
The international trial involved patients with high-risk melanoma, an aggressive form of skin cancer. Participants received either the personalized vaccine alongside Keytruda or Keytruda with a placebo for approximately one year.
The study was double-blind, meaning neither the patients nor the researchers knew who received the vaccine or the placebo.
Researchers said the findings could represent a significant step toward personalized cancer treatment, which aims to stimulate the body's immune system to identify and attack cancer cells remaining after surgery.
“The personalized cancer vaccine uses exciting technology to stimulate the patient’s own immune system to recognise and attack any tumour cells remaining after surgery,” said Professor Pippa Corrie, a consultant medical oncologist in a statement on Friday.
“It is a whole new approach to cancer treatment which is designed to improve outcomes compared with standard anticancer drug treatments that don't take into account individual differences, and this trial was the first proof of principle,” she added.
Tony Chapman, 75, from North Northamptonshire, who participated in the trial at Addenbrooke’s Hospital, described the findings as “groundbreaking.”
Chapman was diagnosed with stage three melanoma in 2019 and underwent surgery to remove a tumour from his chest. Four years later, he discovered a lump under his armpit and required surgery to remove lymph nodes.
After completing treatment at the NIHR Cambridge Clinical Research Facility last year, Chapman remains cancer-free. However, it is not known whether he received the personalized vaccine or the placebo.
Drugmakers MSD and Moderna said the same approach is also being tested against other cancers, including kidney, bladder and lung cancers.
Independent cancer experts welcomed the results but stressed that longer-term studies are needed to determine whether the treatment improves overall survival for most patients.
The findings offer encouraging evidence for personalized cancer vaccines, although further research will be needed to establish their long-term benefits.

Nine in 10 women's organizations assisting people displaced from Sudan's El Fasher report unsafe living conditions and persistent psychological distress a year after the city's fall, the UN Women said on Friday.
Anna Mutavati, UN Women's regional director for East and Southern Africa, told reporters in Geneva that a survey of 50 organizations found 45 reporting continued psychological distress among displaced women and girls, while 49 observed signs of distress.
"One year on, the scars of the violence in El Fasher have not faded," Mutavati said, citing sexual violence, missing relatives, killings and the destruction of homes and livelihoods.
She said 48 organizations reported that women were struggling to sleep because of traumatic experiences, while nine in 10 described unsafe living conditions.
Around two-thirds of the groups were aware of women or girls who had disappeared during or after the city's fall.
Mutavati said 43 organizations had encountered women or girls who received no mental health, psychosocial or legal assistance after fleeing.
She also warned of increasing drone attacks across Sudan, including in Blue Nile, Khartoum, West Kordofan, Gedaref and Kassala states, with women and children accounting for most of those killed or injured.
According to a separate assessment, 84% of 117 households surveyed in El Fasher reported that women avoided marketplaces.
Mutavati called for stronger civilian protection, accountability for abuses and improved access to essential services, while emphasizing the role of women-led organizations in supporting affected communities.
The civil war between Sudan’s army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces erupted in April 2023. It has since displaced more than 14 million people and created one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.

France to deploy 70,000 police ahead of new protests

2026-10-23

Breadcrumb
France to deploy 70,000 police ahead of new protests
France will deploy some 70,000 police nationwide as it braces for new protests this weekend after some of the worst urban violence in years erupted on the sidelines of demonstrations a week ago, the government said Friday.
President Emmanuel Macron, who according to aides is postponing a visit later this month to Nigeria and Senegal amid the crisis, held a meeting of his defence council of top ministers and officials and was to meet security forces.
He also hosted for the first time representatives of high school pupils, whose protests over conditions at their schools sparked the movement that has broadened into a nationwide show of anger against the government at the rising cost of living.
Some 70,000 security personnel will be deployed on Saturday, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said at a press conference in Paris, warning that calls for violence and looting were circulating on social media.
The protests have come at a critical moment for France six months ahead of elections to replace Macron, with a new poll underlining far-right candidate Marine Le Pen as the frontrunner and showing her position has been strengthened by the latest events.
Adding to tensions, Le Pen is at the weekend due to host her National Rally (RN) party congress in Orleans, with thousands of supporters expected but local authorities fearing clashes as opponents head to the city.
Nunez was expected to visit the city Friday to "inspect the security arrangements" at the request of the prime minister's office, it said.
At Macron's meeting with students, "we will present our demands to him -- which remain the same: the state of school infrastructure and an overhaul of the Parcoursup (university admissions) system," Nathanael Combary, president of Renouveau Lyceen (High School Renewal) told AFP ahead of the talks.
Macron's government has sought to draw a line between the legitimate demands of protesters and the looting, burning and ransacking that erupted on the sidelines of protests last Saturday.
In a judicial response of unprecedented firmness, courts have already sent 217 people, half of them first-time offenders, to prison over the events on Saturday, Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said.
On Thursday, Macron called for "the utmost severity" against "acts of delinquency", accusing "ultra-left" groups of having sought to "bring down the republic" last weekend.
'Police have a responsibility'
A fresh wave of demonstrations is expected across France on Saturday, with authorities stepping up security measures and imposing restrictions on protests.
In Orleans, between 20,000 and 30,000 people were expected to come out against Le Pen's National Rally party, but the gathering will be barred from the city centre, the prefecture said.
In the southeastern city of Lyon, central areas will also be off-limits to demonstrators this weekend, while in Paris protesters will only be allowed to march a limited route between Bastille and Nation squares.
Authorities in Marseille had also banned protests but announced Friday that a union-organised demonstration would be allowed on an "exceptional basis" -- the only one authorised in the southern Bouches-du-Rhone department.
They also reversed a decision to suspend all public transport in the city on Saturday. But in the capital, leading museums including the Louvre will be closed on Saturday while the Art Basel art fair is being cut short.
Some 20 percent more members of the security forces will be deployed this weekend after heavy criticism of the anticipation and intelligence gathering of police last week.
"In a country governed by the rule of law, the police have a responsibility both to ensure that protests can take place peacefully and safely and to protect the public from violent disorder," said Eva Cosse, senior Europe researcher at Human Rights Watch, expressing alarm over reports of children being severely injured by crowd-control weapons.
The violence has tarnished the image of France ahead of elections that could be a turning point in its modern history, with the government's debt pile also troubling investors.
A new poll by Harris Interactive for M6/RTL made after the violence showed Le Pen soaring ahead on 33-35 percent in the first round of voting for the presidential elections.
It predicted that hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon was on course to face her in the run-off where Le Pen would emerge as an easy winner on some 70 percent of the vote.

Britain assessing quantum threat to military crypto
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
17:00:52 BST
01:00:52 KST

The Ministry of Defence is assessing its cryptographic dependencies as part of continued preparations for transition to post-quantum cryptography, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Stuart Anderson, the Conservative member for South Shropshire, asked what assessment has been made of the level of vulnerability of military command-and-control networks to quantum-based decryption.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “The Ministry of Defence is assessing its cryptographic dependencies as part of its continued preparations for transition to post-quantum cryptography.
“This assessment remains ongoing in line with wider Government advice and guidance. Necessary replacements will be managed through Defence’s post-quantum migration planning and appropriate equipment refresh cycles.”
A sufficiently capable quantum computer would break the public-key cryptography that secures most military and civilian communications, which has produced the harvest now, decrypt later concern, where an adversary collects encrypted traffic today in the expectation of reading it once the machines exist.
The United States National Institute of Standards and Technology published its first post-quantum cryptographic standards in 2024, and the National Cyber Security Centre has set out a timeline for British organisations to discover their cryptographic dependencies, plan migration and complete the transition, with 2035 as the target for completion of high-priority systems.
Managing replacements through equipment refresh cycles ties cryptographic migration to the normal replacement of hardware. Military platforms have service lives measured in decades, and systems fielded now will still be flying, sailing or driving well into the period when quantum decryption is expected to become feasible.
Anderson asked a series of questions on emerging technology and industrial resilience on the same day, covering intellectual property arrangements in joint international technology projects, the balance between asymmetric capability and platform-heavy procurement, sovereign manufacturing for next-generation combat air, and maintenance resilience in domestic shipyards.
On procurement balance, Pollard said the Defence Investment Plan sets out how the Integrated Force will draw on a more varied mix of equipment and weapons, combining advanced platforms and precision weapons with autonomous technologies and lower-cost, expendable effectors, increasing the mass, lethality and resilience of the force while ensuring investment remains threat-led, affordable and aligned with NATO requirements.
On intellectual property, he said the most common framework for joint international technology development projects is laid out in NATO Allied Acquisition Practices Publication AACP-1, with conditions pre-agreed among NATO members, and that where projects involve non-NATO nations the department will suggest AACP-1 conditions in the first instance.

====================================================================================================

Chest vibrations paired with meditation appears to alter brain wiring in trauma survivors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:00:21 UTC
01:00:21 KST

Combining mindfulness meditation with a gentle buzzing device on the chest can physically alter brain pathways related to body awareness in adults who have experienced trauma. The combination therapy helped participants feel more connected to their bodies, corresponding with increased nerve density in specific brain regions. The research was published in Neuropsychopharmacology.
Many trauma survivors struggle with a debilitating psychological symptom called dissociation. This condition involves feeling detached from one’s own physical form or disconnected from the surrounding environment. Frontline treatments often require patients to vividly confront traumatic memories to process them. This approach can be overwhelmingly distressing and mentally taxing. Consequently, many patients abandon therapy before they can experience any lasting relief.
To help ground patients in the present moment, psychologists often focus on improving a skill called interoception. This is the nervous system’s ability to perceive signals originating inside the body, like a heartbeat or breathing rhythm. Mindfulness meditation is a common tool used to build this internal awareness. However, maintaining focus during meditation requires a sustained effort that can be especially difficult for novices or those experiencing high levels of anxiety.
Researchers Negar Fani, Alexa Kondas, and Timothy J. McDermott at the Emory University School of Medicine wanted to test a novel method to make meditation easier and more effective for trauma survivors. By adding a physical, external sensation to the meditation process, they hypothesized that patients could anchor their attention more easily. This external anchor could provide a tangible point of focus when the mind begins to wander or dissociate.
The researchers utilized a small mechanism placed on the sternum, the central bone of the chest. This device delivers a low-frequency vibration to the skin. Depending on the setting, the vibration is either synchronized to the user’s breathing patterns or pulsed at regular intervals. The physical buzzing acts as a continuous sensory reminder, helping to draw the user’s attention back to their physical body without requiring intense mental effort.
The clinical trial included 116 adults who had experienced trauma and reported elevated levels of dissociation. The participants were randomly assigned to different experimental groups. All participants completed eight brief sessions of mindfulness meditation over a period of several weeks. About half of the participants meditated while receiving the chest vibrations, while the other half completed the exact same meditation exercises without the added vibration device.
The researchers conducted advanced brain scans on the participants before the therapy began and again after the eight sessions were completed. They utilized a specialized magnetic resonance imaging technique that measures the microscopic structure of the brain’s white matter. The brain is broadly divided into gray matter, where information processing occurs, and white matter, which consists of the biological cables that connect different processing centers. These connective cables are primarily composed of axons and dendrites, which are the long, thread-like extensions of nerve cells.
The imaging analysis focused on calculating the density of these nerve extensions within the white matter. An increase in density typically reflects the growth of new connections or the strengthening of existing ones. The ability of the brain to rewire itself in response to new experiences is known as neuroplasticity. By measuring changes in nerve density, the researchers could observe if the meditation practice was genuinely reshaping the brain’s physical architecture.
The brain scans revealed an increase in nerve density within a specific region called the corticospinal tract. This tract is a massive bundle of nerve fibers that carries movement and sensory signals between the brain and the rest of the body. Notably, this increase in nerve density occurred only in the group that received the sternal vibrations. The group that practiced meditation alone did not show the same physical brain changes in this sensory pathway.
To ensure their initial brain mapping was accurate, the researchers ran a secondary validation test. They used a mathematical modeling tool to reconstruct the entire three-dimensional pathway of the corticospinal tract for each participant. This secondary analysis confirmed the initial observation across the study sample. The vibration group consistently developed denser nerve connections along this entire sensory pathway compared to the control group.
Beyond looking at the brain scans, the researchers wanted to know if the participants actually experienced psychological benefits. After each session, the participants filled out questionnaires rating their level of bodily connectedness and awareness. Over the course of the eight sessions, the group receiving chest vibrations reported a much greater improvement in body awareness than the group practicing standard meditation. Both groups showed similar reductions in feelings of dissociation over the sessions.
The most revealing part of the study emerged when the researchers compared the structural brain scans to the psychological questionnaires. In the vibration group, the physical growth of nerve density in the corticospinal tract was directly linked to a reduction in feelings of dissociation. Participants who developed the most pronounced structural changes in their white matter also reported the greatest clinical improvement. This direct relationship between physical brain changes and psychological healing did not appear in the group that meditated without the vibration device.
The researchers suspect that the sternal device works by stimulating the sensory nerves in the chest. This constant, rhythmic buzzing feeds a stream of physical data into the nervous system. This extra stimulation might encourage the brain to build denser nerve connections in the corticospinal tract to process the incoming sensory information. In turn, this strengthened biological hardware makes it easier for the person to perceive their own body at rest, alleviating the symptoms of dissociation over time.
While the experimental setup allows the researchers to link the vibration therapy to the brain changes, the exact biological mechanisms behind this physical remodeling remain somewhat speculative. Human brain scans can reveal structural changes at a macroscopic level, but they cannot show the microscopic chemical processes driving those changes. The study also represents an interim analysis of an ongoing clinical trial, meaning it is currently unknown if these physical and psychological changes will persist for months or years after the therapy sessions end. Finally, the psychological improvements were measured through self-reported questionnaires, which rely on the subjective perspective of the participants.
The study, “Good vibrations: Sternal vibration enhances white matter density and interoceptive awareness,” was authored by Alexa Kondas, Timothy J. McDermott, Vishwadeep Ahluwalia, Greg J. Siegle, Alfonsina Guelfo, Travis M. Fulton, Aziz Elbasheir, Maya C. Karkare, Timothy D. Ely, Amanda Johnston, Rebecca Krawczak, Robert T. Krafty and Negar Fani.

Two ex-FBI officials charged with lying about investigation into Hunter Biden’s laptop

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:00:21 UTC
01:00:21 KST

Two former FBI intelligence officials who specialized in foreign election interference were charged on Friday with making false statements about their roles in investigating the origins of Hunter Biden’s laptop in the run-up to the 2020 presidential election.
Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides surrendered on Friday and made their first appearance in federal court in Washington DC. Floris’s legal team expressed outrage at the development coming from the US Department of Justice, the parent agency of the FBI.
“Nikki Floris is a patriot. She served our nation as a dedicated FBI intelligence officer for nearly 20 years. Yet today, the [justice department] has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts. It’s no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election,” her attorneys said in a statement.
The case was filed 10 days before the 3 November midterm elections and marks the latest in a series of high-profile and politically charged investigative actions the justice department has undertaken in the run-up during the height of campaigning ahead of the vote.
The prosecution, a rare justice department criminal case against a former employee, revisits a tangled and bizarre saga that roiled the final weeks of the 2020 race, in which Joe Biden, Hunter Biden’s father, beat Donald Trump but Trump refused to accept the result and tried numerous ways to overturn it – which ended up in his second impeachment, accused of inciting an insurrection attempt on 6 January 2021, and criminal charges that were ultimately dismissed after Trump’s 2024 election victory.
Friday’s court proceedings also came amid a broader, backward-looking effort by the FBI director, Kash Patel, who before taking over the nation’s premier law enforcement agency was a harsh critic of it, to scrutinize high-profile episodes from the bureau’s recent past that for years have animated Trump’s conservative base.
The revelation of the laptop’s existence in October 2020 injected a thorny storyline in the race between Trump and Biden.
The laptop’s contents were publicized by the New York Post, which said it had obtained from Trump ally Rudy Giuliani a hard drive of a computer dropped off by Hunter Biden at a Wilmington, Delaware, repair shop. The laptop contained emails that appeared to show discussions of the younger Biden’s foreign business dealings.
The peculiar circumstances of the laptop’s discovery raised concerns among Democrats and former intelligence officials about the possibility of Russian disinformation, particularly when the Trump administration’s own intelligence community was assessing that Russia was attempting to interfere on Trump’s behalf in the election and as Giuliani had traveled abroad looking for dirt on the Bidens.

====================================================================================================

Ukraine Ends Blanket Deferments, Ties Full Exemptions to Military Service
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:58:48 UTC
00:58:48 KST

Ukraine’s government, led by Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi, has finalized changes to its worker deferment system, effectively ending automatic exemptions from mobilization for defense and energy companies.
The overhaul aims to create fair rules for those working away from the front, and, above all, for soldiers who have been fighting for nearly five years and need a realistic chance to return home. The number of deferred workers is rising by tens of thousands each month, according to Koretskyi’s estimates.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Unconditional full deferment is unfair to those who serve and opens the door to misuse,” Koretskyi said, adding that some companies had been set up purely to obtain deferments and that “it became a business.”
Four changes to follow
First, a company’s status as critical will no longer depend on its economic performance.
Sectors that directly support defense and the economy – including weapons production, energy, communications, logistics, and housing and utilities – will keep their status. However, the criteria will be updated and checked for misuse.
In an interview with BBC Ukraine on Monday, Oct. 19, Koretskyi said high salaries and the absence of tax debts do not, on their own, make a company critical.
Second, defense and energy companies will no longer be able to automatically defer 100% of their employees. While Koretskyi did not specify the new limit, earlier proposals had suggested lowering it to 85% in the defense and energy sectors, and from 75% to 60% in the utilities sector, according to the New Voice of Ukraine.
Oleshky Evacuation: Russia Announces Kherson Frontline ‘Silence Regime’
Companies that need more workers deferred to keep operating can submit a justified request to the Coordination Center.
Third; tougher enforcement. The Defense Ministry will increase penalties for evading military service, Koretskyi said.
Lastly, the government will work on developing a mechanism that would allow companies to defer all of their employees, should they regularly send some of them to serve voluntarily. Meanwhile, those who enlist would know where they would be sent and for how long, while keeping their jobs and salaries.
The Defense and Economy ministries will draft the terms with businesses, aiming for approval by Dec. 1.
What it means exactly
Men aged 25 to 60 must serve in the military under Ukrainian law, unless they obtain a legal deferment for reasons ranging from critical infrastructure employment to medical reasons.
Under Cabinet Resolution No. 76, which sets out Ukraine’s deferment procedure during martial law, most critical companies can defer up to 50% of their draft-age employees, while defense and energy firms have been allowed to defer up to 100%.
The new approach makes full protection conditional – companies can keep their entire workforce only in case they contribute to the military on a rotating basis.
This would essentially give frontline troops confidence that they will be replaced by others, Koretskyi said, while giving new recruits a clear term of service.
“The ultimate goal is that no one has to search for anyone on the streets,” he said, in an apparent reference to recruiters forcibly detaining men in public, while they are grocery shopping or walking somewhere.
The changes, however, do not signal an immediate escalation. “These decisions do not mean tougher mobilization starting tomorrow,” Koretskyi said, adding that Ukraine must nonetheless be prepared for any scenario, including expanded mobilization in Russia.
Only a month earlier, on Sept. 28, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree No. 700, increasing the size of Russia’s armed forces to 2.4 million, including 1.5 million active-duty military personnel. It marked the fourth time such a decree was signed during this year alone.
The announcement around the same time President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that Russia had already begun additional mobilization, including the expansion of foreign troops, with over 8,000 already in Russia and up to 50,000 more planned.
Industry pushback
Defense manufacturers had lobbied against the measures before they were even finalized.
On Oct. 17, industry groups told UNN that lowering the quota, even to 85%, could halt production lines, delay weapons deliveries and expose companies to penalties for missing state contract lines.
Weapons production runs in sequential stages, so losing a few key engineers or welders at one stage can stall an entire line, with replacements taking months or even years to train, they argued.
The Ukrainian Council of Arms Manufacturers said it had not been consulted and had seen no assessment of how the change would affect production.
Serhii Pashynskyi, head of the National Association of Ukrainian Defense Industry Enterprises (NAUDI) told UNN that several thousand workers who would lose deferments “will definitely not solve the problem of mobilization to the Defense Forces.”
According to the industry representatives, defense workers make up no more than 10% of all deferred conscription-aged civilians, while NAUDI says the sector supplies the military with more than $10 billion in equipment and weapons each year.
Manufacturers have instead called for keeping 100% deferment and carrying out targeted inspections of individual companies suspected of abuse or misuse of the law.
Former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov claimed in January that two million Ukrainian citizens were wanted for alleged mobilization evasion at the time, while another 200,000 servicemen were listed as absent without official leave (AWOL).
On Sept. 1, he had obtained a legal deferment from military mobilization via work with the charitable group “Eastern Europe Foundation,” with some lawmakers casting doubt on the document’s legitimacy.

Roundup: SMEs in Germany post higher profitability in spite of challenges
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
23:57:45 CST
00:57:45 KST

FRANKFURT, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Small- and Medium-Sized Enterprises (SMEs) in Germany turned out to be resilient and posted modest growth of profitability in 2025 in spite of prevailing challenges, a study published on Thursday showed.
German SMEs generated an aggravate turnover of 5.3 trillion euros (about 5.9 trillion U.S. dollars) in 2025, up by 1.5 percent year-on-year and profit margins climbed by 0.5 percentage points to 7.5 percent on average, according to the result of a survey conducted by the KfW Development Bank.
The result is a sign that the German SMEs are "well-positioned" to drive forward the economic recovery in the country, said the bank in a press release.
The findings of the survey also showed that German SMEs in 2025 became more resilient financially to buffer potential shockwaves with improved equity ratio. The share of SMEs with equity ratio higher than 30 percent grew by 1.5 percentage points to more than 51 percent while the share of SMEs with equity ratio below ten percent fell under 24 percent from over 28 percent in 2024.
The strong financial position should, according to Dirk Schumacher, chief economist of KfW, enable them to invest in the future.
Nonetheless, the survey pointed to a reluctance of SMEs to invest, as half of the SMEs invested no more than 5.4 percent of their turnover in their business in 2025 due to high energy and material prices and higher wage burdens.
To sum up the challenges German SMEs are faced up with, a report published by a British consulting company RSM Ebner Stolz concluded that "the economic conditions facing Germany's SME sector have changed fundamentally in recent years."
The global geopolitical tensions tighten and U.S. trade policies became erratic, weighing on the exports on which German SMEs relied on heavily. Meanwhile, surging energy prices and declined competitiveness have eroded the attractiveness of Germany as a destination of investment.
German SMEs are hit "particularly hard", said the "SME Diagnosis 2025" report published by the German Savings Banks Association.
The German SMEs are at "a turning point" and transformation and international business have become decisive for long-term competitiveness, said the report. ■

WINDHOEK, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Namibia's Etango uranium project is expected to raise the country's uranium production capacity and create jobs and business opportunities for local people, Minister of Industries, Mines and Energy Modestus Amutse said Friday.
Speaking at the official launch and progress update of the project in the western Erongo Region, Amutse said the government expected mining investment to drive sustainable economic growth by expanding local employment, skills development and business participation.
The minister said 629 people are working at the Etango site, 99 percent of them Namibians.
Amutse urged Bannerman Mining Resources Namibia, the project's developer, and its partners to give Namibian contractors and businesses more opportunities through local procurement and skills development.
He said local participation was an investment in the country's economic future.
The project is targeting commissioning and first yellowcake production in 2028, with planned output of about 3.5 million pounds of uranium oxide a year.
Amutse said Namibia, currently the world's third-largest uranium producer, could overtake Canada once Etango is operational.
Located about 30 km southeast of the coastal town of Swakopmund, Etango lies in the Erongo uranium belt, which is also home to the Rossing, Husab and Langer Heinrich mines.
The project is being developed by a joint venture between Australian-listed Bannerman Energy and CNNC Overseas Limited, a subsidiary of China National Nuclear Corporation (CNNC).
Under an agreement signed in February, CNNC Overseas took a 45 percent stake in the joint venture and committed about 320 million U.S. dollars to the project's construction, which will be carried out without debt. ■

Major Ebola vaccine trial begins in DR Congo as outbreak continues
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
23:57:37 CST
00:57:37 KST

A medical worker pre-checks a volunteer participating in the Tumaini clinical trial of a vaccine against the Bundibugyo Ebola virus in Bunia, eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Oct. 23, 2026. (Xinhua)
KINSHASA, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- A major clinical trial to evaluate vaccines against the Bundibugyo Ebola virus began Friday in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), with the first participants vaccinated as the country battles the largest recorded outbreak of the virus.
The Phase 2/3 trial, known as Tumaini, was launched in Bunia, the capital of the hardest-hit Ituri Province, said the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations, which is funding and supporting the study.
The trial comes amid a worsening Ebola crisis that has claimed more than 4,600 lives in the DRC since May. Despite the scale of the outbreak, no vaccine has yet been approved specifically against the Bundibugyo virus.
Tumaini, meaning "hope" in Swahili, aims to assess the safety, immune responses and effectiveness of several vaccine candidates, particularly among people who have been in contact with confirmed Ebola patients and face a high risk of infection.
The trial uses an adaptive platform design, allowing multiple vaccine candidates to be evaluated within a single study through a ring vaccination approach targeting contacts of confirmed cases.
The first vaccine entering the trial is Ervebo, which is already licensed to prevent disease caused by the Zaire Ebola virus but has not been proven effective against the Bundibugyo virus.
Two additional vaccines specifically developed against the Bundibugyo virus, one by Moderna and another by the University of Oxford in collaboration with the Serum Institute of India, are expected to join the trial "shortly."
"The launch of the Tumaini trial marks a critical step towards establishing whether candidate vaccines can effectively protect people against the Bundibugyo virus," said Chikwe Ihekweazu, executive director of the World Health Organization's Health Emergencies Program.
WHO Regional Director for Africa Mohamed Janabi also welcomed the launch Friday, saying the trial would generate crucial evidence on candidate vaccines while strengthening the response to the ongoing outbreak and preparedness for future epidemics.
According to the latest figures released late Wednesday by the DRC's health authorities, the country had recorded 9,704 confirmed Ebola cases, including 4,687 deaths, as of Oct. 20, with a case fatality rate of 48.3 percent.
The epidemic was declared in the DRC on May 15 and designated a public health emergency of international concern by the WHO two days later. The Africa CDC subsequently declared it a public health emergency of continental security.
The current Ebola outbreak has become the largest and deadliest ever recorded in the DRC and the second-largest Ebola outbreak globally, after the 2014-2016 West Africa epidemic. ■

China Focus: China grants approval to Citi for wholly-owned securities company in opening-up push
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
23:57:29 CST
00:57:29 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- China's securities regulator on Friday approved Citigroup's plan to establish a wholly-owned securities company in the country, the latest step in the country's broader push to open the financial sector wider to foreign institutions.
The approval allows the U.S. firm to offer capital markets services in China, including equities brokerage, securities investment advisory, securities underwriting and proprietary securities trading, the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) said in a statement.
The firm, Citigroup Securities (China) Company Limited, will be registered in Shanghai, with registered capital of 1.2 billion yuan (about 178.6 million U.S. dollars).
It will become the seventh wholly foreign-owned securities firm approved to operate in China, following J.P. Morgan, Goldman Sachs, Standard Chartered, BNP Paribas, UBS, and Mizuho.
The approval will deepen Citi's long-standing presence in China, allowing the company to better support clients' growth and investment needs, Citi said in an online statement.
"We appreciate the support from regulators to expand our offering in this important market," said Jane Fraser, chair of the board and chief executive officer of Citi. "By adding onshore capabilities to our global platform, we will be able to do more for clients in China's domestic capital markets," she said.
Since the beginning of this year, Citi has helped Chinese clients raise more than 40 billion U.S. dollars in global capital markets, the company said.
The approval came amid China's sustained push to open its financial sector. Since 2020, the CSRC has removed foreign ownership caps on securities firms, fund managers and futures companies, enabling foreign institutions to operate wholly-owned licensed entities.
With policy support, global investment banks have moved from joint ventures to wholly owned operations to tap into the Chinese market, with J.P. Morgan and Goldman Sachs among the first to complete the transition.
Last year, UBS completed its shift to full ownership of its securities unit in China, while Mizuho Securities later obtained approval, further expanding the ranks of wholly foreign-owned brokerages in China.
"The entry of foreign brokerages into China has enriched the competitive landscape of the domestic securities market and reflects foreign institutions' long-term confidence in the Chinese market," said Yang Jingdong, a member of the executive committee at Ping An Securities.
This will push domestic firms to accelerate efforts to strengthen wealth management, derivatives and cross-border investment banking, improve services and better serve the development of the real economy, Yang said.
In a recent interview with Xinhua, Maria Ramos, group chair of Standard Chartered, said that China's orderly advancement of financial opening up has created tangible opportunities for Standard Chartered's China-related business, particularly in RMB internationalization, the global expansion of Chinese corporates, cross-border trade, green finance and wealth management.
Between 2020 and 2026, the bank invested almost 600 million U.S. dollars in China, and Ramos said it would continue to invest in its China franchise and technology. "We are aiming to turn our confidence in China into tangible action on the ground," she said.
In another sign of China's financial opening up, the People's Bank of China, the country's central bank, has approved a subsidiary of U.S. payment giant Visa to set up a bank card clearing institution in China. Visa described this move as "a milestone toward the company serving China's domestic payments market."
During the Annual Conference of Financial Street Forum 2026 held in Beijing this week, CSRC Chairman Wu Qing reaffirmed the country's commitment to expanding high-level opening up.
The CSRC will encourage foreign institutions to leverage their parent companies' expertise and group strengths to further improve product offerings and participate in innovative businesses in China, he said. ■

A man selects fruits at a grocery store in New York, the United States, Oct. 14, 2026. The U.S. consumer sentiment kept falling in October for the third month in a row, as purchasing power continues to dominate consumer views of the economy. (Xinhua/Zhang Fengguo)
NEW YORK, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- The U.S. consumer sentiment kept falling in October for the third month in a row, as purchasing power continues to dominate consumer views of the economy.
According to a final reading released by the University of Michigan (UM) Surveys of Consumers, the Index of Consumer Sentiment weakened to 48 in the October 2026 survey, 0.2 percent below September, and 10.4 percent below a year ago. The sentiment is also 15 percent less than in February, just prior to the Iran conflict.
The Current Economic Conditions Index fell to 46.7, down from 50.9 in September and below last October's 58.6. The Index of Consumer Expectations inched up slightly to 48.8 from 46.3 in September, but was still below last October's 50.3.
The decline in the Current Economic Conditions subindex was driven entirely by buying conditions for durables, which plunged 18 percent on the basis of higher interest rates and rising concerns about the affordability of such purchases. About 69 percent of consumers expect interest rates to rise in the year ahead, the highest since April 2023, suggesting that consumers anticipate further deterioration in buying conditions.
Frustration over high prices eroding consumers' living standards continues to mount, said UM economist Joanne Hsu, director of the surveys.
Year-ahead inflation expectations in October ticked up from 4.6 percent in September to 4.7 percent. Long-run inflation expectations also stepped up from 3.4 percent in September to 3.5 percent. Inflation expectations over both time horizons increased for the second straight month to their highest readings since May. ■

Feature: Fighting fear on front lines of DR Congo's Ebola outbreak
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
23:57:13 CST
00:57:13 KST

BUNIA, DR Congo, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- At an Ebola treatment center in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), saving lives sometimes begins with persuading frightened patients not to flee.
For clinical psychologist Theophraste Tetunabu, fear can be as formidable an obstacle as the disease itself. Some patients are terrified of dying, others struggle with isolation from their families, while some become so distressed that they resist the very treatment meant to save them.
"When patients are told they have tested positive, they fear death. Some may even decide to leave or run away," Tetunabu told Xinhua.
As the epidemic continues to spread across the country and beyond its borders, mental health workers like Tetunabu are fighting a quieter battle against fear, despair and social stigma, which can undermine treatment and leave lasting scars on survivors and their families.
FEAR OF BEING ALONE
For many patients, isolation is among the most distressing aspects of Ebola treatment.
In Congolese communities, illness traditionally brings family members together at the bedside. But Ebola patients must be separated from their loved ones to prevent further transmission, turning a familiar source of comfort into another casualty of the disease.
"In our culture, when someone is sick, there are usually two or three family members at their bedside," Tetunabu explained. "But when they come here, they have to be isolated, away from their families."
That sudden separation, coupled with fears surrounding the disease, can trigger intense anxiety, depression and resistance to treatment.
Tetunabu, who supervises mental health services at the center, said psychological support begins as soon as patients arrive for triage, by explaining treatment procedures, listening to patients' concerns and working the extra mile to reassure them that they are receiving appropriate care.
For some patients, the burden extends beyond their own health. A father undergoing isolation may worry about children left at home, household expenses or unpaid rent.
"If a patient is not psychologically prepared and supported, the situation becomes difficult, even with medical treatment," Tetunabu said, emphasizing the importance of cooperation among doctors, nurses, nutritionists and mental health specialists.
Some patients develop severe psychological distress, including depressive symptoms, agitation or aggressive behavior. In such cases, psychologists work with psychiatrists and other medical professionals to provide additional care.
Esperance, a nurse at the treatment center, has witnessed how a positive diagnosis can devastate patients emotionally.
"When someone is told they are a confirmed case, they think they are going to die," she said. "That is why we call on psychologists to support them, encourage them and give them the strength not to lose hope."
BATTLE AGAINST STIGMA
The psychological suffering does not necessarily end when patients recover. For some survivors, leaving the treatment center means entering another struggle, one against suspicion, rejection and discrimination within their own communities.
Tetunabu said families that have lost relatives to Ebola can find themselves shunned by neighbors and even abandoned by relatives.
"When a person dies of Ebola, there is social rejection. The community pushes you away, and sometimes even family members stop visiting," Tetunabu said.
Misconceptions and rumors about Ebola have also fueled mistrust, discouraging some patients from seeking treatment until their condition has worsened.
Psychologists therefore work to reconnect patients with their families during isolation and accompany survivors back into their communities, helping counter fears and discrimination.
According to the DRC health authorities, the country had recorded 9,704 confirmed Ebola cases, including 4,687 deaths as of Oct. 20, with the outbreak affecting eight provinces.
The World Health Organization said nearly 11,300 people had received mental health and psychosocial support in treatment and transit centers during the current outbreak.
For Tetunabu, seeing a once-terrified patient leave the treatment center is among the most rewarding moments of his work. "It is an enormous joy," he said, stressing that recovery must also mean helping survivors regain their place in society.
"Mental health equals hope," Tetunabu said. ■

WASHINGTON, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a temporary ceasefire in the Russian-controlled southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky starting Oct. 29 to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and civilian evacuations, the White House announced Friday.
"Both nations agreed to temporarily stop all military action in Oleshky to allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway," said a statement issued by the Office of the First Lady Melania Trump.
The White House said the first lady initiated the discussions and worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leaders, alongside her representative, to negotiate the terms of the ceasefire.
"The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster. Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water," said Melania Trump in the statement.
"Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require. Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination," she said.
Oleshky, located across the Dnipro River from the city of Kherson, which remains under Ukrainian control, has been held by Russian forces since the outbreak of the Russia-Ukraine conflict in February 2022. Residents have reported worsening shortages of food and other essential supplies amid continued fighting.
The announcement comes amid renewed U.S. diplomatic efforts to end the Ukraine conflict. Following talks with U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg on Wednesday, Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed in principle to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine in November, according to the Kremlin.
Neither the Russian nor the Ukrainian government has publicly confirmed the ceasefire agreement as of Friday, according to media reports. ■

Yes, Israeli settlers are ripping up West Bank olive trees – but this video is fake
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:56:19 UTC
00:56:19 KST

Yes, Israeli settlers are ripping up West Bank olive trees – but this video is fake
Israeli settlers and soldiers have made a habit of destroying olive trees grown by Palestinian farmers in the West Bank and, in recent days, a video showing some trees being ripped up has circulated online. Just one problem: this particular video was generated by artificial intelligence.
Palestinian olive groves are regularly targeted in the occupied West Bank. This year, the olive harvest was marked by numerous acts of settler violence aimed at Palestinian farmers. Israeli Army bulldozers ripped out olive trees in places like Deir Nizam, a village in the centre of the West Bank, as shown by photos taken by the news agency Reuters in late September.
Since October 14, a video claiming to show olive trees that Israel allegedly ripped up in the West Bank has been circulating on X. The footage shows bulldozers destroying the trees.
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
The video, which was circulated by accounts displaying pro-Palestinian positions, garnered more than 200,000 views across a number of X posts. The video was also shared – before later being taken down – by the Palestinian Authority’s communications team, as noted open source investigator Tal Hagin. It was also shared by the Palestinian ambassador in the Ivory Coast and by the Palestinian media outlet Quds.
A fake video whose origin has been concealed
The video, however, is a fake. When we put it into SynthID – the Google tool that makes it possible to detect images generated by artificial intelligence – the result revealed a watermark on the video indicating that it was produced by Gemini, Google’s chatbot.
It also appears that the video’s creator wanted to hide the video’s artificial origin. An image of a thumbs up has been pasted to the bottom right corner – exactly where the Gemini watermark usually appears.
Anomalies common in AI-generated content
The video also features a number of anomalies common in content generated by artificial intelligence. AI still often struggles to correctly depict specific details.
For example, the shovel on one of the diggers seems to change throughout the video. Initially, it seems to, strangely enough, have spikes on it. Three seconds in, it starts to look normal again.
Another anomaly appears in the background of the video when an olive tree falls to the ground before the digger strikes it.
At least 100,000 olive trees have been destroyed, ripped out or burned in the West Bank since 2023, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Agriculture.

In October 2024 the U.S. State Department offered $10 million for information leading to the identification or location of employees of the Russian media organization Rybar, listing Zvinchuk as its director.
The department's Rewards for Justice program says on its website that Rybar was previously funded by the late Russian mercenary chief Yevgeny Prigozhin and managed social media channels promoting Russian government political interests in the U.S., including by stoking divisions over immigration in the run-up to the 2024 presidential election. Britain imposed sanctions on Zvinchuk and others linked to Rybar in July, having already designated the media company for spreading false narratives about Ukraine and interfering in European elections.
Moscow has regularly denied accusations of misinformation and sabotage campaigns, saying the West is spreading anti-Russian propaganda.
Zvinchuk, a former Russian Defence Ministry official, was detained in Montenegro on charges of spreading "Russian influence," then expelled with three other Russians on Oct. 9.
The State Department spokesperson declined to say whether Washington was involved in Zvinchuk's detention by U.S.-ally Montenegro or whether it had requested his extradition.
Asked to comment on Friday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters Hubbard was not released in exchange for Zvinchuk.
"That's not right," Peskov said of the claim.

Türkiye warns against renewed strikes on Iran as Istanbul hosts high-level talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:54:00 UTC
00:54:00 KST

AA photo.
Türkiye on Oct. 23 warned that any renewed attack on Iran would risk broadening the war and spreading conflict across the region, as Istanbul hosted senior diplomats from key regional powers and European countries for high-level talks.
“We agree that a new attack on Iran would widen the war and spread the conflict across the region. Military intervention in Iran is by no means a solution. No one is endorsing it at this point,” Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan told reporters following the meeting.
Fidan chaired the inaugural joint meeting of the R4 and E3 diplomatic groups, bringing together Türkiye, Egypt, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia under the R4 framework, alongside the United Kingdom, France and Germany, which make up the E3.
Italian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani also attended the talks.
The Oct. 23 gathering marked the first joint meeting of the two groupings, reflecting efforts to strengthen cooperation between European powers and key regional actors amid mounting geopolitical tensions.
Fidan said all countries represented at the meeting opposed any further escalation and supported efforts to end the ongoing conflicts both in the Gulf and Ukraine.
“All the countries around the table want to prevent the war from spreading further. They want the wars in both the Gulf and Ukraine to end,” he said.
“They support a ceasefire and believe diplomacy is the only way forward. This meeting was one of the most significant diplomatic events of recent months,” Fidan said.
His remarks came as several U.S. media outlets reported that the Trump administration was considering resuming strikes on Iran after the country’s midterm elections.
On regional maritime security, Fidan stressed the need to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, warning that disruptions there were driving up prices in Europe.
Fidan also reiterated Türkiye’s support for Saudi Arabia, stressing that the Houthis must halt their attacks in the Red Sea.
“The Strait of Hormuz needs to be reopened immediately, and attacks targeting Saudi Arabia must stop,” he said.
Addressing the Russia-Ukraine war and attacks targeting commercial vessels in the Black Sea, Fidan called for an end to the fighting, or at least safeguards for critical trade.
“Either the war must stop, or, if it does not, the parties must establish exemptions for energy and grain,” he said.
On a question regarding a maritime deal with Libya, Fidan said efforts to ensure stability in the country would continue unabated following the eastern-based House of Representatives' approval of the agreement with Türkiye.
The Libyan parliament in Benghazi unanimously approved the 2019 maritime agreement with Türkiye on Oct. 20, reversing its previous rejection of the deal.
The Turkish top diplomat also said his Egyptian counterpart raised Cairo's reservations about the agreement during the Istanbul meeting, adding that Ankara is ready to address Egypt's concerns.
“We are in a constructive position when it comes to addressing Egypt's reservations,” Fidan said, adding that Türkiye, Italy and Egypt could hold consultations to discuss the issues causing concern.
“We have no problem with holding talks on this matter,” he said.
Fidan also said conditions matured for progress toward unifying Libya's rival administrations in the east and west of the country.
He said ongoing efforts focused on bringing Libya's political and military structures together under a unified framework.
“Soon, you will hear us announce some very good news on this matter,” Fidan said.
The R4 mechanism, established this year by Türkiye, Egypt, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, is intended to promote lasting regional stability and strengthen dialogue on shared challenges through an approach based on regional ownership.
The four countries have held six foreign ministers’ meetings, beginning in Riyadh on March 18, with the most recent taking place in New York on Sept. 21 on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly’s high-level week.
The E3, comprising Britain, France and Germany, emerged from diplomatic coordination on Iran’s nuclear program launched in 2003. Initially focused on the nuclear issue, the grouping has gradually developed into a platform for joint diplomatic initiatives on a broader range of regional and international matters.

‘They took my flower’: Families mourn two soldiers killed near Hebron as IDF braces for escalation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:53:14 UTC
00:53:14 KST

The IDF is still investigating the deadly shooting attack near Hebron in which Staff Sergeant Ron Yonatan Roytman and Sergeant Yuval Shai Svilem were killed. IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, who visited the scene, said that "the outcome of the confrontation with the terrorist cell is painful, but the initial investigation indicates that the force's actions prevented a serious attack against Israeli civilians."
Zamir vowed to pursue and apprehend everyone involved in the attack. He said the IDF had already been preparing for a possible escalation in the West Bank before Friday's shooting. "We reinforced our forces and deployed the headquarters of the 98th Division and many additional troops to the area. Our forces' operations in the region have prevented and thwarted many attacks recently," he said. Ahead of next week's election, Zamir stressed that the entire defense establishment was "at the highest level of preparedness and alert across all fronts."
"Our foremost mission is to thwart terrorism and ensure security and stability for Israel's citizens. We will continue to strike and take the initiative wherever necessary, and we will act with a cool head. We will not be dragged into action or allow our enemies to influence us, especially given the sensitive week ahead. We will also investigate this attack to learn lessons for the future," Zamir said.
The IDF chief expressed his condolences to the families of the two fallen soldiers, who were the first fatalities suffered by the Home Front Command's Ari Battalion.
The battalion was established over the past year to increase the number of combat troops available for different operational sectors, while providing additional forces for missions on the home front. Ari is the fifth battalion of the Home Front Command's Rescue Brigade. Roytman and Svilem were its first fallen soldiers, and their families are struggling to comprehend the loss.
‘I heard about the attack on the radio. Our home has been destroyed’
In the yard of Sergeant Yuval Shai Svilem's family home, a stereo system sits covered in plastic. His father, Amnon, looks at it with tears in his eyes and tells ynet: "It was a regular ritual. Every Saturday evening, after Havdalah, he would play music on it. But that's it. There won't be any more music in this house. Our home has been destroyed."
Yuval's friends and family describe him as one of the kindest people they knew, gentle and friendly toward everyone. "This is a boy who, even now, was still in touch with the babysitter who looked after him when he was three years old. Whenever he came home, he would bring her flowers for Shabbat. And now they've taken my flower," his father said painfully.
Yuval was the eldest of three children. He is survived by his father Amnon, mother Sivan, sister Shira and brother Itamar. "He was a good kid, an angel, always helping and smiling. He went to school here in Hod Hasharon and later graduated successfully from the Torah and Science religious high school in Kfar Saba, where he even earned a two-star diving qualification. That's who he was. He was always ambitious. He also studied biology and wanted to learn about investments later on."
"He was quiet, a homebody, a good kid. He loved going to work and the gym. He always gravitated toward the quiet, good kids, not the troublemakers. He helped everyone. I wanted him to join the Navy, but he wanted to be a combat soldier. He trained extensively for the selection process because he always wanted to be the best."
His parents received the devastating news Friday afternoon when military representatives knocked on their door. Since then, their garden has filled with friends and relatives.
"I heard about the attack on the radio," Amnon recalled. "I was driving, and they mentioned the battalion. I knew it was his battalion. I tried calling him, but he was unavailable. I called and called, and he didn't answer. Eventually I called my wife and told her, 'The boy isn't answering. Maybe he'll answer you.' She tried too, and then they came and knocked on the door."
For now, Amnon says he has no complaints against the IDF, although he wants to understand what happened during the prolonged exchange of fire in which his son was killed. "We still haven't received the investigation findings, and we want to know what happened."
He made just one request to the military representatives who visited his home: "I told them I want to be the last person who ever has to hear the words 'cleared for publication.' My eldest son is gone, and my home has been destroyed."
But Amnon had a different message for Israel's political leadership. "I'm not looking for blood revenge, but I want this to stop. If terrorists take the law into their own hands, the state must make them understand that there are consequences for their actions. It cannot be that they simply demolish their homes while their families remain here and receive money from Hamas or the Palestinian Authority. Their entire immediate families should be expelled from the country, so the next terrorist knows there are consequences for what he does. Not just for him, but for his family too. I'm not looking for blood revenge. We want to stop the bloodshed."
"They took the most precious thing in the world from me. The entire family has been hurt, and they need to take into account that their families will be hurt too. Enough of this bargaining. They'll become martyrs, they'll be glorified, their families will be rewarded, and we'll be left destroyed. Time will pass, but a family never forgets. For us, there are no more holidays or Shabbat. Why should they have them?"
Ron's fight to serve in combat: ‘He dreamed of it’
David Roytman, Ron's brother, told ynet: "He was a star. He was loved everywhere he went. People always say things like that about someone who has fallen, but he really was always number one."
According to David, Ron fought to become a combat soldier. "He wasn't supposed to enlist as a combat soldier at all. He spent a year volunteering with at-risk youth and suffered an injury while playing soccer. They told him there was no chance he would become a combat soldier. And he said, 'That's not going to happen.'"
David said his brother went to extraordinary lengths to achieve his goal. "He went through everyone, from junior officers all the way to the chief medical officer, and he made it into combat service. He became a commander of new recruits and went up to the battalion with them. He always dreamed about it and wanted it. He took every opportunity to serve in the dangerous areas of the West Bank. That's what he pushed for."
David himself served in the Combat Engineering Corps, while their older sister served in the Caracal Battalion. "We're all a family of combat soldiers," he said. Ron attended the Kadoorie Youth Village boarding school in northern Israel. "He was someone who had a real zest for life, someone who loved living. He was my best friend," David concluded.
Staff Sergeant Roytman will be laid to rest Sunday at 11 a.m. at the military cemetery in Ashkelon.
More than 20 minutes of gunfire
The two Hamas-affiliated terrorists behind the attack were Palestinian relatives. Hamouda Wael Mohammed Jaaba and Fares Samir Mohammed Jaaba arrived at the scene, got out of their vehicle and opened fire. The fighting continued for more than 20 minutes, during which additional forces arrived, including the deputy commander of the Ari Battalion and a company commander. The soldiers maneuvered around the terrorists and killed them.
A search of the terrorists' vehicle uncovered a large quantity of ammunition. The assessment is that they intended to carry out a major attack against civilians and planned to reach the main roads before continuing toward populated areas deeper inside Israel. However, investigators are still examining whether the cell was directed by an outside organization or whether the attack was initiated independently by the terrorists.
Because both terrorists were killed, the investigation is continuing in an effort to determine their intended destination. The IDF spokesperson confirmed that the three other people wounded in the attack were also soldiers. All three sustained minor injuries, and their families have been notified.
Ofer Ohana, a medic who arrived Friday morning at the scene of the attack at Yehuda Junction on Route 35, managed to document the gunfire while under live fire himself.
"The terrorist keeps shooting," he can be heard shouting. "There is still an exchange of fire between the terrorist and our forces. We can't get the wounded out. There's been active gunfire for more than 20 minutes."
Following the attack, Israeli forces imposed a closure on Hebron and the nearby town of Halhul, prohibiting entry to and exit from both locations. At the same time, the military implemented a security procedure known as "Gray Bolt" throughout Central Command, under which Palestinian vehicles approaching main roads are checked. The heightened measures were also implemented in the Jenin, Nablus and Jericho sectors as part of efforts to prevent further attacks.
Security forces began extensive searches, engineering operations and preparations to map the homes of the two terrorists, both 27, from Hebron. The men belonged to the same extended family and lived near one another. Investigators are expected to arrest individuals connected to them and examine possible links between the terrorists and additional suspects.
