Lebanon's Fatima Hassan makes history with two Muay Thai golds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:53:13 UTC
00:53:13 KST

Breadcrumb
Fatima Hassan: The Lebanese Muay Thai champion who won two world titles and wants women to be seen
Determined to bring home gold and make her family and country proud, Fatima Hassan stepped into the ring for the final fight of the Muay Thai world championships in Kosovo last month.
Despite feeling unwell, the 27-year-old Lebanese fighter from Baalbek pushed through and launched a relentless attack in the final round. With just 30 seconds left, she delivered the decisive blow to secure her second gold medal of the competition.
Fatima had already won gold in the technical discipline before claiming the title in the main Muay Thai competition, making her the first Lebanese athlete to achieve the double at the IFMA Senior Muay Thai World Championships.
But the medals meant far more to her than sporting success. They represented years of dedication, her family's support, and her determination to prove that women can thrive in a sport long dominated by men.
"Honestly, I'd never been as happy as I was then. I'd worked towards this dream for so long," Fatima tells The New Arab.
Discovering what she loved
Fatima's father introduced her to sport at a young age, encouraged her to try different activities, and taught her the basics of self-defence. She eventually joined a gym near his workplace, where she discovered Muay Thai.
"I didn't really know much about it at the time. They told me it was a nice sport and encouraged me to try it. I went, tried it and loved it," she continues.
At first, she had no ambitions to compete. She simply enjoyed training, but her coaches soon noticed her skills and encouraged her to enter her first competition.
"It hadn't even crossed my mind. I wasn't interested in fighting or hitting people. I didn't like that sort of thing," she recalls.
Her father encouraged her to try it, and after watching another Lebanese female fighter compete, Fatima decided to take the plunge.
She won all three of her first fights, giving her the confidence to pursue Muay Thai more seriously.
But not everyone understood her choice.
As a woman who wears the hijab, Fatima encountered comments from people who considered combat sports unsuitable for girls.
"As long as my father was happy with what I was doing and supporting me, I didn't care what society said or what anyone else thought," Fatima says.
"People would say it was a sport for boys, that I was behaving like a boy, or ask how I could play such a sport when it wasn't meant for girls. But none of it affected me. I loved the sport, and that was what mattered."
Her family's acceptance also took time. Initially uncomfortable with the idea of her competing, they gradually came to understand the sport as they watched her train and fight.
Today, she says, they are among her biggest supporters.
Two gold medals
Fatima's road to the world championships was not straightforward. She had stopped competing for three years because of injuries, although she continued to train and teach Muay Thai.
When the opportunity to compete in Kosovo came along, she knew it was a chance to fulfil a dream she had pursued for years.
Despite her experience, she had only three months to prepare specifically for the tournament.
She worked with several coaches, sought help from a physiotherapist and a doctor, and focused on preparing mentally to return to competition.
She also followed a strict routine, running every day and keeping up with her exercises.
"I went there feeling comfortable and confident. I knew I wanted to come back with an achievement that reflected all the work I'd put in. I kept telling myself that I was going to compete, win and come back with the result I wanted," she tells The New Arab.
Fatima competed in two disciplines: the technical competition and traditional Muay Thai, the main IFMA discipline.
The technical category, in which she competed for the first time, focuses on speed, movement, and technique rather than full-force contact.
She secured her first gold medal there. But the moment she stepped up to receive it stayed with her most.
"When I saw the Lebanese flag being raised, it was a completely different feeling. I actually started crying. I felt such pride. I can't really explain what went through me, but I remember thinking: I want to experience this feeling again in the main competition," she says.
The next day, she entered the main competition with a second gold medal in sight.
Friends and family back home followed her progress, while Lebanese and Arab supporters in Kosovo gathered to cheer on their athletes.
Fatima was also unwell. She had been sick for the three days leading up to the final, with a cough and difficulty breathing.
With each fight consisting of three three-minute rounds, she feared her condition could affect her performance.
"I knew this was my dream, and I was so close to achieving it. This was my last fight, and I had the chance to win a gold medal and make history for Lebanon," she shares.
When she entered the ring, she put her trust in God and focused on the fight. She spent the first round assessing her opponent before becoming more aggressive in the second.
"I was exhausted and struggling to breathe, but I wasn't thinking about that. My mind was focused on winning. The adrenaline was carrying me through."
By the third round, Fatima had decided she needed to finish the fight. Seeing her opponent struggle, she kept attacking, landing powerful punches until she knocked her out with about 30 seconds remaining.
"I had fought over the previous four or five days, competing every day, and I had made it all the way to the final. I told myself that this last fight had to be mine, and I did it," she says.
The two gold medals culminated years of training, setbacks, and a dream she refused to abandon.
"Honestly, I'd never been as happy as I was then. I'd worked towards this dream for so long," she says.
"This was the final dream I had set for myself: winning a world championship."
The physical toll became clear after the fight. Fatima said she struggled to breathe for around three and a half hours after leaving the ring and remained unwell for about a week.
But her focus had been on bringing two gold medals home to Lebanon.
Fighting for recognition
For Fatima, the achievement also highlighted the challenges women athletes in Lebanon face, where she says support remains scarce and male athletes tend to receive more recognition.
"There is practically no support. If someone is able to support themselves, or if they find someone willing to support them, that's already a very good thing," she says.
"I have to be strong and fight for every single achievement I make. And I'm not just talking about one fight. I have to fight for everything."
She believes women are just as capable as men, but their achievements are too often overlooked.
"Look at what I've achieved. No male athlete has done what I've done in this particular category. A woman has achieved it. I'm the first Lebanese athlete to do this, and I think people should pay attention to that. Why shouldn't they recognise women as well?"
Fatima hopes her success will encourage other girls to pursue their ambitions without allowing social expectations or fear of criticism to hold them back.
"I want girls to believe in themselves and have confidence in themselves. Set yourself a goal and pursue your dream," she shares.
"Whatever you do, people will criticise you. But when you succeed, everyone will applaud you and celebrate your achievement. So go after your dream and work towards it. Believe in yourself, have confidence, and give yourself the strength you need. If you do that, I promise you, you will achieve incredible things."
A win for Lebanon
Fatima's achievement carries particular meaning against the backdrop of years of conflict and uncertainty in Lebanon. She says many young people have struggled to imagine a future for themselves amid the country's difficulties.
"We've all felt at times that we can't do anything anymore, that we can't achieve our dreams or build our futures. I think all of us young people, girls and boys, have felt that," she tells The New Arab.
We're trying to pursue our dreams, our goals and our futures, but then everything comes to a standstill because of what's happening in the country," she adds.
Fatima says she eventually stopped following the news as closely, choosing instead to concentrate on her training and future.
"Despite everything we've been going through, I continued training and working towards my goals," she says.
"When I stood there and received the medals, I was overwhelmed. I tried not to cry because there were cameras around, but I felt that Lebanon deserved this. There is so much talent in Lebanon, and we are capable of achieving so much."
Looking ahead, Fatima hopes to fight one or two professional bouts, potentially competing for a title belt, before ending her competitive career.
She also plans to focus on architecture and develop her own gym, where she hopes to train a new generation of young fighters.
Louay Faour is a journalist at The New Arab focusing largely on the Levant, with a particular interest in Lebanese affairs

France Follows Ukraine’s Lead With Helicopter-Launched Interceptor Drone Trials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:52:45 UTC
00:52:45 KST

- Category
- World
France Follows Ukraine’s Lead With Helicopter-Launched Interceptor Drone Trials
France’s 4th Air Combat Brigade is preparing to test helicopter-launched interceptor drones after completing initial flight trials with the French-made AST78, Forces Operations Blog (FOB) reported on October 20.
The 3rd Combat Helicopter Regiment has been evaluating the AST78 since early 2026 as part of a wider effort to integrate drones into French Army aviation. Two remote pilots have now been trained, and testing has expanded from ground launches to flights involving both Gazelle and NH90 Caïman helicopters.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
France’s interest in launching interceptor drones from helicopters mirrors a tactic Ukraine has already begun testing against Russian long-range drones. Ukrainian forces have demonstrated the use of an An-28 aircraft carrying P1-SUN interceptors to hunt Iranian-designed Shahed-type Russian drones, using an airborne launch platform to extend the drones’ reach and position them closer to incoming targets.
The trials have accumulated around 40 flight hours. In one scenario, an AST78 flew alongside a Gazelle for 12 kilometers, reaching speeds of up to 280 kilometers per hour.
“Eighteen months ago, we still thought this would be impossible,” one of the remote pilots told FOB.
The next major step is expected in early 2027, when the regiment plans its first interception trials against a fixed-wing drone at the DGA missile test center on Île du Levant. The tests are expected to focus on launching the interceptor from a helicopter, aligning it with a target, and practicing the interception procedure.
The regiment stressed that the project remains experimental, but noted that the conflict in the Near and Middle East has accelerated French efforts to explore additional options for countering drones, according to FOB.
Launching interceptors from helicopters could extend their effective reach beyond that of ground-based systems and complement existing weapons such as the MISTRAL 3 missile, the Tiger helicopter’s 30 mm cannon, and door-mounted machine guns.
The AST78 can currently reach speeds of up to 300 kilometers per hour. According to the report, adjusting the angle of its propellers could increase that to around 400 kilometers per hour, potentially allowing it to engage faster targets, including Shahed-type drones and some crewed aircraft, FOB reported.
Because the interceptor requires FPV control for highly maneuverable terminal attacks, developers are also considering artificial intelligence and improvements to its optical systems. These upgrades could reduce the workload on the remote pilot during target designation and tracking.
The 3rd Combat Helicopter Regiment is also drawing on lessons from foreign partners, including the United Kingdom, as French Army aviation continues experimenting with drone integration.
France is not alone in adapting helicopter-based counter-drone tactics from Ukraine’s experience. Finland’s military had previously tested NH90 helicopters against drone targets using side-mounted M134 Miniguns and small arms during the MalletStrike125 exercise, explicitly citing lessons from the war in Ukraine.

ISTANBUL, October 23. /TASS/. Gazprom has cut its share of borrowings in international markets by almost six times over the last four years, First Deputy Department Director of the gas holding Ignat Dirks said at the Verona Eurasian Economic Forum.
"Feel the scale of changes. The year of 2022: the share of foreign markets was 77%. Since mid-2026, the share of foreign markets is 13%. It means we complete revised the portfolio structure and certainly, it became possible owing to maturity of the domestic market," he said.
Gazprom’s Eurobonds in circulation reached $25 bln by the start of 2022, which accounted for almost a quarter of the total Russian corporate Eurobonds amount, Dirks said. "I would also like to stress particularly that Gazprom always honors its obligations towards investors, including towards international investors. We continued servicing our foreign borrowers in line with their terms," Dirks added.

Democracy for whom? Palestinians shut out of Israeli vote – RT reports (VIDEO)
Millions of Palestinians living under Israeli control have been stripped of their ability to vote in the upcoming parliamentary election that will shape their lives, RT correspondent Charlotte Dubenskij reports.
Ahead of the October 27 vote, Dubenskij visited East Jerusalem and the occupied West Bank to examine Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s description of Israel as the Middle East’s “only true democracy.”
In East Jerusalem, which Israel captured in 1967 and later annexed in a move rejected by the UN, many Palestinians hold permanent residency rather than Israeli citizenship. They pay taxes, social security, and VAT, but cannot vote for the Knesset, Israel’s parliament.
“We are really helpless, voiceless,” one resident told RT. Another described the frustration of facing the consequences of an election without being able to influence it.
Although Palestinian residents who obtain Israeli citizenship can vote, those who spoke to RT opposed taking that step, arguing it would amount to recognizing Israeli sovereignty.
In the West Bank, around three million Palestinians live with Israeli control over key aspects of their daily lives, including movement and construction. Area C, covering roughly 61% of the territory, remains under full Israeli control.
Palestinian politician Mustafa Barghouti argued that the occupation and different legal systems applied to Palestinians and Israeli settlers contradict Israel’s democratic claims.
“Two different laws for two people in the same area is nothing but the description of apartheid,” he told RT.
Settlements and National Missions Minister Orit Strook, meanwhile, has advocated allowing Palestinians to remain while denying them a parliamentary vote. “They can stay here as human beings, of course,” she said, but stressed that they “shouldn’t be able to vote for the Knesset.”
Barghouti further accused Israel of obstructing internal Palestinian elections. The Palestinian Authority cited Israel’s refusal to guarantee voting in East Jerusalem when it canceled elections in 2021.
For Palestinians interviewed in Ramallah, the priority is to be allowed to hold their own elections rather than voting under occupation.

Breadcrumb
Casualties feared as multi-storey building collapses in Nairobi
A multi-storey building collapsed mid-construction in the Kenyan capital on Friday, with many feared trapped in the rubble and accusations of dangerous building work.
Videos shared online showed a dramatic crash and huge clouds of dust as the building -- thought to have been around 18 storeys high -- came down in the densely populated business and residential area of Eastleigh.
The building was reduced to a pile of rubble as search and rescue teams arrived on the scene, but struggled to start accessing the site which was jammed between other high-rise buildings.
Police said they had already rescued one woman from the rubble, and could hear the voice of another.
"There are lots of people trapped here," Bibiye Mahmoud, president of the Institution of Engineering Technology of Kenya, told AFP at the site of the disaster.
"The contractors and the engineers are supposed to ensure that the works are followed by professionals. But most are not. This is why we are seeing these catastrophes... There is no accountability," she added.
Kenya's National Building Inspectorate report found that 87 percent of buildings audited nationwide last year failed to meet standards or lacked the required approvals.
"Our concern is to save lives," Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja told reporters, adding: "This building has no occupation certificate...this has potentially cost lives."
An occupation certificate is essentially the authority's formal sign-off that a building is safe and legally fit to be occupied.
John Ogallo, vice-president of the Institution of Engineers of Kenya, who was also at the site, said there were warning signs about the building.
"People here are saying distresses were observed, like cracks," before it collapsed, he told reporters.
If you build with the wrong materials, "it becomes a time bomb," he added.
Nairobi is undergoing a rapid construction boom, with high-rise buildings appearing all over the city, particularly in Eastleigh which is known for its busy market areas and as a hub for the Somali community.
Local media reported looting immediately after the collapse, which happened around lunchtime. AFP saw police use tear gas to disperse crowds gathering near the site.
There have been many concerns over safety over the years.
There were 86 building collapses between 2009 and 2019 in Nairobi, killing an estimated 200 people, according to a report by the Kenya Institute for Public Policy Research and Analysis.
The number of buildings completed annually in Nairobi has risen from 20,025 in 2022 to 25,090 last year, according to its statistics bureau, as east Africa's leading business hub sucks in people from rural areas and neighbouring countries.
Corruption has allowed contractors to cut corners or bypass regulations.
Five people were killed when a six-storey building collapsed in a town on the outskirts of Nairobi in September 2022.
In April 2016, 49 people were killed when a six-floor apartment building crumbled in the northeast of the capital after days of heavy rain caused floods and landslides.

‘Foreign policy is the economy’: How Iran war is shaping US midterm vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:51:29 UTC
00:51:29 KST

‘Foreign policy is the economy’: How Iran war is shaping US midterm vote
Democrats are framing the conflict as an affordability issue to criticise Republican candidates backed by Trump.
Detroit, Michigan – The first question in the United States Senate debate in Michigan between Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed and his Republican rival Mike Rogers was about the issue that appears to matter most to voters – the economy.
El-Sayed quickly drew a contrast between himself and Rogers, who is backed by US President Donald Trump. It was not about interest rates, taxes, or trade policy. It was about the US-Israel war on Iran.
“Right now, the cost of gas, the cost of groceries, it all really goes back to this war in Iran,” the progressive Democrat said on Wednesday.
“We need a War Powers Resolution rather than a senator who wants to stand hip-to-hip with Donald Trump on this war that made no sense when it started and certainly makes no sense now.”
El-Sayed was referring to legislative efforts to curb Trump’s ability to continue the eight-month conflict.
Across Michigan, Democrats are emphasising their opposition to the war to woo voters stung by rising gas and grocery prices.
“The war in Iran is a kitchen table issue,” said Jonathan Guyer, programme director at the Institute for Global Affairs (IGA).
“Voters don’t often rank foreign policy as their top issue, but I think it’s so interwoven with the economy right now that essentially foreign policy is the economy.”
IGA released a survey last month suggesting that 60 percent of potential voters disapprove of Trump’s handling of the war. More alarmingly for Republicans, an overwhelming majority of respondents – 81 percent – agreed that the conflict has raised the cost of living.
Higher cost of living
Almost immediately after Israel and the US started attacking Iran on February 28, Tehran began disrupting the flow of energy products through the Strait of Hormuz – sending oil and gas prices skyrocketing.
In the US, the price of diesel – which is used to power heavy machinery, including heavy trucks that ship consumer goods across the country – has reached record highs over the past weeks.
Likewise, petrol or gasoline has become less affordable. Average Americans feel that uptick firsthand almost daily at the gas pump.
The average price of one gallon (3.8 litres) of petrol has gone from less than $3 before the war to more than $4.27 as of Thursday, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA).
The increased cost of energy and transportation has trickled down to the entire economy, fuelling inflation at a time when affordability had become one of the key issues in US electoral politics.
Trump and his allies have argued that the war was necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.
But before the war, Trump himself had said repeatedly that Iran’s nuclear programme had been “obliterated” by the June 2025 US strikes against the country’s uranium enrichment facilities.
And US intelligence officials have testified to Congress that they have no evidence that Iran is building a nuclear bomb.
Rogers, the Michigan Senate candidate, pushed to defend the war during the debate on Wednesday.
“You want to pay $8 [for] a gallon of gas, let Iran get a nuclear weapon. You lose control of that whole region,” he said.
At the same time, Rogers has also called for an end to the conflict.
In a recent campaign commercial filmed in a grocery store, the Republican candidate said, “The war with Iran needs to end, and end quickly.”
The position is echoed by other Republicans in tough House and Senate races.
In neighbouring Ohio, Senator Jon Husted has called for a “quick” end to the war as well. In Iowa, Congresswoman Ashley Hinson, who is running for the Senate, said she told Trump that the conflict should come to an “immediate and successful end”. In Maine, Senator Susan Collins has highlighted her vote in favour of several War Powers Resolutions.
Still, Trump, who is the leader of the Republican Party, has suggested that he may renew all-out fighting with Iran after the midterm vote next month, and he has promoted the war as a historic success.
“I think it’s one of the greatest things we’ve done. We’ve stopped Iran from having a nuclear weapon,” Trump told reporters on Wednesday.
“It’s one of the best things that we’ve done, and it took a lot of courage to do it because no other president was willing to do it.”
‘Death sentence for American economy’
Despite the overall unpopularity of the war, most Republicans continue to support it.
A Pew Research Center poll released earlier this month showed that 63 percent of Republican respondents said they approve of Trump’s handling of the conflict.
The IGA survey, taken in August, put the number at 74 percent. But only 24 percent of Republican respondents said they “strongly approve” of Trump’s handling of the war – down from 40 percent in April.
Guyer suggested that the lack of enthusiastic support for the war in the Republican base may hurt the party in the upcoming elections.
“It means that Republicans aren’t necessarily walking away from the president, but their support for him has a lot less conviction,” he told Al Jazeera.
“That could have implications if they actually show up to vote [and] if they are going to be involved in campaigning.”
With the elections less than two weeks away, it’s apparent that the Democrats see the war as an Achilles heel for Republicans, and they are invoking the conflict incessantly to undermine Trump-backed candidates all over the country.
At a Senate debate watch party attended by dozens of El-Sayed’s supporters in Detroit on Wednesday, Al Jazeera asked Democratic Senator Chris Murphy – who recently returned from a visit to the Middle East – about the war. His answer was all about the US economy, not the geopolitics of the region.
“Well, diesel prices here in Detroit are already above $6 a gallon, and they’re going to go higher if this war restarts. Mike Rogers just said in the debate that he’s going to support the war, which is basically a death sentence for the American economy,” Murphy told Al Jazeera.
“There’s a big choice for Michigan voters to make here. If you want this war to continue for another year, if you want gas prices to climb to $8 a gallon, vote for Mike Rogers. If you want the war to end, if you want prices to come down, then vote for Abdul El-Sayed.”

Cyprus Parliament Reviews Reports on Abramovich-Linked Asset Transfers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:51:00 UTC
00:51:00 KST

The Cypriot Parliament this week discussed recent revelations about corporate maneuvers that allowed firms ultimately owned by Russian billionaire Roman Abramovich to sidestep tax and transparency requirements.
The parliamentary hearings followed an investigation last week by OCCRP, CIReN, BBC, and TBIJ. The reports detailed how the Cyprus affiliate of multinational accountancy firm Deloitte, and corporate service provider MeritServus, worked together to backdate documents relating to companies beneficially owned by Abramovich.
Doing so helped the companies retroactively transfer billions of dollars in assets from Cyprus to the British Virgin Islands, where they would not be subject to Cypriot laws on tax and public disclosure.
OCCRP reached out to Deloitte’s offices in Cyprus and internationally for comment on the parliamentary hearing, but did not receive a response by the time of publication. Deloitte Cyprus previously told OCCRP it "acts in compliance with applicable laws."
MeritServus has been dissolved and it was not possible to obtain a comment.
Lawyers for Abramovich, from the London firm of Kobre and Kim, noted that he “has not been identified as the subject of any investigation, nor has he been charged with any wrongdoing.”
“Our client’s position is that he denies that he evaded tax or concealed his assets,” the firm said in an emailed response to questions.
During the session of Parliament’s Standing Committee on Institutions on Wednesday, representatives of several state bodies were questioned about the findings of the journalistic investigation. Government institutions present included the Finance and Justice Ministries, the Tax Commissioner’s Office, the State Prosecutor and Police, Auditor General, and Central Bank, as well as the Cyprus Securities and Exchange Commission.
An official from the Justice Ministry told the committee that information published by the media outlets would be assessed, and that police investigations would be carried out to determine whether any criminal acts had been committed.
A representative of the Cyprus Public Audit Oversight Board said the body had been in contact with Deloitte Cyprus since the publication of the reports. The representative referred to difficulties Deloitte Cyprus was experiencing in retrieving data and communications from the relevant period, but stated that the company would provide all relevant information as it became available.
Several representatives of regulatory bodies present at the hearings highlighted general improvement made in Cyprus since the period covered by media reports, particularly as a result of E.U. directives being transposed into national law.
Tax reform laws introduced in Cyprus in January increased the possible fine for failure to pay the Special Defense Contribution, one of the taxes the companies beneficially owned by Abramovich were obliged to pay. A fine could be as much as 100,000 euros ($112,200) in addition to four times the originally owed tax for repeat offenders.

Moscow's largest airport, Sheremetyevo, resumed operations on Friday after it was forced to briefly suspend its work and ask passengers to move to safe locations due to a Ukrainian drone threat.

Sheremetyevo said earlier on Friday that it had asked passengers to seek shelter and had evacuated certain areas and got passengers to disembark aircraft during an alert.

Vnukovo and Domodedovo airports were also accepting arrivals and departures in coordination with the relevant authorities following changes to temporary airspace restrictions, Rosaviatsia said. It warned that flight schedules could still change.
At one point during the disruption, 69 flights across Moscow’s airports were listed as canceled and another 164 as delayed, according to the flight-tracking website Airports.ru.
St. Petersburg’s Pulkovo Airport received 25 flights diverted from Moscow, the local news outlet Fontanka reported. Passengers were either kept on board or allowed into the terminal, depending on their airline’s decision.
The Telegram news channel Shot reported that an Emirates Airbus A380 flying from Dubai to Moscow’s Domodedovo Airport was circling over the Penza region as it awaited clearance to land.
Residents and local monitoring channels reported explosions and air defense activity across Moscow’s suburbs, including Khimki, Dolgoprudny, Balashikha and Podolsk. There were also reports of explosions near the Sokol metro station and in the Zyuzino district within the capital.
Photos circulating on social media appeared to show drone debris on a runway at Sheremetyevo.
Authorities also evacuated the IQ Quarter tower in the Moscow City business district, which houses the Digital Development, Economic Development and Industry and Trade ministries, the news outlets MSK1 and Ostorozhno Novosti reported, citing eyewitnesses.
The attack followed several days of major disruptions to air travel in the capital. More than 500 flights were canceled at Moscow’s airports between Oct. 16 and 18, according to Airports.ru data.
Ukrainian drone attacks have repeatedly prompted temporary airport closures in Russia, with aviation authorities restricting flights while air defenses respond.
Reuters contributed reporting.

UK, 31 partners warn of rising famine risk in Sudan, call for urgent action
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:47:00 UTC
00:47:00 KST

Aysu Bicer
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
Sudan is experiencing an alarming deterioration in its food security with 19.5 million people experiencing high levels of acute food insecurity, the UK and 31 international partners warned in a joint statement on Friday.
The statement called for urgent action to avert famine in the coming months, citing warnings from the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC).
An estimated 41% of Sudan’s population is facing acute food insecurity, including 5 million people experiencing emergency levels of hunger, according to the statement.
Without immediate intervention, the number of children suffering from severe acute malnutrition could exceed the projected 825,000, while the number of food-insecure areas, initially assessed at 14, is expected to double.
The civil war between Sudan’s army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces erupted in April 2023. It has since displaced more than 14 million people and created one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
“Conflict is the key driver of Sudan’s hunger crisis,” the statement said, noting that fighting has displaced millions, damaged critical infrastructure and disrupted health care, food production, supply chains and markets.
The crisis has been further aggravated by systematic obstruction of humanitarian aid and the effects of El Nino, which has reduced rainfall and increased drought across more than half of the country, it added.
The partners urged the warring parties to remove all obstacles to humanitarian assistance and ensure “full, safe, rapid, and unimpeded humanitarian access,” while protecting aid workers.
They called for humanitarian operations to be authorized through all cross-line and cross-border routes, including air access into Darfur, and urged measures to reduce bureaucratic delays affecting aid delivery.
The statement also called on the parties to refrain from attacks on civilian infrastructure, including agricultural and food systems, and strengthen coordination to protect humanitarian personnel and sites.
Urging the international community to scale up funding, the partners stressed the need to support the winter cropping season and strengthen locally led responses.
“Together we must act without delay to avert famine,” the statement said, expressing solidarity with Sudanese people and humanitarian organizations working to deliver life-saving assistance under extremely challenging conditions.

bacchus floor mosaic inspires yellow terrazzo and marble apartment renovation in athens

bacchus floor mosaic inspires yellow terrazzo and marble apartment renovation in athens
space is around us redesigns a 100-sqm apartment in kypseli, using an existing bacchus entryway mosaic to guide the reintroduction of dionysus marble, yellow terrazzo, and curved geometry.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
Space is around us redesigns apartment around archaic mosaic
Designed by local studio Space is around us, Bacchus Apartment is a targeted renovation of a 100-sqm residence on Fokionos Negri street in the Kypseli neighborhood of Athens, Greece. Focusing primarily on the kitchen and bathroom, the redesign draws its material and color palette from an existing entryway floor mosaic depicting Bacchus (Dionysus), utilizing butter-yellow tones, curved geometric forms, and period-specific material selections.
MARBLE AND YELLOW TERRAZZO draw from 1960S MATERIAL CULTURE
In the kitchen, design practice Space is around us installs a continuous fitted cabinetry unit along the main wall, maximizing preparation surfaces and storage, terminating in triangular open shelving that adapts to the irregular floor plan. The cabinetry is finished in a butter-yellow hue sampled from the entryway mosaic, paired with Dionysus marble countertops, a material widely used in 1960s Athenian residential architecture.
Opposite the kitchen unit, a custom terracotta dining table with rounded corners and oversized cylindrical legs ensures fluid spatial circulation. The kitchen’s former gray floor was replaced with large-format yellow terrazzo tiles, which extend through the hallway and into the windowless bathroom. In the bathroom, glossy small-format lime-yellow and white tiles reflect ambient light from an internal air shaft, while a rounded vanity mirror and terracotta sconce reinforce the apartment’s geometric motifs.

Landmark E17 motorway stop must close to make way for new service stations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:44:26 UTC
00:44:26 KST

The E17 Snack restaurant on the motorway of the same name between Antwerp and Ghent will disappear among new plans to develop the area with services for travellers and lorry drivers
Landmark E17 motorway stop must close to make way for new service stations
Anyone who drives on the E17 between Ghent and Antwerp knows E17 Snack, the longstanding, family-owned business perched along the motorway. With its tell-tale sign featuring a girl eating a burger, E17 Snack in Waasmunster is one of the oldest motorway restaurants in Belgium.
All good things must come to an end, as they say, and it is no different for the well-known establishment. Flanders’ Roads & Traffic Agency (AWV) manages the land and has awarded the concession to operate on both sides of the motorway to XL Servicestations, which will run new restaurants, EV loading stations and services for families and truckers.
AWV says that it wants to improve the site for travellers, with more parking capacity for lorry drivers and roadside services such as toilets and showers, as well as playground and fitness equipment. There will be no petrol stations, but there will be 28 fast-charging stations for electric vehicles and eight for electric lorries.
There is also a serious problem of illegal dumping on the site, which has plagued the owners of E17 Snack for years. “The parking area will finally be addressed,” E17 Snack owner Kristien De Meulenaer told VRT. “Let’s face it, the parking lot does not make a good impression when you drive in here.”
It’s been my life’s work for 26 years. From sunup to sundown, I worked here with heart and soul.
Kristien De Meulenaere
De Meulenaere has run the small E17 Snack for the last 26 years and has often felt neglected by AWV when it came to the dumping problem. “Especially in the summer months I had to beg them to come and haul the trash from the parking. It was such a shame because it damaged the image of my business.”
She understands the agency’s desire to improve the site and did not bid for the new concession. “They were looking for someone willing to revamp the entire carpark and run larger motorway restaurants. As a small business owner, I simply don’t have the resources to make that happen. It’s a shame, but that’s the way it is.”
XL Servicestations, a daughter company of G&V Energy Group, promises better lighting and security cameras, along with the new services. But it will never have a relationship with customers the way E17 Snack does, says De Meulenaer.
“It’s unfortunate for the customers but also for me,” she says. “I know all of these people; I see children born who have grown up to be lorry drivers themselves and bring their own families here. Sometimes families even hold events here. It’s been my life’s work for 26 years. From sunup to sundown, I worked here with heart and soul.”
New site to open in 2028
De Meulenaere herself spoke to several of the concession candidates and is satisfied with the choice of XL Servicestations. “I’m convinced that it’s a good candidate, they have a bit of the same concept in mind.”
It’s also not impossible that she and her staff could work for the new business. “I’m not sure about that yet,” she says. “We’ll see how it goes.”
Works on the new development will begin in 2027, with an opening date scheduled for the spring of 2028.

Security clearance changes costing firms thousands
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:44:11 BST
00:44:11 KST

One small defence firm lost 163 security clearances on a single date at a cost of £68,000 over twelve months, including fourteen redrafts of a single access letter, according to evidence given to the Defence Committee.
Julian David, chief executive of techUK, raised the issue during a session on the implications of the Defence Investment Plan for British industry.
He said: “In summary, to sponsor someone’s security clearance a company now requires a contract specific sponsor access letter. At the moment, Government Departments do not seem to be able to agree who pays to process that. The impact is real. One provider has estimated that thousands of people are affected. One SME that we know of lost 163 clearances on a single date, costing it £68,000 in 12 months, including 14 redrafts of the access letter to put right.”
Earlier in the session David told MPs that the change is “having a real effect because of the change in the way that it is done on the sponsoring”, and that it affects large businesses as well as small ones, “with people losing 1,600 clearances, and SMEs having to reapply because their sponsor route has gone.”
Kevin Craven, chief executive of ADS, set out two separate problems for the committee, saying: “One is that MOD is currently providing security clearances that can be used by other Departments that do not necessarily have their own security clearing apparatus. That appears to be a source of concern. That is one issue.”
On the second he said: “A separate issue is that the MOD is looking at organisations that provide third-party sponsorship for those security clearances, including my own organisation. We are currently sponsoring some 14,000 security clearances for 700 SMEs and other organisations in the supply chain. If that authorisation were removed, the burden for supplying those clearances would shift in some instances to the primes, which are already struggling with security clearances for their own staff. There are large numbers of SMEs that want direct access to the MOD and are using these third-party clearance houses to obtain their security clearances. That would be a major problem, and it looks like it is a major problem at the moment.”
Tan Dhesi, the committee’s chair, told the witnesses that the committee had been pursuing security clearance already, and that it featured prominently in its report on AUKUS because members thought matters needed resolving before they impeded delivery.
Dhesi said the committee had previously been advised that the situation was much better and all sorted, and asked what had changed and why it had become more difficult.
David told MPs the issue also constrains efforts to bring new sectors into defence, saying the automotive supply chain is made up of small and medium-sized enterprises who are not typically people who have held security clearance, and that obtaining it has become more difficult for a smaller firm.
The government has been seeking to bring non-traditional suppliers into defence work, and Stephen Phipson of MakeUK told the committee that many manufacturing companies outside defence want to enter the market and that MakeUK runs a service helping them make the transition.

Russia confirms Melania Trump-brokered cease-fire in Ukraine
Unknown

2026-10-23
15:42:00 UTC
00:42:00 KST

The Kremlin confirmed Friday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to a temporary cease-fire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky following mediation efforts by U.S. first lady Melania Trump, paving the way for humanitarian aid deliveries and the evacuation of civilians trapped in deteriorating conditions.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Russian and Ukrainian military officials were coordinating the timing of the localized truce, which the White House announced would begin Oct. 29.
"We welcome the efforts of U.S. First Lady Melania Trump, who has made a significant contribution to coordinating the humanitarian operation," Peskov told reporters.
He said the agreement had also been discussed during a recent telephone conversation between Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump.
According to Peskov, all civilians wishing to leave Oleshky would be permitted to do so, with the evacuation operation expected to take several days.
The White House announced the agreement earlier Friday, saying Melania Trump had initiated discussions and worked through a representative directly with Russian and Ukrainian officials to establish the terms of the humanitarian pause.
The first lady described conditions in Oleshky as catastrophic, warning that the city was approaching a humanitarian disaster after years of fighting and severe shortages of essential supplies.
"The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster," she said in a statement.
Under the agreement, civilian representatives from Russia and Ukraine will visit residents to assess their humanitarian needs and coordinate assistance.
Those wishing to evacuate will receive transportation to their preferred destinations, whether in Ukrainian- or Russian-controlled territory.
"I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine," Melania Trump said.
She added that an independent American media organization would accompany the teams to document the operation and help ensure that families' wishes were respected. The organization was not identified.
There was no immediate public confirmation from Ukrainian authorities regarding the agreement.
President Donald Trump welcomed his wife's involvement, saying her priority was protecting children affected by the conflict.
"What she wants to do is save children, and that's her focus. And both sides are cooperating with her, so doing a very good job," Trump told reporters as he departed the White House.
Asked whether the first lady could participate in broader trilateral peace negotiations, Trump replied: "That is not the worst idea I've ever heard."
He said the initiative originated with Melania Trump and that both Moscow and Kyiv had responded positively to her outreach.
The first lady has made the protection of children in conflict zones a central focus of her public work, including efforts to reunite families separated by the Russia-Ukraine war.
Earlier this year, she chaired a United Nations Security Council meeting addressing the plight of children affected by armed conflicts and previously contacted Putin about efforts to reunite displaced children with their families.
Russian officials had also acknowledged contacts with her office before Friday's announcement.
Earlier this month, the Kremlin said Russian human rights ombudswoman Yana Lantratova would communicate with Melania Trump's team regarding the humanitarian situation in Oleshky.
Lantratova subsequently confirmed those contacts, while Russian state news agency Tass reported that she had discussed the situation with her Ukrainian counterpart, Dmytro Lubinets.
The cease-fire announcement comes as conditions in Oleshky, a city along the Dnipro River in southern Ukraine's Kherson region, continue to deteriorate amid prolonged Russian occupation.
Russian forces captured the city, previously home to approximately 24,000 people, during the opening days of Moscow's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Years of fighting have devastated local infrastructure, leaving residents without reliable electricity, heating or running water.
Food and medical supplies have become increasingly scarce, while mined roads, destroyed vehicles and persistent drone activity have made movement into and out of the city extremely dangerous.
Oleshky suffered further destruction in June 2023 when floodwaters engulfed the area following the collapse of the Kakhovka Dam. An Associated Press investigation subsequently concluded that the explosion that destroyed the dam was likely caused by Russian forces.
Hundreds of residents were killed in the flooding, compounding the humanitarian consequences of the war.
With another winter approaching, civilians remaining in Oleshky face mounting risks from hunger, disease and exposure to freezing temperatures.
Ukrainian authorities have repeatedly called for a localized cease-fire to facilitate evacuations, while Russia, as the occupying power, is obligated under international humanitarian law to ensure that civilians have access to essential supplies.
The proposed humanitarian pause would provide a rare opportunity for aid organizations and civilian representatives to reach residents who have remained largely isolated by the fighting.
Although Moscow has acknowledged the agreement, its implementation will depend on military coordination between the two sides and the establishment of conditions allowing humanitarian personnel and civilians to move safely.

We are reclaiming real life after getting rid of Instagram | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:41:58 UTC
00:41:58 KST

I couldn’t agree more with Georgina McNamara (The one change that worked: I deleted Instagram – and embraced the joys of a truly private life, 19 October).
Reading about the sheer relief of stepping away from Instagram resonates deeply with my own feelings over the last few years. There is an incredible quiet joy in reclaiming a truly private life, entirely free from the pressure to document, curate and perform our daily routines for an invisible audience.
This shift immediately brings to mind Jaron Lanier’s compelling points in his 2018 book Ten Arguments for Deleting Your Social Media Accounts Right Now. Lanier warned us that these platforms aren’t just neutral tools; they are behaviour-modification engines designed to hijack our attention and slowly erode our autonomy.
His argument that social media algorithms inherently reward outrage, tribalism and comparison to drive engagement feels truer today than ever. By participating, we unwittingly allow algorithms to alter our moods and warp our sense of reality, stripping away the simple contentment of just being.
In my own life, stepping back from that digital noise has been incredibly grounding. I’ve found that my most meaningful moments – whether I’m spending a few focused hours woodworking in my workshop, sitting down to figure out a new arrangement on the guitar, or just out walking the spaniels – are vastly richer when they exist solely in the present, without the impulse to photograph or share them.
Getting back to tangible, analogue realities has felt like taking a long, deep breath. Even organising a recent social evening at the local pub in Hipperholme reminded me how much more genuine our connections are when we are physically present, sharing a pint and a conversation rather than a screen.
A private life is not a smaller life; it is an unmediated one. As Lanier suggests, opting out isn’t just rejecting technology; it’s reclaiming our free will and our peace of mind.
 
Guy Edmondson
 
Hipperholme, West Yorkshire
Georgina McNamara’s article really resonated with me. I haven’t deleted Instagram, but I check it very infrequently now. While I didn’t post all that often, the compulsion to document experiences and turn moments into posts or stories, rather than being in the moment, was always there – and with it, the eventual anxiety about whether anyone had liked what I had posted.
I also realised that comparing my day-to-day life with others’ carefully curated highlights was making me unhappy: an endless stream of holiday photos made me keenly aware of how long it would be until I would next have a break, while other fitness instructors posting photos taken from strategic angles made me worry that I wasn’t as flexible as them in comparison, or that my technique was poor.
After reading some books and articles on cutting back on smartphone use, I took a number of steps to reduce my phone use, and used the One Sec app to trigger a breathing exercise whenever I opened Instagram.
It made me realise how often I checked Instagram as a reflex, and that I could be devoting this time to other activities that I found more fulfilling. The few occasions that I do check it these days, I find it a bit overwhelming.
I find that my mind is a lot quieter now and that I pay more attention to what is around me, appreciating what I see as a moment that doesn’t have to become a post or a story. And if I take a photograph of something, it’s because I like it, not because I’m concerned about whether someone else will.
 
Laura Dobie
 
Glasgow
I deleted my Instagram account after getting pregnant with my second child. At first, I muted it; when I returned, the algorithm had decided that, with all the information it had gathered on me, I must have taken a break due to baby loss. It bombarded me with images and messages about baby loss, until it realised this wasn’t the reason and started to fill my algorithm with “two under two” narratives. The juxtaposition was stark and insensitive. It felt awful.
I realised I didn’t want this platform having information about not just me but my family as well, and I hated that by feeding into it (with likes on obsessed-over images and funny captions), I was allowing it to dictate some of my parenting decisions through algorithms and advertised content. Since leaving it, my motherhood journey has been much happier, simpler and in my control. I completely agree that it’s the change that works!
 
Stefanie Withey-Jones
 
London
I enjoyed Georgina McNamara’s account of leaving Instagram, particularly her observations about the time spent checking reactions and seeking validation.
However, there is an important distinction to be made between sharing our lives and seeking approval for them. I use social media to share photographs with friends and family because I enjoy letting people I know see what I have been doing. For me, that is about connection, not validation.
There is another pleasure too that is rarely mentioned: unexpected reminders of photographs posted one, five or even 10 years ago. A holiday, a familiar face or an ordinary moment that I had forgotten suddenly reappears, bringing back the feelings associated with it.
It’s not just the memories themselves I treasure, but the unexpected joy of being reminded of them, often when they’re furthest from my mind.
The problem, perhaps, is not posting our lives online, but allowing other people’s reactions to determine how much we value those experiences.
 
Nicky Atkinson
 
Shoreham-by-Sea, West Sussex
I lasted only six weeks on Instagram. Unlike Georgina McNamara, I came to the party late, in my 60s. Almost immediately, I resented the way that posts were pushed into my feed. In no time at all I was spending hours watching posts of horse sanctuaries in the US and feeling depressed and resentful at whole sections of society. So I deleted my account – no small feat in itself, as the process is determined to keep you there.
Afterwards, I felt relief at getting back hours of my own brain time, but for months, I would think: “I could just pop on and look at x, y, z.” I’m glad that I’m off, and scared at how quickly I became addicted. Now when I look around I see that I am the only person on the bus or train who is not looking at a screen but at the outside world, and thinking for myself.
 
Dr Hilary Redden
 
Aberdeen
 The one change that worked? I deleted all social media from my phone and instead installed the Guardian app with a subscription to news and well-curated content. No more time-wasting, bottomless doomscrolling for me. Do it, kids!
 
Cecilia Scott
 
Woking, Surrey

Under Russian suzerainty in 1965, four Afghan women were the first to be elected to the Wolesi Jirga, or lower house of parliament. The two-mile Salang tunnel through the Hindu Kush mountains, linking north and south Afghanistan by road for the first time, is a good example. The problem is: how can we restore such freedom without the use of force, which seldom works.
 
John Griffiths

Algerian urea exports to France under threat as tensions persist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:41:27 UTC
00:41:27 KST

Breadcrumb
Algerian urea exports to France under threat as diplomatic tensions persist, sources say
Algeria has instructed urea producers to stop exporting the fertiliser to France in an intensification of trade curbs that have followed a diplomatic rift between Algeria and its former colonial ruler, according to diplomats and industry sources.
Ties between Paris and Algiers, which have been complicated for decades, deteriorated in 2024 when French President Emmanuel Macron backed a plan for autonomy for the Western Sahara region under Moroccan sovereignty.
The two countries sought to repair relations last year, even at one point declaring that the relationship was back to normal, but the ties have since soured again.
Information about a halt to urea exports emerged early last week and could put at risk Algerian supplies that account for around 30% of French urea imports, French fertiliser industry association Afcome and wheat growers group AGPB said.
Three diplomats also said they were aware of an instruction by Algeria to suspend urea shipments to France. They were among six French and European diplomats who also said that Algiers had in late July imposed a near-blanket ban on French imports.
The diplomats requested anonymity to discuss the issue.
Any disruption to Algerian urea supplies could create fresh concerns for French farmers, who rely on nitrogen-based fertilisers to maintain crop yields and who have already faced higher costs.
Beyond the agricultural impact, the dispute could become politically sensitive for President Emmanuel Macron's government, which is under pressure to shield households and producers from rising costs while managing a sharp deterioration in relations with Algeria, a topic that often polarises the French political landscape.
France experienced some of the worst unrest in years last weekend and a potential confrontation with farmers over fertiliser supplies could only add to that pressure.
Like with previous trade restrictions, including a halt to Algerian imports of French wheat since 2024, the sources said there had been no formal announcement by the Algerian government regarding either urea exports or imports of French goods.
The Algerian embassy in Paris did not immediately respond to emailed questions from Reuters. Algeria's trade and foreign ministries were also not immediately available for comment on Friday, a non-working day in the country.
France's foreign ministry said it had not received notification of such trade restrictions.
Trade matters were a competence of the European Union, it said, adding: "We will, of course, remain particularly vigilant on this issue."

Some Parisians buy pepper spray and tear gas, citing self-defence ahead of protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:36:54 UTC
00:36:54 KST

Some Parisians buy pepper spray and tear gas, citing self-defence ahead of protests
PARIS, Oct 23 - Parisians are buying tear-gas cannisters and pepper sprays to defend themselves and their property during protests, which are expected to continue over the weekend, the owner of a weapons shop in the French capital told Reuters.
France was hit by its worst social unrest in years last weekend as nationwide protests over high prices and declining public services erupted into riots. A town hall was torched, shops pillaged and buildings covered in graffiti as violent groups clashed with police in cities across the country.
Police have authorised only a union demonstration in Paris on Saturday, rejecting requests for rallies lodged by France's main student union, UNEF, and the anti-establishment Yellow Vest movement.
At the Armurerie de la Bourse weapons shop in central Paris, owner Yves Gollety told Reuters he has seen a big increase in the sale of non-lethal weapons since the weekend. Shops just 30 metres (33 yards) away had been looted, with their shutters torn off, he said.
"It's the first time that we've seen such an increase, and with all segments of the population," Gollety said, adding that his customers include shopkeepers, restaurant owners and individuals.
"People have been physically traumatised and are afraid," he said.
The top-selling products are pepper sprays and tear-gas cannisters, which Gollety said could only be used in self-defence. Gollety, who is also president of the national association of gunsmiths, told French newspaper Le Parisien that orders had increased tenfold.
Members of the public are only allowed to buy small cannisters under 100 millilitres in size, Gollety said. Reuters found no evidence that people in Paris were buying other types of weapons in response to the protests.
Alain Di Crescenzo, the president of France's chamber of commerce, urged shopkeepers to refrain from using weapons to defend their businesses. Speaking on the radio station Europe 1 on Friday, he said that he had personally seen shopkeepers arming themselves with baseball bats, crowbars and shotguns. Reuters was not able to independently verify this.
“It’s extremely worrying,” he said. “It’s not their job to do that... It would add suffering onto suffering."
"The police must be left to do their jobs and I recommend the utmost caution," he added.
"YOU HAVE TO BE PREPARED"
A shopkeeper who sells motorbikes and scooters in Paris' 15th arrondissement told Reuters he bought three large tear-gas cannisters, plus another small one, to protect his shop.
"You can be taken by surprise, with people arriving without any prior warning. So you have to be prepared," said the shopkeeper, who asked not to be identified.
France's government has pledged tougher security, and will deploy 70,000 police backed by specialist units for protests on Saturday, but the increase in people considering how to defend themselves illustrates Parisians' fears as the weekend approaches.
One man visiting Gollety's shop, a 58-year-old finance worker who did not want to be identified, said he had researched self-defence options, although he had ultimately not bought anything on this occasion.
"Given what happened last week and the risk it happens again next weekend, I would prefer to be sensible and protect myself," he said, adding he had had a longstanding feeling of being unsafe.
"I've been thinking about this for a long time and I think I'm going to take some steps," he said.
Elsewhere in Paris, Yvan Weiss, who owns a finance consulting firm, told Reuters he was taking steps to avoid his shop's windows being broken.
Asked if he considered getting pepper spray or other defensive gear, he said he had thought about it but in the end decided to get mechanical metal shutters for his shopfront instead. REUTERS

Turkish foreign minister warns new attack on Iran would escalate regional conflict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:35:32 UTC
00:35:32 KST

The Turkish foreign minister warned on Friday that a new attack on Iran would further spread war and conflict across the region.
“Military intervention in Iran is by no means a solution. No one supports this at the moment,” Hakan Fidan told reporters after an R4+E3 meeting in Istanbul, the first-ever meeting in this format.
The foreign ministers from Egypt, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Germany, France, the UK, and Italy came together in Istanbul to discuss the latest regional and international developments.
The US and Israel are said to have developed plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the American midterm elections.
The war that began in late February has yet to be settled despite a ceasefire and a memorandum of understanding to finalize a peace deal.
Fidan said the participating countries shared the view that further military action against the Islamic Republic could intensify regional instability.
He said the countries represented at the meeting wanted to prevent further escalation and supported ending the conflicts in the Gulf region and Ukraine as soon as possible through ceasefires and lasting peace agreements.
“Türkiye has long maintained that diplomacy is the best way forward. This view is also shared by the other countries. They are not only sharing it but also actively advocating it,” he said.
Fidan stressed that the countries in the format needed to maintain a coordinated position on the regional crises.
He called for the Strait of Hormuz to reopen as soon as possible, warning that disruptions to maritime traffic were adversely affecting international markets.
The R4 mechanism was established by Türkiye, Egypt, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia to promote regional ownership, strengthen dialogue and support lasting stability.
The E3 grouping, comprising Germany, the UK and France, emerged from trilateral diplomatic cooperation on Iran's nuclear program launched in 2003.
Fidan described the meeting as one of the most significant diplomatic gatherings in recent months, citing its agenda and the participation of countries from Europe and the Middle East.
He said Istanbul's position at the crossroads of Asia and Europe, near the Turkish straits, gave the gathering additional symbolic importance.
Thanking the foreign ministers, Fidan said their willingness to address shared concerns through solidarity and cooperation was encouraging. He also called for attacks against Saudi Arabia to stop, noting that the participants had discussed diplomatic options for achieving this.
Fidan said the R4 and R4+E3 formats complemented each other by bringing together countries affected by interconnected developments in Europe and the Middle East.
Fidan described the combined platform as informal and flexible, allowing participants to exchange views, develop common policies and identify practical steps where necessary.
He said conflicts in one region increasingly affected the other, making closer coordination between European and Middle Eastern countries essential.
Addressing tensions between Washington and Tehran, Fidan said the situation could develop toward either diplomacy or further warfare, depending on the positions taken by the countries directly involved, regional governments and major international actors.
He said the participants had discussed ways to resolve the crisis without allowing the conflict to spread or cause further destruction.
Fidan clarified that advocating dialogue did not mean accepting violations of other countries' rights or agreeing to the continued closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
He also highlighted the consequences of disruptions to maritime routes, including the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, as well as deteriorating maritime security in the Black Sea.
These developments were affecting global energy supplies, food security and international trade, placing economic and financial pressure on governments, consumers and markets, he said.
Fidan noted that insecurity in the Black Sea had disrupted grain exports, affecting food supplies in regions including the Middle East and Africa. Meanwhile, he said, restrictions in the Strait of Hormuz had contributed to energy concerns and rising prices in Europe.
He said the interconnected nature of these challenges made cooperation between the two regions increasingly necessary.
Turning to the Russia-Ukraine war, Fidan said all participants supported an immediate ceasefire, followed by a peace agreement.
He also emphasized the need to restore freedom of navigation and maritime security in the Black Sea. “Either the war should stop, or, if it does not stop, the parties should introduce exemptions for energy and grain,” he said.
Fidan recalled Türkiye's role in facilitating the 2022 Black Sea Grain Initiative, which helped maintain grain exports during the conflict and reduce the war's impact on international markets.
He argued that although Russia and Ukraine continued to fight, other countries and global markets should not bear the same economic consequences.
Fidan said Türkiye had discussed possible solutions with the relevant parties and was continuing consultations on proposals to transport grain held in Russia and Ukraine to international markets.
He expressed hope that the truce and peace agreement would resolve the issue at its source.
Responding to a question about comments targeting Türkiye ahead of elections in Israel, Fidan said Ankara categorically rejected attempts to use the country as a political target.
“We categorically reject the use of Türkiye in the rhetoric being employed in Israel as the country heads toward elections,” he said.
Fidan criticized attempts by some radical political parties to attract voters by criticizing and demonizing Türkiye, describing such tactics as cheap political maneuvering.
He added that the rhetoric did not warrant being taken too seriously.
Fidan also addressed the maritime jurisdiction agreement signed between Türkiye and Libya in 2019, saying the legally valid agreement should not be turned into a source of political controversy.
He expressed surprise at the debate surrounding the agreement's consideration by Libya's House of Representatives, and said Ankara was aware of Greece's efforts to challenge it within the European Union.
Türkiye would continue its efforts to support stability in Libya, Fidan said.
The foreign minister acknowledged Egypt had reservations about the memorandum of understanding, but noted that Ankara had discussed the issue with Cairo for several years and maintained a constructive approach.
Fidan said Türkiye, Italy and Egypt could hold talks to address the concerns.
“Positive and constructive approaches can certainly be put forward. They should be. We have no problem with that. I also conveyed this to my Egyptian counterpart. This is also the position of our president,” he said.
Fidan argued that the time was right to work toward lasting unity between eastern and western Libya, and that Türkiye and other international actors were pursuing efforts to achieve this goal.
He said the process would require both political reunification and the integration of the country's separate military structures under a national army.
“If the country is to be unified, these structures must come together under a national army,” he said.
Fidan added that a key challenge was determining how military forces currently controlled separately by the two sides could be brought together under a unified framework. “Hopefully, you will soon hear some good news from Türkiye on this matter,” he said.

Volvo shares plummet amid rising losses and job cuts
Kyiv • UNN
Volvo Cars reported a loss of 3.7 billion kronor and will cut another 2,500 jobs. The company's shares fell by nearly 30%.
Shares of Volvo Cars fell by nearly 30% on Friday after the Swedish automaker reported an operating loss in the third quarter that significantly exceeded expectations. The company also announced plans to cut another 2,500 jobs — mainly in its home market of Sweden, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
The publication notes that the drop, which sent the shares to new all-time lows, comes amid serious challenges for the company, whose controlling stake is owned by China’s Geely Holding group. These include unstable demand for electric vehicles, growing tariff pressure, and difficult market conditions in China.
"The third quarter of 2026 was very disappointing and reflects a year that has become much more challenging than initially expected. Therefore, our current recovery plan requires decisive reinforcement," CEO Håkan Samuelsson said.
In the reporting quarter, the automaker posted an operating loss of 3.7 billion Swedish kronor ($373 million), compared with a profit of 5.8 billion kronor a year earlier. According to Citi analysts’ estimates, the consensus forecast had projected a loss of 724 million kronor.
CEO Håkan Samuelsson returned from retirement in 2025, signing a two-year contract to lead Volvo out of its crisis. However, despite aggressive cost-cutting, a regionalization plan, and deeper cooperation with Geely, the situation has only worsened. The company said it needed to cut costs by an additional 5 billion kronor.
The latest measures will affect around 6% of Volvo’s workforce, including approximately 2,000 jobs in Sweden. This will be achieved by ending contracts with consultants, through natural attrition, and via voluntary severance programs. These cuts are in addition to the previously announced layoffs of 3,000 employees.
Samuelsson told Reuters that the reduction process should be completed by mid-2027, although he did not rule out taking additional measures in the future.
In addition
Klaus Zellmer, the former head of Skoda, who will replace Samuelsson next year, must halt the decline of one of Europe’s best-known automotive brands. "Zellmer now faces an even more difficult task than when his appointment was announced a month ago," Bernstein analysts said, adding that, in their view, no improvement in the situation should be expected in the near term.
The launch of the electric Volvo EX60 — a version of the XC60 bestseller that plays a key role in the company’s recovery strategy — has faced serious delays due to problems with battery assembly. According to the company, only around 5,000 units have been produced so far out of the 40,000 planned for this year.
This month, the company abandoned its forecasts for annual sales and cash flow. Volvo said that in its key Chinese market it would prioritize profitability over market share and would not take part in the price war intensifying among local competitors. Meanwhile, the company’s revenue fell by nearly 50% in the third quarter.
According to Volvo, gross margin fell to 14.7% in the third quarter, compared with 20.4% a year earlier.
Six of the 13 models Volvo plans to launch by the end of the decade will be developed specifically for China. According to Samuelsson, until these new models reach the market, no significant improvement in the group’s performance in the region should be expected.
"Perhaps we should have recognized earlier the need for a more regional approach in China; we also should have anticipated the introduction of tariffs earlier, which points to the need for deeper localization of production in the United States," Samuelsson said.
"So for now, this is a weak point that we are working to address."

Silicon Valley Democrats demand investigation into Starlink restrictions in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:33:47 UTC
00:33:47 KST

A group of Silicon Valley U.S. House Democrats on Friday demanded the White House investigate recent interruptions of Elon Musk's Starlink internet service in Ukraine in a letter to White House chief of staff Susie Wiles.
The letter, shared exclusively with CNBC and led by California Democratic Reps. Sam Liccardo, Ro Khanna and Jimmy Panetta, comes after Starshield, the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink, was restricted in Ukraine for a period of time, limiting the besieged country's military capabilities.
Ukrainian officials told CNN on Friday that restrictions remained in place, despite President Donald Trump's claim Thursday that Musk had restored access. The officials said the restrictions were disrupting high-speed military drones, hampering Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian attacks and conduct operations along the front line.
The lawmakers in their letter to Wiles demanded an "immediate, government-wide investigation into the decision to restrict SpaceX's Starshield satellite-based intelligence and military support services in Ukraine." The letter indicates Democrats will make investigating the Starlink interruption a top priority if they win the House in the Nov. 3 midterm election.
"We will ensure that the 120th Congress will closely scrutinize federal funding awarded to Mr. Musk's businesses, including whether these companies meet their contractual obligations, and whether adequate safeguards exist against political interference, arbitrary service restrictions, and misuse of federal resources," the lawmakers wrote.
Asked about the letter Friday, the White House referred CNBC to Trump's comments a day earlier. Trump declined Thursday to say whether he had called Musk about the restrictions, telling reporters, "Whether I called or whether somebody else called, doesn't make any difference." He added, "The bottom line, he put it back," referring to Musk and the Starshield service.
SpaceX did not respond to CNBC's request for comment.
Democrats are widely expected to investigate private businesses that contract with the government if they win control of Congress, which would grant them subpoena power at the committee level.
At the core of the lawmakers' questions is who ordered the throttling of Ukrainian Starshield and whether the direction came from President Donald Trump or Musk, a private citizen.
The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that Musk ordered the restrictions, and the news outlet subsequently reported they were lifted after a phone call between Trump and Musk. Ukrainian forces rely on Starshield to conduct military operations amid a Russian invasion that began over four years ago. Trump has repeatedly denied ordering the disruption of Starlink, despite Musk's public assertions that the order would have come from the White House.
"Despite the resulting loss of human life, and the serious national security implications, neither the Administration nor SpaceX has provided a clear and consistent explanation of responsibility," the lawmakers wrote in the letter. "Either a private contractor independently made life-and-death national security decisions, or President Trump directed the restriction of critical military communications supporting a U.S. ally."
The lawmakers asked Wiles who was behind the decision to restrict Starshield service and to identify any individuals "who authorized, directed, approved, or [were] consulted about the restrictions." The lawmakers also asked how the restrictions were implemented, whether they violated federal contracts and whether similar vulnerabilities exist elsewhere.
"As Silicon Valley's elected members in Congress, we represent hundreds of innovation economy employers and workers whose livelihoods depend on the credibility of American technology abroad," the lawmakers wrote. "Politically motivated service interruptions or erratic throttling will undermine reputations developed through decades of work that Americans have led to support our allies and customers throughout the world."
— Luke Fountain contributed to this report.

Six killed in attack at church in Jordan
Six people were killed and 28 injured on Friday when gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in Jordan's Karak governorate, the country's Public Security Directorate said in a statement.
Security forces had deployed to the church and were pursuing the suspects, the state-owned Al-Mamlaka television station reported. It said gunmen got out of a vehicle and opened fire during a funeral procession at the Hamoud Church in Karak. Al-Mamlaka previously reported seven had been killed in the attack.
A video aired on Al-Mamlaka that appeared to be from a security camera mounted on the church showed three people firing on the church from a sidewalk and hiding behind trees and a low wall, before running towards the church's entrance.
Khaled Burqan, a man who had been attending the funeral, told Al-Mamlaka that dozens of people had been attending the funeral and at least two men — one carrying a rifle and another carrying a pistol — opened fire on them for several minutes.
There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attack and Jordanian authorities did not say who was responsible.
