Melania Trump Brokers Russia-Ukraine Ceasefire in Oleshky
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:30:23 UTC
00:30:23 KST

Romania's President: Russia Escalating the War After Drone Incident Near Constanța
Romanian President Nicușor Dan has described a drone incident involving a merchant ship near Constanța as part of Russia’s escalation of the war in Ukraine
U.S. First Lady Melania Trump has secured a localized ceasefire agreement between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in Ukraine’s Kherson Oblast, intended to enable humanitarian aid deliveries and civilian evacuations starting Oct. 29, the White House said.
According to the White House press service, Melania Trump initiated talks with both countries and coordinated the agreement’s objectives, technical procedures, timing, processes and terms in what it described as her formal role as “Exclusive Intermediary.”
The ceasefire is intended to suspend military operations in and around Oleshky and establish a designated safe passage for residents wishing to leave. The agreement also provides for humanitarian assistance to civilians trapped near the front line.
Oleshky lies on the Russian-occupied eastern bank of the Dnipro River, opposite the Ukrainian-controlled city of Kherson. Before Russia’s full-scale invasion, the city had approximately 24,000 residents. White House estimates put the remaining population at between 1,700 and 2,000, including around 50 children.
The announcement comes as the city faces a worsening humanitarian crisis that has attracted international attention, including from Pope Leo XIV. Residents are struggling with severe shortages of food, clean water and medicine, while people attempting to escape face mines and drone attacks.
Russian forces have effectively blockaded Oleshky, preventing humanitarian aid from entering the area. Civilians trying to flee along the city’s only access roads are frequently targeted by drones.
Speaking exclusively to Euronews on Oct. 13, Tetiana Hasanenko, head of the Oleshky city military administration, described the destruction caused by more than four years of Russian occupation.
“The city is practically destroyed,” Hasanenko said. “There is almost no building that has not been damaged.”
She estimated that around 2,000 people remained in the city, including 35 children who were unable to leave. Residents were surviving on one meal a day, sometimes comprising only a few spoonfuls of grain, while some had resorted to eating weeds.
Melania Trump described the situation as critical, saying the population consisted predominantly of elderly people urgently needing medical care and basic supplies. Limited electricity, mined roads and continuing military attacks have made humanitarian access more difficult.
“The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster,” the First Lady said.
Under the agreement, civilian representatives from Russia and Ukraine will visit residents in their homes to assess their needs and coordinate assistance. Those wishing to evacuate will receive organized support and transportation to their preferred destination. Melania Trump said she expected some residents to choose Russia and others Ukraine.
The White House also said an impartial American media organization would accompany the operation and document the work of both sides, but did not identify the organization. The announcement did not specify the ceasefire’s duration or detail security guarantees for those participating in the humanitarian effort.
The First Lady said she had worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leaders through her representative to negotiate the arrangements. The White House said the initiative began during a private discussion at Melania Trump’s Fostering the Future Together event in New York, held during the 81st United Nations General Assembly. Both countries subsequently appointed teams to coordinate the operation, including demining.
Oleshky has been occupied by Russian forces since the early days of Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022. Flooding after the destruction of the Kakhovka dam in June 2023 submerged large parts of the area and further damaged its already fragile infrastructure.
In her interview with Euronews, Hasanenko said residents fleeing the city had been forced to walk about 25 kilometers toward the village of Radianske through heavily mined territory exposed to drone attacks.
Many were already weakened by hunger, she said. Some people who escaped later returned with food for children and elderly relatives who could not make the journey themselves. Hasanenko said mines had killed people along the route, with some bodies left unrecovered.
“This road really is a road of death,” she said.
Hasanenko also accused Russian forces of targeting food deliveries and punishing residents suspected of receiving assistance from Ukrainian troops. Euronews said it had been unable to independently verify conditions in Oleshky, which remains under Russian occupation and inaccessible to independent journalists.
The White House intervention comes amid strained relations between Kyiv and Washington. The Trump administration has agreed to waive sanctions on Russia and purchase Russian diesel fuel, while the artificial throttling of Starlink terminals on Ukrainian drones continues.
Neither Russia nor Ukraine had commented on the ceasefire at the time of publication.

Free Speech Union hit by internal allegations of racism and sexually inappropriate remarks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:30:07 UTC

The Free Speech Union (FSU) is reeling from internal grievances involving allegations of racism, workplace discrimination and sexually inappropriate remarks by senior members of staff, the Guardian can reveal.
A key figure in the campaign group, the chief operating officer, Sigrun Olafsdottir, departed late last week after employees alleged that she told a junior member of staff she would “never hire a black person” as a part of a one-on-one meeting late last year.
The organisation’s legislative affairs director, Sam Armstrong – who is also head of communications for the Reform MP Robert Jenrick – has meanwhile been accused of making staff members uncomfortable by discussing the American actor Sydney Sweeney’s “assets” in a meeting with more than a dozen staff.
The claims cap a difficult period for the FSU, which was founded by the Conservative life peer Toby Young, and which critics see as a partisan rallying point for anti-woke grievance.
And they may complicate how the organisation seeks to publicly present itself, as a nonpartisan group that seeks to defend “free speech” from the overreach of censorious authorities – one which often raises money from its 50,000 members to do so.
In July, the Guardian reported that the US state department had allocated $5m to the international umbrella organisation that oversees the FSU, part of a larger effort by the Trump administration to promote rightwing causes in Europe. The state department appeared to withdraw this grant after the Guardian reported on the allocation.
In August, the Guardian reported on questions about the organisation’s practices around charity crowdfunding, centred on an instance in which the FSU appeared to raise £60,000 for a legal case that was ultimately fought pro-bono. Much of the FSU’s work consists of raising money for people who it argues have faced inappropriate consequences for exercising their right to free speech.
Lord Young told the Guardian that that case was “not handled on an exclusively pro bono basis”, saying there was another lawyer involved and the person whose case it was had separate legal costs.
These revelations have come alongside a period of internal turmoil. Eight members of the FSU’s small staff have departed within the past year. The Guardian understands that a crucial part of this disquiet has been the allegation of racism against Olafsdottir. The Guardian has spoken to multiple sources about these allegations and viewed documentation related to parts of the claims.
Employees complained that Olafsdottir was frequently “hostile” towards younger members of staff. This alleged hostility was said to occur during the FSU’s in-person gatherings.
The staff of the FSU work remotely but meet regularly for in-person events. These often take place at pubs and hotels, with some personnel said to drink heavily late into the night. Employees of the FSU described blurred boundaries and instances of aggression and discriminatory behaviour on the part of some senior staff during these sessions.
Olafsdottir and Armstrong declined to comment. Young told the Guardian he could not comment on “internal employment matters”. On the incident in which Sydney Sweeney was discussed, he said it related to an FSU member’s case, adding: “There was therefore nothing untoward or unprofessional about the conversation.”
Sources who spoke to the Guardian described Olafsdottir as a prominent presence in an organisation that employs slightly more than two dozen people across the UK and Scotland, and close to Young.
She was not the only senior leader alleged to have made staff members uncomfortable. Several FSU staff members described discomfort at Armstrong’s behaviour. They described an all-staff video meeting during which Armstrong discussed Sweeney’s physique, shortly after Sweeney had appeared in the controversial American Eagle “good jeans” ad. More than a dozen staff were present, and more than half were women. Armstrong joked that Sweeney was the “biggest” story in free speech that week.
“He [went] on to talk about her ‘assets’ at length. It was this continuous joke about her ‘assets,’” said a staff member who was on the call. “It was really stupid and really weird.”
The Guardian has seen FSU text messages referring to the Sweeney episode. In one of them, the FSU’s engagement director ribbed Armstrong and others as “a bunch of chaps so alpha in appreciation of Sydney Sweeney’s assets”.
Armstrong, whose webpage describes him as a political consultant and journalist, attended one high-profile meeting between Young and Sarah B Rogers, a US state department official who has aggressively mocked the UK in public appearances.
The group remains active in raising funds from its 50,000 members, and this week representatives visited 10 Downing Street to deliver a petition on saving jury trials.
Staff who have left the organisation – many of them early in their careers – expressed a sense of betrayal to the Guardian over the workplace climate in the FSU. One suggested the prospect of funds from the state department, and blurred lines around crowdfunders, had eroded internal checks further.
The FSU was “getting a bit cowboy” with “too much money sloshing around”, they said.

Eating too much sugar on antibiotics could squash helpful gut bacteria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:30:00 UTC
00:30:00 KST

Eating too much sugar on antibiotics could squash helpful gut bacteria
For some cancer patients, eating sweets worsens antibiotics’ disruption of gut bacteria
While a spoonful of sugar might help us gulp down a bitter-tasting antibiotic, it also may increase the damage that these drugs cause to the gut microbes.
In patients being treated for blood cancers, eating sugary items during antibiotic treatment was linked to a greater reduction in gut bacteria diversity than taking the antibiotics alone. The combination was also tied to the growth of gut bacteria associated with hard-to-treat infections, researchers report September 30 in Nature.
Cancer patients have lots of variation in their diets and take medications that can damage their microbiome. So, these patients provide a unique opportunity to study dramatic gut changes “that we believe are also relevant in the healthy context,” says Jonas Schluter, a microbiologist at NYU Langone Health.
Previous evidence separately suggested that antibiotics and sugars can disrupt the gut microbiome. But their combined effects, particularly in people at greater risk of infection, was unclear.
Researchers closely tracked more than 9,000 meals eaten by 173 people hospitalized in a treatment center to undergo blood-forming stem cell transplants. “Diet records are one of the biggest black boxes in a lot of diet microbiome studies,” since meals are often self-reported, says Tiffany Weir, a microbiologist at Colorado State University in Fort Collins, who was not involved in the research.
Standardized hospital meals allowed researchers to measure multiple days’ worth of food intake down to the gram, then compare the amounts of various nutrients eaten with bacterial diversity data obtained from stool samples.
For every additional 100 grams of sugar (the equivalent of 2.5 cans of Coke) that patients on antibiotics ate in the two days before sampling, the team found a 24 percent decrease in bacterial diversity. Consuming sweets and sugary beverages during antibiotic treatment was also associated with blooms of Enterococcus bacteria, which can be drug-resistant and are linked to difficult-to-treat infections associated with longer hospital stays and higher mortality.
“Some bacteria, sometimes, survive antibiotics, or perhaps more dangerously, they are resistant to [them],” Schluter says. By giving these bacteria the “universal resource for life, which is simple sugars, we are exacerbating their dominance. It’s almost like burning down the rainforest with a lot of fire, and then trying to extinguish the flames by putting in more petrol.”
The researchers also exposed mice on standard or sucrose-rich diets to a single dose of antibiotics. They found that the sugar exacerbated the enterococcal abundance after antibiotic exposure.
“Reducing sugar intake could be another way for patients to support their gut microbiome during antibiotic treatment,” says Sarah Berry, a nutrition scientist at King’s College London who was not involved in the study. Still, more research is needed to determine whether the findings apply to anyone on these drugs.
Schluter hopes that further studies and clinical trials can help uncover more about the exact relationship between sugar, antibiotics and the gut microbiome.
“You need to take antibiotics to fight infections, but you should also be aware that they have side effects to the microbiome,” Schluter says. “Now, we need to find strategies to mitigate this damage.”

Paris Saint-Germain's Ligue 1 home match against Olympique Lyonnais has been rescheduled from Sunday to Monday due to security concerns surrounding planned protests in the French capital, the French Professional Football League (LFP) announced Friday.
The eighth-round fixture, originally scheduled for Sunday, Oct. 25, at 8.45 pm local time (1945GMT), will instead take place Monday, Oct. 26, at 8.30 pm (1930GMT) at the Parc des Princes.
"The LFP takes note of the Paris Police Prefecture's order prohibiting the organization of the Paris Saint-Germain-Olympique Lyonnais match," the league said in a statement.
The LFP added that the new date and kickoff time had been agreed with broadcaster Ligue 1+, which will televise the match live.
The decision comes as Paris prepares for further demonstrations this weekend following protests on Oct. 17 that were accompanied by rioting and looting.
French authorities are seeking to avoid overstretching police resources, with an NFL game between the Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints also scheduled at the Stade de France on Sunday.
The rescheduled fixture will see Ligue 1 leaders Lyon face defending champions PSG, who sit second on goal difference, with both teams having collected 14 points from seven matches.
The match will also coincide with Monday's Ballon d'Or ceremony in London, where several PSG players are among the nominees.

Polish K2 tank weaponry to be supplied by Norway's Kongsberg

Polish K2 tank weaponry to be supplied by Norway's Kongsberg
The Norwegian defence group Kongsberg announced on Thursday a new contract with South Korea's Hyundai Rotem, the manufacturer of K2 tanks, to equip tanks being built for Poland with remote weapon stations.
Under the agreement, PROTECTOR RS4 systems will be installed on three types of vehicles: K2 tanks, armoured recovery vehicles, and combat engineering vehicles. These remote weapon stations allow the crew to operate mounted weaponry without having to leave the vehicle.
The contract is valued at approximately NOK 700 million (EUR 67 million). The first deliveries are scheduled for the spring of 2027. The agreement also covers spare parts, operator training, and technical support.
Kongsberg has been supplying weaponry to the Polish Armed Forces for many years. In 2008, Warsaw ordered Norwegian NSM anti-ship missiles, with the contract subsequently expanded in 2023. Additionally, under an agreement from January 2026, Kongsberg is set to supply Poland with anti-drone systems, as part of the 'San' programme, in a deal worth PLN 6 billion (EUR 1.4 bln).
Two weeks ago, the Norwegian group announced the construction of a new factory in Pomorskie province, northern Poland. As Eirik Lie, CEO of Kongsberg Gruppen, told PAP at the time, the facility, which is expected to create over 100 new jobs, will manufacture and service anti-drone systems, maritime unmanned vehicles, and weapon stations for combat vehicles. - Ukraine joined NSPA’s Security Cooperation Support Partnership, allowing Ukrainian defense companies to compete for contracts issued by NATO’s main procurement agency.
- About 150 Ukrainian companies attended an NSPA industry day in Kyiv on Oct. 14, the first such NATO event since Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Ukraine has joined a NATO procurement partnership that lets Ukrainian defense companies bid for contracts issued by the alliance’s main buying agency, the NATO Support and Procurement Agency announced on Oct. 22, 2026.
Ukraine is now the seventh member of the agency’s Security Cooperation Support Partnership, alongside Belgium, Luxembourg, Norway, Sweden, the United Kingdom and NATO Headquarters. The partnership, set up in 2025 to give Ukraine sustained support through a structured procurement framework, will also let Kyiv draw on the agency’s expertise and help shape Ukraine’s own defense and industrial requirements. NATO allies in the North Atlantic Council approved the agency’s ability to issue solicitations and sign contracts with Ukrainian industry in April 2026.
The Luxembourg-based agency marked the move with a Ukraine Industry Day in Kyiv on Oct. 14, attended by about 150 Ukrainian companies. NSPA said it was the first event of its kind held by a NATO organization in Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion, bringing together the agency’s director of support to operations, Jacqueline Borsboom, staff from the NATO Representation to Ukraine and NATO Headquarters, and Ukrainian Deputy Defense Ministers Mstyslav Banik and Anna Gvozdiar to discuss future procurement trends and partnerships with companies across Ukraine’s defense industrial base.
“This partnership will help deeper connect Ukrainian industry with opportunities to grow, while enabling Allies and partners to learn from Ukraine’s battle-tested innovation and operational experience. Our aim is to further strengthen Ukraine’s industrial base and bring that expertise into the delivery and sustainment of capabilities,” said Jacqueline Borsboom, NSPA director of support to operations.
“Ukraine is developing its cooperation with NATO in the field of procurement, and participation in this Partnership offers a unique opportunity to access all the services and capabilities of the NSPA for our needs. Ukraine is the first and only country (and not even a NATO member) for which a separate Partnership has been created as a single entry point to the Agency’s work, and Ukrainian industry has also been given broad access to the Agency’s tenders,” said Ukrainian Deputy Defense Minister Mstyslav Banik.
NSPA support partnerships allow two or more NATO countries to pool their demand for goods and services, which can bring economies of scale and lower prices, with the agency acting as the central manager that develops capabilities, handles requirements and oversees delivery on the alliance’s behalf. For Ukrainian manufacturers, the arrangement opens a route into the tenders that NATO uses to buy and sustain equipment for its members.
The agency has already been a major channel for non-lethal aid to Kyiv. NSPA has mobilized around 400 million euros ($448 million) through NATO’s Comprehensive Assistance Package Trust Fund for Ukraine, delivering medical supplies, fuel, critical infrastructure and cybersecurity support, while the IT Capability Coalition has added another 219 million euros ($245 million) to modernize Ukraine’s digital defense capabilities. Allies have also donated millions of liters of fuel, with NSPA staff deployed in NATO countries to oversee quality.
NATO says its allies have provided 99% of all military aid to Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, and with Ukraine now inside the partnership, the agency can issue solicitations and sign contracts directly with Ukrainian companies.

The Atlantic and Pacific Oceans Are Not Trump’s to Rename
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:24:09 UTC
00:24:09 KST

Not content with renaming an international gulf and a cross-border lake, on Oct. 10, U.S. President Donald Trump recently floated the idea of renaming the Atlantic or Pacific Ocean as “Trump Ocean” or the “Ocean of the Americas” at a political rally in Clarksville, Tenn.
“We need an ocean. So, I was thinking of either the Atlantic or the Pacific,” he said to laughter and applause. “We call it ‘Trump Ocean’ or ‘Ocean of the Americas,’ something like that.”
Then, at an Oct. 21 rally in South Carolina, Trump said he asked Google’s CEO, Sundar Pichai, to rename the Atlantic Ocean on Google Maps. According to Trump, Pichai replied, “Please don’t ask us to do that.”
“So, I'll probably pass,” Trump said. “I think let's keep it the Atlantic Ocean.”
While Google has not issued a formal statement on the matter, Trump’s obsession with naming places for himself or America is remarkable. In our view, it reflects a textbook case of “toponymic narcissism”—the use of place naming to remake the world in one’s own image.
Let’s not fool ourselves: Trump knows a thing or two about branding. In fact, his business career has largely revolved around marketing the Trump brand on hotels, golf courses, and even golden sneakers. We shouldn’t be surprised to find him following the same playbook in his second presidential term.
Yet the world map is not a private real estate development. Nor can place names be reduced to a branding exercise. Place names have a greater civic purpose as shared global symbols that should transcend the personal glorification and political interests of any individual leader.
Place names form part of our intangible cultural heritage with cultural significance that will outlive the cartographic whims of President Trump. They shape our geographical imaginations and the way people perceive and understand the world. Geographical naming also has important consequences for education, international relations, and the types of messages we wish to project to the world.
For instance, it is notable that Trump has focused much of his renaming energy on places with Indigenous names, such as Lake Ontario and the Gulf of Mexico. In the case of the Atlantic Ocean, this could also be seen as an attempt to erase an etymology that points through Greece to North Africa. The name derives from the Greek for “Ocean of Atlas,” referring to the mythology of a giant who lives in the Atlas Mountains of northwestern Africa.
As place name scholars, we have spent decades studying the cultural, social, and political aspects of place naming. There is a long history of political leaders and cartographers using place naming to assert raw power by rewriting the world map. In one sense, Trump’s renaming shenanigans are simply the latest flashy example in this broader story of mapping and politics.
But Trump is not merely renaming places to project American power on the world stage. He is also making a mockery of the very act of place naming itself—and, along with it, the international norms that inform the map-making process.
The international community must reaffirm its commitment to respecting the cultural value of place naming and to articulate responsible place-naming principles, especially for geographical features that are shared across international borders. In an open letter co-authored with place name experts around the world, we propose five key principles for responsible place naming:
The first principle is recognizing that place names are culturally significant forms of intangible heritage and shared resources whose stewardship carries responsibilities extending beyond the interests of any particular government, leader, institution, or generation.
Given the cultural significance of place names, our second principle highlights the need for meaningful public participation in place naming decisions. Place names that are changed arbitrarily and without due process should not be recognized by the international community.
Thirdly, place names should not be used to proclaim cultural superiority, advance territorial ambitions, or assert exclusive national ownership over geographical spaces shared among different peoples.
Places should generally not be named for living people. Instead, place naming should serve the public interest rather than promoting the personal legacies of those seeking to commemorate themselves as a form of self-aggrandizement.
Lastly, we recognize that a shared geography need not always have a single name, since multiple place names can bear witness to the layered histories, languages, and attachments through which places acquire meaning. However, this recognition should not extend to condoning the unilateral renaming of shared geographic features without international dialogue among affected countries and communities.
If Trump moves forward with attempting to rename the Atlantic or Pacific Ocean, the international community should stand united in rejecting this attention-seeking act of cartographic malpractice and defend the cultural value of place naming as a cornerstone of our shared world map and geographical imagination.

Hacked e-mails yield revelations on Germany’s far-right AfD party leader
- Hacked AfD e-mails may contradict leader Alice Weidel’s claim that she first learned of an illegal donation in September 2017. Der Spiegel says July e-mails show she knew earlier.
- The leaked payments totalled €132,000 through Swiss intermediaries and led to a €396,000 fine. Germany bans party support from outside the EU.
- The data leak may intensify calls to ban the AfD. The party rejects this, while hackers claim they acted for “transparency and public accountability”.
AI generated
BERLIN – E-mails from a trove of hacked Alternative for Germany (AfD) accounts appear to contradict the far-right party leader Alice Weidel’s previous statements about an illegal campaign donation, Der Spiegel news outlet reported on Oct 23.
The findings emerged from a cache of more than 420,000 internal AfD e-mails published online on Oct 19, which journalists are still combing through.
The e-mails, analysed by Der Spiegel, broadcaster ZDF and Austria’s Der Standard newspaper, suggest that Weidel knew of planned donations linked to her 2017 federal election campaign weeks before she has previously said she became aware of them.
According to the report, Weidel told the treasurer at the time in a July 2017 e-mail that she had been notified of donations. However, after the scandal came to light, Weidel said she had first learnt about the funds in September of that year and had later advocated for their return, it said.
The payments totalling €132,000 (S$188,900) through Swiss intermediaries became one of the most prominent party financing scandals in the AfD’s history.
Parties in Germany are not allowed to receive support from outside the EU, and the AfD was fined €396,000.
The party has said that it will not respond to inquiries on whether e-mails are genuine, and urged the media to refrain from disseminating content linked to data theft.
An AfD spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the e-mails concerning Weidel and the donations.
The hackers told Die Zeit newspaper on Oct 22 that they had published the data, which also includes documents and personal records, in the name of transparency and public accountability. The owners of the website hosting the data did not respond to Reuters’ e-mailed request for comment.
The leaked data could add fuel to calls by some politicians and civil society groups to ban the party that they argue threatens Germany’s democratic constitutional order.
The AfD, which has topped national opinion polls, rejects that accusation as politically motivated.
The domestic intelligence agency, whose assessments could be used as a basis for any possible ban proceedings, said that as a matter of principle it does not comment on its internal work processes when asked if it planned to investigate the matter. REUTERS

Zelensky says ceasefire, security guarantees are conditions for just peace for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:21:00 UTC
00:21:00 KST

Zelensky says ceasefire, security guarantees are conditions for just peace for Ukraine
The head of state made the statement on Friday during an online address to the Hudson Institute in Washington, Ukrinform's correspondent reports.
Among the key conditions for a just peace, he cited a strong Ukrainian army, at least ten years of funding to maintain it, stronger air defenses, and a clear mechanism for responding to possible renewed Russian aggression.
According to Zelensky, the possibility of unblocking negotiations was discussed following a recent visit to Moscow by White House Special Envoy Steve Witkoff. He expressed hope that Ukrainian and U.S. teams would meet in Abu Dhabi in early or mid-November for talks at the technical level. Trilateral talks at the leaders' level could follow, he said.
"In my opinion, first and foremost, we need to move toward the right position. Today, that means a ceasefire. This is point number one, and I believe that only after that will we be able to begin genuine diplomacy, while the working groups can work on the plan," he said.
He stressed that Ukraine would need financial support from its partners to maintain a strong army for at least ten years. This would be necessary, among other things, to rebuild the country after large-scale Russian attacks and revive its economy.
Zelensky also noted that after the war ends, Ukraine will continue to need air defense systems and other technologies to protect itself. He identified the presence on Ukrainian territory of representatives of the European Coalition of the Willing, with U.S. support, as another element of security guarantees.
At the same time, Zelensky said there was still no clear answer to the key question: who would respond, and how, if Russia resorted to aggression again, using drones, missiles or ground forces.
"We need more than just peace. Peace must be just and lasting. And that depends on security guarantees," Zelensky said.
Other important elements of ending the war, he said, include Ukraine's reconstruction, the involvement of American and European businesses, and Ukraine's accession to the European Union.
Zelensky clarified that bilateral security guarantees with the United States and possible NATO membership are different arrangements, but both must ensure reliable protection for Ukraine.
Zelensky said earlier that he would attend the G20 summit in Florida if there were an opportunity to hold talks there with U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian dictator Vladimir Putin to reach peace agreements. However, he has not yet received an invitation to the summit.

UN human rights chief Volker Turk on Friday “strongly” condemned the escalation of drone attacks across Sudan, which have killed at least 306 people and injured hundreds more in the first three weeks of October, Anadolu reports.
“The increasing use of drones, already accounting for the majority of conflict-related civilian deaths in Sudan this year, is deeply disturbing and is exacting a horrifying toll,” Turk said.
“Scores of civilians have been killed and vital infrastructure and services on which they depend eviscerated, driving further displacement and deepening the already severe humanitarian crisis,” he said, reiterating his call on the parties to the conflict to respect their obligations under international law.
Turk said his office had documented strikes attributed to both the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), affecting residential buildings, marketplaces, medical facilities, shelters for displaced people and essential infrastructure.
The office cited recent attacks, including alleged SAF drone strikes on displacement shelters in West Kordofan between Oct. 6 and 10 that killed at least 25 civilians, an alleged RSF strike near a displacement site in Blue Nile on Oct. 9 that killed at least 31 people, and a repeated strike on a transport truck in West Kordofan on Oct. 18 that left at least 139 dead.
Turk urged both parties to comply with international humanitarian law, protect civilians and agree to a ceasefire.
He also called for an end to arms transfers contributing to violations, and stressed that a negotiated settlement centered on human rights and accountability was essential for sustainable peace. The civil war in Sudan continues since 2023 and has led to one of the world’s worst humanitarian disasters.

A missile strike likely hit the Proton plant in the Russian city of Orel, a manufacturer of optoelectronic equipment whose components are used in Russia’s Iskander-M ballistic missiles, Pantsir-S1 air defense systems and Kh-71 cruise missiles, according to the monitoring channel Exilenova+.
Local authorities declared an aviation and missile danger alert in Orel during the attack. Information on the extent of the damage at the plant is still being clarified, and the type of weapon used and the exact time of the strike have not yet been confirmed.
The joint-stock company Proton is part of Russia’s defense industry supply chain and produces optoelectronic equipment and components for military use. Its products include diode modules, switch-inverters and electronic components for onboard weapon systems, which are supplied for the production of the 9M723 missiles of the Iskander-M short-range ballistic missile system, the S-71 Kover air-launched cruise missile and the Pantsir-S1, a truck-mounted system that combines anti-aircraft missiles and rapid-fire cannons to shoot down aircraft, drones and cruise missiles.
The Iskander-M is one of Russia’s main weapons for long-range strikes against Ukraine, firing ballistic missiles with a range of up to 500 km (310 miles). The S-71 Kover belongs to a family of newer Russian air-launched cruise missiles, and Ukrainian military intelligence has previously identified the same R500 turbojet engine in the S-71K Kover and the new Filin ground-launched cruise missile, which Russia began using against Ukraine in late summer 2026.
Orel, the capital of Russia’s Orel region about 160 km (100 miles) from the Ukrainian border, has been the target of repeated long-range strikes. On Oct. 31, 2025, the Ukrainian Navy said it hit the city’s thermal power plant with Neptune cruise missiles, and in May 2025 drones struck the Bolkhov semiconductor plant in the same region, which produces components used by Russia’s defense industry.
Ukraine has increasingly targeted Russian plants that build missiles and their components. In August 2026, Ukrainian Flamingo cruise missiles hit the Progress Rocket and Space Center in Samara, and earlier this month the Ukrainian General Staff confirmed a strike on the Redkino Experimental Plant in Tver region, which produces components for cruise missile fuel.

R4+E3 foreign ministers' meeting begins in Istanbul with Italy's participation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:17:14 UTC
00:17:14 KST

Mehmet Sah Yilmaz and Merve Berker
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
The R4 (Türkiye, Egypt, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia) + E3 (UK, Germany and France) foreign ministers' meeting began in Istanbul on Friday with Italy's participation.
The meeting, hosted by Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, is expected to address regional issues, particularly the Palestinian question, the situation in the Strait of Hormuz, developments related to Yemen and efforts to find a solution to the Ukraine war.
Participants are also likely discuss opportunities for future cooperation and coordination between the R4 and E3 countries.
Fidan to highlight regional responsibilities
In his remarks at the meeting, Fidan, according to diplomatic sources, is expected to emphasize that regional security primarily requires countries in the region to assume responsibility and that Türkiye prioritizes strengthening cooperation mechanisms based on regional ownership.
He is expected to stress the need to prevent existing disputes from fueling one another, conflicts from spreading to new areas and regional tensions from escalating into broader instability.
Fidan is also likely to reiterate that Israel's occupation of Palestine, its uncompromising stance undermining international peace efforts and its aggression across the region are the main causes of tensions in the Middle East.
He will underline that all countries must refrain from actions that could undermine Jerusalem's historical and legal status or damage efforts toward a two-state solution.
The sources said Fidan will highlight the importance of a firm stance by the international community and increased pressure on Israel in response to its steps to expand illegal settlements and encourage illegal settler terrorism.
The Turkish foreign minister is also expected to highlight that the dispute between the US and Iran can only be resolved through diplomacy and dialogue, stressing that military methods do not offer a lasting solution and instead exacerbate regional vulnerabilities and carry the risk of a broader conflict.
He will emphasize that permanently ensuring freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb Strait is vital for regional and global stability, the sources said.
Fidan is likely to reaffirm Türkiye’s support for safeguarding Saudi Arabia's security in the face of Houthi attacks targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure in the kingdom, and highlight the importance of collective security approach embodied in the Mecca Alliance.
Regarding Syria, Fidan will note the valuable contributions of R4 and E3 countries toward strengthening stability and prosperity in the country while drawing attention to Israel's continued actions aimed at destabilizing the country.
The sources suggested he will emphasize that Türkiye, as a Black Sea littoral state, continues to convey warnings and proposals for solutions to the parties to prevent the Russia-Ukraine war from spreading to the Black Sea and to end civilian casualties in the region.
Fidan may also reiterate Türkiye’s readiness to provide all necessary support to end the Ukraine war through dialogue and diplomacy.
R4, E3 mechanisms
The R4 mechanism was established by Türkiye, Egypt, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia to support lasting stability and strengthen dialogue on regional issues based on the principle of regional ownership.
R4 foreign ministers have held six meetings to date, with the first taking place in Riyadh on March 18.
The most recent meeting in this format was held in New York on Sept. 21 on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly High-Level Week.
The E3 mechanism, comprising Germany, the UK and France, emerged in 2003 as part of trilateral diplomatic cooperation concerning Iran's nuclear program.
Over time, it evolved into a framework for joint diplomatic initiatives on various regional and international issues.

New York City Council votes to ban horse-drawn carriages by 2028
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:16:14 UTC
00:16:14 KST

Halis Sunnetci
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
The New York City Council voted Thursday to ban horse-drawn carriages from Central Park and city streets by June 2028, bringing an end to a tradition dating back more than 160 years amid concerns over animal welfare and public safety.
The council approved the legislation, known as Romanch's Law, by a veto-proof majority of 40-7, with two abstentions, following years of debate over the city's horse-drawn carriage industry.
The bill, sponsored by Council Member Christopher Marte, will prohibit horse-drawn carriage operations beginning June 1, 2028.
The legislation is named after Romanch Mahajan, an 18-year-old Indian tourist who died in June after being thrown from a runaway horse-drawn carriage in Central Park.
"Today, the City Council made history. Our landmark vote to pass Romanch's Law is a demonstration of this Council's commitment to animal welfare, public safety, and worker protection," Council Speaker Julie Menin said in a statement.
The legislation requires the city to develop a workforce transition plan by April 1, 2027, including employment assistance, career counseling and training opportunities for affected workers. It also allows for compensation for carriage owners to be considered, although no payments are guaranteed.
The measure also includes protections for retired horses, prohibiting their sale or transfer for slaughter or other inhumane purposes while allowing owners to retain their animals.
The bill now heads to Mayor Zohran Mamdani, whose office said Thursday that he intends to sign it while also ensuring protections for workers and business owners affected by the ban.
However, the decision has drawn opposition from carriage operators and the Transport Workers Union, which has threatened legal action, arguing that the legislation would threaten livelihoods and deprive owners of their businesses.
Horse-drawn carriages have operated in Central Park since 1858, initially serving as transportation before becoming one of New York City's most popular tourist attractions.

Ceasefire planned for occupied Oleshky as residents face starvation and blocked escape routes, White House announces

US First Lady Melania Trump has secured an agreement for a localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, Kherson Oblast, to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and civilian evacuations to begin on 29 October, the White House announced on 23 October.
The proposed truce comes after months of worsening conditions in Oleshky, where Russian restrictions have left residents without reliable access to food, drinking water, medicine, and medical care. Ukrainian officials and international monitors have called for a humanitarian corridor as civilians face hunger, landmines, and regular attacks, with residents unable to leave safely.
Update: Ukraine launches humanitarian mission to occupied Oleshky after US-mediated agreement
Update 21:31: Ukraine’s Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets announced the launch of a humanitarian mission to Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast, saying an agreement had been signed following negotiations coordinated by the US side, with mediation by US First Lady Melania Trump.
The agreement provides for several stages, including preparations for a ceasefire, clearing routes of mines, delivering humanitarian aid, and unblocking evacuation routes.
Lubinets said his office had been raising the alarm about the looming humanitarian catastrophe in Oleshky since late February 2026 and would report on each stage of the mission.
Ceasefire aims to open evacuation route
According to the White House, Trump and her representative worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to agree on the ceasefire's terms, timing, and procedures. Civilian representatives from both countries are expected to visit residents to assess their needs, while those wishing to leave will receive transportation to their preferred destination.
The White House said an American media organization would accompany the teams to document the process and help ensure families' wishes are respected.
Trump said she initiated discussions after learning about the crisis during a private conversation at an event in New York during the 81st United Nations General Assembly. She said the agreement also involves technical preparations, including demining.
Russian troops seize drone-dropped food in occupied Oleshky, accusing recipients of cooperating with Ukraine. Some people go missing, a local official says
Oleshky residents face hunger and isolation
Oleshky, on the Russian-occupied left bank of the Dnipro River, had around 24,000 residents before Russia's full-scale invasion. Recent estimates put the remaining population at roughly 1,700 to 2,000, including about 50 children.
Residents face severe food and medicine shortages, while Russian forces have restricted movement and attacked vehicles attempting to deliver humanitarian supplies. Ukrainian officials have also said Russian troops have seized food parcels delivered by Ukrainian drones and detained or beaten some residents who received them.
Russian troops enter homes and threaten starving Oleshky residents for food and alcohol, officials say
The crisis has drawn growing international attention. Pope Leo XIV appealed to Russian leader Vladimir Putin for a truce to allow aid deliveries and safe civilian evacuations, while Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, said on 18 October that negotiations over a ceasefire and evacuation had advanced to the stage of agreeing on final details.
The White House announcement sets 29 October as the start date for the localized ceasefire. Its implementation will determine whether aid can reach residents and civilians can leave safely after months of isolation.

The Ansarallah also reiterated on Thursday that they had attacked Saudi Arabia in retaliation for deadly Saudi air strikes on the territory they control in western Yemen.
The Ansarallah have been pummeling Saudi Arabia’s aviation and energy infrastructure for weeks, killing at least 22 civilians and roiling energy markets.
The price of oil jumped about 3 percent on Thursday, with the global benchmark topping $112 a barrel, the highest level since mid-May.
Saudi Arabia announced a bombing campaign against the Ansarallah in support of its puppet government in Yemen, which has been at war with the Ansarallah since 2014. That was when the Ansarallah seized the Yemeni capital, Sanaa — which they still hold.
A fragile truce in Yemen unraveled earlier this year. The war resurfaced after Saudi Arabia bombarded Sanaa airport and refused to lift the blockade of their territory.
As the fighting has spilled onto Saudi soil, the United States ordered all “non-emergency government employees and their family members” to leave Saudi Arabia, a State Department spokesman, Tommy Pigott, said in social media post on Wednesday night.
Washington had pulled many diplomatic staff out of the Middle East earlier this year after the start of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. But it started sending some back in late August.
Then in September, the Ansarallah seized areas of strategic territory on Yemen’s Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive, gaining greater control over a crucial choke point for global trade.
The Red Sea has become an increasingly important route for Saudi oil exports since Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway in the Persian Gulf, after the United States and Israel attacked Iran in late February. The Ansarallah’s attacks on Saudi oil facilities and tankers traversing the Red Sea have heaped further pressure on energy markets.
Saudi Arabia, under Mohammed bin Salman, seems adept at getting his country into trouble. In March 2015, when he was serving as defense minister, he ordered an attack on Yemen, expecting to restore the Saudi-backed Yemeni government within weeks and defeat Ansarallah. Instead, he opened Pandora’s box. More than a decade later, the consequences of that decision continue to haunt Riyadh, and it is difficult to imagine the Saudi capital remaining immune to the repercussions of the conflict.
He reopened old wounds when Saudi Arabia bombed Sanaa airport on July 13 in an attempt to prevent a plane carrying a Yemeni delegation from Tehran from landing. The delegation had participated in the funeral procession of Iranian Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was assassinated in a U.S.-Israeli air raid on his office and residence on February 28.

Norway to restart grant payments to Hungary after decade-long hiatus

Norway to restart grant payments to Hungary after decade-long hiatus
OSLO, Oct 23 - Norway has reached an agreement with Hungary allowing the restart of a grants scheme halted over disagreements with the previous Hungarian government, Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide told Reuters on Friday.
Eide, together with his counterparts from Iceland and Liechtenstein, will meet Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orban in Budapest on Monday to sign the €254.1-million ($285-million) agreement under the European Economic Area and Norway Grants scheme.
The deal covers the 2021-2028 funding period, although payments are possible until April 2031, and makes Hungary the fourth-largest of 15 recipients after Poland, Romania and Bulgaria.
There were no payments in the 2014-2021 funding period because of a failure to agree on an independent fund operator with the previous government led by Viktor Orban, Eide said.
"So there has been no transfer from Norway to Hungary in the Norway and EEA grants for 10 years," he said, but the change in government in Hungary now led by Peter Magyar has made a restart possible.
Norway provides 97% of the funding, which seeks to support cooperation between Norwegian and Hungarian organisations in areas including democracy, rule of law, press freedom, combatting corruption and the green transition.
There is now agreement on control mechanisms to ensure the proper use of funds, Eide said.
"We are very much welcoming the direction of travel of the Magyar government because it is important in my view for the Hungarians, but also for Europe, that the Hungarians are coming back to sort of key European values and principles," Eide said.
The move by Norway and its partners follows a decision by the European Commission to unlock €16.4 billion of previously frozen EU recovery and cohesion funds thanks to reforms making progress under the new government in Budapest. REUTERS

Clocks Go Back One Hour in Bulgaria This Sunday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:09:00 UTC
00:09:00 KST

Prices Keep Bulgaria’s Public Tension High Despite Gradual Decline
Bulgaria’s Public Tension Index edged down to 6.10 points in the third quarter of 2026 from 6.22 in the previous quarter, continuing its decline at a slower pace
Clocks across Bulgaria will be turned back by one hour at 4 a.m. on Sunday, October 25, as the country switches from daylight saving time to standard time, the Bulgarian Institute of Metrology has reminded the public.
Under the current European Union directive, all member states must move to summer time on the last Sunday in March and return to standard, or winter, time on the last Sunday in October, BTA reported.
The practice of adjusting clocks is intended to bring daylight hours more closely into line with the working and studying schedules of the population. France requested the introduction of the system in Europe, where it was adopted in 1976, while Bulgaria began observing the practice in 1979.
The EU has considered ending the twice-yearly clock change for years, but agreement among member states remains elusive. In a public consultation held in 2018, 84% of participants supported abolishing the practice. Nevertheless, the current arrangements remain in place, with several obstacles standing in the way of reform.
Following the consultation, the European Commission proposed ending seasonal clock changes across the bloc and allowing each country to choose whether to observe standard time or daylight saving time throughout the year. The European Parliament approved the proposal by a majority, but it also requires agreement from the Council of the European Union, where national governments are represented.
Member states have not reached a majority in favor of abolishing the clock changes, largely because they disagree over which time should be retained year-round. The EU currently operates across three time zones, and existing rules require all member states to change their clocks on the same dates in spring and autumn.
The 2018 consultation, frequently cited in German media, also has limitations. Only about 1% of the EU’s total population participated, with Germany accounting for a significant share of responses. Countries in the far west and east of the bloc, where the choice of time can be particularly consequential, were under-represented.
Responses also showed differing preferences for permanent time arrangements. Across Europe, 56% of participants favored keeping daylight saving time throughout the year, while 36% preferred permanent standard time. The differences between countries make it harder to agree on a common approach.
Permanent summer time would also mean later sunrises during winter. In Aachen, for instance, the sun would not rise until around 9:30 a.m. on December 21.
Germany cannot independently decide to retain either standard time or daylight saving time permanently, as doing so would breach existing EU rules. Although the regulations do not prescribe which time countries must ultimately choose, they require member states to follow common dates for switching to summer time and returning to standard time.
The German government generally supports ending the clock changes across the EU. However, a government spokeswoman told BR24 in response to an inquiry, “Since the choice of standard time falls within the remit of the member states, they must reach a common position in the Council.”
National positions remain substantially different, and many countries have yet to settle on a final choice. Berlin says it is pursuing “harmonised time arrangements in Central Europe” and opposes breaking up the unified system, warning that fragmentation would impede the functioning of the single market.
The European Commission has already published a timetable for clock changes through 2031, indicating that the current system is likely to continue for now, although politicians could decide to change course at any time. The Commission has also commissioned a new study, whose findings are expected by the end of the year.
Supporters of seasonal clock changes point to the benefits of longer summer evenings, which provide more time for outdoor activities and support the restaurant and tourism industries. They also argue that later sunsets during the warmer months improve road safety.
Keeping standard time during winter, proponents say, prevents sunrise from occurring even later in the morning, as it would under permanent daylight saving time. Seasonal changes also mean the sun does not rise as early during summer as it would under permanent standard time, avoiding daylight beginning at 3 or 4 a.m. and better accommodating the body’s natural sleep cycle.
Supporters further argue that common EU rules and synchronized clock changes help prevent disruption to trade, transport and communications across the bloc.
Opponents of the practice cite health concerns, saying clock changes can disrupt sleep and concentration and temporarily increase the risk of accidents. They also question whether the system delivers meaningful energy savings, noting that modern research has found the expected benefits uncertain and any savings potentially negligible.
The twice-yearly adjustments also create administrative and technical complications. Some clocks must still be changed manually, while errors can arise when information technology systems and transport services are synchronized.

Hurricane Vance strengthened to Category 1 on the Saffir-Simpson scale in the Pacific Ocean off Mexico’s coast, the country’s National Water Commission (Conagua) said Friday.
The storm was located 710 kilometers (441 miles) south-southwest of Acapulco in Guerrero state and 930 kilometers (578 miles) south-southeast of Manzanillo in Colima state according to Conagua’s climate service.
The agency announced the hurricane’s intensification in a post on US social media company X.
Vance had maximum sustained winds of 140 kilometers per hour (85 miles per hour) and was moving northwest at approximately 9 kph (6 mph), according to the US National Hurricane Center (NHC).
Forecasters said the storm was expected to intensify rapidly over the following 24 hours and could reach major hurricane strength by Friday night.
The NHC said environmental conditions were favorable for further strengthening, although cooler ocean waters and increased wind shear later in the forecast period could limit its intensity.
The NHC reported no coastal watches or warnings but warned that Vance could generate swells along southern and southwestern Mexico beginning this weekend.
Hurricanes can also bring strong winds, heavy rainfall, high waves and coastal flooding, depending on their trajectory, intensity and proximity to land.
Conagua monitors tropical systems in the region and issues updates on their location and intensity.
Authorities advise residents in potentially affected areas to follow official weather bulletins and civil protection guidance.

Pentagon cracks down on insider betting – AP
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:08:05 UTC
00:08:05 KST

Pentagon cracks down on insider betting – AP
US troops have been warned against using inside information to bet on prediction markets, the Associated Press has reported, citing a directive issued by US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, who said such wagers could expose military plans and influence operational decisions.
The memo, dated Tuesday and reviewed by AP, covers platforms such as Polymarket and Kalshi, where users wager on real-world events, including elections and military action.
The directive bars the use of both classified material and other official information unavailable to the public, with violators facing disciplinary action or criminal charges under military or federal law.
“Our enemies watch movements in these markets,” Hegseth wrote. “When an American service member, intelligence professional, or other Department civilian engages in a financial transaction on a military outcome, they create a signal.”
He also warned that personal financial interests could compromise professional judgment, arguing that “a logistician with money riding on a strike date has an interest in that date” and “an analyst with a position on an outcome has an interest in that outcome.”
The directive follows the prosecution of a US Special Forces soldier accused of profiting from advance knowledge of the January operation to kidnap Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.
Prosecutors allege that Master Sergeant Gannon Ken Van Dyke used information obtained through his involvement in planning and executing the raid to place more than $32,500 in Polymarket bets, earning over $400,000.
Most of the wagers were allegedly placed on January 2, hours before the attack on Caracas. Van Dyke has pleaded not guilty.
The controversy has extended beyond the military. Newly created Polymarket accounts placed suspiciously timed bets shortly before Trump announced an April US-Iran ceasefire, generating hundreds of thousands of dollars in profits. The White House later warned staff against trading on confidential information.
Trump’s former teleprompter operator was separately ordered to surrender more than $107,500 in profits and pay a $65,000 fine after regulators found he used advance access to presidential speeches to bet on which words Trump would say.
The scandals have intensified scrutiny of prediction markets, which several US states have accused of sidestepping gambling laws and consumer protections. The Trump administration, however, has argued that the platforms should remain regulated by federal financial authorities rather than under individual states’ gambling laws.
The president’s family also has business ties to the industry. Donald Trump Jr. serves as a strategic adviser to Kalshi and holds an investment in Polymarket through his venture firm, 1789 Capital.

The maximum exemption level for the energy sector and defense industry will no longer be 100% — when the new rules will be introduced
Kyiv • UNN
The maximum exemption level will no longer be 100%. The Ministry of Defense will strengthen accountability for evasion, while the government is preparing a new mechanism.
The government has finalized changes to the reservation system—the maximum reservation level, including for the energy sector and the defense industry, will no longer be 100%, while the Ministry of Defense is increasing accountability for evading service. Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said this, UNN reports.
Details
According to Koretskyi, the main task is to establish fair and clear rules for everyone working in the rear, and first and foremost for those who are fighting.
Every month, the number of reserved employees grows by tens of thousands. And people who have been defending the country for the fifth year should have the opportunity to return home from service. Therefore, we are making difficult but necessary decisions
Koretskyi also outlined a list of decisions and changes:
First. We are separating an enterprise's critical status from its economic indicators.
Critical sectors should be those that genuinely support defense and the economy: the defense industry, energy, communications, logistics, utilities, and others. Nothing will change for them. At the same time, sectoral and regional criteria for critical status will be updated and checked for abuses.
Second. The maximum reservation level, including for the energy sector and the defense industry, will no longer be 100%.
Unconditional full reservation is unfair to those who serve and creates room for abuse. There were companies established specifically for reservation purposes, and this became a business.
At the same time, we will not weaken the work of those who produce weapons or maintain critical infrastructure. If uninterrupted operation requires reserving more employees, the enterprise will be able to submit a substantiated request to the Coordination Center.
Third. The Ministry of Defense is increasing accountability for evading service. The rules must be the same for everyone.
Fourth. We are preparing a mechanism for 100% reservation provided that the mobilization obligation is fulfilled.
An enterprise will be able to reserve all its employees if it regularly and voluntarily involves some of them in military service. It is essential that a person knows where they are going and for how long. Their job and salary will be retained.
The terms will be worked out by the Ministry of Defense and the Ministry of Economy together with business representatives. The government's goal is to approve a transparent and effective mechanism by December 1. This will give those at the front confidence that rotation is possible and that others will replace them. And those who go to serve will know that they are going for a clearly defined period. The ultimate goal is for no one to have to search for anyone in the streets. There must be an understandable system in which everyone knows their rights and obligations
According to him, these decisions do not mean that mobilization will be intensified tomorrow. They are needed primarily to bring order to the reservation system and eliminate abuses.
At the same time, as a state and society, we must be prepared for any development, including an intensification of mobilization in Russia. We are waging a war for the survival of our state and our people. These decisions are difficult, but they must be made

Top 7 detective films that will keep you on the edge of your seat until the end
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:06:24 EEST
00:06:24 KST

Top 7 detective films that will keep you on the edge of your seat until the end
Kyiv • UNN
UNN has compiled seven detective films about disappearances, murders, and hidden motives. They include "Zodiac," "Gone Girl," and "Se7en."
Mysterious disappearances, baffling murders, hidden motives, and suspects who are difficult to trust—detectives know how to hold your attention until the final scene. UNN has compiled a top 7 list of films in which investigations gradually reveal unexpected details, while the solution is not always obvious.
Zodiac
A serial killer appears in San Francisco, attacking people while also contacting the police and journalists. He sends letters containing mysterious ciphers, turning his own crimes into a dangerous game. While investigators try to identify the perpetrator, journalists also begin their own investigation. At the center of the story are detectives David Toschi and William Armstrong, as well as reporters Paul Avery and Robert Graysmith. The longer the search continues, the more deeply the mystery consumes the lives of those trying to solve it. "Zodiac" is based on the true story of one of the most mysterious crimes of the 20th century.
The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo
Journalist Mikael Blomkvist receives an unusual assignment: to find out what happened to Harriet Vanger, who disappeared approximately 40 years ago. Her wealthy uncle is convinced that one of the relatives was involved in her disappearance, but the mystery has remained unsolved for decades. Lisbeth Salander, a talented hacker with a difficult personality, joins the investigation. Together, they examine old documents, look for links between events in the past, and gradually uncover the dangerous secrets of the family.
Gone Girl
On the day of his fifth wedding anniversary, Nick Dunne returns home and discovers that his wife, Amy, has disappeared. Signs of a struggle remain in the house, and the circumstances of the incident raise more and more questions. Soon, the case attracts media attention, and Nick himself becomes the focus of suspicion. With each new detail, the couple’s story appears in a different light. What initially seems to be an ordinary missing-person case turns into a tangled confrontation in which it is difficult to distinguish the truth from a carefully crafted image.
Knives Out
After the death of renowned writer Harlan Thrombey, his family gathers at the estate. At first glance, it is an ordinary family tragedy, but the circumstances of the death arouse suspicion. Private detective Benoit Blanc takes on the case, and he must sort through conflicting testimonies and complicated relationships between the relatives. As the investigation unfolds, it becomes clear that each family member has their own secrets, grievances, or reasons for concealing the truth. There are many suspects, and outward politeness does not stop them from playing their own game. The film stars Daniel Craig, Chris Evans, Ana de Armas, Jamie Lee Curtis, and other well-known actors.
The Thursday Murder Club
At a retirement home, four residents regularly meet to discuss old unsolved crimes. Their fascination with murder stories changes when a real crime takes place nearby. Now the retirees have the opportunity to put their skills into practice. While the police determine the circumstances of the incident, the quartet begins its own investigation. The protagonists look for clues, speak with people, and try to understand who might have been behind the crime. The film is based on Richard Osman’s novel of the same name. Instead of a gloomy atmosphere, it offers British humor, charismatic characters, and a mystery that is entertaining to unravel alongside the protagonists. This option is ideal for those who enjoy detective stories without excessive violence.
Murder on the Orient Express
During a journey aboard the luxury train "Orient Express," a murder takes place. Snowdrifts bring the train to a halt, leaving the passengers isolated. The investigation is assigned to Hercule Poirot, a renowned detective who must determine which of those present is involved in the crime. As the passengers are questioned, the theories constantly change. Everyone has their own story, and some testimonies contradict one another. To find the answer, Poirot must piece together the facts and unravel the hidden connections between the people involved. Kenneth Branagh not only directed the film but also played the lead role. The cast also includes Johnny Depp, Michelle Pfeiffer, Judi Dench, Willem Dafoe, and Penélope Cruz. It is an adaptation of a novel by the legendary Agatha Christie, returning to the classic detective formula: a limited circle of suspects and a mystery in which every detail matters.
Se7en
Two police officers, the experienced William Somerset and young detective David Mills, investigate a series of brutal murders. The killer chooses victims according to the seven deadly sins and leaves clues intended to explain the logic behind his actions. The further the investigation progresses, the more horrifying the evidence they uncover becomes. The detectives try to anticipate the killer's next move, but he appears to have planned his scheme far beyond what they expected. The leading roles were played by Morgan Freeman and Brad Pitt. The film maintains suspense for all 127 minutes and surprises viewers with a highly unexpected ending.

On the dispute between the US and Iran, he is expected to emphasise that diplomacy and dialogue offer the only path to a lasting resolution, warning that military action deepens regional vulnerabilities and risks a wider conflict.
Following recent attacks by the Houthi militia targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, Fidan is expected to reaffirm Türkiye’s support for safeguarding the kingdom’s security.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"On this disinformation front, there is a silent ally to the Russian bots and the Kremlin’s GRU: social media platforms," Gawkowski declared.
Data from Poland's NASK National Research Institute revealed that social media platforms took action on fewer than a quarter of more than 65,000 reports concerning fake accounts and disinformation submitted during the first half of 2026.

Discord, Google, Meta, X, Telegram, and TikTok did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment.
Poland's confrontation with social media platforms reflects broader European concerns about Russian information operations targeting Western societies. Polish authorities and other Western governments have repeatedly accused Moscow of spreading disinformation to deepen political divisions and destabilize democratic institutions.

====================================================================================================

Feature: Tracing China's Long March through Britain's books, archives, memories
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
23:02:25 CST
00:02:25 KST

LONDON, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- In a reading room at the British Library, a blue stamp dated Jan. 27, 1937 appeared inside a book written by a British missionary who witnessed part of China's Long March.
Nearly 90 years later, the book offers a glimpse into how the extraordinary journey of the Chinese Red Army reached readers thousands of miles away.
As this year marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March, a remarkable revolutionary feat achieved under the leadership of the Communist Party of China (CPC), libraries and archives across Britain, along with the recollections of a writer who retraced the historic route, offer fresh perspectives on a journey that helped shape modern China.
EARLY ACCOUNTS OF THE LONG MARCH
At London's Marx Memorial Library, founded in 1933, two early publications shed light on how the Chinese Red Army was portrayed to British readers.
One is Edgar Snow's "Red Star Over China," published in Britain in 1937. Its orange-red cover bears the words "LEFT BOOK CLUB EDITION" and "NOT FOR SALE TO THE PUBLIC."
Snow's account introduced to Western readers the CPC, its leaders and the extraordinary hardships endured by Red Army soldiers during the Long March.
Another is Agnes Smedley's "China's Red Army Marches," published in London in 1936. Focusing on the Red Army's activities before its historic journey, the book describes villagers making shoes for soldiers and farmers delivering rice to support them.
One passage even reproduces a revolutionary song, complete with musical notation, preserving the voices of Chinese soldiers in a book published thousands of miles away.
The British Library also holds a 1937 edition of Snow's book bearing a stamp from the former India Office Library dated Oct. 30, 1937.
Contemporary British newspapers also reflected growing interest in the Red Army. On Oct. 19, 1937, the Edinburgh Evening News published a review of Snow's book, devoting a section specifically to the Long March.
Together, these publications offered British readers accounts of the soldiers' experiences, their daily lives and the circumstances surrounding their remarkable journey, bringing distant events in China into the view of the British public.
A BRITISH WITNESS AND THREE BOXES OF ARCHIVES
At the University of East Anglia in Norwich, eastern England, three archival boxes preserve the story of Alfred Bosshardt, a British missionary who accompanied the Red Army through parts of southwestern China.
Bosshardt's experiences were later recounted in "The Restraining Hand," published in Britain in 1936, making him one of the earliest Western eyewitnesses to record aspects of the Long March.
The university's collection contains hundreds of items, including correspondence, photographs, newspaper cuttings and audiovisual recordings. Many were collected by British journalist and writer Anthony Grey, who helped bring Bosshardt's story to a wider audience.
Despite their different beliefs, Bosshardt developed considerable respect for the Red Army soldiers, particularly for their discipline and determination.
He recalled that soldiers were instructed to respect villagers, pay for food and compensate residents for damaged property. During breaks from their arduous journey, young soldiers sang songs, wrestled and shared moments of laughter.
Bosshardt also admired Red Army commander Xiao Ke, with whom he later renewed contact. Their friendship continued for decades, forming a remarkable personal link between Britain and China.
RETRACING THE LONG MARCH
Nearly seven decades after the Long March, British-based Chinese writer Sun Shuyun spent 14 months retracing the odyssey. Traveling through remote villages, she interviewed surviving Red Army veterans and their families in an effort to understand the people behind the historical narrative.
For Sun, who studied history at the University of Oxford, the journey became one of the most unforgettable experiences of her life.
In east China's Jiangxi Province, she met an elderly woman who had persuaded her newlywed husband to join the Red Army. He never returned. Nearly 70 years later, she was still waiting for him.
In northwest China's Gansu Province, Sun interviewed a former female Red Army soldier whose life had been marked by poverty, captivity and hardship.
The elderly woman welcomed Sun into her home, wrapped her in thick blankets and prepared a meal unusually rich in salt. Her adopted daughter explained that salt had been extremely scarce during the Long March, leaving the woman with a lifelong habit of cherishing it.
Recalling these encounters at her London home, Sun was moved to tears.
She said the Long March demonstrated the CPC's organizational strength and leadership and laid an important foundation for the eventual victory of the Chinese revolution.
"The Long March is one of the most important events in modern Chinese history," she said, adding that its legacy continues to resonate with China's development today.
Sun stressed that the choices and sacrifices of ordinary people, whose experiences could sometimes be overlooked in historical narratives, deserve to be remembered and passed down to future generations.
From the hardships of revolutionary struggle to the achievements of modernization, the Chinese people have continued to undertake new journeys requiring courage and perseverance, she said.
The great spirit of the Long March "will always deserve to be remembered," Sun added. ■
