SHIJIAZHUANG, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Ding Jianxin, a solo founder, sits at his workstation on a video call with a client. He is among a growing number of artificial intelligence (AI)-powered One Person Companies, or OPCs.
Located inside "Rainforest Space" at the Zhongguancun Science Park in Xiongan New Area, north China's Hebei Province, the workstation is designed for startups like Ding's.
The Chinese government issued an action plan in June for the growth of platform-economy enterprises, calling for accelerated cultivation of AI-powered OPCs. This month, the government proposed in another document to expand AI-related employment and create new models of employment and entrepreneurship in the AI sector.
According to a report on OPCs in China released by a team led by Yao Jianhua, a professor at Fudan University in Shanghai, there were 426 OPC communities nationwide, covering 28 provincial-level regions and 65 cities, as of May 2026.
"Driven by both the deep penetration of AI technology and continued policy support, OPCs characterized by 'one person + AI' are growing from a marginal form of entrepreneurship into an important part of China's entrepreneurial ecosystem, marking a new way of working and employment that is increasingly gaining social recognition," the report said.
Flooded with sunlight, the 2,800-square-meter "Rainforest Space" features stylish co-working areas, shared meeting nooks, a roadshow hall and a cafe. On Floor 3, Building B1 of the tech park, OPC founders tend to their work at their workstations.
In June, Ding registered a creative software company. He has since rolled out several AI-powered products to help small and medium creators gauge the viral potential of AI-generated short drama scripts, flag compliance risks, adapt content for overseas markets and support production workflows.
Established in 2017, Xiongan New Area serves as a key hub for relieving Beijing of its non-capital functions and a core platform for the coordinated development of the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region.
The city has taken initial shape, with relocated projects settling in and innovation resources gathering rapidly. It pursues a dual strategy: attracting headquarters and subsidiaries of state-owned enterprises, and drawing agile, compact OPCs.
Fresh graduate Xue Yang also kicked off her entrepreneurial journey at the Rainforest Space, where she founded an intelligent technology company. The community helped her deploy AI tools and secure computing resources, and matched her with a tailored project.
"I received an order on my second day of business, which greatly boosted my confidence," Xue said.
As a startup accelerator, the community empowers entrepreneurs. More than 40 on-site technology service platforms are open to all OPCs.
The park offers on-demand, pay-as-you-go computing-power access. Founders can tap computing resources much like households draw electricity or running water, without investing in expensive servers. The park has also partnered with social capital to launch a micro seed fund for OPCs.
A one-stop service station sits at the community entrance. Rotating specialists from accounting firms, law firms and intellectual property agencies provide services including company seal engraving, financial bookkeeping, contract review and patent guidance. To date, more than 30 OPCs have settled in the community.
In Xiongan's Rongdong Area, around 10,000 square meters of reserved public service space has been refurbished into an OPC shared service center. It converts underused public space into a live-work setup where founders live upstairs and work downstairs. It complements Rainforest Space, which focuses more on industrial and business matchmaking.
Huo Pengbo heads a technology firm where he is the only human team member. He sits in his office holding a team briefing with his "AI employees". One handles copywriting, another designs visuals, a third edits video content, and a central "smart brain" oversees coordination and decision-making.
"What worries solo entrepreneurs most is not technical challenges, but a flood of administrative chores. Registration, bookkeeping, securing computing power and client negotiations all pull focus from core work," Huo said. The community provides full-chain support "covering computing resources, business leads and daily operational needs," he said, adding that it had encouraged him to launch his venture from scratch.
Xiongan New Area recently released its first batch of accredited OPC communities for 2026, including Rainforest Space and the Rongdong hub. The new area has also rolled out targeted policies to support OPC communities, covering hub construction, one-stop services, factor guarantees and funding support. ■

by Xinhua writers Zheng Jingxia, Liu Yinglun
HONG KONG, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Finance ministers of the Asia-Pacific community have gathered this week in Hong Kong, reaching broad consensus on multiple fronts to propel growth amid increasing global uncertainties and rapid technological shifts.
As one of the core ministerial platforms under the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC), the APEC Finance Ministers' Meeting this year centers on the theme of "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together."
Addressing the meeting, Chinese Finance Minister Lan Fo'an highlighted both the challenges and opportunities of the current international landscape, urging APEC to play a stronger role in strengthening macroeconomic policy coordination.

BEIJING, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- China has rolled out guidelines on adapting to advances in artificial intelligence (AI) to promote employment-friendly development, aiming to harness the technology to create jobs, improve employment quality and stimulate entrepreneurship while mitigating job displacement caused by AI applications.
The guidelines, issued by the General Office of the State Council, set out 18 tasks in six areas, including boosting AI's job-creation potential, making AI adoption more employment-friendly, improving workers' digital skills, enhancing employment services, strengthening labor and social security protections, and monitoring and addressing employment risks.
The guidelines call for expanding employment opportunities in emerging fields, helping micro, small and medium-sized enterprises stabilize and expand employment, fostering new forms of employment and entrepreneurship in the AI sector, and developing new AI-related occupations.
The guidelines urge efforts to tap AI's job-creation potential in traditional sectors, mitigate job displacement caused by AI applications, and establish a mechanism to assess employment risks associated with AI adoption.
The guidelines emphasize improving the framework for protecting workers' rights in human-machine collaboration, strengthening social security for people in flexible employment and those in new forms of employment, and refining income distribution mechanisms to adapt to advances in AI.
The guidelines outline coordinated efforts to cultivate innovative AI talent and implement specialized AI training programs. They also propose using AI to support the implementation of employment policies and make employment services more intelligent, while increasing support for workers transitioning to new jobs.
Further measures include strengthening monitoring and early warning of employment risks associated with AI applications, deepening research into their impact on employment, and improving mechanisms for responding to such risks.
The guidelines come as AI adoption expands across China's economy. The country's core AI industry was valued at more than 1.2 trillion yuan (about 178.62 billion U.S. dollars) in 2025, with more than 6,200 AI companies operating nationwide, according to official figures. By the end of 2025, more than 30 percent of manufacturing enterprises with annual main business revenue of at least 20 million yuan had adopted AI technologies.
A five-year plan for the employment-first strategy highlights promoting employment alongside AI advancements as a key task. It calls for creating new jobs through AI applications and unlocking employment potential in traditional industries.
AI is already reshaping China's economy and transforming its labor market, with demand growing for workers equipped with specialized technical skills.
According to Maimai, a networking and recruitment platform, the number of new AI-related job postings in the new economy on the platform rose 789.47 percent year on year from January to July. Online job-seeking platform Zhaopin also reported particularly strong demand for AI engineers, including those working in automotive manufacturing and intelligent driving. ■

Interview: Stratonex wants to bring Ukraine’s innovation loop to Britain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:02:10 UTC
00:02:10 KST

- British company Stratonex Defence Technologies is developing the VARAN unmanned ground vehicle, which has completed initial mobility and remote-operation testing but is not yet operationally ready.
- Co-founder Ben Everitt told The Defence Blog that Ukrainian feedback pushed Stratonex to prioritize affordable unmanned logistics over autonomy.
British defense technology company Stratonex Defence Technologies is developing a range of unmanned ground vehicles, tactical drones, counter-drone systems and military mobility platforms, with a focus on reducing the exposure of personnel to battlefield threats.
The company’s VARAN unmanned ground vehicle is among its central projects. The platform has undergone initial mobility and remote-control testing, but further engineering and integration work is required before it can be considered ready for operational deployment.
In an interview with The Defence Blog, Stratonex co-founder Ben Everitt discussed the development of VARAN, the company’s relationship with technology partners, its approach to manufacturing and the challenges of moving military hardware from prototypes into serial production.
Everitt also outlined the company’s plans for 2027, including closer cooperation with British manufacturers, universities and military operators. He described lessons drawn from Ukrainian battlefield innovation and explained why Stratonex is placing increasing emphasis on connecting ground vehicles, aerial drones, sensors and other technologies into integrated mission systems.
The following interview is presented in full, with the interviewee’s answers reproduced without editorial changes.
Q: Stratonex Defence Technologies is entering a market where established defense contractors and smaller technology companies are competing to develop autonomous military systems. What specific technological or industrial gaps are you seeking to address, and how does your business model differ from that of traditional defense manufacturers?
A: I think you have to start with what’s actually happening on the battlefield, because it’s changing incredibly quickly.
The traditional idea of a frontline is becoming increasingly meaningless. What you’ve really got is a contested kill zone, potentially 20 kilometres or more either side of the line, where drones, sensors and precision weapons mean that if you can be seen, you can potentially be targeted.
So that’s the problem we’re building Stratonex around. How do you operate in that environment without unnecessarily putting people in it?
That’s where the product set starts to make sense. We’ve got unmanned systems that can move equipment, sensors and other capabilities into that space. Then we’ve got fast, stealthy, relatively inexpensive mobility platforms for those occasions when people do need to go into it and need to get back out again quickly.
The phrase we’ve started using is: keep the humans in the kill chain, but out of the kill zone. I really like it because it sums up what we’re trying to do.
The other thing that’s really struck me is the speed at which all of this is changing. I was recently out in eastern Ukraine, near the frontline, in a car with the manager of a UGV factory. His phone goes and it’s a battalion commander on the frontline who is using his vehicles. He’s basically saying, “This works, this doesn’t, and this is what I want the next batch to do.”
I remember thinking: this is extraordinary. You’re watching the innovation loop happening in real time. The customer is on the battlefield and the factory manager is taking the next requirement directly from him.
Obviously we’re operating in a very different environment in Britain, but that sense of pace and urgency is something we really want to capture at Stratonex. We’re not trying to recreate a traditional defence prime. We want to be agile, work with really good technology partners and get really, really cool technology integrated and into the hands of operators quickly.
Q: Stratonex has presented a portfolio spanning unmanned ground vehicles, tactical aerial systems and counter-UAS technologies. How much of this portfolio is being developed internally, and what role do technology partnerships, licensing arrangements and third-party integration play in bringing these products to market?
A: It’s deliberately a mixture. I don’t think there’s any great virtue in saying that every nut, bolt, sensor and line of code has to have been invented inside the same building.
There are technologies and IP that sit within Stratonex, and then there are areas where we work with partners, licence technology or integrate specialist systems developed by other people.
And that’s exciting, because there is some really, really cool technology being developed by smaller companies in Britain and elsewhere. The problem is often not the technology. It’s getting it integrated, tested, manufactured and ultimately bought.
That’s where I think Stratonex can add a lot of value. We can start with the operational problem and ask: what’s the best combination of platform, sensor, communications, autonomy and payload to solve it?
We’re quite deliberately technology-agnostic about that. If somebody has already invented a brilliant sensor, I don’t want to spend three years and a fortune inventing another one just so we can put our badge on it. I’d rather work with them, integrate it and get the capability out there.
Q: VARAN is presented as a modular unmanned ground vehicle capable of operating in GNSS-denied environments using passive 3D sensing and onboard autonomous navigation. How mature is this technology today, what capabilities have been demonstrated during physical testing, and what engineering challenges remain before the platform can be considered operationally ready?
A: VARAN is a real vehicle. We’ve built it, driven it, tested it and spent quite a lot of time getting it muddy, which is the fun bit.
But we’re also careful not to pretend that having a really good prototype is the same thing as having a fully operationally proven military system. There is still engineering, integration and testing to do.
We’ve demonstrated the fundamental mobility of the platform, remote operation and elements of the sensing and navigation architecture. The next phase is about making all of that increasingly robust across different terrain, payloads, communications environments and operational conditions.
What’s been particularly interesting is the feedback we’ve had from Ukraine. We started out, naturally enough, being really enthusiastic about the autonomy. It’s technically fascinating and there are some really cool things you can do with it.
But the Ukrainians keep bringing us back to something much simpler: the really important thing is that it’s unmanned.
If you can remotely drive ammunition, water, batteries or other equipment those last few kilometres instead of putting people in a vehicle and sending them into the kill zone, you’ve already achieved something incredibly valuable.
So we’re still developing the autonomy, absolutely. But we’re not developing autonomy because autonomy happens to be fashionable. We’re developing the capabilities operators actually want.
Q: Published information describes VARAN as a multi-mission platform capable of carrying reconnaissance, electronic warfare and counter-UAS payloads. How does the vehicle’s modular architecture accommodate different power, communications and payload requirements, and which mission configurations have progressed beyond the design stage?
A: This is one of my favourite things about VARAN because you can get terribly technical about modularity, power, data and payload integration, and I have a tendency to do exactly that.
We took VARAN away for a weekend of testing and filming with a group of former Special Forces guys who our Chairman, Major General John Holmes, knows.
I’m there waving my arms around getting incredibly enthusiastic about all the clever things we can do with it. We can forward-deploy surveillance drones on it. We can remotely recharge them. We can put different sensors and payloads on it. We can use it as part of a much wider unmanned system. All really, really cool stuff.
And the former SAS guys basically looked at it and said: “Yeah, but we can chuck all our kit on that and it’ll carry it for us.”
And they’re absolutely right.
Sometimes the simplest use case is the best one. Logistics is the backbone of successful warfighting. If VARAN can carry the heavy stuff while the operator concentrates on doing his job, that’s incredibly useful.
It also goes back to what the Ukrainians have been telling us. Sometimes we get very excited about the word “autonomy” when the thing the soldier really values is the word “unmanned”.
That’s why modularity matters. VARAN isn’t supposed to be one exquisite vehicle designed around one exquisite mission. The base platform gives you mobility, power and communications and then we can configure it around what the operator actually needs, whether that’s logistics, surveillance, EW, counter-UAS or something we haven’t thought of yet.
Q: VisionWave announced a conditional $20 million purchase order for 200 STRATUM VARAN vehicles in September 2026. What role does Stratonex play in the development, integration and potential production of these vehicles, and what milestones must be achieved before the programme moves into manufacturing and customer deliveries?
A: VisionWave is an important partner of ours and we have a distribution agreement with them, but they are a completely separate company, so I don’t really want to speak for them or get into the detail of their commercial announcements.
What I can talk about is what we’re doing with VARAN.
Our focus is on continuing to develop the platform, testing it, integrating different capabilities and getting it ready for manufacture at scale. And that’s a really exciting challenge in itself.
As I said earlier, the defence technology world is actually pretty good at producing prototypes. The difficult bit is getting from prototype to procurement and then into repeatable, affordable production.
That’s what we’re concentrating on. Making VARAN faster, tougher and more useful, testing it properly, listening to operators and making sure that when demand comes we can actually build the thing at meaningful volume.
Ultimately, I’d much rather be judged on the vehicles we build and deliver than the numbers in a press release.
Q: Moving from prototypes and technology demonstrations to serial production remains a major challenge for emerging defense companies. How is Stratonex addressing manufacturing scalability, supply-chain resilience, unit costs and long-term maintenance, and what production capacity do you realistically expect to achieve?
A: Price really matters to us, particularly with VARAN.
Its three big advantages are its price point, speed and durability. It’s more cost-effective than the heavier platforms in this space, it’s fast and agile, and it’s designed to take punishment.
And you have to be realistic about why the price point matters. These things are going into war zones. At some point some of them are going to get blown up.
One Ukrainian battalion commander put it brilliantly when we were talking about equipment: “If you can make it out of wood, make it out of wood.”
That’s obviously an exaggeration, but there’s a really important philosophy behind it. Don’t add cost and complexity unless they actually give the operator something useful.
There’s a tendency in defence to make everything exquisite. But if making something twice as expensive only makes it ten per cent more capable, and you’re operating in an environment where you’re going to lose platforms anyway, that’s not necessarily a good trade.
So we’re designing around manufacturability, modular components, repairability and supply-chain resilience from the start. We don’t want to build a vast Stratonex factory and manufacture every component ourselves. We’d much rather work with established manufacturing partners and scale production as demand develops.
That’s also why durability and field repair matter. Make it tough. Make it repairable. Make it affordable enough that commanders are actually prepared to use it.
Q: Beyond VARAN, your portfolio includes the D-FLY counter-UAS interceptor and TALON tactical unmanned aircraft. What technical or operational capabilities are you prioritising in these programmes, and can you share any previously undisclosed details concerning prototypes, testing results, new configurations or upcoming product introductions?
A: Again, I think it makes more sense if you look at the portfolio through the kill-zone problem rather than looking at each product individually.
You’ve got this 20-kilometre-plus contested space. So how do I see into it? How do I move equipment through it? How do I operate inside it without unnecessarily exposing people? How do I counter the drones that are creating part of the threat?
VARAN answers part of that. TALON answers another part through tactical aerial capability. D-FLY tackles the counter-UAS problem, including the really important question of cost exchange.
And then you’ve got the mobility platforms, which I think are fascinating. E-bikes and e-scooters might look slightly odd sitting next to drones and UGVs until you think about the operational problem. If somebody does have to enter that kill zone, you want them moving quickly and quietly with as little signature as possible.
That’s the common thread.
What gets me really excited now is joining those things together. A UGV shouldn’t just be a UGV and a drone shouldn’t just be a drone. How do the platforms, sensors, communications and effectors start working together as one mission system?
That’s where I think some of the really, really cool stuff is going to happen.
Q: Looking ahead to 2027, which developments do you expect to define Stratonex’s next phase of growth? Are there any new programmes, industrial partnerships, customer agreements or technological milestones that you are prepared to announce or discuss in greater detail with The Defence Blog readers?
A: There’s loads going on and I’m genuinely really excited about 2027.
Obviously there’s the product side. VARAN will continue developing, we’ve got other products coming through, and we’re increasingly interested in what happens when you connect all these different capabilities together rather than thinking about a UGV, a drone or a sensor in isolation.
But the bigger idea we’re working on is what I’d describe as on-shoring the innovation loop.
That comes directly from what I’ve seen in Ukraine. I keep going back to that phone call in the car between the battalion commander and the factory manager. Operator feedback, engineering, testing and production are happening incredibly close together. That’s one of the reasons they are innovating at such extraordinary speed.
We’re obviously not going to recreate the circumstances that have driven that in Ukraine, but we absolutely can learn from it.
So how do we build our own version of that loop here in Britain? How do we bring operators, engineers, SMEs, manufacturers and academia much closer together, so that an operational problem can become an engineering problem, become a prototype, get tested, generate feedback and go around the loop again quickly?
That’s why we’re looking at academic partnerships as well as product-development partnerships. Universities bring extraordinary engineering expertise, research capability, testing facilities and, importantly, really bright people. Industry brings products, manufacturing and commercial pace. Then you need the operator constantly feeding reality back into the process.
For me, that’s potentially much bigger than any individual product.
Britain doesn’t have an innovation problem. There is some really, really cool technology being developed here. The challenge is connecting it, testing it against real requirements, iterating quickly and then actually manufacturing it.
If we can help build that ecosystem around Stratonex, shorten the distance between the operator saying “I need this” and somebody putting a working solution in their hands, then I think we’ve got something genuinely exciting.
That’s a big part of where I want us to go in 2027: on-shore the innovation loop, build sovereign capability and keep turning really good British technology into things that operators can actually use.
And all of it still comes back to the same mission: keep the humans in the kill chain, but out of the kill zone.

Police reported that the structure collapsed at approximately 1:00 p.m. local time (1000 GMT), immediately raising fears for construction workers and pedestrians trapped beneath the debris.
Emergency personnel quickly cordoned off the area to coordinate rescue efforts as concerns mounted over potential casualties.
The Kenya Red Cross Society confirmed that emergency response operations are ongoing at the site of the collapsed building along 9th Street, First Avenue in Eastleigh, a high-density commercial and residential suburb of Nairobi.
"Kenya Red Cross teams are working alongside multi-agency partners to support search and rescue operations," it said.
The building was still under construction, with shops and rental units already operating on the lower floors, according to initial accounts from the scene.
Emergency responders have deployed heavy machinery to clear debris and assist rescue teams in reaching potential survivors.
Fears persisted that workers and other occupants may have been inside the structure at the time of the collapse, as authorities worked to determine whether anyone remained trapped.
The sudden collapse shook the bustling commercial hub, rapidly drawing large crowds of local traders, shoppers, and residents.
Authorities have yet to determine whether the impact compromised adjacent buildings.
Nairobi Regional Police Commander Issa Mohamud said authorities were still gathering information about the collapse as emergency teams raced to the scene.
Mohamud said police fired tear gas to clear a crowd that had blocked roads and prevented emergency vehicles from reaching the site. Local media reported attempts to scavenge scrap metal from the debris.
Authorities have not said what caused the collapse or whether the building had the required construction approvals.
Dozens of workers have died in similar structural failures across Kenya in recent years.
The latest incident highlights a recurring crisis in Kenya, where several incomplete structures have caved in recent months, frequently resulting in casualties.
Building experts have repeatedly criticized regulatory authorities for lax oversight, citing widespread failures to enforce construction codes and conduct routine inspections.
In response to previous disasters, authorities have repeatedly urged developers, contractors, and regulatory bodies to strictly adhere to safety standards to safeguard workers and the public. ■

ULAN BATOR, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- A total of 188 forest and steppe fires have been reported across Mongolia since the beginning of this year, burning at least 1,907,944 hectares of land, the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) said Friday.
Most of the fires were steppe fires, with the majority occurring in the eastern provinces of Dornod, Sukhbaatar and Khentii. Human negligence was identified as the primary cause of the fires, the NEMA said.
The most destructive of the wildfires was a steppe fire that broke out on Oct. 8 in the core zone of the Numrug Strictly Protected Area in Khalkh Gol soum, Dornod province. The fire was fully extinguished on Oct. 16. Initial investigations indicate that the fire may have been sparked by a convoy operated by Mobicom, a Mongolian telecommunications company with Japanese investment.
The Numrug Strictly Protected Area is one of eastern Mongolia's best-preserved natural ecosystems and provides habitat for a wide range of wildlife, including rare and endangered species. According to the Ministry of Environment and Climate Change, the fire scorched approximately 530,000 hectares of land, including around 470,000 hectares within the protected area -- equivalent to 79.8 percent of the reserve's total area.
Currently, Mongolian firefighters are working to extinguish five steppe fires across the three eastern provinces, the emergency agency said.
Mongolia has a harsh continental climate, with dry and windy conditions typically prevailing in spring and autumn, increasing the risk of wildfires. ■

Greece has temporarily suspended state funding to the Hellenic Basketball Federation (EOK) and ordered financial audits amid a match-fixing and bribery investigation involving federation president Vangelis Liolios.
Sports Minister Yiannis Vroutsis ordered the suspension of legally mandated subsidies and requested an extraordinary financial and management audit covering 2024, 2025, and 2026, according to a ministry statement.
The audit will be conducted by the General Directorate of Financial Audits of the Ministry of National Economy and Finance, while the National Transparency Authority will carry out a separate review.
The ministry said match manipulation can result in financial penalties for sports organizations, alongside criminal and disciplinary sanctions, including restrictions on funding distributed through gambling revenues.
Greek police said Thursday that six people were arrested under judicial warrants over suspected bribery and unlawful interference in basketball matches.
Five suspects were detained during coordinated operations Wednesday in Attica, Achaea, and Katerini, while a sixth voluntarily appeared at police headquarters and was arrested.
Authorities also seized €931,463 ($1.08 million) in cash, 14 mobile phones, six laptops and other electronic devices during searches of the suspects' homes.
Liolios, who denies wrongdoing, was granted additional time to prepare his defense and is expected to appear before an investigating magistrate on Sunday, Oct. 25, alongside businessman Giorgos Mavraganis.
Former referee Petros Papapetrou was scheduled to appear before an investigating magistrate Friday, Oct. 23, to present his defense, while three other defendants, including EuroLeague referee Vasiliki Tsaroucha, are expected to appear Monday, Oct. 26.
According to Greek media reports citing witness testimony, investigators are examining five alleged bribery incidents involving payments to referees, including claims that €5,000 ($5,600) was paid in certain cases.
A witness also reportedly alleged that Liolios was aware of the arrangements, a claim he denies.
Investigators are additionally examining messages allegedly containing advance information about referee appointments.
Separately, Papapetrou has denied wrongdoing and said he can account for €820,000 reportedly discovered at his home during a police search.
The case may involve approximately 50 basketball games played between 2016 and 2026, including professional, youth and school competitions.
 
- Greek basketball legend seeks to testify
Greek basketball legend Panagiotis Giannakis wants to testify in the case and may formally join proceedings in support of the prosecution, his lawyer said Friday.
The 67-year-old former player and coach, nicknamed The Dragon, is expected to address the allegations Monday, Oct. 26, after reviewing the case file.
His name appears in witness testimony concerning a March 2018 game between Faros and Aris, when Giannakis, then Aris coach, was ejected following two technical fouls. A witness alleged that the refereeing decisions were deliberate.
His lawyer, Andreas Mitsainas, said Giannakis wants to clarify the allegations and contribute to establishing what happened.
"This whole situation is a dark cloud over Greek basketball," Mitsainas said.

Ship attacks in Strait of Hormuz hit record high in October

Ship attacks in Strait of Hormuz hit record high in October
- October saw a record high in ship attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waters, with 28 confirmed and reported incidents, according to the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.
- The IMO said more than 30 VLCCs were damaged, including 11 in October, affecting about 3.5% of the global supertanker fleet and raising risks for world oil trade.
- Experts said Iran may be using the attacks to slow shipping recovery and keep pressure on energy markets, while UKMTO warned that poor reporting means some incidents may be missed.
AI generated
OSLO - October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by a Washington-based think-tank that has tracked maritime security incidents worldwide since 2017.
“October has seen the highest number of ship attacks on record,” said Noam Raydan, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.
Raydan, who maintains the institute’s interactive shipping incident map, has recorded 28 confirmed and reported attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waterways in October and 113 since the US-Israeli war with Iran began on Feb 28.
The institute’s map shows most of the attacks that took place in September and October were in the Strait of Hormuz.
Around 3.5% of world supertanker fleet attacked
The tally broadly aligns with data from the International Maritime Organisation (IMO), which recorded a total of 120 incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Middle East since the conflict with Iran began.
The IMO lists more than 30 supertankers, or Very Large Crude Carriers (VLCCs), that were damaged during the attacks, including 11 in October alone, a Reuters review of the IMO list and MarineTraffic vessel data showed.
Each VLCC can carry about two million barrels of crude. The listed vessels account for about 3.5% of the total global VLCC fleet, which exceeds 900.
More tankers came under attack as shipowners became increasingly willing to load cargoes inside the Gulf, lured by daily freight rates exceeding US$1 million (S$1.27 million) and steeper discounts offered by regional producers against dated Brent.
“October 2026 has emerged as the most intense period of maritime attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz since the escalation of hostilities in March,” Greece-based consultancy Marisks said.
Between Oct 5 and Oct 11, a dozen ships were attacked, marking also the highest weekly number of attacks since the conflict began, it also said.
Not all attacks may be captured in data
By intensifying attacks, Iran is seeking to slow the recovery in shipments and maintain pressure on global energy markets ahead of November’s US midterm elections, Raydan said.
Earlier this month, Reuters reported about Tehran adopting such tactics, citing two senior Iranian officials.
UKMTO, the British maritime security service, which recorded 135 incidents related to the US-Iran conflict as of Oct 16, said it was struggling to capture the whole picture due to insufficient voluntary reporting by shippers.
The UKMTO data also showed a sharp rise in ship damage caused by attacks in October. REUTERS

Defence investment must improve lives, says Streeting
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:00:54 BST
00:00:54 KST

Investment in defence will only command lasting public support if people can see that it improves their lives as well as strengthening national defence, and the Telford Gun Hall will inject more than £400 million into the British economy over the next decade, according to the Defence Secretary.
Wes Streeting was speaking at the official opening of the Rheinmetall facility, which returns large-calibre weapon production to Britain.
He said: “And I’m acutely aware that investment in defence comes with trade-offs and choices in other areas of government spending, and at a cost to the taxpayer. So investment in defence will only command lasting public support if people can see not only how that investment strengthens our national defence, but also if they can see how it improves their lives, how it makes sure that we have a Britain that is worth fighting for.”
Streeting said almost seventy per cent of defence investment is already spent outside London and the South East, and indicated that further detail is coming, saying the government is “setting out shortly how people and communities in every nation and region of the UK will feel benefits and do feel benefits from the defence dividend.”
On the region, he said: “Here in the West Midlands, the defence economy is worth £1.8 billion and directly support around 8,000 jobs, with Rheinmetall at the forefront. Defence can also help us to tackle the moral emergency of more than a million young people out of work or education or training.”
He set out four tests for defence spending: “So it’s not just about spending more, although spending more is necessary. Every pound we invest in defence should be judged by what it does for Britain. Does it strengthen our industrial base? Does it push the frontier of innovation? Does it create skilled work, especially for young people? Over the next decade, this facility will emphatically answer yes to all those questions.”
On the figure, he said: “And as it does, it will inject more than £400 million into the UK economy. That’s precisely what I mean when I say that the Ministry of Defence can also be a ministry for growth and a ministry for opportunity, not simply spending more, but investing more wisely, backing the people, places and businesses that strengthen our national security and drive our national renewal.”
Streeting opened by placing the facility in its industrial setting, saying: “As someone who loves our country’s history, it’s not lost on me that we’re a stone’s throw away from the birthplace of British industry, and a part of our country that’s synonymous with engineering and manufacturing.”
He said: “So it feels especially fitting that we’re here to celebrate how we are renewing and reigniting that unique industrial strength. Today is a vote of confidence in our country, a statement of intent on our mission to reindustrialise Britain and create good, well-paid jobs across our country, and proof that we are rebuilding the capabilities of our armed forces.”
The Gun Hall is expected to support more than a hundred highly skilled people as production develops. Rheinmetall currently employs around 685 people in Telford, thirty-five of them at the Gun Hall, and the facility forms part of more than £200 million the company has invested across its British operations over the past five years.
Rheinmetall has said it intends to introduce British steel from Sheffield Forgemasters into production, and that it will continue to work with British small and medium-sized enterprises to build domestic supply chains.
The Apprenticeship Talent Bridge launched this month addresses the same pipeline from another direction, offering strong apprenticeship applicants who cannot be placed by BAE Systems or Babcock to smaller firms in the same communities, with pilots covering Barrow-in-Furness and Devonport.

EU-funded project on digital security and countering disinformation launched in Ukraine
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:00:45 EEST
00:00:45 KST

The non-governmental organisation Detector Media, Kyiv National University of Technologies and Design (KNUTD) and Ukraine Resilience & Recovery Foundation (URRF) are launching a joint project aimed at improving digital security among Ukrainians, countering disinformation and promoting European standards for personal data protection.
Representatives of the three organisations announced the initiative at a press conference entitled "Ukraine on the Path to the EU: Digital Security, Media Literacy and New Challenges of Information Warfare", held on Friday at the Interfax-Ukraine news agency's press centre.
The project, "Digital Security for Citizens: Countering Disinformation, European Data Protection Standards and Media Literacy on Ukraine's Path to the EU", is being implemented with financial support from the European Union under the Resilience and Engagement for Ukraine (REU) programme, implemented by the Institute for Economic Research and Policy Consulting (IER).
According to Yevhen Anhel, Senior Research Fellow at IER, the grant funding mechanism is a pilot initiative. Following a competitive selection process, three consortia were awarded funding, including the partnership between Detector Media, KNUTD and URRF.
Anhel said the initiative is expected to continue after the completion of the pilot phase. He also noted that the European Union places considerable emphasis on supporting the harmonisation of Ukrainian legislation with EU law, including through the involvement of civil society organisations in the relevant reforms.
Halyna Petrenko, Director of Detector Media, emphasised the need for a comprehensive approach to countering Russian disinformation, which remains one of the instruments of information aggression against Ukraine.
According to Petrenko, the spread of manipulative content through social media, digital platforms and emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, poses additional risks to public trust and citizens' ability to make informed decisions.
At the same time, effective efforts to counter disinformation should focus not on restricting freedom of expression but on developing critical thinking, media literacy, fact-checking skills and support for independent media.
The project will include the preparation of analytical and educational materials, thematic events and public discussions, as well as the establishment of a permanent online information platform hosted by Detector Media. The platform is intended to provide a forum for expert analysis, practical guidance and research on digital security, media literacy and European digital policy standards.
Yevheniia Khaustova, Doctor of Economic Sciences and Professor at KNUTD, highlighted the importance of education in building digital resilience and preparing citizens to apply European standards in their everyday lives.
In particular, this concerns personal data protection, citizens' digital rights, the responsible use of digital technologies and a practical understanding of the principles of the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).
KNUTD will be responsible for the project's academic and educational component, involving lecturers, researchers and students in preparing analytical materials, delivering lectures, organising expert discussions and conducting educational activities.
Volodymyr Martsynovskyi, Managing Director of Ukraine Resilience & Recovery Foundation, said that digital resilience is an integral part not only of Ukraine's national security but also of the security of European countries.
According to Martsynovskyi, Russian information operations extend far beyond Ukraine's borders and pose a threat to democratic institutions, public trust and Europe's information environment.
Martsynovskyi stressed that strengthening Ukraine's digital resilience would also contribute to the resilience of Europe's information environment. He identified international cooperation and the promotion of European standards for information security and personal data protection as essential prerequisites for achieving this objective.
Within the consortium, URRF will be responsible for developing partnerships, international communications, stakeholder engagement and facilitating the dissemination of the project's results.
The press conference participants noted that the partnership model brings together the expertise of an independent media organisation, the academic and educational capabilities of a university, and the international cooperation capacity of a charitable foundation.
The project is expected to help improve digital literacy among Ukrainians, develop skills to counter information manipulation, promote European standards for personal data protection and strengthen civil society participation in Ukraine's European integration process.
As previously reported, Resilience and Engagement for Ukraine (REU) programme is implemented by the Institute for Economic Research and Policy Consulting with financial support from the European Union.

How Many Billions Would It Take to Hold Meta Accountable?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Earlier this week, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay a $25 billion fine for violating consumer protection laws dating back to the Cambridge Analytica scandal. $25 billion is a massive fine, the largest Meta has ever faced, but it still had us folks at WIRED wondering: Would Meta even feel the pain?
A quick recap of the case: Filed in 2021, the suit alleged that the company violated the state’s Unfair Practices Act by lying to Meta users about the way it handled their data. (Later, New Mexico’s attorney general also made claims against Meta’s content moderation policies.) In September, a jury ruled in favor of the state. Then came the multibillion-dollar penalty.
“This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” C.J. Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer, said in a statement. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal.”
Meta’s legal troubles have proliferated so much this year that it’s hard to keep track of them. Earlier this year in New Mexico, a jury ruled that the social media company should pay $375 million for violating the state’s Unfair Practices Act. That trial was related to child safety. A second phase of the case resulted in Meta being ordered to pay $567 million.
Meanwhile, a Los Angeles County superior court found Meta—and Google-owned YouTube—liable for harming a user’s mental health with the addictive design features of their apps. The plaintiff, a young woman, was awarded $6 million; Meta is on the hook for the bulk of that payment. Then in August, Meta settled a landmark federal case brought against the company by the majority of US states. This suit, once again, centered on addictive features in its apps that were alleged to be harmful to kids. As part of that settlement, Meta will pay the states between $17 and $18 billion over 10 years.
Added up, that’s a lot of billions. And yet: It’s still just the cost of doing business for Meta. Reuters reports that in the most recent New Mexico trial, the state’s attorneys originally asked Judge Francis Mathew to award the state between $35 and $45 billion. That would’ve been significant for the state, but would that extra $20 billion have kneecapped Meta? Nope.
Even if Meta was forced to pay the total maximum fine of the New Mexico ruling—a whopping $219 billion, or $5,000 across 43 million violations, reduced by the judge to $25 billion—the company would have felt only a mild sting. As of writing, Meta is worth around $1.7 trillion. Its stock took a hit on Thursday, but that was due to a confluence of factors, like Meta’s earnings report on Wednesday, the company’s massive capital expenditures on AI, and AI stocks dragging overall.
At this point, with no immediate monetary damage to Meta, it would take an accumulation of events to force some kind of change, legal experts tell me. For one, Meta has a clear perception problem: Juries are ruling against it, protesters have railed against it, even its own employees have been more vocal about the company’s internal policies.
Every time Meta doesn’t settle a case, the evidence presented during trial can be scrutinized by the public and used in future cases against Meta, says Corban Rhodes, partner at DiCello Levitt, the outside law firm representing New Mexico in this case. “This trial included more than 100 exhibits that we were able to put into public record, things that had been kept secret for more than a decade since Cambridge Analytica,” Rhodes told WIRED.
One such item is a 2018 email that then COO Sheryl Sandberg sent to a few colleagues days after the Cambridge Analytica scandal broke. Sandberg wrote, “The single biggest issue we face—and I really need everyone to know this—is that there were a MILLION developers with access to the data. We are going to have many, many, many more moments like this in the next month and year.”
There are early signals that private insurers may start balking at having to cover the cost of a tech company’s legal defenses. Some experts are suggesting that insurance companies could even end up being de facto governance for AI, as they “inject responsibility into how AI is designed, developed, and deployed as a condition for obtaining insurance.” Meta learned this firsthand in March, when a Delaware judge ruled that insurers do not have a duty to defend Meta against the literal thousands of lawsuits being brought against it.
There’s no well-defined number at which Meta suddenly becomes vulnerable—the company is unlikely to ever fold from legal penalties alone. But problems could crop up if shareholders or board members stop seeing the company as some inanimate entity and start to focus on the individual directors or officers who have been making bad decisions, says Brian Quinn, a law professor at Boston College Law School who studies corporate law, M&A, and transaction law. Like, say, the people who keep appearing in lawsuits.
“The way that indemnification law is written right now, the fact that a person in a company was found to have violated a law doesn’t necessarily make them liable. It can be believed that they were acting in good faith, or in the best interest of their company,” Quinn says. “But problems start to arise if shareholders say, wait a minute, there’s not only evidence that this director or operator is violating the law, but it has appeared in the same set of facts seven times now.”
After a huge accumulation of these kinds of results, Quinn says, some angry shareholders might stand up and say the corporation should no longer be able to indemnify those directors. That’s when you might see change, because Meta’s executives would no longer be as protected.
Finally, since litigation is often behind the curve on society-disrupting technology, Meta’s legal woes are likely far from over—especially as it wades deeper into AI. “Regulators and courts have for a long time been focused on the impact of social media 1.0 and 2.0, and I think we’re moving on from that era,” says Rhodes. “I expect the next wave of litigation will be focused on AI.”
This is an edition of Steven Levy’s and Lauren Goode's Backchannel newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

Cuba: Two years after being named prisoners of conscience, Félix Navarro, Sayli Navarro and Roberto Pérez Fonseca must be released
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

On 23 October 2024, Amnesty International named Félix Navarro, Sayli Navarro and Roberto Pérez Fonseca prisoners of conscience, concluding that they had been deprived of their liberty solely for peacefully exercising their human rights. Two years later, they remain unjustly imprisoned amid the continued politically motivated detention and repression of critical voices in Cuba.
In response, Ana Piquer, Amnesty International’s Americas Director, said:
“Two years after being named prisoners of conscience, Félix Navarro, Sayli Navarro and Roberto Pérez Fonseca remain unjustly deprived of their liberty. That means two more years separated from their families, subjected to the harsh conditions of Cuba’s prison system and punished solely for exercising their human rights. The Cuban authorities must release them immediately and unconditionally. They should not spend another day behind bars.”
That means two more years separated from their families, subjected to the harsh conditions of Cuba’s prison system and punished solely for exercising their human rights. The Cuban authorities must release them immediately and unconditionally.”
Ana Piquer, Amnesty International’s Americas Director.
Félix Navarro is a political dissident and founder of the Pedro Luis Boitel Party for Democracy. He was sentenced to nine years in prison. His current imprisonment marks the third time he has been deprived of his liberty for political reasons.
Sayli Navarro is an activist and member of the Damas de Blanco (Ladies in White) movement. She was sentenced to eight years in prison after being arbitrarily detained amid the repression that followed the July 2021 protests.
Roberto Pérez Fonseca is an activist and human rights defender. He was sentenced to 10 years in prison for his peaceful participation in the 11 July 2021 protests. Among the acts used to convict him was footage showing him tearing up an image of Fidel Castro during the protests.
“Félix, Sayli and Roberto represent many others in Cuba who have been imprisoned for protesting, dissenting or defending human rights. Their sentences illustrate how the authorities continue to misuse the criminal justice system to silence critical voices. Expressing an opinion, taking part in a protest or demanding respect for human rights must never result in years behind bars,” said Ana Piquer.
Félix, Sayli and Roberto represent many others in Cuba who have been imprisoned for protesting, dissenting or defending human rights. Their sentences illustrate how the authorities continue to misuse the criminal justice system to silence critical voices.”
Ana Piquer, Amnesty International’s Americas Director.
Information received by Amnesty International in 2026 shows that the injustice of their imprisonment is compounded by the conditions in which they continue to be held.
Félix Navarro’s situation remains particularly serious. He continues to be held in prolonged isolation and has very limited access to the outdoors. In January 2026, he underwent medical testing after showing possible symptoms of tuberculosis, but neither he nor his family received timely information about the results, raising serious concerns about his health and access to adequate medical care.
Sayli Navarro remains detained in conditions that put her health and physical integrity at risk, including in a prison that has lacked regular access to safe drinking water. The authorities have also repeatedly denied her access to prison benefits on the basis of “re-education” criteria.
Roberto Pérez Fonseca has serious chronic health conditions, whose deterioration during his imprisonment is of particular concern. He has been held in punishment cells, received inadequate medical care and faced difficulties communicating with his family.
In 2026, Amnesty International has also documented obstacles and delays in legal procedures available to people who, because of serious medical conditions, may be eligible for release on health grounds.
“It is deeply alarming that, in addition to being unjustly imprisoned, these individuals continue to be subjected to conditions that may endanger their health, physical integrity and dignity. The Cuban state is responsible for protecting everyone in its custody and must immediately ensure adequate medical care, contact with their families and detention conditions that comply with human rights standards for as long as they remain deprived of their liberty,” said Ana Piquer.
Amnesty International continues to call for the immediate and unconditional release of all prisoners of conscience in Cuba and an end to the detention of people solely for exercising their human rights.
“The Cuban authorities must end the use of imprisonment, harassment and intimidation to silence dissent. Félix, Sayli and Roberto must regain their freedom, but our call does not end with them. No one should be imprisoned in Cuba for peacefully expressing their views, protesting or defending human rights,” said Ana Piquer.

Foes of Gov. Gavin Newsom, who is widely viewed as a likely 2028 presidential candidate, are launching television and digital ads this weekend in early primary states that criticize the governor’s opposition to the proposed billionaire tax on California’s November ballot.
The ad, funded by backers of the wealth tax, castigates Newsom for opposing Proposition 40, the ballot measure that would impose a 5% tax on California billionaires’ assets to offset federal healthcare funding cuts approved by congressional Republicans and signed by President Trump last year.
“We’re all struggling with the high cost of healthcare. In California, Democrats are championing a one-time tax on billionaires that would save coverage for millions,” a narrator says in the 30-second ad. “So why [has] presidential hopeful Gavin Newsom betrayed his own supporters by trying to sabotage the billionaire tax? Maybe it’s because the same billionaires who oppose Prop. 40 also gave millions of dollars to Newsom. Gavin Newsom turned his back on working Californians. Will he do the same to you?”
The ad specifically calls out billionaires Stewart Resnick, who owns several businesses including Pom Wonderful, Fiji Water and Justin Wines; crypto executive Chris Larsen; former Google leader Eric Schmidt; and venture capitalist Michael Moritz, all of whom have backed Newsom’s political ambitions.
Newsom has argued that, although he supports wealth taxes, they ought to be enacted at the national level, rather than a state-by-state patchwork that could drive the rich to leave California, a state with a volatile budget heavily dependent on the state’s wealthiest residents.
The primary funders of the ad are the Service Employees International Union - United Healthcare Workers West, which crafted Proposition 40; Saikat Chakrabarti, a climate change warrior and political advisor who made his wealth in part as a founding engineer at Stripe; and Ross Boucher, an early engineer at Stripe.
Prop 40, which would tax the assets of California billionaires to mostly fund healthcare, has divided Democratic politicians, labor unions and other groups.
The ad buy is six figures but could grow, according to its backers. Among the states where the ad is expected to air are South Carolina, Nevada, New Mexico, Virginia and New Hampshire.
Earlier this month, Newsom stumped for candidates in New Hampshire, his latest foray to early presidential primary states.
The ad launch comes amid a contentious, expensive battle over the proposed wealth tax, which has divided Democrats and their allies. Although Newsom is among Democrats who oppose it, the ballot measure was endorsed by the state Democratic Party and Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.). Voters are closely divided about the measure.

South China Sea Code of Conduct: A Deal Is Not Enough
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:59:00 UTC
23:59:00 KST

As ASEAN and China work toward concluding a Code of Conduct (COC) for the South China Sea in 2026, the central question is not simply whether an agreement can be reached, but whether it will meaningfully reduce tensions. A deal is not enough if it does not address the underlying drivers of tension and shape actors’ behaviors.
The South China Sea is a contested maritime zone, involving China and ASEAN members Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Vietnam. To address the overlapping maritime claims and disputes, ASEAN and China have been negotiating a COC to establish a rules-based framework to manage maritime disputes, reduce miscalculations, and prevent armed conflict.
After nearly two decades of negotiations, Manila, as the current ASEAN chair, has recently signaled that agreement on the COC is at hand. A COC would represent an important diplomatic achievement.
Yet an agreement that lacks credible enforcement mechanisms, preserves ambiguity over compliance, or constrains Southeast Asian countries’ strategic autonomy could do little to address the region’s underlying security challenges.
The substance of the agreement matters more than announcing its completion. A COC that primarily reiterates commitments to dialogue, restraint, and peaceful dispute resolution – like those contained in the existing Declaration of Conduct – would have limited practical value. The COC needs clear procedures for managing incidents, resolving disagreements, and addressing violations.
The South China Sea has seen increased military activities. China has built a network of military facilities in the Spratly and Paracel Islands, some of which are now equipped to host bombers. In 2025, Vietnam commenced its own reclamation work on occupied features, building infrastructure to support a larger military presence.
Naval confrontations between China and the Philippines continue, highlighting the fragility of stability in the contested waters. Diplomatic commitments alone cannot guarantee responsible behavior
If the COC is to improve regional stability, it must include practical measures to prevent escalation and hold parties accountable for their conduct.
This raises a second challenge: ASEAN’s ability to ensure compliance. Even if the agreement includes specific obligations, its effectiveness will depend on whether parties are willing to implement them when doing so conflicts with their strategic interests. ASEAN’s consensus-based approach, while essential to maintaining regional unity, can complicate collective responses to violations, particularly when member states have different economic and security relationships with China.
A credible COC should therefore establish transparent procedures for reporting incidents, conducting consultations, and addressing alleged breaches. Regular reviews and clearly defined dispute-management channels could help prevent disagreements from escalating. Without a meaningful accountability mechanism, the COC risks just becoming a declaration of intent.
The agreement must also protect Southeast Asian states’ strategic autonomy. China may seek arrangements that limit activities it considers destabilizing, such as joint military exercises with the United States. Provisions governing military exercises, defense partnerships, or cooperation with external powers could create constraints that extend beyond managing disputes in the South China Sea. If drafted too broadly, the COC could inadvertently restrict ASEAN members’ ability to pursue their own security interests.
The challenge is to distinguish between measures designed to prevent maritime incidents and provisions that limit legitimate defense cooperation. Southeast Asian states should retain the freedom to conduct exercises, modernize their armed forces, and establish partnerships with countries outside the region, consistent with international law. A COC that undermines these freedoms would risk weakening the very strategic independence ASEAN seeks to preserve.
The Philippines’ expanding defense cooperation with non-Southeast Asian powers such as Australia and Japan illustrates this tension. Manila’s partnerships strengthen its deterrence capabilities and provide additional options for responding to maritime pressure. However, Beijing may view these arrangements as contributing to strategic competition, complicating efforts to reach a mutually acceptable agreement.
Nevertheless, external partnerships should not automatically be regarded as obstacles to a COC. They can strengthen Southeast Asian states’ negotiating position by showing that China and ASEAN alone cannot determine regional security, given the South China Sea’s significance as an international maritime trade route. Extra-regional powers’ participation in maritime security, however, should not obscure ASEAN’s central role in shaping regional norms.
Ultimately, the COC’s credibility will depend on whether it can reconcile three objectives: reducing tensions, ensuring compliance, and preserving the strategic autonomy of Southeast Asian countries. These objectives are not mutually exclusive, but achieving them will require precise language, practical implementation mechanisms, and a willingness to address violations consistently.
The measure of success, then, is not whether ASEAN and China can sign an agreement, but whether that agreement changes behavior at sea. Without credible commitments and meaningful accountability, the COC may secure a diplomatic milestone while failing to deliver the regional stability it promises.

MEP Dan Barna: Bulgaria must clearly name Russia’s aggression in the Black Sea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:58:55 UTC
23:58:55 KST

Author
Irina Nedeva
Interview
MEP Dan Barna: Bulgaria must clearly name Russia’s aggression in the Black Sea
The EU will accelerate the creation of a European Martime Security Center
Friday 23 October 2026 14:58
Friday, 23 October 2026, 14:58
MEP Dan Barna in Radio Studio 2 at the European Parliament in Strasbourg
PHOTO Irina Nedeva
Font size
The Black Sea is no longer merely a trade corridor. It has become a test of European security. In a resolution adopted on Thursday, the European Parliament expresses solidarity with Bulgaria and Romania over the escalation of Russian attacks on commercial shipping, while also voicing serious concern about “the unclear and ambiguous response of the Bulgarian authorities to the escalating Russian threat in the Black Sea”.
How does the Romanian government view the response of the Bulgarian government led by Rumen Radev to Russian threats in the region? And how can Europe protect shipping in the Black Sea without waiting for the next attack? Is a common European response possible when national governments are sending different signals to Moscow?
In Strasbourg, BNR's Irina Nedeva spoke to Romanian MEP Dan Barna, a former deputy prime minister of Romania and one of the driving forces behind the resolution on behalf of the Renew Europe group. Their conversation addressed the need for a European Maritime Security Centre, the protection of commercial vessels, and the role of Bulgaria and Romania in defending NATO’s eastern flank.
But there is also a broader question facing the EU: can Europe finance its defence, maintain support for poorer regions and avoid new political crises within the Union at the same time?
You are calling for a European maritime security centre in the Black Sea. What exactly should this centre do, who will fund it, and when could it become operational? Is there not a risk of creating yet another institution while ships continue to come under attack?
“This resolution is also a very swift response by the European Parliament. I am pleased that, on the very day it was debated in the European Parliament, NATO also brought the Black Sea into focus. The resolution has two main objectives. The first is to recognise the need to designate the Black Sea as a priority area on the eastern flank. The second, as you rightly pointed out, concerns the establishment and funding of a European Maritime Security Centre.
The purpose of this structure, this centre, is to enhance the capacity to respond rapidly to attacks and security threats in the Black Sea. War is no longer just a war of tanks and aircraft. It is a drone war, and in this kind of warfare, time is of the essence. That is precisely why this centre must strengthen NATO’s and the eastern flank’s ability to respond appropriately and in a timely manner. What we are talking about is building technical infrastructure capable of addressing the realities of Russian aggression.”
Romania and Bulgaria are directly exposed to these risks, but the Black Sea is also an external border of both the EU and NATO. What concrete action do you expect from European partners: military surveillance, air defence, escorts for commercial vessels or some other form of presence?
“Everything you have mentioned is important. I mean the ability to identify risks and drones in a given area as quickly as possible. It is also important to have the capacity to scramble aircraft to destroy these drones. In this context, I would like to commend the Romanian and Spanish pilots who have managed to shoot down several drones in recent days. In the near future, we may also have to address the need to protect commercial vessels and provide them with escorts if Russian drones continue to operate aggressively in the region.”
Irina Nedeva and MEP Dan Barna in Radio Studio 2 at the European Parliament in Strasbourg
PHOTO Rositsa Petkova, BNR
Romania has clearly identified the aggressor. For the first time, Prime Minister Rumen Radev has mentioned Russia as being logically linked to the attacks, while adding that there is no evidence confirming their origin. From Romania’s perspective, how do you view the Bulgarian government’s response?
“We must be absolutely clear, and this resolution emphasises the point: Russia is the aggressor and is carrying out attacks against NATO’s eastern flank, including against Romania and Bulgaria. The text of the resolution, which we agreed on only yesterday, also refers to the perception that Bulgaria’s position is unclear and insufficiently categorical. I am optimistic that the Bulgarian government, too, will demonstrate solidarity and determination by acknowledging that these attacks originate from Russia and that a coordinated response is needed.This is one of the main problems associated with these attacks.
Commercial shipping is crucial not only for the countries of the Black Sea region. Food and essential goods are transported by sea to Africa, Asia and many other countries that depend, for example, on Ukrainian grain. The key question is how to protect this commercial traffic. If the Black Sea were to become a situation resembling that in the Strait of Hormuz, brought about by the war with Iran, this would put enormous pressure on the gas and hydrocarbon markets. Agricultural products could also be seriously affected.”
You advocate both stronger European defence and continued support for cohesion policy and agricultural subsidies. When resources are limited, who should make the compromise? Can countries such as Romania and Bulgaria expect more funding for security without losing support for their regions?
“Europe is under intense pressure from anti-European, sovereigntist and extremist movements. Weakening cohesion policy is precisely the argument used by sovereigntist and pro-Russian forces. They are trying to convince European citizens that Europe no longer works. That is why cohesion policy acts as a bond holding European values and European solidarity together. For this very reason, I believe it is important, for Romania, Bulgaria and Europe as a whole, that cohesion policy remains in place and continues to be strong.”
Romania is emerging from nearly six months of political deadlock with a minority government. Is this a temporary arrangement, or are there grounds to expect stability?
“The outlook is relatively optimistic in terms of stability, though not necessarily in terms of the quality of governance. Romania is currently facing a similar situation within its government, and I am sure Bulgaria has been through many such situations as well. We are talking about parliaments divided into three roughly equal blocs, none of which is willing to work openly with the other two. Yesterday, parliament approved a new government. So we now have a new cabinet. That is good news for the country’s stability.”
You have criticised the lack of tangible progress on enlargement. Is the EU ready to admit Moldova and other candidate countries before reforming its own decision-making processes? And how would you prevent a scenario in which new members bring unresolved rule-of-law problems into the Union?
“I must express my deep respect for Marta Kos, the European Commissioner for Enlargement, because she has managed to turn enlargement policy into a consistent and effective one. Two weeks ago in Strasbourg, she announced the new enlargement strategy, under which the four most successful and best-prepared countries were given roadmaps. This is a significant step forward. I am referring to Montenegro, Moldova, Albania and Ukraine. They are receiving roadmaps that set out a clear path forward, with specific conditions and reforms to be completed. These have been presented to their governments. This represents considerable progress because, at the very least, there is now a clear prospect.
I fully agree that Europe needs reforms, including to its voting system and the way its decision-making mechanisms operate. These reforms must prevent a repeat of what happened with Hungary and Viktor Orbán, when Russia managed to block one link in the chain and bring the entire mechanism to a standstill. To avoid this negative experience and this vicious practice, it is clear that Europe must move towards qualified majority voting instead of the current requirement for unanimity.
As regards enlargement, one approach under the new strategy is to retain unanimity only for the first and final stages of the process, while applying qualified majority voting to the intermediate stages. We are working in this direction, too. I am also a member of the European Parliament–Moldova Parliamentary Association Committee. We are working to help the country carry out the necessary reforms.”
Bulgaria is already in the eurozone. When will we stop having to convert our currencies as two neighbouring countries?
“For us Romanians, and for me personally, this is a painful issue. I would like to congratulate Bulgarian citizens, politicians and society on managing to adopt the euro, despite changing seven governments in roughly two years. The fact that all these governments managed to maintain the course and meet the convergence criteria, enabling Bulgaria to join the eurozone at the beginning of this year, is a source of pride.
I know that Romania and Bulgaria have a healthy sense of neighbourly competition on various issues. I know many people on both sides who take pride in their country’s achievements, in the areas where Romania excels and those where Bulgaria performs well. But when it comes to the euro, you have done better than we have. You have my admiration.”
Irina Nedeva’s full interview with MEP Dan Barna was aired on the 12+3 programme on BNR's Horizon channel.

Trump deportees to Sierra Leone risk being forced home, rights group says
DAKAR, Oct 23 - Amnesty International on Friday urged Sierra Leone to halt the expected repatriation of three people deported from the United States, saying they could face serious human rights violations if returned to their home countries elsewhere in West Africa.
• The rights group said Abalo Agba of Togo, Alfred Kamara of Liberia and Fatou Traore of Ivory Coast had each lived in the United States for more than 20 years when they were removed by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement to Sierra Leone on October 12, and that they all have children under 18 still in the US
• They had previously secured a form of protection in the US known as withholding of removal, meaning a US immigration judge found they were more likely than not to face torture or other abuses if forced home
• Since taking office in January last year, the Trump administration has struck several deals with African governments that have agreed to accept migrants from other countries.
• Sierra Leone reached an agreement with Washington to accept up to 300 West African third-country nationals annually
• Amnesty said on Friday that migrants previously deported under the deal had been quickly repatriated, and it criticised what it described as a "revolving door" policy of forcing people home
• A Sierra Leone government spokesperson and the US State Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment REUTERS

Dutch cybersecurity agency probes suspected hacks linked to PHP flaws
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:56:17 UTC
23:56:17 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
The Netherlands’ National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) is investigating reports of successful cyberattacks exploiting critical vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language, warning that the situation could deteriorate rapidly, local media reported Friday.
An NCSC spokesperson told Dutch daily de Volkskrant on Thursday that the reports came through the agency’s international network and were still being verified, according to DutchNews.
There were no indications at that stage that Dutch websites had been successfully targeted, the spokesperson said.
Cybersecurity researchers using artificial intelligence identified at least two serious flaws in PHP, a programming language widely used to build websites.
Details of the vulnerabilities leaked online Monday, prompting PHP developers to announce a security update for Wednesday afternoon.
Attempts to exploit the flaws began before the disclosure, with Amazon reporting an attempted attack on Oct. 17.
US cybersecurity company Cloudflare said the number of hacking attempts rose from thousands before the update to millions afterward, DutchNews reported.
Government, healthcare and news websites were temporarily taken offline while awaiting the security update. DutchNews said its own website was among those affected.
Dutch authorities issued warnings and took numerous websites offline early Wednesday. Governments in Belgium, Germany, France and Finland subsequently took similar steps, according to the report.
The Dutch data protection authority, AP, said Thursday it had not received any reports of data breaches linked to the vulnerabilities.
