What to know as Brazil prepares for tense presidential run-off
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:56:05 UTC
23:56:05 KST

What to know as Brazil prepares for tense presidential run-off
Polls show leftist incumbent Lula closing gap on right-wing rival Flavio Bolsonaro ahead of second round of voting.
Voters in Brazil are headed to the polls for the second time in one month, as Senator Flavio Bolsonaro and President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva square off in a run-off election to decide who will hold the presidency for the next four years.
While Bolsonaro outperformed expectations during the first round of voting on October 4, when he beat Lula by less than two percentage points but failed to secure the majority needed to avoid a run-off, the leftist president has sought to rally supporters ahead of the second round.
The vote on Sunday will decide whether Brazil joins a growing list of countries across Latin America that have handed victories to far-right candidates promising closer ties with the United States, a hard hand on crime and insecurity, and market-friendly economic policies.
Brazil under Lula has emerged as a key holdout against that shift, and a Bolsonaro victory on Sunday would galvanise conservatives in the region seeking to extend their winning streak to the largest country in Latin America.
When is the second round of voting?
The run-off will take place on October 25, 2026.
What happened during the first round?
The first round on October 4 saw Bolsonaro win 47 percent of the vote compared with just more than 45 percent for Lula, with the remainder of the votes distributed among several largely conservative candidates who did not advance to the next round.
While most polls had anticipated a close race that would go to a run-off, Lula had been slightly favoured to win the first round of voting. While Bolsonaro’s margin of victory was small, his overperformance indicated a level of enduring appeal for the political right that caught many Lula supporters off guard.
In addition to Bolsonaro’s success, even as his father, former far-right President Jair Bolsonaro, serves a 27-year prison sentence for his involvement in a coup plot following his loss to Lula in 2022, right-wing candidates also racked up wins in legislative races across the country.
Who is Lula?
Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, simply referred to as Lula, is the incumbent president and the candidate for the Workers Party, or PT.
His time in office has been defined by an effort to pair political democracy with material improvement for the country’s poor and efforts to build ties between developing, non-Western countries on the global stage.
The 80-year-old is seeking his fourth, non-consecutive term, hoping that his record of popularity and support for social programmes, credited by supporters with transforming the country, will help stave off a Bolsonaro win.
Lula clinched a third term in 2022, marking a dramatic comeback following a stint in prison based on corruption charges that were later overturned following revelations of prosecutorial impropriety.
But a highly polarised political landscape has hindered Lula’s ability to usher in ambitious and sweeping reforms during his third term.
Notable successes, such as sharp drops in unemployment and poverty and tackling deforestation in the Amazon rainforest, have been countered by rising household indebtedness that has strained families across the country.
A corruption scandal centring on disgraced banker Daniel Vorcaro has also implicated powerful figures and institutions across the political spectrum, including Bolsonaro himself as well as several members of the country’s Supreme Court, a target of right-wing ire for the conviction and sentencing of the elder Bolsonaro.
Who is Flavio Bolsonaro?
Senator Flavio Bolsonaro is running as the candidate of the right-wing Liberal Party.
The 45-year-old has emerged as the de facto leader of the country’s political right, filling a role previously held by his father before his conviction for a plot to remain in power despite his loss to Lula in 2022.
The younger Bolsonaro has sought to project a more polished image than his father while pledging continuity with many of his beliefs and policy priorities and promising to fight for his release from prison if elected.
He has pledged a militarised approach towards crime and insecurity posed by organised gangs in close partnership with the administration of United States President Donald Trump, who has sought to expand US military involvement across Latin America through ties with right-wing allies in the name of combatting crime.
Bolsonaro has also promised to rein in inflation and government spending, with an adviser stating that he would implement a debt ceiling if elected.
In the days after the first round, Bolsonaro has said he would “redemocratise” Brazil by reforming the constitution. The constitution was put in place after Brazil’s return to democracy in the 1980s, and Bolsonaro’s father has long expressed open nostalgia for the dictatorship period. There’s heavy speculation that Bolsonaro could be seeking to reform the judiciary, after his father’s legal setbacks. He has also promised to restore tax cuts for the events sector.
What has happened since the first round?
While many members of the PT were despondent following Bolsonaro’s first-round victory, Lula quickly urged his supporters to rally for the run-off and threw himself into campaigning.
He has also taken credit for his party’s long-sought constitutional amendment to reduce the six-day work week and promised free public transport on weekends.
Pro-Lula demonstrations in cities across the country have attracted millions of people, helping galvanise the president’s voters and cut into Bolsonaro’s lead. Bolsonaro has held his own rallies, hoping to capitalise on momentum and consolidate support from other conservative parties.
The two candidates held a combative debate on October 18, exchanging insults and accusing each other of corruption.
Questions of outside intervention have also been a theme in the campaign’s closing days, with US social media giant Meta facing allegations that it restricted pro-Lula activity online in a bid to support Bolsonaro.
Concerns about foreign interference, in particular from the US, have loomed over the campaign since the beginning.
The Trump administration has repeatedly sought to intervene in Brazilian politics, previously introducing steep tariffs and penalties against judicial officials in a bid to have the case against the elder Bolsonaro tossed out and mirroring rhetoric on the Brazilian right to cast doubt on the reliability of the country’s voting system.
Trump has himself used false claims of widespread fraud to ignore unfavourable election results, and observers have expressed concern that the US could throw its support behind Bolsonaro based on such claims even if he were to lose the race.
What do polls show?
After his victory in the first round, Bolsonaro emerged as the race’s de facto frontrunner. But polls continue to show a close race, with Lula cutting into Bolsonaro’s lead but continuing to trail within the margin of error.
Speculation that Bolsonaro might pull ahead decisively following the first round, after other conservative candidates failed to advance to the run-off, has not yet appeared in new polls.
A Nexus poll released on Monday showed Bolsonaro winning 46.5 percent of the vote in the second round, with Lula taking 45.9 percent. A poll from the previous week had shown Bolsonaro with 47.9 percent and Lula with 45.1 percent.
Another poll by AtlasIntel and Bloomberg, also released on Monday, showed Bolsonaro with 49.8 percent versus 47.6 percent for Lula. An October 9 poll had shown Bolsonaro with 51.1 percent and Lula with 45.7.
A Quaest poll released on October 21 showed Bolsonaro’s lead continuing to drop, with Lula winning 44 percent and Bolsonaro 45 percent.

6 killed, 28 wounded in shooting at church funeral in Jordan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:56:00 UTC
23:56:00 KST

Seven people were killed and 40 others were injured when gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Jordan's Karak governorate on Friday.
Security forces had been deployed to the church and were pursuing the suspects, the state-owned Al-Mamlaka television station reported. It said gunmen got out of a vehicle and opened fire during a funeral procession at the Hamoud Church in Karak. Al-Mamlaka previously reported seven had been killed in the attack.
Speaking at a press conference, Major General Abdallah al-Maaytah said most of those wounded in the shooting at the Hamoud Church in Karak governorate were still receiving treatment, and that the hunt for the attackers was ongoing. Jordan's health minister said 40 people were wounded.
Interior Minister Mazin Al Farrayeh said the attack had been carried out by "extremists", but that it was too early to tell whether they had any links to known groups inside or outside Jordan.
Khaled Burqan, a man who had been attending the funeral, told Al-Mamlaka that dozens of people had been attending the funeral and at least two men - one carrying a rifle and another carrying a pistol - opened fire on them for several minutes.
There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attack and Jordanian authorities did not say who was responsible.
Jordan's King Abdullah said those behind the attack would be punished "with an iron fist."
"The terrorist attack against Karak will be met with the harshest retaliation. Those who delude themselves into thinking that they can divide Jordanians with their bullets have no chance in the face of our unity," he said in a statement.
Reuters footage from the church after the attack showed blood smeared on the floor near its entrance, where security forces were deployed.
Such attacks are extremely rare in Jordan, which is relatively stable, though Jordanian authorities say they have repeatedly foiled attempted attacks by terrorists in recent years.
Christians make up a minority of Jordan's population. The country is home to several biblical sites that attract Christian pilgrims from around the world.
Jordan's Minister of Endowments and Islamic Affairs Mohammad Khalayleh and several members of Jordan's parliament condemned the attack in comments to Al-Mamlaka.
In a post on X, United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the violence and said attacks against civilians and places of worship are unacceptable.
People who gathered at a Karak government hospital to support the wounded expressed shock.
"What happened today has left people unable to speak or raise our voices. But our only reproach to the state is that it must investigate these dark ideas - where they come from and how they enter the minds of our children," said one of them, Hani Al-Mbaydeen.
Christians make up a minority of Jordan's population. The country is home to several biblical sites that attract Christian pilgrims from around the world.
The U.S. ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz described it on X as a "depraved and brutal attack on a house of worship."
Jordan was among the U.S. allies in the region to be hit by Iranian attacks this year after the U.S. and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February.
Jordan has been increasingly targeted by Iranian attacks this year since the U.S. and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February.

Europe faces threat of organised sabotage, terrorist attacks: Estonian FM Tsahkna
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:55:15 UTC
23:55:15 KST

Europe faces threat of organised sabotage, terrorist attacks: Estonian FM Tsahkna
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
Estonia's counterintelligence service has recently warned that sabotage operations orchestrated by Russian special services have reached a new and dangerous phase in Europe, with targets no longer being purely symbolic. Talking Europe sits down with the country's foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, to discuss the security situation in Estonia and the European Union in general.
Speaking of undercover operations against Estonia attributed to Russian special services, Tsahkna says: "We have witnessed terrorist attacks, sabotage attacks, against the defence industry companies. We just attributed, three weeks ago, one serious attack against our defence industry company organised by the Russian secret services. We caught these three guys. They are in prison now. We see an increase in the number of these attacks. But we also see that they are not against the Baltic States as much as against Europe as a whole. We (in the Baltics) are not at the top of this list. Russia is increasing the pressure on Europe. This is about terror attacks, sabotage attacks, cyberattacks, and any kind of disinformation to divide our unity and to divide our societies as well."
Tsahkna distinguishes between this hybrid war and Russia’s actual military capabilities, which he implies have been degraded by its involvement in Ukraine.
"When I served as a defence minister in 2016-2017, we had permanently 120,000 Russian troops on the other side of our borders, very close, ready to go within 48 hours. These troops were literally sent to Ukraine; they are not existing anymore. They are dead," he says.
Tsahkna goes on: "We know exactly what to do on the military level. We have NATO troops. Actually, French troops are located in Estonia. They are 100 percent integrated with our troops. We have very solid NATO regional defence plans. So this is not the main concern. The main concern now is to keep all of us in Europe united. And we need to understand that [Russian President Vladimir] Putin is testing all of us. He's very carefully watching how we are acting, how united we are, how we are responding."
On diplomatic moves to try to reach a ceasefire in Ukraine, Tsahkna warns that Europe cannot, and should not, become a kind of neutral arbiter.
"Europe is taking part in initiatives, and we just had a meeting in Oslo, together with the US representative and President Zelensky and also the Nordic presidents, prime ministers and the Norwegian prime minister, " Tsahkna says. "So it's not about whether Europe is connected. Of course, we must be there. But we must also understand the position. We cannot let ourselves be dragged into the mediating position that Putin really wants: appointing a special envoy and then trying to mediate between Ukraine and Russia. So we are part of the process, of course, but we are not in the mediating position, a so-called neutral position, in which we would somehow stop our sanctions or give the frozen assets back to Russia. So this is important to understand. "
Tsahkna also has a few observations about the recent protests, violence and unrest in France.
"Elections are coming next year in France that are so important for Europe," he notes. "Of course, using violence is not a solution. And in Estonia we have been paying a lot of attention to keeping our society united, not divided. How to not go to the way of radicalisation. Because divisions in society are making you weaker as a country and as a nation. But of course, it's a matter for France and for the French how to have this dialogue about the future. You know, I'm coming from [the] north. We are very calm people!"

Jordan: Karak church shooting leaves 7 dead, dozens injured

Jordan: Karak church shooting leaves 7 dead, dozens injured
October 23, 2026
A shooting at a church in the southern Jordanian governorate of Karak left seven people dead and another 34 wounded on Friday, Jordan's public security director Obaidallah Maaytah said.
Twenty-seven of the injured are receiving hospital treatment.
What do we know so far?
The shooting occurred at the Hammoud Church and reportedly took place during a funeral.
The attackers' identities and motives remain unclear. Two men opened fire on the funeral procession.
A witness told Jordanian state media there were 150 to 200 people present at the church at the time of the shooting. Videos circulating online showed wounded people on the floor of the church covered in blood, but this footage cannot be verified by DW.
Jordan's Interior Minister Mazen Al-Faraya said a group of "extremists" carried out the massacre. According to Jordanian outlet Roya News, Al-Faraya said authorities already possess the names of suspects behind the attacks but would not publicly disclose their identities as of now.
Jordanian government spokesperson Mohammad al-Momani said security forces have launched a probe into the attack.
Jordan King Abdullah II: 'We will strike with an iron fist'
Jordan King Abdullah II said "the terrorist attack against Karak will be met with the harshest retaliation."
"Those who delude themselves into thinking that they can divide Jordanians with their bullets have no chance in the face of our unity," Abdullah II said, adding, "We will strike with an iron fist against those who dare to threaten our nation."
Jordan's Royal Court later posted footage and photos of the king visiting the hospital where the wounded are being treated.
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun, a Christian, condemned the "heinous terrorist attack" in Jordan and expressed condolences to the victims.
US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz said the news regarding the attack is "devastating."
"Praying for the victims, their families and all those affected by this depraved and brutal attack on a house of worship," Waltz said. "Attacks on Christians continue to escalate worldwide and must be stopped."
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres' spokesperson said the attack at a place of worship during a funeral procession is "especially heinous."
Gun attacks like the one on the church in Karak are rare in Jordan.
Although Jordan is largely a Muslim-majority country of around 11.5 million people, there is a small Christian minority of a couple hundred thousand. The Karak region, about 180 kilometers (110 miles) south of Amman, has a significant Christian population.

Afghan women could lose one of their last paths to a higher education
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:54:00 UTC
23:54:00 KST

Afghan women could lose one of their last paths to a higher education
October 23, 2026
"Laila" awoke in the middle of the night for a glass of water, checked her phone almost by accident, and saw an email that made her stomach drop. The US would stop funding the American University of Afghanistan (AUAF), one of the last places women can still study in the country.
Laila said she sat on her bed, staring, her thoughts racing through the past five years and everything she had endured just to get an education.
It had not been easy to find a way to study in Afghanistan after the Taliban outlawed women's education.
The American University campus was already taken over by the Taliban, but she could study secretly through the university's online program. But now that the university is losing its financing, she told DW she and her classmates fear it will shut down entirely. Her name has been changed for safety reasons.
A hidden education for women in Afghanistan
Laila is in her mid-twenties. She studies political science and international studies and is one of around 1,000 enrolled students at the university, three-quarters of them women.
When the Taliban returned to power in August 2021, Laila was studying at another university in Kabul, with just two final exams remaining to finish her semester. Then, in December 2022, the Taliban announced the ban. Laila's degree was left unfinished.
Laila secured a scholarship to AUAF and started over. "Not every girl got that opportunity," she said.
Laila has told few people outside of her family about her online studies. On most days, she stays home for remote lectures, alongside classmates who use aliases and keep their cameras off for security. "I just know their voices," she said.
Laila speaks English with an American accent. She learned it as a child, watching cartoons. In her early twenties, she was learning even more about the world outside Afghanistan and studying foreign governments.
Then on August 14, 2021, Laila's life changed. She and a friend sat in a restaurant in Kabul. They had just finished an exam and wanted to celebrate passing the test by ordering coffee and cake. Suddenly, a man came in, stopped at the entrance, and shouted "Allahu Akbar." He yelled that the mujahideen would always be victorious.
That was the day the Taliban retook power in Afghanistan, they soon forced women out of public life, banning them from many jobs and from attending school and university.
Laila said she recalls losing feeling in her hands or feet. She pulled money from her purse and slammed it on the table without checking the amount. "We all thought maybe this would be the last day that we are alive," she said.
Since then, some of Laila's peers have received threatening calls and messages. Now, whenever she leaves home, she worries that Taliban authorities might search her phone.
"What if they see my emails from my work, from my university?" she said. "It's always in the back of my head that maybe tomorrow it's my turn. Maybe they will detain me."
Even her home isn't safe. Laila said Taliban authorities have entered on several occasions to search their belongings.
Yet, she has continued studying. For all its limitations and risks, the online program offered a chance to graduate.
A place for Afghanistan's 'future leaders'
With the US pulling out as the university's primary funder, Laila said she doubts whether she has the strength to start over.
The American University of Afghanistan was always intended, largely, for women. Before the campus opened in 2006, former US first lady Laura Bush announced that the US had committed millions to support it.
Appearing in Kabul, Bush said the new university would teach "future leaders," particularly women. Women like Laila, who was four years old at the time.
"These are more than just development projects," Bush said at the time. "They also signify the bond between the American and Afghan people. They are symbols of our shared hopes and dreams."
Patrick Fine was Afghanistan mission director at USAID, the now-defunct American development agency. Fine told DW that many at USAID considered the university idea risky. Critics thought training elites was a waste of money.
But the Bush administration saw an opportunity to stabilize a budding democracy, Fine said.
By 2003, the Taliban had been driven from power. US President George W. Bush wanted to foster goodwill for the US-backed interim government that had replaced the Taliban. The university served that goal, and also offered other "facets of advantage" in educating women, training future politicians, and supporting the Afghan economy.
"It really impacted the lives of thousands of Afghan youth," Fine said, referencing alumni. "The organization has managed to achieve that against incredible odds."
Washington pulls the plug
The university continued with US support. But in Washington, that support started to come under question.
The US government suspected the university of mishandling money. In 2016, US inspectors opened an investigation into its finances. By 2018, investigators said they could not tell exactly how it was spending US aid money, because its accounting was so poor.
John Sopko, a former US federal inspector, oversaw that investigation. When DW contacted him for this story, he replied, "I was surprised they were still funding AUAF."
This year, after the funding was pulled, the US State Department Press Office told DW in an email that the move was made given the university's "history of repeated lack of accountability for millions of American taxpayer dollars."
Fine, the former USAID director, rejected the State Department's fraud explanation.
"Those are just smear tactics," he said. He conceded that past audits found the university struggling to keep up with USAID's extensive rules, "but they didn't find major fraud," he said.
"It is still a useful investment, a worthy investment," Fine said, "and the reason for that is that it's one of the few organizations left that is reaching Afghan women."
The US isn't the university's only funder, but it has long covered most of its costs: nearly 90% as of 2018, according to a US report.
The US State Department told DW that the university is "free to identify other funders and partners, so the end of their receipt of American taxpayer money does not necessarily equate to an end to their operations."
But without the $25 million grant the State Department recently refused, the university's future is in doubt.
What is next for women students in Afghanistan?
"I have lost all my motivation and hope," Laila said, adding that each time she prepares for a lecture, she wonders whether there will be another.
Since she learned about the funding cut, she said she's barely left her room. Her curtains are usually closed, and she's lost her appetite. "Maybe I'm so disappointed that I can't even cry about it," she said.
She said she was supposed to have graduated years ago. She was supposed to be making the world a better place. She was supposed to be studying for a master's degree abroad. Now, she's thinking, maybe she'll find a way in five or ten years.
Edited by: Wesley Rahn

Microsoft says AI system outperforms doctors in simulated disease diagnosis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:53:15 UTC
23:53:15 KST

Halis Sunnetci
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
Microsoft said Thursday that its artificial intelligence system diagnosed complex medical conditions more than twice as accurately as physicians in simulated tests, citing research published in the journal Science.
The company’s AI Diagnostic Orchestrator (MAI-DxO) achieved 83% diagnostic accuracy on complex medical cases, compared with 36% for physicians using textbooks and online resources, according to a Microsoft statement.
Physicians working without external reference materials achieved 22% accuracy.
Researchers evaluated 304 complex cases drawn from The New England Journal of Medicine, using a system in which multiple AI agents work together to assess symptoms, select diagnostic tests and reach conclusions.
The system also achieved 80% accuracy on more typical emergency department cases, compared with 47% for physicians, Microsoft said.
The company said MAI-DxO could also reduce diagnostic testing costs by selecting fewer or less expensive procedures while maintaining high accuracy.
In one cost-optimized configuration, the system achieved 81% accuracy on complex cases at less than half the estimated cost of comparative systems.
Microsoft described the findings as progress toward “medical superintelligence,” its vision of AI systems capable of surpassing leading clinical teams in medical reasoning and care coordination.
However, the results were based on simulated cases rather than real-world clinical practice, and the physician comparison did not include specialist teams.
The company said further evaluation in clinical environments is necessary to establish how the technology performs in actual patient care.
Microsoft plans to evaluate the system through a prospective study with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, comparing its diagnostic assessments with those of physicians in hospital settings.

Drone strike on market town exposes reach of trade fuelling Sudan war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:51:41 UTC
23:51:41 KST

Drone strike on market town exposes reach of trade fuelling Sudan war
NAIROBI, Oct 23 - For Awad Usham Al-Amin and thousands of others, Abyei provides shelter and an opportunity to eke out a living as war rages back home. This week, Sudan's conflict caught up with them there too.
A drone strike believed to be targeting a fuel depot used by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) hit the Amiet market, killing over 150 people in the town, which sits in a territory contested by Sudan and South Sudan.
"I came as a refugee, running from Sudan … but still faced with another conflict here," Al-Amin told Reuters, nursing shrapnel injuries on his right hand and left leg.
The attack flattened shops and stalls in the market where Al-Amin offloads fuel and pushes wheelbarrows to earn a living.
It highlighted how far the tentacles of supply lines linked to the war between the RSF and the Sudanese Armed Forces stretch across the region, sucking neighbours into a conflict involving proxy powers from across the Horn of Africa and broader region.
Five diplomats and analysts following the conflict said the market was an established part of a fuel network serving the RSF fighting across Sudan.
A large volume of the fuel imported into South Sudan is transported through Abyei, where it is collected by RSF networks then transported through Sudan in smaller shipments, the sources said.
"It's clear that the attack in Amiet market targeted fuel storage facilities as well as a truck suspected of carrying fuel," a diplomat said. "The RSF is still present in Abyei... it's difficult to identify them because they are embedded in the community here."
Officials in South Sudan have facilitated the import and transit of fuel to RSF networks, the diplomats and experts said. A spokesperson for the foreign ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment on that.
ABYEI MUST NOT BECOME A THEATRE FOR CONFLICT IN SUDAN
In its first official comments on the incident, Sudan's government said late on Thursday it had "no connection whatsoever to this tragic incident". The RSF-led parallel government has called for a UN investigation without commenting on its presence in Abyei.
Earlier in the week, Yohana Akol Ngor, the caretaker minister of information in Abyei, said Sudan's army was responsible for the attack and Juba summoned Sudan’s ambassador.
On Friday, Apuk Ayuel Mayen, spokesperson for South Sudan's foreign ministry, said the circumstances of the attack, including any connection to the reported presence of the RSF in Abyei, had not yet been established.
"Abyei must not become a theatre for conflict in Sudan," South Sudanese President Salva Kiir said in a statement.
UN aid workers estimate some 25,000 people have fled to Abyei since Sudan's war began in 2023.
UN PEACEKEEPERS HAVE WARNED OF RSF CHECKPOINTS
Al-Amin said no RSF fighters were present when the air strike took place but that they did come from time to time.
The United Nations Interim Security Force for Abyei (UNISFA) has warned in the past that the RSF have mounted checkpoints in Abyei and their presence there had increased insecurity.
Chol Deng Chol, chairperson of the chamber of commerce in Abyei, said the RSF does use the market as a place to stock up on fuel for operations in Sudan’s Kordofan and Darfur regions but none were there on Monday and Khartoum had no right to carry out a strike there.
“If they want to stop this, they must do it in their territory,” he said, adding that 10 tankers were destroyed in the attack. REUTERS

Kneecap, Hozier urge Ireland to act over Gaza student visas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:51:15 UTC
23:51:15 KST

Breadcrumb
Kneecap, Hozier urge Ireland to act over Gaza student visa refusals
A number of prominent Irish figures from film, television and music, including Kneecap, Hozier, Aisling Bea, Siobhán McSweeney and Christy Moore, have urged Taoiseach Micheal Martin to intervene on behalf of 55 Gazan students who have been refused study visas.
The appeal comes amid ongoing legal challenges to the visa refusals, with a High Court hearing examining the government's handling of applications from Palestinian students who secured fully funded scholarships at Irish universities.
In an open letter published by the Irish Examiner on Friday, the artists joined other signatories in urging Martin to “do the decent thing” by the students.
The letter cited Martin’s remarks to the United Nations last month, when he said the international community had failed Palestine, and called on him to intervene on the students’ behalf.
“You have the power to act, to stay true to our principles and promises, and grant these young Palestinians the opportunity of an education far from the rubble of Gaza,” the signatories said.
They added that the students were not taking places away from anyone else and had undergone rigorous vetting.
“They provided every document available to them in a warzone, and yet the minister for justice is refusing to grant them study visas. They are caught in a breakdown of co-ordination between Government departments that they did nothing to cause.”
The open letter follows similar appeals earlier this month from academics and the Ireland-Palestine Alliance Sadaka, who urged Martin, also Ireland’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, to intervene to resolve what they described as an “appalling injustice”.
They called for the applications of all affected students to be reconsidered properly and in time for the students to be evacuated from Gaza.
High Court challenges visa refusals
The continuing appeals come as legal proceedings challenge the Irish government's refusal of study visas to Palestinian students from Gaza.
During a High Court hearing on Tuesday, lawyers representing the students argued that the decisions were unlawful and irrational, highlighting the difficulties applicants faced in obtaining documentation amid the destruction caused by Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
The government argued that the refusals were based on applicants’ inability to provide documentary evidence required for the visas.
The case centred on Shaymaa Abudalu, a survivor of the Gaza genocide who reportedly lost several family members, including her mother and siblings.
She had secured a fully funded place on a four-year engineering degree programme at University College Cork (UCC), but was refused a visa.
During the hearing, the court heard that documents confirming Abudalu’s English-language proficiency had been received by the Department of Justice but had not been considered by the official who rejected her application.
Judge Anthony Barr described this as a “substantial hole” in the government’s case.
However, the proceedings were ongoing, and the court had not yet issued a final ruling that the visa refusal was unlawful or ordered it to be set aside.
Following the hearing, Abudalu’s lawyer, Sarah Jane Hillery, said she hoped the case would clarify the issues affecting all the students.
The Irish Examiner reported that the Irish embassy in Tel Aviv processed Palestinian study visa applications last year, rejecting 13 per cent of them.
This year, the Department of Justice has reportedly refused 114 of 138 applications- a rejection rate of 83 per cent- including 55 applications from students in the Gaza Strip.

racist online chatroom calling for attacks on foreigners and
often second-generation North African heritage Italian street
youth gang members known as maranzas.
                                    
The chat group discovered by the police—uncovered during
investigations following the demonstrations and shocking youth
riots in Milan and other Italian cities on October 17 and 18—was
created for the purpose of gathering in the centre of Crema near
Cremona to conduct "patrols" aimed at "identifying and attacking
foreigners and maranzas."
The group's profile picture featured Benito Mussolini.
                                    
It was managed by a 20-year-old Italian man with a prior record
for theft and making threats.
                                    
The chat contained numerous messages inciting violence,
including racist and xenophobic content such as "let's start
with the n**gers," "let's reopen the ovens," and "long live the
Duce, forever."
The chat was discovered during the analysis of a mobile phone
belonging to the twenty-year-old man.
                                    
He was stopped on October 19th by officers from the Cremona
Police Headquarters—led by Police Commissioner Carlo Ambra—along
with a group of about thirty other young people, most of whom
were dressed in dark clothing and walking in a tight formation
through the streets of Crema's city centre.
                                    
During the encounter, a white balaclava and a hammer were also
seized from a car.

response to threats of violence that had been circulated in
another chat group, titled "Let's Occupy Schools in Cremona
19/10/2026."
Messages found in the chat included: "Let's walk around Crema
all together," "Arm yourselves quickly," "Get your batons out
and come along," and "Put 10 euros' worth of gas in, and you've
got yourselves 10 Molotov cocktails."

Russian losses in the war with Ukraine.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:50:05 UTC
23:50:05 KST

This publication is divided into two parts:
Bi-weekly Summary. A text summary, updated every two weeks, in which we report on what we have learned about recent losses and the frontline events that led to the deaths of Russian soldiers.
Interactive Infographics. The second part provides visualisations of the losses since the start of the war, showing, for example, where the dead served or which regions they came from. We update the data for these graphics, while the accompanying text is refreshed but remains largely the same.
A detailed description of our method for estimating total deaths using Probate Registry data can be found at this link.
Last update to the named list: October 23, 2026.
Last update to the Probate Registry estimate: May 9, 2026; estimate as of late December 2025
Full named list and a map of verified losses is available here: 200.zona.media.
This week, we are only releasing updated numbers for Russian losses in the war against Ukraine.
The map below shows the distribution of casualties across Russia’s regions. These are absolute figures and have not been adjusted for population or number of military units.
You can filter the map to show total losses, losses by branch of service, or the home regions of mobilised soldiers who were killed.
In most cases, official reports or visual cues like uniforms and insignia allow us to determine a soldier’s branch of service, or how he came to be in the army (mobilised, volunteer, prisoner, etc.).
The chart below compares these different groups of servicemen.
From early summer and into the mid-fall season of 2022, volunteers bore the brunt of the losses, which is strikingly different from the situation in the initial stage of the war: in winter and early spring, the Airborne Forces suffered the greatest damage, followed by the Motorised Rifle troops.
By the end of 2022 and the beginning of the next year, losses among prisoners recruited into the Wagner PMC increased markedly. They were formed into “assault groups” to overwhelm Ukrainian positions near Bakhmut.
By March 2023, prisoners became the largest category of war losses. After the capture of Bakhmut, there have been no cases of mass use of prisoners so far.
By September 2024, volunteers once again emerged as the largest category among the KIA. This shift reflects a cumulative effect: prison recruitment had significantly waned, no new mobilisation had been announced, yet the stream of volunteers continued unabated.
By October 23, 2026, the death of 7,920 officers of the Russian army and other security agencies had been confirmed.
The proportion of officer deaths among overall casualties has steadily declined since the conflict began. In the early stages, when professional contract soldiers formed the main invasion force, officers accounted for up to 10% of fatalities. By November 2024, this figure had dropped to between 2–3%—a shift that reflects both evolving combat tactics and the intensive recruitment of volunteer infantry, who suffer casualty rates many times higher than their commanding officers.
Officers killed in Ukraine
To date, the deaths of 15 Russian generals have been officially confirmed: five Lieutenant Generals, seven Major Generals, two who had retired from active service, and one Ukrainian SBU general who had fled to Russia.
Lieutenant General Oleg Tsokov, deputy commander of the Southern Military District, was killed in July 2023—the first officer of that rank to die in the war. In December 2024, Lieutenant General Igor Kirillov, head of the Nuclear, Biological, and Chemical (NBC) Protection Troops, was killed by a bomb in Moscow. Lieutenant General Yaroslav Moskalik, a senior officer in the General Staff’s Main Operational Directorate, was killed by a car bomb in a Moscow suburb in April 2025. In December 2025, Lieutenant General Fanil Sarvarov, head of the Operational Training Directorate of the Russian General Staff, was killed in Moscow by a car bomb. On March 31, 2026, Lieutenant General Alexander Otroschenko, commander of the mixed aviation corps of the Northern Fleet, was killed in the crash of an An-26 transport aircraft in Crimea.
Two deputy army commanders, Major General Andrei Sukhovetsky (41st Army) and Major General Vladimir Frolov (8th Army), were killed in the first weeks of the war. In June 2022, Major General Roman Kutuzov was killed in an attack on a troop formation.
Major General Sergei Goryachev, chief of staff of the 35th Combined Arms Army, was killed in June 2023 while commanding forces against the Ukrainian counter-offensive in the Zaporizhzhia region. In November 2023, Major General Vladimir Zavadsky, deputy commander of the 14th Army Corps, was killed near the village of Krynky.
In November 2024, Major General Pavel Klimenko, commander of the 5th Separate Motorised Rifle Brigade (formerly the “Oplot” Brigade of the so-called Donetsk People’s Republic), was fatally wounded by an FPV drone.
In July 2025, a strike on the headquarters of the 155th Naval Infantry Brigade killed at least six officers, including the Deputy Commander-in-Chief of the Russian Navy, Mikhail Gudkov.
The two retired generals on the list are Kanamat Botashev, a pilot who had been dismissed for crashing a fighter jet and was fighting for Wagner PMC when his Su-25 was shot down in May 2022, and Andrei Golovatsky, a former Interior Ministry general serving an 8.5-year prison sentence (but maintained his rank) who was killed in June 2024.
On March 17, 2026, SBU Major General Volodymyr Lyapkin was killed in the Kherson region. Until February 2014, Lyapkin headed a department in the Ukrainian special services, but after the victory of the Maidan revolution, he fled to Russia. After the war began, he served in the occupation administration of Kherson and then transferred to the “Bars-33” unit.
The date of death is known in 266,700 cases. While this data does not capture the full daily reality of the war, it does suggest which periods saw the most intense fighting.
Please note that data for the most recent months is most incomplete and will change significantly in the future.
The age of the deceased is mentioned in 268,100 reports. For the first six months of the war, when the fighting was done by the regular army, the 21-23 age group accounted for the most deaths.
Volunteers and mobilised men are significantly older: people voluntarily go to war over 30, and the mobilised are generally over 25.

With Strict Agendas and Silent Corridors Kazakhstan’s Kurultai Is Muzzling the Press
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:50:00 UTC
23:50:00 KST

When Kazakhstan’s Kurultai convened in late August for the first time, there were new rules for the media. Journalists in the Kazakh capital’s parliament building were no longer able to question deputies in the corridors. The new rules set firm boundaries not only on where, but what, they could ask members of the country’s new unicameral parliament.
At the opening of the Kurultai’s first session on August 28, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev proclaimed the body would “radically modernize the system of government and provide a powerful impetus to the work of the entire state apparatus.” Later in his speech he urged the Kutultai to become “a platform for national dialogue to develop solutions to key issues in society.”
The boundaries of that dialogue, however, are to be set by the Kurultai itself.
As explained by the Kurultai’s Deputy Chief of Staff Bolat Kalyanbekov in a September 2 Facebook post, “All interactions between journalists and deputies – as well as invited members of the Government – will now take place exclusively within the press center and strictly in relation to the Kurultai’s agenda.”
Kalyanbekov stated that briefings would be held on a regular basis and laid out the rationale behind the decision to bar off-topic questions.
“Our goal is to communicate the substance of the draft laws under consideration by the Kurultai to the public as clearly and comprehensively as possible – explaining the significance of each new legal provision and how the decisions being made may impact the lives of citizens,” he wrote.
Kalyanbekov also argued that the new rules were consistent both with Kazakh law and “established global practices.”
That’s not quite how Fiona O’Brien, the Europe and Central Asia regional director for the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), sees it. “Allowing journalists to informally approach and question deputies in the halls of parliament, and to ask questions not strictly related to the agenda of press conferences, are standard practices of established democracies,” O’Brien told The Diplomat.
Although Kazakhstan deems itself a democratic state, human rights organizations such as Freedom House, classify the country as “Not Free.”
“The kinds of restrictions on movement and questions implemented in Kazakhstan are more common in authoritarian or hybrid environments, where the authorities try to maintain an appearance of democracy while retaining strict control of the information sphere,” O’Brien explained.
***
On October 20, Otkir Kurek – an independent media outlet headed by Nazymgul Kumyspayeva, who also runs a YouTube channel – reported that a group of around 40 journalists accredited to the Kurultai had sent an appeal to Aibek Dadebay, chair of the body, demanding revision of the new media rules.
Otkir Kurek means “sharp shovel” in Kazakh.
Dadebay is also leader of the Adilet party, into which the former ruling party Amanat (née Nur-Otan) merged earlier this year in the runup to the Kurultai elections on August 23. Until May 5, Dadebay headed Tokayev’s presidential administration.
In the recent appeal, as reported by KazTAG, the Kazakh journalists took particular issue with the restriction of questions to agenda-items only.
Under the present rules, “For a question that the moderator deems off-topic, the journalist receives a warning. Two violations mean the loss of accreditation for six months… For a journalist who covers parliament, this is effectively a six-month ban from the profession.”
The appeal noted that the purpose of accreditation is to enable journalists “to inform the public broadly and promptly.”
“Kazakhstan’s parliament and other state organs have long tried to stop journalists asking ‘off-topic’ questions during press conferences,” CPJ’s O’Brien explained. “Introducing sanctions for doing so and preventing journalists from mixing freely with deputies in the halls of parliament essentially closes down the last avenues for journalists to freely question parliamentarians on issues not decided in advance by the authorities themselves.”
“A briefing that repeats what has already been said at the meeting provides no new information,” the journalists argued in their appeal, seeking a revision to the existing regulations to allow journalists to ask questions outside the strict agenda but within the purview of the featured speakers.
“A minister or deputy can always refuse to answer a question, respond later, or respond in writing,” the appeal noted. The journalists characterized the existing policy as unjustified. Journalists, they argued, need to be free to question ministers, deputies, and other officials – who, the appeal pointed out, “rarely appear in public and for whom the public has many questions.”
Kazakh journalists have already run afoul of these rules.
In early October, in the wake of a tragic accident on the Caspian Sea in which 14 servicemembers drowned during a military drill, journalist Asem Gumarova of Ulysmedia.kz asked questions related to the incident during a briefing with a member of parliament, Unzila Shapak, and Deputy Minister of Internal Affairs Sanjar Adilov. The brief was to cover a draft cybercrime law.
Gumarova asked Shapak when the 146 million tenge that had been reportedly collected by Kurultai members would be transferred to the families of the fallen servicemen. She also asked Adilov about reports of pressure being exerted by mysterious callers masquerading as police demanding that the authors of critical posts related to the Caspian accident take their posts down.
Ulysmedia said it received a warning letter threatening to strip Gumarova of her accreditation. The publication cited the “extraordinary nature of the incident and public demand” as justifying Gumarova’s questions.
The recent appeal to Dadebay cited the incident directly, noting that “[t]he question concerned police work online or crimes carried out under the guise of police – that is, the very topic of the briefing.”
***
Accreditation procedures vary country to country. But broadly speaking accreditation confers a degree of legitimacy on a journalist and their outlet and, importantly, provides access to official spaces and proceedings. In Kazakhstan, the Foreign Ministry handles foreign media and individual state bodies, like the Kurultai, as well as the Ministry of Culture and Information, deal with the domestic media.
Kumyspayeva, the editor-in-chief and founder of Otkir Kurek, was earlier this month denied accreditation by the Kurultai. Kalyanbekov provided an official response, which The Diplomat has reviewed, stating that the reason was a mismatch in email addresses on her application materials.
“The official reason given for the denial was that I had provided my professional email address in the accreditation application rather than the email address listed on our media outlet’s website,” Kumyspaeva told The Diplomat. “In my view, this was merely a technicality used as a pretext to deny me accreditation. I suspect the real reason lies in my independent journalism.”
Kumyspayeva takes no government funding, and told The Diplomat that the outlet does not participate in government-funded media contracts.
“As a result, government institutions have no leverage to dictate our editorial policy, determine what subjects we cover, or tell us which questions we are allowed to ask,” she said.
Kumyspayeva has lodged a formal complaint with the Kurultai’s leadership and she intends to pursue the matter in court, if needed. “I believe my professional rights as a journalist have been violated,” she said.
Kumyspayeva also signed the appeal sent to Dadebay regarding the media rules. She told The Diplomat her concerns stretch far beyond her own case.
“In my opinion, these restrictions constitute a form of censorship and contradict Kazakhstan’s constitutional guarantees of freedom of expression and the prohibition of censorship,” she said. “For me, this is not simply a dispute over accreditation for my media outlet. It is about something much more fundamental: the public’s right to information, the freedom of independent journalism, and the accountability of those in power.”
***
The tension here – between the Kutultai leadership and the journalists who cover the Kazakhstan’s legislature – is rooted in diametrically opposed perspectives on the purpose and role of the media.
In the Kazakh government’s view, as implied by Kalyanbekov and the new rules, the media’s role is to disseminate information provided by the government. Based on that, anything not on the agenda just shouldn’t be on the agenda. The government believes that it has the authority to decide what is newsworthy, and pestering officials with questions they’d rather not answer is rank insubordination.
“What concerns me most is that the leadership of the legislative body is effectively assuming the power to decide which journalists and media outlets are allowed to cover its activities and which are not,” Kumyspayeva explained. “In practice, this means access to elected representatives may depend not on a journalist’s professional status, but on how acceptable their reporting and questions are to the authorities.”
The Kutultai’s media rules merely add to a host of challenges faced by independent journalists in Kazakhstan.
“These restrictions are part of a severe constriction of the media sphere in Kazakhstan since the start of this year,” O’Brien argued, noting the cases of Gulnara Bazhkenova and the heads of KazTAG Aset Matayev and Amir Kasenov. Bazhkenova, former editor-in-chief of Orda, was sentenced to eight years in prison in August. Matayev and Kasenov were each given 15-months of “restricted freedom” and banned from journalistic activity for five years in July. The CPJ and other media watchdogs have characterized these cases as politically motivated.
Kazakh courts have increasingly banned convicted journalists from engaging in journalism or engaging in other forms of public activity. The real goal, O’Brien told The Diplomat, “is to ensure that prominent journalists are silenced for years ahead.”
The larger political context is unmistakable.
“This repression appears designed to instill a chilling effect and strengthen control over the press as President Tokayev navigates the final years of his constitutionally mandated single term,” O’Brien told The Diplomat.
Tokayev was first elected in a snap presidential poll in the summer of 2019, following Nursultan Nazarbayev’s surprise resignation that spring. At the time, Kazakhstan’s presidency was limited to two five-year terms. Not even three years into his first term, however, in the wake of Qandy Qantar – Bloody January – Tokayev saw through a wide-ranging constitutional referendum. Later that year, and 18 months early, Tokayev announced another snap presidential election. He paired that announcement with a proposal to limit the presidency to a single seven-year term. In November 2022, Tokayev was elected to his second term, confirming his grip on power until 2029.
The tinkering did not end there. Six months after commenting that haste in changing the constitution again was “completely inappropriate,” Tokayev saw through another constitutional referendum that touched almost every aspect of the document.
As the new constitution went into effect on July 1, Tokayev asked the Constitutional Court to clarify what it meant for re-election, or re-appointment, of term-limited officials, as well as the implications for the timeline on elections. The court replied that the president is eligible to run for another single seven-year term – which would technically be his third. But who’s counting?
Tokayev “is widely thought to be either preparing to run again or attempting to maintain strict control of the succession process,” O’Brien told The Diplomat. “The passing of a new constitution earlier this year and Kurultai elections, which coincided with major waves of pressure on the press, appear to be part of this process. With key journalists in jail or banned from working, the people of Kazakhstan will be less informed as this political process plays out.”
Dadebay has not yet responded officially to the Kazakh Kurultai press corps’ appeal.
“Freedom of the press is not a privilege granted by the authorities,” Kumyspayeva stressed to The Diplomat. “It is a fundamental right, and it is the public – not the government – that ultimately pays the price when that right is restricted.”

Swiss mountain passes close early after first snowfall
Winter is making itself felt in the Alps, forcing the early closure of major mountain roads.
The Swiss Touring Club (TCS) reports on its traffic information portal that the Gotthard and San Bernardino passes are already closed to traffic.
Rainfall and wintry weather conditions have brought forward the closure of several roads which, in a typical year, are closed between late October and early November. No reopening date has been given for some mountain passes. This is the case for the Gotthard, San Bernardino, Nufenen (Novena), Grimsel and Susten passes, which are closed for safety reasons, according to information from the TCS. For other Alpine roads, however, the closures are temporary: the Furka, for example, is impassable only until Monday, unless the relevant authorities issue further updates.
More
Climate change in the Alps: five ways Swiss ski resorts are fighting for survival
Despite the initial closures, a significant part of the Alpine road network remains open to traffic. Among the routes that remain open are the Albula and the Flüela, important links to the Engadine, as well as the Forcola di Livigno, the Bernina, the Julier (Giulia) and the Forno. For some of these routes, the seasonal closure is normally scheduled for later in the year, whilst others remain open all year round, weather permitting.
The situation can change rapidly as the weather evolves. The TCS therefore advises motorists travelling through the Alpine regions to check for the latest traffic updates before setting off.

Many in Serbia’s Youth Movement Fear a Rigged Election on Sunday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:48:00 UTC
23:48:00 KST

Riding an extraordinary wave of public mobilization, Serbia’s student-led opposition heads into Sunday’s snap parliamentary election genuinely believing it can break President Aleksandar Vučić’s 14-year grip on power.
Yet beneath the euphoria of this week’s mass rallies lies a pervasive conviction among its supporters that the contest will be anything but fair—and that the ruling party will resort to outright ballot theft rather than concede defeat.
On Thursday night, that tension was on full display as hundreds of thousands of people flooded into Belgrade’s central Slavija Square, filling the surrounding boulevards in a buoyant, flag-waving display of collective defiance. The assembly marked the movement's final campaign rally ahead of an early vote that serves as the culmination of nearly two years of youth-led unrest against Vučić’s rule.
What began in November 2024 as grief and outrage following the collapse of a newly renovated railway station canopy in the northern city of Novi Sad—a disaster that killed 16 people and was turned by the protesting youth into a lethal symbol of state corruption and crony contracting—has since metastasized into a nationwide rebellion.
Now polling in a dead heat with the governing Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), the youth movement’s “Students’ List” has mounted the most formidable electoral challenge Vučić has faced in over a decade. But across the sea of demonstrators in the capital, few harbored illusions about how the ruling machine will be handling the vote.
“I believe he will do anything he can to steal the votes and remain in power,” said Katarina Zajić, 45, a food technologist who works as an administrative clerk in the Belgrade municipality of Zemun.
That skepticism is informed by years of documented electoral abuse. International election observers, led by the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) and backed by European Union institutions, have consistently found that while Serbian elections offer voters a nominal choice of candidates, the playing field is fundamentally compromised. In report after report, monitors have cited pervasive state capture of broadcast media, intense pressure on public-sector workers to mobilize for the ruling coalition, the routine abuse of public resources for partisan gain, and deep-seated anomalies in the voter register.
Domestic watchdogs have leveled even harsher verdicts. The Center for Research, Transparency and Accountability (CRTA), Serbia’s prominent independent election observation group, concluded that recent election cycles—including the disputed parliamentary and municipal votes in 2023 and 2024—were “not free and fair.” The watchdog documented organized voter migration schemes, the mass registration of “phantom voters,” and the wholesale erasure of the boundary between state institutions and the ruling party.
Vučić and his party have vehemently denied any wrongdoing, routinely dismissing allegations of electoral manipulation as the reflexive excuses of “sore losers” fabricating an alibi for their own political weakness.
“These were by far the cleanest and fairest elections to date, and everyone knows it,” Vučić declared following the 2023 ballot, even as opposition leaders launched hunger strikes and thousands took to the streets to protest organized cross-border voter bussing.
For many of those who massed in Belgrade on Thursday, however, the gap between the government’s assurances and the documented reality on the ground has left them preparing for a confrontation that will not end at the ballot box.
“Vučić never organized fair elections. He never won the elections he didn’t organize, and there won’t be any difference this time,” said David, 45, who attended Thursday’s rally. “The more people come out for the elections, the bigger the chance to win against him. But if he still tries to steal, well, I don’t know... the streets.”
He paused, measuring the consequences of what might follow Sunday night.
“Violence is the last answer,” he said. “But if that’s the answer, we’re probably going to have to go that way.”

IMF sees $50–55 bln Ukraine gap for 2027–28, Russian assets key – Alternate Executive Director Rashkovan
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
17:47:49 EEST
23:47:49 KST

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimates Ukraine's uncovered external financing needs for budget expenditures in 2027–2028 at $50 billion–$55 billion: $30 billion–$35 billion next year and another $20 billion in 2028. Instruments linked to frozen Russian assets are being considered among the key sources for covering these needs, Vladyslav Rashkovan, Ukraine's Alternate Executive Director at the IMF, said.
"I am confident that Russian assets will remain our key issue both now and in the future. It seems to me that over the next two months, the range of options available to us for financing 2027 will lie somewhere between ERA-2 and Ukraine Support Loan-2," he said in an interview with Interfax-Ukraine on the sidelines of the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank Group, held in Bangkok on October 12–18.
Rashkovan clarified that IMF assistance with financing would cover nonmilitary budget expenditures, while additional defense financing needs would remain. Finance Minister Serhiy Marchenko estimates Ukraine's defense financing needs for next year at EUR 40 billion. That is why Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced Ukraine's total need for additional financing next year at EUR 70 billion during a European Council meeting in Brussels on October 14.
The IMF Alternate Executive Director said that Ukraine's international partners are currently more focused on covering financing needs for 2026–2027, although the Fund's Extended Fund Facility (EFF) with Ukraine runs through 2029, and there is an understanding that financing needs in 2028 will also be substantial.
He referred to the Ex-Post Assessment of the previous "wartime" EFF program for 2023–2025, which contained an important conclusion: even if the war ends, for example, in 2027, this does not mean that public finances will return to normal as early as 2028, partly because demobilization cannot happen immediately and social spending will need to increase to support veterans and their families.
"Therefore, even if the war ends in 2028, almost the same amount will be needed. Expenditures will begin to decline only later. This is the model the IMF is working with today... This figure will not come as a surprise to our partners," Rashkovan explained.
As for the main sources of financing other than frozen Russian assets, he pointed to the EU's multiannual budget for 2028–2034, which is being discussed by the European Council.
"European officials assure us that support for Ukraine will be included in it. The current draft allocates EUR 100 billion for Ukraine. We will see what the final structure of the document looks like after the political discussions within the EU. I think it should be agreed by the end of the year," Ukraine's representative at the IMF said, describing the current status of this funding source.
Regarding frozen Russian assets, Rashkovan recalled that most of them are held in Belgium at the international depository Euroclear. They are invested in various instruments of the European Central Bank and the National Bank of Belgium and generate income. In 2024, the G7 established the ERA mechanism, based on discounting future cash flows generated by the continued investment of these assets. Through this mechanism, Ukraine received $50 billion. These are nominally loans serviced using revenues from Russian assets, but for Ukraine they are effectively grants with no repayment obligations or conditions.
After the failure to introduce a EUR 140 billion reparations loan, which European countries lacked the courage to implement at the end of 2025, the EU developed the Ukraine Support Loan mechanism, worth EUR 90 billion for 2026–2027, to provide military and nonmilitary support to Ukraine, Rashkovan added. He clarified that this is also nonrepayable assistance to Ukraine, but it is financed by EU taxpayers.
"I think that over the next two months, discussions within the G7 will revolve around these two instruments (ERA-2 and Ukraine Support Loan-2). Another option would be to look for unused funds in European Union budget programs. I do not have full access to this information, but I am afraid that EUR 70 billion will not be available there," the expert said.
He explained that ERA-2 would again be a financial engineering instrument built around the valuation of future cash flows. While ERA covered a 30-year period, a longer-term model is now being considered, for example, one spanning 50 years. Last December, the European Council decided that the EU would not return Russia's assets until reparations had been paid, significantly reducing the risk associated with this mechanism, Rashkovan said.
According to him, the amount of assistance to Ukraine could also be increased by raising the expected return on investments of Russian assets from the current average of 2.8% annually to, for example, 4% annually, given that yields on U.S. and European government securities are currently around 5%.
"Finally, we know that the assets are not held exclusively at Euroclear. Around EUR 30 billion is held in private French banks. It would be worth provisionally factoring in these funds when developing the model as well," Ukraine's representative at the IMF added.
Summing up, he said that such planning and financial engineering could mobilize around $20 billion for Ukraine, but this would not solve all its problems, particularly given military spending.
"Ultimately, we will still have to turn to G7 finance ministers to cover those costs, because their countries are the ones financing them. (Therefore,) the second option is the Ukraine Support Loan," Rashkovan said.
In his view, it would be possible to increase the size of this instrument beyond the initial EUR 90 billion, the amount determined by the IMF last year.
"If the Fund had identified a need for EUR 140 billion, our partners would have looked for EUR 140 billion. Therefore, it is important now to agree on a common understanding of the total amount: $30–35 billion in nonmilitary needs plus EUR 40 billion in military expenditures, for a total of approximately EUR 70 billion. Accordingly, the ceiling for the Ukraine Support Loan needs to be increased. The instrument and its legal framework already exist; the only thing needed is to raise the lending limit," Ukraine's representative at the IMF said, outlining a possible course of events.
He clarified that in this case, the European Union would have to raise the funds on the market before providing them to Ukraine. At an interest rate of 4%–5%, this would cost approximately EUR 3 billion annually in interest, which European countries would like to cover through assistance from non-European G7 countries. In that case, the mechanism would be almost cost-free for both the European Union and Ukraine.
Among less realistic sources of financing, Rashkovan also mentioned the $5 billion frozen in the United States and the REPO Act (Rebuilding Economic Prosperity and Opportunity for Ukrainians Act), adopted in April 2024. The law allows the U.S. president to confiscate Russian sovereign assets under U.S. jurisdiction and direct them toward assistance to Ukraine.
"Unfortunately, it was not applied even under the Biden administration, and this has still not been done. That is why another initiative, called the PEACE Act, has emerged. It effectively requires the U.S. Treasury secretary, within 90 days after the law enters into force, to seize the relevant assets and transfer the funds to the Ukraine Support Fund. These funds could also be used to purchase defense equipment for Ukraine. The bill has not yet become law, but it is important that discussions on sanctions are continuing," the expert said, describing the current situation.
Another option he mentioned was a levy on Russian oil, similar to the one that existed for Iraq. It could also become a source of funding for the International Claims Commission, established in The Hague.
As for the confiscation of Russian assets, Rashkovan believes it may become possible in the future and that work on the issue should therefore continue.
"Some people propose returning Russia's assets as part of the price of peace. I categorically oppose this: the idea is fundamentally misguided... We know that Russia has no intention of stopping. Therefore, returning the assets would not be the price of peace for Russia, but a prize: it would simply say 'thank you' and carry on," Ukraine's representative said.

He acknowledged that there were problems in Africa as well as all over the world, but defended the decision saying, “I think we really have to approach it with humility”.
“Growing up in England, they never taught us anything about Africa. It needs to be on the curriculum,” he said.
"A lot of the problems they have there are still the results of colonialism and the West intervening, but if you see the people, you see so many designs that are out there today. Top brands come from Africa, and it’s got all the richest resources,” he continued.
He also stated that the culture across Africa is rich and having Formula One there would allow the continent to shine.
Conversations surrounding Rwanda hosting Formula One started in May 2024 when officials met leaders of the International Automobile Federation during the Monaco Grand Prix. Months later, Formula One President and CEO Stefano Domenicali confirmed that Rwanda submitted a proposal and discussions would be underway.
The decision has garnered opposition, with Congolese Foreign Affairs Minister Thérèse Kayikwamba Wagner arguing that the event could improve President Paul Kagame’s international image while conflict rages on.
This is not the first time Hamilton has called for a free Palestine. He has previously called for a ceasefire in Gaza amid Israel’s onslaught which has killed over 74,000 people. He has also used his social media platforms to shed light on the destruction in Gaza as a result of fierce Israeli bombardment.

A marathon EU summit on October 15-16 failed to produce a breakthrough on the European Union's next long-term budget. A farewell to BioWare, maker of some of the best games of the 21st century | Lucy James
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:44:48 UTC
23:44:48 KST

Earlier this week, EA announced the closure of BioWare, a game studio with a 30-year history of compelling role-playing games, complex characters and bold, choice-driven narratives. Its forthcoming game in the Mass Effect sci-fi series has been cancelled, and more than 400 people are losing their jobs. As someone who has worked in the video games industry for 15 years and spent almost 20 as a BioWare fan, I am among millions of mourners today.
It’s not terribly hard to see why BioWare got the chop. Its parent company has been saddled with $20bn of debt thanks to a recent leveraged buyout involving Jared Kushner and the Saudi wealth fund. EA was looking for weight to cut loose, and despite its hardcore fanbase and reputation for genre-defining RPGs such as Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic and Dragon Age, BioWare hadn’t put out a critical or commercial hit in over 10 years. Its forthcoming game, titled Mass Effect: Universe according to a leaked trailer, was announced back in 2020. Despite some flashy teases, it was still years away from release.
The three games that comprise original space-faring Mass Effect trilogy count as my favourites of all time. I first played in 2010, shortly after buying my Xbox 360 and being reassured by my friends that the game was a worthy investment, and have replayed them countless times since. Depending on the day, the top spot fluctuates; more often than not it’s the character-driven sequel Mass Effect 2, which ends with one of the most iconic missions in gaming, that takes the top spot.
Released over a five-year period from 2007-12, the trilogy follows the adventures of Commander Shepard: a lawless Spectre special agent who is empowered by the galactic Citadel Council to use any means necessary to protect its interests and get the job done. Shepard’s appointment as the first human Spectre in a galaxy where humans are the new kids on the block aligns with the arrival of the Reapers, an ancient synthetic race that raze all organic life every 50,000 years. Shepard must convince the galaxy that the threat is real and gather its top soldiers, scientists and scoundrels to defeat it.
When I played Mass Effect for the first time, I didn’t get it. Its controls felt janky and awkward, and I was thrown headlong into a galaxy full of history and politics that I didn’t understand: the game didn’t spell things out, throwing out names and jargon and expecting me to follow. After one exceedingly frustrating encounter with the Mako, the game’s infamously awkward land buggy, I quit entirely. Some months later, something drew me back: the feeling of a job left half done. The galaxy was in peril, and I had to save it.
The second time I tried, something clicked. I focused less on the gameplay quirks and went all-in on its story and characters: the naive archaeologist, Dr Liara T’Soni; the browbeaten Citadel security guard Garrus Vakarian; and Kaidan Alenko, a human enhanced by the military, and suffering because of it. Mass Effect’s story was simple – save the galaxy from a tormenting synthetic race with guns and space powers – but you got to determine how it played out. Players were given the opportunity to make meaningful choices that hugely affected how the story unfolded, and that stuck with me (and millions of others).
Throughout the course of the game, you can shape not only Shepard’s gender and what they look like, but how they react to situations. Would they be friendly, and use some inter-species cooperation to defeat the Reapers? Or take the renegade route, tersely shutting down dissenters, sometimes resulting in hilariously out-of-pocket responses? (My apologies to the intrepid space reporter Khalistah al-Jilani.) Regardless of how you played, it was thrilling to have such agency over how Shepard moved and was perceived in the world. But the real fun was in making decisions that altered the story not only in Mass Effect, but its sequels.
I agonised over every choice, large or small. Across three games and the far flung reaches of the galaxy, my influence was felt. Races lived and died at my whim, and the consequences of my actions showed up in the most unexpected ways. It made my playthrough feel truly mine, guided by the stern hand of its development team, but shaped by me, and me alone. Shepard’s plight was mine, and I would save the galaxy. I hadn’t played anything like it at the time, and even now, I struggle to think of moments that compare. Its missions and story beats are so ingrained in my mind that you’d think I actually lived them. Such is the wonder of a video game, the freedom to explore and affect the world you’re playing in.
Mass Effect’s story wouldn’t have hit as hard if it weren’t for its characters: a motley crew of the galaxy’s toughest and cleverest, drawn to your cause for their own, complex reasons. It questioned whether AI had a soul, the sins of the father, and the heaviness of duty. BioWare wrote missions personalised to your squadmates’ causes, asking you to make agonising decisions that could benefit or harm them, and then forcing you to deal with the results. The writers went one further, allowing you to date some of these characters, slowly building from nervous flirting to ratings-friendly romance scenes. Saying goodbye to your squad, who’d been with you through hell, before the third game’s devastating final act brought me to tears over a decade ago. It still does.
It’s been over a decade since Shepard’s story concluded, and the trilogy is still lauded as among the greatest ever made. I play dozens of games a year, and few have stuck with me as Mass Effect has. Its influence is impossible to shake. It set the standard for action-RPGs for years to come, and despite a furore at its original ending (since changed due to public outcry), is still beloved and widely referenced in gaming culture.
BioWare’s ending feels so final, so abrupt. Despite missteps and mismanagement in recent years, most publicly in the form of failed sci-fi shooter Anthem, getting a glimpse at what the new Mass Effect might have been has left fans bereft. The foundation of the universe was so strong, and in the right hands it could have been another genre-defining story. The loss of BioWare is an enormous one for gaming, a bastion of western role playing games brought down. Its influence will continue to be felt throughout the gaming galaxy.
- Lucy James is founder and curator of lookingfor.game and co-host of the Friends Per Second gaming podcast.
