The long way home: Free after decade in Iraqi prison, Benjamin Hassin begins new life in Jerusalem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:43:47 UTC
23:43:47 KST

Arrested in Iraq in 2015 and subsequently sentenced to death, Canadian-Israeli Benjamin Hassin endured more than a decade of imprisonment. Now, he speaks to The Jerusalem Post about his ordeal, the people who did not abandon him, and his arrival in Israel.
Just over a month ago, on the eve of Rosh Hashanah, Benjamin Hassin landed on Israeli soil for the first time in 12 years.
He was greeted by security officers at the airport, who hugged him and welcomed him home.
The average passenger arriving at the terminal likely had no idea who Hassin was, or why he was being greeted so warmly.
They likely did not know that the 31-year-old Canadian-Israeli had been incarcerated in a prison in Iraq just a couple of days prior. And that he has been imprisoned there since 2015, awaiting execution.
Today, he is studying in Aish Hatorah Yeshiva in Jerusalem, which is where the Post met him to hear his story.
Iraq to Israel and back again
Hassin was born in Iraqi Kurdistan in 1994 to a Jewish family. A year after he was born, in 1995, his family (parents and maternal grandparents) immigrated to Israel, and then in 2002 moved to Canada, where he lived until finishing high school.
At 18, Hassin returned to Israel with the intention of spending time with friends and family before traveling to Sydney, Australia.
But just two days before he was set to fly to Sydney, Hassin decided to cancel his flight and instead travel to Iraq to visit his paternal grandparents.
He chose to stay there for a few months and rented an apartment. During this time, he reported watching videos about the ISIS insurgency and decided to volunteer as a soldier in the Kurdish force.
“It was an American-led brigade, about 200 soldiers,” he explained. “It was led by the Americans, and it was supervised by the United Nations.
“I participated in a few battles, six, I think.”
Volunteering in the army, at just 20 years old and with no military experience, fighting ISIS, was “frightening,” he said. The volunteers received only 10 days of weapons training before they began fighting.
“A lot of terrorists, a lot of bombings, a lot of killings.”
His retelling was delivered in a quiet, matter-of-fact way, a striking juxtaposition to the sheer gravity of the situation being recalled.
After about a year of fighting, Hassin decided he had reached the limit of what he could handle, and informed his unit that he wished to leave – which he was allowed to do given he was only there on a voluntary basis.
But, due to a life-changing turn of events, his decision to leave the fighting would ultimately not mean he would be leaving Iraq.
On June 5, 2015, Hassin was in a taxi on the way to a friend’s house when the driver heard him speaking Hebrew, realized Hassin was Israeli, and threatened to hand him over to ISIS.
The situation became heated, and Hassin, who was armed, drew his weapon and shot the driver in self-defense. The driver died a few days later from his wounds, and Hassin was arrested and charged with murder.
What followed was the beginning of more than a decade in Iraqi custody.
“I spent two months and 27 days in pretrial detention,” he said. “It [his cell] was around 3 feet by 5 feet. I couldn’t stretch my legs fully.”
The treatment during this time was severe. Hassin described emotional and physical abuse, beatings “for no reason,” cigarette burns, a toenail being ripped out, and broken fingers. He showed different scars on his hands and arms and explained what caused them.
He was also handcuffed the whole time, and still bears the physical effects of that 11 years later, with swelling in his hand to this day from the pressure.
“They’d also use sleep deprivation,” he continued. “They’d wake you up in the middle of the night and just say, ‘Go for a walk,’ or ‘go to the washroom.’ So you couldn’t sleep continuously.”
One of the worst forms of abuse that he remembers was being made to wear a blindfold when leaving his room.
“They’d just say ‘Go straight,’ and suddenly I’d fall down the stairs. It was more than the physical pain. Physical pain I knew would go away. But the emotional stuff, that was the worst.”
After the pretrial detention was over, Hassin was moved to a general population prison in Sulaymaniyah. He recalls this being four meters wide and five meters long, with about 20 people in the room at any given time.
This was a holding facility, so he said most prisoners were there for short periods of time, maybe a few days or weeks. Maximum a month.
Hassin was there for five years and two months.
“I still don’t know why I stayed that long there,” he said.
“I had a few lawyers. Two lawyers were actually threatened and resigned from the case. One of them quoted me $100,000 for his lawyer’s fee and said he could get me a 15-year sentence. He was taking advantage of my status, and it was, simply put, manipulation: other prisoners were paying $4,000 or $5,000.”
Hassin refused this. “I told them I’m not going to pay that. I haven’t done anything.”
The years passed slowly, with little to distinguish one day from the next. For the first two years, Hassin said, he was so afraid for his safety that he avoided sleeping at night.
“I’d sleep in the day, like, 10 a.m. to, like, 4 or 5 p.m. At night, I’d just read books or watch TV.”
A friend outside prison would bring him five or six books every few weeks. He read extensively, including Russian literature and philosophy, while much of the rest of his time was spent waiting and thinking.
He was not allowed a Jewish prayer book or any Jewish items, despite requesting them. While praying was forbidden for him, he recalls feeling connected to God spiritually during that time.
Sentenced to death
“Everything happens really slowly there,” he recalled. “It was just listening to people argue about nothing. Fighting about nothing.”
Hassin was finally sentenced on 16 October 2020. He received the death penalty.
This remained in place until November 2025, when his death sentence was annulled after a sulha agreement, with $200,000 in funds raised at the request of the Iraqi authorities (the money was used to persuade the family of the alleged victim to accept the reduced sentence).
However, Hassin was not granted release from prison.
He explained that several executions had taken place in 2014 or 2015, but protests by the families of those executed, along with intervention by the UN and foreign governments, had led to a temporary suspension of executions.
He added that, under the judicial process, a death sentence would be reviewed after 30 days by a panel of 13 judges, including the chief judge. All 13 judges upheld his specific death sentence, he said.
The case was then – according to him – sent to the office of the prime minister or deputy prime minister for final approval, after which an execution could normally take place within 52 days.
However, his execution was never approved, and the case remained pending for years, leaving him waiting without knowing when or whether the sentence would be carried out.
While he can’t say for sure that he received different treatment because he was Jewish and Israeli, he knew that it was a focus for those handling his case.
“On all my case files, the first thing you’d see is a photocopy of my Israeli passport and my ID. And then after that you’d see the statements and what happened throughout the case. So I’m not sure if that affected it, but it probably did.”
Hassin, although somewhat disconnected from the outside world, was aware of October 7 when it happened. Two weeks later, suspecting possible consequences for the Jewish inmate, Hassin’s lawyers asked to have him transferred to a maximum security prison, where he then stayed for a year and nine months.
“It was better there for me. I felt safer.”
He qualified his last statement: “Well, not safe exactly. They all knew I was Israeli. They all knew I was Jewish.”
Throughout his whole time in prison, Hassin was supported by his lawyer Allen Lowy, who would fly to Iraq and visit him in prison. He was also aware of the support of the global Jewish community, particularly the American Jewish community, which was advocating for him and attempting to raise funds.
Despite that support, there were long periods when Hassin understandably struggled to imagine a future outside prison.
During the first five-and-a-half years in prison, he said, he used to call family in Canada once a week or once every two weeks, using the pay phone in the prison cell. After he received the death sentence, Hassin said he stopped calling home.
This reflected the change in his mentality. Prior to the death sentence, he said he held on to hope that he would survive, that he “wouldn’t be that guy who dies in prison.”
But after the sentencing, he said, “Psychologically, I knew it was going to end there, and it was going to be a sad story.”
Nevertheless, he continued to make plans for a life he was increasingly convinced he would not see come to fruition.
“When I was on death row, I said to myself, man, one day, if I do get out, I’m gonna go to the beach.”
Matters changed again when he found out his death sentence had been annulled in November 2025, and that it had changed to a 15-year sentence.
“There’s a law that says you have to finish 75% of the 15 years, which is 11 years and 3 months, and then one can ask to be let off on good behavior.” By this time, he had almost served the 75%, and he became slightly hopeful he would be granted parole.
Gave up hope, then, a breakthrough
However, he said the judge wrote in her two-page report that “according to my crime and according to what happened, I should have been executed years ago, and that I don’t deserve to go back into society.” She rejected his request for parole.
“So I gave up again. I was like, they’re not gonna let me go.”
But after years of expecting the worst, the news he had almost stopped hoping for arrived without warning, on an otherwise nondescript Wednesday, September 16, 2026. Hassin could not sleep, and said he called his lawyer on a whim.
“She said, ‘You’ll be out in 15 minutes.’”
He said the whole process of leaving prison took around an hour and a half, but that he was out the same day.
After that, life has rapidly looked different.
“I met up with the lawyers. They got a five-star hotel [in Iraq]. I didn’t sleep that night.”
The idea of being in prison one day and in a resort hotel the next is inconceivable to most, but Hassin describes it fondly.
“I kept going for a walk, going downstairs, just walking around. I had some tea. I had some ice cream. Small things.”
The group then flew to Dubai, where they had a six-hour layover before flying to Israel.
And when he finally arrived at Ben-Gurion Airport, the welcome described at the beginning of this story brought home a reality that had seemed impossible for more than a decade: he was free, and he was back in Israel.
For the first time in a long time, he “broke down and cried.”
Meeting his family again after so long was jarring but special, he added, tearing up as he spoke.
“When I left my sister in 2012, she was nine. My brother was 12. Now they’re much older. I feel guilty missing out on a lot.”
His siblings, now adults, have since created a family group chat, sending him hundreds of messages and videos throughout the day. It is one of the many ordinary aspects of life that changed during his imprisonment, alongside technology, smartphones, and the rise of AI.
Perhaps one of the most bizarre parts of the story is him ending up at Aish in Jerusalem, studying in yeshiva.
While on the surface it seems to be a peculiar transition, Hassin said it was actually a long time in the making.
“I thought about it even before I got arrested,” he said. “When I was in prison, it became one of those plans like visiting the beach. I thought, if I do get out, I’ll probably go study at Aish.”
He was accepted by the rabbis at the center and arrived almost straight after landing on erev Rosh Hashanah.
He has nothing but good things to say about the yeshiva, and the quiet and thoughtful base it has provided him in the aftermath of his ordeal.
“The classes are amazing. I like the religious debates. Everyone has been so nice and helpful.”
Obviously, it is an adjustment. But Hassin remains positive, and revels in his freedom. He travels to see family in Tel Aviv often, and makes frequent trips to the beach, the thing that he hoped for during those long years in prison.
“It’s a hard transition, but it’s not like I am going from good to bad; I’m going from bad circumstances, life-threatening circumstances, to the safest, most friendly environment. It’s going to take time, but I’ve got all the time in the world.”
While the departure from prison is still fresh, Hassin said it is vital that he shares his story because it is his way of thanking those who helped him and supported him.
“The story’s really not based on me; the story’s based on the people who helped me. There’s nothing special about what I’ve been through. The beauty of the story is the people who helped me get out,” he said, in characteristically humble fashion.
Hassin thanked the thousands of people who contributed to his release, not least the over 6,000 people who raised more than $300,000 in 48 hours to pay for the sulha and legal fees. He also expressed gratitude to Stella Rapp, then head of the consular department at the Foreign Ministry, and her successor Eyal Siso, both tireless advocates for his case.
Since his release, he has also received messages from some of those who helped, including a rabbi who was eager to meet him.
He hopes that just as strangers were willing to help him when he needed it most, he might one day be in a position to offer that same support to somebody else, whether through financial assistance, visiting someone who is ill, or simply showing up for someone in need.
While he wants to stay at Aish for the near future, he is considering going to university and studying computer science.
For now, though, he is in no rush. After more than 11 years in prison, the prospect of an ordinary life, of studying, working, eating ice cream at the beach, is more than enough.
“A normal lifestyle would be good for me, I think,” he mused.
Although he warned the Post that he lost his sense of humor while in prison, there was a clear twinkle in his eye as he said that.
“It’s coming back to me, slowly.”
But like Hassin said, he now has all the time in the world.

UNRWA teacher tells ‘Post’ she was threatened for challenging pro-Hamas rhetoric in Gaza schools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:43:39 UTC
23:43:39 KST

The antisemitic and pro-Hamas indoctrination of Gazan students has a “profound impact” that extends far beyond the classroom, a Gaza-based UNRWA teacher told The Jerusalem Post on Saturday, after school administrators threatened her with scissors for confronting extremist rhetoric being pushed onto young girls.
Speaking to the Post anonymously due to the risks she faces, T. said she decided it was her responsibility to speak out after repeatedly witnessing a colleague attempt to blur the “boundaries between education and political and religious indoctrination within the school environment.”
“I believe that remaining silent in the face of such practices means abandoning our moral and educational responsibilities,” she said, stressing that Palestinian students deserved an environment where they could study and dream of a future uncolored by conflict.
“They have already experienced more than enough war, fear, and death,” T. said. “No one has the right to rob them of their childhood or predetermine that their future must be an extension of the conflict.”
While T. told the Post that she did not consider her attempts to challenge the indoctrination to be anything special, she acknowledged that confronting radicalization had put her at risk. She said she became more aware of the danger recently, when a school administrator threatened her with scissors after she intervened in an attempt by another teacher to promote support for Hamas.
School administrator threatened to cut teacher's tongue for mentioning Hamas
“I had confronted several teachers on more than one occasion over their attempts to indoctrinate children with extremist ideas. During one of these incidents, I became involved in a heated argument with a female teacher who was promoting such views,” she recounted.
“Shortly afterward, a school administrator confronted me, pushed me into a room, pulled a pair of scissors from his pocket, and threatened me, saying: ‘I’ll cut your tongue out if you ever mention Hamas again.’”
T. said she decided not to file a formal complaint with UNRWA because she could not trust that the matter would be handled confidentially or that the organization could guarantee her safety, particularly given the extent of the radicalization she had witnessed within the agency.
“Some people abroad imagine that UNRWA, because it is a United Nations agency, operates in Gaza the same way international institutions operate in Western countries, with an independent administration to which employees can turn for protection. But the reality I experienced was very different,” she said. “I also believe that UNRWA operates in an environment where it cannot simply ignore Hamas’s influence and control on the ground. In my view, employees who openly oppose Hamas may put themselves at risk and potentially create pressures affecting the agency’s operations.”
Even as she explained that UNRWA had to navigate a complex political terrain to be able to operate in Gaza, and was not responsible for the creation of the culture in its facilities, T. argued that the UN agency has not done enough to confront it and has failed to enforce strict boundaries on teachers, allowing the problem to enter the classroom.
T. stressed that not all UNRWA employees supported or were affiliated with Hamas, but argued that the agency lacked adequate structural safeguards to protect her and other whistleblowers.
“If a school administrator could push me into a room, pull scissors from his pocket, and threaten to cut out my tongue because I spoke about Hamas, how could I feel confident that filing a complaint would not expose me to an even more serious threat? What guarantee would I have that next time they would not stop at threatening to cut out my tongue, but might actually kill me?” she asked. “For me, this was not simply a matter of administrative procedures or filing an official complaint. It was a matter of life and death. That is why I did not report the incident. Not because what happened was insignificant, and not because I accepted the threat, but because I did not trust the available system to protect my identity or my safety if I spoke out.”
Hamas uses punishment beyond physical intimidation
Beyond physical intimidation, T. said Hamas could use other means to punish her for speaking out, including accusations against her honor and threats against her family, to silence dissent.
“There are dissenting voices, and there are people who reject these ideas. But most people are afraid for their families. Not everyone can bear the consequences of confronting an organization that holds political power, influence, and security authority,” T. said. “For this reason, I do not believe what happened to me was an isolated incident. In my view, it reflects a much broader problem within Gaza’s educational environment. I believe Hamas understood, from the time it came to power, the importance of education in shaping the minds of future generations.”
Asked how Hamas-oriented education was affecting Palestinian children, T. said antisemitism and the romanticization of martyrdom were shaping their worldviews in psychologically damaging ways.
She added that the schooling system's emphasis on memorization and repetition to answer exam questions failed to equip students with the critical-thinking skills that could help protect them from radicalization.
“When an educational system built around memorization is combined with an ideological discourse that discourages dissent, the problem becomes even more dangerous,” she said. “A child who has never learned to ask questions, challenge assumptions, or examine information critically may become more vulnerable to extremist narratives.”
Nevertheless, T. stressed that Palestinian students should not be defined by the conflict or viewed solely as potential fighters but as children who are also victims of war who have the ability to choose a different future if given the chance.
“The children of Gaza have lived through years of war, fear, destruction, and the loss of loved ones. They need an education that gives them hope and helps them build their lives, not one that makes hatred and conflict permanent parts of their identity,” she shared. “I fear that continued extremist ideological indoctrination could produce generations who believe violence is the natural solution to disagreements, and that a person’s religious or national identity alone is enough to judge them…I want Palestinian children to dream of becoming doctors, engineers, teachers, or artists. I want them to know that their future does not have to be confined to a choice between war and death.
“Reforming education is not simply about changing textbooks. It is an essential part of building a society that can live in peace and dignity, and give its children a genuine opportunity for a better future.”

Most of the victims were from foreign backgrounds and prosecutors are investigating whether the acts targeted the “real or supposed race, ethnicity, nationality or religion” of the victims.
The 12-year-old girl shot eight times was “seriously wounded” but in a stable condition, the mayor of La Verriere, Nicolas Dainville, told AFP.
Police arrested the alleged shooter – a 39-year-old man, according to a source familiar with the case – in nearby Coignieres.
Officers found him in possession of a submachine gun and tear-gas grenades, according to a police source.
He had also booby-trapped his flat with three gas canisters and electric wires “connected to a timer”, according to anti-terrorism prosecutors.
Prosecutors said they had opened an investigation for “murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise”.
Bursts of gunfire
Rabeh said the man was firing sporadically from his car and that the person killed was “of African origin”.
One of the wounded, “in critical condition, is of north African origin”, he added.
It was “objectively a racist, probably Islamophobic attack,” the mayor said, calling for national unity as the toll rose from an earlier count of four wounded.
Dainville said that two of the wounded in his town – cleaners attending to a school Friday morning when the shooter got out of his car to open fire – were of African origin.
Laurent Nunez, France’s interior minister, travelled to the two affected towns. He called the shooting “clearly a terrorist crime”.
A police source told AFP that the man had fired in bursts from his vehicle around 10:30am (0830 GMT).
Adel, a resident of Trappes, about 20 kilometres west of Paris, said his “heart was broken” as he learned the victims might have been targeted for their race.
“I’m north African and it’s frightening for everyone who has the same background,” the 50-year-old told AFP.
Samy, another resident, told AFP he had seen a body on the ground from his window.
His mother, he said, saw a grey Renault Clio car speeding by and heard “loud bangs”.
‘Terrible ordeal’
Writing on X, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the case was “very serious” and that “all resources of the security forces and the judiciary are fully mobilised”.
Macron earlier in the day said “the nation is standing with” the victims of this “terrible ordeal”.
The shooting came with France on edge following last weekend’s riots on the sidelines of mass protests over the cost of living, some of the worst street violence in recent years.
Read moreFrench student groups call for protests to continue after meeting with Macron
More protests are expected this weekend, but police will be out in force after a week of overnight curfews put in place in cities throughout the country.

First Lady of the US, Melania Trump, has secured a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the city of Oleshky, which will begin on October 29, the White House said on Friday.
Both nations have agreed to allow humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway, according to the White House.
The southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky is on the front line of the Russia-Ukraine war and houses approximately 1,700-2,000 of its pre-war population of 24,000 people, the majority of whom are elderly and unable to leave, and approximately 50 children.
Some 90 percent of the city was flooded after the destruction of the Kakhovka Dam, and most of the population has been displaced or evacuated.
Trump worked with Russia, Ukraine to coordinate ceasefire since UNGA
The city came to Trump's attention during a private discussion during the 81st United Nations General Assembly, after which Trump and her representative used a preexisting communication channel established with Russia and Ukraine to aid the unification of 34 children in the past.
Trump has been active in trying to get Ukrainian children seized by Russia during the war returned to their families.
"Both nations promptly assigned teams to coordinate the complex mechanics involved, including demining. All parties have worked around the clock since that moment,” Trump said.
“Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require. Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine,” said Trump.
A US media organization will accompany and document Russian and Ukrainian teams on the ground throughout the ceasefire to ensure the wishes of each family are respected, Trump added.

On October 7, 2023, the State of Israel was turned upside down.
When the government vanished, we – reservists and ordinary citizens – headed south and saved our homeland from an existential threat.
The sense of emptiness we encountered there – the total absence of the state – coupled with the harrowing sights and the pain of loss, left me personally with a profound sense of shame.
I could not fathom that our own people had been massacred in such a way, that the government had simply disappeared, and that the senior military command had effectively evaporated. Yet, alongside this immense pain, a sense of pride in our people also emerged – people who took it upon themselves to save the homeland.
We realized that the responsibility rested solely on our shoulders; there was no one else. Where there was no one to step up, we stepped up.
This is the same spirit we, as reservists, now bring to the political arena. Looking at the numbers, it is clear that everything is at a standstill; the existing political blocs are hurtling toward yet another election.
The only way to prevent this is through the Reservists-Economic Party.
We are the only party remaining in the “third bloc” heading into the elections. With an average of five seats projected in polls and in-depth research, we have the capacity to break the deadlock between the blocs and restore stability.
Our immediate priorities are to tackle the insane cost of living and to ensure universal conscription. We must address the plight of those Israelis who serve for hundreds of days in the reserves, only to return home and face the highest grocery prices in the Western world.
For many years, Israeli citizens have been subjected to a form of brainwashing: the idea that they must choose between a coalition with anti-Zionist haredi (ultra-Orthodox) parties – which view us as heretics and encourage mass draft evasion – and anti-Zionist Arab parties that do not even recognize Hamas as a terrorist organization.
“Compromise on your values for the sake of the bloc.” If that approach worked, they would have kept doing it. The reality is that it doesn’t work; even with such moral compromises, there is no chance of forming a government.
We are telling the political establishment: “Enough.”
Voting this week is a call for change, but it is also a protest against a political system that is racing toward the disintegration of Israeli society.
We cannot survive when, on one hand, we have Arab “autonomous zones” in the Negev and the Galilee – characterized by a lack of governance, polygamy, extortion rackets, illegal construction, and a million illegal weapons – and, on the other, haredi “autonomous zones” that operate without any regard for the authority of the state.
We cannot sustain ourselves – neither socially nor economically.
After such a grueling war and such a heavy toll, we must rebuild Israel with worthy leadership.
While there was an initial assumption – during the first year of the war – that the Knesset would be replaced and a “generation of victory” would take the helm, there is now a sense of resignation – and, among some Israelis, even despair.
We stand against this.
When you lose your way, you must return to the last point you recognized. The State of Israel lost its way – this is the primary reason we reached October 7.
We have a leadership that practices “containment” of threats, focuses on the trivial, fosters factionalism from all sides, and suffers from a loss of vigilance and sheer hubris.
To fix this, we must return to the Zionist foundation: settlement, the absorption of immigrants, and the defense of the homeland.
Anyone who thinks this can be achieved with a “narrow” government simply doesn’t understand the situation. A minority government is not going to be formed here. That is the reality; those are the numbers – it is best not to deny them.
Neither political bloc has the capacity to form a government; they are nowhere near the required threshold. Those are the facts.
Zionist government is the only path forward
The only path forward is what we propose: a Zionist government, excluding both the haredi and Arab parties.
We are fed up with United Torah Judaism’s Yitzhak Goldknopf making decisions that shape the course of our lives. Furthermore, we are unwilling to rely on Arab parties that refuse to recognize Hamas as a terrorist organization.
One bloc in Israel – ranging from People of Israel’s party leader Ofer Winter to National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir – is beholden to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the haredi parties.
Another bloc – ranging from Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot to the Arab parties – lacks the necessary number of parliamentary seats. This dynamic effectively ensures that the current government remains in power through the next election cycle.
We are the only ones left who are not tethered to either bloc.
The reservists – who have carried the nation on their shoulders for hundreds of days, and who sustain the economy upon their return home – have become the solution. This is a discussion about alternatives; the only chance for a Zionist government lies with the reservists and those who prioritize a strong economy.
People will cast their ballots because they are fed up with the high cost of living and with draft evasion. They are fed up with the political deadlock.
We cannot go backward – we cannot afford more rounds of elections or to abandon the prospect of change. Voting for “the largest party” is effectively a vote for yet another election. We are the solution; we have no other country.
The writer is the leader of the Reservists-Economic Party.

Seven people were killed on Friday when gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in Jordan, said the head of the country's Public Security Directorate, in a rare attack on Jordan's Christian minority that authorities described as a terrorist act by extremists.
Speaking at a press conference, Major General Abdallah al-Maaytah said most of those wounded in the shooting at the Hamoud Church in Karak governorate were still receiving treatment, and that the hunt for the attackers was ongoing. Jordan's health minister said 40 people were wounded.
Shooting attack carried out by 'extremists'
Interior Minister Mazin Al Farrayeh said the attack had been carried out by "extremists," but that it was too early to tell whether they had any links to known groups inside or outside Jordan.
Such attacks are extremely rare in Jordan, which is relatively stable, though authorities in the US ally say that in recent years they have repeatedly foiled attempted attacks by Islamist terrorists.
There was no immediate claim of responsibility.
A video aired on Jordan's state-owned Al-Mamlaka television station that appeared to be from a security camera on the church showed three people firing at it from a sidewalk and hiding behind trees and a low wall. The video showed the attackers then running towards the church's entrance. Reuters was able to verify the video from the entry path and wall surrounding the church, as well as other details.
"This is a result of a terrorist ideology and blind extremism, and we will not allow society to go down this path," Jordanian Prime Minister Jafar Hassan said in a post on X/Twitter.
Khaled Burqan, who was at the funeral, told Al-Mamlaka that dozens of people were present and the gunmen opened fire on them for several minutes.
Ihab Ammareen, another witness, told the station he saw bloodied people collapse on the floor after the attack. "People were crying, wailing, screaming — it's hard to describe," he said.
Attackers will be punished with 'iron fist,' King Abdullah says
Jordan's King Abdullah, a major US partner in the fight against militant Islamist groups, visited Karak hours after the attack and said the perpetrators would be punished "with an iron fist."
"The terrorist attack against Karak will be met with the harshest retaliation. Those who delude themselves into thinking that they can divide Jordanians with their bullets have no chance in the face of our unity," he said in a statement.
Reuters footage from the church after the attack showed blood smeared on the floor near its entrance, where security forces were deployed.
In a post on X, United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the violence and said attacks against civilians and places of worship are unacceptable.
People who gathered at a Karak government hospital to support the wounded expressed shock.
"What happened today has left people unable to speak or raise our voices. But our only reproach to the state is that it must investigate these dark ideas — where they come from and how they enter the minds of our children," said one of them, Hani Al-Mbaydeen.
Christians make up a minority of Jordan's population. The country is home to several biblical sites that attract Christian pilgrims from around the world.
The US ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz described it on X as a "depraved and brutal attack on a house of worship."
Jordan was among the US allies in the region to be hit by Iranian attacks this year after the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February.

Yair Lapid: The upcoming election is about what we want Israel to be - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:43:03 UTC
23:43:03 KST

Here’s what I did on a typical morning this week before 8 a.m.
I was interviewed on the radio to discuss someone on Channel 14 calling Gadi Eisenkot a “monkey,” and Yinon Magal describing Ofri Bibas, whose brother returned from captivity after his wife and two babies were murdered, as among “the most vile and despicable people living in the State of Israel.”
I worked out.
I spoke on the phone with Noa Dovev, one of our activists. She is only 25. She had been out campaigning for us when a Likud activist spat on her, shoved her, and was filmed making obscene gestures at her.
I put the kettle on.
While it boiled, I spoke to my son, who had spent two hours stuck in traffic the day before because ultra-Orthodox protesters had blocked the road, screaming, “We’d rather die than enlist.”
Over coffee, I read the daily email report from our team tracking fake news. From late July to mid-October, Likud published more than 1,800 pieces of content created or manipulated using AI. Plenty of racist images. Plenty of attempts to frighten people. Endless lies.
I finished my coffee. At eight on the dot, I headed out.
I want to remind you of something you already know – this isn’t who we are.
The overwhelming majority of Israelis are good, hardworking, law-abiding people who don’t want to live surrounded by this poison and ugliness. The good news is they don’t have to.
Five big questions for Israel
On October 27, we get to choose who we want to be: a violent, extremist, isolated, and divided country, or an optimistic country, united, forward-looking, respected around the world, the best place on Earth to raise children.
That big question comes with four more:
What kind of security will we have here?
Over the past three years, thousands of missiles have struck our cities. Hamas gunmen still control Gaza. Hezbollah terrorists roam free in Lebanon. The Iranian regime has survived with its ballistic missile and nuclear programs. For the first time, more Americans sympathize with the Palestinians than with us, and a majority support ending military aid.
Conspiracy theories are gnawing away at public trust in the IDF. The military is worn down and short thousands of combat troops because the ultra-Orthodox refuse to serve. If this government stays, there will be another October 7 and another flydubai.
Or we can have a government that makes us safer. That drafts tens of thousands of ultra-Orthodox men. That launches a revolution in how we treat those who serve, rewarding reservists instead of draft dodgers. A government that gets Turkey and Qatar out of Gaza and brings Egypt in. That crushes Hamas. That removes the threat of Hezbollah. That does not flinch from striking Iran’s economic infrastructure.
No containment. A strong, swift, decisive response to every threat. A government that understands that real security comes from a combination of military force, economic strength, social solidarity, and international alliances.
What kind of Judaism will we have here?
A Judaism defined by draft dodging, settler violence, soldiers refusing to go into battle alongside a female paramedic, schools that teach religious coercion and educate against Zionism, money for cronies, homophobia, attacks on Reform and Conservative synagogues, a thirst for revenge and corruption?
Or a Judaism that says our responsibility is toward one another, a Judaism that asks, “Shall your brothers go to war while you sit here?” The broad-minded Judaism of Rabbi Joseph B. Soloveitchik and Rabbi Jonathan Sacks, in which the supreme imperative is to take responsibility for your own life. A Judaism that not only created the State of Israel but also makes an incredible contribution to the world around us. A Judaism that sanctifies the search for justice and the striving for peace. A Judaism of hope.
What basic values will we live by?
Will we be a country where, after the worst massacre in our history, the political leadership blocks a state commission of inquiry and blames everyone but itself? A country where people working for Qatar sit at the heart of the Prime Minister’s Office, and instead of firing them on the spot, the prime minister embraces them?
How did we get used to a security cabinet in which a convicted criminal who backs IDF deserters sits alongside a man convicted of supporting terrorism who never served a day in the military? A country where the government attacks the press, the judiciary, the security services, and half the population in an attempt to weaken the foundations of our democracy. A country where women have no role in decision-making and where opponents are branded as enemies.
Or a country with a clear set of values. Anyone convicted of a criminal offense will be barred from serving as a minister. No prime minister will serve more than two terms. Jewish terrorism will be dealt with firmly and without hesitation. The police will fight violent crime and break down protection rackets. The building blocks of liberal democracy will be protected. Women will have equal access to education. Arab citizens will be protected from horrific murder rates.
Political blackmail will give way to a constitution based on the Declaration of Independence, which states, “The State of Israel will be open for Jewish immigration and the Ingathering of the Exiles; it will foster the development of the country for the benefit of all its inhabitants; it will be based on freedom, justice, and peace as envisaged by the prophets of Israel.”
What standard of governance will we demand?
An education system in which Israeli children rank below Turkey in science and below Vietnam in mathematics, and all the education minister does is try to hide the test results? A country where taxes have increased and the cost of living keeps soaring, while tens of billions of shekels keep flowing into coalition slush funds and unnecessary government ministries?
Where Ben-Gurion Airport is buckling, flights are being canceled, and the transportation minister flies off on yet another vacation to Marrakesh? A co-pilot from Oman planned to crash a plane into the terminal at Ben-Gurion, the Omani authorities had known about him since 2024, and to this day nobody here can say who cleared him to land? A country where you are more likely to get a government job if you’re connected than if you’re qualified?
Or we can elect people who know how to run things. People who aren’t there to find jobs for their friends or funders but to build an efficient government that puts education first and treats your tax money with respect because you worked hard for it.
A country led by a team of people who get things done, who have run Israel before and did it very well. A team clean of corruption and free of cronyism, where competence is rewarded and political connections are not.
A team that includes two prime ministers, a foreign minister, a finance minister, a defense minister, ministers of economy, education, and social equality. Women who have run the ministries of transportation and communications, and local authorities. Knesset members you can’t fool or trick, because they’ve seen it all before.
The major choice for Israel
Now we can return to the first question: Who do we want to be?
The choice has never been clearer. This is not a choice between Right and Left: A government dependent on parties of anti-Zionist draft dodgers is not a right-wing government.
This is not a choice between religious and secular Israelis: Anyone who abandons the reservist wearing a kippah for the man screaming “We’d rather die than enlist” is not defending Judaism.
This is a choice between those who carry this country on their backs and those who hitch a free ride.
Deuteronomy says, “Choose life, so that you and your descendants may live.” It does not say, “Choose the Right.” It does not say, “Choose the Left.” It says life. And your descendants are Noa Dovev, attacked at the junction for daring to campaign, my son and thousands like him stuck in traffic, our children and grandchildren who want to build their lives here.
After October 28, I’ll be up early again. Before 8:00 a.m., I’ll work out. I’ll put the kettle on. Talk to my son about something other than chaos. Then I want to go to work for the people of Israel as part of a good, hardworking, decent government that will repair Israel and put us on a better path.
If that’s what you want to see too – vote B’Yachad.
The writer is the Israeli opposition leader and a candidate for B’Yachad.

In Syria, Israel’s female field intelligence soldiers power the IDF's covert operations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:43:00 UTC
23:43:00 KST

The Jerusalem Post recently interviewed female field intelligence soldiers on the Syrian border, overlooking areas where they routinely conduct surveillance and penetration operations.
Meeting at the former Syrian intelligence building, captured during the 1967 Six Day War, near Merom Golan in the Golan Heights, and traveling along the border to the Quneitra lookout, the Post interviewed IDF Capt. ‘O.’ and female intelligence collection soldiers ‘N.’ and ‘R.’ of Battalion 595.
They discussed what it means to be part of a new generation of women who operate inside Syria, monitor increased Iranian activity in the area, and navigate growing tensions with local Syrian residents who were once grateful for the IDF’s presence. They also discussed breaking the glass ceiling for women in combat roles in the IDF. Women now make up more than 50% of their unit.
‘N.’ and ‘R.’ specialize in a combination of direct visual surveillance and drone-based field intelligence collection.
The Post visited Battalion 595 about a year ago in a more southerly part of Israel’s buffer zone in Syria. During both visits, female intelligence soldiers described their efforts to locate and track a range of hostile groups, from Iranian operatives to Hamas members and regime-linked HTS jihadists.
In late 2025, a different group of female soldiers revealed that they had penetrated as far as 18 kilometers beyond the buffer zone into Syria. The operation included providing field guidance for the 890th Paratroopers Battalion.
During one operation, the soldiers studied four individuals who were working for, or associated with, Iran or Iranian agents. Each individual had to be analyzed separately, including their movements, schedules, and habits, one soldier, identified as ‘S.’, said at the time.
By October of this year, however, the soldiers could no longer disclose how far they were penetrating into Syria.
This came amid repeated public pressure from the Trump administration for Israel to scale back its activities in Syria and begin partial withdrawals from its buffer zone.
Nevertheless, all three interviewees, ‘N.’, ‘R.’, and ‘O.’, emphasized that they continued to carry out missions throughout southern Syria, quietly but aggressively.
The IDF has also issued several updates in recent weeks, including an announcement that it killed Iranian-linked Syrian terrorist Yusef Ali al-Hasan on October 9.
According to the IDF, al-Hasan was killed because of his involvement in a series of terrorist activities against Israeli forces, including drone operations and previous rocket fire from southern Syria.
In two separate incidents on October 4 and 5, the IDF also opened fire on three other suspects in Syria.
In the first incident, an IDF reservist from the Carmeli Brigade spotted a suspect attempting to infiltrate an IDF position and shot him dead. The suspect was found to be unarmed, and the incident is under review.
In the second incident, two suspects approached an IDF position in Syria on a motorcycle. IDF soldiers opened fire, wounding one of them, and arrested both for questioning.
These announcements followed a period in which the IDF had been relatively quiet about its activities in Syria, apart from an August 18 attack on a Turkish position. The relative silence came amid pressure from the Trump administration and growing reports of tensions with local Syrian civilians, some of whom have become increasingly frustrated with the IDF’s presence as it approaches its second anniversary.
What do these developments mean for future Israeli-Syrian security relations and intelligence collection along the border?
How female intelligence soldiers track threats in Syria
According to ‘N.’, who has served for two years and eight months, “our job is to guard the civilians, to secure this front, and to collect as much intelligence as possible.”
Asked how she and her unit determine where to focus their intelligence collection efforts within Israel’s extensive security zone in Syria and beyond, she said: “We have technological tools, and we do not work alone. We work with other intelligence partners, there are other IDF forces, and we get intelligence also from higher-ranking headquarters officers.”
Asked how long she had spent in the field on a single deployment, ‘N.’ explained that it varied according to the situation.
“It changes all the time, according to the [character of a specific] period. It could be a few days, or it could be a few hours. The longest was probably around a week, or a bit longer,” she said.
‘N.’ said she had spent longer periods in the field during the June 2025 war with Iran.
“The whole environment was hotter and more unstable, and there was a need for higher readiness, so we did what was required of us,” she said.
While international attention was focused on Israeli airstrikes against Iran and Iranian missiles launched at Israel, activity in Syria also increased.
“Whenever the situation is more tense, there are more incidents, so you need to be more ready in the field,” ‘N.’ said.
She also described an operation in which the unit gathered intelligence on several hostile individuals over a period of days.
“We collected intelligence on multiple hostiles over a period of days. We returned to the same area multiple times – and then an operation was carried out,” she said.
The process involves determining who a target is, whom they meet, and when and how those meetings take place.
“You try to find out who this is, who he meets with, when, and how,” she said, explaining that the soldiers also monitor the times of day or night when a target carries out activities or holds meetings.
‘N.’ emphasized that her unit’s role is to gather the information needed to help other forces carry out operations safely and effectively.
“[Our role is] to collect as much relevant intelligence as possible, so that the [IDF] forces which carry out the operation afterward will be able to do so in the most secure and optimal manner possible,” she said.
The soldiers collect intelligence both during the day and at night, ‘N.’ added, noting that “a lot of activities happen at night,” when people are harder to observe.
Combining drones, surveillance, and field intelligence
‘R.’, who has served for more than two years, described her experience leading teams and managing the unit’s operational readiness.
“I have commanded a few different units, including responsibilities for equipment and technology. I was a team leader [for a small unit] for running the operational activities regarding intelligence and regarding the readiness of the unit, working on their professionalism and their combat knowledge,” she said.
“We carried out many operations to get as much information as the brigade needed. We kept our eyes peeled for [collecting intelligence for] them. Sometimes they also ask for very specific intelligence, and we get as much as we can for them,” she added.
‘R.’ said soldiers must look beyond the immediate target during an operation to understand the broader context.
“Sometimes when you go out to perform an operation, it is easy to just focus on the main mission-target itself, but you can miss some of the important [secondary] things going on around the mission-focus,” she said.
She stressed the importance of connecting the unit’s observations to the overall situation in the area being monitored.
‘R.’ explained that the soldiers do not always know how an operation ultimately unfolds. They therefore try to learn what happened afterward, allowing them to understand how their work contributed to the mission.
The feedback is also important for morale, she said, helping soldiers feel that their work has made a difference even when they do not see the final outcome.
Regarding the choice between direct visual surveillance and drones, ‘R.’ said the decision depends on the mission and the target’s location.
“It depends on the mission. Where is the target? What do you need to do to get [close enough to observe the target] there?” she said.
“We have lots of different tools, and our job is to be skilled enough to choose each time what is the right tool to accomplish the mission in the best way possible,” she added.
Asked whether direct observation was preferable, with drones used when approaching a target would risk exposing the soldiers, ‘R.’ said the priority was to get as close as possible without compromising their safety.
“We want to be as close to the target as possible, without endangering ourselves. We are a clandestine unit. So we do need to keep our distance sometimes, but each time is different,” she said.
Asked about situations in which she and her fellow soldiers had faced danger, ‘R.’ said they could sense when a front was becoming more volatile, whether because of Iranian activity or threats from other groups.
Part of what helped them cope, she said, was the close-knit nature of the unit.
“We are always together, and each of us is there for the next-door soldier. So even if there is a bit more fear or official threat warnings, we have each other's backs, and this is one of the best things [about the unit],” she said.
‘R.’ added that the soldiers supported one another through conversations, body language, and eye signals, particularly when operations required them to remain silent.
“There is a dynamic between the [female] soldiers [in the unit] that they can do this [communicate] even without speaking – this is awesome, and it shows true sisterhood between the women. It is inspiring to see this, and even fun,” she said. “But sometimes with these matters which can cause stress, we need to focus and perform our operations. Then later we get to celebrate it.”
Asked how the unit determines whether a target is linked to Iran, Hamas, HTS, the Syrian regime, or another group, ‘R.’ said the process relies on cooperation with intelligence headquarters.
“These are matters that come to us from intelligence [headquarters]. We also help each other in both directions. They give me guidance in a direction about what I need to search for and look for, and I can help them in another direction, including signs relating to HTS or another group,” she said.
She added that surveillance operations are often repeated to build a more complete intelligence picture of a potential threat.
‘R.’ agreed that activity in Syria had intensified recently, saying that the soldiers could feel the change through sudden mission call-ups and other indications.
“It is felt. It is felt. Whether due to sudden mission call-ups of the unit [or other signs], but we are always ready, whether it [a threat] plays out or not, we are ready to stay here and we are not afraid,” she said.
IDF commander says threats persist despite US pressure
Capt. ‘O.’ commands the larger company to which ‘N.’ and ‘R.’ belong.
He has spent his entire five-and-a-half-year military service in the Golan Heights, including operating in Syria since December 2024, when the IDF established its buffer zone following the fall of the Assad regime.
“Once we understood what was happening with the revolution [against the Assad regime], we saw this was an amazing opportunity,” he said.
‘O.’ said the decision to establish the buffer zone was driven by the opportunity to strengthen Israel’s security by moving its defensive position forward.
“We were ready. It was not a question of whether to go in [to set up a Syrian buffer zone]. It was [only a question of] when do we go in so we can defend from a forward position. Our job is to prevent enemies from getting into Jewish towns which are right next to us here,” he said, gesturing toward nearby residential areas.
Asked about the elevated threat from Iran, including the recent incidents publicized by the IDF, ‘O.’ said the situation involved increased friction.
“There is more friction. There is more ongoing friction. We have no problem with some friction. It is a good thing as it makes us readier for anything and everything [appearing] at any place,” he said.
The Post noted that the IDF spokesperson had issued more updates about Iranian activity and other threats after a period in which IDF sources said Iranian associates had largely left Syria.
‘O.’ responded that attempts to establish terrorist infrastructure in Syria continued.
“There is always an attempt to establish [a terror] apparatus. And they will always remain [at some level]. They want to destroy us, and they will [try to] do this however they can,” he said.
He added that hostile groups would continue to look for different ways to threaten Israel, but said the IDF was prepared to defend residents and visitors to the Golan Heights.
“So sometimes they will try one way, and sometimes they will try another way, but we are ready for everything, ready to defend the civilians and tourists who live in and tour the Golan,” he said.
During the summer, he added, the area attracted many tourists, requiring the soldiers to work harder to protect them. With winter approaching, visitors would again come to see the snow on Mount Hermon, and the IDF would need to protect them as well.
Asked about diplomatic pressure to reduce Israeli operations in Syria and eventually withdraw partially from the buffer zone, ‘O.’ said those decisions were outside his remit.
“I am not part of the political echelon. I am at the tactical level…I receive orders, and I carry them out,” he said.
“What they order me to do, I do. Where they tell me to be, I will be there. If there is an operation which is approved or not, [when it is approved] we will do it as best as possible,” he added. “Whoever decides what the missions will be, that is way over my head. I am not part of these debates…I deal with the here and now.”
Asked whether he had noticed a freeze in operations following US demands, ‘O.’ said such decisions were made at higher levels and that he had not necessarily observed a change in his daily work.
“This is a decision made at the higher levels. I don’t know if I feel this [change]. We have lots of missions every day. I don’t necessarily feel there are more or fewer missions,” he said.
‘O.’ also described the difficulty of distinguishing between hostile operatives and civilians in Syria.
“The people who want to harm us are not fools. They know where to be, when to be there, how to present themselves,” he said, explaining that they also know how to observe others without attracting attention.
He added that hostile operatives can conceal themselves within the civilian population, making it difficult to distinguish between terrorists and civilians.
‘O.’ said the IDF draws on a wide range of capabilities to identify and neutralize threats, with his unit contributing intelligence gathered through clandestine observation and drones.
“The IDF is a very powerful military in all of its sections and on all of the platforms that one can use. We all do this together. In the end, I provide another perspective to complement the broader IDF picture,” he said.
He added that he was part of a larger intelligence apparatus that combines different sources and methods to address specific threats.
“In the end, there is an integration of various kinds of intelligence which collectively provide an answer to more specific issues,” he said.
Syrian civilians grow less patient with the IDF presence
The Post received independent confirmation of increased rock-throwing incidents and tensions between some Syrian civilians and IDF soldiers.
However, neither ‘N.’ nor ‘R.’ believed the situation had deteriorated dramatically. They said the soldiers were still generally received warmly.
“We receive more cherries than rocks,” ‘R.’ said, although she acknowledged that tense encounters sometimes occurred and that the soldiers had to remain prepared for any eventuality.
Field intelligence lessons from Lebanon and Jordan
‘N.’ has also been involved in field intelligence operations relating to Lebanon and Jordan.
‘R.’ described the challenges of gathering intelligence on Hezbollah in Lebanon, noting that the group operates differently from other adversaries.
“Hezbollah is a different organization and it uses different tools and methods. We use different tools and methods [against them],” she said.
‘R.’ added that her unit had been heavily involved in Lebanon during the IDF’s early 2026 invasion, describing the work as more intense in some respects than intelligence collection along a relatively quiet border.
Female combat soldiers still face resistance in the IDF
Asked about serving as a woman in a combat role, ‘N.’ said she had wanted to become a combat soldier since childhood.
“Even as a child, I always wanted to be a combat fighter, so no one was surprised that I went into combat,” she said. “Now I think that the biggest contribution female combat fighters can make is in intelligence collection. I really believe in what I and we are doing.”
‘N.’ said that while her own company was supportive, she had encountered resistance outside the unit.
“My company knows how to deal with this, but I had experiences outside my unit which were not the nicest,” she said.
“There are still both men and women who do not accept this, especially reservists who do not love it. I explained it to them, but we still have a long way to go,” she added.
In some cases, she said, she had managed to reach a “tie” with people who were initially opposed to women serving in combat roles, even if they had not fully changed their views.
‘N.’ said she had generally been admitted to the IDF bases she visited, but there had been occasions when soldiers refused to let her and her fellow soldiers stay overnight because the bases lacked separate sleeping quarters or bathrooms for women.
“It depends on who is the commander and what kind of unit is there at the time,” she said.
‘R.’ said women could perform some tasks as well as men, and in some cases better, pointing to their attention to detail and patience.
“Some things are the same and some things we can do better [than men]. The day-to-day work is less physical,” she said.
Like ‘N.’, ‘R.’ said she generally received cooperation from other IDF bases, although acceptance from male counterparts sometimes depended on the commander in charge.
At higher levels, including the battalion and brigade commands, she said, the unit enjoyed full support because senior officers understood its contribution.
“They understand what we bring to the table,” she said.
‘R.’ recalled an instance in which someone who had initially been skeptical of her role later recognized its value when he needed her help.
“Hopefully, once someone was not excited about me [being a female soldier], but then a week later, he needed me to find something,” she said, describing how their relationship improved.
Such experiences, she added, motivated the soldiers to work harder and demonstrate their capabilities.
“It just motivates us to work harder and in the end we get results,” she said.
The two female soldiers were divided on whether they were ready to see a woman become IDF chief of staff.
‘O.’, meanwhile, said he judged soldiers by their ability to carry out their missions, regardless of gender.
“I expect the same thing from female and male combat soldiers. I do not say a mission is for men or for women. It can be either one for any given mission,” he said.
“We need to remember we are all working toward the same goal: to defend the citizenry – whether a man or a woman doesn’t matter,” he concluded.

jean prouvé’s 1944 demountable house becomes japanese tea pavilion in paris
presented in the garden of the hôtel de maisons, the 1944 prefabricated structure brings together postwar architectural experimentation and a new interpretation of japanese tea culture.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
galerie patrick seguin brings prouvé’s 6×6 house to paris
For this year’s Design Miami.Paris, Galerie Patrick Seguin presents Jean Prouvé’s 6×6 Demountable House (1944) in the garden of the Hôtel de Maisons, as part of Design at Large. Originally conceived as emergency housing for families displaced by World War II, the prefabricated structure reflects Prouvé’s approach to industrialized construction and combines a lightweight steel frame with standardized wooden panels. For the Paris presentation, the gallery reinterprets the interior of the residence as a space inspired by the chashitsu, the traditional Japanese tea pavilion, bringing Prouvé’s architectural principles into dialogue with Japanese culture.
a demountable house designed for postwar reconstruction
Prouvé developed the 6×6 Demountable House in response to an urgent housing shortage in France at the end of World War II. Commissioned to design temporary homes for displaced families in Lorraine and Franche-Comté, he sought a construction system that could be manufactured economically, assembled quickly, and dismantled for relocation when necessary. The house measures six by six meters, a compact footprint intended to accommodate three rooms. Its design allowed families to move in as soon as assembly was complete, without having to wait for permanent reconstruction to finish. The structure builds on his patented axial portal frame, which organizes the house around a bent steel skeleton. Standardized wooden panels fit into the frame, while a roof of bitumen-coated building paper completes the enclosure. With steel subject to strict quotas in postwar France, reserving the material for the primary structure responded to the practical constraints of reconstruction.
Prouvé designed the house to provide shelter quickly, but he also saw potential in the construction method beyond the immediate postwar crisis. The steel frame and wooden panels could be assembled and taken apart with ease, and he hoped the same approach would eventually be used to build permanent homes. At Design Miami.Paris, the presentation by Galerie Patrick Seguin offers an opportunity to revisit these ideas in the setting of the Hôtel de Maisons’s garden. A structure developed for postwar housing is brought into the context of a design event, while the new interior concept introduces another layer to its interpretation.
project info:
 name: 6×6 Demountable House
architect and designer: Jean Prouvé
year: 1944
presentation: Design Miami.Paris | @designmiami, Design at Large

location: Hôtel de Maisons, Paris, France

What States Make of Military Exercises: Ulchi and Beyond
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:42:00 UTC
23:42:00 KST

Just before the South Korea-U.S. Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise began in mid-August, U.S. President Donald Trump ordered a substantial reduction in its scale. Describing the drills as “costly” and an “inappropriate and hostile” signal to North Korea – a state he termed “unthreatening and respectful” – Trump also criticized what he described as Seoul’s lack of support for U.S. operations against Iran.
Trump’s sudden decision raised concerns about South Korea-U.S. defense readiness, alliance reliability, and Washington’s wider commitment to Asia. Several analysts warned that reducing exercises could weaken deterrence and alliance coordination, while others questioned whether the move would secure reciprocal restraint from Pyongyang. Such concerns are understandable: joint military exercises are a visible manifestation of the South Korea-U.S. defense commitment, while North Korea routinely denounces them as rehearsals for war.
The reduction alone, however, does not carry a single, self-evident political meaning. U.S. commanders have since emphasized that other combined training continues and proposed changes to its frequency and geographic distribution. How audiences interpret these changes depends on the wider pattern of cooperation, established relationships, and political context.
Scale, Scope, and Strategic Meaning
Joint military exercises can serve two different but complementary strategic functions. They demonstrate capability and resolve to deter adversaries, but exercises also facilitate defense diplomacy. Repeated military cooperation can help build predictability, trust, interoperability, and institutionalized relationships among participants.
Our research suggests that an exercise’s scale and scope alone cannot reliably distinguish between these functions. Deterrence and defense diplomacy often generate the same observable characteristics, making it difficult to determine where one ends and the other begins simply by examining an exercise’s material features.
Larger and more complex exercises – featuring tens of thousands of troops, sophisticated command-and-control systems, live-fire maneuvers, and complex scenarios – can demonstrate greater warfighting capability and resolve to deter. At the same time, however, those same characteristics may instead reflect years of accumulated defense cooperation and deeper levels of trust and institutional integration between the participating militaries. Their material features reveal what militaries practice and provide evidence of their capabilities but cannot by themselves establish the political messages governments intend or how different audiences will interpret them. Rather, as a political signal, joint military exercises ultimately depend on what participating states and other audiences make of them.
Different audiences will not necessarily derive the same meaning from the same exercise. Washington might intend a reduction in Ulchi as restraint toward Pyongyang, while North Korea might interpret it as a concession, Seoul as uncertainty over U.S. commitment to the bilateral alliance, and Beijing as evidence of Washington’s transactional approach to alliance management. Established relationships and political contexts are therefore essential to interpreting an exercise’s strategic meaning.
Instead, established relationships and political contexts are more important in determining the strategic meaning of exercises than scale and scope alone. The history of Ulchi itself illustrates this.
Ulchi’s scale and scope have seldom increased in tandem with the danger from North Korea. This divergence is significant. If Ulchi’s scale simply tracked the North Korean military threat, as one would expect for greater deterrence, participation should have risen relatively consistently alongside Pyongyang’s expanding nuclear and missile capabilities. Instead, exercise participation has repeatedly risen and fallen according to changes in the diplomatic environment. Participation declined during periods associated with the Six-Party Talks and suspended altogether to facilitate diplomacy with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in Trump’s first term.
The scale of South Korean participation also reflects domestic politics. According to publicly available data, South Korean troop numbers were generally lower under the progressive administrations of Kim Dae-jung and Roh Moo-hyun, increased substantially under conservative presidents Lee Myung-bak and Park Geun-hye, and were again affected by diplomatic engagement under Moon Jae-in. These patterns are consistent with progressive administrations’ greater emphasis on creating diplomatic space for negotiations with the North and conservative administrations’ stronger emphasis on deterrence and alliance cohesion.
Trump’s decision should therefore be understood within this broader political context. Indeed, his own explanations identified several purposes for the same reduction: reducing costs, signaling restraint toward North Korea, and expressing dissatisfaction with Seoul over Iran. The reduction’s material features cannot establish which purpose predominates or how different audiences will interpret it.
Interpreting the Wider Exercise Program
Recent developments illustrate why Ulchi’s reduction should also be understood within the wider pattern of South Korea-U.S. military cooperation. In an interview with the Financial Times, U.S. Army Pacific commander General Ronald Clark emphasized both displaying military capabilities to influence adversaries’ calculations and strengthening military partnerships. His account illustrates how the two functions can reinforce one another: military partnerships help sustain the access and cooperation through which forces demonstrate capability and resolve.
South Korea-U.S. cooperation has continued despite the reduction in Ulchi. Eighth Army commander Lieutenant General Joe Hilbert clarified that other combined training continued, although some activities affected by Trump’s order were conducted by South Korean forces alone. Continued trilateral training through Freedom Edge and South Korea’s observer participation in Keen Sword also demonstrate different forms of military engagement. Observation offers opportunities for familiarity and relationship building without active participation in training. These activities do not cancel out Ulchi’s reduction, but they complicate its interpretation as a broader withdrawal from military cooperation.
Exercise design can also change in response to operational requirements. U.S. Forces Korea commander General Xavier Brunson has proposed more frequent training and geographically dispersed operations, drawing lessons from Ukraine about the vulnerability of concentrated command posts. He suggested the possibility of expanding the scope of exercises from Jeju Island to Gyeonggi Province, while also adjusting the training schedule to include additional smaller-scale drills between the two large annual exercises, Freedom Shield and Ulchi Freedom Shield. Frequency, geographic reach, and the concentration of forces need not change together. Thus, the size of a single exercise therefore provides an incomplete picture of the training program. Whether audiences interpret such changes as reinforcing alliance commitments or altering priorities depends on their political context.
Reducing Ulchi or cancelling a single amphibious exercise does not erase South Korea-U.S. warfighting capability. The institutional defense relationship between the two militaries established over decades – combined command structures, joint planning, interoperability, established procedures, and accumulated experience and “muscle memory” – remains in place. None of this is to suggest that exercises are irrelevant to preparedness; repeated reductions or cancellations over an extended period could eventually erode South Korea-U.S. interoperability and combined warfighting effectiveness. The effects, however, would be cumulative rather than instantaneous. A reduction or cancellation of a single iteration should not be conflated with the disappearance of capabilities built through decades of combined training.
Exercise scale and scope matter, but their strategic meaning is neither fixed nor self-evident. Rather than asking simply whether the United States is exercising more or less and with whom, the more pertinent questions are what particular exercises are intended to accomplish and how Seoul, Tokyo, Washington, Pyongyang, Beijing and other regional audiences interpret them. The deterrent or diplomatic value of an exercise ultimately lies not simply in how many troops participate, but in the political meaning that states attach to their participation – or absence.

Discussing grain initiatives without Russia is pointless, Global South nations agree — MFA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:39:52 UTC
23:39:52 KST

ROME, October 23. /TASS/. International partners within UN forums acknowledge that Black Sea grain initiatives are futile without Russia’s participation and the resolution of the root causes of the conflict in Ukraine, Kirill Logvinov, Director of the Department of International Organizations at the Russian Foreign Ministry, has told the media.
"Our partners from the Global South recognize that discussing any Black Sea Grain Initiative 2.0 without Russia’s participation and without addressing the root causes of the conflict in Ukraine is a dead end," he said after attending a meeting of the Committee on World Food Security at the Rome headquarters of the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO).
Logvinov pointed out that the current situation in the Black Sea is a consequence of actions taken by Kiev, as well as the large-scale military and financial support that the Kiev regime receives from the West. "What is happening must be viewed in a broader historical context, rather than plucking individual events out of the overall picture to use them for yet another political campaign involving sweeping accusations against Russia," he noted.
The Russian Foreign Ministry hopes that the FAO is capable of providing an objective assessment; the organization "should not turn into a platform for issuing 'political verdicts' or become involved in any political games."
"Its task is to provide an objective assessment of the state of food systems and to foster international cooperation in the development of sustainable agriculture. Therefore, Russia has an interest in seeing the FAO remain guided by the goals and objectives enshrined in its founding documents, and in ensuring it acts impartially and objectively. Only through such an approach can the Organization remain effective," Logvinov concluded.
The Russian side holds Ukraine and the UN responsible for the collapse of the "grain deal" - which remained in effect until July 2023 - stating that they failed to fulfill their respective obligations. Meanwhile, Russia continues to meet its own commitments, accounting for 26% of global wheat exports alone and supplying agricultural products to 160 countries.
FAO assessment
As FAO Chief Economist Maximo Torero noted during an event on the impact of the situation in the Black Sea on global food security - held as part of the World Food Forum - the challenges in the Black Sea region represent only one, and not necessarily the most significant, factor threatening food security. He pointed out that the observed price increases and instability are driven by geopolitical conflicts, funding cuts, and extreme weather events.
"In countries dependent on wheat from the Black Sea, there has been no deterioration in the food situation beyond average levels; however, a number of food-importing nations remain potentially vulnerable and require close monitoring," he said.
Earlier, Russian President Vladimir Putin explained that the Russian strikes on Ukrainian ports and export routes were a response to Ukraine’s attempts - beginning in the summer of this year - to target Russian oil refineries and vessels in the Black and Azov Seas. He emphasized that the Ukrainian armed forces of Ukraine had attempted to organize a naval blockade of the Black Sea coast, damaging over 100 Russian and foreign vessels.
