Finland gives Ukraine 10 diesel locomotives that keep trains running when Russian strikes cut the power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:38:22 UTC
23:38:22 KST

Finland will donate diesel locomotives to Ukraine’s state railway, the Office of Ukraine’s President reported. Helsinki also pledged new winter aid, and the two countries signed deals on drones, housing, and satellite communications during Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo’s visit to Kyiv. One of them is a first step toward a satellite link Ukraine would control itself.
With Russia replacing its missiles as fast as it fires them, Ukraine heads into winter needing equipment that works without the grid. Russian strikes have damaged or destroyed almost 600 locomotives of Ukraine’s state railway since the full-scale invasion began, more than 300 of them diesels, the infrastructure minister said. The attacks have reached engines even near the Polish border, on the railway that carries Ukraine’s evacuations, grain, and cargo.
Diesels that keep moving when the grid goes down
Finland will hand 10 locomotives and their spare parts to Ukrzaliznytsia, Ukraine’s state railway, free of charge. Infrastructure Minister Mykola Kalashnyk announced the deal, signed on 22 October at a Ukrainian-Finnish business forum. The engines need no power from overhead lines, so trains can keep running during blackouts.
The engines are Dv12 diesels that VR, Finland’s state rail company, is taking out of service. A VR shareholders’ meeting moved them into state ownership, and the Finnish state is donating them, Yle reported. VR puts their value, spare parts included, at about €2.1 million. Finland’s government said the gift will not affect VR’s ability to run trains at home.
Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi and Orpo signed the donation certificate, one of seven documents signed that day. Two others plan Ukrainian-Finnish drone production in Finland, one for military and dual-use systems and one for heavy drones. Another covers a precast concrete plant for industrial housing construction.
The day’s agreements are worth around €300 million in total, Zelenskyy said. Projects worth €200 million are already under way within the two countries’ Drone Deal, he added. Under an earlier plan, most drones made in Finland would go to Ukraine.
Finland backs €28.5 million power plant project as Ukraine braces for Russia’s next winter energy assault
Winter money now, a 36th military package by year’s end
Orpo announced a new €10 million package. Of it, €5 million goes to the Ukraine Energy Support Fund and €2 million to humanitarian aid for winter. The last €3 million goes to the Ukraine Recovery Program, for energy and water supply. Finland will also deliver mobile heating containers by December.
Finland has given Ukraine five defense packages this year, worth more than €500 million combined, Militarnyi reported. A 36th package is being prepared together with Ukraine’s military. “We plan to make a decision by the end of this year,” Orpo said. In September, Finland approved a package worth about €290 million.
A satellite link Ukraine would own
Ukraine’s Defense Ministry signed a letter of intent with Finnish satellite firm ICEYE and telecom company Nokia, Militarnyi reported, citing ICEYE. The parties will explore building a secure satellite communications system under Ukraine’s control. The aim is to reduce Ukraine’s dependence on foreign commercial operators.
In this model, the state customer owns the satellites, ground stations, and user terminals, RBC-Ukraine reported. The network could serve defense, border protection, emergency services, and disaster recovery. The letter sets out no timeline or funding.
“Modern warfare has proven that reliable communications are a matter of national security,” Zelenskyy said in the companies’ statement. ICEYE CEO Rafal Modrzewski said Ukraine needs “secure, sovereign and high-performance satellite communications systems that it controls.”
The deal comes after a speed cap on Starlink disrupted Ukrainian drone missions this month. The EU, meanwhile, is pushing three European firms to merge into one SpaceX rival. ICEYE has supplied Ukraine with radar satellite imagery for years.
Days before the signing, tracking firm LeoLabs said a Russian government-owned satellite, Cosmos 2612, had spent weeks shadowing an ICEYE radar satellite, coming within 500 meters. The ICEYE satellite is widely believed to provide imagery to Ukraine.
Neither fix is quick. Ukraine’s big locomotive order arrives from 2027, and the first satellites of the ICEYE-Nokia system are expected to launch only in 2028.

UN rights chief 'strongly' condemns surge in drone strikes across Sudan
Unknown

2026-10-23

Beyza Binnur Donmez
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
UN human rights chief Volker Turk on Friday "strongly" condemned the escalation of drone attacks across Sudan, which have killed at least 306 people and injured hundreds more in the first three weeks of October.
"The increasing use of drones, already accounting for the majority of conflict-related civilian deaths in Sudan this year, is deeply disturbing and is exacting a horrifying toll," Turk said.
“Scores of civilians have been killed and vital infrastructure and services on which they depend eviscerated, driving further displacement and deepening the already severe humanitarian crisis,” he said, reiterating his call on the parties to the conflict to respect their obligations under international law.
Turk said his office had documented strikes attributed to both the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), affecting residential buildings, marketplaces, medical facilities, shelters for displaced people and essential infrastructure.
The office cited recent attacks, including alleged SAF drone strikes on displacement shelters in West Kordofan between Oct. 6 and 10 that killed at least 25 civilians, an alleged RSF strike near a displacement site in Blue Nile on Oct. 9 that killed at least 31 people, and a repeated strike on a transport truck in West Kordofan on Oct. 18 that left at least 139 dead.
Turk urged both parties to comply with international humanitarian law, protect civilians and agree to a ceasefire.
He also called for an end to arms transfers contributing to violations, and stressed that a negotiated settlement centered on human rights and accountability was essential for sustainable peace. The civil war in Sudan has continued since 2023 and has led to one of the world's worst humanitarian disasters.

Life’s paths meet at the starting line – three stories from the Sofia Marathon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23

Author
Sevda Dukanci
News
Life’s paths meet at the starting line – three stories from the Sofia Marathon
Shivan Ibrahim from Syria: “I ran this marathon with a smile because I’m in a free country that has given me everything”
Friday 23 October 2026 16:05
Friday, 23 October 2026, 16:05
PHOTO Personal Archive
Font size
Since its first edition in 1983, the Sofia Marathon has become one of the capital’s major sporting events. In 2026, it brought runners together for the 43rd time, once again showing how sport can unite people across borders and differences. More than 12,000 participants from 70 countries took part in an event that is much more than a race for a better time or a test of endurance and willpower. It is a place to meet and connect, where people from different countries, speaking different languages and practising different religions, stand shoulder to shoulder at the starting line.
After the finish, the marathon of life goes on
The Sofia Marathon reminds us that sport is not just about competing. It is also about being together, helping one another and discovering what connects us as people. Once the race is over, the marathon of life continues, with its difficulties, trials and unexpected turns. Sevda Dyukyandzhi introduces us to three participants from very different places and with different interests, who share a passion for sport.
Shivan Ibrahim, Shaban Mustafa and Desislava Pavlova.
PHOTO Radio Bulgaria
Shivan Ibrahim: “Bulgaria is like a mother to me. I love it dearly!”
Shivan Ibrahim arrived in Bulgaria in 2011, crossing borders illegally on his journey from Syria through Türkiye. He spent years without legal status, moving between refugee camps, before his determination and perseverance helped him find his place in Bulgarian society and gain citizenship. The hardships of life as an undocumented migrant are now behind him. Shivan still runs, but these days, as he puts it, “along the same course as everyone else, in a free country, smiling and positive”.
Today, the refugee from Syria is a proud Bulgarian citizen with an established career and two children.
“It was an incredible feeling. We were smiling and full of energy. For us, winning wasn’t about coming first. It was about being together, supporting one another and running together.”
This is the power of sport to bring people together, regardless of age, gender, ethnicity or religion.
“There were so many people. All the time, you could hear different languages and talk to all sorts of people. We were like one body, running along the course together. It didn’t matter who anyone was – young or old. There were disadvantaged people, people from all walks of life. What mattered most was that we were all human,” says Shivan, whose own journey has been far from easy.
Shivan Ibrahim, right.
PHOTO Personal archive
“My journey was a marathon too, but a different kind – a hard one, with a lot of stress and so many doors closed to me. That part of my life was a marathon: fleeing a country at war, passing through several countries and finally reaching a real marathon here in Bulgaria, where you run freely, because you want to! You’re not running from war or escaping something bad and dangerous. Here, you feel you’re really running. Perhaps what matters is to overcome your own limits and take part. To take part because you want to, with love,” says Shivan, who now proudly recites lines every Bulgarian grows up with:
“I am a Bulgarian child and I love
our green mountains!
“I always say it, and I’m proud of it. Bulgaria has given me everything!
“I ran this marathon smiling and full of energy because I know I’m in a free country, a country that has given me everything. If Bulgaria were a person, I’d hug her, kiss her on the head and say: thank you for what you’ve given me!” he says with emotion.
“For me, Bulgaria is like a mother. I love Bulgaria dearly! I can say I love Bulgaria more than Syria, because Bulgaria has given me more than I had in Syria. I’m very grateful to this country.”
Desislava Pavlova
PHOTO Personal archive
Shaban Mustafa – second-fastest Bulgarian in the marathon with a time of 2:32:40, finishing 10th overall
Shaban Mustafa, from the village of Kosten, lives 300 kilometres from the capital. He works for Sungurlare Municipality, farms and tends his walnut trees. Despite his many commitments, he makes time to run early every morning and again in the evening.
“I won the marathon in 2012. I came first that year. But my greatest successes have been in mountain marathons. In 2015, I ran in one of the world’s most competitive and best-known mountain marathons. I finished fourth at the World Long Distance Mountain Running Championships, held at the Gornergrat Zermatt Marathon in Switzerland that year. I’m the only Bulgarian runner to have won the Jungfrau Marathon in Switzerland, also in 2015. I’m also a two-time world mountain running champion, in 2016 and 2023.”
Mustafa believes mass-participation events can encourage children and young people to take up sport. What does it take to get from a small Bulgarian village to the medal podium?
“Sport is good for the health of everyone who takes part. It teaches discipline and respect for others. Sport really does give you so much.
“That’s why I train twice a day, every day. The first thing I do in the morning is go for a run. Then, after work, I run again.”
Desislava Pavlova: “I’m happy to have improved on my previous performances”
Desislava Pavlova is a businesswoman from Sofia, and sport is an essential part of her daily life. For her, taking part in the capital’s biggest sporting event is a lesson in mutual support and determination.
“For me, running is much more than a sport. It’s a kind of therapy. It’s time to recharge, let go of tension and feel free and truly happy. This year’s Sofia Marathon left me with so many good memories and positive emotions. The atmosphere is incredible. It’s so inspiring to see so many people stepping outside their comfort zones and proving, above all to themselves, just how much they can do.”
The marathon may be a race, but it also brings people together.
PHOTO Personal archive
“You can definitely feel people supporting one another. They become kinder, more courteous, more supportive,” says Desi, encouraging everyone to make time for sport.
“What matters is taking the first step,” says the mother of two, who tries to motivate those close to her to stay active.
And on the subject of motivation, we leave you with Shivan Ibrahim’s message to young people:
“Keep following your dreams. Keep thinking positively and stay full of energy. If you really want something, you can achieve it. 
“And love your country! The marathon gave me so much. This was a first moment of joy for me!”

The red-green alliance: How a union of Islamists and Marxists led Palestine to postpone its elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:34:06 UTC
23:34:06 KST

On Oct. 10, Palestinian "president" Mahmoud Abbas announced that parliamentary elections would be postponed. The vote, which had been scheduled for Nov. 28, will now be pushed back all the way to next September. If it takes place, the election will be the first since Hamas defeated Abbas's Fatah party at the polls all the way back in 2006. This time around, Fatah again feared the electoral appeal of the Islamist movement — especially after it managed to form an unprecedented alliance with Palestine's Marxists and liberal democrats.
In 1996, the inaugural elections to the Palestinian Legislative Council saw the moderate Fatah party take 50 of the parliament's 88 seats. The victory came at least in part thanks to the Islamist Hamas movement's choice to boycott the vote. However, in 2006, the next elections saw Hamas take 74 seats in the expanded 132-seat chamber, and the Council was disbanded in 2007 after an armed struggle for control over the Gaza Strip broke out between Fatah and Hamas. Power in Palestine has been divided ever since, with Hamas ruling over Gaza and Fatah retaining its authority in the West Bank.
Elections 2.0
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas of the Fatah party first officially announced new elections in 2021, but they never took place. Abbas said he had postponed the vote indefinitely because Israeli authorities had refused to allow polling stations to open in East Jerusalem, home to around 400,000 Palestinians. Abbas’s critics argued at the time that the president was simply afraid his party would suffer a crushing defeat to Hamas even if the moderates' allies in the Palestinian Liberation Organization (PLO) remained on side.
Nevertheless, even after more than two decades in power, not even Mahmoud Abbas can postpone elections indefinitely. The longer voting has been delayed, the more questions Palestine's foreign partners and donors have raised about the legitimacy of Abbas and his cabinet. Fatah was thus forced to announce parliamentary elections, to be followed several months later by a presidential vote.
The latest attempt to hold elections to choose a new Palestinian Legislative Council was scheduled for Nov. 28, 2026. The veteran Palestinian president appeared to have chosen an almost ideal moment for himself and his party: Hamas had been severely weakened by years of war with Israel in Gaza, and against this backdrop, support for the Islamist group plunged so far that Fatah had its first chance in years of winning a majority. Moreover, the local council elections held in April 2026, including in one municipality in the Gaza Strip, ended in a decisive victory for Fatah candidates. That big win, however, was made possible by the fact that the vote was held under rules devised by Fatah itself and approved by Abbas and his associates.
Against the backdrop of the war in Gaza, support for Hamas has collapsed, giving Fatah its first chance in years to win a majority of the Palestinian vote.
One condition for parties and blocs to participate in local elections was their formal endorsement of the Palestine Liberation Organization’s (PLO) official positions when it came to a peaceful resolution of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict involving the “coexistence” of two states side by side. Hamas and other Islamist groups have never accepted these terms and were therefore barred from participating in the elections. Fatah can certainly claim its victory as an achievement, but it is difficult to call it either fair or convincing.
The rules governing local elections were established by the Palestinian election commission, which is controlled by Abbas, and its judgements apply to all elections. In principle, then, Hamas and similar parties and groups could simply have been barred from the 2026 parliamentary vote as well.
Hamas is working on its own electoral list
However, Palestine’s foreign partners and donors — the United States, the Arab monarchies, and the European Union — repeatedly stressed that only elections involving all significant political forces can restore their confidence in the legitimacy of the Palestinian authorities. At the same time though, foreign governments openly say that Hamas must renounce violence and pursue Palestinian statehood exclusively through peaceful means if it is to return to mainstream politics, leaving Fatah some room to maneuver.
Formally, Hamas has become less radical since 2017, when its new charter declared the group's goal to be the establishment of an independent Arab state not across “all of historic Palestine,” but only within the borders of the Gaza Strip and the West Bank, which the UN recognizes as Palestinian territories. Yet the idea of seeking a peaceful resolution to the conflict with Israel— has still not become the dominant position among the radicals.
A shift to exclusively political methods of pursuing Palestinian independence is being discussed within Hamas as one way to save an organization severely weakened by the war, but no final decision has been made. This appeared to give Abbas's election commission a way to keep Hamas off of the ballot without losing the support of its foreign patrons, who also do not want to see militant thugs in parliament.
Hamas’s strange allies
Yet it seems the "Palestinian street" was less susceptible to such arguments as to why Hamas ought to be kept off the ballot, and the cautious, seasoned Abbas was unwilling to risk mass anti-government protests that could strip Fatah of its remaining levers of power. And so instead of holding pseudo-elections that excluded the most popular party, he chose to postpone the vote once again. The likely reason is that Hamas was already working hard to build a broad coalition of parties and movements willing to run on a joint list.
Cautious Abbas is unlikely to risk barring Hamas from the elections in the face of mass anti-government protests, and the radicals are working precisely toward that scenario
Foremost among the groups ready to back Hamas was Palestinian Islamic Jihad. Although the group isHamas’s closest ideological counterpart, it had never participated in elections and had shown utter contempt for attempts to negotiate a political settlement to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, regarding Israel’s destruction as the only possible path to an independent Palestine. True to its motto — “Islam, jihad, and Palestine” — Islamic Jihad had operated since its founding in the 1980s exclusively as a militant organization, not a political one.
But after a long, exhausting war in Gaza that destroyed the core forces and most of the arsenals of both Hamas and Islamic Jihad, the latter now risks losing its influence altogether. Thousands of its fighters have been killed or fled abroad, along with many of its most experienced commanders and ideologues. In short, Islamic Jihad faced a choice: cling to its longstanding refusal to engage in politics and risk almost certain oblivion, or try to enter parliament, help form the Palestinian cabinet, and thereby survive.
Islamic Jihad is at least a logical ally for Hamas, given the two groups’ closely aligned militant Islamist ideologies. However, the Marxist Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP), a virtually atheistic organization, is a different matter altogether. For the Front’s members, the war against Israel is not religious, but rather part of a global struggle between imperialism and the nations resisting it. Inspired by Mao Zedong and the Vietnamese communists, PFLP members have never dismissed the importance of political means, but have regarded them as secondary to armed struggle.
Ideologically, PFLP was once much closer to secular Fatah, with which it remains affiliated through the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO). Inside the contentious tent of the PLO, however, the Front is the main opponent of Abbas’s party. The Marxists interpret the PLO's commitment to a peaceful resolution of the conflict differently from their Fatah partners, believing that armed struggle can work hand in hand with diplomacy. In this regard, at least, they are indeed closer to Hamas.
The Marxists believe that peace with Israel can be pursued alongside armed struggle for Palestinian independence, bringing them closer to the Islamists
The Islamist-Marxist bloc may have differing visions for Palestine’s future, but its members agree that Israel is the main obstacle to the creation of a truly independent Palestinian state. Fatah, meanwhile, is viewed as an outdated organization that abandoned violence and bet on a “peace process” that has demonstrably failed to deliver genuine Palestinian independence. A joint electoral list, had negotiations to form one succeeded, would therefore have been a natural extension of the longstanding cooperation between the leading Palestinian Marxist and Islamist factions.
The Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine (DFLP) takes a similar position — it remains a member of the PLO but favors Hamas’s methods over Fatah’s. Also Marxist, the DFLP spent years wavering between Fatah and Hamas before ultimately siding with the jihadists. It was reportedly among Hamas’s likely allies in the parliamentary elections.
Particularly noteworthy are potential coalition members that not only share Fatah’s ideological or historical roots but actually emerged from Palestine’s main party of compromise before switching sides to join its principal rival. One such group is the Popular Resistance Committees, founded by Fatah officials who became disillusioned with their party’s commitment to peaceful solutions and turned to radical Islam.
Hamas’s allies include former Fatah officials who grew disillusioned with the party’s pacifism and turned to radical Islam
The most revealing case, however, is that of the Democratic Reform Bloc, led by former Fatah Central Committee member Mohammed Dahlan. In the 1990s, he belonged to the inner circle of Fatah founder Yasser Arafat and headed the party’s branch in the Gaza Strip. He ran it like his personal fiefdom, earning the region the nickname “Dahlanistan.”
In 2007, Hamas seized control of Gaza and drove Dahlan out. He held various posts in the Palestinian government under Abbas for several more years, but Abbas eventually ousted him too, accusing him of murdering Arafat, whose death is officially considered to have been the result of natural causes. Dahlan now divides his time between the United Arab Emirates and Serbia, where he became a citizen in the 2010s. He remains popular in Gaza and is so eager to return to Palestinian politics that he is prepared to forge an alliance with Hamas, which until relatively recently was his chief enemy.
Dahlan’s bloc, incidentally, is the only one of the groups mentioned above that does not appear on the lists of terrorist organizations maintained by Israel, the United States, or the European Union.
What about Israel?
This raises an obvious question: why would Israel, which controls virtually all lawful political activity in the Palestinian territories, allow a bloc of parties and organizations designated as terrorists to participate in elections? Why not simply block the vote if Abbas changes the rules to allow the Hamas-led coalition onto the ballot? Alternatively, why not prevent the elected parliament from functioning properly by arresting or otherwise removing the most notorious Palestinian lawmakers?
There were surely people in the Israeli government who considered these options. But they could hardly ignore the fact that Israel’s rejection of the previous Palestinian elections, held in 2006, had contributed to the current war in Gaza. At the time, Israel did everything it could to prevent a parliament dominated by Hamas from exercising its legislative powers, and the radicals responded by discarding parliamentary norms and simply seizing power in Gaza, killing or driving out hundreds of their opponents. One obvious way to prevent a repeat of this scenario is to bring Islamists into nonviolent politics and demonstrate that parliamentary methods can deliver better results than bombs and guns.
One obvious way to prevent a repeat of the massacre Hamas carried out in Gaza is to bring Islamists into nonviolent politics
Arab countries, too, expected both Abbas and Israel to allow the broad opposition coalition to participate in the elections. Abbas quite literally depends on these Arab partners for his survival, as without their financial backing and diplomatic support, his administration is doomed. Israel, of course, is in a stronger position, but Donald Trump has already included the Israel-Hamas conflict on his list of wars he claims to have personally ended. He could threaten the Israeli government by withholding military and financial aid unless it made certain concessions.
In short, had these disparate forces been allowed to contest the Palestinian elections, a broad coalition of Islamists, Marxists, and defectors might well have taken power. Its members would have been ready to set aside their longstanding grievances against one another simply to oust the thoroughly discredited Fatah and its long-serving leader, Mahmoud Abbas.
With time running out, Abbas decided not to take the risk. Most likely, he secured at least Israel’s agreement regarding the postponement. But although much can change between now and next September, it is hard to imagine Fatah's electoral prospects dramatically improving anytime soon.

Ukraine has engaged an international adviser for the sale of Ukrgasbank and Sense Bank — what the company is known for
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
17:33:23 EEST
23:33:23 KST

Ukraine has engaged an international adviser for the sale of Ukrgasbank and Sense Bank — what the company is known for
Kyiv • UNN
The Ministry of Finance has engaged Rothschild & Co and FinPoint to prepare the sale of stakes in Ukrgasbank and Sense Bank. The banks' owners are not changing for now.
The Ministry of Finance of Ukraine, JSC Ukrgasbank, JSC Sense Bank and N. M. Rothschild & Sons Limited, part of the Rothschild & Co group, have signed tripartite agreements for financial advisory services in preparation for the sale of the state-owned shareholdings in the two banks, UNN reports, citing the Ministry of Finance.
Details
According to the ministry, Rothschild & Co was selected following a competitive selection process. The group has many years of experience advising governments and state-owned companies, participating in privatization projects, and supporting international mergers and acquisitions. Rothschild & Co will provide services in a consortium with FinPoint, a Ukrainian investment banking company.
Under the agreements, the adviser will provide comprehensive financial advice, including:
-  coordinate an analysis of the banks’ activities (due diligence), including for the purpose of determining the initial sale price; 
-  prepare information about the banks for potential investors; 
-  represent the banks on the international market and attract investors; 
-  facilitate the organization of a tender for the sale of the shareholdings. 
Engaging a financial adviser is one of the key stages in preparing for privatization provided for by the Law of Ukraine "On the Specifics of the Sale of Shareholdings Owned by the State in the Authorized Capital of Banks".
"Engaging an international financial adviser is an important step in implementing the strategy of reducing the state’s share in the banking sector. Our task is to ensure a transparent, competitive process for selling the state-owned shareholdings in Ukrgasbank and Sense Bank, attract strategic investors, and create conditions for the further development of these institutions," said Minister of Finance of Ukraine Serhii Marchenko.
The signing of agreements with the financial adviser is a step in preparing for privatization and does not mean a change in the ownership of the banks. Ukrgasbank and Sense Bank are operating as usual, fulfilling their obligations to customers, including under deposits, and ensuring the continuity of banking services. The banks will provide information about the next steps in preparing for privatization on their official websites.
Reference
N. M. Rothschild & Sons Limited is a company of the Rothschild & Co group, registered in England and Wales, with its head office in London. It specializes in financial advisory, corporate finance, and support for mergers and acquisitions (M&A) transactions.
We remind you that on October 1, 2025, the Government adopted an order on preparing for the sale of the state-owned shareholdings in Sense Bank and Ukrgasbank; on October 29, 2025, it approved the Procedure for Engaging an Adviser for the Sale of Shareholdings in State-Sector Banks; and on March 31, 2026, the Ministry of Finance announced a tender to select an adviser for the sale of the shareholdings in the two banks. The Government also established a commission for the sale of state-owned shareholdings in banks.

We’re teenage girls fighting to ban the use of school uniform in porn. Why have you left it up to us? | Rose, Mae, Aylin and Willow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:33:05 UTC
23:33:05 KST

In the Little Feminist Book Club, we don’t read a lot of books. The group, set up by former students at our school, is more about reading poems and articles, analysing song lyrics, discussing the issues that matter to us and, most importantly, campaigning.
Our current campaign – the one you might have heard of – is to ban school uniform from pornographic content. Simply put, we want to end the depiction of school uniform in pornography to ensure that minors are not viewed as anything other than what they are: children. We were shocked when we realised that this content is currently legal – most of the adults we’ve spoken to agree that it is wrong. But apparently it falls to us – students aged 14 and 15 – to take action.
A new law, due to come into force on 6 November, will ban pornography that shows sexual activity involving anyone pretending to be under 16. But it won’t outlaw the depiction of adults dressed as older schoolchildren. We want to remove this grey area in order to stop normalising the sexualisation of school uniforms. We believe children and children’s clothing should not be associated with sexual acts. Therefore, we believe that school uniform should not be shown as something “sexy”, regardless of the actual age of the person wearing it.
Previous members of the Little Feminist Book Club, working with Tools for Change, successfully campaigned for better access to period products in our school. We then heard about another school feminist group who had campaigned to get school uniforms banned from sex shops. We were appalled that they were being sold in that context, yet somehow not surprised. From an early age, some of us had noticed that school uniforms are depicted in ways that sexualise women wearing them. Mae recalls: “For me it started when I was 12, watching TV with my mother. A female character put on a school uniform to turn on a man and I thought, ‘I’m going to have to wear a uniform like that tomorrow.’”
No 12-year-old should feel uncomfortable about going to school in a uniform that is designed to promote unity and community and safety. Yet we did. It made us question how we would be perceived when we left the house in our uniforms. These were women dressing up in school uniform specifically to turn on a man. The only people who should be wearing school uniform are children.
This issue has affected us personally. Members of our group feel too uncomfortable to wear their uniform out of school. One no longer wears skirts at all. When we were asked to speak at a Tools for Change event in parliament in July we unanimously agreed not to wear our uniform. In a world of AI, we were well aware of the dangers of being photographed in uniform while being associated with this campaign. Before we sent our first letters to MPs and charities, we discussed what it might mean if anyone actually paid attention to what we were saying. Would we be prepared to take this on, given all that it might mean? We were, and so we did.
Since starting this campaign, we have been flooded with support. Sadly, this has included other women and girls sharing their experiences of the same issue – dating back generations. Surveys show that one in three girls has been sexually harassed while wearing school uniform, and we have seen comments from many of them. Older women said that they have never been catcalled more than when they wore school uniform as children; others have shared with us their feelings of disgust and horror. One recalled being assaulted by a group of men in the 2000s “explicitly because of my school uniform”. A teenager said that the number of older men who sexually harass her almost every day is “uncountable”.
Getting to hear people’s own personal experiences fuels our passion and drives us forward. The overwhelmingly positive response truly gives us hope that we can make a difference. We want to protect children now and in the future.
As the campaign continues to gain attention, we have received support from important figures including our local MP and an MSP. One has agreed to directly pass our handwritten letter to the prime minister, Andy Burnham, and to table an early day motion. We now also have a meeting scheduled with Alex Davies-Jones, the minister for victims, and another with Jess Asato MP and the peer Gabby Bertin, who was instrumental in the amendments to the crime and policing bill. Our MP is helping us turn our campaign into a law. He suggested that, instead of creating an entirely new law banning school uniform in pornography, it would be quicker and easier to amend existing legislation – meaning that it would take less time for children to be taken out of this harmful and dangerous position that perverted people have placed us in. But these are not decisions we can make. Everyone has a responsibility to end this cycle of sexualisation and objectification of children. We can’t do that as a few kids in the middle of our GCSEs.
We have made a start by launching this petition. Now, we need the adults who vowed to protect us to get behind it. We need the politicians who pledged to halve violence against women and girls to change the law. It’s all well and good to read this article by a group of kids explaining how we’re trying to keep ourselves safe and think this is a fantastic campaign. But that’s not enough. Things will only change when adults take responsibility for ending the disgusting practice of sexualising clothes made for children. Then perhaps one day young people can go to school knowing the only thing our uniforms signify is that it’s time to learn.
- Rose, Mae, Aylin and Willow are students aged 14 and 15

First Russian diesel from Putin-Trump deal heading for US, data shows
- First Russian diesel under a Putin-Trump deal is heading to the US on the Agioi Fanendes, with 40,000 tonnes loaded in Primorsk and due in New York on Nov 7.
- Trump made the deal to cut diesel prices before the Nov 3 mid-term elections, waived parts of a new Russia sanctions law, and promised more Russian exports.
- Russia has resumed wider diesel exports after lifting its own ban, with more shipments planned to the US and traditional buyers such as Turkey and Brazil, Reuters said.
AI generated
The first Russian diesel bound for the US following a surprise agreement reached between Moscow and US President Donald Trump is on board a tanker heading to New York, ship-tracking data showed on Oct 23.
Trump announced the deal in October as part of his efforts to bring down soaring diesel prices ahead of the Nov 3 US midterm elections.
Trump also waived parts of a new US sanctions law against Russia and threatened Europe with a US diesel export ban unless countries released more from their emergency reserves to help ease prices.
The Malta-flagged medium-sized tanker Agioi Fanendes loaded 40,000 tonnes of ultra-low sulphur diesel at Russia’s Baltic port of Primorsk on Oct 22, according to LSEG shipping data. It is expected to arrive in the US on Nov 7.
The buyer and seller were not immediately known. The cargo would be the first to be imported by the US since former president Joe Biden announced a ban on US imports of Russian oil and petroleum products in 2022.
Trump announced on Oct 9 that Russia would immediately export 300,000 tonnes, or 2.25 million barrels, to the US and global markets, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and one million tonnes “immediately thereafter”.
A Kremlin spokesperson confirmed on Oct 23 that the first ship under the deal had departed, but did not specify whether it was bound for the US market or elsewhere.
“As far as I'm aware, there have already been reports from the Ministry of Energy that the first tanker has, in fact, set sail for its recipients, its buyers. Further shipments will continue at a steady pace from here on,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said during a daily conference call.
The deal with the US involved Russia lifting its self-imposed ban on diesel exports.
Russia resuming global exports
Since the European Union imposed a full embargo on imports of Russian oil products in February 2023 over the war in Ukraine, Russia has exported diesel mainly to Turkey, Brazil and African countries.
It also supplies Central Asia by rail.
Shipping data from LSEG and Kpler published this week showed Russian diesel cargoes resuming voyages to their traditional destinations after Moscow lifted its own ban, with at least two tankers signalling trips to Turkey and Brazil.
It was unclear where other tankers were destined for, with cargoes loaded in Primorsk signalling Gibraltar, the Atlantic Coast or Port Said, LSEG data showed.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak has said that additional US shipments would follow as companies from the two countries work out the necessary contracts.
Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who also heads Russia’s sovereign wealth fund, said last week that the US Treasury had asked the fund to help sort out tricky payment issues relating to the agreement.
Novak has said Russia could increase its diesel exports to its usual level of three to 3.5 million tonnes a month by the end of 2026. REUTERS

‘I killed lots of terrorists, but it didn’t make me feel better’: The trauma haunting Israel's elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:32:07 UTC
23:32:07 KST

‘I killed lots of terrorists, but it didn’t make me feel better’: The trauma haunting Israel's elections
From our special correspondent in Tel Aviv – After more than three years of war, the number of Israeli soldiers suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder following bloody campaigns in Gaza and Lebanon has risen drastically. In the lead-up to Israel’s crucial legislative elections, FRANCE 24 speaks with soldiers left shell-shocked by the country’s wars.
The group of Israeli army veterans meets in the departures hall of Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion Airport. They’re anywhere from 20 to 50 years old, and glad to be back together. They hold one another, laughing, and slap each other on the back.
For a year now, these 18 men have come together to give them a chance to speak, and be heard, and to support one another. Accompanied by a team of psychologists, they are all living with varying degrees of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). At the invitation of donors who have funded the programme, they are all on their way to spend a week in New York.
Most of them have no interest in speaking to the media. But Lior Tapicer, a burly blond man with a broad grin, steps forward and lowers his voice.
“They’re all crazy, I love them,” he said. “They make me feel less crazy.”
He agrees to tell us his story – that of a young man traumatised by the Hamas-led attacks on October 7, 2023, and by months spent fighting alongside his combat unit, looking for revenge in the ruins of the Gaza Strip.
‘I could die at any second’
Twenty-nine years old, Tapicer has been discharged from the Israeli Defence Force (IDF) and is now working as a naturopath, he said. He says that the trauma that had made him unfit to keep going as an army reservist first took root in him during the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attacks.
As reports of the attacks on southern Israel spread, he joined his unit and rushed off to the kibbutzim near the border with the Gaza Strip, where combat with Hamas militants and other Palestinian fighters was still raging.
“They gave me an old rifle, I didn’t even have a combat helmet – we were driving in an open jeep,” he said. “The smell of burnt bodies was everywhere, there were bodies everywhere. It was scary as shit – I remember the feeling of being in my own country, and being afraid that I could die at any second.”
Read more‘I don't recognise the country I grew up in anymore’: Some Israelis tempted by exile
The nightmare dragged on into the next night.
“We went into a house – there was shooting, but we were staying silent so they didn’t know we were there”, he said in a detached voice. “And I entered one of the rooms and there was a baby bed, and it was all blood. I won’t describe it.”
A few days later, he entered the Palestinian territory with his combat unit. Having served as a soldier in the Israeli-occupied West Bank since he turned 18, he admits that he was burning for vengeance.
“They attacked us, murdered people, raped,” he said. “To be sincere, when I enlisted the first day, my mind and my body was like, ‘I’m going to kill as many as I can. I’m going to get revenge.’ That’s what I felt in the moment – a lot of hate.”
He broke after four months of fighting. One night, his comrades found him shaking uncontrollably, unable to stand. They decided to have him taken away from the front.
‘I didn’t recognise myself in the mirror’
Although Tapicer was back with his unit 10 days later, he slowly began to realise that his body refused to keep going.
After a few more months, he was declared unfit for service and returned to civilian life. But his mind and his body were still at war. He was wracked with guilt for having left his comrades, who were still fighting in the densely populated territory. He stopped his work as a personal trainer, and began avoiding his family and friends.
“I didn't recognise myself in the mirror,” he says. “I was half a man. My family, my girlfriend, my friends – you know what is to see somebody you love, and feel no love? You feel empty.”
While he says his symptoms have improved since he started treatment for PTSD, the trauma hasn’t left him. Loud noises, the smell of burning, fights with his girlfriend – many things can set off panic attacks, even if they are growing shorter and shorter.
Read moreIsrael marks three years since October 7 attacks with strikes on Gaza, political debate
According to Gaza’s health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israel’s onslaught in Gaza since the October 7 attacks. The Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel killed 1,220 people, with more than 970 Israeli soldiers dying in the subsequent wars launched in Gaza and Lebanon.
When asked about the human cost of Israel’s war in Gaza, Tapicer said that vengeance was a dead end.
“Today, I understand that it’s a problem you’re not going to solve like that. I killed a lot of terrorists and it didn’t make me feel better. It actually makes me feel worse.”
A heavy toll
Since October 7, the wars that Israel has carried out across the Middle East have taken a heavy toll on its soldiers. In January, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said that there had been a 40 percent increase in cases of PTSD among the army’s ranks since September 2023.
Of the more than 22,000 people treated for war-related injuries, 60 percent struggle with PTSD – a struggle that drives some to try to kill themselves. Last year, a Knesset report found that some 279 soldiers had tried to take their own lives between January 2024 and July 2025.
Last July, the Israeli parliament officially recognised “combat trauma” as a disability linked to service in the country’s armed forces, allowing impacted soldiers to benefit from state-funded treatment.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
In Afula in Israel’s north, the Clalit-HaEmek Medical Centre has been overwhelmed by a non-stop flow of patients suffering from severe psychiatric problems.
Psychiatric services director Alon Reshef said he believed the worst was yet to come.
“When the whole stress comes down, we will see a tsunami of people with all kinds of mental problems – and I think we’re on the verge of it,” he said.
“The waiting list for hospitalisation are getting longer and longer and longer. And not only that, but the cases that we meet are much more complex, much more severe. And it's not only PTSD. If you have a mental health problem, let's say depression or schizophrenia, it's also affected, because all these disorders react to what’s happening in society. The number of forced hospitalisations has risen dramatically. So all the signs show that the mental crisis is not only a problem of the practitioners like me or the patients, but a problem of society – and particularly among those soldiers who fought for a long time in Gaza.”
‘Society in Israel is ill’
Reshef hopes that whatever government emerges from the October 27 elections will take the issue of Israelis’ mental health seriously.
“Society in Israel is ill,” he said. “It has lots of vital powers, but right now it is sick. Too much hate, too many confrontations. And nobody listens to the other … It will take years to heal.”
His colleague, Ronen Sidi, has begun carrying out the experimental treatment of severe forms of PTSD with MDMA, more commonly known as ecstasy. By releasing serotonin and dopamine, this synthetic party drug can help patients work through their trauma, learning to live with the feelings that threaten to overwhelm them.
Sidi, a psychologist specialising in psychedelic treatments, said that the treatments were so far yielding positive results, noting a decrease in the intensity of his patients’ symptoms.
Trauma and resilience
Himself a former member of the special forces, Sidi is all too familiar with the trauma that can follow the savage acts that soldiers are often exposed to. But he said that an army’s cohesion in wartime stemmed first and foremost from the legitimacy of the government that sent it to fight.
“There's a lot of studies about PTSD, but there are also quite a few now about resilience,” he said. “What seems to have a lot to do with resilience is a sense of meaning – if you have a reason to do what you do, you can endure a lot of difficulty.”
For the Israeli reservists who have served for sometimes up to 600 days since the October 7 attacks – up from a baseline of 15 to 20 days a year – this point remains fundamental, he said.
“Three years after the October 7 attacks, and with a government that a lot of people don't agree with what they're doing, a lot more soldiers are saying, ‘I have to fight, it's hard – it might even be less hard than it was two and a half years ago – but what am I doing here? Where is this leading?"
‘I want to get better so I can keep serving my country’
In the port of Jaffa south of the sprawling city of Tel Aviv, Or is enjoying a few days of rest between two stretches of military service. A few months ago, the 32-year-old social worker asked to be treated for PTSD.
Serving as a medic in an infantry unit, he has taken part in several missions in war zones and racked up more than 400 days of military service since October 7. Beer in hand, he says, calmly enough, that he is starting to crack.
“It’s a very long war, every soldier has seen horrible things. Sometimes we feel hate. A few months ago, I asked to be treated for PTSD. Many of my friends are doing the same,” he said. “No one comes through three years of war unscathed. Like a lot of people, I feel in control when I’m in the army, but when I get home, I don’t feel well.”
Read moreHow Netanyahu survived the political fallout from the October 7 attacks
His request for treatment came after an experience that left him badly shaken. Four months ago, his combat unit was on patrol when they were surprised by Hamas fighters near a tunnel entrance. The resulting shootout killed one soldier and left several more wounded.
“It was horrible. People told me after that I was screaming, I had lost my mind,” he said. “The soldier who was killed had his face torn off, and it was me who put his body in a jeep. I did everything like a robot, but I remember images, smells.”
Since then, the young man has continued to undertake stretches of military service, but has been assigned to surveillance rather than frontline combat. He is also seeing a psychotherapist.
“I need to take care of myself. I need to get better so I can keep serving my country,” he said.
‘I don’t want to keep fighting wars’
Like many reservists, Or says that he no longer has confidence in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government and its conduct of the war. But as with many Israelis, fear of Hamas rides roughshod over all other considerations.
“I was shocked by the orders that I was given in Gaza, I didn’t think it was the right way to do things. But we had no other choice. We were scared. We knew that Hamas wanted to kill us all, whatever happened, because they hate us. I don’t agree with everything my country has done, especially against civilians, but it’s war,” he said.
“War is bad for Israeli society – it only encourages the extremists,” he added in a resigned tone.
Or doesn’t understand the hostility the rest of the world has towards Israel’s determination to raze the Gaza Strip to the ground, seeing the war in the narrow Palestinian territory as fundamentally defensive in nature. The social worker identifies as a left-wing voter, though he says that the October 7 attacks have shaken his convictions.
He says he hopes that the coming elections will bring about a government that has solutions to the problems facing Israel.
“I don’t want to keep fighting wars,” he said. “I often think that I’ve reached the limits of what I can endure. But they always ask more of me, and I’m able to push those limits back a little further.”

Exclusive: Ukraine fears Trump could grant Russia long-sought relief for fertilizer industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Exclusive: The next Russia deal Trump may be weighing after diesel
U.S. President Donald Trump looks on during an event in the Oval Office of the White House on Oct. 20, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
U.S. President Donald Trump may be considering further sanctions relief for Russia following his recent diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, several Ukrainian and U.S. officials familiar with the matter told the Kyiv Independent.
The potential move would fit an approach in which the Trump administration offers Russia economic benefits in hopes of persuading Moscow to end its war against Ukraine, one U.S. government official and one Senate official said.
Trump's diesel deal with Putin has drawn bipartisan criticism in Washington and strained relations with Kyiv. President Volodymyr Zelensky called the agreement a "weak move," warning that it could pave the way for further sanctions relief.
Now, Ukrainian officials fear the administration could explore a deal involving Russia's fertilizer industry, two people familiar with the matter said.
The U.S. has not directly sanctioned Russia's fertilizer industry or banned imports of Russian fertilizers. But any potential agreement could provide sanctions relief for vessels, companies, banks, and individuals linked to the industry, one senior Ukrainian official said.
Russia has long sought an ease of restrictions affecting its agricultural exports, arguing that banking, insurance, and shipping barriers have limited its access to markets.
Moscow raised the issue repeatedly during negotiations over the Black Sea Grain Initiative (BSGI) back in 2022, but Western governments maintained that Russian food and fertilizer exports were not directly sanctioned.
"The fertilizer story is quite old, and Russians were trying to push it long ago," a Ukrainian intelligence official told the Kyiv Independent.
"Russians always lobbied for fertilizer relief in contacts with Americans and Europeans," the official added. "They actually left BSGI because of no progress on fertilizers."
Russia withdrew from the Black Sea Grain Initiative in July 2023, saying insufficient progress had been made on its demands.
Ukrainian officials now fear Washington could be prepared to offer Moscow concessions on an issue it has pursued for years.
A sanctions-for-peace push
Trump announced the diesel deal on Oct. 9, saying Russia had agreed to supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel to the U.S. and international markets.
"Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter," Trump wrote on Truth Social.
The announcement raised questions in Washington about the deal's legality.
"We view the Russian diesel deal as illegal as per the 2022 law that had passed both chambers and was signed into law," one Senate official said.
Congress passed the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act in 2022, banning imports of Russian-origin energy products, including diesel.
Several people familiar with the matter said Democratic officials were contacting U.S. industries involved in facilitating the deal to ensure they understood the potential legal and investigative risks.
The deal could face further scrutiny in Congress. But as questions over its legality mount, Ukrainian officials fear Washington could seek other ways to offer Russia economic concessions, with fertilizers emerging as one possible area.
"Well, they clearly have some kind of plan," one official said.
Some Senate officials also believe the Trump administration overestimates the scale of the economic deals Russia could offer Washington in return.
The potential fertilizer deal remains unclear, and the officials who spoke to the Kyiv Independent named no specific sanctions Washington might lift.
The Kyiv Independent has contacted the White House for comment and will update the story when it receives a response.
read also
Kyiv warns against further concessions
The Ukrainian president has publicly warned that the diesel deal could be the start of a broader rollback of sanctions against Russia.
"There's intuition, there's intelligence, and there are various details," Zelensky said Oct. 16. "In my view, we cannot accept these agreements. Because gas deals will follow. And I am absolutely certain of this. After gas, they will lift sanctions on other things as well."
The warning shows Kyiv's concern that Washington is shifting toward economic incentives for Moscow even as Russia continues its war against Ukraine.
Before the diesel announcement, Russian officials had repeatedly argued that Moscow and Washington should expand their business ties. The Trump administration, meanwhile, had maintained that economic deals should follow an end to Russia's war.
Ukrainian officials argue that offering concessions before securing a ceasefire is unlikely to persuade Putin to stop fighting. Instead, they say, such agreements could provide Russia with additional revenue while leaving Moscow's military objectives unchanged.
The concern is especially acute because, according to Ukrainian officials, Russia offered the U.S. nothing meaningful in return for the diesel deal.
"It's clear that this only encourages Putin," one senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent.
"He feels that he can go with a war against us, and on top of that, our allies are lifting sanctions against him and striking deals with him."
Speaking to Russian media on Oct. 22, Putin once again made his intentions clear.
Asked whether he would agree to a ceasefire allowing Ukraine to retain the territory it controls, he replied: "It's not their territory; it's the territory of historical Russia."

France to deploy 70,000 police on Saturday to prevent civil unrest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:31:23 UTC
23:31:23 KST

France will deploy about 70,000 police around the country on Saturday as the government seeks to prevent more civil unrest after some of the worst street violence in years erupted on the fringes of cost-of-living protests last weekend.
The interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said on Friday the security forces would include elite units usually used for counter-terrorism operations and hostage rescues, adding that there had been social media calls for violence from “ultra-left” groups.
“We are not talking about a peaceful, friendly demonstration,” Nuñez told reporters after a meeting of senior ministers and officials chaired by the president, Emmanuel Macron. “We are ready tomorrow to be extremely firm and not tolerate anything.”
Macron and his government are struggling to get on top of a crisis that has caught it off guard six months before presidential elections to choose his successor. The government has admitted it “lost control” over widespread rioting on Saturday.
Largely peaceful demonstrations were hijacked by groups of determined rioters, degenerating into rampant violence and extensive looting in Paris, Marseille, Lyon and other cities. In Limoges, the town hall was set on fire and partly destroyed.
“We will be uncompromising with rioters, looters and all who commit violence,” Nuñez said, adding that besides 10,000 more police, the operation would include water cannon, armoured vehicles, mounted police, helicopters and drones.
Demonstrations are expected in several other countries this weekend, triggered by a broader, continent-wide wave of discontent over declining public services, housing affordability, public sector budget cuts and the spiralling cost of living.
Protests over related grievances have been called for Saturday in Milan, Rome and Turin in Italy; in Vienna, Austria; and in Madrid, Barcelona and other cities in Spain, as well as in Lisbon and Porto in Portugal, Dublin in Ireland and Tirana in Albania.
Protests are expected across France on Saturday, although several cities have banned demonstrations or forced them to change their planned routes to protect shops and public buildings, and forecast heavy rain and high winds could dampen turnout.
The centres of Lyon and some other large cities will be off-limits to protesters, while authorities in Paris authorised a union march along a limited route in the east of the capital between the Places de la Bastille and Nation that will avoid the city centre.
But requests for rallies in Paris organised by France’s main student union, UNEF, and the gilets jaunes movement, whose nationwide protests rocked France in 2018 and which plans 600 small-scale events around France on Saturday, were refused.
UNEF said its rallies, which grew from high school protests last month against teacher shortages and dilapidated facilities, would go ahead regardless. Several of the best-known cultural institutions in Paris, including the Louvre, said they would close on Saturday.
Authorities in Marseille had also banned all protests, but announced on Friday that a union-organised demonstration would be allowed on an “exceptional basis”. It will be the only authorised protest in the southern Bouches-du-Rhône department.
Unionists and opposition leaders have criticised the government for refusing to allow more rallies on Saturday, a decision being challenged in court in several cities. Marylise Léon of the CFDT union federation accused Macron of an abuse of authority.
“It’s counterproductive because there is a lot of anger and a demand to be considered and to be listened to,” Léon, the CFDT’s general secretary, told TF1 TV. “It’s not for the president to decide who can legitimately protest.”
La France Insoumise, the radical left party of Jean-Luc Mélenchon, said the government had “crossed the lines that separate a democracy from an authoritarian and police state”, adding that the bans would only “generate more chaos”.
Adding to the tensions, the far-right leader Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner for next spring’s presidential elections, is due to host her National Rally (RN) party congress in Orléans, drawing thousands of supporters – and leftwing, anti-racist opponents.
Nuñez was due to visit the city on Friday to “inspect the security arrangements” at the request of the prime minister’s office. The justice minister, Gérald Darmanin, said 217 people – half of them first-time offenders – had been jailed since Saturday.
On Thursday, Macron called for “the utmost severity” against “acts of delinquency”, saying gangs of rioters had been mainly responsible for the looting but the worst violence was caused by “ultra-left” groups seeking to “bring down the republic”.
Further stoking disquiet, one person was killed and four others injured – including a 12-year-old girl – in a shooting in the town of Trappes, west of Paris, on Friday in an attack that police said could have been racially motivated.

On Saturday, October 24, the Sofia City Prosecutor’s Office will ask the Sofia City Court to order the suspect’s remand in custody as the strictest pretrial detention measure.

The demonstrators are demanding the release of Ahmed Nasser, deputy head of a pro-government Egyptian youth group, who was arrested in the Netherlands on October 10.
He was reportedly detained on suspicion of threatening Anas Habib, an Egyptian activist who lives in the Netherlands, and his pre-trial detention has been extended by 14 days, broadcaster NOS reported.
Habib drew international attention last summer when he filmed himself padlocking the gates of the Egyptian embassy in The Hague, in protest at the Egyptian government keeping the Rafah border crossing with Gaza closed.
His action sparked similar protests at Egyptian embassies in more than 16 countries, after which supporters of President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi began gathering outside embassies to “protect” them.
Days after Nasser’s arrest, Egyptian foreign minister Badr Abdelatty called his Dutch counterpart to demand his release and better protection for Egypt’s embassy in The Hague.
Foreign minister Tom Berendsen said on social media that the two had “discussed the need for progress on the security of our respective embassies and consular affairs.”
It is unclear exactly how Nasser is alleged to have threatened Habib.

A border guard suspected of killing a man in Odesa region extradited from Germany
Kyiv • UNN
A Ukrainian border guard is suspected of fatally shooting a detainee in Odesa region in July 2024. The court remanded him in custody\r\nwithout bail.
A serviceman of the State Border Guard Service suspected of killing a man at the border in the summer of 2024 has been extradited to Ukraine from Germany. This was reported by the Office of the Prosecutor General, according to UNN.
Details
According to the investigation, on July 14, 2024, border guards in Odesa region stopped a taxi in which four servicemen who had left their training unit were traveling toward the Ukrainian-Moldovan border.
The vehicle was stopped approximately 15 km from the border. It is reported that the servicemen planned to cross the border on foot.
Two passengers attempted to flee. One of them was detained, while the pursuit of the other continued. The detained man remained under the supervision of a border guard, to whom his colleague handed over his service pistol
According to the OPG, the suspect shot one of the detainees, although he posed no threat to the life or health of the suspect (the defendant - ed.) or other people. The detained man died at the scene from his injuries.
Several days after the crime, the suspect crossed the border and later left for Germany. He was notified in absentia of suspicion of intentional murder and exceeding official powers (Part 1 of Article 115 and Part 3 of Article 365 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine). The sanctions under these articles provide for up to 15 years of imprisonment.
After being placed on the international wanted list, on October 19, 2026, he was handed over to the Ukrainian side at the border with Poland. The court imposed pretrial detention on the suspect without the right to bail
As a reminder
Employees of the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine were detained at the Ukrainian-Moldovan border. They tried to detain a man, but the boat carrying them ended up on the opposite bank of the Dniester River. There, they were detained by Moldovan border police officers.

Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture designs "fluid" skyscraper Lilli for Miami waterfront
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:30:00 UTC
23:30:00 KST

Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture designs “fluid” skyscraper Lilli for Miami waterfront
US studio Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture has unveiled its latest skyscraper for Miami, designed to display “quiet refinement” on a slender site on the city’s waterfront.
Called Lilli, the residential skyscraper development is the latest in Miami from Adrian Smith + Gordon Gill Architecture (AS+GG). The studio is known for designing some of the world’s tallest buildings, including the world’s upcoming tallest skyscraper, the Jeddah Tower.
At 636 feet tall (193 metres), Lilli is planned for a narrow site in Miami’s Edgewater neighbourhood.
The luxury skyscraper will feature rounded edges and will have terraces on the water-facing side, with larger patios running up the opposite face.
Its design is characterised by rounded edges and large spans of glass interrupted by metallic floor plates.
“Our vision is for Lilli’s interior design to feel inseparable from its architecture,” said AS+GG design partner Juan Betancur.
“The fluidity of the building carries through the interior spaces, while a restrained palette of natural materials allows light, landscape, and views of Biscayne Bay to become part of the experience.”
“The result is a sense of quiet refinement that feels distinctly connected to its waterfront setting.”
The skyscraper will house 117 residences of varying sizes, spread across its 53 storeys, as well as amenities including lounges, pools and spas.
The ground floor will have a lobby for residents with large metallic columns and minimalist detailing.
At the top of the skyscraper, a pool will sit on the edge of a terrace underneath a bulkhead with the same reflective metal treatment seen elsewhere in the exterior.
Lilli is the latest in a series of residential skyscrapers being designed by the studio, which recently completed a “yacht-inspired” building in the city.
Residential skyscraper development has proceeded at a steady pace in Miami, with Bugatti recently unveiling its first branded skyscraper in the city.
The images are by Darcstudio.

NEW DELHI: Former Karnataka chief minister Siddaramaiah on Friday said he had lodged a police complaint over an alleged “fake sting operation” video targeting him, alleging that it was an attempt to blackmail him after he lost power.Speaking to reporters in Mysuru, the senior Congress leader said he wanted the truth to come out and those behind the video to be identified. No matter who sets out to defame me, I know what the truth is. There is no question of me being upset or afraid. This case is 100% created,” he said.Recalling his political career, he said he first became a minister in 1984 and had faced no such incident even when he was chief minister.“Now when I have no power, such a conspiracy is being hatched. It is true that their intention will not succeed,” he asserted.Yathindra alleges Congress links to sting operationMeanwhile, Karnataka minister Yathindra Siddaramaiah alleged that people from within the Congress were behind the purported sting operation, which he claimed was intended to damage his father's image and blackmail him.Speaking to reporters in Mysuru, Yathindra said the video appeared to show the involvement of a woman from the Congress who wanted a party ticket from Puttur, along with the head of a media organisation.“The whole thing was done to damage my father, tarnish his image, destroy his legacy and blackmail him,” Yathindra said.

As she herself says in the video, she wanted a party ticket from Puttur. Prima facie, it appears that the sting operation was conducted for that purpose,” he said.However, Yathindra cautioned against holding the entire Congress responsible for the alleged actions of an individual party worker.“Just because a party worker has done something like this, it does not mean that our entire party is against us,” he said.

Ukrainian drone attack triggers shut down of Moscow airports, drone debris reported on tarmac
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:28:19 UTC
23:28:19 KST

Ukrainian forces strike Oryol electronics plant, drone attacks triggers shutdown of Moscow airports
Ukraine forces struck an electronics plant in the Russian city of Oryol, while drones disrupted airspace over Moscow's airports on Oct. 23.
According to Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+, Ukrainian missiles struck an electronics plant in Oryol, around 160 kilometers (100 miles) from the Ukrainian border. Eyewitness footage from the scene appear to show large explosions and smoke billowing into the evening sky.
Oryol Oblast Governor Andrey Klychkov confirmed that an enterprise had been targeted, while independent Russian media outlet ASTRA, citing its open-source intelligence analysis, identified the facility as the Proton plant.
The plant manufactures semiconductor devices, LEDs, and electronic components for industrial and specialized equipment that could be used in Russian weapons systems. The plant reportedly supplies parts for Russia's S-71 Kover cruise missiles, the 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missiles, and the Pantsir-S1 air defense systems.
Local residents reported hearing at least four explosions, ASTRA said.
326 kilometers (202 miles) to the north, civilian flights at all four of Moscow's main airports were suspended on the afternoon of Oct. 23 amid a Ukrainian drone raid on the Russian capital, local authorities reported.
Restrictions on arriving and departing flights at Sheremetyevo, Domodedovo, Vnukovo, and Zhukovsky airports were announced by Russian civil aviation authority Rosaviatsiya at 2:05 p.m. local time.
At Sheremetyevo, Moscow's largest airport, an air alert was sounded, and waiting passengers were advised to take shelter.
Photos later emerged on social media that allegedly showed debris from a downed drone on the tarmac at Sheremetyevo.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the photos.
Open-source flight tracker FlightRadar24 reported 85 cancelled flights and a further 229 delayed at Sheremetyevo over the day.
According to Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin, 17 drones were shot down while heading toward the city on the afternoon of Oct. 23.
Ukraine had not commented on the reported attack as of the time of publication.
The all-clear was later sounded at Sheremetyevo Airport, Russian state news agency TASS reported at 5 p.m. local time.
An evacuation was also reported at the IQ-quarter skyscraper in the Moscow City business district, which houses offices of several Russian government ministries, including the Digital Development Ministry, Economic Development Ministry, and Industry and Trade Ministry.
Russian state news agency TASS later reported, citing emergency services, that the alarm had been false.
As Ukrainian long-range drones have reached deeper into Russian territory, temporary airport closures across Russia have become increasingly common during Moscow's full-scale war against Ukraine.
On Sept. 1, President Volodymyr Zelensky warned airlines, insurers, and foreign governments that Russian airspace "will be de facto closed" because of Ukrainian drones. Russian President Vladimir Putin responded by accusing Kyiv of "state terrorism," despite Russia's six days of attacks on Kyiv.
Ukraine does not threaten civil aviation, but carriers flying to Moscow, St. Petersburg, and other major hubs must factor in the risk posed by drones in Russian airspace, Zelensky said in an address posted to Telegram.
"Today we want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, everyone who still uses key Russian airports — Russian skies are becoming completely dangerous," he said.
"Although the Russian authorities do not report this as it should, the Russian sky will de facto be closed," he added.

Kenyan world marathon champion Jepchirchir provisionally suspended over doping
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:27:59 UTC
23:27:59 KST

Andrew Wasike 
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
Kenya's reigning world marathon champion and former Olympic gold medalist Peres Jepchirchir has been provisionally suspended after testing positive for a banned performance-enhancing substance, the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) announced on Friday.
"The AIU has provisionally suspended reigning World and former Olympic champion, Peres Jepchirchir, after an out-of-competition sample, collected in Kenya prior to her recent Sydney Marathon victory, returned an adverse analytical finding for EPO," the organization said in a statement.
Erythropoietin (EPO) is a prohibited substance that stimulates the production of red blood cells, increasing the body's capacity to transport oxygen and potentially improving endurance performance.
The AIU said the sample was collected in Kenya before Jepchirchir's victory at the Sydney Marathon in Australia earlier this year.
The provisional suspension prevents the athlete from competing while the case proceeds through the anti-doping disciplinary process. It does not constitute a final ruling on whether she committed an anti-doping rule violation.
Jepchirchir, 33, won the women's marathon title at the 2025 World Athletics Championships in Tokyo, adding to the Olympic gold medal she secured at the Tokyo Games in 2021.
The Kenyan athlete is also a former world record holder in the half-marathon and has won four major international marathons.
According to the AIU, her victories include the New York Marathon in 2021, Boston Marathon in 2022, London Marathon in 2024 and Sydney Marathon in 2026.

Kyiv needs EUR 1.5 bln for winter - energy expert
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
17:27:49 EEST
23:27:49 KST

Kyiv has spent more than UAH 16 billion on strengthening its energy security since the start of 2026, compared with UAH 2 billion last year, and plans to spend another UAH 4.5-5 billion by year-end, Managing Director of the Energy Industry Research Center Oleksandr Kharchenko has said.
However, the city needs a further EUR 1.5 billion to complete the necessary work, Kharchenko said at a discussion hosted by Interfax-Ukraine on Friday.
"This is effectively a tenfold increase in investment, specifically in security measures. This includes protecting high-voltage substations and providing backup power for core sewage and heating systems," he said.
The preparations have been funded mainly from the city budget, with the central government accounting for only about 10%, Kharchenko said.
"The national budget is not in very good shape, and payments through Treasury accounts were blocked for more than a month. This hit all local authorities hard, including their preparations for winter," he said.
As a result, some equipment that cities had planned to install by November or December will be commissioned later because of the four-week pause.
Kharchenko said Kyiv's entire internal generating capacity was physically destroyed in January 2026. Before that, the city had about 1.3 gigawatts of generating capacity, while electricity demand reaches about 2 GW at temperatures of minus 10 degrees Celsius and is around 1.2 GW in milder weather.
Without in-city generation, the metro and water utility pumping stations switch to backup power, limiting their ability to provide full services, he said.
Kharchenko said the city had protected key systems against major technological failures. However, maintaining water circulation and filling reservoirs does not necessarily ensure adequate pressure in elevated districts such as Pechersk. That requires the main power supply lines serving water utility facilities to remain operational, he said.
"Some inconvenience this winter is almost inevitable," Kharchenko said.
Most cities cannot complete energy security projects in a single seven- to eight-month season because of engineering and regulatory requirements. Such projects take two to three years, he said.
Ukraine as a whole may need UAH 250-300 billion annually for at least another two years to strengthen its energy security, Kharchenko said.
