Kyiv needs EUR 1.5 bln for winter - energy expert
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
17:27:49 EEST
23:27:49 KST

Kyiv has spent more than UAH 16 billion on strengthening its energy security since the start of 2026, compared with UAH 2 billion last year, and plans to spend another UAH 4.5-5 billion by year-end, Managing Director of the Energy Industry Research Center Oleksandr Kharchenko has said.
However, the city needs a further EUR 1.5 billion to complete the necessary work, Kharchenko said at a discussion hosted by Interfax-Ukraine on Friday.
"This is effectively a tenfold increase in investment, specifically in security measures. This includes protecting high-voltage substations and providing backup power for core sewage and heating systems," he said.
The preparations have been funded mainly from the city budget, with the central government accounting for only about 10%, Kharchenko said.
"The national budget is not in very good shape, and payments through Treasury accounts were blocked for more than a month. This hit all local authorities hard, including their preparations for winter," he said.
As a result, some equipment that cities had planned to install by November or December will be commissioned later because of the four-week pause.
Kharchenko said Kyiv's entire internal generating capacity was physically destroyed in January 2026. Before that, the city had about 1.3 gigawatts of generating capacity, while electricity demand reaches about 2 GW at temperatures of minus 10 degrees Celsius and is around 1.2 GW in milder weather.
Without in-city generation, the metro and water utility pumping stations switch to backup power, limiting their ability to provide full services, he said.
Kharchenko said the city had protected key systems against major technological failures. However, maintaining water circulation and filling reservoirs does not necessarily ensure adequate pressure in elevated districts such as Pechersk. That requires the main power supply lines serving water utility facilities to remain operational, he said.
"Some inconvenience this winter is almost inevitable," Kharchenko said.
Most cities cannot complete energy security projects in a single seven- to eight-month season because of engineering and regulatory requirements. Such projects take two to three years, he said.
Ukraine as a whole may need UAH 250-300 billion annually for at least another two years to strengthen its energy security, Kharchenko said.

Ukraine frees 270 from Russian captivity in “historic” prisoner swap, including 5 Olenivka survivors and American teacher Stephen Hubbard
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:27:42 UTC
23:27:42 KST

Ukraine has brought home 270 people from Russian captivity, including 261 military personnel and nine civilians, in the third stage of a prisoner exchange process that began on 19 August, Ukraine’s Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War said on 23 October.
Amid Russia’s full-scale invasion, prisoner exchanges remain one of the few channels of communication between Kyiv and Moscow. But with thousands of Ukrainian military personnel and civilians still held in Russian captivity, each swap brings home only a fraction of those awaiting release, while negotiations remain tied to the difficult process of securing the return of captives on both sides.
Most of those released today had been held since 2022, including many defenders of Mariupol. Five survivors of the July 2022 Russian attack on the Olenivka prison barracks are also among those returning home.
The exchange also included American Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old English teacher from Izium, Kharkiv Oblast, who was illegally captured in 2022, then sentenced and tortured by Russia, according to the Coordination Headquarters.
Exchange includes soldiers held for up to eight years
The exchange included members of Ukraine’s Armed Forces, National Guard, State Border Guard Service, and other security and defense units, as well as a State Emergency Service rescuer. Thirty-eight of the released military personnel are officers.
According to Ukraine’s Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets, the exchange was “historic” because it brought home the largest number of Ukrainian military personnel sentenced by Russia: 86 who had been sentenced and one who had faced criminal prosecution.
Two of those released had been held since 2018 and 2020, spending eight and six years in captivity, respectively.
“The priorities remain unchanged: we bring home those who have been in captivity the longest, the seriously ill, and the seriously wounded,” Lubinets said, adding that efforts to return civilians and people held since 2014 also remain a priority.
Nine seriously ill prisoners among those released
Nine of the returning service members are seriously ill, and some are in critical condition, the Coordination Headquarters said. The youngest person released is 24, while the oldest is 63.
Many of those released had faced criminal prosecution in Russia and been sentenced on what Ukraine describes as fabricated charges, including life imprisonment.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said most of those returning had been captured in 2022, and many had defended Mariupol.
The released also include service members who fought in the Donetsk, Luhansk, Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, Kherson, Kyiv, Mykolaiv, and Chernihiv directions, as well as defenders of the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant.
“We remember every man and woman and continue searching for everyone,” Zelenskyy said.
Russia has kept the Red Cross away from Ukrainian POWs since 2024. Now about 1,500 captives it never confirmed as prisoners face prosecution
US and UAE thanked for assistance
Ukraine thanked the United States and the United Arab Emirates for helping secure the releases.
All those released will undergo medical examinations, receive treatment and financial support, and take part in rehabilitation and reintegration programs after prolonged captivity.
Ukraine’s military intelligence chief and head of the Coordination Headquarters, Oleh Ivashchenko, said the return followed months of negotiations. He stressed that efforts to establish the fate of missing Ukrainians and bring everyone home would continue.
The 23 October exchange follows the previous stage on 19 August, when Ukraine brought home 103 servicemembers from Russian captivity.

Nine of the 13 crew members have been rescued.
Attack on merchant shipping on the rise in the Black Sea: What to know
The drone strike on the ship, called Khoryv, is believed to be the fourth merchant vessel to have been attacked off the coast of Romania this month.
Two weeks ago, two merchant vessels were also set ablaze in the western Black Sea, which is a vital shipping corridor heavily used by Ukraine.

Both Romania and Bulgaria have called on NATO to do more to protect commercial shipping in the Black Sea.
NATO said earlier this week that it was sending more maritime patrol aircraft and radar systems to the Black Sea without having blamed any country for the attacks there.
About 23 sailors had been reported dead or missing in incidents in the Black Sea in the 10 days leading up to October 15, according to Reuters.
That tally is higher now.
Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, condemned the increasing attacks on vessels in the Black Sea too, earlier this month calling it "unacceptable" that "the Black Sea has become another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine."

Ukraine tries to shut Moscow's airports with drone strikes on Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:23:00 UTC
23:23:00 KST

Ukraine tries to shut Moscow's airports with drone strikes on Russia
October 23, 2026
For months, drone strikes by Ukraine have forced the suspension of flights to and from airports in Russia. Moscow's Domodedovo, Sheremetyevo, Zhukovsky and Vnukovo airports have had to shut down operations almost daily in October, according to reports from the independent investigative media outlet Agentstvo. On some days, the airports were reportedly closed for up to nine hours.
In early September, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced that Ukraine would seek to cut off the airspace around Moscow and other destinations in Russia. "Today, we would like to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, and everyone who continues to use major Russian airports: Russian airspace will become completely unsafe," Zelenskyy said.
The following day, Ukraine sent a corresponding warning to the International Civil Aviation Organization.
Ukraine's airspace has been closed since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Can Ukraine succeed?
Russia's aviation authority, Rosaviatsiya, has issued an emergency safety "carpet" protocol that is designed to immediately shut down the airspace over a specific region or around affected airports if an aircraft violates Russian airspace, weapons are used, or unidentified objects appear in the skies. Once the protocol is announced, drastic restrictions apply to all air traffic.
"If there is a military threat, a specific section of airspace is closed off, and this carpet is declared," Oleksandr Laneckij, the chief executive officer of the Friendly Avia Support consultancy, told DW. "Essentially, every drone poses a military threat."
Laneckij noted that Yemen's Houthis have managed to significantly disrupt Saudi airspace. "I think Ukraine's military capabilities far exceed those of the Houthis," Laneckij said.
The military analyst Jan Matvejev also said Ukraine would have little trouble severely disrupting Moscow-area air traffic. Though Ukraine has not yet managed to completely shut down Russian airspace as Zelenskyy plans, Matvejev said, its armed forces "remain committed to this idea."
"To close off the airspace and trigger the 'carpet' plan, all you need are simple drones that don't have to be equipped with a warhead or even have a long range," Matvejev said. Ukraine's arms industry can produce hundreds of combat-ready long-range drones in a day, he added. That is why he believes Ukraine could have the necessary resources to shut down Moscow's airports.
Indeed, Ukraine's efforts to shut down Russian airspace are "just getting started," Simon Shuster wrote in October in the US magazine The Atlantic, citing well-informed sources.
Can Russia stop Ukraine's drones?
Matvejev said Russia's air-defense systems were not entirely effective in efforts to prevent Ukrainian drones from penetrating Moscow's airspace. "If it were possible to shoot them down, they would have done so by now," he said. He added that Russia would have deployed additional air-defense troops if they were available.
Laneckij said Russia might lower the threshold for declaring the carpet protocol, which could increase the risk of deadly incidents such as the 2024 Christmas day crash of an Azerbaijan Airlines flight. Investigators say the flight was struck by a Russian air-defense missile that was being used to defend against drones, killing 38 people.
Matvejev seconded the fear that Russia's defenses could again mistakenly target civilian aircraft instead of military objects. He said little had changed about Russia's air-defense protocol since the Azeri flight was shot in 2024.
In an operation against a low-flying drone, the target is visually identified and fired upon with a machine gun. In such a scenario, the danger to aircraft is extremely low, unless they happen to be flying in the immediate vicinity.
The risk to civil aviation increases significantly when anti-aircraft missiles are deployed, Matvejev said. A missile could have defects that are practically unavoidable in mass production and could veer toward an aircraft flying nearby. Matvejev said such defense measures could not guarantee the safety of civilian aircraft during operations.
He said drones did not have to carry explosives to be disruptive. A collision between an airplane and a basic drone can have serious consequences — and, he said, a drone sent from Ukraine all the way to Moscow must be relatively large, "weighting dozens of kilograms."
In the summer of 2023, Ukrainian armed forces attacked the airport in the Russian city of Pskov, where both military and civilian aircraft were parked. Earlier this month, drone debris fell on the Sochi airport, on Russia's Black Sea coast.
Russia also attacks Ukraine's airports. In September, Zelenskyy said Kyiv's airport had been struck, as well as the Boryspil airport near the capital.
How will international airlines react?
Laneckij said three factors would determine whether international airlines suspend their flights to Russia: the military threat, the degree of demand and the insurance cost.
He said issues could emerge around insurance. When insurers rate the security risk of flying to Russia as very high, they could significantly raise their rates for aircraft headed there. This would cause ticket prices to skyrocket.
Competition within Russia's aviation market has already declined because many airlines are no longer in business, Laneckij said. This has increased demand for tickets from the remaining foreign airlines.
"Whether they stay or not depends on the price they have to pay for the danger faced," he said.

23:22:00 KST

French and British fighter jets simulated a nuclear strike over the Mediterranean Sea in the first joint exercise involving France’s airborne nuclear capabilities, Paris announced, as the two allies deepen military cooperation amid tensions with Russia, Reuters reported.
The exercise followed an agreement reached by France and the United Kingdom in July 2025 to strengthen cooperation on their nuclear arsenals in response to growing threats to Europe and uncertainty over their shared ally, the United States.
French Minister of the Armed Forces Catherine Vautrin said the two countries could coordinate their nuclear forces while maintaining their independence.
“Our nuclear cooperation with the UK continues to deepen: on Tuesday evening, British Typhoon fighter jets participated for the first time in a French nuclear exercise alongside Rafale aircraft,” Vautrin added.
According to a statement from the French Ministry of the Armed Forces, French jets took off from Saint-Dizier airbase in northeastern France, accompanied by British Typhoon fighters, and simulated a nuclear strike during the exercise, codenamed “Rummy.”
British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said the joint mission demonstrated the allies’ commitment to European security.
“In an increasingly dangerous world, our adversaries must be left in no doubt: the UK and France are united in their commitment to European security and to maintaining the deterrence that has helped preserve peace for generations,” Streeting said.
French President Emmanuel Macron announced in March that France would increase its nuclear arsenal. He also launched an initiative enabling European partners to take part in joint exercises and potentially host French nuclear-capable military assets on their territory for short periods.
France spends approximately 5.6 billion euros annually maintaining its stockpile of around 290 nuclear warheads, which can be deployed from submarines and aircraft. According to Reuters, France has the world’s fourth-largest nuclear arsenal.
The United Kingdom possesses 225 nuclear warheads, while Russia and the United States each have more than 5,000.

Israeli elections: Arab voters weigh participation against abstention in bid to oust Netanyahu

23:21:49 KST

Amid fears over hardline Israeli policies, Palestinian citizens of Israel see the upcoming Israeli elections as a chance for change, with calls for higher Arab turnout to prevent incumbent Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from forming another government, Anadolu reports.
In a series of field interviews conducted by Anadolu on the streets of various Arab cities and towns in Israel, citizens emphasized that participating in this election is particularly crucial, given the “worsening racism and marginalization” against them.
While some plan to vote for the first time in hopes of bringing about political change, others continue to abstain, questioning whether elections can alter their circumstances and arguing that successive governments have failed to address their demands.
Arab citizens make up around 20% of Israel’s population of more than 10 million.
Many say they have faced discrimination for years, but view the current government as a more dangerous phase, strengthening their desire to replace it through the ballot box.
Polls suggest Arab parties could win around 15 seats in the 120-member Knesset, while Arab politicians hope higher turnout will weaken the chances of small right-wing parties seeking to support Netanyahu.
Calls for participation, change
Palestinian Imad Bashnaq said the upcoming election was “decisive and extremely important,” particularly for Arab society.
He argued that the rise in racism and fascism since Oct. 7, 2023, had made conditions intolerable.
“I have always maintained that we — as Arabic speakers — are the only ones capable of bringing about change in the Middle East, not just here within this country,” Bashnaq said, arguing that “a few madmen” have taken control of the government and now seek to dictate the course of an entire region.
“We are the original rightful owners, and there is no dispute about that.
“But we are a minority in a state, and this state is a reality we have to deal with,” he added.
OPINION: Israel’s election: The Arab vote and Netanyahu’s politics of exclusion
‘Every vote makes difference’
Areen Ghanayem said she would vote for the second time, maintaining that “every vote makes a difference.”
She said Arab society needed broad participation given the problems it faces and what she described as the government’s failure to pay sufficient attention to its concerns.
“We need to have a voice and someone who speaks on our behalf and demands the rights that should be ours,” she said.
Ghanayem expressed concern that the current government could return to power, saying it marginalized Arab society.
Citizens, she added, did not want to feel excluded from political life but sought to assert their presence and ability to influence decisions.
Occupier attacks
Mohammed Ahmad Abboud said he would take part in the upcoming election, as he had in the past, with the aim of “removing the racist government.”
He said the current election differed from previous ones because of what he described as “escalating violations,” pointing to Israeli occupiers’ attacks in the occupied West Bank.
Abboud also voiced concern over statements by Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich regarding the “Judaization” of the Negev and the Galilee — regions located in the south and north of Israel, respectively.
Occupier attacks against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank have escalated since Israel launched its genocidal war on the Gaza Strip in October 2023.
The attacks have included the killing of Palestinians, the burning of homes, vehicles, and mosques, the destruction of agricultural land, preventing farmers from reaching their land, and the forced displacement of Palestinian communities.
These attacks have coincided with Israeli military operations involving arrests, the demolition of Palestinian homes and structures, and the expansion of illegal settlements.
Between hope and despair
In the northern city of Acre, a resident known as “Jojo” urged Arab citizens to participate in the election, arguing that voting was necessary to bring about change.
“We must vote to bring about change — real change,” he said, expressing optimism that the upcoming election could produce better results.
READ: Racism controversy erupts in Israeli election campaign after broadcaster calls Eisenkot a ‘monkey’
Separately, Saeed Abu Sultan, also from Acre, said that many years of participating in elections have not brought about any change in the reality faced by citizens.
“Some people might be able to make a difference, but as for us, we’ve grown accustomed to things as they are. We haven’t felt any change for 30 years,” Abu Sultan added.
Arab voter turnout expected to rise
Experts expect Palestinian citizens’ participation in the upcoming election to increase compared with the 2022 vote.
Experts and politicians estimate turnout among Palestinian citizens could reach 60% to 61%, up from 53% in 2022, while Arab parties hope participation will rise even further.
Arab politicians say higher turnout could alter the balance of power and reduce the chances of small Israeli right-wing parties crossing the electoral threshold and entering parliament, potentially weakening Netanyahu’s ability to form a government.
The Joint List, comprising the Democratic Front for Peace and Equality, the Arab Movement for Change, and the Balad party, is contesting the election under the leadership of Yousef Jabareen. Polls project it could win nine seats.
The United Arab List, led by Mansour Abbas, is also running, with projections suggesting it could win between five and six seats.
The election is scheduled for Tuesday, Oct. 27, to choose the 120 members of the Knesset, with Netanyahu’s bloc competing primarily against the Jewish opposition parties led by Gadi Eisenkot.
The election comes as Netanyahu’s bloc has been losing ground in opinion polls.
Forming a government in Israel requires the support of at least 61 of the Knesset’s 120 members.
Cooperation between the Jewish opposition and Arab parties could prevent Netanyahu from forming a government.
However, most opposition leaders reject such cooperation, while Netanyahu and Eisenkot have so far also ruled out alliances with Arab parties.
Arab lawmakers have outlined conditions for supporting any government, including ending wars, advancing a political process with the Palestinians, and ending discrimination against Palestinian citizens of Israel.

Romania Blames Russia for Deadly Drone Attack on Cargo Ship

2026-10-23

23:21:15 KST

Romania said Friday that one sailor had died and three were missing after a drone struck and sank a ship in the Black Sea, with the country's president blaming Russia for the attack.
The cargo ship Khoryv, flying the Comoros flag, was "struck by a drone and sank near Romanian territorial waters," President Nicușor Dan wrote in a Facebook post.
Speaking to reporters, Dan said the attack was "clearly part of the escalation that Russia is carrying out in the context of the war in Ukraine."
Romania launched a rescue operation after the Khoryv sent a distress signal around 10:00 am local time, 13 nautical miles from the Romanian port of Constanta.
Romanian authorities said 10 Ukrainian and three Azerbaijani crewmembers were on board.
"Of the 13 people on board, 10 were rescued by another commercial vessel in the area, nine of whom were alive and one of whom had died. Three others are still missing," Romania's interior ministry said in a statement.
It added that the vessel "sustained major damage and capsized."
"Due to adverse weather conditions and poor visibility, an aerial rescue operation by helicopter is not possible," the Romanian Naval Authority said in a separate statement.
Romanian Prime Minister Luca Niculescu said on Facebook the attack was "unacceptable and constitutes a flagrant violation of international law."
The strikes on civilian shipping in the waters off NATO and EU members Bulgaria and Romania have left scores of sailors missing or dead.
Seven ship crewmembers went missing on Oct. 15 off the coast of Romania when the Wine Trader, a chemical tanker, caught fire after a drone attack.
Romanian fighter jets also shot down two Russian drones over the Black Sea last weekend.
On Thursday, following a meeting of Romania's Supreme Council for National Defense, the presidency said that "threats to freedom of navigation and critical infrastructure have increased significantly."
Romania is looking into "accelerated development of maritime surveillance capabilities, mine countermeasures and effective countermeasures against drones that intrude unauthorized into national airspace and territorial waters," the presidency said.
NATO said after talks on Black Sea security on Tuesday that it was deploying additional planes, drones and radar systems to the area because of the attacks on ships.
Foreign Minister Dan Neculăescu said Romania was working with NATO allies including Bulgaria and Turkey to "fast-track the additional surveillance capabilities."
In his Facebook post, Dan said it was "time for Russia to take the peace initiatives put forward by the United States and Europe seriously, to accept the proposals for a ceasefire and to bring the war to an end."

Melania Trump coordinated Russia-Ukraine ceasefire in frontline town – Kremlin

Melania Trump coordinated Russia-Ukraine ceasefire in frontline town – Kremlin
Moscow and Kiev have agreed to a temporary ceasefire in the frontline town of Alyoshki in Russia’s Kherson Region to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and civilian evacuations following mediation co-ordinate by US First Lady Melania Trump, the Kremlin has confirmed.
Located near the front line in Kherson Region, which voted to join Russia in a 2022 referendum, Alyoshki has been largely cut off from essential supplies and basic services for months under a Ukrainian siege. Drone attacks and remotely laid mines have hampered aid deliveries and evacuation efforts, leaving an estimated 1,500 to 2,000 civilians in the town trapped, many of them elderly.
The White House announced the agreement earlier on Friday, saying both sides had agreed to suspend all military operations in Alyoshki from October 29 to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and prepare for civilian evacuations through a designated safe passage.
Melania Trump, who had previously expressed willingness to support humanitarian efforts in Alyoshki, described the situation as “dire,” calling the town a “frontline war city on the brink of disaster.”
“The remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water,” she said.
Civilian representatives from Russia and Ukraine will assess residents’ needs and help organize evacuations to either country, depending on the residents’ wishes, the first lady said.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said military officials were working to coordinate the timing of the ceasefire. He welcomed Melania Trump’s efforts, crediting her with making a “significant contribution” to the humanitarian operation.
Peskov also acknowledged the work of Russian human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova and her Ukrainian counterpart Dmitry Lubinets in arranging the operation.
Moscow has accused Kiev of deliberately creating the humanitarian crisis by targeting civilian supply routes and obstructing aid deliveries. Russian Foreign Ministry envoy Rodion Miroshnik previously described the situation as a “medieval blockade using modern methods,” accusing Ukrainian forces of preventing residents from leaving.
Russian President Vladimir Putin and his US counterpart, Donald Trump, discussed the crisis during a phone call earlier this month. According to the Kremlin, the two leaders agreed that Russian human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova would maintain contact with Melania Trump’s office over humanitarian efforts.

The restriction on protests means that people who are not in the marches are breaking the law, and is aimed at ensuring the rule of law, a French official said.

France is struggling to reduce the budget deficit ahead of elections in six months, pushing up spreads between French and German government bonds into territory associated with the euro-area debt crisis.

Karakoram 2026: Inside China-Pakistan Joint Military Training in Xinjiang
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:17:00 UTC
23:17:00 KST

On October 14, China and Pakistan began joint military training known as Karakoram 2026. According to official sources, the training’s opening ceremony was held in Korla city, Xinjiang, China. The main objective of this training is to focus on joint counterterrorism operations in high-altitude areas, according to China’s Ministry of National Defense.
The nine-day exercise encompassed a range of operational and tactical training activities that are significant not only for bilateral military cooperation but also in the context of a changing regional security environment.
Bilateral military exercises between Pakistan and China are a well-established and recurring feature of their defense cooperation. The two countries conducted the Sea Guardian IV naval exercise earlier this year to enhance interoperability and maritime cooperation. Joint counterterrorism drills are also a constant feature of their defense cooperation, with the previous example being Warrior IX held in December 2025.
Karakoram 2026 particularly focused on joint counterterrorism in high-altitude areas, with “skills training in UAV [unmanned aerial vehicle] operation, on-the-move target search and firing, and long-range sniping, and joint command and live-force exercises,” according to a Chinese Defense Ministry spokesperson.
China Central Television’s military channel said that China provided all the equipment, including Type 191 rifles, Type 201 squad machine guns, Type 11 armored assault vehicles, Type 08 infantry fighting vehicles, artillery, and both unmanned and anti-unmanned systems. The use of Chinese equipment and subsequent Pakistani familiarization with equipment could boost the likelihood of future Pakistani procurement.
However, the most notable feature of Karakoram 2026 is that this is the first time both countries are moving away from counterterrorism training by specialized units to regular army forces. This development will further strengthen defense cooperation and reinforce the broader all-weather strategic partnership between Pakistan and China. The main aim of this is to increase interoperability and joint cooperation on terrorism-related issues.
Karakoram 2026 is a reflection of broader convergence between China and Pakistan over shared security concerns in the region. Their respective threat perceptions may not be identical, but they have a shared interest in preventing terrorist organizations from exploiting territorial vulnerabilities. Beijing continues to have concerns about the potential for attacks in China, while Chinese nationals operating in Afghanistan and Pakistan have faced attacks on occasion. Joint counterterrorism training provides an institutional mechanism to translate these shared concerns into practical military cooperation.
One key component of these exercises was UAV operations. The motivation is obvious considering the emergence of drone warfare in the Afghanistan-Pakistan border region, especially the use of UAVs by terrorist outfits. Training in this domain will increase situational awareness while simultaneously supporting surveillance operations. At the same time, mobile target detection and engagement will strengthen coordination under dynamic battlefield conditions.
Long-range sniping and live-force exercises further test tactical proficiency, decision-making, and interoperability. For participating forces, this exercise would be helpful in coordinating response and improving communication during complex operations.
Looking at all the capabilities involved in Karakoram 2026, it is evident that the exercises were specially designed in relevance to the difficult terrain of northern Pakistan and the bordering Chinese region of Xinjiang. The China-Pakistan border region has difficult, mountainous terrain with extreme weather conditions complicating security operations. However, one should not perceive these exercises as evidence of China and Pakistan preparing for a specific operation in the region. Rather, Karakoram 2026 is significant mainly due to improved preparedness for shared counterterrorism contingencies and strengthening military-to-military familiarity.
Another major dimension setting the scene for these exercises is the fraught security environment between Afghanistan and Pakistan, which has complicated Pakistan’s counterterrorism efforts. Islamabad has repeatedly raised concerns about the presence of Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) militants on Afghan territory and their ability to conduct cross-border attacks. For Pakistan, the recent surge in drone attacks especially by the militants across the border raises another challenge that needs to be addressed.
A 2026 report by the U.N. Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team documented escalating cross-border attacks involving Pakistan and Afghanistan and reported continued support for the TTP by Afghanistan’s de facto Taliban government. In this context, joint training in drone operations may help Pakistan improve both surveillance and defense. The value of such experience will greatly depend on whether the units and police forces bearing the brunt of these attacks, received practical training in counterdrone defense.
The biggest implication of Karakoram 2026, however, is not the specific training received; it is the institutionalization of cooperation. With air, naval, and now army training exercises, China and Pakistan have developed a framework covering all three services. Pakistan used Chinese platforms during the May 2025 conflict with India, and army-level interoperability is a natural and logical next step in defense cooperation.
Karakoram 2026 is not merely a military training but a broader reflection of evolving security priorities of China and Pakistan. With the resurgence of terrorist attacks, counterterrorism cooperation sits at the forefront of Islamabad’s national security concerns. On the other hand, Beijing remains heavily invested in Pakistan under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), and the security of Chinese nationals in Pakistan remains an important dimension of bilateral relations.
The deteriorating security environment in the region thus reinforces the importance of China-Pakistan military cooperation. The UAV-related training, coordination in command, and realistic field exercises at Karakoram 2026 can be understood against the broader need to improve situational awareness, tactical coordination, and responsiveness to emerging threats.
However, the effectiveness of military training cannot be measured solely by the completion of an exercise. Its lasting value will depend on the extent to which the participating forces incorporate lessons from joint training into their operational practices and adapt to emerging security challenges.

Several killed, dozens wounded in Jordan church shooting
At least seven people have been killed and 34 others wounded in a church shooting in Jordan, authorities said Friday. The unidentified assailants allegedly attacked the Greek Orthodox church during a funeral in the Karak directorate in the central part of the country.
Seven people were killed and 34 injured on Friday when gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in Jordan’s Karak governorate, the head of the country’s Public Security Directorate told reporters, in a rare attack on the country’s Christian minority.
Speaking at a press conference in Karak, Major General Abdallah al-Maaytah said most of those wounded in the shooting at the Hamoud Church in Karak were still receiving treatment, and that the hunt for the attackers was ongoing.
Interior Minister Mazin Al Farrayeh said the attack had been carried out by “extremists”, but that it was too early to tell whether they had any links to known groups either inside or outside Jordan.
There was no immediate claim of responsibility.

A video aired on Jordan’s state-owned Al-Mamlaka television station that appeared to be from a security camera mounted on the church showed three people firing at it from a sidewalk and hiding behind trees and a low wall. The video showed the attackers then running towards the church’s entrance.
Khaled Burqan, who was at the funeral, told Al-Mamlaka that dozens of people were present and that the gunmen opened fire on them for several minutes.
Ihab Ammareen, another witness, told the station that he saw bloodied people collapse on the floor after the attack. “People were crying, wailing, screaming – it’s hard to describe,” he told the station.
King Abdullah II said on X that Jordan “will confront the terrorist act that targeted Karak with the harshest penalties” and offered his “deepest condolences to the families of the martyrs, and our wishes for recovery to the wounded”.
In 2016, gunmen ambushed police in a series of attacks in Karak, including at a Crusader castle popular with tourists, killing 10 people, including seven officers, and wounding dozens. Jordanian security forces killed the gunmen after a long standoff.

EU vies to expand role in Ukraine-Russia peace talks to influence US thinking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:15:39 UTC
23:15:39 KST

Brussels wants to turn the next round of trilateral peace talks betwen Ukraine, Russia and the US into a multilateral format with European representation.
The European Union is seeking a greater role in peace talks to end Russia’s war on Ukraine, potentially including direct contact with Moscow.
The United States wants to resume trilateral talks at the technical level in November, after its midterm elections. Ukraine says it welcomes any format at any time, while Russia has said it is “ready in principle”.
The peace process stalled in February after the US launched its war on Iran, shifting much of its diplomatic focus to the Middle East.
Brussels sees a possible resumption of talks as an opportunity to move from a trilateral to a multilateral format, bringing European representatives to the table and giving the EU a chance to influence Washington's thinking, which has recently shifted sharply in Moscow’s favour, setting off alarm bells.
Europeans, however, have a track record of being blindsided, dismissed and even ignored by their American counterparts, so there is no guarantee of success.
“Now, there is an expectation that there will be a multilateral-level discussion with representatives at senior official level, and the EU will be present at these talks,” European Commission deputy chief spokesperson Arianna Podestà said on Friday.
“We have always worked to have Ukraine in a position of strength, and we have always worked for a just and lasting peace for Ukraine. We’re doing so on every occasion.”
Podestà said the EU should be represented jointly by the European Commission, the bloc’s executive arm, and the European Council, which represents member states.
Asked whether this could involve European officials meeting Russian representatives face to face, she left the door open.
“At this stage, I wouldn’t have further details to provide. The expectation is that there would be a joint Commission-Council representation that would attend the meetings,” she said. “Beyond that, I don’t have other elements to share.”
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov did not immediately oppose European participation, as Moscow has done in the past, but stressed that the next round of talks under preparation would remain trilateral.
“Nothing can be ruled out a priori,” Peskov said.
“But these talks we are discussing, which are scheduled for the first half of November in Abu Dhabi, will take place in a trilateral format.”
A seat for two?
It remains unclear whether both EU institutions will have a place at the table.
The last rounds of talks involving Ukraine, Europe and the US, first in Miami and later in Oslo, included only Bjoern Seibert, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s powerful chief of cabinet.
Pedro Lourtie, chief of cabinet to European Council President António Costa, was not invited.
National security advisers from Germany, France and the UK — the so-called E3 — and NATO attended the Miami talks. In Oslo, Italy took France’s place.
Discussions focused on security guarantees for Ukraine, sanctions against Russia and post-war recovery. After the Oslo talks, US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Saint Petersburg for nearly three hours.
The Kremlin later dismissed Witkoff’s proposals as offering “little of real value” towards ending the war, while signalling its readiness to resume technical-level talks.
EU officials and diplomats say Moscow has yet to show signs of abandoning its maximalist demands or engaging meaningfully in the peace process. But with the stakes so high, they argue, Europe cannot afford to sit on the sidelines.
US President Donald Trump’s decision to strike a diesel supply deal with Putin and ease long-standing sanctions on Russia has alarmed European capitals, reinforcing their view that the EU’s presence at the table is essential as a counterweight to Washington.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, whom Trump has repeatedly criticised, has urged European leaders to establish their own diplomatic channel with Moscow.
Earlier this year, Costa quietly opened a line of communication with Russia, but the initiative failed to yield results and was put on hold.
The idea of appointing a special envoy was discussed again by EU leaders at last week’s summit. No consensus candidate emerged, but Finnish President Alexander Stubb has returned to the conversation after co-hosting the latest round of talks in Oslo.
Moscow later said it could accept Stubb as an intermediary, provided he did not “parrot” the European position — a condition unlikely to sit well with the Finnish president, a staunch supporter of Ukraine.

The cult Japanese writer and “rebellious genius” Ryu Murakami has died at the age of 74
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
17:14:31 EEST
23:14:31 KST

The cult Japanese writer and “rebellious genius” Ryu Murakami has died at the age of 74
Kyiv • UNN
The cult Japanese writer and filmmaker Ryu Murakami died on October 17 at his home. He wrote more than 40 works.
Ryū Murakami, the cult Japanese writer and filmmaker whose provocative novels, filled with black humor, found millions of readers, has died at the age of 74. According to the Japanese publishing house Gentosha, he passed away at his home on October 17, UNN reports, citing The Guardian.
Details
Murakami, who was called the "enfant terrible" (rebel genius) of contemporary Japanese literature, wove scenes of violence, explicit drug use, and sex into his works, using them to offer sharp criticism of Japanese and American cultures.
"It was a tremendous honor for us to present English-speaking audiences with many of Ryū Murakami’s strange, distinctive, and cinematic novels," said Adam Freudenheim, publisher and managing director of Pushkin Press, which publishes translations of Murakami’s works in the United Kingdom together with Bloomsbury.
Ryū Murakami was born in 1952 in the city of Sasebo (Nagasaki Prefecture) to a family of teachers. In high school, he played drums in a rock band, and after taking part in a protest on the roof of a building, he was placed under house arrest for three months. He published his first novel, "Almost Transparent Blue," in 1976. Written while he was still a student, the book is narrated by a character named Ryū and depicts the hedonistic lifestyle of a group of disillusioned young people gripped by nihilism. The work won the Gunzo New Writers’ Prize, as well as the Akutagawa Prize—the most prestigious literary award in Japan.
Ryū Murakami was not related to his more famous namesake—Haruki Murakami. Ryū Murakami’s books are "sharper and more vicious," journalist David Pilling wrote in 2013. "If Haruki is the Beatles of Japanese literature, then Ryū is its Rolling Stones."
Over the course of his life, Murakami wrote more than 40 novels and collections of short stories, including "Coin Locker Babies," "In the Miso Soup," "Audition," "Piercing," and "Popular Hits of the Shōwa Era." Most of his books have still not been translated into English.
Many of the author’s works were adapted for the screen—both with his own involvement and by other filmmakers. His best-known work is "Audition"—a 1999 feature film directed by Takashi Miike. The plot follows a widower who stages fake auditions in order to find a new partner. In 2009, writing about the novel in The Guardian, Irvine Welsh described its prose as "elegiac and touching, yet at the same time sharp and palpable on a physical level—like the touch of a butcher’s knife or a surgical scalpel."
Murakami’s third novel, "Coin Locker Babies"—the story of children abandoned in coin lockers—was recognized with the Noma Literary Prize in the "New Face" category. In 2020, Russell Thomas, selecting the work for a list of the best books set in Japan, wrote in The Guardian: "It is a surreal coming-of-age horror story that hurtles the reader from the heights of love and stardom to the depths of madness and murder." "In his works, Murakami never shies away from the opportunity to shed light on the darkest corners of society," he added.
"All of us at Pushkin Press are deeply saddened by the news of his death and extend our condolences to the writer’s many readers around the world," Freudenheim said.

Ukrainian Troops Battle Russians Inside Gas Pipeline for Months Near Kupiansk in “Operation Impossible”
Ukrainian troops from the 425th Separate Assault Regiment “Skelya” spent several months fighting inside an underground gas pipeline near the eastern Ukrainian city of Kupiansk in Kharkiv region, the regiment reported on October 22.
Skelya detailed the operation, which its troops called “Operation Impossible,” in footage published on its YouTube channel. The regiment stated that its troops cleared Russian forces from several kilometers of the pipeline and blocked further infiltration toward the city.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“During the months-long operation, our soldiers conducted assault operations underground, living and fighting in darkness, cold, and dirt,” the regiment stated. “At the same time, assault groups held positions in Radkivka to prevent the enemy from using the entrance to the pipeline near the settlement.”
Skelya troops eventually cleared the section of pipeline of Russian forces and prevented them from continuing to use it as an underground route toward Kupiansk.
The conditions inside the pipeline forced soldiers to remain in extremely confined spaces for days at a time. “For several days, we were constantly in a horizontal position, so the first thing we wanted to do after getting out was simply stand up,” one of the operation’s participants described.
The operation was aimed at denying Russian troops an underground approach to Kupiansk while Ukrainian assault groups simultaneously held the surrounding ground positions needed to secure access points to the pipeline, according to Skelya.
The fighting inside the pipeline came as Ukrainian forces increasingly turned underground infrastructure into an active part of operations around Kupiansk. On October 22, the 2nd Khartiia Corps reported that troops had traveled more than 15 kilometers underground during the separate Operation VELES before emerging behind Russian positions, while Ukrainian units attacked simultaneously on the surface.

Finland Prepares 36th Military Aid Package for Ukraine, Decision Expected by Year-End

- Category

Finland Prepares 36th Military Aid Package for Ukraine, Decision Expected by Year-End
Finland is preparing its 36th military aid package for Ukraine, with a decision on its approval expected before the end of 2026, Militarnyi reported on October 23.
Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo announced the plans during a joint press conference with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv on October 22.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"We are currently preparing the 36th package in close cooperation with the Ukrainian military. We plan to make a decision by the end of this year," Orpo stated.
The Finnish government is coordinating the contents of the upcoming package directly with Ukraine's military to address its operational requirements. Details of the equipment and weapons under consideration have not yet been disclosed.
Orpo noted that Finland had already provided Ukraine with five military aid packages in 2026. He confirmed that Helsinki would continue supplying military equipment and supporting the training of Ukrainian personnel.
The planned delivery is part of Finland's continued military assistance to Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Previous shipments have included artillery ammunition, armored vehicles, and other military equipment.
Among the Finnish weapons already deployed by Ukrainian forces are 120 KRH 85 92 mortars and Crotale air defense systems, designated ItO 90M in Finnish service. The Crotale systems are designed to intercept low-altitude aerial targets, including aircraft, helicopters, and drones.
Finland approved its 35th military assistance package on October 9 in response to an urgent Ukrainian request. That shipment contained a single type of defense equipment from Finnish military stocks, while preparations for a larger follow-up package were already underway.
The upcoming package builds on a sharp increase in the scale of Finnish assistance earlier this autumn.
On September 15, Finland allocated its 34th package, worth approximately $335 million, its second-largest defense allocation to Kyiv since the full-scale invasion began. Part of the equipment was purchased directly from the Finnish defense industry, while the contents and delivery schedule remained confidential for operational security.
That decision raised the total value of Finnish defense aid to roughly $4.15 billion, up from about $3.68 billion after President Alexander Stubb approved the $138.5 million 33rd package on May 29.

Russia Has Lost 241 More Square Kilometers Than It Captured Since September, ISW Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:13:30 UTC
23:13:30 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Has Lost 241 More Square Kilometers Than It Captured Since September, ISW Says
Russia’s offensive in Ukraine has effectively gone into reverse in recent weeks, with Moscow losing more territory than it has captured since the beginning of September while its personnel losses continue to climb, according to an October 22 assessment by the Institute for the Study of War (ISW).
ISW estimates that since September 1, Russian forces have lost a net 241 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory—meaning Ukrainian gains have exceeded Russian advances by that amount.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The pace of Russia’s territorial progress has also slowed sharply compared with 2025. During 2026, Russian forces have advanced at an average rate of only about 0.25 square kilometers per day.
At the same time, Ukrainian forces have increasingly regained the initiative on several sections of the front.
One of the most significant recent examples was Operation Vivaldi on the Lyman axis. Ukrainian forces recaptured more than 270 square kilometers of territory during the operation and disrupted Russian plans to threaten Ukraine’s so-called Fortress Belt in the Donetsk region.
Russia’s manpower situation is also deteriorating. ISW noted that monthly personnel losses are rising while recruitment is struggling to keep pace.
Since the beginning of October 2026, Russia has already lost nearly 37,000 troops, according to Ukrainian estimates cited in the assessment. For comparison, Russia’s personnel losses during the entire month of October 2025 totaled 31,270.
ISW assessed that the Kremlin could face increasing pressure in the coming months if Ukraine continues to seize the initiative and disrupt Russian offensive plans.
If current trends persist, Russian commanders may push more aggressively for some form of additional mobilization as battlefield losses increasingly outpace Moscow’s ability to replace personnel.
The broader picture, according to ISW, is that Russia is continuing to expend large numbers of troops without producing corresponding territorial gains—a trend that could become increasingly difficult for Moscow to sustain if Ukraine maintains its recent momentum.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces traveled more than 15 kilometers through underground infrastructure before emerging behind Russian positions during Operation VELES, a counteroffensive operation on the Kupiansk axis coordinated by the 2nd Khartiia Corps of Ukraine’s National Guard.

Emre Demiral and Rania Abushamala

Saudi Arabia announced Friday that the UN World Data Forum and the Saudi Statistics Forum, scheduled for November in Riyadh, have been postponed until 2027.
The Saudi General Authority for Statistics said in a statement on the US social media company X that the decision was made “in coordination with the United Nations Statistics Division.”
Both forums were due to take place from Nov. 9 to 12. New dates will be announced later through official channels, it added.
The authority said the postponement reflects its commitment to delivering an experience that meets the expectations of the data and statistics community and enables broad international participation by speakers, experts and partners.
This would strengthen the intended impact of the UN World Data Forum, it said.
The authority confirmed that the Road to Riyadh activities leading up to the UN forum will continue.
The postponement came amid an ongoing escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi group since July, alongside renewed fighting between the Houthis and Yemen’s internationally recognized government.
Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting Yemen’s government against the Houthis since March 2015.

Allegations against Thomas Markle Sr challenge media’s Meghan narrative
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:11:26 UTC
23:11:26 KST

The depiction of the Duchess of Sussex by certain sections of the media has often been one of a fame-hungry daughter casting off an elderly father in his declining years and keeping him from his grandchildren as she embraces the international celebrity stage.
Their estrangement has been the subject of countless headlines since her marriage to Prince Harry. But her statement today, released after child sexual abuse image allegations made against Thomas Markle Sr, 82, suggests deeper, darker fears as the cause.
“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them,” she said.
It has been speculated that the source of the estrangement between Meghan and Markle Sr, an award-winning TV lighting director, was over his decision to collude with a photographer and be paid for setting up shots of him preparing to attend the Sussexes’ wedding at Windsor Castle where he was due to walk her down the aisle.
In the end, Markle Sr pulled out of the wedding due to health issues, and it was Harry’s father, now King Charles, who lent the bride his arm on her final steps to the altar of St George’s chapel after she walked the first part of the aisle alone.
Since that day in May 2018, the relationship between daughter and father has never recovered. Now it appears the reasons why are contained in a letter from the same year, sent to the Metropolitan police and containing “troubling and disturbing allegations” against Markle Sr and shared with Meghan in the summer after her wedding.
The precise nature of those allegations has not been clarified, though they were enough for Meghan to want to keep her own family at a distance from him, her statement makes clear.
The fact she says that “the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine”, suggests the 2018 letter did not go as far as what has now been alleged.
Markle Sr has vigorously denied the latest allegations, which are made by his son Thomas Markle Jr, 60. First published by the Sun newspaper, they claim Markle Sr downloaded child sexual abuse images to computers and mobile phones found at his former home in the Philippines.
He has called the accusations “sick lies” from a son with whom he has a troubled relationship, and claims to have had no access to the computers and phones in question in the two years since he left Mexico, where he was previously living, for the Philippines, according to the Daily Mail.
Meghan clearly hopes to reframe the narrative of her estrangement from her father, which has often been shaped by his loquacious tendencies in many media interviews.
When speaking to journalists, Markle Sr has frequently lamented the breakdown of his relationship with his youngest daughter (he has two other children, Samantha Markle and Thomas Jr, from an earlier marriage). He has spoken of how he has been unable to reach Meghan, and of how he has never been allowed to meet his grandchildren, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five.
The media depiction has often leaned towards that of an uncaring daughter, whose father paid for her education, helped her to cultivate her interest in acting through his television work, and found himself abandoned in his time of need.
For the most part, Meghan has not publicly acknowledged his many health woes – he has suffered a series of strokes and recently had a leg amputated due to complications with a blood clot – and she clearly believes this has been weaponised against her.
However, in 2025, Meghan’s spokesperson confirmed that the duchess had “reached out” privately to her father when he was hospitalised and very unwell. He is now understood to be in a rehabilitation centre in Florida undergoing physiotherapy after the amputation of his leg.
Whatever the outcome of this latest development, it adds a new dimension to the complicated, fractured relationship between Meghan and her family.

BEIJING, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping sent a message to the 2026 Global Governance Forum (Xiongan) on Friday.

CANBERRA, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- The Australian government announced on Friday that construction has begun on a new laboratory wing at the Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness (ACDP) to strengthen the country's ability to detect and respond to emerging disease threats.
The facility, operated by Australia's national science agency CSIRO in Geelong, Victoria, plays a key role in protecting human and animal health, agriculture and the economy from infectious diseases.
In a joint statement, the government said the upgrade would enhance Australia's scientific and biosecurity capabilities, including its response to threats such as H5 avian influenza.
Minister for Science Tim Ayres said the bird flu outbreak demonstrated the importance of having the expertise and facilities needed to detect and respond quickly to serious disease threats.
The project will be delivered in two stages to ensure the center's diagnostic and research operations continue during construction.
The first stage is expected to be completed in 2029, allowing selected activities to move into the new laboratory wing before refurbishment of existing facilities begins.
The government said it had allocated an additional 387.4 million Australian dollars (about 252 million U.S. dollars) to CSIRO in its latest budget, on top of the agency's annual funding of nearly 1 billion Australian dollars. ■

IN BRIEF: What to know about restrictions at Moscow airports, evacuation at Sheremetyevo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:10:00 UTC
23:10:00 KST

MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. Temporary restrictions on aircraft arrivals and departures were imposed at Moscow’s Vnukovo, Domodedovo, Zhukovsky, and Sheremetyevo airports, Russia’s Federal Air Transport Agency (Rosaviatsiya) reported.
At present, Vnukovo and Domodedovo airports are accepting and dispatching flights in coordination with the relevant authorities. Restrictions at Zhukovsky and Sheremetyevo airports have been lifted.
Passengers were evacuated from the Sheremetyevo International Airport following an air raid alert issued due to the threat of a drone attack, the press service reported.
TASS has compiled the key information on the situation at the airports.
Restrictions imposed
- Temporary restrictions on aircraft arrivals and departures were imposed at Vnukovo, Domodedovo, Zhukovsky, and Sheremetyevo airports, the Federal Air Transport Agency (Rosaviatsiya) said.
- According to its statement, the restrictions were necessary to ensure flight safety.
- Moscow’s Sheremetyevo Airport warned passengers about possible changes to flight schedules and longer wait times due to the restrictions, the press service noted.
- As of now, Vnukovo and Domodedovo airports are accepting and dispatching flights in coordination with the relevant authorities, Rosaviatsiya said in a statement on its Max channel.
- Zhukovsky and Sheremetyevo airports have also resumed accepting and dispatching aircraft.
Evacuation at Sheremetyevo
- An air raid alert was declared at the Sheremetyevo Airport, the press service reported.
- Passengers were evacuated, and access to the secure areas of all terminals was restricted.
- Sheremetyevo Airport staff assisted passengers in moving to safe areas and provided updates on the current situation, the press service noted.
- Airport officials clarified that instructions for staff and passengers were displayed on screens throughout the terminals.
- The air raid alert has now been lifted.
Situation at airports
- The situation in the terminals is calm.
- Passengers have access to drinking fountains, water purifiers, water coolers, and free mother-and-child rooms in the terminals of Moscow’s airports.
- Airport information desks and call centers are operating.
- More than 20 flights bound for Moscow airports were diverted to other cities due to current restrictions, Moscow airports told TASS.
Airline actions
- Airlines are adjusting their schedules due to restrictions at airports in the Moscow Region, Rosaviatsiya noted.
- Aeroflot and Rossiya airlines confirmed that they are adjusting their schedules due to airport restrictions.
- Rossiya noted that the schedule changes are related to restrictions at Moscow and other Russian airports.
- According to Aeroflot, some flights have been diverted to alternate airports and will resume once the restrictions are lifted.
- Pobeda is adjusting its schedule due to ongoing restrictions in Russian regions and at Moscow hub airports, the carrier’s press office said.
- It operates at full capacity, providing information and assistance to customers in accordance with all regulations and standards.
- Passengers are asked to check their flight status before heading to the airport via the chatbot, on the departure airport’s website, and via the email address provided at the time of booking.
- The forced change and refund service allows passengers to change or refund their tickets on their own with just two clicks, even for non-refundable fares, the airline noted.
Monitoring
- Civil aviation operations in the Moscow region are under special monitoring by the Transport Ministry and Rosaviatsiya.
- The Transport Prosecutor’s Office is monitoring compliance with passenger rights in connection with restrictions at Moscow’s airports, the press service told TASS.
Handling of flights bound for Moscow
- Nizhny Novgorod’s Chkalov Airport, which serves as the main alternate airport for Moscow’s air hub, handled 13 flights bound for the capital, the press service said.
- St. Petersburg's Pulkovo Airport served as an alternate airport for 25 flights bound for Moscow, the company that operates the airport pointed out.

====================================================================================================

Africa CDC calls for urgent Ebola funding as cases spread
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
22:09:58 CST
23:09:58 KST

ADDIS ABABA, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) has called for enhanced regional preparedness and immediate release of pledged funds to avert further spread of the rapidly expanding Ebola outbreak.
Wessam Mankoula, head of the Continental Incident Management Support Team for the Ebola response at the Africa CDC, warned at an online press briefing Thursday evening that the Bundibugyo outbreak is expanding rapidly across geographic boundaries.
"With the evolving Ebola outbreak in our continent, unfortunately, the virus keeps moving, crossing from one country to another," said Mankoula, highlighting Nigeria as the latest African country to be affected by the deadly virus.
Nigeria on Tuesday confirmed its first case of Ebola, involving a woman who recently arrived in the country on an international flight from Uganda. The West African nation became the fifth country to have recorded a confirmed case, with the list also including the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Uganda, France, and Kenya.
Noting that Nigeria initially listed 44 close contacts, Mankoula highlighted that an additional number of contacts have been identified by the country's health authorities, while efforts are also currently underway to identify more contacts and bring them under quarantine.
The latest data from the Africa CDC showed that confirmed cases in the ongoing Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak have reached 9,735, with more than 4,690 deaths and a case fatality rate of 48.2 percent. Some 2,614 patients have recovered from the deadly disease.
Noting that the Ebola virus is only infectious when the patient starts developing symptoms, Africa CDC officials stressed that at-risk countries need to have multiple layers for detection. They highlighted the urgent need to bolster national and continental preparedness and surveillance capabilities.
"We need to have strong point of entry screening, strong surveillance capacity, and also strong laboratory capacity. This is in addition to looking for different pillars related to strengthening the preparedness capacity in all countries that do not have Ebola at this stage," said Mankoula.
Africa CDC data showed the current outbreak at week 23 has recorded 3.2 times more cases and three times more deaths than the next-highest comparator, the 2014-2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak.
Recalling a total of around 3 billion U.S. dollars in funding pledges, Mankoula noted that only 35 percent of the pledged amount has been disbursed from the donors so far.
"Ebola outbreak will not be controlled with pledges, as long as those pledges are not disbursed and used to push actions on the ground," he said. "While this outbreak is evolving, this is a time for the urgent release of those pledges." ■

FACTBOX: What we know about latest reciprocal prisoner exchange between Russia, Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:09:39 UTC
23:09:39 KST

MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. Russia has brought home 270 servicemen from territory controlled by the Kiev regime in exchange for 270 Ukrainian servicemen captured in combat, the Russian Defense Ministry said.
TASS has compiled the key information available so far.
Prisoner exchange
- Today, Russia returned 270 servicemen from territory controlled by the Kiev regime in exchange for 270 captured Ukrainian servicemen, the Defense Ministry said.
- The returned Russian servicemen are currently in Belarus.
- Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova is working with them.
- The Russian servicemen will receive further treatment and rehabilitation at Russian Defense Ministry medical facilities after receiving the necessary psychological and medical care and traveling back to Russia.
- The United Arab Emirates provided humanitarian mediation to facilitate the return of Russian servicemen from captivity, the Defense Ministry added.
Family reunifications
- Six families are reuniting in Russia and six more in Ukraine through a humanitarian initiative led by the two countries’ human rights commissioners, a TASS correspondent reported.
- Russian citizens will return home soon.
Efforts to arrange exchanges
- On September 15, Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova told TASS that talks with Ukraine on a new prisoner exchange were actively ongoing.
- She noted that dialogue with Ukraine’s human rights commissioner on exchanges and other humanitarian issues was difficult but important.
- Lantratova said the two countries’ human rights commissioners were working extensively to reunite families separated by conflicts and exchange documents.
- Cardinal Matteo Zuppi, president of the Italian Bishops’ Conference, expressed hope that he could help move the exchange process forward during a visit to Moscow in late September as the Pope’s special envoy for Ukraine.
- Zuppi also said that during the visit, he discussed various humanitarian cases requiring the sharing of information with Russian representatives.
Difficulties with exchanges
- Ukrainian authorities treat exchanges of captured servicemen like "trading at a market" and selectively take back their own troops, leaving hundreds of Ukrainian soldiers in captivity for years, Rodion Miroshnik, the Russian Foreign Ministry’s ambassador-at-large, has said.
Previous exchanges
- Since May 2025, Russia has handed over 3,976 captured Ukrainian servicemen to Kiev, while Kiev has returned 3,886 Russian servicemen, Miroshnik said on October 14.
- On August 19, Russia returned 103 servicemen from Ukrainian captivity, including 31 wounded, in exchange for 103 captured Ukrainian servicemen.
- On June 26, Russia returned 160 servicemen from Ukrainian captivity in exchange for 160 Ukrainian servicemen.
- On June 5, Russia and Ukraine exchanged captured servicemen as part of a reciprocal swap involving 185 servicemen on each side.
- On May 15, Russia returned 205 servicemen from territory controlled by Kiev in exchange for 205 captured Ukrainian servicemen.
- Russian Presidential Aide Yury Ushakov said on May 8 that Russia had agreed to US President Donald Trump’s proposal for a ceasefire with Ukraine from May 9 to 11 and an exchange of 1,000 captured servicemen on each side during that period.
- Russian President Vladimir Putin said on May 9, in response to reporters’ questions, that Moscow had proposed an exchange of captured servicemen to Ukraine before Trump made his proposal.
- On May 9, Ushakov noted that the relevant Russian and Ukrainian agencies were actively working on lists of captured servicemen and that an exchange would begin if they reached an agreement.

What do we know about the collapsed building?
Videos spreading online showed a dramatic crash and huge clouds of dust as the building came down in a busy business-residential mixed-use district.
The Red Cross sent teams to the site, posting on social media: "At around 1340 hours, a multi-story building under construction collapsed on 9th Street in Eastleigh, Nairobi."
There were conflicting reports on the size of the unfinished building. Nairobi Police Chief Issa Mohamud said the building had more than 10 floors under construction, while other accounts range from 12 to 18 stories.
Governor Johnson Sakaja's office said only the building's ground floor was occupied.
"There were some businesses in the basement, and workers who were busy building," local resident Abdi Aziz, 25, told the AFP news agency. "But since it was Friday prayers, a lot of them were at the mosque."
Rescue work underway at Nairobi building collapse site
A video published by Reuters news agency showed people gathered at the scene as an excavator moved rubble.
But rescue operations were proving complicated. Police officers sought to clear the area and provide access to emergency response teams but had to fire tear gas at people who had begun looting neighboring shops.
Eastleigh is a densely packed residential and market area, known as a hub for the Somali community.
It was not clear what caused the building to collapse.  Nairobi is undergoing an extremely rapid construction boom, with high-rise buildings shooting up all over the city as Kenya's population expands.
Kenya: How common are building collapses?
Building collapses are a recurring problem in Nairobi.
County officials responsible for issuing building permits have been accused of failing to conduct adequate inspections to ensure developers comply with construction standards and safety guidelines.
There were 86 building collapses between 2009 and 2019, killing an estimated 200 people, according to a report by the Kenya Institute for Public Policy Research and Analysis.
Meanwhile, a separate audit of almost 15,000 buildings by the National Building Inspectorate found that 4.8% were very dangerous while 72.3% were classified as unsafe.

Mucahithan Avcioglu
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
Türkiye plans to announce a revised National Energy Plan on Nov. 5, with stronger targets extending through 2040, a senior energy official said Friday.
Speaking at a panel at the Investment Summit Towards COP31 in Istanbul, Ahmet Ozkaya, director general of energy affairs at the Energy and Natural Resources Ministry, said renewable energy is essential to securing supplies, reducing import bills and achieving Türkiye’s 2053 net-zero emissions goal.
Combined wind and solar installed capacity has exceeded 44 gigawatts, he said, recalling the target announced in 2024 to increase capacity to 120 gigawatts by 2035.
“We anticipate stronger targets, particularly revised targets extending from 2035 to 2040,” Ozkaya said.
Grid investment essential
Ozkaya said integrating renewable energy with growing electrification requires stronger transmission and distribution infrastructure, alongside storage, interconnections and greater grid flexibility.
An earlier estimate put transmission and distribution investment needs at $80 billion through 2035, he said, adding that requirements would rise as the planning horizon extends to 2040.
Without grid upgrades, renewable energy ambitions would remain “just numbers and targets,” he warned.
The transition is also supporting domestic manufacturing, with local content approaching 100% in hydropower equipment, nearly 90% in solar and 60%-65% in wind, according to Ozkaya. He said the ministry is working on additional incentives to address competitive pressures facing the sector.
Technology and cleaner mobility
Basar Vural, chairman of ABB Türkiye, said technologies needed for electrification already exist, but deploying them requires coordinated action and an ecosystem capable of supporting growing demand.
He stressed the need for infrastructure investment to ensure electricity systems can meet rising demand.
Karin Gilges, president of Bosch Türkiye and the Middle East, highlighted digitalization and artificial intelligence as central to more sustainable manufacturing, alongside opportunities to reuse water and return it to production systems.
Murat Bulbul, CEO of Toyota Automotive Industry Türkiye, said reducing carbon dioxide emissions should remain the central objective of the automotive transition.
Differences in energy infrastructure, costs and socioeconomic conditions require multiple technologies, including hybrids, plug-in hybrids, battery-electric vehicles and hydrogen, he said.
Relying on a single solution would limit emissions reductions to particular regions, Bulbul argued, saying Toyota’s approach aims to provide suitable mobility options worldwide while leaving no one behind.
