Delicate operation carried out on explosives-packed WWII shipwreck
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:06:13 UTC
23:06:13 KST

Engineers perform delicate operation on explosives-packed World War II shipwreck, but bombs remain in place
Sheerness, England — A delicate operation aimed at preventing an 82-year-old U.S. shipwreck packed with tons of World War II explosives from unleashing a potentially catastrophic tidal wave on London has been completed. But while the most imminent danger has been addressed, the explosives remain inside the rusting wreck of the SS Richard Montgomery on the riverbed, and experts aren't taking their eyes off it.
The Montgomery, one of about 2,700 Liberty ships built in the U.S. to support the Allied war effort, was grounded on a sandbar off the town of Sheerness in the Thames Estuary, just 40 miles from the British capital, in August 1944. It was carrying munitions intended to support the Allies following the D-Day landings.
The vessel broke apart during salvage efforts and sank, with an estimated 1,500 tons of explosives in its cargo holds.
The ship's three rusting masts protruding from the water had been a familiar sight to residents and passing vessels for decades. But recent surveys revealed increasing deterioration in the structure, raising fears the masts could collapse and trigger an explosion.
"The vessel was starting to lean and deteriorate, so they could see some of the structures around the mast starting to collapse," Nolan Conway, a naval architect with Florida-based marine salvage firm Resolve Marine Group, which was contracted to remove the masts, told CBS News.
"The fear is the masts could have fallen onto the cargo itself, causing it to detonate," he said. "Some of the munitions are believed to be fused munitions with pressure fuses, so something like an impact could potentially set them off."
U.K. maritime minister Keir Mather told lawmakers in the House of Commons this week that the "complex project requiring specialist program, engineering and risk management expertise" had been completed ahead of schedule and on budget, with all three of the masts removed at a cost of just under $13 million, according to The Guardian.
Mather said in the U.K. Parliament that the masts had put "significant load on the structure and their removal has reduced that risk and supports the long-term safe management of the site."
The government has long maintained an exclusion zone around the wreck, which is about 1.5 miles off the Sheerness coast.
Mather told lawmakers the wreck would "continue to be subject to continuous monitoring and control via the established exclusion zone."
Removing the remaining explosives would carry considerable risks, and the consequences of an explosion remain the subject of debate among experts.
"The impact of this wreck detonating is unpredictable," Conway said. "Estimates range from impacting the shoreline, to creating a tidal wave that could travel up the Thames, to a rather minor event that could potentially just close a nearby shipping channel. There's a large range of impacts, but none of them are really good."
Officials continue to assess the overall risk of an explosion as low, but the deteriorating condition of the masts prompted authorities to act.
Conway said the challenge for the firm was to devise a way to remove the masts without disturbing the sunken ship's hull and the perilous cargo inside, or putting the people doing the work at risk.
"How can you cut off that mast without vibrating or impacting the wreck?" he said. "We designed a custom lifting frame to safely pick it up without the mast swinging or swaying as we lifted it free of the wreck."
Engineers used a remotely operated underwater diamond-wire saw that clamps "around the mast with hydraulic arms and passes the saw through without getting divers in the water," Conway explained.
The removal of the masts marks the end of a distinctive chapter in the wreck's history. The masts, visible above the estuary since World War II, are expected to be preserved for public display.
Mather, the U.K. maritime minister, said the masts had been moved to a local museum, the Historic Dockyard Chatham, and would be displayed "in recognition of the historic significance of the SS Richard Montgomery and its role in supporting the Allied forces' efforts during World War II."
More than eight decades after the ship failed to reach the battlefields of Europe, the Montgomery and its dangerous cargo will remain where it came to rest, now entirely hidden from view, but far from forgotten.

45 seconds of voting in the Lviv Oblast Council sparked a new dispute with Poland: Warsaw says Kyiv promised the UPA year decision will not take effect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:05:34 UTC
23:05:34 KST

On 20 October, the Lviv Oblast Council voted to declare 2027 the year of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), its commander Roman Shukhevych, and Oleh Olzhych, a poet and member of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN). The vote on the UPA and Shukhevych took 45 seconds, Ukrainska Pravda reported, citing the council's online broadcast. It reopened a dispute Kyiv and Warsaw had only just settled. In May, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy gave a special operations unit the honorary name "Heroes of the UPA," and Polish President Karol Nawrocki later stripped him of the Order of the White Eagle in response.
Poland is the main hub for Western aid to Ukraine, and that role rests on Polish trust, which every new fight over the two nations' shared past erodes. Since 2022, Poland has also paid for nearly 30,000 Starlink terminals for Ukraine, Rzeczpospolita reported. The sorest point is the UPA. Poland recognizes the UPA's 1943 Volhynia massacres of Poles as genocide, a classification Ukraine disputes, pointing to the broader Polish-Ukrainian conflict of World War II, in which both sides killed civilians.
A batch vote, then a "catastrophe"
The resolution honoring the UPA commander and his fighters passed with 52 of the 55 deputies who voted, none against. The one on Olzhych passed 49 of 54. A source in the council told Ukrainska Pravda that, after a lunch break and an air raid alert, deputies voted through 30 to 40 minor items one after another without discussion, and the UPA year passed among them.
A source in the Office of the President called the situation a "catastrophe."
"Ukraine looks irrational. We only just settled the previous crisis, and now this. Everyone knew it was not allowed, the head of the oblast knew about it personally. But the chase for cheap one-day hype won out. The consequences are already here, and they will only grow," the source told Ukrainska Pravda.
The same source said the decision put the next Polish military aid package at risk. Polish Defense Ministry spokesperson Janusz Sejmej said this was "not true," and Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk said Poland would keep helping Ukraine.
Ukraine's Foreign Ministry called the decision counterproductive, noted that oblast deputies are not subordinate to central authorities, and urged Poland to refrain from sharp steps that could hinder the normalization of relations. "Only Russia stands to gain from tension in our relations with Poland," Iryna Vereshchuk, deputy head of the Office of the President, wrote.
“Heroes of UPA” unit will keep its name, Budanov’s office says despite Polish pressure
Warsaw holds Kyiv to its word, but Lviv won't budge
Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz called the decision unacceptable. Deputy Foreign Minister Marcin Bosacki told Polsat News on 21 October that it was hard to imagine a worse decision for Polish-Ukrainian relations. He said Zelenskyy's aides had assured Warsaw it would not take effect, and that the resolution had disappeared from the council's website after Poland intervened, which he called promising. Warsaw would hold the Ukrainian authorities to their word, he added.
The council itself does not plan to revoke or revise the decision, its representatives told Liga on 21 October.
On 23 October, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said he had received a signal from Zelenskyy that he "will in no way support this decision" if further steps depend on him. "Ukraine will simply have very serious problems with integration if it does not also respect our sensitivity," Tusk said.
Poland bans proposal's initiator, who took part in search in Łasków, from Schengen Area
Poland has barred Sviatoslav Sheremeta, the Lviv Oblast Council deputy who initiated the decision, from entering the Schengen Area for five years, until 20 October 2031. Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński announced the ban on 21 October at the request of Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski. Sikorski described Sheremeta as a reenactor of the Galizien Waffen-SS division.
Before the ban was announced, Sheremeta told Zaxid.Net that he had never taken part in military-historical reenactment, and noted that Sikorski's post had at first named a "P. Sheremeta." He found Polish officials' reaction strange, since Lviv and other oblast councils had declared years of the UPA and Shukhevych before. "This is nothing new," he said. He added that the decision was not aimed at anyone, least of all Poles or Poland, and that a ban would hurt the two countries' cooperation on commemoration.
Ukrainians have the right to choose their own heroes and honor them, Sheremeta believes. He suggested that recent statements by Polish officials may be linked to the discovery of Ukrainian civilians killed by Polish armed groups in Łasków in 1944.
Sheremeta also directs Dolia, a memorial search center. In October, Dolia carried out a search in Łasków, a village in Poland's Lublin Voivodeship, and found the remains of more than 40 Ukrainians, including women and children. The Ukrainian Institute of National Memory, which commissioned the search, says they were killed by units of the Polish Home Army and the Peasants' Battalions in an attack on 10 March 1944 in which more than 300 people died. Exhumation is planned for spring 2027.
The dispute over shared memory has shaped relations between Kyiv and Warsaw for a decade. After local authorities in Hruszowice removed a UPA monument in 2017, Ukraine's Institute of National Memory halted exhumations of Poles in Ukraine. Despite a 2019 pledge by the institute to stop blocking them, the first exhumation took place only in April 2025, in Puzhnyky, after Tusk announced a breakthrough.

Poll shows Netanyahu’s bloc losing 3 seats as opposition leads with 54 to 48 ahead of Israeli elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:05:24 UTC
23:05:24 KST

A recent Israeli opinion poll published Friday showed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc losing three seats ahead of the upcoming legislative elections, falling to 48 seats compared with 54 for the Jewish opposition bloc, Anadolu reports.
The poll’s results were published by the Maariv newspaper four days before the election scheduled for Oct. 27.
Neither bloc would be able to form a government based on the projected results.
According to the poll, Netanyahu’s bloc lost three seats compared with the last week’s, in which it was projected to win 51 seats.
The poll found that Netanyahu’s bloc would secure 48 seats if elections were held today, including 19 for his Likud party, seven for Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power party, seven for the ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism party, eight for the ultra-Orthodox Shas party, and seven for Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism party.
The Jewish opposition bloc would win 54 seats, including 21 for Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party, 15 for Naftali Bennett’s Together party, 10 for Yair Golan’s Democrats party, and eight for Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu party.
Arab parties would secure 14 seats, with nine going to the Joint List, led by Yousef Jabareen, and five to the United Arab List, led by Mansour Abbas.
Separately, the Reservists party, led by Yoaz Hendel, would win four seats, though the poll did not specify which bloc it would support.
Forming a government requires the support of at least 61 of the Knesset’s 120 members.
Most leaders of Jewish opposition parties have ruled out cooperating with Arab parties to form a government.
Maariv attributed the decline in Netanyahu bloc’s projected seats to the failure of the “Your Israel” party, led by Ofer Winter, to cross the electoral threshold after polls in recent weeks had projected it would win four seats.
In recent days, Winter has faced pressure from Netanyahu’s camp to withdraw from the race, on the grounds that his continued candidacy would harm right-wing votes that could otherwise go to parties more likely to win seats.
Preferences for prime minister
The poll showed Eisenkot maintaining his lead over Netanyahu as the preferred candidate for prime minister, with 49% support compared with 41% for Netanyahu.
Bennett also led Netanyahu, receiving 45% support against 43% for the incumbent prime minister.
Israel’s prime minister is not elected directly by the public.
The position goes to the candidate who can form a government that wins the support of at least 61 Knesset members.
Possibility of another election
Should the current deadlock persist, Israel could find itself facing another round of elections — unless a unity government or a narrow-based government, supported from the outside by Arab lawmakers, is formed.
According to Maariv, 60% of Israelis prefer a unity government if the Knesset election produces no clear outcome.
Of those, 33% favor a government led by a figure from the “Change Bloc,” while 19% want Netanyahu to lead it. Another 8% said they were not interested.
The newspaper added that 23% favor holding another election if no decisive result emerges, down from 27% in the previous poll, while 17% said they did not know.
The outlet stated that the poll was conducted by the private Lazar Research Institute among a random sample of 580 Israelis, with a margin of error of 3.7 percentage points.

Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) warned that Russia may stage sabotage in Central and Eastern Europe, including the Baltic states, and blame Ukraine for the attacks, in a Telegram post on 23 October.
The warning comes three days after The Wall Street Journal reported that US intelligence traces Europe’s sabotage wave to Putin’s personal order. If Russia stages new attacks and pins them on Ukraine, as HUR warns, European anger could turn on Kyiv rather than the Kremlin. This goes further than HUR’s statement on 2 October, which named potential Russian targets in Europe but did not mention a plan to blame Ukraine for attacks.
HUR says Moscow wants to discredit Ukraine’s army
Russia is stepping up its hybrid strategy to destabilize the European Union, according to HUR. The agency identified two aims: reducing foreign support for Ukraine by discrediting its Defense Forces, and intimidating European governments and societies.
The accusations would be spread through Russian propaganda channels and international platforms accessible to the Kremlin.
Potential targets include infrastructure and Russian Orthodox Church sites
HUR listed several potential targets for Russian provocations:
- critical infrastructure and areas bordering Russia;
- the Kaliningrad exclave;
- areas of EU countries with Russian-speaking populations;
- Kremlin-controlled sites, including properties belonging to the Russian Orthodox Church network;
- historical sites associated with Russia.
The list reflects HUR’s assessment of potential targets, not confirmation that attacks at these locations are planned.
Earlier warnings and reported sabotage
On 2 October, HUR said Russian intelligence services had been ordered to increase activity in EU and NATO countries. It named military facilities, critical infrastructure, communications systems, and Starlink ground stations as potential targets and said it had alerted partners.

A European government official separately told the agency that the CIA had warned countries in the region of a possible Russian attack. The Journal cited European officials briefed on the intelligence findings.
According to the newspaper, at least three drones carrying military-grade Semtex explosives were involved. One struck an Antonov cargo plane used to transport military aid to Ukraine but failed to explode. Another collided with a different aircraft, while a third detonated near the airport perimeter. German newspaper Welt am Sonntag has since named two suspects, citing German investigation files. Earlier German media reports described the sequence differently.
The Journal also reported sabotage attacks on Starlink stations in Poland, Lithuania, and Bulgaria in recent weeks. In August, Slovak authorities said they had foiled a planned arson attack on a Ukrainian drone factory, the Journal reported.
Russia denies involvement in sabotage in Europe. Responding to Berlin’s accusations over the Leipzig incident in early September, Putin asked where the evidence was.

France deploys 70,000 police for new protests as Macron delays Africa trip
Massive law enforcement mobilised ahead of Saturday’s demonstrations amid calls online for violence and looting
France will deploy some 70,000 police nationwide as it braces for new protests this weekend after some of the worst urban violence in years erupted on the sidelines of demonstrations a week ago, the government said on Friday.

France to field twelve SAMP/T NG air defence units
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:00:55 BST
23:00:55 KST

France has ordered four additional SAMP/T NG firing units, taking its total order for the ground-based air and missile defence system to twelve, according to eurosam.
The Organisation for Joint Armament Cooperation, known as OCCAR, placed the contract on behalf of France with eurosam, the Franco-Italian grouping formed by MBDA France, MBDA Italy and Thales. The units will be delivered to the French Air and Space Force in a multi-layer configuration combining Aster and MICA VL missiles.
The company said: “This order is an additional step towards the renewal of the European Long-Range Air and Missile Defence ground capabilities, following the SAMP/T NG development launched in 2021.”
It added: “OCCAR-EA, eurosam and its members, MBDA and Thales will continue to lead the way in state of the art and sovereign air and Missile defence systems for the benefit of European defence. These advanced air defence systems are crucial in the current global context to respond to increasingly challenging threats.”
A SAMP/T NG firing unit holds up to forty-eight Aster missiles ready to fire, carried across up to six launcher modules of eight rounds each, alongside a multi-function radar and identification module able to detect and identify targets beyond 350km, and an engagement module. The whole system is mobile and eurosam says it can be operational in under thirty minutes, offering 360-degree coverage and engaging targets beyond 150km.
The system is designed around the Aster 30 B1 and the newer Aster B1NT. The B1NT uses a Ka-band seeker and new interception algorithms to give what the company describes as a hit-to-kill capability against short and medium range ballistic missiles, low manoeuvring targets and hypersonic missiles.
Britain has a stake in the wider programme, since the United Kingdom is a participant in the FSAF-PAAMS arrangement that OCCAR manages, and the fourteenth amendment to that contract, signed in Paris in January 2024, covered supplementary procurement of equipment allowing Britain to carry out mid-life upgrades to its own Aster missiles. Aster is the weapon carried by the Royal Navy’s Type 45 destroyers as part of the Sea Viper system, which HMS Diamond used against Houthi missiles and drones in the Red Sea.
France and Italy have supplied SAMP/T systems to Ukraine, where the type has engaged Russian ballistic missiles.
The order lands while Britain has no ground-based long-range air defence system assigned to the defence of the United Kingdom. Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, confirmed this week that a further £790 million will be invested in homeland integrated air and missile defence, covering enhanced command and control, improved sensing and radar systems, counter-drone capabilities and more effective layered defences.
The Defence Committee reported yesterday that anti-strike capabilities for shooting down ballistic, hypersonic and cruise missiles and drones are among the capabilities European NATO members lack in sufficient numbers, and that replacing American military capabilities with European weapons has been costed by the Kiel Institute at an extra €50 billion each year over the next decade.
Sky Sabre gives the British Army a medium range ground-based system, currently deployed in Poland and the Falkland Islands. This publication has reported on continuing work on the potential of British destroyers in the ballistic missile defence role and on when those destroyers will receive their missile upgrades.

Testosterone may help new brain cells survive, and timing could matter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:00:33 UTC
23:00:33 KST

New research in male rats suggests that the timing and duration of testosterone exposure may influence whether newly born brain cells survive to maturity. The study, published in Neuroscience, indicates that testosterone may be most effective at boosting the survival of young neurons during the later stages of their development, particularly within a part of the hippocampus involved in spatial learning and memory. These findings offer new insight into how male sex hormones support brain plasticity in adulthood.
Adult neurogenesis is the biological process by which the mature brain generates new functional nerve cells, or neurons, from dividing stem cells. This process takes place largely inside the hippocampus, a seahorse-shaped structure located deep within the brain’s temporal lobe that is essential for learning, memory formation, and stress regulation. Specifically, new cells are born along a thin band of tissue called the subgranular zone, located within a subregion of the hippocampus known as the dentate gyrus.
Once these precursor cells divide, they migrate into the neighboring granule cell layer and begin extending communication fibers to other parts of the hippocampus. Over several weeks, the surviving cells mature into functional neurons that are highly excitable and adaptable, helping the brain form new circuits and store new memories. However, roughly half of all newly generated cells in the hippocampus naturally die off within the first month before they can fully integrate into the brain’s network.
Hormones are among the major internal factors that regulate how many of these young cells survive. Testosterone, the primary male sex hormone, naturally declines as men age, and low circulating levels of the hormone are associated with an elevated risk of age-related memory decline and dementia, although results from clinical trials testing testosterone treatment for memory in older men have been mixed. In the body and brain, testosterone can act directly on androgen receptors or be converted by enzymes into other active hormones, such as estradiol, a form of estrogen, or dihydrotestosterone, a potent androgen.
“Growing clinical evidence has shown that testosterone can improve or sustain memory in aging men, potentially reducing the risk and severity of age-related memory loss, including Alzheimer’s disease,” senior study author Mark D. Spritzer, a professor of biology at Middlebury College, told PsyPost. “One mechanism by which testosterone may be having these effects is by acting as a neuroprotectant in the brain. The hippocampus is a region of the brain that is essential for learning and memory, and it is an area that degrades with age.”
Previous experiments in male rats have shown that removing the testes, and with them the main source of testosterone, does not change the rate at which new hippocampal cells are born, but it substantially reduces how many of those new cells survive. Restoring testosterone through daily injections for 30 consecutive days reliably rescues these young neurons. In contrast, several studies using shorter treatment windows of 15 to 21 days found no benefit for cell survival, while a recent experiment by the same research group showed that a brief five-day burst of testosterone given between days 11 and 15 after cell birth did improve survival.
This pattern raised questions about whether testosterone needs to build up over a full month to protect new neurons, or if young cells are simply more sensitive to the hormone during specific developmental stages. Between 11 and 30 days after birth, maturing neurons go through a sensitive window where they begin forming active connections, or synapses, with other brain regions. During this same timeframe, chemical signals from a neurotransmitter called GABA shift from exciting the young cells to inhibiting them, a transition that promotes proper maturation.
“We had previously shown that testosterone injections can improve levels of adult neurogenesis (proliferation and maturation of new neurons) within the hippocampus,” Spritzer explained. “However, we did not know whether or not specific periods of neuron development were more strongly influenced by testosterone. Therefore, the current experiment involved giving rats testosterone during different stages of neural development to assess the effects on adult neurogenesis. The ultimate goal is to better understand how testosterone influences the brain and cognition.”
To resolve the contradictions in earlier work, Spritzer, lead author Tatum W. Hamilton, and their colleagues at Middlebury College designed an experiment to test how different windows of testosterone exposure affect neuron survival at 30 days of age. They directly compared a full 30-day treatment against two 15-day treatments covering either the first half or the second half of the cells’ 30-day maturation period.
The researchers worked with 43 adult male Sprague-Dawley rats that were approximately 60 days old at the start of the study. All rats were housed individually to control for social variables, as prior work showed that testosterone’s effects on the brain are easier to detect in individually housed animals. One week after arriving at the laboratory, all of the rats underwent surgical castration to remove their natural source of testosterone, allowing the scientists to precisely control hormone levels through injections.
Eleven days after surgery, every rat received a single abdominal injection of bromodeoxyuridine, a synthetic compound commonly known as BrdU. When cells divide, they incorporate BrdU into their newly synthesized DNA, which permanently tags the exact batch of cells born during the brief window after the injection. By waiting 30 days and then counting how many BrdU-tagged cells remain in the brain, scientists can measure the survival rate of that specific generation of cells.
Starting the day after the BrdU injection, the rats were divided into six groups of six to eight animals each. Half of the groups received daily injections of testosterone propionate at a high physiological dose of 0.500 milligrams per rat; earlier work by the same group found that a lower dose of 0.125 milligrams had no effect on new neuron survival. The other half received inert sesame oil injections as a comparison control. These injections were administered during one of three time windows following the BrdU tag: an early period (days 1 to 15), a late period (days 16 to 30), or the full period (days 1 to 30).
On day 31, the researchers collected blood samples to verify hormone levels and extracted the rats’ brains for microscopic analysis. They sliced the entire hippocampus into thin sections and used chemical staining techniques to make the BrdU-tagged cells visible under a light microscope. A researcher who was blinded to which treatment each rat received counted the labeled cells across the granule cell layer and subgranular zone, as well as in an adjacent area called the hilus to check whether any changes were specific to the neurogenic zone.
The team also divided their cell counts between the dorsal (top/front) and ventral (bottom/back) portions of the dentate gyrus, because these two zones serve different functions. The dorsal hippocampus is primarily involved in spatial navigation and memory, whereas the ventral hippocampus mainly regulates stress and anxiety. Finally, using a laser-scanning confocal microscope and fluorescent markers, the researchers examined 50 randomly selected BrdU-tagged cells per rat to see how many also contained NeuN, a nuclear protein found in mature neurons.
Blood tests confirmed that rats receiving testosterone during the late period and the full 30-day period had elevated serum testosterone concentrations at the end of the experiment, averaging about 5.7 nanograms per milliliter, compared to less than 0.3 nanograms per milliliter in the oil-treated groups and the early-period testosterone group, which had stopped receiving hormone injections 16 days earlier.
Across the entire dentate gyrus, rats treated with testosterone had higher numbers of surviving BrdU-labeled cells in the neurogenic zone than rats given oil. Planned statistical comparisons between the hormone and oil groups within each time window showed that only the full 30-day testosterone treatment produced a statistically significant increase across the whole structure. Rats given testosterone during the late window (days 16 to 30) showed a trend toward higher cell survival across the whole dentate gyrus that fell just short of statistical significance, while early treatment (days 1 to 15) had no effect.
“The results suggest that testosterone may have an additive effect, which is a novel finding,” Spritzer noted. “Namely, longer exposure to testosterone increased neurogenesis to a greater degree.”
When the researchers examined the dorsal and ventral regions separately, a more specific pattern emerged. In the dorsal dentate gyrus, testosterone increased cell survival in both the full 30-day group and the late 16-to-30-day group, while the early 1-to-15-day group showed no benefit over oil injections. In the ventral dentate gyrus, testosterone had no effect on cell survival during any of the three treatment windows, although rats injected during the early period unexpectedly had fewer surviving cells in this region than rats injected during the late or full periods regardless of whether they received hormone or oil.
Fluorescent microscopy confirmed that roughly 79 to 87 percent of the surviving BrdU-tagged cells had matured into NeuN-positive neurons across all groups, regardless of whether the rats received testosterone or oil. Because the hormone did not alter the proportion of new cells that became neurons, the higher BrdU counts can be read as a greater number of surviving new neurons. No treatment differences were found in the overall tissue volume of the dentate gyrus or in cell counts within the neighboring hilus region.
Together, these results suggest that maturing neurons in the dorsal hippocampus are especially responsive to testosterone when they are between two and four weeks old. Because the dorsal hippocampus governs spatial learning, the authors note that this regional sensitivity aligns with past behavioral experiments showing that testosterone improves spatial working memory in male rats. The hormone may help preserve new cells during this late window by blocking programmed cell death, boosting supportive growth proteins like brain-derived neurotrophic factor, or aiding the transition of GABA signals as young neurons wire into existing brain circuits.
“We demonstrated that testosterone enhances adult neurogenesis, with the effects being strongest during the later stages of neuronal development,” Spritzer said. “These results suggest that testosterone may be a useful therapeutic target for helping to sustain neuroplasticity, among men in particular.”
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. First, the experiment was conducted in surgically castrated young adult rats housed in social isolation, which does not mirror the gradual, partial hormone decline experienced by aging men in daily life. Second, the blood and brain tissue were collected 24 hours after the final testosterone injection for the full and late groups, but 16 days after the final injection for the early group. The authors raise the possibility that this gap helps explain why early treatment showed no benefit, but note that this explanation would require new cells to die off at a steady rate throughout development, which earlier research does not support.
“This was preclinical research conducted with rats, so it cannot be extrapolated directly to humans,” Spritzer cautioned. “However, it is suggestive that testosterone may have therapeutic value. Of importance was that we used a high physiological dose of testosterone, and the effects of dose levels have not been considered carefully in past human clinical studies involving testosterone.”
Spritzer also pointed out that boosting cell survival without limit is not necessarily the goal. “One challenge with neurogenesis research is the assumption that more is always better,” he added. “There is likely an optimal level of adult neurogenesis for best brain functioning.”
In addition, the overall statistical analysis did not show that testosterone’s effect differed across the three time windows, so the conclusions about timing rest on separate comparisons within each window, each involving only six to eight rats per group. The study also did not directly measure the molecular pathways inside the cells, so it remains uncertain whether testosterone acted through androgen receptors, estrogen receptors, or downstream growth factors during that 16-to-30-day window. Nor did it test whether the extra neurons translated into better learning or memory. Future research will need to test these specific molecular mechanisms and examine whether similar timing effects apply to older animals or females.
“Now that we know more about the stages of neural development that are influenced by testosterone, assessing the molecular mechanism will be important,” Spritzer said. “Testosterone is metabolized in the brain and likely has many effects on neuronal development, which should be explored.”
The study, “Effects of testosterone upon the survival of new neurons in the dentate gyrus of adult male rats,” was authored by Tatum W. Hamilton, Ezra J. LeMole, Grace K. Nadecki, Jordan M. Gardner, Quinn P. Kennedy, Kathryn A. Blek, and Mark D. Spritzer.

British premier urges UK households to stockpile water, food amid rising risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:00:30 UTC
23:00:30 KST

Aysu Bicer
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
UK households are being urged to stock up on bottled water, canned food, and other essential supplies to prepare for emergencies amid growing concerns over severe weather, cyberattacks, and potential disruptions to food supplies.
Speaking at a wildfire resilience summit in Liverpool, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Friday that people should take sensible measures to ensure they have enough supplies at home to cope with difficult situations as storms batter parts of the country.
He said "unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common," adding, "it's not about panic buying... It's about just taking sensible measures to have enough in the house to tide you over should there be a difficult situation."
The government's recommendations advise households to keep enough essential supplies to last three days, including nine liters of water per person and non-perishable food such as canned meat, vegetables, and dried fruit.
The guidance also recommends keeping a battery-powered or wind-up FM radio, a torch, blankets, a first aid kit, hand sanitizer, wet wipes, toiletries, and a charged power bank.
Households are also advised to keep cash on hand in case electronic payment systems fail, alongside copies of important documents, and essential supplies for babies and pets.
The advice comes after the National Audit Office warned that Britain's food supply chain faces growing risks from cyberattacks and the climate crisis, saying the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs had not done enough in recent years to strengthen resilience.
Burnham, however, rejected the claims that the government had failed to prepare adequately.
He pointed to the need for greater public preparedness amid increasingly frequent unexpected events, including severe weather and power outages.
Burnham said he kept beans and soup in his cupboard and also recommended Twiglets as part of his personal emergency supplies.

====================================================================================================

The alleged attack on Helen Haines shocked the nation. It shouldn’t have
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:00:30 UTC
23:00:30 KST

“Thoughts and prayers.” After each soul-destroying mass shooting in the United States, this is the platitude invariably trotted out by every impotent politician unable to confront the stranglehold reality of the country’s gun lobby.
“Turn the temperature down,” risks becoming Australia’s equivalent. The plaintive cry to hold back a rising tide of hatred and anger, incubated, amplified and legitimised online, now spilling into grotesque real-world violence.
Helen Haines, the independent member for Indi, remains in hospital. She has lost both legs after a driver allegedly deliberately drove into her twice, outside her electorate office. A man has been charged. The motivation for his alleged attack remains unclear. But the horrific incident has sparked an urgent national reckoning about the safety of public figures, especially women.
Haines’s life will never be the same. But what of political life? What of the lives of women who seek to claim their place in shaping the future of their country?
‘Targeting women because they are women’
In the days since the alleged attack on Haines, politicians have detailed their own experiences of abuse and threats.
The minister for women, Katy Gallagher, has had her children threatened. A man told Pauline Hanson online he would “hunt her down and kill her”.
The social services minister, Tanya Plibersek, received an anonymous note slipped under the door of her home, telling her they hoped her children “die of painful cancers”. The number of death and rape threats she has received over years in public life is beyond counting, she said.
Male politicians face threats too. ACT senator David Pocock has moved house several times because of safety concerns for himself and his young family. Barnaby Joyce says a driver performed a u-turn to drive directly at him.
But the attacks and threats are overwhelmingly gendered.
Last year, then AFP commissioner, Reece Kershaw, told senate estimates that “the nature of threats and comments directed at female parliamentarians and high office holders is particularly troubling, with a common feature being offensive material centred on derogatory language about their appearance”.
“Some of this material also contains extremely violent themes, including threats of graphic, sexual violence,” he said.
“These threats, which are being made online or are being sent in the post or over the phone, are sometimes also directed at their children.”
Kershaw said politicians were targeted because of their public profiles or policy positions. “However, in some cases, it appears male offenders are targeting women because they are women.”
A parliamentary report last year found 85% of surveyed parliamentarians and their staff reported dealing with constituents “behaving in a violent, threatening or volatile manner”.
Australia is not alone. The Inter-parliamentary Union (of more than 180 parliaments around the world) found “parliamentarians around the world are facing growing levels of intimidation, harassment and violence from members of the public”. A global survey found the odds of a politician experiencing online violence were more than twice as high for women as for men.
While members of Australia’s political class are the victims of a rising hostility online erupting into the real world, they are part of establishing a baseline for the tenor and tone of political debate.
The week before Haines was allegedly attacked, the member for Moncrieff, Angie Bell, stood in the House of Representatives and said that the small business minister, Anne Aly, and the prime minister, should be “stoned in the square” for a decision made by the tax office.
That evening, Aly posted on Instagram a devastated, wearied, riposte.
“This is not just something that we should just turn away from.”
Aly then, almost as an afterthought, revealed: “this past week alone, I’ve had 19 death threats on my social media. And in the past I’ve had death threats that are couched in that exact same language: ‘stone her’.” Bell withdrew the comment and has since apologised.
‘An environment has been created’
There is a bleak irony that Aly took to social media – responsible for incubating and amplifying so much violent political rhetoric – to speak out against the attack made against her on the ostensibly more dignified floor of the parliament.
The chair of the Centre for Journalism & Democracy at City St George’s University of London, Prof Julie Posetti, is lead author of a series of UN Women reports, which began with last year’s publication, Tipping Point: The chilling escalation of online violence against women in the public sphere.
Surveying more than 600 women across 119 countries – with a particular focus on human rights defenders, activists and journalists – the report found more than 70% of respondents had experienced online abuse in the course of their work, and 41% had experienced real-world attacks, abuse, or harassment that they linked to online abuse.
British-Australian Posetti, familiar with the political culture of both countries, says attacks on politicians were both “entirely predictable and utterly shocking”.
“Women are being forced out of public-facing roles … including representative office, because of the serious threats that are being delivered at scale with virtual impunity.”
This pressure comes after years of hard-fought improvements for women in political power. While women’s representation in government has increased dramatically over the past decades, and in Australia women make up about half of federal parliament, globally women hold just 22% of cabinet level positions, and that proportion is now falling.
More than 100 countries have never had a female leader.
Posetti describes the online-to-offline trajectory of violence as a “vicious, self-perpetuating” cycle. Online threats beget offline attacks, and offline abuse – such as politicians attacking female journalists during press conferences – can trigger a tsunami of online harassment, further exacerbating the risk of offline attacks.
“It’s a fire where fuel is just continuously loaded into the mix. It elevates perpetually and it’s amplified online … through those algorithmic drivers, which are tuned to do what they do for profit, because we know that engagement is more likely to be driven by anger and rage than it is by support for some kind of positive action, for example.”
The rising tide of violent rhetoric and action is occurring alongside a broader democratic erosion, one being witnessed around the world.
Posetti said decades of progress on gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls were backsliding at an alarming rate under a rising tide of authoritarianism, in which “strong man” leaders decry everything from diversity, equity and inclusion, to low birthrates, and whose acolytes joke about male control over female bodies.
“An environment has been created where there is tolerance for slut-shaming women in politics who are routinely threatened with being ‘raped to death’, for threatening violence against women journalists, and for threatening the families of women human rights defenders with violence,” Posetti says.
“If you push women out of public life, you are less likely to get women’s issues represented effectively, you are less likely to see nuanced stories about women covered empathetically: there are real implications for women’s participation in democratic deliberation, not just in being elected to office, but women are being driven out of public debate entirely because there is no safe way to engage.”
Posetti argued misogynistic rhetoric “which just five or 10 years ago would have been viewed as repugnant and unpalatable” was being legitimised and reinforced online.
In the US, so often the grim indicator of the direction of Australian politics, in 2024 the president threatened a female political opponent with “nine barrels shooting at her … when the guns are trained on her face”. Violence is celebrated: this week Donald Trump congratulated a supporter at a rally for punching a protester.
Law follows language. Rhetoric has real-world consequences.
The case that established abortion rights in the US, Roe v Wade – settled law of the land for nearly 50 years – was overturned in 2022. Even now, a decade-old tenacious right-wing movement has swung back into vogue in that country – #Repealthe19th – which overtly argues that women be banned from voting.
Addressing the crisis
Fuelling so much is the isolating duality of the online world: the platforms that promise connection but offer only an ersatz counterfeit, while peddling invitations to the darkest corners and reinforcement of the basest of instincts.
Users are bombarded all by relentless “feeds” that feel public but are, in fact, uniquely private, carefully curated by deliberately arcane algorithms.
Violent memes are posted for all the world to see, but the algorithms hold each viewer in an individual self-reinforcing silo.
If those violent posts generate “engagement”, even a moment’s attention, more and more like it are offered, are imposed. Each feed is its own incubator, under constant singular refinement, making social media ever more isolated, more idiosyncratic, more dangerous to vulnerable people.
Posetti says there were two key elements to addressing the deepening crisis. The first is the human element: “There needs to be a commitment from organisations, from political and corporate leaders, and from others in public life, to treat other human beings with decency and dignity”.
The second is regulation of the technology platforms on which vitriol is allowed to flourish, amplify and spread. “No matter how effective the political leadership is, unless you address the technological drivers for the escalating hate towards women, minorities, other marginalised groups in society, then you are … sticking a used Band-Aid on a gaping wound, trying to address the aftermath.”
Australia, the global vanguard on social media bans for children, and the development of a proposed digital duty of care, “has a rare opportunity to take some global leadership on this”.
Focus on misogyny
After the alleged attack on Haines, New Zealand MP Tamatha Paul saw parallels in the killings, 10 years apart, of female British politicians Jo Cox and Ann Widdecombe. (Male MP Sir David Amess was murdered in 2021).
“These were women in politics who were walking down the road, standing outside of their electorate offices, walking to their homes, being in their homes, when they have been attacked or murdered.”
Paul argued the well-meaning counsel from security agencies on how politicians could keep themself safe – don’t advertise social engagements, change routines and routes to work and home – undermined democratic engagement and missed the fundamental problem.
“Focus on the fact that misogyny and rape culture, and allowing it to manifest and fester in our society, is what normalises violence against women: either violence against high profile women in politics and all of the invisible violence that happens behind closed doors.
“Why do women have to pay with our lives?”
Paul said she had a message for men: “this is on you to call out your friends”.
“When they make jokes, when they say that politicians look like pigs, when they make comments that they would never make about another man, call them out.
“Call them out because this is what happens.”

CICA members look to turn regional dialogue into action

For more than three decades, the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia (CICA) has provided a platform for dialogue among countries with different political and economic priorities. Its 28 members are now looking at ways to strengthen cooperation on regional security, economic development and emerging challenges.
Under Azerbaijan's chairmanship, which began in 2024, discussions have focused on strengthening the organisation's institutional framework and making cooperation more practical. Migration, climate change and artificial intelligence were among the issues raised, alongside finance, education and business. As CICA enters a new phase, attention is turning to how member states can translate discussions into lasting cooperation.

High housing prices in Bulgaria have driven around 20% of potential buyers out of the market over the past year, while annual property price growth could slow to between 5% and 7% in 2027, Miroslav Vladimirov, a board member of one of the country’s leading real estate brokerage firms, told Bulgarian National Radio (BNR).
Property prices are currently increasing by approximately 15% year over year, but a continued decline in transactions could bring a substantial slowdown in that growth, Vladimirov said.
“The annual price growth remains consistent with 2024 and 2025 levels - hovering around 14–15% year-on-year as of the end of the second quarter. If the decline in transaction volume persists, we are likely to see a slowdown in the rate of price growth; rather than a 15% annual increase, we might see figures in the 3–7% range,” he explained.
The number of property transactions has dropped by 14,086, with the decline beginning in the final quarter of 2025 and continuing through the first two quarters of 2026. Although transaction volumes had remained relatively stable over the previous five years, property prices rose significantly. The latest year-over-year decline amounts to approximately 17% to 18% compared with 2025.
Vladimirov said prices are still rising because demand has not fallen enough to put downward pressure on the market. Mortgage affordability also remains relatively high, he added.
“The mortgage market is what is sustaining this level of transactions. It is primarily buyers using their own funds, their savings, who have withdrawn from the market,” Vladimirov said, noting that some potential buyers are unwilling to pay current prices.
“Inevitably, households will become more cautious and will be less inclined to take unreasonable risks,” he added.
Vladimirov expects property prices to undergo a correction if the decline in transaction volumes continues.
Speaking on BNR’s Horizon Before Noon (Horizont do obed) program, he also forecast a modest increase in mortgage interest rates, although the rise is expected to remain below 1%.
Meanwhile, sellers are continuing to demand prices comparable to those seen last year, keeping properties on the market for longer as the number of transactions falls by 18%.
The residential property market is showing signs of returning to more typical levels after a record 18.
Housing prices remain on the rise, but the number of completed transactions is falling, pointing to signs of a gradual cooling in the property market.
Property tax valuations in Bulgaria will increase by 30% next year and by 35% in each of the following two years, while the change will not affect the household waste fee, Deputy Finance Minister Lyudmila Petkova said
Housing prices in Bulgaria climbed 15.5% year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, according to National Statistical Institute (NSI) data

Yemen’s army said Friday that more than 35 fighters of the Houthi group were killed or wounded in a military operation targeting the group’s positions in southwestern Taiz province, Anadolu reports.
In a statement, the army’s 35th Armored Brigade said its forces carried out a “swift and targeted operation” against Houthi positions and fortifications along the Aqrouz front in the Al-Misrakh district.
It said the operation targeted positions at Jabal Al-Manara, Kour, Wadi Kour, Al-Maqda, Al-Dabaya and Kahlan, leaving “more than 35 Houthi fighters killed or wounded.”
The statement did not specify the number of fatalities or injuries.
The operation also disabled a military vehicle equipped with weapons and destroyed Houthi fortifications at the targeted sites, it added.
The Houthis did not immediately comment on the Yemeni army’s account.
Taiz province has witnessed fierce fighting between the Yemeni army and the Houthis for weeks, killing and wounding hundreds on both sides.
READ: 1,574 killed, 6,939 injured in Yemen escalation since August: WHO
Taiz holds strategic importance as a geographic bridge and a vital link between Yemen’s northern provinces.
Control of the province would mean control over supply routes and key transport corridors connecting the interim capital, Aden, with the country’s central and northern provinces.
These developments are part of a military escalation that began in July and is considered the most extensive since the relative calm that followed a truce launched in April 2022.
Since Oct. 5, Yemeni government forces have been conducting Operation Dawn of Yemen, which Presidential Leadership Council Chairman Rashad al-Alimi said aims to regain control of state institutions from the Houthis and recapture the capital Sanaa.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized Sanaa and several other provinces in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.
The Houthis control much of northern and western Yemen, while government forces and their allies hold Aden and large parts of the country’s southern and eastern provinces.

Estonian employers get right to test employees' sobriety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:56:00 UTC
22:56:00 KST

Estonian employers get right to test employees' sobriety
Amendments to the Occupational Health and Safety Act that take effect on October 26 will give employers the right to test employees for intoxication.
However, according to the Labor Inspectorate, this does not mean that every workday can now begin with a breathalyzer test. Under the new rules, employers may test employees for intoxication if there are reasonable grounds for suspicion. For example, suspicions may arise if an employee behaves unusually, slurs their speech or displays other signs of possible intoxication.
An exception applies to workplaces where working while intoxicated could have particularly serious consequences. If an employee's duties involve operating potentially hazardous equipment or they work in an environment involving such hazards, the employer may conduct intoxication tests even without reasonable suspicion. This could apply, for example, to bus and truck drivers, operators of dangerous machinery and construction workers.
The aim of the amendment is to prevent workplace accidents and protect employees, their colleagues and others.
Employers cannot conduct intoxication tests at their own discretion. Before conducting tests, they must establish written procedures and inform all employees of them. These procedures must clearly specify how testing will be conducted, what constitutes a positive result, the potential consequences of such a result and what happens if an employee refuses to be tested. Employees' rights must also be protected and they must have the opportunity to challenge test results.
Employers may retain intoxication test data for up to three years from the date of testing.
The Labor Inspectorate emphasizes that the purpose of intoxication testing must be to ensure workplace safety, not to subject employees to unjustified checks.

Melania Trump secures ceasefire in Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, White House says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:55:52 UTC
22:55:52 KST

The agreement, due to take effect on 29 October, is intended to allow humanitarian aid and civilian evacuations in a city where residents have endured years of Russian occupation, severe food shortages and dangerous attempts to escape.
US First Lady Melania Trump has secured an agreement between Russia and Ukraine to temporarily halt military operations in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, the White House announced on Friday. The intent is to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and evacuate civilians trapped near the front line.
The localised ceasefire is scheduled to begin on 29 October, with both sides agreeing to suspend military action in the southern Ukrainian city and establish a designated safe passage for residents wishing to leave, according to the White House.
Oleshky lies on the Russian-occupied eastern bank of the Dnipro River, opposite the Ukrainian-controlled city of Kherson. Before Russia's full-scale invasion, it had approximately 24,000 residents. According to White House estimates, only 1,700 to 2,000 remain, including around 50 children.
The announcement comes amid a deepening humanitarian crisis in Oleshky, where residents face severe shortages of food, clean water and medicine, while attempts to escape have exposed civilians to mines and drone attacks.
Speaking exclusively to Euronews on 13 October, Tetiana Hasanenko, head of the Oleshky city military administration, described a city devastated by more than four years of Russian occupation.
"The city is practically destroyed," she said. "There is almost no building that has not been damaged."
Hasanenko estimated that around 2,000 people remained in Oleshky, including 35 children who, she said, were unable to leave.
She described residents surviving on a single meal a day, sometimes consisting of only a few spoonfuls of grain, while others had resorted to eating weeds.
Melania Trump's role in the agreement
According to the White House, the First Lady and her representative worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leaders to negotiate the terms of the humanitarian pause, including its timing, technical procedures and implementation.
Melania Trump initiated discussions with both sides, acting in what the White House described as the formal role of "Exclusive Intermediary".
"The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster," she said.
The First Lady described the remaining population as predominantly elderly residents in urgent need of medical attention and basic supplies, with limited electricity, mined roads and continuing military attacks complicating humanitarian access.
She argued that her intervention had been essential to securing the agreement and making aid deliveries and evacuations possible.
Under the proposed arrangements, civilian representatives from Ukraine and Russia will visit residents in their homes to assess their needs and coordinate assistance.
Those wishing to leave will be offered transportation to their preferred destination, with Melania Trump saying she expected some to choose Ukraine and others Russia.
The First Lady also said she had secured the participation of an impartial American media organisation to accompany and document the operation, although the White House did not identify the organisation.
The statement did not specify how long the ceasefire would last or provide detailed security guarantees for those involved in the humanitarian operation.
A 25-kilometre 'road of death'
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the first days of Moscow's full-scale invasion in February 2022. The city was further devastated by flooding following the destruction of the Kakhovka dam in June 2023, which submerged large parts of the area and damaged already fragile infrastructure.
In her exclusive interview with Euronews, Hasanenko described how residents attempting to flee had been forced to walk approximately 25 kilometres towards the village of Radianske, crossing heavily mined territory exposed to drone attacks.
Many were already physically weakened by hunger, she said, while some who managed to escape subsequently returned with food for children and elderly relatives unable to make the journey themselves.
Hasanenko said people had been killed by mines along the route, with some bodies left unrecovered.
"This road really is a road of death," she said.
She also accused Russian forces of targeting food deliveries and punishing residents suspected of receiving assistance from Ukrainian troops.
Euronews has been unable to independently verify conditions inside Oleshky, which remains under Russian occupation and inaccessible to independent journalists.
A humanitarian operation in occupied territory
The White House said the initiative originated during a private discussion at Melania Trump's Fostering the Future Together event in New York, held during the 81st United Nations General Assembly.
Both countries then assigned teams to coordinate the arrangements, including demining, according to the White House.
The agreement, if implemented, could provide a rare opportunity to reach civilians who have spent years largely cut off from regular humanitarian assistance.
But with Oleshky remaining under Russian military control, questions remain over how safe access will be guaranteed, how the suspension of hostilities will be monitored and whether residents will be able to leave freely for their chosen destinations.

Türkiye eyes COP31 to attract green investment, advance industrial transformation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:55:00 UTC
22:55:00 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
Türkiye sees COP31 as an opportunity to attract international green investment and accelerate industrial transformation, officials said on Friday, highlighting opportunities in renewable energy manufacturing, electric mobility and recycling.
Speaking at the Investment Summit Towards COP31 in Istanbul, Ahmet Burak Daglioglu, president of Türkiye’s Investment and Finance Office, said the conference would help present the country’s investment potential to global businesses and financing providers.
“We have a very strong story,” he said, adding that Türkiye needs to communicate its green transition policies more effectively to international partners.
Climate-friendly investment gains momentum
Climate-friendly investments are a priority under Türkiye’s international direct investment strategy through 2028, with 94 projects attracted under that heading so far, Daglioglu said.
The office also assesses and scores projects in its portfolio against sustainability principles, he added.
Türkiye’s ambitions extend beyond generating renewable energy to manufacturing equipment needed for the transition.
The country has Europe’s largest solar panel production capacity and an extensive wind energy equipment manufacturing ecosystem serving domestic and international markets, Daglioglu said.
Battery production capacity is expected to expand, while automotive policies support existing manufacturers’ transformation and new players such as electric vehicle producer Togg, he added.
Daglioglu highlighted recycling and upcycling opportunities arising from Türkiye’s industrial base and integration into global supply chains.
Under the Zero Waste initiative launched in 2017, 90 million tons of waste has been recycled, while the recovery rate has reached about 37%, he said. Türkiye aims to raise that rate to 60% by 2035.
Green development can support growth
Mehmet Emin Birpinar, Türkiye’s special representative for COP31 at the Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Ministry, said climate action presents an economic opportunity.
“Climate change is not an obstacle to our development,” he said, pointing to the direction of global financing flows.
Birpinar compared green development with earlier waves of industrialization and information technology that helped countries build wealth, warning that missing the transition could leave Türkiye further behind.
He stressed the need to reduce emissions while adapting infrastructure and economic activity to changing climate conditions.
Rising cooling demand illustrates how climate impacts can increase energy consumption and potentially emissions when electricity comes from fossil fuels, he added.

Shamonda virus: first human case is ‘an alert’, not a reason to panic, says EU health agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:54:42 UTC
22:54:42 KST

The first human case of Shamonda virus, confirmed in France, poses no wider threat to Europeans, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) told Euronews.
Europe’s public health authorities need to be aware of the first human case of Shamonda virus confirmed in France, but not “panic,” the ECDC told Euronews, as investigations into the patient’s death continue.
French authorities confirmed on Thursday a Shamonda virus infection in a patient in Lyon who died in early October, marking the first time the virus, previously seen only in animals, mainly cattle, has been reported in a human.
“This is a very special case,” Tamás Bakonyi, principal expert on vector-borne and zoonotic diseases and one health-related issues at the ECDC, told Euronews.
The affected patient had leukaemia and was “severely immunocompromised,” making it easier for the virus to infect the person. “The whole process of viral infections or other kinds of infections are behaving differently in those [immunocompromised] individuals than in healthy people,” Bakonyi said.
While it cannot be excluded that the virus can spread to other humans, “it does not mean that now we should be concerned, that we should be in panic,” he said, adding that there is limited evidence of a broader threat.
“The studies [in France] indicated that it was a quite long period that the patient had already been carrying the virus and then developed encephalitis and died,” Bakonyi said.
The Shamonda virus belongs to a group of viruses transmitted by biting insects called midges.
The virus was first detected in Nigeria in the mid-1960s and has since been reported sporadically in cattle in West, East and southern Africa and in Japan.
This summer it was also detected in Western Europe. Cases were reported in Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland, as well as the island of Jersey.
Investigations are ongoing
Although it had never been reported in humans before, Bakonyi said that experts and public health institutes in European countries had already been looking into whether the virus can cause infections in humans.
“This is an alert, but we have seen this,” Bakonyi said, adding that millions of people have lived in an environment where the virus is present and it has never been reported as a problem.
“It cannot be excluded that it also propagates in other humans, so that is the alerting part and that is why now there are ongoing investigations to clarify every aspect,” he said.
Those include clinical, laboratory and epidemiological investigations to determine whether the virus caused or contributed to the patient’s death and how the infection was acquired.
Some of these studies include testing for antibodies in people who may have been exposed to the virus, such as veterinarians and farmers, to see if they have been infected even without developing symptoms.
The case underlines how closely animal and human health are linked. That’s why ECDC together with European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) are taking one health approach — working together in the fields of animal and human health they have begun gathering scientific data and other relevant information, including input from experts across different countries, to inform its risk assessment.

OPEC Fund approves record $250M loan for Istanbul North Rail Crossing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:51:23 UTC
22:51:23 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
The OPEC Fund for International Development has approved a $250 million loan for the Istanbul North Rail Crossing project, marking the largest single financing commitment in the institution’s history.
According to a fund statement, the loan is part of a broader approved package of up to $500 million to build a new railway bypassing the Istanbul metropolitan area.
The 127-kilometer (79-mile) double-track, electrified line will run between Cayirova on the Asian side and Catalca on the European side, crossing the Bosphorus via the Yavuz Sultan Selim Bridge.
Carrying both passengers and cargo, the link addresses a critical bottleneck in Asia-Europe rail traffic. Currently, freight trains only use the Marmaray tunnel during limited nighttime hours, restricting annual capacity to 3 million tons.
The new line will expand this to 50 million tons, cutting freight journey times between Cayirova and Catalca from 13 hours to 3.6 hours.
It will also link Istanbul Airport and Sabiha Gokcen Airport to the national rail network, reducing inter-airport transit time from two hours to 65 minutes.
Strengthening global trade corridors
The railway provides an integral missing link for three international rail-served trade corridors crossing Istanbul: the Trans-Caspian Middle Corridor linking China and Central Asia with Europe; the Iraq Development Road connecting Asia and the EU via the Middle East and Türkiye; and the Türkiye-EU corridor, which accounts for a third of Türkiye’s international trade.
Shifting freight from road to lower-carbon electrified rail will ease congestion and strengthen Türkiye’s position as a logistics hub linking Europe, Asia, and the Middle East.
The $8.3 billion project is backed by the Turkish government and a World Bank-led consortium including the Asian Development Bank (ADB), Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB), Islamic Development Bank (IsDB), European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), and European Investment Bank (EIB).
"Türkiye has been an important partner of the OPEC Fund for nearly five decades," said OPEC Fund President Abdulhamid Alkhalifa, noting the record financing supports infrastructure that boosts connectivity and sustainable growth.
Since 1979, the OPEC Fund has approved nearly $850 million for Turkish projects across transport, agriculture, health, and energy.

UK government to make unprecedented intervention in setting of water bills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:51:10 UTC
22:51:10 KST

Ministers will make an unprecedented intervention in water bills and how companies prioritise investment, directing bosses to bring down costs and stop leaks and sewage overflows.
Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, has told suppliers in England and Wales she plans to intervene in the next price review – conducted by the water regulator, Ofwat.
Sources at the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said Andy Burnham’s 10-year plan, which will follow next week’s budget, would hand the government more robust powers to keep bills affordable and direct local investment. But sources close to Eagle said there also needed to be immediate action as companies began to make decisions before the next price-setting process, expected to conclude in 2029.
There has never been government intervention in the five-year review process. It is run by Ofwat, which analyses companies’ business plans and determines how much can be charged to customers in their bills to fund investment and running costs.
Eagle has written to regulators and water company chief executives, saying that the process must meet specific government priorities, including offering bill payers much better value for money – though stopping short of demanding bill cuts.
The letter to companies and regulators says they must be focused on investment in new technology to save money, and early intervention on leaks and sewage. It also called for far better communication and decision-making power handed to local communities and leaders.
The first priority must be affordable bills, the letter says, adding: “Affordability means a laser focus on value for money for customers.”
The letter says the public is clear about what the objectives for the industry should be. “They want clean rivers. They want reliable water services. They want to know that their money is being spent wisely, and that bills are kept affordable. And they want confidence that the system is working in their interests.”
The letter warns company bosses that it will “not be a business-as-usual price review … it is the beginning of a long-term transition to a different model for the water sector”.
Defra sources said Eagle intended it to be the first in a series of changes that will be announced in the coming months on the water industry, calling it “one of the clearest symbols of public frustration with Britain’s infrastructure”.
A Defra source said the intervention by Eagle was a down payment on bigger changes that would come in the 10-year plan. The source said: “Angela will take a much more bullish approach to telling water companies and regulators what is expected from them. This is the start of a journey to a very different water system and one that delivers for the public.
“There are also things we want regulators and companies to be doing now and so Angela is using the levers she’s got to influence their investment decisions at an early stage and make sure they’ve got no excuses. As well as looking at ownership structures, there are other ways we can go further than what came before.”
The new intervention from Eagle comes as the government continues to explore more radical options for the stricken company Thames Water. The Guardian reported earlier this week that Burnham had told officials to contemplate options that were not previously considered feasible, even if that meant spending taxpayer money and going to court.
Burnham previously said he would nationalise Thames Water – which is running out of cash and recently asked its creditors for an additional £2.4bn – but is struggling to find a way to do so without spending billions of pounds, getting tied up in a lengthy court battle, or both.
The outcome of the last price review process in 2024 led to highly controversial bill rises, after Ofwat authorised a £104bn modernisation programme, funded in large part through progressive annual rate increases that will see average water bills surge by 36% over the second half of the decade. The biggest increase was allowed for Southern Water, whose customers will pay 53% more by 2030, at an average of £642 per year.
Over the summer, several major suppliers requested permission to charge billions more to cover mounting capital costs and debt obligations, sparking fury from campaigners and from politicians, including Burnham.
The prime minister criticised the decision, warning that bill payers must no longer be treated as a “blank cheque” or a “bottomless source of funding for other people’s failures”, saying ordinary households were being forced to plug massive corporate balance-sheet deficits.
However, campaigners for public ownership have warned the move will do little in practice to reduce bills or the environmental impact of sewage or leaks. Sophie Conquest, the lead campaigner at We Own It, said: “These proposals are yet more reshuffling of the deckchairs on the Titanic, and fall far short of Burnham’s promise to end 40 years of neoliberalism.
“This government should be intervening on behalf of households to stop bill hikes. If water companies can’t function without siphoning more and more money out of our pockets, then this government should let them go bust.
“From there, we can bring water affordably into public hands. Under public ownership, we can put people and the environment ahead of the interests of faraway shareholders and hedge funds.”

Bora was taken into preventive detention on October 16 while on her way to participate in the Cockroach Janata Party's (CJP) ‘Lehra Do Tiranga’ march at Central Park in Connaught Place. She was released the following day.According to her petition, the police initiated proceedings based on alleged sloganeering at Mandi House on October 16, repeated protests around Jantar Mantar despite prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the BNSS, and allegations that she had instigated people to join a demonstration at Connaught Place on the same day.

The petitioner’s call and the incident alleged were different. The petitioner called for a peaceful gathering at Mandi House at 5.00 pm on Oct 16, and it is a matter of record that she was detained from Mandi House,” Bora’s petition said.
