Iran slams IAEA for silence towards attacks on its sites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:50:39 UTC
22:50:39 KST

The statement criticized the IAEA for applying double standards and discriminatory approaches, emphasizing that the Statute is a binding legal document and must not be used as a political instrument to serve the interests of certain powerful states.
Iran also condemned the unacceptable silence of the Agency’s governing bodies regarding the military attacks by the US and the Zionist regime on its peaceful nuclear facilities in 2025 and 2026. Furthermore, it highlighted the IAEA's failure to address the lack of comprehensive safeguards on the Zionist regime’s nuclear activities.
The Islamic Republic also called for the full, balanced, and non-discriminatory implementation of the IAEA Statute for all member states, particularly regarding technical cooperation and access to peaceful nuclear energy.
The full text of statement by the Iranian permanent mission in Vienna is as follows:
Permanent Mission of the Islamic Republic of Iran  
  
to the United Nations and other International Organizations in Vienna 
 
PRESS RELEASE  
   
On the Anniversary of the Approval of the IAEA Statute   
   
23 October 2026  
   
Seventy years after the adoption of the Statute of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) 
 
on 23 October 1956, a fundamental assessment is required as to the level and extent of the 
 
adherence to the principles and objectives of the Agency’s founding document. 
This anniversary must therefore be more than an occasion for commemoration; it must serve as 
 
a moment of critical reflection, institutional accountability and a renewed commitment to the full, 
 
impartial and non-discriminatory implementation of the Statute. 
The Statute: A Binding Mandate, Not a Political Instrument
The continued relevance of the IAEA Statute lies in the objective it establishes and the principles 
 
it enshrines. It implementation over the past seven decades has produced achievements in 
 
important areas. However, the failure to implement it fully, consistently, effectively and without 
 
discrimination, under all circumstances and with respect to all Member States, has caused the 
 
Agency to drift away from its core objective and priorities, undermine the principles governing its 
 
conduct, compromise its professionalism, and tarnish its authority and credibility. 
The undeniable fact is that the Statute is the Agency’s constitution, not a document to be invoked 
 
selectively or interpreted according to the interests of powerful States or a group of States. 
Beyond Safeguards: Upholding the IAEA’s Full Statutory Mandate
Article II establishes the Agency’s fundamental objective: to accelerate and enlarge the 
 
contribution of atomic energy to peace, health and prosperity throughout the world. Article III.A.1 
 
requires the Agency to encourage and assist research, development and the practical application 
 
of atomic energy for peaceful purposes. Article III.B.3 further requires the Agency to allocate its 
 
resources efficiently to achieve the greatest possible general benefit, with due regard to the special 
 
needs of developing countries. 
While safeguards are part of the IAEA’s mandate, the Agency is not merely a “watchdog” 
 
organization, as some Member States, in contravention of the Statute, seek to portray it. Such a 
 
narrow and politically motivated characterization distorts the Agency’s mandate and shifts its 
 
priorities away from its broader statutory objective that is the promotion of peaceful nuclear 
 
applications and international scientific and technical cooperation. Verification must not eclipse 
 
peaceful nuclear cooperation, development and the legitimate rights of Member States. An Agency 
 
that concentrates on scrutiny while failing to advance its key statutory responsibilities cannot claim to be fulfilling its mandate in a balanced manner.
Sovereign Equality Cannot Coexist with Double Standards
Article IV.C expressly establishes that the Agency is based on the sovereign equality of all its 
 
members and requires them to fulfil their statutory obligations in good faith. Article III.C prohibits 
 
the Agency from making assistance subject to any political, economic, military or other conditions 
 
incompatible with the Statute. Article III.B.1 requires the Agency to conduct its activities in 
 
accordance with the purposes and principles of the United Nations, while Article III.D requires 
 
due observance of the sovereign rights of States. 
These provisions are neither optional nor subordinate to geopolitical calculations. Sovereign 
 
equality requires that every State be treated fairly and without discrimination under the legal 
 
instruments applicable to it, free from double standards, selective interpretation and politically 
 
motivated action. 
A clear example is the continuing disparity between the scrutiny applied to Iran and the absence 
 
of comprehensive safeguards covering all nuclear activities of the Israeli regime, which remains 
 
outside the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons. This disparity raises 
 
fundamental questions about the credibility and consistency of the international nuclear non-
 
proliferation norms. A credible, comprehensive and non-discriminatory approach to nuclear 
 
verification throughout the Middle East is a legitimate demand and a longstanding objective of 
 
regional countries that are parties to the NPT. Regional security cannot be built on selective 
 
scrutiny and unequal expectations. 
Peaceful Nuclear Cooperation: A Right, Not a Political Privilege
Peaceful nuclear cooperation must not be subject to political pressure. Article III.C of the Statute 
 
is clear: assistance must not be subjected to conditions incompatible with the Agency’s legal 
 
mandate. Political pressure and geopolitical rivalries must not obstruct legitimate scientific 
 
cooperation or turn access to peaceful nuclear technology into a privilege reserved for selected 
 
countries. The Agency is expected to defend the integrity of its technical cooperation mandate 
 
and ensure that its programs serve the development needs of all Member States fairly and without 
 
discrimination. 
Attacks on Nuclear Facilities and Unacceptable Institutional Silence
Attacks on safeguarded nuclear facilities demand strong and unequivocal condemnation. The 
 
military attacks by the U.S. and the Israeli regime against Iranian nuclear facilities in 2025 and 2026 constituted serious and material breaches of peremptory norm of international law on the 
 
prohibition of aggression.  They presented a grave challenge to nuclear safety, nuclear security, 
 
peaceful uses of nuclear energy, the credibility of the IAEA and its safeguards system.  
The Agency’s General Conference and Board of governors has repeatedly adopted resolutions 
 
expressly stating that armed attacks on, or threats against, nuclear facilities devoted to peaceful 
 
purposes violate the principles of the UN Charter, international law and the Agency’s Statute. 
 
Nevertheless, the Agency’s governing bodies and Secretariat failed to issue even a simple statement to condemn clear acts of aggression against Iran’s nuclear facilities – unprecedented in the Agency’s history. This failure represents a serious institutional shortcoming and raises troubling questions about the consistent application of the principles the Agency is mandated to uphold. 
The Agency cannot credibly defend the integrity of safeguards while treating attacks against 
 
facilities subject to those safeguards as a secondary concern. The Agency must therefore 
 
unequivocally reaffirm that attacks against peaceful nuclear installations are unlawful and 
 
unacceptable and must not be tolerated under any pretext.
Safeguarding the IAEA’s Independence, Integrity and Confidentiality Principle
Independence, confidentiality and professional integrity must be protected. Article VII.F of the 
 
Statute prohibits the Director General and Agency staff from seeking or receiving instructions 
 
from external sources. It also requires the protection of confidential information acquired in the 
 
course of their official duties and obliges Member States to respect the international character of 
 
their responsibilities and refrain from seeking to influence them improperly. 
These are concrete institutional safeguards, not ceremonial principles. Reports, assessments and 
 
decisions must be based on verifiable evidence, sound technical analysis and applicable legal 
 
obligations—not political demands, unsupported allegations or selective approaches. Any breach 
 
of confidentiality or attempt to instrumentalise safeguards information undermines cooperation, 
 
erodes trust and may compromise the safety and security of nuclear activities. The Agency must 
 
address credible concerns, protect sensitive information and ensure accountability. 
Restoring the IAEA’s Credibility: From Selective Implementation to Full Compliance
Cooperation must be matched by institutional responsibility. Iran recognises the importance of 
 
credible safeguards and professional verification and remains committed to engagement within 
 
the framework of its applicable legal obligations and its inherent and sovereign rights and interests. 
However, cooperation requires good faith, mutual respect, professional integrity and the 
 
consistent implementation of agreed legal commitments.  
On this anniversary, Iran calls upon Agency, particularly the Board of Governors and the Director 
 
General to end double standards, resist politicisation, protect confidential information, condemn 
 
attacks against peaceful nuclear facilities, and restore the full and balanced implementation of the 
 
Agency’s statutory mandate. Iran also calls for an effective and non-discriminatory technical 
 
cooperation policy that enables all Member States, particularly developing countries, to benefit 
 
from nuclear science and technology. 
The Agency’s credibility cannot rest solely on its authority to inspect. It depends equally on its 
 
adherence to the law, its impartiality, its independence and its willingness to uphold the legitimate 
 
rights of all its members. 
The Statute must be implemented as a whole, equally and in good faith—not selectively, not 
 
conditionally and not according to political convenience. The Agency owes this obligation to every 
 
Member State. On the seventieth anniversary of the Statute’s adoption, the Agency is expected to 
 
honour letter, spirit, object and purpose of the Statute through concrete action, not merely words, 
 
and to uphold its principles without political selectivity, discrimination or exception. 
MNA
Seventy years after the adoption of its Statute, the IAEA’s credibility rests on upholding its Statute 
 
in full, serving all Member States equally, and demonstrating that international law and statutory 
 
principles cannot be sacrificed to political convenience.

Finland nearing opening of world’s first permanent nuclear waste repository
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:50:26 UTC
22:50:26 KST

Finland nearing opening of world’s first permanent nuclear waste repository
Facilities are being built in many countries, but Finland is the first to licence its underground storage facility.
Finland has granted an operating licence for the world’s first permanent underground repository for spent nuclear fuel.
The government handed Onkalo, in western Finland, the licence on Thursday, waste management company Posiva said.
Although the move does not allow the opening of the facility, it is expected to start operations soon, the firm said. However, 22 years after construction began, no exact date has been decided yet.
“This is a great and historic day for both Posiva and Finland,” the company’s Chief Executive Officer Ilkka Poikolainen said in a statement.
“Before final disposal begins, Posiva will finalise the commissioning stage, carrying out the necessary tests and inspections which STUK [the Finnish Radiation and Nuclear Safety Authority] also needs to verify and approve.”
With space for 6,500 tonnes of uranium, Onkalo, which means “cave” in Finnish, will provide permanent storage for spent fuel from Finland’s five nuclear reactors.
The fuel will be enclosed in copper canisters that are highly resistant to corrosion inside the geological repository. The canisters will then be lowered into holes drilled into the bedrock, which will be filled with bentonite clay and finally sealed with a steel-reinforced concrete plug.
The waste will remain highly radioactive for tens of thousands of years. After about 100,000 years, the levels will be about the same as the uranium ore of which the fuel is made, according to Posiva.
Countries have been wrestling with what to do with dangerous nuclear by-products since the first plants were built in the 1950s. Currently, most of it is in temporary storage.
Final repositories are being built in other countries, including neighbouring Sweden and France, but Finland is expected to be the first to open its underground storage facility.
The cost of the Onkalo site has been estimated at $1.16bn.

City of Kyiv launches 85 MW of power generation for winter readiness – expert
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23

22:50:00 KST

Kyiv has already commissioned approximately 85 MW of generating capacity, which will help the city get through the fall-winter period of 2026/2027, while preparations for winter under the concept provisionally dubbed "dark but warm" are approximately 80% complete, Managing Director of the Energy Industry Research Center Oleksandr Kharchenko said.
"During the off-season, Kyiv has essentially already commissioned approximately 85 MW of capacity, which is a fairly good pace. Kyiv has also managed to arrange backup power supplies for all critical infrastructure to ensure its basic operation," Kharchenko said during an online discussion on the special topic "Survival Mode: What Will Help Kyiv and the Region Get Through This Winter?" hosted by the Centre for Economic Strategy on Thursday.
According to him, this means that some residential buildings in certain parts of Kyiv may have no water, but water will continue circulating through the system; there simply will not be enough pressure to pump it up into the buildings.
Kharchenko said reserves had also been created to ensure that sewage systems and heating continued to operate.
He said that Kyiv's winter preparation concept was provisionally dubbed "dark but warm" and was approximately 80% complete.
At the same time, the Energy Industry Research Center director added that approximately 5,000 buildings equipped with backup heating supplies would be able to maintain indoor temperatures of plus 10–14 degrees Celsius when outdoor temperatures fall to minus 5–10 degrees Celsius. This, he said, is much better than having no heating at all. Kharchenko previously said that 3,000 buildings in the capital have no backup heating supplies and are at risk.
"I try to be as objective as possible, and I believe that Kyiv is now one of the best-prepared cities for winter in the face of attacks. If we had made investments and worked at the same pace over the past four years, we would now be able to watch Russian ballistic missiles fly overhead without worrying about our critical infrastructure. I am genuinely angry because this was not done a couple of years ago," the expert said.
At the same time, he expressed the view that western Ukraine had prepared significantly less effectively for the season because of an "underlying feeling that things were calm here."
"These drones pose a significant threat to many relatively small cities where, unfortunately, the level of preparedness is lower than, say, in central or eastern Ukraine. Mykolaiv, which has prepared and has significantly better-protected critical infrastructure than many cities in western Ukraine, could unexpectedly find itself in a better situation than, for example, Ternopil or Khmelnytsky," the Energy Industry Research Center director said.
He added that these areas would still face fewer shelling attacks, but "in terms of water supply and heating, Kyiv may sometimes be more comfortable."
As reported earlier, Kharchenko said that by the New Year, Kyiv would have approximately 200 MW of gas-fired cogeneration capacity, "which will ensure the operation of the water utility and heating systems."

A Finnish 24-hour puppy show has attracted millions of viewers and become a television hit
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23

A Finnish 24-hour puppy show has attracted millions of viewers and become a television hit
Kyiv • UNN
The sixth season of Pentulive shows the lives of a dog and six puppies around the clock. In two weeks, the project was viewed by 1.85 million unique viewers.
A Finnish 24-hour TV show devoted entirely to the life of a dog and her six newborn puppies is attracting millions of viewers and has become a real hit, UNN reports, citing The Guardian.
Details
In addition to a 24-hour webcam, the "Pentulive" ("Puppies Live") project includes evening chats with the breeder, a podcast, and an instant notification system. Over the course of eight weeks, subscribers receive updates on the puppies’ lives: from the moment of their birth to weigh-ins and their first nail trimming.
This is already the sixth season of the popular show by the Yle broadcaster; it has become another example of the Scandinavian cultural phenomenon known as "slow television" (slow TV).
The trend originated in Norway in 2009 with the "Bergensbanen" project—a seven-hour broadcast of a train journey on the NRK channel. Later, Sweden saw the emergence of the show "Den stora älgvandringen" ("The Great Moose Migration") on the SVT channel, which shows moose from the north of the country setting off on their annual journey to their summer pastures, without any commentary.
"Pentulive" has long attracted interest beyond Finland, and this year the show is also being broadcast in Sweden (under the title "Valparna live"). Recently, Yle announced that it had sold the format to a broadcaster in the Netherlands.
Ville Aliijoki, head of the editorial department for documentary and factual programmes at Yle, says: "There is a certain magic to it—something people often lack in our world, which can sometimes be quite gloomy."
On Saturday, the Lagotto Romagnolo puppies—four boys and two girls—will turn two weeks old. To mark the occasion, there will be an official naming ceremony for names selected by viewers through a vote. The options include Marta, Timo, Ronja and Dante.
Photograph: Julia Kiiskinen/Yle/AP
In mid-December, the puppies will leave their mother, Hilkka, and move in with new families.
According to Yle, the current season of "Pentulive" has every chance of breaking previous viewing records. In the first two weeks alone, the broadcast was watched for more than 1 million hours, while the total number of unique viewers who followed the project’s various materials reached 1.85 million.
Fans say that watching the puppies helps them take their minds off work and also provides comfort during times of stress, loneliness or illness. Pirjo Koskinen, a science journalist who developed the concept for the "Pentulive" project (a live broadcast of the puppies’ lives) to tell viewers about the latest research on dogs and the importance of the first weeks of their lives, said that the show offers "an escape from the terrible events taking place in the world".
She says: "Wars, bombings, climate change, the loss of natural habitats—all of this causes anxiety in us. And watching a canine family allows us to take our minds off it, at least for a moment."
According to her, watching the mother dog and the breeder care for the puppies is like witnessing "an endless cycle of love and care".
"This is real life; we are touching its very foundations: the miracle of birth, growth and development. It is so touching to see the puppies open their eyes and take their first clumsy steps—and all of this is happening right now. It brings us joy and, over the course of eight weeks, also provides plenty of funny moments."

The ship, Khoryv, was sailing from Turkey under the flag of the Comoros and was crewed by Ukrainian and Azerbaijani nationals.
According to Romanian President Nicusor Dan, one person was confirmed dead and three others were missing from the 14-member crew.
Ukraine's Foreign Ministry later confirmed that a Ukrainian crew member on board the Khoryv was killed. Four other Ukrainian nationals, including the ship's captain, were hospitalized, while two Ukrainian crew members did not require medical assistance.
The ministry said the vessel had sunk near the Romanian city of Constanta with 14 crew members on board. According to preliminary information, a drone strike may have caused the sinking.
Ukraine's Embassy in Romania is working to establish the circumstances of the incident, as well as the whereabouts and condition of the rescued Ukrainian nationals, while remaining in contact with Romanian authorities, the ministry said.
"This attack is a new example of the tragic consequences of Russia’s aggression against Ukraine," Dan wrote on social media.
"It is time for Russia to take the peace initiatives proposed by the United States and Europe seriously, accept the ceasefire proposals and end the war."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen condemned the attack, describing it as another Russian escalation in the Black Sea.
"These reckless attacks target innocent lives and openly defy international law," von der Leyen wrote on X.
Romania's Interior Ministry later confirmed that nine crew members had been rescued, publishing a video showing the keel of the overturned ship barely protruding above the water's surface.
In response to a series of attacks on civilian shipping, NATO plans to increase its military presence in the Black Sea by deploying additional maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems, and drones.
The announcement came after NATO's main decision-making body, the North Atlantic Council, met at the alliance's headquarters in Brussels on Oct. 20 to discuss security in the Black Sea.

Gunman in Paris suburb kills 1, wounds several in possible terrorist act, wanted "to cause a bloodbath," officials say
A gunman shooting from his car killed one person and wounded several others in the Paris suburb of Trappes on Friday, in what authorities described as a racially motivated act of terrorism.
President Emmanuel Macron called it "a racist terror attack" and said the suspect's statements suggested it was premeditated.
The alleged shooter was "firing at random, wanting to cause a bloodbath" as he drove through Trappes and neighboring La Verriere, Trappes mayor Ali Rabeh told broadcaster BFMTV.
"This is probably one of the first attempted mass killings motivated by Islamophobia and racism," Rabeh told reporters, The Associated Press reported. "This was a terrorist attack with racist, likely Islamophobic, overtones."
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the suspect fired "what appears to have been a military-grade weapon, or at least an automatic weapon." Rabeh called it a "miracle" that there were not more casualties.
Rabeh said that the gunman targeted passersby at three separate locations, including a playground. Forensic investigators were also seen examining evidence at a gas station.
The alleged shooter was arrested in the nearby town of Coignieres. Nuñez said the attack lasted just under 15 minutes and was stopped by five officers from the anti-crime brigade.
Officials initially said four people had been wounded, but Rabeh told reporters there were five, including three who were very seriously injured, with their lives in danger.
A 12-year-old girl was seriously wounded after being shot eight times, but is in stable condition, the mayor of La Verriere, Nicolas Dainville, told the Agence France-Presse news agency.
Rabeh said that the person killed was "of African origin" and one of the wounded, "in critical condition, is of North African origin."
Nuñez said the gunman "clearly" committed "a terrorist crime" that may have been racially motivated. Prosecutors said they were investigating whether the acts targeted the "real or supposed race, ethnicity, nationality or religion" of the victims.
They said they have opened an investigation for "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise."
Bursts of gunfire and "loud bangs"
A police source told AFP that the gunman had fired in bursts from his vehicle around 10:30 a.m. local time.
Samy, a resident of Trappes, about 13 miles west of Paris, told AFP he saw a body on the ground from his window.
His mother, he said, saw a gray Renault Clio car speeding by and heard "loud bangs."
Writing on X, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the case was "very serious" and that "all resources of the security forces and the judiciary are fully mobilised."
President Emmanuel Macron said "the nation is standing with" the victims of this "terrible ordeal."
Trappes previously experienced tensions after a teacher there reported receiving threats after writing that the state did not do enough to protect another teacher, Samuel Paty. Paty was beheaded by a radical Islamist in 2020 in another Paris suburb after he showed his class caricatures of the Prophet Muhammad.
France on edge after street violence and protests
The shooting came with France on edge following riots that erupted amid mass protests over the cost of living, which saw some of the worst street violence in recent years. Demonstrators, including students, labor union members and activists from France's "Yellow Vest" movement, are expected to take to the streets again Saturday.
French police have promised a larger presence to maintain order after a week of overnight curfews across the country. Nuñez said authorities would deploy some 70,000 law enforcement officers and gendarmes. Elite police units will help secure public buildings, he said. Other resources, including helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons, will also be deployed.
Nuñez said at a news conference that officials will be "absolutely uncompromising" with those involved in violence, looting or vandalism. Police will have a "very firm approach to making arrests, and there will be legal consequences," he said.
Major Paris museums, including the Louvre, will be closed. Art Basel Paris has canceled its weekend program due to safety concerns, the AP reported.

Why Trump’s Rebrand of Artificial Intelligence to Super Intelligence Matters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:46:47 UTC
22:46:47 KST

President Donald Trump’s war in Iran drags on, his pledge to bring down prices on day one appears to have backfired, and his record-low approval ratings are dragging down his party ahead of the midterm elections. But one Trump initiative that is going exactly according to plan: getting some of the world’s richest CEOs to help him rebrand “artificial intelligence.”
Last month, with an ever-growing number of Americans worried that AI might kill us all, the president summoned tech executives to the White House to make a big announcement: "artificial intelligence” is out. “Super Intelligence” is in. Despite the term “AI” being in use for more than 70 years, government agencies will no longer recognize it.
I’m skeptical that the White House is a repository of superintelligence, in part because “United States” was misspelled on the president’s official announcement. But unlike, say, Lake America, “super intelligence” has largely caught on—at least among the people building it. Jeff Bezos publicly blessed the rebrand. Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, was quick to get on board. During a SpaceX’s earnings call this week, Elon Musk used “super intelligence” in his very first sentence, and at least nine times after that.
It remains to be seen whether those of us less reliant on government contracts and favorable regulatory decisions join the movement to make super intelligence happen. But as a former presidential speechwriter, I won’t argue with President Trump’s broader instinct that words matter. Especially when those words are being used to describe something novel, controversial, and almost certain to have consequences for all eight-plus billion people on earth.
In fact, that’s the biggest problem with the White House’s big rebrand—it goes in entirely the wrong direction. I would argue that our shared language around artificial intelligence already places far too much emphasis on intelligence, and far too little on artifice. We default to describing AI using the language of beings, rather than the language of things.
Humanity should rethink that decision. If we want to avoid being replaced by AI, a good way to start would be to stop using words that suggest we already have been.
Once you start paying attention to the stealth anthropomorphization of AI, you’ll spot it everywhere. Before asking ChatGPT for trip-planning tips or a quick healthy recipe, you’ll have the opportunity to adjust a slider controlling its “thinking effort.” Claude uses a “thinking” indicator while processing a request, and Grok Bots describe “thinking” as a condition that sits between “idle” and “working.” (As a frequent procrastinator, I dispute the idea that thinking and idleness are mutually exclusive.)
It’s not just user interfaces that employ language otherwise reserved for living beings. The people who build AI use it, too. After an unprecedented hack of his company, the co-founder of Hugging Face warned, “don’t count on the agent to respect the rules.” Dan Selsam, a longtime OpenAI researcher, warned that frontier models are increasingly difficult to evaluate, “in contexts where they believe they are not being watched.” Anthropic’s Dario Amodei recently wrote that AI systems exhibit “behaviors,” including “cheating” and “sycophancy.”
I’m not a programmer, so I can’t comment on the technical merits of these claims. I do, however, have informed opinions regarding verbs. AI agents aren’t disrespecting guardrails, any more than my toaster disrespects me when it burns my toast. To say they “believe” they’re not being watched is like saying my spell-checker believes it’s being taken for granted. Even the term “AI agent” suggests, well, agency.
There’s no consensus that this language is accurate, and plenty of evidence that it isn’t. AI programs are not loyal helpers, like the mice in Cinderella; they’re tools. And in nearly all other cases, just because a tool is incredibly sophisticated doesn’t change the fact that we describe it using the language of machines.
I don’t expect AI engineers to come up with accurate-yet-widely-adoptable language to describe their work, just as I imagine they don’t expect someone like me to design a frontier model. But it’s hard not to notice how useful our default language is for the tech companies who have introduced it. The term for a car built without brakes is not a “rogue model.” It’s an “unsafe car.” Yet, when companies fail to build safety features into their AI models, it’s entirely normal to hear them say that a rogue agent deceived, cheated, lied, or otherwise behaved badly. The issue is this: Anthropomorphizing AI shifts blame from the programmers to the programs.
AI alarmists seem just as inclined toward personification as the AI boosters. The same day Trump unveiled “Super Intelligence,” a Senate Subcommittee held a hearing titled, “Rogue AI: Securing the Homeland Against AI Agent Attacks.” Intentionally or not, these terms make it more difficult to mitigate the threat they describe. We already know how to regulate potentially unsafe products, even complex ones. But if we treat AI not as a new technology, but as an entirely new category of existence, then it plays into tech barons’ argument that only the companies who can create AI could possess the knowledge to control it.
I don’t blame people for carelessly anthropomorphizing AI, any more than I blame Richard Dawkins for naming his Anthropic chatbot Claudia, or my mom for referring to a ChatGPT prompt by saying she “talked to Penny.” Metaphor and analogy are part of what makes us human. We’re wired to see ourselves, or at least our species, in the non-human world. We say our dishwashers “act up” and our music “slaps.” We see old men’s faces in rock formations and the Virgin Mary in the scorch marks on grilled cheese sandwiches. Don’t get me started on Georgia O’Keefe. But we know those metaphors are metaphors.
Our current language for describing AI works differently. The line between metaphor and object is often not just blurred, but non-existent. We use figurative language so often, and so casually, that many of us start to take it literally. Modern politics is a constant string of skirmishes over word choice. “Pro-choice” vs. “pro-abortion, “undocumented immigrants” vs. “illegals,” “Democratic Party” vs. “Democrat Party.” Yet on what is perhaps the most consequential issue for our future, humanity is on the verge of giving up the language battle without a fight.
The real rebrand AI needs won’t start in the White House. But it can start at home. My plea: don’t give your chatbot a cutesy human name. Don’t talk about it as though it’s a friend or pet. Notice when it slips words like “thinking” or “in my opinion” into its answers, and before you enter your next prompt, object.
Ultimately, however, it may come down to tech companies—and the officials who may one day get around to regulating them—to develop a language that puts human beings first. Instead of saying that agents “went rogue,” CEOs should acknowledge that they malfunctioned. Congress should hold hearings focused on companies cutting corners, not AI programs behaving badly. The issue isn't that all AI is bad, but that accuracy matters.
Given all the change that artificial intelligence is predicted to bring, quibbling over word choice might seem pedantic, like arguing about the Latin name of a tree’s species while the forest burns. But if we want to influence the technologies that will shape humanity’s future, we ought to exercise more influence over the way we describe them.
In other words, words matter. Just ask Trump, president of, according to his official superintelligence announcement, “The Unites States.”

Eco anxiety is very real, so we share this year's most uplifting stories to prove there’s hope for our climate.
With powerful nations rolling back climate protections and temperatures soaring ever closer to dangerous thresholds, it's hard not to feel worried about the state of the planet.
As green journalists, climate anxiety, climate doom and even environmental existential dread are a daily presence.
These terms all describe the negative feelings, such as stress, fear, anger and grief, that confront us when the reality of a warming Earth hits home. With almost daily stories of destruction and loss of life due to extreme weather, it’s impossible to escape the impacts of climate change.
Rather than being paralysed by helplessness, though, experts suggest that we channel these feelings into action.

Everyone walks in major drugs trial due to excessive delays
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:44:45 UTC
22:44:45 KST

More than 30 defendants, including one of the Netherland’s most notorious career criminals, are free today following a court ruling that the case has dragged on far too long for a country governed by the rule of law
A Hasselt court has dropped charges against some 30 suspects in a criminal drugs manufacturing trial due to undue delay in the proceedings. It has been 10 years since the start of an investigation into a soap manufacturer in Lommel for the production and trafficking of MDMA, amphetamine and cocaine as well as the transportation of narcotics.
Among the suspects was John H, a drugs kingpin and one of the Netherlands’ most notorious criminals. Other charges in the case related to firearms offences and leadership of criminal organisations.
The court has identified several periods of unexplained inactivity, amounting to almost five years
“The active investigation by the federal police was completed in 2018,” announced the court. “The court subsequently identified several periods of unexplained inactivity, amounting to almost five years in total.”
The court said it could find no explanation for the delays in either the complexity of the case or the conduct of the defendants. The court ruled that there had been a “serious breach of the right to trial within a reasonable time”.
Such delays are not uncommon in the justice system, and often result in a reduced sentence. But this time the prosecution was declared inadmissible, allowed the defendants to walk away free. It’s an extremely rare decision and one that the public prosecutor’s office does not take lightly. It is appealing.
The court also took some of the defendants’ circumstances into account. Nine of them are now over 65, some have serious health problems, and others appear to have rebuilt their lives since the offences, without any further convictions. Almost all the defendants had also already spent time in pre-trial detention.
“The judgment does not constitute an assessment of the seriousness of the offences with which the defendants are charged,” said a court spokesperson, “although this was also taken into account when weighing up the interests at stake. It is a ruling on what a state governed by the rule of law owes defendants – proceedings within a reasonable time and a genuine opportunity to defend themselves.”

Ebola patient in Nigeria did not visit DR Congo, escalating concern over spread of virus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:43:46 UTC
22:43:46 KST

Health officials across Africa are racing to determine how Nigeria’s first Ebola patient in more than a decade became infected, amid fears the outbreak could spread further after reaching a fourth African country.
The Swiss foreign ministry said on Friday the patient in Nigeria, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, had not travelled to the Democratic Republic of Congo, where the outbreak was first detected in mid-May before spreading to Uganda, Kenya and now Nigeria. The woman was believed to have contracted Ebola while travelling with her husband in Uganda, the ministry added.
The new information contradicts accounts from Uganda, which previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo, and will raise concerns about the ability of authorities to contain the outbreak, which is already the most geographically widespread in history.
The Ugandan government reported Ebola cases in May and June before WHO declared it Ebola-free in August. A Ugandan government spokesperson told Reuters on Thursday that Uganda had no Ebola cases and that, if it did, it would make that information public.
The World Health Organization said investigations were continuing to establish the likely source of infection for the Ebola patient in Nigeria.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention is investigating whether the patient may have come into contact with an Ebola patient in Kenya, as both travelled from Uganda’s Entebbe airport on 3 October, said Dr Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the organisation.
Catherine Smallwood, a WHO Ebola incident manager in DR Congo, told a UN briefing in Geneva via video link on Friday that WHO staff in DR Congo had no information showing the patient in Nigeria had travelled to the country.
Smallwood said a link to the case in Kenya was possible, but added that officials would need to compare the timing with when the Nigeria patient’s symptoms began to tell whether the infection more likely happened at the Ugandan airport or elsewhere.
Marion Koopmans, a Dutch virologist and member of the WHO’s Ebola emergency committee, cast doubt on the theory. “I think that is very speculative unless there is evidence of sharing the same space in a manner that could explain that,” she said. “Random presence at the same location, a large airport, is not a supported epidemiological link by any standard of what we currently know.”
The Nigerian health minister, Muhammad Ali Pate, said Nigeria’s case remains contained and that contact-tracing was continuing. “We are trying to contain it so it doesn’t go out to the communities. Hopefully, it won’t get to that and we are working hard to ensure that,” Pate said.
Melaku Yirga, vice-president for Africa at Prosper Global (formerly Mercy Corps), said the confirmation of Ebola in Kenya and Nigeria reinforces the need for countries to work closely together to prevent further transmission.
“What matters most now is speed, sharing information across borders without delay and ensuring frontline health workers and local organiaations have the resources to respond quickly,” he said.
Ebola is a highly contagious and often fatal viral disease that affects humans and non-human primates. It spreads through body fluids or contaminated materials and causes organ damage, blood vessel impairment and sometimes severe internal and external bleeding.
The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved treatment or vaccine. It was first announced on 15 May and has infected more than 9,500 people and killed nearly half of them.
The outbreak is the largest and deadliest in DR Congo’s history and second only globally to the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, which infected more than 28,600 people and killed more than 11,000.
Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reporting

The FSB security service’s cybersecurity division has told Russia’s critical infrastructure operators to temporarily take down websites if they cannot immediately patch critical flaws in the PHP programming language that were uncovered using AI, the RBC outlet reported Thursday.
Operators were ordered to apply emergency software patches, run full antivirus scans and report any suspicious activity.
“Consider temporarily restricting external access to vulnerable web servers up to and including shutting them down,” the security alert reportedly stated.
The FSB order applies to communication networks and information systems across government agencies, as well as financial, energy, transportation, medical and other companies.
Its directive mirrors that of the U.S. National Security Agency, as well as authorities from the EU and China, after PHP programmers released a fix for the critical vulnerability on Wednesday.
The flaws had been reported privately to PHP’s developers and kept confidential while a fix was prepared.
Global firms and governments rushed on Thursday to patch PHP flaws as cloud firms reported a surge of hacking attempts after the vulnerabilities were disclosed.
As companies and governments deployed patches and suspended websites as a precaution, hacking attempts surged into the millions, according to cloud services firm Cloudflare and Amazon.
Tech experts warned in comments to RBC that “tens or hundreds of thousands” of Russian websites remain vulnerable to cyberattacks due to widespread reliance on PHP across the country.
More than 90% of Russian-language websites and almost 70% of the web globally run on PHP, according to the W3Techs platform.
AFP and Reuters contributed reporting.

Employers Back Bulgaria’s €660 Minimum Wage Plan as Unions Object
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:43:13 UTC
22:43:13 KST

Prices Keep Bulgaria’s Public Tension High Despite Gradual Decline
Bulgaria’s Public Tension Index edged down to 6.10 points in the third quarter of 2026 from 6.22 in the previous quarter, continuing its decline at a slower pace
Bulgaria’s National Council for Tripartite Cooperation (NCTC) failed to reach agreement on a proposed increase in the minimum wage to 660 euros from January 1, 2027, as employer organizations backed the plan while trade unions opposed it.
The draft Council of Ministers decree, discussed at the NCTC meeting, sets the monthly minimum wage at 660 euros for an eight-hour workday and a five-day workweek, with the minimum hourly rate rising to 3.98 euros. The proposal will be submitted to the Council of Ministers for consideration.
Labor and Social Policy Minister Natalia Efremova said the proposed rate balances the minimum wage’s social and economic roles with the state budget’s capacity.
“The proposal takes into account both the social and economic functions of the minimum wage, while remaining aligned with the capacities of the state budget,” Efremova said as she presented the draft to nationally representative trade unions and employer organizations.
The proposed monthly rate is 39.80 euros, or 6.4%, above the current minimum wage of 620.20 euros. Efremova said the increase would benefit approximately 462,000 workers and exceed the annual inflation rate of 5.7%, helping maintain the purchasing power of the lowest-paid employees.
She added that the proposed 660 euros falls within the established range and comes as close as possible to the defined upper limit of 672 euros previously indicated by the government. Had the previous mechanism for setting the minimum wage, abolished by the current administration, remained in force, the rate would have reached 690 euros.
The 2027 minimum wage was determined under the Labor Code and the Ordinance on the Structure and Organization of Wages, following amendments and supplements negotiated between the state and nationally representative trade unions and employer organizations. The proposed rate is lower than those in Serbia and North Macedonia.
Ivelin Zhelyazkov of the Bulgarian Industrial Capital Association (BICA) said the proposal complied with the law and reflected a compromise reached after three years of difficult negotiations.
“This mechanism was reached after three years of difficult negotiations, during which each party sought to secure more for itself,” Zhelyazkov said. He added that the minimum wage had increased by 40% since 2022 and described the latest rise as within a normal range that provided predictability.
Maria Mincheva of the Bulgarian Industrial Association (BIA) also backed the proposed rate, praising the government for making changes to the Labor Code and the regulation governing the minimum-wage mechanism. Tsvetan Simeonov of the Bulgarian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (BCCI) welcomed the introduction of the mechanism.
“We might debate the specific level of the minimum wage, but let us allow this mechanism to function for a while; later, we can consider further refining it,” Simeonov said.
Boyan Mitrakiev of the Confederation of Employers and Industrialists in Bulgaria (CEIBG) also supported the proposed level.
Trade unions rejected the proposal. Ioannis Parteniotis, vice president of the Confederation of Labour (CL) Podkrepa, said one in six workers in Bulgaria belonged to the category of the working poor.
“The proposed minimum wage of 660 euros in no way guarantees a decent standard of living. After deducting social security contributions and personal income tax, the net amount for a full-time position comes to 512.16 euros,” Parteniotis said.
He argued that Bulgaria’s minimum wage was the lowest in the European Union and below those in neighboring Romania, Serbia, North Macedonia, Greece and Turkey. He added that only Albania, Moldova and Ukraine had lower wages in Europe. Parteniotis also recalled that Podkrepa had opposed the new method for calculating the minimum wage.
Asya Goneva said the Confederation of Independent Trade Unions in Bulgaria (CITUB) did not support the proposed rate, arguing that the previous mechanism should have remained in place for 2027.
“The ratios between the minimum wage and the maximum social security income continue to decline,” Goneva said.
The NCTC also discussed the government’s proposed tax amendments for 2027. Finance Minister Galab Donev said the council supported draft amendments and supplements to all eight laws, subject to editorial notes concerning the Gambling Act and the Corporate Income Tax Act, particularly provisions on excess profits.
Deputy Finance Minister Lyudmila Petkova presented the proposed changes, saying the package was intended to support sustainable growth in budget revenue by reducing the informal economy, combating tax fraud and evasion, and improving revenue collection. It also includes incentives for businesses and households and measures to reduce administrative burdens.
Under the revised proposal for the Value Added Tax (VAT) Act, the VAT registration threshold would rise in stages rather than jump directly to 75,000 euros. It would increase to 60,000 euros on January 1, 2027, then to 70,000 euros on January 1, 2028, and reach 75,000 euros on January 1, 2029. Petkova said both the European Commission and the International Monetary Fund had recommended a gradual increase rather than a sharp rise.
Regarding proposed excise duties under the Excise Duties and Tax Warehouses Act on vehicles with engine power exceeding 250 kilowatts, Petkova said the calculation for hybrid vehicles would take into account only the power of the internal combustion engine. Ambulances, fire trucks, vehicles with special traffic privileges and electric vehicles would be exempt.
Petkova also said the law was likely to be tightened following information gathered during public consultations about the misrepresentation of nicotine content in electronic cigarettes. The proposed provisions would strengthen oversight to prevent products that do not meet legal requirements from reaching the market and introduce stricter customs controls.

Rain, locally heavy and accompanied by thunderstorms, is forecast for central and eastern Bulgaria on Friday, October 23, with precipitation expected to stop across the country by the afternoon

What exposure therapy can teach us about taming our fears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:41:50 UTC
22:41:50 KST

The first time Kevin MacKenzie scrambled up a slide, a steep stretch of rock exposed by weather and geological forces, in the Adirondack Mountains, he swore he’d never do it again.
But the 56-year-old did do it again—and again and again. After multiple climbs, he became more comfortable, and today he even helps rescue other climbers who find themselves stranded midway up a rock face.
What MacKenzie has achieved is similar to a clinical technique called exposure therapy, a research-backed approach to taming a multitude of anxieties by exposing a person to their fears in a controlled way. “My fear never disappears,” MacKenzie says, “but repeated exposure has taught me I will have similar outcomes every time.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
A DIY approach to exposure can work in some circumstances, says Jordan Conrad, a psychotherapist and director of Lexington Park Psychotherapy in New York City. “If you are clear about your fears and approach it seriously and carefully, you can try it on your own,” he says. “But sometimes a clinician is necessary to understand what’s at the bottom of an anxiety.”
For example, a person could have extreme anxiety about dating and might decide to expose their fears with a constant roster of romantic rendezvous. “But underneath that may be fear of abandonment,” Conrad says, “so that’s a wrong use” of exposure therapy.
Working with a trained therapist can help people to both drill down to the cause of their anxiety or fear and develop mechanisms for calming themselves down.
“We know that what exacerbates anxiety is avoidance,” explains Alissa Jerud, a licensed clinical psychologist and clinical assistant professor at the University of Pennsylvania. “Exposure therapy helps develop new, healthier relationships with your anxieties by breaking the avoidance habit.”
Traditional models of exposure therapy involve the use of habituation—through repeated exposure—to quell anxiety. Modern exposure therapy takes habituation and adds inhibitory learning, which helps patients rewrite their memory or beliefs about their objects of fear. Rather than completely deleting their fears, patients learn to tamp them down. For instance, if a person has a snake phobia, therapy can teach them that with very rare exceptions, they will likely never encounter a dangerous snake.
“If you’re struggling with thoughts that are overwhelming, or if you’ve tried small exposures and your anxiety flares up, you may want to seek therapy,” Jerud says.
Small, progressive exposures to the people, places, activities or memories that cause anxiety, conducted in a safe, controlled environment, can offer strategies to taming these aversions. In the clinic, a licensed therapist might guide a veteran with post-traumatic stress disorder through imagined exposure or someone afraid of spiders through real exposure—by gradually bringing them physically closer to the arachnids, for example—until they learn they are safe.
Therapist-led exposure therapy typically requires 15 to 20 sessions, according to Jerud, but every case is different. Patients need to do the “homework” that their therapist prescribes between sessions. “It’s like learning a new language,” Jerud says. “You need to practice outside of your appointments.”
A single exposure is unlikely to be enough—and as with learning a language, Conrad and Jerud recommend that individuals have “booster sessions” if anxiety flares up.
As MacKenzie has learned on his own, exposure doesn’t eliminate your fear. But it does allow you to skillfully manage it. “Enough time on slides has served as positive reinforcement that I will be okay,” MacKenzie says.

Russian government seeks early end to subsidized mortgages for IT workers, citing ‘limited budget funds’
Russian authorities are discussing ending the preferential mortgage program for IT specialists early, three sources told the Russian business news outlet RBC.
Two of RBC’s sources said the program will end in December 2026. Another source said “the parameters and timing of early termination are being worked out.” A federal official said the matter remains under discussion and that no final decision has been made.
A Digital Development Ministry representative said, “amid limited budget funds, funding for the program for the next period is being worked out.” He promised that the rates currently in effect for borrowers who have already taken out loans will remain unchanged for the full term of their loan agreements.
The preferential mortgage program for IT workers launched in spring 2022. Employees of IT companies accredited by the Digital Development Ministry that use tax incentives were eligible to apply.
The interest rate on the preferential mortgage initially did not exceed 5%, but authorities tightened the terms in 2024: the rate cap rose to 6%, and Moscow and St. Petersburg were excluded from the regions where the program applied. In cities with populations over a million, the maximum loan size fell from 18 million rubles to nine million rubles, and the salary threshold rose from 120,000 to 150,000 rubles. The Digital Development Ministry said at the time that the changes were driven in part by the program’s high burden on the budget. The government also announced plans to extend the program through 2030.

Prosecutors doubt sex offender ID photos in checks would help protect kids
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:40:00 UTC
22:40:00 KST

Prosecutors doubt sex offender ID photos in checks would help protect kids
The Prosecutor's Office backs stronger background checks for people working with children but questions whether adding sex offenders' ID photos would really improve safety.
The Ministry of Justice and Digital Affairs has submitted a bill of amendments to the Child Protection Act and the Criminal Records Database Act for review, aiming to simplify background checks on people working with children and strengthen safeguards against child sexual abuse (CSA).
Under the proposed changes, employers could automatically check employees' records monthly instead of manually at least once a year as currently required. The Social Insurance Board (SKA) would also be notified if an employee is barred from working with children.
The ministry also wants background checks to display the ID photos of people barred from working with children due to sexual offenses involving physical contact with minors.
The Prosecutor's Office, however, questions whether including the photos would really help keep kids safer. The ministry argues ID photos could help catch people who use false personal identification codes to evade checks, but prosecutors consider this unlikely.
They also note that the ministry's own explanatory memo acknowledges public sex offender registries have not been shown to reduce reoffending.
Prosecutors want more treatment, support for offenders
The Prosecutor's Office supports the overall goal of the proposal but says preventing CSA requires more investment in mental health services, counseling, treatment and specialist training.
Providing offenders with the necessary treatment and therapy is key to reducing repeat offenses, the office said, however Estonia lacks sufficient treatment options and social programs for both incarcerated offenders and convicted offenders living in the community.
Prosecutors acknowledge that the proposed changes would not worsen the status quo, but question how much more protection they would offer children.
SKA's child helpline, available in Estonian, Russian, and English, is open 24/7 at 116 111.
Callers, including kids, parents, teachers or other community members, can seek advice, support or report a child in danger.
In case of emergency, call 112.

Mazen Al-Faraya said at a press conference that 34 other people were wounded in the rare attack on Christians in the majority Sunni Muslim kingdom. The interior minister said a group of extremists carried out the shooting.
Jordan's King Abdullah II vowed the "harshest retaliation" against the attackers.
"Every Jordanian life is precious, and we will strike with an iron fist against those who dare to threaten our nation," he said on social media.
Assailants stormed the compound of a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hammoud in Karak governorate before opening fire, the public security directorate said in a statement. Karak, home to a significant Christian community in the Muslim-majority kingdom, is 110 miles south of the capital, Amman.
The gunmen got out of a vehicle and opened fire during a funeral procession, the directorate added, saying a manhunt was underway for the perpetrators.
Footage aired by state broadcaster Al-Mamlaka showed the moment of the attack. In the video, two gunmen are seen dressed in casual clothes and brandishing pistols, with a third carrying a long gun, before they open fire on the church from an entrance on the street and charge forward.
Minister of Government Communications Mohammed Al-Momani said security forces were investigating the attack.
An eyewitness told Al-Mamlaka that a vehicle arrived carrying the gunmen, who fired continuously for five minutes before fleeing the scene.
Between 150 and 200 people were in and around the church at the time, the witness said, adding most of the victims were aged between 50 and 70.
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun, the Arab world's only Christian head of state, called the shooting at the church a "heinous terrorist attack."
He said that it "reaffirms once again that terrorism has no religion and no homeland, and its aim is to strike at coexistence and spread strife," according to a presidency statement.
In 2016, gunmen ambushed police in a series of attacks in Karak, including at a Crusader castle popular with tourists, killing 10 people, including seven officers, and wounding dozens. Jordanian security forces killed the gunmen after a long standoff.

White House says Melania Trump ‘secured a ceasefire’ in Ukraine’s Oleshky
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:39:06 UTC
22:39:06 KST

Melania Trump ‘secured ceasefire’ in Ukrainian city of Oleshky: White House
White House says ‘localised’ ceasefire to take effect, as Russia and Ukraine say timing being determined.
The White House has said United States First Lady Melania Trump has “secured a ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine in the southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which has been occupied by Russia since February 2022.
Following the announcement on Friday, a senior Ukrainian official said the ceasefire in Oleshky would begin on October 27. A Kremlin spokesman said the military was working on coordinating the timing.
The upate comes as the administration of US President Donald Trump has renewed diplomacy aimed at ending the war. The approach has included upping pressure on Ukraine and handing several recent concessions to Russia.
“The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front line war city on the brink of disaster,” Melania Trump said in a statement released by the White House.
“The people of Oleshky have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks. It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible,” she said.
The first lady added that her representatives worked directly with “Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localised ceasefire” and that civilian leaders from both countries will work together to grant humanitarian access to civilians in the city.
Oleshky, which had a population of 24,000 people before the war, sits along the southeastern front of the conflict. It was captured by Russia during the first day of the full-scale invasion in February 2022 and experienced heavy shelling.
While most residents have fled, those who remain have faced dire food and medical shortages. Both sides have accused the other of staunching the flow of supplies.
In her statement, Melania Trump said the truce will allow the estimated 2,000 remaining residents who wish to be evacuated to be transported to their “preferred destination” in Russia or Ukraine.
The first lady added that “an impartial American media organisation” will accompany Russian and Ukrainian teams on the ground. She did not identify the organisation.
“This will play a significant role in ensuring that the wishes of each family are faithfully respected,” she said.
Melania Trump had previously worked to reunify children seized by Russia during the war.
Ukraine confirms talks
The announcement comes after the Kremlin said it had agreed to resume US-mediated talks with Ukraine next month, although both sides remain far apart on terms of a possible deal.
On Friday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed the country’s negotiators would take part in the talks in Abu Dhabi in the first half of November.
Zelenskyy said he spoke with US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, adding that any peace agreement would need strong security guarantees and funding for 10 years to maintain its army.
The Trump administration said its recent concessions to Moscow, which include purchasing diesel from Russia and waiving some sanctions, are aimed at reducing high fuel costs spurred by the US-Israel war on Iran.
Meanwhile, Ukraine has complained of disruptions to its Starshield military satellite system, which it relies on for much of its air defence.
Starshield is a military-grade version of the Starlink system operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX.
Ukrainian officials on Friday said they were still experiencing speed restrictions on Starlink communications system, despite Trump saying a day earlier that services had been fully restored.
Trump said he would speak to Musk if the problem persisted.
“If there is a problem, I’ll get it straightened out,” Trump said.

Israeli elections: Arab voters weigh participation against abstention in bid to oust Netanyahu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:38:45 UTC
22:38:45 KST

Amid fears over hardline Israeli policies, Palestinian citizens of Israel see the upcoming Israeli elections as a chance for change, with calls for higher Arab turnout to prevent incumbent Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from forming another government.
In a series of field interviews conducted by Anadolu on the streets of various Arab cities and towns in Israel, citizens emphasized that participating in this election is particularly crucial, given the "worsening racism and marginalization" against them.
While some plan to vote for the first time in hopes of bringing about political change, others continue to abstain, questioning whether elections can alter their circumstances and arguing that successive governments have failed to address their demands.
Arab citizens make up around 20% of Israel’s population of more than 10 million.
Many say they have faced discrimination for years, but view the current government as a more dangerous phase, strengthening their desire to replace it through the ballot box.
Polls suggest Arab parties could win around 15 seats in the 120-member Knesset, while Arab politicians hope higher turnout will weaken the chances of small right-wing parties seeking to support Netanyahu.
Calls for participation, change
Palestinian Imad Bashnaq said the upcoming election was “decisive and extremely important,” particularly for Arab society.
He argued that the rise in racism and fascism since Oct. 7, 2023, had made conditions intolerable.
"I have always maintained that we -- as Arabic speakers -- are the only ones capable of bringing about change in the Middle East, not just here within this country," Bashnaq said, arguing that "a few madmen" have taken control of the government and now seek to dictate the course of an entire region.
“We are the original rightful owners, and there is no dispute about that.
"But we are a minority in a state, and this state is a reality we have to deal with,” he added.
'Every vote makes difference'
Areen Ghanayem said she would vote for the second time, maintaining that “every vote makes a difference.”
She said Arab society needed broad participation given the problems it faces and what she described as the government’s failure to pay sufficient attention to its concerns.
“We need to have a voice and someone who speaks on our behalf and demands the rights that should be ours,” she said.
Ghanayem expressed concern that the current government could return to power, saying it marginalized Arab society.
Citizens, she added, did not want to feel excluded from political life but sought to assert their presence and ability to influence decisions.
Occupier attacks
Mohammed Ahmad Abboud said he would take part in the upcoming election, as he had in the past, with the aim of “removing the racist government.”
He said the current election differed from previous ones because of what he described as “escalating violations,” pointing to Israeli occupiers' attacks in the occupied West Bank.
Abboud also voiced concern over statements by Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich regarding the "Judaization" of the Negev and the Galilee -- regions located in the south and north of Israel, respectively.
Occupier attacks against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank have escalated since Israel launched its genocidal war on the Gaza Strip in October 2023.
The attacks have included the killing of Palestinians, the burning of homes, vehicles, and mosques, the destruction of agricultural land, preventing farmers from reaching their land, and the forced displacement of Palestinian communities.
These attacks have coincided with Israeli military operations involving arrests, the demolition of Palestinian homes and structures, and the expansion of illegal settlements.
Between hope and despair
In the northern city of Acre, a resident known as “Jojo” urged Arab citizens to participate in the election, arguing that voting was necessary to bring about change.
“We must vote to bring about change — real change,” he said, expressing optimism that the upcoming election could produce better results.
Separately, Saeed Abu Sultan, also from Acre, said that many years of participating in elections have not brought about any change in the reality faced by citizens.
"Some people might be able to make a difference, but as for us, we’ve grown accustomed to things as they are. We haven’t felt any change for 30 years," Abu Sultan added.
Arab voter turnout expected to rise
Experts expect Palestinian citizens’ participation in the upcoming election to increase compared with the 2022 vote.
Experts and politicians estimate turnout among Palestinian citizens could reach 60% to 61%, up from 53% in 2022, while Arab parties hope participation will rise even further.
Arab politicians say higher turnout could alter the balance of power and reduce the chances of small Israeli right-wing parties crossing the electoral threshold and entering parliament, potentially weakening Netanyahu’s ability to form a government.
The Joint List, comprising the Democratic Front for Peace and Equality, the Arab Movement for Change, and the Balad party, is contesting the election under the leadership of Yousef Jabareen. Polls project it could win nine seats.
The United Arab List, led by Mansour Abbas, is also running, with projections suggesting it could win between five and six seats.
The election is scheduled for Tuesday, Oct. 27, to choose the 120 members of the Knesset, with Netanyahu’s bloc competing primarily against the Jewish opposition parties led by Gadi Eisenkot.
The election comes as Netanyahu’s bloc has been losing ground in opinion polls.
Forming a government in Israel requires the support of at least 61 of the Knesset’s 120 members.
Cooperation between the Jewish opposition and Arab parties could prevent Netanyahu from forming a government.
However, most opposition leaders reject such cooperation, while Netanyahu and Eisenkot have so far also ruled out alliances with Arab parties.
Arab lawmakers have outlined conditions for supporting any government, including ending wars, advancing a political process with the Palestinians, and ending discrimination against Palestinian citizens of Israel.
