MEP Dan Barna:
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:38:24 UTC
22:38:24 KST

Author
Irina Nedeva
Interview
MEP Dan Barna: Bulgaria must clearly name Russia’s aggression in the Black Sea
The EU will accelerate the creation of a European Martime Security Center
Friday 23 October 2026 14:58
Friday, 23 October 2026, 14:58
MEP Dan Barna in Radio Studio 2 at the European Parliament in Strasbourg
PHOTO Irina Nedeva
Font size
The Black Sea is no longer merely a trade corridor. It has become a test of European security. In a resolution adopted on Thursday, the European Parliament expresses solidarity with Bulgaria and Romania over the escalation of Russian attacks on commercial shipping, while also voicing serious concern about “the unclear and ambiguous response of the Bulgarian authorities to the escalating Russian threat in the Black Sea”.
How does the Romanian government view the response of the Bulgarian government led by Rumen Radev to Russian threats in the region? And how can Europe protect shipping in the Black Sea without waiting for the next attack? Is a common European response possible when national governments are sending different signals to Moscow?
In Strasbourg, BNR's Irina Nedeva spoke to Romanian MEP Dan Barna, a former deputy prime minister of Romania and one of the driving forces behind the resolution on behalf of the Renew Europe group. Their conversation addressed the need for a European Maritime Security Centre, the protection of commercial vessels, and the role of Bulgaria and Romania in defending NATO’s eastern flank.
But there is also a broader question facing the EU: can Europe finance its defence, maintain support for poorer regions and avoid new political crises within the Union at the same time?
You are calling for a European maritime security centre in the Black Sea. What exactly should this centre do, who will fund it, and when could it become operational? Is there not a risk of creating yet another institution while ships continue to come under attack?
“This resolution is also a very swift response by the European Parliament. I am pleased that, on the very day it was debated in the European Parliament, NATO also brought the Black Sea into focus. The resolution has two main objectives. The first is to recognise the need to designate the Black Sea as a priority area on the eastern flank. The second, as you rightly pointed out, concerns the establishment and funding of a European Maritime Security Centre.
The purpose of this structure, this centre, is to enhance the capacity to respond rapidly to attacks and security threats in the Black Sea. War is no longer just a war of tanks and aircraft. It is a drone war, and in this kind of warfare, time is of the essence. That is precisely why this centre must strengthen NATO’s and the eastern flank’s ability to respond appropriately and in a timely manner. What we are talking about is building technical infrastructure capable of addressing the realities of Russian aggression.”
Romania and Bulgaria are directly exposed to these risks, but the Black Sea is also an external border of both the EU and NATO. What concrete action do you expect from European partners: military surveillance, air defence, escorts for commercial vessels or some other form of presence?
“Everything you have mentioned is important. I mean the ability to identify risks and drones in a given area as quickly as possible. It is also important to have the capacity to scramble aircraft to destroy these drones. In this context, I would like to commend the Romanian and Spanish pilots who have managed to shoot down several drones in recent days. In the near future, we may also have to address the need to protect commercial vessels and provide them with escorts if Russian drones continue to operate aggressively in the region.”
Irina Nedeva and MEP Dan Barna in Radio Studio 2 at the European Parliament in Strasbourg
PHOTO Rositsa Petkova, BNR
Romania has clearly identified the aggressor. For the first time, Prime Minister Rumen Radev has mentioned Russia as being logically linked to the attacks, while adding that there is no evidence confirming their origin. From Romania’s perspective, how do you view the Bulgarian government’s response?
“We must be absolutely clear, and this resolution emphasises the point: Russia is the aggressor and is carrying out attacks against NATO’s eastern flank, including against Romania and Bulgaria. The text of the resolution, which we agreed on only yesterday, also refers to the perception that Bulgaria’s position is unclear and insufficiently categorical. I am optimistic that the Bulgarian government, too, will demonstrate solidarity and determination by acknowledging that these attacks originate from Russia and that a coordinated response is needed.This is one of the main problems associated with these attacks.
Commercial shipping is crucial not only for the countries of the Black Sea region. Food and essential goods are transported by sea to Africa, Asia and many other countries that depend, for example, on Ukrainian grain. The key question is how to protect this commercial traffic. If the Black Sea were to become a situation resembling that in the Strait of Hormuz, brought about by the war with Iran, this would put enormous pressure on the gas and hydrocarbon markets. Agricultural products could also be seriously affected.”
You advocate both stronger European defence and continued support for cohesion policy and agricultural subsidies. When resources are limited, who should make the compromise? Can countries such as Romania and Bulgaria expect more funding for security without losing support for their regions?
“Europe is under intense pressure from anti-European, sovereigntist and extremist movements. Weakening cohesion policy is precisely the argument used by sovereigntist and pro-Russian forces. They are trying to convince European citizens that Europe no longer works. That is why cohesion policy acts as a bond holding European values and European solidarity together. For this very reason, I believe it is important, for Romania, Bulgaria and Europe as a whole, that cohesion policy remains in place and continues to be strong.”
Romania is emerging from nearly six months of political deadlock with a minority government. Is this a temporary arrangement, or are there grounds to expect stability?
“The outlook is relatively optimistic in terms of stability, though not necessarily in terms of the quality of governance. Romania is currently facing a similar situation within its government, and I am sure Bulgaria has been through many such situations as well. We are talking about parliaments divided into three roughly equal blocs, none of which is willing to work openly with the other two. Yesterday, parliament approved a new government. So we now have a new cabinet. That is good news for the country’s stability.”
You have criticised the lack of tangible progress on enlargement. Is the EU ready to admit Moldova and other candidate countries before reforming its own decision-making processes? And how would you prevent a scenario in which new members bring unresolved rule-of-law problems into the Union?
“I must express my deep respect for Marta Kos, the European Commissioner for Enlargement, because she has managed to turn enlargement policy into a consistent and effective one. Two weeks ago in Strasbourg, she announced the new enlargement strategy, under which the four most successful and best-prepared countries were given roadmaps. This is a significant step forward. I am referring to Montenegro, Moldova, Albania and Ukraine. They are receiving roadmaps that set out a clear path forward, with specific conditions and reforms to be completed. These have been presented to their governments. This represents considerable progress because, at the very least, there is now a clear prospect.
I fully agree that Europe needs reforms, including to its voting system and the way its decision-making mechanisms operate. These reforms must prevent a repeat of what happened with Hungary and Viktor Orbán, when Russia managed to block one link in the chain and bring the entire mechanism to a standstill. To avoid this negative experience and this vicious practice, it is clear that Europe must move towards qualified majority voting instead of the current requirement for unanimity.
As regards enlargement, one approach under the new strategy is to retain unanimity only for the first and final stages of the process, while applying qualified majority voting to the intermediate stages. We are working in this direction, too. I am also a member of the European Parliament–Moldova Parliamentary Association Committee. We are working to help the country carry out the necessary reforms.”
Bulgaria is already in the eurozone. When will we stop having to convert our currencies as two neighbouring countries?
“For us Romanians, and for me personally, this is a painful issue. I would like to congratulate Bulgarian citizens, politicians and society on managing to adopt the euro, despite changing seven governments in roughly two years. The fact that all these governments managed to maintain the course and meet the convergence criteria, enabling Bulgaria to join the eurozone at the beginning of this year, is a source of pride.
I know that Romania and Bulgaria have a healthy sense of neighbourly competition on various issues. I know many people on both sides who take pride in their country’s achievements, in the areas where Romania excels and those where Bulgaria performs well. But when it comes to the euro, you have done better than we have. You have my admiration.”
Irina Nedeva’s full interview with MEP Dan Barna was aired on the 12+3 programme on BNR's Horizon channel.

Switzerland disputes Ebola claims – media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:38:20 UTC

Switzerland disputes Ebola claims – media
The woman diagnosed with Nigeria’s first Ebola case in more than a decade did not travel to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DR Congo), the Swiss government has said. The statement contradicts claims by Ugandan authorities that she had visited the country where the current outbreak began.
The patient is a 42-year-old Ugandan-born Swiss national married to a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja. She is believed to have contracted the virus while traveling with her husband in Uganda, the Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs told Reuters on Thursday.
Uganda’s Health Ministry initially reported that the woman was a Nigerian national who had visited eastern DR Congo on business before traveling through Uganda. The ministry said the source of her infection remained unknown and stressed that Uganda had no active Ebola cases. However, the Swiss government later denied that the woman had traveled to DR Congo, while the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) said they had received no confirmed information about such a visit.
“The information supplied to WHO did not include travel to another country (other than Uganda),” WHO representative in Nigeria Pavel Ursu said.
The Africa CDC is also investigating whether the woman may have come into contact with a Kenyan Ebola patient, as both traveled through Uganda’s Entebbe airport on October 3.
Nigeria confirmed the infection on October 20. The woman returned to Nigeria on October 3 after spending about two and a half weeks in Uganda, the BBC said. According to the WHO, she developed symptoms four days later and sought medical care on October 11. She remains in isolation and is showing signs of improvement, while her husband is also isolated but has no symptoms. Nigerian Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate warned from “any panic,” stressing there was “no evidence that it has gone into the communities,” as authorities stepped up contact tracing and monitoring.
Uganda recorded 20 Ebola cases earlier this year, mostly imported from DR Congo, before being declared free of the disease in August.
The outbreak has affected DR Congo, Uganda, Kenya, Nigeria, and France. According to the latest figures from DR Congo’s Health Ministry, the country had recorded 9,704 confirmed Ebola cases and 4,687 deaths as of October 20, with a fatality rate of 48.3%. The outbreak has affected 66 health zones across eight provinces.

Late invitations and spats leave Hungary’s 1956 commemoration with ‘modest’ guest list
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:38:15 UTC
22:38:15 KST

Hungarian PM Péter Magyar had hoped to host top leaders in Budapest for the 70th anniversary of the 1956 revolution. But last-minute invitations and spats with Paris and Kyiv kept Macron, Tusk and Zelenskyy away, leaving only EU chiefs Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa attending.
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar sought to bring European leaders to Budapest for a major commemoration of the 70th anniversary of the 1956 revolution.
In the end, only European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa are attending on behalf of the EU leadership.
Late invitations and diplomatic tensions contributed to the absence of key figures, including French President Emmanuel Macron, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Magyar had planned a major international commemoration on 23 October to mark the anti-Soviet uprising, saying the day after his landslide election victory that he wanted to welcome some of the world’s most senior leaders to Budapest.
“We really hope that on the 70th anniversary of the 1956 revolution, on October 23, when we will welcome world leaders here, either the US Secretary of State, the Vice President, or the President will be able to visit here,” Magyar told reporters on 13 April.
In June, Magyar personally invited Macron in Paris, extending similar invitations to Tusk in Warsaw, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Around 40 countries sent delegations to Budapest, though most EU member states were represented by ministers or parliamentary speakers rather than heads of government. Moldovan President Maia Sandu and Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze also travelled to the Hungarian capital.
“It was a mistake that they set expectations so high,” István Szent-Iványi, a foreign affairs expert and former diplomat, told Euronews.
“Europe and its individual member states are struggling with a thousand problems, and they didn’t feel that it would be worth coming,” he said.
Euronews reached out to the Hungarian government but had not received a response by the time of publication.
Late invitations
Sources close to the Hungarian government, speaking on condition of anonymity, said said the ceremony was complicated by delays in sending official invitations, many of which were not dispatched until September, when leaders’ schedules were already full.
Tusk had already scheduled a trip to India, while Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni had planned a visit to Kuwait.
One source said the government had acted in good faith but that communication between the prime minister’s office and the foreign ministry had been poor.
“We will do better in the future,” the source added.
Remarks irk Paris and Kyiv
Magyar’s comments linking riots in France to migration may have contributed to Macron’s decision not to attend.
“Seeing this senseless destruction and unjustified violence, perhaps it is now clear to everyone why Hungary takes the toughest possible stance on migration,” Magyar wrote in a social media post last Sunday, drawing criticism in Hungary and France.
The following day, the French embassy in Budapest announced that Macron would not attend, adding that his visit had never been confirmed by France.
On Wednesday, Macron criticised what he called “stupid comments” by foreign leaders linking migration to the unrest. Besides Magyar, US President Donald Trump and Tusk had made similar remarks.
“We’ve had people claiming that we were invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false,” Macron said. “The fact is that all those speaking ill of our country right now are people who don’t love our country. And those people irritate me.”
Magyar has also faced criticism over his invitation to Zelenskyy, as Euronews first reported last week.
At the EU summit in Brussels, Zelenskyy expressed openness to visiting Budapest, but Magyar downplayed the possibility just days later. Zelenskyy’s adviser Dmytro Lytvyn also pushed back against the remarks.
Ukraine is represented at today’s commemoration by its parliamentary speaker. The Ukrainian president’s office said the visit was arranged independently and was not intended to replace Zelenskyy’s attendance.
Dániel Hegedűs, deputy director of the Institut für Europäische Politik, said Magyar’s public comments had not helped the commemoration.
“Those social media appearances can be interpreted as interference in French domestic politics, and obviously did not facilitate Macron’s visit,” he said.
He added that Magyar’s response to Zelenskyy’s invitation, saying everyone had been invited, “sends the message to the partners that whether they come or not is not a strategic issue”.
Georgian prime minister’s presence stirs controversy
The guest list also includes Irakli Kobakhidze, Georgia’s controversial prime minister. suppression of dissent.
Brussels has criticised Kobakhidze’s Georgian Dream party for its close ties to Russia, its role in derailing Georgia’s EU integration path and its crackdown on dissent.
“We know it’s a pro-Russian oppressive regime, so it doesn’t really belong here, in the vicinity of a memorial to the 1956 revolution. But they say here that it’s protocol, everyone was invited, and he said he would come,” Szent-Iványi said.
This week, Georgia’s Constitutional Court began hearings on a request by the governing party to ban five pro-Western parties.
Von der Leyen and Costa attend
Von der Leyen and Costa are the most senior EU figures attending, signalling Brussels’ support for Magyar’s pro-European policies following the end of Viktor Orbán’s tenure.
"Six months ago the people of Hungary voted for a new chapter. To turn the page on years of division, of trust eroded, freedoms rolled back, prosperity undermined" von der Leyen said in Budapest.
Von der Leyen and Costa had initially been expected to miss the commemoration due to an EU-Gulf Cooperation Council meeting scheduled for Saturday in Riyadh. Its postponement last week cleared the way for both to attend in Budapest.
Szent-Iványi said that leading European missing the ceremony does not mean that they are turning their backs on Magyar.
“This is a modest list of participants; that’s a fact. But I think the presence of von der Leyen confirmed the message that this election meant Hungary returning to Europe”.

On the 23rd of October, the Austrian Foreign Ministry announced that it would expel four Russian diplomats based in Vienna for engaging in activities incompatible with their diplomatic status—a term typically used to refer to espionage, reports Reuters.

Romanian President Nicusor Dan has accused Russia of escalating its attacks on NATO's eastern flank, after a drone strike sank a cargo ship off the Romanian Black Sea coast, killing at least one sailor, with three still missing.
Video released by Romanian authorities on Friday showed only a small part of the capsized tanker's hull still visible above the waves as it sank.
Emergency vessels searched the surrounding waters for survivors in choppy seas and high winds.
Romania's naval authority said the Comoros-flagged Khoryv, with a crew of 13 Ukrainian and Azerbaijani sailors, had sent a distress signal 13 nautical miles off Romania's port of Constanta, just beyond Romanian territorial waters.
Nine sailors were rescued from the water, three were missing, and one body was recovered.
Part of ‘Russian escalation process’
The past two weeks have seen a sudden surge in deadly attacks on commercial ships off the coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria, with at least seven cargo ships hit and some 30 sailors reported dead or missing.
"It is part of Russia's escalation process in its war in Ukraine," President Dan told reporters, later saying the ship had been hit by a drone.
NATO said on Tuesday it would send more maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems and drones to the Black Sea. The alliance has not specified what capabilities would be sent.
On Saturday, Romanian jets shot down two of the latest generation of Russian drones over Romanian territorial waters.
The vessels that have been struck lately have either been anchored near or headed towards the Sulina Canal, which links the Danube River to the Black Sea.
The canal has become the primary export route for Ukraine, one of the world's biggest grain and food oil exporters, which has relied on Danube River ports and Romanian territorial waters as Russia has attacked Ukraine's own Black Sea ports.
Ukraine, Romania and Bulgaria have called on NATO to do more to protect commercial shipping in the Black Sea.
EU ‘alarmed’ about escalation in Black Sea
EU chief Ursula von der Leyen said on Friday she was "deeply alarmed" after Russia was blamed for the drone attack.
"Deeply alarmed by yet another Russian escalation in the Black Sea. A civilian vessel carrying Ukrainian and Azerbaijani crew has been struck off the coast of Romania. These reckless attacks target innocent lives and openly defy international law," von der Leyen posted online.

Türkiye urges stronger financing partnerships to turn COP31 pledges into investment

Mucahithan Avcioglu
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
Türkiye aims to turn climate commitments into investments through COP31, officials and business leaders said on Friday, urging stronger cooperation between governments, banks and international investors.
Speaking at the Investment Summit Towards COP31 in Istanbul, Halil Hasar, head of climate change at the environment ministry and COP31 chief climate diplomacy officer, said the country seeks to build consensus and translate agreements into action.
Organized by the presidency’s Investment and Finance Office and the International Investors Association (YASED), the summit gathered policymakers, financiers and businesses ahead of COP31 in Antalya.
Hasar said Türkiye aims to bring its experience in peace diplomacy to climate negotiations, helping countries with different priorities work toward common goals.
“Let us not just establish dialogue; after talking around the table, let us reach a consensus,” he said. “Let us turn that consensus into action.”
As the Paris Agreement enters its second decade, implementation must accelerate, with private capital essential to meeting developing countries’ financing needs, he added.
Banks support energy transition
Ziraat Bank CEO Alpaslan Cakar said green transition is a strategic priority for Türkiye’s competitiveness, while developments around the Strait of Hormuz underscore the importance of reducing dependence on imported energy.
Turkish banking sector loans to the energy industry have exceeded 1 trillion Turkish liras, energy investments financed through project finance have surpassed 695 billion liras, and renewable energy loans have topped 340 billion liras, he said.
“Finance should be seen not only as providing resources, but as a tool that enables investments to be implemented,” Cakar said.
Clear targets, credible transition plans and transparent reporting can help industries cut emissions while preserving production and exports, he added.
International investors seek predictable conditions
YASED Chairman Ali Fuat Orhonoglu said international investment brings capital, technology and expertise to Türkiye’s green transition.
The association represents 280 companies from 35 countries and supports Türkiye’s target of reaching 120 gigawatts of combined wind and solar capacity by 2035, he said.
Developing countries face an annual investment gap of around $4 trillion to achieve sustainable development goals, roughly half related to energy transition investment, Orhonoglu said.
COP31 offers an opportunity to attract partnerships, but lasting gains require predictable investment conditions, modern infrastructure and reforms, he added.

An excerpt of the book released Thursday details allegations encompassing Kushner's time as a senior White House adviser during the first Trump administration, which included a lead role in U.S. policy in the Middle East. Kushner had a major hand in negotiating key foreign policy deals that involved Israel, the Gulf states, China and Russia during that period.

Kushner said, "The allegations made by this author are completely insane and never happened." The new book, "Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed's Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East," alleges Kushner had access to billions of dollars in undisclosed foreign bank accounts intended to pay for "influence within the U.S. government."
An excerpt from the book that was published in "Vanity Fair," but not independently verified by CBS News, says Dutch intelligence agents learned the Russians had hacked Kushner's iPhone in 2017 after flipping a Russian spy and subsequently gained access to Kushner's phone as well.
According to the report, "when Kushner used the phone, they could see his screen. Almost as soon as they got inside, the intelligence service began capturing every image of Kushner's screen as he used it."
At the time, Kushner served as a senior White House adviser to President Trump, including on Middle Eastern diplomacy.
The report alleges Dutch spies witnessed him log into a United Arab Emirates account that had allegedly received hundreds of millions of dollars from a bank in Azerbaijan, and claims the leaders of Saudi Arabia and the UAE put at least $2 billion into multiple bank accounts linked to Kushner, including an account with Israel's Central Bank.
According to the book excerpt, the owners and managers of the accounts were often disguised as official government entities or charities, but the funds were actually intended for "off-the-books diplomatic objectives" such as striking a deal to end the Israeli-Palesteinian conflict.
The report also claims Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman put roughly $1 billion into at least one account for Kushner, citing a "person with knowledge of the money" saying "its allocation was for Kushner's personal benefit."
Kushner forcefully denied the accusations leveled in the "Vanity Fair" excerpt, writing in part, "The allegations made by this author are completely insane and never happened."
"We denied every claim on the record, yet the author provided not a single shred of verifiable evidence to substantiate them," he said.
"No bank statements, wire transfer records, account numbers, transaction dates, or other verifiable details were provided to support these extraordinary accusations," he said.
CBS News reached out to the White House, which referred us to a statement from Steven Cheung, who is assistant to the president and White House director of communications.
Cheung said the "bull**** Vanity Fair article comes from a book that is complete fiction, and was fabricated from the warped mind of failed spy thriller writer."
"He presents no evidence or even a shred of documentation. Just mysterious words from unnamed sources," Cheung said on X.

At least seven killed after gunmen open fire at church in Jordan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:32:40 UTC
22:32:40 KST

At least seven killed after gunmen open fire at church in Jordan
Survivors say two masked gunmen began shooting as dozens attended a funeral procession.
At least seven people have been killed, and 34 others wounded, in an attack in Jordan’s Karak governorate that saw gunmen open fire during a funeral at a church.
Director of Jordan’s Public Security Directorate Obaidullah Al-Maaytah told a press conference on Friday that seven people are confirmed dead after the assault on a Greek Orthodox Church in the village of Hamoud.
Twenty-seven of the wounded were receiving treatment in hospitals, he said.
The search for the gunmen is ongoing, Al-Maaytah added, pledging that “the perpetrators will be caught and our national unity will not be hit”.
Survivors said they heard an explosion when the funeral procession started, after which masked attackers broke into the church and began shooting for several minutes.
State-owned television station Al-Mamlaka reported that security forces were deployed to the church and were pursuing two suspects, who got out of a vehicle and opened fire.
Funeral attendee Khaled Burqan told Al-Mamlaka that dozens of people were at the procession. One of the assailants carried a pistol, he said, and the other carried a rifle.
There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attack.
Without naming a specific group, Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya told the press conference that the “terrorist” attack was “unprecedented” and was perpetrated by a group with “no relationship to humanity”.
“This country will never be dragged into terrorism and violence,” he said, adding that “Jordanians have never seen something like this before”.
Earlier, Jordan’s King Abdullah II vowed authorities would confront the attackers “with the harshest penalties”.
“The blood of Jordanians is precious, and we will strike with an iron fist against anyone who overreaches against this country,” he said in a post on X.
The United Arab Emirates foreign ministry meanwhile condemned what it described as “terrorist and criminal acts”, and said it rejected all forms of violence “that aim to undermine security and stability”.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres also strongly condemned the attack, his spokesman Stephane Dujarric said. “It goes without saying that an attack not only on a place of worship but during a funeral procession is especially heinous,” Dujarric told reporters on Friday.
Such attacks are extremely rare in Jordan. Christians, numbering about 300,000 people, make up a minority of Jordan’s population of roughly 11.5 million, though the country is home to several biblical sites that attract Christians from around the world.
Previous attacks
This is not the first time that Karak has come under attack.
In 2016, a deadly ISIL (ISIS) assault saw a group of fighters hole up in a Crusader-era castle and kill 10 people, including security officers and a Canadian tourist. Jordanian security forces ultimately shot and killed the attackers.
Karak, located about 120km (75 miles) south of the capital Amman, is home to “Christians and Muslims who have lived side by side for generations”, Taylor Luck, senior Middle East correspondent at the Christian Science Monitor, told Al Jazeera.
“This community prides themselves on its interfaith solidarity and coexistence,” Luck said.
If the attack was “intended to create divisions, we are likely to see this community come back even stronger”, he added.
More broadly, the shooting holds significance not just for Jordan’s Christian population, but also Amman’s “public diplomacy” as a custodian of both Christian and Muslim holy sites in Jerusalem, political analyst Xavier Abu Eid told Al Jazeera.
For years, King Abdullah has been a vocal critic of Israel’s systemic attacks against religious sites in occupied Palestinian territory.
“This is something that goes totally against the message that Jordan wants to give to the world,” Abu Eid said.

In a statement, the army’s 35th Armored Brigade said its forces carried out a “swift and targeted operation” against Houthi positions and fortifications along the Aqrouz front in the Al-Misrakh district.
It said the operation targeted positions at Jabal Al-Manara, Kour, Wadi Kour, Al-Maqda, Al-Dabaya and Kahlan, leaving “more than 35 Houthi fighters killed or wounded.”

The Houthis did not immediately comment on the Yemeni army’s account.

Taiz holds strategic importance as a geographic bridge and a vital link between Yemen’s northern provinces.
Control of the province would mean control over supply routes and key transport corridors connecting the interim capital, Aden, with the country’s central and northern provinces.
These developments are part of a military escalation that began in July and is considered the most extensive since the relative calm that followed a truce launched in April 2022.
Since Oct. 5, Yemeni government forces have been conducting Operation Dawn of Yemen, which Presidential Leadership Council Chairman Rashad al-Alimi said aims to regain control of state institutions from the Houthis and recapture the capital Sanaa.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized Sanaa and several other provinces in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.
The Houthis control much of northern and western Yemen, while government forces and their allies hold Aden and large parts of the country’s southern and eastern provinces.

A low-pressure front brought 179kmh winds and rains across Europe overnight, with towns facing power outages as trees and debris littered roads, causing traffic issues, airport and train delays and reduced access to bridges.
Utility Enedis said in an update on Oct 23 that nearly 300,000 clients had no electricity due to the storm, with most of the disruptions in Brittany on the western coast and Normandy in the north. Britain’s National Grid said engineers had to restore power to more than 12,000 homes.

Meteo France, France’s weather agency, issued orange alerts for much of the country’s north-west, saying that heavy wind and thunderstorms would continue into late Oct 23.
A second storm named Boelo is expected to impact Northern Ireland, Scotland and parts of northern England over the weekend, Britain’s Met Office said.

Former German President Roman Herzog visited Pakistan in 1995. The two countries established diplomatic relations in 1951 and have maintained close political and economic ties since then.

Japan Needs Higher Interest Rates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:28:00 UTC
22:28:00 KST

On a recent visit to Sapporo, the city on Japan’s northern island where my parents came from, my wife and I found gentle people, mild autumn days, and excellent food. As tourists who live and work in the United States, we also enjoyed very low prices: lunch at a high-quality restaurant cost only about $20 per person. While that was convenient for us, like so many other tourists who have headed to Japan to take advantage of favorable exchange rates, the cheap yen (yen yasu) has been hard on Japan’s economy.
To understand the pressure Japan is under, it is worth looking at the purchasing-power-parity equilibrium exchange rate – the rate at which a representative basket of goods and services would cost the same across two countries. This month, the OECD reports a PPP equilibrium exchange rate between Japan and the United States of around 93 yen per dollar. That is a far cry from the actual yen-dollar exchange rate, which has been hovering in the 150–160 range.
This means that goods produced in Japan cost much less than goods produced in the United States. As a result, Japanese exporters enjoy high demand and strong profit margins, but importers are under severe pressure. The weak yen also hurts Japanese consumers, as it creates strong incentives to raise prices: With imported goods more expensive, domestic producers know that their output will find buyers, and importers might pass their mounting costs on to buyers.
Japan used to have the opposite problem. In the early 1980s, it was a dominant economy experiencing strong growth. But the 1985 Plaza Accord, under which major economies agreed to take coordinated action to strengthen their currencies vis-à-vis the U.S. dollar, changed everything. After the accord was implemented, the PPP exchange rate was higher than the actual exchange rate, reaching almost double in 1995.
The strong yen (yen daka) persisted for decades, contributing to chronic deflation and stagnant growth. During this period, a visit to Tokyo strained tourists’ pocketbooks, Japanese goods found few customers abroad, and Japan’s once-formidable industries struggled. The situation deteriorated further around the 2008 global economic crisis, when the United States embraced monetary easing.
In the decades after the Plaza Accord, Bank of Japan (BOJ) governors (with the possible exception of Fukui Toshihiko) consistently failed to loosen monetary policy in line with changing economic conditions. Deflationary pressures intensified.
After returning to power in 2012, Prime Minister Abe Shinzo sought to turn things around with an economic-reform package, which came to be known as Abenomics. (I served as an adviser to Abe.) This package included a recommendation for monetary expansion, which then-BOJ Governor Kuroda Haruhiko embraced.
Now, conditions have changed. After the COVID-19 pandemic, the United States experienced a surge in inflation, which forced the U.S. Federal Reserve to abandon monetary expansion and raise interest rates. As the dollar strengthened, and the Japan-U.S. interest-rate differential widened, the yen depreciated in value, and deflationary forces gave way to inflationary pressures.
When circumstances change, so, too, must policy. For the BOJ today, this means pursuing monetary tightening in order to reduce the domestic money supply, and raising the interest rate.
To some extent, Japanese policymakers seem to recognize this. After keeping the short-term interest rate around 1 percent for some time, the BOJ raised its policy rate to 1.25 percent last month. This is high for Japan – the highest in 31 years, to be precise. But with the U.S. short-term money market pushing the interest rate close to 4 percent, and more U.S. rate hikes likely, it is not nearly enough. Speculators continue to exploit the interest-rate differential via the so-called carry trade (borrowing cheaply in yen to invest in higher-yielding assets abroad).
Under the gold standard or a fixed exchange rate, if a major country pursued monetary expansion, another, weaker country might need to reduce its money supply and raise its interest rate. Under a flexible exchange-rate regime, however, an expansion in one country should be met with a (moderate) expansion in another, just as tightening should be met with tightening.
We know that U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Japanese Finance Minister Katayama Satsuki are communicating about fiscal and monetary matters. Ultimately, however, monetary policy must be pursued autonomously, with BOJ Governor Ueda Kazuo doing what is best for Japan’s economy. Under the current circumstances, that means reducing the money supply and raising interest rates more aggressively.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said he was concerned about SpaceX’s manipulation of the Starlink satellite system, which made Ukraine’s defense more difficult, and suggested that reports of Elon Musk’s involvement show why he is focused on making Canada less dependent on any one country or technology. UNN reports this, citing Bloomberg.
Details
The Wall Street Journal reported this week that Musk ordered the speed of the military version of Starlink to be limited, hindering the capabilities of Ukraine’s defense forces in the fight against Russia. The Journal also reported that U.S. President Donald Trump called Musk to ask him to lift these restrictions.
"I’m looking for the right adjective to describe the person who made this decision, or the group of people who made this decision against a country—and this is against a country that is literally fighting for the lives of its citizens against open aggression," the Canadian prime minister told reporters in Istanbul on Friday, October 23. "So, are we concerned? Yes, we are concerned."
Carney said the incident shows why his government is focused on diversifying Canada’s trade relations, particularly in technology, in order to strengthen the country’s sovereignty.
"As Canadians, we do not want to find ourselves in a situation where we depend on a single supplier that can change its point of view, or where we can be forced to change our point of view by a single nation-state that puts Canadians at risk or threatens our sovereignty," Carney said.
But the diversification process will take time, since "we are starting from a position where we are very, very dependent on certain systems in certain countries."
Carney’s visit is the first official visit by a Canadian prime minister to Turkey and is part of his government’s efforts to expand Canada’s diplomatic and trade relations, as U.S. tariffs continue to harm some of its industries, the publication writes.
Meanwhile, the European Union is preparing to ask Canada and the United Kingdom to increase their support for Ukraine to help address a funding shortfall, according to a report by Politico.
Carney said that Canada "does not need the EU to carry out these requests" and that his government is working directly with Ukraine, adding that he had spoken with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy during the past week, including about the situation with Starlink.

The men, who were driving a car with Israeli number plates, opened fire after they were stopped by soldiers at a temporary checkpoint outside Hebron. They were killed after a 20-minute gunfight.
An AFP photographer who was on the way to another assignment and witnessed the gun battle saw two Palestinian men armed with a handgun and an automatic rifle exchanging fire with Israeli forces.
Prominent Israelis, including a candidate for the far-right Amcha Yisrael party, shared conspiracy theories groundlessly accusing the AFP photographer of links to the gunmen after he documented the Hebron attack.
The Foreign Press Association (FPA) said it was deeply alarmed by claims the photographer had been tipped off, describing them as “dangerous and defamatory”. “He is a longtime professional who was on his way to another assignment and courageously documented what he saw in keeping with his professional duties,” the FPA said in a statement.
The incident came a week after settlers severely injured the photographer Heidi Levine as she documented attacks on Palestinians attempting to harvest olives in the occupied West Bank. Israel has also denied entry to several European journalists and an academic.
Since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks there has been a surge of Israeli settlement expansion, ethnic cleansing and violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed there by Israeli forces or settlers.
Attacks have intensified further since the start of the annual olive harvest in late September. Israeli settler militants have used violence to stop Palestinians bringing in a crop that is economically and culturally vital to their communities.
Israel holds elections on Tuesday. The current far-right coalition, which backs settlers politically and financially, is seeking to shore up voter support in the face of polls that show it is likely to loose its majority.
Itamar Ben-Gvir, the far-right national security minister, also travelled to Hebron on Friday and demanded the dismantling of the Palestinian Authority and restrictions on Palestinians’ freedom of movement, which is already heavily curtailed by Israeli controls, checkpoints and roadblocks.

Hundreds to defy Palestine Action ban in protest at US embassy in London

Hundreds to defy Palestine Action ban in protest at US embassy in London
Campaigners plan Halloween mass action days before the UK Supreme Court hears a challenge to the group’s ‘terrorist’ proscription.
More than 400 people are expected to gather outside the United States embassy in London on October 31 in the latest act of mass defiance against the British government’s ban on the Palestine Action group.
Protesters plan to hold placards reading: “I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action,” and campaign group Defend Our Juries said a parallel action will take place outside the US consulate in Edinburgh, Scotland.
More than 3,850 people have been arrested for publicly backing Palestine Action since the United Kingdom’s government proscribed it as a “terrorist” organisation in July 2025, Defend Our Juries said.
The timing of the demonstrations is calculated. In June, the Court of Appeal sided with the government and overturned a High Court ruling that had found the proscription unlawful.
On November 4 and 5, the UK Supreme Court will hear an appeal by Palestine Action cofounder Huda Ammori.
‘Arrested again and again’
Among those Al Jazeera spoke to at the group’s previous action outside Westminster Magistrates’ Court was Teresa, a former teacher-turned-activist who has been arrested multiple times for protesting against the proscription.
“It’s a badge of honour, to be able to do this for Gaza” she told Al Jazeera.
She is not alone. Those arrested at recent actions include Massive Attack’s Rob del Naja, 94-year-old human rights barrister Margaret Owen, former government adviser Jonathan Porritt and the Reverend Sue Parfitt.
Why the US embassy?
Organisers want to raise the possibility that the UK move to ban Palestine Action came under pressure from US President Donald Trump.
The proscription followed an incident in which activists spray-painted Trump’s Turnberry golf course in Scotland. The US president labelled the action “terrorism” on his Truth Social platform and praised then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s response.
During the legal challenge, it emerged that Trump and Starmer had spoken by phone twice about Palestine Action in March 2025. Starmer had requested updates from Police Scotland on the arrests and briefed Trump on developments.
The US president’s son Eric Trump also met Scottish First Minister John Swinney before the ban was announced, and documents released under the Freedom of Information Act showed the Turnberry protest was discussed.
The Halloween protests will also come three days after a hearing in the trial of the Turnberry protesters at the High Court in Glasgow. Prosecutors are now seeking to have the seven defendants sentenced as “terrorists”, a move critics called “completely disproportionate”.
The same week that the prosecutors made that call, Washington designated Palestine Action a “terrorist organisation”.
Defend Our Juries said the resulting sanctions have blocked Ammori from crowdfunding for her Supreme Court challenge.
Growing opposition
This week, actors Paul Mescal, Jessie Buckley and Susan Sarandon along with broadcaster Gary Lineker signed a letter published on the cover of the New Statesman magazine urging Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government to drop the “draconian” legislation.
Campaigners said the ban on the group has also in effect halted UK sales of books by the Irish novelist Sally Rooney, a Palestine Action supporter.
However, when author Sarah Helm, wife of National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell, publicly declared her support for Palestine Action, the Metropolitan Police took no action. Defend Our Juries said that exposes a ban that cannot be enforced evenly.
Shami Chakrabarti, a senior figure in the ruling Labour Party, has urged the home secretary to lift the ban.
Speaking to the LBC radio station, the former shadow attorney general said it “makes a mockery” of counterterrorism law and the power to proscribe should be exceptional and kept under constant review.
“I’d better be careful what I say, or I’ll be arrested,” she added.
The government’s case
The government argued that Palestine Action’s campaign of break-ins and criminal damage at defence sites, including those linked to Israeli arms maker Elbit Systems, meets the legal threshold for proscription. The Court of Appeal described it as a covert organisation operating through secret cells.
Defend Our Juries insisted its own protests are entirely peaceful.
“This mass defiance and the mass arrests expected to follow will lay bare the fundamental rights to free expression at stake in the Supreme Court hearing just days later,” a spokesperson said.

Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov has accused the European Parliament of using a resolution on Bulgaria’s participation in a NATO anti-drone project to launch a political attack on the government, alleging that the effort was orchestrated by what he called “assembly arrangement 2.0.”
Stoyanov made the remarks to journalists at Cheshnegirovo Airfield near Plovdiv, where he was observing a capability demonstration during the multinational experimental exercise OPEX “BOLD ADRA 26” (BOAD-26), BGNES reported.
“This is a political attack on our government, organized by 'assembly arrangement 2.0' - the same entity that was active in Bulgaria during the protests, and is now operating within the European Parliament. This is a fact; this is the truth,” Stoyanov said.
He argued that members of the European Parliament criticizing Bulgaria for delaying its participation had overlooked the fact that Sofia had already submitted the required documents. He also questioned why lawmakers from the Baltic states, Poland, the Czech Republic and Slovakia were pressing Bulgaria to join a project their own countries had not joined.
Stoyanov noted that the initiative had been in place since February 2025 and said Bulgaria’s current leadership had evaluated the necessary funding and filed the documentation for participation, which can also be approved through “tacit consent.”
“Countries that are not NATO members, but are members of the European Union, are telling us to join a NATO project. This is nonsense. It is simply incomprehensible,” the defense minister said.
On attacks against commercial vessels in the Black Sea, Stoyanov said Bulgaria could not reach a definitive conclusion until the drones’ origin had been established. He referred to an attack on the airport in Leipzig, saying Germany had taken 28 days, in his assessment, to declare that the attack had come from Russia.
“One cannot expect an immediate conclusion the very next day,” Stoyanov said.

The minister said Bulgaria would identify Russia as responsible if the investigation established that the attack originated there, and would take the appropriate subsequent steps. The same approach would apply if the drones came from another source, he said, stressing that national security decisions would be guided by Bulgarian interests rather than double standards.
Stoyanov said Bulgaria had increased surveillance in the eastern sector and was using all available military resources to protect the Black Sea region. The measures include Air Force fighter and reconnaissance aircraft, as well as the Navy.
He warned that counter-drone capabilities were struggling to keep pace with the rapid development of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).
“Counter-UAV systems are lagging significantly behind the technology, failing to keep pace with developments,” he said.
Stoyanov said drones were evolving so quickly that equipment could become obsolete soon after being acquired. He expressed hope that the defense industry, including Bulgaria’s own sector, would respond rapidly to the emerging threats.
He also identified legislation as a key issue, saying the rules must allow authorities to make faster decisions when unmanned aircraft are detected. The Defense Ministry has prepared amendments to the Law on Defence and the Armed Forces, while the Transport Ministry has drafted a related regulation.
“Events involving unmanned aerial vehicles unfold very quickly. This necessitates rapid action and swift decision-making,” Stoyanov said.
He added that decision-making powers would have to be delegated to lower-level commanders because current procedures require the defense minister to authorize an engagement.
“If we have to wait for the Minister of Defence to grant permission to act against a drone, by the time the entire chain of command is involved, it will simply be too late,” he said.

Gallup International Balkan puts presidential candidate pair Iliana Yotova and Kiril Valchev at 43.2% support ahead of Bulgaria’s October 25 election, with Andrey Gyurov and Georgi Kandev trailing at 29.7%, according to a nationally representative survey conducted from October 14 to October 22, 2026.
The poll indicates that the lead of the top pair is shrinking but remains substantial. Projected turnout is approximately 2.6 million voters, or around 39%.
Kostadin Kostadinov and Petar Volgin rank third with 12.4% support. The other candidate pairs receive the following shares: Ivan Hristanov and Stoyanka Cherkezova, 3.4%; Radostin Vasilev and Krasimir Manov, 2.5%; Ivaylo Simeonov and Kosyo Stoychev, 1.9%; Nikolay Nenchev and Tsveta Kirilova, 1.6%; and Ivelin Mihaylov and Yuliana Mateeva, 1.3%.
The survey also points to widespread dissatisfaction with the campaign. Asked about its appeal, 41.1% of respondents took a neutral position, selecting “Neither,” while 38.7% described it as boring and uninteresting. Only 16.6% considered the campaign interesting and dynamic.
Overall, 79.8% of respondents said they saw no positive momentum in the campaign, while 3.6% answered that they did not know. The findings suggest that most citizens have formed an opinion of the campaign, but that sentiment is largely negative. The survey links the limited public engagement to the expected turnout of around 38%.
Gallup International Balkan conducted 1,001 standardized, face-to-face interviews with adult Bulgarian citizens using tablets. The quota sample was stratified by age, gender, education and type of settlement, and fieldwork took place between October 14 and October 22, 2026.
The survey is nationally representative of Bulgaria’s adult population and reflects its demographic structure by gender, age, education and type of settlement. The maximum margin of error for the main sample is ±3.1 percentage points at a 50% share, with a 95% confidence level. The study is part of Gallup International Balkan’s independent research program and was funded from the agency’s own resources.

Kazakhstan and Czech Republic expand agricultural cooperation
Kazakhstan and the Czech Republic intend to broaden trade and economic cooperation in the agro-industrial sector, develop livestock breeding, and introduce modern agricultural technologies, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing Kazakh Agriculture Ministry.
Over the first eight months of 2026, bilateral trade in agricultural products between the two countries increased by 31%.
During a meeting, Kazakh Vice Minister of Agriculture Yermek Kenzhekhanuly and Czech Deputy Minister of Agriculture Jaroslava Špalková discussed prospects for increasing mutual agricultural exports, expanding cooperation in livestock and crop production, and strengthening collaboration in veterinary and phytosanitary safety.
“We highly value the steady development of Kazakh-Czech relations in agriculture. Expanding cooperation with Czechia is one of the most promising avenues for strengthening the position of Kazakhstan’s agricultural products in the European market. To realize the existing potential, it is important to develop direct business contacts, broaden the range of exported products, and ensure compliance with European quality and safety standards,” the vice minister said.
For her part, Jaroslava Špalková outlined key priorities for the development of Czech agriculture. Among them, she highlighted cooperation in pedigree livestock breeding, aquaculture, and organic agricultural production.
The Kazakh side emphasized the importance of diversifying the trade structure, increasing supply volumes, and expanding the range of products of mutual interest.
Promising areas of cooperation also include supplies of pedigree cattle and genetic material from high-value breeding bulls, improvements in breeding programs, the development of artificial insemination technologies, and the exchange of expertise in herd reproduction.
Plant quarantine and protection issues, as well as the digitalization and automation of related processes, also featured prominently on the agenda.
The parties discussed opportunities for sharing experience and technological solutions to enhance phytosanitary control of agricultural products and improve the efficiency of related procedures.
Following the meeting, both sides reaffirmed their commitment to further developing cooperation in the agro-industrial sector. The implementation of the agreed initiatives is expected to strengthen Kazakhstan-Czech trade and economic ties, expand business contacts, and foster long-term partnership in agriculture.
To note, Kazakhstan, Mongolia also expand cooperation in energy, agriculture and mining.

CineCrossroads: What to watch this weekend - “Clayface,” “The Mask,” and “Megamind”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:20:13 UTC
22:20:13 KST

CineCrossroads: What to watch this weekend - “Clayface,” “The Mask,” and “Megamind”
The weekend is approaching, bringing three stories about characters whose transformations force them to question who they really are. In this edition of CineCrossroads, a disfigured actor undergoes a terrifying experiment, a timid bank clerk discovers a mask that unleashes his wildest impulses, and a famous supervillain finds himself searching for a new purpose. Qazinform News Agency correspondent wishes you an enjoyable viewing.
Movie of the Week: Clayface (2026)
Behind every face is a story, but Matt Hagen is about to lose both.
Directed by James Watkins, Clayface presents the origin of one of the most unusual villains from Batman’s rogues gallery. Tom Rhys Harries stars as Hagen, a rising actor whose promising career is destroyed after a violent attack leaves him severely disfigured.
Desperate to recover his appearance and return to the screen, Hagen turns to scientist Caitlyn Corr, played by Naomi Ackie, and agrees to undergo an experimental treatment. The procedure initially appears successful, but its effects soon transform his body into an unstable, clay-like form capable of assuming other identities.
Rather than following the structure of a conventional superhero film, Clayface combines psychological thriller, tragedy and body horror. Hagen’s transformation gives him extraordinary abilities, but it also weakens his grip on reality and drives him towards revenge.
Written by Mike Flanagan and Hossein Amini, the film also stars Max Minghella, Eddie Marsan and David Dencik. Released in cinemas on October 23, Clayface explores identity, ambition and the dangerous pursuit of physical perfection.
Classic Pick: The Mask (1994)
What if putting on a new face allowed you to become everything you were too afraid to be?
Directed by Chuck Russell, The Mask stars Jim Carrey as Stanley Ipkiss, a shy and frequently overlooked bank clerk whose life changes when he discovers a mysterious wooden mask. After placing it over his face, Stanley transforms into a green-faced figure with extraordinary powers, unstoppable confidence and the energy of a living cartoon.
The mask gives Stanley the courage to pursue singer Tina Carlyle, played by Cameron Diaz, but it also attracts the attention of dangerous criminals. As his second identity becomes increasingly difficult to control, Stanley must decide whether real confidence can exist without magic.
Combining comedy, romance and inventive visual effects, The Mask became one of the defining films of Carrey’s career. Like Clayface, it explores physical transformation and hidden identity, but approaches those ideas with color, humor and playful chaos.
Family Pick: Megamind (2010)
What happens when a villain finally wins?
Directed by Tom McGrath, Megamind follows a blue-skinned alien who has spent his life trying to defeat Metro Man, the celebrated protector of Metro City. When Megamind unexpectedly succeeds, he discovers that ruling the city is far less satisfying than fighting for it.
Without a hero to oppose him, Megamind creates a new one. However, the experiment quickly goes wrong, forcing the self-proclaimed villain to decide whether he is capable of becoming the person he always believed he could never be.
Featuring the voices of Will Ferrell, Tina Fey, Brad Pitt and Jonah Hill, Megamind combines superhero action with comedy and family adventure. Like Clayface, it explores how public labels can shape a person’s identity, while suggesting that individuals are not permanently defined by the roles assigned to them.

FACTBOX: Bank of Russia holds key rate at 14%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:19:51 UTC
22:19:51 KST

MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. The Bank of Russia has decided to maintain its key rate at 14% per annum, stating that current price pressures remain elevated, according to the regulator's press release.
TASS has compiled the key details of the decision.
Regulator’s press release
- The Bank of Russia's Board of Directors has decided to maintain the key rate at 14% per annum.
- The economy as a whole is growing at a moderate pace in the second half of 2026.
- Current price pressures remain elevated, and inflation expectations remain high.
- According to the Bank of Russia's assessment, underlying price growth is not slowing and remains within the 5-6% range on an annualized basis, primarily due to the impact of temporary capacity constraints in certain industries.
- This requires restrained growth in aggregate demand to resume a decline in underlying inflation, the Central Bank emphasized.
- The Bank of Russia noted that it will make further decisions on the key rate depending on inflation dynamics and inflation expectations, as well as an assessment of risks from domestic and external conditions.
- In Q3 2026, seasonally adjusted price growth averaged 8% on an annualized basis, up from 4.8% in Q2 2026.
- The corresponding core inflation rate increased to 6.2%, up from 4.5% in the previous quarter.
- Price dynamics continued to be influenced by volatile items, primarily motor fuel, the regulator noted.
- Annual inflation stood at 6.8% as of October 19 and is projected to settle within the 7.1-7.6% range by year-end.
- High inflation expectations are hindering a slowdown in inflation.
- Despite a slight decline in household and business expectations in October, overall, they have remained near their highest levels in two years in recent months, the Central Bank emphasized.
- The expectations of financial market participants and analysts have increased.
- According to high-frequency data, the economy is growing at a moderate pace in the second half of 2026.
- Business sentiment improved slightly in October following the low levels of previous months.
- Consumer demand growth is slowing but remains elevated, the Central Bank pointed out.
- Investment activity continues to recover compared to levels at the beginning of the year.
- Tensions in the labor market are gradually easing.
- According to surveys, the supply of workers at enterprises continues to improve, but the situation remains uneven across industries, the Central Bank noted.
- Wage growth is slowing and gradually converging with productivity growth.
- However, the gap in their dynamics remains significant, the regulator emphasized.
- At the same time, companies plan more moderate wage indexations in 2027 compared to 2026.
- Unemployment remains near historical lows.
- Lending activity was elevated on average in Q3 2026, driven primarily by the corporate segment.
- The retail loan portfolio grew moderately, the regulator noted.
- Households' propensity to save has declined somewhat but remains high.
- The Bank of Russia is proceeding from the announced fiscal policy parameters.
- Over the medium term, this will contribute to a slowdown in inflation.
- If fiscal policy parameters change, monetary policy may need to be adjusted, the regulator pointed out.
Ruble reaction
The ruble slowed its gains on the Moscow Exchange following the Bank of Russia's decision to maintain the key rate at 14% per annum, trading data showed.
Prior to the announcement, the yuan was trading at 12.037 rubles, down 12.8 kopecks, according to data as of 1:25 p.m. Moscow time.
By 1:30 p.m. Moscow time, the yuan paired its losses to 11.45 kopecks, trading at 12.05 rubles.
MOEX reaction
The MOEX Index turned lower following the central bank's decision to hold the key rate at 14% per annum, trading data showed.
As of 1:25 p.m. Moscow time, ahead of the rate announcement, the MOEX Index was up 0.22% at 2,434.74 points.
The RTS Index stood at 945.44 points, up 0.22%.
By 1:30 p.m. Moscow time, the MOEX Index reversed its gains to trade down 0.45% at 2,418.68 points.
The RTS Index also slid 0.45% to 939.21 points.

UNDP urges faster green investment as Istanbul hosts pre-COP31 summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:19:19 UTC
22:19:19 KST

A senior UN Development Programme official has called for faster action to turn available capital and technology into green investments, as Istanbul hosts an investment summit ahead of COP31.
Speaking at the summit on Friday, UNDP Deputy Assistant Administrator Nick Rene Hartmann said the challenge was connecting financial resources with viable climate and development projects.
“We do not lack the capital,” he said. “Time is not our friend.”
Jointly organised by the Turkish Presidency’s Investment and Finance Office and the International Investors Association, the summit brought together government officials, international organisations and global companies at Ziraat Bank’s headquarters in the Istanbul Financial Centre.
Discussions focused on mobilising international investment in clean energy, sustainable industry, infrastructure and the circular economy ahead of the UN climate conference, which Türkiye is set to host in Antalya in November.
Hartmann estimated the value of the global financial system at $305 trillion, comparing it with an annual financing gap of $4.3 trillion for achieving the Sustainable Development Goals in developing countries, roughly 1.4 percent of that total.
Yet clean energy projects in developing countries can face financing costs up to seven times those in advanced economies, he said.
Since 2010, solar energy costs have fallen by 90 percent and battery storage costs by 93 percent, he added, stressing the need for effective regulation, reliable infrastructure and risk sharing to translate those gains into investment.
Turning climate commitments into projects
Hartmann welcomed Türkiye’s ambition to make COP31 an “implementation COP”, saying investment must advance at speed and scale.
The Climate Bridge initiative, to be presented at COP31, aims to turn climate commitments into investment opportunities, with initial demonstration projects envisaged in Ethiopia, Fiji, Indonesia, Pakistan and Uzbekistan.
The approach would combine concessional finance, grants, guarantees, risk-sharing instruments and private capital, he said.
UNDP has identified 700 sustainable development investment opportunities across 50 countries, Hartmann said. Since 2022, it has supported initiatives helping align more than $920 billion in public and private financing with the Sustainable Development Goals.
Strengthening Turkish suppliers
In Türkiye, UNDP and the Industry and Technology Ministry have developed a resource efficiency programme backed by $5 million in EU support, Hartmann said.
The programme aims to prepare investment-ready projects and strengthen Turkish suppliers’ competitiveness as low-carbon partners for international investors and European buyers.
Hartmann urged investors to look beyond projects already close to securing financing, invest in skills and local suppliers, and incorporate sustainability from the outset.
“Sustainability should therefore not be treated simply as a compliance cost,” he said. “It is an increasing source of economic value and an investment worth making.”

Polish PM says Zelenskyy will not support Lviv Oblast's move to declare 2027 Year of UPA
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said during a press conference as part of his visit to India that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had made it clear he would not support any further steps by Lviv Oblast Council concerning the designation of 2027 as the Year of the UPA The UPA, or Ukrainian Insurgent Army, was a nationalist paramilitary organisation that fought for Ukrainian independence during and after World War II, primarily against Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union and Roman Shukhevych, one of its commanders-in-chief.
Source: European Pravda, citing Ukrinform;
Details: Tusk said Zelenskyy had signalled that, if the subsequent procedure depended on him, he would not support the initiative in any way. Tusk added that Zelenskyy had been very unhappy about what had happened.
Tusk also said he had made considerable efforts to resolve the "orders crisis" and to explain why decisions of this kind harmed Ukraine's interests and needed to be considered in the context of the two nations' difficult shared history.
He acknowledged the complexity and ambiguity of the history of both countries, while stressing that Ukrainians could not seek any justification regarding the Volyn tragedy The Volyn (Volhynia) tragedy was a series of events that led to the ethnic cleansing of the Polish and Ukrainian populations in 1943 during World War II. It was part of a long-standing rivalry between Ukrainians and Poles in what is now Ukraine's west. Poland considers the Volyn tragedy a genocide of Poles and Shukhevych.
Tusk said he understood all the complexities and wanted Poles to understand that there was considerable ambiguity in both Polish and Ukrainian history. However, he stressed that genocide could not be justified in any way. He warned that Ukraine would face serious difficulties with its integration into the EU if it failed to respect Poland's sensitivities on the issue, adding that Poland was not demanding anything extraordinary in the first place.
Tusk added that he had spent many hours explaining the Polish perspective on the issue to Zelenskyy and had come away with the impression that the Ukrainian president understood it.
Meanwhile, Tusk said he could hardly be held responsible for decisions taken by individual members of Lviv's district or oblast councils. He described the move as resembling a planned provocation by a local nationalist and called it very unwise and unnecessary.
Background:
- On 20 October, Lviv Oblast Council voted to designate 2027 as the Year of Roman Shukhevych, the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) and Oleh Olzhych. The decision immediately drew criticism from Polish officials. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, in particular, said the move was helping Ukraine's adversaries.
- European Pravda previously reported that Poland had suspended the delivery of a military aid package to Ukraine over Lviv Oblast Council's decision to designate 2027 as the Year of the UPA and Roman Shukhevych. The information was provided by a source in the Ukrainian government.
- Poland's Ministry of National Defence later denied reports that the delivery of a major aid package had been suspended because Lviv Oblast Council had designated 2027 as the Year of the UPA and Roman Shukhevych.

Black box sheds light on fatal ferry sinking off Turkish Cyprus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:18:40 UTC
22:18:40 KST

A crisis center is set up at Taşucu Port following the ferry disaster off Turkish Cyprus.
Black box recordings from the Filo Jet ferry, which capsized and sank off the coast of Turkish Cyprus, have revealed that crew members discussed multiple technical problems aboard the vessel and expressed concerns that its failures could lead to disaster, according to information presented to a court.
In one recording, the ship’s second engineer was heard saying, “We’re the only thing on this ship that’s sound; everything else is half-broken,” as reported by media on Oct. 23.
The recordings also indicated that the captain continued the voyage despite discussions among crew members about water entering the vessel.
The ferry sank on Aug. 30 while sailing from Kyrenia in Turkish Cyprus to Taşucu Port in Mersin, southern Türkiye, carrying 259 passengers and eight crew members.
Search and rescue teams recovered 27 bodies. The body of three-year-old passenger Anni Asel Hilaloğlu has yet to be found.
With an investigation into the sinking ongoing, authorities have examined 32 days of recordings from the vessel’s voyage data recorder (VDR), which serves as a black box, out of a total of 68 days of recorded data.
According to information presented during court proceedings, crew members discussed technical problems involving the steering system, radar, cameras and the vessel’s starboard side.
The recordings also revealed complaints about what crew members described as insufficient investment in the ship by its operating company, as well as concerns that existing malfunctions could cause it to sink.
Nine suspects, including the operating company’s director, captains, engineers and other crew members, appeared before Kyrenia District Court again as part of an investigation into alleged deaths caused by negligence and carelessness.
At the request of investigators, the court ordered their detention to be extended by a further seven days to allow the investigation to be completed.
Police said inquiries were continuing into individuals suspected of bearing responsibility for the disaster. With another person added to the investigation, the number of suspects being sought rose to six.

TenPayGo and China’s Digital Opening to Foreigners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:18:00 UTC
22:18:00 KST

Attracting foreign visitors to China takes more than easing visa rules or improving transport links; visitors also need to navigate the country once they arrive. In an economy where much of daily life runs through digital platforms, seemingly small tasks – from paying for a meal to accessing everyday services – can become obstacles that shape how accessible the country feels to outsiders.
China’s effort to make itself more welcoming to tourists has thus also extended into its digital ecosystem. Tencent’s TenPayGo offers a glimpse of how one of China’s largest technology companies is approaching that challenge.
TenPayGo is a standalone payment app built around Tencent’s existing Weixin Pay network. Tencent publicly launched the app on September 24, allowing foreign visitors to pay using supported international bank cards and overseas e-wallets, like Apple Pay. It also offers translation and travel-related features, with additional transport and lifestyle services being introduced gradually.
The ability to pay with international bank cards on China’s digital platforms is not entirely new: WeChat Pay and Alipay have supported such payments for years. TenPayGo’s main distinction is that it gives foreign visitors a dedicated entry point to Tencent’s existing payment services. This could lower the barriers to using Tencent’s services and make them more visible to foreign visitors.
China recorded more than 150 million inbound visits in 2025, with spending exceeding $130 billion. Spending through mobile payment platforms reached more than $11 billion. Tencent reported that, between January and August 2026, the value of transactions made through overseas wallets in China rose 80 percent, while the volume increased 81.8 percent. These figures point to rapid growth in cross-border payment activity.
Other Chinese fintech giants are already in this market. Ant Group, the parent company of Alipay, said in September 2024 that the number of international visitors using its mobile payment services in China had quadrupled over the previous six months. Both companies have already spent years adapting their payment services to foreigners. TenPayGo therefore looks less like the creation of a new payment service than a move to make Tencent’s existing network more accessible and competitive.
TenPayGo also arrives as Beijing seeks to address a problem its own officials have already acknowledged: Visitors still face barriers when navigating China’s digital services. On February 5, 2026, 11 government agencies issued a policy plan aimed at making these services more accessible. By 2027, China wants to significantly improve the convenience of digital services for visitors, largely removing barriers in areas including accommodation, healthcare, payments, tourism, and public services, while expanding the range of situations in which these services can be used.
By 2030, it seeks to establish a more interconnected digital ecosystem aligned more closely with international practices. The plan also calls for multilingual services, integrated digital service platforms, more convenient digital payments and stronger data security and personal information protection.
In July, authorities launched a year-long initiative in Beijing, Shanghai, Shenzhen, Hangzhou, Chengdu and Sanya to improve digital services for foreign visitors.
TenPayGo reflects this broader effort, but it also illustrates the difference between making China’s digital ecosystem easier to access and making it more open. TenPayGo uses Tencent’s existing merchant network while simplifying the way outsiders enter it. This is a first step. But whether China can achieve digital openness will depend on how far it goes beyond the individual apps.
