====================================================================================================

People who believe conspiracy theories overestimate how many others agree, new research finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:00:32 UTC
22:00:32 KST

Reading a conspiracy theory does more than just introduce a suspicious narrative; it also inflates a person’s estimate of how many other people believe the claim is true. According to new research published in the European Journal of Social Psychology, this exaggerated sense of public agreement may help explain why people come to accept conspiracy theories after encountering them. In one of the experiments, showing people concrete statistical data about how few others actually endorsed these claims reduced their own belief in them.
Conspiracy theories are explanations for events that assume multiple actors are secretly working together to achieve a harmful or unlawful goal. When people feel uncertain about how to interpret events, they often look to others for cues on what to think or do. Psychologists refer to these cues as descriptive norms, which are perceptions of how common a particular belief or behavior is within a group. Relying on descriptive norms is a form of social proof, where people assume that if many others hold a view, that view is likely valid.
Although conspiracy theories frequently draw massive attention online, actual believers usually represent a minority of the broader public. Still, those who endorse these narratives often assume their views are widely shared. For example, a 2021 study of British participants found that people consistently overestimated how much their peers believed in conspiracy theories, and that thinking peers endorsed these ideas strongly predicted a person’s own belief. Similarly, a 2023 study in Turkey indicated that people who believed local conspiracy theories overestimated how many ordinary citizens and experts agreed with them.
Correcting these misperceptions can alter how people think. In a 2021 experiment with British parents, showing participants that most other parents rejected anti-vaccine conspiracy theories reduced their own endorsement of those claims. Building on this foundation, the new research was led by Jan-Willem van Prooijen, head of the Social Psychology section at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, senior researcher at the Netherlands Institute for the Study of Crime and Law Enforcement, and endowed professor of radicalization, extremism, and conspiracy thinking at Maastricht University.
He and his colleagues wanted to test whether simply encountering a conspiracy theory inflates perceived descriptive norms, and whether providing hard data on public skepticism can reduce belief in a wide variety of general conspiracy theories.
“People often encounter conspiracy theories, for instance online,” van Prooijen told PsyPost. “One problem is that extreme voices that spread conspiracy theories (e.g., online influencers) sometimes get excessive exposure. That might raise the impression that these conspiracy theories are more widely believed than is actually the case. We wanted to examine these dynamics in our research: Do conspiracy beliefs depend on how normative people think they are, and can we use these insights to develop an intervention?”
To investigate these questions, the researchers conducted six online studies totaling 2,906 participants from the United States and the United Kingdom. All six studies were preregistered, meaning the researchers publicly recorded their hypotheses and analysis plans before collecting data.
In the first pair of studies, the researchers examined the relationship between personal conspiracy beliefs and perceived norms using 300 American participants in Study 1a and 299 British participants in Study 1b. Participants rated how plausible they found 10 popular conspiracy claims, such as the idea that the 9/11 terrorist attacks were an inside job by the U.S. government, on a scale from 0 to 100, and then used the same scale to estimate the average plausibility rating given by the other participants in the study.
In both countries, the actual average belief in these 10 theories was relatively low, sitting at 33.09 out of 100 in the American sample and 34.16 in the British sample. However, participants estimated the group average to be higher, guessing 39.85 in the United States and 42.30 in the United Kingdom. Those who strongly endorsed the conspiracy theories themselves were much more likely to think other participants believed them too, with strong correlations of 0.65 in the U.S. sample and 0.71 in the U.K. sample, and their estimates of the group average were less accurate than the estimates of skeptics.
The researchers also tested whether conspiracy believers saw themselves as standing out from the crowd, given that past research has linked conspiracy belief to a desire to feel unique. By comparing each person’s own rating to their estimate of the group rating, the team found that stronger believers saw the gap between their own views and the group’s as no larger than skeptics did.
These initial findings align with research covered by PsyPost in 2025, which found that individuals who are overconfident in their thinking abilities tend to hold stronger conspiracy beliefs and vastly overestimate how many others agree with them.
Because the first two studies only looked at correlations, the researchers next tested whether reading a conspiracy theory directly causes people to think the idea is popular. They recruited 505 American participants for Study 2a and 501 British participants for Study 2b. In each study, half of the participants were randomly assigned to read an anonymous blog post claiming that pharmaceutical companies secretly suppress medical cures to boost their profits, while the other half read a blog post arguing that pharmaceutical companies do not hide cures.
After reading and summarizing the text, participants rated their own belief in four statements about pharmaceutical conspiracies on a 0 to 100 scale, and estimated how the other participants in the study rated them. In the American sample, reading the conspiratorial blog post raised personal belief to an average of 61.78, compared to 49.46 among those who read the non-conspiratorial text. It also pushed estimates of other people’s belief up to 62.64, compared to 51.00 in the control group.
The British sample in Study 2b showed the same pattern. Personal belief averaged 59.78 after reading the conspiracy post versus 41.99 in the control group, while estimates of others’ beliefs rose to 60.28 compared to 46.41 in the control condition. Statistical mediation analyses were consistent with the idea that the increase in personal belief ran through this heightened sense that others believed the claim. But the reverse pattern, in which people’s newly strengthened beliefs shaped their guesses about others, also fit the data, so these analyses cannot establish which came first.
“One reason why people believe conspiracy theories is because they assume many others believe them as well,” van Prooijen explained. “Conspiracy beliefs thus spread via social influence processes. Understanding these processes can help design effective interventions to reduce conspiracy beliefs.”
To test whether changing perceived norms can directly alter conspiracy beliefs, the researchers manipulated the norm information given to participants in Studies 3 and 4. In Study 3, 501 American participants were presented with six popular conspiracy theories, such as the claim that the government uses subliminal messages on television. Half were told that “especially many” previous participants found the statements plausible, while the other half were told that “only a few” found them plausible.
This vague wording did not produce a statistically significant difference between the two groups. Participants told that many others believed the claims scored an average of 44.48 out of 100 on personal belief, compared to 41.65 among those told that few others believed them. The authors noted that words like “many” and “few” are open to personal interpretation; for instance, learning that even 10 percent of the public believes an extreme claim might still register as a large number to some people. Because this study did not measure whether participants’ sense of the norm actually shifted, the authors acknowledge another possibility: that people do not take their cues from norm information at all, and that the link seen in earlier studies reflects people projecting their own beliefs onto others.
In Study 4, the team tested whether providing specific, factual statistics would be more effective. They recruited 800 American participants and showed them eight conspiracy theories from the first study. Half of the participants saw a bar chart for each theory displaying the actual distribution of ratings from Study 1a, along with the median score and a note explaining that most participants did not find the statement plausible at all. The other half saw the conspiracy statements without any statistical data.
Providing concrete data shifted how participants viewed both the public consensus and the theories themselves. Those who saw the charts estimated the previous group’s average belief at 20.95 out of 100, compared to 38.34 among those who received no data. In turn, personal endorsement of the conspiracy theories dropped to an average of 24.06 in the group that saw the factual charts, compared to 33.70 in the control group.
“We have done two studies testing the intervention, but it only worked if we gave people factual statistical information of how few people believed a conspiracy theory,” van Prooijen noted. “If we provided more abstract information, only stating that ‘few people’ believe the theory without providing concrete numbers, the intervention did not work. It remains speculative why that is the case, but it is nevertheless informative for future interventions based on this research.”
“The practical significance is that these insights quite directly suggest an intervention to reduce conspiracy beliefs,” van Prooijen said. “We have tested the effects of exposing people to factual statistical information of how widespread belief in a particular conspiracy theory is. Such information often clarifies to people that a conspiracy theory actually is not widely endorsed at all, which decreases the likelihood that people will believe the theory themselves.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these results. Participants in brief online experiments may partly respond the way they think researchers expect, which the authors note could mean these effects are smaller in everyday life, and the “others” in these studies were fellow online participants rather than the broader population. In addition, social media algorithms and online communities can surround users with like-minded believers, creating environments where conspiracy theories genuinely are the local norm.
“It is important to keep in mind that in everyday life, these processes are likely to be more complicated,” van Prooijen said. “For instance, we examined the effects of exposing people to conspiracy theories on their perceptions of how normative belief in these theories is. But in real life, people to some extent also choose what information they wish to be exposed to. People may for instance actively search the Internet looking for conspiracy theories, and be motivated to think belief in these theories is widely shared.”
The authors also point out that factual norm interventions could backfire if applied to the rare conspiracy theories that actually are endorsed by a majority of the public, such as theories surrounding the assassination of John F. Kennedy. Future studies could examine how these social processes operate in real-world online networks and in more collectivistic cultures, where pressure to conform to group norms may be even stronger.
“An important caveat is that the intervention that we tested might only work in communities where a particular conspiracy theory is indeed not so widespread,” van Prooijen added. “Some conspiracy theories ARE widespread, for instance in the general population (e.g., about the Kennedy assassination), or in specific groups (e.g., online anti-vaccination groups). These are complications that need to be investigated further, and are important to take into account before putting these insights into practice.”
“We were excited to see that our findings almost naturally suggested an intervention, which indeed had the anticipated effects,” he continued. “At the same time, the intervention was successful in only one experiment. We need more testing to assess the effectiveness of this approach. One possible goal is to examine these issues in a longitudinal design: What is the long-term effectiveness of an intervention based on information about descriptive norms?”
The study, “Everyone Knows It’s a Hoax: The Role of Perceived Descriptive Norms in Conspiracy Beliefs,” was authored by Jan-Willem van Prooijen, Paul K. Bergmann, Vladimira Čavojová, and Jakub Šrol.

Gunmen kill 7 at Jordan church, king vows retaliation

AMMAN – Gunmen killed at least seven people and wounded dozens at a church in southern Jordan on Oct 23, with the king vowing retaliation for the rare attack on Christians in the majority Sunni Muslim kingdom.
Assailants stormed the compound of a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hammoud in Karak governorate and opened fire, authorities said.
The gunmen got out of a vehicle and started shooting during a funeral procession, the public security directorate said in a statement, adding that a hunt was under way for the perpetrators.
“The terrorist attack against Karak will be met with the harshest retaliation,” King Abdullah II said in an English-language post on X.
“We will strike with an iron fist against those who dare to threaten our nation.”
After authorities gave a death toll of six, director of public security Abdullah Al-Maaytah said it had risen to seven with 34 injured, 27 of whom were still receiving treatment.
Images from state broadcaster Al-Mamlaka showed the king visiting Karak on the evening of Oct 23 after the attack.
The Royal Court also shared a video showing the monarch at a local hospital in military uniform to check on the wounded.
“This country is ours and we will not abandon it - we will never abandon it,” an injured man told him.
Footage aired by Al-Mamlaka also showed the moment of the attack.
Two gunmen are seen dressed in casual clothes and brandishing pistols, with a third carrying a long gun, before they open fire on the church from an entrance on the street and charge forwards.
“A terrorist group has carried out a horrific act, one that is condemned in every respect, and the security services are working round the clock to track them down,” Interior Minister Mazen Al-Faraya told a press conference.
“Jordan has been targeted by a terrorist attack carried out by a group of extremists.”
He said the perpetrators had “absolutely no connection whatsoever to human values” and it “only serves to strengthen the Jordanians’ resolve... to combat and fight terrorism in all its forms”.
Mohammed Al-Khalayleh, minister of awqaf, Islamic affairs and holy sites, said “the sanctity of places of worship is inviolable and any violation of this is unacceptable on religious, moral and national grounds”, calling national unity “a red line that must not be crossed”.
‘Heinous terrorist attack’
Minister of Government Communications Mohammed Al-Momani said security forces were investigating the attack.
A witness told Al-Mamlaka the gunmen fired continuously for five minutes before fleeing the scene.
Between 150 and 200 people were in and around the church at the time, the witness said, adding that most of the victims were aged between 50 and 70.
Karak is home to a significant Christian community in the Muslim-majority kingdom, where Christians make up 2% to 3% of the population.
The Greek Orthodox Archdiocese in Jordan said that if the attack was aimed at driving out Christians from the holy land, “it will only make us cling to it more firmly and deepen our roots in it”.
“We are absolutely certain that Jordanian society will remain impervious to every dark, extremist ideology, and that this criminal act is far removed from - and alien to - the moderate Islam of our country,” it said.
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun, the Arab world’s only Christian head of state, called the shooting a “heinous terrorist attack”.
He said it “reaffirms once again that terrorism has no religion and no homeland, and its aim is to strike at coexistence and spread strife”, according to a presidency statement.
A spokesman for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said “an attack not only on a place of worship, but during a funeral procession, is especially heinous”.
Attacks on houses of worship in Jordan are rare.
In 2016, an attack in Karak targeted a security centre and police patrols, leaving 10 people dead.
The victims included seven security personnel and a female tourist, before four militants who had barricaded themselves inside Karak’s historic castle were killed. AFP

The Real Child Protection Cases That Loosely Inspired Fjord
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:00:03 UTC
22:00:03 KST

From the Palme d’Or-winning abortion drama 4 Months, Three Weeks, and Two Days (2007), to the institutional corruption-themed Graduation (2016) and beyond, Romanian auteur Cristian Mungiu’s body of work has always concerned itself with the human cost of systemic oppression and bureaucratic faultlines. With the searing legal and familial drama Fjord, which earned Mungiu his second Palme at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival in May, the filmmaker once again brings his signature sense of slow-burning tension to the clash between individual and societal codes of morality. Except this time, he shrewdly flips the script. With the story of a religious immigrant family of seven facing an uphill battle against Norway’s child protection services (known as Barnevernet), Fjord dares to imagine a scenario where well-intentioned progressive values can backfire as severely as rigidly conservative ones if they disregard basic human principles like empathy, compassion, and respect.
Written by Mungiu, Fjord follows Mihai and Lisbet Gheorghiu, a Romanian engineer and Norwegian nurse played by Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve, respectively. Set in their modest ways, the couple tries to settle into their lives in Norway, having moved there after the death of Mihai’s parents to be closer to Lisbet’s family. Raising their five children with a conservative ethos, they don’t quite mesh with the liberal community that surrounds them. But their eager kids still build close friendships with the children of their progressive neighbors, Mats and Mia Halberg, a development that further underscores the two families’—and consequently, the two belief systems’—political and practical differences.
Tensions rise in town when the kids’ school raises child-abuse allegations against the Gheorghius after teachers notice some mysterious bruising on one of their kids. While the film never spells out their precise origins, Barnevernet steps in at once, separating their five kids (including a baby, still breastfeeding) from Mihai and Lisbet, placing them in foster care after the couple admits to some physical discipline that would be considered mild in Mihai’s culture, but is against the law in Norway. Claiming that they are being harshly discriminated against due to their religion and conservative beliefs, the couple asks help from Mia, an attorney, to represent their case in the Norwegian court.
The real court case that loosely inspired Fjord
Joining TIME on Zoom recently, Mungiu emphasizes that “the film is fictional. It’s not a reenactment associated with any one particular case.” Still, there were a number of real-life court cases that intrigued him as a storyteller with a journalism background. Chief among them was that of the Bodnariu family, who occupied international headlines for several months after they were separated from their five children in November 2015. Pentecostal parents Ruth and Marius were accused of domestic violence, with worldwide protests criticizing what dissenters called harsh and hasty steps taken by Norwegian social workers without proper evidence. In Romania, one of the indirect results of the wildly popular case went as far as a constitutional referendum in 2018 that aimed to alter the definition of a traditional family and prevent same-sex marriages. (The referendum eventually failed due to low turnout.)
“So you couldn’t avoid the Bodnariu case,” recalls Mungiu. He followed the story as it remained in the papers, and during that time and the years that followed, Mungiu began to notice other cases that displayed a similar pattern. “Whenever there was this encounter between, let's say, families coming to Scandinavia from more conservative parts of the world, there was a cultural clash.” What eventually convinced him to pursue the topic through a film was a recent-enough realization that the world somehow became more illiberal than it used to be. “I thought that through this story, I could talk about the [confrontational] state of the world today. People are not listening to the other group. I hope that the world can be a bit more rational than this.”
Upon deciding to write Fjord, Mungiu read everything he could online, moving to Norway for several extended periods to investigate the country’s child-protection laws and relevant cases on the ground. His process involved talking to several families involved with child protection cases and their relatives, as well as journalists who covered cases like the Bodnarius’, court interpreters, police officers, NGO representatives, and various different religious groups. “Finally, I talked to Barnevernet about these cases in general,” he adds. “They were willing to also give details about how things have changed.”
One key tool Mungiu didn’t have access to was the recording and transcription of the Bodnariu trial, which is among the reasons why Fjord had to be largely fictional. “Norwegian authorities said only the family could have access to the recording if they came over. But the family knew that they couldn’t come over. Because if they did, they could be arrested,” he explains. “The family was trying to get their justice in the European Court of Justice, but they first had to utilize all the legal procedures [in Norway]. And because they left Norway before having a final decision about their proceedings, they couldn't get a positive answer from the European Court of Justice.”
The audience is on trial too
Mungiu draws a direct connection between Fjord and his previous film, R.M.N. “In that film, I was trying to investigate how a conservative society reacts when someone who’s different from them comes into their world. We know that they’re not very welcoming or willing to accept differences. They don't understand that there's a bigger world out there. In Fjord, I really wanted to reverse this paradigm and to understand what happens when the conservatives are the minority in a progressive, liberal society.” According to Mungiu, we might expect that type of society to be more empathetic and inclusive, treating minorities with more compassion. But through his investigations, he got the sense that whoever’s in the majority feels entitled to impose their own point of view onto others. “This is not a good example that we wish to set for the conservative part of the society,” Mungiu reflects. “We shouldn't be behaving the same way they behave.”
On these grounds, the central question of Fjord is whether anyone can be truly objective toward people whose values they don’t share. The Gheorghius’ conservatism, for example, means they oppose same-sex marriage. So can viewers both disagree with the couple on those grounds, while also feel that they are being treated unfairly by Barnevernet? It is a challenge that is essentially at the heart of the American justice system, which asks potential jurors to set all their biases aside and only assess the case in hand through proven facts. “I noticed that saying, ‘I'm here to [only] judge if they are guilty of what they are charged with’ isn’t easy, because you are biased by your own point of view of the world. But I hope that this is what the audience is going to do. The reason why I wanted to tell this story from this neutral perspective is that it is a rare opportunity of inviting not just one bubble that you sympathize with in your regular life. The other bubble exists and dialogue is needed to make the society a little bit more peaceful again. So I took this position of a mediator, if you will.”
A visual style in service of the film’s thesis
To accentuate the connection between Fjord’s searching themes and lean visuals, Mungiu purposefully embraced long shots and continuous takes beginning during the scripting phase, in order to fully immerse the audience in the conflicting world of the characters in a neutral fashion. Indicating that he avoids many of the mainstream filmmaking methods that he finds manipulative, “I don't use anything [distracting] within the scene,” Mungiu says. “I don't use coverage. I don't use music. I don't have funny angles. The camera doesn't move unless it follows a movement in the shot. I try to do this in a sober way, just with the actors and their emotions. I think it's a respectful way of telling the audience, ‘You are adults like we are, you are as smart as I am, so feel free to see [for yourself] what's more important in this shot, or who the main character is.’”
Similarly, he carefully scouted locations in sync with his ideas around isolation and lack of communication. “It was important for us to set this story in a small community, with two houses at the end of this fjord in a lovely but somehow curled world,” he explains. “It’s very majestic, and [it’s a location where] people will have to talk to one another eventually because there's nobody else around.”
He remembers an anecdote about the real inhabitants of the two houses he uses in the film for the Gheorghius and Halbergs, who were in fact not communicating with one another. That all changed shortly after the production convinced one of them to allow the film crew to shoot in his house. Mungiu recalls the homeowner saying, “I will let you, but my neighbor is very grumpy. He hasn’t talked to me in the 10 years that we have been neighbors, so you are going to have problems with him." But when the crew contacted the owner of the other house, they found that he was quite open-minded. “We asked him, ‘Do you have a conflict with your neighbor?’ He said, ‘No, but none of us have started a conversation, so I let him enjoy his privacy.’ At the end, they were communicating normally, and we had a very good relationship with both of them.”
Can a person ever really be fully objective?
No matter how neutral Mungiu tried to stay throughout his research process, there were some moments that made him face his own biases. “I went [to Norway] with this idea that I will meet a society that is not at all religious. This is the idea that we project onto the Protestant north.” As such, he was surprised to notice deeply rooted religious leanings there, especially among older people with a connection to the Norwegian church. He also learned about the younger population’s attraction to new neo-cult movements. “I watched at least a couple of documentaries about this phenomenon. People are really worried that the younger generations are [drawn to] these new cults. So I noticed that the people there are just as inclined to have religious beliefs as any other.”
With this discovery, Mungiu eventually eliminated various scenes in Fjord which would have insinuated that Norwegian people saw the world in a more rational way only because they weren’t religious. “Making decisions on rational grounds is of course a very good thing to do,” Mungiu explains. “But [there is also] this need of belonging to something bigger than just [rationality] that we all feel. Some people still long for the discomfort that there's something bigger than them. And as long as this belief places them on the right side of the world through [tolerance] and [inclusivity], I think we should be tolerant to it.”
“You shouldn't answer radicalization with radicalization”
His time in Norway also led Mungiu to learn more about the Sami people. “I didn’t know much about them before, but the Sami population sets a good [historical] example about how bigger communities and countries were not acting in an ethical way towards minorities. You can see this in the U.S. as well, [in the way] Native Americans were treated,” he adds. “And I think that we should learn from this [that] maybe this ‘we want to civilize you’ idea is not the most ethical one,” he reflects, clarifying that while everyone should obey the laws and respect the culture of the country they live in, real integration cannot happen by enforcing one’s own values onto others. “That won't change [the way] someone thinks. You will just frustrate them, [reinforcing] that there is a hypocrisy in the world.”
Mungiu cautions against the ongoing ideological war that he says is moving in the wrong direction across the globe. “I don't want to be preachy, but hopefully there's something that stays with you after you watch a film like Fjord,” he reflects. “I took the risk of talking about things that people need to listen to even if they’re not nice. Don't kill the messenger. It's time to start to have a dialogue and this is what cinema can do.”

E9X: The battery-powered plane with 90 passengers on board and a range of 1,000 kilometres
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Flying without kerosene is no longer just a dream, with pilots being trained to fly electric planes in the Netherlands. Before long, these battery-powered planes could be carrying 90 passengers and flying distances of up to 1,000 kilometres.
Johannes, Peter and Floris are thrilled. The pilots are carrying out the first test flights for the scaled E9X demonstrator. It’s a world premiere — and if all goes to plan, their electric model plane could soon become a big passenger aircraft.
After a soft landing, the aircraft is still in one piece — and now the real adventure can begin: analysing the flight data in the Elysian Aircraft laboratory, which sits beside Amsterdam’s Schiphol Airport.
Over the next two decades, the global number of air passengers could double. This is bad news for the global climate, so the young Dutch start-up Elysian is working on a solution.
The world’s first battery-powered passenger aircraft
Daniel Jacobson is one of the founders of Elysian Aircraft. With ten million euros in start-up capital, his team now aims to develop one of the world’s first big, battery-powered passenger aircrafts.
“The design pretty much stands”, Jacobson tells Euronews in his workshop. “There will be 6 engines. And we have folding wingtips, so that we fit into the current gates’ infrastructure of the airports, because the wings are very large. We are talking about more than 50 metres.”
Battery-packed wings
Jacobson shows Euronews the first full-scale model of the innovative wing. The battery packs are integrated into the wing’s structure. To give a better idea of the scale, there are roughly 40 battery packs across the entire wing, each pack weighing around 1000 kg.
“Yes, we are an obese plane”, the Elysian manager admits. Yet he smiles confidently: “We are always on a diet, trying to reduce weight. How can you use different materials, how can you combine things, how you do thermo-management. And it’s also IP (intellectual property) that we are generating here.” There are no further details — it’s top secret at this stage.
Battery-wings — a revolutionary idea, and the key to success. The co-founder and co-CEO of Elysian Aircraft sounds rather proud: “There was really this consensus in the academic world and in the industry that flying electrically with a large aircraft would never be possible. We have disproven that with our research on our design.”
Reducing global aerospace emissions
But what are the benefits? “By being able to transport 90 passengers for initially 800 kilometres and eventually 1000 kilometres you can reduce emissions to zero, from half the world’s flights”, Jacobson says. “That is a very large amount of flight activity in the world. And you reduce total emissions from aerospace by 20%.”
The E9X is due to be operational by 2034. Europe is doing rather well in the race for the future of aviation, Jacobson believes. “But comparing it to the US or even China, we should fund start-ups and innovation much more aggressively when we want to keep our advantage”, the top manager urges with regard to the EU.
Pilots prepare for electric take-off
We stop at the small regional airport of Teuge. Here, flying on electricity is already a reality. The E-Flight Academy trains pilots from several airlines in an environmentally friendly way at a low altitude.
Co-founder Merlijn van Vliet takes Euronews on a ride in a small 2-seater: “In this aircraft we have two batteries with 11 kilowatt-hours each. So, in total we have 22 kilowatt-hours on board. We can fly 45 to 50 minutes with them and still have ten minutes of reserve capacity.”
We follow the banks of a river through green meadows where Dutch cows are grazing. “We are now flying towards the old city centre of Deventer. They don’t hear us. So, we can fly wherever we want and they don’t hear us on the ground”, Merlijn beams.
What is his vision for the future? “In ten years, this will grow big and we will fly electric with 40 or 60 passengers — or even more.”
Charging infrastructure
Jurjen de Jong is a pioneer. He is developing a European charging infrastructure for electric aircraft.
“We will expand from the Netherlands to the Nordic States, to France, to Germany and Switzerland”, the co-founder of NRG2fly tells Euronews. “And then we will have a fully-fledged network of low-emission, low-noise electric mobility and that is really what we’re going for”.
Airports are surrounded by huge car parks. Solar panels, tens of thousands of electric cars and stationary energy storage systems could be connected to form a network — “the inter-net of energy”, as Jurjen calls it.
Teuge airport is testing the scaled concept. “We have 500 solar panels on the rooftop”, Jurjen explains, “their energy is stored in a battery. So basically, we have a whole energy hub which is providing energy instead of taking energy from the grid.”
NRG2fly co-founder Jurjen de Jong has a broader vision too: “My dream is to have all regional electric planes powered by the sun. And then we can leave a better world for me, my children and everybody.”

Electric stoves could help people with asthma breathe easier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Electric stoves could help people with asthma breathe easier
Swapping polluting gas stoves for electric ones reduced asthma symptoms, a study finds
Biomedical Writer
For people with asthma, switching from a gas stove to an electric one might be a breath of fresh air. The combustion that creates the flame of a gas stove or oven releases pollutants, including nitrogen dioxide, which can trigger asthma symptoms. After a research-backed electric stove replacement, people reported more symptom relief than is often achieved with asthma medications.
“We were really surprised at how large the benefit was,” says Ashwini Sehgal, a clinician who studies community health at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland. With funding from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency during the Biden administration, Sehgal and colleagues spearheaded a project to install electric stoves in Cleveland households that had at least one person with asthma.
Eighty-five participants who had poorly controlled asthma were given a questionnaire a few months after the switch. They reported symptom improvement that was roughly two to three times as large as what’s typical with medication. Those with the worst symptoms saw the biggest improvement. Participants also reported fewer emergency room or hospital visits and said they missed work or school less often.
One 38-year-old woman told Sehgal’s team that whenever she cooked on her gas stove, she felt like her throat was closing. But the sensation disappeared after she switched to electric. Another participant, a 36-year-old man, found it difficult to walk uphill and play with his kids. With the stove swap, “he described how much better he felt as ‘magical,’ ” Sehgal says.
While heating, steaming or frying on a gas stovetop, nearby NO2 levels can skyrocket, reaching hundreds of parts per billion. That’s much higher than the EPA’s one-hour outdoor air quality standard of 100 parts per billion. NO2 exposure is linked to increased asthma symptoms. For example, research in children has found the pollutant can boost wheezing, coughing and asthma attacks.
The project was initially funded to follow 1,200 households for 12 months. But the Trump administration terminated the EPA’s Community Change Grants early, which drastically reduced the number of study participants. Yet even with this small group, the symptom improvement was significant.
The decision to replace a gas stove “depends on how much you are struggling with your own illness,” says environmental epidemiologist Carrie Breton of WashU Bursky School of Public Health in St. Louis. As a trial run, Sehgal suggests using an electric hot plate and a toaster oven to see if keeping the gas stove off helps improve symptoms.
If a stove swap isn’t in the budget, reducing NO2 exposure is still worthwhile, says pulmonologist Laura Paulin of Dartmouth Health. She recommends using kitchen ventilation, either via an exhaust hood that vents to the outside or an open window. A HEPA filter with a carbon insert can trap NO2 to decrease airborne concentrations. And try to keep children with asthma out of the kitchen when the stove is on, Paulin says. “It is a daunting task to replace a stove, but it doesn’t have to be an all-or-nothing thing.”
For researchers, the next step would be to measure lung function before and after a stove switch, Breton says. It would also be helpful to account for more factors, such as seasonal effects. “Many things can trigger people’s asthma,” Paulin says. Researchers could do a randomized trial in which some people get the electric stove right away while others wait for six months, Sehgal says, to allow time for comparison.
If electric stoves continue to be linked with fewer trips to the emergency room, fewer hospitalizations and better symptom control than medication can provide, “health insurance companies should consider paying for or subsidizing” stove swaps, Sehgal says. “If it truly works this well,” Breton says, “it’s got a bigger bang for your buck.”

Russian sabotage and reconnaissance groups step up activity in Sumy and Chernihiv regions – SBGS
Andrii Demchenko, Spokesperson for the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine, said this in a television interview, according to Ukrinform.
“If we compare it with a period when there was virtually no activity by enemy sabotage and reconnaissance groups, several cases have now already been recorded both in the Sumy and Chernihiv regions. The task of such groups is to gather intelligence on how our defenses are organized and find out where our positions are located. If they succeed, they also try to attack Ukrainian positions with their own forces,” Demchenko said.
In addition, the Spokesperson said that attempts to mine the area are frequently detected during counter-sabotage operations.
“In other words, when withdrawing, the enemy tries to make sure that our soldiers are blown up by the devices that the enemy plants during their operations,” he added.
Demchenko emphasized that the Defense Forces use drones to detect such groups in a timely manner. Border guards also receive advance intelligence about possible attempts by sabotage and reconnaissance groups to infiltrate along certain sections of the border and conduct counter-sabotage operations.
Demchenko noted that in the Kharkiv region, the enemy is attempting to expand its area of control.
“The enemy is trying to destroy the positions held by Ukrainian defenders, hoping that infantry groups will subsequently be able to advance more easily. But once again, the enemy is suffering heavy losses,” the spokesperson said.
As reported by Ukrinform, Russian troops are currently most frequently captured in the Kharkiv region during enemy attempts to expand their area of control.

Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainian officials said that the Starlink restrictions for drones were still in effect as of the morning of October 23.
As of Friday morning, October 23, Ukrainian interceptors still could not use high-speed internet to shoot down Russian attack drones or conduct mid-range operations, Ukrainian officials and drone operators said, despite U.S. President Donald Trump saying that SpaceX founder Elon Musk had lifted the speed restrictions for his Starshield service, Politico reports, UNN writes.
Details
"Morning tests show the speed limits of 140–160 km/h are still there, and the navigation isn’t working properly," a Ukrainian government official told on condition of anonymity.
"As of this morning, instances of connectivity loss at speeds of 161 km/h are still being observed. There is currently no confirmation that the restrictions have been lifted," a defense ministry official told reporters on Friday.
Ukrainian drone units, the publication writes, began testing the speed restrictions on Thursday evening, shortly after Trump told reporters that Musk had restored Starlink. "While some tests recorded speeds of up to 200 km/h over the Black Sea and noted an improvement, the drones still rapidly lost signal once flying above the 160 km/h speed limit," the report states.
"So, the key point is: We accelerate above 180 km/h, fly for a couple of minutes, the connection drops. It falls to 140–150 km/h and then is re-established — but the situation is better," a drone pilot told the publication. "So it works better, but with constant connection interruptions."

At least seven killed in attack at church in Jordan, state-owned outlet says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:57:33 UTC
21:57:33 KST

Seven killed as gunmen open fire at church in Jordan, authorities say
Oct 23 - Seven people were killed and 34 injured on Friday when gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in Jordan's Karak governorate, the head of the country's Public Security Directorate told reporters, in a rare attack on the country's Christian minority.
Speaking at a press conference in Karak, Major General Abdallah al-Maaytah said most of those wounded in the shooting at the Hamoud Church in Karak were still receiving treatment, and that the hunt for the attackers was ongoing.
Interior Minister Mazin Al Farrayeh said the attack had been carried out by "extremists", but that it was too early to tell whether they had any links to known groups either inside or outside Jordan.
There was no immediate claim of responsibility.
A video aired on Jordan's state-owned Al-Mamlaka television station that appeared to be from a security camera mounted on the church showed three people firing at it from a sidewalk and hiding behind trees and a low wall. The video showed the attackers then running towards the church's entrance. Reuters was able to verify the video from the entry path and wall surrounding the church, as well as other details.
Khaled Burqan, who was at the funeral, told Al-Mamlaka that dozens of people were present and that the gunmen opened fire on them for several minutes.
Ihab Ammareen, another witness, told the station that he saw bloodied people collapse on the floor after the attack. "People were crying, wailing, screaming — it's hard to describe," he told the station.
BLOOD SMEARED ON THE GROUND
Jordan's King Abdullah visited Karak hours after the attack and said the perpetrators would be punished "with an iron fist".
"The terrorist attack against Karak will be met with the harshest retaliation. Those who delude themselves into thinking that they can divide Jordanians with their bullets have no chance in the face of our unity," he said in a statement.
Reuters footage from the church after the attack showed blood smeared on the floor near its entrance, where security forces were deployed.
Such attacks are extremely rare in Jordan, which is relatively stable, though Jordanian authorities say they have repeatedly foiled attempted attacks by Islamist militants in recent years.
Christians make up a minority of Jordan's population. The country is home to several biblical sites that attract Christian pilgrims from around the world.
Jordan's Minister of Endowments and Islamic Affairs Mohammad Khalayleh and several members of Jordan's parliament condemned the attack in comments to Al-Mamlaka.
The US ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz described it in a post on X as a "depraved and brutal attack on a house of worship."
Jordan was among the US allies in the region to be hit by Iranian attacks this year after the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February. REUTERS

All four Moscow airports shut down, one declares air raid alert and begins evacuating passengers
All four of Moscow’s airports — Sheremetyevo, Domodedovo, Vnukovo, and Zhukovsky — closed to arrivals and departures, Rosaviatsia said.
Sheremetyevo declared an air raid alert and told passengers to head to the nearest safe zones and shelters.
Domodedovo announced that, because of temporary restrictions, “flight schedules are being adjusted.”
Vnukovo also reported the closure, explaining that the measures “were due to security considerations.” Passengers were advised to “be prepared for a lengthy wait,” including on board aircraft.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said over the past several hours that at least 11 drones had been shot down approaching the capital.
Update: Restrictions at all four Moscow airports were lifted several hours later, but the airports closed again by 9 p.m. At around 11 p.m., Vnukovo and Domodedovo resumed handling arriving and departing flights “subject to approval.” The Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ posted a photo of drone debris on a runway at Sheremetyevo Airport. Passengers were evacuated, though Russian authorities made no official statement about debris falling there. The air raid alert at the airport was later lifted. An evacuation was also ordered at the IQ Quarter complex in Moscow City during the attack. The tower houses several federal government agencies, including the Economic Development Ministry, the Industry and Trade Ministry, and the Digital Development Ministry.
On September 1, Volodymyr Zelensky warned airlines that Russian skies are “becoming unsafe,” saying that “drones will appear in Russian skies in a way that will have to be reckoned with.” He added that Ukraine “doesn’t threaten civil aviation as such,” but that because of Ukrainian drone attacks, “Russian airspace will de facto be closing.” Vladimir Putin called Zelensky’s statement “a declaration of terrorism” and added that “if such tragedies occur, we will find a way to respond.”
Over the past two months, Moscow’s airports have repeatedly closed due to the threat of Ukrainian drone attacks. Dozens of flights have been delayed as a result, and in some cases airports descended into chaos.

Andy Burnham says he has emergency stockpile of beans, soup and Twiglets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:57:06 UTC
21:57:06 KST

Andy Burnham has said he has stockpiles of beans, soup and Twiglets in case of a civil emergency, as he said a new government campaign was not a reason for panic buying.
The prime minister was questioned on his domestic supply situation after the Be Ready campaign advised households to have enough bottled water and long-life food to keep going in case of an emergency, such as one caused by a weather event or a cyber-attack.
Asked on BBC Radio 5 Live whether, like Angela Rayner, he would make sure his emergency supplies included a bottle of sauvignon blanc, Burnham said: “I’m not sure a bottle of wine is your best first port of call if you’re in a slightly crisis situation, but it probably helps when you’ve done the hard work.
“I’ll stick to the basics, I think. I do like my beans, so I have plenty of those in the cupboard, and soup. I think those are the kind of things that I would recommend people to have, as well as Twiglets. I’m not sure I can get by for too long without those.”
The campaign says people should ensure they have at least three days of supplies, including water, in case of an emergency, which is similar to advice given to citizens in some other European countries.
Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said the nation also needed to prepare for the threat of “state-sponsored terrorism” by Russia or other hostile powers targeting everyday infrastructure.
The advice was general and longer-term, Burnham told 5 Live, rather than urgent. “It’s not about panicking, is it? It’s just about being prepared and having a sensible amount of supplies in the home … These events, sadly, in the world that we’re in are becoming more likely, and therefore it’s just sensible to be prepared.”
Asked about a message from a listener who was worried about supplies running low as people tried to stock up, Burnham said: “It’s not about panic buying. I understand what your listener is saying there, but it’s about just taking sensible measures to have enough in the house to tide you over should there be a difficult situation.”
Speaking earlier to the BBC, the Treasury minister James Murray admitted to being less prepared. He said: “I’ve got quite a lot of coffee in my house … it’s for individual people to take choices. I’m not going to say: ‘Here’s a government shopping list.’” He added: “I’m not going to pretend I’ve followed all that advice myself yet.”
He said the advice was in part a matter of bringing the UK into line with other countries. He told BBC Breakfast: “If you look at, say, Ireland or other countries in Europe like France and Netherlands, they’ve had this system for quite a long time, the idea of having a bit of stuff at home to protect yourselves in case something goes wrong.
“So it’s quite normal in other countries. I think it’s a bit more interesting here because we haven’t really talked about it as a country in recent years.”

Syria's Suweida: Analysts warn of Israeli agenda behind unrest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:56:27 UTC
21:56:27 KST

Breadcrumb
'Israeli agenda' behind National Guard moves in Suweida, analysts warn
The activities of the "National Guard" militia in Syria's southern province Suweida, led by Druze spiritual leader Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri, are increasingly coinciding with violations committed by Israeli forces occupying southern Syria and moves by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to win over Palestinian Druze voters ahead of the upcoming elections.
Militia members recently threatened to attack Umm Walad, a town in eastern rural Daraa near the administrative boundary between Daraa and Quneitra governorates, according to video recordings. The threats came as the militia carried out a drone attack early on Wednesday targeting a government-affiliated internal security checkpoint near Tal Hadid, west of Suweida.
Wael Alwan, a researcher at the Jusoor Centre, said military operations by the National Guard and affiliated armed groups in Suweida were expected.
Speaking to The New Arab, Alwan said the activities would serve Netanyahu's aim to secure votes from Druze communities in the occupied Palestinian territories. They also provided him with an opportunity to demonstrate his alleged commitment to protecting Syria's Druze, as he claims to be doing within Israel, while supporting and arming them.
Alwan said these actions by militias in the governorate, as well as calls for Israeli intervention, were primarily political and media-driven and were part of their continuing attempts to create unrest and block efforts to resolve the situation in Suweida.
Israeli arms openly supplied in Suweida
Israeli arms supplies to militias opposed to the Syrian government are no longer being concealed, according to Charles Lister, director of the Syria programme at the Middle East Institute.
On 19 October, Lister wrote on X that National Guard members had obtained US-made M16 and AR-15 rifles, suggesting Israel had supplied them.
Rashid Hourani, a researcher specialising in security and military affairs, told The New Arab that the National Guard's escalation was linked to efforts on the ground to return the Suweida issue to square one.
These efforts had intensified followed the militia's takeover of Waqm willage in western rural Suweida on 8 October, he said—with the group seeking to expand its areas of control in the province while the Syrian government worked to restore stability and facilitate residents’ return.
Hourani also linked the developments to continuing Israeli military operations on the "Sufa 53" road project, which aims to extend a route through western rural Daraa to the Jordanian border.
He said these activities were an attempt to undermine efforts by Jordan, the US, Turkey and Saudi Arabia to reach a solution to the Suweida crisis, particularly the implementation of the Syrian-Jordanian-US roadmap.
Hourani said the National Guard had recently received weapons and ammunition from Israel, transported by military helicopters. Israeli reconnaissance aircraft had also increased their aerial coverage of the militia, particularly over areas controlled by the Syrian government.
Israeli reconnaissance flights had also covered Daraa governorate and the skies over Damascus and its countryside, he added.
Hourani said Israel's movements and support for the National Guard were part of its efforts to impose a new reality on the ground that will strengthen its hand in negotiations with the Syrian government.
Damascus, meanwhile, was relying on diplomacy and US pressure to curb Israeli violations and intervention in Syria.
He said Israel's main current objective was establishing a security buffer zone along the Syrian side of the occupied Golan Heights.
US concern over renewed escalation
The Suweida crisis returned to the forefront after al-Hijri declared on 25 August that the Unitarian Druze, were "an inseparable part of the State of Israel".
The remarks prompted objections from Druze figures and religious authorities in Syria, Lebanon and the occupied territories, and saw an increased crackdown within Suweida against voices opposing al-Hijri.
Tom Barrack, the US special envoy to Syria, expressed Washington's concern over renewed escalation in Suweida in September, when armed militias also intensified their military activities, calling on all sides to exercise restraint.
Barrack called for Suweida's reintegration in accordance with the roadmap agreed by the US, Jordan and Syria approximately a year earlier.
He urged dialogue, understanding and cooperation between the Druze, tribal communities and neighbouring countries, warning that the alternative to dialogue was not victory but another round of mourning.
He said he had signed a tripartite peace roadmap for the governorate a year earlier with Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani and Jordanian Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi, the aim of which was to reintegrate Suweida into Syria in a dignified manner, while guaranteeing full citizenship rights and ensuring that all obligations were met.
Journalist Samer al-Miqdad told The New Arab that the danger posed by the National Guard's military movements extended beyond changes in territorial control or the spread of fighting into rural Daraa. The greater risk was a return to widespread chaos across southern Syria and the reignition of the crisis.
"People in eastern rural Daraa fear the consequences of this militia's military operations," he said. "We had reached an acceptable level of calm and de-escalation, but the militia is trying to undermine it."
He added that the group continued to marginalise opponents in Suweida who called for a resolution, even if that meant using force and repression. Any further escalation would directly harm residents, he warned, and an extension of the fighting into Daraa would be disastrous, given the militia members' threats.
The roadmap for resolving the Suweida crisis was signed on 17 September 2025, following meetings in Amman in July and August that year between the Syrian government, Jordan and the US.
It affirmed that any solution must preserve Syria's territorial unity and that Suweida's affairs could not be addressed outside the Syrian national framework. The roadmap called for the withdrawal of security forces, the establishment of local administration with security and administrative arrangements, the delivery of humanitarian aid, the release of abductees and the return of displaced residents.
It also called for an end to foreign interference alongside regional security understandings, and an investigation into the deadly events in Suweida in July 2025, when clashes erupted between Druze gunmen on one side and government forces and Bedouin fighters on the other.

Greece joins push to ban social media for minors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:55:16 UTC
21:55:16 KST

Greece joins push to ban social media for minors
A growing number of countries are tightening rules governing children’s online activity amid fears of addiction.
The Greek parliament has passed a law banning the use of social media by people under the age of 15.
Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis’s party, New Democracy, used its majority to pass the bill on Friday. None of the other political parties backed the bill in a heated debate that started on Thursday, despite the fact that a growing group of countries worldwide have introduced restrictions on minors.
Greece’s new laws will come into effect on January 1 2027. It will require age verification on social networks and impose harsh penalties should companies fail to comply.
Mitsotakis previously announced plans for the ban in April, taking to TikTok, one of the most popular social networks with young people in Greece, to explain the “difficult but necessary” measure that his government planned to take.
The opposition socialist PASOK party abstained from the vote, after seeking an alternative bill that would have banned social media for under-13s and parental controls for 13- and 14-year-olds.
The ban brings Greece into line with about 20 countries that now restrict access to social media apps for young people. Australia, France, Brazil, Indonesia, Austria, Denmark, and the UK are among those that have either introduced or plan similar restrictions.
Critics say social networks use addictive algorithms to glue kids to their screens, and warn excessive scrolling can damage their mental health.
Bans have also faced pushback though, with questions about their enforcement and how effective they really are.

In 2021, Meghan won a UK High Court privacy and copyright claim against Daily Mail publisher Associated Newspapers over articles that reproduced parts of a “private” letter she wrote to him, asking him to stop talking to the press.
The latest controversy follows a turbulent few years for the royal family, which has been hit by both scandal and ill health.

Then in February 2024, Charles, now 77, revealed he was undergoing treatment for cancer.
Weeks later came another blow: Catherine, Princess of Wales and wife of heir William, announced she too was being treated for cancer. She is now in remission.
Most recently, police in February arrested the king’s disgraced younger brother Andrew Mountbatten Windsor on suspicion of misconduct in public office related to his links to late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. AFP

Where Intuitions Conflict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:54:48 UTC
21:54:48 KST

If you ask a group of people a philosophical question or present them with a challenging thought experiment, it’s often the case that they will express very different views about it. We quite naturally interpret this as different people having different intuitions. But is that what’s going on?
In “Conflicting Intuitions,” published earlier this year, Joshua Knobe (Yale) takes up this question. Having imagined posing a question about free will to a group of students who express disagreement over its answer, he writes:
[I]t might be that some people have compatibilist intuitions, while others have incompatibilist intuitions, and similarly for each of the other traditional questions of philosophy. Then the puzzlement we feel regarding these questions might be explained in terms of the conflict between the intuitions of different people.
But that’s not the only possible explanation:
I will argue that experimental research has been providing evidence for a very different hypothesis. On this hypothesis, the difficulty is in large part a matter of individual people having conflicting intuitions. Thus, when a person encounters a thought experiment designed to get at one of the traditional questions of philosophy, she will often have an intuition pulling her in one direction but also an intuition pulling her in the exact opposite direction. This might seem like an obvious hypothesis, and perhaps it is. Still, I think that its implications haven’t been fully appreciated. If true, it would have important implications both empirically and philosophically.
On the empirical side:
The conflicting intuitions hypothesis has important implications when it comes to what exactly our theories about people’s intuition are supposed to explain…
If we assume that the difference in responses is due to different people having different intuitions, we would naturally assume that the theory should explain why different people have different intuitions regarding this case. So we might think that our theory of the underlying cognitive processes should explain why [some] have one intuition and the other[s] have the opposite intuition.
However, if we conclude that the difference in responses is due to each individual person having conflicting intuitions, there is an important sense in which there is more that needs explaining. An adequate theory would not merely have to explain why half of the participants have the intuition that it is a case of causation; it would have to explain why those people are conflicted…
There are various issues on the philosophical side. Here’s one, mentioned after the discussion of some empirical work on cases about which respondents say that apparently conflicting intuitions are both correct:
Independent of anything that could be settled through further empirical work on ordinary intuitions, we need to know whether there is some way of working out a philosophical theory that makes sense of what people seem to be saying in these cases. For example, within the philosophy of law, we can ask whether there is any way of developing a theory on which it can be right to say something like: there is a sense in which this action clearly violates the law, but there is a deeper sense in which it does not violate the law. Similarly, within the work on personal identity, we can ask whether there is any way of developing a theory on which it can be right to say: there is a sense in which this person is clearly Phineas, but there is also a deeper sense in which he is not truly Phineas.
Here again, I suspect we will arrive at different answers for different philosophical issues. For some, we may find that it is possible to develop such a theory, and philosophical work along these lines might lead to important new insights. For others, we will presumably arrive at the opposite conclusion. We will find that there is simply no possible way for both intuitions to be true.
Additionally, “we would need a clear answer to the… question as to how conflicting intuitions can have a larger philosophical significance even when we recognize that there is no possible way that both intuitions can be true.”
The whole article is here. Discussion welcome.

Russia-Ukraine talks planned for November in UAE: Kremlin

Russia and Ukraine say talks planned for November in UAE
The US-brokered talks are the first planned since negotiations stopped earlier this year.
Moscow and Kyiv have confirmed that trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States have been scheduled for November.
The planned negotiations, aimed at ending Russia’s war on its neighbour, will be held in the United Arab Emirates, the Kremlin’s spokesperson said on Friday.
US-brokered talks were held earlier this year, but made little progress. The meetings then lapsed as the Trump administration was focused on its war on Iran.
However, Russia signalled its willingness to reengage after US special envoy Steve Witkoff travelled to meet with President Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg this week.
The next round of talks is now “planned for the first half of November in Abu Dhabi” and “will take place in a trilateral format,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the Hudson Institute think tank on Friday that he spoke with Witkoff after the envoy’s meeting with Putin, and that technical negotiations will take place “in the first half of November, and as early as possible”.
But much would depend on Russia, he warned, noting that a similar meeting expected earlier this month never materialised.
Hopes of making significant progress are slim. Previous talks have struggled to produce results, with Russia maintaining a list of hardline demands, including that Ukraine hands over large parts of its territory and agrees not to join NATO.
In a televised interview aired late on Thursday, Putin said that any trilateral talks should focus on the long-term security arrangements for a final peace deal, not a “short” truce.
Zelenskyy, for his part, said that any peace agreement would need strong security guarantees for Ukraine and funding for 10 years to maintain the Ukrainian army. He also called for Europe to be involved in the talks.
Shifting ties
Confirmation of the November talks comes amid growing strain on relations between Kyiv and members of the US government, and signs of improving ties between US President Donald Trump and Putin.
Trump, whose war on Iran has provoked rising energy prices that have dented his political support in the run-up to midterm elections, has criticised Ukraine’s targeting of Russian energy infrastructure and given Russia several key concessions in his administration’s latest diplomacy push.
The White House said on Friday that First Lady Melania Trump brokered a “localised ceasefire” between Moscow and Kyiv in the southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which has been occupied by Russia since February 2022.
Meanwhile, Trump has eased sanctions on Moscow and made a deal to buy 300,000 tonnes of Russian diesel. Moscow announced on Friday that the first shipment was on its way to New York.
European leaders have said that the deal made peace between Ukraine and Russia harder to achieve by giving Russia “hope”.
Ukrainian forces have since reported problems regarding access to satellite technology from Starlink and crucial intelligence, despite US assurances that speed restrictions had been removed.
Ukraine is also waiting for shipments of air defence interceptors that had been previously promised, Zelenskyy said, making Ukrainian defensive efforts against near-daily Russian drone and missile attacks more difficult.
Such attacks have killed more than 19,000 Ukrainian civilians – including 762 children – since Russia launched its full-scale war more than four years ago, Ukraine’s acting prosecutor general, Anton Kovalsky, said Friday.
So far this year, prosecutors have confirmed the deaths of 2,960 civilians, including 668 children, Kovalskyi added.
Separately on Friday, Russia’s Ministry of Defence announced that Moscow and Kyiv had each exchanged 270 prisoners of war.
The ministry was quoted by state media as saying that the freed Russian servicemen were in Belarus and would be transported to Russia once they had received psychological and medical assistance.
Prisoner swaps are rare ground on which Russia and Ukraine have maintained contact throughout the conflict, with thousands exchanged since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
