The Next Chapter of Africa-China Climate Cooperation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:38:00 UTC
21:38:00 KST

Nearly five years have passed since the adoption of the Declaration on China-Africa Cooperation on Combating Climate Change at the Eighth Forum on China-Africa Cooperation (FOCAC 8) in 2021. Since then, discussions have often centered on simple indicators to reflect on the progress made – for example, the number of projects announced, the size of new investments, and the scale of renewable energy commitments.
At first glance, Development Reimagined’s China-Africa Climate Action Tracker provides just this. The tracker captures 246 publicly announced climate actions across 50 African countries between 2022 and the first half of 2026, including nearly 49 GW of renewable energy in the development pipeline, clean technologies, clean transportation, and, more recently, critical minerals. However, while these results are important, they capture only part of a partnership that has evolved significantly over the past five years.
Beyond the numbers, the tracker reveals three structural shifts that have been taking place since FOCAC 8: that cooperation is becoming more investment-led; more closely linked to green industrialization; and increasingly focused on building long-term institutions. As FOCAC 10 approaches in 2027, these shifts have important implications for how future Africa-China climate cooperation should be designed and evaluated.
From Infrastructure Delivery to Long-term Investment
The first shift is a move from contractor-led cooperation toward longer-term investment partnerships.
For many years, Africa-China cooperation in the energy sector was largely associated with engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) projects. Often having bid and won procurement processes funded by African governments or banks, Chinese companies built power plants, transmission lines, and other infrastructure that supported African countries’ energy ambitions. That model remains important and continues to contribute to Africa’s energy transition.
However, the China-Africa Climate Action Tracker suggests that the partnership is evolving. Investment and equity-led projects, EPC-plus projects, and technology transfer are becoming increasingly prominent, while the share of traditional EPC-only projects is declining. And, although Chinese state-owned enterprises such as Power China and Energy China continue to play a dominant role in project delivery in Africa, a growing number of Chinese private firms are expanding their presence through investments in local manufacturing and production capacity.
For example, in Zambia, a Chinese firm announced a lithium battery manufacturing project in 2024 with an investment of approximately $30 million. The facility, located in the Zambia-China Jiangxi International Economic and Technical Cooperation Zone, is now operational. This illustrates how Africa-China climate cooperation can extend beyond infrastructure delivery to support local green manufacturing and industrial development.
Climate Cooperation Is Becoming a Green Industrial Agenda
The second shift is even more interesting. Africa-China climate cooperation is increasingly extending beyond individual renewable energy projects toward the development of integrated green industrial value chains
Hence, although new solar, wind, and hydropower energy infrastructure continue to dominate Africa-China climate cooperation, the tracker also highlights the rapid emergence of critical minerals as an essential component of climate cooperation.
Development Reimagined began systematically tracking Africa-China critical minerals projects in 2025 and has already identified close to 20 projects involving lithium, graphite, rare earth elements, and other strategic resources. More significantly, eight of the nine countries hosting these critical mineral projects also have renewable energy projects. This overlap points to opportunities that Chinese and African firms are taking up to extend cooperation beyond mineral extraction.
African countries are increasingly pursuing and implementing national industrial strategies that connect renewable energy, mineral processing, and manufacturing. The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is developing battery value chains. Nigeria is expanding clean technology manufacturing. Tanzania is positioning itself as a multi-mineral processing hub.
Looking at Africa’s green manufacturing progress, projects that involve Chinese stakeholders span electric vehicle assembly, battery manufacturing, energy storage, solar PV production, and related supply chains. These examples demonstrate growing interest among Chinese companies in localizing production in Africa markets rather than relying solely on exports of finished products.
That said, some of this manufacturing pipeline remains at the memorandum of understanding, feasibility, planning or pre-construction stage. Announced projects don’t always become operational manufacturing capacity. In addition, feasibility studies often miss the opportunity presented by the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), which could help make green manufacturing investments more commercially viable through access to the much larger continental market.
Cooperation Is Moving Beyond Individual Projects
The third trend is perhaps the least visible but could prove the most important. Climate cooperation is increasingly being built through and reinforcing African initiatives and institutions, not just project-by-project.
Since 2022, the tracker has recorded more than 40 climate “exchanges,” including strategic partnerships, technology cooperation, capacity-building initiatives, and industry collaborations. These initiatives receive less attention than utility-scale renewable energy projects, but they could prove fundamental in building the institutional foundations necessary for long-term economic transformation.
For example, pairing Chinese expertise in solar technology and energy storage with training for African engineers and technicians could do more than bring new clean-energy systems online. It could help build the local skills needed to operate and maintain these systems, support local businesses and expand access to reliable electricity over the long term.
Looking Ahead to FOCAC 10
So what do these three trends suggest for the next phase of Africa-China climate cooperation?
Our view at Development Reimagined is that while the number of megawatts installed will remain an important measure of progress – especially in the context of the 300 GW 2030 renewable energy goal announced by African leaders in the 2023 Nairobi declaration – the next stage of Africa-China climate cooperation presents an opportunity for FOCAC 10 to do more than announce the next generation of projects. It can help shape the conditions under which these projects deliver lasting value.
The first priority could be turning a growing pipeline into projects that are delivered. The real test for any announced project comes afterwards – including the need to securing affordable finance, reach construction, begin operations and ultimately deliver economic and climate benefits. FOCAC 10 could place greater emphasis on this implementation journey, including clearer mechanisms to track progress and identify where policy, financing, or technical support is needed. This would help shift the focus from the volume of commitments towards the results they generate.
The second priority could be to continue to connect individual projects to the bigger opportunity of green industrialization. Investments in renewable energy, critical minerals, EVs, batteries, and solar PV are beginning to form the building blocks of new green industrial value chains across African countries. More energy projects need to be directed to support local production, technology transfer, skills development, and value addition. Chinese companies are already exploring this shift, while African countries are developing policies to attract and anchor these investments. FOCAC 10 can help strengthen this convergence, with the AfCFTA providing an important platform for linking national manufacturing investments to a larger continental market.
The third is to invest even after a project is built. A solar farm, manufacturing facility, or battery plant can create important economic and climate benefits, but its longer-term contribution depends on the capabilities around it, including skilled workers, local suppliers, research institutions, effective regulators, and access to finance. These foundations are less visible than a new project, but they determine whether investments can be sustained, replicated and scaled.
Future Africa-China climate cooperation therefore has an opportunity to put greater emphasis on building these capabilities alongside physical infrastructure, while also responding more fully to African countries’ priorities on climate adaptation.
These three priorities, although they might be new, do not, in fact, require a departure from the progress made since FOCAC 8. Rather, they build on how the partnership is already evolving.
FOCAC 10, to be held in 2027, can help move Africa-China climate cooperation into its next active phase: one where success is measured not simply by what is announced or built, but by what actual power is delivered, what industrial goods are produced locally and what industrial capabilities are growing on the continent.

At the same time, the developer has confirmed that football will continue to be played at the stadium for another five years.
Invego founder and CEO Kristjan-Thor Vähi believes Latvia will have a new national stadium in the coming years. Once that happens, he argues, the existing Skonto Stadium, which has reached the end of its useful life, will no longer be needed.
Vähi explained that Invego has developed a concept for transforming the area into a district connecting Riga’s historic centre with the newer Skanste neighbourhood.
He added that preparing a development project of this scale would take at least three to five years.
According to the company's CEO, the existing Skonto Stadium will remain available for football for the next five years.
Vähi said he had informed key officials involved in the development of Latvia's new national stadium about this commitment, including the president of the Latvian Football Federation (LFF), the chair of Riga City Council's Urban Development Committee and the city's chief architect.
"I am confident that these five years will give them sufficient time to find a solution for developing the new national stadium," Vähi said.
Skonto Stadium is currently owned by SIA Adventika Group.
As previously reported by LETA, the Latvian Football Federation signed a letter of intent with Adventika Group in early 2026 concerning the acquisition of Skonto Stadium for the national football stadium project.
The proposal involved reconstructing the existing stadium while making use of its current infrastructure.
The national stadium project was intended to be developed in cooperation with the Latvian government, Riga City Council and international football organisations, including the Union of European Football Associations (UEFA) and the International Federation of Association Football (FIFA).
LFF Secretary General Arturs Gaidels previously confirmed to LETA that both options, constructing a stadium in Lucavsala and redeveloping Skonto Stadium, remained under consideration.
He emphasised that one of the main criteria for choosing between the projects would be their economic viability.
Meanwhile, Edgars Bergholcs of the United List (AS), chair of Riga City Council's Urban Development Committee, has proposed reviewing the existing football infrastructure development plans.
He has suggested relocating the planned national football stadium from Lucavsala to the Skanste neighbourhood, next to Xiaomi Arena.
Under this proposal, the area could eventually develop into a multifunctional sports and events centre supported by appropriate infrastructure.
The Invego group comprises more than 60 companies operating in Estonia, Latvia and Portugal and is currently implementing 30 development projects.
The company has developed more than 150,000 square metres of residential space, representing approximately 1,500 homes, as well as 50,000 square metres of commercial property.
A further 500,000 square metres of residential and commercial space is currently under development.
In recent years, Invego has built new homes for more than 1,000 families in Tallinn and its surrounding areas.
Its largest completed developments include Vana-Peetri, Tiskreoja and Tabasalu Kodu.
Other major residential projects currently under development include Luccaranna, Uus-Järveküla, Keila Pargikodud and Verve.
In Riga and the surrounding region, Invego is developing eight residential districts, including three in partnership with Reterra and one in cooperation with EfTEN Special Opportunities Fund.
The company is also developing Silves Hills, a 65-hectare residential district in southern Portugal.
In Latvia, the group operates through SIA Invego Latvia, which has 17 additional subsidiaries registered in the country.
According to information from Firmas.lv, Invego Latvia was registered in 2023 and has share capital of five million euros.
The company's sole shareholder is an Estonian company of the same name, Invego Latvia, while Kristjan-Thor Vähi is listed as its ultimate beneficial owner through ownership rights.

The new owners of the Daily Telegraph have made large numbers of staff redundant, telling them the title will be transformed from a newspaper “into a global, AI-powered premium media and intelligence business”.
In an all-company briefing and email on Friday morning, staff were told the title would rely increasingly on technology, data and AI to “reinvent the reader experience”. Newsroom insiders said they expected as many as 100 people to lose their jobs.
The “next chapter” of the Telegraph will focus on new revenue streams including “video, audio, puzzles, events, B2B, licensing, commerce and new products”, the CEO, Carolin Hulshoff Pol , wrote.
It will also focus on growing its audience internationally, “particularly in foreign affairs, defence and business”, she said.
Some staff were told on Thursday they were being fired, while others received calls and emails on Friday morning. Some senior staff were said to be in tears as they told colleagues their fate.
The culture and sports departments have been particularly hard hit, according to insiders. A source from inside the Telegraph said the atmosphere in the newsroom was “like a morgue”.
The Telegraph was bought in June by the European media group Axel Springer for £575m, ending three tortuous years for the title and its staff, during which potential owners were blocked, fell through or faced fierce internal opposition.
The paper joined a stable of media brands including the German titles Bild and Die Welt, as well as the digital outlets Politico and Business Insider. Mathias Döpfner, Axel Springer’s chief executive and controlling shareholder, said he intended to invest in the Telegraph to make it the “leading centre-right media outlet in the English-speaking world”.
However, heavy job cuts have been expected at the paper amid an internal staff consultation in recent weeks into the future of the business.
Pol said that during the lengthy sale process, “the Telegraph had limited ability to invest, adapt and move at the pace the market demanded”, adding that “the media world and technology have changed at extraordinary speed”.
“Our ambition is to transform the Telegraph from a leading British newspaper into a global, AI-powered premium media and intelligence business – built on trusted journalism, direct relationships with our audiences and expertise that sets us apart.
“To deliver on this ambition, we need to change how we are organised, how decisions are made, where we focus our resources and create efficiencies. We need clearer accountability, faster decision-making and a simpler, more effective organisation.”
She said the organisation would “use AI confidently while enhancing what technology cannot replace: judgment, originality, courage and trust”.
A spokesperson for the Telegraph Media Group reiterated Pol’s remarks, adding: “Today marks the start of a formal consultation process. These are difficult choices that we believe are necessary for the future of the business.”
TMG would not confirm the number of redundancies.

My Word: When Europe fiddles and burns - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:33:33 UTC
21:33:33 KST

It was a searing image. The sight of the historic city hall in Limoges, France, going up in flames, and the spire collapsing into the blazing building was haunting.
Two different news clips captured two sides of the story: In one, the crowd of onlookers could be heard cheering as the tower fell; in the other, someone called out in a shocked voice: “It’s fallen!” I wondered whether he was referring just to the spire or to French civilization in general.
According to Smithsonian Magazine, the city hall first opened its doors on Bastille Day in 1883, and “has been celebrated as an architectural wonder. Well-known for its tall spire and ornate metal belfry, the 143-year-old building gained historic monument status in 1975 as a prime example of late 19th-century French architecture and civic pride.”
There’s something sadly symbolic in the beautiful building that opened on the French National Day all those years ago being burned down in the 2026 French riots. Beautiful architecture and civic pride are being willfully destroyed.
For the masked assailants, arsonists, and looters rampaging throughout France – and elsewhere in Europe – this is a modern version of Bastille Day. The mobs are ruling through fear and violence.
Whatever initially triggered the riots – ostensibly highschoolers complaining about their conditions – the flames are being fanned from other directions. This is not about the cost of living, the price of fuel, or crowded classrooms.
News footage showed shocked storekeepers along the iconic Champs-Élysées helplessly looking on as their stores were looted and trashed. Not only were their livelihoods being stolen, but their very way of life.
It’s not by chance that symbols of the government, and of France itself, were attacked. The Statue of the Republic was defaced in Paris; the marble bust of Marianne was damaged in an attack in the historic Marseilles City Hall building; and the tourist office in Lyon, housed in a 19th-century architectural gem, was also destroyed – not that the city can expect an influx of tourists any time soon.
France has seen demonstrations before, even violent ones, but “vive la difference” – these were not French students holding philosophical discussions as they marched in May 1968; nor were they “the Yellow Vests,” protesting fuel prices in the mass rallies that petered out with COVID 19 restrictions; and today’s rioters are not the workers who took to the streets three years ago to protest the planned rise of the retirement age.
The Yellow Vests have made a comeback, but these riots are not quintessentially French. Thanks to immigrants and illegal migrants, and their children and grandchildren, foreign flags of former colonies like Morocco and Algeria rival the French tricolor, and Palestinian flags and keffiyehs are prevalent.
I couldn’t help but note the guest appearance last week by keffiyeh-clad, omni-activist Greta Thunberg. She is now absorbed by the global political climate rather than the world’s weather.
More than ever, when protesters chant, “From the river to the sea,” the question is which river and sea they are referring to. Anarchists and jihadists are agents of chaos and destruction – they create a lethal combination.
In some French cities, the lingua franca of the rioters was Arabic. There’s a word for it: “Intifada.” The Intifada has been globalized, and the results can be seen on the streets of France, where hundreds of protesters and police officers have been injured, and damage could reach a billion euros.
The current conflagration in France is not (yet) specifically an attack on Jews, but the writing was spray-painted on the wall years ago, along with the slogan “Free Palestine.”
When French President Emmanuel Macron last year declared his unconditional recognition of a State of Palestine, he did not strengthen France and French values; he rewarded terrorism and violence. No wonder there are jokes and memes about first implementing a “Two-state solution” in France.
Newsweek and other media noted the appearance of protest videos featuring the song “MRH” by rapper BORO700, which refers to jihadist Mohamed Merah, who murdered 30-year-old teacher Rabbi Jonathan Sandler and his two young sons along with eight-year-old Myriam Monsonego at a Jewish school in Toulouse in 2012, as well as killing French soldiers in other attacks.
The lyrics also praise a perpetrator of the November 2015 jihadist assault in Paris, in which 130 people were murdered, including those at a concert at the Bataclan hall, at a football stadium, and at cafés and bars. The victims were not chosen specifically, but the targets were carefully selected to include all that the young, carefree, French way of life represents.
What's causing the French riots?
As Abe Greenwald put it in Commentary, trying to explain “the real cause” of the riots in France is “kind of like trying to determine the official cause of death in someone who suffered from multiple fatal conditions at the end of his life. That someone is Europe, and the conditions are progressive, in more than one sense of the word.
“There are the real crises: welfare-state failure, education collapse, the disappearance of community, an unsustainable old-age dependency ratio, and unassimilated immigration. Then there are the isms, the activist theologies ensuring that solutions remain out of reach: socialism, anarchism, Islamism, Palestinianism, and antisemitism…
“This indecipherable convergence of radical pursuits is now everywhere in the West, and it’s been with us for a while…
“In the years since 2011, the storm has been fueled by Black Lives Matter, Antifa, gender radicalism, anti-Israel mania, and jihad fandom… The riots in France will add something new, too.”
Macron had his “let them eat cake” moment last week, attending a Celine Dion concert with his wife Brigitte as the riots worsened. Perhaps it was more like Nero fiddling as Rome burned. The French president is quacking like the lame duck he is ahead of the scheduled April 2027 elections.
Both far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon and far-Right front-runner Marine Le Pen are hoping to gain from the current protests. Neither bodes well for the Jewish community.
Marseilles-born rector of Bar-Ilan University Prof. Cyrille Cohen, speaking on Reshet Bet’s “International Hour” radio show, pointed out that polarization is not a byproduct of the riots but an aim.
Whether the Right or the Left wins, there is likely to be a wave of aliyah. Bar-Ilan, like other Israeli universities, is already absorbing more French-speaking students, he noted. Cohen quipped about a French cartoon ahead of the presidential elections showing Jews “undecided how to vote: whether to choose Jerusalem or Netanya.”
Those Israelis threatening to leave the country if next week’s general election doesn’t bring about their desired results, should keep in mind that there is no guarantee of a safe haven and a warm welcome for Jews anywhere in the global village, no matter which camp they belong to.
Israelis also need to be aware that outside forces – including Iran, Russia, Turkey, and Qatar – are happy to foster Israeli divisions and foment unrest as a way of weakening the Jewish state.
The attacks on Israel have long morphed into an assault on Judeo-Christian values. Ahead of November 11, the British Commonwealth’s Remembrance Day for its war dead, it is customary to wear poppy pins. Indeed, November 11 is also known as Poppy Day.
This year, the Palestinians and their supporters have hijacked that too, selling a poppy badge in Palestinian colors while claiming the poppy-anemone is the Palestinian national flower. It’s not; it’s Israel’s national flower, and the red anemones that carpet the Negev in the spring have come in particular to symbolize the 1,200 slaughtered in the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led invasion and mega-atrocity.
Europe is discovering that the nightmare wasn’t a bad dream but reality of its own making. It needs to wake up and smell the burning buildings. Violent riots are not demonstrations of free speech and democracy. This is war. But the world has yet to internationalize the message of the French maxim, “En la guerre comme en la guerre.”

Israel Police officials clarified on Friday that there was no suspicion that a Palestinian photographer working with the French news agency AFP had advance knowledge of a shooting attack near Hebron earlier in the day, Walla learned, following reports that the photographer had prior information about the incident.
The clarification came after professional photographs of the terrorists at the scene were published, reportedly taken by the photographer in real time, according to foreign media reports.
Meanwhile, the IDF told Walla in response that "The entire incident is under investigation."
Following a situational assessment led by Judea and Samaria District Police Commander Maj.-Gen. Moshe Pinchi, the investigation into the attack was assigned to the district's Minorities Division, part of its Central Investigations Unit. Police will also assist the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) in investigating the incident.
During the assessment, attended by the commander of the Hebron area police and senior district officers, officials presented preliminary findings from the scene and reviewed the actions taken by police officers who assisted IDF troops.
Police to increase enforcement against vehicles used in terrorism
Pinchi instructed investigators to place particular emphasis on the use of a vehicle that had been taken off the road and was used in the attack. Known in Hebrew as a mashtuba, the vehicle was no longer legally permitted to operate on public roads.
He stressed the need to combat the use of such vehicles for terrorism and criminal activity throughout the West Bank.
Following the attack, district police will step up operations along major roads, including inspections of vehicles and suspects and the seizure of vehicles that have been taken off the road. Operational cooperation with IDF troops in the area will also be increased.
Police also addressed the timing of a statement distributed to the media earlier in the day and expressed regret over its release.
The statement said that even when an investigation is conducted professionally and independently, authorities must exercise judgment, demonstrate sensitivity to developments on the ground, and understand the public implications of when information is released.
Two terrorists killed following shooting attack near Hebron
A shooting attack took place on Friday morning near the Yehuda Junction, close to Hebron. Following a manhunt, IDF troops killed two terrorists involved in the shooting.
Five people were wounded in the attack, including two who were reported to be in critical condition.
The terrorists arrived at a scrapyard in the area in a vehicle bearing Israeli license plates and observed the soldiers before carrying out the attack.
According to the IDF's preliminary investigation, the attackers were two terrorists from Hebron who arrived carrying a large quantity of ammunition, an M4 rifle, and a handgun.
They reached the area of the Yehuda Junction, where an IDF squad-level outpost belonging to the Ari Battalion had been established two months earlier.
The deployment was the soldiers' first operational assignment.
Following a situational assessment, the soldiers set out to establish a checkpoint and prevent terrorists from accessing Routes 35 or 60 to carry out an attack. Similar precautions were taken at other junctions in the area.

IDF, Defense Ministry drafting resolution to protect reservists and families' benefits through 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:33:10 UTC
21:33:10 KST

The IDF and Defense Ministry are drafting a government resolution to protect the benefits and entitlements of reservists and their families whose service spans 2026 and 2027, following a Walla investigation that exposed gaps in eligibility, Walla learned on Thursday.
Alongside the government resolution, the IDF and Defense Ministry are advancing legislation in the Knesset, which they hope to expedite after the elections, during the Knesset's first session.
The move follows Walla's revelation that reservists could lose benefits and entitlements despite serving for extended periods. Because their reserve duty is divided between two calendar years, some soldiers fail to meet the minimum number of service days required to qualify for grants and benefits in either year.
As a result, a reservist serving nearly 100 consecutive days could fail to meet the eligibility requirements, despite having completed a substantial period of service.
The IDF and Defense Ministry are pursuing two parallel approaches: drafting a government resolution to regulate the calculation of reserve duty days and eligibility for benefits, while also advancing legislation in the Knesset.
While the legislative process is expected to take longer, the government resolution is intended to allow eligibility issues to be resolved sooner, subject to government approval.
Despite these efforts, the wives of reservists have criticized the proposed timetable. They argue that there is no justification for forcing families to wait until the legislative process is completed while soldiers continue accumulating reserve duty days and their families contend with the financial and personal consequences of prolonged service.
They are demanding that the IDF and Defense Ministry bridge the eligibility gaps during the interim period, providing assistance similar to that available to families of reservists who accumulate a large number of service days within a single calendar year.
Tank battalion reservists face loss of benefits
At the center of the controversy are soldiers from Battalion 363 of an armored brigade, some of whom have been called up for their fifth or sixth round of reserve duty since the start of the war.
As Walla previously reported, the soldiers received orders for 99 days of reserve duty beginning November 22, 2026, with 40 days falling in 2026 and another 59 days in 2027.
The division between the two years could affect their eligibility for various benefits, including reimbursements for mental health treatment, grants related to extending maternity leave, student grants, and vacation vouchers.
Some benefits require 45 to 50 days of reserve duty per year, while others require 60 days or more.
In response, the soldiers' wives sent a letter to IDF Personnel Directorate head Maj.-Gen. Dado Bar Kalifa and Chief Reserve Officer Brig.-Gen. Benny Ben Ari, demanding a solution to prevent their families from losing their entitlements.
"It is unacceptable that families who continue to shoulder the burden time and again should be harmed because of bureaucracy and dates over which they have no control," the women wrote.
They also emphasized that the benefits were not luxuries but assistance intended to help families cope with the price they pay for prolonged reserve duty.
IDF promises eligibility will not be affected
In response to an inquiry from Walla, the IDF Spokesperson's Unit said the issue was known and being addressed, and that reservists' eligibility for benefits would not be harmed because their service was divided between calendar years.
The IDF said the military and Defense Ministry were finalizing a draft government resolution concerning benefits for reservists.
Once the process is completed, the resolution will be submitted for government approval, after which the IDF will work to implement the entitlements in accordance with the approved framework.
Regarding battalions whose reserve duty spans two calendar years, particularly Battalion 363, the IDF clarified that service days completed in 2026 and those scheduled for 2027 would be taken into account under the framework to be established.
For a battalion that accumulated 40 days of reserve duty in 2026 and continues serving in 2027, service days will be calculated across both years, allowing eligibility for benefits in 2027 to be assessed based on the total number of service days and the provisions ultimately approved.
The IDF also clarified that reservists who have already exercised their eligibility for benefits based on service in 2026 and perform additional reserve duty in 2027 will remain eligible for benefits under the conditions to be established.
The proposed framework also addresses eligibility for emotional support and treatment when reserve duty is calculated across calendar years.
The IDF is preparing to advance the government resolution to allow reservists to receive their benefits as soon as possible.
At the same time, a dedicated briefing will be held for commanders and relevant personnel. The briefing will outline the assistance currently available, clarify the eligibility mechanism, and provide answers to reservists' questions.
Despite the IDF's commitment that reservists' rights will not be affected, the government resolution has yet to be approved, and the legislative process remains ahead.
Reservists' wives are demanding an interim solution to ensure that their families are not left without the benefits and assistance to which they are entitled.
Wives say no solution has been provided for 2026
The wives of reservists serving in Battalion 363 responded to the IDF Spokesperson's Unit's statement, arguing that despite the impression that a solution had been found, they had yet to receive an answer concerning their entitlements for 2026.
According to the women, the battalion is preparing for its sixth round of reserve duty after hundreds of days of service, during which their husbands are expected to be away from home for 99 consecutive days.
The women described the difficulties of raising children, working, and managing their households alone.
"We are not looking for special treatment, but are asking to receive support and assistance from the IDF and the state in dealing with our situation," they said.
According to the women, they even requested that the call-up be brought forward by five days to preserve their entitlements.
They are demanding a clear commitment that no benefits or rights belonging to reservists and their families will be affected in either 2026 or 2027.

France likes to speak in the name of the human conscience. It lectures other countries, hands out moral grades, and proudly invokes its national promise of liberty, equality, and fraternity.
But when its streets are burning, stores are being looted, and Jews fear for their safety, the disgraceful gap between France’s international posture and its domestic reality is exposed. A world power that seeks to teach others how to manage conflicts is struggling to protect its citizens’ storefronts.
This is more than a governance crisis. It is an indictment of French President Emmanuel Macron and a leadership that has replaced responsibility with empty rhetoric.
The student protests and anger over the cost of living may have originated in genuine hardship. Precisely for that reason, allowing them to become a pathway to arson and looting is a betrayal of the public that came to protest.
No shortage of classrooms justifies burning businesses, and no electricity bill justifies attacking police officers. Anyone who wraps criminality in the flag of social justice is not a revolutionary. He is granting legitimacy to lawlessness.
A government that cannot protect both the right to protest and the victims of violence has failed in its most basic duty.
Amid the chaos, the question arises once again: Why are Jews expected to pay the price?
Rioters vandalized a synagogue in Paris’ 19th arrondissement. The Torah ark was forced open, and religious items were thrown to the floor. There is no moral path leading from student hardship to attacks on Jews. When such a path emerges, protest has become a refuge for hatred and antisemitism.
There is no reason to condemn all the protesters. But the Palestinian flags and chants of “Free Palestine” provide ample evidence of what parts of the demonstration became. Once again, French Jews are expected to answer for the actions of the IDF and the Israeli government.
The citizenship of French Jews has been subjected to racist tests before, during the infamous Vichy regime. Nor should anyone forget the Dreyfus affair.
The figures on antisemitism demolish the excuses offered by the French leadership. France recorded 1,320 antisemitic acts in 2025. The synagogue in La Grande Motte was attacked, and a police officer was injured in an explosion.
These are not isolated incidents. They constitute a reality demanding national introspection. When the state must place security around Jewish institutions, it should begin examining its own failures. Jews do not need another emotional speech after the next attack.
Evasion is not tolerance when confronting Islamism. According to a survey conducted in 2025, 44% of Muslim respondents said they placed the rules of their religion above French law, while some expressed a preference for Sharia law.
A country cannot accept a situation in which its laws become recommendations and a minority seeks to dictate the legal rules. There must be no street where the law retreats in the face of threats or where police officers fear to enter certain areas. A Paris whose streets are in flames is the victim of state failure.
In France, as in Britain, politicians fear losing the Muslim electorate. When politicians exchange principles for electoral calculations, and when a leader softens his opposition to extremism for fear of losing support, he also abandons moderate Muslims.
A leadership that purchases temporary calm through moral ambiguity is selling its country’s future.
Macron’s presidency will be remembered with disgrace. The riots, the burning of stores, and the resurgence of antisemitism are the consequences of his failed leadership and that of the government he heads.
The importance of the presidency
Macron has forgotten that the presidency is more than a title, a palace and a flag. The images coming from France are a political humiliation for the president and the French leadership.
Anyone seeking to embody European leadership must explain why citizens in his own country are forced to pray that the next protest will pass over their businesses.
Israel remembers French moralizing all too well. On the eve of the Six Day War, France imposed an arms embargo and withheld Mirage aircraft ordered by Israel. Fifty Mirage 5 jets ordered in 1966 were never delivered under the agreement and instead entered French service.
From an Israeli perspective, this was a betrayal of trust by a major supplier at a moment of danger. Behind the lofty language of balance and responsibility stood a decision demonstrating how friendship can become conditional on diplomatic convenience.
France does not enter this debate with clean hands.

Behind the slogan of a civilizing mission stood a reality in which demands for independence were answered with military force. The liberty France presented as a universal value ended when people under French rule sought to exercise it themselves.
It is difficult to imagine a sharper contradiction between declaration and action: liberty for the ruling nation and subjugation for the people it ruled.
The depth of that betrayal was also exposed in Senegal. In December 1944, French forces opened fire on African soldiers at the Thiaroye military camp after those men had served France and demanded the pay owed to them.
Men who had risked their lives for France discovered that their service did not guarantee equal treatment. Macron recognized the incident as a massacre in 2024, 80 years after it occurred.
That recognition was important, but the delay remains painful. It took decades to call the killing by its proper name. This was not only colonial brutality. It was also state-sanctioned ingratitude.

France is paying, and will continue to pay, the price of its arrogance. Human rights were presented as a noble promise but were repeatedly subordinated to the interests of those in power.
There is now a simple demand of France’s leaders. Before presenting yourselves as judges of the world, acknowledge your own responsibility. Open the archives and give the victims a place more dignified than a footnote in a ceremonial speech.
Even if France eventually withdraws its support for the forces of evil represented by Palestinian terrorists who murdered, raped, mutilated, and abducted approximately 1,500 innocent Israeli and foreign civilians, history will not forget.

The conference would also feature a cultural programme.

The ICC called on the European Commission to urgently determine its position on US sanctions
Kyiv • UNN
The ICC is asking the European Commission to clarify the rules for companies operating amid US sanctions. The uncertainty threatens assistance to victims in Ukraine.
The European Commission must clarify as soon as possible how European companies should act in light of US sanctions against the International Criminal Court, its Secretary Osvaldo Zavala Giler said. According to him, the uncertainty threatens the work of the Court and organizations that help victims, particularly in Ukraine. Politico reports, writes UNN.
Details
ICC Secretary Osvaldo Zavala Giler said that the European Commission should provide recommendations as soon as possible to enable the court to continue operating in Europe. He warned that delays in consultations with Washington must not hinder the protection of the institution.
The United States began imposing sanctions on ICC judges and prosecutors in February 2025, and on October 9 announced an expansion of the restrictions. The new sanctions are due to enter into force in April 2027. The EU expressed its support for the court, but has not yet applied a mechanism that would prohibit European companies from complying with certain US sanctions.
To reduce its dependence on the United States, the ICC has already switched to open-source software and restructured its financial operations so that they do not depend on the dollar or US banks. The court has also reduced the number of partner banks to several institutions willing to process payments without ties to the United States.
According to Zavala Giler, the problem extends beyond the operations of banks and technology companies. The uncertainty is already affecting non-governmental organizations that assist the court, particularly in their work with victims in Ukraine and Uganda.
As one possible step, the ICC Secretary proposed that the European Commission provide companies with official guidance on their obligations. He also called for consideration of applying the blocking statute, which would protect European companies from the effects of certain extraterritorial US sanctions.
If the International Criminal Court cannot conduct financial operations in Europe, in euros, within the SEPA area without ties to the United States, then this calls European financial sovereignty into question
The European Commission currently favors dialogue with the United States. At the same time, the leaders of EU countries declared their readiness to take the necessary measures to support the court.

====================================================================================================

Hammersmith Bridge is a symbol of our dysfunctional times. The money is there, the joined-up thinking isn’t | Simon Jenkins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:30:26 UTC
21:30:26 KST

London’s Hammersmith Bridge is a metaphor for all that is wrong with British government. Closed to motor traffic and inert for seven years, it is a victim of the anarchy that seeps into every tier of public administration. The bridge sits today on a sublime bend in the Thames, guarded by what looks like Checkpoint Charlie in iron curtain Berlin. With Albert Bridge also now closed, 37,000 extra vehicles seeking to cross the river have brought south London close to perpetual gridlock. No one cares.
London may be the richest, smartest, coolest place in Britain. Yet it is run like a high street vape shop. Its buses are ever slower, homeless people are ever more prevalent, waiting times in hospitals ever longer. No one can decide if they want an HS2 terminus or a Heathrow runway. A robotic Whitehall algorithm has just declared, ludicrously, that the borough of Kensington’s “housing target” must be 5,107 homes a year, up from a previous target of 1,381.
The first thing you notice about a city is its traffic. In other cities, it moves. In London, it crawls. Its congestion is officially rated the worst of any capital in the world. Efforts to improve the sclerotic traffic lights have failed. The recent installation of computer-assisted “smart” lights – the much-vaunted road time optimisers – has contrived to cut just 27 seconds off individual bus journeys. A Guardian investigation last month timed a series of trips, and found the average speed for a No 22 bus between between Putney Common and Oxford Circus was under 6mph, or 16% slower than a decade ago.
The principal reason for this appears to be London’s epidemic of roadworks. In most cities such infrastructure is subject to intense regulation and coordination. The reason is obvious: that the disruption can restrict movement and thus impose costs on third parties. There is no regulation worthy of the word in London.
In 2017 the Economist published what became a notorious map showing roadworks in Paris and London. The first had a scatter of sparse red dots; London’s map was a sea of blood. Estimates are that vehicles in London navigate 1,300 roadworks every day, with the total for 2024 at 490,893. There is no evidence of the slightest coordination of hold-ups.
The chief reason is that a quarter century of privatising utilities has given water and cabling companies virtually unlimited freedom to dig where and when they please. Streets in the most afflicted inner boroughs now awake each morning to what looks like an overnight blitz. A mass of road closures and detour signs have turned the London street into what looks like a permanent construction site. Seeing any work being done is rare and there is no sense of anyone being in charge.
Hammersmith Bridge is a tough case. It legally belongs to the local Hammersmith and Fulham council – not Richmond on the south bank – but it has decided it “cannot absorb” the cost of restoring its decaying structure, put at £300m. It merely allows pedestrians and cyclists to cross. Yet it claims to have spent £54m on it over seven years. Merely doing next to nothing costs millions of pounds a year.
The bridge’s predicament is serious. Built by Sir Joseph Bazalgette in 1887, it was one of the world’s first iron suspension bridges – and the iron’s life has expired. Repair could only be temporary, or over the longer term astronomical. As architecture it is a noble if rather ungainly structure, compared with graceful Albert Bridge downstream. A growing body of opinion is that it would be common sense to replace it.
Designing a new bridge should be a competitive challenge. It needs to respect the buildings and natural environment of Barnes and Hammersmith on either bank. A work of style and dignity should have nothing to do with the concrete gashes of the 20th century’s London and Waterloo bridges. It needs to be very special.
As for who should take the lead, in any other city a river crossing would be the responsibility of its mayor. British mayors spend their time trying for headlines or Downing Street. London’s Sadiq Khan appears to have no view on Hammersmith Bridge, any more than he does on the capital’s roadworks, building conservation or policy on tall buildings.
As for paying for a new bridge, there is an answer. The so-called City Bridge Foundation was formed in the middle ages to maintain London bridges and later City crossings. Its charter limits its responsibility to just five crossings: Tower, London, Southwark, Millennium, and Blackfriars bridges. However, its trustee, the City of London Corporation, could amend the charter so that it could reinvest in infrastructure. It is one of London’s richest charities – with assets in the order of £1.5bn. The foundation currently spends lavishly on causes that have nothing to do with bridges.
This needs changing. The City of London is an out-of-date relic of medieval local government. The legacy of London’s past wealth should be at the disposal of the whole metropolis. The money is there. A new Hammersmith Bridge should rise across the Thames’s most exquisite western reaches, and soon.
- Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist

China, Europe should coordinate on carbon pricing, border tax: energy transition expert
Adair Turner urges Beijing and Brussels to unite on emission fees as the US pulls back from climate commitments
China and Europe should jointly introduce a system like the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), a levy on carbon-intensive imports designed to account for the carbon costs domestic producers face, which “applies against the rest of the world,” the co-chair of a global energy transition organisation says.
“The biggest single thing which I would love China to do is to say, ‘We want to join with Europe in a climate club’,” said Adair Turner, co-chair of the Energy Transitions Commission, during a panel discussion at the Bund Summit in Shanghai on Thursday.
Turner, who is also the former chairman of the UK’s Financial Services Authority, called on the two economies to commit jointly to carbon prices high enough to drive the decarbonisation of heavy industries such as cement and steel.
Calls for closer China-Europe climate cooperation have grown louder as the US retreats from international climate efforts under the Donald Trump administration, including its withdrawal from the Paris Agreement.

Why jaw-jaw is the best route EU leaders can take right now
Amid a proxy war with Russia, growing acrimony with the US and roiling protests at home, it is madness for European leaders to pick a trade fight with China
3-MIN READ3-MIN
15
 Listen
Alex Lo has been an SCMP columnist since 2012, commenting on China and international affairs. 
Beijing has told Brussels not to “fantasise” that pressure will extract concessions. This came after China made a goodwill gesture in the recent hybrid-car trade deal. The European Union responded by doubling down on a proposed trade “kill switch”.
The instrument follows a Franco-German proposal. It would let the bloc swiftly restrict single-market access in response to economic coercion. EU chief Ursula von der Leyen says all 27 leaders back it. Chemicals and machinery are priority sectors. French President Emmanuel Macron wants to add plastics and ferroalloys. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and others want a tougher, unified line on Chinese trade practices, currency depreciation and critical dependencies. The formal proposal is expected in December.
Unanimity among 27 leaders is itself a rare thing. It is usually reserved for communiques about how much everyone values unanimity. At a time when a proxy war with Russia, a likely trade war with China and acrimony with the United States are pushing the cost of living and livelihoods of ordinary Europeans to the brink, this is starting to look like a case of collective madness, a communal death drive. But China is the least of its problems.
The union faces what may be its most precarious moment. Its leaders are deeply unpopular, and its economy is sluggish. No wonder angry Europeans are hitting the streets. I have read a description of a “European Autumn”, with citizens turning on their rulers in one capital after another, much like the Arab Spring. Could Europeans become as fed up with incompetent and arrogant leaders as Arabs did?

Why the US can’t cut India off from Russian crude
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:29:48 UTC
21:29:48 KST

Why the US can’t cut India off from Russian crude
India will not cut off Russian crude supplies even if the current US push for it to take in more Venezuelan oil to cool global fuel prices masks the larger goal of weakening New Delhi’s energy ties with Moscow.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in Mumbai on Tuesday that India diversifying its energy supplies is a “smart thing to do.”
Some analysts see a hidden geopolitical and economic goal behind those words and Rubio’s push for Indian conglomerate Reliance to buy and refine more Venezuelan oil.
“A key US goal is to weaken the Indo-Russian relationship by steering India farther away from Russian crude,” geopolitical analyst Brahma Chellaney posted on X on Thursday.
“Washington’s underlying diplomatic objective is to get India to substitute Russian oil with US crude and US-controlled Venezuelan oil.”
Washington imposed an additional 25% tariff on Indian goods in August 2025 to pressure New Delhi over its Russian oil purchases, arguing that Moscow’s energy revenues were helping finance its military in the Ukraine conflict. The penalty was withdrawn in February this year.
Last week, US President Donald Trump also waived separate sanctions and steep tariffs targeting major buyers of Russian energy under a recently passed law, citing ongoing US efforts to negotiate an end to the Ukraine conflict.
During his Indian tour, Rubio sought to get India to buy more U.S. energy as well as more oil from Venezuela, whose export revenues are directly deposited into an account controlled by the U.S. Treasury, with Washington determining when, how much and for what purposes the funds are released. Rubio wants the world’s largest oil-refining complex in Jamnagar to process more Venezuelan crude. Washington appears not to be content with India’s rapid emergence since May as a top global buyer of U.S.-sourced and U.S.-controlled energy supplies. The U.S. has already become India’s largest supplier of both liquefied natural gas (LNG) and liquefied petroleum gas (LPG). At Washington’s urging, India has also become the largest destination for Venezuelan oil exports. A key U.S. goal is to weaken the Indo-Russian relationship by steering India farther away from Russian crude. While Rubio framed India’s efforts to diversify its energy portfolio as a “smart thing to do,” Washington’s underlying diplomatic objective is to get India to substitute Russian oil with U.S. crude and U.S.-controlled Venezuelan oil.
— Dr. Brahma Chellaney (@Chellaney) October 21, 2026
“What America is trying to do is gain greater control over the international oil market,” Jindal School of International Affairs adjunct professor and former Jawaharlal Nehru University professor, Anuradha Mitra Chenoy, told RT.
“India will continue purchasing Russian oil,” she added.
Russia remains India’s largest oil supplier amid global energy disruptions. Russian crude made up more than half of India’s oil purchases in July, although the share fell to 33.5% in September as Middle Eastern supplies recovered and competition from China intensified, Reuters reported.
The scale of available supplies in the global market makes replacing Russian oil difficult, especially for a country such as India, Chenoy explained. The world’s most populous nation imports more than 85% of its energy.
“Venezuela alone cannot provide all the alternatives,” Chenoy said. “There are only a limited number of major sources available internationally, and Russia remains one of the most important suppliers.”
Venezuela produced approximately 1.16 million barrels per day of crude in September, compared with Russia’s 8.43 million, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA). India’s Russian imports alone exceeded Venezuela’s entire output that month.
India, looking to widen its crude basket amid the global uncertainty, has already expanded Venezuelan purchases substantially. New Delhi’s Venezuelan imports surged from $255 million in all of FY2026 ended March, to $3.6 billion in the April-August period this year, data shared by the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI) think tank showed.
India is a fast-growing major economy and one of the few bright spots amid the macroeconomic headwinds blowing across the world. The IMF forecasts it to grow at 7% this year and next.
Sustaining that growth depends heavily on the availability and affordability of energy, Chenoy pointed out. “India cannot simply abandon Russian oil because Washington wants it to.”
Why Venezuelan oil cannot easily replace Russian crude
Venezuela’s Merey grade is being offered at around $25 per barrel below benchmark Brent, but that cost advantage disappears when the $35-a-barrel freight to India’s west coast is added in, energy analyst Natalia Katona told the Indian Express.
The discounts on Russian crude have also narrowed and freight costs risen, making its delivered price comparable to some Middle Eastern grades, particularly Iraqi oil, reports said.
Still, it would be tough for Venezuelan oil to compete with Russian crude, let alone replace it for Indian buyers, because of the limited production, higher cost, and specialized equipment needed to refine the heavy grade.
Reliance’s Jamnagar complex, which can process around 1.4 million barrels daily, is among the refineries equipped to handle the Venezuelan grade.
From the American perspective, Merey has one advantage that likely prompted Rubio to rush to India amid higher fuel prices back home: it can produce a higher volume of diesel.
However, that is not a great reason for India to replace Russian crude with Merey.
The sanctions that were levied on Venezuela by Washington – before US forces kidnapped Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January – had forced India to stop buying oil from the South American country and froze billions of dollars in Indian investments in oil fields there.
“India must consider whether another shift in US policy could again put its investments and earnings at risk,” said GTRI founder Ajay Srivastava.
The time-tested and deep friendship between India and Russia must also be considered.
Chenoy pointed out that there is a broad consensus across Indian society and politics about the friendship with Russia. “India’s relationship with Russia has been among its most stable international relationships for decades,” she said.
Any designs the US has on India-Russia ties are bound to fail because of that one reason alone.

Japanese writer Ryu Murakami dies at 74
Japanese writer Ryu Murakami died on October 17, 2026, at the age of 74, according to a notice released by GENTOSHA publishing house on October 23, Qazinform News Agency reports.
Murakami made his literary debut in 1976 with Almost Transparent Blue, which won the Gunzo Prize for New Writers and the prestigious Akutagawa Prize. The novel became a bestseller, selling approximately 3.5 million copies.
His other notable works include Coin Locker Babies, In the Miso Soup and Kyoko. His writing explored social issues and the darker aspects of contemporary society, earning recognition in Japan and internationally.
For around 20 years, Murakami also served as the principal interviewer on the economic talk show Kanburia Kyuden (Canbria Palace).
His funeral was held privately, with only family members in attendance, in accordance with the family's wishes.

China earmarks 80 mln yuan for Xizang quake relief, recovery efforts
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:28:43 CST
21:28:43 KST

A villager receives a folding bed at a temporary resettlement site of an earthquake-hit village in Maru Township of Baqen County, Nagqu City, southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, Oct. 23, 2026. China has allocated 50 million yuan (about 7.5 million U.S. dollars) in emergency disaster relief funds and earmarked another 30 million yuan for recovery efforts following a 7.0-magnitude earthquake in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region. The earthquake struck Baqen County of the city of Nagqu at 10:33 p.m. on Thursday, leaving 16 people dead and 54 injured. (Xinhua/Tenzin Nyida)
BEIJING, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- China has allocated 50 million yuan (about 7.5 million U.S. dollars) in emergency disaster relief funds and earmarked another 30 million yuan for recovery efforts following a 7.0-magnitude earthquake in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region.
The earthquake struck Baqen County of the city of Nagqu at 10:33 p.m. on Thursday, leaving 16 people dead and 54 injured.
The Ministry of Finance and the Ministry of Emergency Management jointly allocated 50 million yuan to support rescue operations and assistance to affected residents, while the National Development and Reform Commission earmarked the additional 30 million yuan from the central budget to help restore damaged infrastructure and public service facilities.
The country has upgraded its national earthquake emergency response from Level IV to Level III.
On Friday afternoon, the emergency management ministry, in a separate statement, also announced an upgrade of the national natural disaster relief response to Level III, saying that additional joint working groups were dispatched to disaster areas to guide relief efforts.
It said that on top of the 5,000 relief items previously allocated by the central government, an additional 5,000 central relief items, including tents, coats and folding beds were allocated.
By coordinating efforts with other relief agencies and companies, the ministry said it has also promptly allocated 43,000 other relief items, including mobile toilets, heating stoves, food and fuel, to ensure that affected people are properly resettled.
China's national comprehensive fire and rescue force has dispatched a total of 350 rescuers and 83 vehicles for rescue operations. The emergency management ministry has guided Xizang's emergency management department in arranging for Wing Loong drone deployment to the quake-hit area for disaster reconnaissance.
As of 6:30 a.m. on Friday, 120 rescuers and 27 vehicles had arrived in the quake-hit area, while the remaining 230 rescuers and 56 vehicles from the Xizang fire and rescue corps were en route as reinforcements, having all entered Nagqu's administrative area.
The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology said it has worked swiftly to organize local telecom operators to carry out emergency repair and restoration work on affected communications facilities.
As of 10:30 a.m. Friday, all of the 628 base stations that went out of service due to the quake in the city of Nagqu have been restored, it said. "At present, emergency command communications at all levels of government are unimpeded, and public communications services are functioning normally."
Earlier, as of 4:30 a.m. on Friday, authorities had mobilized relief supplies at the central, regional, municipal and county levels, and delivered them in batches to the affected area.
These supplies included 1,000 prefabricated housing units, 3,239 tents, 2,821 folding beds and 4,280 quilts, among other essentials. ■

ALMATY, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- The Monetary Policy Committee of the National Bank of Kazakhstan on Friday lowered the base rate to 15.75 percent per annum, the central bank said in a press release.
Annual inflation in Kazakhstan has declined for 12 consecutive months, reaching 9.3 percent in September. IDF names two soldiers killed in deadly shooting attack near Hebron
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:28:36 UTC
21:28:36 KST

The IDF cleared for publication the names of two soldiers killed in the shooting attack near Hebron: Staff Sgt. Ron Yonatan Roytman, 23, from Ashkelon, a squad commander in the Ari Battalion (775) of the Search and Rescue Brigade, and Sgt. Yuval Shai Svilem, 20, from Hod Hasharon, a combat soldier in the same battalion. Both were killed in the attack at Yehuda Junction.
The IDF said three other people wounded in the attack were also soldiers and that their injuries were classified as minor. The families of the casualties have been notified.
David Roytman, Ron's brother, said: "He was a star. Everyone loved him wherever he went. People always say things like that about someone who has fallen, but he was always number one. He fought to become a combat soldier. He wasn't even supposed to enlist in a combat role. He spent a year volunteering with at-risk youth and was injured while playing soccer. They told him there was no way he could become a combat soldier. He said, 'That's not going to happen.'"
His brother added: "He went through everyone, from junior officers all the way to the chief medical officer, and he managed to become a combat soldier. He was a commander of recruits and went with them to the battalion. He was always dreaming and striving for more. He took every opportunity to serve in the most dangerous areas of Judea and Samaria. That's what he pushed for."
David himself served as a combat soldier in the Combat Engineering Corps, while their older sister served in the Caracal Battalion, a mixed-gender combat unit.
"We're all a family of fighters," David said.
Ron attended the Kadoorie Youth Village boarding school in northern Israel.
"He was someone with a zest for life, someone who loved living. He was my best friend," his brother said.
Staff Sgt. Roytman, 23, will be laid to rest Sunday at 11 a.m. at the military cemetery in Ashkelon.
Hod Hasharon Mayor Amir Kochavi paid tribute to Sgt. Yuval Shai Svilem.
"With profound sorrow and heavy hearts, we received the devastating news that Hod Hasharon resident Sgt. Yuval Shai Svilem had fallen in battle with terrorists at Yehuda Junction," Kochavi wrote.
"Yuval was the son of Sivan and Amnon, a loving brother to Shira and Itamar, a devoted grandson, cousin and beloved friend. He was born and raised in Hod Hasharon.
"The Hod Hasharon municipality and community bow their heads in grief and share in the profound sorrow of our colleagues Amnon and Sivan, their children Shira and Itamar and the entire family."
Two Palestinian terrorists arrived at the scene, got out of a vehicle and opened fire. The gunbattle lasted more than 20 minutes, during which additional forces arrived, including the deputy commander of the Ari Battalion and a company commander from the battalion. The soldiers worked together to flank the terrorists and killed them.
A search of the terrorists' vehicle uncovered a large quantity of ammunition. Authorities believe the attackers had planned a major attack against civilians and intended to reach the main roads before proceeding into Israel's interior.
However, investigators are still examining whether the attackers were part of a cell directed by an outside organization or acted on their own initiative. Because both terrorists were killed, the investigation is continuing in an effort to determine their intended destination.
Magen David Adom paramedics and emergency medical technicians, working alongside an IDF medical team, treated the wounded at the scene before evacuating them to Shaare Zedek and Hadassah Ein Kerem hospitals in Jerusalem.
Ofer Ohana, a medic who arrived Friday morning at the scene of the attack at Yehuda Junction on Route 35, managed to film the exchange of fire while under live fire himself.
"The terrorist keeps shooting. The exchange of fire between the terrorist and our forces is continuing. We can't get the wounded out. There has been active gunfire for more than 20 minutes," he can be heard shouting in the footage.
Meanwhile, a photographer for the French news agency AFP captured footage of the two terrorists reloading their weapons during the exchange of fire and later filmed their bodies lying on the ground after they were killed.
The IDF will examine the AFP photographer's account to determine whether he happened upon the scene by chance or had received advance information about the attack.
AFP categorically denies that the photographer who captured images of the terrorists in the West Bank had any prior knowledge of the attack, insisting that he has not even been questioned by security forces.
Moshe Butavia, Kiryat Arba's security chief, took part in the gunbattle with the terrorists.
"We received a report of a shooting attack targeting a military force on Route 35, with casualties. Security forces from the area rushed to the scene, including me," Butavia told ynet. "The terrorists arrived in a vehicle, stopped at a spot where they couldn't be seen, quickly got out and opened fire."
He added: "In the morning, residents are traveling along the road, including buses taking students to schools in Kiryat Arba. I arrived at the scene about 15 minutes after the incident began. When I got there, I joined the fighting. Two terrorists were firing from an elevated position, and we engaged them for about 20 minutes until a force commanded by the sector's deputy battalion commander killed them."
Describing the scene, Butavia said: "The terrorists arrived in a decommissioned vehicle with yellow Israeli license plates. The soldiers at the scene prevented the attack from spreading to the main road and endangering passing motorists. That prevented a much greater disaster."
Butavia praised the security forces, saying: "The army works hard every night, carrying out numerous operations to maintain residents' security and protect the roads and communities. We must remain vigilant."
IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir praised the soldiers of the Home Front Command's Ari Battalion who killed the two Palestinian terrorists in the shooting attack near Hebron.
"The soldiers' swift actions prevented an even more serious attack and additional casualties among civilians and security forces," Zamir said during a situational assessment at the IDF's Judea Brigade headquarters.
Following the attack, Israeli forces imposed a closure on Hebron and Halhul, prohibiting entry to and exit from both cities.
At the same time, the military implemented a procedure known as "Gray Bolt" throughout Central Command, under which Palestinian vehicles entering main roads are subjected to security checks. The measures also apply to the Jenin, Nablus and Jericho areas as part of efforts to prevent further attacks.
Security forces began extensive searches, engineering operations and mapping the homes of the attackers, Hamouda al-Jaaba, 27, and Firas al-Jaaba, 27, both from Hebron. The two belonged to the same extended family and lived near each other.
As part of the investigation, authorities are expected to make arrests among people connected to the attackers while examining possible links to other individuals or organizations.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who visited the scene with Defense Minister Israel Katz, said: "We warned several weeks ago about attempts by our enemies to harm us, our civilians and our soldiers ahead of the elections. That is what they tried to do here. IDF soldiers stopped them with their own bodies and were also hit. The soldiers not only stopped the terrorists but also charged at them heroically and killed them."
Netanyahu added: "First, we will act to demolish this place and completely transform it. But we will also do something that has not been done until now. We are going to implement the successful, aggressive model we used in the refugee camps, which are effectively terrorist strongholds.
"That is exactly what we will do here, in a neighborhood of Hebron from which the terrorists came. We will evacuate the residents, go house to house, remove the weapons and deal with and destroy all terrorist infrastructure."
The Home Front Command's Ari Battalion was established over the past year in response to the need to increase the number of combat troops deployed across various operational sectors, while also providing additional forces for missions on the home front. It is the fifth battalion in the IDF's Search and Rescue Brigade.
Shortly after the battalion's first company completed its operational training, the unit was placed on rescue alert as part of Operation Roaring Lion to provide support in northern Israel.
Once its formation was complete, the battalion joined the brigade's other battalions conducting routine operations in the IDF's Judea and Samaria Division.
Over the past week, the battalion's soldiers began their first operational deployment after completing several months of initial training, including specialized instruction for the unit's combat soldiers.
The battalion commander, Lt. Col. L., said Friday morning: "The battalion's soldiers acted professionally and were deployed effectively throughout the area as part of the effort to protect the residents of the State of Israel."
He added: "Already during their first operational deployment, the battalion's soldiers demonstrated the importance of their mission and their operational readiness. The soldiers maintained a high level of alertness and operational readiness, engaged the enemy and acted swiftly and decisively to neutralize the threat. They prevented harm to civilians, protected the population and successfully completed their mission.
"We will continue to operate responsibly and remain vigilant as part of our mission to defend Israel's residents."

Greek parliament approves social media ban for under-15s from January
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:28:36 CST
21:28:36 KST

ATHENS, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- The Greek parliament has approved legislation banning children under 15 from accessing social media from Jan. 1, 2027, Greek media reported Friday.
The legislation requires social media platforms to implement age-verification measures to ensure compliance. Companies that fail to meet the requirements could face fines of up to 6 percent of their global annual turnover.
Addressing parliament ahead of the vote on Thursday evening, Digital Governance and Artificial Intelligence Minister Dimitris Papastergiou described the measure as a necessary step that is compatible with the European Union's (EU) existing regulatory framework.
"It would have been very easy to do absolutely nothing today and wait for the perfect European law. But the challenge is here. Children are sinking into the internet every day, and I believe a responsible government must do what it is obliged to do," he said.
Minister of State Akis Skertsos said technology should be regulated in ways that give children greater freedom to grow up safely.
Meanwhile, Health Minister Adonis Georgiadis described digital addiction as a public health challenge. Excessive use of social media can negatively affect children's sleep, concentration, social relationships and psychological development, he said.
The legislation forms part of broader government efforts to protect children from harmful online content, cyberbullying and platform features that encourage excessive use.
Greece aims to become the first EU member state to introduce such a ban, the government has said.
The French parliament passed legislation on July 21 aimed at protecting minors from the risks associated with social media use. However, the French Constitutional Council ruled on Aug. 14 that the key provision banning under-15s from accessing social media was unconstitutional. ■

CANBERRA, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Australia's health care and social assistance sector has become the country's largest industry in current-price terms, generating 265.2 billion Australian dollars (about 172 billion U.S. dollars) in gross value added in 2025-26, new data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics showed on Friday.
The sector accounted for 9.6 percent of Australia's total economic activity and was also the country's largest employer, with 2.58 million jobs, or 15.8 percent of total employment.
The ABS said the latest estimates incorporated more detailed industry surveys and administrative data, allowing it to better measure market-based services such as private health care, aged care and disability services.
The revised methodology lifted the sector's estimated economic value by 13.9 billion Australian dollars for 2023-24 compared with previous estimates.
In real terms, the sector has more than tripled in size over the past three decades. ■
