====================================================================================================

Economic Watch: Chinese automakers shift gears in Brazil with local production push
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:27:58 CST
21:27:58 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- From assembly lines in northeastern Brazil to hybrid engines tailored to the country's ethanol-rich fuel market, Chinese automakers are putting more of their manufacturing and innovation on the ground, moving beyond vehicle exports as they deepen their presence in Latin America's largest economy.
The growing local manufacturing presence is expected to gradually reshape Chinese automakers' export strategies in Brazil and open up new opportunities for industrial cooperation, Cui Dongshu, secretary-general of the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA), told Xinhua.
According to CPCA data, China exported 337,104 new energy vehicles (NEV) to Brazil in the first eight months of 2026, up 159.4 percent year on year, making the South American country the largest destination for Chinese NEV exports.
The growth comes amid expanding demand for electrified vehicles in Brazil. Battery electric vehicle registrations rose 172.3 percent year on year to 22,246 units in September, according to the Brazilian Electric Vehicle Association.
Cui attributed the appeal of Chinese NEVs in Brazil partly to their competitive pricing and diverse product offerings, ranging from battery electric models for urban commuting to plug-in hybrids suited to longer journeys. He noted that such vehicles could meet the needs of Brazilian consumers who value affordability, driving range and lower operating costs, particularly as public charging infrastructure remains underdeveloped.
Brazil has also been pursuing policies to strengthen its domestic automotive industry. Its Green Mobility and Innovation Program, known as Mover, encourages investment and technological innovation.
Against this broader backdrop, Chinese automakers are expanding their local manufacturing presence. In June, BYD began testing the welding, assembly and calibration of dashboard crossbeams at its plant in Camacari, in northeastern Brazil's Bahia state, replacing a process in which the parts previously arrived fully assembled, according to the state government. BYD aims to produce or source more than half of its vehicle components locally in Brazil by January 2027.
By September, the plant had more than 8,000 direct employees, making BYD the second-largest industrial employer in Bahia state, according to the company.
Great Wall Motor (GWM) is also expanding its manufacturing operations in Brazil. In August, the company said its plant in Iracemapolis, Sao Paulo state, had produced more than 15,000 vehicles in the first eight months of 2026 and employed over 1,800 workers. The automaker is also working with Brazilian suppliers to increase the use of locally made components.
Beyond local manufacturing, Chinese automakers are also adapting their technologies to Brazil's unique energy landscape, where ethanol is widely used as an automotive fuel.
BYD brought together more than 100 Chinese and Brazilian engineers who spent two years developing a plug-in hybrid system compatible with both gasoline and ethanol. The technology is used in BYD's Song Pro, a plug-in hybrid SUV launched in Brazil in August. The model can run on gasoline or ethanol.
GWM has made similar adaptations for the Brazilian market. In June, the company introduced locally produced hybrid vehicles that can run on gasoline or ethanol. The technology, developed with Brazilian engineers, underwent more than 400,000 km of testing under local driving conditions.
Cui said Brazil's established automotive industry offers considerable scope for cooperation with Chinese automakers. Brazilian suppliers have strengths in areas such as vehicle bodies, chassis and interiors, while Chinese automakers can provide key NEV components. Such complementary strengths could pave the way for closer cooperation in local sourcing, joint research on technologies adapted to Brazilian conditions, and supply chain development, Cui added.
"This is a phased transition: first exporting vehicle kits and equipment, then encouraging auto parts suppliers to make greenfield investments or establish joint ventures, creating a model in which automakers lead the overseas expansion of entire industrial supply chains," Cui said.
In March, BYD announced plans to invest 300 million Brazilian reals (about 59.4 million U.S. dollars) in an automotive research and testing center in Rio de Janeiro, where it plans to develop, test and validate vehicle technologies.
The Bahia state government also held talks with China's Minth Group in June, an automotive components supplier, to explore a possible investment in the state, with discussions focusing on opportunities created by BYD's local production.
Aecio Moreira, acting secretary of economic development of Bahia state, said BYD's investment had opened new opportunities to attract automotive suppliers and strengthen the state's auto manufacturing supply chain. ■

China strengthens protection for growing snow leopard population
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
20:27:46 CST
21:27:46 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- China's snow leopard population has doubled to about 5,000 from around 2,500 in 2013, reflecting progress in protecting the species and its habitat.
The latest figures were released by the National Forestry and Grassland Administration on Friday on the occasion of the International Day of the Snow Leopard which falls on Oct. 23.
Snow leopards typically inhabit rugged terrain at elevations of 3,000 to 5,000 meters and serve as an important indicator of the health of high-altitude mountain ecosystems. The species is classified as "vulnerable" on the International Union for Conservation of Nature Red List of Threatened Species and receives the highest level of wildlife protection in China.
China has the world's largest snow leopard population and protects more than 60 percent of the species' global habitat, according to the administration. Its habitat covers about 2.08 million square kilometers across eight provincial-level regions.
China has taken a systematic approach to snow leopard conservation since 2013. Its protection network includes two national parks and 78 other important protected areas in key snow leopard habitats. More than 800,000 square kilometers of habitat are under strict protection, while nearly 40 percent of the species' potential habitat is under standardized management.
The country is also using technologies such as infrared cameras and DNA analysis of fecal samples to monitor snow leopard populations, track their movements and study their breeding activity.
Sustained conservation efforts have improved snow leopard habitat quality and ecosystem integrity, alongside growth in the population and its reproductive vitality, the administration said.
In April, infrared cameras in the Helan Mountains in northwest China captured a reintroduced female snow leopard with her cub, marking the first time a snow leopard reintroduction project worldwide has resulted in cubs being born and successfully raised in the wild.
Native to the Helan Mountains, snow leopards disappeared from the area in the 1950s due to habitat destruction and human disturbance. To restore the population, eight snow leopards have been introduced to the mountains so far. Several snow leopards, including those arriving naturally, have since established territories and hunt independently.
Signs of the species' presence are also emerging elsewhere. In Muli County of Liangshan Yi Autonomous Prefecture, southwest China's Sichuan Province, footage recorded this year confirmed the first sighting of a snow leopard in the prefecture, extending the known southeastern edge of the species' range, the administration said.
Looking ahead, China will focus on improving connectivity between habitats, protecting genetic diversity and refining measures to prevent and address human-wildlife conflict to sustain snow leopard population recovery, the administration said. ■

====================================================================================================

Countering China’s web of spies and proxies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:26:26 UTC
21:26:26 KST

After a car struck comedian Huang Yi-hao (黃逸豪) while he rode a scooter near his home in New Taipei City on Sept. 11, prosecutors said the collision was staged and a person in China identified only as “K” paid five Taiwanese men NT$450,000 (US$13,900) to seriously injure him.
They did so to allegedly prevent him from performing on Sept. 20 after he mocked Chinese leader Xi Jinping. The case illustrates a broader danger.
Beijing’s campaign against Taiwan increasingly relies not only on military pressure but on covert networks that exploit an open society: surveillance, influence operations, recruitment, criminal facilitation and transnational repression. Taiwan should treat these sub-threshold threats with the same seriousness as a conventional military attack.
Chinese Communist Party organs and intelligence services operate through layers of intermediaries. The United Front Work Department helps cultivate political, religious, business and diaspora contacts, while the Ministry of State Security and Ministry of Public Security conduct intelligence, security and repression operations.
These agencies do not merely gather information. They seek local collaborators who can map communities, move money, monitor critics and amplify divisions.
Taiwan’s counterintelligence agencies have described a spectrum of activity. Professional intelligence officers operating under nonofficial cover, “white glove” intermediaries who conceal funding and instructions, talent spotters who identify vulnerable targets, local collaborators who provide logistics or amplify narratives, and informants who pass along unclassified but useful information. Some networks also use criminal groups for intimidation or violence.
Executive security and coercion
The Huang case fits this pattern. Prosecutors said the alleged organizer used local proxies to track Huang with a GPS device, collect personal information and stage the collision. It was transnational repression carried out through deniable local intermediaries.
Beijing also seeks leverage over Taiwan’s leadership. In October, the FBI arrested Wanying “Heather” Zhang, a California real estate agent, at Los Angeles International Airport on charges that she acted as an unregistered agent of China.
Federal prosecutors allege that Zhang and another person traveled to the Seattle area in September 2025, surveilled the home of Lai Ting-yu (賴廷與), the adult son of President Lai Ching-te (賴清德). They allegedly sent photographs, video and vehicle license-plate information to a Chinese government official.
The case remains pending, and the allegations have not been tested at trial. But if proven, they would show how Chinese intelligence can extend pressure beyond Taiwan’s borders and seek information useful for coercion.
In August, New Taipei District Court sentenced Hsu Chun-ying (徐春鶯), a Taiwan-based advocate for spouses born in China, to seven years in prison. The court found that she conspired with Chinese officials and proxies to influence Taiwanese politics and illegally transferred NT$24.5 million (US$760,000) outside regular banking channels.
The case shows how foreign-linked funding can enter domestic politics through informal financial channels. It does not prove that every recipient of such money knowingly acted as a Chinese agent, but it demonstrates why Taiwan needs stronger transparency rules for political financing, lobbying and cross-border money flows.
Money and legislative pressure
Beijing also benefits when Taiwan’s own democratic processes delay defense spending. Opposition lawmakers have repeatedly delayed or altered parts of the defense budget.
Critics argue that some changes have weakened operational readiness, while supporters describe them as legitimate legislative oversight. The more defensible point is that Beijing has an interest in exploiting political division, and Taiwan’s parties should avoid actions that create avoidable gaps in defense readiness.
Frontline agencies have also been penetrated. Chuang Tsung-hui (莊宗輝), former director of the duty command center of the Coast Guard Administration’s Kinmen-Matsu-Penghu Branch, was detained in May 2025 and indicted in August 2025 on national security and corruption charges. Authorities said he leaked duty rosters, personnel files, vessel deployment schedules and radar-related data to Chinese officials in exchange for bribes. He was convicted in March.
Such leaks can help Beijing understand patrol patterns, radar coverage and deployment routines. In a blockade or quarantine scenario, that intelligence could reduce Taiwan’s ability to detect and respond to coercive maritime activity.
Taiwan has also confronted attempted defections. Prosecutors said an Army lieutenant colonel surnamed Hsieh (謝) was recruited through a retired officer and offered NT$488 million to fly a CH-47 Chinook helicopter to a Chinese naval vessel near the median line of the Taiwan Strait.
The plot was not merely about stealing an aircraft. A successful defection could have provided China with a Western-made heavy-lift helicopter and delivered a psychological blow to Taiwan’s military and public.
Technology and academia
China also targets Taiwan’s semiconductor sector and universities. Taiwanese investigations have accused Chinese-linked entities of using shell companies and recruitment schemes to obtain semiconductor expertise and proprietary information.
The policy concern is straightforward: Taiwan’s “silicon shield” depends not only on fabrication capacity but on the protection of engineers, intellectual property and supply-chain knowledge.
Academic exchanges also create exposure. The 2017 case involving Zhou Hongxu (周泓旭), a Chinese national who studied at National Chengchi University and was later convicted of espionage, showed how student or professional cover can be used to identify and approach politically connected targets.
Taiwan should preserve academic openness while applying consistent security screening, transparency requirements and counterintelligence awareness to high-risk exchanges.
Taiwan cannot meet this challenge by treating every Chinese national, Taiwanese businessperson, temple group or China-born spouse as a spy. Such an approach would damage social cohesion and play into Beijing’s strategy of division.
Instead, Taiwan should:
- Prosecute coercion, espionage, illegal political financing and transnational repression firmly and impartially
- Require greater disclosure of foreign funding in political campaigns, lobbying, civil society organizations and media
- Harden protection for political figures, military personnel, Coast Guard and other frontline agencies
- Improve counterintelligence training for universities, technology firms and local governments without stigmatizing entire communities
- Treat cognitive warfare and influence operations as national-security threats, while protecting free speech and due process
The Huang Yi-hao case is a warning. Beijing does not need to invade Taiwan to weaken it. It can use money, intermediaries, intimidation and information operations to make Taiwan more fearful, divided and difficult to govern. The response must be firm, lawful and democratic.
Guermantes Lailari is a retired US Air Force Foreign Area officer who holds advanced degrees in international relations and strategic intelligence.

Kindergarten shelters reserved exclusively for education participants – Cabinet
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:25:49 EEST
21:25:49 KST

The Cabinet of Ministers has regulated the use of civil protection shelters at kindergartens and general secondary education institutions by people other than participants in the educational process.
Under Resolution No. 1288 of October 15, the government amended the procedure for establishing and maintaining the civil protection shelter fund.
In particular, in accordance with the law on preschool education, shelters at preschool institutions are to be used exclusively to protect participants in the educational process.
School shelters are also available exclusively to participants in the educational process while in-person classes are being held, the resolution says.
At the same time, school shelters may be used to accommodate both participants in the educational process and other members of the public only by decision of local executive authorities or local self-government bodies, and in accordance with procedures established by the institution's owner or operator.
If a decision is made to use a school shelter for both students and other members of the public, the operator must ensure that teachers, a psychologist if available, and police or security personnel if available remain with the children throughout the shelter period. It must also separate the areas occupied by students and other people where possible, minimize or eliminate overlapping routes to and from the shelter, provide separate functioning toilets, and make available a separate room or designated area for children with special educational needs to help regulate their emotional state and provide psychological support, as well as psychological, pedagogical and developmental services. The operator must also ensure the safety of all participants in the educational process.

Expert: Estonian party ratings could shift as election campaigning ramps up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:24:00 UTC
21:24:00 KST

Expert: Estonian party ratings could shift as election campaigning ramps up
The Center Party and Social Democrats topped Emor's October poll as long-time leader Isamaa slipped, with voters' party loyalties still far from firm, said expert Aivar Voog.
Voog, a polling expert at Emor, told ERR on Friday that party ratings had remained largely unchanged over the last year, but shifted more sharply in recent months as parties ramp up campaigning ahead of the March 2027 Riigikogu elections.
He noted that new members may also be influencing support.
Isamaa had long led the rankings, but its supporters' loyalty was never particularly firm, Voog said, commenting on the party's slide to third place. "They have a significant mass of incidental [voters] and that has started to redistribute itself," he added.
He expects a clearer picture to emerge early next year, as some parties begin to stand out and attract undecided voters.
Longtime Foreign Ministry secretary general and security expert Jonatan Vseviov announced Thursday that he is joining the Social Democratic Party (SDE) and intends to run next spring as their candidate for prime minister. His move could affect the party's next poll result.
"He's certainly well known among opinion leaders and educated people, but little known to the wider electorate," Voog said, adding that while Vseviov has strong foreign and security policy chops, he still needs to prove himself on economic issues.
Mobilizing support
The Social Democrats, previously most popular among younger voters, are now also the top choice among middle-aged voters, narrowly overtaking Isamaa among ethnic Estonians. Voog said this could help offset a weakness, as younger supporters are less likely to vote than middle-aged voters.
Voog said the Conservative People's Party of Estonia (EKRE) may also struggle to mobilize its supporters in March, as its typical supporter is a man over 60 who lives outside the capital.
EKRE supporters tend to rely on alternative media and the party's own channels, making them less susceptible to major media outlet influence and potentially more loyal.
Emor's latest poll put the party above 13 percent, but Voog said it remains unclear whether EKRE can not just broaden its appeal, but also convert support into votes at the ballot box.
Fight for voters
Voog said right-leaning voters in Estonia may split between Isamaa, EKRE, the Reform Party and Parempoolsed, while more conservative voters may choose between EKRE, Isamaa and the Center Party, setting several major parties up to compete for the same voters.
The Social Democrats, meanwhile, might benefit from voters abandoning the poorly rated Eesti 200, though some may instead shift their support to the Reform Party.
Voog said more conservative voters tend to be less active and turn out to vote at lower rates than those with more liberal views. Less active voters tend to be less educated and find it harder to decide whom to vote for, he explained, adding that they are also likely to consume less media.
While liberal voters dominated the 2023 Riigikogu elections, conservative forces had the upper hand in 2019, and Voog expects conservative parties will likely come out on top again next spring.

Divers exploring oldest warship off Sweden find "new clues"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:23:32 UTC
21:23:32 KST

Divers exploring oldest warship found off Sweden find "new clues"
Bubbles rise through the murky green water as divers tenderly explore a rare 15th-century shipwreck off Stockholm's coast, believed to be the oldest warship found off Sweden.
"It's a very big ship, it was around 40-45 meters when it sailed probably," project leader and marine archaeologist Hakan Altrock from Sweden's Museum of Wrecks said, overseeing the dives down to the skeletal remains of what is known as Vrak 5, or Shipwreck 5, on a cool October day.
Located off Haringe Castle south of Stockholm, the vessel is thought to be the oldest warship found off Sweden or Denmark, which were joined in a union with Norway in the 15th century.
First discovered in the late 1800s, the shipwreck is one of five lying on the seabed in the Landfjarden sound, most of which have been dated to the 1600s and 1700s.
But in February 2025, researchers were able to date Vrak 5 to the 1480s, or possibly even the 1460s.
"It's not possible to say if it is Swedish, it could also be Danish," Altrock said, noting that the timber used to build it comes from the area that is now southeastern Sweden.
"This is the first example of a ship in the Baltic that has been built with the carvel technique... in Scandinavia that we know of," he said.
He was referring to a boat-building technique where hull planks are laid edge-to-edge rather than overlapping, which made it possible to build bigger and sturdier vessels — necessary with the advent of heavy cannons on ships.
Researchers have produced a 3D scan of the wreck, which can be seen here.
"This is the most historically interesting wreck in the area," Altrock said. "Every time we can examine part of it, we have the opportunity to find new clues."
Sunk in battle?
Marine archaeologists excavated the wreck this week in order to better document it, find out more about how it was built, and as part of a special project about food on board.
Archaeologists aim to "search for the ship's kitchen and gain new clues about how the ship was built and sank," the museum said in a statement.
Among other things, they used special pumps to vacuum up sediment and expose parts of the construction.
Divers found bricks that suggested they had found the galley, in addition to parts of the ship's rigging.
Matilda Jarl, a PhD student in marine archaeology also at the site, said the crew would have eaten fish, meat and porridge on board.
"A lot of the food would be boiled. So there would be a lot of pottage, which is basically anything that is cooked in a pot," she said.
"With the food they would also drink beer. The people with a higher status on board would be drinking wine also, but the general crew would be drinking beer instead of water as it kept better," she added.
It is not yet known why the ship sank where it did.
Altrock said rumors from when the wreck was found in the 19th century referred to a fire on board.
"Perhaps it was sunk when they (the Danes) attacked the Haringe Castle behind us in 1501," he said. "That's one theory."
"Maybe we'll find traces of where it burned. We'll see."
Other shipwrecks found in region
Several other wrecks and relics have been found in the region recently.
In April, officials announced that a 16th century shipwreck providing "unique historical and archaeological information" had been discovered off Sweden's southeastern coast. The ship is believed to have been built in the late 1500s, which would make it older than Sweden's iconic 17th century warship "Vasa" on display in Stockholm after being salvaged in the 1960s. The navy vessel HMS Belos found the wreck during a military exercise.
In February, a Swedish Navy shipwreck buried underwater in central Stockholm for 400 years became visible due to unusually low Baltic Sea levels.
In July 2024, a team of divers discovered a massive haul of champagne and wine on a shipwreck on the floor of the Baltic Sea off Sweden. The precious cargo was later declared off limits by the government.
That same year, researchers exploring an ancient shipwreck off the coast of Sweden discovered centuries-old artifacts, including a weapons chest and pieces of armor.

Denmark to buy cheap U.S. cruise missile built in Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:22:11 UTC
21:22:11 KST

- Denmark will buy Covenant’s ground-launched Anthem cruise missiles, to be built in Leipzig, Germany, alongside Kongsberg Joint Strike Missiles for its F-35s.
- Germany’s defense ministry is also in talks with Covenant as the Bundeswehr evaluates low-cost cruise missiles for its own long-range strike needs.
Denmark will buy Anthem ground-launched cruise missiles from U.S. defense company Covenant Industries, giving the Danish military its first land-based option for striking targets deep inside enemy territory, the Danish Ministry of Defense announced on Oct. 22, 2026.
The ministry said the purchase is meant to strengthen Denmark’s national and collective deterrence, describing the new missiles as long-range precision weapons that NATO has asked allies to provide. They use advanced navigation to hit targets accurately over long distances and can both deter an attack and strike back deep inside an enemy’s territory if necessary, and the acquisitions follow a recommendation from Denmark’s chief of defense.
“The acquisitions are a significant step in making Denmark better able to defend itself and carry our share of the burden in NATO, and at the same time we are sending a strong signal that we have the ability to strike back,” said Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus, in remarks translated from Danish.
Officials told reporters at the announcement that the contracts have already been signed, but withheld quantities, prices and delivery dates for security reasons. They said one reason for choosing the weapon was that it can be delivered relatively quickly and at a competitive price, and the Anthem missiles for Denmark will be built in Leipzig, Germany, where Covenant is setting up its European production line.
Anthem is a jet-powered cruise missile designed from the start for low cost and mass production. Covenant says it can carry a 200 kg (440-pound) warhead for precision strikes deep in enemy territory, and the missile reportedly has a range of more than 1,000 km (620 miles), with some media reports putting it as high as 1,500 km (930 miles). The company plans to sell it for a six-figure sum, under $1 million per missile, compared with the several million dollars typically charged for comparable cruise missiles.
Anthem first flew in August 2025, and Covenant says it has since been used in more than 200 tests, including several flight tests with U.S. forces in the United States and abroad, although the missile has not yet been used in combat. Choosing it marks a departure for Denmark, which has traditionally bought proven, production-ready systems for its armed forces.
Covenant opened a 10,000-square-meter (108,000-square-foot) plant in Leipzig earlier this month to build missiles for European NATO allies. Production is set to begin in 2027, with the company planning 1,000 missiles in the first year and 5,000 in 2028, and Covenant aims to source more than 95% of the components for its European version from inside Europe, with the Leipzig facility handling assembly and warheads integrated later at customer locations.
Germany is also studying the missile, and the German defense ministry has said it is in talks with Covenant about closing its own long-range strike gap, although no German order has been publicly confirmed. Lt. Gen. Christian Freuding, the head of the German Army, has confirmed that the Bundeswehr wants to buy new low-cost cruise missiles for mass use and is evaluating two systems already on the market, though he did not name them. Anthem has been reported as one of the candidates, alongside the Flamingo cruise missile from Ukrainian company Fire Point, and Covenant has brought in Andreas Marlow, a retired lieutenant general and former deputy commander of the German Army, as an adviser.
Denmark is pairing Anthem with a second, air-launched weapon, the Joint Strike Missile, built by Norway’s Kongsberg with Raytheon. The stealthy JSM fits inside the internal weapons bays of Denmark’s F-35 fighters, weighs 416 kg (917 pounds) with a 120 kg (265-pound) warhead and has a range of more than 350 km (217 miles). It is derived from Kongsberg’s Naval Strike Missile, which Denmark already operates on its frigates and for coastal defense.
Russian Ambassador to Denmark Vladimir Barbin responded quickly to the announcement, saying Danish policy is built on confrontation and preparation for a possible conflict with Russia, and calling it a dangerous illusion to think precision strike weapons could pose a military threat to a nuclear power.
Denmark’s military planning has traditionally focused on defending its own territory, and the new missiles give it a way to strike targets in an adversary’s rear areas for the first time. With Covenant’s Leipzig line due to start production in 2027, the first Anthem missiles for Denmark are expected to come from that plant.

“We have noted numerous calls from far-left and radical far-left movements,” Nunez told a news conference, adding that the deployment would include elite police units, “around 20” armored vehicles and 15 water cannon vehicles.
Macron, who on Oct. 22 announced that only union demonstrations would be authorised this weekend, was to hold a meeting of his defence council of top ministers and officials and also meet security forces.
He was also set to host for the first time representatives of high school pupils, whose protests over conditions at their schools sparked a movement that has broadened nationwide into a show of anger against the government at the rising cost of living.
The protests have come at a critical moment for France six months ahead of elections to replace Macron, with a new poll underlining far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is the frontrunner and showing her position has been strengthened by the latest events.
Adding to tensions, Le Pen is at the weekend due to host her National Rally (RN) party congress in Orleans, with thousands of supporters expected but local authorities fearing clashes as opponents head to the city.
Macron's government has sought to draw a line between the legitimate demands of protesters and the looting, burning and ransacking that erupted on the sidelines of protests last on Oct. 17.
In a judicial response of unprecedented firmness, courts have already sent 217 people, half of them first-time offenders, to prison over the events on Oct. 17, Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said.
On Oct. 22, Macron called for "the utmost severity" against "acts of delinquency", accusing "ultra-left" groups of having sought to "bring down the republic" last weekend.
Demonstrations in Marseille in the south and Lyon in the southeast have been banned at the weekend, while in Paris protesters will only be allowed to march a limited route between Bastille and Nation squares.
Marseille authorities however reversed a decision to halt all public transport in the city on Oct. 24. But in the capital, leading museums including the Louvre will be closed on Oct. 24 while the Art Basel art fair is being cut short.
"In a country governed by the rule of law, the police have a responsibility both to ensure that protests can take place peacefully and safely and to protect the public from violent disorder," said Eva Cosse, senior Europe researcher at Human Rights Watch, expressing alarm over reports of children being severely injured by crowd-control weapons.
The violence has tarnished the image of France ahead of elections that could be a turning point in its modern history, with the government's debt pile also troubling investors.
A new poll by Harris Interactive for M6/RTL made after the violence showed Le Pen soaring ahead on 33-35 percent in the first round of voting for the presidential elections.
It predicted that hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon was on course to face her in the run-off where Le Pen would emerge as an easy winner on some 70 percent of the vote.

Shelters in schools and kindergartens are no longer for everyone: who will be allowed to take shelter from shelling
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:21:13 EEST
21:21:13 KST

Shelters in schools and kindergartens are no longer for everyone: who will be allowed to take shelter from shelling
Kyiv • UNN
Members of the public will be allowed into school shelters only by decision of the local authorities and under separate safety rules. In kindergartens shelters are intended for participants in the educational process.
Ukraine has clarified the rules for access to shelters located in schools and kindergartens. From now on, people who are not involved in working at these institutions may take shelter there from shelling only by a separate decision of the local authorities and subject to compliance with specified safety requirements.
UNN explains what the new rules provide, who will be able to use school shelters, whether people will be admitted there at night, and where to turn in the event of a refusal.
The Cabinet of Ministers has changed the rules for access to shelters in schools and kindergartens
By Resolution No. 1288 dated October 15, 2026, the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine amended regulations governing the use of civil defense protective structures. The document was officially published on October 21, and all the new provisions entered into force on that date.
The changes concern, in particular, shelters located directly in the buildings of preschool and general secondary education institutions or on their premises. The main principle is that during in-person education, children and employees of educational institutions have priority in using such structures. However, in the case of schools, government officials have nevertheless provided for the possibility of jointly using shelters with other residents of the community.
It should be noted that it would be incorrect to call this provision an entirely new ban on access for the public, as it is portrayed on social media and in some Telegram channels. Restrictions on access by outsiders to shelters at educational institutions during in-person education were already in effect: the relevant provisions were established by Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 1331 dated December 19, 2023. The government's new decision primarily details the procedure for jointly using school shelters, child-safety requirements, and the duties of responsible persons.
Who can take shelter in kindergartens and schools
Separate rules apply to kindergartens in Ukraine. Pursuant to Part Five of Article 52 of the Law of Ukraine "On Preschool Education," protective structures located on the balance sheet or premises of such institutions are used exclusively to protect participants in the educational process. These include kindergarten pupils, educators, teacher assistants, other institution employees, and the pupils' parents. This list is established by Article 18 of the Law of Ukraine "On Preschool Education."
During in-person education, shelters in schools are also intended for participants in the educational process. This primarily refers to students, teaching staff, and other employees. At the same time, Article 52 of the Law of Ukraine "On Education" includes students' parents among the participants in the educational process, whereas each kindergarten regulates their presence separately.
Earlier, the Education Ombudsman's Service explained that parents who were caught by an air raid alert directly at a school have the right to remain in the shelter together with other participants in the educational process. At the same time, the administration must take the capacity of the protective structure into account.
Different conditions will apply to outside citizens, including residents of neighboring buildings. They will be able to use a school shelter in accordance with the established access procedure.
Under what conditions will other citizens be allowed into school shelters
Resolution No. 1288 provides for the possibility of students, institution employees, and other categories of the population being in school shelters simultaneously . However, this requires a separate decision by a local executive authority or local self-government body. In addition, the procedure for using a school shelter is determined by the entity responsible for its maintenance, in particular the founder or head of the educational institution, taking into account the requirements of the relevant military administration.
Before allowing the shelter to be used jointly, it is necessary to assess whether its area, equipment, and access arrangements can ensure adequate protection for everyone. In particular, there must be separate zones for students and other citizens, movement routes, rules of conduct, and a procedure for admitting outsiders. In addition, restrictions on access to other premises of the educational institution must be established. In other words, residents who have been allowed to use the shelter do not thereby acquire the right to move freely around the school.
It is important that the availability of vacant spaces in a school shelter in itself does not mean automatic permission for outsiders. If there is no corresponding decision by the local authorities, access to the shelter for other civilians will be restricted during in-person classes.
How school shelters will operate at night, on weekends, and during holidays
Resolution No. 1288 stipulates that at night, on weekends and public holidays, civilians must also be accompanied into the shelter in the school building (on the school grounds). This may be done by security guards or maintenance workers.
During school holidays, residents of nearby buildings who plan to use the school shelter will also need to take into account the facility’s actual operating schedule and the approved conditions for using the shelter. Therefore, people should find out in advance whether the nearest school shelter operates at night and who is responsible for opening it.
Another important change concerns the curfew. Resolution No. 1288 provides for an exception for people heading to a shelter during an air raid alert or returning from one after the all-clear. However, this exception does not mean a general permission to move around the city during curfew for any other purpose.
How children’s safety will be ensured in shared shelters
One of the main conditions for allowing outsiders into school shelters remains ensuring students’ safety. If the local authorities have permitted schoolchildren and other community residents to stay there simultaneously, the institution’s administration must organize the space so that different categories of visitors are separated as much as possible.
First and foremost, this involves allocating separate areas for people to stay. Where possible, separate rooms may be arranged for students and other civilians. In addition, the routes used by schoolchildren and outsiders to and from the shelter should intersect as little as possible.
Teachers must be present throughout the entire time children remain in the shelter. The involvement of a psychologist and a police officer (or a security service employee, if the school has one) is also предусмотрено.
Particular attention is paid to sanitary conditions. Separate restrooms must be provided for participants in the educational process.
For children with special educational needs, a special room or a separate part of the premises must be arranged where they can receive psychological support and the necessary psychological and pedagogical services. The needs of people with disabilities and other groups with reduced mobility must also be taken into account when organizing access.
How to find out whether the shelter at the nearest school can be used
Information about school shelters available to outsiders must be published on the official web portals of the founders of educational institutions or of the educational institutions themselves.
First of all, people should check the official website of the nearest school, the local council, or the relevant education department. If the necessary information is not available, they can contact the school administration or the local government body directly. It is advisable to clarify not only whether access is possible, but also the specific entrance to the shelter, its operating hours, and the procedure for entering during an alert.
Alternative protective structures can also be found through the "Diia" app. The "Unbreakability" section contains a map of shelters where users can view their locations and plot a route.
What to do if you are not allowed into a school shelter during an air raid alert
If access is denied, first of all it is necessary to find out whether the specific shelter is intended for use by outsiders. If the school is holding in-person classes and the local authorities have not adopted a decision on the shared use of the protective structure, restricting access for outsiders is lawful.
If the shelter has officially been authorized for use by other civilians but is locked or people are refused entry, they can contact the institution’s administration, the entity responsible for the shelter, or the local authorities. They can also report this to the police by calling 102 or to the State Emergency Service by calling 101.
If possible, the shelter’s address, the time of the incident, and the circumstances of the refusal should be recorded. Photo or video materials may help during the further review of the appeal.
When access to a school shelter is impossible during shelling, the nearest available protective structure should be used as quickly as possible. There is no point wasting time arguing at locked doors when there is a threat of a missile strike. If it is impossible to reach an equipped shelter, it is necessary to look for the safest available place in accordance with the recommendations of the State Emergency Service of Ukraine, avoiding windows, glass structures, and other hazardous areas.
We remind you
Earlier, UNN reported that at one of the capital’s schools, people were not allowed into the shelter during an air raid alert.

Are parents in France and Italy liable for damage caused by student protesters?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:18:01 UTC
21:18:01 KST

Are parents in France and Italy liable for damage caused by student protesters?
Parents in Italy could face financial penalties if their children participate in vandalism or looting during protests.
As high school student protests began in France last month, footage soon spread on social media of angry parents dragging their children away from demonstrations.
They may have good reason for doing so as France considers plans to impose fines on those whose children vandalise or damage property following a similar measure introduced this week in Italy.
As young protesters across France were joined by others angry about the rising cost of living and proposed public spending cuts, similar youth-led demonstrations have begun in Italian cities. Many have turned violent with protesters burning barricades, and police accused of using excessive force.
Here’s what we know.
What are the protests in France and Italy about?
In late September, high school students in the northern Paris suburb of Seine-Saint-Denis began protesting about the state of their school buildings and teacher shortages. They were particularly angry about the proposed government budget which includes millions of euros in cuts to public spending.
Students in Paris, and later in other French cities, erected barricades around their schools and caused hundreds of closures during the first week of October.
Later, the protests spread nationwide as public sector workers joined demonstrations to oppose planned pay freezes. Now the protests have widened again, with those angry about the rising cost of living, petrol shortages and fuel prices joining demonstrations which have frequently descended into rioting, looting and arson.
French President Emmanuel Macron said last week that “nothing justifies” violence and that local officials could ban certain street gatherings if deemed necessary. French authorities also announced curfews.
But last Saturday, hundreds of thousands of protesters in France, Italy, Spain, Belgium and Portugal took part in largely uncoordinated demonstrations against rising living costs.
Initially peaceful weekend protests in Milan descended into riots, with groups of mainly young people looting shops, smashing windows and clashing with police. Masked protesters threw stones, paving blocks and other objects at riot police and set fire to barricades made from bar tables.
Riots were also reported in the Italian cities of Bologna and Turin.
Official figures on the expected costs of the damage in both France and Italy have yet to be established.
What has Italy announced?
On Tuesday, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government approved a series of measures in response to the unrest, including sending 500 soldiers to Milan until the end of the year and increasing financial liability on parents whose children were involved in vandalism and looting.
Under new rules, anyone taking part in a group of at least five people and endangering public safety during protests faces up to five years in prison and a maximum fine of 20,000 euros ($22,460).
Protesters aged 14 to 18 can now be subject to administrative detention, even if they have not committed a crime, provided there is evidence that they pose a danger, extending powers that previously applied only to adults.
In part of the decree, which includes the phrase “You break it, you buy it”, Italy also strengthened the law holding parents responsible for criminal damage by their children.
Article 2048 of the civil code already states that parents and guardians are liable for damages caused by the “unlawful act of unemancipated minor children or persons subject to guardianship who live with them. The same provision applies to the foster parent”.
In Italy, authorities may enforce these laws through asset and wage attachments.
The new measure permits the state to directly fine parents or claim damages for any resulting loss against parents’ property or by deducting public subsidies the family receives.
What is the situation in France?
Under article 1242 of the French Civil Code, parents who live with their children and exercise parental authority also have a civil liability for damage that their children cause.
“Parents, in their capacity as holders of parental authority, are by right jointly and severally liable for damage caused by their minor children, except when the latter have been entrusted to a third party by an administrative or judicial decision,” the law states.
Last year, a new law amended article 1242 to strengthen parents’ role during youth justice proceedings. It removed the cohabitation requirement for parents for civil liability to apply.
In France, compensation from parents for damage caused by children can be enforced through civil proceedings, and can include the seizure of assets if not covered by civil liability insurance, which is often tied to housing insurance, subject to the terms of the policy agreement.
On Friday, French radio station RFI reported that a new bill known as “rioters pay” is now also being proposed by the government in response to the violent protests.
The government is scheduled to debate the draft bill on October 27.
If the law is passed, those found responsible for vandalism could be required to pay up to 10,000 euros ($11,200) in compensation. In the case of criminal damage by minors, parents could be held responsible.
A provision to the bill could also introduce collective civil liability, potentially requiring someone in a group responsible for damage to pay, even if they did not cause it themselves, on the same financial terms as those who caused the damage, RFI reported.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu described the legislation as “absolutely essential” to ensure taxpayers do not pay for damage caused by protests.
Where else does this happen?
Several other countries also hold parents financially liable for damages their children cause.
For example, in Sweden, parents or legal guardians may be held financially liable, subject to statutory conditions and limits, for certain injuries or property damage caused by a child who commits a crime.
In the United States, subject to state-specific conditions and limits, laws addressing parental responsibility specify that if a minor intentionally destroys public property, businesses, or vehicles, victims or local government can sue the parents in civil court.

Denmark to ban mink farming in government U-turn
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:17:45 BST
21:17:45 KST

Denmark to ban mink farming in government U-turn
- Published
Mink farming will end in Denmark by August 2029 after the government decided to drop plans to pursue an exemption to an EU-wide ban on the practice.
Denmark was once the largest producer of mink fur in the world, but the industry has declined due to global bans on fur farming, a decline in the fur trade and an earlier outbreak of a Covid strain in the nation's mink population.
The ban is due to come into effect on 7 August next year, and is followed by a two-year transition period to phase out the practice.
Danish Nature Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen said the government had chosen animal welfare.
"A business should not continue just because it has existed for a long time. It should also make sense for society, for the economy and for the animals," he said.
The Danish government had initially sought an exemption for its mink industry when the EU added the mammal to its list of invasive species in 2025, prohibiting people from keeping them.
However, the current coalition government, elected in June, reversed this decision and decided not to proceed with the application on Friday.
Social Democrat MP Brigitte Vind said it was "a good day for animal welfare".
"It is absolutely the right decision not to apply for a special scheme for mink breeding in Denmark," she said.
The Danish Mink Association, which represents breeders, has been approached for comment.
Denmark is one of the few European countries to still produce mink fur, one of the more common pelts used in making fur garments.
However, its production has slipped behind that of other countries, such as Poland and China, in recent years.
The industry faced a crisis during the coronavirus pandemic, when the government ordered a mass cull of mink after a mutated strain of Covid-19 was found in the animals. Approximately 15 million were killed.
At the time, the country had huge export markets to China and Hong Kong. The government later admitted it had no legal basis for the culling.
There are now approximately 15,000 mink left in Denmark.
No costs have yet been determined for closing Denmark's seven remaining mink farms, but an animal welfare spokesperson for one of the governing coalition parties previously estimated it would be around 14m Danish krone (£1.56m), local media report, but the final amount could be higher.
The wearing of fur is a controversial subject within fashion circles, with publications and fashion brands choosing not to use or promote it several years ago.
But it re-entered the spotlight last year, with celebrities and fashionistas wearing both vintage and so-called faux fur.

Political analyst's view: Why is Kulbergs in no hurry to form a government? Rajevskis explains what lies behind the prolonged pause
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:17:02 UTC
21:17:02 KST

This weekend, it became known that negotiations on forming Latvia's new government will begin on the 28th of October, three weeks after President Edgars Rinkēvičs entrusted Andris Kulbergs with the task. With the United List holding 41 seats in parliament, potential coalition partners have little room to demand political concessions, influential positions or other benefits. Nevertheless, the election winner is taking his time. BNN asked political scientist Filips Rajevskis, co-founder of Mediju tilts, to explain the reasons behind the delay.
"I think he is doing the right thing," the political scientist says. "Everyone is trying to operate according to the principles we have always been accustomed to, when coalition-building begins on election night as soon as the first results come in. Under the usual procedure, the president invites representatives of all parliamentary groups for consultations before nominating a candidate for prime minister. First, the president consults the parliamentary groups, negotiations between parties take place in parallel, and then the president names a candidate for prime minister. That is the normal procedure we have become accustomed to since Latvia regained its independence. However, Latvia has never experienced a situation in which one political force holds 41 seats. These 41 seats have completely changed the political paradigm. We can now see who is ready and capable of adapting to the new situation and who is not."
Rajevskis argues that Kulbergs' decision to take a pause is justified by the circumstances. "The first thing he publicly promised was a package of 100 laws that would need to be amended to reduce government expenditure. One hundred laws in one hundred days. Even before the election, he said that anyone wanting to join his coalition would have to sign up to these changes. When he made that statement, he could not have imagined, even in his wildest dreams, winning 41 seats. But now he has those seats, and his words sound almost remarkably prophetic. 
It seems that the political parties are not simply waiting. They are waiting for him to come and explain his plans.
 It does not appear that anyone has proposals of their own to present to Kulbergs. That is the first point. The second is that he needs time to prepare his action plan. That is precisely what he publicly calls it – an action plan. It would form the basis of the government declaration and the framework for cooperation with other parliamentary groups to establish a majority in the Saeima."
The political scientist also points to what he describes as a psychological challenge that some parties previously in power are struggling to overcome.
"There are parties that are taking the situation very emotionally and finding it painful to accept that they have suffered a fundamental defeat, despite their high expectations and the enormous amounts of public money channelled into various media outlets through institutions such as the Society Integration Foundation, the Media Support Fund and other organisations that have invested money in the media. The first is New Unity, which entered the current Saeima with 26 seats, lost one MP along the way, and has now seen its representation fall from 25 to just seven seats. It is extremely difficult for them to come to terms with losing 18 seats. I imagine the atmosphere within the parliamentary group is rather unpleasant. Those seven who have been elected are probably viewed with a certain amount of resentment by the others. 
And for those whose parliamentary careers end on the 3rd of November, when they must leave their comfortable offices in parliament, emotions are undoubtedly running high."
"The second is the Progressives, who were widely expected to win 17 or 18 seats but ended up with exactly the same number as in the previous Saeima – ten. It can be said with considerable confidence that the next four years will be lean years for them, spent in opposition. Naturally, they are losing their nerve. They are trying to create the impression that there is some urgent question to answer: where is Kulbergs? In reality, Kulbergs has no reason to rush. The president has given him a mandate, and he can use this time to prepare for negotiations. Once the president formally asks him to form a government in accordance with the law, he will not actually need much time. He can choose his coalition partner because he does not need many additional votes to secure a parliamentary majority."
BNN pointed out that Progressives leader Andris Šuvajevs has already suggested that Kulbergs appears confused and that his party is overwhelmed by its electoral success. Rajevskis responded that it is the Progressives themselves who currently appear confused, arguing that they were "absolutely not prepared for four lean years".
Asked whether Kulbergs could form a government with the National Alliance alone or would also need to invite New Unity, the political scientist emphasised that holding 41 parliamentary seats gives the prime minister considerable room for manoeuvre. 
"I think he needs one partner, and the National Alliance looks like the most natural coalition partner.
 At the same time, he has the opportunity, and indeed the need, to build relationships with Šlesers, with Latvia First and with New Unity, so that he has strategic flexibility and greater freedom of action. Because we understand perfectly well that having only the National Alliance in the coalition, with a total of 51 seats in parliament, would be complicated."
Rajevskis stressed that Kulbergs should focus on expanding his political options rather than limiting them. "What he needs to do strategically is broaden his room for manoeuvre, not narrow it. Normally, forming a coalition reduces those options. He should do everything possible to expand them and ensure that he can rely on the largest possible number of votes in parliament under different circumstances. For example, Raivis Melnis would certainly be suitable as defence minister in the next government. He appeared as a leading figure on New Unity's election posters. People who voted for New Unity were effectively saying that they supported Raivis Melnis becoming defence minister. I have the impression that Kulbergs would be comfortable with Raivis Melnis serving as defence minister, which would create additional opportunities for cooperation and political manoeuvring with New Unity. He should do everything possible to maintain a broad network of potential partners, giving him the flexibility to work with different parliamentary majorities depending on the situation."

Blue disc OK to use if parking machine not working, says highest court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:13:43 UTC
21:13:43 KST

A woman who fought her parking ticket all the way to Belgium’s supreme court has won her case, which is expected to have implications for local parking regulations across the country
Blue disc OK to use if parking machine not working, says highest court
Let it never ben said that you should not fight a parking ticket: The Court of Cassation has ruled in favour of a driver who was fined for not paying for parking on the street as the payment machine was defective.
It took four years for the case to reach the highest court in the land, the decision of which has implications for parking regulations across Belgium. The court ruled in favour of a woman from Charleroi, who displayed her blue parking disc in her car when the nearest payment machine didn’t work.
According to the city, motorists must either find another machine in the area that does work or pay via an app. No sirree, said the Court of Cassation.
The Flemish government has already indicated that there is in fact no obligation to look for another parking meter first
Traffic lawyer Laurens Guinée
“In fact, the traffic laws have always stated that you are allowed to use the blue disc if the parking machine is out of order,” traffic lawyer Laurens Guinée told VRT. “But some municipalities have introduced a stricter rule requiring drivers to look for another working machine first. The Court of Cassation has now made it clear that such an additional obligation cannot override the general rules of the road.”
The decision could have implications for other cities and towns. Several local authorities currently have parking regulations requiring motorists to find another machine if the closest one is out of order, or to pay via an app. “This ruling now calls that into question,” says Guinée.
Simple choice for motorists
According to the lawyer, the ruling is also in line with forthcoming regional traffic regulations. “The Flemish government has already indicated that there is in fact no obligation to look for another parking meter first. The Court of Cassation states in very clear terms that if a local authority expects motorists to pay for parking, then they are entitled to expect the parking meter to be working.”
So the choice for drivers is simple, Guinée says. “If the parking machine is out of order, put your parking disc in your windscreen straight away. On weekdays, you can then park for up to two hours. You don’t have to look for another machine or take any further steps.”

Rubio’s Unusual Visit to India Marks a Paradigm Shift in India-US Ties

Since the February 2025 inauguration of the second Trump administration, New Delhi has struggled to find a way to deal with the constantly swinging moods in Washington. Although the still-emerging strategic partnership between the two has, at times, seemed to take center stage, on most occasions, U.S. President Donald Trump appears to have expressed very little affinity for India, his vice president’s matrimonial ties to the country notwithstanding.
The tariffs imposed on India – at one time among the highest for targeted countries – and the failure to arrive at a trade deal despite prolonged negotiations are among the many irritants that have seeped into the relationship.
Beyond all else, there is the stark reality that in Washington’s calculations India appears to matter only to the extent it episodically can be played off against China. In this context, U.S. Secretary of State Mark Rubio’s two-day visit to India on October 20-21 may not have provided the positive breakthrough New Delhi was earnestly looking for, highlighting instead the contours of the changing strategic partnership and the increasingly erratic nature of U.S. foreign policy under Trump 2.0.
Rubio broke a protocol of sorts. His first stop was Mumbai, India’s financial capital. As a result, there was no meeting between him and Prime Minister Narendra Modi, which would have been a foregone conclusion had he included New Delhi in his itinerary. In Mumbai, he met the top two industrial chiefs of the country: Gautam Adani of the Adani Group and N. Chandrasekharan of the Tata Group. India’s External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar, who recently aired his grievances against the U.S., flew down to Mumbai to meet Rubio as well as visiting UAE Foreign Minister Abdullah bin Zayed.
That the U.S. secretary of state could decide the venue of his meeting with his Indian counterpart while in India has been criticized by the opposition parties. It also dovetails squarely with emerging assessment that U.S. strategy is divorced from any cogent calculations, responding rather to rapidly shifting whims and fancies of a transactional leader.
Following the meetings – bilaterally between Jaishankar and Rubio, another between Jaishankar and bin Zayed and finally, all three together – a readout of cooperation was issued. Curiously missing were two important initiatives involving all three countries: the I2U2 and the India-Middle East Economic Corridor (IMEC).
The I2U2 was formed by the three countries along with Israel in 2021, and the IMEC was announced in 2023. Both projects have stalled due to a variety of reasons including the war in Iran. Jaishankar’s summation of the trilateral meeting as a “useful exchange of perspectives on energy, connectivity and contemporary developments” was a clear indicator of the limited outcome of the confabulation and served only to raise questions concerning U.S. intentions.
Rubio and U.S. Ambassador to India Sergio Gor did try to sound optimistic while predicting the future of the India-U.S. trade deal. Rubio said that the deal, which is allegedly 99 percent complete, could be only “weeks away” from being signed. This kind of temporal signaling is de rigor in Trump administration communications, but generally has little connection to real time. Rubio, in fact, uttered those same words on June 4 while testifying before the U.S. Senate Foreign Relations Committee. “We can wrap up the negotiations on our trade agreement, which we think we’re a few weeks away from being able to conclude,” he said roughly 20 weeks ago.
The latest statement of reassurance comes amid pessimistic Indian assessments, including that of the country’s finance minister. Speaking at the Munich Leaders Meeting on October 5, Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said, “The negotiations are still ongoing but we would like to believe that both sides have reached a plateau beyond which giving or taking might be very difficult.” Trump’s October 20 prediction about a “much different” trade deal with India hasn’t cleared the air of the ambivalence surrounding the future of the deal.
Rubio’s second and final stop was Jamnagar in the western Indian state of Gujarat, to visit the refinery of Reliance Industries to discuss energy cooperation and push for Indian imports of heavy Venezuelan crude. The latter may point to the true heart of the visit: seeking a way to involve India in transactional U.S. foreign policy by offering select Indian players a chance to profit from the questionable finances of ventures such as those in Venezuela. Jamnagar, which possesses the specialized high-capacity infrastructure required to process thick and high-sulfur heavy Venezuelan crude, is also the world’s largest single-location refining complex. A further tradeoff from the trip thus could also be to provide Rubio with a reason to claim, just before the impending U.S. mid-terms, that there is impending relief from high domestic diesel and energy prices.
Reliance Industries, led by Mukesh Ambani, is also embracing the prospect of such closer cooperation. Rubio and his wife were welcomed by the entire Ambani family, consisting of Mukesh’s wife, his sons, daughters, and their spouses. Apart from touring the oil-refining complex and Reliance’s emerging clean-energy manufacturing hub, Rubio also visited the Vantara, a controversial wildlife rescue and conservation center curated and led by one of Mukesh Ambani’s sons.
Although Rubio explained his trip as a measure to strengthen bilateral trade ties, the thrust of the trip seems more focused on American domestic politics, a search for mid-term talking points by courting new buyers and markets for expanded Venezuelan oil production. The opaque finances of the entire Venezuelan escapade notwithstanding – it has been widely reported that there has been no public accounting of just where Venezuelan oil profits are going – Reliance Industries is also planning investment in a new refinery in Texas, which Gor tweeted is “an opportunity to expand U.S. energy production and create jobs.”
Indeed, during the visit, Rubio termed India the “refining superpower of the world.” This was music to select Indian media, owned by Reliance Industries, which doubled down on the point that India, which imports 89 percent of its energy requirements from different countries, is the fourth largest exporter of refined petroleum products.
What India stands to gain out of the possible deal between Reliance Industries and the United States isn’t clear. Who will bear the cost if U.S. policies shift again remains an unanswered question. Given the fact that the U.S. is now importing Russian diesel against the will of the U.S. Congress – with its composition up for grabs in a matter of weeks – that would seem to raise questions concerning the rationale behind putting New Delhi’s import of Russian crude under permanent scanner and possible sanctions.
For decades, India has treated strategic, defense, and technology cooperation as the core of its partnership with the United States. But under Trump 2.0, the relationship is being recast as a transaction built on trade and energy, with India now viewed as buyer, refiner, and market. Rubio’s itinerary, which skipped the corridors of power for boardrooms and a refinery, made the point amply clear. Whether dancing to the American tune is a prudent strategy for India remains to be seen as transactionalism is gradually eroding what could have been the defining strategic partnership of the 21st century.

A skin cancer vaccine was tested in the U.S. — how much did it reduce the risk of recurrence?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:12:55 EEST
21:12:55 KST

A skin cancer vaccine was tested in the U.S. — how much did it reduce the risk of recurrence?
Kyiv • UNN
A vaccine created based on tumor mutations, combined with Keytruda, reduced the risk of melanoma recurrence by 42%. The drug is still experimental.
American pharmaceutical companies Moderna and Merck reported successful trials of a vaccine against melanoma — a dangerous form of skin cancer, UNN reports, citing Bild.
Details
According to the results of a study involving more than 1,100 patients, combining the vaccine with Keytruda reduced the relative risk of disease recurrence or death by 42%, and the risk of distant metastases or death by 38%. The study results are planned to be presented at the congress of the European Society for Medical Oncology in Madrid.
The vaccine's distinctive feature is that it is created individually for each patient, taking into account the genetic mutations of their tumor. The drug is intended to "teach" the immune system to recognize and destroy cancer cells.
Two years after treatment, more than 82% of patients who received the vaccine together with Keytruda remained alive without disease recurrence. In the control group, where Keytruda was administered with a placebo, this figure was 70%.
The new therapy is intended for patients whose melanoma has already been surgically removed, in order to prevent the disease from returning. It is not a preventive cancer vaccine.
The drug remains experimental and has not yet been approved for widespread use.

- A drone strike sank the Comoros-flagged merchant ship Khoryv about 13 nautical miles off Constanța, Romania, killing one sailor and leaving three missing.
- Ursula von der Leyen blamed Russia, while Romanian President Nicușor Dan accused Moscow of escalating attacks on NATO’s eastern flank.
A drone strike sank a merchant ship carrying Ukrainian and Azerbaijani sailors off Romania’s Black Sea coast on Oct. 23, 2026, killing one crew member and leaving three missing, prompting European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to condemn what she called another Russian escalation in the Black Sea.
The Comoros-flagged Khoryv sent a distress signal at around 10 a.m. local time about 13 nautical miles (24 km) from the Romanian port of Constanța, just outside Romania’s territorial waters, the Romanian navy said. Rescuers pulled nine sailors from the water and recovered the body of a tenth, while the search continued in rough seas and strong winds for the three still missing. The ship had been sailing from Ereğli, Türkiye, to the Romanian port of Sulina with a cargo of ferrous metals, and its 13-member crew included 10 Ukrainian and three Azerbaijani nationals.
Von der Leyen addressed the attack in a post on X, writing that she was deeply alarmed by yet another Russian escalation in the Black Sea and that her thoughts were with the family of the sailor who was killed and the families of the three crew members still missing.
“These reckless attacks target innocent lives and openly defy international law,” wrote European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
Romanian President Nicușor Dan said the Khoryv was struck by a drone and sank near Romania’s territorial waters, and he accused Russia of escalating attacks on NATO’s eastern flank. Video released by Romanian authorities showed only a small part of the capsized hull still above the waves before the ship went under.
The sinking is the latest in a string of drone attacks on merchant shipping off Romania and Bulgaria. Romanian broadcaster Digi24 reported that drones have hit 11 merchant vessels in the Black Sea in recent weeks, seven of them near Romania. Earlier this month, the Turkish-owned Royad Mammadov caught fire and sank after a drone strike while carrying grain from the Ukrainian port of Izmail to Ravenna, Italy, killing two crew members, and a separate attack on the commercial vessel Wine Trader left several crew members missing, including a Croatian citizen.
The attacks have drawn a growing response from NATO allies on the Black Sea. Romania’s Supreme Council of National Defence discussed the situation at a meeting on Oct. 22, and a NATO committee had previously met at the request of Romania and Bulgaria, as the alliance stepped up military aircraft deployments over the area. The Croatian Seafarers’ Union has called for the waters off Bulgaria and Romania to be declared a combat zone.
Romanian rescue teams were continuing the search for the three missing sailors on Oct. 23.

77‑year‑old Crimean activist sentenced to 18 years by Russia.

Photo: Erik Romanenko / TASS
The Southern District Military Court in Rostov-on-Don has handed down a sentence to 77-year-old Crimean civil activist Volodymyr Ananiev on terrorism charges. According to information obtained by Mediazona, Ananiev was sentenced to 18 years in a maximum-security prison. Before the hearing began, he said that any actual prison term—“whether two or twenty-two years”—would be a “death sentence” for him.
The prosecution had sought a 22-year prison term for Volodymyr Ananiev under charges of “illegal trafficking of explosives” and “preparation for a terrorist attack.”
According to the FSB, Ananiev, along with Volodymyr Bodnar and Oksana Shevchenko, was a member of an underground group that, on behalf of Ukrainian special services, was preparing an assassination attempt in Simferopol against Sergei Aksyonov, the head of the annexed Crimea. To this end, they monitored the official’s car “using a surveillance camera installed in a rented non-residential premises.”
The court had been hearing the case against Ananyev since February 2025. According to the Crimean Human Rights Group, the elderly man’s health problems worsened while he was held at Rostov’s Pretrial Detention Center No. 5, and he received virtually no medical care. During court hearings, he leaned on a cane, complained of high blood pressure, and asked for a doctor to be called.
Krym.Realii describes Ananiev as a “grassroots activist” who, since the early 2000s, had collaborated with the Union of Landowners and helped Crimean farmers with privatizing land plots and establishing businesses.
After Russia’s annexation of the peninsula, Ananiev lived in Kyiv; however, in November 2023, he decided to travel to Kerch “to visit his parents’ graves” and from there went to stay with an acquaintance in Simferopol.
On 5 February 2024, security forces reported that they had foiled an “SBU terrorist attack against one of Crimea’s leaders.” In a video distributed at the time by state agencies, Bodnar stated that he had brought an “American- or German-made mine” into Crimea via Melitopol and then hidden it in a garage. In surveillance footage included in the same video, at least six security officers with assault rifles, wearing helmets and body armor, can be seen storming into a private home and pinning Ananiev to the floor.
In 2025, Bodnar and Shevchenko were sentenced to 13 and 10 years in prison, respectively. As a result of a plea deal, heir cases were heard by the court under a special procedure—that is, without an examination of the evidence. At the same time, as attorney Refat Yunus noted during closing arguments, in Ananiev’s case, “the prosecution cited the final judgments against Bodnar and Shevchenko as evidence of guilt.” The defense attorney added that, according to Bodnar’s testimony, neither he nor Shevchenko knew Ananiev prior to their arrest; they had only heard from their “supervisor” that a certain “old man” would be helping them in Crimea.
The investigation claimed that Ananiev rented commercial space in Simferopol, installed a video camera there “to monitor the road,” and granted Bodnar access to the live feed via a special app; he later purchased and stored explosives in the same premises.
The defendant did not deny that in December 2023 he had indeed been “commissioned” to organize a kitchen with delivery service at one of Simferopol’s cafes. He signed a lease for the adjacent space, found workers to carry out the renovation and setup—including the installation of video surveillance—but subsequently, those workers communicated directly with the client.
In his closing arguments, attorney Yunus added that investigators had neither seized nor examined the camera itself, nor had they questioned the workers who installed it.
The defendant insisted during his closing arguments that the seized explosives did not belong to him either. According to Ananiev, the rented space was connected to the café by a door, and on the day before his arrest, he saw the owner’s wife “fiddling” with some kind of bag near that door. The next time, Ananiev said, he saw the same bag “in the bare hands of a bomb disposal expert who was conducting the search without gloves.” The investigation did not conduct fingerprint analysis or biological testing of the bag, defense attorney Yunus clarified.
