Uganda says it has no active Ebola cases, but infections in Kenya and Nigeria are prompting fresh scrutiny
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:11:00 UTC
21:11:00 KST

Ebola cases in Kenya and Nigeria raise concern in Uganda
October 23, 2026
The first confirmed Ebola patients in Kenya and Nigeria may have crossed paths at Uganda's Entebbe International Airport, according to African health officials, as new information from Switzerland contradicts Uganda's account of the Nigerian patient's travel history.
Uganda, a country reporting no active Ebola infections, has become a focus of investigations into cases thousands of kilometers apart.
Uganda insists that it has no confirmed active cases of the deadly virus. Yet health authorities in Kenya and Nigeria are investigating Ebola infections involving people whose travel histories or contacts are connected to the East African nation.
Both patients passed through Entebbe International Airport on October 3, according to Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC).
Health officials say the two may have crossed paths, although it has not been established whether they encountered each other or whether any transmission occurred at the airport.
The differing accounts have raised questions about whether Uganda was simply a transit point for infected travelers. Or could infections be going undetected along some of Africa's busiest cross-border routes? 
The latest developments come after Switzerland disputed claims that the Nigerian patient had visited the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where an Ebola outbreak is underway.
Did the two Ebola patients cross paths in Uganda?
Nigerian Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate confirmed an Ebola case in the capital, Abuja, involving a woman who had recently traveled to East Africa, including Uganda.
"Today we are confirming that there has been one imported case of Ebola virus disease in the Federal Capital Territory," Pate said.
The woman developed symptoms on October 7 and visited a private health facility on October 11. Further laboratory testing confirmed Ebola, and she was subsequently isolated for treatment.
Pate said the patient was stable and health officials had identified 44 contacts, including health care workers, caregivers, patients and people who may have encountered her during her travels.
But the woman's journey has become central to the investigation.
Speaking on Thursday, Mankoula said the first confirmed patients in Kenya and Nigeria were both known to have traveled through Entebbe International Airport on October 3. Investigators are examining whether the two patients were at the airport at the same time and whether their movements overlapped.
Switzerland contradicts Uganda's account
Uganda's Health Ministry says preliminary findings indicate that the Nigerian patient traveled to eastern DRCfor business before passing through Uganda without symptoms and returning to Nigeria.
"Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation," the ministry said in an October 20 statement.
But, on Friday, Switzerland's Federal Department of Foreign Affairs directly disputed the account.
"She and her husband did not travel to the Democratic Republic of the Congo," the department said in a statement to Reuters news agency.
The woman, identified by Swiss authorities as a Swiss national of Ugandan origin, is married to a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja.
On Thursday, the Swiss government told Reuters that she was believed to have contracted Ebola while traveling with her husband in Uganda, although that assessment has not been independently confirmed.
The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Africa CDC also said Thursday that they had not received confirmed information establishing that the woman had traveled to the DRC.
The conflicting accounts raise fresh questions about where the woman was exposed to the virus and how accurately her movements were initially reconstructed. They do not, however, establish that she contracted Ebola in Uganda.
Uganda maintains that it has no confirmed active Ebola cases and says it is awaiting more detailed information from Nigeria about the woman's movements.
Kenya's missing contact complicates investigation
In Kenya, Uganda has emerged in a separate investigation involving the country's first confirmed Ebola patient, who died in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, on October 5. The patient had traveled from the Democratic Republic of Congo through Uganda before reaching Kenya.
Health officials have now established that the patient passed through Entebbe International Airport on October 3, the same day as the woman subsequently diagnosed in Nigeria. Kenyan authorities have since reported additional infections linked to the initial case.
But one aspect of the investigation remains unresolved.
According to Kenya's Daily Nation, health officials are searching for a Ugandan national identified as a contact of the deceased patient.
"We know him (the Ugandan) by name and passport number and from his phone but we are not able to reach him," Kenya's director-general for health, Patrick Amoth, told the newspaper.
The Daily Nation reported that the man was using a South Sudanese telephone number, complicating efforts to establish his whereabouts.
Being an untraced contact does not mean that he is infected. However, locating potentially exposed individuals is essential to preventing further transmission.
Can border screening stop Ebola?
Uganda shares a lengthy border with the Democratic Republic of Congo, where Ebola outbreaks have repeatedly challenged health authorities.
Cross-border trade, population movements and international travel make it difficult to establish where someone was exposed to the virus.
Ebola symptoms typically develop two to 21 days after infection. According to the WHO, people infected with Ebola are not considered infectious until symptoms appear.
Even well-functioning border surveillance systems cannot identify every infected traveler.
The discovery that both patients traveled through the same international airport on the same day illustrates the complexity of tracing potential exposures across multiple countries. It also highlights the importance of reconstructing travel histories and identifying close contacts.
Uganda says it is strengthening screening and public health controls at points of entry. Nigeria has intensified contact tracing and infection prevention measures.
The challenge is ensuring that authorities across different countries can exchange accurate information quickly enough to identify potential exposures.
Anxiety grows in Nigeria
In Abuja, the confirmed infection has revived memories of previous Ebola outbreaks. Resident Peace Kolawole expressed concern about the consequences of another outbreak. "So here is my hand sanitizer, so I'm actually very concerned about it," she told DW.
Others fear that Nigeria's health care system may struggle to respond while many citizens face economic hardship. "Because now people are not even worried about sickness anymore, people are worried about surviving," Abuja resident Jonathan Steven told DW.
Nigeria's health authorities say the patient is receiving medical care and contact tracing is continuing.
What remains unanswered?
Uganda's position between the DRC and other regional destinations offers one explanation for its appearance in both investigations.
But the latest findings have added two significant questions: Did the patients from Kenya and Nigeria come into contact at Entebbe International Airport on October 3? And where did the Nigerian woman contract the virus if, as Switzerland insists, she never traveled to DR Congo?
The conflicting accounts from Uganda and Switzerland have made establishing the Nigerian patient's travel history an urgent part of the investigation. The WHO and Africa CDC have yet to confirm the disputed DR Congo travel history.
Uganda's declaration of zero confirmed active cases does not establish that all infections have been ruled out. Equally, the travel histories do not prove an undetected outbreak.
For Kenya and Nigeria, the immediate priority is containing confirmed infections. For Uganda, the challenge is demonstrating that its surveillance systems are effective and reassuring both its citizens and neighboring countries.
The Africa CDC will convene an "extraordinary virtual meeting" of national health officials on October 28 as the continent's latest Ebola outbreak continues to spread.
Edited by: Keith Walker

Ukraine troops report ongoing problems with Starlink satellite network
Unknown

12:09:08 UTC
21:09:08 KST

The White House has said that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, where a deepening humanitarian crisis has left thousands of civilians struggling to survive.
In a statement on Friday, the White House said both sides had agreed to halt all military operations in the city from 27 October to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and preparations for the evacuation of civilians.
Residents of the southern Ukrainian city, which has been under Russian occupation since February 2022, have described increasingly desperate conditions amid severe shortages of food, water and electricity. An estimated 2,000 people remain in the city, with some reportedly forced to survive on weeds, boiled grass, bread and meagre rations.
Both Russian and Ukrainian officials said all sides were close to agreeing to a ceasefire.
The White House statement said the ceasefire was brokered by Melania Trump, and her representative worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms. “Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine,” the first lady said.
Despite the claim the ceasefire had been brokered by Melania Trump, there had already been protracted efforts to organise a humanitarian ceasefire, with claims by Ukrainian officials that it had been Russia that had rejected previous calls.
Calls for a ceasefire had been issued by Pope Leo XIV – who discussed the issue with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy – the United Nations, EU officials and the Council of Europe. As recently as 18 October, Ukraine’s ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, had also said he thought agreement was close without any mention of the first lady’s involvement.
Ukraine has for weeks been pushing for a civilian evacuation from Oleshky and nearby settlements, at times using drones to airdrop emergency food and medical supplies into town.
Lubinets told Reuters on Friday that the mission to Oleshky would involve demining roads leading into the town, delivering food and evacuating civilians. “A sufficient quantity of humanitarian aid will be delivered to meet the needs of everyone who requires it. What’s more, we are working to ensure that this is not just a one-off event, and that it is not limited to Oleshky alone,” he said.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian forces continue to report widespread disruptions to the Starlink satellite network, despite Donald Trump’s claim that Elon Musk had lifted restrictions on the service.
The slowdown, which has affected the communications system used by Ukrainian troops, began last week after Trump and Elon Musk, the founder of Starlink, publicly criticised Zelenskyy over continued strikes on Russian oil refineries.
The restrictions have raised questions and confusion about who ordered the slowdown and why, with Trump and Musk denying responsibility. Asked about the Starlink slowdowns on Friday, Trump said he would speak to Musk if the restrictions remained in place.
“I’ve heard it was fixed, but if it’s not, I’ll speak to him,” he told reporters.
The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, “underlined the importance for Ukraine to have full access” to Starlink in a phone call with Trump on Friday, Downing Street said.
Ukrainian officials said throughout the day on Friday that speeds remained capped at about 100mph, with no indication that the restrictions had been lifted.
“At present, we have not observed any lifting of the restrictions on Starlink,” said Serhii Beskrestnov, a military expert who advises Zelenskyy.
“There have been isolated cases in which Starlink has operated at speeds slightly above the imposed limits, but this is likely due to SpaceX’s algorithms or specific conditions of use, rather than any lifting of the restrictions,” Beskrestnov added.
The speed restrictions have prevented Ukrainian military equipment, including drones, from maintaining a connection to the satellite network when travelling at high speeds, hampering offensive drone operations and efforts to intercept incoming Russian attacks.
The slowing down of Starlink, coupled with Zelenskyy’s complaints that Washington had temporarily suspended intelligence-sharing with Kyiv, has plunged relations between Ukraine and the US to a new low in recent days.
Tensions first flared after Washington’s surprise decision to lift sanctions on Russia and begin importing Russian diesel, as Trump sought to bring down US energy prices before the midterm elections. Maritime tracking data showed that the first tanker carrying Russian diesel was en route to New York on Thursday, and on Friday the Russian deputy prime minister, Alexander Novak, said three tankers were en route to the US and claimed Russian companies could supply 500,000 metric tonnes in October.
Meanwhile, Russia launched another overnight barrage against Ukraine, even as Moscow said a fresh round of US-brokered talks aimed at ending the war could take place next month.
The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said on Friday that trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US were expected to resume in Abu Dhabi in November. Previous rounds of negotiations have failed to produce a breakthrough, with Moscow and Kyiv far away over the terms of any peace settlement.
Among Russia’s maximalist demands are that Ukraine withdraw its forces from territory it still controls in the east of the country, drastically reduce the size of its military and adopt a neutral status that would rule out Nato membership.
Speaking to a Russian state television reporter late on Thursday, Putin once again questioned Ukraine’s sovereignty, echoing claims he has repeatedly made throughout the war. “The lands lost by Kyiv are not their territory, they are Russia’s historical lands,” Putin said.
The Russian president also cited unspecified genetic research to revive his longstanding claim that Russians and Ukrainians were “one people”, before insisting that Moscow would achieve all the objectives of its full-scale invasion.

“There is always a door open to diplomacy, even in the most difficult disputes,” he said, adding that the key is demonstrating “the will, courage and sincerity to keep that door open.”
Erdogan said Turkiye remains committed to diplomacy despite increasing global conflicts, escalating tensions, and declining trust in international institutions.

He also criticized the structure of the international system, particularly the UN Security Council.
“A structure in which the will of more than 190 countries depends on the discretion of five countries is neither fair nor capable of fully restoring trust,” he said.

He reaffirmed Turkiye’s commitment to bringing conflicting parties together, mediating fair solutions and assuming responsibility for peace efforts.

Czech government fast-tracks public media revamp criticised as power grab
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:06:46 UTC
21:06:46 KST

Czech government fast-tracks public media revamp criticised as power grab
PRAGUE, Oct 23 - The Czech ruling coalition moved on Friday to fast-track legislation that would move public media financing into the state budget and cut funding, a plan critics say threatens press independence.
The populist government, led by billionaire Andrej Babis and backed by a pro-Russian far-right party, has frequently attacked public and private media critical of its policies.
The proposal, which had been flagged previously but was unexpectedly brought to a first parliamentary reading on Friday, would cut funding for Czech Television and Czech Radio by about 15%, possibly during next year.
It would also scrap the licence fee system under which households pay 205 crowns ($9.44) a month and instead finance the broadcasters through the state budget.
Critics say the changes would weaken the broadcasters and leave them more vulnerable to political influence. Czech Television is the country's most-watched broadcaster across the main age groups.
In another unusual move, the lower house voted to extend debate, the first of three required readings, into Saturday in a bid to overcome opposition obstruction.
Zdenek Hrib, leader of the opposition Pirate Party, likened the government's behaviour to Hungary under former prime minister Viktor Orban, whose rule was marked by disputes over media freedom and the rule of law.
"We are seeing here that Andrej Babis and his entourage... have embarked on the trajectory of installing an authoritarian regime," Hrib said in the opening debate in parliament.
GOVERNMENT SAYS PLAN FOLLOWS EUROPEAN TREND
ANO, the leading party in the coalition, pledged before last year's election to abolish licence fees so households would no longer pay directly for public broadcasting.
"The government is led to this change by a European trend under which ever more European countries depart from the fee-funded principle," the proposal submitted to parliament said.
The government has argued that savings are needed at the broadcasters and that the changes would not affect editorial coverage.
The move sits uneasily with the government's efforts to curb budget deficits. The 2027 budget projects a wider deficit but makes no provision for public media funding.
Journalists and media organisations see the changes as an attempt to increase political control over coverage.
They say the proposals have not been subjected to sufficient public debate, lack safeguards against political interference and would make funding more dependent on politicians.
Reporters Without Borders, the International Press Institute and the European Broadcasting Union are among the organisations that have criticised the plan. REUTERS

Felix Savon: From Olympic boxing legend to convicted sex offender facing poverty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:04:44 UTC
21:04:44 KST

Felix Savon, a heavyweight boxer who won three Olympic gold medals and six consecutive world amateur championships, is one of the greatest amateur boxers in history. He brought tremendous honor to his native Cuba, a country whose leaders have always been eager to use sports to showcase the strength of the regime and the nation.
Savon was a loyal citizen, fiercely devoted to his homeland and communist ideology. He received dozens of offers to defect, turn professional and face opponents such as Mike Tyson and Evander Holyfield. He turned them all down. No one could buy him, not even for tens of millions of dollars. According to several reports, legendary boxing promoter Don King offered Savon an eight-figure sum to turn professional, but Savon remained loyal to Fidel Castro.
But in recent months, reports have mounted about Savon's deteriorating health and personal hygiene. He has appeared abandoned, dirty and unkempt. Last week, a 17-second video surfaced online showing a man said to be Savon rummaging through garbage bins. The man filming recognized him and asked what he was doing. Savon replied that he was looking for food. It should be noted, however, that despite the video's millions of views, the man's identity has not been conclusively verified, nor is there clear documentation of when the footage was recorded.
The images of Savon apparently searching for food in garbage bins sparked outrage among Cubans. Some collected food, clothing and Bibles to provide immediate assistance. Others expressed anger that the Cuban authorities were no longer looking after an athlete who had brought so much honor to the country and resisted the temptation to leave.
Before shedding any tears, however, it is worth remembering who Savon is. In 2018, he was sentenced to 11 years in prison for sexual assaults involving at least one child under the age of 12. He was released on parole in 2024.
When the spotlight fades
Savon, nicknamed "Ninote" ("the big kid") by his fans, celebrated his 59th birthday last month. He is one of only three boxers in history to win three Olympic gold medals, claiming his titles in 1992, 1996 and 2000. The other two are Hungary's Laszlo Papp and fellow Cuban Teofilo Stevenson, whom Savon idolized.
Savon was also a clear contender for gold at the 1988 Seoul Olympics, but Cuba decided to boycott those Games. He finished his career with a record of 362 wins and 21 losses, having managed to avenge his defeats against all but two of the boxers who beat him.
In 2001, the Manic Street Preachers became the first Western rock band to perform in Cuba. With Fidel Castro in the audience, the band dedicated its song "You Love Us" to Savon, who had recently retired from boxing.
Savon is not the only famous Cuban athlete facing severe poverty and hunger. As long as he and other athletes were useful to the government, they received generous stipends and housing. But once they were no longer of use, their financial support dwindled to a pittance — around $25 a month, an amount insufficient to cover even two weeks of living expenses, particularly given U.S. sanctions and the rising cost of living.
Savon holds a university degree awarded to him by the regime, but he cannot even write his own name. The only work he is qualified to do to earn a living is coaching children, an option that is clearly no longer available to him in light of the crimes for which he was convicted. From there, the descent into hunger and destitution is a short one.
It is hardly unusual to find athletes who earned hundreds of millions of dollars only to lose their entire fortunes after retirement. The reasons vary. Athletes financially support their entourages and families, fall prey to bad business deals and fail to hire professionals to guide their financial decisions. They also continue living the same lifestyles they enjoyed at the height of their careers.
That means extravagant spending on homes, cars, restaurants, entertainment and vacations, both for themselves and their entourages. The difference is that millions of dollars are no longer flowing into their bank accounts every month.
Usually, however, the outcome is bankruptcy, financial hardship, the need to find new employment and a major adjustment in lifestyle. The case of a legendary boxer searching for food in the trash is an extreme one.
It is true that Savon never earned millions, but the government took care of him — and also ensured he received a remarkably short period of imprisonment for the crimes he committed. Nevertheless, the video was shocking. And even in this respect, he is not alone.
The video that sparked an outcry:
Unlike athletes such as Michael Oher, Dennis Rodman, Jimmy Butler and even Kurt Warner, who experienced homelessness at one point or another before overcoming the odds to become professional athletes and earn millions, there are plenty of athletes whose lives have followed the opposite trajectory.
Former NBA player Delonte West earned more than $16 million during his career in the league. He was diagnosed with bipolar disorder while still playing professionally and has also said he suffers from clinical depression. He attributed some of his struggles to the pressures of competing in a demanding professional sports league.
After his career ended, West, who had been involved in drug and weapons offenses since his teenage years, was seen on several occasions wandering the streets, dressed like a homeless man. Those painful images of West were also among the reasons the NBA decided to introduce programs and seminars designed to help players dealing with psychological distress.
Boxers Mike Tyson and Iran Barkley also lost their fortunes, were evicted from their homes and were forced to sleep in homeless shelters or even subway stations.
Former football player Kevin Johnson lost the millions he had earned during his career and spent an extended period homeless. He was eventually murdered at a homeless encampment earlier this year, at just 55 years old.
Savon, as noted, is a different case. His loyalty to his country "cost" him tens of millions of dollars. After all, this was a boxer who once claimed that Mike Tyson would not have stood a chance against him.
He did not lose a fortune he had accumulated. Rather, the country to which he had been so fiercely loyal simply failed to show him the same loyalty in return.

Bulgaria’s CEC Confirms All Voting Machines Repaired Ahead of Sunday Vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:03:00 UTC
21:03:00 KST

Bulgaria’s Central Election Commission (CEC) is ready for Sunday’s elections, with all voting machines repaired and the final plan for counting votes and processing election documents approved, CEC spokesperson Stoyanka Balova said on BNT.
Balova said the Commission had adopted the final procedures for tabulating results, processing votes from abroad and receiving documents from district election commissions, leaving only a few minor details to be addressed before election day.
One issue that drew discussion ahead of the vote was the CEC’s decision to require stamps on receipts printed by voting machines. The measure was not included in the Commission’s initial methodological guidelines but was subsequently introduced to ensure a uniform procedure across polling stations, particularly because partial local elections are also taking place in some areas.
Balova explained that receipts had been stamped at all polling stations during partial local elections in recent weeks. Runoff elections are now being held in several parts of the country, requiring two separate Sectional Election Commissions (SECs) to operate in the affected localities. Voters must visit one commission to vote in the local elections and another to cast their ballot in the presidential election.
She said the standardized procedure was intended to prevent disagreements over whether votes were valid. Although the change came shortly before the elections, SEC members already had experience with the process from previous votes.
Balova stressed that machine-printed receipts are used only to verify the vote count, while the official results are established from the machine-generated protocol.
“The receipts are for verification purposes and will be counted by the Sectional Election Commissions as a control measure; however, the official result is derived from the protocol - we do not base the vote count on the receipts,” she said.
The machine-voting procedure was also demonstrated in the studio of The Day Begins. Before voting starts, an SEC member switches on the machine, enters the required code and prints a zero report confirming that no votes have been recorded.
During the demonstration, Balova explained that the polling station should open at 7 a.m., after which the commission member enters the machine’s PIN code and checks the zero report to verify that no vote has been cast.
Voters identify themselves with an ID card before receiving a card for the voting machine, which they insert into the designated slot. Once they hear a click, the ballot appears on the screen, allowing them to select their preferred presidential candidate pair and review their choice.
Voters can return to the previous screen and change their selection before pressing the “Vote” button to confirm it. The machine then prints a receipt, which must be removed after the beep to prevent the printer from becoming blocked.
The voter folds the receipt so that the marked choice cannot be seen, has an SEC member stamp it and places it in the ballot box. The voter then signs the voter list and receives their ID card back.
Balova said SEC members could guide voters who encounter difficulties with the machines, but they must preserve the secrecy of the ballot and cannot operate the equipment on a voter’s behalf.
“A member of the Section Election Commission must maintain a distance of at least two meters so as not to compromise the secrecy of the vote,” she said, explaining that assistance must be limited to verbal guidance, such as telling a voter to insert the card until it clicks.
Commission members are not permitted to stand immediately beside voters or operate the machines for them.
Voters with visual impairments have additional options. At polling stations where paper ballots are used, special templates are available to help them vote, with information about the locations providing them published on the websites of the respective District Election Commissions.
Voters whose condition prevents them from voting independently may be accompanied by an assistant. However, assistants cannot be SEC members, observers, authorized representatives, or representatives of political parties or initiative committees. Balova also clarified that illiteracy alone is not grounds for voting with an assistant.
She confirmed that all voting machines had been repaired and were scheduled for delivery to the relevant municipalities and polling stations by the following day. Under the contract between the CEC and the contractor, the machines will be inspected again after the elections, with further repairs carried out if needed. Balova added that the machines have a one-year warranty.

“They say they want to be in NATO and enjoy protection from a nuclear umbrella but not have it based in Scotland. They say they support our armed forces but stop Cadet units from building valuable community links by banning activity inside state schools.
“This is the same story from the SNP. Secrecy, fantasy and no serious plan for Scotland’s security.”
Dave Doogan, the SNP’s Westminster leader and the member for Angus and Perthshire Glens, told this publication that he drafted and costed the plan about two and a half years ago, that it now needs a refresh, and that he would publish it once enough people were asking the question. “Why not release the defence plan now? Well, a good reason is that it needs a refresh, but it’s designed to answer a question when enough people are asking that question, and that will come when we’re having the next independence referendum debate,” he said.
The plan assumes a budget of around five and a half billion pounds a year, drawn from Scotland’s existing share of British defence spending, and a conventional three service structure generated over time. Doogan also said an independent Scotland would not press a claim on British military equipment if doing so damaged what remained of the United Kingdom, telling this publication that “if we were to claim our share of eight per cent or whatever of UK assets, and that caused major difficulties for the UK, well, we just wouldn’t do it because it’s not intelligent.”
On skills, the Scottish Government confirmed this month that it will match fund two Defence Technical Excellence Colleges, one on each coast, after Luke Pollard offered the money in March as part of a £50 million Scotland Defence Growth Deal. The Scottish Affairs Committee reported in September that progress on the colleges had fallen behind equivalent work in England and urged both governments to act with greater urgency, and this publication has reported that Scotland risks missing out on the defence spending boost without a bigger skills base.
Downie has been among the more active Scottish Labour members on defence since the election, pressing on submarine dismantling at Rosyth and on the industrial base. Wes Streeting told the Commons yesterday that he wants the Defence Technical Excellence Colleges backed with £50 million in England to expand to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, and offered to work with the Scottish Government on the defence of the United Kingdom regardless of constitutional differences.

270 Ukrainian POWs return home in latest swap with Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23

21:00:51 KST

Editor's note: The story initially reported that five people previously believed to have been killed in the 2022 Olenivka prison massacre had returned to Ukraine. However, President Volodymyr Zelensky's social media post was later edited to clarify that those who returned were survivors of the terrorist attack.
Ukraine and Russia exchanged prisoners of war on Oct. 23, with 261 Ukrainian service members and nine civilians returning home, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced.
The exchange, the first in two months, also saw 270 Russian prisoners of war returned to Russia from Ukrainian captivity.
According to Zelensky, most of the Ukrainians returning home had been captured during the Siege of Mariupol in spring 2022. They included service members from the Ground Forces, Navy, and Air Assault Forces, as well as border guards and fighters from the Azov regiment, which led the city's defense.
Five of the released POWs survived the Olenivka prison massacre in July 2022, when a thermobaric munition was detonated inside a prison barracks housing Ukrainian prisoners of war.
According to Ukraine's Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, a "significant portion" of the released prisoners had been found guilty on sham criminal charges while in Russian captivity.
Seven Ukrainian civilians were also brought back from Russia with the help of Ukrainian authorities on Oct. 23, Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said in a Facebook post. Lubinets added that another seven civilians had traveled to Russia as part of family reunification efforts supported by the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC).
Zelensky, as well as the Coordination Headquarters later said that nine civilians had been released.
Lubinets called the prisoner exchange "historic," saying it brought home the largest number of convicted Ukrainian service members since 2022: 86 convicted soldiers and one person who had been facing criminal prosecution.
Ukraine, international human rights organizations, and the U.N. have described such trials in Russia as war crimes. The Third Geneva Convention grants POWs protected status under international humanitarian law and prohibits prosecuting them solely for their participation in hostilities, subject to the rules governing lawful combatant conduct.
Lubinets added that the exchange marked the return of Azov Regiment service members for the first time "in a long while."
Two of those released had been held in Russian captivity since 2018 and 2020, spending eight and six years in captivity, respectively, Lubinets said.
The youngest released POW was 24, while the oldest was 63, he added.
Ukraine's Interior minister Ivan Vyhivskyi said that among the returned prisoners were a father and son, both called Volodymyr, both in Ukraine's National Border Guard, that were taken prisoner in Mariupol's Azovstal and saw each other for the first time in four years.
"Today is full of heartbreaking footage: hugs, calls to relatives and joy from the fact that you can hold the Ukrainian flag in your hands again," he said.
While intermittent U.S.-mediated "peace talks" between Russia and Ukraine have failed to secure even a partial ceasefire, prisoner exchanges remain one of the few channels of regular cooperation between Moscow and Kyiv.
The latest swap was the 11th reported prisoner exchange of 2026. The previous two exchanges took place in August.

Sugar restriction in early life is linked to lower dementia risk and slightly slower brain aging decades later
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:00:28 UTC
21:00:28 KST

An analysis of UK Biobank data found that people who were exposed to Britain’s sugar rationing in the womb and during their first years of life had a 27% lower risk of dementia, a 46% lower risk of Alzheimer’s disease, an 11% lower risk of depression, and a 20% lower risk of anxiety compared with people born after rationing ended. Brain scans also suggested slightly slower brain aging in this group. The paper was published in npj Aging.
Neurological and psychiatric disorders such as dementia, depression, and anxiety place a growing burden on individuals, healthcare systems, and societies worldwide. Increasing evidence suggests that some of the factors influencing these conditions may begin acting very early in life, during sensitive periods of brain development.
The first 1,000 days of life, beginning in pregnancy and continuing through infancy, are considered especially important for shaping long-term health. Nutrition is one of the major environmental influences during this period because the developing brain depends heavily on an adequate and balanced supply of nutrients. At the same time, modern diets often expose pregnant women, breastfeeding mothers, and young children to large amounts of added sugar.
This has raised concerns that high sugar intake early in life could have lasting effects on brain development and later mental health. Biological studies suggest that excessive sugar exposure may promote inflammation and disturb systems involved in the body’s response to stress. Poor maternal metabolic health, including elevated blood glucose, has also been associated with a greater risk of conditions such as attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and anxiety in children.
Study author Xingji Lian of Guangzhou First People’s Hospital and Guangzhou Medical University in China and colleagues set out to examine whether limited sugar exposure early in life was linked to mental and brain health in older age. Because randomized trials restricting sugar during pregnancy and infancy would be impractical and unethical, the researchers turned to history. The U.K. rationed sugar between 1942 and 1953, limiting intake to levels in line with current dietary guidelines and providing no sugar ration for children under two years of age.
Sugar rationing ended in September 1953, and average adult sugar consumption nearly doubled almost immediately, while intake of other major foods remained stable. This allowed the researchers to treat the policy change as a natural experiment, comparing people conceived while rationing was in place with people conceived after it ended. A previous study using the same natural experiment, published in Science, linked early exposure to rationing to lower risks of type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure.
The researchers drew on the UK Biobank, a large long-term research project that has collected genetic, health, lifestyle, and medical imaging data from about half a million people in the United Kingdom. They examined diagnoses of dementia, Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, depression, and anxiety, along with brain scans that allowed them to estimate each person’s brain age.
The analysis included 60,394 participants born between October 1951 and March 1956. Of these, 38,227 were conceived while rationing was in place (born between October 1951 and June 1954), including 9,963 born between October 1953 and June 1954, who were exposed to rationing only in the womb. The remaining 22,167 participants, born between July 1954 and March 1956, served as the comparison group, and a subset of 9,053 participants without brain disorders had brain scans.
People exposed to rationing both in the womb and after birth had lower risks of dementia, Alzheimer’s disease, depression, and anxiety than the comparison group, after the researchers accounted for factors such as region and month of birth, socioeconomic status, education, family history, and genetic risk scores. Those exposed only in the womb had a 10% lower risk of anxiety but showed no meaningful differences for the other conditions. Rationing was not associated with Parkinson’s disease.
Because participants were only in their late 60s or early 70s by the end of follow-up, the dementia findings rested on relatively few cases: 307 people had been diagnosed with dementia and 123 with Alzheimer’s disease. By comparison, 7,015 had been diagnosed with depression and 4,011 with anxiety.
Longer exposure to rationing after birth was associated with progressively lower risks of depression and anxiety, with the associations becoming more pronounced after six months. For example, participants exposed to rationing for 12 months after birth had a 23% lower risk of depression and a 28% lower risk of anxiety, and the lowest risks were seen in those exposed for 24 months. No such pattern appeared for dementia or Alzheimer’s disease.
The associations were most consistent in women, who showed lower risks of Alzheimer’s disease, depression, and anxiety. In men, the only reliable reduction was for anxiety.
In the brain imaging analyses, people exposed to rationing after birth had brains that looked about 0.39 years, or roughly five months, younger relative to their actual age than those of the comparison group. They also tended to have larger volumes in several deep brain structures, including the hippocampus, thalamus, and putamen, and lower contrast between gray and white matter across much of the cortex, a finding the authors say could reflect several different tissue changes and should be considered preliminary. Exposure only in the womb showed few associations with brain structure.
“These quasi-experimental findings suggest that early-life sugar restriction is associated with attenuated neurobiological aging and lower risks of dementia and psychiatric disorders, suggesting sugar intake as a potential modifiable factor of lifelong brain health,” study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of the long-term consequences of early nutritional patterns. However, it should be noted that the end of sugar rationing coincided with broader post-war economic recovery, improved maternal healthcare, and changing infant feeding practices, all of which may have independently influenced brain development. Rationing of other foods also ended by July 1954, although consumption of those foods changed only slightly. Because of this, it remains uncertain how much of the observed differences are due to sugar alone.
Individual sugar intake was not measured; exposure was inferred from participants’ birth dates. Diagnoses of depression and anxiety relied partly on self-reports and primary care records, and participants grew up in a post-war, predominantly white British setting that may not reflect the experiences of children today. The authors say the findings need to be replicated in contemporary groups with detailed dietary information before informing clinical or public health recommendations.
The paper, “Early-life sugar rationing, brain aging, and long-term neurodegenerative and psychiatric health outcomes: a population-based natural experiment study,” was authored by Xingji Lian, Amei Chen, Xiaoyan Zhu, Yuyu Huang, Chongzhe Yang, Yan Huang, Meilong Ran, Longyan Yin, and Bing Zhang.

A Democratic win in Texas is a long shot – but Ken Paxton’s weakness is obvious | Moira Donegan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:00:26 UTC
21:00:26 KST

It’s a bit like Lucy with the football. Every few years, Democrats convince themselves that a Texas Senate seat might finally switch from red to blue. On paper, it makes sense. Texas is a large and urbanizing state with an increasingly educated – and increasingly non-white – population.
Other one-time Republican strongholds that have undergone similar demographic shifts have turned purple or even blueish – think Georgia, for example. The border counties along the Rio Grande valley, with their deep poverty and big Latino populations, were long thought to be fertile ground to nurture a kind of anti-Trump populism that could be converted into pro-Democratic sentiment. The state Democratic party is anemic there, but a few talented candidates have emerged.
Who else remembers Beto O’Rourke, the former Texas Democratic congressman and onetime presidential hopeful, who appeared on a 2019 cover of Vanity Fair, photographed in muted Annie Leibovitz tones along a desert dirt road, promising to deliver his home state, and a crucial Senate vote, from the clutches of Republican control?
Does that hope seem naive now? Even almost childish? Given what we know of O’Rourke’s subsequent success – or of the voting trends in the Rio Grande valley – does the past hope of a blue Texas begin to seem at all arrogant?
Forgive me, then, for harboring doubts about whether Texas will vote, as some pollsters and many hopeful Democrats now say it will, for James Talarico, the Democratic Senate nominee, over his Republican opponent, the odious state attorney general, Ken Paxton.
The excitement of Democrats in the Texas US Senate race this year carries with it the aftertaste of past disappointments. Lucy swears that this time, she’ll let Charlie Brown kick, and Charlie Brown – a slave to his own optimism – draws back his leg.
But if there was ever a cycle where optimism from Texas Democrats seemed reasonable, it might be this one. Polls have put Talarico, a former seminarian, at a steady, though narrowing, lead. And there is reason for his appeal: Talarico speaks in eloquently religious terms that are well-tailored to his Bible belt audience; at 37, his relative youth will probably appeal to voters fatigued by gerontocracy.
But the real deciding factor in the election may well be his opponent: Paxton is an uncommonly dishonorable man, even by the very low standards of a Republican Senate candidate. He’s been indicted on various fraud charges by Texas grand juries (he denied wrongdoing and eventually paid $300,000 in restitution).
He was sued over similar fraud claims, subjected to multiple whistleblower complaints, nearly disbarred, and impeached in his capacity as attorney general by members of his own Texas Republican party. (He was later acquitted.)
He is also going through a messy, public divorce after his wife of several decades, Angela, finally began proceedings against him after an alleged extramarital affair.
He subjects women to systematic mistreatment in public life, too: as Texas AG, he has presided over one of the most maximalist and sadistic abortion ban regimes, leading to one of the highest maternal and infant mortality rates in the country. He is unlikable, and unliked. Republican Texans who would have come out to vote for another candidate are more likely to stay home rather than vote for him.
If winning a Texas Senate seat has long been a pipe dream for Democrats, the possibility that they might do so seems to be frightening Republicans.
A loss in Texas would not just be a strategic defeat for the GOP, but a psychic one – a failure to hang on to unified power in a state that is supposed to be both the geographical center and the cultural linchpin of conservatism. It presents a risk to the emotions and morale of the Republican party much more than other potential losses in states such as, say, Maine, Michigan or Alaska.
In a word, it would be emasculating. And in characteristic fashion, Republican power players have sought to assert masculinity as their central line of attack in the race.
Over and over, Republicans have sought to keep Texas by insinuating that Talarico is gay, a woman or a pedophile – sometimes all three – and persistently linking him to the issue of gender transition treatment for minors. They have implied that he’s weak, that he’s either asexual or sexually threatening, depending on the occasion, and, weirdly, that he’s vegan.
JD Vance, who has used the midterm cycle to informally launch his 2028 bid for the Republican presidential nomination, has seemingly decided to imitate Trump in vulgarity even where he lags him in charisma and humor. Like many, he’s been trying to get a 2016-style nickname for the Democrat to stick: “Talafreako.” It doesn’t quite roll off the tongue.
But Vance has also suggested that Talarico is gay – and that he would somehow be disqualified from the Senate if he was. At a rally in Tyler, Texas, Vance told a male audience member that he loved him. “In a totally platonic way, to be clear. I’m the vice-president, not James Talarico.” He paused and waited for the crowd to laugh.
Before that, he had insinuated that Talarico was a pedophile. “A guy that age who is so obsessed and focused on transgender children, I don’t know about you, but I never want to see that guy’s web browser history,” Vance said.
Elon Musk – nominally a resident of Texas, though billionaires don’t really “reside” anywhere – has looked to rescue Paxton’s candidacy with a massive infusion of cash, dumping $158m into the race late last month on the Republican’s behalf. On his social media platform, X, he has taken on a similar tone to Vance in attacking Talarico, alternating between casting vaguely sexual aspersions about Talarico’s character – Musk has repeatedly called him “creepy” – and making specific, incendiary and false claims about the Texas Democrat. “Talarico would vote to take away your kids and transition them,” Musk wrote. “Not just in Texas, but nationwide. Pure evil.”
These kinds of low-brow, sexualized smears are the kind of thing Republicans do to make themselves look tough. The name-calling is supposed to evoke the power of the schoolyard bully in the form of a man in a suit, to conjure the image of someone so powerful that rules, and decorum, don’t apply to him.
But I think that really, these kinds of juvenile taunts are a sign of the party’s weakness. Republicans have no answer to mainstream Americans’ economic pain; all they can offer are titillating little libidinal gratifications for their base.
They are betting that the grim satisfaction of dominance, of cruelty, will be more important to voters than $5 gasoline. They’re leaning into being mean, in short, because they don’t have anything else.
- Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist

Potholes, bus fares and headphone dodgers: will Burnham’s strategy of ‘everyday fixes’ succeed?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:00:25 UTC
21:00:25 KST

In the first episode of Armando Iannucci’s political satire The Thick of It, the hapless minister Hugh Abbot is in the back of a taxi, frantically brainstorming for an on-the-hoof policy he can announce to the assembled national press.
“So you want something sexy and eye-catching, and that is free and universally popular and instantly applicable. No one can possibly object to it,” says the addled junior adviser Ollie Reeder. “Well, really, you should have said something before then, because I’ve got a file about that fucking thick of that back in the office.”
After a three-month micro-policy blitz from Downing Street, the question now being asked is: did Reeder pass said file on to the government’s battalion of special advisers? In the past week Andy Burnham has vowed to clamp down on social pariahs blaring out TikTok videos on public transport, outlaw “rip-off” private car park fines and – on Thursday – fill in potholes in 7,000 miles of England’s roads.
Before that, as part of the focus on “everyday fixes”, the prime minister announced a plan to remove VAT from electricity bills, a £2 cap on single bus fares across England and take action on “auto-renew” subscriptions. There’s also promises to crack down on pricey branded school uniforms, ban specious discounts, limit vape and betting shops and stop airlines charging families to sit together on planes. At this rate all minor annoyances in the UK will be eradicated by Christmas.
The idea is simple, says one policy adviser. “People expect the government to be able to do something about things which are unfair – big or small,” they said. “It sends a message that the government is on people’s side, its ready to act, and it can genuinely make a difference.”
Government insiders say the policies are not the product of standing around in a circle, throwing a stress ball and shouting out ideas. “There isn’t someone with a whiteboard brainstorming new bicycles for special constables,” says one, furthering the Thick of It comparison. Instead, the everyday fixes were a central policy strategy from Burnham’s first day in office. “We did this sort of thing under Keir too,” said another source. “But under Andy it’s a whole different thing; he’s put rocket boosters under it.”
In the first days of his premiership, Burnham gave his close ally Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, the job of establishing taskforces for three core areas – cost of living, public control and regeneration. One government source said: “There is a very intentional drumbeat of those because they do make a difference, but also it’s constantly showing people that we understand where those frustrations and low-level pressures are.”
Ideas are “kicked around” between the cost of living taskforce in the Cabinet Office and the policy unit in No 10, with all departments encouraged to feed in. “There’s a sort of filtering up process,” the source said. “It’s quite a sprawling sort of cross-government approach.”
Another said that while some departments were better placed to find “not hugely spendy” fixes, every minister was encouraged to contribute. “I think a lot of people had sort of resigned any hope that the government can actually get things done – and this is showing them that, yes, actually, we can,” another source said.
The small policy announcements have been, one delighted adviser said, a roaring success. Another source said: “Some people are very snotty about it, but in a world where it’s really hard for a government to cut through, this is working. You put some ideas through the grid and you often don’t know if they’re going to fly. But when you see one go gangbusters, it’s kind of like Christmas morning.”
One single fact policy idea dominated the news cycle for an entire day. Another generated tens of thousands of posts on X. Burnham’s faintly hokey video on antisocial phone use garnered 2m views. “It helps that he’s just really good at it,” the source said.
The small-fix policies have not been appreciated by everyone. Reform UK’s Robert Jenrick said the UK was “going down the pan and our prime minister is faffing around tweaking parking tickets” – despite trying to implement the policy himself when he was a Conservative minister. The former Olympian Sharron Davies said: “As Paris burns our prime minister has stopped people playing loud music on buses & trains,” leading some to question whether she expected Burnham to invade the French capital.
Kemi Badenoch, meanwhile, has been dismissive, saying in a speech this week that cracking down on loud music on public transport was a “job for ticket inspectors, not the prime minister”. Reprising the theme at prime minister’s questions on Wednesday, the leader of the opposition implicitly accused Burnham of fiddling while Rome burns. “We are spending more on interest payments than we do on schools, the army and the police combined,” she said. “Meanwhile, the prime minister is worrying about loud music on trains. This is not serious.”
Across the dispatch box, Burnham hid his delight at her response behind a disappointed look. “I’m not going to apologise for doing the small things that help people have better lives,” he said sombrely, while his advisers likely high-fived in private.
Regardless of the reaction of Burnham’s opponents, the focus on minor grievances is a canny strategy that appears to be working, said the pollster Luke Tryl, the director of More in Common. In recent polling, when people were asked whether Burnham understood the pressure of high energy bills on ordinary people, 45% said he did. When the same question was asked about Starmer, that figure was 23%. “I think the Tories and Reform have got it dead wrong on this,” Tryl said. “People bring this sort of stuff up in focus groups all the time. It cuts across left- and rightwing voters. People care about immigration, about the NHS – but they also care about everyday frictions.”
But behind the scenes there is an acknowledgment that a focus on ticking off small things from the PM’s to-do list will be significantly more challenging in moments of crisis. There has to be a “twin-track” approach, said one insider. “It’s combining a big picture, long term, dismantling 40 years of neoliberalism and addressing questions about ownership and control, but at the same time tackling more immediate daily bugbears,” they said. “What you’ve seen so far is these smaller level interventions, but the bigger structural, longer term piece will be in the 10-year plan.”
While the everyday fixes may be popular, the sugar-high they produce could be short-lived, said Ed Shackle, the head of qualitative research at the policy consultants Public First Global. “The government should be under no illusion that as soon as any real substantive event rears its head, any small popularity boost will be instantly blown away,” he said. “Quick fixes are popular, but they are a poor substitute for fixing the big issues the public care about.”

Rich tamarind chutney gives this vibrant tequila sour a sweet-sour depth that pairs brilliantly with crisp apple juice.
Spiced tamarind and apple sour
Serves 1
45ml blanco tequila – we use Olmeca Altos Plata
 
25ml apple juice 
  
25ml fresh lime juice 
  
20ml sugar syrup 
  
½ tsp tamarind chutney – any decent brand will do 
  
1 egg white 
 , or 3 drops cocktail foamer
 
1 star anise, to garnish
Put everything bar the star anise in a shaker and shake vigorously without ice to set the egg white and build a smooth foam. Add a good handful of ice, shake again until well chilled, then strain into a tumbler filled with fresh ice. Garnish with a star anise.

====================================================================================================

Trump, the peacemaker, can make peace in Israel - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:00:13 UTC
21:00:13 KST

If the polls are close to being right, voting stations across the country will close on Tuesday night at 10 p.m. without answering the most important question facing the country: Where does Israel go from here?
Neither political bloc will have a majority – neither Benjamin Netanyahu nor Gadi Eisenkot – and Israel will once again face the prospect of political paralysis and potentially another election.
In that scenario, much of the responsibility would fall on President Isaac Herzog. He would meet with the different party leaders, hear their recommendations, and decide who should receive the mandate to try to form a government.
He might also attempt to bring the sides together, hoping to find a formula that could prevent Israel from returning to the destructive cycle of elections as we had in the years before October 7.
But there is another president whose role in this process could be just as consequential: Donald Trump.
Trump’s endorsement of Netanyahu this week was interesting not only because of its timing – just days before Israelis go to the polls – but because of the reasoning behind it. Trump made clear that his support for Netanyahu was tied to Iran.
Netanyahu, he said, is the partner he needs to finish the job and topple the Iranian regime. With someone else in power, Trump warned, America might have to finish the job alone, and that is something he does not want to do.
Whether that is true is a good question. But the endorsement revealed something else about how Trump sees what happens next. For him, the Israeli election is not only about who wins in Israel. It is also about what the US will do when it comes to Iran.
Imagine the following scenario: The election here ends without a decisive victory for either side, and amid attempts to build a minority coalition or attract defectors from one side to the other, Trump invites Netanyahu and Eisenkot to the White House.
Netanyahu would happily accept. Eisenkot would be less enthusiastic, knowing what he would be walking into. But he would not be able to refuse the invitation. The two Israeli politicians would arrive in Washington, and Trump would present them with a proposition: I need both of you to form a government so we can finish the job in Iran.
For Netanyahu, it would be a dream come true, while for Eisenkot, the political cost would be huge. The Yashar leader promised just on Wednesday that he would not agree to a rotation agreement with Netanyahu.
Trump could guarantee an agreement
But Trump could offer him something that might force him to reconsider: a national unity government built around a shared strategic objective of taking on Iran, alongside Trump serving as the guarantor that Netanyahu would honor a future transfer of power.
Could Trump actually enforce such an agreement? Not legally. But if Netanyahu were to break a commitment made at the White House, he would risk not only embarrassing Trump but also damaging his relationship with a president whose support he considers essential to Israel’s security.
What Trump could do is force Netanyahu to agree to only 18 months as prime minister. That would leave Trump roughly another six months in office to exert pressure if Netanyahu tried to block the transition.
Is this imaginary scenario difficult to see happening, considering the personal animosity and broken trust between Netanyahu and Eisenkot? Yes. But is it impossible? No.
For this to happen, though, Israelis would need to be able to trust their leaders, something that is very hard right now as Netanyahu beats the war drums on a daily – and even hourly – basis with just days left to the election. His threats reached a point this week that raised concerns that Israel might attack Iran at any moment or might even be trying to provoke Iran to attack first.
On the one hand, there is no question that the danger is real. Iran’s pursuit of nuclear weapons and its development of long-range ballistic missiles pose a grave threat to Israel. The question is not whether this needs to be confronted but rather whether it needs to be confronted right now.
The public does not know the answer, and neither do most members of Israel’s political establishment. Only a handful of people have access to the intelligence needed to determine what Iran is actually doing, how immediate the threat is, and whether military action can wait.
If Iran is actively building a nuclear bomb and intelligence indicates that it is approaching a point of no return, Israel may have no choice but to act, regardless of the election. But if the threat is likely to be essentially the same in a few weeks or months, then the current government needs to exercise extreme caution.
If Netanyahu decides to attack, even for the best and most legitimate of reasons, most Israelis will suspect that his motives are political. Even if the attack is entirely justified, people will believe that its timing was designed to influence the outcome of the election.
This brings us to the heart of the problem. Israel is suffering from a deep crisis of trust. An operation that might genuinely be necessary to strengthen the country’s security could end up further undermining public confidence in the government and even the IDF, simply because so many Israelis would not believe that it had to happen.
This is where Trump could play another important role.
If the US decides to participate in another military operation against Iran, that would provide Israelis with an indication that the threat is serious and that the decision is not simply a political move by Netanyahu. American participation would not eliminate the questions, but it would give the decision a level of credibility that Netanyahu cannot provide on his own.
There is another person whose voice could be even more important to Israelis: IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir.
Zamir was appointed under Netanyahu, but he is not seen as a political loyalist and has already proven that he is ready to challenge the cabinet when he believes that Israel’s security interests are in jeopardy.
A public address by Zamir, explaining what he can about the danger, its urgency, and the military considerations behind any decision to act, would provide assurances that are currently missing. It is obviously not Zamir’s job to endorse Netanyahu’s political arguments, but he is responsible for protecting the IDF and preserving public trust in it.
Without that trust, even the right decisions can come at a terrible cost.
The writer is a co-founder of the MEAD policy forum, a senior fellow at the Jewish People Policy Institute, and a former editor-in-chief of The Jerusalem Post. His newest book is While Israel Slept.

Swiss motorists flock to cheaper Austrian fuel pumps
Swiss shopping tourism in search of bargain prices outside "high price" Switzerland now also extends to filling up with cheaper petrol.
Due to soaring prices caused by the conflict in the Middle East, many Swiss motorists are crossing the border to find cheaper fuel, primarily in Austria.
With petrol prices hitting record highs, many motorists are on the hunt for the cheapest petrol station, even if it means driving a little further and crossing the Austrian border.
“I live in Switzerland, near the border. I often come to fill up in Vorarlberg [Austria’s westernmost state]. The price difference is about 30 cents a litre,” said one motorist.
More
Swiss border towns to combat ‘shopping tourism’
“It’s a good deal. In Switzerland, you pay a lot more. I don’t know why,” said another driver. “It’s shocking to see how much we have to pay,” one motorist told Swiss public broadcaster SRF.
In Austria, petrol costs €1.85, or CHF1.72. Diesel is priced at €2.18, or CHF2.03. Austrian prices are around 20% lower than in Switzerland.
“One in two cars, and one in two customers, are Swiss. At present, petrol stations near the border generate the bulk of their turnover from Swiss customers,” said Petra Girardi, spokesperson for the Vorarlberg Chamber of Commerce.
On Tuesday morning, the price of a barrel of Brent crude once again exceeded the $110 mark, but prices at the pumps in neighbouring countries are often more favourable thanks to the government subsidies in place there.
More
Why Switzerland’s fuel stockpiles are for Swiss use only
Backlash from politicians
This price difference encourages “petrol tourism”, argues Markus Schnyder, a Swiss People’s Party politician. “In neighbouring countries, this sort of fuel discount is widespread. We are now at a disadvantage.”
“This is very damaging to our competitiveness and it also leads people to fill up abroad and then do their shopping there, which further stimulates shopping tourism.”
In parliament, several motions from the centre-right parties are calling for a reduction in fuel prices. Left-leaning parties, including the Greens, oppose this. In their view, it would create false incentives in terms of climate policy and favour heavy users.

‘Burden and loss’ builds in DR Congo, as Kenya strengthens Ebola containment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

‘Burden and loss’ builds in DR Congo, as Kenya strengthens Ebola containment
As Ebola continues to spread in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), more resources are needed to fight the disease and feed patients and families, UN agencies said on Friday.
“If we lift the foot off the pedal, the virus will resurge very quickly, will continue to spread to newly affected areas and pose a threat for the country, the region and the world at large,” warned Dr. Catherine Smallwood, World Health Organization (WHO) incident manager in the DRC.
The country remains the epicentre of an outbreak of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease that was officially declared in mid-May. It began in the volatile eastern region and has now spread to eight provinces, the latest being Nord-Ubangi in the northwest.
There have been 9,765 cases to date and nearly half – 4,727 – have died. Additionally, 30,000 contacts are being monitored each day over a three-week period.
A smaller outbreak in Uganda was officially declared over in August, while cases have also been confirmed in Kenya, Nigeria and France.
Lives and livelihoods lost
In the DRC, “we’re seeing an incredible permanent burden and loss of livelihoods in those families that are affected”, said Dr. Smallwood, speaking from the eastern city of Bunia to journalists in Geneva.
At nearly six months in, the outbreak “is occurring in an area that is geographically vast and moving into ever hard to reach locations and remote locations”, she noted. Some places can take several days to reach by boat or motorcycle and are inaccessible by car or plane.
The crisis continues to unfold amid ongoing conflict, hunger and displacement, and the World Food Programme (WFP) is working to ensure that families get enough to eat. The UN agency is also building Ebola treatment centres, among other operations.
Feeding hungry families
WFP’s Representative in the DRC David Stevenson shared stories of the people who depend on its support.
One woman, Francine Birungi Amoti, lost a child to Ebola and is raising her six surviving children and a baby entrusted to her care. She is unable to attend to her fields due to violence.
“For Francine, food assistance means being able to feed the children in her care when reaching her fields could cost her life,” he said, speaking from the capital Kinshasa.
“This is what a crisis on top of a crisis looks like: disease and bereavement, compounded by insecurity and hunger.”
Concerns and challenges
Dr. Smallwood also pointed to another concern as the number of people dying from Ebola outside recognised treatment centres “remains a big flag of late detection of cases at the community level”.
The past week has seen a decline in the number of people dying in the community or outside Ebola treatment centres which indicates that actions to increase early detection and quick referral to care have been working.
However, WHO understands that in some parts of eastern DRC, “patients are visiting between two to five different health facilities before they're referred to Ebola treatment centres”, representing “a really, really big challenge”.
Beds for patients
Dr. Smallwood said there have been significant improvements in the quality of care provided at Ebola treatment centres. WHO had set a target of 3,000 beds across affected areas and currently over 2,000 are available.
She also highlighted the positive fact that 2,600 people in the DRC have survived Ebola. Clinics are being opened where they can access care, including to monitor presence of the virus and any related conditions that may arise, as well as psychosocial support.
Update from Kenya
There is also good news on the Ebola front in Kenya following the country’s first case and fatality earlier this month – a Kenyan man who had been working in the DRC before flying back to Nairobi via Uganda.
More than 100 contacts were identified, some of whom will complete their 21-day quarantine on Sunday and will be heading home to their families.
WHO representative in Kenya Dr. Neema Rusibamayila Kimambo welcomed the development.
“I think their sacrifice has been important in ensuring that the community is protected and that we don’t have community spread today,” she told UN News.
Listen to the full interview here.
Support, not stigma
She stressed that these people should not be stigmatised as being released from quarantine does not mean that they had Ebola, only that they had contact with someone who did.
With Ebola now confirmed in four African countries, Dr. Kimambo underscored that governments must remain vigilant.
“Africa is very interconnected and nobody is safe until everyone is safe,” she said. “So, as long as we have Ebola in DRC at the scale that it is, or in any other country, it means that we are not safe. Therefore, the key message is preparedness.”

Yemen: Deepening concerns for Taiz City as aid is blocked from entering
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23

Yemen: Deepening concerns for Taiz City as aid is blocked from entering
Aid agencies warned on Friday of the fast-developing humanitarian emergency inside Taiz City in Yemen, which has been encircled by de facto Houthi forces fighting government troops along the country’s west coast.
“It’s 20 days and counting since Taiz has been cut off…we are seeing increasingly that the fighting makes it impossible for us to get in and impossible for people to get out,” said Jens Laerke, spokesperson for the UN aid coordination office, OCHA. “Access roads have been cut off and that means that very little fuel, food or other supplies have reached the city since.”
The escalation between Houthi separatists and the Aden-based Government began in early September, ending the relative calm brought about by a 2022 truce.
Among the agencies responding to chronic and acute needs across Yemen, the UN World Food Programme (WFP) reported that more than 800,000 people in Taiz have been cut off from assistance. This includes 600,000 people who depend on humanitarian assistance and 200,000 women and children. “We’re desperately trying to regain access to Taiz and we continue to support the broader operations across Yemen,” said Azfar Deen, WFP Regional Communications Officer for Eastern and Southern Africa.
Water price hike
There is growing concern about dwindling water supplies inside Taiz City because most residents depend on water delivered by trucks, OCHA spokesperson Mr. Laerke explained. But “with the roads closed and the diesel to run the trucks very scarce, water production in the city has fallen by about half. And the cost of the truck water has roughly tripled. You can imagine what that does to these people who are trapped there,” he told journalists at a scheduled briefing in Geneva.
The UN Children’s Fund, UNICEF, highlighted deepening concerns about widespread hunger in Yemen. In Taiz alone, the agency has screened more than 168,000 children this year, with more than 52,000 found to be acutely malnourished, including more than 11,500 children suffering from severe acute malnutrition.
The agency has pre-positioned nearly 8,000 cartons of ready-to-use therapeutic food across Taiz governorate to help treat children with severe acute malnutrition. This is enough to sustain services for approximately three months, but “even when stocks are available, access constraints and disruptions to supply routes can make it more difficult for partners to transport supplies and for families to safely reach treatment”, said spokesperson Ricardo Pires.
Displacement grows
Between 7 June and 19 October 2026, the UN migration agency, IOM, recorded approximately 258,679 displaced individuals, the majority in Taiz and Lahj governorates. Many families are experiencing repeated movements and seeking refuge in already overstretched displacement sites and host communities.
In addition, as of 17 October, 3,836 Yemeni nationals arrived in Djibouti, reportedly fleeing the deteriorating security situation.
Reports indicate that at least 1,574 people have been killed and 6,939 others injured in the Yemen conflict since August.

Soil mapping aims to boost agricultural production in Kenya
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Soil mapping aims to boost agricultural production in Kenya
A new Kenyan initiative is helping farmers better understand their soils in a bid to improve crop yields amid intensifying climate shocks.
The Soil Mapping for Resilient Agrifood systems (SoilFER) programme supports farmers to develop reliable soil information that will inform agricultural decisions such as which fertilizer to use and how much.
So far, more than 3,600 soil samples have been collected and mapped across 45 counties, contributing to a digital soil map designed to provide farmers with location-specific information about their land.
Select farmers also receive training to diagnose and fix soil degradation – earning the title “soil doctor” – who then go on to teach their peers.
SoilFER was launched through a partnership between the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and the Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization (KALRO) in Kabete, with financial support from the United States Department of State and Japan.
‘Now we know better’
For Agness Munialo, a farmer from Kakamega county in western Kenya, learning about soil composition and fertility has changed how she thinks about farming.
“Farmers would use excessive chemicals, sometimes even more fertilizers in an attempt to get more yields. Now we know better,” she said.
Ms. Munialo, a trained soil doctor who participated in the SoilFER programme, said the initiative was helping farmers, particularly in rural areas, better understand soil composition, pH levels and fertility.
According to Barrack Okoba, FAO-Kenya’s national coordinator of the programme, making soil information accessible is essential to building resilience in agriculture.
“Part of resilience is to make sure that our information system is available and supporting farmers to build sustainable farm management,” he said.
Through the support of FAO, KALRO has renovated three labs and equipped them with state-of-the-art technology to support analysis of soil samples collected across the country.
The samples are georeferenced, with the findings transmitted directly to farmers’ mobile phones.
Gen Z in agriculture
The initiative is also attracting interest from young people exploring opportunities in agriculture.
Jackline Kioko, a KALRO intern who participated in the launch, said the information shared had given her a better understanding of how soil testing could inform decisions on her family’s farm.
“I'd love to do farming more, now that I have the information that you can actually test your soils to know what nutrients it requires,” she said.
Collaboration and information sharing
Kenya’s Cabinet Secretary for Agriculture, Mutahi Kagwe called for stronger collaboration among agricultural institutions to promote coordinated decision-making, enhance information sharing, and ensure that soil health is integrated into the work of all relevant institutions.
“I want to urge Kenyans that before thinking about what to plant or the fertilizer to use, think about soil testing,” he said.
The event also marked the launch of the Kenya Soil Partnership, the Kenya Soil Laboratory Network and the national rollout of the Global Soil Doctors Programme.
The SoilFER programme is currently being implemented in six other countries: Ghana, Guatemala, Honduras, Mozambique, Tunisia and Zambia.

West Bank: Guterres alarmed as Israel imposes sweeping closures after deadly Hebron attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
