West Bank: Guterres alarmed as Israel imposes sweeping closures after deadly Hebron attack
The UN said on Friday it was “extremely alarmed” by intensifying violence in the occupied West Bank, as Israel moved to seal off the territory following a deadly attack on its soldiers in Hebron.
Two Israeli soldiers were killed and at least five injured when gunmen opened fire near a military checkpoint outside the city, according to news reports. The two Palestinian attackers were also killed.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered Hebron sealed, pledged house-to-house raids and home demolitions, and reportedly threatened a wider assault on a scale not seen since the Six-Day War. It is the fourth time in a month that Israel has imposed restrictions across the territory.
Speaking at the noon briefing in New York, UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said Secretary-General António Guterres was deeply concerned by the closures and by reports of home demolitions and possible displacement in Hebron.
“Those closures severely restrict Palestinians’ freedom of movement, access to basic services and livelihoods,” he said.
Record settler violence
Mr. Guterres condemned “the violence caused by record numbers of attacks by Israeli settlers against Palestinians in 2026”, recalling Israel’s obligation as the occupying power “to protect the Palestinian population from such attacks and to hold perpetrators to account”.
Mayy El Sheikh, spokesperson for the UN human rights office (OHCHR) in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, said the lockdown was “yet another episode in a never-ending stream of suffocating measures making life more and more unbearable for Palestinians.”
‘Pattern of collective punishment’
“It follows a pattern of collective punishment whenever Palestinians commit acts of violence against Israeli settlers or soldiers,” she said, noting that similar incidents had previously brought lockdowns, intensified raids and arbitrary detentions.
Hebron’s entrances and exits were closed after Friday’s attack, she said, and the Ibrahimi Mosque was shut, leaving worshippers unable to perform Friday prayers.
The closure comes at the height of the olive harvest.
“Israeli movement restrictions are already preventing thousands of Palestinian farmers from reaching their olives for the harvest,” Ms. El Sheikh said. “This is bound to have devastating effects on the season.”
OHCHR has documented more than 160 settler attacks in the first two weeks of October alone, involving live ammunition, arson, crop theft and damage to olive groves.
Settlers also targeted European Union diplomats, and a Washington Post photojournalist was badly assaulted a week ago by masked settlers while covering the harvest near Ramallah.
Gaza deaths
Mr. Guterres also remained deeply concerned about civilian deaths in Gaza, including children, and severe aid restrictions ahead of winter.
He called on all parties “to immediately cease all acts of violence, to exercise restraint and refrain from action that could further inflame tensions”.

Sudan: Drone strikes killed at least 306 people in three weeks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Sudan: Drone strikes killed at least 306 people in three weeks
UN human rights chief Volker Türk on Friday strongly condemned an escalation in drone strikes across Sudan this month, which killed at least 306 people and injured hundreds more in the first three weeks of October alone.
The strikes, attributed to both the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), hit homes, markets, hospitals, displacement sites, power stations and water sources in Kordofan, Darfur, Blue Nile, Khartoum and other states, according to the UN human rights office (OHCHR).
“The increasing use of drones, already accounting for the majority of conflict-related civilian deaths in Sudan this year, is deeply disturbing and is exacting a horrifying toll,” Mr. Türk said.
Targeted by both sides
In a particularly disturbing trend, the office documented numerous strikes on displacement sites, where people who had already fled the fighting had sought shelter.
Between 6 and 10 October, alleged drone strikes attributed to military government forces on shelters for displaced people in Ghubeish and El Nuhud in West Kordofan killed at least 25 civilians, including women and children.
On 9 October, an alleged RSF drone struck a crowd of displaced people engaged in artisanal gold mining near a displacement site in Abu Shendi, Blue Nile, killing at least 31 people, most of them women and children.
On 18 October, at least 139 people were killed when a transportation truck was hit in a “double tap” repeat strike in Dibab, West Kordofan, an area controlled by the RSF militia.
Markets and hospitals have also been hit, including an RSF-attributed strike on Um Darfa hospital in Blue Nile on 11 October that seriously injured two health workers and left the facility non-operational.
“Scores of civilians have been killed, including internally displaced persons, and vital infrastructure and services have been eviscerated, driving further displacement and deepening the already severe humanitarian crisis,” said OHCHR Spokesperson Seif Magango.
Deadly strike
Peacekeepers with the UN Interim Security Force for Abyei (UNISFA) this week visited communities affected by a drone attack on 19 October on Amiet Market and the Todach area in Abyei, the disputed oil-rich region between Sudan and South Sudan. The attack killed more than 80 people.
UNISFA troops were the first to reach the scene, where “every shop was burning”, said Lieutenant Colonel Muhammad Farooq, commander of the Mission’s Pakistani battalion.
The Mission deployed quick reaction and firefighting teams to stop the fire spreading and took more than 27 injured people to its hospital in Todach, according to Acting Force Commander Brigadier General Adebowale Ajabge.
Angelina Musa Diaw, a trader and mother of three, said she had lost everything. “No work, everything is gone,” she said. “I am here with my children. But I need help.”
Security Council demands accountability
In a statement released Friday, the Security Council condemned the Abyei attack “in the strongest terms”, warning that the death toll is expected to rise as UNISFA continues to verify casualties. They stressed that attacks on civilians could amount to war crimes and called for a full, transparent and prompt investigation, with those responsible held to account.
The council reaffirmed that Abyei must remain demilitarized and free of all forces except UNISFA, and called on all actors to end military operations and occupation in the area. Members urged all parties to work with the Mission to protect civilians, aid workers and peacekeepers.
Call for ceasefire
Mr. Türk called on the parties to respect their obligations under international humanitarian law (IHL), including by not directing attacks against civilians and civilian objects.
“Broader peace efforts must squarely address the continued influx of arms that is fuelling the conflict and press for an end to the transfer of arms that are used in manifest disregard of the IHL obligations protecting civilians,” he said.
“I urge both parties to the conflict, and their affiliates, to commit to a ceasefire,” the High Commissioner added, stressing that a negotiated settlement with human rights at its core, underpinned by accountability, is the only feasible pathway to sustainable peace in Sudan.

World News in Brief: Iran nuclear inspections, deadly church attack in Jordan, El Fasher – one year on
The head of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), Rafael Grossi, called on Friday for a swift return of inspectors to Iran, warning of growing fragility in the global nuclear non-proliferation regime.
The technical groundwork has been done and “the bases on which a diplomatic agreement could be concluded exist,” he told the UN General Assembly.
He urged the parties to “redouble efforts”, adding that inspectors’ return “requires a return to the negotiating table”.
Iran has sharply restricted access since the June 2025 strikes on its nuclear sites during a 12-day war with Israel.
Non-compliance concerns
The IAEA estimated in March that just over 200 kilogrammes of uranium enriched to 60 per cent remained at Isfahan, with more at Natanz.
In September, the agency’s board of governors referred Iran’s non-compliance to the Security Council, which Tehran contests.
“The global non-proliferation regime…depends on dialogue,” Mr. Grossi said, pointing to successful efforts in Syria and war-torn Ukraine, where IAEA has brokered eight localised ceasefires to repair power lines at the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant and deployed 287 missions since Russia launched a full-scale invasion in 2022.
UN chief condemns deadly church attack in Jordan
The UN chief António Guterres on Friday strongly condemned a deadly attack on a church in Hmoud, Jordan.
The terrorist attack on a funeral service at a church in Hmoud in Jordan left seven people dead and many more injured, UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said.
“The Secretary-General expresses his deep condolences to the families of the victims and wishes a speedy recovery to all those injured,” he added.
“An attack not only on a place of worship but during a funeral procession, is especially heinous.”
The Secretary-General also called for all those responsible to be found and to be held accountable, Mr. Dujarric said.
“Attacks against civilians and places of worship are unacceptable,” he said. “Places of worship must be places of peace and must be safe for all.”
Read his full statement here.
Sudan’s El Fasher survivors, one year since city fell
One year since paramilitary forces rampaged through Sudan’s El Fasher, the legacy of fear and trauma continues to haunt thousands of survivors.
That’s the message from gender equality agency UN Women, which reported that nine in 10 Sudanese aid organizations it surveyed had found women or girls in distress who had received no mental health, psychosocial or legal support since fleeing the Darfuri city.
The war in Sudan erupted in April 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), former allies who had jointly seized power in a 2021 coup.
On Friday, UN Women regional director Anna Mutavati told reporters in Geneva that some people have started to return, “but the fear of violence is constant”.
‘Scars have not faded’
“The scars of the violence in El Fasher have not faded,” she said. “Women and girls continue to live with the trauma of sexual violence, the disappearance of their daughters, their sisters, their mothers, their husbands, and their sons, the killing of family members, and the loss of their homes, property, and livelihoods.”
Reports of deadly strikes on civilians, rape and violence continue, said Ms. Mutavati, emphasising that drone attacks are increasing across Blue Nile, Khartoum, West Kordofan, Gedaref and Kassala.
“Most of those killed or injured are women and children,” she said. “Many had already fled violence, including sexual violence.”

Eight candidates in race to become Switzerland’s next government minister
Seven men and one woman have put themselves forward as candidates to replace Guy Parmelin in the governing Federal Council.
The Swiss People’s Party’s nomination committee announced the candidates after the deadline had passed at noon on Friday. Two candidates from French-speaking Switzerland, one from Ticino and five from German-speaking Switzerland are standing for the Federal Council seat.
Parliamentarians Thomas Aeschi (Zug), Michael Graber (Valais), Rémy Wyssmann (Solothurn), Céline Amaudruz (Geneva), Marco Chiesa (Ticino), and cantonal government members Jean-Pierre Gallati (Aargau), Franz Ruppen (Valais) and Pierre Alain Schnegg (Bern) are standing for election to the Federal Council.

Guy Parmelin bows out after a remarkable final act
According to a statement, hearings with all candidates will be held over the coming weeks under the chairmanship of former Swiss People’s Party parliamentary group leader Caspar Baader. The committee reserves the right to approach other individuals if necessary, it was stated.
According to the party, this assessment will focus on the candidates’ positions on the party’s core political issues, namely armed neutrality and Switzerland’s self-determination, the EU treaty package, asylum and migration policy, the armed forces and internal security, financial relief for the middle class and businesses, and a secure and affordable energy supply.
The selection committee noted that the candidates’ leadership experience and skills are also of central importance in the assessment, particularly with regard to the Justice and Defence ministries. On November 20, the parliamentary group will decide on the list of candidates to be put before parliament for election to the Federal Council.

Ukraine has brought home 270 people in a prisoner exchange with Russia, including military personnel and nine civilians, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Friday, Oct. 23.
Most of those released had been held in Russian captivity since 2022. Among them were five Ukrainian prisoners of war who survived the July 2022 Russian attack on the Olenivka prison.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“270 of our people are home. A very important result,” Zelensky wrote on Telegram.
Those released include members of Ukraine’s National Guard, including fighters from the Azov unit, as well as border guards, Territorial Defense members, and personnel from the Navy, Ground Forces, Air Assault Forces, and State Special Transport Service.
According to Zelensky, most of those returning are soldiers who defended the besieged southern port city of Mariupol. Others served in the Donetsk, Luhansk, Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, Kherson, Kyiv, Mykolaiv, and Chernihiv sectors.
Many of the released Ukrainians had been illegally convicted in Russia, Zelensky said.
Among those returning are five people who were previously believed to have died during Russia’s July 2022 attack on the Olenivka prison, where Ukrainian prisoners of war were held.
According to open-source data, more than 53 Ukrainian defenders were killed and over 130 wounded in the mass killing of Ukrainian prisoners of war at Penal Colony No. 120 in Russian-occupied Olenivka (Donetsk region) on the night of July 29, 2022. Most of the victims were members of the Azov Regiment who had defended the Azovstal steel plant in Mariupol.
Ukraine Expands Satellite Cooperation With Finland as Starlink Doubts Linger
“We remember every single person and continue the search for everyone,” Zelensky wrote, thanking those involved in securing the exchanges.
He also thanked Ukrainian troops on the front lines for capturing Russian personnel, which he said helps Ukraine bring its own people home through prisoner exchanges.
150 Russian soldiers traced by families through Ukrainian project
Meanwhile, the Ukrainian state project I Want to Find (Khochu Nayti), which provides information about Russian military personnel captured, missing, or killed in Ukraine, reported on Telegram that 270 Russian soldiers had returned to Russia in the exchange.
More than half of those released – 150 people, or 56 percent – had been located by their relatives through the project. It helped their families confirm their captivity, enabling them to secure official prisoner-of-war status for the soldiers in Russia.
According to the project, 40 percent of those exchanged had spent less than a year in captivity, while another 43 percent had been held for one to two years. Only 17 percent had been in captivity for more than two years.
“For comparison: in the August exchange, more than half of the military personnel whom Russia brought back from captivity had spent less than a year there,” the report stated.
Half of those returned were between 35 and 44 years old, while young men aged 19 to 24 accounted for the next-largest group, at 21 percent. The exchange also included 11 prisoners of war aged over 55.
Ahead of the elections, Russian authorities announced they were prepared to include residents of the Russian-occupied parts of Donetsk and Luhansk regions who had been recruited into the Russian Armed Forces on prisoner-exchange lists. Before that announcement, Russia had refused for years to facilitate the return of these prisoners of war.
“As soon as the elections were over, officials predictably tried to ‘forget’ their promises. However, the prisoners of war themselves and their families continued to push for them to be honored,” the project said.
POWs from the so-called “LDNR” (Donetsk and Luhansk People’s Republics) recorded video appeals and repeatedly asked Russia to include them in exchange lists during interviews.
Many had been in captivity since the beginning of the full-scale war. During that time, they had witnessed numerous exchanges in which Moscow brought home service members who had spent only a few months in captivity, the project noted.
Following public pressure, Russian authorities included dozens of Russian Armed Forces personnel from the so-called “LDNR” in Friday’s exchange. Among them were Dmitry Ryabtsev and Sergey Kharitonov, who had been held in captivity for more than four years.
First major POW exchange in two months
The most recent known return took place on Aug. 24, when Ukraine brought home 10 servicemen via Belarus as a special stage of an exchange previously agreed between the two sides. All 10 had fought in the Donetsk sector and had been listed as missing – two since 2024 and eight since 2025.
Earlier, on Aug. 19, Ukraine and Russia exchanged 103 prisoners each. Those released to Ukraine included members of the Armed Forces, Border Guard Service, and National Guard who had fought in Mariupol and other sectors.
In April, Kyrylo Budanov, head of Ukraine’s Presidential Office, announced preparations for another exchange shortly after Ukraine brought home 182 people in its 72nd prisoner swap.
The group included 175 military personnel and seven civilians, many of whom had been held in captivity since 2022. Among them were defenders of Mariupol and the Chornobyl Nuclear Power Plant.
At the time, Budanov said a larger group could not be returned immediately because of what he described as bureaucratic delays on the Russian side.

Europe will have to accept dependence on us – US tech giant

Europe will have to accept dependence on us – US tech giant
European governments should stop worrying about their growing dependence on American AI, US tech giant Palantir’s top executive for the UK and Europe has said. Instead, they should focus on the advantages the products offer, particularly against Russia, Palantir UK CEO Louis Mosley believes.
The European Commission is frantically trying to reduce reliance on American tech and the US in general.
“Europe is going to have to accept some dependency,” Mosely told Bloomberg News this week.
The Commission estimates that the bloc relies on foreign providers for over 80% of its digital products, services, infrastructure, and intellectual property. However, many are skeptical that replacement is possible. In a Wire’s 2025 survey cited by the European Parliament, only 16% of regional IT leaders said the bloc could achieve digital sovereignty within five years, with almost 60% citing US dominance as a key obstacle.
Nevertheless, this year several European governments have rejected Palantir products or announced plans to phase them out. France’s domestic intelligence agency, the DGSI, which adopted the company’s analytical software in 2015, has plans to drop it over the coming years in favor of a domestically developed alternative from ChapsVision.
“We cannot depend on the goodwill of certain partners who, as we’ve seen in recent days, are capable of cutting off access to models,” Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said when announcing the decision in June.
Berlin has reportedly chosen the same French competitor over Palantir for Germany’s domestic intelligence agency BfV.
Similar moves to ostracize the American firm have been reported in Spain and Denmark, as well as the non-EU nations of Switzerland, Norway, and the UK.
Mosley cited Palantir’s extensive use of the Ukraine conflict as a testing ground for its military solutions, saying “the questions around sovereignty are secondary” for Kiev. The company got involved in Ukraine following the escalation of Kiev’s conflict with Russia in 2022, supplying what it calls “targeting packages.”
One of Palantir’s flagship products is Maven, an AI-powered system that processes vast amounts of intelligence data to help identify targets and generate strike recommendations for troops. It accelerates the so-called “kill chain,” allowing the military to consider substantially more potential targets than human personnel previously could.
Originally developed as a Pentagon project, Maven involved Google until 2018, when employee protests prompted the company to withdraw from the initiative. NATO purchased its own version of the system for use at its European headquarters in March 2025.
“I can provide categorical reassurance that where customers have bought our software, they are in full operational control of that software,” Mosley assured in a separate interview with Reuters concerning NATO’s purchase.
There are no kill switches. There’s no ability for Palantir or the US government to reach in and switch it off.
The US government has a track record of restricting foreign access to flagship AI models. The French prime minister’s remark about a lack of goodwill was a reference to Washington’s blockage of Anthropic’s Mythos 5 tool, which lasted for almost three weeks.

OMA turns potato head’s bali store into creative workshop for recycled materials and traditional craft

OMA turns potato head’s bali store into creative workshop for recycled materials and traditional craft
rammed earth architecture, recycled materials, and traditional indonesian craftsmanship come together in a circular retail space with hands-on workshops.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
OMA AND POTATO HEAD REIMAGINE RETAIL IN BALI
In Bali, Potato Head and OMA have opened the Good Times General Store, a retail space where buying something is only part of the experience. Located within Desa Potato Head in Seminyak, Indonesia, the hospitality brand’s first permanent store doubles as a craft center, bringing together Indonesian-made objects, fashion, furniture, and hands-on workshops. Rather than separating production from consumption, the project invites visitors to discover how things are made, where their materials come from, and what happens to them after their first life.
The architecture follows the same philosophy. Developed by OMA in collaboration with Ade Herkarisma, Potato Head’s Group Head of Architecture and Development, the building draws on Balinese construction traditions through an alang-alang thatch facade, rammed-earth walls made from local clay, reclaimed wood, and terrazzo floors incorporating recycled bamboo offcuts. Fragmented earthen blocks organize the interior while blurring the boundaries between its different functions. The result is a tactile environment where the materials do much of the talking, without needing to hide behind elaborate finishes.
FIVE BAYS BRING INDONESIAN CRAFT AND RECYCLED DESIGN TOGETHER
Inside, five interconnected bays trace different stages in the lifecycle of objects. Designed by OMA, the spatial layout brings together retail, craftsmanship, and material experimentation within a single environment. The first introduces artisan souvenirs, books, records, and lifestyle pieces by independent makers, while the second showcases Potato Head’s clothing and travel collection inspired by Bali. The third is dedicated to the Wasted collection by Max Lamb, which transforms discarded plastics and other waste materials into functional furniture and homeware. Together, these spaces present different approaches to design, from traditional Indonesian craftsmanship to contemporary experiments in material reuse.
The remaining two bays shift the focus from finished products to the processes behind them. A working natural dye studio extracts pigments from plants and food waste collected across Desa Potato Head, inviting visitors to experiment with dyeing, painting, and pattern-making. Next door, a wall of shredded HDPE plastic, recovered through collectors and upcyclers in Bali and Java, anchors a workshop space dedicated to plastic molding and material experimentation. The program will continue to evolve, with additional ateliers for weaving, upcycling, and sewing planned for 2027.
OMA CONNECTS CIRCULAR ARCHITECTURE WITH HANDS-ON WORKSHOPS
Beyond its retail program, the Good Times General Store is connected to Potato Head’s existing sustainability infrastructure, including the Waste Lab, where discarded materials are investigated and repurposed, and the Follow the Waste Tour, which traces how resources move through the resort. The relationship extends to the architecture itself, conceived as an example of how locally sourced and reclaimed materials can shape contemporary spaces. ‘Retail can be more than a transaction,’ says Potato Head founder Ronald Akili, emphasizing the importance of understanding who makes an object, what goes into it, and what its next life might look like.
For OMA, the project continues a long-standing collaboration with Potato Head that has already produced several spaces across Desa, including the hotel and Klymax Discotheque. This time, however, the emphasis moves from hospitality and entertainment to the everyday relationship between people and the things they consume. By bringing craft, recycling, and public participation into a single architectural setting, the Good Times General Store proposes a different kind of shopping experience, one in which visitors might leave with a handmade object, a new skill, or simply a better understanding of waste. The shopping bag, for once, is not necessarily the main takeaway.
project info:
name: Good Times General Store
designers: OMA and Potato Head | @oma.eu and @potatoheadbali
location: Seminyak, Indonesia

Yesterday I received a photograph showing one of our fighters, call sign “Kazak.” He’s from the Espanola battalion. He died after drawing a drone away from his fellow soldiers, a heroic act. 5 signs Iran war is escalating
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:54:08 UTC
20:54:08 KST

The US and Israel launched their war on Iran on February 28, and the conflict is now in its eighth month, with a series of developments suggesting the fighting could widen.
The opening US-Israeli strikes killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and other senior officials, and Iran retaliated with attacks on US military bases and oil facilities in the Gulf, alongside repeated disruptions of shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. A memorandum of understanding was reached between the US and Iran in June, aimed at halting hostilities and restoring commercial shipping, but it has now largely broken down.
With Israel heading to the polls on October 27 and the US midterm elections following in November, reports say both countries have drawn up plans for renewed strikes.
Here are five developments that point to a possible new phase of the war.
Trump hints at more strikes
US President Donald Trump has signalled that the war may intensify. He said Washington had "knocked the hell out of" Iran and "may do it a little bit further".
On Wednesday he said the US was not negotiating with Tehran and that "something one way or the other" would happen "fairly soon".
Tehran has answered with threats of its own. Iran's Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei warned that Iran could target US-linked energy, data and AI facilities across seven Gulf states, citing a "zero red lines" strategy.
Iran has also vowed to hit regional data centres, undersea internet cables and Saudi oil refineries, including Aramco facilities.
Attacks on shipping around Hormuz surge
Before the war, the Strait of Hormuz handled about 125 large commercial vessels a day and about 20 percent of global crude and LNG supplies. Now it is effectively closed to normal traffic.
The International Maritime Organization has recorded 27 attacks on commercial ships this month, the highest since the war began. At least 24 sailors have died in attacks on 100 commercial ships since February.
Both the US and Iran claim control of the waterway.
US and Israel reportedly draw up strike plans
The New York Times reported that the US and Israeli militaries have developed plans for a short but intensive offensive after the US midterm elections, with possible targets including energy, nuclear and missile sites.
They have stepped up exercises, including flights across Iraqi airspace, and US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth made an unannounced visit to Israel.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has reportedly pushed for renewed strikes, although Trump has opposed restarting the war before the midterms.
Officials said both militaries were ready to strike earlier this month before Trump called off the operation at the last moment. Analysts suggest Netanyahu could use the prospect of war to press rivals into a unity government after Israel's 27 October election.
Negotiations remain stalled
The memorandum of understanding signed in June after Pakistani and Qatari mediation has stalled amid disagreements, including over navigation in the strait. There is no clear path forward on the US naval blockade, sanctions relief or Iran's nuclear programme.
Rezaei said Iran has set seven conditions through intermediaries and will not reopen Hormuz or resume talks until they are met. Attacks on ships have increased since Trump rejected a Tehran proposal late last month to end the war and open the strait.
Rezaei also cautioned that energy markets may not stabilise for up to three years.
UK deploys fighter jets to Saudi Arabia
On Tuesday, the UK government said it will deploy Royal Air Force (RAF) Typhoon fighter jets on defensive missions to help protect Saudi Arabia from escalating attacks by the Iran-allied Houthi militia. London said the jets would not carry out offensive strikes.
The move adds to a wider Western military presence in the region. UK jets have already flown defensive sorties over other Gulf states and Jordan.
The US State Department has ordered non-emergency staff and families to leave Saudi Arabia amid Houthi strikes.

UK tells public to keep three days' emergency supplies at home
The British government advised the public on Friday to keep three days of emergency supplies at home, a message it said had been hammered home by this week's PHP software glitch, as well as a record-setting summer of heat, drought and wildfires.
Governments and businesses worldwide have rushed to secure systems running the PHP programming language after flaws were disclosed on Wednesday, forcing some services offline and triggering millions of hacking attempts in one of the most significant cybersecurity incidents in recent years.
The British government said the internet outage showed the importance of its newly launched "Be Ready" campaign, which advises the public to keep three days of bottled water and non-perishable food in the house.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham, hosting a meeting on the response to wildfires, said that in the past Britain had been "on the back foot" responding to emergencies and that it needed to be more proactive. The government announced a new wildfire response plan that includes deploying military aircraft.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said cyber incidents such as the PHP outage would become more common as AI made it easier to find ways to thwart traditional defences. He also cited risks from hostile states, organised criminals and climate change.
The UK was facing a greater level of threat "than we have certainly for most, if not all, of my lifetime", he said during an appearance on the BBC's "Question Time" programme broadcast overnight.
Britain's advice is similar to that issued by the European Commission, which told EU citizens last year to keep a 72-hour emergency kit containing supplies such as food, water, cash and power banks.

Singapore's longevity industry: The quest for eternal youth
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
In Singapore, the quest for eternal youth is no longer just a billionaire's fantasy. It's becoming big business. High-tech clinics, longevity labs and specialist companies all promise the same thing: slowing down the ageing process. From continuous metabolic monitoring and genetic testing to supplements and oxygen therapy, every aspect of the body is measured and optimised.
For some, the ambition is clear: to shave 20 years off their biological age and stay fit, sharp and competitive for as long as possible.
The global healthy-ageing market was worth between $19 billion and $20 billion in 2023, and is expected to more than triple by 2035. Singapore may offer a glimpse of what lies ahead: a world where healthcare becomes a subscription service, and where every cell can be measured, improved and even corrected.
FRANCE 24's Theo Collet, Antoine Morel, Aruna Popuri and Adam Hancock report.

Kunstnik Silver "SBoy" Seeblum kujutab teosel Ülemiste vanakest, kes legendi järgi elab lähedalasuvas Ülemiste järves ja küsib aeg-ajalt, kas Tallinn on valmis. Maalil istub vanake järve ääres sülearvuti taga.
Kunstniku sõnul oli maali lõpetamine juba päris raske, aga ta teeks seda uuesti.
Eesti rahvatantsijate video kogus kiiresti üle miljoni vaatamise
Sotsiaalmeedias kogus üle miljoni vaatamise Tallinna Ülikooli rahvatantsurühma Soveldaja video, kus tantsitakse Eesti rahvariietes ameerika räppar Future'i loo "Mask Off" saatel.
Sellega liitus Eesti ülemaailmse "Born From Culture" trendiga, mille algatas koreograaf James Fenwick. Video filmimiseks Tallinnas kulus kaheksa tundi ja selle tegemiseks polnud rühmal eelarvet.
Koreograaf Elo Unt ütles, et tema hinnangul tuli tantsuvideos toredasti välja eestlaslik olek, meie olemise viis.

New exchange: Ukraine brings back 270 more defenders from Russian captivity – photos
On Friday 23 October, 270 military personnel returned to Ukraine from Russian captivity as part of a new exchange.
Source: Zelenskyy on social media; Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War
Quote from Zelenskyy: "270 of our people are home. A very important result. National Guard members, including Azov warriors, border guards, warriors of the Territorial Defence Forces, the Navy, the Land Forces, the Airborne Assault Forces, and the State Special Transport Service, as well as nine civilians, are returning home. Most of them had been in captivity since 2022."
Details: According to the president, most of those released are warriors who defended Ukraine in Mariupol. People who defended the Donetsk, Luhansk, Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, Kherson, Kyiv, Mykolaiv, and Chernihiv fronts are also returning.
"Many were illegally convicted in Russia. Among those returning are five people who were believed to have been killed in the Russian terrorist attack in Olenivka in July 2022," Zelenskyy wrote.
Background: Ukraine and Russia held their last prisoner of war exchange in August, when 103 service personnel from the National Guard, the Armed Forces of Ukraine, the Navy, the Territorial Defence Forces and the State Border Guard Service were brought back to Ukraine.

Alpha Research poll shows Iotova’s lead narrowing as rivals gain ground

Iliana Iotova
PHOTO Ani Petrova
Font size
President Iliana Iotova and her running mate Kiril Valchev retain their lead ahead of the 25 October presidential election, but their support has fallen by a statistically significant margin, according to a poll funded by Alpha Research itself.
The poll put their support at 41.1% among those certain to vote. Andrey Gyurov and his running mate Georgi Kandev have gained ground, with 28.3%, as have Kostadin Kostadinov and Petar Volgin, with 12.8%.
The polling agency expects turnout of around 40%, or 2.6–2.7 million people, slightly higher than at the start of the campaign.
Asked about the government’s response to drone attacks in the Black Sea, 19% of respondents said it had been entirely appropriate. Another 37% said the government should have sought more active assistance from the European Union and NATO, while 24% said it should have maintained complete neutrality.

Unions, employers and government fail to agree on minimum wage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:51:00 UTC
20:51:00 KST

Friday 23 October 2026 13:19
Friday, 23 October 2026, 13:19
PHOTO BTA
Font size
The National Council for Tripartite Cooperation failed to reach a consensus on a proposal to raise the minimum wage to €660, BTA reports. Employers’ organisations support the proposed increase.
The minimum wage in 2026 is €620, Social Minister Natalia Efremova said. She said the proposal was in line with what the state budget could afford and would affect around 462,000 people. The 6.4% rise would exceed the annual inflation rate of 5.7%, Efremova stressed.
Trade unions said that one in six workers in the country is considered to be among the working poor. A minimum wage of €660 in no way guarantees a decent standard of living, they said, adding that after income tax is deducted, take-home pay falls to €512.

Regional powers, European heavyweights meet in Istanbul for 1st joint talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:51:00 UTC
20:51:00 KST

The R4 meeting was attended by Pakistani Foreign Minister Muhammad Ishaq Dar (2nd L), Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty (L), and Saudi Arabian Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan (R). (AA Photo)
Istanbul hosted high-level diplomatic talks on Oct. 23, bringing together foreign ministers from regional and European powers to discuss the Iran conflict, maritime security, the Palestinian issue and the Russia-Ukraine war. 
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan chaired the inaugural joint meeting of the R4 and E3 diplomatic groups, bringing together Türkiye, Egypt, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia under the R4 framework, alongside Britain, France and Germany, which constitute the E3.
The Oct. 23 meeting marked the first joint gathering of the two mechanisms, reflecting efforts to expand cooperation between European powers and key regional actors amid mounting geopolitical tensions.
Italian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani was also expected to attend the talks, bringing the number of participating countries to eight.
Fidan held separate meetings in Istanbul with British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and Pakistani Foreign Minister Mohammad Ishaq Dar.
The discussions were scheduled to begin in the R4 format before being expanded to include top diplomats from the E3 group and Italy.
According to Turkish diplomatic sources, Fidan was expected to emphasize that regional security requires countries in the region to assume primary responsibility for addressing their own challenges.
Within this framework, he was expected to highlight Türkiye's commitment to strengthening cooperation mechanisms founded on regional ownership.
Fidan was also expected to stress that existing disputes must not exacerbate one another, conflicts must not spread to new fronts, and regional tensions must not escalate into wider instability.
The Turkish foreign minister was expected to identify Israel's policies toward the Palestinian territories, which he considers an obstacle to peace efforts, and its expanding military actions across the region as major drivers of instability in the Middle East.
Fidan was also expected to underline that tensions between the United States and Iran could be resolved only through diplomacy and dialogue, warning that military approaches fail to deliver lasting solutions and instead deepen regional vulnerabilities.
Ensuring freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on a lasting basis was another key priority on the agenda, given the waterways' significance for regional and global stability.
The discussions were also expected to cover Houthi attacks targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia. Fidan was expected to reaffirm Türkiye's support for Saudi Arabia's security and highlight the principle of collective security and solidarity underpinning the Mecca Defense Agreement.
Ahead of the talks, Miliband's office said the discussions would focus particularly on the Strait of Hormuz and the security situation in Saudi Arabia.
He was also set to warn that Iranian tactics were being replicated elsewhere in the region, with attacks on Saudi Arabia further destabilizing the Middle East and placing additional pressure on strategic maritime routes, including Bab el-Mandeb and the Suez Canal.
The meeting was also expected to address the security implications of the Russia-Ukraine war, particularly the risk of the conflict spreading into the Black Sea.
Fidan was expected to reiterate that Türkiye, as a Black Sea littoral state, would continue presenting proposals to the parties to prevent further escalation and contain the conflict's impact on regional security.
Attacks on commercial vessels, frequently involving drones, have increased in recent months as the conflict has extended its reach across the Black Sea, placing Turkish shipping at growing risk.
Türkiye submitted a proposal to Russia and Ukraine last month aimed at halting attacks on maritime targets. However, strikes have continued in recent weeks, particularly in waters near Romania and Bulgaria.
NATO announced on Oct. 20 that it was deploying additional aircraft, drones and radar systems to the Black Sea to improve regional surveillance and situational awareness through enhanced sensor coverage and greater information-sharing.
The R4 mechanism, established this year by Türkiye, Egypt, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, is intended to promote lasting regional stability and strengthen dialogue on shared challenges through an approach based on regional ownership.
The four countries have held six foreign ministers' meetings, beginning in Riyadh on March 18, with the most recent taking place in New York on Sept. 21 on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly's high-level week.
The E3, comprising Britain, France and Germany, emerged from diplomatic coordination on Iran's nuclear program launched in 2003. Initially focused on the nuclear issue, the grouping has gradually developed into a platform for joint diplomatic initiatives on a broader range of regional and international matters.

Denmark sends ammo to Ukraine for F-16 guns to down drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:50:33 UTC
20:50:33 KST

- Denmark delivered more than 50,000 rounds of 20 mm ammunition to Ukraine on an expedited basis for the cannons on its F-16 fighters.
- Ukrainian pilots are already using the rounds to shoot down Russia’s jet-powered Shahed-type attack drones, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said.
Denmark has rushed more than 50,000 rounds of 20 mm ammunition to Ukraine for the cannons on its F-16 fighter jets, and Ukrainian pilots are already firing them at Russia’s jet-powered Shahed-type attack drones, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said on Oct. 23, 2026.
The ministry announced the delivery on X, saying Denmark sent the rounds on an expedited basis in response to a Ukrainian request. It described aviation, and the F-16 in particular, as one of the most effective tools against jet-powered Shaheds, and said destroying them requires sufficient stocks of ammunition.
“We are grateful to Denmark for its quick and effective response to our request for additional ammunition. This speed matters directly for strengthening Ukraine’s air defence and protecting people from Russian air attacks,” said Minister of Defence Evgeniy Khmara.
Every F-16 carries an internal M61A1 Vulcan, a six-barrel rotary cannon that fires about 6,000 rounds per minute. Using the gun against drones lets pilots save their far more expensive guided missiles for cruise missiles and other high-priority targets, and 20 mm rounds are held in much larger quantities around the world than Patriot interceptors or Western air-to-air missiles.
The guns burn through ammunition quickly, with Bloomberg reporting that destroying a single jet-powered drone can take about 150 rounds and that, at the current intensity of Russian attacks, Ukraine could need around 10,000 rounds a day. At that rate, the Danish shipment would cover roughly 330 engagements.
Russia began using jet-powered versions of its Geran drones, the Russian-built derivatives of the Iranian Shahed-136, in significant numbers in early 2026. The newer jet models can carry up to 90 kg (198 pounds) of explosives, fly up to 1,000 km (620 miles) and reach speeds of up to 600 km/h (373 mph), making them much harder to catch than the earlier propeller-driven drones. Ukrainian Air Force spokesman Yurii Ihnat has said Ukraine shoots down about 60% of the jet-powered drones, compared with roughly 90% to 95% for other types.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said combat aviation, primarily the F-16, accounts for 55% to 60% of all intercepts of jet-powered Shaheds, and that Ukraine has expanded contracts to keep its F-16 squadrons supplied with 20 mm rounds. Germany has delivered its first batch of F-16 ammunition for countering the drones, and Belgium and Spain have also sent urgent shipments.
Denmark has been one of Ukraine’s main F-16 partners, pledging 19 of the jets and hosting early training for Ukrainian pilots. Ukraine is also testing several domestically built interceptor drones designed to catch jet-powered Shaheds, while its F-16 pilots continue to use their cannons against the drones with the new Danish rounds.

Trump Says Starlink Limits Are Gone—Ukraine Says the Signal Still Dies at 100 MPH
Ukraine’s Defense Ministry has not confirmed that Starlink speed restrictions have been removed, despite US President Donald Trump saying SpaceX had already lifted the limits affecting Starshield terminals in Ukraine, ministry sources told UNITED24 Media on October 23.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukrainian specialists are continuing to monitor both the civilian Starlink network and its military-focused Starshield service.
As of the morning of October 23, tests were still recording cases in which connectivity disappeared once terminals reached speeds of around 161 kilometers per hour—roughly 100 mph.
That leaves uncertainty over whether the restrictions have been fully removed, partially relaxed, or are still affecting some terminals and configurations.
The findings come a day after Trump said SpaceX had already eliminated the speed restriction for Starshield terminals operating in Ukraine.
For now, however, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry says it has no confirmation from its own monitoring that the limitation has disappeared.
Earlier, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Starlink and Starshield services used by Ukrainian forces remain restricted, although US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has promised to work to resolve the issue.
The President also confirmed that the US had restored intelligence sharing with Ukraine, including information about Russian ballistic missile launches.

Trump to rally in Florida after stoking Ramaswamy ad furor – US politics live
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:48:31 UTC
20:48:31 KST

Ramaswamy accuses Acton of ‘lying’ about attack ad, but court records contradict mother’s claim – live
Vivek Ramaswamy campaign ad features Democrat Amy Acton’s estranged mother accusing her of lying about her childhood, but a copy of a 1978 arrest warrant suggests Acton told the truth
Ramaswamy accuses Acton of 'lying' about attack ad, but court records contradict claim made by Acton's mother in ad
Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for Ohio governor, accused his Democratic opponent, Dr Amy Acton, of “lying about lying” in her outraged response to an attack ad released by his campaign.
“We ran an ad about lying,” Ramaswamy argued on Friday, “it had nothing to do with childhood abuse”. Instead, the Republican claimed, his opponent was lying “about her history”.
The Ramaswamy campaign ad features Acton’s estranged mother, Donna Arthur, accusing the daughter she lost custody of in 1978, after her second husband was charged with raping her then 12-year-old daughter, of lying about her childhood.
According to police and court documents obtained by the Associated Press, Arthur’s second husband, Cledith Arthur, was arrested and charged with the rape of his stepdaughter in July 1978, after Acton’s biological father reported him to authorities. The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978, when Acton was between 10 and 12 years old.
Cledith Arthur pleaded not guilty and was indicted by a grand jury that September, but failed to show at a court hearing and remained a fugitive until at least 1981. Donna Arthur fled the state with her husband, who later died.
Philip Stearns, Acton’s brother, said in a statement denouncing the ad that after his stepfather was arrested “and Amy and I were removed from their custody, our birth mother stayed married to Amy’s rapist until he died.”
In the attack ad, Donna Arthur called her daughter “a liar” and said “she lies about her past; she says she grew up living in a tent, none of that is true.” That part of the ad uses stock video of a tent that had previously appeared in a biographical ad from Acton’s campaign, in which the candidate described her troubled upbringing. “I think it was somewhere off Route 7,” the candidate recalls. “I was 12, and we were living in a tent.”
A copy of the 1978 arrest warrant for Cledith Arthur, posted online on Friday by Nick Evans, a reporter for the Ohio Capital Journal, suggests that Acton was telling the truth. The warrant lists a campground off Ohio Route 7 in Rogers, Ohio as Cledith Arthur’s address.
“In 1982, after the Arthurs had skipped bail and fled Ohio, a deputy attempted to serve a warrant at” the same campground, Evans reports. “In a hand written note, the deputy relays that the park’s manager said Arthur ‘has not camped here for over two years.’”

'We’ll take care of Cuba on our way back from Iran', Trump tells Florida crowd
Donald Trump casually hinted at likely US military action against Cuba during a campaign rally in Fort Myers, Florida on Friday.
About midway through his 90 minute speech, as he described the toll inflicted on Iran by the Pentagon, Trump’s remarks were interrupted by a supporter shouting “What about Cuba?”
“He wants to know what about Cuba. Give me a break,” Trump said. “Don’t worry, we’ll take care of Cuba on our way back from Iran. We’ll just- we’ll do a little stopover”.
“Actually, what we’re going to do with Cuba is we’re going to come back from Iran,” Trump went on, making a swerving gesture with his hand. “Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. “We’ll have Marco – Marco!” he continued. “We don’t even have to stop, we could just put him in there and he’ll figure it out.”

Susan Collins, the vulnerable Republican senator in Maine vying for a sixth term in office, said that she had secured additional tariffs exemptions on Canadian products that are crucial to her state’s agricultural industries.

Collins has positioned herself as a moderate Republican, comfortable breaking with Donald Trump, and touted the millions in federal funds she’s directed back to Maine as chair of the powerful Senate appropriations committee.

'I'm the one that said do it': Trump touts lawsuit to block Senate race certification in Alaska
Speaking to reporters in Florida, Donald Trump touted the justice department lawsuit that attempts to block the Senate race certification in Alaska, if the incumbent Republican that he has endorsed there loses.
“I’m the one that said do it,” Trump said, while standing alongside Ron DeSantis, the GOP governor of Florida.
Without evidence, the president claimed that Daniel J Sullivan, the retired schoolteacher and registered Republican running against the incumbent GOP senator Daniel S Sullivan, was “put up” by Democrats to siphon the vote against the Trump-endorsed candidate.
“I don’t think he ever voted before,” Trump said of the Republican challenger. “All of a sudden he decides to run for the Senate, and his name is Dan Sullivan. One is Daniel S. One is Daniel J. The Daniel J is the fake. And he wants to change his middle initial to Daniel S, but he said this has nothing to do with politics.”
David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation & Research, said that the justice department’s lawsuit against Alaska – seeking to pause the US Senate race’s certification in the event that the Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses – is “an unprecedented intervention by the federal government”.
In a statement, Becker added that the administration had “absolutely no authority to tell Alaska when or how to certify the results of its Senate election”.
Attempting to intervene “at this late stage” is “entirely against department policy”, Becker said. “There is no legitimate enforcement of federal law here, and it raises serious concerns about political interference”.
Becker also said that he could not recall an administration “ever attempting to stop the certification of an election – and certainly not 11 days before polls close”.

Turnout is being driven in part by widespread voter frustration, reflected in Donald Trump’s record-low approval ratings.
Democrats lead in early returns: Registered Democrats account for 45% of early ballots cast, compared with 30% from Republicans (tracking returned ballots, not candidate selection). The party gap is particularly pronounced in North Carolina, Kansas and Iowa. While Republicans traditionally favor election day voting, strategists worry this widened margin signals a “red undertow” – GOP voters staying home due to frustration over high gas prices, the conflict in Iran and sweeping tariffs.
Early votes are pacing well ahead of 2022: In Georgia, early votes already represent more than 37% of the total turnout from the 2022 midterms. Texas and North Carolina sit at 33%, while Florida is at 27%. We’re seeing similarly high paces recorded in Michigan and Ohio too.
Mail-in voting remains resilient: Almost 57m mail-in ballots have been requested or sent nationally – greater than the 52m requested in 2022, according to NBC News (using data from TargetSmart). Russia’s 2027 Budget Under Scrutiny as Auditors Flag $288 Billion in Spending Discrepancies
Russia’s draft federal budget for 2027–2029 contains major inconsistencies, unsupported revenue projections, and large pools of unallocated spending, Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service reported on October 22.
According to the service, Russia’s Accounts Chamber found that budget justifications covering $288.24 billion, or 77% of the open portion of 2027 federal spending, did not match the parameters of the draft budget. The documents also lacked calculations for 13 revenue categories worth a combined $9.72 billion.

More than 35% of measures and planned outcomes under Russian state programs would be assessed only on whether they were formally completed, without quantitative measures of effectiveness. Programs without specific performance criteria account for $64.71 billion in planned spending in 2027 and $81.18 billion in 2029.
Around 85% of reserved funds have not been allocated to specific areas of spending, while auditors also identified problems with investment programs and project preparation.
Russia’s debt-servicing costs are projected to rise 45.7% from the expected 2026 level to $66.82 billion by 2029. That would account for 10.5% of federal expenditure and leave fewer resources available for other state needs.
The draft budget also lacks a complete distribution of intergovernmental transfers to Russia’s regions. Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service assessed that the opacity surrounding state finances allows Moscow to continue prioritizing both its war against Ukraine and opaque handling of public funds.
The findings come as pressure on Russia’s federal finances mounts from the war’s costs, weaker energy revenues, and rising borrowing needs. Earlier in October, Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service reported that Russia’s budget deficit had reached $61.08 billion in the first nine months of 2026, already 37% above the Kremlin’s original full-year target, while oil and gas revenues fell 17.2%.

Is unity government Netanyahu’s ultimate survival tactic?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:45:03 UTC
20:45:03 KST

Benjamin Netanyahu, the longest-serving prime minister of Israel, has been pushing the idea of establishing a “broad national government” after the October 27 general election.
Analysts say a so-called unity government might be the only way Netanyahu can stay in power while stalling progress on his drawn-out corruption trials.
Netanyahu’s popularity has suffered since the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led blitz – – an attack he could have prevented by acting on intelligence tips in a timely manner – and the prolonged wars he has launched on multiple fronts.
Pre-election public polls show Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc tied with the Zionist opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot.
Each bloc is projected to win 51 seats. It means both Jewish blocs are 10 seats short of the 61-seat simple majority required in the Knesset to form a government.
In other words, neither of the two main Jewish blocs can form a government without support from Arab parties – typically backed by Palestinian citizens of Israel comprising one-fifth of the country’s population of 10.3 million.
Despite legal challenges mounted by Zionist groups to keep them from taking part in the election, Arab parties are projected to win roughly 14 seats, electoral strength that can play a decisive role in government formation.
But nearly all Jewish parties have ruled out forming a coalition government with the help of Arab parties, which they consider radioactive, especially after the Hamas-led blitz into Israel on October 7, 2023.
Opposition figures such as Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Liberman have already announced plans to pass term limits and ban defendants in criminal cases from serving as prime minister, moves that would eliminate any chance of Netanyahu continuing as prime minister.
Tugce Ersoy-Ceylan, a professor of international relations at Izmir Katip Celebi University, tells TRT World that a national unity government can certainly ensure Netanyahu's political survival given the current parliamentary arithmetic.
“While such a government might be presented as a solution to Israel's political instability, it could also allow Netanyahu to retain power without addressing the underlying institutional crisis,” she says.
Ersoy-Ceylan notes that a unity arrangement would not automatically suspend Netanyahu’s corruption trials. However, staying in office could give him “greater political leverage” to seek procedural delays.
“Therefore, political survival is a plausible motivation, but the outcome of his legal proceedings cannot be predicted with certainty,” she says.
The cases against Netanyahu, indictments for bribery, fraud, and breach of trust, have faced years-long delays for so-called security and diplomatic reasons.
Gokhan Cinkara, an academic and director of Necmettin Erbakan University Global and Regional Studies Application and Research Centre, says Netanyahu is preparing to use every political manoeuvre to stay in power.
“One such tactic is to create alarm in order to fracture the opposition bloc,” he tells TRT World.
The Israeli occupation forces said on October 23 that it had killed two Palestinians following a reported shooting attack near the occupied West Bank’s Hebron.
The incident, which happened three days before the general election, revived the security concerns, leading to a call by far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir to dismantle the Palestinian Authority (PA).
So far, no evidence suggests the PA, which has only partial control in parts of the occupied West Bank, was involved in the incident.
Cinkara says the Jewish opposition cannot form the government alone.
“One way or another, it will need the support of Palestinian-Israeli political actors,” he says.
Nimrod Goren, president and founder of the Israeli Institute for Regional Foreign Policies, tells TRT World that Netanyahu would ideally like his current coalition to govern again.
“If that will not be the case – as polls indicate – a political stalemate, in which no side can establish a coalition and the current government stays as caretaker until another election in the spring, will also be a satisfactory model for him,” he says.
Goren acknowledges that Netanyahu may try to bring on board “one of the opposition parties”, even though none are currently willing to join hands with Likud.
Eisenkot has publicly rejected serving under Netanyahu even under a rotation agreement. Similarly, Liberman has insisted on a Zionist-only coalition and the so-called defendant law that would bar Netanyahu from the premiership.
Analysts say the idea of unity has gained currency of late precisely because of this deadlock. Netanyahu has pushed for it ostensibly to end the frequent “boycotts and political vetoes”.
What about Palestinian-Israeli representation?
A central obstacle to a unity government remains the status of Arab parties.
Ersoy-Ceylan says Jewish blocs' reluctance to rely on them reflects both ideological divisions and electoral calculations.
“Most mainstream Jewish parties operate within a Zionist political framework and remain reluctant to grant Arab parties decisive influence over questions of national identity and security,” she says.
Opposition leaders also fear alienating Zionist voters. However, cooperation is still possible, she says, citing Palestinian Israeli politician Mansour Abbas’s Ra’am party, which joined the Bennett-Lapid coalition government in 2021.
The deeper problem is that even though Palestinian citizens of Israel are formally represented in the Knesset, their parties are frequently treated as “illegitimate coalition partners”, she says.
This creates a structural limitation on political inclusion and democratic representation, she adds.
Cinkara attributes much of the current exclusion of Arab parties to Netanyahu’s own framing of the issue.
“Netanyahu has succeeded in portraying Palestinian Israeli political actors in Israel as outsiders and a threat to the system – and more and more people have bought into that narrative,” he says.
He says the opposition is unlikely to exclude Arab parties after the election, as they are expected to win “close to 13 seats” in the Knesset.
Goren says the opposition will need “some sort of reliance” on the Arab parties to govern.
“Hopefully, once the numbers are in following the election, all opposition parties will act responsible and enable this to happen,” he says.
Experts say the issues of judicial independence and equal citizenship of Palestinian Israelis will bear the longer-term costs of Netanyahu’s deadlock strategy, which is centred around a “unity government” excluding non-Jewish citizens.
Ersoy-Ceylan says that Netanyahu’s repeated attempts to weaken judicial oversight risk normalising executive interference in the Israeli judiciary and undermining public confidence in democratic institutions.
The systematic delegitimisation of Palestinian Israelis means formal citizenship does not necessarily translate into equal political influence, she tells TRT World.
“Even a change of government would not automatically resolve this contradiction since the exclusion of Arab parties extends beyond Netanyahu's coalition.”

Breadcrumb
Who is Amer Ghalib, Donald Trump's new advisor on Arab-American affairs?
Amer Ghalib, the first Arab-American and Muslim elected official to endorse Donald Trump in the 2024 election, announced on Wednesday that he has been appointed to a new role as advisor to the president on Arab-American affairs.
The former mayor of Hamtramck, Michigan, said in his announcement that he was grateful to Trump for the opportunity, and that while he could not promise to solve every challenge Arab-Americans face, he would try his best to be a voice for the community in the White House.
Ghalib, who was born in Yemen, immigrated to the US in 1997 and was the first in his family to graduate from high school, made headlines in 2024 when he met with Trump and described their conversation, where they discussed various topics, from Arab American concerns to the situation in Yemen and poll updates.
The New Arab takes a closer look at who Ghalib is and some of the things he has been outspoken on.
Former mayor of Hamtramck, Kuwait ambassador
Ghalib, a physician-turned politician, was elected mayor of Hamtramck, Michigan in 2021and then was nominated in March 2025 by Trump to be the US ambassador to Kuwait.
During his time in Kuwait, he faced scathing criticism from senators such as Ted Cruz and Jeanne Shaheen for ‘liking’ social media posts that were reportedly interpreted to be antisemitic in nature—actions he distanced himself from and said were not reflective of his views.
His actions as a private citizen were also criticised by staunch pro-Israel groups, including the Israel Anti-Defamation League (ADL) and some right-wing news outlets.
In January, Ghalib started work as senior advisor for strategic partnerships at AmeriCorps, following a consultation with Trump where they discussed him exploring different career paths.
At the time, Ghalib said he chose AmeriCorps after debating several options because he believed it closely aligned with his background in public service.
“I chose this position so I can serve as a bridge between the federal government, local communities and the White House,” Ghalib told reporters at the time.
Relationship with Trump
Ghalib has long had what appears to be a good relationship with Trump, and has met him several times over the years.
Earlier this year, he said: “My relationship with the president is strong, and I have direct communication with him and his administration”.
When Ghalib endorsed Trump, many commentators suggested that the reason could have been their shared positions when it came to culture war debates, gender identity, and gay rights. The city has been known for its social conservatism, especially after it banned the pride flag on public property in 2023.
During the run-up to the 2024 presidential elections, Ghalib accompanied Trump on some of his presidential campaign rallies.
Stance on Israel
Ghalib has been outspoken about Israel’s war on Gaza, determined to be a genocide by leading rights groups and scholars.
He has also expressed his rejection of the 2020 Abraham Accords, which saw several Arab states normalise relations with Israel, and has targeted former president Joe Biden’s support for Israel.
Hamtramck also became the first American city to adopt a Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) policy against Israel. Despite criticism from pro-Israel groups, Ghalib defended the move, highlighting that the resolution had been drafted by Jewish Voice for Peace and was approved unanimously by the city council.
“It wasn’t my idea. We don’t have any companies that deal with Israel in our city,” he said at the time.
When quizzed on whether he believes Israel is a homeland for the Jewish people, he said: "I believe it can be a home for the Jewish and the Arabs and the Muslims and the Christians as well."
However, he has also faced backlash over contradictions, with many questioning the various stances he has held.
In July, Ghalib doubled down on his support for Trump, despite him calling for Palestinians to be blocked from returning from Gaza if it is taken over and redeveloped.
“Yes, I disagree with the president on the idea of evacuating indigenous people of Gaza from their homeland,” Ghalib wrote in a Facebook post. “But I still support him for many other reasons, and I don’t regret supporting him in the election.”
Some have also called him out for supporting Trump during a time when he was pushing Islamophobic policies and introducing the travel ban on several Muslim-majority countries, including Ghalib’s birthplace of Yemen.

US-Iran war, then and now: How the landscape has changed since February
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:43:53 UTC
20:43:53 KST

US-Iran war, then and now: How the landscape has changed since February
The positions of Washington and Tehran have changed dramatically since US-Israeli strikes began the war, analysts say.
Iran says seven oil tankers have caught fire or sustained damage in and around the Strait of Hormuz as its Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) warns that renewed US attacks could trigger a wider response and the world braces for the possibility of renewed hostilities.
Although analysts consider a US attack before the November 3 midterm elections unlikely, sabre-rattling on both sides has raised fears that escalating rhetoric could give way to renewed attacks with control of the Strait of Hormuz and Iranian nuclear facilities at the heart of the conflict.
But the critical Gulf waterway, through which one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies were shipped before the war, was not even an issue before the United States and Israel first launched strikes on Iran on February 28. Furthermore, talks over Iran’s nuclear programme were under way at the time.
As the US wrestles with depleted defensive weapons stocks and a global energy crisis mounts, how does the land lie now before potential renewed strikes and how does it differ from February before any of this began?
Here is what we know:
How has the geography of the war changed?
Unlike in February before the war began, the US and Iran would be fighting it out on several different fronts if attacks resume.
Iran’s regional allies and Lebanon
While the objective of US-Israeli strikes on Iran was initially to topple its leadership, another aim was to weaken Iran’s regional allies, including Hamas and Hezbollah. Announcing the offensive, Trump pledged to prevent Tehran-backed groups from attacking US forces and destabilising the region.
While the offensive failed to force a change in Iran’s government, Hamas has been severely weakened as Israel continues to attack Gaza – with more than 1,400 Palestinians killed since a US-backed “ceasefire” was announced in October last year.
Hezbollah’s retaliation against targets in northern Israel after the killing of Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei in the first US-Israeli air strikes brought Lebanon into the war in early March.
Israel launched a bombing campaign against sites in southern Lebanon and the suburbs of Beirut it considers Hezbollah strongholds and, at one point, occupied about one-fifth of the country, displacing more than one million people. It still occupies significant land on Lebanon’s southern border.
Waterways, energy facilities now battlegrounds
The biggest geographical change, however, has been the emergence of the Gulf’s waterways and energy infrastructure as key targets. Iranian attacks on US military assets and civilian infrastructure have exposed Gulf countries to the consequences of a war they had hoped to avoid.
Urban Coningham, a research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, told Al Jazeera: “US-Iran negotiations had previously centred on Iran’s regional allies and nuclear programme. The Strait of Hormuz and attacks on the Gulf have now become central points of contention.”
While the Gulf has experienced attacks before, Coningham said the scale and “velocity” of recent Iranian strikes, including on oil and gas infrastructure, have marked a significant shift.
The Strait of Hormuz between Iran and Oman, which had been freely open to international shipping before the war, now gives Tehran a means of imposing costs far beyond its borders. Iran continues to threaten and attack shipping there while the US maintains its own blockade of Iranian ports. Traffic has been severely disrupted and supplies of oil and gas have been sharply reduced.
In March, CNN reported that the Pentagon and US National Security Council had significantly underestimated Iran’s willingness to restrict passage through the strait and the consequences of that. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth rejected the reporting, insisting the military had planned for that possibility.
Renewed fighting in Yemen
Renewed fighting between the forces of the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government of Yemen and the Iran-backed Houthis has added another front to the regional crisis. Yemen’s war has expanded to Saudi Arabia as Houthi missile and drone attacks target Saudi airports and oil infrastructure.
This front has brought another trade chokepoint into sharper focus – Bab al-Mandeb, the strait that links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. Houthi threats against Saudi-linked shipping there could compound transportation disruptions in Hormuz, undermine efforts to move Gulf exports through alternative routes and place additional pressure on the US.
How have the political stakes changed?
The two countries’ leaders face different constraints. Iran’s rulers remain concerned about unrest and their own survival but do not face the same electoral reckoning as Trump’s Republican Party, which faces midterm elections in less than two weeks.
In Iran
Before the February strikes, Iran’s government faced deep public anger after its deadly crackdown in January on nationwide protests against high inflation and the plummeting value of Iran’s currency. US-Israeli attacks subsequently killed Khamenei, who had ruled since 1989, and security chief Ali Larijani. But they did not topple the Islamic Republic.
Khamenei’s son Mojtaba succeeded him. His elevation and the influence of the IRGC has reinforced the position of hardliners within the government.
Coningham cautioned that the absence of demonstrations during a war should not be interpreted as support for the government.
“While the conflict had produced a rallying effect around resistance to foreign attacks, that did not mean Iran had emerged stronger,” he said.
In the US
Meanwhile, Trump faces much tougher political pressure before any renewed strikes. His approval rating has fallen from 40 percent in a Reuters/Ipsos poll reported days before the war began to just 31 percent in a survey released on Monday – the lowest recorded by the pollster across either of Trump’s presidential terms – amid frustration over high petrol prices and the deep unpopularity of the war on Iran among Americans.
How has the economic balance changed?
In Iran
Iran’s economy was already struggling before the war, weighed down by sanctions and assets frozen abroad. The conflict has deepened those pressures as the US combines military force, more sanctions and a naval blockade to squeeze the country further.
In April, Iran’s government estimated the direct and indirect damage from US-Israeli attacks at $270bn. The pressure intensified in late August when Washington launched Operation Economic Outcast, seeking to isolate Iran from international trade by imposing penalties on those doing business with it.
Official figures showed Iran’s gross domestic product contracted by 10.1 percent year-on-year from March 21 to June 20. Energy exports have been severely curtailed by the US blockade while the rial has plunged in value.
In the US
The US has also incurred substantial costs. In September, the Congressional Budget Office estimated that the conflict had cost the Department of Defense $38bn as of August 1. It said continued operations were expected to cost about $2bn to $3bn a month, depending on the intensity of fighting.
As a result of the additional costs of the war, US government debt surpassed a record $40 trillion in August – two years before it had been expected to reach that level.
How has the military balance changed?
For the US
While the US has demonstrated its ability to strike deep inside Iran, that destructive capacity has not brought down Iran’s political system nor has it finished off Tehran’s ability to retaliate with strikes on US assets and energy infrastructure in neighbouring countries.
Coningham said the difficulty for Washington is “translating military superiority into strategic results”. He also described recent troop redeployments as possible military posturing, but he added that the deployments do represent a shift from earlier efforts to reduce the US military footprint in parts of the region.
US media reports suggested there is now a severe shortage of weapons in the US arsenal in the Middle East as expensive defensive missiles have been depleted against a bombardment of cheap Iranian drones.
Fox News reported that the USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit were expected to reach the Middle East by the end of November, bringing about 10,000 military personnel. The deployment would expand Trump’s military options as he weighs further action.
For Iran
Coningham said, for Iran, the conflict fits a longstanding narrative of resistance against what its leadership portrayed as US and Israeli colonialism and imperialism.
Since February 28, the IRGC has demonstrated its skill at “asymmetric warfare” as it has held off expensive US military might with cheap, mass-produced drones.
Furthermore, its use of “decentralised structures” has allowed it to continue operating despite disrupted communications and the loss of senior decision-makers, Coningham said.
US strikes have severely damaged Iran’s navy and increased its reliance on smaller vessels, including speedboats used in recent attacks in the Strait of Hormuz. On that front, geography is on Iran’s side as it can fire at ships in the Strait of Hormuz from ground positions along its coast. It can also place sea mines in the strait using rockets to drop them.
These are tactics the US had not necessarily expected to contend with when it initiated the strikes on Iran but will certainly face now.
How has global trade changed?
A mounting global energy crisis was not on the cards in February, but it is certainly looming now.
Disruptions to Gulf energy supplies caused by the war and fears of further escalation have pushed oil prices sharply higher. Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil prices, settled at $72.48 a barrel on February 27, the day before the war began.
It hit $126.41 on April 30, its highest level in four years. By early trading on Friday, it stood at $114.47.
But the crisis extends beyond crude oil. Damage and disruptions to fuel production in the Middle East alongside sanctions on Russian supplies have tightened diesel markets while the global supply of liquefied natural gas has also been heavily affected. The International Energy Agency warned in October that supply constraints could persist well into 2027.
Diesel, which has doubled in price in the US, is a big problem for Trump because farmers and businesses in the US, key voting blocs for him, rely on it for production and transport.
Alternative ports, pipelines and ship-to-ship transfers have helped Gulf producers restore exports but at higher logistical costs and with continuing exposure to attacks.
Re-establishing shipping through vital waterways in the Middle East, therefore, has now become a primary objective in the war.
