One of Earth’s most powerful supervolcanoes is refilling with fresh magma
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:23:19 UTC
20:23:19 KST

One of Earth’s most powerful supervolcanoes is refilling with fresh magma
- Date:
- October 23, 2026
- Source:
- Kobe University
- Summary:
- Deep beneath Japan’s Kikai caldera, a massive magma reservoir is refilling 7,300 years after one of the most powerful volcanic eruptions in Earth's recent geological history. Scientists used underwater seismic surveys to reveal a vast store of magma that appears to have accumulated since the ancient catastrophe. The discovery could help explain how supervolcanoes like Yellowstone and Toba rebuild their magma supplies.
- Share:
One of Earth's most powerful supervolcanoes is slowly refilling its enormous underground magma reservoir, thousands of years after producing one of the largest volcanic eruptions in recent geological history. Scientists at Kobe University have discovered evidence that fresh magma is accumulating beneath Japan's Kikai caldera, which unleashed a catastrophic eruption about 7,300 years ago.
The discovery offers a rare look at how giant volcanic systems rebuild their magma supplies after massive eruptions. It could also provide important clues about the behavior of other supervolcanoes, including Yellowstone in the United States and Toba in Indonesia, potentially helping scientists improve their ability to recognize warning signs of future eruptions.
How Supervolcanoes Store Enormous Amounts of Magma
Some volcanic eruptions are so immense that they dramatically reshape the landscape. The amount of magma released can be staggering, enough to bury all of New York City's Central Park beneath a layer roughly 12 kilometers (7.5 miles) thick.
When such enormous volumes of magma escape from underground, the rock above the emptied reservoir can collapse, leaving behind a broad, relatively shallow depression known as a caldera. These features are associated with some of the most powerful eruptions in Earth's history.
Famous examples include Yellowstone, Toba, and Japan's Kikai caldera, most of which lies beneath the ocean. Kikai last experienced a giant eruption approximately 7,300 years ago, producing the largest known volcanic eruption of the Holocene, the geological epoch that began roughly 11,700 years ago and continues today.
Although scientists know that giant caldera volcanoes can erupt more than once, they still have an incomplete understanding of how the enormous quantities of magma required for these events accumulate underground. This makes it extremely difficult to anticipate when another major eruption might occur.
"We must understand how such large quantities of magma can accumulate to understand how giant caldera eruptions occur," says Kobe University geophysicist Nobukazu Seama.
Scientists Discover a Massive Magma Reservoir Beneath Japan
Kikai's underwater location might seem like an obstacle to studying the volcano, but it actually gives researchers an important advantage. The surrounding seafloor allows scientists to carry out extensive geological surveys across the volcanic structure.
"The underwater location allows us to implement systematic, large-scale surveys," Seama explains.
To investigate what lies beneath Kikai, researchers from Kobe University collaborated with the Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology (JAMSTEC). They used powerful airgun arrays to generate seismic pulses that traveled through the crust beneath the ocean floor.
Instruments called ocean bottom seismometers recorded how these waves moved through the underground rock. Because seismic waves travel differently through solid rock and regions containing molten material, scientists can analyze their behavior to investigate structures that cannot be observed directly.
The findings, published in Communications Earth & Environment, revealed a substantial region containing a high proportion of magma directly beneath the site of Kikai's massive eruption 7,300 years ago.
By examining the seismic measurements, the team was able to determine the approximate size and shape of the underground reservoir. Its position and extent suggest that it occupies the same magma storage system involved in the ancient eruption.
"Due to its extent and location it is clear that this is in fact the same magma reservoir as in the previous eruption," Seama says.
Fresh Magma Is Recharging the Ancient Supervolcano
Perhaps the most intriguing finding is that the magma currently beneath Kikai does not appear to be simply leftover material from its catastrophic eruption thousands of years ago.
Previous investigations revealed that a new lava dome has been developing near the center of the caldera over approximately the past 3,900 years. A lava dome forms when relatively thick, viscous lava accumulates around a volcanic vent rather than flowing freely across the surrounding landscape.
Chemical analyses also showed that volcanic material from this dome and other more recent activity differs in composition from the material released during Kikai's giant eruption.
That difference provides an important clue. It suggests that the magma now stored beneath the volcano was supplied by new injections of molten rock from deeper within Earth's crust or mantle, rather than remaining unchanged since the previous eruption.
"This means that the magma that is now present in the magma reservoir under the lava dome is likely newly injected magma," summarizes Seama.
Together, the seismic observations and chemical evidence help researchers develop a clearer picture of how a giant volcanic system can gradually rebuild its underground magma supply following a massive eruption.
This replenishment process does not mean that another catastrophic eruption is imminent. Instead, it reveals how a magma reservoir can be recharged over thousands of years, an important process that scientists need to understand before they can reliably assess the long-term behavior of supervolcanoes.
What the Discovery Could Reveal About Yellowstone
The findings could have implications far beyond Japan.
Researchers believe the process identified beneath Kikai may help explain why other enormous caldera systems, including Yellowstone and Toba, also contain large magma reservoirs relatively close to Earth's surface.
"This magma re-injection model is consistent with the existence of large shallow magma reservoirs beneath other giant calderas like Yellowstone and Toba," says Seama.
The proposed model suggests that, following a giant eruption, new magma can gradually enter and replenish an existing underground reservoir. Understanding how this happens could reveal important patterns in the long-term cycles of magma accumulation, volcanic activity, and major eruptions.
Researchers now hope to improve the seismic techniques used at Kikai so they can investigate the movement and storage of magma in greater detail.
"We want to refine the methods that have proved to be so useful in this study to more deeply understand the re-injection processes. Our ultimate goal is to become better able to monitor the crucial indicators of future giant eruptions."
By revealing how fresh magma accumulates beneath a volcano responsible for one of Earth's most extraordinary eruptions, the research brings scientists closer to understanding the processes that eventually make such colossal events possible.
This research was funded by the Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT) (The Third Earthquake and Volcano Hazards Observation and Research Program (Earthquake and Volcano Hazard Reduction Research)) and the Japan Society for the Promotion of Science (grant 20H00199). It was conducted in collaboration with researchers from the Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology (JAMSTEC).
Story Source:
Materials provided by Kobe University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Akihiro Nagaya, Nobukazu Seama, Gou Fujie, Satoru Tanaka, Hiroko Sugioka, Shuichi Kodaira. Melt re-injection into large magma reservoir after giant caldera eruption at Kikai Caldera Volcano. Communications Earth, 2026; 7 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s43247-026-03347-9

Parashat Lech Lecha: There is no wisdom like that gained through experience
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:22:58 UTC
20:22:58 KST

Parashat Lech Lecha opens with the first test through which God puts Abraham, the father of the Jewish nation. He is commanded to leave his home, his surroundings, and his homeland, and to journey to an unknown land, as the verse states (Genesis 12:1): “To the land that I will show you.” The Mishnah in Pirkei Avot (5:3) states accordingly: “Abraham our forefather, may he rest in peace, was tested with 10 trials.”
These trials are among the defining foundations of the Jewish nation. They are not merely historical events in the life of the nation’s founding father, but chapters in the shaping of the believing individual, whose influence remains evident to this day. Each trial presented Abraham with a new challenge, requiring him to discover additional inner strength, deepen his faith, and elevate his life to a higher level.
His struggles belong not only to the past; they also laid the foundations for the ability of future generations to face their own challenges.
What is a 'test'?
To understand the deeper meaning of these trials, we must examine the very concept of a “test.” Our sages, in the Midrash, explore the connection between a test and elevation, between facing a challenge and the ability to grow through it.
The Midrash states: “It is written: ‘You have given those who fear You a banner to raise, because of the truth, forever’ (Psalms 60:6). One trial after another, and one stage of growth after another, in order to test them in the world and to elevate them in the world, like the mast of a ship” (Bereishit Rabbah, Vayera 55:1).
According to this understanding, a trial is not merely an examination intended to test a person, but also a means of helping that person grow and rise to a higher level. Just as a ship’s mast rises high and can be seen from afar, so too can a person rise through the trials he experiences and discover strengths within himself that he never knew he possessed.
Precisely when he feels confronted by a difficulty that exceeds his abilities, an opportunity may be presented to him, so that he can reach a level he could never have attained by any other means.
To understand why Abraham was given these trials and what their purpose was, it is worth examining Nachmanides’s commentary on the verse describing the trial of the Binding of Isaac (Genesis 22:1): “And God tested Abraham.”
According to the Ramban, God does not need a test to know what lies in a person’s heart; the test is intended for the person himself. There is a difference between a capacity that exists within someone as a potential that has not yet been realized, and a capacity that has already been revealed through an actual deed.
A person may believe himself to be courageous, loyal, or deeply faithful, but only when called upon to act with courage do these qualities become a tangible part of his character.
Trials are not just for personal growth, there's more at play
THIS IDEA takes on an even broader significance in the words of Rabbi Yaakov, author of the Ba’al Haturim, who draws a connection between Abraham’s 10 trials and the 10 utterances through which the world was created. The trials are not merely a personal journey of spiritual growth, but part of a broader process of repairing the world and bringing it toward its ultimate purpose.
According to this interpretation, the first trial, “Lech Lecha” (“Go forth”), corresponds to the first divine utterance in Creation: “Let there be light.” This parallel offers an important key to understanding how a person should face life’s challenges.
When a person encounters a trial, he may feel as though darkness has enveloped him and the light has disappeared from his world. The familiar path is no longer clear. The answers he once had no longer suffice, and he struggles to see how he can move forward.
It is precisely in these moments that he must remember that just as Creation began with light, so too a trial may mark the beginning of a new revelation. This does not mean that every difficulty quickly disappears, or that we can always understand why events unfolded as they did.
However, we can believe that even amid uncertainty, a path exists, and that facing a challenge may open up possibilities within a person and his world that would otherwise never have emerged.
Abraham, our forefather, is commanded to journey to an unknown land, and God tells him, “that I will show you.” God’s light will illuminate the way for him, provided he believes that God watches over and guides everything, for He is the master of the universe.
A person is not always given a complete map of the future. To move forward, he must take one step at a time, seeking clarity along the way, and trusting that what he does not yet understand may become clear later.
Sometimes, life’s trials are the light that a person must follow, for hidden within them is a great light that he is called upon to discover. ■
The writer is the rabbi of the Western Wall and holy sites.

Parashat Lech Lecha: Having the courage to stand alone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:22:52 UTC
20:22:52 KST

It takes courage to stand alone against the beliefs of an entire society. Few experienced this loneliness as deeply as Abraham. In a world steeped in idolatry, he introduced humanity to belief in one God. Abraham was the first lonely man of faith.
The other side
His radical ideas enraged those around him, who tried to burn him alive. Miraculously, he survived. He later left his homeland and journeyed toward the land of God, crossing treacherous terrain and the great rivers of the Tigris and Euphrates.
He became known as Avraham Ha’Ivri, a name that reflected three aspects of his identity. By ancestry, he descended from Eber, a descendant of Noah. The word Ivri also means someone from the other side, “ever.”
Geographically, Abraham had traveled from beyond the great rivers, leaving his homeland to settle in a new land. Ideologically, he stood on one side of a great divide, bravely opposing an entire civilization that could not imagine a single God. Abraham came from the other side of the river and had the courage to stand on the other side of the world.
Soon after arriving in the Land of Israel, Abraham found himself caught up in a regional war. The conflict became personal when his nephew Lot was taken captive. Abraham joined the battle and defeated four powerful warlords who had conquered and enslaved five neighboring populations. With his small force, he confronted armies far more powerful than his own.
The name Avraham Ha’Ivri now took on another meaning. Beyond his ancestry and journey across rivers, he stood on one side against powerful enemies on the other. Significantly, the only time the Torah explicitly calls him Avraham Ha’Ivri is during this war.
A nation apart
Abraham’s willingness to stand alone would become a defining feature of our nation. As his descendants, we would desperately need that same strength. We were meant to be a different people, committed to the values God taught us even when others challenge them.
We were chosen for responsibility rather than privilege, expected to live by higher standards and reflect the dignity of a life lived in God’s presence. Throughout history, we would face a choice between Abraham’s courage to remain different despite our loneliness and the temptation to surrender that difference for acceptance.
Exile intensified this loneliness. Scattered in small communities, we lived as guests in other people’s homelands, often regarded as outsiders. Empires rose and great religions spread while we remained small and vulnerable. Yet we preserved our identity and faith, following Abraham’s example. Wherever we lived, we held firmly to our faith and traditions, even when doing so set us apart from the surrounding society. The price of remaining different was often high.
With the birth of Israel, that loneliness began to ease in two ways. We could finally live together in our homeland, speaking a common language and sharing a national identity. We could preserve our distinctiveness while enjoying the dignity of sovereignty. We no longer had to explain why our lives were different.
At the same time, Israel gradually gained acceptance abroad. Over 75 years, our military strength, economy, and technological achievements earned international respect. Diplomatic relationships expanded. Countries sought our expertise, welcomed our innovations, and increasingly treated Israel as a valuable partner even when old prejudices lingered. We felt less alone both because we had one another and because the wider world seemed increasingly willing to accept us.
Alone again
Oct. 7 shattered much of that confidence in our “acceptance.” The massacre in the South had barely ended, yet by October 8, protesters were already condemning Israel and portraying us as the aggressors. As we fought a just war against those who attacked us, we faced fierce condemnation and spurious accusations of terrible crimes. Israel has been sidelined, marginalized, and boycotted. Even our right to exist has been questioned, a challenge rarely directed at other nations.
After decades in which we believed that our legitimacy had become an accepted fact, we discovered how quickly old arguments could reappear. Once again, we find ourselves in the footsteps of Avraham Ha’Ivri, standing on the other side of a world that struggles to accept us.
This renewed Ivri status extends far beyond Israel. Across the Western world, opposition to Israel has frequently spilled over into antisemitism. Jewish students face intimidation on campuses, Jewish institutions require heightened security, and many Jews feel increasing pressure to conceal their identity. Generations of hard-won acceptance suddenly feel fragile. Jews who once felt completely at home in their countries are discovering how quickly they can be made to feel like an outsider.
Whether in Israel or abroad, we are once again being called upon to follow in the footsteps of our common ancestor Abraham and summon the courage to be Ivrim, even when that means standing alone.
The courage to be different
Most Jews are answering the Ivri call. Since Oct. 7, hostility toward Jews has only strengthened the Jewish identity of many who had previously felt disconnected from our people. Many Jews who had placed great faith in liberal democracies and their promises of equality have begun to reconsider that confidence.
We cannot always rely on others to defend our rights nor can we assume that social justice movements will also stand up for Jews. Sadly, many who champion the rights of other minorities show little concern for Jewish vulnerability. This painful awakening has drawn many Jews closer to their people.
While many Jews have embraced the courage of Avraham Ha’Ivri, standing firm in the face of a hostile world, others remain uncomfortable with the prospect of standing apart. Eager for acceptance, some have distanced themselves from Israel, even turning against its very legitimacy. There is a painful irony in disavowing a state that has become a vital anchor of Jewish identity and security. In their desire to be accepted by others, they are distancing themselves from their own people.
The price of acceptance
This sad pattern has tragic precedents. Throughout history, many Jews seeking acceptance in the wider world have been willing to sacrifice their faith and surrender core elements of their Jewish identity. In their desire to belong, they sometimes abandoned the core traditions and beliefs that had sustained our people for generations.
In the Hellenistic era, some Jews concealed their circumcision to fit into Greek society. During the Christian Middle Ages, some Jews converted to Christianity, viewing baptism as a ticket of entry into a Christian-dominated world.
In the 19th century, as Jews were invited to participate more fully in European society, many surrendered aspects of their Jewish culture and identity to feel more comfortable in the emerging culture of modern Europe. Later, in Eastern Europe, some Jews enthusiastically joined the Communist revolution, exchanging their Jewish identity for a place in a movement they believed would usher in a new era of equality and progress.
Today, we are witnessing another version of this familiar pattern. In some social and cultural circles, public opposition to Israel has become a badge of acceptance. Some Jews feel that gaining approval in these environments, particularly on social media, requires them to distance themselves from Israel or even openly condemn it. The barter has changed, but the tragedy remains: Jewish identity is once again being traded for public acceptance.
Abraham taught us that standing alone requires courage. After Oct. 7, we are once again discovering that our identity and our future cannot depend upon the approval of others. To be an Ivri is to remain faithful to our convictions even when the world stands against us.■

France: 1 killed, 4 wounded after shooting near Paris
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

France: 1 killed, 4 wounded after shooting near Paris
October 23, 2026
One person was killed and four others were injured when gunshots were fired from a vehicle outside Paris on Friday, according to local authorities.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said the shooting was "clearly a terrorist crime."
He said shots were fired at the total of three locations in the towns of Trappes and La Verriere, which are located about 20 kilometers (13 miles) west of the French capital, close to Versailles. The "rampage" lasted for 15 minutes, according to the minister.
Nunez said the shooter fired "what appears to have been a military-grade weapon, or at least an automatic weapon."
Three of the wounded remain in critical condition.
Commenting on the shooting, President Emmanuel Macron said the attack "marks a turning point" for France.
"What happened today was a terrorist and racist attack," he told reporters, noting that the victims were targeted due to their religion and the color of their skin.
What do we know about the suspect?
Shortly after the Friday attack, authorities detained a man in the neighboring town of Coignieres and took him into police custody.
The authorities later identified the suspect as Kevin T., born in 1987. They said the alleged shooter already had a criminal record.
France's anti-terrorism prosecutor said the authorities found a Sten Gun — a British-made WWII-era submachine gun — and a tear gas grenade in his car. The alleged shooter had also booby-trapped his apartment, according to the authorities.
Mayor: 'Miracle' that more were not killed
"An individual fired shots from his vehicle at multiple people along his route," the mayor of Trappes, Ali Rabeh, wrote on social media.
He later told French broadcaster BFM TV that one of the locations at which shots were fired was a playground.
"It is a miracle that there were not more victims," he said.
Rabeh said the person killed was of African origin, while one of those critically wounded was of North African origin.
The mayor also told reporters the attack had "racist, likely Islamophobic, overtones."
“This is probably one of the first attempted mass killings motivated by Islamophobia and racism,” he said.
A 12-year-old girl injured in the attack
Aurore Berge, the French minister in charge of gender equality and antidiscrimination, said a 12-year-old girl was very seriously injured in the incident.
"If a racist motive is established, I hope that the whole nation will stand alongside the residents of Trappes, La Verriere, and the victims. We cannot tolerate even the slightest racist remark in the French republic," she said.
French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu called the incident "very serious" and said that "all available resources of the security forces and judicial authorities have been fully mobilized."
He added that France's National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor's Office (Pnat) is monitoring the situation.
Pnat itself said it had opened an investigation into "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise, with the aggravating circumstance that the acts were committed on the basis of the victim's actual or perceived membership of a specific race, ethnicity, nation or religion."
France shooting: What else do we know?
The shooting came as France braces for yet another day of protests against the high cost of living on Saturday, with major museums in Paris and other major cities closing their doors and the government deploying a significantly larger security presence.
"We are not talking about a nice protest," Interior Minister Nunez told reporters, announcing the deployment of 70,000 security personnel. "We are ready tomorrow to be extremely firm and not tolerate anything."
France has also seen a spate of Islamist terrorist attacks in recent years and, although the number of incidents has fallen, authorities have warned that risks remain.
The town of Trappes has experienced its own share of tension, with a local teacher reporting receiving threats after saying that the state did not do enough to protect Samuel Paty, a teacher in another Paris suburb who was beheaded by a radical Islamist in 2020 after he showed his class caricatures of the Prophet Mohammed.
There was no immediate suggestion that Friday's shooting was linked either to the current protests or Islamist terrorism.

Three killed in mine explosion in northern Türkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:21:30 UTC
20:21:30 KST

Rescue teams were dispatched to the area following the report. (AA Photo)
Three miners were killed and five others injured in a firedamp explosion at a private coal mine in Zonguldak, northern Türkiye, on Oct. 23, with rescue teams recovering the body of the last worker trapped underground.
The explosion occurred at around 10 a.m. in the Gelik town of Kilimli district, prompting the deployment of firefighters, the Disaster and Emergency Management Authority (AFAD), gendarmerie and Turkish Hard Coal Enterprises (TTK) rescue teams.
Eight workers were affected by the blast. Two miners were initially confirmed dead, while five were rescued and taken to hospital. The body of the eighth worker, who had been trapped underground, was later recovered.
Health Minister Kemal Memişoğlu said one of the five injured miners was in critical condition. Zonguldak Governor Osman Hacıbektaşoğlu said two workers had suffered burns and were intubated, with plans to transfer them to the capital Ankara for further treatment.
The incident comes less than a month after another fatal mining accident in western Türkiye. Five miners died following a collapse at the İmbat Mining operation in the Soma district of Manisa province on Oct. 1.
Seven workers were initially trapped in that incident. Two were pronounced dead after being pulled from the site, while two others were hospitalized. Rescue teams recovered the bodies of the remaining three miners in the early hours of Oct. 2.
Three prosecutors were appointed to oversee a judicial investigation, while the Labor and Social Security Ministry launched a separate inquiry.
Firedamp is an explosive mixture of methane and air that can accumulate in underground coal mines. Methane can ignite when exposed to a spark or other ignition source, causing a blast that can devastate confined mine workings.

Czech firm develops patrol drone armed with interceptors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:20:44 UTC
20:20:44 KST

- Czech company KBP International unveiled GRYF, a long-endurance drone that carries interceptor drones or small missiles to counter hostile UAVs.
- GRYF can fly up to 12 hours with a 500 km range and a 50 kg payload across four hardpoints.
Czech company KBP International has unveiled GRYF, a long-endurance drone designed to carry interceptor drones and small missiles aloft so it can hunt down hostile unmanned aircraft, presenting the aircraft on Oct. 21, 2026, at the Future Forces Forum in Prague in the presence of Czech President Petr Pavel.
GRYF works as a flying weapons carrier: the aircraft itself is not the weapon but a platform that patrols for long periods and brings counter-drone effectors into position, where they can be launched at incoming threats. KBP said the platform is built for long-endurance operations as a carrier for interceptors and mission-specific payloads, as part of a layered approach to air defense.
The company told visitors at the unveiling that GRYF can stay airborne for up to 12 hours and has an operational range of 500 km (310 miles). The drone is powered by a four-cylinder piston engine, cruises at 150 km/h (93 mph) and has four hardpoints with a maximum payload of 50 kg (110 pounds), Militarnyi reported from the show floor, enough to carry a lightweight interceptor missile of around 5 kg (11 pounds) on each hardpoint.
KBP displayed GRYF in two configurations at the Prague exhibition, one armed with small interceptor missiles and the other with interceptor drones, showing that the same airframe can switch between effectors depending on the mission.
The company presented the aircraft as an answer to the demand for effective and affordable ways to protect airspace against drones. Using a cheap, long-endurance carrier to loiter near a protected area and release small interceptors is intended to engage drones at a lower cost per shot than firing conventional ground-based air defense missiles, while extending coverage beyond the reach of fixed sites.
GRYF draws on KBP Group’s more than 30 years of experience building composite aircraft structures. The group combines in-house design and production of unmanned aircraft, piston aero engines and advanced manufacturing, and it says it can handle the full process from initial design and prototyping to series production of key drone components. KBP is expanding its facilities to support both its own products and work with other European aerospace and defense manufacturers.
The company used the same Prague exhibition to show two one-way attack drones, the piston-powered TARON and the jet-powered SABRE. KBP International was also a main partner of this year’s Future Forces Forum, the 16th edition of the event, which brought together around 530 exhibitors and official delegations from 65 countries at the PVA Expo Prague exhibition grounds.
KBP’s announcement focused on the platform’s design and role, with production timelines and first customers for GRYF still to be announced as the company moves the new carrier beyond its public debut.

Russia has kept the Red Cross away from Ukrainian POWs since 2024. Now about 1,500 captives it never confirmed as prisoners face prosecution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:20:10 UTC
20:20:10 KST

About 1,500 Ukrainians held in Russia and occupied Ukraine are facing criminal prosecution even though the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has never confirmed them as prisoners, Petro Yatsenko, representative of Ukraine's Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, said on 19 October at an event on missing persons at UN headquarters in New York. The event was organized by the permanent missions of Ukraine and Poland to the UN.
Without ICRC confirmation, there is no official record that a person is alive or held, which leaves captives without proper protection, the headquarters said. Amnesty International calls this enforced disappearance, a practice that puts people outside the protection of the law. The ICRC itself has been shut out. Under the Geneva Conventions it is supposed to visit prisoners of war, but on 18 September it told Reuters that Russia has given it no access to Ukrainian POWs since 2024. UN investigators have gathered evidence of systematic torture in the detention centers where they are held. Russia denies torturing or mistreating POWs.
Families lose track of captives as Russia moves them between prisons
Kateryna Nazarii, who coordinates families of the 24th Mechanized Brigade, is the wife of a Ukrainian serviceman held by Russia. The ICRC has not been able to confirm his status as a prisoner of war. Russia does not let the ICRC or other humanitarian organizations into the prisons where Ukrainians are held, and does not hand over complete lists of prisoners, Nazarii said at the event. When families do find out where a relative is held, she said, that person is moved to another prison, and contact is lost again.
Many of those whose captivity Russia has not confirmed are civilians. Among them, Yatsenko said, are about 200 young people born after 2000 and nearly 400 people over 60. None of them has been confirmed through the ICRC, according to the headquarters.
Secrecy and torture in Russian captivity
Most Ukrainian POWs are cut off from the outside world. In a March 2025 report, Amnesty International found that 24 of the 43 families of confirmed POWs it interviewed had received no word at all from their relative. Counting prisoners allowed only one brief call or text at the start of captivity, 72% of those 43 were held incommunicado. The UN monitoring mission found that only 21 of 174 former POWs it interviewed had been able to correspond with their families, Amnesty noted.
Silence is what makes the abuse possible, Amnesty argues. The UN monitoring mission found that 97% of former POWs it interviewed had been tortured or ill-treated, the report notes, and methods include beatings, electric shocks, burns, and sexual violence. A UN commission of inquiry concluded in 2024 that the torture amounted to a "coordinated state policy," the report adds.
When the Red Cross did get in, it saw what Russia chose to show. An OSCE expert mission reported in September 2025 that, according to former prisoners, Russian staff presented only prisoners in relatively good physical condition during ICRC visits and kept the sick and tortured out of sight. The experts also found that Russia blocked visits to some facilities and gave incomplete prisoner lists.
The unconfirmed are not a small group. A quarter of the 3,767 POWs who returned to Ukraine by November 2024 had never been confirmed by Russia as captives, the Coordination Headquarters said, as cited by Amnesty. Hundreds or possibly thousands more may still be held without Russia notifying the ICRC, Amnesty concluded.
Those who come back describe the conditions. Anatolii Zemlianyi, a soldier of the 2nd Assault Brigade released in the May 2025 exchange, told Frontliner that he spent eight months in a hospital in occupied Donetsk with a grenade wound in his leg and got no proper treatment. In captivity, he said, prisoners drank water from puddles.
Russia continues to hold Ukrainian civilians unlawfully
Nobody knows how many Ukrainian civilians Russia holds. "It is not known," the UN human rights office said in a September 2025 report, which cites Ukraine's Prosecutor General's Office as having identified 15,250 civilians detained by Russia between February 2022 and August 2025. Exchanges bring very few of them back: of 5,941 people released from Russian captivity between February 2022 and 14 August 2025, 352 were civilians, Ukraine's human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets told The Week.
Under the Fourth Geneva Convention, an occupying power may intern civilians only for imperative reasons of security, and only under a regular procedure with periodic review, the same UN report notes. Russia instead treats detained civilians as criminals, Oleksandr Kononenko, a representative of Ukraine's human rights commissioner, told relatives of civilian hostages in 2023.
"This convention clearly states that civilian hostages should not be detained. They should be released. What is Russia doing? It 'makes all these people criminals' and accuses them of terrorism, opposition to a special military operation, and assistance to the Ukrainian Armed Forces, which is completely absurd from the point of view of an independent state and those people who are patriots of their state," Kononenko said.
Kyiv believes Russia detains civilians partly to trade them. Regular civilian swaps risk signaling to Russia that by detaining more Ukrainians it could get more Russians released, so it may seize more people to replenish its "exchange fund," Lubinets said. Ukraine therefore demands that civilians be released unconditionally. Amnesty sees a second motive. It concluded that Russia has long used arbitrary arrest, torture, and enforced disappearance to intimidate civilians in areas it controls.

Katarzyna Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, the leader of a junior party in Poland’s ruling coalition, has announced that her resignation from the government and the leadership of her party, the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), in protest over a parliamentary vote on Thursday.
Poland 2050 (Polska 2050) is set to remain in the government, thereby maintaining Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s parliamentary majority. However, the dispute has highlighted tensions within the ruling coalition just a year ahead of parliamentary elections at which it will seek another term.

— Katarzyna Pełczyńska (@Kpelczynska) October 22, 2026
Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, who serves as minister for funds and regional policy, made her decision in the wake of an unusual voting result in the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, on Thursday.
Another junior partner in the ruling coalition, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), had proposed a bill abolishing two-term limits for mayors. Those limits had been introduced in 2018 with the aim of reducing corruption and cronyism by preventing local officials from becoming entrenched in power.
However, PSL, which has a strong presence in local politics, argues that the limits prevent effective, popular mayors from being re-elected, thereby denying voters the right to decide who they want to represent them.
Although the government has a majority in the Sejm, the bill was narrowly defeated, with 213 votes in favour and 215 against, after 15 MPs from the ruling coalition joined with the right-wing opposition in voting against it.
Pełczyńska-Nałęcz herself is not a member of parliament, so did not vote. Her party was split, with six MPs voting for the bill, three against, three abstaining, and three not voting at all.
Aftewards, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz made clear that she opposed the bill and celebrated the fact that it was blocked. She also announced her resignation from the government and the leadership of her party.
“The coalition, unfortunately including a significant portion of MPs from Poland 2050, stood against the people and in favour of backroom political deals,” she wrote. “I am leaving Donald Tusk’s government because values are more important to me than positions.”
“I am leaving the party in the hands of its founder, who stepped away but then returned,” she added, referring to Poland 2050’s founder, Szymon Hołownia. “I hope that he remembers what values he came to power in the name of.”
Pełczyńska-Nałęcz’s decision follows a year of turmoil for Poland 2050. In September 2025, Hołownia, who had led the party since founding it in 2021, announced that he was stepping down.
However, a first attempt to choose a new leader was invalidated in January after technical problems with voting. Hołownia then hinted that he may reverse course and seek to continue leading the party, though in the end that did not happen.
In February, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz was chosen as the new leader. That prompted her rival candidate, Paulina Hennig-Kloska, to quit the party, taking half of its MPs with her. They formed a new group called Centrum (Centre).
Both Poland 2050 and Centrum remain in the ruling coalition. However, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz has had an uneasy relationship with Tusk.
Around half the MPs from Poland 2050, a junior member of Poland’s ruling coalition, have split from the party and formed a new parliamentary caucus.

The episode highlights the tensions within the ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right and contains parties that disagree on a number of issues.
It also points to the pressure smaller coalition partners are feeling ahead of next autumn’s parliamentary elections. Only parties that win at least 5% of the vote nationally can enter parliament. But Poland 2050 has been polling at around 1% and PSL is on 3%.
In the 2023 election, Poland 2050 and PSL in fact stood together as an alliance called the Third Way (Trzecia Droga), helping ensure that the two parties won enough votes to enter parliament. However, in 2025, they split from one another and confirmed that they would not stand together again.

The fact that the bill to end two-term limits for mayors was defeated has also caused tension between PSL and its coalition partners.
In the wake of yesterday’s vote, PSL immediately announced that it would push for the introduction of two-term limits for members of parliament, arguing that the same rules should apply to national and local elected representatives.
The right-wing opposition has long hoped that it could tempt PSL, the most conservative element of Tusk’s coalition, to quit the government. A recent report even claimed that US President Donald Trump had, at the behest of Poland’s opposition, suggested to PSL’s leader that he leave Tusk.

FSB orders Russian critical infrastructure websites taken offline over PHP vulnerabilities

FSB orders Russian critical infrastructure websites taken offline over PHP vulnerabilities
Russia’s Federal Security Service’s cybersecurity center has ordered organizations that run the country’s critical information infrastructure to temporarily shut down their websites if they cannot quickly update their software to protect against the PHP vulnerabilities.
The National Coordination Center for Computer Incidents (NKTsKI) sent the directive on October 22 through the state cyberattack defense system GosSOPKA. The Russian business news outlet RBC obtained a copy, and three recipient organizations confirmed the document’s authenticity.
NKTsKI instructed organizations to install the patched version of PHP, scan servers with antivirus software, and review logs for signs of intrusion. If the system cannot be updated quickly, the FSB instructs them to “consider temporarily restricting external access to vulnerable web servers, up to and including taking them offline.”

Germany wants to buy thousands of missiles from European and Ukrainian manufacturers, Bloomberg reports
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

Germany wants to buy thousands of missiles from European and Ukrainian manufacturers, Bloomberg reports
Germany is negotiating the purchase of thousands of European-made high-precision long-range missiles to replenish its arsenal amid delays in the delivery of US Tomahawk missiles.
Source: European Pravda, citing Bloomberg
Details: Manufacturers that could win German contracts include Dutch company Destinus SA with its Ruta cruise missiles and German-British defence startup Hypersonica, which is developing the ultra-fast HS1 missile.
Negotiations are also underway for a contract worth over €1 billion with US defence startup Covenant to supply thousands of its ground-launched Anthem cruise missiles.
Furthermore, sources indicate that the German Ministry of Defence is holding talks with Ukraine regarding the co-production and procurement of Ukrainian Bars cruise missiles.
Their manufacturer has not yet been disclosed. The idea behind acquiring thousands of new, inexpensive missiles is to saturate enemy air defences, thereby ensuring that strikes reach their targets.
The German armed forces currently only use the air-launched Taurus cruise missile, which has a relatively short range of about 500 km.
Germany's plan to purchase the powerful BGM-109 Tomahawk missile and the Typhon ground-launch system from US manufacturer Raytheon could be delayed for up to five years.
Background:
- The German government expects that creating a new arsenal of long-range weapons designed to deter Russia will require nearly €12 billion.
- The day before, Denmark announced a billion-dollar deal for the purchase of high-precision long-range missiles for the first time in history, amid intentions to strengthen its security.

This man has quit Badenoch’s increasingly hard-right Tory party – others should be brave enough to do the same | Polly Toynbee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:16:16 UTC
20:16:16 KST

The chair of the London Assembly, Andrew Boff, resigned this week from the Conservative party after 53 years of membership. He quit after being blocked from entering the race to be Tory candidate for London mayor because he supports the European convention on human rights (ECHR), putting him at odds with Kemi Badenoch’s hardline position.
Messages of support for one of the capital’s longest-serving Conservative politicians quickly poured in from fellow Tories. Gavin Barwell, Theresa May’s Downing Street chief of staff, has backed Boff, warning Badenoch that others would follow him over the ECHR edict. But the rest sent messages privately, not daring to reveal themselves under a leadership that doesn’t tolerate dissent. In an interview last year, Badenoch decreed that rebels “should not and cannot stand as a Conservative candidate” if they do not agree with leaving the ECHR. She also bars anyone supporting net zero.
When Boff applied, for the seventh time, to be considered as Conservative candidate for London mayor, he didn’t really expect to be selected – but nor did he expect to be summoned to be told he was barred from entering the race. In a statement he pointed to the fact that Winston Churchill helped found the ECHR after the second world war, arguing “it was never a leftwing project” but a “safeguard against arbitrary government”. What’s more, he points out to me, the “convention doesn’t even mention asylum seekers”, Badenoch’s main justification for leaving the treaty.
The time may come, he warned, when extremists win an election on an even smaller vote share than Labour’s 34% in 2024 – and overturn all human rights legislation without the protections the ECHR affords. “That’s what authoritarian governments do,” Boff said. But he insisted that the committee, which vets Conservative candidates, didn’t listen. “They just repeated the same tropes, that activist judges are using the ECHR against parliament.”
Now he is free of the party straitjacket, Boff is planning to stand for London mayor as an independent, allowing him to say what he thinks about Badenoch.
He complains to me that the energy and resources that should promote the party “all go to promoting Kemi, Kemi, Kemi”. Thinking well of her in 2015, he says he had encouraged her to stand for the London assembly, where she served until 2017 before being elected to parliament. He says he found her “lazy and combative”.
Few will be surprised by Boff’s departure. But many will be wondering what took him so long. He was ejected from the Tory conference in 2023 for quietly heckling the then home secretary Suella Braverman’s speech, accusing her of homophobia and transphobia. “It is a signal to people who don’t like people who are LGBT+,” Boff, who is gay, said at the time as he condemned her speech as “trash”. Boff said that Braverman “was basically vilifying gay people and trans people by this attack on LGBT ideology”.
He was not alone in voicing criticism over the party’s direction. The former Tory MP Robert Buckland, fellow one-nationer and director of the Tory Reform Group, hurried out to defend Boff after his ejection from the conference, saying heckling was “part of the democratic debate” and that his treatment by security staff was “heavy-handed”.
Buckland was among the many one-nationers who lost their seat at the 2024 general election. But that traditional strand of Conservatism has not vanished – nor have those who used to vote for the Tories but now turn to the Liberal Democrats or simply boycott the ballot box.
Boff’s views represent a growing centre-right moderate strand that has been expelled or silenced under Badenoch’s leadership. Facing this hostile climate, one nation Tories have gone to ground in parliament; but outside the Commons, Prosper UK, a centrist Tory grouping led by the former mayor of the West Midlands, Andy Street, and the former Scottish Tory leader Ruth Davidson quietly gains strength.
Its mission statement is to win back moderate voters who snubbed the Conservatives at the last general election, and this message seems to have struck a chord, with the group attracting nearly 30,000 supporters since its launch in January.
It is worth examining Boff’s views, as many Conservatives who have signed up to Prosper UK are likely to share them. He calls himself a Thatcherite, strongly opposing Labour’s renationalisation plans, backing low taxes and a small state. He voted for Brexit, believing the words of the likes of Daniel Hannan, who claimed “absolutely nobody is talking about threatening our place in the single market”. But instead the Tories delivered a hard Brexit after what he calls an “atrocious” campaign.
Times have changed; as the political analyst Peter Kellner pointed out this week, Britain’s pro-Brexit majority has literally died out. Any so-called betrayal of the referendum is only betraying the dreadful legacy of the departed.
If the Conservative party has any future as a government, it won’t be under its present leader. A small bounce for improved performance in parliament will never overcome Badenoch’s growing distance from voters, including those who should be natural Tories.
Boff may be a throwback to an irretrievable, more moderate Conservative brand, like that of the Macmillan era – a voice from the good old days when traditional party allegiances were clearly defined. Or possibly he and Prosper UK are the vanguard of a reconstituted centre-right able to attract new voters as well as those who have deserted the Tories.
That won’t be easy: already there are gloating Spectator-aligned Tories who say that the party is better off without the likes of Boff, or any real concession to centrism. But we should have a care. The success of a respectable right matters to all in the left bloc of progressive parties, too. A centre right is needed to fight off the dark forces of the hard right and worse, here and across Europe. That Overton window framing politics needs a firm shunt towards a more rational debate on our future in Europe – and on saving the planet.
- Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

Estonia has a higher education gender gap and few plans to fix it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:16:00 UTC
20:16:00 KST

Estonia has a higher education gender gap and few plans to fix it
Men make up just 40% of students in higher education in Estonia. Experts say raising the compulsory school attendance age to 18 alone won't close the gender gap.
Education and Research Minister Kristina Kallas (Eesti 200) and Kadri Täht, a professor of work and education sociology at Tallinn University (TLÜ), agree that the gender imbalance is not necessarily a problem in itself. It becomes one, Täht said, when educational choices limit people's future opportunities, reinforcing gender segregation in the labor market.
"Traditional jobs in manufacturing, where men typically found work and where engineers were required to have degrees, have declined," Kallas said. Automation has reduced demand for such jobs, she added, with artificial intelligence (AI) expected to accelerate the trend.
The imbalance is particularly pronounced in health and welfare majors, which encompass everything from healthcare to social work. Last academic year, women outnumbered men in these programs by more than four to one, with 5,553 female students compared with just 1,246 men.
Gender Equality and Equal Treatment Commissioner Christian Veske has likewise warned that the divide could leave society less prepared for crises.
"In a crisis, society needs everyone's skills, but the way people are distributed across educational fields limits that," he said, pointing to Ukraine's experience.
Gap starts much earlier
Both Kallas and Täht said the imbalance has roots in earlier stages of education.
"The education system likely already favors girls a bit more at the basic education level already," Täht acknowledged, citing differences in study habits and learning styles.
She said boys are also more likely to pursue vocational education after basic school. Men accounted for 54 percent of vocational students in Estonia last academic year, and have made up at least half of the total every year for the past eight years.
The professor stressed, however, that this does not mean the education system is designed for girls. Rather, social expectations may be contributing to differences in learning skills and motivation.
According to Estonia's latest PISA results, girls outscored boys in reading by 25 points, while boys led in math by 13 points. Täht said it is difficult to determine whether social or biological factors are at play.
Estonia also has one of the euro area's largest gender pay gaps, with men earning an average of 12.2 percent more than women last year, according to Statistics Estonia, and Täht said even that could be encouraging young men to enter the workforce sooner.
"Even when girls are better educated, we still see men ultimately earning more on average in the labor market," she explained.
Health impacts of higher ed
At the ministry, Kallas pointed to Estonia recently raising the compulsory school attendance age from 16 to 18 as one step toward narrowing the education gap.
She said one of the goals of the change, which will keep teens in school until they've earned either a high school or vocational education diploma, "is to reduce the education gap between boys and girls."
Lower education levels are also associated with other issues, such as poorer health, the minister said.
Taavi Tillmann, an associate professor of public health at the University of Tartu (TÜ), has also discussed this link, telling Novaator that people with higher education levels tend to be healthier and have lower rates of cardiovascular disease — though exactly why remains unclear, even to Tillmann.
Täht agreed that raising the attendance age to 18 could help more boys finish school at the upper secondary level and go on to continue their education, but cautioned that it's still no guarantee more men will actually enroll.
"What matters is that more [boys] actually end up in upper secondary education and then go on from there to pursue higher education," she said.
Few measures target boys directly
Other government efforts include a regulation adopted by the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communication (MKM) last November to reduce gender segregation in education and the labor market — although more broadly, the regulation serves to underpin the EU's funding system.
This spring, the State Shared Service Center (RTK) also distributed nearly €2.3 million to projects aimed at addressing the divide, with about 30 percent coming directly from the state budget.
Among the recipients, Taavi Kotka's HK Unicorn Squad received nearly €215,000 to promote girls' interest in technology and engineering, while the Estonian Business School (EBS) received €214,000 for a project to empower girls in STEM and leadership.
Of the 12 funded projects, only three directly encourage boys to pursue higher education: two focus on teachers and one on healthcare workers.
At TLÜ, Täht said the education system should identify earlier what causes teen boys to lose interest in school and continuing their education.
"That way they could be provided with better support and guidance, and they could find their education more meaningful, exciting and useful," she added.
While the compulsory school attendance age was only just raised to 18 this year, women have accounted for around 60 percent of higher education students since at least 2010.
Asked why the state hadn't acted sooner, Kallas said, "Better late than never."
The minister added that there are already so many major initiatives underway in Estonia's education system that the ministry simply lacks the capacity to take on anything new, including addressing the gender education gap.

How did Mars get its moons? Japan’s MMX mission is about to find out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:13:09 UTC
20:13:09 KST

Roaring away on top of a tongue of flame, the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency’s (JAXA’s) ambitious Martian Moons Exploration (MMX) spacecraft launched on its way to Mars on October 19. Its mission: to study the Martian moons Phobos and Deimos, setting down on the surface of the former (along with a small rover) and even returning a 10-gram sample of Phobian material to Earth for later study.
The two tiny moons—Phobos is a lumpy space potato that is about 26 kilometers in length, and Deimos is an oddly shaped rock that is about 16 km long—were discovered in 1877 but still hold many mysteries tight. Despite close-up images taken of both by various Mars missions over the decades, there is much we still don’t understand about them, even basics such as how they formed. In fact, this is such a big question that answering it is actually MMX’s primary goal.
I’m excited about this mission! MMX will take a year to voyage to the Red Planet and, once there, will slip into an orbit around Mars that will keep it close to Phobos. It will map Phobos’s surface to measure the moon’s shape and scout for potential landing sites (and will also occasionally observe Deimos from a distance). Once engineers back on Earth choose an appropriate spot on Phobos, MMX will deploy a rover to roam the surface, and soon thereafter, the mission’s main spacecraft will touch down. It will collect a small sample of the surface regolith—the powdery material made from rocks pulverized by meteorite impacts and thermal weathering—and eventually blast off into space once again. The plan is to then fly by Deimos for some close-up observations and to subsequently head back to Earth to return the surface sample in 2031.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The rover’s design is pretty clever. It’s a joint effort by France’s National Center for Space Studies (CNES) and the German Aerospace Center (DLR). Called Idefix (after the dog in the French Asterix comic), it has a mass of about 24 kilograms. It’s not much bigger than a large shoebox, although, once the solar panels extend, it will span just more than a meter across.
The deployment is pretty gutsy—if successful, it will make Phobos the smallest body ever visited by a wheeled rover. It starts with MMX slowing to a stop about 40 to 100 meters above Phobos and then releasing Idefix. From there, the moon’s weak gravity (only about a thousandth as strong as Earth’s) will pull the rover slowly down; the descent could last several minutes even from such a low height. The impact will be gentle, probably less than one meter per second, roughly human walking speed.
After that, the locomotion system is designed to flip the rover upright no matter how it lands, putting the wheels down so it can move. Even that is tricky; Idefix will weigh only about 15 grams, or roughly half an ounce, on Phobos! A house sparrow on Earth weighs twice as much. Idefix is designed to measure the moon’s surface temperature and mineralogy, but it will also snap pictures of its wheel tracks on Phobos to better understand the cohesion strength and size of the regolith grains.
So why is there interest in the Martian moons? Mostly it’s because their origin story is so baffling.
Mars sits on the inner edge of the main asteroid belt, so some scientists have proposed that these wee moons are captured asteroids. One point in this idea’s favor is that the compositions of both moons resemble those of common asteroids.
It’s difficult, however, for a planet to grab a passing rock and keep it; orbital mechanics dictate that an asteroid must shed a lot of velocity in order for Mars to ensnare it. Such an object would have to be on a fantastically lucky trajectory to, say, dip down and drag through the upper Martian atmosphere to slow to just the right speed for capture.
It’s far easier, though, if the incoming asteroid is binary: two rocks in orbit around each other. In that case, one of the pair falls into orbit while the other is ejected from the system and carries away the excess energy. That means there must have been two separate events to snag both moons; their orbits are very different, with Phobos a mere 6,000 km above the Martian surface and Deimos a little more than 20,000 km up, so they were unlikely to have been captured together.
Also, both moons have circular orbits directly over Mars’s equator, whereas captured asteroids would be expected to fall along more elongated trajectories around the planet. Such highly elliptical orbits could have been circularized via atmospheric drag and tidal forces from Mars acting on the moons. But this process takes so long (billions of years) that it’s not clear that enough time would have elapsed for Deimos to have settled onto its current path that way.
Another possibility is that a large asteroid impact on Mars could have thrown material into space that then coalesced as the moons. This mechanism has precedent; our own moon came to be that way when a small planet (about the size of Mars, ironically enough) slammed into Earth not long after the formation of our world,: the impact ejected huge amounts of rock that rapidly condensed to form our faithful companion.
Indeed, there are hints that, in some ways, the Martian moons’ compositions resemble that of the Red Planet. But if they formed from the same event, why are they in such different orbits? Perhaps many such objects were formed from the event, and the current moons are the only survivors. A more recent hypothesis is that one moon formed (either together with Mars or from a later impact) but was itself blown apart by an impact to create the extant pair; this idea can explain the circular equatorial orbits, as well as the current differences in their orbital heights.
Phobos is lower-density than expected for a solid rock, so it’s likely to be at least partially a rubble pile, composed of countless smaller rocks held together by their mutual gravity. Many, if not most, smaller asteroids are rubble piles, and we’re still not completely sure how this happens. It almost certainly results from impacts, with the leading candidate being a smashup energetic enough to shatter the asteroid but not quite sufficient to dissipate it. Afterward, the broken pieces fall back together via gravity. If this is true for Phobos, MMX will tell scientists a lot about how it’s changed over time.
There have been previous attempts to send dedicated spacecraft to Phobos (such as the former Soviet Union’s Phobos 1 and 2 missions and the Russian-Chinese mission Phobos-Grunt), but they all failed in different ways to get there. In fact, many missions to Mars have failed, prompting the dark joke in the space community that a monster on Mars called the Great Galactic Ghoul was eating them. Mind you, Phobos and Deimos are named after the minor gods of fear and terror, both sons of Ares!
I hope MMX has more luck. It’s well past time humanity was successful in sending a dedicated probe to these weird little Martian moons. The images and data will be wonderful, and hopefully many mysteries will be unraveled—as inevitably more will pop up. That’s science, and that’s why we explore. There are always more fun things to discover.

Dental implants can hijack your immune system, scientists discover
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:12:28 UTC
20:12:28 KST

Dental implants can hijack your immune system, scientists discover
- Date:
- October 23, 2026
- Source:
- Rutgers University
- Summary:
- Researchers have uncovered a surprising reason dental implant infections often resist antibiotics: the implants themselves can contribute to the problem. Bacteria corrode titanium implants, releasing microscopic particles that hijack immune cells, trigger destructive inflammation, and accelerate jawbone loss.
- Share:
For tens of millions of people, dental implants have provided a way to replace missing teeth with a full set of fixed, functional teeth rather than removable dentures. However, an estimated 10% to 20% of implant patients eventually develop peri-implantitis, a serious infection that damages the surrounding jawbone.
Antibiotics frequently fail to control this condition, and scientists have struggled to understand why. Now, researchers believe they have uncovered the mechanism responsible.
A new study published in PNAS Nexus by scientists at the Rutgers School of Dental Medicine reveals that bacteria can gradually corrode dental implants, releasing microscopic titanium particles into nearby tissues. These particles interfere with the immune cells responsible for fighting infection, trapping them in a state of excessive inflammation that progressively destroys jawbone.
The researchers examined human tissue samples, studied human immune cells in the laboratory, and conducted experiments using genetically engineered mice. Their investigation identified a calcium channel in macrophages, the immune cells that engulf bacteria, that becomes activated by titanium particles. When this channel was disabled in mice, the disease was prevented.
This discovery provides the first credible drug target for a condition that affects as many as one in five dental implant recipients and costs healthcare systems worldwide more than $1 billion annually.
"For the first time, we show why all the antibiotic treatments that work around teeth do not work around implants," said Georgios Kotsakis, senior author of the study and assistant dean for clinical research at Rutgers School of Dental Medicine. "Now that we know the cause, we can start developing therapeutics."
Why Dental Implant Infections Resist Antibiotics
One of the biggest mysteries surrounding peri-implantitis has been its similarity to periodontitis, the gum disease that develops around natural teeth. Both conditions begin with the same types of bacteria found in the mouth, yet they respond very differently to treatment.
For natural teeth, antibiotics combined with routine professional cleaning can resolve the infection. Around dental implants, however, the same medications are successful in fewer than half of cases. Even when treatment is attempted, the underlying jawbone may continue to deteriorate.
For the past two decades, scientists have largely concentrated on the bacteria responsible for these infections. Researchers in Kotsakis' laboratory decided to investigate another possible contributor: the implant material itself.
Their work showed that bacteria accumulating on implant surfaces create acidic biofilms that slowly damage the titanium. Over time, this corrosion can release billions of microscopic metal particles, each smaller than a red blood cell.
Titanium particles can also be dislodged during routine dental cleaning. This is particularly concerning when instruments designed for natural teeth are used on implants, because they can scrape and damage the metal surface.
How Titanium Particles Hijack the Immune System
Once released into the gums, the tiny titanium fragments attract a bacterial toxin known as lipopolysaccharide, which coats their surfaces. This combination creates a deceptive target for the immune system, making the particles resemble unusually large bacteria that cannot be broken down.
Macrophages, the white blood cells responsible for engulfing and destroying harmful microorganisms, attempt to consume these particles. But because the cells cannot digest titanium, they become stuck in a prolonged state of excessive inflammation.
As a result, the macrophages produce large quantities of inflammatory signaling molecules, including interleukin-1 beta. This protein is also associated with inflammatory processes involved in rheumatoid arthritis and Alzheimer's disease.
The resulting immune response gradually breaks down the bone supporting the dental implant. At the same time, the macrophages become less effective at fighting the bacteria that triggered the infection in the first place.
Laboratory experiments revealed just how severely their defenses were disrupted. Macrophages exposed to titanium particles engulfed fewer than half as many bacteria as immune cells that had not encountered the particles.
"These particles are little magnets that attract the bacterial toxin, and they hijack the immune system, preventing it from clearing bacteria," said Kotsakis. "You have a perfect storm that defies antibiotics."
Scientists Identify a Potential New Treatment Target
After uncovering how titanium particles disrupt immune defenses, the researchers investigated the molecular pathway responsible for the damaging reaction.
They traced the process to TRPC1, a calcium channel (a specialized, pore-forming protein structure within cell membranes) found in macrophages. This channel plays a central role in the inflammatory response triggered by titanium particles and bacterial toxins.
To test its importance, the team used genetically engineered mice that lacked TRPC1. When these animals were exposed to the same combination of titanium particles and bacteria, their immune systems responded much more effectively.
The mice developed dramatically smaller abscesses, produced fewer inflammatory signaling molecules, and regained the ability to clear bacteria. Disabling the channel prevented the destructive disease process observed when TRPC1 was present.
The results point toward a potentially new approach to treating peri-implantitis by targeting the immune system response rather than relying exclusively on antibiotics.
With funding from the National Institutes of Health, Kotsakis and his colleagues are now evaluating potential drugs that act on the same molecular pathway in human cells.
Why Proper Dental Implant Cleaning Matters
Although the research opens the door to future therapies, it also reinforces an important preventive measure for people who already have dental implants.
Regular professional cleaning remains the strongest known protection against peri-implantitis. However, the instruments and techniques used during those appointments can make a significant difference.
Until approximately a decade ago, many dentists routinely cleaned implants with the same metal scalers used to remove deposits from natural teeth. Research by the Rutgers team and other scientists has since demonstrated that these tools can damage and corrode titanium surfaces, potentially releasing additional particles and accelerating the disease.
Today, nonabrasive cleaning methods have become standard practice, helping protect implant surfaces while reducing the risk of complications.
By revealing how corroded titanium can interfere with immune defenses, the findings offer a new explanation for why some dental implant infections are so difficult to treat and identify a promising direction for developing more effective therapies.

Journal Reference:
- Juliana Girón Bastidas, Danyal A Siddiqui, Viviane Nascimento Da Conceicao, Yuyang Sun, Mashael Al Thunayan, Brij B Singh, Georgios A Kotsakis. Implant-derived titanium particles impair macrophage bacterial clearance via TRPC1 and lysosomal dysfunction. PNAS Nexus, 2026; 5 (4) DOI: 10.1093/pnasnexus/pgag081

His mother, he said, saw a grey Renault Clio car speeding by and heard “loud bangs”.

Writing on X, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the case was “very serious” and that “all resources of the security forces and the judiciary are fully mobilised”.
Macron earlier in the day said “the nation is standing with” the victims of this “terrible ordeal”.
The shooting came with France on edge following last weekend’s riots on the sidelines of mass protests over the cost of living, some of the worst street violence in recent years.
Read moreFrench student groups call for protests to continue after meeting with Macron
More protests are expected this weekend, but police will be out in force after a week of overnight curfews put in place in cities throughout the country.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP, Reuters)
