Deaths of 2 CIA agents in Mexico lead to treason charges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:07:39 UTC
20:07:39 KST

Deaths of 2 CIA agents in Mexico lead to treason charges against former state attorney general
A former Mexican state attorney general could face trial for treason over accusations that he illegally launched a joint operation with the CIA without telling the federal government.
The operation to dismantle a drug lab in the state of Chihuahua in northern Mexico in April drew attention after two CIA agents and two state officials died in a car accident on their way back.
That raised questions about the Trump administration's actions on Mexican soil, and outraged President Claudia Sheinbaum, who has made a strong defense of national sovereignty a centerpiece of her administration. The state district attorney, César Jáuregui, resigned, saying he wanted to clear the way for an inquiry into the operation.
He was arrested Oct. 17 on state charges of illegal exercise of public office, which a judge ruled Thursday can go to trial. Federal officials later added the treason charge, and a federal judge will decide Saturday whether to allow the indictment.
Earlier this year, a statement from Mexico's Ministry of Security said one U.S. agent entered Mexico as a visitor while the other entered with a diplomatic passport.
"None had formal accreditation to participate in operational activities in national territory," the security ministry said.
 Mexico has long worked with the U.S. in its fight against organized crime, but that's caused fears at times that American agencies do not respect the country's sovereignty. Sheinbaum and her predecessor Andrés Manuel López Obrador have made legal changes that aimed to stop foreign agencies from operating in Mexico without the federal government's consent.
Jáuregui held at a maximum-security prison
Héctor Villasana, one of Jáuregui's defense attorneys, said federal prosecutors told the court in a closed hearing this week that they were seeking an exemplary punishment to prevent a situation like the United States' removal of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.
The U.S. State Department told The Associated Press that it is aware and watching Jáuregui's case but didn't make a link between the case and the CIA deaths.
Here's how a traffic accident in the mountains of Chihuahua led to a charge of treason - a crime Mexico has not successfully brought to trial in decades despite one recent attempt.
An accident in the Chihuahua mountains
On April 19, the Chihuahua Attorney General's Office reported the dismantling of a drug lab in the municipality of Morelos, in the mountains of that state. On the way back, a vehicle in the convoy veered off the road and fell into a ravine. Two state agents and two Americans were killed.
In a news release, the state attorney general's office identified the two Mexican casualties as first commander of the state investigation agency Pedro Román Oseguera Cervantes and officer Manuel Genaro Méndez Montes. The U.S. agents killed were "instructor officers" who "were carrying out training tasks" as part of binational anti-drug cooperation, Jáuregui told reporters at the time. Jáuregui called the targeted labs "one of the largest sites found in the country where chemical drugs were produced."
The Federal Security Cabinet reported the dismantling of laboratories there during a joint operation by the state prosecutor's office and the army but did not provide details.
The operation ended without arrests because the criminals fled.
Treason is a hard-to-prove crime
According to the federal prosecutor's office, Jáuregui endangered national security by authorizing the participation of U.S. agents in the field operation, a decision that only the federal government can make. Experts say it is a political decision ahead of the 2027 Mexican midterm elections.
The charge carries from 5 to 40 years in prison, but it is very difficult to prove.
Samuel González, a former chief prosecutor for organized crime and an analyst, said that Jáuregui may have failed to fulfill his obligations by not informing the federal government or by allowing the foreign agents to carry weapons in violation of the law. But "even if that were the case, it would not constitute treason," a wartime crime.
Luis Villegas, the former prosecutor's defense coordinator, said it was unacceptable for the federal prosecution to compare the presence of the agents to a foreign "invasion."
Carlos Pérez Ricart, a professor at the Mexican university CIDE and author of the book "A Hundred Years of Spies and Drugs," said that even if the case is ultimately dismissed, its public impact will be huge.
Mr. Trump has repeatedly said Mexico isn't doing enough against the cartels. Sheinbaum's opponents, including Chihuahua's governing National Action Party, have claimed that she's running a "narco-government."
Pérez Ricart said the case could set back the country's fight against drugs and organized crime because it "sends a very bad signal to Washington," while the discussion should center on "more or better" collaboration with the U.S.
Official contradictions about the agents' role
Villegas said that the two Americans who died were officials providing training related to intelligence and drones. U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson just stated that they were "embassy personnel." Multiple people familiar with the matter later confirmed to CBS News they were CIA agents. The CIA declined to comment.
According to Jáuregui's defense team, the federal prosecutor's office said the agents were close to the person who led the operation, the Chihuahua investigations chief, who was one of two deceased Mexicans.
The day of the operation there were two other U.S. agents in the convoy traveling in another vehicle, who were later expelled from the country. The president said none of them had permission to operate in Mexico and that the military was unaware of the foreigners' presence.
The next day, Sheinbaum said she was unaware of the operation. Jáuregui clarified that the Americans had joined the group after it.
Presence of U.S. agencies in Mexico
The presence of U.S. agencies in Mexico has been a constant for decades, although former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador (2018–2024) limited their activities, and Sheinbaum amended the Constitution to prohibit field operations without the express authorization and cooperation of the Mexican government. The law does not allow members of U.S. agencies to be armed.
Ricart, the professor, said that, beyond official relations, there have always been anti-drug agents involved in operations of this kind, "often without the federal government's knowledge."
"These actions happen, have happened, and will continue to happen" because they are based on U.S. trust with state or local officials and facilitate ongoing collaboration," he said.
"However, since there are no clear rules, they can lead to abuses."
Mexico has announced the dismantling of numerous drug labs in recent months after Mr. Trump threatened possible military action to curb drug trafficking.
In February, Mexican naval personnel discovered a hidden drug laboratory in the country's Durango region and "neutralized" over 5,000 pounds of methamphetamine. In January, authorities announced more than 1,500 pounds of meth were seized from clandestine laboratories in the states of Durango, Sinaloa and Michoacán.

Russian Diesel Tanker Heads to New York After Trump-Putin Deal

A tanker carrying 40,000 metric tons of Russian diesel has set sail for New York under a deal between Washington and Moscow, with the shipment set to arrive on Nov. 7 – four days after the US mid-term elections.
The Malta-flagged Agioi Fanendes loaded ultra-low-sulfur diesel at Russia’s Baltic port of Primorsk on Thursday, Oct. 22, Reuters reported, citing LSEG shipping data. It added that the shipment’s due in the US on Nov. 7.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
US President Donald Trump has sought to reduce diesel prices before the Nov. 3 midterms to help his party win the by waiving parts of a new sanctions law against Russia. He also threatened to ban US diesel exports unless European countries release more emergency reserves.
Russian leader Vladimir Putin said on Wednesday, Oct. 21, that the first tanker under the Kremlin’s diesel agreement with the White House would sail in two to three days.
First cargo is a fraction of Trump’s initial pledge
The shipment is about 13 percent of the initial 300,000 metric tons (about 330,700 US tons) Trump said Russia would release immediately under the agreement.
Trump announced the arrangement on Oct. 9, saying larger volumes would follow in November and afterward. He claimed the deal would bring down fuel prices for US farmers, truckers and consumers.
Putin said Russia was preparing several tankers, suggesting the first cargo would be part of a wider series of shipments.
The timing he gave refers to departure, rather than delivery to a US buyer. Shipping and unloading would still have to take place after the vessel sails.
Ukraine Still Recording Starshield Connectivity Losses at 161 Kph, Defense Ministry Source Says
While Trump initially boasted of up to 2 million tons of Russian diesel to the world market upon announcing the deal, a Russian minister raised the figure to 3.5 million tons by year-end in a later remark.
Kyiv Post recently estimated that the planned 300,000-ton shipments to the US would last a bit over half a day, based on known consumption data. Ukraine’s sanctions envoy, Vladyslav Vlasiuk, said the 40,000-ton shipment would last less than two hours.
Sanctions relief draws criticism from Kyiv, US Congress
The diesel agreement has become a source of friction between Washington and Kyiv.
After Trump announced the deal, the US Treasury authorized transactions involving Russian diesel through April 7, 2027, easing restrictions imposed over Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Trump later signed an Oct. 16 executive order waiving sweeping new Russia-related sanctions and tariffs shortly before they were scheduled to take effect.
The suspended measures included additional 500% tariffs on Russian imports and 100% duties targeting major buyers of Russian oil and gas.
President Volodymyr Zelensky has criticized the diesel arrangement and broader sanctions relief, arguing that additional energy revenues would help Russia finance its war rather than persuade Putin to stop it.
Opposition has also come from US lawmakers. A bipartisan group of 12 senators urged Trump to rescind the diesel agreement, warning that it would reward Moscow while offering limited relief to Americans.
The senators called for stronger enforcement of economic pressure on Russia as attacks on Ukraine continued.

Leaked trove reveals extent of far-right AfD’s efforts to court Trump and Maga allies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:07:00 UTC
20:07:00 KST

A data leak from Germany’s far-right German Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has revealed the extent of efforts by the party to court Donald Trump and other leading figures in the Maga movement, stretching back more than a decade.
The trove reveals the pains the AfD took in wooing the president, whom they saw from the beginning as a potential ally, with senior party officials agonising over the wording of an obsequious congratulatory telegram when he was elected in 2016, which included the wish that his “hopes as a person be fulfilled”.
The AfD became a home for anti-immigration voters after 1.2 million refugees arrived in Germany in 2015 and 2016. It entered the Bundestag, Germany’s parliament, in 2017 with 12.6% of the vote, came second in the February 2025 federal election with 20.8%, and now leads national polls at about 30%. In September it won 43.8% of the vote in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, and it is now trying to form Germany’s first far-right state government since the second world war.
Trump hailed the win in Saxony-Anhalt in a post on his Truth Social, concluding his message with a German version of his Make America Great Again acronym, “MGGA!!!”
Germany’s domestic intelligence agency monitors the party as a suspected rightwing extremist organisation, and state agencies classify five of its regional branches as confirmed extremist.
Its leader in the central Thuringia region, Björn Höcke, was convicted in 2024 of knowingly using a slogan of the SA, the Nazi party’s paramilitary wing. AfD politicians also attended a meeting with extremists at which a mass-deportation “masterplan” was discussed. Its 2025 election programme calls for lifting sanctions on Russia and repairing the Nord Stream gas pipelines programme. Nearly all of Germany’s other parties have kept a “firewall”, refusing to govern with it.
Media outlets including the Guardian have reported on the apparently friendly contacts between the party and the US state department during Trump’s second term.
The leaked documents show AfD officials quickly moving to requests for support from the White House on policy issues when he first won the 2016 election.
Others show a burgeoning political courtship between senior figures including the AfD’s now leader, Alice Weidel, and the key Trump ideologue Steve Bannon.
The data, provided to reporters by the transparency organisation Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets), covers more than 420,000 emails, along with documents and personnel records, from the party’s foundation in 2013 to the present, with most coming before 2019.
The AfD said in a statement on Monday that a hosting provider used by the party had been attacked at the end of September and that “only a few mailboxes” had been copied. It told the news agency dpa that most of those mailboxes had not been used for years, and party sources were quoted as saying the published material appeared to be authentic.
The cable
AfD figures praised Trump ahead of his first election in 2016, with then leader Frauke Petry calling him a “refreshingly alternative proposition” in the spring of 2016. On the day after Trump won the presidency, Petry said the victory was “encouraging for Germany and for Europe”.
The hacked documents reveal that in the wake of his election, the party scrambled to send an ingratiating telegram to the new president.
Mainstream German politicians greeted Trump’s election with skepticism. On 9 November 2016, the then chancellor, Angela Merkel, offered Trump “close cooperation” only “on the basis of … values” including respect for human dignity “regardless of origin, skin colour, religion, gender, sexual orientation or political views”. The then defence minister, Ursula von der Leyen, called the result a “huge shock”. The next day the vice-chancellor, Sigmar Gabriel, reportedly called Trump the “forerunner of a new authoritarian and chauvinist international”, and he counted the AfD among its forces.
On 10 November, Petry emailed the party’s federal board proposing “an official and brief congratulatory telegram to the future US president”. German politics, she wrote, was “once again outdoing itself in politically unacceptable behaviour”; the AfD was “already perceived as the ones who don’t join in the majority howl of the political establishment” and, “as the only German party welcoming a new beginning in the US”, should say so officially.
Eleven of the board’s 13 members replied, all in favour. Current leader Weidel wrote “Yes:-)”. Beatrix von Storch, now deputy leader of the party’s Bundestag group, wrote: “Couldn’t be more of a yes.”
Board member Dirk Driesang added that Trump should also receive, “by post (?)”, the party’s manifesto in English.
The telegram went out on 11 November under Petry’s name, “on behalf of the federal board”, and was released to the press. It told the president-elect: “We are confident that you will readjust the transatlantic relationship and end the wars in Syria and Ukraine by mutual agreement with Russia.”
A second message, for the inauguration, was planned more carefully, and included a concrete request for a political favor. On 11 January 2017, Driesang asked for it to be put on the agenda of the board’s next conference call, “this time faster and better prepared”, and proposed adding a request: “Please support us in our efforts to remove the enemy-state clause from the UN charter.”
The “enemy state” clauses were written into the UN charter in 1945, and exempted action against “any state which during the second world war has been an enemy of any signatory” from the charter’s normal rules, so that the wartime allies could move against any “renewal of aggressive policy” by Germany, Japan or their allies. The general assembly declared them obsolete in 1995 and resolved to repeal them, but the text has never been amended, because changing the charter needs ratification by two-thirds of member states and all five permanent members of the security council.
No German party currently defends the clauses, but the Bundestag’s own research service wrote in 2017 that international lawyers unanimously regard the clauses as having no practical relevance. On the German right, however, the clauses are totemic, and viewed as a limitation on German sovereignty. The AfD’s Bundestag group demanded its deletion in a 2020 motion that called it a “relic of the past” which “indirectly designates Germany an ‘enemy state’”, and every other party voted it down.
AfD’s federal board adopted the enemy state request on its call of 16 January, according to the federal office’s record of the decision contained in the leaked documents.
When the office circulated an English draft on 19 January, Georg Pazderski, then the party’s Berlin leader and a member of its federal board, objected to the tone and to the request for support: “You don’t address the president as Mr Trump, he is Mr President. Otherwise a bit wordy and flowery. I stand by it: the enemy-state clause doesn’t belong in this letter at all. You don’t do that in a letter of congratulation. It looks like a begging letter.”
Driesang replied at 6.16 the next morning: “Personally I of course find the style appropriate, otherwise I wouldn’t have written it that way.”
The office also wanted to know how the telegram should reach Trump: “directly to Trump’s campaign team … or through official diplomatic channels (e.g. the US embassy in Berlin)?”
André Poggenburg, then the party’s leader in Saxony-Anhalt, answered: “all available channels.”
The text released on the afternoon of 20 January, signed by Petry and her then co-leader Jörg Meuthen, kept the request. It told Trump that the clause stood in Germany’s way “as a strange anachronism”, and asked him to see the AfD “as natural allies at your side, because we are the only German party in clear opposition to the wrong policies of Chancellor Merkel”. The Guardian reported the telegram’s wording the next day.
Frauke Petry subsequently left the party in 2017 in the wake of a bitter internal power struggle.Meuthen, Pazderski and Driesgan have also left the party.
Frohnmaier and the embassy
Markus Frohnmaier entered the Bundestag in 2017 and is now a deputy leader of the AfD’s parliamentary group and a member of the foreign affairs committee. Before that he led the party’s youth wing, the Junge Alternative. At a rally in Erfurt in October 2015 he told the crowd: “I say to these leftwing thought-terrorists, this party cartel, quite clearly: when we come, there will be a clear-out, there will be a mucking-out!”
Germany’s domestic intelligence agency classed the Junge Alternative as “confirmed extremist” in 2023. The Junge Alternative dissolved in March 2025, and a successor organisation, Generation Deutschland, was founded in November 2025.
In April 2019 the BBC and several European partner outlets reported on documents emailed in 2017 by Petr Premyak, a Duma staffer and former naval counterintelligence officer, to a senior official in Vladimir Putin’s administration in 2017 proposing support for Frohnmaier’s candidacy, with the assessment: “We will have our own absolutely controlled MP in the Bundestag.”
Frohnmaier’s lawyers said he “was never under the control of any third party”, and he told the BBC the documents were fake.
Five weeks after those reports, on 13 May 2019, his parliamentary assistant wrote to a Gmail address in the name of Daniel Pipes, the founder of the Middle East Forum (MEF).
The US civil rights organization the Southern Poverty Law Center writes of Pipes that he has “spent the better part of three decades actively promoting anti-Muslim rhetoric”, and has reported his argument that western leaders should consider “working with” far-right parties such as Austria’s Freedom party, “not marginalizing it”. Pipes had met Frohnmaier in Berlin two months earlier, on a tour of what he calls Europe’s “civilizationist” parties; the far-right site PI-NEWS published a photograph of the two.
The email thanked “Dr Pipes” for sending his interview with the rightwing weekly Junge Freiheit, then came to the point: “On behalf of Mr Frohnmaier I should also contact you with the request to arrange a contact in the US Embassy. Mr Frohnmaier would like to meet the Ambassador in person or the Head of the Department of Economic Cooperation and Development Policy.”
The ambassador was Richard Grenell, who had told the rightwing news outlet Breitbart within weeks of taking up the post in 2018: “I absolutely want to empower other conservatives throughout Europe, other leaders.” Grenell, whose praise in the same interview for Austria’s rightwing politician Sebastian Kurz as a “rock star” prompted calls from German politicians for his expulsion. Grenell went on to serve as Trump’s acting director of national intelligence in 2020 despite having no background in intelligence, to front the evidence-free claims of “illegal votes” in Nevada two days after the 2020 election, and, in Trump’s second term, to run the Kennedy Center through its renaming as the Trump Kennedy Center, until he stepped down in March.
The archive holds no reply from the Pipes address and no record of a meeting.
Responding to a request for comment, Pipes wrote in an email: “I received that request. I did not pass the request to anyone at the US Embassy in Berlin. If Markus Frohnmaier had a meeting there, it took place without my involvement. I do not recall Mr Frohnmaier among the many politicians I met on that trip. I show no subsequent contact with him after 13 May 2019.”
Pipes added: “The Southern Poverty Law Center distorts my views, which can be summed up by my well-known adage: ‘Radical Islam is the problem, moderate Islam is the solution.’ I oppose Islamism and Islamists, not Islam and Muslims … Representing my views and work otherwise is a calumny.”
Pipes concluded: “In 2019 in Berlin, I constantly argued with AfD members and leaders, encouraging them to adopt an anti-Islamist rather than an anti-Islamic outlook, without success. Indeed, I made that point in the Junge Freiheit interview you referenced.”
Two months earlier the same office had approached Breitbart itself. On 12 March 2019 the assistant asked the Bundestag group’s press spokesman whether he happened to have “a contact at Breitbart”, then wrote to the Breitbart reporter Chris Tomlinson, describing his boss as a “young star” of the party and an expert on the UN’s “2030 Agenda” and Global Compact for Migration: “Are you maybe interested in doing an interview with Mr Frohnmaier for Breitbart about these topics and the situation in Germany?” No reply is in the archive.
There is no evidence that this pitch was successful, and no mentions of Frohnmaier on Breitbart outside quotes in a story the previous year about anti-immigrant riots in the German city of Chemnitz.
In an email replying to a request for comment, Frohnmaier wrote: “Regarding the correspondence you refer to, it must first be noted that we have so far had no opportunity to independently verify its authenticity and completeness. This applies all the more given that, according to the information available to us, the documents were obtained unlawfully.”
He added: “The contacts you refer to are to be seen in the context of the usual cultivation of international political contacts. Exchanges with international interlocutors are part of everyday political work and are, in themselves, nothing out of the ordinary. As a matter of principle, we do not comment further publicly on internal matters.”
‘We came to listen’
A year earlier the AfD’s Bundestag group had announced its first contacts with the Trump administration. A press release on 13 June 2018 said the group’s foreign affairs spokesman, Armin-Paulus Hampel, and Jens Kestner, a member of the defence committee, had travelled to the US “to inform themselves about the state of German-American relations”.
“We came to listen,” Hampel was quoted as saying in the release. “In talks at the state department, on Capitol Hill and at the Pentagon,” the release went on, “the two AfD politicians also set out the foreign-policy positions of the AfD Bundestag group.”
It named two of their interlocutors: Justin Stebbins, “security policy adviser to the influential senator Ron Johnson”, who it said “showed understanding” for the AfD’s position on Nato; and Ken Toko, “head of the ‘German desk’ in the state department”, who pressed Germany on defence spending. The Frankfurter Rundschau reported at the time that it was the group’s first official US trip and that the talks were at mid-level working level.
The AfD’s founding manifesto, adopted in 2016, says Nato membership serves Germany’s interests “insofar as Nato confines itself to its task as a defensive alliance” and calls for the withdrawal of all allied troops stationed in Germany, “and in particular their nuclear weapons”. Its 2025 manifesto keeps Nato membership only “until an independent and capable European military alliance has been built”, and rejects Nato’s eastward expansion. The 2025 manifesto also says that the party envisions Ukraine as a neutral state, aligned neither to Russia nor the west.
Steve Bannon
The most direct line into Trump’s circle was through Harris Media, a Texas digital firm that had worked for the Republican senator Rand Paul, Marine Le Pen and Benjamin Netanyahu, and ran the AfD’s online campaign for the 2017 federal election, as Der Spiegel reported at the time.
On 28 February 2018 the firm’s founder, Vincent Harris, emailed Alice Weidel, by then the AfD’s co-leader in the Bundestag, to say he would be in Berlin in March and would “love to connect” about “the database for the party, and maximizing donations, and lead generation efforts”. Weidel replied the next day: “Sure! My office will get in touch with you. Btw. Do you have Steve Bannons cell phone number? I need to see him.”
Bannon, the former White House chief strategist, had left the post seven months earlier and had been forced out of Breitbart in January. On 3 March Harris wrote to both of them: “Alice, Per your email, wanted to introduce you to Steve Bannon. I believe you two will get along incredibly well, and share common vision and ideals.” He was, he added, “looking forward to seeing what you will cook up together”.
Bannon answered two minutes later from his BlackBerry, “Thanks vince”, and “Alice let me know when u can chat”. Weidel replied: “Steve, any time. I am in Berlin tomorrow, in Zurich Monday and Tuesday. Let me know.” Bannon: “I’m in zurich tuesday, wednesday”, and “Would love to meet”. Weidel: “Tuesday afternoon Zurich. When and where?” Bannon: “Perfect.”
The meeting was reported by the news agency dpa the same day, citing Weidel’s office, which said Bannon’s experience of political communication and alternative media had been of particular interest to her. What the emails add is who arranged it, and why. On 12 March Harris wrote to Weidel: “I am glad to see the other meeting went well!”
Three days later Thor Kunkel, the party’s campaign creative director, had a suggestion for Weidel. “Why not hire Bannon? For AfD-TV,” referring to the party’s in-house media organization. “Why not? The man is desperately looking for a job. I know this by chance from Dietrich Mateschitz,” name-checking the co-founder of Red Bull. Weidel forwarded it to her Bundestag office; the archive does not show that anything came of it.
By that summer the party was keeping its distance from the former White House aide in public. On 11 August 2018 Alexander Gauland, a former Christian Democrat who co-founded the AfD and was then one of its deputy leaders, told German newspapers that Weidel “had met once with Bannon” but that she saw no possibility of cooperating with him. The emails show what that looked like from inside: when CNN wrote to the AfD’s press office on 7 August asking about Bannon’s Movement foundation, and noting that “some other news outlets have been reporting that Ms Weidel met Mr Bannon in Switzerland in March”, Meuthen replied: “I will not give CNN an interview on that.” A week later the Bundestag group’s press office told every AfD MP that, “after consultation with the two parliamentary group leaders, we ask you politely to leave these requests unanswered”.
On 26 March 2019 Bannon told a press conference in Rome, at which he called Italy “the centre of the universe” because of Matteo Salvini, that he had met representatives of several parties there, including the AfD. When a Stuttgarter Zeitung correspondent asked the party who had met with Bannon, the federal office told the board it knew nothing about it. Pazderski, the party’s Berlin leader, complained of a “wild growth” in the party in foreign relations, and said that the board had to “put a stop to these will-o’-the-wisp self-promoters, because their completely uncoordinated ‘private diplomacy’ reflects negatively on the entire party”.
The second administration
The leaked mail thins out after 2019, but the party’s ongoing contacts with the second Trump administration appear through the public record and its politicians’ own newsletters.
On the eve of the January 2025 inauguration Von Storch, the party’s deputy leader and her husband Sven were at Trump’s “Make America Great Again Victory Rally” in Washington. She told her newsletter subscribers the next day, “together with many celebrities and Trump supporters”, and “met Steve Bannon and Donald Trump Jr there, among others”.
On 14 February the vice-president, JD Vance, met Weidel on the sidelines of the Munich security conference. On 23 February the AfD doubled its vote and became the largest opposition party in the Bundestag.
In September 2025, the New York Times reported that in April, Von Storch and the AfD politician Joachim Paul had met the state department official Samuel Samson in Washington. “They took a lot of notes,” Paul said.
On 1 October Darren Beattie, then the acting under-secretary of state for public diplomacy, posted that he had met Frohnmaier and a second AfD MP, Jan Wenzel Schmidt, “to discuss U.S.-Germany relations, as well as shared priorities on cultural exchange and migration”. Beattie was fired as a White House speechwriter in 2018 after it emerged he had spoken on a panel with the white nationalist Peter Brimelow. On 13 December his successor, Sarah B Rogers, met Frohnmaier too; Frohnmaier posted on X that the exchange had “made clear that Washington is looking for a strong German partner that is ready to take on responsibility”.
The Guardian reported in February that Rogers, asked about the 2019 Russian documents, which argued for supporting his candidacy in the 2017 German election, said she had “sought guidance within the state department and determined” that the allegation was “unsubstantiated – and in any event, not a bar to a meeting”.
In an emailed response to a request for comment on the meeting, Rogers wrote “Mr Frohnmaier is the foreign policy spokesman for the most popular political party in Germany. He delivers AfD’s foreign policy positions in the Bundestag, and is the person German media call when they want a policy statement from AfD. For this reason, we talk to him in his official capacity to understand AfD’s positions.”
Rogers added: “During the ‘cancel culture’ era, there was a manic focus on reputational contagion that probably hurt American civic life, and is a poor fit for American diplomacy.”

At Cuba's special ed schools, teachers keep classes going despite crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:06:49 UTC
20:06:49 KST

At Cuba's special ed schools, teachers keep classes going despite crisis
HAVANA, Oct 23 - Yarnelys Bec Abalela arrived at the Abel Santamaría School for the Blind in Havana when she was just 3 years old. At that time, a congenital cataract threatened her vision.
After completing ninth grade, she enrolled in a higher-level special education program and then returned to help children with a condition similar to her own.
“Thanks to what I learned at this center, I was able to become a teacher,” said Bec, who has worked at Abel Santamaria for 21 years and is currently a fifth-grade teacher and therapist.
Now, massive power outages and a lack of everything from eyeglasses to Braille paper mean she needs to confront a whole new set of challenges.
Cuba's already inefficient state-run economy — long plagued by shortages — has descended this year into a full-blown crisis in the wake of hardened sanctions and a fuel blockade by the administration of US President Donald Trump.
Thousands of students in special education schools across Cuba are suffering fuel, electricity and transportation shortfalls.
But the schools are improvising, and keeping going. Many have reduced in-person classes, introduced virtual schooling, or installed solar panels.
At the Abel Santamaría school, enrollment remains at 44 students, all blind or vision-impaired students from Havana. Though the school maintains transportation to and from its facility, the fuel shortage has forced it to reduce in-person classes to four days a week. On Fridays, students work from home on exercises assigned by their teachers.
“Receiving instruction from a family member, at home, is not the same as in person, with trained teachers," said school director Suramis Rodríguez.
Power outages, which often exceed 18 hours a day in the capital, pose an additional challenge in a school where lighting is crucial for students with low vision. During blackouts, teachers move the children closer to the windows or relocate activities to courtyards and hallways to take advantage of natural light, Rodriguez said.
The US says the now nine-month fuel blockade is necessary to upend Cuba's government, which it calls inept and corrupt. The United Nations has called the blockade illegal and a violation of the human rights of all Cubans.
Despite the challenges, Cuba keeps the doors open at 330 special education schools, according to government statistics.
“In the midst of this situation, this is still the best place to provide these children with the tools they need for their lives,” said Bec. REUTERS

Inburgering with Dutch News: the great cycle path squeeze
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:06:15 UTC
20:06:15 KST

Inburgering with Dutch News: the great cycle path squeeze
Hanneke Sanou
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
You can’t have failed to notice that Dutch cycle paths are no longer the preserve of old-fashioned cyclists. E-bikes, fatbikes, scooters, snorfietsen, speed pedelecs, disabled vehicles – a seemingly never-ending stream of other road users have moved in. But what exactly are the rules and regulations?
Lesson 64: what is allowed on the cycle path?
Fatbike
The fatbike, with its characteristic thick tyres and frequently thick riders, has become wildly popular. It’s not surprising because at the moment, riders do not need a helmet, driving licence, or third-party liability insurance. The fatbike is officially an e-bike, and therefore there is no age limit, but measures are afoot to make helmet-wearing compulsory for riders up to the age of 18.
Fatbikes are allowed to travel at up to 25 kph. However, many are doctored to go faster – as you will notice when you see them whizzing past cars that keep to the 30 kph limit, mandatory for cars in some Dutch cities.
Electric bike
The electric non-fat bike, so to speak, is literally overtaking the person-powered bike, and that is partly due to its popularity among older riders – who are also well represented in the annual traffic death toll. The same rules of the road as apply to fatbikes apply to ordinary e-bikes – none. You will, however, see more and more elderly riders with a helmet.
Electric cargo bike
The cargo bike, or moedermobiel, deserves a separate mention because of the riders’ mistaken opinion that everyone has to make way for this space-hogging vehicle because it carries cute little toddlers. A good place to spot cargo bikes is outside primary schools at 3pm, when they cause a veritable jam of their own.
Speed pedelec
Speed pedelecs are electric bikes as well, but unlike normal electric bikes, they can legally reach speeds of up to 45 kph. This makes them motorcycles in the eyes of the law, with the rules that then apply, such as mandatory helmet-wearing, a driving licence and insurance. Speed pedelecs can travel on cycle paths, but only at a maximum of 25 kph.
Snorfiets, or moped
No pedalling is needed for this motorised bike or moped, which has a maximum speed limit of 25 kph and is allowed on cycle paths. Although snorfietsen have the same speed limit as electric bikes, they are technically considered to be motorcycles, and riders need a helmet, a driving licence and insurance.
The introduction of helmets for all types of mopeds several years ago led to the downfall of the snorfiets – after all, if you need a helmet, why not drive a proper motorbike – or a fatbike?
Scootmobiel
The motorised wheelchair or scootmobiel is possibly the most dangerous vehicle on the cycle path. According to statistics agency CBS, the traffic death rate among mobility scooter riders is over six times that of motorbike riders and over 20 times that of cyclists.
Users don’t need to pass any tests or learn the rules of the road, and they can go pretty much wherever they like – shopping centre, pavement, cycle path, ordinary road – just not the motorway.
The Canta
The Canta looks like a brommobiel – a small electric vehicle with four wheels – but because it is considered a mobility aid for people with a disability, it is treated in the same way as a scootmobiel.
The Canta is not supposed to go faster than 30 kph on the cycle path and 45 kph on the road, but is allowed to mount the pavement and annoy pedestrians at 6 kph. It can also park anywhere and does not need a number plate.
The minimum age is 16, and you’ll need to take out insurance, but you don’t need a driving licence. The Canta became popular with youngsters who could not be bothered to cycle and has since spawned a surge in far hipper micro cars.
Micro cars
The Birò and its ilk are small, fashionable and, according to many, extremely annoying electric vehicles which are banned from cycle paths but whose drivers use them anyway – particularly as a sneaky escape when faced with a traffic jam.
Popular with estate agents and PR people, micro cars have a maximum speed of 45 kph. If you want one, you will need a brommobiel driving licence and must be 16 or over.
Electric scooter
The step, or scooter, used to be a children’s plaything, but since the invention of the electric version, they have been taking over cities throughout Europe. Steps which have been officially approved have been allowed on Dutch cycle paths since July 1 this year. In Dutch terminology they are known as “light electric vehicles”.
The step has a maximum speed of 25 kph, and riders have to be 16 or over. You will need third-party liability insurance, and the base must have a number plate which is clearly visible.
The e-step is predicted to rival the fatbike in popularity and ability to provoke cycle-path rage – as long as helmets are not compulsory.

Ukraine is still recording satellite connectivity losses at speeds of 161 kph (100 mph), with no confirmation that restrictions on Starlink and Starshield have been lifted, a source in Ukraine’s defense ministry told Kyiv Post on Friday, Oct. 23.
“Ukraine’s Defense Forces and defense ministry specialists are continuously monitoring Starlink/Starshield connections and recording the results. As of this morning, cases of connectivity loss at speeds of 161 kph are still being observed,” the source said.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“There is currently no confirmation that the restrictions have been lifted,” the person added.
Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, an adviser to the Ukrainian president, also said in a Facebook post that there was no evidence the restrictions had been removed.
“We are not currently seeing the restrictions on Starlink being lifted. There are occasional cases when Starlink can move somewhat faster than the limit, but these are likely the result of SpaceX’s algorithms or specific operating conditions, rather than the removal of the restriction,” Beskrestnov wrote.
The latest assessment comes a day after US President Donald Trump said Elon Musk had restored Ukraine’s satellite service, but did not confirm whether he had personally intervened to lift the restrictions.
“I guess the bottom line, he put it back,” Trump told reporters on Thursday, responding to a Wall Street Journal report that he had called Musk and asked him to restore the service.
Russian Diesel Tanker Heads to New York After Trump-Putin Deal
It remains unclear whether the reported restoration has significantly improved Ukraine’s satellite communications capabilities.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told CNN’s Christiane Amanpour in an interview published Thursday that restrictions were still affecting Ukraine’s military satellite communications.
“Now it’s still limited,” Zelensky said.
CNN reported that some Ukrainian military units saw higher connection speeds after the reported restoration, but improvements were uneven, and restrictions remained.
A source familiar with the situation told CNN that the available speeds were “clearly not enough to intercept jet-powered drones.”
Starlink restrictions undermine Ukraine’s interceptor drones
On Oct. 17, Zelensky said Starlink speeds in Ukraine had been capped at 161 kph, making the system unusable for some interceptor drones designed to destroy Russian jet-powered Shahed attack drones and endangering Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian attacks.
“When an Iranian drone goes with a speed of 450 or 500 kph [280 to 311 mph], and you limit [the speed] one night to 70 or even 100, you cannot intercept anything,” Zelensky told CNN. “And this is terrible.”
Zelensky said Ukraine does not use Starlink to attack Russian military or energy targets inside Russia.
“We don’t attack Russian military targets or energy targets using Starlink. Never,” he said. “That’s why it was strange they limited us in Ukraine. It means limiting our ability to defend ourselves.”
The inability to intercept Russian drones effectively has become a major threat to Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.
Ukraine’s acting chargé d’affaires in the United States, Denys Senik, previously said Kyiv was awaiting an official response from the Pentagon and SpaceX on the full restoration of Starshield services. The system’s performance remained unstable, he said.
According to The Telegraph, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk proposed that Trump restrict Starlink speeds in Ukraine.
The Wall Street Journal subsequently reported that Trump called Musk and asked him to lift the speed restrictions imposed by the SpaceX chief.
Responsibility for restrictions remains unclear
Asked who ordered the restrictions, Zelensky said he did not know whether the decision came from SpaceX or US government institutions.
“I don’t know,” he said. “Technically, I think SpaceX can do it. But whether the decision comes from them or from some institutions, I don’t know.”
Musk said Starshield, SpaceX’s military-grade satellite service, is controlled by the US government.
But US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has maintained that Starlink is a commercial product whose operating decisions are made by SpaceX, while saying Ukraine’s request for broader access to Starshield remained under discussion.
The Pentagon has denied issuing instructions to slow the system.

Motorsport Day in Tokyo: Italy and Japan United by a Passion for Motorsports
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:05:25 CEST
20:05:25 KST

A bridge between Italy and Japan built on a shared passion for motorsports, as well as for fashion, design, technology, and lifestyle. This is the central theme of “Motorsport Day 2026,” held at the Italian Embassy in Tokyo to mark the 160th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the two countries. During the event, a new initiative linked to the Mille Miglia was unveiled, scheduled for April 2027 between Nara and Kyoto to celebrate the centennial of the historic Italian race. Princess Yōko of Mikasa was the guest of honor. Approximately 200 people attended, including Akio Toyoda, president of Toyota, along with representatives from automakers, racing teams, industry companies, drivers, the media, and the business community. For Toyoda, this was his first visit to the Italian ambassador’s residence—a significant occasion symbolizing Japanese-Italian exchange through the world of motorsports. On display at the residence were vehicles and products that showcase the history and technology of motorsports in both countries: from the Toyota 2000GT to the Nissan Nismo GT500, from the Ferrari 296 GT3 to the Haas F1 car, and including Pagani and historic cars associated with the Mille Miglia. Among the motorcycle manufacturers, Ducati and Aprilia participated. Speaking alongside Ambassador Mario Vattani and Princess Yōko, Toyoda focused on “automotive culture,” in which Italy plays a leading role, describing it as a “master” in terms of history, tradition, and technological innovation, as well as a “source of inspiration” for the future—including for the Japanese industry. The initiative aims to promote the technical expertise and appeal of Japanese motorsports worldwide, while creating opportunities for exchange and business between companies and brands from both countries.

France tightens security in anticipation of weekend protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:05:13 UTC
20:05:13 KST

France to deploy 70,000 police as country braces for weekend protests
Interior minister pledges crackdowns on violence as cities issue curfews, crowd restrictions.
French authorities are preparing for a massive police deployment and warning of crackdowns on violence as the country prepares for nationwide demonstrations on Saturday.
President Emmanuel Macron was due to hold a meeting on Friday with his defence council – made up of top ministers and officials – and was planning to meet with security forces, as cities across the country issued restrictions on gatherings and public transport. Macron, who has blamed “seditious” ultra-left groups for the unrest, was due to announce “additional decisions” following the defence council meeting, his office said.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said about 70,000 police would be deployed nationwide on Saturday, roughly 10,000 more than last weekend, with elite units, mounted police, helicopters, drones, armoured vehicles and water cannon.
“We will be uncompromising with rioters, looters and all those who commit acts of violence,” he told reporters, adding that “ultra-left” groups were urging activists online to target public buildings.
“We are not talking about a nice, friendly demonstration,” he said. “We will be extremely vigilant, extremely firm, and we will let absolutely nothing pass.” Curfews imposed in some sensitive areas this past week will remain in force.
Macron’s announcement on Thursday that only union demonstrations would be authorised at the weekend has prompted harsh criticism from student groups whose demonstrations in recent weeks against conditions in schools were joined by groups denouncing high living costs and other grievances.
More than 500,000 people gathered across France last Saturday for demonstrations that were marred by violence and looting.
Paris has extended a nighttime curfew until Monday, while France’s third-largest city, Lyon, has banned gatherings in central areas and introduced curfews and public transport restrictions for Saturday. In the coastal city of Marseille, which had also banned protests, authorities said on Friday they would allow one union-organised march on an “exceptional basis”.
In advance of the planned protests, Macron met with high school students for the first time on Friday.
Nathanael Combary, president of the campaign group High School Renewal, said Macron had been “attentive”, but that students were awaiting proposals in talks with the prime minister on Monday.
“We are not satisfied,” he said, urging pupils to “continue to mobilise”.
‘Trampling on freedoms’
Despite the restrictions, France’s national student union, UNEF, has called for rallies on Saturday. The Yellow Vest movement, an anti-establishment force that first emerged in 2018, was planning a march through central Paris.
Police have authorised only one union demonstration along a limited route in Paris and rejected requests for rallies organised by UNEF and the Yellow Vest movement, the Reuters agency reported. UNEF said its rallies would go ahead.
In the city of Orleans south of the capital, 20,000 to 30,000 people are expected to protest against Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally as it holds its party congress there, but the prefecture said the gathering would be barred from the city centre.
Amnesty International called the restrictions “a slide toward authoritarian practice” that jeopardise the right to demonstrate peacefully, and Human Rights Watch expressed alarm over reports of children severely injured by crowd-control weapons. Marylise Leon, general secretary of the French Democratic Confederation of Labour union, said the bans were “counterproductive” given the level of anger.
“Macron is trampling upon the freedom to protest in our country, and is spitting on the values of the republic he claims to defend,” UNEF said.
Shops and businesses in major cities have been urged to close. The Louvre and the Louis Vuitton Foundation will be closed on Saturday, while the Paris edition of the Art Basel fair will end on Friday, two days ahead of schedule.
Since last Saturday’s violence, 2,700 people have been arrested, according to the Ministry of Justice.

Israel’s election is being cast as a historic showdown - but four trends tell a different story
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:04:33 UTC
20:04:33 KST

Night after night, or at least on the nights he anchors Channel 12’s nightly news, Danny Kushmaro introduces the election segment by calling them the most fateful elections in Israel’s history.
And he is not alone. “Israel’s most important elections” or “Israel’s most fateful elections” has become a refrain of this campaign.
It brings to mind a verse from Ecclesiastes (7:10): “Don’t say, ‘How was it that the former days were better than these?’ You would be asking an unwise question.”
Kohelet cautions against romanticizing the good old days. Here’s a related lesson for Tuesday’s election: don’t assume that the current one is more fateful or important than all those that came before. That would be an unwise assumption.
Besides, we seem to say that about almost every election.
What about the December 1973 election, two months after the Yom Kippur War? That wasn’t critical? The 1977 election, which forever changed this country’s political landscape and brought Menachem Begin to power, wasn’t fateful? How about the 1996 election, just months after Yitzhak Rabin’s assassination? Or Ariel Sharon’s defeat of Ehud Barak in 2001, as the peace process with the Palestinians unraveled and the Second Intifada gathered force?
Every election feels like the most fateful and important one. Ever.
But perspective is needed.
How 'fateful' elections turns political battles into existential wars
And why does that matter? Because calling this the most important and fateful election ever turns the political competition, the battle between the pro-Netanyahu and anti-Netanyahu blocs, into nothing less than an existential matter. Defeat becomes harder to regard as a setback that can be corrected next time. Instead, it begins to sound like something the country cannot survive.
And that can make accepting the outcome harder.
Therein lies the problem.
Since Naftali Bennett formed his government in 2021, Israel has struggled with more than the question of who should govern. It has struggled with whether the losing side will give the other side a chance to do so.
Before Bennett’s government was even sworn in, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu branded its formation “the greatest election fraud.” He meant broken campaign promises, not stolen ballots. But the message cast a government formed legitimately through the parliamentary process as fraudulent and, therefore, illegitimate.
From the minute Bennett’s government took office, the opposition worked tirelessly to bring it down. The main arena was the Knesset, where the coalition’s slim majority made every vote consequential.
As a result, the opposition sometimes voted against legislation it supported, believing it would weaken the government. In recordings published in May 2022, Likud MK Miri Regev defended voting against measures benefiting soldiers and vulnerable groups because the overriding objective was to topple the coalition.
The government spent much of its short life fighting for survival.
Then Netanyahu won the 2022 election and formed his hard-right government. Suddenly, the shoe was on the other foot.
Yair Lapid conceded the election and arranged an orderly handover. But as opposition to the judicial overhaul brought masses into the streets, the language of illegitimacy crept in again.
For instance, at a massive demonstration in Tel Aviv in April 2023, former Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) director Yuval Diskin said that while the government had been elected legally, it was morally illegitimate because of its “appalling composition and reprehensible actions.”
By August, the Kaplan protest leadership was also calling the government illegitimate, amid questions about whether Netanyahu would obey the High Court. Once again, the distinction between fighting a government’s policies and denying its legitimacy was becoming blurred.
Will Israel's next government have room to govern?
That leaves a question hanging over Tuesday’s vote: will whichever government emerges be given room to govern, both in the Knesset and in the streets?
Calling this election “the most fateful ever” hardly prepares the ground for that.
If voters are told that the future of the country, and indeed the Jewish people, hangs in the balance, accepting defeat becomes that much harder.
Are these elections consequential? Of course. So were many of those that came before. But at this critical juncture, the country also needs to accept and live with the results. Israel desperately needs a government given the space to govern.
Accepting the outcome does not mean supporting the next government, abandoning opposition, or refraining from protest. Nor does winning an election give a government a blank check.
But opposing a government’s policies is different from treating its very existence as illegitimate. There is a difference between working to replace a government and, from the outset, seeking to make governing impossible.
That distinction must hold for whichever side wins.
Magnifying the stakes may bring voters to the polls. But it may also do something this country can ill afford: make it harder afterward for the losing side to accept the results and let the winners govern.
That is one takeaway from this campaign. Here are three more.
Election's fiercest battles taking place within blocs
Despite the characterization of these elections as the most fateful ever, the campaign has been relatively subdued: no televised debates between the leading candidates, no massive outdoor rallies. Much of the action has consisted of social media clips, interviews, and leaks to the press.
And some of the fiercest fighting has taken place inside the blocs: Netanyahu vs Ofer Winter, Gadi Eisenkot vs Avigdor Liberman.
In the anti-Netanyahu bloc, three candidates who regard themselves as worthy of the premiership have periodically sniped at one another: Eisenkot, Bennett, and Liberman. They share an interest in replacing Netanyahu, but each wants to be the one to do it.
The sharper fighting, however, has been on the Right, where Netanyahu and Religious Zionist Party head Bezalel Smotrich have spent considerable energy trying to persuade Winter and his People of Israel party to withdraw.
The stated concern is the electoral threshold. If Winter fails to cross the 3.25% bar, votes coming predominantly from the Right will not translate into seats.
The cautionary tale is April 2019, when Bennett and Ayelet Shaked’s New Right narrowly missed the threshold. Had it crossed, Netanyahu could have formed a coalition, and the country would have been spared the dizzying spiral of repeat elections.
But Winter also presents Netanyahu with an uncomfortable challenge from within his own political camp.
The anti-Netanyahu parties say this government failed: failed to prevent October 7 and failed to achieve its declared objectives afterward, with Hamas, Hezbollah, and the Iranian regime still standing. Netanyahu can dismiss those charges as the familiar carping of his opponents.
That is harder when Winter delivers a similar message from the Right.
Winter’s emphasis on new faces – his list includes no one who has previously served in the Knesset – reflects his contention that the political leadership associated with October 7 needs to be replaced. His indictment extends across the Knesset, but it also challenges Netanyahu’s claim to be the leader best equipped to keep the country safe.
The competition is therefore about more than whether Winter will waste right-wing votes. It is also about whether he will persuade right-wing voters that their own leadership has failed.
The rival across the political divide challenges your policies. The rival on your own side challenges your claim to speak for your own camp.
Polls are shaping Israel’s election, not just measuring it
Polls are supposed to measure public opinion. Good polls reflect what the public thinks.
In this campaign, however, polls don’t merely reflect opinion. They help shape it. And Israel’s electoral threshold gives them particular power to do so.
Israelis famously don’t want to be freiers – suckers. They don’t want to vote for a party that falls below the 3.25% threshold and wins no representation, because they will feel, and are repeatedly told, that they wasted their vote.
So voters wait to see whether polls show Winter’s party, or Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha’s party, crossing the threshold before deciding whether to support them. If the party looks likely to pass, they may vote for it. If not, they look elsewhere.
The result is a circular process: voters consult the polls to decide whether a party is viable, while its viability depends on whether they will vote for it.
A poll showing a small party below the threshold can frighten away the very voters who might otherwise put it over. One showing it above the threshold can give hesitant supporters the confidence to vote for it.
At that point, the polls are doing more than reflecting opinion. They are shaping it.
Their influence also extends to the choices available on the ballot. Benny Gantz’s withdrawal this week followed polls consistently showing his party below the threshold. The fledgling party led by Gilad Erdan and Yuli Edelstein withdrew before the lists were finalized, against a similar polling backdrop.
Polls are critical in elections. They become a problem when they start to decide those elections.
The airwaves and newspapers have been filled with candidate interviews. Netanyahu, Eisenkot, Lapid, Winter – everybody is getting airtime.
And everybody is being asked a version of the same question: whom will you refuse to sit with in a coalition?
It is a natural and legitimate question. Voters are entitled to know which government their vote might help bring into being.
But insisting on unequivocal answers encourages candidates to make commitments before they know the parliamentary arithmetic they will have to work with.
If candidate X promises never to sit with party Y or candidate Z, and then does precisely that, the recording of his promise will be played on an endless loop. The candidate will be branded a liar.
Bennett’s signed pledge before the 2021 election not to allow Lapid to become prime minister, even through a rotation, and not to form a government dependent on Mansour Abbas is the obvious example. He subsequently formed precisely such a government.
Did he break a campaign pledge? Obviously. But his defense was that the election results left a choice between breaking that promise and sending the country into yet another election. So here’s a formula for understanding politics: politicians don’t break promises; they encounter changed circumstances.
That line might invite a knowing smirk, but it makes a serious point: coalition government requires compromise, and the election results determine which compromises will be necessary.
If everyone adheres to every coalition veto issued during this campaign, the country may end up with plenty of promises intact and no government for a very long time. Politicians should leave room for compromise before the election, rather than making absolute promises they may have to abandon afterward for the good of the country.
Changing course does not necessarily mean a lack of backbone. Sometimes it is what separates a functioning government from yet another round of inconclusive elections.

A gunman killed one person and wounded five others, including a 12-year-old girl, in a shooting in a Paris suburb that French President Emmanuel Macron described as a "terrorist and racist" attack.

Some far-right politicians have blamed immigration for looting and vandalism in a number of French cities on October 17.
Macron said the gunman had deliberately chosen not to fire upon some people due to their skin color and appearance.
The anti-terrorism prosecutor's office, known as PNAT, formally opened an investigation into the shooting.
PNAT can take over any criminal investigation it believes meets the criteria for terrorism, including violence inspired by far-right ideas. Terrorism sentences are tougher, and counter-terrorism forces have greater investigative powers.
Broadcaster BFM said the wounded girl had been hit eight times and was in serious condition.

Trappes Mayor Ali Rabeh, whose parents came from Morocco, said the shooting was "racist" and "Islamophobic."

Netanyahu bloc falls to 48 seats as opposition reaches 54, days before election - poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:03:56 UTC
20:03:56 KST

The gap between Israel's coalition and opposition blocs has widened to six seats ahead of Tuesday's Knesset election, despite the two largest parties being separated by just two seats, according to a Maariv poll by Lazar Research published Friday.
The coalition bloc receives just 48 seats this week, following the failure of Ofer Winter's People of Israel party to cross the electoral threshold. The party receives 3% of the vote, below the required 3.25%. Meanwhile, the opposition's change bloc has strengthened to 54 seats. Recent polling averages have shown the two political blocs nearly tied, highlighting the fluctuations in the election race.
The poll also shows that United Torah Judaism and Otzma Yehudit each lost one seat, polling 7 mandates, while Likud (19), Shas (8), and the Religious Zionist Party (7) each gained one. Overall, the coalition bloc has weakened by three seats compared with the previous week's poll.
Within the opposition bloc, the most significant change is the two-seat jump by Naftali Bennett's B'Yachad party, which rises to 15 seats. The Democrats also gained one seat this week, reaching 10. In contrast, Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party (21) and Yisrael Beytenu (8) remain unchanged. Other election surveys published on Wednesday also placed Eisenkot's party ahead of Likud.
The poll also shows that the Reservists or the New Economic Party narrowly crosses the electoral threshold, winning four seats.
This distribution of seats between the blocs depends on the Reservists-Economic Party crossing the electoral threshold. Given its narrow margin above the threshold in the current poll, if the party fails to qualify, the distribution is expected to shift to 50 seats for the coalition, 56 for the Zionist opposition, and another 14 for the Arab parties.
In addition to People of Israel (3%), the Haredi Public party (0.9%), Noam LeYisrael (0.5%), and Tzomet Beit Yisrael (0.5%) also fail to cross the electoral threshold.
Voter turnout intentions continue to rise
The Maariv poll also found that the proportion of Israelis who are certain they will vote in Tuesday's Knesset election continues to rise, reaching 81%. The figure suggests a potential increase in voter turnout compared with the 2022 election, when turnout stood at 71%.
As in the October 8 poll, the percentage of respondents certain they will vote is higher among opposition party supporters (87%) than among those intending to vote for coalition parties (83%).
Of particular note is the significant increase in the proportion of Arab party supporters who say they are certain to vote, rising from 74% on October 8 to 81% in the current poll, matching the national average.
These figures could result in the Arab party bloc winning significantly more seats in the upcoming election than it holds in the current Knesset. Arab voter turnout has emerged as a significant issue in the election campaign, amid concerns over crime and political distrust in Arab communities.
Eisenkot maintains lead over Netanyahu
The Maariv poll also found that Gadi Eisenkot continues to lead Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in a head-to-head matchup for prime minister, with 49% support compared with Netanyahu's 41%.
Naftali Bennett, who was tied with Netanyahu at 43% in the previous poll, now leads him by 45% to 43%.
Against Avigdor Liberman, Netanyahu continues to lead, although the gap has narrowed slightly, with Netanyahu receiving 44% compared with Liberman's 39%.
Majority of Israelis prefer unity government over new election
As in the previous poll, most Israelis (60%) would prefer a unity government to be formed if the Knesset election produces no clear result.
Of those surveyed, 33% want such a government to be headed by a leader from the change bloc, while 19% want Netanyahu to lead a unity government. Another 8% have no preference regarding who leads it, provided that a unity government is established.
Only 23% would prefer another election in the event of a deadlock, down from 27% in the previous poll. Another 17% said they did not know. A previous Maariv poll published on October 16 also found majority support for a unity government, with 27% preferring another election.
A breakdown of the findings by political bloc shows a decline in the proportion of coalition voters who would prefer another election, from 32% to 25%.
Opposition voters, meanwhile, remain consistent in their preferences, with a majority (55%) favoring a unity government headed by a leader from their own bloc.
The poll was conducted between October 19 and 22 among a representative sample of Israel's population aged 18 and older, including Jewish and Arab respondents. The initial sample consisted of 1,000 participants, while the final sample included 1,048. Data were collected from the general population using Panel4All's online respondent panel. A total of 580 people were contacted, 188 responded (30%), and 78 completed the survey (41%). The researchers also conducted supplementary telephone polling among the Arab population. A total of 687 telephone calls were made, 308 people responded (45%), and 100 completed the survey (32%). The poll's maximum margin of sampling error was 3%.

Energy winter to be difficult but not catastrophic, no worse than last – CER director
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:03:04 EEST
20:03:04 KST

The upcoming winter of 2026-2027 in terms of energy supply will be difficult, but not catastrophic and no more difficult than the last one, and it will be successfully navigated, believes Oleksandr Kharchenko, Director of the Center for Energy Research (CER).
"I am absolutely certain that we will get through the season. Despite all the challenges, there is an understanding of how to proceed. There are a sufficient number of scenarios, people who are ready to execute these scenarios, and the means with which they will be carried out (...) And I do not think that the winter will be more difficult than the last one. Rather the opposite," he said during a discussion on "Ukraine on the Threshold of Winter: Energy, Defense, and the New Diplomatic Reality" at the Interfax-Ukraine news agency on Friday.
According to the expert, the main factor of uncertainty for the energy sector right now is the weather. At temperatures of minus 10 degrees Celsius, scheduled power outages can reach 10-12 hours. In energy-deficient regions such as Kyiv, Odesa, and parts of Sumy and Chernihiv regions, scheduled outages may be quite long. At the same time, with milder weather, the restrictions will correspondingly be softer.
"Another truly risky component is heating. There are high risks that there will be attacks on large thermal facilities in Kyiv; they will undoubtedly happen, they happen constantly," Kharchenko emphasized.
However, according to him, a significant part of the capital's heat infrastructure is protected, and power engineers understand how to act after facilities are damaged.
"Whatever we could protect, we protected; whatever we couldn't – well, let's say, we know how to maneuver with that," he added.
At the same time, in those cities where there are actually only two or three boiler houses, if they are destroyed, a significant threat to heat supply will arise, and much in critical conditions will depend on how these cities prepared for winter.
In turn, as Kharchenko explained, energy engineers have more or less come to terms with the factor of Russian missile and drone attacks and understand that the intensity of these attacks will neither increase nor decrease cardinally.
"That is, they are not capable of inflicting more massive strikes than they are currently inflicting," he believes.
The expert added that these strikes have their own periodicity and a certain rhythm, and energy engineers understand how to respond to them, how to restore power supply to consumers as quickly as possible, and how to return core municipal infrastructure systems to operation as soon as possible.
