US renews push for EU to soften Big Tech rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:57:51 UTC
19:57:51 KST

Customers browse as Apple's new iPhone 18 and related products go on sale at their Regent Street store on September 18, 2026 in London. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images
BRUSSELS — The United States has renewed a warning that it will not lower tariffs on EU steel products and a range of other goods unless Brussels softens its enforcement of the Digital Markets Act, the bloc’s rulebook for Big Tech.
The European Commission relayed the message from the Trump administration to EU capitals at a meeting last week, two people with knowledge of the matter told POLITICO. They were granted anonymity to discuss the closed-door conversation.
The warning risks reigniting transatlantic trade tensions ahead of U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3, after a spell of calm following the EU’s implementation of the trade agreement struck at President Donald Trump’s golf resort in Turnberry, Scotland, last year.
Advertisement
Under the EU regulation enacting the trade deal, the Commission must report to the European Parliament and EU governments before the end of the year on whether Washington is keeping its side of the bargain on steel tariffs.
European lawmakers insisted on the additional safeguard because U.S. tariffs on steel and aluminum still go up to 50% — above a general ceiling of 15% for tariffs on EU goods agreed at Turnberry. Brussels has also asked for a range of goods, including pasta, cheese, wines and spirits, to be exempted from U.S. duties.
If the Commission concludes that the U.S. is not complying, it would be empowered — but not obliged — to remove the preferences that the EU granted under Turnberry in cutting tariffs on U.S. industrial goods to zero. Despite pressure from MEPs, there is little appetite in the Commission or EU governments to do so, for fear of reigniting a trade war.
It’s not the first time Washington has tried to tie steel relief to the EU’s digital rules.
During a November 2025 visit to Brussels, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick offered to address the EU’s steel and aluminum concerns if the bloc softened its digital rules. Competition chief Teresa Ribera, who oversees the DMA, denounced that offer at the time as “blackmail” and said the rules were not up for negotiation.
The DMA imposes obligations on very large tech companies — most of them American — that it has designated as gatekeepers. Brussels has fined Apple, Meta and Google a combined €1.59 billion under the law since April 2025, most recently €890 million for Google in July.
Advertisement
The European Commission declined to comment.
The U.S. Mission to the EU did not respond to a request for comment, but Ambassador Andrew Puzder recently questioned the EU’s motives in implementing the DMA.
“You start to wonder, are we trying to deal with the competition in the digital marketplace or are we trying to generate revenue from American companies to benefit Europe?” he told the Financial Times.
Francesca Micheletti contributed reporting.
This article published on Oct. 22 has been corrected to make clear that the Digital Markets Act is an EU regulation.

Rosoboronexport to unveil 'Anti-Drone Dome' UAV defense concept
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:57:47 UTC
19:57:47 KST

MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. Russia’s state arms exporter Rosoboronexport (part of the Rostec State Corporation) will showcase for the first time its latest air defense system designed to protect the population, troops, and facilities from drones, called the Anti-Drone Dome, the company’s press service reported.
The Anti-Drone Dome is designed to shield the civilian population, as well as strategic and infrastructure facilities, bridges, buildings, fuel and energy complex enterprises, and troop deployment sites from unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) attacks. "Options are also available for protecting convoys and vehicles transporting VIPs or sensitive cargo," the press service stated. It said that the project will be presented at the third Russia-Africa Summit, which will be held at Moscow’s Gostiny Dvor fairground on October 28-29.
The project was developed by specialists from Rosoboronexport in collaboration with leading Russian manufacturers of counter-UAV systems and representatives of specialized law enforcement agencies. It draws on practical experience in countering UAVs gained during military and counterterrorism operations in recent years.
"Protecting critical infrastructure from unmanned aerial vehicles has today become the cornerstone of national and economic security, as well as the foundation for further technological development. The proper design and implementation of such a system makes a significant contribution to demonstrating the effectiveness of government and business operations, maintaining supply chains, and signaling to investors that their investments are secure. Rosoboronexport offers the implementation of reliable site-specific protection against UAVs, tailored to each specific partner and facility. All the equipment and solutions used in this system have proven their effectiveness in real conditions," said Rosoboronexport CEO Alexander Mikheyev, quoted by the press service.
It added that the project is a multi-layered system comprising airspace reconnaissance capabilities, firepower capabilities, and electronic countermeasures against UAVs, a geoinformation system based on an automated control system, as well as engineering (physical) protection measures.
Concept and solutions
The company said that during the third Russia-Africa Summit, Rosoboronexport will present the concept itself to its partners, along with solutions designed for the development of the Anti-Drone Dome. These include physical UAV destruction systems such as the Pantsir-SMD-E air defense missile system and the Pantsir-S1M air defense missile and gun system developed by the High Precision Systems Holding Company, the Verba man-portable air defense system (MANPADS) and the TKB-1167 air defense system, as well as the Citadel anti-aircraft artillery system with programmable-detonation ammunition, developed by Rostec.
The company is also showcasing the Silok, Repellent-Patrol, Sky-Hunter 4PC, and Radescan (in its anti-drone version) systems for detecting and electronically jamming the control and navigation channels of unmanned aerial vehicles.
The Anti-Drone Dome is a comprehensive system whose configuration and functionality are adapted to a specific customer, taking into account the characteristics of the protected facility.
All of its components are developed and manufactured at facilities in Russia.

Health Insurance Week to highlight 'health along path of life'
TEHRAN – Under the theme “Health Along the Path of Life,” National Health Insurance Week will be held from October 24 to 30, focusing on “Innovation and Transformation in the Basic Health Insurance System: Shifting from Treatment-Oriented to Health-Oriented Care.”
The themes for each day of the week are as follows:
 
* Saturday, October 24: National Consensus and Universal Health Insurance for Health Equity
 
* Sunday, October 25: From Government Support to Philanthropic Contributions: Ensuring Sustainable Support for Patients with Hard-to-Treat Diseases
 
* Monday, October 26: Data Mining and Smart Monitoring to Safeguard Resources and Ensure Families’ Financial Protection
 
* Tuesday, October 27: Smart Innovation, Transparency, and Easy Access to Services
 
* Wednesday, October 28: Health Literacy, Family Physicians, and Sustainable Prevention Through Public Participation
 
* Thursday, October 29: Joining Forces with the National Health Team for a Healthier Nation
 
* Friday, October 30: Supporting People from Healthy Childbearing to Healthy Aging
According to the health ministry, the Health Insurance Organization covers about two million patients with rare and hard-to-treat diseases.
All resident and non-resident foreign nationals with legal stay in Iran must have basic health insurance coverage under a new Cabinet of Ministers enactment.
To safeguard the patients’ health and lower financial burden on households, tens of specialized healthcare service packages have been defined for them, with some more being continuously developed.
The packages include diagnostic, therapeutic, pharmaceutical, rehabilitation, and dental services, whether in the form of outpatient or inpatient services, which are provided with minimal deductibles or free of charge.
In 2024, seven more anti-cancer drugs were added to the list of rare diseases fund, with health insurance covering 70 percent of the costs.
“Currently, with the inclusion of these seven drugs, a total of 90 anti-cancer drugs are covered by the rare and hard-to-treat diseases fund, and the health insurance is paying 70 to 95 percent of their costs,” IRIB quoted Kameli, an official with the health insurance organization, as saying.
The number of health centers that have concluded contracts with the Health Insurance Organization increased by seven percent in the past Iranian calendar year (ended on March 19) compared with the year before.
In 2025, more than 53,000 centers concluded contracts with health insurance organizations, IRNA quoted Keivan Tajbakhsh, an official with the Organization, as saying.
Health insurance contracts have been signed with government, non-government, private, and charity centers for services.
The centers include doctors’ offices, hospitals, pharmacies, rehabilitation centers, and all medical centers.
“We hope to witness an increase in the number of health centers that are parties to the contract with Health Insurance Organization as new forms of the contract, approved by the Supreme Council of Insurance, are announced,” Tajbakhsh said.
He stated that 13,931 pharmacies, 20,804 doctors’ offices, 2,049 clinics, 2,446 independent laboratories, and 4261 rehabilitation centers, both independent and affiliated with other organizations, have concluded contracts with the Health Insurance Organization.
Efforts to enhance intl. cooperation
In August, the head of the Iranian Health Insurance Organization, Mohammad-Mehdi Nasehi, and officials from the International Conference on Public Health (ICOPH) committee explored avenues to enhance collaborations.
The Conference chair, Hematram Yadav, and its convener, Isanka Gamage, held a meeting with Iranian officials to discuss ways to boost cooperation in the fields of health insurance research and the exchange of managerial expertise, Borna news agency reported.
The officials met on the sidelines of the 12th International Conference on Public Health (ICOPH) held from August 5th to 7th in Bali, Malaysia. An Iranian delegation led by Nasehi attended the conference.
Lauding Iran’s active participation, Yadav said enhancement of scientific cooperation with Iran would be a valuable opportunity for ICOPH members.
For his part, Nasehi voiced the country’s readiness for the promotion of scientific cooperation with ICOPH. Referring to the scientific and practical capabilities of Asian countries, he stated that fostering ties with universities, research institutes, and health organizations in the ICOPH member states could pave the way for broader scientific, research, and managerial cooperation in health and health insurance sectors.
In May, Iran and Tajikistan signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) in the health sector focusing on six parts, including medical education, research, healthcare, treatment, medicine, and health insurance.
According to Nasehi, the MOU was signed on the sidelines of the 18th session of the Joint Commission on Trade, Economic, Scientific, Technical, and Cultural Cooperation between the Republic of Tajikistan and the Islamic Republic of Iran which was held on May 26, in Dushanbe under the chairmanship of the co-chairs of the commission — Minister of Energy and Water Resources of the Republic of Tajikistan Daler Juma and Minister of Energy of the Islamic Republic of Iran Abbas Aliabadi, IRNA reported.
Fostering ties in the health sector, particularly health insurance, is a part of Iran’s six-point roadmap for water diplomacy.
Referring to Iran’s expertise in health insurance, the official said the country’s experiences in implementing health insurance, referral systems, and other fields of health will be shared with Tajikistan through consultation and implementation.
In December 2025, Nasehi and the Minister of Health and Social Protection of Tajikistan, Jamoliddin Abdullozoda, agreed to promote cooperation between the two countries in the field of medical health insurance.
During a meeting held in Tajikistan, the two sides discussed the potential for expanding ties by launching joint investments in the health sector, ihio.gov.ir reported.
For his part, Nasehi announced the organization’s readiness to share experiences with Tajikistan to help strengthen its insurance system.

Free dental services offered during national oral health week
TEHRAN – The health ministry provided different dental services during the week-long national oral and dental health campaign, held from October 17 to 23 nationwide.
The campaign centered on training, self-care, prevention, and raising awareness about the importance of oral health. The health ministry, in cooperation with the Ministry of Education, conducted oral health education at schools to improve the knowledge of children and families about oral health.
Dental screening at schools focused on proper tooth brushing, applying fluoride varnish, promoting oral health habits, and referring those who need further treatment to medical centers.
With the help of student health ambassadors and healthcare providers at school, they would teach students about proper nutrition and how to brush and floss their teeth correctly.
“Apart from schools, dental services are being offered in rural and urban areas with a population of less than 20,000 individuals; pregnant mothers, mothers with children under two years old, and children aged under 14 are receiving free oral health packages and dental treatment,” IRNA quoted Zahra Qorbani, an official with the health ministry, as saying.
In other cities, dental services were also offered with health insurance covering 70 percent of the total costs. The dental services included tooth extraction, filling, scaling, and preventive care.
The official said that the health ministry programs are not limited to oral and dental health week; the health ministry is endeavouring to enhance both access to and the quality of services through upgrading equipment, supplying needed materials, and dispatching dentists to areas where there are not enough specialists.
Referring to the high costs of dental treatment, Qorbani highlighted that the main responsibility of the health ministry is to prevent diseases and reduce the need for costly medical care. To preserve natural teeth, promote oral health, and reduce the burden of costs, dental services need to target individuals at early ages of life while simultaneously increasing access to necessary treatments.
The week-long event was held under the theme ‘Don’t forget two times two, brushing your teeth for two minutes twice a day’, the health ministry’s website reported.
The health ministry also benefited from the capacity of dental offices, mass media, and social media to hold educational and preventive programs related to oral health for the promotion of self-care and enhancement of oral health literacy among the public.
In the past Iranian year, the program was held in some 34,000 schools, providing services to more than three million students across the country, Qorbani said in January.
World Oral Health Day (WOHD) is celebrated every year on March 20 to empower people with the tools and knowledge to prevent and control oral diseases, which affect nearly 3.5 billion people worldwide.
It encourages people to look after their oral health by adopting a good oral hygiene routine and managing risk factors.
Themed ‘A Happy Mouth Is… A Happy Life’, WOHD 2026 spotlighted oral health as the foundation of lifelong well-being — from a baby’s first teeth to maintaining a healthy smile in older age.

Since then, the occupation authorities have forced the child to appear in various videos. In them, the girl can be seen thanking Russian soldiers and saying that her relatives had supposedly been killed by the Ukrainian military.
"We established all the circumstances back in the summer. Sofia has close relatives in Ukraine who were looking for her, waiting for her and asking for her to be returned. But the Russians kept the child in a residential institution for months, with no possibility of returning to them," Dvoretska wrote.
Lvova-Belova recently said that Sofiia was being placed in the care of an "uncle" who lives in Russia with his wife.
The Russian official claimed that the child herself had expressed a desire to live with her "uncle". Dvoretska, however, says Sofiia had not known that this "relative" existed before she was abducted.
A video was subsequently posted on Lvova-Belova's Telegram channel showing the "uncle" and his wife collecting Sofiia. In the footage, the girl is wearing a camouflage cap bearing the Russian flag and the word "Spets" [short for "specialist" or "special forces"]. The "guardian's" face is blurred.
"The Russians suddenly remembered the child's privacy. In the new video, they carefully blurred the face of the uncle to whom Sofiia is being handed over, as well as those of the other adults. But this was not done to protect the child. It was done to make it difficult to establish who these people are and exactly who the Ukrainian child has been handed over to.
"When they needed to film propaganda, no one cared about the privacy or safety of 10-year-old Sofia. She was simply needed as a tool for propaganda," Oleksandra Dvoretska said.
Background: A Ukrainian girl with a disability who had been abducted by Russian forces from a residential institution in Oleshky was previously reported missing in Russia.

UK makes quiet shift to prepare for supply chain shortages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23

19:48:00 KST

UK quietly warns citizens to stock up on emergency supplies
- The UK government told households to be ready for emergencies and keep three days of supplies, as it warns of weather, cyber and hostile threats.
- The guidance was quietly launched on Oct 22, with Paymaster General James Murray saying households and government both have a role in resilience.
- Ministers want to avoid panic buying, recalling Covid-19 shortages, while also preparing for supply chain disruption and bigger spending choices on defence and infrastructure.
AI generated
LONDON – Britain is trying to get its citizens to prepare for the worst – without descending into a panic.
The British government has quietly published guidance for households to “be ready” in the event of a national emergency.
The advice that they should have enough supplies to be self-sufficient for three days represents a subtle shift towards more urgent messaging amid growing concern about threats ranging from Russian hybrid attacks and AI-driven cyberwarfare to climate change.
The recommendations were slipped onto a government website on Oct 22, along with a written statement to Parliament by Security Minister Dan Jarvis.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting separately said he wanted people to be “alert, but not alarmed” in a 21st-century update to Britain’s wartime slogan: “Keep Calm and Carry On”.
The nature of the roll-out highlights the government’s concern about overdoing the worries, with memories of the empty supermarket shelves of the early days of the Covid-19 pandemic still fresh.
However, the UK faces an expanding list of threats, including droughts and flooding, and the head of MI5 said earlier in October that the security service devotes more resources to countering actions by hostile states, such as Russia and Iran, than during the Cold War.
The preparedness campaign had been planned for earlier in the year by former Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
However, his successor Andy Burnham delayed its launch due to concerns that it could be seen as an overly pessimistic start to his premiership, as reported by Bloomberg in August.
Burnham has spent his first four months in office trying to build optimism across the country. Policy announcements have focused more on feel-good steps such as bus fare caps and greater devolution than on thorny issues such as defence spending and the threats facing the UK.
But the decision to publish guidance on Oct 22, telling households to “take a few simple steps to stay prepared if everyday services are temporarily disrupted”, suggests the government is now seeking to build voter awareness of the difficult decisions facing John Healey in his Budget next week.
“Individual households can play their role in making sure that they’re more resilient, but government has a role in making sure we’ve got the right defences,” Treasury Minister James Murray told Sky on the morning of Oct 23.
“The big focus, rightly for many years and into the future, is on our military capability, our defensive capability.”
The online checklist advised Britons to stock up on three days’ supply of bottled water and non-perishable foods, as well as hand sanitiser, a torch and batteries, and a radio. It also advised them to keep cash at hand, copies of important documents, and blankets and warm clothing.
“The storms last winter and the wildfires this summer have shown how severe weather events can cause disruption to our everyday lives and impact the services we rely on, like phones, power, water and the internet,” Jarvis said in his statement.
They “are a reminder that we can all play our part to keep ourselves, our loved ones, and our communities safe in times of emergency”.
The move comes at a time when ministers are under pressure to take significant steps to modernise infrastructure and prepare for the future.
Hotter summers and plans for data centre construction are increasing demand for water, but the UK has not built a new reservoir since 1992, shortly after the privatisation of the water sector.
Britain has also been warned by its top defence experts that it needs to invest heavily in its military, as it is unprepared to defend itself in the event of a full-scale war.
Healey quit his job as defence secretary under Starmer in a row over military spending, and now as chancellor faces the conundrum of getting defence spending to 3.5% of GDP by 2035.
Jarvis said the move “brings the UK into line with many of our European peers who also have the three-day message at the heart of their campaign”.
No government ministers had been scheduled to speak on the launch of the resilience campaign this week.
Streeting only revealed the launch was imminent when asked by journalists about preparation for resilience when he appeared at the opening of a new weapons factory in the West Midlands on Oct 22.
He said the public needed to be prepared for supply chain disruption caused by “hostile state actors or terrorists”.
UK shoppers rushed to stockpile essentials in March 2020 as the Covid-19 pandemic stoked fears of lockdowns and shortages. Toilet paper, pasta and cleaning products vanished from shelves in many stores, forcing supermarkets to ramp up restocking efforts.
Tesco, Sainsbury’s, Asda and Morrisons joined the BRC that month in urging shoppers to buy only what they needed, warning that panic-buying risked leaving others without essentials.
Speaking in front of the House of Commons Public Accounts Committee last week, Jim Bligh, corporate affairs director of the British Retail Consortium, said he was concerned about being too alarmist.
“Panic-buying is quite easy to generate, particularly if you tell people to buy a particular type of product – they will go out to buy it,” he said.
“If the government were to say to you, ‘Go and buy x liters of water,’ would we run out of water? I do not know.” BLOOMBERG

Digested week: If you were under house arrest, would you be wishing for more books about soil?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:47:30 UTC
19:47:30 KST

Monday
“Who’s Nicole Kidman?” asked my 11-year-old. For God’s sake. “You know Nicole Kidman,” I said. “She’s in ...” I tried to think of a single thing she might have seen her in. “She’s that witch queen with the hair in Aquaman.” Blank stare. “She’s in … she’s an icon, she’s really famous. She used to be married to Tom Cruise.” A pause. “Oh for God’s sake, Tom Cruise, from Top Gun.” “Oh yes.” “She was the villain in Paddington!” Thank God.
Kidman had come to her attention, and that of every other 11-year-old girl in the land, via Adéla, the Slovakian singer whose song, Nicole Kidman, from her debut album, Prima, has caused a minor TikTok sensation and went to No 1 on Spotify earlier this month.
“Do you mean Adele?” I said, when we got to this part of what already seemed like a very long conversation. Excoriating, alright-grandma look. “It’s Adéla. With an ‘a’. She was in Dream Academy, she went out in the first round.” I knew what this meant and got briefly excited. “So she’s a Katseye reject!” More stern looks. “She’s in trouble for mocking Christians.” I gave up at this point.
The Nicole Kidman song, given a discreet nod by Madonna in a TikTok, was inspired by a corset Adéla wore to the Golden Globes and contains the lyrics: “Babygirl in control / I feel like Nicole,” and: “Every single night / I pray that my tits are sittin’ right / Moulin Rouge, my corset is so tight.” Hmm.
Kidman has graciously accepted the compliment and this week, when the song played at a runway show for Victoria’s Secret in LA, the actor, in the front row, laughed and put her head in her hands. I thought the whimsy of the song was quite clever, then made the mistake of watching the video and, after having a full Mary Whitehouse moment, am rehearsing remarks I intend casually to launch over dinner on the relationship between thongs and UTIs.
Tuesday
What do we think of King Charles sending Aung San Suu Kyi, the imprisoned Burmese leader, two books about soil? Suu Kyi, who is 81 and has been under house arrest at an undisclosed compound since her government was ousted by a military coup in Myanmar in 2021, was pictured receiving the books and smiling in a photo apparently staged by her captors.
It’s either a genius move on the part of the king – bringing to the gated leader visions of rolling English countryside and vistas she has, at present, zero chance of enjoying – or else, a little tactless. Soil to Table by gardeners Bridget Elworthy and Henrietta Courtauld, has been described as “a celebration of soil and its connection to the food we eat”. And the second title, Soil: The World at Our Feet, is a catalogue from an exhibition held in London last year.
Gift diplomacy is, of course, always tricky. You may recall the king’s father’s blunt knockback of a gift from a wellwisher during a walkabout with his wife in 2016. Offered a framed picture of Elizabeth II, the then Duke of Edinburgh snapped: “I don’t want that and neither does the queen. She knows what she looks like.” (The Lady Mayor of Windsor briskly stepped forward to accept the gift and smooth things over.)
Wednesday
Larry David’s new essay in Air Mail, the online newsletter, caused enough division this week to provoke coverage in the New York Times. “In our Socialist America,” David went after the Democrat Socialists of America (DSA), aping the style of Jonathan Swift’s A Modest Proposal to write: “Everyone will be so fulfilled spiritually and financially that the police department will be dramatically reduced to where an officer’s only job will be to adjudicate domestic disputes. Toward that end, stands will be set up at local farmers markets, where they will work to resolve marital issues in a folksy, farm-to-table manner. Fresh berries will be provided.”
It’s a weaker effort on David’s part than when he went after Bill Maher in the New York Times last year, savaging him in an essay entitled My Dinner with Adolf for approving remarks made after a meeting with Donald Trump. (“This private Hitler was a completely different animal. And oddly enough, this one seemed more authentic, like this was the real Hitler. The whole thing had my head spinning.”) Predictably, it’s David’s final section on the Middle East that has triggered a lot of take-the-phone-off-gramps fury from gen Z.
“We strongly believe in a two-state solution,” David writes in his mock manifesto. “To this end, we propose that Palestinians should be given all the land currently occupied by Israel and that Israel should be given Pitcairn Island in the South Pacific, where the weather is beautiful and grapefruits are aplenty.” Zohran Mamdani and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez are great advocates for the DSA, but for a fuller picture it’s worth returning to DSA co-chair Megan Romer’s side-splitting efforts to explain her party’s policies to David Remnick, earlier this year. “Yeah. You know, again, I don’t have, like, a solid …”
Thursday
Andrew Scott is everywhere promoting Elsinore, his Oscar-bait movie about the Shakespearean actor Ian Charleson, who died of Aids in 1990, and which I can’t wait to see. (Even though, occasionally, I feel about Scott the way I have come to feel about Nicola Walker – that the acting tics are visible enough to pull me out of the performance.)
Elsewhere in gay content, it’s worth stopping by a much-overlooked and very good show, Fellow Travelers, currently airing on Channel 4, in which Matt Bomer and Jonathan Bailey’s characters fall in love in 1950s Washington, right in the middle of Senator Joe McCarthy’s various purges. Alongside the well-known anti-communist witch-hunt, McCarthy also went after gay and lesbian federal workers in what came to be called the Lavender Scare, ruining lives as he went. Bailey, who looks like a young Gregory Peck and as an actor just gets better and better, is heartbreaking in this show about an underdocumented episode of history. Highly recommended.
Friday
News this week of Andy Burnham’s appearance on Gogglebox raises the happy, theoretical spectre of what previous incumbents at No 10 might have looked like on equivalent shows. Thatcher on The Weakest Link? Churchill on Bake Off? One feels that Blair would have actively enjoyed scaling the bouncy houses on It’s A Knockout. Someone alert the AI!

Taiwan September unemployment falls to lowest level in 26 years

19:46:31 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) –The unemployment rate fell to 3.36% in September, the lowest level for the month in 26 years, the government said Friday.
The 0.05% drop compared to August was the result of recent graduates finding jobs, according to the Directorate General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics. The September work participation rate of 59.59% was the highest in 34 years for September, per Liberty Times.
Women and middle-aged people had also returned to the workplace in higher proportions, the government said. The forecast for October is a continuing decline in the unemployment rate.
In September, 11.64 million people were employed, a decline of 15,000 from August, but an increase of 10,000 compared to September 2025. An estimated 405,000 people were out of work in September, a decline of 6,000 from the previous month, Liberty Times reported.
Looking at age groups, the highest jobless rate was for recent graduates and new jobseekers, registering 11.59% for the group from 15 to 24 years of age. The group from 25 to 29 experienced a jobless rate of 5.69%, while the rate fell to 3.4% for those aged 30 to 34.

Turtle Beach Vulcan II XP Review: Clicky Compromise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:45:00 UTC
19:45:00 KST

Highly customizable, both physically and through software tweaks. Great to type on. Reliably responsive inputs. Excellent macro manager.
TIRED
No Hall effect keys. Inverted media wheel and some non-functioning LEDs. Plastic basin underside feels cheap.
Turtle Beach is no stranger to competitive-grade gaming keyboards. In recent years, it has focused on its mid- to high-tier Vulcan range, with the Vulcan II XP as its newest entry.
It has a lot going for it—Titan HS mechanical switches, easy modification and customization options, and a suite of pro-tier gaming features available through its support software. However, while it arrives as a full-size keyboard (NumPad included!), a series of trade-offs and compromises ultimately make it feel very middle-of-the-pack.
Measuring 462 x 153 x 32 millimeters, it looks undeniably sharp thanks to its low profile and floating-key approach, all sitting atop a premium brushed-aluminum top plate. Unfortunately, the first compromise is the disappointing underside: a cheap-feeling basic plastic shell basin. Thankfully, the legs feel sturdy when popped up, adding around 10 mm in height and a comfortable angle to the board.
I also like the included soft foam wrist rest, which snaps to the front underside and adds nice support when gaming or typing. It's not memory foam, though, so I fear it might lose some of that cushion over time. The Vulcan also has integrated media controls on the top right with back, play/pause, and forward buttons, plus a media wheel with a push-to-mute feature.
It’s a $150 wired-only device (Turtle Beach is launching a wireless version, the Vulcan II XP Air for an extra $50) that connects via a detachable 1.8-meter USB-C to USB-A cord. A physical connection means zero input latency, which competitive gamers will benefit from.
Swarm Mode
The corded approach does make the Vulcan II XP a breeze to set up. Plug it into a Windows PC, and that's it. But you’ll need Turtle Beach’s Swarm II app to get the most out of it, especially given that the default RGB lighting is a blinding rainbow cascade.
Swarm II brings out the best in this keyboard. Visually, it offers 10 built-in customizable light effects—you can adjust brightness, pattern speed, and colors for some templates. They're pretty gimmicky—especially the Snake one—but it makes for a fun showcase. What's cooler is that you can adjust every LED, perfect for the 11th “custom” slot where you can choose colors, speed, and one of six patterns. You can turn the LEDs off entirely, but only through the app.
Beyond the eye candy, Turtle Beach packs in an impressive slate of features. You can remap inputs down to the individual key and store those configurations as one of five onboard profiles—perfect if you want layouts tailored to specific games, or a more work-oriented profile.
Critical to the keyboard’s gaming credentials, it includes a macro manager that lets you create custom inputs and command combos, down to how many milliseconds of input it should take before activating a keypress. It supports dozens of popular games by default, from competitive favorites like Counter-Strike and Overwatch to single-player epics like Skyrim, which have popular modding scenes and can benefit from bespoke controls. It even has presets for office apps and Photoshop, adding to the Vulcan’s overall versatility. You can easily import new layouts, too.
Touch Typing
I’ve been testing the version with linear switches—Turtle Beach also offers a model with tactile switches, both available in black or white. If you’re new to mechanical keyboards, the main difference is that linear keys press all the way down smoothly, while tactile ones have a little “bump” of resistance as the internal switch activates, which you can feel as the keystroke registers. It’s ultimately personal preference.
For the most part, this is a joy to type on, with precise spacing between keys, and the keys themselves having a satisfying “clackiness” when fully pressed. The only small issue is that the factory-lubed linear keys are so smooth and silent until you get that clack as they hit the base, that it’s easy to accidentally long-press a key. Until you’re used to that, it can catch you off-guard—not an issue when typing, where the worst is an errant stretch of letters whennnnnnnn pausing to think mid-sentence, but it tripped me up a couple of times in games until I was used to it.
Unfortunately, unlike Turtle Beach’s earlier Vulcan II TKL Pro, the keys here aren’t Hall effect, but they are hot-swappable—another trade-off, exchanging long-term reliability and accuracy for the ability to replace or upgrade keys easily. The board supports three-pin or five-pin mechanical switch keys and makes swapping them easy. The flat keycaps also pop off without trouble, which makes cleaning simple. Turtle Beach claims the switches last 50 million keystrokes, which should be plenty, but only a third of the TKL Pro's 150 million.
In gaming, the Vulcan II XP offers a 1,000-Hz polling rate for a 1-millisecond response time, which is competition-grade but falls short of the higher-end 8,000-Hz keyboards on the market. Hopping back to Swarm II, you can activate its more advanced features, like Easy-Shift, allowing for key duplication—basically putting commonly used features within easier reach—and ReacTap, assigning two commands to the same key, useful for games that require very swift inputs. (This might be banned in some competitive scenes under automation rules, though.)
These features can be a little fiddly to set up and map, but with a little experimentation, you can build layouts and input fields that work exactly as you want or need. I tailored a bunch of controls for Borderlands 3 and was dropping Psychos like never before. A minor annoyance, though: Reverting a specific input while trying to create a custom setup would sometimes revert the entire profile, which meant I had to redo everything.
Back to the Drawing Board
While the Vulcan II XP offers great performance for the price, I do have concerns about the overall build quality. On the unit I received, the media wheel was inverted by default—turning it counter-clockwise toward the minus symbol turned the volume up. This was even after I updated the board’s firmware through the Swarm II app, and I had to remap the inputs for it to work as intended. It’s good that the Vulcan II XP’s customization is specific and nuanced enough to remap even the dial direction, but I shouldn’t have had to.
I also found that the LEDs below the “0” and “.” keys on the NumPad don’t seem to work properly, glowing a stubborn, glaring white no matter what color or pattern is assigned. I even tried turning off every other key’s light and manually assigning colors to just those—to no avail.
It’s another reason the board feels middle-of-the-road. Like the shiny metallic top plate hiding the cheaper plastic base, the Vulcan II XP dazzles at a glance, but the closer you look, the more flaws and small annoyances are revealed.
For the price, some of those annoyances are forgivable. For anyone who hasn't upgraded to a mechanical keyboard, this is a decent entry without breaking the bank, delivering a lovely typing experience backed up by enough pro-tier gaming features to feel like a real upgrade—but more demanding or professional players will want to aim higher.
Matt Kamen is a freelance journalist specializing in media, video games, and technology coverage. Beyond WIRED, his work can be found in The Guardian, Empire, and elsewhere. ... Read More

19:44:36 KST

MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. The Bank of Russia has decided to keep its key rate at 14%, as current price pressure remains elevated, according to a press release from the regulator.
"On 23 October 2026, the Bank of Russia Board of Directors decided to keep the key rate at 14.00% per annum. The economy as a whole is growing at a moderate pace in 2026 H2. Current price pressures remain elevated. Inflation expectations stay high. According to the Bank of Russia’s estimates, underlying price growth has not yet decreased and remains in the range of 5-6% in annualized terms, primarily due to the impact of a temporary reduction in production capacities in certain sectors. This requires aggregate demand to grow moderately for underlying inflation to resume its decline," the regulator said.
The Bank of Russia notes that it will make further decisions on the key rate depending on the dynamics of inflation and inflation expectations, as well as the analysis of risks posed by domestic and external conditions. According to the Central Bank, the current seasonally adjusted price growth averaged 8.0% in annualized terms compared to 4.8% in 2026 Q2. The similar indicator of core inflation rose to 6.2% from 4.5% in 2026 Q2. Price dynamics were still affected by volatile components, primarily motor fuel. As of 19 October 2026, annual inflation stood at 6.8% and is expected to come in at 7.1-7.6% as of the end of 2026
"High inflation expectations impede a slowdown in inflation. Despite a slight decrease in the expectations of households and businesses in October, they have generally remained near two-year highs in recent months. Expectations of financial market participants and analysts have increased," the regulator added.
The Bank of Russia noted that according to high-frequency data, the economy is growing at a moderate pace in 2026 H2.
"Business sentiment improved somewhat in October compared to low levels of the previous months. Growth in consumer demand is slowing but remains elevated. Investment activity continues to recover compared to the levels of early 2026," the regulator said.

Eritrea detains Yemeni fishermen for forced labour
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:44:23 UTC
19:44:23 KST

Eritrea's Gulag: detention camps and forced labour for Yemeni fishermen
Driven by painful memories of his detention in an Eritrean prison, Yemeni fisherman Tareq al-Nahari instinctively raised his left hand to protect his head from a barrage of bullets fired by an Eritrean naval boat.The gunfire severed his ring and middle fingers, while one bullet pierced his skull.
Yet he survived, thanks to a medical miracle. However, the projectile that struck his temporal lobe erased his past, identity, and even his future, leaving him unable to form new memories, a condition known as anterograde amnesia.
Despite this, al-Nahari, who is in his forties, remains alive among his family, having escaped death. This is a better outcome than that suffered by his peers, including two fellow fishermen who were aboard the same boat and died in the same incident. One of them was his maternal cousin.
Yemeni fishermen face repeated acts of violence and successive crimes at the hands of Eritrean naval personnel, who intercept them and take them to a network of prisons and detention centres resembling Soviet Gulags.
Eritrean detention centres are no different. Abducted Yemenis are forced to perform arduous labour, including cutting roads through mountains, paving them and constructing military and civilian facilities, without pay or even adequate meals.
This is confirmed by the reports received by Majed Abdo, the sheikh of fishermen in Yemen's Hodeidah governorate. He holds his fellow countrymen responsible for what happens because they enter the territorial waters of a neighbouring sovereign state in their boats.
Amjad al-Omaisi, director-general of al-Khawkhah, a district in the Hodeidah governorate that faces Eritrea on Yemen's western coast, rejects this view. Former Eritrean Supreme Court judge Abdullah Khayyar shares al-Omaisi's assessment.
Life in the Gulag
Tens of thousands of people earn their living from fishing in villages and settlements along Yemen's western coast.
Salem Alyan, a member of the Fisheries Cooperative Union, which organises and oversees the sector, estimates that there are 100,000 traditional fishermen supporting around one million people. However, the sea has become an immediate source of danger amid Eritrean attacks, he told our Arabic-language sister publication, Al-Araby Al-Jadeed.
This is borne out by the account of Issam Mohammed al-Nahari, who is accompanying his brother Tareq, now suffering from memory loss, on a medical trip to Sanaa. He is one of over 20 fishermen we interviewed during this investigation.
Issam said that when the boat incident occurred on Sunday, 25 January 2026, 50 fishermen were aboard the wooden vessel with his brother.
They were taken to the port of Massawa in southern Eritrea, despite insisting that they had been attacked in Yemeni territorial waters.
They were imprisoned for periods ranging from two months to one year. Issam said his brother arrived at Hodeidah hospital alongside the bodies of the two fishermen killed in the incident.
Tareq remained in intensive care for two months before being discharged with memory loss. He could no longer recognise any of his family members apart from his four-year-old daughter, Aya.
Issam said similar incidents frequently occurred to his fellow fishermen, who faced crimes, abuses, and enslavement in detention centres in Asmara without those responsible being held accountable.
"We were tortured to coerce us into forced labour and deprived of food, except for one meal of poor-quality lentils," he said.
He recalled another experience in the summer of 2024, when he was arbitrarily detained by the Eritrean navy alongside his father, Mohammed al-Nahari, and others.
"Throughout the month, I was subjected to severe beatings in front of my father. In the end, I gave in and agreed to work breaking stones from a nearby mountain in the city of Assab, in southeastern Eritrea, so they could be transported and used to pave the roads," he said mournfully as he sat beside his brother Tareq.
He said he spent daylight hours working alongside 20 fellow fishermen under close surveillance by Eritrean naval soldiers armed with rifles and batons.
Medical reports obtained by Al-Araby Al-Jadeed indicate that Tareq al-Nahari is suffering from a concussion and has undergone two head surgeries.
His treatment has cost more than seven million Yemeni rials ($12,500), and he can no longer afford further medical expenses.
Some of his fellow fishermen were also detained in 2023 and forced into hard labour, breaking stones and building a school in Assab under the supervision of naval soldiers.
The soldiers repeatedly beat them whenever their performance declined because of the scorching heat.
They were fed only flour bran, normally used as animal feed, in addition to a meal of lentils.
As a result, Yemeni fishermen flee immediately whenever they sense an Eritrean naval boat approaching. This has led to repeated cases of drowning and injuries at sea.
The consequences of division and war
On 18 May 2023, Mwatana for Human Rights, a Yemeni non-governmental organisation, announced that Eritrean naval forces had detained 69 Yemeni fishermen in three incidents between 2019 and 2022. Minors were among those detained and subjected to forced labour.
Meanwhile, fishermen whose testimonies were documented by this investigation, said 184 of their colleagues had been detained between the beginning of 2023 and January 2026. Of these, 95 remain in captivity.
However, sources agree that the actual number is much higher and that no official body has documented the total number of fishermen detained over the past years.
This is due to the political and security crises that have gripped Yemen for more than a decade, with serious consequences for traditional fishing.
While politicians have been preoccupied with the war, attacks by the Eritrean navy have escalated amid the difficult economic conditions facing fishermen and their families.
Fishermen either lose their lives or have their equipment seized by Eritrean naval forces before being taken to detention centres in Marsa Fatima, Assab, Massawa, Dahlak and Tiro, as well as Terma Island in eastern Eritrea.
Accounts also indicate that some detainees are transferred to Lesser Assab and forced to work for Eritrean project contractors.
They work throughout the day and return to detention centres only in the evening. They are not repatriated to Yemen until the project is completed.
Their return takes place in stages, beginning with the injured, the sick, the elderly and younger detainees unable to endure the hardships of the work.
Among them is Abdul Salam Bishara, a fisherman from al-Khawkhah in the southern Hodeidah governorate. He suffered a slipped disc after being forced to break stones on a mountain near Assab in 2017.
He received no medical assistance before being deported to Yemen.
"They left me only because I was no longer able to work," he said.
He added that when Eritrean authorities decide to release detainees, another crime reportedly follows.
Large numbers of released fishermen are crammed into unseaworthy boats and sent towards the Yemeni coast without any consideration for their safety.
Between 50 and 60 fishermen are placed on a boat that would normally accommodate no more than 30 people.
Al-Omaisi, the director-general of the al-Khawkhah district, described this as one of the crimes against humanity committed by the Eritrean armed forces.
Speaking to Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, he said Yemeni human rights organisations should defend the rights of these victims and file lawsuits against the Eritrean regime in international courts.
Violations of international law
Mohammed Amin, a lawyer at the Court of Appeal in Hodeidah, said the arbitrary detention, torture, enforced disappearance and coercion of fishermen into working under threat constituted serious violations of international law.
These acts could amount to enslavement and crimes against humanity when committed on a widespread or systematic basis.
To secure justice for the victims, Amin told Al-Araby Al-Jadeed that each case should be documented separately through the testimonies of survivors and witnesses, medical reports, photographs and documents, while identifying the date and place of detention and the authorities, individuals or officials responsible.
"After gathering the evidence, human rights organisations and victims' lawyers can submit case files to the relevant international bodies or explore the possibility of prosecution before national or international courts with jurisdiction. This would help ensure investigations, accountability, compensation and reparations for the victims," he added.
This view is shared by Colonel Abdul Ghani Abu Halfah, who has been tasked by the Sanaa authorities with following up on the treatment of injured people in government hospitals, both military and civilian.
He cited the case of Tareq al-Nahari, who was transferred to the military hospital in Sanaa. Abu Halfah noted that he is facing extremely difficult financial circumstances after becoming unable to work.
Between August and September, during this two-month-long investigation, 26 fishermen, most of them from al-Khawkhah, managed to return to Yemen. Port Director-General Ghali Qashr, the head of the Red Sea Fisheries Authority, Wael Abdul Wadoud, and al-Khawkhah Director-General Amjad al-Omaisi received them.
During their meeting with the officials, the returning fishermen confirmed that they had been in Yemeni territorial waters aboard two traditional wooden boats known as jalbah vessels when Eritrean naval boats attacked them and took them at gunpoint to Eritrean prisons.
Held in a prison in Assab, they endured torture and starvation before being forced into hard labor.
The Eritrean forces had seized a tonne of fish they had caught before their arrest, in addition to looting their fishing equipment.
They also took one of the boats, removed its engine and replaced it with an old, dilapidated one. Upon their return, the fishermen were forced to sail the vessel back to Hodeidah's shores, said al-Omaisi.
Seizing fishermen's livelihoods
Yemeni fisherman Musad Yusuf Zakhm, from Al-Khawkhah, said he was detained in June 2023 for two months alongside nine other fishermen in a prison in Assab.
During their detention, they were forced to cut and pave a road with stones near the city port after their boats had been intercepted and confiscated. They were also tortured and transferred to Lesser Assab, where they spent about 15 days before being released and deported to the city of Mokha.
He added that he had previously been detained in another incident, when he was abducted to Dahlak Island in mid-2022 and held for two months alongside 15 fishermen.
Their fishing equipment and supplies, including nets, refrigerators, the boat engine and its contents, were confiscated. The value of the seized property amounted to $10,000.
In another case, a fisherman estimated his losses at 18 million rials ($33,000), according to documentation examined by Mwatana for Human Rights.
For fishermen, confiscation means more than simply losing property: their boat represents their livelihoods and the means to provide for their families.
A timid official response
According to an official memorandum (No. 355) sent by Hussein Hamed al-Attas, chairman of the General Authority for Red Sea Fisheries, to Hodeidah Governor Abdullah Abdu Ahmed Ateifi on 21 February 2026, at least 95 Yemeni fishermen remain detained in Eritrean prisons.
Al-Omaisi, the director-general of al-Khawkhah, confirmed that violations against fishermen "take place almost daily, without any genuine official action to compensate the victims or prosecute the Eritrean authorities in international courts".
However, al-Omaisi emphasised that these crimes have no time limit for prosecution.
According to lawyer Amin, since Yemeni fishermen conduct their work under the ruling issued by the International Court of Arbitration in The Hague in 1998-1999, which demarcated the maritime boundary between the two countries, the abductions, torture, and forced labour they face constitute violations requiring accountability.
He explained that "what is happening to these fishermen violates Eritrean law, as they are subjected to abuses, have everything they own confiscated and are forced to work. It also violates international human rights law, which prohibits subjecting anyone to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, and to arbitrary arrest or detention without a legal charge or a fair trial."
If Yemeni fishermen commit an offence, the appropriate measures under Eritrean law would be to confiscate any fish they are carrying and return them to their country, according to former Eritrean Supreme Court Judge Abdullah Khayyar.
He pointed out that Eritrea has no clear laws and that, even where laws exist, they are not enforced.
"Military rule and its consequences dominate the functioning of state institutions. Everything that happens is dealt with [...] through administrative and military procedures that fall outside the law," he told Al-Araby Al-Jadeed.
In light of all this, the internationally recognised Yemeni government has limited its response to calling on Eritrea to release the fishermen held in its custody.
However, these appeals do not always receive a response, according to a source at the Ministry of Agriculture, Irrigation and Fisheries in Aden, who declined to be named because they were not authorised to speak to the media.
The source cited a request made by the government in June 2020 for the release of detained fishermen and confiscated equipment.19 fishermen were released, while another 100 remained in detention.
Their suffering continues, with no solution in sight. Yet, as Issam al-Nahari said, fishermen cannot abandon their only source of livelihood.
"Death while searching for food to feed your children is better than dying of hunger."

Cities end contracts with Go Church following shocking Pano report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:41:48 UTC
19:41:48 KST

Flemish politicians have spoken out and cities have ended their relationship with Go Church following a VRT investigation uncovering exploitation, manipulation and sexual assault of young people involved in the religious organisation
Officials in Leuven, Mechelen, Sint-Niklaas and Turnhout, among other Flemish cities, have ended their rental contracts and other agreements with the religious organisation Go Church following a scathing report by VRT investigative programme Pano in collaboration with daily newspaper De Morgen.
The programme, which can be seen on VRT Max, interviewed more than 30 of the church’s former followers and went undercover to discover that the church recruits mostly vulnerable young people – often minors – and then manipulates them into giving money, working for free and cutting ties with family and friends who might question the church.
Pano began an investigation following an appeal on TikTok by a schoolteacher who teaches religious studies. “I want to warn young people,” she told VRT. “Go Church is destroying children. They pressure them into going to the church, and they manipulate them. This should not be allowed.”
What is Go Church?
Go Church is part of the Lighthouse Group of Churches, an international network with more than 7,600 churches worldwide and millions of online followers. In Belgium, the movement previously operated under the names Pleasant Surprise Church International (PSCI) and Mustard Seed Chapel International (MSCI).
The group is led by Dag Heward-Mills, a Ghanaian bishop who is highly revered within the movement. Followers address him as “Daddy” or “Prophet.” Go Church recruits new members at busy spots, such as train stations, specifically targeting young people.
According to the organisation itself, Go Church is active in Antwerp, Boom, Bruges, Brussels, Duffel, Ghent, Leuven, Mechelen, Sint-Niklaas and Turnhout. Around 450 people attend its services every week.
Go Church recruits young people on the street at busy locations such as train stations. It offers a fun atmosphere and personal attention, which appeals to teenagers and 20-something who are seeking connection.
Church leadership build personal relationships with its young members, visiting their homes and inviting them to theirs. The 20-year-old “Anna” is a typical example of how the church uses its youthful membership. She and other members of the church would go to their pastor’s home on a daily basis to “cook for him, do the grocery shopping and take him to work.”
When I didn’t answer their messages for a few days, they showed up at my door at 23.00
At one point, Anna sought comfort and advice from the pastor, and he sexually assaulted her. “I don’t even know how long it lasted; my head was in shutdown,” she said. It began a months-long experience of sexual abuse. “At one point, it turned into rape. Sometimes he raped me multiple times a week.”
The pastor, who had come from the UK to help grow the church in Belgium, opened bank accounts for a few girls and coerced them to putting all their money in the accounts, with which he paid his own expenses. When he was eventually called back to the UK, their money disappeared with him.
Many young people report similar grooming by church leaders. They are asked to provide their phone numbers and addresses. “When I didn’t answer their messages for a few days, they showed up at my door at 23.00,” one young woman said.
The church also insisted on approving any marriages, and they were encourage to marry only within the church, being told that outsiders would lead them straight to hell. Women were told that they needed to do the cooking and the cleaning and could not refuse their husbands sex.
If members dared to try to speak out, the church convinced other members to harass them on social media. Former church members continue to suffer trauma, and religious experts say that Go Church meets the criteria to be considered a cult.
Lack of judicial follow-up
Belgium has an agency where cult activity can be reported (IACSSO), but, according to federal parliamentarian Stefaan Van Hecke (Groen), the information collected there has not been followed up by State Security for a few years now. “There used to be 15 people in the State Security department who followed up on this,” he said, “but now there is literally no one.”
According to Van Hecke, State Security sees the problem as “from another century”. But that’s not the case, he says. “It’s always been here, but we just don’t have a view on it anymore.” He does recommend reporting any criminal activity to the IACSSO and to the local police.
In the meantime, cities are shutting down all ties with Go Church. “They meet in a city-owned neighbourhood house under the name of an individual,” said Mechelen mayor Bart Somers (Voor Mechelen). “We have ended that contract. There was an immediate response from a lawyer, very aggressive, trying to intimidate us. But we’re having none of that.”

Duchess of Sussex ‘deeply distressed’ over child sexual abuse image claims against father

The Duchess of Sussex has said she is “deeply distressed” over accusations involving child sexual abuse images against her estranged father, Thomas Markle Sr, and revealed she was made aware of “disturbing allegations” against him in 2018 by the Metropolitan police.
Meghan issued a statement after the Sun newspaper published claims that her half-brother Thomas Markle Jr alleged he had found a stash of images belonging to their father at his former home in the Philippines.
In an interview with the Daily Mail, Markle Sr denied possessing child sexual abuse images, calling the accusations “sick lies”.
It is understood that authorities in the UK previously told Meghan that allegations made about her father in a 2018 letter sent to Scotland Yard, and subsequently shared with her by the police, were being investigated.
Meghan was informed by the Met of the allegations in the summer shortly after her wedding, it is believed.
In a statement through her spokesperson, Meghan said: “I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed.
“In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan police and Royalty and Specialist Protection [Rasp]. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.
“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them. I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.
“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.”
Sources said although Meghan was made aware of the allegations in 2018, she had been unable to speak publicly to avoid jeopardising any future investigation and because speaking out could have resulted in legal action against her.
The 2018 letter was understood to have been shared with Meghan by the Rasp unit within the Met police.
It is understood the Met has not previously investigated Markle Sr, nor is it currently doing so. The force said it was making internal inquiries regarding officers from Rasp being involved in the passing on of a letter.
A Met spokesperson said: “We are aware of media reports that officers from the Met’s royalty and specialist protection command were involved in the passing on of a letter in 2018. We are undertaking inquiries internally in an effort to confirm this.”
Markle Sr has been estranged from the duchess since he failed to attend her wedding to Prince Harry on health grounds, and he has never met his grandchildren Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five.
The Sun reported that Markle Jr told detectives in the Philippines he had discovered “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sexual abuse images on computers and mobile phones stored in four large boxes at the home in Cebu where Markle Sr was living until he returned to the US in May after having a stroke.
Markle Jr, 60, said he had also contacted the FBI in the US, the Sun reported.
The FBI said in a statement: “The FBI is aware of the allegations and will provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities. We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of US law.”
The undersecretary for the Philippines’ justice department, Nicholas Ty, told the BBC the matter was being investigated by a human trafficking and child sexual exploitation taskforce in Cebu.
The interior secretary, Jonvic Remulla, separately told the BBC that national police had secured Markle Sr’s computer to conduct a comprehensive digital forensic examination. Remulla said it would take “one week to get the forensic [results]”.
Meghan’s father has denied possessing child sexual abuse images, telling the Daily Mail that the accusations were “sick lies”.
He told the newspaper that the computers had not been in his possession since he left Rosarito, Mexico, with his son in January 2025 and moved to the Philippines “for a fresh start”.
Speaking from a rehabilitation centre in Florida, where he is learning to walk with a prosthetic limb after his left leg was amputated because of a blood clot, he told the Mail: “I’m shocked, I’m hurt and I’m very upset that my son is making these accusations against me. I could never do what I’m being accused of. It’s the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.
“This is bullshit. It’s just a bunch of lies. It’s sick. I have no idea why Tom is trying to destroy me with these lies.”
Meghan’s half-sister Samantha Markle has defended their father, accusing her brother Markle Jr of “making up lies” to make money.
She told the Mail: “There is no merit in these disgusting allegations whatsoever and my brother is disgusting for making them up. He wants to destroy our dad. Shame on him.”
She alleged her brother made the allegations days after their father cut off his funds, “and once the money stopped he made up the most outrageous lies he could to make money from the media”.
She alleged the computers were not in her father’s possession for two years and he could have been set up. “That leaves a lot of room for tampering,” she said.

EU envoy signals progress on visa-free travel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:40:07 UTC
19:40:07 KST

European Union Ambassador to Türkiye Aivo Orav addressed members of the press at the EU Delegation’s headquarters in Ankara. (AA Photo)
European Union Ambassador to Türkiye Aivo Orav said Turkish officials had received instructions at the highest level to resolve outstanding issues related to six criteria required for visa liberalization, expressing cautious optimism about progress on the long-standing issue.
Speaking at a press conference, Orav said visa-related difficulties, including lengthy waiting lists and problems securing appointments, had been raised in almost all his meetings in Türkiye. “These issues need to be addressed systematically,” he said, adding that EU member states were trying to assign more staff to their consular services to ease the pressure on visa applications.
Orav stressed that visa liberalization remained important for both sides and said his recent discussions with Turkish politicians and public administration officials had been encouraging. “In my meetings in Türkiye, they say they have received instructions at the highest level to resolve the problems related to these six criteria,” he said.
The six outstanding criteria concern anti-terrorism legislation, data protection, Europol cooperation, anti-corruption measures, judicial cooperation and the implementation of the EU-Türkiye readmission agreement.
Visa liberalization would allow Turkish citizens to travel to the Schengen area for short stays without obtaining a visa.
Orav also called for a forward-looking approach to EU-Türkiye relations, acknowledging the difficult history between the two sides while emphasizing their mutual interests. “Türkiye needs the EU, and the EU needs Türkiye,” he said, urging diplomats to help political leaders focus on future cooperation.
He said the EU was ready to move forward, pointing to an increase in high-level contacts over the previous six months. In June and July, two EU leaders visited Türkiye within a two-week period, while the bloc’s high representative for foreign affairs and security policy visited twice. Four European Commission members also made visits, he added.
Orav said the frequency of these contacts demonstrated that both sides had the tools and mechanisms needed to advance their relationship.
