Hijab ban in Azerbaijan raise fears over religious freedom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:39:35 UTC
19:39:35 KST

Breadcrumb
'I have a right to study': The Azerbaijani schoolgirls shut out of class over their hijabs
"I want to study. I have my hijab on, but they are not letting me study. I have a right to study," a distressed Azerbaijani schoolgirl was filmed saying in a video posted online, passionately advocating for her right to attend school like other children while wearing an Islamic headscarf.
Across Azerbaijan, pupils and teachers wearing hijabs have reportedly been denied entry to schools since new regulations were implemented earlier this month.
The restrictions have prompted emotional scenes captured in online footage, with schoolgirls seen in tears and students looking on in distress as a visibly veiled teacher was dismissed from school premises.
The decision, approved last month, has sparked outrage both domestically and internationally, with human rights groups such as Amnesty International describing the restrictions as discriminatory.
Speaking to The New Arab, Amnesty International’s Eastern Europe and Central Asia director, Marie Struthers, emphasised that excluding pupils and teachers who wear the hijab from schools "violates their rights to education, and the freedoms of religion and expression."
School exclusions
The restrictions have also sparked protests across Azerbaijan, with local reports documenting demonstrations against the headscarf rules, involving girls wearing Islamic headscarves and boys joining their classmates in solidarity.
On Monday, the Ministry of Internal Affairs said it had detained 37 people for disrupting public order during the protests.
Struthers also called for the release of those detained.
"The international community should call upon Azerbaijani authorities to: reverse these discriminatory restrictions and ensure that affected pupils and teachers can return to school; immediately and unconditionally release anyone detained solely for peacefully exercising their rights; and respect the right to peaceful protest and all human rights," she said.
Struthers cited recent Amnesty reporting on the detention of Shahizyar Huseynova, the wife of Azerbaijani Muslim activist Aga Huseynov.
She was reportedly arrested last Wednesday after protesting outside a school in Baku, where their daughter had been refused entry the previous day.
"According to [Huseynov], she has been detained for four months, and the charges against her have not been provided."
Struthers also cited other reports the organisation received, including one about activist Matanat Turan (Mahmarzayeva), who is affiliated with the Azerbaijan People’s Front Party (APFP).
On Sunday, a court in the Azerbaijani city of Sumgayit reportedly imposed a two-month preventive measure on Turan after she protested against the headscarf restrictions in Khirdalan.
She added: "Ilkin Huseynov, an activist who had launched a free online platform connecting volunteer teachers with children excluded from school, including for wearing hijabs, went missing on 14 October after leaving his Baku home accompanied by unidentified people."
Growing protests amid a regional fallout
Smuthers’ urgent calls reflect concerns voiced across the country, as the controversial ban has escalated into a regional dispute, with ally Turkey declaring its firm opposition to Baku’s decision.
Oktay Saral, an adviser to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, criticised the restrictions on hijabs in Azerbaijani schools, prompting President Ilham Aliyev’s ruling party to accuse Turkish figures of interfering in Azerbaijan’s domestic affairs.
Ankara’s condemnation of the hijab ban has prompted a fierce backlash from the Azerbaijani government, which has barred 31 Turkish nationals from entering the country, including Fatih Erbakan, leader of Turkey’s New Welfare Party.
Caught in the middle of the public feud, however, are Azerbaijan’s women and girls, whose lives are being affected by the new school regulations in a country where 96 per cent of the population identifies as Muslim.
Rafig Shahbazov, a Georgia-based journalist covering developments in Azerbaijan, told TNA that there was currently “no publicly available comprehensive official figure showing how many students or teachers have been affected nationwide” by the restrictions.
He said there was also no comprehensive information on how many schools had implemented the rules, how many pupils had missed classes or whether the restrictions were being enforced consistently across the country.
However, Shahbazov stressed that continuing reports of hijab-wearing pupils and teachers being turned away from schools suggested that "the issue has not been confined to one school or a single district."
"The first protest videos I encountered came from Jalilabad, after which reports and footage emerged from Baku and surrounding villages, as well as Sumqayit and other locations," Shahbazov added.
"Baku’s School No. 69 and the school in Mollaoba village in Masalli district are among the locations mentioned in reporting and discussions surrounding the restrictions."
Shahbazov also noted that, based on publicly available evidence, students, teachers, and parents responded in various ways, including expressing solidarity with girls and women who wear the hijab.
"Some students have continued to attend school wearing hijabs despite the restrictions, while others have reportedly been prevented from entering classrooms," Shahbazov told The New Arab.
In some locations, male classmates have reportedly refused to attend lessons in solidarity with girls who were denied access.
Protesters have used slogans such as ‘Freedom for the hijab’ and ‘Let the girls go to school’, framing the issue as one of access to education as well as religious freedom.
"Parents have also challenged the restrictions. Some have protested outside schools after their daughters were reportedly refused entry," Shahbazov added.
"For many families, the central concern is not simply whether a particular item of clothing is permitted, but whether girls should have to choose between practising their faith and continuing their education. Teachers have expressed concern about the impact on their professional lives and personal religious choices."
Protests involving schoolchildren are unusual in Azerbaijan. The demonstrations have also prompted a social media campaign, with protest footage spreading online.
However, local users have since reported disruptions to access to Instagram and TikTok in the country, raising questions about the authorities’ response to the growing controversy.
Internet monitoring groups have also documented restrictions on access to the platforms, but Azerbaijani authorities have not explained the reported disruptions.
Legal questions
The growing controversy follows a series of legal changes, beginning with amendments to Azerbaijan’s general education law that reaffirmed the principle of secular education and required pupils and teachers to comply with school dress codes.
Subsequent regulations prohibited additional clothing deemed to disrupt the standard uniform or conflict with secular education.
Although the school rules do not explicitly mention the hijab, they have since been interpreted in ways that restrict the wearing of Islamic headscarves.
Emin Abbasov, an Azerbaijani human rights lawyer and chair of the Independent Lawyers Network (ILN), told The New Arab that the secularism requirement introduced under the new regulations "amounts to a ban on expressing religious belief through clothing in state schools."
He added: "Wearing religious clothing is a protected manifestation of belief which is a core part of freedom of religion both in national and international law. Restrictions must therefore have a sufficiently clear legal basis, pursue a legitimate aim and be necessary and proportionate. A general reference to secularism does not, by itself, establish that excluding pupils or teachers wearing a hijab meets these requirements."
Abbasov continued: "The vague requirement to dress ‘in accordance with secularism’ also raises questions about foreseeability and the scope for arbitrary enforcement and its impacts."
The ILN chief also cited reports by his organisation, which found that pupils and teachers wearing hijabs were reportedly denied entry to schools across Azerbaijan since October 12, sparking warnings that such restrictions raise serious concerns about freedom of religion, equality and access to education.
"The justifications appeared in state officials and pro-governmental media refer to social equality, secular education and protecting girls from religious coercion require careful scrutiny," Abbasov told The New Arab.
"However, protecting children from coercion is a legitimate concern, as is ensuring neutrality and secularity in education, but the authorities failed to demonstrate the problem of coercion and alternative — less intrusive measures such as education at schools on secularism, increased civil society role in promoting secularity, etc."
He added: "Excluding a girl from school because of her clothing risks punishing the very child the state claims to protect. It can interrupt her education, deepen isolation and undermine her future independence."
Abbasov argued that an outright ban "is a clear intervention in the right to believe of citizens," adding that it also infringes on the right to education and, for teachers, constitutes “a breach of employment rights."
The head of the ILN cited constitutional protections and international law safeguarding freedom of belief and the right to education.
He added that Azerbaijan’s government must, under both international law and the country’s constitution, adhere to key legal principles, including necessity and proportionality.
Rights at risk
In response to the backlash, Azerbaijani authorities have blamed Iranian influence for stirring division in the country — in addition to alleged Turkish influence.
More ethnic Azerbaijanis live in Iran than in Azerbaijan itself.
Azerbaijan’s State Service for Special Communications and Information Security alleged that a "foreign hacker group" had attacked more than 100 state websites on the night of 13 October.
Abbasov criticised the government’s "divisive narratives," describing the accusations of foreign influence involving Iran, Turkey and people of Arab backgrounds as "absolutely unacceptable and very harmful."
He warned that such rhetoric risked deepening isolation and perpetuating harm against the women and girls affected by the ban.
"From what we see from the protests, mostly by the secular parts of Azerbaijan, supporting religious people or the young girls and women wearing hijabs, it shows that society is not convinced that it faces any religious fundamentalism or any harm," Abbasov told The New Arab.
"The Azerbaijani government now wants to divide society between secular and religious people. And it needs somehow a foreign influence, a foreign enemy and new threats in society in order to govern or to continue governing Azeris with coercive and repressive methods that society does not want to continue."
He continued: "There are no threats; there is no reason to take any measure for protecting secularity in Azerbaijan."
The New Arab contacted Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Science and Education for comment but had not received a response by the time of publication.
However, Azerbaijani officials have continued to defend the ban in public statements.
MP Nigar Arpadarai alleged that children did not choose to wear the hijab themselves but were influenced by their families.
"A child has no freedom to choose a religion. This is a conscious prerogative of adults," she told the 1news.az website.
After decades of Soviet rule, Azerbaijan emerged as one of the most secular states in the Muslim world.
Under President Ilham Aliyev, the country has maintained a poor human rights record, with the government repeatedly targeting journalists, activists and independent politicians.
Human rights organisations have long accused Aliyev’s administration of intensifying its crackdown on freedom of speech.
Assiah Hamed is a staff writer at The New Arab

Kazakhstan approves 2026-29 plan to develop unmanned systems
Kazakhstan has approved a comprehensive plan to develop unmanned systems between 2026 and 2029, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports.
The relevant government resolution was signed by Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov on October 13, 2026.
The plan aims to establish the legal framework, infrastructure and incentives needed to advance unmanned technologies across Kazakhstan, improve economic efficiency and strengthen the country’s export potential.
Under the plan, Kazakhstan intends to launch a unified digital platform for unmanned systems and introduce an Unmanned Aircraft System Traffic Management (UTM) system. It also provides for the establishment of at least two research and development (R&D) centers.
Workforce development is another key priority. The plan calls for training at least 1,000 specialists, including drone operators, design engineers, embedded software developers, UTM specialists, cybersecurity professionals and maintenance technicians.
Kazakhstan also plans to expand domestic production capabilities by developing the assembly, testing and servicing of unmanned systems. Additional measures will focus on manufacturing critical components, secure software and artificial intelligence models locally.
Unmanned technologies are expected to be introduced across agriculture, transportation and logistics, public services and industry.
The plan also seeks to establish a sustainable domestic market involving government agencies, businesses, universities, national companies and the Astana Hub autonomous cluster fund.
Implementation will be overseen by the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development. The responsible authorities will be required to report regularly on the progress of planned activities and the achievement of established targets.

Across China: Herder photographers document snow leopards and beyond in China's "water tower"
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:36:38 CST
19:36:38 KST

XINING, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- On a craggy rock in a grand canyon in northwest China's Qinghai Province, Sangdrup raises his camera, scanning the rugged cliffs for a glimpse of wildlife.
From the forests flanking the gorge, white-lipped deer, blue-eared pheasants and blue sheep emerge from time to time, becoming the subjects of Sangdrup's lens. The autumn air carries the scent of grass and trees, while the Lancang River rushes below.
The 32-year-old Tibetan is among a cohort of herders who have taken up cameras at the Sanjiangyuan National Park, serving as wildlife photographers, grassroots guardians and caretakers for injured animals.
Established five years ago as part of China's first batch of national parks, Sanjiangyuan is the largest and highest. Covering 190,700 square km in the heart of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, it guards the headwaters of the Yangtze, Yellow and Lancang rivers at an average elevation exceeding 4,700 meters.
On his daily patrols, Sangdrup has made a habit of photographing wild flowers and animals, both as a record of his rounds and as a precious gift for future generations.
What he wants to capture most is the snow leopard, dubbed "the king of snow mountains."
Born and raised on the grasslands, Sangdrup first heard about snow leopards from his family as a child.
"All I knew was that they were beautiful and mysterious, like a big cat, but none of my pals around had ever seen one," he recalled.
His first encounter came in 2018, when he was on patrol at dawn and a grayish-white animal darted across the slope in front of him. In that instant, Sangdrup realized it was a snow leopard. He froze, then fumbled for his phone and pressed the shutter.
"I felt nothing but sheer awe," he later recalled. "I was so thrilled that I forgot there could be danger."
Looking at the blurry figure on the small screen, Sangdrup felt both excitement and regret: the phone's low resolution had spoiled a rare close-range opportunity.
Soon after, he spent a substantial sum on his first professional camera. At first, he knew little about technique -- aperture, ISO, shutter speed -- and could only fumble his way through, as few people around him knew photography then.
"I was afraid of breaking the camera by messing with the settings, so I basically stuck to auto mode," he said. "But I just loved taking pictures."
On every patrol, he would head out with his camera and keep shooting until the battery died before going home.
With constant trial and error, his photos kept improving. White-lipped deer, leopards, vultures, golden eagles, and blue sheep began appearing frequently in his photographs, but snow leopards remained his main subject.
To capture better images, Sangdrup has come to know the snow leopard's habits well. "Blue sheep are their main prey. Where you see a large herd, a snow leopard won't be far away," he said, adding that the best months are January through May.
In Sanjiangyuan National Park, 20,800 herders have been hired as rangers. Together with professional rescue teams, they have found and helped rescue many wild animals in need, including two snow leopard cubs that were not suitable for release and have now become public favorites at the Xining Wildlife Zoo in Xining, the provincial capital, drawing tens of millions of views online.
The snow leopard is under first-class national protection in China and is listed as vulnerable by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.
China is home to about 60 percent of the world's snow leopard habitats. The Sanjiangyuan area is one of the areas with the highest snow leopard density in the country and the world.
According to survey results released in early 2025, the average snow leopard population density in the Sanjiangyuan area is about 0.9 individuals per 100 square km, with an estimated total population of around 1,002.
The herder photographers' images are no longer private keepsakes. In 2023, a documentary film "Snow Leopards and Friends," partly filmed by three local herders, won the Best Documentary award at the 36th China Golden Rooster Awards, one of the country's top film awards.
For 35 days, the team camped near a den, capturing rare close-up footage of a mother snow leopard nursing her cubs without disturbing them.
"We wanted the world to see the snow leopard in its most natural state," said Konchok Choephel, one of the filmmakers.
In 2021, China established its first national parks: the Sanjiangyuan National Park, the Giant Panda National Park, the Northeast China Tiger and Leopard National Park, the Hainan Tropical Rainforest National Park and the Wuyishan National Park.
The five national parks cover a total area of 230,000 square km and incorporate more than 120 nature reserves of various types and levels.
By implementing a series of measures such as habitat restoration, ecological corridor connectivity, and regulation of human activities, the five national parks have delivered notable ecological successes over the past five years.
For example, as "the water tower of China," Sanjiangyuan National Park has significantly enhanced its water conservation capacity, channeling an average of 80 billion cubic meters of high-quality water downstream annually. Degraded grasslands have turned green, rivers run clearer, and populations of Tibetan antelopes, also under China's first-class national protection, have rebounded from less than 20,000 to over 70,000.
As China marks the fifth anniversary of the national parks, a photography exhibition was held in Qinghai earlier this month, showcasing 100 images by ecological photographers and rangers. The photos depicted snow-capped peaks, rare wildlife and the harmonious coexistence of herders and nature in the province.
"We hope these images help more people understand the achievements of national park construction and encourage wider participation in protecting our shared home," said an official from the provincial forestry and grassland bureau. ■

7.0-magnitude Xizang quake an extensional fracture: expert
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:36:24 CST
19:36:24 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- The 7.0-magnitude earthquake that struck Baqen County of the city of Nagqu in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region on Thursday was an extensional rupture, according to experts with the China Earthquake Networks Center (CENC).
The quake occurred at around 10:33 p.m., causing heavy casualties. Focal mechanism solutions show the event was basically consistent with regional tectonic characteristics.
"An extensional fracture, in simple terms, occurs when the crust is stretched horizontally and, under tension and gravity, faultage slides downward along existing faultage, forming fractures and rupture surfaces," said Han Yanyan, a senior engineer with the earthquake prediction department of the CENC.
The CENC explained that the collision between the Indian and Eurasian plates had caused the uplift of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, crustal shortening and thickening, and widespread plateau deformation. These processes are the main dynamic mechanism controlling tectonic deformation in the western part of the Chinese mainland.
The interior of the plateau is subjected to both north-south compression and east-west extension, and two typical fault systems, trending roughly north-south and east-west, have developed there.
"The epicenter is located within the Changtang block of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, about 2 km from the nearest fault, the Baqen-Riwoqe fault," Han said.
Under such intense crustal deformation, the Changtang block and its surrounding fault zones are particularly active. Since 1900, the block has experienced six earthquakes of magnitude 7 or above, including this one. The largest was a 7.5-magnitude earthquake in Shuanghu on Nov. 8, 1997.
"Therefore, this earthquake was an energy release of the Changtang block," Han said. ■

Thailand to mandate safety standards for EV batteries

Unknown Publisher

18:36:22 CST

BANGKOK, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Thailand plans to impose mandatory safety standards on electric vehicle (EV) batteries covering their manufacture, import and sale, the government said on Friday, as the country seeks to build confidence in its growing EV industry.
The standard applies to non-lead-acid rechargeable batteries in battery-electric passenger and goods vehicles with at least four wheels. It requires protection against overcharging, overheating, and short circuits, said deputy government spokesperson Lalida Periswiwatana.
Under a draft ministerial regulation, manufacturers and importers would need licenses under Thailand's Industrial Product Standards Act, while retailers would only sell products that are licensed and meet the standard.
The rules would take effect 180 days after publication in the official Royal Gazette. Businesses are advised to follow the progress of the regulation and prepare for product standards, testing, and licensing requirements, Lalida said in a statement.
Beyond pre-market safety controls, the Ministry of Industry has also been asked to study how to track batteries after their service life ends. Lalida said the work remains at the consideration stage and is not yet a take-back or mandatory recycling scheme.
The government wants Thailand's EV industry to grow with quality, not just by increasing production capacity or sales, she said, adding that this approach would build consumer confidence, strengthen the competitiveness of the Southeast Asian country's EV industry, and drive the economy alongside sustainable environmental care. ■

He also drew attention to the priorities of the Russian side: first of all, the return to Russia of diplomatic property in that country illegally confiscated under previous US administrations, as well as the resumption of direct air traffic between the two countries. At the same time, according to him, there is not yet sufficient political will on the part of American colleagues, who often try to link these matters with far-fetched regional and international issues.
"As for future rounds [of talks concerning irritants], we assume that before the end of the year, probably another such round could take place. Its specific dates will be agreed upon through channels," he said.

The Secretary of State for Defence has declined to discuss reported ballistic shelters at Faslane in open session, telling the Defence Committee there is a difference between what others report and what the department is willing to say.
Wes Streeting was giving evidence to the committee on the work of his department.
Michelle Scrogham, the Labour member for Barrow and Furness, raised air and missile defence, noting the committee had heard that covering what is needed would cost a billion pounds per city. She said: “I am interested to hear it reported that Faslane is getting ballistic shelters. Are you looking at rolling that out in other areas?”
Streeting said: “There is a danger of my being dragged into a level of operational security detail that I would not want to share in this format.”
Scrogham replied: “It is public knowledge. It is in the UK Defence Journal.”
Streeting said: “There is a difference between what others report and what we are willing to say. Given the spirit in which we engage with this Committee, first, I would always be happy to try to share with the Committee in a closed format as much as we can of that which we would not want to share in an open session. Given your constituency interest in this, I can reassure you that the security of our nuclear deterrent and the enterprise that underpins it is obviously of the highest importance to us. I would be very happy to make sure that we properly brief you as the Member of Parliament for Barrow.”
Faslane on the Clyde is the base for the Vanguard class ballistic missile submarines that carry the continuous at-sea deterrent, and for the Astute class attack submarines. Coulport, a few miles away, stores and loads the warheads. Barrow-in-Furness, which Scrogham represents, is where the submarines are built by BAE Systems.
Earlier in the same exchange Streeting addressed homeland air defence more generally, saying the government is putting £790 million into integrated air and missile defence to modernise older systems and that a layered approach is needed. He noted that Luke Pollard had described the idea of an iron dome for Britain as an iron sieve.
Ministers confirmed in Parliament this month that a future requirement for hardened aircraft shelters across Royal Air Force bases in the United Kingdom has been identified, and that hardened shelters may form part of future infrastructure considerations at RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus.
The Defence Committee reported this week that Russian submarine and sabotage forces in the High North pose direct risks to the North Atlantic and to Britain, including to the nuclear deterrent, and that failure to deter Russia from underwater threats puts subsea data cables and energy pipelines in British waters at particular risk.

China Cannot Remain the World’s Factory. What Comes Next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

For four decades, China’s rise was built on an extraordinary bargain with the world. China offered labor, scale and, eventually, an industrial ecosystem of unparalleled depth. The world supplied technology, capital and markets. China became richer. The rest of the world got cheaper and increasingly better goods. By the middle of this century, that bargain will have to change. Not because China’s manufacturing model has failed, but because it has become too successful.
Over the past few years, the United States has imposed tariffs and export controls. Multinational companies have adopted “China plus one” strategies. Supply chain resilience has become a boardroom obsession. Yet China’s exports have continued to grow, helping to cushion its weakening domestic economy. Its goods trade surplus reached a record $1.2 trillion in 2025. But it would be a mistake to assume that this can carry on indefinitely. Increasingly, what is economically efficient is no longer politically tenable.
China’s manufacturing dominance is generating resistance. And not only in America. Europe worries about the erosion of its industrial base. Developing countries welcome Chinese investment and admire aspects of China’s development experience, but still ask a reasonable question: where, in this model, is our development?
Most countries do not simply want to buy Chinese electric vehicles, batteries, solar panels, machinery and robots. They want factories of their own. They want their workers to acquire new skills and their suppliers to move up the value chain. They want technology and know-how. For years, Western companies complained that access to China’s enormous market came with demands for technology transfers. Now, China finds itself on the other side of the table, being asked to share its own expertise.
China cannot indefinitely remain the world’s manufacturer indefinitely. Its great economic challenge over the next few decades will be to remain deeply embedded in a global economy increasingly shaped by protectionism and national security. The answer may lie in a new role: a shift from being the factory of the world to an exporter of industrial and technological capabilities.
The new China model
China’s real advantage lies no longer in cheap labor or subsidies, but in the accumulated learning embedded in perhaps the densest industrial ecosystem the world has ever seen. What China can now export is not just what it makes, but what it has learnt about how to make it.
The industrial ecosystem that China built around smartphones accumulated expertise in batteries, sensors, precision manufacturing and power electronics. Those capabilities then migrated into electric vehicles. EVs, in turn, spurred further advances in batteries, chips and automation. Automation fed into robotics. Knowledge compounds as it moves between industries, suppliers, engineers and firms. Each industry creates capabilities that make the next one easier to build. This is China’s innovation flywheel.
The important question now is whether that learning can travel. Neither Brazil nor Indonesia can recreate Shenzhen by decree. But they need not retrace the 30 years China spent building it. They can build on what China has already learnt. Chinese companies can bring machinery, engineers, production processes and supply-chain expertise with them. Local workers learn; local suppliers improve.
Knowledge that took decades to accumulate in China can thus accelerate development elsewhere. That would be a very different model of Chinese globalization: not simply exporting the products of China’s industrial ecosystem, but giving other countries access to the knowledge embedded within it.
Such a shift is already under way. In Brazil, BYD is moving from importing cars to manufacturing them locally and developing local suppliers. In Hungary, it is pairing its first European passenger-car factory with a research and development center that will work with Hungarian universities and companies.
In Indonesia, Chinese investment is helping to build an integrated battery industry stretching from nickel processing to battery production and recycling. These early examples point to a different relationship with the world: one based less on exporting what China makes than on exporting the capability to make it.
At first glance, this may sound like a loss for China. Why give up production at home? Why train tomorrow’s competitors? Because the alternative may be worse. Countries increasingly want options. They do not want their economic future to depend overwhelmingly on any single supplier, Chinese or American.
The greater the dependence, the greater the political pressure to unwind it. A similar logic applies to artificial intelligence. The competition between the United States and China over AI is usually described as a race: who has the most powerful chips, the most computing power and the best frontier models? But another contest may matter just as much: whose AI is used most widely?
America retains formidable advantages at the technological frontier. China’s constraints have pushed its ecosystem in a somewhat different direction: toward efficiency, lower-cost deployment, open models and rapid downstream application. Chinese developers have strong incentives to spread their models widely, allow others to adapt them and capture value from the ecosystem that grows around them. The world’s most downloaded family of open AI models is Chinese: Alibaba’s Qwen.
From China, with love
Technologies that transform economies are not always the most advanced ones. Adoption and the intensity of use matter as much as proximity to the technological frontier. For much of the world, the AI that would matter most may not be the most intelligent model ever built. It may instead be one model that is cheap enough, open enough and adaptable enough to be used everywhere.
Openness is not simply an act of generosity. It can also be an economic strategy. Open systems surrender some rents at the core while creating larger markets for applications, integration and services. If China cannot monopolize the technological frontier, it can compete by making technology cheaper, more adaptable and more ubiquitous.
China itself offers the greatest modern demonstration of what technological diffusion can accomplish. After it began reforming and opening up its economy in the 1980s, foreign companies brought capital, manufacturing methods, management expertise and technology. Chinese workers and engineers learnt from them. Domestic suppliers emerged. Chinese companies adapted foreign technologies and eventually became innovators in their own right. themselves.
China has now reached the other side of that development process. By 2050, the most important measure of China’s economic success will not be how much it sells to the rest of the world, or how much of the world’s manufacturing remains within Chinese supply chains or whether a Chinese model tops every AI benchmark. It will likely be whether China’s success can help generate success for other countries.
Speaking in Shanghai in July, Xi Jinping argued that AI technologies should be “shared” so that countries could benefit from them more equitably. He also called for greater efforts to build AI capabilities in the Global South. The instinct is the right one. Dominance breeds resistance. Diffusion gives a reason for others to remain connected. For four decades, China benefited enormously from a world willing to share capital, technology, knowledge and markets.
The question for the next few decades is whether China can do the same for others.

TDM Neo Hybrid Headphones Review: Two-in-One Woes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Unveiled at CES 2026, the TDM Neo is a pair of on-ear headphones that transform into a Bluetooth speaker. It caught the imagination of the attending media, won a handful of awards, and inspired countless column inches.
Given the current state of the portable audio industry, it's easy to understand why. Most designs seem to revolve around incremental updates and new colorways rather than genuine technical innovation. Neo is an exciting alternative, and it’s little wonder the startup brand went on to smash its Kickstarter targets.
I’ve spent the past couple of weeks listening to the headphones and Bluetooth speaker, and have lost count of the number of times I’ve showed off the clever twist-and-fold mechanism to friends. But has TDM managed to produce a genuine tech twofer, or designed a novelty product that gives you the worst of both worlds?
Twist and Shout
The twist-and-fold mechanism on the Neo is clever and addictive. Rotate the ear cups around the cushioned but flexible headband, bring them together, and strong magnets snap everything firmly in place. Once connected, the headphone drivers disable, and the outward-facing Bluetooth speakers kick in. Twist them apart and you've got your headphones back.
It’s innovative, and the engineering is impressive. Once in speaker mode, the two rubber TDM logos sit closely together and form a protective base, while the asymmetrical twisted headband cocoons the ear cups together. It works well—it never once popped open accidentally. The action is smooth, the connection reassuringly solid, and switching between modes works exactly as intended.
The Neo has four 40-mm drivers—two for the headphones and two for the speakers. The outward-facing speakers are each rated at 5 watts (for a total of 10). Ten watts is not a lot for a modern Bluetooth speaker, but wattage doesn't automatically tell you how loud or good a speaker will sound, especially in the current age of digital signal processing. The highly regarded $55 JBL Go 5 has just 4.5 watts of output, for instance.

Loader Monteith expands red-brick bungalow within "remarkably compact footprint" near Manchester

Loader Monteith expands red-brick bungalow within “remarkably compact footprint” near Manchester
Scottish architecture studio Loader Monteith has transformed a two-bed, red-brick bungalow into a four-bedroom family home in Prestwich, UK.
Described by the studio as “squeezing a quart into a pint pot”, the project involved expanding and reorganising the 69-square-metre home in the town near Manchester to accommodate a growing family and improve connections to a rear garden.
Loader Monteith designed a rear brick extension that opens up the home’s living spaces to the garden, while a new upper floor has been nestled beneath a dormer roof.
“The challenge was to maximise the space without compromising on architectural ambition,” studio co-founder Matt Loader told Dezeen.
“We developed the design in response to the existing house and its local context, creating appropriately scaled additions that respect the surrounding architecture,” Loader added.
“This delivers four bedrooms and two bathrooms within a remarkably compact footprint.”
The extension was designed by Loader Monteith for clients Matt and Angie Maurer, who took on much of the project’s construction themselves.
“Taking on so much of the work ourselves meant we also had to find the right contractors and suppliers who understood our vision and cared about the details in the same way we did,” Matt Maurer told Dezeen.
“Both clients were keen to embrace an ambitious architectural solution,” Loader added.
The home’s front elevation is marked by a green-toned, copper entryway that contrasts with its red-brick walls and clay roof tiles.
This is complemented by the angular red-brick extension at the home’s rear, which is also framed by copper detailing and topped with a sedum roof.
“We began by analysing the local architecture of Prestwich, where red brick predominates,” Loader said.
“We used brick for the new extensions, incorporating decorative corbelling and folded details inspired by local architectural patterns.”
At the front of the home, the living spaces have been relocated to accommodate two street-facing bedrooms, including one ensuite, along with a study, utility room and toilet.
Behind this, the kitchen, living and dining spaces are organised as a trio of interconnected spaces within the rear extension.
Steps between the spaces lead down to the sunken dining and living area, which sit level with the garden and open onto it through sliding doors.
“The challenge was fitting so much accommodation into such a small house while making it feel generous and improving its connection to the garden,” Loader said.
At the centre of the plan, a skylit staircase leads up to the newly-added first floor, where the primary ensuite bedroom and an additional bedroom and bathroom are located.
A pared-back material palette is used throughout the home, including concrete floors and white walls set off by exposed timber joinery.
Other UK home extensions recently featured on Dezeen include the expansion of a Grade II-listed rectory in the Cotswolds by Prest Vale Architects and the renovation of a terraced home in London by Polysmiths using “light as the primary material”.

Ukraine&apos;s economy is approaching a critical threshold: experts warn that reducing employee deferments will intensify the decline
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:29:34 EEST
19:29:34 KST

Ukraine's economy is approaching a critical threshold: experts warn that reducing employee deferments will intensify the decline
Kyiv • UNN
Tightening restrictions on employee deferments threatens production, employment, and business. Advanter Group forecasts a 0.5% decline in GDP in 2026.
The Ukrainian economy risks facing a new wave of production cuts, job losses and declining business activity if restrictions on reserving employees of strategically important enterprises are tightened. According to modeling by Advanter Group, Ukraine's GDP could contract by 0.5% by the end of 2026, while business losses from Russian shelling have already exceeded $10 billion. Against this backdrop, additional staffing restrictions could deepen the economic crisis, UNN writes.
The snowball effect: how cuts to employee reservations threaten the economy
The discussion surrounding the government’s proposed changes to the rules for reserving conscripts has gone far beyond the staffing policies of individual enterprises. Amid the war, constant Russian shelling, a labor shortage and limited access to financing, additional restrictions could affect the economic resilience of the state as a whole.
As UNN was told by Andriy Dlihach, founder of the Advanter Group of companies and the Board community, and co-founder of the Center for Economic Recovery, modeling conducted by analysts indicates that Ukraine’s economy is approaching a critical threshold. According to him, negative trends are already being observed in a number of key sectors, while additional restrictions on businesses could accelerate the economic downturn.
Our modeling shows that Ukraine’s economy is already approaching a critical threshold. According to our estimates, GDP could contract by 0.5% by the end of this year. Business losses from Russian shelling have already exceeded $10 billion
The destruction of production facilities, damage to energy infrastructure and disruptions to logistics are already creating significant financial burdens for businesses. An additional shortage of skilled workers could make restoring damaged enterprises economically impossible.
According to Advanter Group estimates, under current conditions only about 60% of enterprises will be able to recover after Russian strikes. The rest risk facing prolonged downtime or being unable to fully resume operations.
All of this could trigger a snowball effect: worsening business conditions will lead to staff reductions, declining business activity and a further slowdown in the economy
The loss of workers limits enterprises’ production capabilities, leading to reductions in the volume of goods and services. Lower production, in turn, means lower business revenues, resulting in reduced tax receipts and weakened domestic demand.
Such a scenario is particularly dangerous for the economy during wartime, when the state is simultaneously seeking ways to increase defense funding, support critical infrastructure and preserve its own production capacity.
Representatives of 16 analytical centers have already appealed to the President of Ukraine, the Prime Minister, relevant ministries and other government bodies, calling on them to review the government’s proposed changes to the procedure for reserving conscripts.
Which sectors could suffer the most
According to Andriy Dlihach, the labor shortage is already having a negative impact on construction and logistics. At the same time, retail trade, the manufacturing sector and industry have suffered significant losses in recent months.
As for modeling the impact of the proposed changes on various sectors of the economy, construction and logistics are already suffering the most. The defense-industrial complex and the energy sector could also potentially come under additional pressure
For the construction sector, a shortage of workers could mean slower restoration of damaged housing, industrial facilities and infrastructure. For logistics, it could mean more difficult transportation, longer delivery times and additional costs for enterprises that depend on the stable operation of transport companies.
The situation in industry is no less sensitive, as training qualified workers there often requires considerable time. Losing even part of a workforce with specialized expertise could lead to the suspension of individual production processes.
A separate threat is posed by possible restrictions on enterprises in the defense-industrial complex and the energy sector. Their work directly affects the state's defense capability, the stability of energy supplies, and the functioning of other sectors of the economy.
At the same time, negative consequences may also spread to related industries that provide strategic enterprises with components, materials, transportation, repair, and other services. Even if such companies do not directly produce weapons or electricity, their work may be critically necessary for the continuity of the relevant production processes. In addition, they often also carry out government orders.
Moreover, businesses operating abroad that are strategic for the state bring foreign currency into the budget. For example, airlines that, because of the full-scale war, were forced to relocate their operations abroad in order to preserve their fleets and personnel return foreign-currency revenue to Ukraine, which is an additional source of budget income.
According to the Ukrainian Air Transport Association, in 2022–2025, Ukrainian aviation enterprises paid almost UAH 27 billion in taxes and fees. The companies continue to carry out international transportation and specialized aviation operations abroad, ensuring the export of services and foreign-currency revenues for the budget.
Andrii Dlihach reported that Advanter Group was directly involved in developing the concept of economic reservation and the reservation of critical personnel. However, the approach proposed by the government differs from the analysts' recommendations.
Thus, potential economic losses from reducing reservations will not be limited to enterprises whose employees will directly lose their deferments. Due to production and logistics links, the negative effect may spread to entire industries.
Parliament recommended that the government not reduce reservations for the defense-industrial complex and critical infrastructure
The Verkhovna Rada also shares concerns about the possible consequences of the government's initiatives.
As Fedir Venislavskyi, a member of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on National Security, Defense and Intelligence, told UNN, the parliamentary committee has already considered the issue of a possible reduction in the number of reserved employees and recommended that the Cabinet of Ministers refrain from making such decisions concerning the defense-industrial complex and critical infrastructure.
At the committee's extraordinary meeting, which took place exactly one week ago, on Thursday, we expressed our concerns and adopted a decision recommending that the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine not reduce the number of reserved employees in these areas
At the same time, the lawmaker emphasized that the final version of the government resolution is not yet available, so it is currently impossible to assess its specific provisions.
According to him, there is indeed a need to streamline the reservation system. The increase in the number of reserved employees is linked both to the growing number of critically important enterprises and to possible abuses.
However, in Venislavskyi's view, addressing this problem should begin with verifying the validity of granting the relevant statuses, analyzing staffing tables, and auditing the existing system, rather than automatically reducing the number of employees necessary for the functioning of strategic enterprises.
Businesses need stable rules, not constant revisions to reservation conditions
The conditions for determining critical status cannot be revised just a month and a half after the previous changes. Businesses need predictability and stable operating rules
Constant changes in regulatory conditions make it more difficult for enterprises to plan their activities over the long term. Companies that enter into contracts, invest in production, and build a personnel reserve need to understand whether they will be able to fulfill their obligations.
Uncertainty about the possibility of retaining key employees creates additional risks for investment, the fulfillment of government orders, and the development of production.
Executive Director of the European Business Association Anna Derevyanko told journalists in a comment that the changes proposed by the government had caused serious concern among both Ukrainian and foreign companies.
The mobilization problem requires a comprehensive solution
Experts and members of parliament interviewed by UNN emphasize that the issue of mobilization cannot be considered separately from the needs of the economy and the country's defense capability.
According to Dligach, instead of creating additional problems for businesses, it is necessary to review approaches to managing human resources in the military, develop recruitment, and seek other ways to replenish personnel.
A separate area should be improving the system for rotating servicemembers and creating conditions for veterans to return to the civilian economy. Veterans themselves could strengthen businesses' operations. This would partially compensate for the staff shortage and allow enterprises to take a more flexible approach to reserving employees from mobilization.
At the same time, according to Andriy Dligach, there is currently practically no systematic return of specialists to civilian employment.
Fedір Venislavskyi also emphasized that the state must use all available mechanisms to meet mobilization needs without creating additional risks for the enterprises on which Ukraine's defense capability depends.
It is important that the government address not only the review of cases in which reservations from mobilization were granted without sufficient grounds, but also all the other components of this problem. This concerns people who evade mobilization, servicemembers who arbitrarily leave their units, as well as possible abuses in obtaining deferments and other similar issues
He emphasized that the parliamentary committee shares the business community's concern about the possible consequences of reducing reservations from mobilization, especially for enterprises in the defense-industrial complex.

AI-discovered bugs may soon trigger fresh disruptions, cyber experts say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:26:46 UTC
19:26:46 KST

News analysis
AI is unearthing internet’s hidden flaws – and more outages may follow
- AI is finding more hidden software flaws, with VulnCheck saying discoveries have doubled year-on-year and experts warning of more internet outages.
- Recent problems hit PHP and other tools like Node.js, Plex, LiteLLM, Railway and eMudhra, forcing some operators to take sites offline to avoid attacks.
- Experts say AI shortens the time to find and weaponise bugs, but some argue many flaws are hard to exploit, and the clean-up could still improve internet safety.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – Advances in artificial intelligence have uncovered a stream of new software vulnerabilities that are almost certain to trigger more disruption along the lines of the outages that percolated across global government websites this week, cybersecurity professionals have warned.
AI helped drive a doubling of the number of digital flaws discovered year-on-year, according to research due to be published in the coming days by VulnCheck, a Massachusetts-based threat intelligence firm.
Matthew Prince, chief executive of digital infrastructure firm Cloudflare, said he is aware of “a bunch of additional severe vulnerabilities that are present in other pieces of critical software”, and predicted busy months ahead as AI surfaces long-hidden weaknesses in the fabric of the internet.
“I think we’re going to have a couple years where every single week it’s going to feel like the sky is falling,” Prince said.
The outages that spread across government sites in Europe and elsewhere beginning on Oct 21 happened after the discovery of weaknesses in PHP, a venerable programming language that powers a huge swathe of the internet.
Operators have been rushing to fix their software in anticipation of mass exploitation and, because some felt they could not patch before hackers jumped in, a subset simply yanked their sites offline until they could make them safe.
VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity said the scramble to fix PHP came during an already busy week in cybersecurity.
The week also brought disclosures of vulnerabilities PHP alternative Node.js and streaming program Plex, breaches tied to AI gateway LiteLLM and development platform Railway, and the revelation that the Indian certificate authority eMudhra used an extraordinarily flimsy cryptographic key that potentially put users across the internet at risk.
“If we just saw four or five things like this, this week, I would expect we’re going to see a lot more,” Garrity said. “I think there’s going to be a lot more fire drills for anything that’s internet exposed.”
Timelines shortening
The codebases that run modern programs are sprawling and mistakes, or “bugs”, that open up potential avenues for exploitation often crop up in unexpected places.
Previously, finding bugs required a baseline level of skill, and taking advantage of those bugs to build digital lockpicks – called “exploits” – could be expected to take weeks or months of work by an experienced professional.
That would, in the past, have provided defenders a little breathing room to fix bugs and gently roll out software updates.
AI has effectively thrown those assumptions out the window. Models can find one bug after another by subjecting codebases to round-the-clock scrutiny, and can turn around exploits in hours.
Shane Fry, chief technology officer of Virginia-based RunSafe Security, said the demonstrated performance of AI models over the past few months has effectively laid to rest any doubts over whether they would change the industry.
“What’s fundamentally, and unquestionably, changing is the timescale for not only finding vulnerabilities, but how quickly adversaries can weaponise them,” Fry said.
Scary monsters
While all the experts agree that defenders’ timelines are getting shorter, they are split on whether AI will lead to a hacker free-for-all.
Daniel Stenberg, lead developer of file transfer tool curl, argued the vulnerabilities found by AI models tend to be exotic bugs that are difficult for rogue actors to take advantage of.
Ramy Rahman, a senior principal solutions engineer at cybersecurity company ArmorCode, said “more disclosed vulnerabilities do not automatically mean more successful attacks”.
There was tentative evidence of that around the PHP vulnerability that drew worldwide concern this week.
Threat intelligence firm Hunt.io said that – like Amazon and Cloudflare – it has seen aggressive attempts to take advantage of the bug. But the firm’s head of research, Esteban Borges, said cybercriminals he tracked appear to have failed to cobble together a working tool to take advantage of it.
Prince, of Cloudflare, said he has seen anecdotal evidence of compromises linked to the PHP vulnerability.
The deluge of AI-driven discoveries might rattle the industry, but would be a net positive in the end, he said, comparing it to slaying the monsters in a haunted house.
The confrontation may be scary, he said, but leaving the monsters to lurk quietly behind closed doors is far worse.
“The reality is, we’re going to get a lot of this stuff cleaned up,” he said. REUTERS

Can you train your brain to handle uncertainty better?
Unknown

2026-10-23
10:25:48 UTC
19:25:48 KST

Rachel Feltman: For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman.
There’s a lot of uncertainty in the air right now, whether you’re trying to predict the outcome of an upcoming election or just trying to guess how much it will cost to gas up your car come next week. You don’t need a degree in neuroscience to know that all those unknowns are tough for the human brain to handle. But some experts think there’s actually a lot of nuance to explore about the cognitive burden of uncertainty—and that you might actually have the power to change how well you tackle it.
Our guest today is Maia Szalavitz, a contributing opinion writer for the New York Times and the author or co-author of eight books. She’s also the author of a feature in the latest issue of Scientific American that explores the emerging science of the human brain as a prediction engine. She’s here to tell us more about what that means in a world that feels increasingly unpredictable—and what we can do to make our minds more adaptable to chaos.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Thank you so much for coming on to chat with us.
Maia Szalavitz: Thanks for having me.
Feltman: So how did you first get interested in this topic?.
Szalavitz: Sure. So our world seems to be becoming increasingly uncertain, and it’s not the kind of uncertainty that we’re used to dealing with in modern America because we’re used to the law being predictable. We’re used to the government’s actions being reasonably predictable. We’re used to all kinds of norms that are being violated. We’re used to being able to think of “What do I wanna be when I grow up?” and that be an actual thing that you can choose rather than perhaps losing all jobs to AI.
So I was in the midst of my own uncertainty, and I’ve been thinking a lot about this idea of how the brain works as a prediction engine, and I was really interested in hearing from people with that perspective about, like, how to manage in this really unusual situation—I mean, I didn’t even get to mention climate change. You’re used to, like, summer being summer and winter being winter—so it’s really unsettling and really, you know, because our brains do work, as far as we can tell, as prediction engines, and we’re constantly having to update prediction errors, when there’s uncertainty, it gives your brain a lot more work.
Feltman: What exactly do we mean when we say we’re modeling the brain as a prediction engine?
Szalavitz: So essentially, all of our experience of reality is a hallucination under this perspective, which is really weird to think about just in itself. But essentially, in order to solve the problem of avoiding entropy and avoiding death and ideally successfully reproducing, biological creatures need a way of managing risk and figuring out what to do next.
And so our brains sort of optimize on, okay, we get this general sense—and it’s based on experience, and there’s obviously some genetics—but you start out with this general, you know, way of perceiving the world, and then you update it when there’s an error. And so, you know, my example that I use in the piece is that, like, if you are in your room, and you have a cat, and you look, and you see something out of your corner of your eye, and it’s curled up, and it’s gray, you have a pretty full picture of that cat in your head when you, you know, do that. And then you look, and, oh, it’s actually the towel that you forgot to put in the laundry, right? But there’s no, like, glitch in it going from cat to towel, right? It’s, like, completely seamless, and this is the way our entire world works. And there’s all kinds of really interesting implications of it for things like pain and how you act psychologically.
But that is kind of the fundamental idea, that we are always making predictions, revising predictions, and, you know, with major prediction errors, it becomes seriously problematic because we may not be able to, you know, eat and survive and do the things we need to do.
Feltman: So what are some of the implications for, you know, what this means in terms of, like, how we think things through and how we process the world? I guess what I’m getting at is, like, “Why is it helpful to use this prediction engine idea?”
Szalavitz: If you think about it, if your entire life is based on predictions, there are certain things that you are going to be good at and certain things you are going to be bad at. Staying in the moment is going to be a very difficult thing if your entire world is predictions, right? And if you’re constantly predicting things, then what you’re predicting has a very big influence on what you will perceive.
And so if you are constantly seeing the world in a really negative way, that will skew it even further. Or if you are constantly just trying to avoid things, it’s really, if you think about it, it has implications for absolutely every aspect, which is why I’m sort of struggling of, like, narrowing it down here.
Feltman: Yeah, absolutely. What about the implications for how cognitive stress impacts our bodies?
Szalavitz: Sure. So Bruce McEwen was the great researcher on the impact of stress and health, right? And he talks about, like, how stress gets under the skin. And at this very moment, I am having a personal experience of this because I had to take a course of prednisone to deal with a hearing issue, and that’s basically massive amounts of stress hormones, like, coursing through me and making me feel like bad coke or something.
But those stress hormones are really good in an emergency because what they do is keep you awake and alert and focused on dealing with what you need to deal with in front of you to escape the emergency. And that has a physiological cost because you spend more energy doing it, and therefore you produce more waste, and therefore there’s all kinds of different things that your body needs to manage that can get out of whack.
And when you look at the data, severe chronic stress, starting in childhood with things like abuse or neglect or other forms of trauma, raise risk for everything from, you know, obesity, heart disease, stroke, all of the mental illnesses, virtually. And it’s because of the way these hormones impact your brain, because if you have too much of these glucocorticoids, it can eat your hippocampus a little bit, and so it makes memory weird.
And a lot of these things are all about trade-offs, because in the short term, if you don’t survive, then the rest doesn’t matter, right? But in the long term, you are generating a debt in some sense.
Feltman: Well, speaking of mental illness, in your piece, you outlined how a few mental illnesses could be reframed as sort of disruptions in this predictive machinery. Could you tell us a little bit more about that?
Szalavitz: Sure. So the most obvious one is anxiety, because anxiety is worrying about the future.
Feltman: Sure, yeah.
Szalavitz: And so uncertainty is not going to be good for anxiety. And one of the things that was really interesting about this is that if we’re in this predictive world, then one of the key ways of dealing with anxiety is to get your predictions in line with reality as much as possible. But you can get stuck if you try to do that by just escaping because if you go in a dark room and curl up, yeah, you’re gonna reduce prediction error ’cause nothing’s going on, but you are not going to get the information you need to be able to manage the world. And so people with anxiety disorders tend to have a very high intolerance of uncertainty. We just don’t like it.
I am on the autism spectrum, and I like things to be predictable. I am not into extreme variability most of the time, except for in intellectual pursuits. But if you’re constantly having to worry about what’s gonna happen—am I gonna go out the door and get hit by a car? Or, does that person hate me?—then you’re spending a lot of mental energy, and if you start avoiding, then you will think that, like, you know, “Oh, I’m scared of dogs. I will avoid dogs. Didn’t get bitten. It worked. My strategy’s good. I will continue avoiding.” And so that creates a negative cycle that you can really get stuck in. And so while everyone with anxiety does not want to stop avoiding the things that they are avoiding, that is inevitably part of overcoming it.
Feltman: The researchers that you spoke to, published something about four phenotypes for managing uncertainty. Could you tell us what those are?
Szalavitz: The first one is probably where I would constitutionally fall, which is fragile. And what that means is: does not like uncertainty, tries to hide in a dark room, is congenitally oversensitive to stimulation. Or there’s another way to get into the fragile pathway, which is by, like, abuse or neglect or growing up in a really unpredictable situation. And so you kind of turn toward dysfunctional strategies like just hiding rather than actually exploring the world and resolving the prediction errors in a productive way.
And so the second type is called durable, and these are people who are growing up in a very, very predictable world, which would seem to be good, but if it’s so predictable that you never experience prediction errors, and you rarely experience the stress of having to deal with unexpected things, then you’re obviously, by nature, not going to be good at it, and you may underlyingly be fragile.
The third type is resilient, and this is what people tend to think is, “oh, this is, like, the best possible type,” because you don’t hide, you manage stress, you go and are curious about the world and learn, and by learning you build up your muscle of dealing with stress, right? But the authors of the paper argue that there’s a fourth type, which they very annoyingly call proentropic—which I would think it would be antientropic because you don’t want to die in entropy—but anyway, the point is that such people actively seek challenge and actively seek to, you know, deal with uncertainties and manage them successfully. And when you do that, you know, like anything else, the more you do something, the better you get at it generally.
Feltman: Yeah. Could you give some examples of, you know, what that would look like in the real world?
Szalavitz: You could think of it as anything from, you know, a firefighter who’s going into these very intense, dangerous situations and managing extreme stress very regularly. Or you could say, well, a scientist, you know, somebody who is, daily, challenging the way they see the world and, like, putting ideas to various tests and that sort of thing. So it could just look like anybody who really is trying to not avoid the world too much. Now the thing is: sometimes avoidance is productive, and you asked earlier about other mental illnesses that can be affected by this predictive thing, and depression is really one of them. You can kind of think of depression as being “let’s curl up in a dark room,” like a strategy of that. And, you know, people argue that, evolutionarily, that may be why we have this thing that we call depression in the sense that if you’re failing, sometimes withdrawing and, like, getting out of the situation is a good idea. And if you have a mechanism to make that happen, if you’re, like, failing, like, socially or in whatever ways, then that could be productive. However, if you get stuck there, then it becomes unproductive, and obviously the feelings of it can just escalate such that it’s very difficult to escape from without, you know, chemical or therapeutic help.
Feltman: So can understanding the brain as a prediction engine actually help us cope better with uncertainty? Your piece certainly had a very compelling narrative lead that got into this a little bit. So maybe you could start by sharing that with our listeners.
Szalavitz: When I was interviewing the authors of the paper that described those various phenotypes, they had just survived the Eaton Fire in Los Angeles, and they had been working on the paper during that, and the fire actually threatened their homes very significantly, and they had to, like, evacuate in a smoky, messy, scary hell.
And to top it all off, one of the co-authors was injured in a childhood diving accident, and so he is quadriplegic, and he uses a wheelchair, and the mobility van that transports his wheelchair was undergoing service. So he couldn’t get into his wife’s car, and they had to leave, and he had to, like, drive his electric wheelchair through, you know, the falling debris and the howling winds and the smoke and all of that to get to a place where a vehicle could get to that would be capable of him getting picked up.
Feltman: Yeah. That’s a tough one for the old prediction engine, I got to say. [Laughs.]
Szalavitz: No, exactly. And so that was why, like, when I was interviewing them, Laura Harrison brought it up because she was like, “This got put to the test for us very seriously, you know, in these circumstances.”
And so, you know, I wasn’t originally gonna write about any of that. I was just writing about the paper, and so then I had the anecdote that would, like, allow us to get into, you know, the very real-world implications of how we manage uncertainty. And, you know, they were talking about, while they were in that moment, like, thinking about these ideas and thinking about, like, “Okay, well, how do I respond in a proentropic or at least resilient way?” and, you know, “How do I manage the odds of, like, is it safer to stay or go?”
And so it was really fascinating to think about that. And when you do that, the other thing that becomes very clear is that managing your emotions is very important because your emotions are kind of there, they’re kind of decision-making algorithms to, like, guide you when under uncertainty, right? Like, this has worked in the past, so this will feel good. This doesn’t, so it won’t, right? So you have to be aware of those influences and whether they are guiding you in the right direction or not. And you also have to be aware that, like, when your brain is flooded with stress hormones, you are not thinking about the future the way you ordinarily do because you’re very narrowed in on where you are now, which is important when you’re getting out of a fire.
But it means that you’re not going to be at your most creative or at your most able to deal with abstraction. And so, you know, this is why, like, in national emergencies, it’s so difficult to manage because we just freak out. [Laughs.] I mean, I sort of feel like what happened, you know, with the pandemic is that that massive social stress moved everybody a notch higher away from planning and abstraction and deeper thought and into a more reactive and often aggressive, unfortunately, mode. So kind of understanding all of this in this context is really useful when you want to try to, like, cope with either on a personal or a, you know, political level the challenges that we are facing now.
Feltman: Well, and speaking of that shift in the wrong direction that I think we all feel very aware of, you made the point that these phenotypes aren’t really fixed, and that we can change the way our prediction engines work. Could you talk a little bit about how that’s possible?
Szalavitz: So obviously, we are limited, to some extent, by our temperament. Like, I’m never gonna be the chillest person in the world. That probably will not happen. But we can move away from our default responses toward, if they have become dysfunctional, toward more appropriate and, and helpful ones. And you do that by explicitly facing it—not in a way like tough love or force or any of that. And this is a lot of what cognitive-behavioral therapy is. It’s like, you know, “Okay, I walk into the room; I assume they hate me.” That’s my brain doing the assumption. It’s not them doing anything. So I have to be aware of that, and I have to say, “Well, what’s the evidence for my belief that they’re going to hate me?” And there probably isn’t any. And so I need to, like, let go of that and just go into the room with a better expectation. When you face these kinds of things, you have to not assume your perception is automatically correct or real, and you have to assume that it’s provisional.
And the more you can, like, expect surprise and, you know, work toward having the surprises ideally be pleasant ones, then you can get better at managing the whole thing—because it’s kind of amazing how much stuff is, like, building muscle, where it’s just, like, you start with, like, the lower weights, and you suck, and you’re bad at it, and then you repeat it, and then you actually see that you can really get a lot stronger, right? So this is true whether it’s managing stress or, you know, learning anything. But what we tend to do is, sort of, push people into the deep end, and then they’re like, “Well, I can’t do this. I’m bad at this.” It’s like, if you, for your first [time] trying to lift weights, [you] tried to lift 300 pounds, you would not succeed, and you would probably injure yourself, right? But you can, I can attest, build up to this by a lot of practice over many, many years. When it is stress or when it is, like, some of our psychological tendencies, a groove gets worn into your brain because it’s easier and because otherwise we couldn’t possibly handle the complexity of the world.
So one of the interesting things and implications of the predictive brain stuff is that if you can increase brain plasticity, you can interrupt some of these patterns and help people predict in a more functional way. And it’s really interesting to me that everything, with a few minor exceptions, that has antidepressant effects, whether it’s, like, SSRIs [selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors], exercise, ECT [electroconvulsive therapy], psychedelics, all of these things increase plasticity. And psychedelics do it in an especially interesting way because they seem to open up windows of plasticity that are only open at certain points during development. And so I find that fascinating.
Feltman: Well, thank you so much for coming on to talk to us. Your article was fascinating and it was great talking to you.
Szalavitz: Thank you as well.
Feltman: That’s all for today’s episode. You can read Maia’s feature online or in the latest issue of Scientific American, which is on newsstands now. We’ll be back on Monday with our weekly science news roundup.
