RFK Jr. promised to define ‘ultraprocessed’ food. What's taking so long?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:25:38 UTC
19:25:38 KST

In August Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., took the stage at the Department of Health and Human Services headquarters in Washington, D.C., and announced what would be a first for the U.S. government: an upcoming formal definition of “ultraprocessed foods.” The reason for defining the term, Kennedy said, was to help bring healthier food options to Americans. But Kennedy held back sharing what, exactly, the definition would be.
Processed foods have been a target for Kennedy’s “Make America Healthy Again” agenda. Some scientists and health organizations, including the American Heart Association, support a federal definition, too. But a consensus definition on ultraprocessed foods has been notoriously difficult to reach.
The lack of a clear definition can create “ambiguity” in how to enforce or monitor food regulations, says Lindsey Smith Taillie, a nutrition science professor at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. “It can leave manufacturers and retailers confused,” in addition to consumers.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Now, more than two months later, the federal effort to define ultraprocessed foods has reportedly stalled. According to Bloomberg Law and the Wall Street Journal, Kennedy’s plan was met with a wave of pushback from the food industry and the White House because of concerns about the legal ramifications of such a definition.
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, ultraprocessed foods make up some 55 percent of the average American’s daily calories—the percentage is even higher among young people aged one to 18. Researchers say defining these foods would make it easier for the government to limit ultraprocessed foods in school lunches, for example, or to put labels on food packaging to better inform consumers about what they are eating.
That matters, because evidence suggests ultraprocessed foods are bad for us: they are linked to the risk of chronic diseases, such as type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, as well as worse mental health outcomes. But it’s unclear whether these ill effects are entirely linked to the foods’ ingredients or nutritional value, the way in which they were processed or something else.
Ultraprocessed foods may also be addictive and tend to be convenient, portable and heavily marketed to children, Taillie says.
We asked the experts what they consider to be ultraprocessed foods, why these foods are often considered “unhealthy” and why it’s so hard to agree on a definition—on the federal level and in the field.
How do scientists define ultraprocessed foods?
Imagine an ultraprocessed food: whatever you are thinking of, you are probably right on the money, says Marion Nestle, a nutrition expert and a professor emerita at New York University.
“In my experience, consumers ‘get’ the concept easily, so easily that they start avoiding them,” Nestle says.
To Nestle, ultraprocessed foods are those that are “industrially produced, designed to be irresistible, if not addictive, and are usually formulated with lots of sugar, salt, and flavor, color and texture additives.”
“An operating definition is ‘you can’t make them in your home kitchen,’” she adds.
“If you think about what a lot of these ultraprocessed foods are, they are designed for consumption,” says Matthew Landry, an assistant professor of global health and biobehavioral sciences at the University of California, Irvine. They might come in textures and flavors designed to keep us snacking.
Some scientists have sought to categorize processed foods with tools, such as the NOVA food classification system.
Under this system, foods are sorted into four categories: Group 1 includes unprocessed and minimally processed food, such as fruits, vegetables, grains, nuts, legumes and meat. Group 2 includes “culinary ingredients,” such as salt, sugar and fats. Group 3 includes processed foods that are canned or fermented, such as cheese. The fourth group represents ultraprocessed foods and is comprised of items that have undergone “extensive chemical or physical processing,” Taillie says.
Foods in this fourth category are typically high in added sugar, sodium, and saturated fats and may include artificial ingredients such as flavors, colors or emulsifiers, Taillie says. Chips, candies and frozen meals might fall under Group 4.
Where things get tricky are the edge cases: What category should a flavored yogurt fall under? What about granola bars or tofu?
NOVA only classifies foods based on processing levels, not nutritional value. Other classification systems, such as one called FPro, attempt to take nutritional information into account. But scientists haven’t agreed on one shared system.
Why is it so hard to come up with a consensus definition?
There are several reasons. For one, companies aren’t required to disclose how a food product was processed on its label, Taillie says. Using other sources of information—such as ingredients lists—can serve somewhat as a proxy, she says. For example, if a product’s ingredients include added colors, sweeteners, thickeners or chemical names that you don’t recognize, then it’s probably ultraprocessed.
Complicating matters further is that, as with any food classification system, drawing a line between what is “processed” and what is not is somewhat arbitrary, Taillie says.
“You have to set a threshold somewhere, which means that there are going to be some products that are captured that people will look at and inherently feel that should not be captured, or vice versa,” she says.
Under systems such as the NOVA scale, foods that experts might consider beneficial to our health, such as some yogurt, could be categorized alongside less healthy ones. In a July journal article, for instance, Landry and a co-author argued that ultraprocessed, plant-based meat alternatives such as soy burgers can act as a “gateway” to eating whole, plant proteins, such as beans or lentils. In turn, making a clear definition for foods that are processed but have other “redeeming nutritional qualities” is challenging, Landry says.
There’s also a layer of complexity when considering how a definition may be used. Not everyone has access to whole foods—people who are food-insecure, for instance, might rely on shelf-stable foods, such as frozen meals. Landry argues that any federal action to define ultraprocessed foods should take that into account.
And then there’s opposition from the food industry, which has “absolutely” been a roadblock, Nestle says. Food companies’ antagonism toward reaching a consensus definition has been “strong and well coordinated,” Taillie agrees, with actions that have included lobbying at the state and federal level.
“These are among the most profitable products on the market,” Nestle adds.
If you’re interested in cutting down on ultraprocessed foods, there are benefits to doing so. But there’s no need to sweat over a single cupcake or cup of instant noodles, experts say.
“As a consumer, I’m not too worried about whether this slice of bread that I have in the morning is ultraprocessed or not,” Taillie says. “I’m really looking at the course of the entire day. How many foods am I consuming that might fit into that criteria?”

NEW DELHI: Delhi Police detained several protesters on Friday as a march against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls headed towards the Election Commission (EC) headquarters in central Delhi. Authorities imposed prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), banning mass gatherings, sources said.The demonstration was called by the Delhi Coordination Committee of People Against SIR, a people's collective, and drew students, youth, farmers and activists carrying the national flag and banners of the group.The Krantikari Yuva Sangathan (KYS) and the Students' Federation of India (SFI) also extended their support, with activists from Delhi, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh joining the march.
Amid slogans such as “Gyanesh Kumar, resign”, “Halt SIR” and “Won’t tolerate vote theft”, the protesters were joined by senior CPI(M) leader Brinda Karat and members of the All India Democratic Women's Association (AIDWA) and the All India Democratic Students' Organisation (AIDSO), among others.The march began near Gole Dak Khana, at the intersection of Kalibari Marg and Bhai Vir Singh Marg, and proceeded towards the ECI headquarters.
When police stopped the protesters, they sat down and held a 'People's Parliament', as announced by the organisers.“The protest has begun! We won't let go our right to vote and the right to protest for it! Our's is a democratic country and we will ensure that spirit remains alive!” the All India Students' Association (AISA) said in a post on X.
“This is not about reclaiming Jantar Mantar; this is about saving democracy and the country,” a protester said, as cited by PTI.Another protester said that since Jantar Mantar had been denotified as a protest site, every street in the country would become a Jantar Mantar, pointing to several organisations announcing demonstrations across India.Protests planned across 88 citiesPeople Against SIR has launched a website providing information about demonstrations being held in different cities. According to the collective, protests have been planned in 88 cities across 18 states, involving 145 organisations.The collective has listed demonstrations scheduled for Friday, with programmes extending until November 1 as part of its campaign against the SIR exercise. Organisers have appealed to farmers, workers, youth, women and people from different sections of society to participate while carrying the national flag.The organisers said the Delhi march would remain peaceful and conclude with the adoption of resolutions and the singing of the national anthem. The SFI has also called for solidarity protests in central Delhi and at district headquarters on Friday.Security tightened, traffic diversions in placeSecurity was tightened in central Delhi, with Delhi Police and Rapid Action Force (RAF) personnel deployed in large numbers.
Traffic diversions were enforced in parts of central Delhi from 1 pm and were scheduled to remain in place until 5 pm. Congestion was expected around Bangla Sahib Gurudwara, Connaught Place, Parliament Street and Jantar Mantar.The Delhi Traffic Police advised commuters to avoid unnecessary travel along the affected stretches, plan their journeys and follow instructions issued by traffic personnel.The protest comes amid concerns raised by opposition parties and various organisations over the SIR exercise and the alleged deletion of voters from electoral rolls.

SIMFEROPOL, October 23. /TASS/. European leaders have undermined their credibility as partners in dialogue, making their presence at the negotiating table with Russia inappropriate, while US President Donald Trump could convey their views, State Duma member representing the Republic of Crimea Mikhail Sheremet told TASS.
Politico previously reported that European Union countries were concerned about their status in the Ukraine negotiations and were trying to find someone who could represent the bloc’s interests. According to The Telegraph, candidates for the role include Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, Finnish President Alexander Stubb, Czech President Petr Pavel, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.
"The frenzied, revanchist and Russophobic policies of the leaders of several European countries have led them into a political and economic dead end, leaving them entirely incapable of engaging in constructive dialogue with their key neighbor and economic donor, peace-loving Russia," Sheremet said. "That is why I am convinced that, under the difficult circumstances now emerging, Europe’s interests at the upcoming talks could be represented by its strategic ally, US President Donald Trump, who commands authority and enjoys the trust of the European Union."
The US president and European Union politicians have repeatedly exchanged harsh remarks. Sheremet believes that disagreements between the White House and several European capitals are not as deep as they appear publicly. "I am convinced that America remains Europe’s key partner and most important ally," he emphasized.
The lawmaker also noted that, as Europe is repeatedly rocked by unrest, "one cannot help but recall the times of European prosperity under the leadership of level-headed, civilized politicians such as Silvio Berlusconi, Angela Merkel and Viktor Orban," who were capable of redirecting Europe’s confrontational agenda toward a constructive and peaceful course.
"Today, public support for the leaders of major countries such as Germany and France does not exceed 15%, and they are afraid to meet their own citizens in public, raising serious questions about their legitimacy," Sheremet said.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov previously said that Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates was currently being considered the main venue for trilateral talks between Russia, the United States and Ukraine.

South Korea invites North for military talks over border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:20:31 UTC
19:20:31 KST

South Korea invites North for military talks over border
The proposal comes days after Pyongyang says it moved new military units into ‘firing positions’ along the border.
South Korea has proposed holding military talks with North Korea in a bid to calm rising tensions over their heavily fortified border.
Seoul said on Friday that it had invited Pyongyang to discuss restoring communication channels. The offer was made as military activity on the border increases.
Talks with North Korea would aim to “mutually confirm” the precise location of the land Military Demarcation Line (MDL), “discuss ways to restore military communication lines and prevent accidental clashes in border areas”, Kim Hong-cheol, deputy minister for national defence policy, told reporters.
“Specific dates and locations could be discussed through Panmunjom,” Kim said, referring to the symbolic truce village on the North-South border where soldiers from both Koreas stand face to face.
He added that the South was open to three-way talks involving the United States-led United Nations Command and hoped for “a positive response from North Korea”.
It remains unclear whether North Korea would agree to talks. Leader Kim Jong Un has taken a hardline approach towards Seoul and suspended virtually all dialogue and cooperation with the South in recent years.
Meanwhile, Pyongyang has raised its military activity along the border and continues to do so.
On Wednesday, Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of the North Korean leader, announced that new military units have been moved into “firing positions” along the border.
Mines, barbed-wire fences, tactical roads, antitank walls and other fortifications have also been added to one of the world’s most heavily armed borders.
Tensions have worsened since last month when three South Korean soldiers were injured by explosions near the military demarcation line in the western section of the Demilitarized Zone, the buffer zone that runs between the Koreas, commonly known as the DMZ.
The South blamed the blast on landmines laid by the North and demanded an apology. Pyongyang has fiercely rejected the accusation.
Seoul’s Ministry of National Defence said on Friday that it was difficult to predict “what further incidents could occur if this situation is allowed to continue unaddressed”.
The ministry noted that a proposal for talks last year did not receive a response from Pyongyang.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung has called for the North to return to dialogue. However, Kim Yo Jong responded by slamming the suggestion of bilateral talks as “the climax of the farce”.

Austria expels four Russian diplomats over suspicion of espionage

Austria has declared four Russian diplomats persona non grata over suspicions of espionage. This was reported by the Austrian publication Heute, writes UNN.
Details
Three of the diplomats worked at the Russian Embassy in Vienna. According to the Austrian Foreign Ministry, they engaged in activities incompatible with their diplomatic status. All three were declared persona non grata in accordance with Article 9 of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations.
The decision also concerns a Russian diplomat who worked at the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) in Vienna. He was part of the Russian delegation on military security and arms control. He was also declared persona non grata and ordered to leave Austria.
This is not the first expulsion of Russian diplomats from Austria. In the spring, the country had already taken such a step, and now diplomatic tensions between Vienna and Moscow have resurfaced.
At the same time, the Austrian Foreign Ministry did not specify exactly what actions the diplomats were accused of. No details were released regarding the information obtained by the Austrian security authorities either.

Ukraine reports problems with Starshield after Trump said access restored
KYIV – Ukraine said on Oct 23 that it was still having problems using the Starshield military communications service, a day after US President Donald Trump said tech titan Elon Musk had restored access.
“As of this morning, instances of signal loss are still being observed,” a source in the Defence Ministry told reporters.
“There is currently no confirmation that the restrictions have been lifted.”
Trump on Oct 22 said that Starshield was “back”, following a Wall Street Journal report that the President had asked Musk to restore the service vital to Kyiv’s forces.
The Journal reported earlier this week that Musk had capped the speed at which Ukrainian equipment could connect to the system, making some Ukrainian drones useless.
Musk had previously said that “any limits on speed or usage” of Starshield systems – which are operated by his SpaceX company – were “decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS”, referring to Trump.
But Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Oct 20 that the Pentagon had not directed any changes to Starshield, and Trump said last week he had not either.
Kyiv last week reported restrictions to the service, which it considers crucial to fending off Moscow’s invasion, shortly after Trump criticised Ukraine and urged it to stop targeting Russian oil refineries.
Ukraine uses Starshield, Starlink’s military-grade satellite service, for battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russia-occupied territory, and its interceptor drones.
It also uses the Starlink civilian satellite system, but not for military operations.
Washington-Kyiv relations have become tense again, with Trump calling for President Volodymyr Zelensky to be replaced after he criticised a US deal waiving some sanctions to allow more Russian diesel into global markets.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Friday that Ottawa is "in need of Turkish expertise" to strengthen its defences and reduce reliance on foreign military systems.
Speaking to reporters a day after meeting Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Ankara, Carney said Canada was interested in both Turkish military technology and joint industrial partnerships, with an emphasis on developing capabilities together.

Canada will maintain controls on arms exports and dual-use technologies, he said, adding that officials would be clear about how those rules apply as the two countries explore opportunities for cooperation.

Over 83% of Ukrainian manufacturers face labor shortages — poll

10:17:52 UTC
19:17:52 KST

MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. Labor shortages have become the primary challenge for Ukrainian enterprises, with over 83% of companies reporting the issue, the NV news outlet reported, citing data from the GRC.UA recruitment agency.
According to GRC.UA’s analytical report, titled "Labor Market Barometer," "83.3% of production managers cited labor shortages among the main problems reported by the surveyed companies." Meanwhile, the outflow of people abroad was cited by 66.7%, and a general shortage of workers across various categories stood at 50%.
Amid the severe workforce deficit, the report notes that 100% of the surveyed employers now hire individuals aged 50 and older for various positions. Furthermore, 66.7% of respondents recruit women for "traditionally male occupations" and employ people with disabilities.
The survey data was collected in September-October, polling 6,160 respondents across various regions of Ukraine.

Trump's diesel price relief efforts grow costlier as election nears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:16:46 UTC
19:16:46 KST

Trump’s diesel price relief efforts grow costlier as election nears
- Trump is using costly measures to cut diesel prices before the November midterms, including farm aid, trucker rule changes, and pressure on allies, but prices still rose to US$6.28 a gallon.
- The plan has brought political and financial risks. It adds strain on federal spending, creates diplomatic friction, and faces scepticism from experts and industry groups.
- Farmers and truckers remain under pressure from high fuel and fertiliser costs. Critics say the aid is temporary and may not fix the market problems driving the price rise.
AI generated
With the November midterm elections fast approaching, US President Donald Trump is throwing an array of costly and politically fraught solutions at one stubborn problem: the price of diesel.
His administration has offered billions of dollars to farmers, relaxed rules for truckers, eased sanctions on Russian fuel and pressured European allies to release emergency stocks. Yet diesel prices rose again last week, leaving Trump spending political and financial capital without delivering the relief his party wants as voters go to the polls.
Republicans are defending narrow majorities in Congress, and high costs are a major concern for voters. Nearly 80% of Americans blame Trump for higher costs, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos poll.
US diesel prices rose nearly 10 cents a gallon in the latest week to an average of US$6.28, reversing two weeks of declines and remaining near record highs, according to the Energy Information Administration.
The political pressure is particularly acute in traditionally Republican Farm Belt states like Iowa and Kansas, where rising fuel and fertiliser costs, trade disruptions and weak farm economics have fueled discontent among some of Trump’s core supporters.
Trump has promoted his diesel measures at campaign rallies across the region. He signed an executive order onstage in Nebraska allowing red-dyed diesel to be used in highway vehicles and announced US$8 billion (S$10.2 billion) in new farm aid during a rally in Kansas on Oct 19.
The measures illustrate the trade-offs Trump is accepting in pursuit of near-term relief. The new aid adds fresh strain on federal spending, while the Russian fuel move risks helping Moscow finance its war in Ukraine. Pressure on European allies to release emergency stocks, backed by a threat to restrict US diesel exports, has created diplomatic friction.
“The President tends to discount long-term losses over short-term gain, and I am skeptical if there is any short gain to be had here,” said Chris Borick, a pollster and political scientist at Muhlenberg College in Pennsylvania.
The White House attributed high diesel prices to “pre-existing issues”, including years of refinery closures and damage from Russia’s war in Ukraine, while defending Trump’s efforts to ease costs.
“The President wants diesel prices to fall, which is why he has taken historic actions to save American farmers, truckers, and workers every hard-earned penny,” White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said.
Scepticism and unanswered questions
One of Trump’s most direct attempts to lower diesel costs has struggled to gain traction.
Trump signed an executive order in October allowing truckers to use red-dyed diesel, typically intended for off-road use such as farm equipment, for highway driving while temporarily avoiding certain federal tax reporting and record-keeping requirements.
But the Internal Revenue Service has not eliminated the federal diesel tax, instead temporarily waiving related reporting requirements and penalties through year-end, leaving uncertainty for truck stops and fuel sellers.
David Fialkov, top lobbyist at NATSO, a trade group representing the largest US truck stop operators, said members appreciate Trump’s effort to tackle diesel costs but that the guidance remains “murky” and carries too much risk.
“I really don’t see any of these dyed diesel announcements making a meaningful dent in diesel prices,” Fialkov said.
Trump is also turning to federal payments to cushion some of the constituencies feeling the pain.
Government payments to farmers were already expected to top US$47 billion in 2026, buoyed by commodity payments and US$12 billion in tariff relief distributed by the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) earlier that year. The US$8 billion farm relief programme would push the total to a record US$55.4 billion, exceeding the previous high of US$45 billion in 2020, when farmers received pandemic assistance.
The payments can help farmers manage higher costs and lost sales but do not directly address the market disruptions driving up fuel and fertiliser prices. They also raise questions about taxpayer spending to compensate producers for damage that farm groups say is linked partly to the administration’s own trade and foreign policies.
“This is the second round of emergency aid this year to address losses that were largely foreseeable,” National Farmers Union President Rob Larew said. “Trade disruptions and rising fuel costs tied to conflict abroad have put family farmers in a difficult position, and one-time payments can’t provide the stability they need to plan for the future.”
It is unclear how quickly the latest aid will reach farmers. USDA could not immediately say how the money would be allocated, when payments would reach farmers or whether congressional approval would be required.
Friction over Russian fuel
Some of Trump’s efforts to increase diesel supplies carry geopolitical trade-offs.
His decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel that were designed to restrict Moscow’s energy revenues and limit its ability to finance its war in Ukraine has drawn bipartisan criticism – and raised questions about whether the move will meaningfully lower US fuel prices.
Trump has defended the sanctions relief as necessary to draw Russian President Vladimir Putin into negotiations to end the war in Ukraine and to release American prisoner Stephen Hubbard.
As the administration’s intervention efforts have failed to lower fuel costs, Trump has sought to shift blame towards Ukraine and President Volodymyr Zelensky rather than the Iran war ahead of the Nov 3 elections.
Analysts say the Iran conflict has been the much bigger driver of the diesel price spike, disrupting global oil flows and refined-fuel supplies, while Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have helped tighten supplies but played a more limited role on the price.
“I sort of see it as a blame-shifting kind of scapegoating operation, more than a genuine attempt to moderate prices in the lead-up to the election,” said Edward Fishman, director of the Maurice R. Greenberg Center at the Council on Foreign Relations. REUTERS

READ: Israeli opposition leaders accuse Netanyahu of clinging to power at country’s expense
The Israeli prime minister claimed that approximately 150,000 Palestinians had left Gaza during the war and suggested that at least 60 percent of the territory’s population would leave if given the opportunity.

Netanyahu also reiterated that Israel intends to retain military control over more than 60 percent of the Gaza Strip, signalling that his government does not plan to withdraw from areas currently held by Israeli forces.

Trump-Kim summit prospects fade as North Korea remains silent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:16:42 UTC
19:16:42 KST

The chances of a meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un this year are fading, with Pyongyang yet to respond to Washington's outreach and little time remaining before a regional summit in China where the two leaders could meet, according to five people familiar with the matter.
Trump has expressed interest in reviving diplomacy with North Korea, having met Kim three times during his first term. But Pyongyang has shown little enthusiasm for renewed talks aimed at curbing its nuclear program, leaving the prospect of another high-profile summit increasingly uncertain.
The United States has received no response to its efforts to arrange a meeting, according to the five people, four of whom were briefed by senior U.S. and South Korean officials. A South Korean official also said there were no signs that North Korea was preparing for a meeting.
The leaders could still meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 18-19, but the window for arranging such an encounter is narrowing.
In August, Trump said he planned to meet Kim later this year and indicated that the North Korean leader had responded to his outreach.
South Korea's intelligence agency told lawmakers late last month that there was a 50% chance the leaders would meet during the APEC summit. But Trump struck a more cautious tone Monday, playing down the likelihood of a meeting during the gathering or a regional summit in the Philippines later in November.
"I get along with him very well, and I'm not sure that anybody's asking for a meeting," Trump told reporters at the White House.
A White House official said Trump remained willing to engage Kim without preconditions, while emphasizing that no meeting had been scheduled.
"President Trump remains open to talking with Kim Jong Un, without any preconditions. No meetings to announce at this time. The leaders will meet at the appropriate time," the official said.
Last week, South Korean Ambassador to Washington Kang Kyung-wha said there had been no concrete progress toward a summit. A senior U.S. official had similarly said last month that Trump was ready to speak with Kim and that the initiative now rested with Pyongyang.
North Korean state media has indicated that any bilateral summit would come with tough conditions, potentially including sanctions relief. Kim's influential sister, Kim Yo Jong, has described the two leaders as having an "excellent" relationship, but that has not translated into renewed diplomatic engagement.
Ankit Panda, a senior fellow in the Nuclear Policy Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, estimated that the chance of a Trump-Kim meeting at the APEC summit was below 10%.
He said Pyongyang was likely seeking a significant public gesture from Washington before agreeing to another meeting, adding that a recent U.S. decision to scale back military exercises with South Korea had not been enough.
Washington has periodically sought China's help in facilitating talks with North Korea, which maintains close ties with Beijing. But cordial relations between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping have yet to produce a breakthrough with Pyongyang.
Despite three historic meetings in 2018 and 2019, Trump and Kim failed to reach a lasting agreement on North Korea's nuclear weapons program.
The two Koreas remain technically at war under the armistice that ended fighting in the 1950-53 Korean War. The United States maintains about 28,500 troops in South Korea as part of its joint defense posture against the North, which continues to develop nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles. South Korean officials have cited estimates from private research groups putting North Korea's nuclear arsenal at between 80 and 120 warheads.
U.S. Ambassador to South Korea Michelle Steel said Wednesday that the timing of any meeting remained uncertain but suggested it could come together quickly if both sides agreed.
"If it happens, then it's going to happen the next day or within a couple of days' notice," she said at an event organized by the American Chamber of Commerce in Korea.

Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Mao Ning’s Regular Press Conference on October 23, 2026
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:16:28 CST
19:16:28 KST

At the invitation of President Xi Jinping, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier will pay a state visit to China from October 27 to 31.
Xinhua News Agency: On German President Steinmeier’s visit to China that you just announced, could you share the program? How does China see the current state of relations with Germany? What are your expectations for the visit?
Mao Ning: President Steinmeier will visit China again after nearly eight years. During the visit, President Xi Jinping will hold talks with him and Premier Li Qiang and Chairman of the NPC Standing Committee Zhao Leji will meet with him to exchange views on bilateral relations and issues of mutual interest. Besides Beijing, President Steinmeier will also visit Anhui Province.
The sound and steady growth of the comprehensive strategic partnership between China and Germany, the world’s second and third largest economies, not only serves the interests of both countries, but is also what Europe and the world hope to see. The past 54 years since diplomatic ties were established have shown that mutual respect and mutual trust are the bedrock for a stable relationship and mutual benefit the key to success in bilateral cooperation. Our two countries have built strategic consensus through close collaboration and achieved shared prosperity in practical cooperation, delivering tangible benefits to both peoples.
President Steinmeier, an old friend of the Chinese people, has actively contributed to the development of China-Germany relations. We hope to work with the German side to take this visit as an opportunity to cement mutual trust, deepen cooperation and seek joint innovation, so as to make greater progress in bilateral relations, contribute to steady and sustained growth of China-Europe relations, and bring fresh energy to the world.
CCTV: October 25 will mark the 55th anniversary of the restoration of the lawful seat of the People’s Republic of China in the United Nations. How does China see its relationship with the UN over the past 55 years, and how will it enhance its cooperation with the organization in the future?
Mao Ning: On October 25, 1971, the UN General Assembly adopted at its 26th session Resolution 2758 with an overwhelming majority, deciding to restore all rights of the People’s Republic of China in the United Nations. This marked the return of the Chinese people, one-fourth of the world’s population, back to the UN stage, which is of great significance and far-reaching impact for China, the wider world and the United Nations itself. The Chinese people shall always remember the invaluable support and help we received from friendly countries and individuals.
Over the past 55 years, China has always been a builder of world peace, a contributor to global development, and a guardian of the international order. We firmly support the UN in playing a central role in international affairs, actively participate in the work of the UN in various fields, and faithfully fulfill our duties as a permanent member of the UN Security Council. Through the UN, we work to strengthen solidarity and cooperation with other countries, advocate for common security, promote shared development, foster dialogue among civilizations, and advance the reform and improvement of global governance.
Standing at this new starting point of history, China will continue to shoulder its responsibility as a major country, further deepen cooperation with the UN across the board, jointly tackle global challenges, and build a community with a shared future for humanity.
Reuters: The U.S. Treasury has proposed to add biotechnology as a new “prohibited technology” under the U.S. Outbound Investment Security Program. This could restrict American investments in Chinese biotechnology companies. How does the ministry view this measure?
Mao Ning: It serves no one’s interest to take discriminatory measures targeting specific countries or putting restrictions on economic, trade and investment activities based on overstretching the concept of national security. The U.S. should abide by the principles of market economy, stop disrupting normal business cooperation, and help keep global industrial and supply chains stable through concrete actions. China will closely follow relevant developments and take necessary measures to safeguard its legitimate and lawful rights and interests.

Trump Invokes Defense Production Act to Boost Oil Production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:15:00 UTC
19:15:00 KST

President Donald Trump has invoked a Cold War-era law in an effort to boost oil production and lower energy prices.
In a presidential memorandum issued Thursday, Trump determined that petroleum production, refining, and related activities are essential to national defense under the 1950 Defense Production Act. The determination follows Trump’s declaration of a national energy emergency in January 2025.
“Ensuring resilient domestic petroleum production, refining, and logistics capacity is central to United States defense readiness,” the memo reads. “Without immediate Federal action, United States defense capabilities will remain vulnerable to disruption.”
The memo comes as the price of gas and diesel has soared across the country amid supply disruptions caused by the U.S. and Israel’s war against Iran. Brent crude futures rose 1.2% to $114.47 a barrel early Friday, extending gains after Thursday hit a five-month high. U.S. diesel pump prices averaged $6.32 a gallon, slightly higher than Thursday but below the September record, according to AAA. The high energy prices, and related inflation, have become a defining issue for voters in the coming midterm elections.
Here’s what to know.
What does the memo mean for energy production?
The memo means that energy production shortfalls are seen as a national defense risk.
The memo invokes Section 303 of the Defense Production Act, a law that allows the federal government to intervene in private industry for national defense. Section 303 allows the President to make purchases, purchase commitments, provide financial support and equipment, and expand production through other measures.
The memorandum also removes certain Section 303 requirements through an emergency waiver, including ordinary congressional notification and authorization constraints.
While the memo does not specify which projects could be funded, Vice President J.D. Vance said last week that the Administration would use the Defense Production Act to expand capacity at a Delek U.S. Holdings-owned refinery in Texas.
Without taking action, the memo said, U.S. industry would be unable to provide sufficient energy services in a “timely manner due to constrained financing, long lead times, permitting and infrastructure bottlenecks, and supply chain limitations.”
Has the Defense Production Act been invoked before?
Enacted during the Korean War, the Defense Production Act was first used to expand domestic industries in critical materials, such as aluminum and titanium, for national defense.
Section 303 of the act was also used during the pandemic to fund domestic production of medicines and vaccines. Former President Joe Biden also invoked the statute to support clean energy manufacturing and supply chains, including minerals used in electric vehicle batteries and the production of of energy-efficient heat pumps and insulation.
In April, more than a month after Iran began disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz in retaliation for U.S.-Israeli Feb. 28 strikes, Trump invoked the act to declare petroleum, natural gas, coal, electricity grid, and other energy infrastructure essential to national defense. Citing April’s natural gas determination, the Department of Energy on Monday committed up to $42 million to advance the proposed Constitution Pipeline linking Pennsylvania and New York. The department also announced up to $50 million last week for transmission upgrades in Virginia and West Virginia, citing April’s grid determination.
Last year, Trump signed legislation providing $1 billion for Defense Production Act activities, including energy projects deemed critical to national security.
Trump’s use of Section 303 of the act for fossil fuel projects has drawn criticisms from environmentalists, with the Center for Biological Diversity calling the April memoranda, which waived congressional notification, “unlawful.” Nevertheless, the statute expressly includes energy production and construction in its definition of national defense.
How else has Trump tried to lower energy prices?
The Trump Administration has pursued a number of other measures aimed at lowering energy prices since the Iran War began. Earlier this month, Trump signed an executive order temporarily expanding access to tax-exempt dyed diesel, which is typically reserved for off-road farm and construction vehicles. The Group of 7 countries, including the U.S., also agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil reserves to the world over four months.
In August, the Administration extended the Jones Act waiver for another 90 days, allowing foreign-flagged ships to transport oil and certain other commodities between U.S. ports.
Trump also announced an agreement with Putin earlier this month to import diesel from Russia, alongside temporary sanctions relief. The deal has faced significant backlash from lawmakers.
For many of these measures, industry analysts and stakeholders have said the reduction in energy prices is likely to be limited and possibly short-lived. Analysts estimated that the Jones Act waiver was expected to reduce gasoline prices by only pennies per gallon. Capital Economics economist Hamad Hussain said the reserve release could lower diesel prices temporarily, but would not resolve the underlying supply crunch. And analysts warned that the dyed diesel measure would have a limited effect on most consumers since the tax-exempt fuel isn’t widely available at ordinary commercial pumps. A Council on Foreign Relations analysis also suggested that damaged Russian refining capacity may make a near-term effect of the Russia deal on diesel markets unlikely, although Trump said the agreement would supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to U.S. and global markets immediately.
Meanwhile, oil exports from the Middle East topped prewar levels last week, marking a rebound in regional oil shipments despite continuing security risks. Ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz, however, still face attacks from Iran, while the Bab el-Mandeb Strait near Yemen has been threatened by the Houthi rebels. Analysts previously told TIME in June that the risk of further attacks and damage to facilities could delay a full-scale recovery.
Thursday’s memorandum could support investment in fuel capacity, but it’s uncertain how quick or measurable an effect it will have on energy prices. Gas prices still depend heavily on globally traded crude, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, although they can be influenced by domestic refining and distribution conditions. The U.S. was the largest crude producer globally last year, averaging 13.6 million barrels of crude a day.
Analysts warned, after the April memorandum, that federal support would not necessarily translate into immediate price relief.
“Until the pipes are in the ground and the fuel is flowing or transported, it may not be able to be called a true structural shift,” Cyrus Brooks, director of marketing at energy research firm RBAC, wrote in April.
Still, Brooks said of the April action that federal recognition of energy as important to national security could support important infrastructure investment, potentially relieving a bottleneck in domestic fuel production, refining or transportation.
“Energy security seems to be the brightest neon sign flashing,” he wrote. “Not because it’s everything, but because nothing works without it.”

A Dating App Is Offering ‘Chivalry Mode’ and ‘Marriage Timeline’ to Get Gen Z Married
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:15:00 UTC
19:15:00 KST

When Adreanna Pulliam signed up for the Christian dating app Upward over the summer, she was prepared to come across men who identified as hyperconservative.
So when she swiped on a guy’s profile that listed “a progressive donkey or a ‘Trump is King’ elephant” as his relationship deal-breaker, she was shocked. “I hadn’t expected to see a moderate libertarian” on the app, she says.
It only got more bizarre from there. There was the guy advertising his Snapchat with the username “Yaboi Blaze reallysexgod.” Another dater, for reasons she still can’t fathom, included a photo of him at a funeral, standing in front of a poster-size image of the deceased.
While Pulliam was apprehensive about the prospects, she wanted to see how different Upward, one of the lesser-known apps in Match Group’s sprawling portfolio of dating platforms, was from Hinge and Tinder. She hadn’t had much luck with either of them. Many of the profiles she encountered on Upward, she tells WIRED, were “MAGA types of men” who “fit more of that red-pill, trad wife, conservative values” category of dater.
A 25-year-old opera singer in Bloomington, Indiana, for whom marriage has always been “the end goal,” Pulliam is the kind of person Upward is trying to appeal to since relaunching last month.
The relaunch was redesigned around two key data points from Match Group’s 2026 Singles in America study: 72 percent of Gen Zs want to get married, and a quarter of singles aged 18 to 34 “identify with a combination of traditional values around family, faith, and community,” a news release about the survey noted.
The pivot away from an app exclusively for Christian daters was about opening up its doors for people “who share those same goals, but may not lead with a faith-first mindset,” says Lauren DeFord, director of brand marketing at Match, of the app’s new focus on Gen Z singles.
Upward’s expansion is representative of the ongoing change in the dating market. Dwindling engagement and the introduction of AI have pushed companies to reassess user growth. For some, that means abandoning their original mission.
Upward, which runs on a tiered subscription, works similarly to Tinder. You can swipe left or right on profiles, and users are encouraged to include a Faith Statement on their page, explaining what they value most about their relationship to God. Among its new features are Chivalry Mode, which, if you’re familiar with how Bumble used to operate, persuades men to message first, and Marriage Timeline, which lets daters share when they hope to get married with potential suitors.
But while a marriage-focused app like Upward may be tapping into a genuine desire for commitment, that doesn’t mean young people are returning to traditional relationship norms en masse, says Daniel Cox, author of Generation Uncoupled: America’s New Gender Divide and the Crisis of Human Connection. In fact, the opposite is happening.
In his book, Cox argues that Gen Z is entering adulthood with a less clear sense of their “relational priorities,” and a decline in social and civic life has given rise to a “hyperindividualistic culture” that doesn’t always prioritize things like marriage. As a result, fewer Gen Zs are coupling up today. An American Institute for Boys and Men survey found that 44 percent of Gen Z men have had no relationship experience at all during their teen years, double the rate for older men. “This movement makes it a lot harder to ... want to sacrifice and to be there for someone,” he says.
Upward’s relaunch framed the app as the “home of modern courtship,” including video testimonials of singles who’d found love on the app. But aesthetically, there wasn’t anything “modern” about its promotional rollout. In one video, newly married Zach donned a cowboy hat and blue jeans, doing all the things men should presumably do for their significant others: gift them flowers, carry her through a meadow, open the car door. A bold text overlay on the video read “chivalrymaxxing.” According to the company, branding was inspired by an “Americana” theme, and its “Wanted: For Life” campaign draws on Western-style imagery.
Cox, who is the director of the Survey Center on American Life, is convinced that the trad trend is “a reaction to the lack of cultural norms around courtship. People are wanting something over nothing,” he says, adding that daters are desperate for “a script” with direction and defined roles, given how nontraditional approaches to partnership, such as polyamory and relationship anarchy, are increasing among young people. “And something that’s nice about the trad script is it’s very clear. Though I don’t think it’s close to ideal for a lot of young people.”
A 2023 Pew Research survey found that only 23 percent of adults considered being married “extremely” or “very important” to living a fulfilling life, compared with 61 percent who said the same about having close friends. In the last 30 years, the percentage of high school seniors who said they were likely to marry someday had fallen from 80 percent in 1993 to 67 percent in 2023, according to Pew. The decline was driven mostly by changing views among young women who, despite the portion of married adults slightly increasing from 50 percent to 51 percent between 2019 to 2023, remain more likely than men to be unpartnered.
The trend is likely to continue in that direction. “There’s increasingly a belief among young women that marriage makes them less happy,” Cox says. “So it’s not only that they have less of a desire to get married. There’s a concern that if they get married, they won’t be as happy as if they are single. That seems like a view that is potentially not going to change.”
Upward, which declined to share information regarding the number of active users on the platform, is betting that it will.
When setting up her account, Pulliam was baffled to find out that Upward let users list their body type, ranging from “fit” and “curvy” to “chubby,” a feature typically reserved for hookup apps. She was also confused that Upward allows married people on the app. Some of the stranger options for relationship type included “it’s complicated” and “I’m not into labels.” “I’m not knocking open relationships or anything like that, but it was interesting to see such a progressive take from a more of a conservative demographic,” she says.
Tauti, a social work student who lives in California, lasted less than 48 hours on the app, disturbed by the overwhelming conservative majority looking for domesticated partners. Sometimes the hook with mission-specific apps like Upward is that the religious identity associated with the platform can create an assumption of compatibility before users have really gotten to know one another. “I did not know me being Christian and leaning liberal was a big ask,” she said on TikTok. “It’s turned me off from Christian dating altogether.”
Some users believe the recent pivot is diluting the experience for daters who joined seeking out people with purely Christian beliefs. “Why are you on there if you’re agnostic?” Heidi Marais, a teacher and single mom, asked on TikTok in September. “And Upward, why is it an option?”
DeFord, who maintains that Christian singles remain at the core of Upward’s mission despite describing the relaunch as a “brand shift,” pushes back against the assertion that the experience is worsening. “Those users can still interact and match with people who share the same denomination, the same religious views, the same cadence of how they like to practice.”
Since its debut in 2020, Upward has struggled with various hiccups that include everything from functionality issues to user perception. Many reviews in the Apple App Store complain of terrible user support, poor filtering features, and automatic bans, with one user calling the app “janky as hell.”
Cox notes there is ample reason to be wary of Match’s claim that a majority of Gen Z want to get married. Given that Gen Z is younger, it is likely that more people have never tied the knot. “So if they’re comparing Gen Z to millennials or Gen Xers in the survey, it could be that they have already been in relationships, maybe even divorced, so they are not as eager to get married again.” Match’s survey, which the company says is “demographically representative” of the US Census, sampled 5,000 US singles over the age of 18 who were not married, living with a partner, or in a committed relationship. In any case, Cox says, the “norm around what is the ideal age to get married” has vanished.
Pulliam still wants to get hitched but doesn’t consider it a priority right now. She attended a Christian college and recognizes the potential for Upward to be a hit “within communities of Christian private universities,” she says. “But I think the only way that the app works is for maybe someone who has a little bit more of a closed mind.”

Saudi missile plant expansion may produce more powerful missiles, study says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Saudi Arabia expanding missile plant to build bigger weapons, satellite image researchers believe
- Saudi Arabia appears to be expanding its al-Duwadimi missile plant, with satellite images showing new casting pits and storage buildings for larger solid-fuel missiles.
- US researchers said the work could help Riyadh build longer-range or heavier weapons, boost defence against Iran, and widen its role in the Yemen conflict.
- The move may deepen fears of missile proliferation and increase US political opposition to a Saudi nuclear deal, while the plant could be ready by year-end.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - Saudi Arabia appears to be expanding its ballistic missile factory to build larger solid-fuel missiles that could fly farther or carry heavier payloads, according to two US researchers who analysed more than a year of commercial satellite images.
More capable missiles could help Saudi Arabia to deter attacks by Iran and make its military more self-reliant, while possibly strengthening its position in a deadly conflict with Yemen’s Tehran-backed Houthi fighters.
But they risk fuelling a regional missile race and could deepen opposition in the US Congress to a US-Saudi civilian nuclear agreement that has already raised concerns about proliferation.
Satellite company Planet Labs, based in the US, took images of the al-Duwadimi complex about 200km west of Riyadh between April 2025 and September 2026.
The two researchers, Sam Lair and Michael Duitsman of the Foreign Policy Research Institute, assessed that those images show a new building that houses casting pits - wells in which a mixture of fuel ingredients is poured into missile motor casings and allowed to harden.
The Saudi embassy and Information Ministry did not respond to requests for comment.
The building, flanked by what appear to be walls to protect nearby structures from accidental explosions, is at least twice as large as the one believed to house the plant’s existing casting pits, Lair and Duitsman said in their assessment.
The Foreign Policy Research Institute (FPRI) is a non-partisan research organisation in Philadelphia.
A second new building could be used to store fuel ingredients or finished missile components, they said.
The imagery “suggests that Saudi Arabia is expanding the infrastructure at the missile production complex, likely to produce larger missiles which could deliver larger payloads or reach longer ranges,” they wrote.
Militaries favour solid-fuel missiles because they can be stored for long periods and launched more quickly than liquid-fuel systems.
Lair and Duitsman and experts from the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) and the CNA research and analysis organisation told Reuters that the makeup of Saudi Arabia’s missile force suggests that the al-Duwadimi complex relies on Chinese technology.
Lair and Duitsman said that its characteristics also are similar to Chinese missile plants.
Saudi Arabia secretly acquired about 40 liquid-fuel DF-3 ballistic missiles from China in 1987, according to a 1991 declassified CIA estimate. It displayed two of them for the first time in an April 2014 military parade, according to a Youtube video and photographs of the event.
The FPRI team also recently identified from social media videos and photos what they assessed was the wreckage in Yemen of a Saudi-fired Chinese-designed DF-15 missile.
Lair said the kingdom may now be producing the solid-fuel DF-15, and that the expansion of a1-Dumadimi is likely for the production of the longer-range DF-21 or a similar missile.
Riyadh is believed to have turned to Beijing because Washington has long restricted exports of longer-range missile systems.
The Chinese embassy and defence ministry did not respond to requests for comment.
The CIA declined to comment.
The White House did not respond to a request for comment.
Missiles would alter balance of power
Sascha Bruchmann, a research fellow at IISS, said longer-range missiles would allow Saudi Arabia to strike Iran without risking its US-supplied F-15 jet fighters against Iranian air defences.
“You’d want a system to threaten whatever is holy to Tehran... if you don’t have the political will to send an F-15 with JDAMs over Tehran,” said Bruchmann, referring to US-made satellite-guided bombs.
“Iran has a lead because its missiles and drones can strike Saudi wherever it wants. The Saudis could close that capability gap a bit.”
Bruchmann, who reviewed the FPRI analysis at Reuters request, concurred that the expansion of al-Duwadimi could be for producing more powerful solid-fuel missiles.
Janes, the defence intelligence company, also reviewed it and said the buildings “may suggest an effort to expand production capability or support the development of longer-range missiles.”
Saudi Arabia’s apparent pursuit of more powerful missiles comes as other Gulf powers are also seeking to expand their offensive and defensive arsenals, said Decker Eveleth, a CNA analyst who has been tracking the al-Duwadimi construction with commercial satellite imagery and concurred with the FPRI assessment.
“This is being replicated across the Middle East,” he said.
“You see exactly the same thing happening in the UAE. You see the exact same thing happening in Turkey. Everybody is doing this now.”
The expansion of al-Duwadimi could have political consequences in the US by stiffening bipartisan congressional opposition to a US-Saudi agreement under which the US would help Riyadh establish uranium enrichment for power generation.
Opponents say that the deal lacks sufficient safeguards to prevent Riyadh from secretly building a nuclear weapon. The kingdom has denied any such plan.
Work on the plant began in 2025
The FPRI assessment said the Planet Labs imagery showed that the expansion at al-Duwadimi began in April 2025 with ground-clearing and digging for the suspected storage building. Work on the suspected casting-pit building began later that month or in early May, it said.
A Dec 12, 2025, photo showed what researchers assessed were two deep pits inside the building that had no roof yet.
A Sept 18, 2026, photo shows the roof still partly missing and “heavy duty blast diverting walls” on either side to prevent accidental explosions from damaging adjacent structures.
The walls, the researchers said, are somewhat similar to those depicted in imagery of US and Iranian missile plants and “further evidence the building is for casting solid propellant motors.”
Finishing the roofs would not take long, the FPRI said, but installing casting equipment may take several months. The facility could be ready to start producing missiles as early as the end of the year. REUTERS

Scientists discover a surprising double benefit of exercise for Parkinson’s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:10:11 UTC
19:10:11 KST

Scientists discover a surprising double benefit of exercise for Parkinson’s
- Date:
- October 23, 2026
- Source:
- American Academy of Neurology
- Summary:
- A seven-year study found that people with Parkinson’s disease who were more physically active experienced slower declines in memory, thinking, and movement abilities. Those exercising more than eight hours per week showed almost no average cognitive decline, suggesting that staying active may offer important benefits as the disease progresses.
- Share:
People with Parkinson's disease who are more physically active may experience slower declines in memory, thinking, and movement, according to a new study published October 7, 2026, in Neurology, the official medical journal of the American Academy of Neurology.
The findings suggest that staying active could offer two important advantages for people living with Parkinson's. However, researchers emphasize that the study identified a connection between physical activity and slower symptom progression. It does not establish that exercise directly causes the disease to progress more slowly.
"Parkinson's disease is a brain disorder that causes movement and cognitive problems that gradually worsen leading to disability and a loss of independence," said study author Dong-Woo Ryu, MD, PhD, of the University of Cincinnati in Ohio. "Previous research has shown associations between physical activity and movement symptoms. Our study found physical activity may have dual benefits, with associations with slower declines in movement and cognition."
Tracking Exercise and Parkinson's Symptoms Over Seven Years
The research involved 294 adults with mild to moderate Parkinson's disease. Participants were 66 years old on average, and researchers monitored their health for up to seven years.
To understand their activity habits, participants completed questionnaires estimating how many hours each week they spent being physically active. The questions covered activities performed at work, around the home, and during hobbies or recreation.
Researchers classified activities by their intensity. Moderate activities included brisk walking, doubles tennis, leisurely swimming, and household tasks such as cleaning windows, vacuuming, or mowing the lawn. More demanding activities included running, cycling at higher speeds, participating in team sports, playing singles tennis, shoveling, and carrying heavy objects.
The team examined physical activity in three ways. First, they calculated the total time participants spent doing moderate or vigorous activities. Second, they estimated overall activity volume by combining duration with intensity, giving greater weight to strenuous exercise. Third, they separately measured the amount of time spent doing vigorous activities.
Based on total weekly activity time, participants were placed into three categories. Those in the least active group reported up to four hours per week, the moderately active group reported four to eight hours, and the most active group reported more than eight hours.
Each year, participants also completed assessments designed to track changes in thinking and memory, along with tests evaluating the severity of their Parkinson's symptoms.
More Activity Linked to Slower Memory Decline
One of the most striking differences emerged in cognitive performance. Researchers used a 30-point test of thinking and memory, with lower scores reflecting poorer cognitive function.
Among participants in the least active group, scores fell by an estimated average of 0.478 points each year. The moderately active group experienced a much smaller annual decline of 0.090 points.
For the most active participants, the estimated average yearly decrease was only 0.007 points, indicating that their cognitive scores remained nearly unchanged over time.
The researchers also examined changes in Parkinson's movement symptoms using an assessment scored from zero to 132. Higher numbers represented more severe symptoms, and participants began the study with an average score of 23.
In the least active group, symptom scores increased by an estimated 0.143 points annually, indicating a slight worsening. By contrast, scores decreased by 0.225 points per year in the moderately active group and by 0.783 points in the most active group.
Even after accounting for participants' age, sex, and how long they had been living with Parkinson's, the researchers found that the most active group experienced slower cognitive decline and less worsening of movement symptoms than the least active group.
The connection was not limited to one measure of exercise. Higher total activity time, greater overall activity volume, and more time spent exercising vigorously were each associated with slower deterioration in both thinking abilities and movement symptoms.
Why Consistent Physical Activity May Matter
The results suggest that remaining physically active over time could be especially important for people with Parkinson's disease. Researchers noted that even relatively small differences in the rate of decline might become more significant when they accumulate over several years.
"The possible benefits of physical activity for people with Parkinson's disease may depend on how long they stay active and whether they continue exercising over time," said Ryu. "While our study found small differences between activity levels, these differences may become more meaningful over time. Since participants generally had good thinking and memory skills at the start of the study, our results should be interpreted with caution and further studies are needed."
The researchers also identified an important limitation. Physical activity levels were based on participants' own reports rather than direct measurements, meaning some estimates may have been inaccurate.
Although the findings strengthen the evidence connecting physical activity with better long-term outcomes in Parkinson's disease, additional research will be needed to determine whether exercise itself can slow the progression of symptoms.
Funding for the study came from a grant provided by the Gardner Family Foundation and the Precision Medicine in Neurodegenerative Diseases Fund.

MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. Russian specialists have created the Titan advanced robotic demining system, the system’s developer told TASS.
"To address the challenge of clearing mine and explosive obstacles using robotic systems amid the enemy’s widespread use of anti-personnel mines and improvised explosive devices in the special military operation zone, the latest robotic demining system, Titan, has been developed. The use of electric motors, a low-profile design, and all-round fragmentation protection against all known performed fragments of anti-personnel engineering munitions ensure stealth during missions and the necessary survivability. The system has increased blast resistance. According to our information, there are no counterparts with comparable quality of equipment and protection being used on either side of the line of contact," a company representative stated.
The system is designed to clear a continuous route through anti-personnel minefields by sweeping away the main types of anti-personnel mines. "The Titan enables the sweeping of mines equipped with pressure-action, pull-action, and break-wire target-sensors," he noted.
He specified that the system has successfully completed testing and is expected to be deployed in the special military operation zone. "Work is currently underway to improve the level of protection, add new controls, and refine the design of the sweeping equipment," he added.
The system’s total weight is 2.3 metric tons, and its payload capacity is one ton. "The Titan’s maximum speed with the sweeping equipment is seven km/h, and without it - 14 km/h. The system is capable of operating autonomously for at least 3.5 hours. The sweep width is two meters. If necessary, the Titan can be equipped with electronic warfare capabilities. The system’s control range depends on the type of communication used but is at least 500 meters," the developer added.

Foreign diplomats in Brazil discuss quick recognition of runoff winner
Unknown

Foreign diplomats in Brazil discuss quick recognition of runoff winner
BRASÍLIA, Oct 23 - Foreign diplomats in Brasilia are discussing a rapid recognition of whoever wins Sunday's presidential runoff, four ambassadors told Reuters, seeking to ward off any attempts from outside the country to call the election prematurely for either candidate.
However, they have yet to formalize a plan, with multiple missions still in discussion with their capitals on how best to proceed, the sources said.
Right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, former President Jair Bolsonaro's son, holds a small but narrowing lead in polls over leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
Two ambassadors told Reuters that they are worried that US President Donald Trump, or his administration, might question the result if Lula wins by a small margin.
"It wouldn’t surprise me if Trump or (right-wing Argentine President Javier) Milei declare Bolsonaro the winner before electoral authorities do,” said one ambassador, who worried such a scenario could provoke a major institutional crisis.
The ambassador, who spoke on condition of anonymity given the sensitivity of the subject, said they were not involved in discussions with other governments.
The State Department and US Embassy in Brasilia did not respond to questions on whether Trump would commit to recognizing the runoff's winner as confirmed by Brazil's electoral tribunal.
The tribunal did not reply to a request for comment.
One ambassador said their concern about Trump comes after the US leader's comments on recent elections in Latin America, including Honduras’ 2025 presidential election. Amid delays in that vote count, Trump alleged fraud without providing evidence and said there would be "hell to pay" if Honduras changed preliminary results that had put his preferred candidate ahead.
A premature recognition from Trump or someone else “could lead to an institutional crisis that nobody wants," the ambassador said.
'FAITH IN THE BRAZILIAN SYSTEM'
Memories are still fresh from Brazil's 2022 election, when foreign governments, including the United States, the European Union, and many Latin American countries, played an important role recognizing in Lula’s win over former President Bolsonaro, who refused to concede for days.
The elder Bolsonaro received a 27-year-sentence for plotting a coup after his 2022 election loss lead to his supporters violently storming the capital.
"Our main objective is to recognize the outcome of an election that we expect to be held according to good standards. We have faith in the Brazil voting system," one European ambassador told Reuters, adding that "speed is the main concern."
Bolsonaro finished ahead of Lula in the election's first round on October 4, which sent markets soaring on optimism that he was well positioned to win and push through tough economic reforms that favor business with the help of a new Congress packed with allies.
Bolsonaro holds a small lead over Lula in polling heading into the runoff, but polls suggest it is narrowing as the vote approaches.
“If Lula wins, particularly by a small margin, it’s inevitable that at least some will say that the vote was somehow rigged in his favor,” said one ambassador, who said the hypothetical scenario increases the pressure on Brazilian electoral authorities and international observers to quickly confirm the vote’s outcome.
Oliver Stuenkel, a professor at Sao Paulo’s Getulio Vargas Foundation, said a Trump refusal to quickly recognize a Lula victory would be a nadir in bilateral ties.
“I think that is a scenario that one has to keep on the radar," he said.
Ambassadors expressed faith in Brazil’s electoral process and institutions, and said concerns were not about any single candidate but about possible election denialism affecting declining confidence in Brazil’s democratic institutions.
“I don’t care if Lula or Bolsonaro wins,” one ambassador said. “I do care about the shape of Brazilian democracy after this election.” REUTERS

Black Sea: Drone Strike Sinks Ship off Romania, Leaving One Dead and Three Missing (UPDATED)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:06:00 UTC
19:06:00 KST

The merchant ship Khoryv, flying the Comoros flag, was reportedly struck by a drone and caught fire before sinking about 13 nautical miles off Romania’s Black Sea port of Constanța, leaving one sailor dead, three missing and nine rescued.
The vessel had 13 people on board: 10 Ukrainian citizens and three Azerbaijani citizens, according to Romanian naval authorities. The Maritime Coordination Center received the ship’s distress signal at around 10 a.m., prompting Romanian authorities to launch a rescue operation.
The Romanian Naval Authority is coordinating the response, with the Coast Guard and the Romanian Agency for the Rescue of Human Life at Sea taking part. Rescue vessels have been sent to the area to search for the three missing sailors.
Authorities also requested a Black Hawk helicopter, but heavy rain and unfavorable weather conditions near Constanța prevented it from reaching the scene.
Romanian authorities have not yet established the definitive cause of the incident. Initial reports indicate that the Khoryv was hit by a drone, which sparked a fire on board. The ship was outside Romania’s territorial waters but close to the country’s maritime border, Digi24 reported. The origin of the suspected drone has not been confirmed.
The specialized website VesselFinder identifies the Khoryv as a 43-year-old ore-oil carrier built in 1983. The vessel had departed from the Turkish port of Ereğli and was heading toward Sulina, where it was scheduled to arrive on October 23 at around 11 p.m. Its last recorded Automatic Identification System (AIS) position was in the Black Sea.
The incident adds to a series of attacks on merchant vessels in the western Black Sea in recent weeks. Rear Admiral (Ret.) Sorin Learski told Digi24 that such attacks pose security risks and have economic consequences, affecting the insurance market and trade through the Port of Constanța.
Learski said the vessel’s proximity to the Romanian coast was an additional cause for concern, highlighting the need for stronger protection of commercial shipping and anti-drone systems.
The incident followed a meeting of Romania’s Supreme Council for National Defense, which discussed threats arising from the changing security situation in the Black Sea, Romania’s readiness to respond, the protection of maritime borders and the security of critical infrastructure.
About 10 days earlier, another commercial vessel flying the Comoros flag was struck by a drone near Sulina.

Swiss government accepts it could have handled F-35 procurement better
Following criticism of the alleged fixed price for the F-35 fighter jets, the governing Federal Council has accepted six out of seven recommendations made by the parliamentary oversight body. At the same time, it has rejected the accusation that the US contracts had scarcely been read.
In its statement published on Friday, the government announced measures in response to criticism of the F-35 procurement. In future, defence procurement is to be conducted more transparently, risk management is to be improved, and the legal department of the Federal Office for Defence Procurement (Armasuisse) is to be strengthened.
At the same time, the Federal Council has rejected allegations that the contracts were barely scrutinised. It regrets the impression that only the then project manager had read the contracts in full. In addition to the former head of armaments, other Armasuisse experts had studied the texts in their entirety, whilst the defence ministry and former Defence Minister Viola Amherd, had examined the pricing clauses in depth.
More
Renewed controversy in Switzerland over US fighter jets – explained
In September, the parliamentary oversight body had criticised the fact that the promised fixed price for the jets had never materialised. Defence Minister Martin Pfister had previously admitted that the funds would probably only be sufficient for 30 fighter jets rather than 36. Parliament recently approved a supplementary credit of CHF394 million ($476 million).

Pope Leo XIV will skip an interfaith peace gathering in the Italian town of Assisi next week as he continues recovering from lung cancer surgery, with doctors advising him against the helicopter journey from the Vatican.
The 71-year-old pope had been scheduled to attend Tuesday's event, titled “Disarmed and Disarming Peace,” which marks the 40th anniversary of a landmark interfaith prayer meeting convened by St. John Paul II in 1986.
The Vatican said Friday that a follow-up chest X-ray showed Leo was recovering well, but his medical team recommended avoiding the trip as a precaution because of the short time since his operation.
Instead, Leo will send a message to organizers, religious leaders and other participants, expressing his support for the gathering and reaffirming the importance of dialogue and peaceful coexistence amid ongoing conflicts.
The meeting brings together representatives of different faiths to pray for peace and renew the spirit of the 1986 gathering. Assisi, the birthplace of St. Francis of Assisi, has long served as a symbol of interfaith dialogue.
The cancellation is the latest adjustment to Leo's schedule following surgery last week to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, where doctors had found a malignant nodule. Tests confirmed adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer.
The Vatican said subsequent examinations found that the cancer was localized and that Leo would not need further treatment. His activities, however, will continue to be guided by medical advice as he recovers.
Leo returned to the Vatican on Saturday after the operation. Although he has appeared in good health during public appearances since his return, speaking clearly and with a strong voice, doctors are taking precautions while his lungs heal.
The decision to avoid the Assisi trip also comes as the pope prepares for a planned visit to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from Nov. 6 to 17. The trip is expected to involve about a dozen flights and two helicopter rides to high-altitude destinations.
His surgeon previously said there were no clinical reasons to rule out the Latin American journey. Thoracic surgeons often advise patients to avoid flying for about three weeks after lung surgery, a recovery period that would leave Leo little margin before his scheduled departure.
The Vatican said the pope remains close to those attending the Assisi gathering and believes its message is particularly relevant at a time of international conflict.
