Train Scots workers to seize defence billions, says Marra
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:00:59 BST
19:00:59 KST

Billions of pounds of defence investment heading for Scotland will only translate into skilled jobs if colleges, employers and councils are handed the power to decide what training their local economies need, according to the Scottish Labour leader.
Michael Marra made the argument during a visit to Babcock’s Rosyth yard, where the Royal Navy’s five Type 31 frigates are being built, and said the centralised approach taken at Holyrood had failed. He called for regional leaders to be given greater powers to bring colleges, employers and training providers together so that people are equipped with the skills industry actually wants.
He said: “Scotland has world-class shipyards, outstanding engineering expertise and the talent to lead the next generation of British industry.
“Here at Rosyth, Babcock is building the next generation of Royal Navy frigates. Across Scotland, billions of pounds of defence investment offer a huge opportunity to create skilled jobs, strengthen our industrial base and open up new careers for young people.
“But investment alone is not enough. We must make sure people in our communities have the skills to take advantage of these opportunities.
“In this area Holyrood’s centralised approach to skills has failed. We need to hand over power to local people and communities.
“Local colleges, employers and councils can work together to train people for the jobs their local economies actually need.
“Decisions about the skills needed in our shipyards, our energy industry and our advanced manufacturing sector should be shaped by the people who understand those industries best.
“There are billions of pounds of investment on the table here. Scottish workers should be given the skills to grab it. Let’s turn that investment into opportunity: good jobs, stronger local economies and a new generation of skilled workers building Scotland’s future.”
The figures published alongside the visit show apprenticeship starts by people aged sixteen to twenty four in Scotland falling from 20,506 in 2015/16 to 13,891 in 2025/26, a drop of more than six thousand, or 32 per cent. Starts in the twenty to twenty four bracket are down 41 per cent, from 7,669 to 4,491, and the sixteen to nineteen bracket is down 27 per cent, from 12,837 to 9,400. Starts by people aged twenty five and over more than doubled over the same period, rising from 5,312 to 10,958. Scottish Labour took the numbers from Scottish Government modern apprenticeship supplementary tables for the fourth quarter of 2025/26, and said one in six young people in Scotland is not in education, training or employment.
The Type 31 programme supports around two and a half thousand skilled jobs across Scotland and the wider United Kingdom supply chain, including four hundred apprenticeships. A shortage of trained welders in Scotland has meant Babcock using workers from overseas, the party said.
Marra’s call follows the commitment of £6 billion to three new floating docks for the submarine service at His Majesty’s Naval Base Clyde, work that has been reserved for British shipyards, alongside wider investment in maritime industries. Babcock is building five Type 31 frigates at Rosyth under a contract worth around £1.25 billion, based on the Iver Huitfeldt design, with the first of class named HMS Venturer.

snøhetta and barth create six spaces for exploration at le rosey boarding school
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:00:49 UTC
19:00:49 KST

snøhetta and barth create six spaces for exploration at le rosey boarding school
the renowned swiss boarding school works with barth to create learning spaces that depart from the conventional classroom.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
Le Rosey creates new spaces to learn
A glance at the new rooms at Swiss boarding school Le Rosey inevitably brings back memories of childhood mornings. For much of Western society, those long days unfolded in monotonous, almost institutional spaces that could have been photocopies of the school next door, were it not for the occasional murals a teacher with a creative itch had insisted on using to decorate the classroom.
Le Rosey’s students already experienced a somewhat different environment before this intervention. Founded in Rolle in 1880, it is Switzerland’s oldest and largest boarding school and one of Europe’s most famous. Its 450 students, drawn from more than 70 countries, experience an educational model known for its progressive learning methods. The recent transformation of six of its rooms is proof of this.
all images @ tobias kaser
An architectural statement of intent
The school’s commitment to fostering creativity, collaboration and discovery as ways of learning is amplified in its Impact Space, an environment created to nurture entrepreneurial thinking and encourage meaningful contributions to the wider world. It is here that Snøhetta has designed six new spaces with the collaboration of barth.
Each space focuses on a way of learning. Conceived as immersive environments with personalities of their own, the rooms invite exploration, reflection or dialogue through their names, chosen color palettes and textures, and furniture arrangements.
challenge of creating six rooms in historic boarding school
The starting point was a series of structurally irregular spaces with barely any parallel walls. Collaboration with barth, which engineered, manufactured and installed the custom joinery for each space, was essential to realizing the architects’ vision.
Throughout the process, the company and the architects worked together to resolve the unforeseen challenges posed by the original spaces, finding innovative solutions to bring the products of Snøhetta’s imagination to life.
The first room in this ecosystem is the Knowledge Room. Inspired by a forest and centered on self-directed discovery as a learning method, the room is dotted with inclined, tree-like columns that incorporate bookshelves, seating and displays through cantilevered platforms.
Next is the Actis Virtus Room, which reimagines the Harkness method, an approach to learning through discussion on equal terms. Dominated by a large oval table, the room features an overhead structure that mirrors the table’s shape, integrates lighting and supports seats that hang like swings.
The Rooted in Peace Room, meanwhile, draws inspiration from a Japanese tea house to encourage introspection, while the Reflection Room, with mirrored surfaces that return distorted images, invites users to look beyond tangible reality.
In the Curiosity Room, an S-shaped curtain system plays with the concept of privacy by revealing and concealing different areas. Finally, the Unafraid to Be Room offers a small, immersive amphitheater in which to practice public speaking.
How the project’s challenges were resolved
To realize the architects’ vision, barth took responsibility for almost all the custom-built interior elements, providing an unusual degree of flexibility that allowed an abstract, creative idea to become a tangible project.
Each of the six rooms presented its own challenge, and all required technical solutions tailored to their particular characteristics. In the Knowledge Room, for example, surfaces had to withstand substantial loads while appearing exceptionally light; in the Actis Virtus Room, the suspended chairs were a feat of design; and in the Curiosity Room, extensive technical coordination made it possible to support heavy fabric from only a few attachment points.
The greatest challenge, however, was the Unafraid to Be Room. Central to the concept was the creation of a fully immersive orange landscape, requiring transitions between materials to be as imperceptible as possible and construction elements to remain concealed. Together, Snøhetta and barth created a continuous surface that flows throughout the room without obvious interruptions.
From the setting to what happens within it: a space conceived to foster critical thinking, spur creativity and inspire innovative ways of learning has itself been built through a collaboration in which innovation and lateral thinking were essential. This is not a traditional classroom. Nor will it host conventional lessons. It is a new way of creating, conceived precisely to shape tomorrow’s creative minds.

LSD pushes brain activity toward a more fractal, complex state, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:00:23 UTC
19:00:23 KST

A new neuroimaging study indicates that lysergic acid diethylamide, commonly known as LSD, alters human brain activity not just by weakening regular brain waves, but also by speeding them up and making neural signals more complex. The weakening of brain waves and the rise in signal complexity were most pronounced in regions tied to sensory processing, language, emotion, and mental imagery, while areas that control physical movement were largely spared. The findings, published in Communications Biology, also hint that listening to music may dampen rather than amplify these drug-induced changes, though that trend did not hold up after statistical correction.
LSD is a potent psychedelic drug that temporarily alters perception, mood, and the sense of self. Like other classic psychedelics, it works primarily by attaching to and activating serotonin 2A receptors on brain cells, though LSD also binds to dopamine receptors. Studying how this compound changes large-scale brain activity helps scientists understand the biological processes that generate conscious experience.
In human studies, researchers often use magnetoencephalography, or MEG, to track the fast-paced electrical activity of the brain. MEG is a non-invasive procedure where a participant sits with their head inside a helmet-like scanner containing sensitive magnetic detectors. As groups of neurons fire together, they produce tiny magnetic fields that the scanner records at a millisecond-by-millisecond scale.
This electrical activity consists of two main types of signals: rhythmic brain waves and background noise. Rhythmic waves, or neural oscillations, happen when thousands of brain cells fire in a synchronized beat, much like a choir singing a specific note. Two of the most common resting rhythms are alpha waves, which cycle at about 8 to 13 times per second (measured in hertz, or Hz) during relaxed wakefulness, and beta waves, which cycle faster at 15 to 30 Hz and relate to active thinking and alertness. These rhythms ride on top of non-rhythmic, background electrical activity that naturally loses strength at higher frequencies.
Previous psychedelic studies consistently showed that drugs like LSD and psilocybin cause a widespread drop in the strength of alpha and beta waves, a process called cortical desynchronization. Because traditional brain wave analyses measure activity within fixed frequency windows, they can confuse a change in wave speed with a loss of wave strength, or mistake shifts in the background noise for changes in actual rhythms. If an alpha wave speeds up against a background that naturally falls off at higher frequencies, it can look as though the wave lost strength when it actually just shifted to a faster tempo.
Beyond brain wave speed and strength, psychedelics also change the unpredictability and structure of brain signals over time. Scientists measure this using two mathematical tools: Lempel-Ziv complexity, which counts how many new and distinct patterns appear in a signal over time, and Higuchi fractal dimension, which measures how “rough” or self-similar a signal looks when zoomed in and out across different time scales. Higher scores on both metrics indicate richer, less predictable brain activity.
The physical and social environment also plays a major role in shaping a psychedelic experience, with music frequently used in both traditional rituals and modern psychedelic-assisted therapy. For example, a study covered by PsyPost in 2018 showed that LSD heightened brain responses to music across regions tied to auditory processing, emotion, and memory. The new research was led by first author Venkatesh Subramani, who holds a doctorate in neuroscience, and senior author Karim Jerbi, a full professor in the psychology department, both of the Cognitive and Computational Neuroscience Laboratory (CoCo Lab) at the Université de Montréal. The team aimed to separate true changes in brain wave strength from shifts in wave speed and background activity, while also testing how music interacts with these electrical signatures.
“A characteristic effect of classic psychedelics is the desynchronization of rhythmic brain activity (that is, reduced coordination of activity among neural populations) in the alpha (8-13 Hz) and beta (15-30 Hz) bands,” Subramani told PsyPost. “LSD, however, appears somewhat unique because it also speeds up these intrinsic oscillations, by up to 2 Hz for alpha and up to 5 Hz for beta. This acceleration creates an ambiguity: it is unclear whether LSD genuinely desynchronizes these rhythms, or whether the previously reported desynchronization is an artifact of shifts in the spectral peaks.”
To investigate these questions, the researchers analyzed existing MEG data originally collected from 17 healthy volunteers. The experiment used a within-subject, single-blind, placebo-controlled design with a counterbalanced session order, meaning each participant completed two separate scanning sessions spaced 14 days apart without being told which treatment they were receiving. In one session, participants received an intravenous injection of 75 micrograms of LSD, and in the other, they received an inactive saline placebo.
Roughly four hours after the injection, participants underwent MEG brain scans under two different conditions, each lasting seven minutes. In the first condition, they rested with their eyes closed in silence. In the second condition, they kept their eyes closed while listening to ambient music excerpts. The research team used anatomical MRI scans of each participant’s head to map the MEG signals onto 360 distinct regions across the outer surface of the brain.
The authors then used a specialized mathematical tool to separate the rhythmic brain waves from the non-rhythmic background activity in each brain region. Instead of measuring wave strength inside rigid frequency boxes, they tracked the exact peak frequency where each participant’s alpha and beta waves were strongest. They also calculated Lempel-Ziv complexity and Higuchi fractal dimension for each region, and trained machine learning algorithms to see which brain features best distinguished the LSD state from the placebo state.
When the researchers separated the rhythmic waves from the background noise and accounted for shifting frequencies, they found that LSD still caused a genuine drop in the strength of alpha and beta waves. Alpha wave weakening was most pronounced in the temporal lobes, while beta wave weakening occurred broadly across the brain’s surface. However, ignoring the shifting frequencies made the wave weakening look much more widespread than it actually was, confirming that standard methods can inflate the apparent spatial extent of the drug’s effect.
“This study clarifies the ambiguity,” Subramani explained. “It shows that the weakening of oscillations, the usual marker of desynchronization, is genuine even after accounting for the peak shifts, a potential confound.”
Separating the signals also clarified what was happening in the posterior cingulate cortex, a major hub for self-reflection and daydreaming. In standard analyses that mix all signals together, this hub showed large drops in brain wave power under LSD. Once the background noise was removed, those rhythmic differences vanished, indicating that LSD mainly altered the background electrical activity in this region rather than its synchronized waves.
Alongside weakening the waves, LSD systematically sped them up across large portions of the brain. On average, the peak frequency of alpha waves increased by about 2 Hz, while beta wave peaks shifted upward by roughly 5 Hz. Machine learning models trained solely on these frequency shifts were able to correctly identify whether a scan came from an LSD or placebo session with over 82 percent accuracy, where chance would be 50 percent.
The background electrical activity also flattened out across the brain, meaning there was less slow background activity relative to fast activity. At the same time, both Lempel-Ziv complexity and fractal dimension rose substantially, especially in the back of the brain where visual information is processed. Machine learning decoders using these complexity and fractal measures distinguished the LSD state from placebo with over 76 percent accuracy, compared to a 50 percent chance level.
“In plain terms, LSD makes the brain’s main rhythms faster and weaker, and makes its activity more complex,” Subramani noted.
These results align with research covered by PsyPost in 2024, which examined brain activity under microdoses using EEG rather than full psychedelic doses using MEG, and similarly found that LSD increases neural signal complexity. The broader shift away from slower rhythms is also in line with a study covered by PsyPost in March 2026, which examined scalp EEG activity following psilocybin rather than source-resolved MEG following LSD and found that the drug weakened slower theta and alpha waves while strengthening faster beta and gamma activity. That study measured the strength of different frequency bands rather than the speed of individual rhythms, however, and the authors of the new paper note that a clear speeding of alpha and beta peaks has not been consistently observed with psilocybin.
To understand how these electrical changes relate to everyday mental functions, the researchers compared their brain maps against a massive database of over 14,000 prior brain imaging studies. They found that LSD’s effects followed distinct functional hierarchies across different brain systems. Reductions in alpha and beta wave strength, background flattening, and complexity increases were strongest in networks tied to vision, hearing, language, emotion, and mental imagery, while the motor cortex, which controls physical movement, remained largely unaffected.
The weakening and speeding of brain waves did not always line up. The functional systems that showed the largest drop in alpha wave strength, such as auditory and language networks, showed only minimal alpha speeding, while motor and attention networks retained relatively more of their alpha strength but showed the largest increases in alpha speed. In the beta range, the pattern reversed, with the biggest speed-ups occurring where beta strength dropped the most. Because the two effects were not statistically linked across the brain, the authors suggest that wave weakening and wave acceleration may reflect separate processes happening at the same time.
When the researchers examined the effect of music, they did not find any results that survived strict statistical corrections for multiple comparisons across the whole brain. However, uncorrected trends pointed in the opposite direction of what the team initially expected. Instead of boosting the brain effects of LSD, listening to music tended to slightly calm them down, resulting in less background flattening and lower signal complexity compared to experiencing LSD in silence.
The authors suggested that music might act as an external attentional anchor. Building on a 2024 analysis of this same dataset that found psychedelic-induced signal complexity was highest with eyes closed and dropped when attention turned outward, they propose that resting in silence allows the mind to wander freely into unconstrained internal states, whereas focusing on an external structured sound may gently ground and stabilize the brain’s electrical activity.
“Music can be very emotionally powerful, and music and psychedelics have been used together in rituals across many cultures,” Subramani said. “We wanted to formally test how music modulates the way LSD affects the brain. We hypothesized that music potentiates the effect of the drug. Somewhat surprisingly, and albeit not statistically robust, we found the opposite trend: music appeared to reduce the drug effect, which could suggest that the stimulus acts as an anchor that keeps subjects from fully experiencing the psychedelic state.”
“As noted in the paper, this is only hypothesis-generating,” he added. “It calls for studies with more subjects and targeted experimental designs with better controls.” He cautioned that “the music result is exploratory and should not be over-interpreted.”
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these results. The study relied on a relatively small sample of 17 participants, which limits the statistical power needed to detect subtle interactions between the drug and external factors like music. In addition, the MEG scans were recorded about four hours after the LSD injection, roughly two and a half hours after the drug’s subjective effects had peaked. This timing gap may explain why the researchers found few strong links between the brain measurements and participants’ questionnaire ratings.
Looking at music over a single seven-minute average also treats a dynamic song as if it were a static event. Future studies with larger groups could track how brain waves respond to changing musical moments in real time, and use muscle sensors to help rule out muscle activity as a source of the fastest brain signals. Comparing LSD directly with other psychedelics using these same signal-separation methods will also help determine whether speeding up alpha and beta rhythms is a unique signature of LSD’s pharmacology.
The team is already extending their analytical approach to see how these faster brain wave frequencies might affect other common measures of brain communication, such as functional connectivity, which tracks how closely pairs of brain regions coordinate their activity over time.
“This study shows that LSD shifts the oscillatory peaks and that there is a genuine weakening of oscillations beyond these shifts,” Subramani said. “Power is one measure that could be confounded by peak shifts. Another is functional connectivity between pairs of brain regions. We have been actively working on this, and a preprint will be out shortly!”
The study, “LSD reconfigures cortical dynamics through faster brain rhythms and increased fractal dimension,” was authored by Venkatesh Subramani, Timothy Nest, Annalisa Pascarella, Jérémy Brunel, Yorguin José Mantilla Ramos, Yann Harel, Suresh Muthukumaraswamy, Robin Carhart-Harris, Giulia Lioi, Nicolas Farrugia, and Karim Jerbi.

Governors Have an Opportunity to Give Civics Education a Badly Needed Boost
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:00:03 UTC
19:00:03 KST

Governors have no shortage of ideas about how to improve education. But before deciding what to change, they need an honest answer to a more basic question: How are our students doing?
That sounds simple. It isn’t.
We governed Tennessee at different times and from different political parties. But we learned the same lesson: you cannot improve what you are unwilling to measure honestly.
Governors will get the chance to see how students in their state are doing in a critical,often-overlooked subject: civics. But they have to sign up by the end of January to get state-level results on the National Assessment of Educational Progress civics assessment, also known as the Nation’s Report Card, or NAEP.
For newly elected governors, that will mean making a quick decision shortly after taking office. It shouldn’t be a hard one, though.
U.S. students get limited instruction, particularly in early grades, about how our government works, the rights and responsibilities of citizens, and how to apply civics knowledge beyond the classroom. Governors can help change that by prioritizing and measuring what students know and can do in civics.
What we know now is limited but concerning: only 1 in 5 eighth graders in U.S. schools reached the NAEP Proficient level on the most recent Nation's Report Card in civics, meaning the vast majority of students likely struggle to identify the separation of powers and checks and balances spelled out in the Constitution.
Unlike in subjects like reading and math, we don't have state-specific information about how our own students are doing compared to students in other states in civics. That puts leaders at a disadvantage when trying to improve schools and communities and help young people develop the civic knowledge and skills they need to excel academically, in the workforce, and in their communities.
But beginning in 2028, if they meet the January deadline, states can get state-specific results in eighth-grade civics rather than just national averages. Tennessee's academic progress over the past two decades serves as an example of why all states should capitalize on this opportunity. In 2007, Tennessee’s extremely low Nation's Report Card scores in reading and math, which contradicted our own state assessment results, served as a wake-up call. Our state got to work raising K-12 expectations, increasing the rigor of our end-of-year state tests, and improving classroom practices.
The strategy worked: Between 2011 and 2015, Tennessee became the fastest-improving state on NAEP. And progress continues. Recently, for the first time, the state ranked in the top quarter of states for reading and math achievement.
This is why we believe NAEP is a particularly valuable tool. It’s considered the gold standard in assessments and is the only common yardstick that measures student learning across the country. It lets us know whether students today are doing better or worse than kids in those same grades did two years or two decades ago and how students in our state are doing compared to other states.
We didn't always have the benefit of state-level NAEP results. NAEP didn’t produce any state-specific data at all until the 1980s, when Tennessee joined other southern states in a pilot program to determine whether valid state results could be obtained from NAEP data. That paved the way toward a federal requirement 25 years ago that results for all 50 states in 4th- and 8th-grade reading and math be reported publicly.
That was a win for states and kids. But today, we have to ask ourselves, what about those other essential things that children learn in school besides reading and math?
States now have an opportunity to answer that question in civics. We hope they'll take it. We know from experience how valuable it is to have an honest, independent measure of how students are doing. Good policy requires good information. And good leadership requires being willing to confront what that information tells us.

Corruption is voters' top issue ahead of midterm election, CNBC survey shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:00:01 UTC
19:00:01 KST

Voters are now more concerned about government corruption than any other issue, including high grocery and gas prices, according to the final CNBC All-America Economic Survey before the Nov. 3 midterm election.
The finding follows a monthslong messaging effort by Democrats to link widespread economic dissatisfaction with what they allege is rampant corruption by President Donald Trump and his Republican allies.
CNBC's survey of 1,000 registered U.S. voters found 36% of respondents pointing to government corruption as one of the most important issues facing the country right now. The cost of food and groceries came second with 34%, followed by protecting democracy and the price of gas, which garnered 23% each.
The nationwide poll, which gauged attitudes about the economy, Trump, Congress, artificial intelligence, the Iran war and more, was conducted Oct. 14-18. It was co-led by Democratic pollster Hart Research Associates and Republican pollster Public Opinion Strategies, and carries a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1 percentage points.
Read the full survey results here.
To be sure, the question asking voters to name their top concerns lists several economy- and cost-related topics separately, subdividing an issue that might otherwise rank higher if lumped into a single category.
But the results nevertheless align with other recent polls showing corruption has shot to the top of voters' list of pressing worries.
A Fox News poll published last week found 60% of registered voters are extremely concerned about government corruption, surpassing concerns about inflation and high prices. A Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll released Sunday found some two-thirds of respondents think Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself, up 10 percentage points since September 2025. Gallup recently found perceptions of government corruption in the U.S. have hit multi-decade highs. And an August poll from Reuters/Ipsos found nearly 7 in 10 Americans believe Trump's businesses influence his presidential decisions.
Republicans have also tried to seize on growing anti-corruption sentiment. The Trump administration has launched a task force led by Vice President JD Vance aimed at cracking down on fraud, while the president frequently accuses his Democratic enemies of crookery.
"I just want to say that from day one of my administration, we've waged an unprecedented war on corruption and fraud, and will not let our country be looted and plundered by thieves and pirates and foreign fraudsters and basically scum," Trump said Tuesday while unveiling a new reward program for whistleblowers.
But with Republicans in charge of the federal government — and as high costs linked to Trump's tariffs and the Iran war have put the GOP on defense — Democrats have been able to cast blame more directly.
"Americans have spent well over $100 BILLION extra on gas because Trump chose to go to war with Iran," Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., said Wednesday on X. "His ego-fueled decisions cost you thousands."
Their arguments often spotlight Trump, attempting to draw a contrast between Americans' widely felt financial struggles with the president's surging net worth, his family's lucrative business dealings and his focus on pricey construction projects.
Other Democratic candidates have widened the scope of the message, delivering a pitch that the system itself is broken.
"The problem is that the people's elected representatives don't represent the people. They represent the donors and special interests," Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., said in an April campaign video. "Corruption is why things don't work for ordinary people."
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., has hammered the claim that Republicans have betrayed their vow to bring down costs.
"The wealthy and well-connected are cashing in. What are Republicans doing to lower costs for everyone else? Absolutely nothing," Jeffries wrote Friday.
Rhetoric and results
Democrats' push appears to be resonating with voters, even as large swaths remain skeptical of both parties.
Respondents to the CNBC survey gave Democrats a 4-point edge over Republicans, 35% to 31%, when asked which party would do a better job dealing with government corruption.
But that gap grew to 17 points in Democrats' favor among voters who said corruption was their most important issue.
And independents, by a 15-point margin, said Democrats would address corruption better than Republicans – though 41% of those respondents think neither party would do a good job.
The apparent rise in concern about corruption is welcome news to critics of the president who have long lamented that Americans have become numb to scandal in the Trump era.
That shift is taking place because voters are feeling the impact of inflation and connecting it to what they see in Washington, said Brian Lemek, executive of the Democrat-backing political action committee Defend the Vote, in an interview.
"It's the only thing people are talking about right now," said Lemek, whose group briefed candidates on the issue in June.
Voters are "looking at the reality that their costs are high" and "making the connection between this corrupt and broken system and their high costs," he said.
Additionally, survey respondents overwhelmingly opposed the idea of elected officials, including the president and members of Congress, personally owning or trading stocks in individual companies that have contracts with the federal government. That should not be allowed, 93% of voters said in the poll.
A similar proportion – 89% – said that companies owned, or invested in, by a sitting president's immediate family members should not be allowed to receive contracts from the federal government.
"This definitely ties back to the corruption issues that we've been talking about," said Alicia Simmons of Hart Research Associates.

MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. These stories topped Friday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
Izvestia: Putin signals readiness for Ukraine peace talks as EU risks being sidelined
The goal of negotiations with the United States and Ukraine will be to achieve a lasting peace settlement and guarantee Russia’s security, President Vladimir Putin said. A joint US-Israeli military operation against Iran is entirely possible amid a stalemate in negotiations caused by irreconcilable differences between the parties’ positions, research fellow at the Center for Middle East Studies at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Primakov National Research Institute of World Economy and International Relations (IMEMO) Alexey Yurk said.
"It is difficult to say whether such a strategy could break the negotiating deadlock. It might only lead Washington and Tehran to harden their positions. But both sides understand that there are currently no other options for breaking the impasse," the expert said.
Yurk did not rule out that reports in Western media about a planned US-Israeli strike on Iran could be deliberate information leaks intended to undermine Trump and the Republicans in the midterm elections, given the negative attitudes toward the war among undecided American voters. However, the political scientist believes this does not in itself mean that such plans are not being discussed at the White House and the Pentagon.
Izvestia: Hungary ignores Rosatom’s requests for talks on Paks II nuclear plant
Hungarian authorities have not responded to Rosatom’s requests for negotiations over the Paks II nuclear power plant project, the Russian state corporation’s CEO Alexey Likhachev told Izvestia. He stressed that Rosatom intends to build the plant as quickly as possible and avoid legal proceedings. However, the Hungarian authorities have effectively suspended progress on the project to conduct an audit and determine its future.
"We have officially informed the Hungarian government, repeatedly informing it of our readiness and our requests for negotiations, but so far we have received no response," Likhachev stressed.
As a result, uncertainty still surrounds the future of the project. "In the absence of any concrete signals from the Hungarian government, there is currently a nonzero probability of both the project moving forward with even greater momentum and its complete suspension," Likhachev said. "Our objective, of course, is not to end up in court and establish grounds there for holding our partners financially liable. Our objective is to build the plant as quickly as possible," he added.
Foreign media previously reported that Hungary’s new government was allegedly considering replacing Rosatom as the project’s contractor. However, Hungarian company Paks II Zrt, which commissioned the Paks II plant, denied reports of Rosatom’s possible replacement, according to Portfolio.
The company stressed that a comprehensive review of Paks II was still underway and that a final decision on the investment project had yet to be made. Paks II Zrt also stated that there was "no room for speculation" regarding such a complex project.
It would be extremely difficult for an outside contractor to take over the Paks II project because of the time required to review documentation and renegotiate contracts, leading analyst at the National Energy Security Fund and an expert at the Financial University under the Russian Government Igor Yushkov told Izvestia.
Moreover, Rosatom is the only corporation in the global nuclear industry capable of providing a full range of services, from design to decommissioning. Therefore, if Rosatom is replaced, Budapest will have to bring in a team of separate contractors, Yushkov explained.
Although the Hungarian economy is not currently experiencing a critical energy shortage, the new nuclear power plant project is strategically important for the country, Artyom Ilyinsky, junior research fellow at the Department of European Political Studies at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Primakov National Research Institute of World Economy and International Relations (IMEMO), told Izvestia. According to him, the plant could provide a reliable safety net for the country’s energy system, particularly given Budapest’s plans to phase out Russian gas supplies by 2027.

Vedomosti: Novatek CEO calls on EU to reconsider plans to phase out Russian LNG
The European Union (EU) should rethink its decision to completely phase out imports of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) from January 1, 2027, in light of current economic realities, Novatek CEO and co-owner Leonid Mikhelson said on October 22 at the 19th Verona Eurasian Economic Forum. He warned that the situation on the global gas market would worsen if the EU’s decision remained in force, Vedomosti writes. Russian LNG cannot be excluded from the global economy, so the volumes currently supplied to Europe will be diverted to other markets, Mikhelson stressed.
The Novatek chief pointed out that growing global gas demand cannot be met without Russian resources. According to Novatek’s forecast, global gas consumption will rise from the current 4.3 trillion cubic meters per year to 5.5 trillion cubic meters by 2050. Meeting this demand will require producing 120-135 trillion cubic meters over the next 25 years, compared with a total of just 87 trillion cubic meters extracted over the previous 25 years, Mikhelson noted.
Novatek’s Yamal LNG plant is currently the only supplier of Russian gas to the EU, Igor Yushkov, an expert at the Financial University under the Russian Government, told Vedomosti. Once the complete ban on supplies to the EU takes effect, the company could redirect exports to countries in South, East, and Southeast Asia, as well as Turkey, the analyst said.
After ending imports of Russian LNG, Europe will have to compete for available gas supplies from the United States and Qatar, Yushkov noted. This could indeed push up gas prices on the global market, the expert said. Sergey Suverov, an investment strategist at Aricapital Management Company, and Sergey Kaufman, an analyst at Finam Financial Group, shared his assessment.
Suverov forecasts that the average gas price in Europe will rise to $650 per 1,000 cubic meters in 2027. Kaufman believes prices could reach $800 per 1,000 cubic meters. According to Vedomosti’s calculations based on World Bank data, the average gas price in Europe was approximately $600 per 1,000 cubic meters in January-September 2026. In 2025, gas in Europe cost around $427 per 1,000 cubic meters.

Foster + Partners designs pair of skyscrapers connected by garden bridges in Armenia
A pair of skyscrapers joined by three bridge elements will form the centrepiece of World Trade Center Yerevan, a development by British studio Foster + Partners set to be built in Armenia.
Situated in the Armenian capital of Yerevan, one of the towers will house offices and the other will contain apartments and a hotel.
Foster + Partners plans to connect the skyscrapers with enclosed bridges that will provide amenities for occupants of both buildings, including landscaped terraces.
Wrapped in glazed facades, the pair of skyscrapers will have a concrete structural frame with steel bracing and a split core, catering for open, flexible interior spaces.
The towers will be angled to give views of notable landmarks, including the National Assembly of Armenia, the Armenian National Opera and Ballet Theatre, the Armenian Genocide Memorial and Mount Ararat.
The World Trade Center Yerevan development will also feature low-lying buildings at the base of the skyscrapers containing entertainment, hospitality and shopping spaces arranged around a public square.
“Our new development is in close dialogue with the country’s history and culture,” said Foster + Partners senior partner Niall Dempsey.
“The low-rise buildings seamlessly stitch into the wider urban fabric, while the towers are elevated above ground level, freeing up 50 per cent of the site and making an important contribution to the life of the city.”
The central green axis of the nearby park will be extended to form a route leading to a podium at the base of the skyscrapers.
Foster + Partners aims for the public spaces to reference the area’s architectural heritage in its design for World Trade Center Yerevan.
The development is set to be built in an area of Yerevan that was masterplanned in 1924 by Armenian architect Alexander Tamanian, who had ambitions to transform the Armenian capital into a garden city.
“Our scheme celebrates the outdoor life of the city by connecting the urban fabric with public spaces, ensuring our new interventions work in harmony with the historic grain,” said Foster + Partners partner Juan Frigerio.
“To the north of the towers, the events plaza responds to the significant St John the Baptist Church and its forecourt, creating a seamless connection between old and new.”
Other designs recently unveiled by Foster + Partners include its plans for the Two World Trade Center skyscraper in New York and a masterplan to transform the area surrounding an airport near Luanda, Angola.
The images are by Foster + Partners.

Traction!
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Listen to this essay
16 minute listen
In conversations, few words catch my attention faster than ‘friction’ – and especially talk of making things frictionless. From the workplace to grocery shopping, our societies seem to be striving to remove friction from everything. The motivation appears to be that decreasing resistance makes life easier and smoother.
Having spent a career as a tribologist, studying friction, wear and lubrication scientifically, I have some opinions on this. I’ll confess that, in most of my career, I too have sought to reduce friction, developing new materials, designs or even instrumentation in order to lower friction in a jet engine or reduce emissions from your car. However, I’ve also found myself trying to figure out how to increase friction to remove plaque on teeth.
The reality is that friction, despite seeming so antagonistic, is necessary and even productive. The force that resists motion has, since humans first struck a spark from a stone, been the very thing that propels us forward. And this paradox offers a lens through which to reread humanity’s entire technological history.
In order to appreciate all that an understanding of friction has helped us to accomplish, it’s necessary to start at square one and state what friction actually is. We define friction as the force that resists motion, and that means friction is rather ubiquitous. If things are moving, whether they’re sliding around or rolling, there’s friction. Solids, liquids, gases? Doesn’t matter. If there’s movement, friction is there to resist it. Unfortunately, because friction’s job is to resist, we’ve developed an aversion to it as a nuisance. But it’s a very important force, and we’ve thrived by expanding our understanding of it. By the 1960s, after millennia of evolving with friction, we finally accepted that friction is such a critical part of our world that a scientific field of study needed to be devoted to it: tribology.
Tribologists like me study this force in all its forms. Tribology is the science of interacting surfaces in relative motion, concerned with the wear of materials, friction and lubrication. Basically, tribology is the specialisation of things rubbing against each other. You may raise an eyebrow at a field of science focused on this, but when you pause to consider how much motion is going on inside us, around us and throughout the Universe, you can appreciate that tribology is vast. More than anyone, tribologists know the problems friction can cause. But they also know the achievements that have followed as we’ve come to understand resistance better.
Although tribology as a formalised field is relatively modern, friction has long shaped humanity’s technological innovations. For example, consider its pivotal role in people’s journeys from A to B over the centuries. I’m willing to bet that whenever you need to move unwieldy furniture or carry home that giant bag of cat litter, your instinct is to find a cart to help you. Early humans had a similar thought, turning to log rollers to move heavy objects, and coming up with one of our greatest inventions: the wheel. Rolling makes it easier to move objects because it reduces friction between the object and surface you’re moving it against. There are far fewer surface interactions in the process of rolling versus sliding. Plenty can be said about the wheel, including the fact that even in 2026 we can’t seem to agree on the origin of its discovery, but there is zero doubt that it’s a brilliant innovation for dealing with friction. But wheels also need friction: when we exert a force to move a wheel forward, the force between the ground and the wheel – static friction – keeps it from spinning freely, which would result in us going nowhere. Once forward motion begins, the resistance to motion becomes dynamic friction, which is just as important. If you’ve driven on ice, you know the danger of too little friction.
However, if people hadn’t continued improving on these basic principles, even the wheel would be rather inefficient due to friction.
The Vikings’ longships minimised form drag so they could cut through the water quickly
The ancient Romans discovered this in their amphitheatres. Roman chariot races didn’t come without their headaches. Or rather, foot aches. I’m certain the drivers likely complained about their hot feet, caused by friction between the wheels and axle heating up the surrounding parts. In Odes, a collection of lyric poems, the poet Horace described how chariot wheels would glow during racing. Today, scientists know that this glow is from turning the energy of motion into thermal energy. Roman designers eventually figured out that they could temper the problem by putting axungia (animal fat) grease between the wheel and axle. By doing so, they were applying tribological knowledge already exploited by the Sumerians: that fats and oils work more effectively than water as lubrication between surfaces. However, that created a new conundrum: if the grease got hot enough, it risked catching fire. The solution? A coolant. In this case, they splashed water on the chariots, in the ancient equivalent of a pit stop.
While all roads led to Rome, you could say all seas led to the Vikings. They, too, cleverly adapted to the resistance that met them as they journeyed through the oceans. Moving through fluids produces a type of friction known as drag. Even within drag there are subsets. Skin drag is from the friction between the surface of the ship and the water, whereas form drag stems from the shape of the hull as it moves through the water. When they had to transport cargo safely, the Vikings used sturdy ships with wide hulls. This wider hull increased form drag and slowed them down, but the stability provided was more critical. Their famous longships, however, were long and slim, minimising form drag as much as possible so they could cut through the water quickly.
As with all friction scenarios, however, the Vikings found themselves having to balance some competing demands. Faster longships are better, yes, but it was also imperative that the ships not break apart into pieces from the waves. They needed flexibility and strength, while keeping the ships as light as possible to ride higher in the water to reduce drag. To do this, the Vikings used their ‘clinker’ technique of nailing together long planks of wood. The rivets and overlapping planks would increase drag compared with a more polished, smoother design but these individual planks gave the ships the ability to twist and flex to weather storms. If I was on a boat trip in the middle of the ocean, I too would be happy to sacrifice a little bit of drag reduction to avoid capsizing from a rogue wave.
Looking at boats and ships today, it’s clear that we didn’t just accept these Viking designs as the culmination of nautical perfection. Likewise, we aren’t driving around in Roman chariots today. We have since made incredible leaps forward in understanding how to quantify friction and thus design for it, finally approaching friction scientifically. In the 1920s, Chrysler’s head of engineering Carl Breer had the idea to design cars with aerodynamics in mind. Planes seemed to slice seamlessly through the air. Shouldn’t cars do the same? Breer tasked the engineer William Earnshaw to consult with none other than Orville Wright to learn how to design a car in a wind tunnel. The resulting teardrop-shaped Chrysler Airflow was considered a flop, as many disruptive designs can be when they’re just too jarring for taste, but that flop revolutionised how we design cars. Wind-tunnel testing remains a standard today, and friction’s presence is as expected as the air itself.
Tribology testing is routine for the automotive industry today, and there are tribology labs scattered throughout a variety of industries, from medical to food. In these labs, you’ll find instruments designed to measure friction at macro-scales down to the atomic level. My PhD lab at the University of Florida had tribometers measuring friction in force ranges that covered three orders of magnitude. I’ve even worked in a lab that had a tribometer built to test an actual train wheel against a railway. Tribologists are incredibly clever with innovating ways to measure friction, given how persnickety friction is. Friction is dependent on the conditions of the operation – how fast things are moving, how much force they experience, and what temperature and environment they’re in.
Temperature in particular is a fun variable to contend with, because friction itself leads to temperature changes; indeed, frictional heating can be extreme in some cases. Like with Roman chariots, greases can ignite at certain temperatures making it imperative to control friction heating in order to avoid accidentally reaching that temperature. And for applications like jet engines, which get very hot anyway, we have engineered solid materials with low friction to withstand the heat.
When tribologists run into a wall, we develop a new instrument to understand what friction is trying to tell us
You may think tribology is already a niche field, but we have specialisations within it. Mine was solid lubrication, and I worked on developing and testing materials for jet engines and automobiles. In some cases, the conditions of the end use were so aggressive that the steel I was running my material against would experience enough friction heating to completely change the colour of the steel. That’s how you know you’ve reached the extremes in tribology, but those extremes must be met and they obviously are. After all, we have space stations orbiting Earth and landers on Mars.
Which brings us to another critical point about friction’s role in human progress: resistance is a consequence of progress, and its existence is a sign of progression itself. We wouldn’t have the now-robust business of solid lubricants if we had not advanced technologically to design turbine engines, which themselves were the result of us figuring out powered flight. By achieving that, our progress led us to new resistance. I think this is critical to remember anytime we find ourselves confronting unexpected resistance, and it’s something I remind myself of whenever I get halted in my work. I wouldn’t be stumped by this new resistance if I hadn’t managed to advance myself to this position where the resistance exists.
Often when tribologists run into a wall, we find ourselves developing a new instrument to help us understand what friction is trying to tell us. Tribometers have been designed to mimic all of the variables mentioned above, and that alone is quite a feat of human engineering, but now we also couple them with other techniques that allow us to somehow see what is happening while it’s happening. From maps of frictional heating during operation to how friction is influencing cellular movement, instruments and techniques have enabled us to usher friction into a new era to drive us forward, doing more than just finding clever ways to overcome friction. We can harness it as a tool.
In terms of friction, the 20th century can be thought of as the century in which humans accepted the resistance, and established engineering rigour around friction to propel our technological advances forward. Critically, it’s when we formalised how to overcome friction to be more efficient. As a tribologist, however, I’m far more excited about what the 21st century has brought us. Instead of just overcoming friction, we began fully realising how to harness that resistance to bring in a new era of progress. Exhibit A is once again found in our cars, where friction has been deployed as a tool in sustainability. Braking requires friction, so engineers asked: why don’t we use the consequences of that friction to our advantage? The heat from friction in braking is now used to create electricity in regenerative braking in EVs and hybrids. We must continue to use this creative and fresh perspective when dealing with friction, as opposed to always driving towards frictionlessness. Imagine if those engineers had been so fixated on the negatives of friction that they didn’t harness its power.
Using friction as a tool has come to us only as we’ve evolved to understand the depths of friction, including its behaviours and where it may be lurking. We know it is involved in dynamic processes, so let’s use it to control such processes. Yes, we’ve done so for a while with mechanisms like brakes and dampeners, but expanding this beyond machines has really taken hold in recent decades. Now, we’re looking at how friction may be a tool in perhaps the most impressive machine there is: the human body. It’s possible friction may be a lever to help us better model and understand biological processes and, in turn, help in the development of therapeutics. The rate at which a virus ejects from its protein shell or capsid can dictate whether it results in an active infection or instead remains dormant in the cell. If we want to use viruses to intentionally infect and defeat other viruses or bacteria, then controlling the virus’s ejection rate is crucial. Friction is the key to unlocking this possibility. In 2023, researchers found that, by packing the coils of virus DNA in certain ways, they could increase friction during ejection and slow down its rate of ejection.
Every advance we make generates new friction. We solve one problem, and friction presents another
Recently, our knowledge of friction has taken us to even more surprising places, extending even to helping us understand dark matter. The concept of ‘resistance is your reward for progress’ may be best illustrated by the astrophysicist Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar. Despite the fact that established scientists mocked his theories, Chandrasekhar would go on to become a founder of astrophysics, and is the reason we understand the evolution of stars and interstellar dynamics. In the 1930s, he was interested in how the interactions between stars could lead to their collisions. He calculated the timescales of such collisions and realised, though only after publishing, that things weren’t adding up quite right. This led him back to the drawing board, where he spotted there was a resistance present that no one before had identified: dynamical friction. This friction is a gravitationally induced drag that acts on objects as they interact and move through space.
Fast-forward to the 21st century, and dynamical friction has been used as a tool to infer the presence of dark matter. In 2024, researchers in Hong Kong realised that orbital times weren’t matching up with a couple of stars they were studying that were believed to be circling around black holes. They looked at Chandrasekhar’s concept of dynamical friction and wondered what would happen if they incorporated the contribution of friction from the dark matter surrounding the black hole. Voila! Suddenly, the predicted and calculated orbital times of the stars matched with what they were measuring. Friction was present when humanity first started experimenting with fire and the wheel. Now it’s there as we probe the frontiers of our Universe.
We need friction to move. Without its resistance, Earth’s plates would be in constant motion. We could not walk, or drive, or even hold objects. Understanding how to achieve what we want, in a world requiring this resistance, has been essential in our development.
Yet there is a deeper paradox at work, one that William James captured when he wrote that life is built ‘in the self-governing resistance of the ego to the world’. Every advance we make generates new friction. We solve one problem, and friction presents another. We step forward, and new resistance awaits. This is what progress means: that we have moved into territory that demands new understanding.
Roman engineers learned it when their chariot wheels caught fire. Chandrasekhar discovered this when his calculations didn’t add up. And we will continue to encounter resistance as we push forward.
When people speak of a frictionless world, they imagine ease. But ease without resistance is a wheel spinning in place, motion without progress.

Many Latinos are over Trump. The shift is especially striking in Texas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- President Trump’s approval rating among Latino registered voters has fallen to 24% from 38% at the start of his second term, polls show.
- Tejano singer Bobby Pulido is trying to flip a Texas congressional seat in a district Trump won by 18 points in 2024.
EDINBURG, Texas — Clad in pressed jeans and cowboy hats, dozens of riders on horseback and drivers in pickups kicked up dust along a dirt road in Edinburg, near the southern tip of Texas. They were there for a cabalgata, a traditional horse procession, with a political message: Send Tejano singer Bobby Pulido to Congress.
Some were lifelong Democrats. Others had voted for President Trump two years ago. But on this Saturday, they all rode for Pulido, a Democrat trying to flip a House seat Trump carried by 18 percentage points in 2024.
Among them was David Lopez, 54, astride his brown horse, Black Jack. He voted for Trump because he saw him as a good businessman. But now, Lopez says the president’s tariffs have hurt his truck and trailer repair shop in nearby McAllen, and business is down about 20% from last year.
“I am voting Democrats all the way. Trump is no longer doing a good job,” Lopez said. “We need to find a way to make it out of this together.”
Lopez is part of a shift rippling through Latino communities across the country. Two years after helping return Trump to the White House with a Republican-controlled Congress, Latino voters are souring on the party in power, fueled by frustration over rising costs and the administration’s aggressive approach to immigration enforcement.
In 2024, Trump won the support of 48% of Latino voters, expanding Republican gains with a group that has long leaned Democratic. Now, that support is cratering. The president’s approval rating among Latino registered voters has fallen to 24% from 38% at the start of his second term, polls show.
Among Latinos who voted for Trump, 65% say they plan to back Republicans on Nov. 3, while more than a third said they were ready to vote for a Democrat or were undecided, according to a Pew Research Center poll released this month.
More broadly, Latino voters favor Democrats in House races 51% to 24%, and those who sat out the 2024 election are leaning toward Democrats. Those shifts could help decide control of the House, in part because Republicans in Texas and Florida redrew their congressional maps betting that their 2024 gains among Latino voters would last through the midterms.
The race between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton is hotly contested and enormously expensive, with total ad spending topping $500 million.
Nowhere is that test sharper than in the borderlands of the Rio Grande Valley, where voters say that Trump has failed to deliver on his economic promises and that his administration has gone too far on immigration enforcement, an issue they wanted addressed, but humanely.
In more than two dozen interviews in the Latino-majority region, voters say they are driven less by party loyalty and more by frustrations that they have been taken for granted, and want to elect politicians who take their votes seriously.
They say it has become harder to keep up with rising costs, including for the diesel that fuels their trucks and their weekly grocery runs. Builders say construction projects have ground to a halt as workers are detained or deported. And small-business owners say sales have dropped, either because customers are afraid to leave their homes or because tariffs have driven up their costs.
1. Sebastian Guevara, 65, poses for a photo at a political rally on Oct. 16, 2026, in Mercedes, Texas. “Trump forgot about Latinos as soon as he won,” he said. 2. Luis Sustaita, 49, a mariachi musician who had voted Republican in previous years, says he will be voting for Bobby Pulido.
Nidia Olivarez, 48, and her husband, Arnulfo, 55, voted for Trump in 2024 but have grown frustrated with how he has handled the economy and immigration raids in their community. This year, they’re backing Pulido over GOP Rep. Monica De La Cruz in Texas’ 15th Congressional District. But not because they’ve had a change of heart about the Democratic Party.
“We are only voting for Pulido, not other Democrats,” Olivarez said. The couple are still unsure whether they’ll support any Republicans.
For them, the vote is personal. They’ve long loved Pulido’s Tejano music and like that he’s a familiar figure in their community. They trust him, she said. They’re less sure about the Republicans at the top of the ticket: Ken Paxton, the Senate nominee running against Democrat James Talarico, and Gov. Greg Abbott, who is seeking reelection.
“We want to see who continues to show up in the area,” Olivarez said. “That matters to us.”
Latino voters in Texas are increasingly willing to consider candidate over party, said Brandon Rottinghaus, a professor of political science at the University of Houston.
“They are not just looking for what party to align with. They want to know that they can trust the person they’re voting for,” Rottinghaus said.
That dynamic will play a role in the competitive races for Texas’ 15th, 28th and 34th congressional districts and in the Senate seat, which has proved to be one of the most expensive and high-profile contests this year. In a sign of GOP concerns, Trump and Vice President JD Vance have repeatedly traveled to Texas this month to rally voters.
In recent weeks, Trump has brushed off polls that show him losing ground with Latino voters.
“I think we are doing great, I won Hispanics,” Trump told reporters on Monday. “I’ve done more than any other Republican in history, I got tremendous Hispanics.”
In early October, Trump was asked about Latino voters who say they feel betrayed by his administration’s immigration and economic policies. His message to them was that “we have to do what we have to do,” in reference to his immigration crackdown.
1. People dance during Bobby Pulido’s concert. 2. A man rides his horse before a parade in support of Bobby Pulido on Oct. 17, 2026, in Edinburg, Texas. 3. Bobby Pulido, in brown vest and white cowboy hat, upper left, takes a photo with rallygoers after speaking on Oct. 16, 2026, in Mercedes, Texas.
Gloria Rodriguez, a social worker in Edinburg, has seen the impact the immigration raids have had on children. Since Trump returned to the White House, she has helped coordinate services for hundreds of kids whose parents or caregivers have been detained or deported. She worries many of them will develop post-traumatic stress disorders.
“Everything they are doing with immigration is too much,” said Rodriguez, 50, who is voting for Democrats down the ballot. Her 15-year-old daughter, Angelina, says she told her mother to vote for Democrats, in part because she is scared her friends will be deported.
Luis Sustaita, 49, a mariachi who owns a music store that sells instruments to school districts, is voting Democrat this year because he says he is disheartened by the values of the modern-day Republican Party.
In the latest “The De Los Podcast” episode, Times columnist Gustavo Arellano talks with hosts Fidel Martinez and Suzy Exposito about how the Latino vote will influence the 2026 midterm elections.
“There are no old-school Republicans anymore. It is all MAGA,” said Sustaita, who lives in Weslaco. “They used to be about the people. Trump is all about himself and making himself rich.”
In South Texas, Republicans and Democrats alike are trying to court voters on a more personal level. It is about identity more than political affiliation in many ways.
In the majority-Latino 15th Congressional District, Pulido’s campaign slogan is “Not team red, not team blue — South Texas I am team you.” In an interview, Pulido added that his message to Latino voters is: “I hear you loud and clear, and I believe I share values with you.”
De La Cruz, a former insurance agent and a staunch Trump ally, said Latinos are “tired of being taken for granted” and said Pulido “has some nice records, but he’s a product of the same corrupt system that got rich and made us poorer.”
“I grew up in South Texas watching the compadre system steal from us while our families struggled to get by,” De La Cruz said in a statement. “You work hard and want a little more for your family and safe communities. I cut your taxes, protected Social Security and Medicare, stood with Border Patrol agents, and I’m fighting every day to bring down gas and grocery prices.”
Whether that message will resonate with voters will be seen on Nov. 3.
Tina Treviño, 61, said she hopes “la raza” — a term used in the Mexican American community that is widely understood as “the people” — will deliver political change to Texas. She says the system is not working for Latinos, and believes Democrats will be able to bring that change.
“It’s about Chicano power,” Treviño said. “We need that more than ever.”

Trump ramps up fraud investigations of immigrants as election approaches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Trump ramps up fraud investigations of immigrants as election approaches
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- As the midterms approach, the Trump administration is expanding fraud investigations involving immigrants.
- Studies and state reviews find noncitizen voting is rare. California officials say many registrations flagged by federal authorities as possible fraud appear to belong to U.S.-born voters.
- Immigration attorneys say minor inconsistencies in applications are increasingly triggering fraud findings, the denial of benefits and deportation proceedings.
WASHINGTON — President Trump has alleged that elections, public benefit programs and federal grants to nonprofits are rife with fraud. Now, he is increasingly focusing on fraud in his effort to detain and deport more immigrants.
Recent, high-profile flash points include 28 lawful permanent residents accused this week of illegally voting in California and the federal investigation into Somali-born Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.).
The broader crusade takes many forms, including allegations of fraud in immigration applications, illegal voting by noncitizens and misuse of federal benefits by immigrants who don’t qualify.
“This administration has purposefully mischaracterized immigrants and asylum seekers as fraudsters,” said Royce Murray, a former senior official at the Department of Homeland Security under the Biden administration. That, she said, “serves a narrative that immigrants are not to be trusted and are here to take something rather than contribute, with an end goal of trying to make Americans less welcoming and more comfortable with a mass deportation agenda.”
On Tuesday, Trump and Vice President JD Vance announced a $25-million program under the Justice Department to encourage the public to report suspected fraud in the U.S. government.
 This administration has purposefully mischaracterized immigrants and asylum seekers as fraudsters
— Royce Murray, former Department of Homeland Security official
The White House said the first check, for $10,000, will go to right-wing influencer Nick Shirley, who posted a video last year alleging that Somali residents in Minnesota were running fake child-care centers to collect federal subsidies. Dozens of people were convicted in connection with a sprawling, $250-million children’s food assistance scheme that predated this administration, though more charges have been announced in recent months.
Also Tuesday, administration officials launched another nationwide anti-fraud crackdown, this time targeting immigrants who they allege have illegally collected SNAP benefits. Homeland Security highlighted the arrests of five people, calling them “the opening salvo in a sustained, large-scale ICE operation.”
“From day one of my administration, we’ve waged an unprecedented war on corruption and fraud, and will not let our country be looted and plundered by thieves and pirates and foreign fraudsters and basically scum,” Trump said during a news conference announcing the Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program.
Earlier this year, the White House created a task force to eliminate fraud and the Department of Justice created a fraud enforcement division, in part, to target immigration-related offenses. Prosecutors have put aside thousands of other cases to zero in on immigration enforcement.
The focus on fraud has noticeably accelerated in the weeks leading up to the election.
Federal authorities charge 28 people in California with alleged illegal voter registration or voting, escalating the Trump administration’s fight with state election officials.
In California, some of the green card holders arrested this week over voter fraud said they didn’t remember registering to vote. The daughter of one defendant, Omar Muñoz, 72, of Belize, said she wondered whether her father had been confused with his U.S.-born son of the same name, who is a registered voter.
California officials pounced on the small number of people alleged to have cast illegal ballots. Illegal voting by immigrants “is so rare that the Trump admin is parading around town about .0001% of California voters,” Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office wrote on X.
In the last seven weeks alone, the State Department said, 112 noncitizens across 20 states have been charged with illegal voting and registration offenses. Overall, since Trump returned to the White House, 155 people have been charged with voting fraud-related offenses.
Mullin and Atty. Gen. Todd Blanche said earlier this month that Homeland Security agents had secured 10 convictions and detained 100 others for civil immigration violations since August.
During the Biden administration, voter fraud charges were brought in just 13 cases, Blanche added.
Studies and audits of state voter rolls have repeatedly found that voting by noncitizens is rare and hasn’t swayed any elections.
Last week, with mail-in voting already underway, the Justice Department sued California, asking a federal court to bar the state from counting the ballots of 20,000 voters who were flagged by federal officials as “likely noncitizens.” Los Angeles County officials reviewed a sample of 200 of those voter registrations and found that nearly 40% indicated they were born in the U.S.
That number of flagged ballots — 20,000 — is a substantial reduction from the 190,000 noncitizens the administration alleged were on state voter rolls earlier this year, though federal authorities this week said they had found a “separate batch of 17,000 voting records potentially tied to noncitizens.”
California leaders pointed to other states, such as Nevada, where similar accusations have proved meritless.
Murray, the former Homeland Security official, said she believes the administration is “trying to sow the seeds of doubt that the midterm outcomes will be trustworthy, so that if the Republican Party loses as badly as they’re predicted to, they can characterize it as due to fraud.”
Murray said the Trump administration has largely misconstrued what it means to commit fraud.
“Fraud is a very specific thing — it’s essentially lying,” she said. “Because you don’t get asylum does not mean you committed fraud, it just means you were ineligible.”
In September, a Homeland Security whistleblower told Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) that hundreds of U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services employees had been tasked with quickly reviewing the voter information of thousands of people in search of suspected noncitizen voters, and were given a quota of investigating 40 subjects per day.
On Wednesday, a federal judge restricted Homeland Security agents from carrying out sweeping field operations aimed at rooting out voter fraud in nine states, including California.
It is against federal law for immigrants who are not naturalized citizens to vote or register to do so. Penalties can include fines, jail time and even deportation, though authorities rarely pursued that option.
Eric Balliet, a former special agent with Homeland Security Investigations, the criminal investigative arm of ICE, said he takes no issue with investigating fraud, but the timing of this operation and significant resources dedicated show it is “highly politically charged.”
Balliet worked for various administrations, including Trump’s first, before retiring in 2024. Homeland Security Investigations agents typically focused on transnational criminal investigations such as drug smuggling and human trafficking.
Instead of initiating investigations based on tips or specific information, agents are now taking aggregated data and using algorithms to produce suspect lists, Balliet said. That’s not how law enforcement should operate, he said, calling it a massive privacy overreach against millions of law-abiding citizens.
“It’s the epitome of Big Brother,” he said.
Beyond the allegations of voter fraud, the Trump administration has also increasingly targeted immigrants on suspicion of lying to obtain a visa, green card or citizenship.
Omar’s family fled civil war in Somalia and immigrated to the U.S. in 1995 when she was 12. After agents searched her residence this month looking for evidence that her immigration paperwork contained falsehoods, she called the allegations baseless.
Last month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Muillin suggested the outcome of the investigation could be deportation. Years ago, the agency declined to move forward with a probe based on similar allegations against Omar, according to the Washington Post.
The congresswoman is not alone.
Emiliano Andrade-Covarrubias, 56, who died of unknown causes last week at an ICE facility in Texas, was arrested because the agency alleged he had fraudulently obtained his green card. ICE sought to deport him, saying he had failed to disclose a 2004 arrest for theft, but his daughter told the Texas Tribune that he did bring up his criminal record during the application process for his permanent residency.
Immigration lawyers say their clients are facing more intense scrutiny and that some have battled false accusations of fraud after applying for a green card or citizenship.
U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services spokesperson Zach Kahler blamed the Biden administration for lax vetting that allowed bad actors to exploit immigration programs.
“These abuses are not harmless,” he wrote in a statement. “Meritless claims clog the system, drain limited resources, and delay relief for legitimate victims of crime. USCIS is taking aggressive action to identify, expose, and eliminate fraud.”
Erin O’Neil, an attorney based in Connecticut, said some of her clients are now in deportation proceedings triggered by allegations of fraud over minor inconsistencies that have no bearing on the case. In one case that resulted in a denial based on fraud, she said, the allegation was simply that her client failed to disclose a two-week work assignment in another state.
“In the past, the worst that would happen is your citizenship application would be denied,” O’Neil said. “Now we have seen through several of my clients that, not only is the citizenship application denied, but they are placed into removal proceedings.”
