Earthquake kills 16, injures 76 in Tibet as rescue efforts continue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
09:59:45 UTC
18:59:45 KST

A magnitude 7 earthquake in Tibet has killed at least 16 people and injured 76, with hundreds of homes destroyed as rescuers search remote, high-altitude communities for survivors amid freezing temperatures, dangerous aftershocks and rockslides.
Rescue teams have searched villages and damaged homes in China's Tibet region after a magnitude 7 earthquake killed at least 16 people, injured 76 and forced more than 12,000 residents to evacuate, state media and local officials said Friday.
The earthquake struck Nagqu, a sparsely populated city in northern Tibet about 4,800 meters (15,750 feet) above sea level, late Thursday. At least 339 homes collapsed, while other buildings developed cracks or began leaning, raising fears they could fall during aftershocks.
Authorities warned that the remote terrain, low temperatures and potential rockslides were complicating rescue operations. Intermittent snowfall is forecast over the next three days, adding to concerns for residents displaced by the disaster.
Nagqu's acting mayor, identified by his surname, Dunzhu, said rescuers had completed three rounds of searches by Friday afternoon, checking individual households and villages for survivors.
More than 5,000 people from three local counties were deployed to support the response. Authorities also sent more than 300 police officers, including traffic and community police, to assess damage, assist evacuations and help residents reach safer locations.
Emergency supplies arriving in the region included 2,000 prefabricated housing units, about 3,400 tents, 2,000 folding beds, flashlights and winter clothing.
More than 12,000 people had been safely relocated, according to the official Xinhua News Agency. Videos released by local media showed residents fleeing their homes and taking shelter outdoors or in parked cars as the earthquake shook buildings.
The U.S. Geological Survey said the earthquake occurred at 10:33 p.m. Thursday local time, with its epicenter 191 kilometers (119 miles) east-northeast of Nagqu and a depth of 18 kilometers (11 miles).
China's Earthquake Networks Center reported 413 aftershocks. The U.S. agency separately recorded at least seven aftershocks measuring between magnitude 4.3 and 5.2, each at a depth of about 10 kilometers (6 miles).
The tremors and resulting rockfalls disrupted transportation and communications. Local railway authorities halted trains passing through the affected region, while officials closed part of National Highway 317 to clear debris. Only emergency, rescue and official support vehicles were permitted through the restricted section.
Communication and power supplies were gradually being restored, local officials said.
Chinese President Xi Jinping called Friday for all-out rescue operations and medical assistance, underscoring the seriousness of the disaster.
The earthquake was China's strongest since a magnitude 7.1 tremor struck neighboring Qinghai province in January 2024, according to the report. A magnitude 7.1 earthquake hit Yushu in Qinghai in 2010, killing at least 2,698 people and leaving nearly 300 others missing.

New electronics reach Iran, but prices soar as gov’t fees, US sanctions hit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
09:56:28 UTC
18:56:28 KST

New electronics reach Iran, but prices soar as gov’t fees, US sanctions hit
Latest smartphones are finding their way into Iran despite sanctions and trade restrictions, but many can’t afford them.
Tehran, Iran – When the latest iPhone 18 lineup was released by Apple in the United States on September 18, it only took a couple of days for the new models to go on sale in downtown Tehran.
That is despite Apple not having a physical presence in Iran due to years of international sanctions, and the ongoing months-long US naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports, through which the bulk of the country’s imports previously entered.
“These things can’t stop a mobile phone seller,” a phone and accessories trader in Tehran’s Charsou Mall, a major electronics hub, told Al Jazeera, asking to remain anonymous for security reasons.
But he explained that the process of bringing in phones has become much more complicated, time-consuming and costly, due to both external pressures and domestic conditions imposed by the Iranian government.
Many electronics manufactured internationally are imported into Iran via Dubai in the United Arab Emirates, but the nearly eight-month-long war with the US and Israel has disrupted trade through the Strait of Hormuz. Iran has also repeatedly attacked the UAE throughout the conflict, and the UAE also announced a halt to trade, commercial exchanges and financial transactions with Iran on August 19.
Some Iranian traders then pivoted to using passengers coming in from Oman to bring in phones and other items. But after US sanctions on all Iranian airlines – and anyone who provides services for them – came into effect in September, few flights are landing in the country.
“Most of the phones are now smuggled into the country. Many go to Sulaimaniyah and then come in by land,” the trader said, referencing the northeastern city in the Kurdish region of northern Iraq, which borders western Iran.
A similar story has also been true for many other electronics currently found in the Iranian market, including laptops, graphics and processing units, PlayStation devices and even Starlink terminals.
This week in Tehran, a MacBook Air 15-inch M4 sold for the rial equivalent of more than $1,450, about 6 percent higher than an average retailer in the UAE. A one-terabyte PlayStation 5 Slim disc-edition console was going for about $730, or 11 percent more expensive than some retailers in the US.
‘Registration’ and other fees
Things are much worse when it comes to mobile phones.
Mobile phone service on imported devices only works for 30 days if a registration fee to the Iranian government is not paid.
The fee was introduced nearly 10 years ago, ostensibly aimed at fighting smuggling and corruption. The amount varies depending on the value of the phone, with the government charging import duties of up to 6 percent for phones worth below 600 euros ($673), up to 15 percent for phones between 600 and 900 euros ($673 and $1,010), and up to 30 percent for phones with a value above 900 euros.
After adding other levies and “warranties” from domestic companies, extra charges for some phones can amount to more than half of the total price paid.
But even a registered phone cannot be used to freely access the internet, as the government imposes severe internet filtering and shutdowns, while global payment methods are off-limits to Iranians and international firms refuse many services to Iranian nationals because of US sanctions.
According to the state-linked Tasnim news site, about $1.6bn worth of mobile phones were imported commercially during the previous Iranian year ending in March 2026, up to 20 percent of which were phones priced at more than $600. Phones worth $470m were brought in by aeroplane passengers, most of them higher-spec phones. There are no clear figures for smuggled phones.
In mid-August, customs chief Foroud Asgari told state media that approximately one million phones had been imported during the first five months of the current Iranian year, versus 3.16 million in the corresponding period of a year earlier. He said the import value of the phones had fallen by approximately 70 percent.
The government can also decide to stop the registration of phones whenever it deems necessary.
That was the case between 2023 and 2024 for newer iPhone models, which authorities said could not be registered under any circumstance because they were made by an American company and were gobbling up precious foreign currency reserves for imports. Authorities did not take issue with similarly-priced high-end models.
Skyrocketing government charges and local restrictions are making it harder for Iranian customers to afford new phones at a time when the monthly minimum wage and basic government subsidies for an average married worker amount to the equivalent of just $83 in Iran.
The rial, the country’s national currency, has continued on its downward spiral. It changed hands for about 2.64 million per US dollar in Tehran on Monday, slightly improved from an all-time low reached earlier this month.
Prices have been surging across the board, especially for food and other essentials, as domestic mismanagement, war damage, sanctions and blockade squeeze the Iranian economy and make most of the country’s 90-million population poorer.
Afsaneh, a 27-year-old teacher from Tehran, said she has been thinking about replacing her iPhone 13 with last year’s 17 model, but balks when she sees the prices.
“The only way to get it is to sell my current phone, use my small savings and also borrow from my parents,” she told Al Jazeera.
She pointed out that many among her peers and acquaintances are also forced to keep old devices alive by repairing them or replacing parts, if possible, since they cannot afford to upgrade.
“A lot of people are one failure of a major electronic device away from getting into serious debt,” she said.

Ukrainian soldier clings to hope of seeing his children after surgery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
09:53:37 UTC
18:53:37 KST

Mykola Kasiuk refused to give up on his remaining eye, even after doctors told him he had lost his sight and recommended removing it. Two years after a land mine left him nearly blind, the Ukrainian soldier was placing his hopes in a team of U.S. surgeons working to repair the damage.
Lying in a hospital bed in Kyiv before surgery, Kasiuk crossed himself and prayed.
“I want to be able to see my children again,” he said.
Russia’s war in Ukraine has left soldiers and civilians with devastating eye and facial injuries, while specialists capable of treating complex cases remain scarce.
Before Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, eye care at many Ukrainian hospitals was largely limited to routine procedures such as cataract surgery.
A visiting team of American surgeons is helping fill that gap by treating severely injured patients and training Ukrainian doctors in oculoplastic surgery, which repairs the structures around the eyes. The procedures range from reconstructing damaged eye sockets and eyelids to fitting artificial eyes.
For Kasiuk, the operation offered a chance to preserve an eye that local doctors had considered beyond saving.
“No, I won’t let them,” he told his wife, Tetyana, when she relayed the recommendation to remove it. “This is my last hope.”
Kasiuk had trained as a military cook, not an infantryman. But after joining the military, he was given a rifle and sent into some of the fiercest fighting in eastern Ukraine.
His final memories of the world around him are scenes of devastation in the Donetsk region: fellow soldiers killed in combat, homes reduced to rubble and dogs wandering through the ruins. He remembers hearing Russian soldiers nearby and the pervasive smell of death.
On April 16, 2024, Kasiuk was walking with fellow soldiers when he stepped on something and fell. His commanders later told Tetyana that he had triggered a land mine.
The evacuation vehicle carrying him came under fire. Almost everyone inside was killed.
When Tetyana arrived at the hospital, she struggled to recognize the swollen, bandaged man covered in shrapnel wounds. His teeth had been shattered, and his face was barely recognizable.
“This is not my husband,” she told a hospital attendant.
Then she noticed the tattoos on his hands. They were his.
Doctors removed one eye after shrapnel pierced it and raised concerns about infection. They operated on the other but suspected the optic nerve had been damaged. Kasiuk was transferred between hospitals and underwent repeated operations, with little improvement in his vision.
He gradually learned to navigate life without sight. He uses an old mobile phone to make calls and listen to the news, and recently learned to style his own hair. When Tetyana switches on a lamp, he tells her that the faint light he can still perceive becomes brighter.
That small trace of vision has kept hope alive.
The American surgeons came to Kyiv through Vision for Ukraine, a medical mission organized by the Christian Medical Association of Ukraine. They would not know the full extent of the damage until they operated on Kasiuk’s eye socket.
Stuart Seiff, an oculoplastic surgeon from San Francisco, approached the case cautiously. The immediate priority was to reconstruct the socket and eyelids, improve the eye’s protection and restore some of Kasiuk’s appearance and sense of normality.
“The socket on the right is very contracted,” Seiff said.
Surgeons can rebuild the damaged lining using tissue taken from inside the mouth or behind the ear, or a specially prepared amniotic membrane that helps healing and reduces scarring. If vision cannot be restored, an artificial eye can provide a more natural appearance.
That was the outcome for Artem Deresh, another wounded Ukrainian soldier. His prosthetic eye, meticulously hand-painted in a Kyiv laboratory, looks almost real.
“I don’t want to stand out from the crowd. I also don’t want to make people uncomfortable,” Deresh said.
For Kasiuk, the stakes extended beyond his appearance. He wanted to regain even a small measure of independence and, if possible, see his family again.
On the day of surgery, a nurse helped him into scrubs and wheeled him toward the operating room. He prayed aloud along the way, repeatedly asking questions about the procedure and whether it would work.
The nurse tried to reassure him, telling him not to worry and that he would be beautiful.
The operation unfolded under the constant threat of Russian attacks. An air-raid alert interrupted the hospital’s routine, potentially delaying procedures for hours. When the alert ended, applause broke out across the ward as staff rushed to resume their work.
During the hourslong operation, a major strike hit Kyiv’s National Sciences Building, sending plumes of smoke into the air. Hours later, another strike hit a medical facility in the city.
Back home in Chernivtsi, in western Ukraine, Tetyana waited anxiously, knowing that the surgeons’ findings could shape the family’s future.
The man she had known before the war was gone, she said. Kasiuk had worked in factories to support the family, and together they had raised three daughters.
“He lives in his own little world now,” Tetyana said.
Kasiuk lives with almost constant pain, and his days and nights have lost their rhythm. Sometimes he sleeps through the day and remains awake all night.
His daughters are growing up, each moving toward a future he cannot see. His eldest is studying psychology, while his middle daughter is pursuing art and has won awards for her paintings. The youngest, now in sixth grade, remembers a father who could see, play with his children and take them on trips.
His condition has traumatized the children, Tetyana said.
She tries to shield her husband from worries she fears he cannot bear while navigating disability paperwork, pursuing further treatment and holding the family together. The burden has left her exhausted.
“Sometimes I wish someone would understand that I get tired, too,” she said.
The surgeons found more potential for recovery than they had expected.
They restored movement in Kasiuk’s eye and used skin grafted from behind his ear to help the eyelid protect it. The procedure also opened the possibility of a corneal transplant.
“He has a fantastic result at this point, absolutely fantastic,” Seiff said.
Whether Kasiuk will regain his sight remains uncertain. Doctors suspect scarring on the cornea, the transparent front surface of the eye, is clouding his vision. They still do not know how much damage lies deeper inside the eye or whether it can transmit visual signals to the brain.
His recovery will depend partly on how the eye heals. Scar tissue could form again and cloud the cornea, potentially undermining the gains made during surgery.
“That’s the big enemy. We try to control it, but there’s only so much you can do,” Seiff said.
Doctors plan to monitor Kasiuk for up to six months before deciding whether he needs another intervention. Options could include using stem cells to support a corneal transplant or implanting an artificial cornea.
For now, Kasiuk is holding on to the possibility that some of the world he remembers might return.
“I remember what the world looked like: the sun, the blue sky, the clouds,” he said. “I hope I’ll be able to see this beautiful world again, even if only a little.”

Serbia’s snap election: What’s at stake and can students unseat Vucic?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
09:52:20 UTC
18:52:20 KST

Serbia’s snap election: What’s at stake and can students unseat Vucic?
A snap parliamentary vote on October 25 will determine whether a student-led group can loosen Vucic’s grip on power.
Serbia will hold a snap parliamentary election on October 25 .
The vote is seen as a test of whether President Aleksandar Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) can extend its 14-year grip on power and stave off a student-led movement born out of mass anti-government protests.
Here’s what you need to know:
How did Serbia get here?
In November 2024, the collapse of a concrete canopy at a railway station in Novi Sad killed 16 people. What began as demands for accountability over the disaster grew into a nationwide movement against alleged corruption and the government’s handling of the tragedy.
Students emerged as the movement’s driving force, organising some of Serbia’s biggest demonstrations since the overthrow of Slobodan Milosevic. Their campaign has channelled deep frustration with the SNS, which has governed since 2012, and with a conventional opposition seen as fragmented and ineffective.
The parliamentary election was not due until late 2027. But Vucic resigned from the presidency in September, ahead of the end of his second and final constitutional term, and is leading the SNS campaign for prime minister. The manoeuvre has made the parliamentary contest central to his effort to retain political power before a separate presidential election must be held.
Who is challenging the ruling party?
The main challenger is the student-backed Student List–Students Win (Studentska lista–Studenti pobeduju), which brings together candidates with little or no previous political experience, including academics, teachers and other professionals.
It is campaigning on restoring the rule of law, ending corruption and rebuilding institutions, rather than focusing on divisive questions such as Kosovo, European Union membership or relations with Russia.
“The political dynamic has changed from the ground up,” Jelena Vasiljevic, a senior research associate at the University of Belgrade’s Institute for Philosophy and Social Theory, told Al Jazeera.
Young people, long considered the country’s most politically disengaged group, have become the core of its largest social mobilisation in decades, she said.
Some opposition parties have chosen not to run and instead support the student list.
Others are contesting the election but face the prospect of failing to clear the threshold for parliament. As a result, many see the vote as not simply a contest between parties, but a referendum on whether the SNS system should continue.
Why does the election matter?
The outcome will shape whether Serbia attempts to reset institutions that critics say have been hollowed out by years of party control. The SNS rejects allegations of abuse and corruption, but its opponents and rights groups accuse it of putting pressure on independent media, electoral malpractice and using state resources to maintain power.
For Vasiljevic, turnout will be decisive. The SNS retains a disciplined core electorate, supported by a clientelist model of government, in which goods and services are exchanged for political support, she said. The student list must not only unite opposition-minded voters but also mobilise habitual non-voters and the undecided.
A student list breakthrough would also remake the opposition.
Vasiljevic said parliament could contain a large group of politically inexperienced and ideologically diverse student-backed politicians, while traditional opposition parties could be greatly reduced. The result may therefore start a wider reorganisation of Serbia’s political landscape, regardless of who forms the government.
But winning power would be only the beginning.
Srdan Majstorovic, chair of the governing board of the European Policy Centre, said a new government would face the far harder task of rebuilding a democratic system after what he described as 14 years of systematic damage to institutions, the rule of law and public trust, compounded by deep social divisions and rampant corruption.
After years of what critics call a captured-state system, he said, Serbia would need a broad reset of its democratic governance.
What’s at stake for foreign policy?
Serbia’s stalled EU path is a part of the backdrop.
Majstorovic said progress has been blocked by concerns over the rule of law, Serbia’s limited alignment with EU sanctions, including those against Russia, and the stalled normalisation process with Kosovo.
A change in government would not automatically transform foreign policy, he said.
The student movement has avoided detailed commitments, instead treading carefully to unite left, centre and right-leaning voters.
But Majstorovic said democratic reform, judicial independence, free media and tackling corruption could renew cooperation with Brussels and revive the accession process.
Igor Bandovic, director of the Belgrade Centre for Security Policy, said foreign policy remained the biggest unknown in the student list’s programme. Its candidates have taken a hard line on Kosovo, proposed reviewing agreements reached under EU auspices and floated a referendum on EU membership within six months of taking office. They have also signalled continuity in relations with Russia.
Bandovic said a new government would probably face more immediate domestic priorities and the constraints of the Balkans’ security environment. But a referendum on EU membership could slow or halt accession further. If the SNS stays in power, he expects further deterioration in relations with Brussels.
External actors are watching closely.
Bandovic said Moscow has offered explicit support to the government, portraying the protests as a Western-backed “colour revolution”. The United States Congress has voiced concern about democratic standards and Serbia’s ties with Russia, while the US administration has been more restrained.
China, which has commercial interests in Serbia, has avoided public comment but is likely to prefer continuity.
How does the election work?
Voters will elect all 250 members of the National Assembly in a single nationwide constituency.
One ballot is cast for a party or coalition list, with seats allocated proportionally.
Electoral lists generally need at least 3 percent of votes to enter parliament, while recognised minority lists are exempt from the threshold.
The list or coalition able to command a majority in the 250-seat assembly will form a government.
But with the result expected to be close and the campaign taking place amid deep mistrust, the legitimacy of the process may prove as consequential as the final seat count.
Polls will close on Sunday at 8pm local time. Preliminary results are expected about two hours later.

Smart TVs may keep tracking viewers even after privacy settings are turned off
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
09:51:46 UTC
18:51:46 KST

Smart TVs may keep tracking viewers even after privacy settings are turned off
Some smart TVs continue sending network traffic consistent with viewing recognition after users disable the feature, raising questions about privacy controls, reports a Qazinform News Agency correspondent.
Researchers at Northeastern University conducted 5,943 controlled experiments involving 12 televisions from 10 manufacturers. The devices covered eight operating systems representing approximately 95% of the US smart TV operating system market, according to their study.
Automatic content recognition, or ACR, identifies programmes by sampling audio or video and comparing digital fingerprints with a content library. Viewing information can support audience measurement and targeted advertising.
On Samsung’s Tizen, traffic consistent with ACR persisted after opting out in all 30 tests of its built-in streaming service, 41 of 60 antenna tests and 18 of 30 HDMI tests.
On Vizio’s SmartCast, the privacy setting produced no observable reduction in traffic to an Amazon Kinesis endpoint identified as consistent with ACR activity. Roku’s opt-out did not cover its own streaming service, a limitation disclosed in its policies.
However, encryption prevented researchers from establishing what the continued transmissions contained or how companies handled them.
“These behaviors indicate potential privacy violations; however, we cannot know for certain without access to payload content,” the report states.
Opting out fully suppressed identified ACR traffic on four tested platforms: LG’s webOS, Amazon’s Fire TV OS, Sony’s Google TV implementation and VIDAA OS. The findings reflect the tested devices and software versions and do not necessarily apply to other models or regions.
On the project website, researchers urged manufacturers to explain which inputs ACR monitors and protect its transmissions. They also published a blocklist of ACR network addresses and suggested disconnecting televisions from the internet and using an external streaming device without ACR.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Chinese e-commerce platform AliExpress had allegedly used users’ audio systems as part of a browser fingerprinting technique to distinguish devices, according to an investigation by the Brave browser team.

TSMC seeks rare-earth-free motors to reduce risk from China restrictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
09:51:32 UTC
18:51:32 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — TSMC is exploring factory motors that do not require rare-earth magnets to reduce supply risks from China's export restrictions, Reuters reported Thursday.
The chipmaker has asked suppliers about motors that can operate without rare-earth magnets in its automated factories. Three industry executives familiar with the discussions said the company was considering alternatives, but no large-scale changes have been made yet.
Rare earths are metals used to make powerful magnets found in many industrial machines. These magnets are used in motors that power automated equipment, including machinery found in semiconductor factories, per the International Energy Agency.
TSMC relies on automated equipment to produce advanced semiconductors. A shortage of specialized motors or replacement parts could disrupt chip production for customers in the smartphone, artificial intelligence, data center, and defense industries.
In 2025, China introduced export controls on certain rare-earth materials and related technologies. The restrictions require government approval for affected exports and have raised concerns about higher costs and supply disruptions for manufacturers.
Taiwan could face indirect supply disruptions because many rare-earth materials reach manufacturers through the US, Europe, and Japan. Hsu Tsun-tzu (徐遵慈), a researcher at the Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research, said China's export restrictions could raise costs and create uncertainty for the country's businesses, per CTEE.
Taiwan and the US have also stepped up cooperation to secure alternative supplies of critical minerals. The two sides endorsed a US-led initiative in January to strengthen supply chains for advanced technologies, including semiconductors and artificial intelligence.
Taipei is developing its own rare-earth processing technology to reduce dependence on imports. Economy Minister Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫) said that the government planned to establish a pilot production line within three years that could meet about half of domestic demand, per CNA.
The country is also working on technology to recover rare earths from industrial and electronic waste. A government-backed research institute said it plans to begin transferring recycling technology to private companies this year, focusing on producing high-purity materials for industrial use.
The government is looking overseas for additional rare-earth supplies. Officials visited mining sites in Australia in May and planned an eight-day trip to the US in late October to meet mining companies and government officials.
Taiwan has also identified Canada as a potential source of rare-earth materials. The economics ministry aims to meet 50% of domestic rare-earth demand through local supply and processing by 2030.
Finding alternative sources remains difficult because China dominates the global rare-earth industry. The International Energy Agency said China accounted for 91% of global refined production of rare earths used in magnets and 94% of powerful permanent magnet production in 2024.

IEA chief expects energy crisis to persist into 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
09:50:33 UTC
18:50:33 KST

International Energy Agency Executive Director Fatih Birol
International Energy Agency Executive Director Fatih Birol said on Oct. 23 he expects the energy crisis to continue into 2027, warning that the world will still be dealing with its consequences as governments seek alternative energy sources and strengthen supply security.
Addressing the Investment Summit Towards COP31 in Istanbul remotely, Birol said developments worldwide and countries’ energy policies offered little reason to expect normalization next year.
“I am not optimistic about normalization in 2027,” he said. “Even when I try to look at things optimistically, I cannot find an argument that convinces me.”
“This crisis will continue in one form or another in 2027. The world will still be trying to heal its wounds, provided no new wounds emerge,” he added.
Birol said the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz was affecting the economy, agriculture, and energy, prompting governments, companies, and investors to reconsider their short- and long-term strategies.
He drew parallels with the oil crises of 1973 and 1979, which he said spurred nuclear energy development and improvements in vehicle efficiency.
Birol described COP31 as a “golden opportunity” for Türkiye and a major opportunity for the world, arguing that the current crisis could help build support for concrete outcomes.
He outlined a proposed commitment to increase electricity’s share of global energy from 23 percent to 35 percent by 2035, with countries encouraged to sign on at the Antalya summit.
Greater electrification would strengthen energy security while reducing emissions, he said, offering a common objective at a time of deep international divisions.
Adoption would also send an unequivocal signal to investors and capital markets, he added.
Birol said participation levels and an agreement on electrification would be two key measures of COP31’s success, expressing optimism about both the number of governments attending and their level of representation.

BAQEN, Xizang, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Sixteen people have been killed and 76 others are injured following a 7.0-magnitude earthquake which struck Baqen County of the city of Nagqu in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region at 10:33 p.m. on Thursday, local authorities said.
Casualty figures were updated as of 1 p.m. on Friday, according to a press conference held by the information office of the Nagqu municipal government.
More than 5,000 personnel have been deployed to the front lines of the disaster relief operation, working in teams responsible for search and rescue, medical treatment, temporary shelter and the provision of essential supplies.
Rescue operations are in full swing, while an emergency command headquarters has been established on the front lines to coordinate relief efforts.
Local authorities have launched round-the-clock intensified monitoring of key sites, including mountainsides, reservoirs, power stations, rivers, structurally unsafe buildings and telecommunications base stations. Emergency repairs are also underway, with damaged telecommunications and power facilities gradually being restored.
Earthquake monitoring, meteorological and emergency management departments, meanwhile, are coordinating closely to issue timely warnings of aftershocks and adverse weather conditions.
Police and transport authorities have inspected more than 1,700 kilometers of roads, 201 bridges and 324 culverts to ensure access for rescue operations, identifying 11 potential hazards and clearing fallen rocks from seven road sections, the press conference revealed.
The Red Cross Society of China has dispatched a working team to the disaster-hit area to guide local relief efforts. It has also allocated 3,800 sets of supplies, including family relief kits, hygiene kits, heaters, tents, jackets, folding beds and quilts.
The China Charity Federation, one of the country's most influential charity organizations, has urgently allocated 3 million yuan (about 446,561 U.S. dollars) to support emergency rescue endeavors. ■

Eberechi Eze replaced Saka on Wednesday and could start in his place again on Saturday, while Viktor Gyokeres, Mikel Merino, Max Dowman and Myles Lewis-Skelly give Arsenal coach Mikel Arteta further options to rotate his side.
The round of matches gets underway on Friday night when Ipswich Town hosts Nottingham Forest, with Ipswich having made a promising start to life back in the Premier League.

Manchester United's 4-1 defeat away to Como in the Champions League on Wednesday night has increased the pressure on coach Michael Carrick. Analysis: Four things to look out for in Sundays 'Clasico' between FC Barcelona vs Real Madrid
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
17:43:40 CST
18:43:40 KST

MADRID, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- The first 'Clasico' of the season between FC Barcelona and Real Madrid is the highlight of the weekend in La Liga. Barcelona has the chance to increase its lead over its historic rival, while Jose Mourinho's side will look to confirm its recent improvement. Here are some things to look out for on Sunday night.
1: A feast of attacking talent
Both sides are packed with talent, with Lamine Yamal leading Barcelona's attack and Kylian Mbappe spearheading Real Madrid's forward line.
The match features two of the favorites for this season's Ballon d'Or, and both will be keen to impress. However, Yamal and Mbappe are far from the only attacking threats. Raphinha, Anthony Gordon, Pedri and Karim Adeyemi also give Barcelona plenty of options, while Yan Diomande and Jude Bellingham will support Mbappe for Real Madrid, with youngsters Endrick and Carlos Espi among the substitutes.
With so much attacking talent on show, a goalless draw looks unlikely.
2: Contrasting tactics from Hansi Flick and Jose Mourinho
The game should also highlight the tactical differences between the two coaches. Barcelona's game is based on possession and moving the ball quickly to create and exploit space in the opposition defense, while Mourinho prefers his teams to remain compact before launching quick attacks.
Expect Barcelona to dominate possession and try to stretch Real Madrid down the flanks, with Yamal and either Adeyemi or Gordon operating on the wings, while Raphinha looks to press Real Madrid when it has the ball.
The good news for Barcelona is that Rodri is expected to start, although Real Madrid has the pace to exploit any mistakes.
3: Defensive concerns for Barcelona?
Barcelona goes into the game following an entertaining 4-2 defeat away to Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League, in which the French side exploited the space between Barcelona's midfield and defense.
Flick will be without Eric Garcia and Andreas Christensen, while Jules Kounde is doubtful with an ankle injury, leaving Barcelona short of defensive options. Garcia is expected to be sidelined for three to four weeks, while Kounde's availability will depend on his recovery.
Unless Kounde recovers in time, Flick will have to field a makeshift defense. Although Rodri could provide additional protection in midfield, Diomande, Mbappe and Bellingham will fancy their chances of finding the net.
4: A difficult game to referee
Anyone who has followed the Spanish press recently will have seen the controversy surrounding the match, with Real Madrid's television channel criticizing refereeing decisions and raising questions about the treatment of the two clubs.
Real Madrid has also pursued the ongoing Negreira case, which concerns payments made by Barcelona to companies linked to Jose Maria Enriquez Negreira, the former vice president of Spain's Technical Committee of Referees.
All of this means the referee for Sunday's game will be under intense scrutiny, with every decision likely to be closely analyzed.
With Real Madrid potentially looking to use tactical fouls to disrupt Barcelona's passing game, the match could be difficult to officiate even under normal circumstances. On Sunday, the pressure will be greater than ever. ■

Bulgaria Faces Years of Fiscal Pressure, Finance Minister Says
Bulgarian Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Galab Donev has called for realistic budget planning and financial discipline in the coming years, citing a 2025 budget deficit of 4% of gross domestic product and the consequences of accumulated fiscal imbalances.
Speaking ahead of a meeting of the National Council for Tripartite Cooperation, which brings together representatives of employers and trade unions, Donev said the agenda covered different issues linked by the challenge of reconciling public needs, economic growth and social justice with the state’s financial resources.
He stressed that tax policy should serve purposes beyond generating revenue, including supporting families and children, promoting responsible behavior, safeguarding public health and distributing the financial burden more fairly.
“When discussing amendments to tax legislation, it is important to consider not only their budgetary impact but also the objectives they aim to achieve - specifically, the positive outcomes for society and the economy,” Donev said.
The finance minister also stressed the need for a responsible approach to public finances, pointing to the excessive deficit procedure and data published by Eurostat. He said these showed that Bulgaria’s actual budget deficit for 2025 had reached 4% of GDP, confirming the “hidden” deficit he had flagged during the summer.
Donev warned that the effects of the accumulated fiscal imbalances would continue to affect budgets in the years ahead, rather than being confined to one fiscal year. Differences between the actual state of public finances and preliminary estimates, he said, also influence the preparation and implementation of subsequent budgets.
The deputy prime minister said restoring the sustainability of public finances required “realistic budget planning and financial discipline.”
“We must strike a sensible and feasible balance between financial sustainability and social responsibility,” Donev said.
Bulgaria’s Debt Ratio Climbs Despite Ranking Among EU’s Lowest
Bulgaria’s budget deficit widened to 4% of gross domestic product in 2025, while government debt climbed to 29.9% of GDP, according to the latest data from the National Statistical Institute (NSI)
Bulgaria Targets 3% Deficit as 2027 Budget Debate Exposes Divisions
Bulgaria will seek to keep its budget deficit within the 3% limit, Deputy Prime Minister Ivo Hristov said on BNT, adding that the final budget figures would depend on parliamentary discussions and subsequent revisions
Bulgaria’s Current Account Deficit Hits Highest Level Since 2009, BNB Says
The Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) has reported that the country's current account deficit reached 8.1% of gross domestic product over the 12 months to July, its highest level since 2009, while forecasting economic growth of 2.8% for 2026
Bulgaria’s Annual Inflation Reaches 5.7% in September
Bulgaria’s annual consumer price inflation rose to 5.7% in September from 5.1% in August, according to figures released by the National Statistical Institute (NSI) on October 14, while monthly inflation was negative 0.2%
Radev Presents Draft Budget With Pension Increases and More Defense Funding
Bulgaria’s draft 2027 budget aims to curb spending, reduce the government deficit and lower the nominal amount of new public debt compared with 2025 and 2026, while increasing pensions
IMF Cuts Bulgaria’s 2026 Growth Forecast to 2.6%, Raises Inflation Estimate
The International Monetary Fund has cut its forecast for Bulgaria’s economic growth in 2026 to 2.6% from 2.8% projected in the spring, according to its October World Economic Outlook report, while raising its estimate for average annual inflation to 4.9%

Sanctioned Investor in Cambodian Scam Compound Owns California Mansion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
09:40:00 UTC
18:40:00 KST

Brendon Luo was sanctioned in June by the U.S. Treasury Department, which alleged he was an investor in a cyber-scam compound operated by Cambodia's Prince Group. Property records show he still owns a mansion in a gated community in southern California.
The Prince Group is widely accused of involvement in compounds in Cambodia where thousands of trafficked workers were forced to commit industrial-scale cyberfraud. The Prince Group has strongly denied the accusations, but the U.S. has sanctioned more than 140 allegedly-associated entities and individuals, including Luo.
The sanctions have not disrupted Luo’s ownership of a five bedroom mansion in Yorba Linda, a city of about 68,000 people that is part of the Los Angeles metropolitan area. Although no sale price was identified in property records, online real estate portals value the property at roughly $5 million.
Luo was born in China and acquired passports from Cambodia, Vanuatu and Cyprus, according to information from sanctions notices as well as immigration records obtained by OCCRP.
A Cambodian government factsheet distributed to the media in September stated that Luo was the “registered owner” of Legend Innovation Co. Ltd. That company allegedly operated a scam compound named 8Park, which was dismantled this year by Cambodian authorities.
The U.S. sanctions notice alleged that Luo and another individual were “major investors in a Prince Group... scam compound that was used to facilitate fraud operations.”
A Prince Group spokesperson said in an emailed response to questions that the conglomerate has "never had any relationship with Legend Innovation."
“Brendon Luo had no role within the Prince Group of companies, nor was he associated with their operations throughout South Asia,” the spokesperson added.
Legend Innovation was sanctioned separately by the U.K. government in March. The U.K. Treasury said 8Park was “believed to be Cambodia’s largest scam compound, with capacity to accommodate 20,000 trafficked workers”.
Luo did not reply to requests for comment sent to multiple company email addresses, and no one answered calls to phone numbers listed for his Cambodian firms. However, a representative for Luo did respond to questions via the Prince Group spokesperson.
“Mr. Luo did not own Legend Innovation and had no role in it, or the construction or operation of any business that was conducted by it on the land in question,” Luo's representative said. “Mr. Luo has never been associated with, nor had any ownership interest, in the companies referenced, or in their alleged scam operations.”
The representative added that Luo “never held a role of any kind with Prince.”
Luo's California mansion in the “Enclave at Yorba Linda” development is down the street from a property that was owned by Chen Sokly. OCCRP recently identified Chen Sokly as the person referred to as “co-conspirator 2” in a U.S. federal court indictment of Prince Group founder and chairman Chen Zhi. The indictment charges Chen Zhi with alleged wire fraud and money laundering conspiracy.
American authorities alleged that co-conspirator 2 was a Prince Group “enforcer” who protected the conglomerate’s scam operations from police. Chen Sokly has not been charged in the case.
The Prince Group spokesperson previously told OCCRP that the conglomerate and its chairman were innocent of the U.S. allegations, adding that it was “not a criminal syndicate but a collection of legitimate businesses serving millions of people and employing tens of thousands of people across the globe.”
Luo was listed as a director of Prince Plaza Investment Co. Ltd. In October 2025, the U.S. Treasury Department included that company on a list of sanctioned firms it said were “owned or controlled by, or purport to act for or on behalf of, members of Prince Group TCO [Transnational Criminal Organization].”
As previously reported by OCCRP, Luo’s real estate portfolio also includes a luxury condominium in downtown Tokyo.

Iran War Updates: Trump's U.N ambassador says war could last another year as oil prices continue rising
What to know about the Iran war today:

- The price of Brent crude oil briefly crossed $117 a barrel Friday, its highest level during the war, after Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed to have disabled seven tankers near the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian president to meet with Putin next week in Moscow
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian will travel to Moscow next week for talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said, according to a report by Reuters.
It hasn't been long since Pezeshkian spoke to Putin in person, but this will be the first meeting between the two in Russia during the ongoing war.
The two leaders met with each other on the sidelines of the Caspian Environmental Summit in Turkmenistan on Oct. 8. The two also met at a summit in Kyrgyzstan in September.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov visited Tehran earlier this week as the two sides continue to strengthen relations. Araghchi said Russia and Iran were closer than ever, despite President Trump saying Russia was doing little to help Iran a day prior.
U.N. sounds alarm on besieged Yemen city of Taiz
Time is running out to get aid into Taiz, besieged by pro-Iran Houthi fighters who are preventing supplies from reaching Yemen's third-largest city, the United Nations said Friday.
Houthi fighters have encircled Taiz since early October, blocking the road that links it to Aden, interim capital of the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government.
"Safe, sustained and unimpeded humanitarian access is urgently needed so that essential supplies and life-saving assistance can reach people in need," said the U.N. humanitarian agency OCHA.
"It's 20 days and counting since Taiz has been cut off," said OCHA spokesman Jens Laerke.
"We are seeing increasingly that the fighting makes it impossible for us to get in and impossible for people to get out," he told a press conference in Geneva.
Laerke said the dwindling water supply was a growing concern, as most residents depended on water brought in by trucks.
"With the roads closed and the diesel to run the trucks very scarce, water production in the city has fallen by about half," he said.
U.S. envoy leaves open possibility of striking Iran this weekend, despite Trump's prior midterm promise
A U.S. official left open the door for the possibility of a strike on Iran this weekend, despite President Trump previously saying there would be none before the midterm elections in less than two weeks.
"Could there be a strike this weekend? Absolutely," Tom Barrack, the U.S. ambassador to Turkey and point man on Syria, who does not have a direct role on Iran policy, told Israeli army radio in response to a question.
"(President Trump) is very clear. He's open and available and accessible to a deal and we've been at the table for months and months and months," Barrack said.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces elections Tuesday, in recent days has repeatedly vowed to topple the clerical state in Iran, following two major bombing campaigns against Iran since last year.
Mr. Trump has also signaled an openness to resuming strikes on Iran after a long deadlock in diplomacy although he earlier said it would not happen before midterm elections on Nov. 3.
Earlier Friday, Mr. Trump repeated a common refrain that the U.S. could choose to end the war anytime it wants through a renewed military campaign, but could also let the country "wither" under sanctions.

European, Mideast foreign ministers push peace and diplomacy at Istanbul talks
Foreign ministers from eight European and Middle Eastern countries met in Istanbul on Friday in an unprecedented format, urging diplomacy and peaceful solutions to prevail across the Middle East as well as the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
Ministers from Britain, France, Germany and Italy met counterparts from Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt to discuss Hormuz — a crucial trade route blocked in the Iran war — as well as Yemen and ways to end the Russia-Ukraine conflict.
At the heart of the talks was the situation in the Straits of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, which is paralyzing global trade and driving up energy prices as well as the attacks on Saudi Arabia by Houthis from Yemen, allies of Tehran.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said a new escalation between Iran and the United States "would create nothing but losers and would undoubtedly have very serious consequences for hydrocarbon prices."
"The first thing this group of eight countries ... will do is call on both sides to exercise the utmost restraint, because we cannot afford another escalation in the region," he told journalists.
Italy's Antonio Tajani said the regional problem cannot be solved "from a purely military standpoint."
Wall Street mostly loses ground under pressure from rising oil prices
Stocks slipped Friday on Wall Street under increasing pressure from rising oil prices.

Trump says U.S. could take all of Iran's oil: "We could take the whole country"

Tanker involved in UAE oil spill identified, analysts say
The tanker involved in an oil spill off the coast of the United Arab Emirates has been identified, according to analysts who spoke to the Reuters new agency.
Emirati authorities have not named the vessel, but Martin Kelly, CEO of Orbital Risk Intelligence, told Reuters the oil slick was coming from a vessel called the Gem No. 2.
Another analyst told the news agency that satellite imagery appears to show a large spill coming from the tanker.
"The slick is considerably larger, covering approximately 160 square km (60 square miles), and looks to be coming from the ship," Leon Moreland, a researcher at the Conflict and Environment Observatory, said.
"Furthermore, a slick this close to shore increases the chance it could impact nearby beaches and ecologically sensitive habitats," he said.
The Gem No. 2 was hit by an unidentified projectile 13 nautical miles west of Al Jazeera in the UAE on Oct. 9, shipping sources told Reuters.
No group claimed responsibility for the incident at the time, but maritime security sources told the news agency that it took place outside of the Strait of Hormuz.

Any further escalation between Iran and the U.S. "would leave no winners," France's foreign minister said Friday.

Residents in the north of the United Arab Emirates have described smelling gas after an oil spill off the country's coastline.

"I was on my balcony and panicked thinking gas was leaking in my house and I will blow up everyone."

Iranian state TV claims movement of "non-compliant" vessels in Strait of Hormuz completely halted
Iranian state TV claimed Friday, citing an unnamed source close to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy, that all movement of "non-compliant" vessels through the Strait of Hormuz had been completely halted following a series of Iranian attacks on ships and navigational support systems.
The report cited the source as saying that if U.S. military escorts and ship-to-ship transfers - all of which the Iranian regime refers to as "oil smuggling" - resumes, action against the vessels and technical systems supporting them will be "much more forceful."
Iran has repeatedly warned commercial ships not to use the long-established shipping lanes through the strait, through which about 20% of global oil supplies passed before the war. Tehran demands that all vessels seek authorization and use a northern route, close to its coast, and it has attacked ships for months that refuse.
The Trump administration, however, has encouraged shippers to use an alternative southern route, close to Oman, to avoid Iranian tolls.
Iran claimed Thursday to have struck four ships that used that route, and said three others hit sea mines in the U.S.-designated shipping lanes.
President Trump on Thursday dismissed Iranian claims about striking vessels as lies aimed at increasing global oil prices ahead of the looming U.S. midterm elections.
Both Iran and the U.S. have claimed at various times during the war to have completely halted traffic that violates their respective blockades of the waterway.

Iran's foreign minister has called Israel's relationship with the United States "parasitic," citing alleged American taxpayer funding for missile defense in Israel.

CBS News has not been able to independently verify the figures.
Semler is the founder of the Security Policy Reform Institute, a think tank that, according to its website, is "driven by empiricism and guided by progressive values" to promote "the meaningful reform of U.S. foreign policy to break the cycle of endless war and serve the most pressing economic, social, and political needs of working-class Americans."
Araghchi also said the U.S. had "fired more interceptors defending Israel than Israel has," a claim supported by a Washington Post story from May that cited U.S. Defense Department data and U.S. officials.
"That is not a symbiotic relationship," Araghchi said. "It is a parasitic one."

Many residents in the north of the UAE have reported oil smells on social media in recent days, including residents in northern districts of Dubai.

The British maritime security UKMTO reported on Oct. 9 that a vessel was hit by a projectile off the UAE coast, causing a fire that was later brought under control. According to the maritime security company Vanguard, the vessel in question was the Panama-flagged oil tanker GEM NO.2.

U.S. ambassador to the U.N. says Iran war could last another year
U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz has said the war with Iran could drag on for another year.
In an interview with the Financial Times published Friday, Waltz said the U.S. could still be fighting the war President Trump initially said would last "four to five weeks" 12 months from now.
Waltz told the FT the U.S. will not have achieved its key goals in Iran until the country disposes of its highly enriched uranium and accepts a "meaningful agreement on their domestic enrichment."
"I'm not going to put out hypotheticals. One would hope that they'll come to the table in a meaningful way before that," Waltz said, referring to the possibility of another year of war.
He added that Mr. Trump "and the U.S. Navy can maintain this blockade [on Iranian ports] for the foreseeable future," and said the administration was still "tightening" its economic pressure campaign against Iran.
Mr. Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have renewed their threats to launch new strikes on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3.
Foreign ministers from Europe and Gulf region to discuss Strait of Hormuz and Iran conflict
Foreign ministers from seven nations in Europe, the Middle East and elsewhere will hold talks in Istanbul Friday focused on the Strait of Hormuz and the interlinked crises in the Middle East, as well as the Ukraine war.
Ministers from the so-called E3 group – Britain, France and Germany – will meet counterparts from the newly created R4 group, composed of Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt, to discuss the Israel-Palestinian crisis, developments in Yemen and the Strait of Hormuz, and ways to end the Russia-Ukraine war, a Turkish foreign ministry source told AFP.
British Foreign Minister Ed Miliband's office said the talks would revolve around "the Strait of Hormuz and the situation in Saudi Arabia," as the Saudis back Yemen's beleaguered government in its decade-long civil war, which has flared up amid the U.S. war on Iran.

"The U.K. is stepping up to help stabilize the region, having this week committed RAF Typhoons to defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks in their airspace," it added.
CBS/AFP
Saudi Aramco says volume bypassing Strait of Hormuz via pipeline has surged
The president of Saudi state-owned oil company Saudi Aramco, whose facilities have been targeted by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militants repeatedly for weeks, says the amount of oil moving through a pipeline that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz has more than tripled.
The East-West pipeline's capacity has surged from 2 million to 7 million barrels each day, President and CEO Amin Nasser said in an interview with Saudi-owned television Al Arabiya Business.
Built in the early 1980s, the pipeline has played a crucial role in Saudi Arabia's ability to export oil amid disruption to shipping via the Strait of Hormuz during the Iran war. It carries crude from Saudi oil fields and production facilities in the east, on the Persian Gulf, to the Yanbu oil terminal on the Saudi Red Sea coast on the other side of the vast kingdom, from which it can be shipped to global markets.
That route, which, unlike the Gulf, has two available exits, has also been threatened and attacked by the Houthis, who have vowed to stop Saudi shipments via the Red Sea's southern gateway, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Nasser said Saudi Aramco has used drones to assess damage caused to infrastructure, including sites key to the East-West pipeline, by Houthi attacks, and to help with firefighting.
CBS/AP
Trump accuses Iran of lying about strikes on ships to drive up oil prices
As crude oil prices hit their highest levels since May, President Trump accused Iran on Thursday of lying about attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz to drive up global energy prices.
"Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of Oil prior to the U.S. Midterm Election," Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social. "They are even making up fake hits, mines, and everything else, because more Oil is coming through the Hormuz Strait now than it did even prior to the beginning of the Conflict."
Brent crude, the international standard for oil, hit $112 a barrel Thursday morning, its highest price since May 18.
Iran claimed to have struck four vessels in the Persian Gulf Thursday after they transited the Strait of Hormuz using a U.S.-endorsed route that Tehran rejects, and it said three others hit sea mines in the region after using the same shipping lanes. All of the ships were damaged along or after using southern shipping lanes in the strait near the Omani coast, which the Trump administration has insisted for weeks is open to traffic.
The U.S. military has escorted tankers out of the Persian Gulf using that route, boosting the quantity of oil leaving the region, but it is a costly process. Overall instability in the Middle East has kept energy prices high despite the recently increased supplies.

Bulgaria to Maintain Enhanced Black Sea Air Patrols, Air Force Chief Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
09:37:04 UTC
18:37:04 KST

Bulgarian Air Force Commander Major General Nikolay Rusev said on BNT that enhanced patrolling over the Black Sea would continue for as long as necessary as a preventive response to the war north of Bulgaria.
Rusev said Bulgaria had the trained personnel and aircraft needed to carry out the missions, although existing radar coverage had limitations, especially when detecting low-flying objects.
The heightened patrols were introduced as a precaution against incidents similar to those taking place north of Bulgaria. “The Bulgarian skies are protected, but we must still take preventive measures to ensure that nothing similar occurs further south - towards Bulgaria, our sea, and our airspace,” Rusev said, noting that media reports kept the public informed about the difficult situation to the north, where people were losing their lives.
He stressed that the increased flights were not an independent Air Force initiative, but part of a coordinated military effort involving several branches of the armed forces.
“These are coordinated, well-thought-out actions involving various branches of the armed forces. We are working together and interacting; the Land Forces, the Navy, and the Special Forces are all involved,” Rusev said, adding that each branch had a specific role but shared the same objective.
Asked how long the military could maintain the increased patrols, the Air Force commander said the country had enough operational aircraft and pilots to sustain them.
“We will keep this up for as long as necessary. We have sufficient aircraft, with the required operational lifespan, and we have the pilots; this is simply our job,” Rusev said, adding that the mission would continue for as long as the situation required.
Bulgaria has also deployed additional surveillance and engagement systems, while receiving information about the air situation from neighboring countries.
Rusev said the country maintained constant contact with its partners to build a comprehensive picture of activity across Bulgarian airspace, the Balkan Peninsula and the Black Sea.
He explained that fighter jets were tasked not only with monitoring the skies but also with remaining ready to respond if necessary. Within the Air Force, coordination between aircraft, radar stations and surface-to-air missile systems is handled through a unified command-and-control system. Communication channels have also been established with the other branches of the armed forces.
Rusev emphasized that effective air defense depended both on the equipment available and on having personnel trained to use it.
He said Bulgaria had qualified personnel and identified the MiG-29, F-16, Su-25 and L-39 as aircraft available for combat missions, airspace protection and, if required, engagement of targets.
The radars currently in service are more than 30 years old, Rusev said. Although they are maintained in good working condition, their data is supplemented with information from allies and neighboring countries.
Bulgaria has already signed a contract to purchase new radars, with the first system expected to arrive in the country in about a year and a half. Work is also underway to procure new surface-to-air missile systems, and a contract for them is expected to be signed soon.
“The Air Force, the Defense Staff, and the Ministry of Defense are working actively on this. We haven't stopped,” Rusev said.
Asked whether radar systems could detect low-flying drones and jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles such as the Geran type, he said detection depended on the altitude at which the target was flying. He added that the military also detected objects that were not made public.
“We see quite a few things that we don't announce publicly - there is no need to frighten people, and it simply isn't worth causing them alarm,” Rusev said, adding that monitoring the airspace and taking action when necessary were the military's responsibilities.
Rusev also addressed the presence of an allied Poseidon aircraft in Bulgaria, saying it would remain for an extended period to carry out its assigned tasks. He stressed that the aircraft was not the only asset allies had provided to support the Bulgarian military.

Cable saboteurs to face up to fourteen years in jail
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:36:42 BST
18:36:42 KST

Those who intentionally damage critical undersea energy and telecoms infrastructure would face prison sentences of up to fourteen years and unlimited fines under proposals published today, which also place new security and resilience duties on subsea telecoms providers and give ministers power to intervene where national security is at risk, according to the government.
A White Paper published by the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology sets out proposals to update 140-year-old legislation, and marks the start of a twelve-week public consultation.
Ian Murray, the Telecoms Minister, said: “Undersea cables are the hidden backbone of modern Britain, carrying the data we rely on every day to message friends and family, do our banking, and run our businesses.
“The threats we face have changed dramatically, with suspicious Russian activity around critical undersea infrastructure, yet some of the laws protecting these vital connections date back more than a century.
“We intend to modernise those laws with tougher penalties, stronger requirements on industry and new powers to protect our national security, making sure the UK’s critical infrastructure is fit for the threats of today and tomorrow.”
Dan Jarvis, the Security Minister, said: “Undersea cables carry the energy and data our country relies on every day. Protecting them is vital to our national security.
“We’re toughening the law to stay ahead of those who seek to do us harm. Those who deliberately or recklessly damage our undersea infrastructure will face tougher penalties, including longer prison sentences and unlimited fines.
“These measures are part of the work underway across government to protect our critical infrastructure and keep our country safe.”
Michael Shanks, the Energy Minister, said: “Undersea pipelines and cables are critical to keeping energy flowing to homes and businesses across the UK.
“This legislation will further strengthen deterrence and help ensure we can prevent, detect, and respond to threats against our energy supply.”
The fibre-optic cables running along the seabed carry around ninety-nine per cent of Britain’s international data. Undersea pipelines provide seventy-four per cent of the country’s gas supply, and undersea electricity cables carry supply from Europe and from the growing offshore wind sector.
The proposals cover four areas, the first of which would modernise criminal law on harmful conduct against telecoms and energy undersea infrastructure through new offences, stronger penalties and new enforcement measures; introduce statutory security and resilience duties for subsea telecoms cable infrastructure providers; create a national security direction power allowing the Secretary of State to direct providers of subsea cable infrastructure and repair capabilities where necessary and proportionate; and establish a regulatory regime covering sensing technologies installed on subsea fibre optic cables.
Fibre optic sensing can detect activity at sea, and the government says it could pose national security risks if sensitive data fell into the wrong hands.
The government states that Britain already has a highly resilient subsea cable network, and that where cable faults occur they are due to accidents involving anchors or trawler nets dragged across the cables, environmental hazards or technical failures. It adds that suspicious activity around critical undersea infrastructure is increasingly being observed, and that in April the British armed forces exposed a covert Russian submarine operation around critical undersea infrastructure in and around British waters.
The Royal Navy has tracked the Russian vessel Yantar in waters around Britain, which this publication covered when the United Kingdom tracked the Russian spy ship amid cable concerns.
The Defence Committee reported yesterday that failure to deter Russia in the High North, particularly from underwater threats, puts subsea data cables and energy pipelines in and around British waters at particular risk during peacetime. Its report records that Russia’s Main Directorate for Deep-Sea Research holds assets designed specifically to degrade or destroy critical infrastructure and technological networks, including undersea energy pipelines and data cables.

Otherwise, our regulatory framework is generally in place and functioning. Therefore, the introduction of any new mechanisms is not under discussion," Chebeskov said.

US Court Orders Lebanese Ex-Minister to Pay $35M in Torture and Fraud Case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
09:32:00 UTC
18:32:00 KST

A U.S. district court has ruled against four Lebanese individuals, including a former minister, finding them liable for fraud, torture and civil conspiracy and ordering them to pay $35 million in damages, for orchestrating the kidnapping and torture of a Lebanese-American couple.
Speaking to OCCRP about the verdict from the Florida court, Lara Samaha, a U.S. green card holder, said the couple filed in the U.S. because “the justice system in Lebanon is so corrupt it is impossible to obtain justice.”
According to the default final judgment seen by OCCRP, a binding court order issued when defendants fail to respond to a lawsuit, the court ordered Gebran Bassil—a sitting member of parliament, Lebanon’s former foreign minister, and the son-in-law of former President Michel Aoun—to pay millions in damages, along with three co-defendants.
“I feel justice has been served after 7 years in court and more than 300 court filings,” Lara Samaha told OCCRP. She confirmed that there will be a follow up on a related lawsuit in Lebanon, though she declined to detail the next steps.
The Florida court heard that the defendants kidnapped and tortured Lara and her husband Elie Samaha, a U.S.-Lebanese citizen, to force them to dismiss a lawsuit they had raised in Florida in 2017, against Lebanese government officials who had stymied Lara’s efforts to obtain her inheritance. The couple alleged to the court that Bassil had worked to ensure the dismissal in order to protect one of those officials. The court found that Bassil and the other defendants had lured the couple to Lebanon under the pretext of a settlement discussion of the inheritance dispute.
Bassil’s office denied any connection to the case or the parties involved. In a statement issued on October 16 after reports of the ruling, his office said Bassil has no relationship with the parties involved and objected to what it called a selective and fragmented presentation of the legal proceedings. The office claimed that the Florida court had previously dismissed a lawsuit in March 2023 for lack of jurisdiction, and that the Lebanese judiciary had issued a ruling in Bassil’s favor against Elie and Lara Samaha.
Commenting on the statement, Lara dismissed Bassil’s office claims, saying that what matters is the US court orders and final judgement.
The office did not say whether or not Bassil plans to challenge the Florida court judgement.
The couple’s legal battles began in 2015, when they filed a lawsuit in Beirut alleging that politically-connected family members had stolen millions of dollars Lara was due to inherit. With that case delayed but still active, they filed a parallel suit in the U.S. on November 17, 2017, seeking to recover the inheritance.
In 2019, the couple traveled to Lebanon hoping to settle the dispute. That, they say, is when their ordeal began.
Lara Samaha told Daraj, OCCRP’s partner, that she and her husband were detained —she for 11 days and he for nine. The legal complaint alleged that Lebanese security forces detained the couple upon their arrival in Beirut. She alleged that each spent part of that time in an underground military prison, where they were denied food, medicine and light. She also alleged they were forced to withdraw their lawsuits in both the U.S. and Lebanon.
Bassil, who heads the Free Patriotic Movement (FPM), an influential Christian party in Lebanon allied with the Shiite movement Hezbollah, has been under U.S. sanctions since November 2020 for playing a major role in corruption in the country.
Bassil's office did not respond to OCCRP's request for comment.
