Pulaku: The two faces of Nigeria’s vigilantes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
09:30:05 UTC
18:30:05 KST

Adamawa State, Nigeria - The night they came for Daniel Musa*, the dogs were barking.
At about 11:30 pm on May 23, 2023, Musa looked out of a window overlooking the gate of his home in Adamawa State, northeastern Nigeria.
The intruders wore all black, like the night. Their faces were uncovered.
Musa, 49, usually left his dogs loose in the compound at night. But the men who had climbed over the fence drove them back into their cage and locked it, clearing a path to the house.
Then they broke the padlock on a smaller gate and moved towards the main door. There, they began trying to force it open with a digger.
Musa, a local pastor, knew they were coming in. Rather than wait for them to break down the door, he opened it himself; he didn’t want any trouble.
He had already told his wife and his then 13-year-old daughter to stay in their bedroom. The men entered his home, pointed a gun at him, and ordered him to sit on the floor.
One went into his bedroom and took money and phones. Another walked to the fridge and helped himself to bread, milk, and water.
Then, at gunpoint, they led Musa out of his home; he did not struggle. He feared that if they did not take him, they might take his wife or daughter instead.
For six hours, Musa walked blindfolded with his captors through bushland, crossing shallow streams until they reached the mountains. There, he heard the familiar voice of his neighbour and discovered he had also been abducted.
He would remain in captivity for three days.
By then, negotiations with his relatives over ransom were under way. The kidnappers demanded 15 million naira (about $11,256 at the time) for his release. But after contacting Musa's family members, they switched off their phones. The family could only reach them when the kidnappers chose to make contact, leaving them unable to negotiate a lower ransom.
Musa, whose name has been changed to protect his identity, says he remained blindfolded throughout his captivity. His only drinking water came from a river, and even then, his captors allowed him just a few sips at a time, whenever they chose.
The captives, still blindfolded, were warned by their abductors that if they detected police officers or vigilantes approaching, they would kill their hostages before attempting to escape.
At about 4am on Friday, gunfire erupted.
For roughly 15 minutes, shots rang out around the camp.
Musa lay on the rocky ground between two other captives, urging them not to move. They could hear voices approaching but had no way of knowing whether they belonged to their abductors or the people trying to rescue them. Were the kidnappers returning? Had the security forces found them? Or were they about to be killed, as their captors had threatened?
“We were confused. We didn’t know who was coming, so I told the others not to move,” he said.
The voices told them not to be afraid, as they removed their blindfolds. Several men stood before them; he can’t recall how many, all dressed in olive-green uniforms.
They belonged to Pulaku, a predominantly Fulani vigilante organisation fighting kidnapping and cattle rustling in northeastern Nigeria. Musa had heard of the group, but this was his first encounter with its members.
The kidnappers had fled, leaving behind food, phones and other belongings. Musa recalled that the rescuers also discovered what appeared to be a national identity card belonging to one of the suspects.
The captives then made their way down the mountain with their rescuers before the police took them to headquarters in Yola, the Adamawa State capital. There, Musa was reunited with his wife and daughter.
He recalls being filled with joy when he saw them again. He credits Pulaku with making that reunion possible.
“They saved my life,” says Musa. His church would later present Pulaku with an award, recognising its work in the community.
But the group’s growing role in fighting kidnapping has also brought the organisation under scrutiny. While some residents credit its members with saving lives, others accuse them of serious abuses. One man says they held him for more than two months and beat him so badly that he lost consciousness.
The two accounts reveal the uneasy place occupied by armed community vigilantes in a region where formal security forces have struggled to contain kidnapping and cattle rustling.
On a Tuesday afternoon in late September, three Toyota Hilux trucks make their way out of Yola and into the open savanna of northeastern Nigeria.
Inside, about 30 men wear the same olive-green uniforms. Some wear combat boots; others wear rubber shoes. They carry an assortment of weapons: Locally made firearms, machetes, and long wooden sticks more commonly associated with herding cattle.
After about an hour, the convoy reaches an area of scattered trees and sparse woodland. Here, away from the city, the men exit the vehicles and begin drills, moving through the terrain and rehearsing patrol tactics. Several crouch on the reddish, sandy ground, aiming their firearms towards the open area, while others stand and watch.
Among them is Mahmud, who only gave his first name. He is a former cattle herder and farmer in his late 20s. He has closely cropped hair, a faint moustache and a cap pulled over his head. A firearm rests in his hands.
Mahmud is local to Malkohi, Adamawa State, and is one of Pulaku's newer recruits. He has yet to confront kidnappers himself, but speaks confidently about the dangers that may lie ahead.
“We are ready to fight day in, day out,” he says.
For men such as Mahmud, the threat of kidnapping and cattle theft is not an abstract security problem.
Across Adamawa and neighbouring Taraba State, analysts say armed groups have preyed on communities for years, abducting residents for ransom and stealing livestock. The mountains and forests that stretch across parts of the region offer places for kidnappers to hide and make it difficult for security forces to reach them.
The scale of the violence is reflected in figures compiled by SBM Intelligence, a Nigerian research and market intelligence firm. Between July 2025 and June 2026, it recorded 21 kidnapping incidents in Adamawa, involving 77 abducted people, and four incidents in Taraba, involving 14 people.
Cattle theft has also taken a heavy toll. A 2024 study published in the University of Jos Journal of Political Science estimated that 134,182 cattle were stolen in Taraba between 1999 and 2022. Over the same period, researchers reported that more than 113,000 stolen cattle were recovered in Adamawa.
For Fulani pastoralists, whose livelihoods have long been tied to livestock, cattle theft can mean losing far more than animals. At an estimated 700,000 naira ($525) per animal, a herd of 50 cattle could be worth about 35 million naira ($26,254) - a substantial investment for a family whose livelihood depends on its animals.
But Fulani communities face another struggle: The association of their ethnic identity with kidnapping, banditry and farmer-herder violence in parts of Nigeria's media.
A 2021 study published in African Journalism Studies, which examined 598 articles from three Nigerian newspapers, found that reports sometimes used the terms "herdsmen" and "Fulani herdsmen" interchangeably, while employing labels such as "Fulani terrorists" and "killer Fulani herdsmen".
For Alhaji Bello Ardo, a Fulani community leader in Adamawa State, such portrayals contribute to the suspicion faced by people who have no involvement in crime.
"It's painful to see an entire ethnic group being stereotyped. Every ethnic group has individuals involved in crime, but in our case, people make accusations without confirmation," he says.
"If people are robbed, they say it's Fulani without knowing who the perpetrators are."
Ardo points out that Fulani pastoralists are themselves victims of cattle theft and violence.
"We are also not safe. Our cattle are being stolen, and we are also being killed," he said.
"People don't understand that not all Fulani are terrorists."
According to its leaders, Pulaku began taking shape more than a decade ago, as Fulani community members organised to confront cattle theft and kidnapping.
Based in Malkohi, Yola South Local Government Area, the organisation was founded by the late Alhaji Abdu Bali; Musa Usman Malkohi, the group's current commander; and other Fulani community leaders as a voluntary response to kidnapping and cattle rustling.
Its name invokes a cultural ideal that has long shaped Fulani identity.
Pulaaku, as the concept is commonly written, encompasses values including dignity, patience, self-control, modesty, courage and respect for others.
Professor Abubakar Abba Tahir, a mass communication scholar who holds the traditional title of Kakaki Fombina, is a spokesperson for the Adamawa Emirate, a traditional Fulani institution in northeastern Nigeria.
He explains that pulaaku is not a fixed code but a living tradition, shaped by the experiences of different Fulani communities.
"Pulaaku is a living cultural concept whose interpretation has always been influenced by community traditions, social circumstances, historical experiences, and individual understanding," he tells Al Jazeera.
The concept can inspire collective responsibility and community protection, Tahir explains, but it also places importance on restraint and respect for human life.
And there is a distinction between pulaaku, the cultural ideal, and Pulaku, the vigilante organisation that has adopted its name, spelling it with a single "a".
"The mere use of pulaaku in an organisation's name does not, by itself, establish that its activities fully reflect the broader cultural ideal," Tahir says.
Whether an organisation upholds those values, he argues, depends on its conduct, accountability and respect for human rights.
Pulaku's leadership says the organisation now has more than 500 members operating across parts of Adamawa and neighbouring Taraba State. Although predominantly Fulani, its ranks also include members of other ethnic groups, including Verre and Chamba.
Unlike the police or military, Pulaku is not part of Nigeria's formal security establishment.
"The group is not on the government payroll," says its grand commander, Musa Usman Malkohi, an older man with a short grey beard and moustache. He refuses to share his age.
He says members contribute their own resources, with additional support from communities and local authorities. Local government chairmen have provided financial assistance towards running costs, while the Adamawa State government has supported the group with vehicles.
On the side of one of the trucks, a message painted in black reads: "Thank you Governor Ahmadu Umaru Fintiri."
It refers to the governor of Adamawa State, who donated the vehicle to Pulaku - a visible sign of the support the volunteer group receives from the state government, despite not being part of Nigeria's formal security forces.
Membership is voluntary, and the organisation's leadership decides which members are permitted to carry firearms.
For the police, one of Pulaku's greatest assets is its members' knowledge of the terrain. Many come from communities familiar with the forests and mountains where kidnappers establish hideouts.
But the story of how this volunteer organisation grew into a force of hundreds begins with a man whose own family was touched by the violence the organisation was formed to confront.
Musa Usman Malkohi wears a traditional patterned Zanna Bukar cap and a kaftan. Unlike the men training in front of him, he carries no weapon.
A farmer and cattle breeder, Usman speaks predominantly Fulfulde, the language of the Fulani people, as well as Hausa with a noticeable Fulani accent.
From his position behind the armed men, he watches the exercise unfold. He explains his involvement in the fight against kidnapping is not just a matter of community security; it’s personal.
In 2018, gunmen attacked Usman's home and abducted his 24-year-old son.
Usman believes he was the intended target, describing the attack as one of the challenges he faced while fighting what he calls "bad people".
By then, he was already leading Pulaku. The violence he had spent years confronting had reached his own home.
For about seven days, Usman worked to secure his son's freedom.
He says members of his own vigilante team eventually rescued the young man without a ransom being paid.
The group's cofounder, Alhaji Abdu Bali, was killed in October 2019 when suspected kidnappers attacked his residence in Lakare, Yola. Local news reports said four people were killed and another injured in the attack.
By then, Pulaku was seeking a closer relationship with the state.
Following Ahmadu Umaru Fintiri's election as governor of Adamawa in 2019, the organisation approached the government about working more formally with security agencies.
"The government subsequently brought the police and military into discussions with the group," Usman said.
The arrangement offered Pulaku access to cooperation with the institutions legally responsible for public security.
For the authorities, it meant gaining assistance from men who knew the remote areas where kidnappers could hide.
Yet that cooperation also created a difficult boundary.
Pulaku was a volunteer organisation, not a police force. Its members were expected to apprehend suspected criminals and hand them over to the police for investigation and possible prosecution.
They were not authorised to hold suspects in their own custody, conduct interrogations or impose punishment.
But allegations that Pulaku members detained people themselves raised questions about whether they were observing those limits - and who was responsible for enforcing them.
"Pulaku are taking a front line because they know the terrain, the mountainous and the forest areas better than we do," explains Suleiman Yahya Nguroje, spokesperson for the Adamawa State Police Command.
According to Nguroje, the vigilantes provide intelligence, help security forces navigate difficult terrain and participate in joint operations targeting suspected kidnapping networks.
Nguroje says joint operations disrupted four suspected criminal hideouts, including sites around the Bagale Mountains and the Kojoli and Yadim areas of Fufore.
Several suspects were arrested, he said, with cases proceeding through the courts.
In February 2024, hunters and vigilantes participated in an operation that freed 40 hostages in neighbouring Taraba State, according to a report by TVC News. Police also attributed a role to Pulaku in the rescue operation around Zing and Yorro.
The police confirmed Pulaku's involvement in the operation that freed Daniel Musa in May 2023.
For Nguroje, the cooperation is a practical response to the limitations of conventional policing.
"There's no way we can effectively perform our responsibilities without cooperation, without collaborations from sister security agencies, critical stakeholders and members of the public," he said.
But working with the police is not the same as being the police.
Hakeem Abubakar Abba, a Nigerian legal practitioner in Yola, said no specific federal or state law expressly establishes Pulaku as a security force with independent policing powers.
"There is no express law that is sanctioning their functions," he told Al Jazeera.
Although the organisation's cooperation with police could fall within broader community-policing arrangements, Abba said its members have no special statutory powers of arrest beyond those available to citizens.
They may apprehend suspects in circumstances permitted by law, but cannot conduct criminal investigations, determine guilt or impose punishment.
He also questioned the safeguards governing the organisation's activities.
Abba said he was unaware of any formal written agreement setting out Pulaku's relationship with the Nigeria Police Force.
He alleged that members sometimes deal with suspected offenders without referring them to the authorities.
"At times, they settle matters at their own end, which I believe is not within the ambit of the law," he said.
He also said several members had reportedly faced court proceedings over alleged human rights violations, including torture and inhumane treatment, although he did not provide case details or judgements that would allow those claims to be independently verified.
The police say Pulaku members are expected to hand suspects over to officers for formal investigation and possible prosecution.
For people such as Daniel Musa, cooperation between the police and armed volunteers can mean the difference between remaining in captivity and returning home.
For Haruna Hamza, however, the question is what happens when the volunteers themselves are accused of acting as captors.
But there’s another side to this.
Sitting in the office of a human rights organisation in Adamawa, Haruna Hamza carefully raises his kaftan and turns around to expose his back.
Raised scars form darkened, swollen patches that look like dried leeches, where the skin healed unevenly. Pulling his kaftan back down, he begins describing what happened to him; his voice drops.
Hamza, a man in his late fifties, said they were the marks of a beating by Pulaku members.
In March 2025, he says, members of the vigilante organisation arrested him and his eldest son, without telling either of them what they were accused of doing.
"I asked them what my offence was, but no one told me. Up to today, I still don't know my offence," he said.
According to Hamza, he and his son were taken to Pulaku's base in Malkohi. He says his son was also detained but was not physically assaulted.
Hamza, however, alleges that his hands were tied with rope. Several men physically suspended him by his arms while others beat him with canes made from tamarind tree branches.
He said the beating continued until he lost consciousness.
"I was beaten into a coma. I fainted, and I don't even know when the rope on my hands came loose," he said.
Hamza's description of a coma refers to his account of losing consciousness; Al Jazeera has not established that he was medically diagnosed as being in a coma.
He could not identify any of the individual men he says attacked him.
But he attributes the assault to Pulaku members.
He alleged that he remained detained at the group's base for two months and one week, without being transferred to police custody.
He said injuries on his back became severely infected.
"The scars you see on my back decayed. Maggots were coming out of them," he said.
Hamza also alleged that a slap damaged one of his ears, causing it to bleed for about a week.
As he recounts the experience, his voice softens and becomes more subdued. At other moments, he sounds agitated.
Months after his release, he can finally sleep on his back without pain, but the marks on his body are still visible.
He said he has continued to live with the physical consequences of the alleged assault. He also said his hopes of obtaining justice had diminished, and that he now tries to avoid discussing the experience.
He would not wish what happened to him on anyone, he said.
But the organisation he accused of detaining and torturing him disputed his account.
Its commander had a very different explanation for the marks on Hamza's back.
Musa Usman Malkohi rejects Hamza’s account that Pulaku members had tortured him.
"The scars on his back were drawn with a marker. We don't abuse humans," he said.
The commander had been shown photographs of the marks on Hamza's body.
He maintained that the injuries were not genuine, suggesting that closer examination of the wounds would reveal they had been drawn onto the skin.
He also accused Hamza of defaming the organisation.
"We were planning to take legal action against him, but we collectively decided to just forget about him," he said.
Usman did not deny that Pulaku members had detained Hamza.
He said the organisation dealt with suspects whom he believed could pose a threat to its members, but did not specify what Hamza was suspected of or provide evidence linking him to criminal activity.
He did not clarify whether Pulaku kept records of people detained at its base, nor did he confirm that Hamza had been handed over to police.
Hamza maintains that he was never transferred into police custody during his detention.
The Adamawa State Police Command said it had not received a formal complaint from Hamza or his family about the alleged detention and torture.
However, police said they were investigating the allegations but did not provide further details.
Nguroje said officers had organised workshops and training sessions for vigilantes and hunters, covering issues including extortion, unnecessary demands and human rights violations.
"We taught them about violations of human rights. We taught them about extortion and unnecessary demands," he said.
The command did not provide figures on previous complaints against Pulaku or details of criminal or disciplinary proceedings involving its members.
For Hamza, the unresolved questions that no one is willing to answer are more immediate.
Why was he detained? Under whose authority was he held? And who will establish what happened during the more than two months he says he spent at the vigilante group's base?
The tension surrounding Pulaku reflects a much wider dilemma in Nigeria, where communities facing kidnapping, banditry and other violence have increasingly turned to armed volunteer groups for protection.
Kabir Adamu, managing director of Beacon Security and Intelligence Limited, a Nigeria-based security and intelligence firm, sees the growth of vigilantism as a consequence of deeper failures in public security.
"The reason why we have a lot of vigilante groups is because of the failure of public security in Nigeria," he said. "And that failure has led to self-help, vigilantism and the securitisation of different environments."
Nigeria's security crisis has deepened over more than a decade, driven by overlapping conflicts. In the northeast, Boko Haram's armed rebellion has devastated communities since 2009. Elsewhere, disputes over land and water, cattle rustling and the spread of armed criminal gangs have led to killings and kidnappings.
Climate pressures and competition for resources have intensified a number of these tensions. Meanwhile, overstretched police and military forces have struggled to secure vast rural areas, leaving communities exposed to repeated attacks.
In the northeast, the Civilian Joint Task Force has fought alongside security forces against Boko Haram and other armed groups. In the southwest, the Amotekun security network was established to combat violence, while Benue State, in central Nigeria, set up its own Community Volunteer Guards.
Their powers and relationships with authorities differ, but all reflect a growing reliance on local groups to protect communities.
But that reliance has brought its own dangers.
In southeastern Nigeria, Amnesty International documented the killing of 14 young people by operatives of Ebube Agu, a state-backed paramilitary outfit, in Imo State in July 2022. The rights organisation also recorded allegations that local vigilantes in neighbouring Anambra State detained about 80 people in a makeshift prison and demanded money from their families for their release.
The allegations against Pulaku remain disputed. But the contrast between Daniel Musa's rescue and Haruna Hamza's account of detention and abuse exposes the difficult position of communities that depend on armed volunteers for protection while having limited means to hold them accountable.
Adamu warns that the consequences extend beyond individual allegations. When armed groups become closely associated with particular ethnic identities, they can deepen mistrust between communities and further weaken the authority of the state.
"The risks are that it erodes the authority of the state, it leads to depleted social cohesion, and it accentuates the fragility that Nigeria is in at the moment," he says.
*Daniel Musa is a pseudonym; his name has been changed to protect his identity.

You know who doesn’t care about AI, recession indicators, or You Can See Everything FOMO? Birds.
Birds don’t even know you exist, nor would they care about you if they did. In this era of everything all the time, it’s almost life-affirming to interact with a being who has a brain the size of a garbanzo bean, that isn't able to drive or vote.
There are probably entertaining dramas playing out in your yard right now that you don’t even know about. Mine include a crow with one eye and a greedy Steller’s jay that fills his crop with peanuts until it’s translucent.
Now that smart bird feeders have been around since 2020, even moderately priced models come with high-resolution cameras, 4K video recording, and AI ID that rarely misses. Many of them require minimal maintenance other than filling the seeds. (As long as you're following the 5-7-9 rule of pole-mount placement, to keep squirrels away.)
Below are some early Black Friday sales on models I have been using and enjoying for years and would not hesitate to buy for a gift (or myself).
Top Picks
Birdfy Original (Blue) With Solar for $127 (29% Off)
For some reason, this deal is only on the blue version of this feeder; the yellow costs an extra ($13). Anyhow, if you've only got $130 to spend, Birdfy's enduring original is your best bet. Sure, there are sturdier, better-designed feeders (like Kiwibit, below), and feeders with better camera quality (like Camojojo's 32MP Hibird), but you will either pay extra or run into janky apps and paywalled features.
If you're just looking for a reliable feeder that will last through the seasons and sports a high-quality, easy-to-use app without major features being paywalled, you won't do better than this model. It comes with an auxiliary solar panel that mounts separately, but if you don't want solar, you can pay even less—just $110. I would recommend it, though—Birdfy's panels have been very reliable in my experience, and I think it's worth the extra $17 to not have to worry about bringing it in to charge. (Note: This model only supports 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi.)
Kiwibit Feeder 2 With Solar Roof for $170 (29% Off)
This isn't the latest and greatest Kiwibit model (that would be the Feeder 2 Pro, $220), but the regular Feeder 2 is still exceedingly well designed, and this is the lowest price I have ever seen it. The generously sized, 1.5-liter seed hopper is bifurcated for two different types of feed and pulls right out of the body via a handle on the top—no need to take the whole feeder down to refill.
The 8-megapixel photos and 4K video quality are top-tier at this price point, and the solar roof kept everything charged through all kinds of weather during my test. The app is easy to navigate and functional without a Kiwibit Plus subscription, but more and more features are starting to be paywalled, as I found when I recently reviewed the Feeder 2 Pro, which I don't love. Note that this feeder only works on 2.4-GHz Wi-Fi and the warranty is only one year, compared with the above Birdfy's two-year warranty.
Kiwibit 4K Feeder With Auxiliary Solar for $140 (26% Off)
Despite the different name, this Kiwibit model has the same camera and hardware as the Feeder 2, just without the built-in solar roof. Still, I had no issues installing the included 3-watt solar panel on the back of the wall mount (I always pole-mount my feeders to keep squirrels away), so if you're interested in Kiwibit's sturdy build quality and high-resolution imagery and want to save $30, this is a totally viable option.

Austria expels four Russian diplomats
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Austria has taken the decision to expel four Russian diplomats.
Source: Austrian media outlet ORF, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Three of the diplomats expelled by Austria are accredited to the Russian Embassy in Vienna, while another is a member of the Russian delegation to the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe.
The ministry reported that the diplomats engaged in activities incompatible with their diplomatic status. They were therefore declared personae non gratae and ordered to leave the country.
These measures were based on intelligence gathered by security agencies, according to the ministry. No additional details regarding the reasons for the expulsion were provided.
Background: In September Hungary took the unprecedented decision to expel 10 members of staff of the Russian Embassy – for the first time since 2018. In response, the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs stated that the country would expel employees of Hungarian diplomatic missions.

repurposed shipping container becomes 24-sqm birch plywood micro-cabin
custom BB-grade birch panels with flush joints form an unbroken interior shell, embedding furniture, a fireplace, and concealed storage along a glazed axis that opens directly onto the terrace.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
Flacon Cargo Module turns SHIPPING CONTAINER INTO MICRO-CABIN
Designed by architects Evgeny Makarenko and Andris Shneps-Shneppe, this 24-sqm micro-cabin transforms an intermodal steel shipping container into a self-contained, relocatable residential module. Located within the ‘Derevnya’ creative community, an experimental rural settlement established by the Flacon Design Factory team, the project accommodates a double bedroom, kitchen, living area with a fireplace, and a full shower room within a compact footprint.
BIRCH PLYWOOD SHELL INTEGRATES FLUSH JOINERY AND BUILT-IN FURNITURE
The interior is lined in an unbroken shell of hand-selected, second-grade (BB) birch plywood, chosen for its natural grain variations. Built-in furniture, work surfaces, and concealed storage integrate directly into the wall and ceiling planes to leave the central circulation path clear. Wall panels are installed using a hidden mounting system with flush joints, eliminating exposed fasteners and hardware to reduce visual clutter. A semi-matte lacquer finish reflects natural light entering through an expansive glazed end-wall, which connects the indoor living space directly to an outdoor wooden terrace. Fitted with radiant floor heating, the off-site prefabricated cabin, designed by the collaborative team between architects Evgeny Makarenko and Andris Shneps-Shneppe, was completed in two and a half months.

That's the main issue," he said.The NIA had alleged that VanDyke and the six Ukrainian nationals entered India on tourist visas, travelled to the northeastern region without mandatory permits and subsequently crossed from Mizoram into Myanmar, where they allegedly trained ethnic armed organisations.The agency had initially invoked provisions of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), including those relating to conspiracy.It had also alleged that the accused disclosed details about the network and were involved in assembling equipment and targeting a passenger aircraft in Myanmar.However, in its charge sheet, the NIA did not invoke the UAPA provisions and instead proceeded under Sections 21 and 23 of the Immigration and Foreigners Act, which provide for offences that can be compounded before the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO).The agency had earlier indicated that its investigation into the alleged terror-related aspects was continuing and that further allegations could be included in a supplementary charge sheet.

Bulgarian Journalist Koltuklieva Hospitalized, May Need Surgery After NSO Officer Assaults Her
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

18:24:34 KST

Bulgarian Journalist Koltuklieva Hospitalized, May Need Surgery After NSO Officer Assaults Her
Journalist Sonya Koltuklieva remains hospitalized at St. Sofia Hospital after being shoved to the ground by a National Security Service (NSO) officer during an encounter outside the headquarters of Progressive Bulgaria in Sofia, prompting political demands for the resignation of Parliament Speaker Mihaela Dotsova and NSO chief Emil Tonev.
Koltuklieva said on Facebook that she was receiving painkillers and that doctors would decide whether she needed shoulder surgery. She added that further examinations were needed to determine whether she had sustained internal injuries, while Prof. Nikolay Gabrovski had offered to monitor her condition. A follow-up scan may be necessary in four to five weeks to check for hidden injuries.
“Thank God I’m still alive! It was brutal - truly cruel. How exactly did I pose a threat to Mihaela Dotsova?! With a phone, perhaps?” Koltuklieva wrote on Facebook.
The incident occurred on Thursday in central Sofia, as Koltuklieva tried to question Dotsova about parliamentary hearings concerning the pardon granted by Iliana Yotova, then vice president, to Ognyan Atanasov, known as the “Escobar of Petrich.”
Footage circulated on social media shows the journalist opening the door of a car in which Dotsova was sitting before an NSO officer pushed her backward onto the pavement. The security officers and the vehicle carrying the speaker then left the scene. The incident took place outside Progressive Bulgaria’s headquarters.
Koltuklieva was initially examined in the emergency department of the Military Medical Academy and discharged to recover at home. She was subsequently questioned at the Military Appellate Prosecutor’s Office and later returned to St. Sofia Hospital. The Military Prosecutor’s Office has initiated pretrial proceedings, and the officer involved, Martin Varadinov, has provided a statement.
The journalist described the encounter in a detailed account on social media, saying she had waited for Dotsova to emerge from the party headquarters before asking why hearings had been derailed. According to Koltuklieva, the speaker did not respond before entering her car. The journalist then opened the door and continued asking questions while holding up her phone, after which an NSO officer rushed toward her and shoved her in the shoulder.
Koltuklieva said she next remembered lying on the ground with a headache, nausea and severe shoulder pain. She also recounted that Dotsova later arrived to express regret but repeatedly explained that she had been stressed after seeing the journalist outside the headquarters.
Dotsova described the incident as unacceptable and said she respected journalists regardless of their political views. She stated that the NSO follows its own rules and procedures and that she cannot issue orders to its officers, but pledged to seek a full investigation and transparency.
“I told her that, both as an individual and as a woman, I express my deepest regret regarding what happened,” Dotsova said, adding that she valued the work of journalists in a democratic society. She said Koltuklieva’s opening of the car door had startled her and that she did not see exactly what happened after the security personnel stepped out and closed it. She learned the subsequent details through media reports.
The NSO announced an immediate inquiry into the conduct of its personnel and said strict measures would follow if officers were found to have breached established procedures. The service confirmed to NOVA that the officer had appeared before the Military Prosecutor’s Office.
President Iliana Yotova, who oversees the service, firmly condemned the officer’s actions, saying they could not be justified by the performance of official duties. She stressed that journalists must be able to work freely and without fear and called for the investigation to establish whether violations had occurred and for the law to be strictly observed.
The incident has prompted demands from several parliamentary parties for accountability. GERB announced that it had collected 39 of the 80 signatures required from lawmakers to request an extraordinary sitting of the National Assembly and seek Dotsova’s removal. The party invited all opposition parliamentary groups to support the initiative.
“We find Mihaela Dotsova’s behavior, leaving the scene of the incident completely unperturbed following the aggressive reaction of her NSS security detail, to be unacceptable,” GERB said in a statement. The party argued that her conduct was incompatible with the office she holds and that she could no longer command respect for Parliament or continue representing it.
Under the National Assembly’s rules, one-third of lawmakers, or 80 MPs, can submit a written proposal to remove the speaker in cases involving an objective inability to perform her duties, systematic overstepping of authority or repeated failure to fulfill her responsibilities. The proposal is put to a vote at the first sitting after submission, with the speaker entitled to be heard, and requires the support of more than half of the lawmakers present.
GERB leader Boyko Borissov had already called for Dotsova’s resignation following the incident. DPS leader Delyan Peevski called on Prime Minister Rumen Radev to remove Dotsova and urged Yotova to dismiss Tonev.
“We Continue the Change” and Democratic Bulgaria also condemned the incident and demanded Tonev’s resignation. Both parties pointed to the NSO’s place under presidential authority, with Yotova currently serving as president and seeking a full term in office.
Atanas Atanasov of Democrats for a Strong Bulgaria, speaking in his personal capacity, said Dotsova should resign because a journalist had suffered bodily injuries in an assault in front of her, while she had failed to show a human response. Representatives of We Continue the Change told Club Z that they were meeting to discuss whether to join the removal petition.
Democratic Bulgaria issued a separate statement demanding the immediate voluntary resignations of Dotsova and Tonev, arguing that the incident did not warrant prolonged political debate.
“Incompetence and a lack of professionalism do not constitute a political stance open to debate; rather, they are grounds for vacating one’s post,” the party said in its statement, urging both officials to step down.
The party also criticized the lack of a clear response from those in power and said Yotova bore institutional responsibility because the NSO falls under the presidency, whose head exercises general oversight and control. It said requesting a report and condemning the incident were only initial steps, and called on Yotova to dismiss Tonev if he did not resign voluntarily.
Democratic Bulgaria further argued that Radev could not avoid political responsibility for the NSO’s operating model and personnel appointments made during his presidency, saying responsibility did not disappear when a person left office.
Radev also faced criticism from other political figures. We Continue the Change leader Asen Vassilev wrote that the incident showed a “Complete loss of all sense of proportion.” Revival leader Kostadin Kostadinov said, “That is simply not how things are done,” condemned the NSO’s behavior and demanded Yotova’s resignation. Kostadinov, who is also a candidate for president, called on Dotsova to explain her actions.
Koltuklieva said she intended to return to work after recovering, criticizing the conduct of Radev’s security detail and arguing that the incident was about basic humanity rather than political divisions.

Girl arrested after taking US$111 from Russia to poison Ukrainian troops
Unknown

Tom Hunter and Willie Haughey back Fife weapons plant
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:24:04 BST
18:24:04 KST

Two of Scotland’s best known business figures have backed the proposal to turn the former Mossmorran chemical plant into a weapons components factory, with Sir Tom Hunter saying Europe cannot depend on America for its protection and that Donald Trump has a point about NATO burden sharing, according to comments made on the Go Radio Business Show.
Hunter, who became Scotland’s first home-grown billionaire after selling Sports Division and now runs the Hunter Foundation, co-presents the programme with Lord Willie Haughey, the Labour peer who built City Facilities Management in Glasgow. Haughey raised the Mossmorran proposal on Sunday’s edition and put it to Hunter that Scotland needs to take a more pragmatic view.
Hunter said: “I mean, the fact is, you know, we live in a world where we need defence. We didn’t think we were going to need it, but once again, we cannot depend on America to protect us. And I actually think Donald Trump’s got a point about NATO. We haven’t been paying our way. So we need to get a European wide defence industry to keep us safe. We can’t depend on the Americans.”
Haughey’s reply to that was “got a point for once”, before he turned to the politics of building armaments in Scotland. He said: “What people have to know is that the first rule of government is to keep your citizens safe and secure. And whether we like it or not, we are living in a more dangerous place at the moment than we have been maybe for decades.”
The proposal they were discussing comes from TBG International Limited, a Hampshire-based defence contractor, which submitted a pre-application screening request to Fife Council last month for an energetics manufacturing facility on the site of the former Fife Ethylene Plant near Cowdenbeath. Energetics covers explosives, propellants and pyrotechnics, the chemical heart of almost every munition, and the plans set out process buildings, earth-covered storage magazines and the earthworks that go with them, alongside the reuse of existing offices and warehouses.
Fife Council has told the company that a full environmental impact assessment will be required, because an integrated chemical installation producing explosives falls under Schedule 1 of the assessment regulations. ExxonMobil stopped production at Mossmorran in February after concluding the plant was no longer financially viable, putting more than 400 jobs at risk, and expects decommissioning to run until 2028.
Haughey also made a wider claim about European industry, telling listeners that around half of the car manufacturers are approaching governments for help to remodel and re-equip their factories to make armaments, because Chinese producers have taken the volume out of the car market. Fewer cars to build means fewer jobs, he argued, at the same moment that Europe cannot say where the next conflict will come from.
“See the people who are complaining about not wanting to build armaments factories, they’ll be the first people to complain if they don’t feel as if they’re being protected.”
Finding work for the Mossmorran workforce has been a live question since the closure was announced, and Douglas Alexander, the Scottish Secretary, said in November last year that Babcock had signalled a willingness to explore whether it could in time employ some of the plant’s skilled workers. The site sits a short drive from Rosyth, where Babcock is building the Type 31 frigates.
Scotland’s place in the defence spending increase has been contested all year, with the Scottish Affairs Committee warning that skills shortages could stop the country benefiting and this publication reporting that Scotland risks missing out on the defence spending boost. The Scottish Government confirmed this month that it will match funding for two Defence Technical Excellence Colleges, one on each coast, having been offered the money in the spring.
Wes Streeting told the Commons yesterday that he wants the colleges backed with £50 million in England to expand to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, and offered to work with the Scottish Government on the defence of the United Kingdom regardless of constitutional differences.

Nurseries offer lifeline to DR Congo’s youngest Ebola victims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
09:21:43 UTC
18:21:43 KST

A caregiver wearing a protective gown and gloves bottle-fed a baby, one of hundreds of children orphaned by the Democratic Republic of Congo’s Ebola outbreak.
Five months into the epidemic, the virus continues to spread, and the nursery in the country’s remote east is among 12 facilities caring for children whose parents have died from the highly contagious disease.
“Many children have lost both their father and mother because of Ebola,” Marie Bakikula, a caregiver at a UNICEF-supported nursery in Mongbwalu, told Agence France-Presse (AFP).
The mining town in Ituri province, near the Ugandan border, is considered the epicenter of the outbreak.
Children account for about one-third of deaths and more than one-quarter of infections in the current crisis, which has recorded more than 2,000 cases, according to UNICEF.
A short distance from the nursery, workers in white protective suits loaded a child-sized coffin into the back of a pickup truck.
Other children survive but lose their families. Those arriving at the emergency nurseries have witnessed their parents die and seen burial teams in protective suits remove their bodies.
Others were separated from their families after their infected parents were transferred to Ebola treatment centers.
“They all believe that by coming here they will never see their parents again,” said Monique Ndjangosi, a psychologist at the Mongbwalu nursery.
Nearby, a young girl and three boys played among stuffed toys that had recently been disinfected with chlorine. Their mothers had tested positive for the virus.
The children will remain under observation for 21 days, the disease’s incubation period, in case they develop symptoms.
“One of them showed symptoms seven days after arriving and was admitted to the Ebola treatment center,” said Bakikula, who volunteered to work at the facility after surviving Ebola herself.
The only contact many children maintain with their infected parents is through photographs and videos taken by health care workers.
“We cannot take them inside the treatment center to visit their parents. It’s too risky,” Ndjangosi said.
In some cases, child protection teams succeed in locating relatives, including distant family members, who can care for orphaned children. In others, finding relatives proves impossible.
“We still have children we have not been able to identify because they are too young and their parents arrived in a coma,” said Celine Lusinde, head of provincial child protection services.
Her office has registered 8,200 newly orphaned children since the outbreak began.
Marie-Therese Tsesi, a 63-year-old nurse, has taken in five children orphaned by Ebola at her modest mud-brick home near Mongbwalu hospital.
“Their father was the only parent they had left. He died of Ebola,” she said.
“They were sleeping outside and showing signs of malnutrition.”
The current Ebola epidemic, the Democratic Republic of Congo’s 17th, quickly became the deadliest on record in the central African country and remains uncontrolled despite months of efforts. Cases have also been detected in Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria.
The disease spreads through contact with bodily fluids and causes severe hemorrhagic fever. It has infected 9,704 people and killed 4,687 in the DRC, according to the latest health authority figures, giving it a fatality rate of nearly 50%.
A clinical trial is underway, but there is currently no approved vaccine or specific treatment for the Bundibugyo strain responsible for the outbreak.
Health authorities continue to face resource shortages, while insecurity caused by armed groups in Ituri province, the area hardest hit by the epidemic, restricts access to some communities.
Many deaths occurring outside health facilities are believed to go unreported.

Swiss population growth is slowing and shifting away from major urban centres
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
09:19:00 UTC
18:19:00 KST

Swiss population growth is slowing and shifting away from major urban centres
Population growth is slowing down and, driven by high rents and a persistent housing shortage, is shifting from major cities towards the outskirts of urban areas.
This is the conclusion reached by an analysis by UBS published on Friday. Driven by strong labour demand and the arrival of 70,000 refugees from Ukraine, Switzerland’s population rose by almost 460,000 people over the five-year period from 2021 to 2025, according to the bank’s experts. This increase corresponds to around 240,000 additional households. However, only around 220,000 new homes were built during the same period. The supply of housing has therefore failed to keep pace with the rise in demand.
According to UBS, however, the growth rate has now peaked. In 2025, the permanent resident population rose by around 76,000 people, which corresponds to an increase of just over 0.8%. For the current year, the bank forecasts a further slight slowdown to 0.7%.
More
New arrivals make do with the dregs of the Zurich’s housing market
With average annual growth rates of between 1.4% and 1.6%, the cantons of Schaffhausen, Valais, Fribourg, Aargau and Thurgau have recorded the strongest growth over the past five years. They are all situated on the outskirts of major urban agglomerations. These cantons have not only attracted numerous new residents from abroad but have also drawn many families from other Swiss regions, UBS analysts point out. Consequently, the cantons of Basel-City, Geneva, Neuchâtel and Vaud have experienced a net loss of population to neighbouring regions.
This trend was particularly evident in the Zurich. Between 2021 and 2025, the city recorded high net immigration from abroad, totalling almost 38,000 people. At the same time, however, the pandemic, the housing shortage, the growing prevalence of remote working and the marked disparity in rents between the city centre and the suburbs meant that Zurich, in net terms, lost a record number of 21,500 people to other municipalities.

8 Things to Know About the iPhone Duo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
09:15:00 UTC
18:15:00 KST

The iPhone Duo is finally here. Apple's first folding smartphone arrives seven years after Samsung pioneered the category with the Galaxy Fold. That gave Apple plenty of time to refine the hardware behind closed doors rather than in public view—and the results show: The Duo is a pretty dang good foldable.
Whether your Duo just landed on your doorstep or you're still weighing that $1,999 price, here's what you need to know before unfolding it.
Apps Aren’t Optimized—Yet
The iPhone Duo is a new shape and size for Apple, so many of your apps likely aren't optimized to show up properly on the unique 5.4-inch outer screen or the 7.6-inch inner display. Apple also changed how navigational elements appear on the Duo, aligning them on the right rail instead of centering them on the bottom like every other iPhone.
Apple apps, redesigned for the Duo, look great. Many third-party apps look like the Google Home app in the picture above: a strip down the middle with thick, black bars on the sides. Several major app developers have already optimized their apps for iOS 27.1—Slack, Instagram, DoorDash, and WhatsApp, for example—but I've noticed that even some optimized apps like Instagram can still have broken user-interface elements. It will take time for every app in your library to work perfectly across these new screens.
It might be a good thing that the Duo is back-ordered for several weeks. By the time you snag yours, app developers will likely have caught up to the new device, and you might enjoy a richer folding experience.
Say Goodbye to Face ID
Nearly a decade ago, Apple introduced Face ID as the future of the iPhone, eventually replacing the fingerprint-based Touch ID. So it might be confusing to hear that Apple's first folding phone doesn't have Face ID at all and instead relies on the older biometric authentication method. (Likely because Face ID tech takes up too much space in the thin iPhone Duo.) Touch ID never disappeared—Apple has used it on the iPhone SE and still features it on iPads and MacBooks—but this is the first time it has returned on a flagship iPhone.
Using your thumb again will take some getting used to, but it's not a deal-breaker. Some folks will miss the convenience and speed of Face ID, where all you needed to do was stare at the screen, instead of now reaching for the Touch ID sensor on the right side. Others who hated facial authentication might actually like the return of the fingerprint sensor.
Apple also introduced the Dynamic Island a few years ago—the pill-shaped island around the Face ID camera sensors that shows live app activities, like the next turn on your navigation or music currently playing, giving a second job to the camera cutout. Without Face ID, Dynamic Island hasn't disappeared from the iPhone Duo. Instead, Apple moved it to the top-right edge around the outer selfie camera; on the inner display, it appears at the top-right edge when a live activity is in progress.
You Need a New MagSafe Wallet
The iPhone Duo supports MagSafe just like the rest of the iPhone lineup, so you can magnetically stick your favorite phone grip on the back, or attach the phone to a magnetic car dock, bike mount, or wireless charger. One thing to note: If you unfold the Duo and attach it to a car dock or tripod, the phone will tip to one side because the magnet can’t keep it held straight given the uneven weight distribution. Third-party accessory makers could address this with anti-rotation magnets, but it might mean upgrading your current accessories.
Wallets, unfortunately, are the one accessory that won't really play well with the Duo. Yes, you can still attach a MagSafe wallet, but because the Duo is shorter than other iPhones, the wallet sticks out awkwardly past the lower edge. Apple doesn't have an official solution, so if you want to use a magnetic wallet with your iPhone, you'll have to look at third-party accessories.
Use the Rear Camera for Selfies
Everyone knows the rear cameras on your smartphone are better than the selfie camera on the front. One of the best features on a folding phone is the ability to take a selfie with those superior rear cameras and still be able to see a preview with the outer screen.
Don't confuse this with “Duo Preview” as I did, though. That's a feature that lets you show the person you're photographing the camera's viewfinder, so they can make sure they look picture-perfect before you tap the shutter. The setting to enable this is on the left edge of the camera app, where you can also turn on “Kids Cue” to have Snoopy animations play on the outer screen to get the attention of a kid for the perfect photo.
But if you're taking a selfie yourself and want the camera controls on the front screen, all you need to do is launch the camera and flip the phone around—you'll see a slider that says, “Slide to show camera.” Slide it, and the full camera app will show up on the outer screen, so you can switch modes and access Photographic Styles right there and enjoy the higher-quality results from the superior cameras. Doing this also crucially disables the inner screen, so your fingers won't accidentally switch modes.
You Can Create App Pairs
Filling the inner 7.6-inch screen with two different apps running side by side is incredibly handy and one of the cornerstone features of any folding phone. Whether you're on a phone call and want to pull up a confirmation email, or want to browse two different Safari webpages, you can drag an app from the bottom and pull it to the left or right side to enter the split-screen state.
One trick that isn't immediately obvious is that you can create app pairs. Just tap the middle bar between the two apps once, and it'll glow white, meaning that those two apps are now locked and can be accessed at any moment from the Recent apps menu. You can't save that as an app icon combo, though. This is still very handy if you know you'll always want to open two apps simultaneously on the big screen.
Be Careful of the Inner Screen
I get it, you're going to want to protect the fragile screens of your $1,999 iPhone. A case is smart—folding phone cases aren't like normal cases, as they usually come in two shells that attach to each side of the phone. You can also totally add a screen protector to the outer 5.4-inch screen.
But for the 7.6-inch matte inner screen, exercise some caution. You might see chatter online that you can “remove” the Duo's nano-texture finish, but it's an “integral” component of the inner display—as Apple says on this support page. “Don't attempt to remove it,” Apple writes. (Apple also has a page on cleaning the nano-texture display properly here.) Attempting to remove the finish is likely a surefire way to void your warranty. Apple doesn't say anything about using third-party screen protectors, but using one could compromise the display performance.
If you scratch or damage the nano-texture finish, Apple says you can take it to any Apple Store or an Apple Authorized Service Provider and have it replaced for $19 (or $49 if the phone is out of warranty). That's not the same as if there's an actual crack in the inner display—that'll run you a cool $999 if you don't have AppleCare+.
You Can Split the Keyboard
The iPhone Duo is a wide phone. If you've complained about the size of modern smartphones and how it's hard to reach the top of the screen, well, you might still have some issues reaching the sides of the Duo. There's some good news, though. Apple lets you split the keyboard to make typing on the inner display a little easier.
Later this year, Apple will also issue a software update bringing Reachability to the Duo. On other iPhones, this brings the top of an app down, making it easier to reach. On the Duo, it will move an app to the left or right so you won't have to stretch those fingers as much.
Apple Pencil Support Is Coming
Have you always wanted to use a stylus on an iPhone? Soon! Steve Jobs is probably rolling in his grave.
Apple will bring support for the USB-C Apple Pencil (and only that Apple Pencil model, not others) in a software update later this year. Paired with the 7.6-inch screen's nano-texture finish, it should make writing and drawing on the iPhone Duo feel paper-like. Sadly, there's no place to store the stylus on the iPhone like you can on an iPad. I'm sure someone will make an accessory for it.

War-ravaged Sudan on brink as El Nino fans new flames of hunger
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
09:12:58 UTC
18:12:58 KST

Farmers across Sudan are facing a devastating harvest as drought and soaring temperatures compound the effects of a civil war that has already pushed millions toward hunger, raising fears of a worsening famine.
El Nino, the climate pattern threatening parts of Africa with extreme weather, has brought higher temperatures and drought to Sudan, where pockets of famine have emerged during more than three years of fighting.
Rain-fed agriculture, which supplies much of the country’s food, is suffering as crops wither, livestock weaken and farmers struggle to salvage their fields.
Rainfall during July through September, Sudan’s peak rainy season, was the lowest in more than three decades nationwide, according to U.S. Geological Survey data.
North Darfur recorded its lowest rainfall since 1984, the year a devastating famine struck Sudan and Ethiopia. North Kordofan experienced its lowest rainfall since 1990, while southeastern Gedaref state recorded its lowest since 1991.
“The risk of famine is growing in many conflict-affected areas of Sudan, with the impact of El Nino-induced drought compounding already dire conditions,” the U.N.-backed Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) said in an Oct. 12 alert.
In June, the IPC estimated that 5.1 million people faced severe hunger. The figure is being updated, but the drought threatens to reverse expected improvements as the harvest season begins.
The World Food Program forecasts that drought will leave an additional 350,000 people facing severe hunger by the end of 2026, rising to 1.2 million more by August 2027, Samuel Clendon, the agency’s head of program for Sudan, told Reuters in October. Darfur and Kordofan are expected to be hardest hit.
Crops wither as livestock lose value
In North Kordofan, Mariam Omar pulls weeds from her smallholding near Um Ruwaba, where crops that should be nearing harvest have shriveled in the dry, sandy soil.
“This year is terrible,” she said.
Mohamed Abdelrahman, a farmer who operates about 420 hectares and finances smallholders through his sesame trading business, estimated that about 40% of farmland around Um Ruwaba would produce no harvest. Many farmers displaced by the war are returning to drought-stricken land, he said.
Livestock markets are also suffering. At El Obeid, North Kordofan’s capital, cows stand with their ribs protruding beneath dusty hides.
“Usually at this time the cattle are fat and everyone is making a profit. But now, with this autumn’s scarcity, the cattle became skinny,” trader Sirajaldeen Abdellateef said.
A rapidly depreciating currency and rising inflation are adding to farmers’ losses, making food and other essentials increasingly expensive.
The WFP has prioritized 5 million people most in need but says it cannot reach everyone requiring assistance. For those it serves, the agency has cut food rations to stretch limited supplies.
As of Oct. 17, the WFP had $276 million available for its Sudan operation, less than half of last year’s budget. It needs another $134 million to address hunger caused by drought.
The simultaneous decline in food aid and agricultural production is a “recipe for disaster,” the WFP’s acting executive director, Carl Skau, told Reuters after visiting Darfur.
In Tawila, a sprawling Darfur displacement camp sheltering about 700,000 people, food rations have been halved even as thousands more arrive, Skau said. Aid workers reported that 9,000 people reached the camp between early September and mid-October.
Suad Ahmed, a teacher who has been displaced several times during the war, fled her village east of al-Fashir, North Darfur’s capital, to seek food in Tawila.
“As I was coming here on the road, so many people said: ‘If you find food and drink there, please tell us,’” she said.
Adam Rojal, spokesman for the General Coordination of Displaced Persons and Refugee Camps in Sudan, said hunger was increasingly driving people from their homes.
“It’s no longer just about bullets,” he said.
Even Gedaref, a southeastern state that has largely escaped the fighting and become an important source of food during the war, has been hit by drought.
Emad Kabsoor, who operates farms covering 14,700 hectares, said scorching temperatures and a lack of rain had devastated his fields.
“Even if we get rain going forward, I’ll only have about 25% of last year’s crop,” he said. “We’ve never had a season like this.”
Temperatures in Gedaref on Oct. 20 were between 7 and 9 degrees Celsius above the historical average, according to the Reuters Climate Monitor.
Sudan’s government has downplayed the threat. Agriculture Minister Esmat Qureshi said Oct. 8 that this year’s harvest would be smaller but “not significantly less than last year’s.”
The drought is worsening conditions in a country where fighting between the military and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has devastated communities, disrupted agriculture and displaced millions.
Humanitarian agencies have repeatedly accused both sides of blocking or hindering aid deliveries. Both deny the allegations.
Abdelrahman Ismail, head of the RSF’s humanitarian aid authority, told Reuters the group had sought to coordinate an early response and could do more with sufficient resources.
The IPC declared pockets of famine in Sudan in 2024 and 2025, including in al-Fashir, where government forces and their allies, along with as many as 250,000 civilians, endured an RSF siege for about 18 months before the city fell.
Famine expert Alex de Waal said Sudan’s current crisis was in many respects worse than the famine that devastated the region in 1984, killing hundreds of thousands. While the international community mobilized substantial assistance then, humanitarian budgets are now being cut.
“The situation today is in most respects much, much worse because of the conflict,” de Waal said.
Sirajaldin al-Tahir, a farmer in Um Ruwaba, remembers the 1984 famine, when failed harvests and dying livestock forced people to flee. He said U.S. food aid helped his village survive.
“But God took pity on us, and the US government brought in aid and distributed it to our village,” he said.
More than four decades later, failed rains and collapsing harvests are again threatening Sudan’s food supply, while war and shrinking aid budgets leave millions increasingly vulnerable.
“This year, 2026, we don’t know how it will end,” al-Tahir said.

‘Who’s responsible for this mess?’ India slams West over climate-linked trade barriers (VIDEO)
India has questioned Western nations for imposing climate-related trade barriers on developing economies despite Europe’s historical contribution to the climate crisis the world is facing now.
Wealthy countries built their economies using fossil fuels but are now imposing additional costs on poorer nations, Indian Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal told the Berlin Global Dialogue on Thursday.
“Who’s responsible for this mess in the first place?” Goyal asked, referring to the West’s carbon emissions, and challenged the European Union’s environmental trade restrictions.
India accounts for around 17% of the world’s population but has significantly lower per capita emissions than Europe, Goyal pointed out.
The minister questioned the $100 billion annual climate finance commitment made by wealthy countries to help developing economies address climate change. The target, first agreed upon during UN climate negotiations in 2009, was extended through 2025 under the Paris climate process.

— RT_India (@RT_India_news) October 23, 2026
“Eleven years later, we haven’t seen a nickel or dime of that. It’s all promises,” Goyal said.
He argued that the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) fails to recognize the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities, under which developed countries are expected to shoulder a greater burden in addressing climate change.
The mechanism places carbon-related costs on imports of steel and other emissions-intensive products. Brussels has justified it by saying it ensures imported goods face carbon costs comparable to those paid by European manufacturers.
India’s concerns echo a position adopted by BRICS leaders at their September summit in New Delhi. The declaration opposed unilateral and discriminatory carbon border measures that could undermine developing countries’ efforts to address climate change.
Goyal warned that the EU’s 50% duty on steel imports exceeding specified quotas could raise costs for European industries and consumers.
The restrictions have implications for India, which sent nearly 40% of its steel exports to the EU last year, according to government think tank NITI Aayog.
India’s trade agreement with the EU, concluded in January, does not exempt Indian exporters from the bloc’s carbon levy, Reuters reported. The agreement is expected to be signed by the end of this year and could take effect in early 2027, Goyal said.

Belarus convicts at least 419 people for supporting Ukraine during Russia's full-scale war
Criminal cases have been brought against at least 419 people in Belarus in connection with the war in Ukraine.
Source: Belarusian human rights centre Viasna, as reported by European Pravda
Details: According to Viasna, at least 419 people, including 73 women, have been convicted for supporting Ukraine since February 2022. Of these, 142 are currently in detention. The centre noted that the actual number of criminal cases could be significantly higher.
Of those convicted, 222 were sentenced for "facilitating extremist activities", including for sharing photographs and videos showing the movements of Russian military equipment.
Another 44 people were convicted of "treason" in connection with their support for Ukraine during the war. A further 17 foreign nationals were convicted of "espionage" in Belarus.
Another 29 people were convicted of "terrorism" in cases involving acts of sabotage, including on railways and at a military airfield, while 45 were convicted for donating to the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
The largest number of convictions, Viasna noted, are linked to the so-called Hajun case – a wave of arrests connected with the activities of the independent monitoring project Belaruski Hajun, which tracked the movements of Russian and Belarusian troops.
At the time, Ukraine's Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned a new wave of repression by the Lukashenko regime in connection with the so-called Hajun case.
Background: On 16 September, US Special Envoy for Belarus John Coale announced during a visit to Minsk the release of 25 Belarusian political prisoners.

Ultra-Orthodox conscription debate ignites Israel’s election battleground
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
09:03:39 UTC
18:03:39 KST

Ultra-Orthodox conscription debate ignites Israel’s election battleground
Israel’s election heats up over the ultra-Orthodox conscription debate, reflecting deep societal and political divides.
From the fallout of multi-fronted wars and demands for accountability over security failures to mounting concerns over the cost of living, Israelis are grappling with a series of crises ahead of the October 27 election.
Yet one contentious issue has come to dominate headlines during the campaign: whether Israel’s ultra-Orthodox Jewish minority should serve in the military.
An estimated 80,000 ultra-Orthodox, or Haredi, men aged between 18 and 24 are currently avoiding military service, a figure whose significance grows with every report of staff shortages in the Israeli army.
For their political supporters in the Knesset’s Haredi Shas and United Torah Judaism (UTJ) parties, they are helping preserve the essential character of Israel through Torah study and prayer.
But for their detractors, they are draft dodgers refusing to undertake their share in the multiple wars Israel has embarked upon in the wake of the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023.
Critics include the self-styled Zionist opposition bloc that is locked in a tight race with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu‘s Likud Party and the far-right coalition it leads.
In May, as Haredi anger over the jailing of draft evaders spilled into street protests following a 2024 Supreme Court ruling that the military must begin drafting ultra-Orthodox men, the issue proved toxic enough to threaten Netanyahu’s government.
His ruling coalition has relied on the support of the Haredi parties in return for softening measures aimed at forcing their supporters to serve in the army. But after Netanyahu told the parties that he lacked the votes to pass an exemption bill, they pushed to dissolve the Knesset and effectively weakened the government.
On Tuesday, Netanyahu said he opposed the arrest of 40 Haredim – plural for Haredi – who were taken in for evading the draft after returning to Israel from the United States, despite a law this year meant to temporarily halt such arrests.
“We must preserve the world of Torah because it preserved us,” Netanyahu told the Haredi Kol Barama radio station. “These arrests are a deliberate attempt to harm the process of drafting Haredim without coercion.”
However, how well Netanyahu’s comments will land with the rest of the population is unclear, with the issue seen as offering an opportunity for those seeking to oust him as well as opening up divisions within his own base.
A September poll by the Israel Democracy Institute found an overwhelming 72 percent wanted to see the Haredim drafted alongside other Israelis eligible for military service.
In early October, a group of Haredim clashed with Israeli forces seeking to arrest a draft dodger in Modi’in, drawing condemnation from Netanyahu’s opponents. Former Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, whose Yashar (“straight” or “honest”) party currently holds a narrow lead over Netanyahu’s Likud, described the incident as reflecting “the same dangerous world view that seeks to make draft evasion the norm and portray those who fulfil their duty to the state as suckers”.
He added: “That is what the upcoming election is about: Netanyahu’s draft-dodging government, or a government of conscription led by me.”
Critics of the Haredim’s refusal to serve have even found voice within Netanyahu’s party, with Likud lawmakers arguing the issue of ultra-Orthodox non-conscription could pose a threat to the future of the State of Israel.
“It is a paradox,” said Daniel Bar-Tal, a professor of psychology at Tel Aviv University.
“On the one hand, the issue of equal service unites all the secular and Zionist religious public,” he said. “On the other side, the ultra-Orthodox are rightist … This does not go together, so [Netanyahu] has a dilemma.”
Despite popular anger over the refusal to serve, and the potential consequences for their allies in the Knesset who are striving to protect that exemption, Haredi intransigence shows no sign of easing.
The two Haredi parties – Shas and UTJ – have ruled out joining any coalition that does not pass laws exempting members of their community from military service, even if it makes forming any coalition sympathetic to the ultra-Orthodox impossible.
“This is a big deal,” said Israeli pollster Mitchell Barak. “The opposition parties are trying to pitch the election as the draft dodgers versus those who protect and serve – and that is the decisive point of the election.”
Politically toxic
Next week’s polls are the first since Israel’s genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip began in October 2023, killing nearly 74,400 people and leaving most of the besieged territory in ruins, as well as the multiple conflicts across the region that followed it.
The military campaigns have placed a big burden on the state’s finances, with the high cost of living being a major source of public discontent ahead of the polls. Higher taxes have added to the economic pressure, with surveys showing that families of reservists deployed to Israel’s war zones face increased emotional and psychological strain, alongside stagnant household incomes.
According to an August survey, 42 percent of Israelis said their finances had worsened since the war on Gaza began three years ago, with the families of reservists hit hardest.
That squeeze comes as the Haredi population keeps expanding, with 1.26 million, or 12.5 percent of Israelis identified as Haredi. Projections suggest that by 2065, somewhere between 20 percent and a third of the population will be Haredi, with a large portion refusing to either work or serve in the army in place of Torah study.
“The great burden of having to serve became much more pronounced – and at the same time the Haredi sector keeps growing,” said Shmuel Rosner, a senior fellow at The Jewish People Policy Institute, “which means that a large cohort of potential soldiers does not ease the burden on others.”
He added: “The blunt refusal of Haredi leaders to even consider a change in times of such dangers demonstrated to many Israelis that this community is one that depends on Israel financially and otherwise contributes little.”
