"Getting people into space is one thing. Creating somewhere they actually want to live is quite another"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

“Getting people into space is one thing. Creating somewhere they actually want to live is quite another”
For most of the space age, architects could fantasise freely about building off-world. Inflatable lunar villages and glass Martian domes could be sketched out without anyone having to worry too much about who cleaned the toilets.
That luxury is disappearing as we start to seriously consider the possibility of living in space. Next year, the first commercial space station will be launched – Haven-1 – and will be joined by a second, Axiom, a few months later.
NASA will return to the moon in 2028 with plans to start building a semi-permanent base. A nuclear reactor will follow by the end of the decade, as might the Chinese, and by the time the International Space Station (ISS) is retired in 2030, there will be tens of private stations available to replace it.
The elegant visions of 2001: A Space Odyssey are now giving way to the messy business of everyday existence
And that’s before we talk about Elon Musk and his ambition to create a city of a million people on Mars by the 2050s.
But getting people into space is one thing. Creating somewhere they might actually want to live is quite another.
That is where architecture comes in, and firms such as Foster + Partners, BIG, SOM (pictured top) and others have already turned their attention to what might be possible beyond Earth. The elegant visions of 2001: A Space Odyssey and the like are now giving way to the messy business of everyday existence and the problems of extraterrestrial construction.
The obvious challenges are formidable but well-rehearsed: how do you shield people from radiation? Where does the oxygen come from? How do you recycle water?
Engineers have mostly answered these questions. But once people are asked to live somewhere for years rather than just visit, other questions arise. Such as: who gets a window? It may sound trivial. It isn’t.
A window in space is both expensive and a potential point of failure. The engineers would prefer a solid metal tube.
Yet astronauts value their views of Earth enormously and “Earth-gazing” is a favourite way to unwind aboard the ISS. In fact, being able to see out is considered essential for morale.
So imagine the first lunar settlement. There are six bedrooms but only two windows. Who gets them? The commander? The tourist who pays the most? Does everybody receive 10 minutes of Earth-gazing a day?
History should certainly make us wary of who gets to dictate what extraterrestrial living looks like
Or, does the window belong to everyone, because something so precious cannot become private property?
The same applies to almost every spatial decision. Who gets a room with a door? How large is it? Can inhabitants personalise it? Where can somebody go to be alone? Where must they encounter other people? Who controls the thermostat, lighting or music?
In a lunar base containing 30 people these are potentially bones of contention. There has been at least one stabbing in the Antarctic, so the danger is real.
And that’s before we even decide who gets to run the place. Would you prefer a government body or a corporation like SpaceX or Blue Origin, which, after all, are manufacturing the rockets that are likely to haul people and materials to the moon and Mars?
History should certainly make us wary of who gets to dictate what extraterrestrial living looks like. Take Henry Ford’s Fordlandia, established in the Amazon in the 1920s to secure rubber.
That was conceived not simply as an industrial settlement, but as an attempt to export Ford’s version of American life: workers received company housing – segregated, of course – but had prescribed diets and had to follow strict behavioural rules. The American managers had running water and got the best views, while the Brazilians had to rely on wells.
The company town is an old model: housing, employment, shops and infrastructure controlled by the same organisation. On Earth, at least, you can leave. What does “leaving” mean when the exit is miles across the moon and stepping outside without permission might mean dying?
This matters because the economics of space point towards precisely this danger. The first extraterrestrial settlements will require immense investment. Governments will fund some, but corporations will provide most of the transport, communications and habitats.
Architects should be arguing about (and hopefully agreeing) extraterrestrial design standards before settlements exist
Commercial necessity can gradually become governance. The East India Company provides an extreme historical precedent: a trading firm that accumulated taxation, administrative and military powers as business slid into tyranny.
Space could easily witness a 21st-century version. Imagine a Martian settlement where one corporation supplies your employment, accommodation, oxygen, water, communications and return ticket. You are simultaneously worker, tenant and customer. Architecture could make that unequal relationship physical, as in Fordlandia.
None of this is an argument against commercial spaceflight. Without private capital, much of the extraordinary acceleration now taking place would be impossible.
Nor can architects wish away physics. A window genuinely is more dangerous than a wall.
But if we are to start producing extraterrestrial architecture, it must do more than ensure survival. A habitat that maintains oxygen while steadily degrading its inhabitants’ mental health has failed.
Circadian lighting, vegetation, privacy, views, places for leisure and for ritual are not decorations to be value-engineered away. They contribute to people’s ability to function and remain sane.
This is why architects should be arguing about (and hopefully agreeing) extraterrestrial design standards before settlements exist. I would argue the time for that is now.
The danger is not that our first extraterrestrial settlements will look insufficiently futuristic. It is that they will reproduce the worst terrestrial arrangements: workers’ barracks, gated communities, company towns and luxury enclaves – only this time with airlocks.
If we leave those questions until the rockets arrive, someone else will already have answered them for us
Conversely, architects rarely get to establish the principles of an entire built environment before it exists. Here we can.
We should use that opportunity to ask difficult questions now, while the answers are still cheap. Who owns the habitat? Who can modify it? What constitutes an acceptable home in space?
What must remain communal? What degree of privacy ensures dignity? And, yes, who gets a window?
If we leave those questions until the rockets arrive, someone else will already have answered them for us. You might not like who that person is.
Jonathan Morrison is an architecture journalist based in London. He was previously the architecture correspondent for The Times. His first book, How to Build a Space Station, was published in September 2026.

The ‘Exotic Physics’ Behind a Mysterious 1,000-Mile Cloud on Mars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Every morning during the Martian spring and summer, a thin and extremely long cloud emerges, only to disappear again. The wispy formation appears near the volcano Arsia Mons and gradually elongates until it reaches over 1,000 miles—about the distance from New York to Kansas City as the crow flies—before dissipating. This cycle then repeats for several months.
Since it was first recorded by a probe in 2018, scientists have been unable to find a plausible explanation for the existence of this cloud, often referred to as the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud (AMEC). Until now. Recently, researchers successfully modeled the cloud’s formation for the first time, their results suggesting that it may be driven by a physical process that has never been directly observed in any planet's atmosphere.
"We found that we needed to include some exotic physics … physics that, while included in textbooks, is treated as theoretical and usually thought not to happen in nature. It certainly hasn’t been seen in action before," Jorge Hernández-Bernal, a planetary scientist at Paris’ Sorbonne Université and lead author of the study, said in a press release. "Once we included this physics in our simulations, the AMEC emerged just as we hoped.”
On Earth, clouds usually form when water vapor creates droplets or ice crystals in the presence of tiny particles, such as dust or salt. The new study, published in Nature Geoscience, instead suggests AMEC could be forming through so-called homogeneous nucleation, where vapor changes directly into ice crystals on its own without any help from debris.
“It’s akin to droplets of condensation appearing in the middle of a room, rather than on a window," Hernández-Bernal explained. “It’s wholly unexpected.”
This phenomenon requires extreme conditions—a sharp temperature drop of 30 degrees Celsius within 10 minutes and high relative humidity. The Arsia Mons volcano also plays a key role. When wind current hits the 65,000-foot-tall volcano, it creates a powerful wave that launches moist air high in the atmosphere in a matter of minutes.
Scientists have assumed a similar phenomenon could occur in the upper atmospheres of other planets, including Venus and even Earth, but it has never been observed. That’s not too surprising given the extreme air humidity required for this phenomenon, which is more than 100,000 times greater than any value measured on Earth.
Before this modeling, it was not known that these humidity levels existed on Mars either. “We don’t have nearly as much information about Mars’ atmosphere as we do about Earth's, so reproducing the AMEC to this degree is a big success,” said Hernández-Bernal, adding, “the result is remarkable.”
This story originally appeared on WIRED Czech Republic and Slovakia and has been translated from Czech.

Tokayev says GDP per capita exceeded $15,000
Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev outlined the country’s key economic and social achievements during a ceremony marking Republic Day, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing Akorda.
The President highlighted economic growth, an expansion in housing construction and the development of small and medium-sized businesses.
“Since 2019, our economy has grown by around 30%. GDP per capita has exceeded $15,000. Under the National Fund for Children program, $2.5 billion has been transferred to the accounts of seven million children.
Last year, more than 20 million square meters of housing were commissioned, an unprecedented figure. Life expectancy has approached 76 years. According to the World Bank, Kazakhstan leads the region in this indicator.
“Our top priority is to strengthen the national economy. We have entered the ranks of the world’s most influential countries, taking 34th place. Kazakhstan’s gross domestic product is approaching $350 billion, placing us second among the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) countries,” Tokayev said.

The President emphasized the development of high-tech manufacturing and industrial production.
“Over the past five years, the share of manufacturing in total exports has exceeded 45%. Kazakhstan’s industry is therefore moving to a new level of development.
In recent years, we have made a major breakthrough in railway engineering. We have begun producing almost everything needed for the sector, from rails and railway sleepers to freight and passenger cars and electric locomotives. Automobile production is also gaining momentum, with more than 150,000 passenger and commercial vehicles rolling off assembly lines annually. All strategic sectors of the economy are receiving a strong boost,” he said.
Tokayev also highlighted the role of foreign investment in the country’s continued development. Over the past seven years, Kazakhstan has attracted $155 billion in investment.
He added that participation in high-level international events and visits abroad had strengthened Kazakhstan’s political standing while delivering tangible economic benefits.
“Since the beginning of this year, 355 commercial agreements worth a total of $60 billion have been signed,” the President said.
Tokayev also stressed Kazakhstan’s growing role as a major transport and logistics hub in Eurasia. Airports, railway stations, bridges and seaports are being built and modernized, while cross-border infrastructure is being upgraded.

Kazakhstan’s National Bank cuts base rate to 15.75%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

17:58:51 KST

Kazakhstan’s National Bank cuts base rate to 15.75%
The Monetary Policy Committee of the National Bank of Kazakhstan has set the base rate at 15.75% per annum, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports.
The regulator attributed the decision to a slowdown in annual inflation and easing inflation expectations. In September, inflation stood at 9.3%, marking its 12th consecutive monthly decline.
Food inflation slowed to 8.5%, while non-food inflation fell to 11%. Services inflation remained unchanged at 8.9%. Meanwhile, public inflation expectations for the next 12 months decreased from 12.1% in August to 11.8% in September.
However, the balance of risks remains tilted toward higher inflation. The National Bank cited strong domestic demand, changes in fuel and lubricant prices and regulated tariffs, as well as elevated global energy and food prices among the main inflationary factors.
The regulator warned that annual inflation could rise slightly toward the end of the year due to the low-base effect from the previous year.
The National Bank said future decisions on the base rate would depend on inflation trends, inflation expectations and changes in the balance of risks. Its target is to bring inflation down to 5% by 2028.
The next scheduled decision on the base rate will be announced on December 4.
Earlier, it was reported Türkiye's Central Bank lowered the policy rate to 36% after 5 consecutive holds.

Trump turns to Cold War-era law to tackle fuel crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
08:58:37 UTC
17:58:37 KST

Trump turns to Cold War-era law to tackle fuel crisis
US President Donald Trump has invoked a Cold War-era national security law to boost domestic oil production and refining, as rising fuel prices threaten the Republicans’ chances in November’s midterm elections.
Speaking on Thursday at a Republican campaign rally in Iowa – an agricultural state where farmers have been hit hard by the oil crisis – Trump announced that his administration would use the Defense Production Act (DPA) to provide up to $150 million to expand American refining capacity and produce diesel and gasoline “at record levels.”
He also predicted that the Iran and Ukraine conflicts would end soon, sending gasoline and oil prices “tumbling down.”
Enacted in 1950, the DPA allows Washington to financially support industries deemed essential to national defense. In a presidential memorandum, Trump designated domestic petroleum production, refineries, pipelines, and storage facilities as critical to national security, arguing that private companies could not expand capacity quickly enough without federal intervention.
Energy Secretary Chris Wright promised the funds would be deployed in cooperation with private companies, while the Department of Energy separately projected the initiative would increase refining output by millions of gallons of gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, and other products per day.
Vice President J.D. Vance had earlier announced plans to invoke the law to expand a Delek-operated refinery in Tyler, Texas, although such projects typically take months, if not years, to complete.
Trump’s announcement comes as his approval rating has plunged to a record low of 31% – compared with 47% when he began his second term – ahead of the midterm elections on November 3, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll published Monday. The survey also found that 68% of Americans disapproved of his handling of the economy.
Fuel prices in America sharply rose after the US and Israel launched their war against Iran in late February, disrupting global energy supplies. According to the US Energy Information Administration, average gasoline prices have climbed from $2.94 per gallon immediately before the conflict to $4.28 in the week ending October 19, while diesel has jumped from $3.81 to $6.28 over the same period.
The Trump administration has sought to tackle the fuel crisis through several emergency measures, including releasing 172 million barrels from strategic oil reserves, relaxing gasoline-blending requirements, temporarily easing diesel regulations, and announcing additional subsidies for struggling farmers.
In early October, Trump also announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to release more than 300,000 tons of Russian diesel onto global markets, with additional supplies expected later. He has also repeatedly pressed Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, which he blamed for rising fuel prices.
The president’s pressure sparked pushback from Zelensky, who called Trump’s diesel deal with Moscow “a weak decision” and “not fair and not honest” while refusing to comply with the refineries ultimatum. In response, Trump suggested that Ukraine should “get a new president” instead of Zelensky, whose term expired more than two years ago, while calling continued Ukrainian strikes a “disgrace.”

first drive: rolls-royce spectre series II brings more range, speed and material craft to stockholm
rolls-royce tests the 390-mile range of its gradient-painted spectre series II on the streets of stockholm and beyond.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
NORDIC DRIVE EXPOSes MATERIAL CRAFT of rolls-royce spectre
Following the 2023 debut of its first all-electric vehicle in Napa and a subsequent drive of the darkened Black Badge edition in Barcelona, Rolls-Royce brings the Spectre Series II to the streets of Stockholm. The updated super-coupé extends its range by 18% to 390 miles (627 kilometers) while introducing highly intricate material finishes, shifting the focus toward deep bespoke personalization, gradient exterior treatments, and intricate textile development.
all images courtesy of Rolls-Royce Motor Cars
rolls-royce unlocks more range and speed with less charging time
Where the Napa drive highlighted the transition from a V12 engine to silent electric torque, and Barcelona exposed the aggressive acceleration of the alter-ego Black Badge, Stockholm provides a cool, crisp environment to test the Series II’s electric endurance. Engineers at the British marque refined the battery cell technology to unlock a longer driving distance and reduce charging times by 14%. The dual electric motors produce 442 kW of power and 1,015 Nm of torque, which increases to 1,100 Nm when Spirited Mode is engaged, all whilst maintaining the characteristically silent magic carpet ride over the city’s cobblestones and coastal highways.
series II delivers deeper bespoke personalization
The physical presence of the Series II retains the fastback profile but moves away from the brand’s traditional horizontal color split. A new Gradient Two-Tone exterior treatment transitions a single color from the front of the motor car to the rear over a black base coat, altering how light hits the sheer surfaces. Developing the paint chemistry and application process took six months, and each vehicle requires four days in the paint shop to achieve the correct visual depth across the expansive body panels.
To further accentuate the sweeping lines of the coupé, Rolls-Royce developed a new solid exterior finish named Ethereal Blue. Grounding this profile are newly designed 23-inch forged alloy wheels that introduce a faceted, multi-spoke geometry. The wheels are cut with unusually sharp 2.5-millimeter (0.1-inch) radii, allowing the metallic surfaces to maintain a crisp, diamond-like reflection. Each wheel undergoes up to six hours of hand-polishing and is offered in both part-polished and fully polished variations.
Inside the spacious cabin, the material palette moves beyond traditional leather to integrate complex textiles and perforation patterns. The Series II introduces Duality Twill, a rayon fabric made from bamboo. The textile features a graphic pattern echoing the interweaving rope lines of sailing yachts. Producing a full Duality Twill interior requires 16 kilometers (10 miles) of thread and up to 2.6 million individual stitches, taking 25 hours to construct. Alongside the twill, a Placed Perforation leather option maps 78,138 precision-cut holes in three different sizes across the seats, referencing the shifting silhouettes of clouds in moonlight.
Across the dashboard, a new Brindled Walnut veneer combines non-fruiting walnut wood with residual eucalyptus fibers to form a layered tiger-stripe pattern. This wood is sealed in a clear lacquer infused with glass flakes, suspending the particles beneath the surface for a multidimensional finish. The interior panel and clock gallery now span the entire width of the fascia, joined by an illuminated artwork composed of 8,108 individual pixel-like lights that mimic mist settling over a landscape. An aviation-inspired timepiece with cast metal hands and an up-lit Spirit of Ecstasy figurine encased in a unique inset vitrine complete the tactile dashboard.
Tracking driver habits since the super-coupé’s initial 2022 launch reveals that owners utilize the electric vehicle extensively, often driving it daily and charging at home rather than treating it as an occasional exhibition piece. By extending the driving range to 390 miles and introducing highly labor-intensive material finishes, the Series II shifts the Spectre from a silent electric debut into a deeply personalized, long-distance driver’s car.

Heineken document reveals worries over weight-loss drugs and beer sales
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23

Heineken document reveals worries over weight-loss drugs and beer sales
- Heineken warns GLP-1 weight-loss drugs may cut beer and cider sales, as users feel fuller, drink less and choose smaller serves, low-alcohol drinks and premium products.
- The brewer told British pubs and bars to adapt with half-pints, low- and no-alcohol drinks and small plates, or risk lower visits and spending as use grows.
- Evidence from surveys, spending data and interviews shows many GLP-1 users drink less. Experts say the drugs may also help alcohol use disorder treatment, but threaten beer makers.
AI generated
LONDON – Heineken has urged British pubs and bars to adapt to the booming use of weight-loss drugs or risk losing customers and revenue, according to a company presentation seen by Reuters, in a rare acknowledgement from a major alcohol maker that the medicines pose a threat to beer sales.
The warning comes as GLP-1 use has surged, with some 10 million people taking medications like Novo Nordisk’s Ozempic and Wegovy in the US in 2025, according to JPMorgan research.
Their growth is having ramifications across the consumer goods industry, hitting cravings for sweets and snacks, driving up demand for clothing alterations and prompting a scramble to sell products that counter side-effects.
Heineken, the world’s second-largest brewer after AB InBev, told hospitality customers that GLP-1 drugs can reduce the desire to drink and put pressure on beer and cider sales from “fullness and fewer serves”, while warning that traditional multi-pint drinking occasions could become harder to sustain.
The previously unreported presentation, sent to hospitality customers in October, advised venues to promote half-pints, low- and no-alcohol drinks and pair drinks with small plates, or risk declines in customer visits and spending as use of the medicines becomes increasingly mainstream in Britain.
The alcohol industry is already grappling with years of falling sales in some major markets as consumers cut back on drinking for health and economic reasons.
Heineken told Reuters that the presentation was shared as part of its regular engagement with UK hospitality businesses to help them understand how the market is evolving.
“We see some changes in consumption behaviour among (GLP-1) users and will continue to monitor how these behaviours evolve in 2027,” Heineken said.
GLP-1 users were not abandoning alcohol altogether but were increasingly opting for smaller serves, lower-alcohol drinks and more premium products, aligning with broader ongoing trends, it continued, adding its portfolio is well positioned to meet these demands.
Evidence of reduced consumption grows
Europe is the Dutch brewer’s largest market by revenue, but growth has been sluggish. Heineken has singled out Britain, where it owns more than 2,000 pubs, as a relative bright spot.
Beer generated nearly £14 billion (S$23.9 billion) of sales in British pubs, bars and restaurants in the year to February 2026, with less than £300 million of that from no- and low-alcohol beers, according to a Heineken UK report.
Although drinks companies have largely played down the threat from GLP-1 medicines, emerging spending data points to an impact on purchases.
A group of US households with a GLP-1 user tracked by market research firm Circana between 2024 and 2026 reduced spending on alcohol for both at-home and out-of-home consumption compared with households without a user.
After two years on the drugs, they spent about 7% less per month on alcohol versus non-using households, including around 13.5% less on beer.
Top spirits maker Diageo has told investors any impact from GLP-1 drugs should be manageable even if use becomes more widespread.
Carlsberg told Reuters existing data did not yet support the view that the drugs were a clear driver of beer consumption trends. Anheuser-Busch InBev declined to comment.
Surveys in Europe and the UK by Circana, market researcher NIQ and specialist UK-based hospitality researcher KAM have also pointed to reduced drinking by GLP-1 users.
Ten of 11 GLP-1 users Reuters interviewed said they had reduced their drinking, sometimes significantly, saying it left them feeling uncomfortable or unwell, or they simply no longer had any desire to drink.
Britain-based Daniel Cornwell, founder of hospitality executive recruitment business SPE Resourcing, said he used to drink regularly at work events and on weekends but now finds alcohol causes him discomfort and results in a multi-day hangover.
GLP-1’s effects on the brain may also affect users’ motivation to drink, said Joseph Schacht, a professor at the University of Colorado Anschutz, who led a randomised controlled trial on the impact of GLP-1s on people with alcohol use disorder (AUD). He said trials have consistently shown a reduction in cravings and consumption for people with AUD.
Schacht said the medicines could create a potential “Prozac moment” for AUD treatment, while also posing a challenge for alcohol producers if broader groups of drinkers cut back too. REUTERS

Türkiye’s crop production is expected to increase significantly in cereals and fruits in 2026, while vegetable output is projected to edge lower, according to the second production estimate released by the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) on Oct. 23.

Households turn more optimistic on inflation, survey shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
08:53:14 UTC
17:53:14 KST

Inflation expectations diverged across sectors in October, with households and businesses becoming more optimistic about the inflation outlook while market participants turned slightly more cautious, according to surveys released by Türkiye’s Central Bank on Oct. 23.
The bank’s Sectoral Inflation Expectations survey showed that 12-month-ahead inflation expectations rose by 0.19 percentage points from the previous month to 23.89 percent among market participants, while declining by 0.70 points to 31.8 percent for the real sector and by 1.85 points to 43.75 percent for households. The share of households expecting inflation to decline over the next 12 months also edged up to 16.56 percent.
A separate Household Expectations Survey indicated that consumers continued to see fuel and energy, followed by food, as the product groups recording the strongest price increases. The share of respondents citing fuel and energy among the categories with the highest price increases rose by 2.7 percentage points from the previous month to 38.9 percent.
The survey also showed that gold remained households’ preferred investment choice, with 43.3 percent of respondents saying they would buy gold, up 0.3 percentage points from a month earlier. Real estate ranked second, with the share of respondents opting for a house, shop or land increasing by 2 percentage points to 35.6 percent.
Households’ expectation for house price growth over the coming 12 months eased by 0.33 percentage points from the previous month to 30.36 percent, while their forecast for the U.S. dollar/Turkish Lira exchange rate one year ahead rose by 0.96 lira to 56.86.
The Sectoral Inflation Expectations survey compiles 12-month-ahead consumer inflation forecasts from financial and real-sector experts, manufacturing firms and households. The Household Expectations Survey for October was completed by 3,152 households.
The survey results came a day after Citi said the Central Bank’s 100-basis-point rate cut to 36 percent reflected a carefully calibrated return to monetary easing, adding that policymakers appeared increasingly confident that underlying inflation was moderating. Citi forecasts inflation at 28.4 percent at the end of 2026, 21 percent in 2027 and 13.5 percent in 2028, and expects the policy rate to end this year at 35 percent.
HSBC Global Investment Research, meanwhile, forecasts inflation at 30 percent by the end of 2026 and 15 percent by the end of 2027. It expects the one-week repo rate to fall to 35 percent by the end of 2026 and 21 percent by the end of 2027.

Macron to meet student groups: Where are France’s protests heading?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
08:50:23 UTC
17:50:23 KST

Macron to meet student groups: Where are France’s protests heading?
President to meet for first time with student representatives on Friday before further protests.
Paris, France – President Emmanuel Macron plans to meet with high school student representatives as the country braces for further protests over the weekend.
The meeting on Friday marks the first time the French leader has held talks with the student groups that have been calling for an overhaul of the education system since September.
Students have called for more demonstrations to maintain the pressure while Jean-Didier Berger, the minister delegate to the interior minister, said the police presence on the streets would be increased by 20 percent.
Last weekend, largely peaceful demonstrations gave way to violent riots. Authorities were accused of failing to prepare adequately and are taking no chances before further protests expected on Saturday. A partial urfew in Paris will limit movement while protest bans are in place in Marseille and Lyon.
‘We’ve been given promises that were never kept’
High school students have made their demands clear: better-funded schools, more teachers and a greater say in decisions affecting their future.
With protests showing little sign of abating, a government weakened by political deadlock and mounting debt faces a difficult question: What can it do to bring young people off the streets?
“For years, we’ve been given promises that were never kept,” said Soumaya Sarre, an 18-year-old student and a leading figure in the Federation of High School Students from Working-Class Neighbourhoods. “What we want is for promises to be backed by concrete results. We want to see real change in our high schools.”
Since mid-September, high school students have been protesting against teacher shortages; overcrowded classrooms, sometimes with more than 40 students; and dilapidated school buildings. Their grievances have grown into a nationwide movement at a tense moment for France as it gears up for its presidential election in six months.
“Let’s be clear: Our demands are not all impossible to meet,” said Nathanael Combary, 18, president of the board of directors of the student organisation Renouveau Lyceen. He identified two priorities: a comprehensive overhaul of Parcoursup, the university admissions system, which many students consider discriminatory, and a 1.5-billion-euro ($1.7bn) emergency plan to improve school infrastructure before winter and summer.
Other student organisations and unions are calling for an additional 10 billion euros ($11.2bn) for education, more teachers on permanent rather than precarious contracts and 250,000 additional university places. “My primary goal is to provide very concrete solutions,” Combary said.
So far, the government has announced 3,000 additional substitute teachers and an online consultation while its 2027 budget allocates an extra 1.1 billion euros ($1.2bn) to national education.
But beyond these practical demands, one message emerged repeatedly in interviews with students: They want to be heard. “It is clear that this crisis points to one thing: a breakdown in dialogue between the government – and politicians in general – and young people,” Combary said. “We need a government that listens to us and is capable of responding to our demands.”
‘Wealthy family has replaced the welfare state’
Higher Education Minister Philippe Baptiste is not considering abolishing Parcoursup, calling the idea “pure demagogy”, but he said he was ready for “profound changes”.
After a meeting with student organisations on October 7, the Union etudiante, a national student union federation, said the minister could not give them any guarantees. Another meeting is set for Monday at which the government said it will present a first set of decisions on staffing, teacher replacements and Parcoursup.
Some observers doubted that these measures alone can address the deeper causes of the unrest: a sense of anxiety linked to a diploma that no longer guarantees a job, an ever-increasing cost of living and a sense that the state is not capable any longer of providing services.
“Young people’s prospects depend on the social status and wealth of a family. This is the root cause of these protests, and it can’t be fixed with a few measures, such as improving heating in schools and toilets,” said Jacques Reland, a senior research fellow at the Global Policy Institute. “The wealthy family has replaced the welfare state,” he said.
On top of that, students and unions are asking for a level of support that the government can’t give, even if it wanted to. On a political level, Macron has a minority in parliament, which makes it impossible to pass any meaningful reforms.
But the biggest obstacle for any concessions to the protesters is finances. France has long spent on a generous welfare system. Macron offered a cheque of 10 billion euros ($11.2bn) in tax cuts to quell the ‘yellow vest’ movement, which ripped through France in 2018. A similar response may be more difficult this time. Public debt is projected to reach 121.7 percent of France’s gross domestic product in 2027, up from 119.3 percent this year, according to the government’s budget bill.
“They are demanding things that the government is not in a position to satisfy unless they increase the deficit, or touch social security – two aspects that would push people in the streets,” Reland said.

European, Mideast foreign ministers hold talks in Istanbul
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
08:50:14 UTC
17:50:14 KST

Breadcrumb
European, Middle East foreign ministers hold security talks in Turkey's Istanbul
Foreign ministers from eight European and Middle Eastern countries are set to meet in Istanbul on Friday in an unprecedented format for talks on the Strait of Hormuz and wars across the Middle East.
Ministers from Britain, France and Germany—the so-called E3—as well as Italy will meet counterparts from the newly created R4 group comprising Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt to discuss the Palestinians, developments in Yemen and Hormuz, and ways to end the Russia-Ukraine war, a Turkish foreign ministry source said.
British foreign minister Ed Miliband's office said the talks would essentially revolve around "the Strait of Hormuz and the situation in Saudi Arabia".
It said Miliband "will advocate for a diplomatic solution to the (Hormuz) crisis that restores full navigational rights and freedoms".
He will also stress "how Iranian tactics are being replicated across the region, with attacks on Saudi Arabia further destabilising the region and increasing pressure on vital waterways and global chokepoints, such as Bab al-Mandeb and the Suez Canal", it added.
France confirmed the talks on "the Iranian crisis in its various ramifications", hailing it as a first "in this format... against a backdrop of extreme instability and uncertainty in the region."
The meeting will aim to "strengthen coordination between Europeans and Middle Eastern countries in the face of crises that we did not choose and that affect us all," the French foreign ministry said.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan is hosting the meeting, as Turkey steps up efforts to strengthen its regional role, including through the Mecca Defence Alliance, a defence pact launched with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia in August.
Turkey has said the pact is not aimed at any specific country and remains open to others, including Egypt.
Cairo has yet to decide whether to join the alliance. On Wednesday, President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said Egypt would "defend Saudi territory" and would not take part in any attack on Yemen.
Intensifying attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis have forced Saudi Arabia to close its main airport and postpone a major investment conference, while a maritime blockade has threatened oil exports from the world's largest crude exporter.
Riyadh has since secured backing from its allies.
During a surprise visit on Wednesday, President Emmanuel Macron said French forces would help protect the Red Sea oil terminal of Yanbu.
Britain announced a day earlier that it would deploy fighter jets to help Saudi Arabia defend against the growing threat of Houthi attacks.
'Chance of success'
Fidan praised regional cooperation Friday, saying, "Lasting solutions cannot be imposed from outside."
During the talks, Fidan is expected to stress that regional security requires countries in the region to "assume responsibility" and that Turkey prioritises cooperation mechanisms based on "regional ownership", according to Turkish officials.
He is also expected to say that "existing disputes should not be allowed to feed one another, conflicts should not be allowed to spread to new areas, and regional tensions should not be allowed to turn into broader instability".
Fidan is expected to call for increased international pressure on Israel over settlement expansion and what Ankara describes as "settler terrorism".
He will also reiterate Turkey's support for Saudi Arabia's security in the face of Houthi attacks and underline the need to safeguard freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandeb.
The Black Sea is also expected to feature prominently, with Fidan highlighting Turkey's efforts to prevent the Russia-Ukraine war from spilling into the region.

Iranian film Head to Head asks: What if men wore the hijab?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
08:49:51 UTC
17:49:51 KST

Breadcrumb
Head to Head: Iranian filmmaker Ghasideh Golmakani on making men confront sexism through hijab role reversal
What if the hijab were mandatory for men? That is what happens to the male actors in Head to Head, the debut feature by Iranian director Ghasideh Golmakani.
The premise is not quite as straightforward as it sounds. Head to Head is a mockumentary about making a fictional film in which men must wear skirts and headscarves. It may have several layers, but Ghasideh is clear about what she wanted to achieve.
"I never wanted to make a conventional film. I wanted to make exactly what I made. It became just what I had imagined," Ghasideh tells The New Arab.
Although Head to Head doesn't necessarily fit the category of a documentary, the film was fully scripted, with every scene carefully planned. That said, the rehearsals allowed some flexibility.
"The structure and the dialogue were already written, but we rehearsed a lot with the actors beforehand. During those rehearsals, I gave them space to improvise a little," she explains.
This flexibility helped Ghasideh capture the film's central reactions. We see a woman directing a production on a male-dominated set, where the actors agree to wear women's clothes and headscarves but begin to complain when the experience becomes uncomfortable.
To capture their reactions, Ghasideh asked the actors to wear the clothing during rehearsals, even before they had fully familiarised themselves with the script.
"I didn’t give them the script at the beginning. They read it before each rehearsal session, so it was very fresh in their minds when they performed it," she explains.
"During the rehearsals, I asked them to wear headscarves and dress as women. They were obviously bothered by it. It was warm, and they reacted exactly as I had written."
Beyond the veil
In this sense, Head to Head works like a sociological experiment, with predictable results, at least for Ghasideh.
By exposing the discomfort of actors, whose profession involves stepping into other people's shoes, the film goes beyond challenging an oppressive law to reveal how deeply ingrained gender discrimination is in society.
As she puts it, "What I’m pointing to is our failure, as human beings, to put ourselves in other people’s shoes. Nowadays, we judge each other so easily because of religion, nationality, gender or whatever else. I find that increasingly frightening. For me, this film goes beyond Iran. I could have made it in another country, using something other than the veil, and I think it would have carried the same message."
In sharing this, she notes that the hijab, which has been at the centre of many demonstrations, serves as a symbol of the restrictions imposed on women.
For instance, there is a scene where the director shouts 'cut' because the men dressed as women are dancing in ways that women are not allowed to in Iran. But as Ghasideh points out, discrimination against women is hardly exclusive to Iran.
"Women in other countries may not have to wear a hijab, but they still generally face more restrictions than men and are subjected to much greater scrutiny," she says.
"I left Iran when I was 18 and went to France hoping to find liberté, fraternité, égalité," she says. "To my unpleasant surprise, I discovered that we were still very far from equality. In Iranian films and Iranian society, this is more obvious because the contrast is so stark. But it also exists in other societies."
Finding humour in injustice
The restrictions women face also raise questions about the limits of activism, another theme Head to Head explores. In one scene, the crew's van is about to be stopped by the morality police.
Bahar resists putting on a headscarf, seeing it as a humiliation that would also bring the film's role-playing to an abrupt halt.
She is torn between staying true to her principles and avoiding a direct confrontation with the authorities. The reversal of power relations made possible within the film suddenly clashes with the reality outside it.
For Ghasideh, confronting such inequalities has strengthened her determination to challenge them, even if she prefers to do so through her films rather than direct confrontation.
"Somehow, that feeling of injustice between men and women became even stronger in me. I’m not doing things on a large scale, but I always try to reduce inequality in my surroundings as much as I can, and a little through my films as well," she says.
"But I don’t shout too loudly. I’m afraid that shouting can sometimes frighten the listener or the audience. That is also why I chose comedy: it stays with you differently from slogans shouted at full volume."
But how much of Ghasideh is there in Bahar? The similarities between the fictional director and the filmmaker herself are hard to ignore.
"It took me a long time to find the actress because, for different reasons, none of the people I met convinced me. Someone said, ‘Why don’t you play the role yourself? It’s you!’ But I didn’t want to take on that responsibility," she notes.
"It was my first feature, and I needed to concentrate on directing. Luckily, I found her. I think Bahar is very much like me, although she is a little more exaggerated."
The parallels between the two help reinforce the film's approach to sexism. Rather than confronting entrenched discrimination through direct political denunciation, Head to Head relies on irony and comedy to make its point.
"For someone who responds to this kind of irony, I think it works better than a serious treatment of the subject," she explains.
Making a film in Iran can itself be an act of resistance. For Ghasideh, this was particularly apparent in her debut feature, which she wrote, directed, and produced herself despite the lack of financial support.
"I think writing, directing and producing my debut feature was the craziest thing I could have done. What was really difficult was the lack of financial support. It weighed on me so much that I couldn’t think about anything else. I live in Hamburg, so I bought a camera here, went to Iran and said, ‘I’m going to make a film. No matter what.’"
Should men try wearing the hijab?
Despite censorship, conflict and countless other difficulties, Iranian cinema continues to produce a remarkable number of films, some of which circulate widely on the international festival circuit.
"I think we have a very strong culture of resistance. I saw a documentary about Iranian film history in which a producer described filming during the Iran-Iraq War in the 1980s. When sirens warned of an Iraqi bombing raid, they would stop. After the bombing, they would continue shooting," she shares.
"For me, that was beautiful and sad at the same time. It is a form of resistance: art resisting war, conflict and our problems. I think this is deeply rooted in our culture.”
Ghasideh is now preparing her second fiction feature, about an Iranian-German couple in Hamburg. She describes it as "another black comedy, questioning cultural clashes." With another film in the works, we ask whether she believes art, and cinema in particular, can change the world.
She answers with conviction, saying, "I hope the film can make people pause, even briefly, and stop judging each other so easily" and that "this power game between men and women also has to stop at some point. Otherwise, we will never achieve a balanced society anywhere."
Her answer brings us back to the question at the heart of Head to Head: should all men wear a hijab, even for just one day, to better understand women’s experiences?
"No," she says. "They can do whatever they want," she adds, saying she would definitely recommend they at least watch her film.
After premiering at the Toronto International Film Festival and receiving a Best Screenplay nomination at the Asia Pacific Screen Awards, the film is now set to screen at the Chicago International Film Festival
Manuel Halpern is a journalist and film critic, founder and editor of Wild at Heart, and a member of FIPRESCI
Follow him on Instagram: @manuelhalpern_

The 24 solar terms, consisting of 12 major solar terms and 12 minor solar terms, were created thousands of years ago by the ancient Chinese to guide agricultural production.
The culture behind the terms provides useful guidance to people's lives as each term features special food, cultural ceremonies and healthy living tips.
Frost's Descent, or "Shuangjiang," the 18th solar term, falls on October 23 this year. As the last solar term in autumn, Frost's Descent signifies the upcoming winter. It's the harvest time for most crops and the weather is gradually getting colder.

Support for U.S. to be seen as "hostile act" toward Iran: official

MOSCOW/TEHRAN, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Iran has warned regional countries that any support for the United States in the event of a renewed armed conflict would be regarded as a hostile act toward Tehran, an Iranian official said on Friday.
Iran would be able to identify which regional states are prepared to back American forces if military action resumes, Fada Hossein Maleki, a member of the Iranian parliament's National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, told RIA Novosti in an interview.
"In that case, the decisions taken by Iran may go beyond strikes on the military bases of those countries, and those countries themselves will be classified as hostile states," he added.
Iran's Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi said on the same day that the United States has spent 11 billion U.S. dollars in taxpayers' money on missile defense for Israel within the past three years.
"It has fired more interceptors defending Israel than Israel has," Araghchi said. "That is not a symbiotic relationship. It is a parasitic one." ■

Japan's Sagawa Express says up to 53.23 mln personal data records may have leaked
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:47:15 CST
17:47:15 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Sagawa Express Co., a major Japanese parcel delivery company, said Friday that up to 53.23 million records containing personal information may have been leaked following unauthorized access to its parcel tracking system.
The potentially compromised information includes names, addresses and telephone numbers of parcel senders and recipients, as well as email addresses registered with the company's membership service, Smart Club. Information related to corporate customers with freight service contracts may also have been exposed, the company said.
Sagawa Express said the potentially affected data covers shipments handled from June 21 through Sept. 30, as well as information registered with Smart Club and data on corporate clients.
No credit card information or sign-in passwords for the tracking service were exposed, the company said.
The company confirmed on Sept. 30 that its parcel tracking service, known as the Parcel Inquiry Service, had been accessed without authorization by a third party, and partially suspended its internet-based services to prevent further damage.
Following a detailed investigation, the company disclosed Friday that the number of potentially affected records could reach 53.23 million.
However, Sagawa Express cautioned that the figure includes a considerable number of duplicate records and does not represent the number of individual people affected. The company said it is organizing the data to determine the precise number of affected records. ■

China completes first demo unit of next-gen heavy-ion cancer therapy accelerator
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:47:15 CST
17:47:15 KST

This photo taken on Oct. 20, 2026 shows the first demonstration unit of China's new-generation, domestically developed medical heavy-ion accelerator in Huizhou, south China's Guangdong Province. (Xinhua/Yu Fei)
GUANGZHOU, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- The first demonstration unit of China's new-generation, domestically developed medical heavy-ion accelerator has been completed in Huizhou, Guangdong Province, southern China, according to the Institute of Modern Physics (IMP) under the Chinese Academy of Sciences.
The completion marks a milestone in China's precision radiotherapy field and is expected to bring advanced cancer treatment to more patients while boosting the country's ion radiotherapy industry, the institute said.
The unit has entered the equipment testing stage and is expected to begin clinical trials by the end of this year, said IMP.
Heavy-ion therapy is widely recognized as an advanced form of precision radiotherapy. It can deliver radiation precisely to tumors, limit damage to healthy tissue, and cause DNA double-strand breaks in cancer cells, which helps prevent recurrence. It is especially suitable for some solid tumors that are unsuitable for surgery, insensitive to conventional radiation, or prone to recurrence.
China became the fourth country, after the United States, Germany and Japan, to independently develop a heavy-ion therapy system and apply it clinically. Its first fully independent heavy-ion accelerator for clinical treatment began treating patients in Wuwei, northwest China's Gansu Province, in 2020.
Across China, ten domestically developed medical heavy-ion accelerators have been promoted, and by the end of September 2026, nearly 5,000 patients had been treated, with stable operation and notable results.
The new-generation system, known as SIMM, is an ultra-compact rotating-beam heavy-ion therapy system. It uses a series of new technologies, including a compact high-current linear injector, a short-circumference rapid-cycling synchrotron, and an intelligent rotating beam delivery system.
Its core technologies have received patent approvals in the United States, Europe, Japan and South Korea. One of its inventions also won a gold award at the 26th China Patent Award, IMP said.
The new system reduces the floor area from 4,600 square meters to 1,200 square meters and cuts energy consumption to about one-third of previous levels. Its annual treatment capacity can rise from about 1,000 patients to 2,000-5,000, which is expected to lower construction and operating costs and help reduce treatment fees, IMP added. ■

"Too little, too late": Netizens slam Japan's slow reaction to Mongolian reserve fire
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:47:12 CST
17:47:12 KST

ULAN BATOR, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Public frustration is mounting among Mongolian and Japanese social media users over a massive steppe wildfire in the Numrug Strictly Protected Area, as netizens criticize the slow response from the Japanese-linked company and raise questions over perceived double standards in public discourse.
The fire ignited on Oct. 8 in the core zone of the high-value protected reserve in Dornod Province, eastern Mongolia. Official figures from Mongolia's Ministry of Environment and Climate Change showed the blaze scorched roughly 530,000 hectares of land, of which some 470,000 hectares sit inside the reserve -- equivalent to 79.8 percent of the protected area's total territory.
The fire was fully extinguished on Oct. 16 after eight-day round-the-clock operations by Mongolian emergency teams. As flames advanced toward the bilateral frontier, China mobilized over 3,400 emergency personnel along the Inner Mongolia section of the China-Mongolia border for round-the-clock fire-prevention patrols.
Mobicom, a major Mongolian telecom firm invested in by Japan's KDDI, has been linked to the fire. KDDI on Tuesday issued an apology, acknowledging that Mobicom executives were present inside the reserve when the incident occurred. The parent firm said it took the grave environmental impact "extremely seriously," yet offered limited details about how the fire actually started, noting it would await outcomes of Mongolia's official investigation.
Mobicom maintained the convoy entered the zone for 4G-network testing with prior notifications, a claim that Mongolian government officials have publicly cast doubt on. Local Mongolian media have alleged alternative motives for the incursion, though such reports remain unconfirmed by formal probes.
The huge ecological toll has sparked fierce online pushback. Mongolian social media users called for full accountability and comprehensive restoration of the damaged reserve.
"Hopefully, the Japanese company will be responsible for paying to restore the wildlife!" One comment read on a Facebook post by Japan Daily. Another user wrote: "Many Mongolians had never even laid eyes on the breathtaking wilderness before this tragic incident unfolded."
Many Mongolian netizens stressed that environmental destruction of this scale cannot be offset merely by money or apologies, urging legal punishment for those responsible and thorough assessment of soil, vegetation and wildlife losses.
Criticism also surfaced on Japanese social platforms. Some Japanese netizens pointed to apparent double standards in Japanese public opinion. They drew comparisons with widely circulated domestic narratives about foreigners damaging Japan's environment, questioning the relative silence within Japan over the large-scale ecological harm caused by a Japan-linked corporate activity overseas.
"The natural environment cannot instantly recover just through apologies or compensation payments," one Japanese social media user commented. Others highlighted cross-border spill-over risks, noting the burned area is more than twice the size of Tokyo, warning that intensified dust storms generated by the damaged steppe could potentially affect not only Mongolia and China but also the Korean Peninsula.
Several online voices also criticized the Japanese administration's conspicuous lack of public remarks regarding the disaster.
Mongolian authorities have handed the case over to national police for full-scale investigation. Officials have pledged to pursue liabilities for involved company staff as well as relevant administrative personnel who authorized access permits, and to claim full compensation for both economic costs and long-term ecological harm. A special working group is conducting field surveys to quantify multi-faceted environmental damage and work out restoration plans.
The Embassy of Japan in Mongolia on Thursday released a statement on the incident on social media, saying that it is closely following the serious damage caused by the blaze, and pledged to actively push Mobicom to put in place remediation measures.
"Wasn't this response far too late? You turned a blind eye and stayed silent all this time," a netizen replied under the post. ■

China's innovation gains pace, powering new growth drivers: report
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:47:10 CST
17:47:10 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- China's innovation capacity continued to strengthen last year, with the innovation environment improving and new growth drivers expanding, providing solid support for high-quality development, official data showed on Friday.
The country's innovation index stood at 185.5 in 2025, up 6.4 percent from a year earlier, according to an annual report released by the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS). The sub-indices measuring the innovation environment, input, output and impact all kept rising last year.
The report noted that multiple indicators performed well, including the share of science and technology appropriations in government budget spending, business R&D spending as a share of operating revenue, R&D spending as a share of GDP, the number of high-value invention patents per 10,000 R&D personnel, overall labor productivity, and high-tech products' share of goods exports.
In China, innovation is gathering pace across the board. From DeepSeek's global splash to humanoid robots that wowed audiences, China's scientific achievements have been translating rapidly into industrial applications. Artificial intelligence (AI), new energy and new materials are among the sectors maintaining strong growth momentum.
In the first three quarters of 2026, new drivers of growth, represented by high-end manufacturing, the digital and intelligent economy, and modern services, contributed more than 40 percent of China's economic growth.
"The rapid growth of new drivers is a standout feature of this year's economic performance," Mao Shengyong, an NBS spokesperson, said.
Separately, tax invoice data released by the State Taxation Administration on Friday also revealed that industries tied to new growth drivers have expanded faster this year, with those related to AI picking up speed especially quickly.
In the third quarter of 2026, sales revenue of core industries of the digital economy, and patent-intensive industries rose 9.9 percent and 14.4 percent year on year, respectively, a clear acceleration from the second quarter, the tax data showed. Sales in the integrated circuits and semiconductor equipment manufacturing sectors surged 77.9 percent and 35.9 percent, respectively, from a year earlier.
Innovation has long held an important place in China's development strategy. The latest major step comes as the guidelines on developing new quality productive forces were released earlier this month, spelling out the overall goals and key tasks for the 2026-2030 period.
As China actively cultivates future industries, expands emerging sectors and upgrades traditional ones, the momentum built through innovation is steadily converting into economic growth, experts said. ■

Singapore private home prices rise 1.4 pct in Q3
China

SEOUL, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's appellate court on Friday acquitted Seoul Mayor Oh Se-hoon of charges involving the illegal acceptance of political funds, overturning a lower court's guilty verdict.
The Seoul High Court cleared Oh of violating the political funds act, reversing the lower court's ruling that sentenced him to a fine of 10 million won (7,540 U.S. dollars) and a forfeiture of 21 million won.
The team of Min Joong-ki, independent counsel who led investigations into corruption allegations involving former President Yoon Suk-yeol and his wife Kim Keon-hee, sought a prison sentence of one and a half years alongside a forfeiture of 33 million won for Oh during the appeal.
The appellate court ruled that sufficient evidence was not offered to prove Oh's charges, concluding that testimony from self-proclaimed political broker Myung Tae-kyun, which was the sole direct evidence, was unreliable.
Oh was indicted without detention in December 2025 on charges of receiving opinion poll results on 10 occasions ahead of the Seoul mayoral by-election in 2021 from Myung and having his long-time financial supporter, Kim Han-jung, cover the costs.
If Oh is fined over 1 million won in the final ruling, he will lose his mayoral post.
On July 13, Yoon was sentenced to two years in jail for conspiring with his wife to receive customized opinion polls free of charge from the same political broker on 58 occasions ahead of the 2022 presidential election. ■

Russia ready to resume trilateral Ukraine talks in November, Putin says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
08:46:14 UTC
17:46:14 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin reaffirmed Moscow’s readiness to resume trilateral peace talks on the war in Ukraine, saying the negotiations would focus on ways to ensure postwar security for both sides.
In an interview on Thursday with Vesti news outlet, Putin discussed Russia’s negotiations with representatives of US President Donald Trump’s administration, recalling an agreement to resume trilateral talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine.
“The objective of these talks will be to discuss how to ensure the security of both Ukraine and Russia following the conclusion of peace agreements – specifically definitive, long-term agreements rather than merely a temporary cessation of hostilities,” he added.
Putin said they are ready to resume contacts to achieve this goal, noting that during their meeting in St. Petersburg on Wednesday, US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff stressed they must address the broader architecture of European security if they are to discuss future security arrangements for both Russia and Ukraine.
“I agree with that too. Well, let’s see how the situation develops over the coming days,” he added.
His remarks came a day after he hosted the US envoy at St. Petersburg’s Constantine Palace, after which Russian presidential aide Yury Ushakov told reporters that Putin conveyed Moscow’s readiness "in principle" to resume trilateral peace negotiations on Ukraine in November.
“Our president informed Steve Witkoff that we are, in principle, prepared to resume the aforementioned trilateral negotiations around the 10th of November,” Ushakov said following the talks, adding that Moscow’s readiness for trilateral negotiations particularly concerned the issue of building a post-war “security system” for Russia and Ukraine.
Separately, Witkoff announced on X that he and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner held “constructive” discussions in St. Petersburg and the Norwegian capital Oslo, the latter of which took place on Tuesday, and that these discussions will continue with trilateral talks “at the technical level.”
Russia and Ukraine last held US-mediated peace negotiations earlier this year, with three rounds of talks on January 23-24, February 4-5, and February 7-18. The first two were held in Abu Dhabi, while the third took place in Geneva.
Commenting on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's remarks on Wednesday to Fox News on being open to freezing the front line in Ukraine in an effort to end the war, Putin argued that it seemed "inappropriate" to describe the issue as amounting to "any territorial losses."
"To begin with, my view on this matter is that this is not their territory. It is the territory of historical Russia," Putin said, further arguing that the residents of these territories "chose" to be part of Russia through referendums in September 2022.
The referendums were widely condemned as illegal by the international community.

Unknown

2026-10-23
08:44:43 UTC
17:44:43 KST

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has said Türkiye will continue its diplomatic and mediation efforts to help resolve conflicts, warning that declining trust in international institutions is deepening global instability.
In a video message to the 9th Istanbul Mediation Conference, Erdogan thanked the foreign ministry for organising the event and welcomed Istanbul’s growing role as a diplomatic hub.
“I am pleased that Istanbul, which has brought people and cultures together for centuries, has today become one of the centres of diplomacy,” he said.
Erdogan stressed the importance of maintaining diplomatic engagement amid rising conflicts, escalating tensions and declining confidence in international law and institutions.
“As Türkiye, we have made it our principle never to abandon diplomacy, even when parties refuse to talk to one another and hopes are fading,” he said.
He cited prisoner exchanges between Russia and Ukraine and mediation efforts across Africa as examples of Türkiye’s work to open pathways to peace.
Erdogan criticises global power imbalance
Erdogan reiterated his call for reform of the United Nations, repeating his message that “the world is bigger than five” — a reference to the five permanent members of the UN Security Council.
He said the UN General Assembly had recently convened under the theme “Building Trust Again”, focusing on restoring confidence in the international system.
“Today, millions of people in Palestine, Lebanon, Sudan and other crisis zones, who have placed their hopes in the United Nations, are deeply disappointed,” Erdogan said.
“A structure in which the will of more than 190 countries depends on the discretion of five countries is neither fair nor capable of fully restoring trust,” he added.
Erdogan said Türkiye rejected an approach to international politics built on mistrust and maintained that diplomacy remained possible even in the most difficult disputes.
“The issue is whether we can demonstrate the will, courage and sincerity to keep that door open,” he said, adding that Türkiye would continue bringing parties together, mediating to achieve fair solutions and assuming responsibility for peace.

German immigration office hit by human smuggling scandal – Bild
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
08:43:51 UTC
17:43:51 KST

German immigration staff charged with smuggling immigrants – Bild
An employee of a German immigration office and her husband have been arrested for allegedly assisting a human smuggling ring which brought Indian men into the country through sham marriages in exchange for hefty payments, Bild has reported.
The Cologne branch of the immigration office told the tabloid on Thursday that it has revoked the residence permits illegally issued by the criminal group, which involved two other people.
According to Bild, the smuggling ring exploited the EU’s family reunification program to bring in the Indians.
The foreign nationals arrived in Cyprus, where they entered fictitious marriages with Bulgarian women whom they had never met before, it said.
A member of the Cologne immigration office, identified as Subha L., then processed and approved the applications for residence permits by the Indian males despite the irregularities in their paperwork, the report read.
The employee and her husband earned at least €76,000 (around $85,000) from the scheme, Bild said.
A lawyer for one of the suspected smugglers told the WDR broadcaster that the scheme had allowed more than 20 Indian men to enter the EU.
Subha L. was arrested along with her husband in December 2025 and remains in per-trial detention. She has been dismissed from her job, the Cologne immigration office said. The trial for the four suspected members of the criminal group is scheduled to begin in February.
The immigration office said it tightened workflow controls following the scandal to ensure any suspicious cases are identified more promptly.
An MP for German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party accused the Cologne immigration office of failing to execute its duties and called for it to be audited by the Federal Office for Migration and Refugees.
“We are witnessing a growing loss of control within an agency that views itself as a ‘welcoming authority’ rather than an immigration authority,” Seif told the Kolner Stadt-Anzeiger newspaper.
In 2023, another employee of the Cologne immigration office was sentenced to four-and-a-half years in prison for falsifying the documents of Syrian refugees applying for residence permits.
Illegal immigration has again become a contentious topic in the EU this year after more than 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into the Spanish North African enclave of Ceuta in late July. Up to 8,000 foreigners still remain scattered throughout the territory, straining local resources and prompting protests by residents.
Despite the number of arrivals subsiding since the EU migrant crisis of 2015, the foreign-born population in the bloc reached a record 64.2 million last year, expanding by 20.2 million since 2010, according to a report published by the Center for Research and Analysis on Migration at RFBerlin in April.
Germany continues to have the largest number of immigrants in the EU, with 18 million foreign-born citizens, making up 21.2% of the country’s population, the paper said.

Finland donates 10 diesel locomotives to Ukraine
Finland has become the first country to donate locomotives to Ukrzaliznytsia, Ukrainian Railways, following the signing of an agreement to transfer 10 Dv12 diesel locomotives and spare parts.
Source: Ukrzaliznytsia, the Ukrainian state railway company
Details: The agreement was signed by Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo and Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi in the presence of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The formation of an international coalition to provide the Ukrainian railway with more locomotives was initiated during the Carpathian Eight summit. Agreements were reached at that time with a number of partners regarding the transfer of second-hand locomotives to Ukrzaliznytsia.
Ukrzaliznytsia is currently in desperate need of additional locomotives, as Russia is systematically and deliberately attacking them. Nearly 600 Ukrzaliznytsia locomotives, including over 300 diesel locomotives, have been damaged or destroyed since the beginning of the full-scale invasion.
"Repairing them requires significant funds and time and, in some cases, is impossible. Therefore, it is important to promptly replenish the locomotive fleet," the company noted.
Ukrzaliznytsia added that diesel locomotives are also of particular importance for ensuring the stability of transport operations amid intensifying Russian attacks on energy infrastructure and power outages.
Background:
- It was previously reported that Russian strikes had damaged 492 locomotives and 249 railway carriages since the beginning of the full-scale invasion. The government's action programme envisages repairing 70% of the damaged locomotives.
- An agreement in principle was also reached during the Carpathian Eight summit for US$100 million in grant funding under the RELINC project jointly with the IBRD. These funds will be used to purchase second-hand locomotives.
- Ukraine's Ministry for Restoration previously stated that it would simplify the import of locomotives and the repair of damaged traction power during martial law.

Israeli strikes and gunfire killed at least four Palestinians across the Gaza Strip on Thursday, as continued attacks underscored the fragility of a U.S.-brokered ceasefire that has failed to halt the violence or pave the way for reconstruction, health officials said.
In Gaza City, an Israeli strike hit a vehicle in the Tel al-Hawa neighborhood, killing at least one person, according to medics.
Earlier reports put the death toll at two. Images from the scene showed crowds gathering around the burning wreckage as emergency crews in orange vests sprayed the vehicle with water.
Gaza’s Hamas-led Interior Ministry said the strike killed a noncommissioned officer from the drug-control police department and wounded another officer. The two were returning from an assignment when their vehicle was hit, according to the ministry.
Elsewhere, strikes killed a Palestinian man riding a bicycle in the southern city of Khan Younis and another man near the Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza, medics said. Gunfire killed a woman near the Jabalia refugee camp in the north.
Israel’s military claimed it had struck Hamas members in Khan Younis, Nuseirat and Gaza City. It said it was unaware of the reported shooting in Jabalia.
The latest deaths come amid renewed Israeli attacks on targets it identifies as Hamas positions.
Israel accuses the Palestinian group of rebuilding its arsenal and carrying out attacks in violation of the cease-fire. Hamas denies the allegations and accuses Israel of undermining the agreement through continued military operations.
The cease-fire, brokered by the United States and implemented in October 2025, envisioned an eventual end to the Gaza genocide, the withdrawal of Israeli forces and the reconstruction of the devastated territory.
However, negotiations have made little progress on key issues, particularly Hamas’ disarmament and the extent of an Israeli military withdrawal.
Israeli airstrikes, gunfire and other military operations have continued despite the truce, leaving Palestinians exposed to further casualties and delaying efforts to rebuild homes and essential infrastructure.
Gaza health officials say at least 1,500 Palestinians have been killed since the cease-fire began. Israel, meanwhile, says four of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza over the same period.
The continued violence has deepened concerns about the agreement’s ability to deliver lasting security or meaningful relief to the territory’s population, much of which has been displaced by more than two years of war.
Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 people have been killed in Israel’s military campaign in Gaza, which began following Hamas' incursion into southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, killing about 1,200 people, according to Israeli figures.
The Gaza Health Ministry has also reported more than 175,000 injuries. The figures are widely cited by the United Nations and international organizations, although the full toll remains uncertain, with victims believed to remain buried beneath destroyed buildings.
