France mounts major security operation for fresh wave of protests
PARIS, Oct 23 - France will deploy 70,000 police backed by specialist units for protests on Saturday, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said on Friday, accusing ultra-left groups of encouraging violence and looting after unrest shocked the country last weekend.
The government is seeking to prevent a repeat of last week's demonstrations that descended into riots, looting and arson in several cities, triggering widespread criticism of authorities for not preventing the mayhem.
"We will be uncompromising with rioters, looters and all those who commit acts of violence," Nunez told reporters on Friday after meetings involving President Emmanuel Macron, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu and senior security officials.
Nunez said authorities had identified numerous online calls from hard-left groups encouraging attacks and urging activists to target public buildings.
"We are not talking about a nice, friendly demonstration," Nunez said, adding: "We are ready for tomorrow. We will be extremely vigilant, extremely firm, and we will let absolutely nothing pass."
MUSEUMS, MAJOR EVENTS SHUTTERED AS PRECAUTION
Anger over living costs and strained public services has drawn students, workers and unions onto the streets of France in recent weeks, but authorities say radical militants and bands of young looters have taken advantage of the dispute to sow chaos.
Police have authorised only a union demonstration in Paris on Saturday, rejecting requests for rallies lodged by France's main student union, UNEF, and the Yellow Vest movement, an anti-establishment force that first emerged in 2018.
Many French cities beyond Paris have also banned protests, including France's second and third largest cities, Marseille and Lyon.
UNEF said its rallies, which grew from high school protests last month against teacher shortages and shabby facilities, would go ahead regardless.
Fears of renewed turmoil prompted several of Paris' best-known cultural institutions, including the Louvre, to close on Saturday, while the city's normally bustling Art Basel fair will remain shut throughout the weekend.
Business groups also urged shops to stay shut after some 3,000 stores and businesses were ransacked last weekend.
Nunez said 10,000 more police would be on the streets than a week ago, while the specialist RAID and GIGN units, mounted police, helicopters, drones and anti-drone systems would be deployed across the country.
Armoured vehicles and water cannon vehicles would also be available, while curfews imposed in some sensitive areas this past week would remain in force.
FAR-RIGHT CONGRESS A POSSIBLE FLASHPOINT
Authorities are also concerned that the annual congress of Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally in Orleans this weekend could become a flashpoint, with left-wing and anti-racist groups announcing counter-demonstrations.
The upsurge of violence has boosted poll ratings for Le Pen, who is the frontrunner for next year's presidential election. She has portrayed the unrest as evidence of a collapse in state authority.
Adding to tensions, one person was killed and four injured in a shooting west of Paris on Friday in an attack that police said could be racially motivated.
Macron is due to meet student representatives later on Friday for the first time, seeking to de-escalate a crisis that has exposed deep social and political tensions.
Marylise Leon, the general secretary of the CFDT, one of the nation's largest trade unions, criticised him on Friday for refusing to grant permission to more rallies on Saturday.
"It's counterproductive because there is a lot of anger, a lot of anger and a demand to be considered and to be listened to," she told French broadcaster TF1. "It's not for the president to decide who can legitimately request to protest."
The social turbulence has intensified scrutiny of France's economic outlook and ratings agency Moody's is widely expected to cut the French credit rating on Friday, underscoring concern that the government had not reined in public spending. REUTERS

Gender pay gap stubbornly remains among one-quarter of employers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

08:05:15 UTC
17:05:15 KST

Women are still earning an average of 5% less than men in management functions in Belgium, according to the latest research by Randstad
In some 25% of companies in Belgium, women in management functions still earn an average 5% less than men. The figure takes into account comparable functions and ages of the employees.
The latest study by HR expert Randstad compared the salaries among more than 1,000 companies. “We see the difference particularly in leadership positions,” says Wouter Beuckels of Randstad, who offers two explanations for the phenomenon.
“Only one-quarter or one-third of management positions are held by women,” he says. “This means that fewer women are also involved in making decisions about salaries or promotions. In addition, we also see that women negotiate their salaries less frequently. As a result, they are less likely to get the best deal.”
Belgium postpones EU guidelines
The pay gap is less acute in functions outside of management. “In those cases, representation is more equal, and the gender pay gap falls under that 5% margin,” says Beuckels.
He points out that large companies with more structured pay scales have far less of a gender pay gap than small and medium-sized companies.
The EU has been trying to tackle the gender pay gap in companies for some time and has drawn up guidelines requiring companies to be more transparent about salaries. “Incorporating these guidelines into Belgian law was postponed by six months last June,” notes Beuckels. “Due to the uncertain economic situation, companies may have less budget available to address the gender pay gap.”

French companies plan to invest €1.5 billion in Kazakhstan over the next three years

Unknown Publisher

French companies plan to invest €1.5 billion in Kazakhstan over the next three years
French companies plan to invest an additional €1.5 billion in Kazakhstan over the next 3 years, with projects expected in renewable energy, hydropower, urban utilities and tourism, France’s ambassador to Kazakhstan, Sylvain Guiaugue, said at a briefing at the French Embassy’s residence, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports.
The planned investments reflect French companies’ continued interest in the Kazakh market, the ambassador said, noting that businesses also intend to expand local hiring and production.
French companies currently employ around 200,000 people in Kazakhstan. They plan to hire another 1,000 local workers over the next 3 years, according to the ambassador.
Renewable energy and infrastructure
Renewable energy is among the main areas attracting French investment. Potential projects include wind farms and hydropower facilities, as well as the modernization of existing dams.
French companies are also exploring opportunities in urban infrastructure, particularly water management and heating networks in major cities.
Tourism is another area of cooperation. French company Poma has signed a contract to supply cable car systems for a project in the Almaty region. The company is also expected to localize part of its equipment production in Kazakhstan.
The ambassador said French businesses increasingly seek local suppliers and partners. Major projects can create opportunities for Kazakh small and medium-sized enterprises to join supply chains.
Nuclear energy cooperation
France and Kazakhstan are also exploring opportunities to expand cooperation in nuclear energy, building on existing partnerships.
The ambassador cited the long-running cooperation between Kazakhstan’s Kazatomprom and France’s Orano through the joint venture KATCO, as well as nuclear fuel production in Kazakhstan using Framatome technology.
French engineering company Assystem has also been selected as an adviser to Kazakhstan’s government on nuclear power plant development.
The ambassador said contacts between the two countries were continuing as Kazakhstan plans to build at least two nuclear power plants. Potential cooperation could also include research and university training to prepare specialists for the sector.
Kazakhstan as a regional hub
The ambassador said French businesses were interested in using Kazakhstan as a base for reaching wider regional markets.
He also highlighted the importance of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, which he said was becoming increasingly significant for trade and connectivity between Europe and Central Asia.
The investment plans are outlined in a new study, French Business in Kazakhstan: A Lasting Impact, published by the French Embassy’s Economic Department in October 2026. It examines the economic contribution of French businesses, including their investment, employment, local production and exports.
Earlier, Qazinform reported that Kazakhstan showcased its agricultural exports at SIAL Paris 2026, held on October 17-21. The national pavilion was presented by the National Association of Oilseed Processors of Kazakhstan (NAOPK) and its member companies. Kazakhstan is among the EU’s top three suppliers of sunflower seed meal.

Iran war could worsen after US midterms

Iran war could worsen after US midterms
- Vali Nasr says the US-Iran war is in an “inconclusive holding pattern” and may worsen after the US midterms, as Tehran now wants more than it did in June.
- He says Trump has a three-month window to negotiate peace or strike, but any new attack could trigger wider conflict and damage the global economy.
- Nasr says US weakness in the war has hurt its security image in West Asia, while China benefits from less American influence and countries now must rethink their defence plans.
AI generated
SINGAPORE – The US and Iran war is in an “inconclusive holding pattern”, and there is no knowing which way the situation might go once the United States midterm elections are over, more so since Tehran’s demands have hardened.
That is the word from Professor Vali Nasr, one of the world’s most renowned experts on Iran and a former adviser to the US State Department.
“President Trump was forced into a memorandum of understanding which actually looked very much to be in Iran’s favour. Since then, he has been trying to claw back what the US lost in those first 40 days,” said Nasr, referring to the failed June agreement for a 60-day ceasefire.
“This can be resolved by them going into another bout of war. Or they can do what they have been doing, grinding this (out) going forward. The Iranians are now asking for more than they asked for in June.”
The 14-point agreement, reached in Islamabad, undertook to release substantial frozen funds of Iran, allowed Iran to resume oil exports, and envisaged a massive reconstruction fund for Iran. Tehran reaffirmed its commitment to never acquire or develop nuclear weapons and to allow the International Atomic Energy Agency to supervise the blending down of its uranium stockpile.
Asked whether he thought Tehran may be overplaying its hand, he responded: “They don’t think they are overplaying their hand. They think they have a winning hand, and they want to get something big out of this war.”
At the same time, he pointed out that Iran could not withstand the economic blockade indefinitely, nor continue resisting military attacks as it has. Neither is the war sustainable for the global economy with the Strait of Hormuz all but closed and Gulf economies held hostage to inconclusive hostilities.
Interviewed for The Straits Times Asian Insider podcast, Nasr noted that US President Donald Trump will either have to negotiate peace with Iran, or strike forcefully – and he has a three-month window between the midterm elections and before the US Congress convenes next January to do things his chosen way, without legislative oversight.
“My own sense is that it is not easy for the US and Iran to arrive at an agreement,” said Vasr. “So, we are inching our way to a resumption of conflict.”
The Iran-born scholar, educated in the UK and the US, is a senior academic at Johns Hopkins University's School of Advanced International Studies. He is also a visiting professor at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies.
Nasr served the Obama administration as an adviser on Iran and has been a member of the State Department’s Foreign Affairs Policy Board.
Speculation is mounting that Trump, chafing from the ignominy of the battlefield reversals that Iran’s drones and missiles have wreaked on American bases in the West Asian region, will unleash the most heinous weapons on Iran.
There is also talk that the US and Israel have agreed to escalate, particularly after the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. On Oct 19, US War Secretary Pete Hegseth reportedly held unannounced discussions with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at an air force station in the Negev desert.
After Trump backed Netanyahu to win next week’s Israeli national polls, the Premier responded warmly about “completing the mission we had started together”. The US midterms are scheduled for Nov 3, and surveys suggest a Democratic victory is on the cards. Israelis go to the polls on Oct 27 to elect a new Parliament.
Depleted ammunition stocks notwithstanding, the US retains the firepower to inflict crippling damage on Iran. While the use of nuclear weapons has been ruled out by Trump, his options include dumping massive ordnance – “the Mother of All Bombs” – on Iranian infrastructure such as power and desalination plants.
Yet, doing so is tempered by the knowledge that it would embolden Russia and China to consider similar means themselves, in their respective domains. Besides, the inevitable Iranian retaliation would be devastating for the Middle East region.
“Iranians have been saying it very openly... that when the dust settles, we won’t be the only people going down. Others will, too, and that will have great consequences for the global economy,” Nasr said, adding that Trump is caught between governments advising caution and others egging him on to “finish the job”. He is also conscious of his legacy.
“Americans are not comfortable with the image of losing.”
As for US influence in the West Asian region, Nasr said Washington’s inability to protect Gulf states – most recently Saudi Arabia – has evaporated confidence in the American security umbrella.
“The US brought a war to their doorsteps in which the Gulf states became collateral damage. Then, the US proved incapable and unwilling to defend them... they could not (even) defend their own bases.”
A result of all this is that every country in the region will recalculate its security requirements. Indeed, it is time to think of the West Asian region as you would of Nato and Europe, with Trump “jumping over Europe to shake hands with (Russian President Vladimir) Putin, and wanting Ukraine to surrender”.
While outside powers such as China and Russia will not hasten to fill this gap until they define their interests in the region more clearly, the setback to US influence is considerable.
“Already, China has won,” said Nasr. “(The) Chinese do not need to step in and do what the Americans did – the very fact that there is less American influence is to their benefit.”
It is the same with the rest of Asia, including East and South-East Asia.
“(Trump) has left many countries around the world sort of exposed because they had built their security under assumptions of the old American security order, which is in question because of this war... Every country will have to do its own calculation about its security needs and its interests.”
Besides, the way the US fought this war also revealed fundamental shortcomings in its military, including its inability to match China in producing weapons at scale. Moreover, it is unclear what sort of America will emerge after the inevitable period of retrospection on both military and strategic fronts.
What are the global implications if the US and Israel tried one more devastating strike on Iran? Nasr said a wider conflagration could not be ruled out, with North Korean soldiers fighting alongside Russians in Ukraine, Russia supporting Iran, Pakistani troops in Saudi Arabia helping to defend the kingdom, Ukraine itself assisting some Gulf monarchies with defence technology and counter-drone expertise, and Britain saying it will move fighter jets to help protect Saudi Arabia.
“Big wars don’t stay localised,” said Nasr. “If you have more than one of them happen at the same time, inevitably they get connected.”

Military horses could carry loads in the field again
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher

09:00:53 BST
17:00:53 KST

Exercise COPPER HORSE found that Military Working Horses may be able to support a limited range of field tasks under controlled training conditions, with further development needed on equipment, load carriage and operating endurance, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked the Secretary of State for Defence what findings were made on the feasibility of the operational use of horses during Exercise Copper Horse.
Louise Sandher-Jones, the Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “Exercise COPPER HORSE found that Military Working Horses may be able to support a limited range of field tasks under controlled training conditions. It also identified areas requiring further development, including equipment, load carriage and operating endurance before any judgement can be made on potential operational use.”
Britain’s forces keep around five hundred horses, almost all of them in ceremonial roles with the Household Cavalry Mounted Regiment in London, the King’s Troop Royal Horse Artillery at Woolwich, and the Defence Animal Training Regiment at Melton Mowbray, which trains horses and military working dogs.
A horse can carry around a fifth of its body weight, and United States special forces operated on horseback in northern Afghanistan in 2001, and the French, Italian, Austrian and Swiss armies retain mules or horses for mountain logistics.
We reported recently that the British Army has been experimenting with the use of horses for reconnaissance, patrol and security tasks in terrain where military vehicles may struggle to operate, according to imagery released by the Ministry of Defence.
Soldiers and Military Working Horses from the Household Cavalry Mounted Regiment took part in a mounted combat capability experiment on the Barossa training area at Sandhurst, exploring how mounted troops could support battlefield activity beyond the Regiment’s familiar ceremonial duties.
The training was conducted across difficult terrain and focused on environments where conventional vehicles could face restrictions, giving soldiers an opportunity to examine how horses might provide an alternative means of moving personnel during reconnaissance and security operations.

Iran, Tajikistan private sector ties strengthened with tripartite chamber memorandum
TEHRAN- A tripartite cooperation memorandum was signed among the Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture of Khorasan Razavi Province, the Iran-Tajikistan Joint Chamber of Commerce, and the Chamber of Commerce of Khatlon Province.
According to a Thursday report by IRNA from the Khorasan Razavi Governorate, the memorandum was concluded with the aim of developing trade relations, facilitating communication among economic actors, identifying investment opportunities, and expanding private-sector cooperation between Iran and Tajikistan.
The signing of this memorandum is considered a step toward strengthening economic cooperation, increasing trade exchanges, and paving the way for the implementation of joint projects between economic actors of the two countries.
The Governor of Khorasan Razavi also participated and delivered a speech on Thursday at the “Khatlon 2026” investment conference and the exhibition of agricultural, industrial, and handicraft products of this province in the city of Bakhtar.
Gholamhossein Mozaffari also met and held talks with Davlatali Said, the head of Khatlon Province of Tajikistan, on the sidelines of the “Khatlon 2026” international investment conference.
During this meeting, the Governor of Khorasan Razavi, referring to the extensive economic capacities and the sisterhood agreement between the two regions, emphasized Iran’s readiness to develop inter-provincial cooperation in the fields of agriculture, food industries, pharmaceuticals, and building materials.
The head of Khatlon Province of Tajikistan, while thanking the Khorasan Razavi delegation for attending this international event, expressed satisfaction with the significant activity of Iranian entrepreneurs and investors in Tajikistan and the signing of fruitful memoranda between the two countries, and emphasized the necessity of practical implementation of these agreements.
Davlatali Said also, referring to Khatlon’s capacities in cotton production, agriculture, textile industries, transportation and logistics, tourism, and food industries, emphasized benefiting from the experiences and technical and engineering capabilities of Khorasan Razavi, especially in the field of water resources management and the development of irrigation systems.
According to him, the annual production of about 100,000 tons of cotton in Khatlon Province was also cited as an important capacity for expanding industrial and trade cooperation.
The two sides also emphasized the necessity of forming a joint working committee to follow up on previous memoranda, drafting a roadmap for future cooperation, and creating a platform for direct dialogue between private-sector actors of both sides.
This meeting was held in line with strengthening historical and cultural ties, developing economic diplomacy, and expanding joint cooperation between Khorasan Razavi and Khatlon Province.
The Governor of Khorasan Razavi, heading a delegation, arrived in Dushanbe, the capital of Tajikistan, on Tuesday (October 20) to participate in the “Khatlon 2026” international investment conference and exhibition.
Tajikistan is among the three export destination countries of Khorasan Razavi. In line with developing trade relations between Iran and Tajikistan, plans have been made for coordinating future trips and participation in permanent exhibitions.
Khatlon Province is one of the four provinces of Tajikistan, the most populous of the four first-level administrative regions of the country, and is located in southwestern Tajikistan.
Meanwhile, during the trip of the Governor of Khorasan Razavi Province and his accompanying delegation to Tajikistan, a cooperation memorandum was signed between the Chambers of Commerce of Mashhad and Dushanbe with the aim of developing trade interactions and facilitating the activities of traders and businessmen of the two countries.
At the signing meeting, held at the Dushanbe Chamber of Commerce, the issue of Iranian and Tajik traders using the domestic forex rates of the two countries to attend exhibitions and develop exhibition cooperation was discussed and agreed upon.
Also, the ground for the presence of Tajik businessmen in the Mashhad Mining Exhibition, which is held in the next Iranian month, was reviewed, and emphasis was placed on providing the possibility of attendance and allocating booths to Tajik traders.
Acceptance of Iran’s national standards for goods imported into Tajikistan was another topic raised at this meeting, and it was decided that the necessary follow-ups in this regard would be carried out through the Dushanbe Chamber of Commerce.

Galerie Patrick Seguin shows demountable Jean Prouvé house with Japanese tea room interior at Design Miami.Paris
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23

17:00:00 KST

Galerie Patrick Seguin shows demountable Jean Prouvé house with Japanese tea room interior at Design Miami.Paris
Galerie Patrick Seguin in Paris has brought a 1944 house by architect Jean Prouvé to Design Miami.Paris, where it was reinterpreted as a Japanese pavilion.
The 6×6 Demountable House was designed in the 1940s to be assembled at speed and function as housing for those who had been made homeless by war.
It is currently for sale via Galerie Patrick Seguin and on show in the gardens of the Hôtel de Maisons during Design Miami.Paris.
“This house was designed at the end of the second world war to provide temporary accommodation for displaced families whilst their homes were being rebuilt,” the gallery’s founder Patrick Seguin told Dezeen.
“Its exposed structure showcases all of Prouvé’s ingenuity; he was able to respond to the urgency of post-war reconstruction with a design that could be assembled in a single day,” Seguin continued.
For Design Miami.Paris, the gallery reimagined its interior as a contemporary chashitsu – a traditional Japanese pavilion used for tea ceremonies.
“This new reading creates a dialogue between Prouvé’s architecture and Japanese aesthetics and reflects the close ties he maintained throughout his life with Japan, where he was invited to give lectures on several occasions,” Seguin said.
“Japanese architect Reiko Hayama was also one of his closest collaborators, joining his atelier in the early 1970s.”
Because it had been designed to be demountable, taking the wooden house to Paris for the show was easy, according to the gallery.
“Prouvé designed the houses to be easily assembled and dismantled; that’s the ingenuity of these structures,” Seguin said. “The 6×6 house only requires a single day to be assembled by three people.”
After the end of Design Miami.Paris, the Prouvé house “will no doubt be moved to its new owner’s home,” the gallerist concluded.
This year’s edition of Design Miami.Paris also saw Apple unveil its Designers of Tomorrow.
The Jean Prouvé house is on show at Design Miami.Paris 2026 from 21 to 25 October 2026 at L’hôtel de Maisons, 51 Rue de l’Université, 75007 Paris, France. See Dezeen Events Guide for more design events and exhibitions around the world.

Radev Blasts the European Parliament for “Dictating” to Bulgaria
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

Radev Blasts the European Parliament for “Dictating” to Bulgaria
Prime Minister Rumen Radev has sent an open letter to political groups in the European Parliament (EP), accusing Bulgarian MEPs of using the institution for a domestic election campaign after a resolution criticized Sofia’s response to drone attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea, the government press service said.
Addressed to the EP political groups through Parliament President Roberta Metsola, the letter challenges the last-minute addition of what Radev calls baseless and manipulative allegations against the Bulgarian government to a resolution expressing solidarity with Bulgaria’s investigation into the attacks and its efforts to rescue endangered crews.
The resolution, adopted with 432 votes in favor, 52 against and 88 abstentions, expresses concern over what MEPs describe as Sofia’s hesitant diplomatic response to Russia and calls on Bulgaria to confirm its participation in a NATO initiative to counter drones by October 30. The document is not legally binding.
Radev said the addition of Point 6, formally proposed by the Greens, undermines the resolution’s earlier recognition of Bulgaria’s rapid response and rescue operations. The provision alleges a weak diplomatic reaction toward Russia and a lack of concrete action.
The prime minister said it was regrettable that Bulgarian MEPs had submitted the resolution, naming Andrey Novakov, Andrey Kovatchev, Eva Maydell, Emil Radev, Iliya Lazarov, Radan Kanev and Ilhan Kyuchyuk among those involved.
"It is absurd for Members of the European Parliament to call upon us to join NATO’s anti-drone initiative, given that the Bulgarian Minister of Defence has already announced the decision for Bulgaria to join it," Radev said in the letter. He added that the initiative had been announced in February 2025, but governments associated with the MEPs now pressing for Bulgaria’s participation had done nothing to facilitate it.
The prime minister also rejected what he described as a patronizing attempt by MEPs to dictate Bulgaria’s sovereign decisions. He said an investigation into the attacks was underway and that Bulgaria was working with its NATO and EU allies to identify those responsible.
"We have always viewed the European Parliament as a respected institution, the purpose of which is to strengthen the pro-European consensus within our societies, rather than to create fertile ground for manipulation and division," Radev said.
He listed measures taken by his government, beginning with appeals to NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa for joint action to stop attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea.
On October 13, 2026, when two commercial vessels were attacked again near Bulgarian territorial waters, Radev summoned the Russian ambassador in Sofia and described the attacks as unacceptable, saying their logic pointed toward Russia.
Bulgaria joined the multinational European Sky Shield initiative in 2022, during a caretaker government appointed by Radev when he was president. At the European Council meeting on October 15-16, Radev held a trilateral meeting with Rutte and Romanian President Nicușor Dan and proposed a moratorium on attacks against commercial shipping in the Black Sea.
The government has introduced extensive security measures around Bulgaria’s territorial waters, including preventive steps to protect maritime areas and strengthen surveillance in the air and at sea. Additional aircraft have been deployed for aerial patrols, with Bulgarian Air Force crews flying F-16, MiG-29, Su-25 and L-39 aircraft on surveillance, patrol and reconnaissance missions over Bulgarian waters. Three unmanned aerial vehicle surveillance systems have also been deployed in the Black Sea.
Following an extraordinary North Atlantic Council meeting on October 20, 2026, NATO allies expressed solidarity with Bulgaria and Romania and readiness to assist them. Allied forces have since increased surveillance and reconnaissance in the Black Sea, including through additional maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems and drones. A Boeing P-8A Poseidon reconnaissance aircraft arrived in Bulgaria within hours of the decision and began patrolling the western Black Sea.
A joint mine-countermeasures mission involving Bulgaria, Turkey and Romania is also underway to survey Black Sea shipping lanes and address the threat posed by drifting mines. It is the first initiative of its kind involving the three NATO littoral states.
Despite adverse weather, one of the vessels hit by drones was towed to the port of Burgas for a detailed investigation. An international team of experts invited by the Bulgarian government has arrived with advanced equipment to determine the type of drones used.
Radev said accusations concerning attacks on commercial vessels within Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone must be based on conclusive evidence rather than assumptions.
The EP resolution also calls for stronger EU support for Bulgaria and Romania, including faster implementation of the Black Sea Maritime Security Centre initiative, the reallocation of unspent funds under the Security Assistance for Europe (SAFE) instrument, stronger protection of underwater telecommunications, power and data cables, and adequate funding for Black Sea defense needs in the EU’s future long-term budget.
MEPs condemned Russia’s escalation of its war against Ukraine in the Black Sea, holding Moscow responsible for deadly attacks on civilian commercial vessels off the Bulgarian and Romanian coasts and repeated incursions into Romanian airspace. The resolution calls on the EU to consider a naval operation in the Black Sea and urges NATO to examine a defensive initiative modeled on the Black Sea Guardian concept, emphasizing cooperation among Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey.
Of Bulgaria’s 17 MEPs, eight voted in favor of the resolution: Andrey Kovatchev, Iliya Lazarov, Eva Maydell, Andrey Novakov and Emil Radev from GERB and the European People’s Party; Ilhan Kyuchyuk from DPS and Hristo Petrov, known as Itso Hazarta, from PP; and conservative Taner Kabilov.
Stanislav Stoyanov and Rada Laykova, representing Vazrazhdane and the Europe of Sovereign Nations group, voted against. Elena Yoncheva, Kristian Vigenin and Tsvetelina Penkova abstained. Radan Kanev, Nikola Minchev, Ivaylo Valchev and Petar Volgin did not take part in the vote.
The dispute unfolded as Radev also addressed domestic political issues after a meeting of the Executive Council of his Progressive Bulgaria party. He reiterated the party’s decision to support Iliana Yotova and Kiril Valchev in the presidential election.
"The world is currently in flames, and this is no time for amateurs at the helm of the state. Bulgaria must be in safe hands," Radev said in a statement following the meeting, adding that the party would back Yotova and Valchev for the sake of peace and security.
He also called on voters to end the period of the so-called “assembly,” referring to the informal coalition between PP-DB and GERB-SDS that had the support of DPS, and prevent parties he described as representing the status quo from obstructing political change.
Radev said recent operations by the Interior Ministry against the mayors of Kardzhali, Belitsa and Sungurlare, all affiliated with DPS, were based on reports and evidence of corruption. DPS leader Delyan Peevski and GERB leader Boyko Borissov had accused the government of using the police and security services to intimidate political opponents.
"I truly expect the Ministry of the Interior and the security services to continue their work in this direction, while avoiding any actions that could be exploited for political purposes - especially during this election campaign," Radev said.
He dismissed allegations that the operations amounted to a “new Revival Process,” arguing that the actions targeted suspected corruption rather than people from a particular ethnic group. He cited the Burgas district prosecutor’s remarks that evidence supported a 72-hour detention.
Radev also said the investigation in Sungurlare had produced witness testimony pointing to people and circumstances beyond the municipality. He declined to identify those involved, saying it was for law enforcement authorities to determine whether any currently active politicians were implicated.
Asked about Borissov’s disclosure that the two had spoken, Radev said he had invited all former prime ministers to a ceremony marking the arrival of Tsar Samuel’s relics. He said the conversation with Borissov lasted only a minute or two and was limited to extending the invitation.

TCCIMA energy committee chairman raises 6 demands to facilitate exports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
07:58:08 UTC
16:58:08 KST

TCCIMA energy committee chairman raises 6 demands to facilitate exports
TEHRAN- Saeed Tajik, Chairman of the Energy and Environment Committee of the Tehran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture (TCCIMA), and Chairman of the Board of Directors of Iran Quality and Standard Inspection Company, at the 30th National Export Day ceremony, raised six demands from the 14th government and emphasized the need to end the “neither war nor peace” situation and to use upcoming opportunities to develop exports.
The government’s exit from the pricing process and the exchange of export proceeds, the removal of currency contracting, and the elimination of non-tariff export barriers were among the demands he raised.
The Chairman of the Board of Iran Quality and Standard Inspection Company took the podium at the National Export Day ceremony, held at the Summit Hall, as one of the country’s selected exporters for the year 1405, and, in the presence of President Masoud Pezeshkian, addressed the need to remove export barriers.
In his remarks, Saeed Tajik described the past year as one of the hardest years the country has experienced in the last 50 years and said: “The resilience of Iranians in the conditions of crisis and the Ramadan war is one of the wonders of the world in 2026.”
Referring to the costs imposed on the country during the war, he said: “The resistance of the Iranian nation and the armed forces in this period has caused people and trade parties in different parts of the world to speak with greater respect about Iran and Iranians. Now that the world has realized Iran’s importance more than before and the country has borne heavy costs, this exceptional opportunity must be used for Iran’s return to the global economic cycle.”
He, stating that “the 14th government is at a historical juncture,” emphasized the need to use the opportunities ahead and called for an end to the neither-war-nor-peace situation.
He added: “This situation must end so that we, the economic soldiers, can demonstrate Iran’s economic authority and export capacity on the global stage. Until we return to the world economic cycle, the government’s budget deficit will not be resolved, inflation will not be curbed, the exchange rate will not be controlled, and the country’s trade balance will remain defective, disrupted, and unbalanced.”
The Chairman of the Energy and Environment Commission of the Tehran Chamber enumerated three main obstacles to the development of exports of Iranian goods and services and said: “Sanctions and restrictions on access to the international trade system; domestic policies and regulations restricting exports, referred to as ‘domestic sanctions’; and weakness in competitiveness and compliance with the requirements of target markets are among these obstacles.”
Tajik, explaining the effects of sanctions and restrictions on access to the international trade system, referred to sudden export bans, currency contracting, and government intervention in pricing the foreign currency obtained from exports and its exchange, and said: “What concept and achievement has the limit and ceiling on commercial cards for exports had other than increasing the number of rented cards?”
Tajik then stated that “the country’s export process does not have the required quality due to restrictions” and added: “The problem of acceptance of quality conformity and standard certificates for Iranian goods in destination countries still persists. Iran’s inspection, testing, and certification network must still be approved by destination countries, and this problem has caused non-tariff barriers such as standard certificates, quarantine, and similar measures to obstruct exports, despite the signing of preferential trade agreements with many countries, including the Eurasian Union, and the removal of tariffs on many goods.”
The Chairman of the Energy and Environment Committee of the Tehran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture considered another problem of the country’s exports to be the Law on Combating the Smuggling of Goods and Currency in the current and wartime conditions and stated: “In this law, the boundary between intentional smuggling, document deficiencies, or delays caused by conditions is not clear, and this situation sometimes causes economic actors to be identified as violators.”
Tajik, stating that “today, transportation restrictions, customs, and technical and quality controls of Iranian goods in target markets are more evident than ever,” noted: “If national determination is formed to support the issuance of guarantees, economic diplomacy, and international recognition of Iran’s conformity assessment system, technical and engineering services can become the main driver of the trade balance and the flag-bearer of Iran’s credibility and quality in international and regional markets.”
He referred to the testing, inspection, and certification (TIC) industry as one of the fields of technical and engineering services that plays an important role in ensuring quality, safety, health, and trust in international trade, and called for the assistance of the Minister of Industry, Mine and Trade in amending ISIC codes.
He continued by criticizing the neglect of “technical and engineering services” in support systems and proposed six demands to facilitate exports, including “suspension of the Law on Combating the Smuggling of Goods and Currency in wartime conditions” and “the government’s exit from the pricing process and the exchange of export proceeds.” Tajik also emphasized the necessity of determining commodity priorities for the allocation and exchange of exporters’ foreign currency, removing currency contracting for exporters, and eliminating the complicated bureaucracy of order registration for importers.
He listed strengthening the capacity of export management companies with the aim of improving the quality of export processes among his other demands and called for recognition of technical and engineering services companies as service producers in the International Standard Industrial Classification (ISIC). Removing non-tariff export barriers, including through concluding bilateral agreements and accepting standard certificates issued in Iran in target countries, was among the other demands of the Head of the Energy and Environment Commission of the Tehran Chamber at the ceremony.

China Focus: China's "city of the future" takes center stage at global governance talks
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:55:27 CST
16:55:27 KST

SHIJIAZHUANG, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Xiongan New Area, China's "city of the future" built on the North China Plain, is drawing wide attention with the 2026 Global Governance Forum (Xiongan) scheduled to kick off there on Friday.
The forum brings together leading figures in strategic affairs, politics, academia, business, media and youth affairs from around the world, particularly those working on issues related to the United Nations, climate change, artificial intelligence and multilateral trade.
While the attendees discuss frontier topics ranging from climate change and AI governance to multilateral trade and sustainable urban development, the host city Xiongan, located in north China's Hebei Province, itself serves as a living laboratory for global governance, with hands-on experience in urban governance, green transition and digital governance.
Located about 100 kilometers southwest of Beijing, the new city that is still taking shape has covered 222 square kilometers of developed urban area. Over 5,300 buildings have been completed, with a total floor area exceeding 62.14 million square meters.
In April 2017, China decided to establish the Xiongan New Area as part of a strategy to promote the coordinated development of the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region. Serving as a hub to accommodate non-capital functions relocated from Beijing, the city was designed to be smart, green, innovative, livable, and free from "urban ills."
DIGITAL CITY
When it comes to digital governance, the Xiongan Urban Computing Center, notably, holds more than 40 billion high-quality data records. The city has built over 500 kilometers of smart roads, leveraging 5G technology for intelligent connected vehicle trials. The roads are equipped with lampposts that integrate traffic lights and various sensors.
The computing center, with its facade reminiscent of the shape of an eye, is considered the city's "brain." On a huge electronic screen, real-time data show the city's operation in nearly every respect. Which road has more traffic? Anything unusual in the underground pipes? Are the neighborhood trash cans full? In Xiongan, every building has its digital model, and every pipe is fitted with sensors.
Xiongan has been planned and built as three synchronized cities. Beyond the urban surface buildings, there is a city in the cyber cloud and another underground.
Beneath the ground run utility tunnels. Water, electricity, gas and heating pipelines are all placed inside these tunnels, with reserved lanes for logistics.
On Tuesday, China National Data Group Co., Ltd., a new state-owned enterprise (SOE) directly administered by the central government, was officially inaugurated in Xiongan.
It is positioned as a national team for data services, a leader in data infrastructure connectivity, and a strategic force for national data sci-tech innovation.
GREEN DEVELOPMENT
Above ground, Xiongan is a garden city. Residents can reach a park within a 300-meter walk, and a woodland within three kilometers.
Xiongan's urban development places the natural landscape at the heart of the city's design, laying a solid foundation for an eco-friendly future city to ensure quality of life.
Since 2019, Xiongan has embarked on a comprehensive initiative to treat rural sewage, garbage and toilet waste in the vicinity of Baiyangdian Lake, one of northern China's major wetlands.
Latest figures reveal that the city has completed 484,500 mu (roughly 32,300 hectares) of new afforestation, bringing its total green area to 744,500 mu and lifting its forest coverage rate to 35.2 percent.
According to Xiongan's planning and construction bureau, green buildings account for 100 percent of new projects, with some achieving ultra-low energy consumption.
ALLEVIATING BEIJING'S PRESSURE
After nine years of construction, Xiongan has become a key hub for the relocation of Beijing's non-capital functions.
Among these relocated projects, the headquarters of China Satellite Network Group Co., Ltd. operates steadily. Headquarters of Sinochem Holdings and China Huaneng Group Co., Ltd. have settled and begun regular operations in Xiongan. Also, China Mineral Resources Group Ltd. has seen the near completion of the main structure of its headquarters in the city.
Four universities and several hospitals from Beijing, including Beijing Jiaotong University and Peking University People's Hospital, are under construction in Xiongan.
To date, more than 400 branches of state-owned enterprises (SOEs) directly administered by the central government and over 600 high-tech firms have settled there.
"The forum held in Xiongan builds an important platform to exchange urban governance ideas and share cutting-edge insights with the world," said Li Huaxia, head of the publicity, cyberspace affairs and information bureau of Xiongan New Area.
By hosting this international forum, Xiongan is putting its capacity to the test, while demonstrating its pivotal role in the coordinated development of the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region and its unique geographic advantages.
In terms of transport, it sits close to Beijing Daxing International Airport. A direct expressway opened in 2023 connecting Xiongan and this airport.
Xiongan is just a 30-minute high-speed rail ride away from Beijing. Last month, China also opened a high-speed rail section connecting Xiongan with Shangqiu in central China's Henan Province.
Noting that the Xiongan-Shangqiu section fills a gap in Xiongan's southbound high-speed rail corridor, Liu Yanhong, deputy general manager of Xiongan high-speed railway corporation, said the line facilitates commuting and business exchanges for relocated enterprises and institutions, and supports stronger industrial cooperation along the route. ■

Australia's largest renewable energy project to face 12-fold increase in cost
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:54:53 CST
16:54:53 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Australia's largest renewable energy project will cost up to 12 times more than originally forecast, a major review has found.
A reassessment of the Snowy 2.0 pumped storage power station, a major expansion of the existing Snowy Mountains hydro scheme in the east coast state of New South Wales, found that the project will cost at least 22.2 billion Australian dollars (15.6 billion U.S. dollars), with an allowance for up to 25 billion AUD (17.5 billion USD).
The federal government originally estimated in 2017 that the project would cost 2 billion AUD (1.4 billion USD) and start operating in 2021.
A 2023 review estimated that the power station would cost 12 billion AUD (8.4 billion USD) and be fully operational in late 2028.
The project is now expected to be commissioned in late 2029.
The project will connect two existing dams through a 27-km underground tunnel and a new underground pumped hydro power station.
When completed, it will be able to generate 2,200 megawatts of electricity and provide 350,000 megawatt hours of storage.
The review found that 65 percent of tunneling and 90 percent of cavern excavation for the project has been completed, with work to build the underground power station underway.
It attributed the cost blowout to the rising cost of labor and construction material and to unexpected problems drilling a key tunnel.
Minister for Climate Change and Energy Chris Bowen and Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said in a joint statement on Friday that completing the project remains the responsible course.
"Once completed, Snowy 2.0 will be an incredible national asset, supporting Australia's energy security, price stability and the transition to renewable energy," they said. ■

Xinhua Commentary: Global governance must keep pace with a changing world
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:54:45 CST
16:54:45 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Global governance must evolve to reflect the realities of today's world and respond more effectively to the needs of all countries, especially developing ones.
As the 2026 Global Governance Forum (Xiongan) convenes, China's Global Governance Initiative (GGI) offers a timely framework for addressing this challenge through reform and improvement of the existing system.
The need for change is growing ever more urgent. Development gaps remain wide, inequalities persist, and challenges ranging from climate change to debt distress continue to weigh heavily on developing countries.
Yet, the current international institutions and global governance mechanisms tasked with addressing these issues do not always adequately reflect the changing distribution of global economic strength or give all countries an equal voice in making decisions that affect them.
At the core of the current strain on the system lies a glaring representation gap. While emerging economies have become increasingly important drivers of global growth, their representation in some key decision-making bodies remains inadequate. As the global economic and demographic center of gravity shifts, this disparity is becoming difficult to ignore.
The Global South should not remain a passive recipient of rules shaped by others. It must have a greater say in setting the global agenda and shaping international rules. Improving the representation of developing countries in global governance institutions is not a concession by the West, but a necessary adjustment to make the system more inclusive, representative and effective.
Such reform would benefit the international community as a whole. The world is a single ship carrying all nations; its stability depends on their ability to meet shared challenges together. A governance system that fails to accommodate the legitimate concerns of a large part of the world will struggle to muster the collective response that global challenges require.
Fairer representation, however, is only part of the answer. Global governance must also be judged by whether it improves people's wellbeing and delivers tangible results. International cooperation should serve ordinary people, and commitments made at the global level must translate into practical progress on the ground.
These principles are central to the GGI, which sets out five core concepts: adhering to sovereign equality, abiding by the international rule of law, practicing multilateralism, advocating a people-centered approach, and focusing on taking real actions. The Initiative has gained support from nearly 160 countries and international organizations, while more than 60 countries have joined the Group of Friends of Global Governance.
At its core, the GGI calls for global governance to keep pace with changing times while upholding the purposes and principles of the UN Charter. It seeks to reform and improve the existing global governance system, rather than to overturn the international order. The objective is to make multilateral institutions more responsive to today's challenges and better equipped to deliver results for the international community.
This distinction matters. Reforming global governance is not a zero-sum game in which a greater role for the Global South must come at the expense of other countries. Nor is it about replacing one set of rules with another. It is about making international institutions more representative of the world as it is today, while strengthening the common rules and cooperation needed to address shared challenges.
At a time when the world faces mounting uncertainties and increasingly interconnected challenges, the task is not simply to discuss what needs to change, but to build greater consensus on how to make global governance more inclusive, effective and action-oriented.
By giving all countries a greater voice, putting people at the center and turning commitments into concrete results, the global community can build a system tailored to better meet challenges of our time. ■

Across China: Rare songbird makes comeback in China's village woodlands
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:54:42 CST
16:54:42 KST

NANCHANG, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- In the wooded hills around villages in east China's Jiangxi Province, a critically endangered songbird is being seen in growing numbers.
The blue-crowned laughingthrush, distinguished by its blue crown, black facial mask and yellow throat, numbered fewer than 200 in the wild in 2006. Its population has since risen to about 660, with roughly 320 living in Jiangxi's Dexing City, according to conservation authorities.
Earlier this week, volunteer bird protector Hong Taiping was walking near Banqiao Village in Dexing when a burst of calls made him stop. Several of the birds were moving through the branches, feeding on wild persimmons. He raised his camera and waited.
"They spend so much time feeding in the bushes that they blend into their surroundings," Hong said. For him, listening is often more useful than looking.
Blue-crowned laughingthrushes often breed in trees near villages and rivers, where food is plentiful and predators may be fewer. Their preference for habitats close to human settlements makes protecting these areas particularly important.
In Dexing, local authorities have hired seven dedicated bird guards to patrol breeding areas, mobilized village officials and volunteers to remove trapping nets, and planted fruit-bearing trees, including mulberries and bayberries, to improve feeding habitats.
Researchers from Jiangxi Agricultural University and other institutions are studying the birds' breeding habits, habitat preferences and responses to human disturbance. Dexing established a local conservation center in 2024. When the species was first recorded in the city, only a handful of breeding sites were known. Today, its local numbers have grown to about half of the global wild population.
The species was first documented in neighboring Wuyuan County by a French collector in 1919 and formally named in 1923. After decades without confirmed sightings in Wuyuan, it was rediscovered in the wild there in 2000.
Despite its recovery, the bird remains classified as critically endangered on the International Union for Conservation of Nature's Red List. Its limited distribution and vulnerability to habitat disturbance make continued protection essential.
Conservation efforts have extended overseas. The blue-crowned laughingthrush is covered by a Global Species Management Plan approved in 2012 by the World Association of Zoos and Aquariums. In North America, zoos have expanded their captive populations partly by importing birds from European institutions, according to the association. At France's Mulhouse Zoological and Botanical Park, staff have kept in touch with Jiangxi Agricultural University professor Zhang Weiwei, seeking information about the wild population and ways to improve captive breeding.
More than 300 blue-crowned laughingthrushes are now kept in captivity across Europe, Asia and the Americas.
At a scientific exchange meeting held in Wuyuan in October 2023 as part of the Franco-Chinese Month of the Environment, the two countries discussed closer cooperation on captive conservation and the development of ecological communities.
In August, China's National Forestry and Grassland Administration reported stable or growing populations among 19 nationally protected bird species.
In Dexing, a birdwatching competition in June recorded 162 bird species, including the blue-crowned laughingthrush and the crested ibis, both under China's highest level of state protection.
The latest monitoring has brought another surprise.
"In previous years, we rarely spotted them after late July. But this year, we're still seeing them in late autumn," said Xie Zhihua, head of the local conservation center. "We didn't expect that." ■

Study warns of pathogen risks from healthcare handbasins
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:54:40 CST
16:54:40 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Contaminated handbasins in healthcare settings may put patients at risk of infection and contribute to outbreaks of drug-resistant bacteria, a study has warned.
The study, led by Australia's Flinders University, compared healthcare handbasin design guidelines across 39 countries and regions with available scientific evidence, finding substantial inconsistencies and limited evidence on which design features best reduce pathogen spread, according to a university statement released on Friday.
"Microbes can build up in taps and drains. When water hits contaminated surfaces, splashing can carry them onto nearby equipment and surfaces," said Mikaela Todarello, a PhD candidate at Flinders University, lead author of the study published in the Journal of Hospital Infection.
The researchers said improved basin engineering could reduce splashing, limit biofilm buildup and prevent contamination from spreading, particularly in areas caring for patients most vulnerable to infection.
The study found that flat or shallow basins, drain positions directly beneath taps, water flow and bowl slope can affect splashing and microbial spread.
Further research was needed to determine which combinations of design features best reduce infection risks in real healthcare settings, Todarello said. ■

Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand to develop common approaches for cross-border digital money
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:54:35 CST
16:54:35 KST

SINGAPORE, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- The central banks of Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand will work with industry players in their respective jurisdictions to develop common approaches for the cross-border use of digital money, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) said Friday.
The approaches may cover how different forms of digital money can be accepted, exchanged and settled across institutions, networks and jurisdictions, MAS said in a statement.
The cooperation will take place under the BLOOM initiative, which stands for Borderless, Liquid, Open, Online, Multi-currency. The central banks of Malaysia and Thailand have joined the initiative as policymaker members, alongside MAS.
The initiative aims to bring together policymakers, financial institutions, payment networks and technology providers to advance the use of digital money in cross-border financial activities.
Participants will focus on three areas: acceptance and settlement across jurisdictions, interoperability among digital money arrangements, and programmable controls, according to the statement. ■

Gaza faces starvation as Israel blocks commercial trucks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
07:52:03 UTC
16:52:03 KST

Breadcrumb
Gaza faces spectre of starvation as Israel continues to block commercial trucks
The war-torn coastal enclave may go hungry again as Israeli restrictions on the entry of commercial goods deepen shortages, drive up food prices and threaten to shut down remaining operational bakeries.
Abdel Nasser al-Ajrami, head of the Bakery Owners Association in Gaza, warned on Thursday that the seven remaining operational bakeries could close within 48 hours as flour stocks run low.
Speaking to The New Arab, he said several other bakeries that had operated in partnership with the World Food Programme (WFP) and received fuel support had already closed in Gaza City, central Gaza and the south.
Although the Kerem Shalom crossing reopened after several days of closure, no flour shipments had entered Gaza by Thursday, al-Ajrami said. Efforts to secure essential supplies had also yielded no response by late Wednesday.
Commercial shipments have been blocked since mid-October amid disruptions linked to an Israeli festival. Trucks expected to enter Gaza on Thursday were reportedly prevented from doing so by Israeli settlers, further worsening shortages in local markets.
In a press statement, Gaza's Ministry of Social Development warned that the closure of bakeries and restrictions on flour and other essential food supplies could have catastrophic humanitarian consequences.
The ministry said the shortages threatened to worsen malnutrition, particularly among children, sick people and older residents.
It called on the international community to pressure Israel to open the crossings and allow humanitarian aid and commercial goods to enter.
Soaring prices
The disruption to commercial supplies has already driven up prices and made basic goods increasingly difficult for residents to afford.
Radi Kamal, a resident of al-Zawaida refugee camp in central Gaza, told TNA that a 250-gram packet of coffee now costs $10, up from $6. A kilogram of tomatoes costs around $6, potatoes $4 and frozen red meat about US$20. Eggs and fruit have also become scarce.
"Almost everything has become more expensive, and we can no longer buy as much as we used to," Kamal said. "Even when goods are available in the market, many families cannot afford them. We have to choose what we need most and go without other things because we do not have enough money."
He said families feared the situation would deteriorate further if commercial trucks continued to be blocked.
"If supplies do not arrive, prices could rise further, and some goods may disappear from the markets," he said. "Families are already struggling to buy food. If bread also becomes unavailable, feeding our children will become even harder."
Um Mohammed, a 42-year-old mother of five from Gaza City, told TNA that rising prices had forced her to cut back on household purchases to ensure her children had enough to eat. "When I go to the market, I buy only what we need most, but even these things have become expensive," she said. "I put my children's needs first and give up other things so I can provide food for them."
In Deir al-Balah, in central Gaza, Abu Ahmed, 51, who supports a family of six, said many households could no longer afford the goods available in local markets.
"We have to buy less and put other needs aside because prices keep rising," he told TNA. "If the bakeries close, things will become much worse because bread is a basic food that we depend on every day."
While Israeli restrictions on the entry of goods remain a major obstacle to supplies reaching Gaza, a apparent dispute over commercial imports and alleged financial demands on merchants has added another layer to the crisis.
Before Israel's genocidal war, around 1,500 merchants and importers operated in Gaza. Commercial-sector sources say Israel has since restricted the coordination of commercial shipments to just eight merchants, leaving supplies vulnerable to disruptions when disagreements arise.
Merchants have accused Hamas of imposing fees of up to 10,000 shekels (around US$3,300) per truck. Disagreements have also emerged over the proportion of sales that merchants must collect in cash rather than through bank transfers.
Hamas and Gaza's Government Media Office have denied imposing mandatory fees on goods. The Ministry of Economy has said the proposed contribution is voluntary and intended to support a national fund providing social assistance, including help for orphans, widows and displaced families.
Riyad al-Sawafiri, head of the Economic Committee at the Gaza Chamber of Commerce and Industry, told TNA that the chamber opposed imposing additional fees or taxes on merchants.
Some traders said they were required to pay 30 per cent of their sales in cash, while Nahed Shuhiber, head of the Private Transport Association in Gaza, put the figure at 25 per cent.
Shuhiber told TNA that the dispute was linked to measures taken against one of the eight merchants authorised to coordinate commercial shipments into Gaza following disagreements over sales procedures.
The situation is further complicated by a cash shortage. Merchants struggle to obtain money for transactions, while residents face difficulties withdrawing their savings.
Despite these internal disputes, the entry of commercial trucks remains subject to Israeli approval and border procedures, leaving the flow of essential goods vulnerable to restrictions and interruptions.
Food insecurity
Political analyst Mustafa Ibrahim told TNA that the suspension of commercial shipments could not be understood solely as a dispute over import procedures or financial contributions.
"Restrictions on the entry of goods have direct and severe consequences for the lives of Gaza's population," he said. "Disruptions to supplies worsen the food crisis, drive up prices and make it harder for people to secure their basic needs."
He added that low-income families and displaced people were bearing the heaviest burden, particularly as bakeries warned of closure and flour stocks dwindled.
"Even if disagreements exist between merchants and local authorities, resolving them should not come at the expense of the population or leave people without access to food," Ibrahim said.
He also questioned the gap between images of trucks at the crossings and the shortages in Gaza's markets, arguing that the presence of vehicles at the border did not guarantee that goods would reach consumers.
With commercial supplies blocked by Israel, food prices soaring and bakeries warning they may soon run out of flour, Gaza's residents face mounting difficulties in securing basic necessities.

Why is Gen Z revolting?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
07:51:31 UTC
16:51:31 KST

Why is Gen Z revolting?
From France to India, young people are taking to the streets over growing inequality, failing public services and bleak prospects for the future.
We are currently experiencing a wave of protests across Europe and beyond. Many have been dubbed “Gen Z protests”, with young people aged roughly 13 to 29 leading demonstrations over issues that particularly affect their generation.
In France, protests started several weeks ago over deteriorating conditions in severely underfunded schools. They have been growing in strength, with between half a million and 800,000 protesters reportedly taking part in them across the country last weekend.
In India, the Cockroach movement has emerged as the strongest challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s increasingly authoritarian leadership. Last week, its leader was arrested as anger grew over the removal of more than 130 million names from electoral rolls.
In Spain, anger has arisen over a broken housing system and laws that fail to protect households against eviction. First there was the forcible eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal. Then parliament voted down widely popular legislation that would protect households against evictions, prompting Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to call snap elections. Maricarmen died two weeks after her eviction.
While the context in each country is different, grievances over inequality are at the centre of the current protest wave. This inequality has two aspects. One is about class and one is about generation.
Across Europe, inequality has increased significantly since the 2008 crisis. This can be seen in growing income inequality and spiralling wealth inequality. The effect on people’s lives is worsened by the erosion of the once-proud European welfare states. High-quality public services for all were once meant to offer a guaranteed minimum standard of living and a meritocracy in which everyone had the chance to succeed. But years of austerity have eroded the state’s capacity to deliver good education, healthcare, social care and other services. The gradual retreat of the state exacerbates growing income and wealth inequalities, as some can pay for better services while many cannot.
These growing inequalities are often felt more acutely by young people and are compounded by other challenges they face. In one area after another, young people are experiencing failures in governance that give them a bleaker outlook and much worse prospects than their parents and grandparents had.
Underfunded education systems have no doubt played a significant part in the sharp decline in reading and maths skills laid bare by the most recent PISA results. A common explanation for this decline is worsening mental health and associated school absences, with social media often cited as a contributing factor.
Another driver of declining educational attainment is the rapidly increasing use of AI. These are governance failures of another kind. Efforts to regulate both social media and AI have been slow and hampered by strong lobbying from tech giants.
The AI revolution also affects young people as they seek to establish themselves in the labour market. While AI’s impact on employment is still in its infancy, it is already clear that entry-level work in particular is increasingly being done by machines.
Housing is another essential aspect of life in which young people are disadvantaged. Today’s young people spend a much higher proportion of their income on rent than any previous generation did. This is, again, a failure of governance.
On top of all this comes the climate crisis, which perhaps represents the largest governance failure of them all. The latest IPCC report illustrates starkly how much more precarious life will be for those born in 2020 than for their parents and grandparents.
More equal societies would be much better placed to withstand the instability that climate change brings as they would offer collective forms of adaptation. Instead, the increasingly unequal societies we now see will put the burden of adaptation on individuals and households.
In other words, multiple governance failures and the erosion of state capacity have created an explosive situation for young people. This is the anger being expressed on the streets of Paris, New Delhi, Rome and Madrid.
Predictably, the main government response has been repression. This follows a global trend of criminalising and repressing protest. Whether through anti-protest laws, arrests or police violence, repression is on the rise. Repression sometimes succeeds in killing off protest movements. At other times, it instead inflames them. That has certainly been the case in both France and India so far.
What is really needed are genuine efforts to address the inequalities and governance failures that motivate young people to take to the streets. Without them, political crises are bound to ensue.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Serbia’s Student Opposition Holds Final Rally Before Parliamentary Vote
Around 150,000 people joined an opposition student-led rally in central Belgrade on Thursday, calling for an end to the rule of Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) in the parliamentary election scheduled for Sunday, according to the independent Archive of Public Gatherings.
The Student List, a movement of student-backed candidates without a single leader, is seeking to end more than 14 years of SNS rule. The right-wing populist party has been in power since 2012.
Civil society organizations have warned that the election campaign has been marred by intimidation, arrests and the misuse of public resources.
Marija Nedeljkovic Radic, 47, said she had come to support the students because their movement had restored her hope for the country.
"I came to support the Student List because young people finally gave me hope that it is possible to live in a normal country," she said. "Really, for the first time in my life, I believe that it is possible."
Sunday's election follows nearly two years of student-led protests triggered by the collapse of a canopy at the newly renovated railway station in Novi Sad in 2024, which killed 16 people. The disaster, widely attributed to corruption, prompted some of Serbia's largest demonstrations since Slobodan Milošević fell from power in 2000.
The protests, initially focused on demands for a transparent investigation into the tragedy, grew into a broader anti-corruption movement calling for an early election.
On Thursday, demonstrators marched through Belgrade waving flags bearing the words "Students are winning," chanting slogans and blowing whistles before gathering at Slavija Square, a focal point of some of their largest previous protests. The Archive of Public Gatherings, an independent organization that monitors crowd sizes, estimated that approximately 150,000 people attended.
University professor Jugoslav Gasic, one of the Student List's 250 candidates, told the crowd that the movement intended to end years of what he described as humiliation and betrayal, as well as decades of politicians placing personal and party interests above those of the public.
"You deserve better, and we know how to deliver it. Students are winning!" Gasic said, prompting chants of "Victory, victory!"
Vucic has dominated Serbian politics for more than a decade, serving as both prime minister and president. Facing mounting pressure, he announced a snap election last month, setting up his biggest electoral challenge since the SNS came to power in 2012.
Vucic, 56, addressed his own supporters at a sports hall in Belgrade on Thursday. He has repeatedly accused the student movement of being a foreign-funded attempt to overthrow the government.
"Let us never forget how they tried to bring down our state. Let us always protect and defend it," Vucic said.
He resigned as president to run for prime minister and urged his supporters to defeat the opposition decisively, before white ticker tape and balloons were released over the crowd.
Many of the Student List's 250 candidates for the 250-seat parliament come from academia or are deliberately positioning themselves as political outsiders. Although the movement has a broad policy platform, its central commitment is to combat corruption.
Reliable independent polling is lacking in Serbia, and surveys have offered widely divergent assessments of the race. In the days before the election, civil society organizations warned that the conditions needed for "free and fair elections" were not in place.
On Wednesday, prosecutors in Belgrade questioned six people arrested on suspicion of plotting "violence, riots and attacks" on election day.
Reports of threats and intimidation against student demonstrators have increased in recent months, although their rallies have remained largely peaceful since the movement began.
Igor, a 35-year-old student who attended Thursday's gathering, said he had followed the movement's struggle from its outset.
"Today is the last rally, and it’s important that we all come here to send a message of love and peace and that we see each other on the 25th at the polling stations," he said.

Cambodia Cracked Down on Banks Allegedly Linked to Cyber-Scams. The IMF Says the Problem Persists.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
07:40:00 UTC
16:40:00 KST

Earlier this year, the NBC revoked the license for Panda Bank, saying its “financial condition” had “continuously deteriorated, leading to an inability to provide normal banking services.”
Panda Bank had not been sanctioned, but the U.S. did target two other institutions that the NBC shut down last year: Prince Bank Plc. and Huione Pay.
Both institutions were targeted as part of sweeping sanctions related to the Prince Group, a Cambodian conglomerate that the U.S. alleged ran “industrial scale cyberfraud operations” out of “compounds reliant on human trafficking and modern-day slavery.”
The Prince Group has adamantly denied allegations of any illegal activity. A spokesperson previously told OCCRP that the conglomerate was “not a criminal syndicate but a collection of legitimate businesses serving millions of people and employing tens of thousands of people across the globe.” 
The U.S. accused the conglomerate’s companies, including Prince Bank, of laundering the proceeds of scams. Prince Group companies mixed “illicit revenues with the legitimate Cambodian economy,” the U.S. Treasury Department alleged.
While the Huione Group was sanctioned alongside "146 targets within the Prince Group," the Treasury Department did not allege that it was part of the Cambodian conglomerate. Huione Pay, also known as H-Pay, was part of the Huione Group, which the U.S, alleged had laundered the proceeds of “virtual currency investment scams.” 
The NCB stated it had ordered the liquidation of Huione Pay after having “observed transactions involving the purchase, sale, or payment using crypto assets,” which violated Cambodian regulations. The NBC did not provide a specific reason for its decision to liquidate Prince Bank.
Rath Sophoan, chairman of the Association of Banks in Cambodia — which includes all licensed lenders in the country, but not crypto institutions like Huione Pay — argued that accusations against a handful of institutions should not be overstated.
He noted that the four lenders on the U.S. sanctions list accounted for less than 1 percent of the roughly $100 billion in assets held across the country's 59 commercial banks as of December.
“Allegations involving individual institutions should not be generalized to Cambodia’s wider banking sector, which remains broad, diverse, and subject to licensing and supervision by the National Bank of Cambodia,” Rath Sophoan said.
In its statement earlier this month, the NBC attempted to counter what it said was “the dissemination and intentional fabrication of false information aimed at causing economic sabotage.”
But the IMF and others are urging the NBC to do more to build trust in the financial sector.
“An immediate priority is for the NBC, with support of other regulators, to identify banks with potential links to criminal activity and take action to address them,” the IMF said in its review last month.
Jacob Sims, a visiting fellow at Harvard University's Asia Center and a leading expert on transnational crime in Southeast Asia, was even more direct in comments to OCCRP.
“The National Bank of Cambodia can complain about unfair reputational damage, but the most effective way to defend the reputation of the sector would be to show that regulations and enforcement standards are being applied seriously,” he said. “That simply hasn’t occurred.”
