Since September 2024, Russia has imposed a duty on imported alcohol from unfriendly countries at a rate of 20% of the customs value of the products, but not less than €3 per litre.
The duty increase will naturally lead to a rise in the cost of imported alcohol. Wholesale prices at the current exchange rate will rise by about 70-100 roubles (roughly €0.65-0.95) per bottle, the newspaper states. A 70 cl bottle in the mass-market segment will increase in price by over 200 roubles (roughly €1.90).
For expensive imports, the duty increase will be less noticeable to consumers.
Retail chains' stocks of alcohol already imported will only last until the end of the year.
Background: It was previously reported that although Latvia unequivocally supports Ukraine in the war, it has not stopped supplying goods to Russia: last year, its exports amounted to more than €962 million, half of which was alcohol.

Are global oil reserves sufficient to withstand renewed US-Iran war?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
07:37:12 UTC
16:37:12 KST

Are global oil reserves sufficient to withstand renewed US-Iran war?
With emergency stocks at multidecade lows, analysts say the world may have only a month or two if Hormuz shuts again.
Oil prices have climbed towards their highest levels in five months as attacks on tankers in and around the Strait of Hormuz mount and efforts to end the United States-Israel war on Iran are deadlocked.
Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose by more than $2 to $110.85 a barrel on Wednesday, close to a five-month peak.
A day earlier, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said two tankers were “set ablaze” after hitting mines at what it called an illegal crossing point in the strait. Then, on Thursday, the IRGC said it hit seven more tankers although Washington dismissed the claim. In a statement, the IRGC said four of the vessels were transferring oil when they were targeted and caught fire overnight.
In September, the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), seized territory in Yemen close to the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a critical chokepoint into and out of the Red Sea and a gateway to Egypt’s Suez Canal.
The escalation came as the world’s emergency oil stocks, already tapped heavily since the Iran war began on February 28, sit at their lowest levels in decades.
Al Jazeera put a question to analysts: If fighting resumes in full, the Strait of Hormuz is shut off completely and Houthi attacks choke off Bab al-Mandeb, how long could the world’s reserves last?
Here’s what you need to know:
What emergency oil reserves are there?
Strategic oil reserves are stockpiles of crude oil and fuel held by governments or by companies on their behalf for use in a supply emergency.
The International Energy Agency (IEA), which was established in 1974 after the Arab oil embargo, coordinates most of them. Its importing members must hold at least 90 days of net imports. China and India are not members.
How much of the reserves has already been released this year?
A record amount.
On March 11, days after the start of the US-Israel war on Iran, the IEA’s 32 members agreed to make 400 million barrels available from emergency supplies, more than double the volume released after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The US pledged 172.2 million barrels from its Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) and Japan 79.8 million, according to IEA figures.
The SPR has since fallen to 283 million barrels, its lowest level since October 1982, according to the US Department of Energy.
Much of that oil was lent rather than sold and must be returned with extra barrels, according to the US Energy Information Administration.
How much oil is left?
Far less than before the war began in February, and not all of it can be used.
Aaron Kildow, a senior crude oil analyst at Sparta Commodities, told Al Jazeera that global strategic stocks excluding China and Iran have fallen by nearly 327 million barrels since the end of December 2025 with the US, Europe and Japan accounting for about 95 percent of the draw.
He estimated that leaves only about 400 million barrels of usable reserves worldwide, excluding China’s stockpile, which is unlikely to be exported, and Gulf stocks, which could be cut off by a total closure of Hormuz.
Nearly half of these available stocks are in Japan.
Europe has about 76 million barrels uncommitted, but members such as Germany are holding some back for a local emergency, Kildow said.
“Europe is the real wildcard, both on timing and willingness,” Kildow said.
Meanwhile, China’s onshore crude stocks stand at 1.13 billion barrels, down from 1.23 billion in late February but still enough for about 80 days of refinery intake, Muyu Xu, a senior crude oil analyst at the analytics firm Kpler, told Al Jazeera.
India’s reserves cover just eight days of its imports, the Reuters news agency reported.
What would a full closure of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb mean?
Before the war, about one-fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas supplies, or roughly 20 million barrels of oil a day, passed through the Strait of Hormuz.
Saudi Arabia has increased the amount of crude it transports from its oilfields in the east to its Red Sea port of Yanbu in the west via the East-West Pipeline, thereby bypassing Hormuz.
But there have been strikes on that pipeline, and tankers heading south from Yanbu must pass through Bab a-Mandeb, where the Iran-backed Houthis declared a blockade on Saudi shipping in July.
Only a confirmed 373,000 barrels a day of Saudi crude have transited Bab al-Mandeb so far this month, the lowest level since February, Xu said, with most Yanbu cargoes now heading north via Egypt instead.
If Hormuz were shut and the Houthis blocked all Saudi tankers, Gulf producers could export only through a few pipelines and Yanbu’s northbound route, Xu said.
That would leave about 7.5 million barrels a day of Middle Eastern crude, against 16.8 million now, a shortfall of about 9.3 million barrels a day, she estimated.
“If such attacks occur, the supply disruption could be even more severe and prolonged,” Xu said, referring to strikes on oilfields, terminals and pipelines.
So how long would reserves last?
Not for long – possibly just weeks, according to experts.
If Kpler’s estimated shortfall had to be covered entirely from the roughly 400 million usable barrels that Kildow identified, they could not, in practice, be released that fast. Japanese and South Korean reserves can move quickly, Kildow said, but US barrels are staged over three months, and Europe’s contribution is uncertain.
Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG Group, said the world was fortunate after the first closure. “The salient feature of March and beyond was how a crisis didn’t actually develop. We got away with it,” he said.
“I don’t think the global economy will be as lucky next time if there is a protracted conflict,” Beauchamp said. “A month or two is all we have.”
The world would not literally run out of oil. Instead, prices would rise until enough demand disappeared. “One hundred fifty dollars [per barrel] becomes a very distinct possibility, which then sees significant demand destruction,” Beauchamp said.
The sharpest squeeze would be on diesel, which is already nearly double the price of crude, the IEA said.
Refiners would compete for crude grades rich in diesel, “a cost that ultimately lands on consumers,” Kildow said.
Who would feel it first?
Asian importers with thin reserves.
Most Gulf exports in September and October went to Asian buyers, and India and Pakistan are among the most exposed, Kildow said, adding that their nearest alternative supply, from West Africa, is 25 to 28 days away by sea, compared with two days from Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates.
“The squeeze won’t hit uniformly. It lands fastest and hardest where reserves are thinnest and substitute supply is farthest away,” Kildow said.
Who would gain?
Oil producers far from the Gulf.
In the second quarter of this year, as the US-Iran war was under way, ExxonMobil reported earnings of $14.5bn, its highest in four years while Chevron posted $12bn, its best in six years and Shell more than doubled its earnings to nearly $10bn. Their profits are largely down to the high oil prices.
A second shock would send refiners scrambling for supplies from the US, Latin America, West Africa and Russia, Xu said.
“This would allow non-Middle Eastern producers to benefit from higher crude prices, potentially alongside lower transportation costs,” she said.
In August, US President Donald Trump said companies such as ExxonMobil and Chevron were “making too much money based on a shortage”.

Scaffolding as Interior Architecture: The Longevity of Temporary Structures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

Scaffolding is perhaps one of architecture's most familiar temporary structures. It accompanies buildings through construction, maintenance, and renovation, only to disappear once its work is complete. Yet its apparent impermanence conceals a different kind of longevity. Scaffolding systems are designed to be assembled, dismantled, transported, and reused, with standardized components robust enough to withstand repeated handling and changing site conditions. Their temporary character lies less in the material itself than in the duration of each assembly.
This logic is not unfamiliar in furniture design. Dieter Rams's 606 Universal Shelving System, designed for Vitsœ in 1960, established a modular approach in which shelves, cabinets, and other components could be rearranged, expanded, or transported as circumstances changed. Similarly, IKEA's modular storage systems popularized and demonstrated how furniture can be understood as a collection of interchangeable parts rather than a singular, finished object. Although different in material and intended lifespan, these systems share an important principle: longevity can be achieved through adaptability rather than permanence of arrangement.

Residents asked to stay indoors as Storm Austen rages through Belgium today

The first storm of the autumn is making its way across Flanders and the whole of the country. Storm Austen will mostly affect East and West Flanders, with winds up to 100kph
Residents asked to stay indoors as Storm Austen rages through Belgium today
A storm with winds up to 90kph – and potentially to 100kph on the coast – will move through Flanders today. East and West Flanders has a code orange storm alert, while the rest of the country is on code yellow alert.
“Storm Austen” also comes with dark clouds and rain, beginning this morning and continuing into tonight. After 22.00, winds and rain will ease up, with the code alerts remaining in place until after midnight. Clearing is expected overnight.
Residents of East and West Flanders are warned to stay indoors as much as possible and close doors and windows. All parks, provincial domains and nature reserves are closed, and all outdoor public activities have been cancelled.
Storm Austen is the first storm of the autumn, and it is a fiery one
Meteorologist Jacotte Brokken
On the coast, visitors centres including Duinpanne in De Panne and Atlantikwall Raversyde in Ostend are closed, and only the indoor section of Zwin Nature Park in Knokke is open.
Across the country residents and businesses are asked to secure outdoor furniture and other objects, or bring them inside. “We see more storms happening during this time of the year,” said VRT meteorologist Jacotte Brokken. Storm Austen is the first one this autumn, and it is a fiery one.”
A storm is a low-pressure system, she explains, and the pressure within that system has dropped significantly in a short period of time. “This has everything to do with the position of the jet stream intersecting with the storm’s position. This interaction gives the storm an extra boost. We call this a ‘bomb cyclone’, or ‘weather bomb’.”
That is indeed as bad as it sounds; Storm Austen is expected to pack quite a punch, particularly in terms of wind. The storm is affecting neighbouring countries as well, with some 161,000 households in France currently without electricity, and ferries cancelled between France and the UK.

Rubio’s India Visit Focuses on Energy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
07:24:00 UTC
16:24:00 KST

During U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to India on October 20-21, the two sides discussed stepping up energy cooperation and increasing procurement of American technologies and weapon systems as part of a stocktaking of their bilateral relationship.
Unlike his trip to India in May, Rubio did not visit the Indian capital, New Delhi. Instead, he visited India’s commercial capital, Mumbai, and Jamnagar, where the world’s largest oil refinery run by Reliance Industries Ltd. (RIL) is located.
An Indian readout of Rubio’s visit to Mumbai said that “the two sides reviewed the entire gamut of India-U.S. relations and discussed ways to further strengthen the Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership.” They exchanged views on trade, defense, technology and energy security, and Rubio and Jaishankar welcomed “the progress made in negotiations on the India-U.S. Bilateral Trade Agreement (BTA) and reaffirmed their commitment to working towards its early conclusion.”
According to a U.S. statement on the talks between Rubio and his Indian counterpart S. Jaishankar, Rubio “reiterated that increased energy trade with the United States can play a transformative role in diversifying India’s supply chains while meeting its sizable consumer demand.” Commending recent progress in bilateral defense and civil nuclear cooperation, Rubio advocated the increased purchase of U.S. technologies and systems. No details were provided about which technologies the United States wants India to purchase.
In addition to Jaishankar, Rubio met representatives of three top Indian business houses – the Tatas, Adanis, and Reliance – in Mumbai. He also participated in a trilateral meeting with Jaishankar and the UAE’s Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan that focused on energy security and regional issues.
Rubio’s visit to Jamnagar was linked to the RIL-run refinery’s capacity to refine heavy crude oils and its plans to construct a refinery near the U.S. border in Texas.
The Rubio visit’s focus on energy is not surprising, as India is one of the top importers of petroleum products. The U.S. has been pressuring India to stop fuel imports from Russia, which surged after the outbreak of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, and to buy Venezuelan crude oil instead, especially after the Donald Trump administration took over Venezuela’s oil industry following its abduction of President Nicolás Maduro.
As Indian strategic affairs analyst C. Raja Mohan wrote in a recent opinion piece in Indian Express, “Washington wants greater energy cooperation with India and more Indian investment in the U.S. Reliance offers a substantial private-sector partner. The question is how Delhi can turn the company’s growing importance in American calculations into an asset for India-U.S. relations.”
Rubio’s latest visit to India came at a time when India-U.S. relations have plunged to their worst in several decades. In addition to imposing unprecedented levels of tariffs on India, the Trump administration has tightened immigration and visa rules that are likely to hit Indian professionals hard. Besides, it has cozied up to Pakistan.
Last month, the U.S. Congress passed a bill authorizing Trump to punish countries buying energy from Russia, which has major implications for India. However, days ahead of Rubio’s visit to India, U.S. President Donald Trump announced a waiver on sanctions and tariffs related to Russian exports for a 60-day period, after he reached a deal on purchasing Russian diesel. The suspension of sanctions will give India some respite, albeit temporarily.
At a time when India-U.S. ties are strained, “Rubio’s visit seeks to shift the focus to energy security, corporate partnerships and resolving trade standoffs,” Indian analyst Brahma Chellaney observed in a post on X. By visiting Mumbai and Jamnagar rather than New Delhi, “Rubio is emphasizing pragmatic cooperation over diplomatic friction. The approach could help sustain momentum in energy, private-sector investment and economic ties, thus keeping the broader bilateral partnership productive,” Chellaney pointed out.
During his visit to India, Rubio made several statements that sought to reassure Delhi.
At an event to mark the 250th anniversary of American Independence, Rubio acknowledged differences between India and the U.S. “No two nations on Earth will ever be perfectly aligned on every issue, and of course there will be times and points of disagreement.” But on core issues “that define the national interest of both India and the United States – the alignment between our countries is extraordinary,” he said.
On the stalled India-U.S. trade deal that has cast a shadow over bilateral ties, Rubio said both countries were “incredibly close” to an agreement. “The way I would say it is we are weeks, not months away from I think, finalizing it. I think 99 percent of the work is done… I feel very positive about the trajectory that it’s on.”
In an interview published in Indian Express, Rubio sought to assure India that improved ties with Pakistan would not be “at the expense of our relationship with India.” On the new immigration rules, he said that the regulations were “not unique to Indians or India; it is tied more broadly to the world… We are trying to fix 20 years of neglect of an immigration system that was simply not being enforced. And that’s not targeting India.”
Reassuring as Rubio’s statements may be, it will take a lot of work to bring the troubled India-U.S. relationship back to an even keel, especially since Trump is known for unpredictable policy changes. Therefore, Rubio’s visit may be the first step on a long and winding road to rebuilding trust.

National Protection Service (NSO) officer Martin Varadinov has been detained after pushing journalist Sonya Koltuklieva to the ground during an incident involving Parliamentary Speaker Mihaela Dotsova, with the case now under investigation by the Military Prosecutor’s Office.

After Dotsova entered the vehicle without answering and the door was closed, Koltuklieva pulled it open and continued asking questions while holding up her phone.
She recalled that an NSO officer then rushed toward her and shoved her in the shoulder. Her next memory, she said, was lying on the ground with a headache, nausea and severe shoulder pain.
Koltuklieva said Dotsova later repeated that she had been distressed because the journalist was the only person outside the party headquarters when she left. The reporter said she asked the Speaker to go away.
President Iliana Yotova, to whom the NSO reports, also condemned the officer’s response.

The poll was conducted Oct. 18-21 among 1,075 respondents. It has a margin of error of plus or minus 2.99 percentage points at a 95% confidence level.
Tung commented on the survey, saying that the more than 50% support for an alternative mayor signaled public dissatisfaction with the lack of development, per NOWNews. He said he would continue reaching out to voters to communicate his vision for the city.
Asked about the survey, Hsieh declined to comment, saying he would prioritize preparations for Typhoon Champi, per Liberty Times.
The KMT released its own Keelung mayoral poll on Tuesday, showing that 41.3% of respondents favored Hsieh, giving him a 5.6-percentage-point lead over Tung, per UDN. When asked who was more likely to win the election, 45% picked Hsieh, putting him 18.5 percentage points ahead of Tung.
The KMT poll was conducted Oct. 13-16 among 1,071 respondents. It has a margin of error of plus or minus 2.99 percentage points at a 95% confidence level.

Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir sharply criticized Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s alleged desire to form a “unity government” with Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot in an interview with The Jerusalem Post this week, warning that such a coalition would severely “harm Israel.”
“Netanyahu wants a unity government with Eisenkot and various other figures,” Ben-Gvir said. “Maybe that would look a little better to certain people around the world, but it would not actually benefit Israel. It would harm Israel.”
The remarks come amid growing tensions between the prime minister and national security minister over the composition of the next government and Ben-Gvir’s political ambitions.
On Sunday, Ben-Gvir claimed that Netanyahu had promised European officials he would be excluded from the next coalition – an allegation the Likud party denied. Netanyahu has also openly ruled out giving Ben-Gvir the Defense Ministry, a portfolio the minister has openly sought.
Ben-Gvir’s far-right Otzma Yehudit party has been a key member of Netanyahu’s coalition. Recent polling has projected Otzma Yehudit to win approximately eight seats in the next Knesset.
Ben-Gvir calls for right-wing government as Eisenkot, Netanyahu unable to hit 61-seat coalition
“We cannot have a government that is split down the middle,” the national security minister added. “The government needs to be able to make decisions in one direction or another. I want a right-wing government,” the national security minister told the Post.
Most recent polling, though, has shown neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition bloc as managing to secure a 61-seat majority in the upcoming October 27 elections.
Asked how such a government could be formed, Ben-Gvir expressed confidence that another right-wing government was possible, saying that voter turnout on election day would enable Netanyahu’s bloc to secure a Knesset majority.
“I think we can form a government … if we get all our voters out into the streets,” he said.
Despite the tensions between Netanyahu and Ben-Gvir, the minister said he wanted the prime minister to remain in his position after the elections.
Ben-Gvir added that rather than pursuing a partnership with Eisenkot, Netanyahu would need to “stand with” him.
“I love Netanyahu very much,” Ben-Gvir said. “I don’t want Eisenkot to be prime minister.”
“Netanyahu needs to stand with me on the Right and pursue a full, full right-wing government. Only that way will we be able to save the State of Israel.”
When asked about red lines on whom to partner with, Ben-Gvir first condemned the Arab parties, Ra’am and the Joint List, stating that they “side with terrorists” and that they seek to harm the country.
He said that a government with other party leaders in the opposition bloc, such as former prime minister Naftali Bennett, would also harm the country.
Ben-Gvir also said he still believed that the haredi (ultra-Orthodox) parties – Shas and United Torah Judaism (UTJ) – could also still be coalition partners, despite recent tensions over their stance regarding haredi conscription.
Ben-Gvir, whose views are often characterized as extreme, has been criticized for rhetoric opponents say has contributed to the deterioration of Israel’s international image. He has also faced criticism over rising crime rates, particularly in the Arab sector, during the government’s term.
Ben-Gvir tells 'Post': I want to do for the IDF what I did for the police
Speaking about his plans to become defense minister, Ben-Gvir said, “I want to do for the IDF what I did for the police.”
“I believe that, if I become defense minister, I can dismantle the Palestinian Authority, encourage emigration, recruit many haredim who are not currently enlisting in the IDF, and change the rules of engagement,” he added.
“There are many things I want to do as defense minister. That is why I want to put forward my candidacy for the position.”
Asked what qualified him for the defense minister role despite criticism that he had not served in the IDF, Ben-Gvir pointed to his warnings about Hamas before October 7.
“That is exactly what they told me before October 7, when I said we should bomb Gaza. All the generals sitting in the room told me, ‘You don’t understand. You haven’t served in the military. We understand Hamas. Hamas wants quiet. Hamas wants to lower the flames. Hamas just wants to get its economy in order. You don’t understand; you haven’t served in the military.’”

Amid criticism of Ben-Gvir’s approach to Israel’s international standing, he said that, as defense minister, he would challenge critics to consider how they would respond to similar threats in their own countries.

“Would you be willing to have Hamas on your border, coming to destroy you, wanting to murder you and kill your babies? Every leader would tell you, ‘No, I would not accept that.’ So why should we accept it?”
Ben-Gvir pointed to his visit to the United States, saying he had received a “very warm welcome” at US President Donald Trump’s home and remained in contact with American officials in Israel.
“I actually think that many diplomats and ambassadors can understand what I am saying, particularly in the United States,” he noted.
“There is an understanding that we are fighting a war against jihadists, against ISIS, against people who hate us and want to destroy us.”

Uzbekistan introduces annual psychological diagnostics at educational facilities for pupils, students and their teachers and workers of kindergartens, Qazinform News Agency reports.

Why Durga Puja’s Celebration in West Bengal This Year Was Different
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
07:11:00 UTC
16:11:00 KST

Amid the festive fervor that engulfs India in autumn, the eastern Indian state of West Bengal is immersed in the 10-day celebration of Durga Puja.
Durga Puja, or the worship of the ten-armed goddess Durga, who slayed a demon king, symbolizes the victory of good over evil. It is the biggest festival for Bengalis and for the Bengali diaspora. It is much more than a religious festival and has metamorphosed into the largest public art festival in the world as well.
Given the significance of Durga Puja in the lives of Bengalis, ruling parties in the state have always leveraged the festival for political purposes. This was the first Durga Puja held under the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which came to power in Bengal just five months ago, after defeating the regional Trinamool Congress (TMC).
This year, however, the festival was in the news for all the wrong reasons. For the first time in Bengal, a stampede in a puja pandal (venue for worship) in north Kolkata left 19 dead and over 25 injured on October 17. The dead included 11 women and five children; the youngest was aged seven. A pall of gloom descended upon Bengal’s largest socio-cultural celebration. Kolkata has never witnessed such a tragedy during Durga Puja.
On the evening of the stampede disaster, there was another shock in store for Kolkata. Images of bulldozers demolishing bookstalls adjoining puja pandals in south Kolkata emerged.
For decades, leftist parties had set up bookstalls selling Marxist literature during the puja days. This time, Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari declared that his government would not allow communist culture to flourish. His government used bulldozers to flatten the stalls. In north Kolkata’s Dum Dum area, Hindutva goons vandalized a leftist-run book stall and even tore great classics of Bengali literature. Kolkata is famous for its love for intellectual banter and books.
Although Durga Puja revolves around the worship of a Hindu goddess, in Bengal it is a cultural phenomenon rather than a ritualistic-religious one. Unlike North India, where Navaratri (nine days) is observed through strict fasting, prayers, consumption of only vegetarian fare, and worship of the Mata Rani (Mother Goddess), in Bengal the connection with Durga is more personal. She is perceived as a loving daughter coming to her parental home and is therefore pampered with the best food and sweet offerings, including sacrificial meat.
What makes the Durga Puja of Bengal unique is the pantheon of gods it includes — Saraswati and Lakshmi, the goddesses of learning and wealth, respectively – regarded as Durga’s children along with the male gods, Ganesh and Kartik. Her annual arrival on earth, accompanied by her children, is the rationale behind the celebration. This celebration is marked by cultural dance, music, theatrical performances, publication of literary magazines, new clothes, revelry, and feasting. It is an inclusive, secular approach to an ostensibly religious festival, which the Hindutva-dominated North Indian psyche cannot comprehend.
Under former Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee of the TMC (2011-2026), the festival expanded both in scale and budget. Banerjee inaugurated thousands of community pujas every year in Kolkata, patronizing neighborhood clubs that organized the festival. Organizers would unleash their creativity and artistry through the pandal decorations and portrayal of Durga. Known as “theme pujas,” pandals depicted topical issues ranging from social problems to contemporary subjects like climate change, and even abstract concepts.
The dizzying creativity in the art installations attracted domestic and foreign tourists to Bengal during the puja season. As per a British Council study in 2021, the Durga Puja creative economy was worth around $4.53 billion, contributing 2.5 percent of the state’s GDP.
Bengal’s Durga Puja even earned the prestigious UNESCO tag for being an “Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity” in 2021. In its citation, UNESCO stated: “Durga Puja is seen as the best instance of the public performance of religion and art, and as a thriving ground for collaborative artists and designers.” Banerjee considered the UNESCO recognition a major achievement of her government and even started a Durga Puja Carnival to showcase the festivities.
Several ministers of Banerjee’s TMC became synonymous with their neighborhood pujas, which acquired political clout and prominence. Even prominent TMC leaders like former mayor Farhid (Bobby) Hakim, a Muslim, were famous for their patronage of the Durga Puja. In fact, this secular celebration of Durga Puja, where Muslims also participate, is what rankled the Hindutva organizations. The TMC under Banerjee was known for its secular credentials and its patronage of festivals of all major religions, be it Durga Puja, Christmas or Eid.
In contrast, the BJP has always harped on retaining the purity of the “sanatan dharma” (literally, universal truth, i.e., Hinduism). It has always encouraged sectarian and communal politics with scant regard for minorities. Even before it came to power in Bengal, the BJP and its ideological mentor, the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), had stoked the vegetarian versus non-vegetarian debate, projecting the Bengali tradition of offering meat to Durga as an aberration.
Not surprisingly, much before the festival, Adhikari issued a stern warning to puja organizers with a list of dos and don’ts, including strict adherence to religious rituals. Organizers were also given diktats not to take creative liberties with the idol and the pandal in any way that can defile the sanctity of the worship. Earlier Durga Puja pandal themes like taboos surrounding menstruation were anathema to the BJP government.
It was obvious that the BJP government in Bengal is intent on stripping Durga Puja of its cultural, secular, and artistic character and imposing a rigid ritualistic norm of worship in its stead. The state administration was more focused on such extraneous issues rather than basics like ensuring crowd management; this critical lapse led to the stampede on October 17. The Telegraph newspaper observed that the Adhikari government had replaced police personnel, who in the past were lauded for their efficient crowd control measures, with a new team of inexperienced officers.
Even the Left Front government, which ruled Bengal for 34 years (1977 to 2011) and was avowedly atheist, never interfered or restricted the festive celebrations of Durga Puja. Rather, it termed the puja as a “sharad utsav” (autumnal festival) and participated in it by setting up bookstalls at the venues.
The BJP’s victory in pluralistic Bengal surprised many. Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah had been desperate to oust the proud Banerjee, who had publicly challenged the prime minister several times. Therefore, Durga Puja 2026 was, to many Bengalis, an attempt by the BJP to erase the TMC’s contributions to the Durga Puja spectacle.
Soon after forming the Bengal government, BJP leaders replaced TMC politicians heading prominent puja committees across Kolkata. Banerjee’s government used to give around $1,000 to puja committees. This year, the BJP government provided a grant of $1,000 as well as free electricity to each puja committee across Bengal.
The BJP, which valorizes the deity Ram, celebrates the Dussehra festival as Ram’s conquest of the demon, Ravana. In Bengal, the party had to make an uncomfortable compromise; it had to worship goddess Durga, and in the way Bengalis celebrate the festival.
In keeping with its communally divisive agenda, Chief Minister Adhikari announced on Wednesday that only those who believe in “sanatan dharma” will be allowed to touch the Durga idols during immersion in the river. The opposition has accused him of advocating untouchability. But Adhikari is unperturbed.

Texas startup aims to field gene-edited military dogs by 2028
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
07:08:28 UTC
16:08:28 KST

- Warhound emerged from stealth with $200 million to clone and gene-edit working dogs for the U.S. military, police and first responders.
- Palmer Luckey defended the project on X, citing protective gear, health-focused gene edits and the American Humane Society’s support.
Anduril founder Palmer Luckey has pushed back against critics of Warhound, a new Texas startup he conceived with Colossal Biosciences CEO Ben Lamm that plans to clone and gene-edit working dogs for the U.S. military, law enforcement and emergency responders.
Warhound emerged from stealth on Oct. 22, 2026, with a $200 million seed round, which values the company at $1.2 billion. As the announcement drew criticism online, Luckey defended the project in a post on X, pointing to the protective gear and health-focused gene edits at the center of the plan.
“Which part of this do you object to? The hearing protection? The eye protection? The body armor? Or gene edits that makes them less likely to develop cancer and joint problems? There is a reason the American Humane Society is supporting this,” wrote Luckey.
The company is built around a supply problem in the U.S. military’s working dog program. The Army created the K-9 Corps in 1942, and the Department of War’s Military Working Dog Program now has more than 2,200 dog teams, according to Warhound. More than 80% of U.S. military working dogs are bought from Europe, and fewer than half of the dogs purchased are judged fit for service after a roughly three-year acquisition and training pipeline, which means the military has to buy and train about 200 dogs to field 100. Lamm told Fortune that the United States is competing with other governments, including China and Russia, for the same animals.
Warhound plans to work in stages. It will identify top-performing dogs that have completed training, biobank their genetic material and clone those proven animals, while also pursuing targeted gene edits. The company’s starting point is the two breeds most used in military service, the Belgian Malinois and the German Shepherd, and it says it will screen out known harmful variants tied to muscle degeneration and other inherited diseases so that no dog enters service carrying genetic markers for common career-ending conditions such as hip dysplasia.
Lamm said the company is still working out which other traits can be edited responsibly, and he has pointed to possible future improvements in speed, agility and sense of smell for tasks such as bomb detection. The first group of dogs has already been biobanked and is being edited, with Colossal-owned cloning company Viagen helping produce the animals. Lamm expects the first dogs to be born early next year and to enter service in about two years.
Anduril’s role sits “on top of the dog, not in the dog,” as Lamm described it. The defense company is supplying eye and ear protection, body armor and integration with its Eagle Eye system, so that dogs, handlers and autonomous systems can operate as a single team, with sensor-equipped vests that send information back to handlers.
The American Humane Society will certify Warhound’s training programs and help reunite retired dogs with their former handlers through its Military Working Dog Reunification Program. Luckey and Lamm developed the concept after a discussion at Peter Diamandis’ Moonshots Summit, but Luckey holds no equity in Warhound and Anduril has no ownership stake, while Colossal licenses its technology to the company and holds an economic interest.
Warhound is led by CEO David Spirk, a former Marine who served as the first chief data officer of U.S. Special Operations Command and later of the Department of War. Its backers include In-Q-Tel, Sequoia Capital, ARK Invest, Franklin Templeton, 8VC and Lux Capital.
The company has briefed government groups but has no signed customers yet and has not set a price per dog. It is discussing a “Canine-as-a-Service” model in which the government would buy a steady supply of trained dogs, and plans to build national-scale kennel and training infrastructure starting with private capital.

Europe needs a war economy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
07:08:10 UTC
16:08:10 KST

Europe needs a war economy
With US support increasingly uncertain, Europe must mobilise its financial and industrial power to defend itself and counter Russia.
For the past four-and-a-half years, the war on Europe’s doorstep has haunted policymakers. Yet they have treated it as a looming threat rather than one already eroding the very foundations on which Europe stands.
Russia’s war has devastated much of Ukraine’s south and east, even as the front lines have shifted only slowly. For Europe, however, the challenge has never been confined to the battlefield. Supporting Ukraine and constraining Russia have tested the continent’s economic resources and political unity. Now, as United States President Donald Trump seeks to force a disadvantageous settlement on Kyiv and repeatedly threatens to withdraw US support, Europe faces the prospect of shouldering even more of that burden alone.
Even if the latest crisis is averted, Europe can no longer assume that Washington will guarantee its security. It must develop the financial capacity to sustain Ukraine’s defence, the industrial strength to defend itself and the economic leverage to constrain Moscow. To meet these challenges, Europe must build a war economy.
The past four years offer lessons in how Europe can finance such an effort, but also warnings about the divisions that could undermine it. The European Union has already been at the forefront of Ukraine’s recent financing, moving from an 18.1-billion-euro ($21bn) share of the G7’s $50bn Extraordinary Revenue Acceleration (ERA) loans in 2024 to finalising a new 90-billion-euro ($100bn) loan this April, one that came without US commitment. Yet internal divisions remain over numerous issues, particularly as they pertain to constraining Russia. This month, the EU adopted its largest-ever round of sanctions listings. But while the measures added a record number of designations, they did little to broaden the scope of restricted activity and did not accelerate the phase-out of Russian energy imports, with pipeline gas imports still permitted until autumn 2027. European leaders have also expressed concern over Trump’s decision to waive new Russia-related sanctions as he seeks to grapple with the costs his foreign policy has wrought.
However, the US-Israel war on Iran has, if anything, shown that Europe’s measures against Russian hydrocarbons could have gone further. Before February, some 20 million barrels per day (bpd) of crude and oil products and roughly 110 billion cubic metres (bcm) a year of liquefied natural gas (LNG) passed through the Strait of Hormuz. By comparison, Russia exported about 6.5 million bpd of oil and products in September, and some 43bcm of LNG last year – about a third of Hormuz’s oil and two-fifths of its LNG. As the crisis continues and Trump seeks additional Russian supplies, Europe must complement its efforts to constrain Moscow with greater investment in its own security.
The first and most important step is to establish a standing framework for joint EU borrowing – not only to finance Ukraine’s continued defence, but also to fund the defence industry Europe will need to sustain its own defence and, if necessary, prevail against future threats from Russia. Crisis begets innovation, as demonstrated during the COVID-19 pandemic, when EU member states pushed past their long-held aversion to mutualised borrowing, creating the 750-billion-euro NextGenerationEU recovery fund in 2020. The EU’s contribution to the ERA loans and this year’s 90-billion-euro facility, both financed by common EU borrowing, extended that logic to wartime finance. But these remain crisis-by-crisis improvisations. Deepening fiscal and capital markets union and building a genuine fiscal-military state would provide the foundations of Europe’s power and its ability to deter and win wars.
The same logic plays out in the US today, where deep capital markets have given companies such as SpaceX, which invested heavily for years before seeing returns, the space to develop technologies such as its Starlink network that have reshaped modern warfare. The importance of this technology is now keenly felt on Ukraine’s battlefields, where Kyiv’s communications have rested on a network subject to the whims of one man, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. Europe therefore needs the fiscal capacity to fund its own technological development and procurement.
There are understandable jitters about the existing indebtedness of European states such as France and the United Kingdom. However, Russia’s frozen sovereign assets offer a potential way to support further borrowing. Divisions remain over using these assets, with Belgium, which hosts the lion’s share at Euroclear, opposing such a move over fears of Russian legal action and damage to its position in the global financial system. The bloc must come together to share that risk, which is overblown in any case. Not all EU fiscal support needs to come in the form of direct joint debt either. Greatly expanding the EU capital markets union and creating tax-advantaged structures across the region for defence firms and technological innovators may prove even more effective.
Beyond the assets themselves, Europe must also take greater control over its continued economic linkages with Russia. That means intervening far more actively in cases such as that of Austria’s Raiffeisen Bank. In 2025, following a Russian court ruling, more than 2.1 billion euros were taken from Raiffeisen’s Russian subsidiary to compensate Rasperia, a company tied to the sanctioned oligarch Oleg Deripaska. A Vienna court’s ruling last month now paves the way for Raiffeisen to seek compensation from Rasperia’s frozen assets in the EU – using the same sanctions derogation through which Euroclear released some $3bn in 2025. It is precisely this kind of legalised dealing with Moscow that keeps threats like those levelled at Belgium credible: if the Kremlin can seize European assets and prompt the release of Russian-linked assets frozen in the EU, every expropriation becomes a bargaining chip.
Furthermore, the UK and the EU have increasingly made use of measures against circumvention that share some features with US secondary sanctions. Europe should now be more assertive in making it clear that firms helping Russia evade its sanctions risk losing access to European financial systems and markets. US firms will choose Europe over the Kremlin, even if Trump waives more sanctions.
Finally, Europe should seek to reduce US influence over its foreign and security relationships. Speaking in Qatar this week, US Ambassador to Turkiye Tom Barrack said Washington was moving away from its decades-old bargain of security for Gulf oil. Europe may not be able to offer the same level of security, but it can offer a mutually beneficial partnership that addresses both sides’ concerns. And it is Europe that is now stepping up in the Gulf, with the UK and France deploying jets, air defences and refuelling support to help Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks. Unlike Washington, Europe can promise a deeper partnership in the future and serve as a reliable buyer of Gulf oil and gas exports in exchange for Gulf states doing more to address Europe’s security concerns about Russia through enhanced sanctions compliance and, first and foremost, ending the Kremlin’s role in OPEC plus.
Europe has the means to finance its own security. It must now find the will to borrow for it.

Eisenkot offers hawkish alternative to Netanyahu for Israeli PM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
07:06:57 UTC
16:06:57 KST

Eisenkot offers hawkish alternative to Netanyahu for Israeli PM
JERUSALEM, Oct 23 - Reserved, media-shy, and a relative newcomer to Israeli politics, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot presents a clear contrast to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the veteran leader he aims to defeat in an election next week.
His image as a straight-talking security hawk from humble roots has resonated in a nation going to the polls on October 27 for the first time since Hamas attacked Israel three years ago.
Eisenkot offers a break with Netanyahu's leadership and far-right allies, but not with the hawkish security views that have hardened since October 7, 2023: He opposes Palestinian statehood and says Hamas' military wing must be destroyed or dismantled.
Opinion polls show Eisenkot's Yashar party leading Netanyahu's Likud, though Israel's fractured politics mean neither is assured of forming the next government.
Eisenkot has emphasized his security credentials on the campaign trail, citing his "Dahiyeh doctrine" of responding to attacks with disproportionate force, which he deployed as a commander during Israel's 2006 war with Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon.
His austere public style also sets him apart from Netanyahu, a flamboyant and combative politician who is on trial for corruption and remains widely blamed for the security failures surrounding the October 7 attack, according to opinion polls.
Eisenkot's public standing is also bound up with the personal price his family has paid since 2023: a son and two nephews were killed fighting in Gaza.
"He's very likable, not a politician, an everyday person," said Eitan Shamir, director of the Begin-Sadat Center for Strategic Studies at Bar-Ilan University. "He's not too sophisticated. People feel they can relate to him."
Beyond his call to eliminate Hamas' military capabilities, Eisenkot has said Israel's next government must prevent Iran from acquiring a military nuclear capability, either by force or through an "arrangement" such as a US-backed diplomatic solution.
He also favours Jewish settlement in the occupied West Bank, where settlements expanded under Netanyahu. Most countries consider the settlements illegal and an obstacle to peace.
But settlement should serve Israeli national interests and must be “legal”, he told Israel's Channel 7, a comment suggesting opposition to settler outposts established without state approval.
Eisenkot has criticised settler violence against Palestinians, which has surged since 2023, raising tensions in Israel’s ties with Western states, and he opposes Netanyahu's far-right coalition partners Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, who have both faced sanctions by some Western countries for inciting violence against Palestinians.
MOROCCAN ROOTS
A son of Moroccan immigrants, Eisenkot would be the first prime minister from Israel’s Mizrahi community, Jews who trace their roots to the Middle East and North Africa.
An important constituency for Netanyahu, the Mizrahi community has sometimes been disadvantaged in Israel, particularly in the state’s early decades, which were dominated by Ashkenazi Jews, who trace their roots to Europe.
Eisenkot served in the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) for 41 years, commanding troops in the West Bank during the second intifada, or uprising, and during the 2006 war against Hezbollah in Lebanon.
The "Dahiyeh doctrine" he deployed in 2006 was a deterrent strategy of responding to attacks by militant groups with overwhelming destruction, even of civilian infrastructure, in areas they use. The name refers to Beirut's Hezbollah-controlled southern suburbs. The UN emergency relief coordinator at the time said the Israeli bombardment of Dahiyeh had breached humanitarian law.
Eisenkot rose to become chief of staff from 2015 to 2019.
The party he founded in 2025 is called Yashar, meaning straight or honest in Hebrew.
JOINED WAR CABINET
After Hamas launched the October 7 attacks, killing 1,200 people and taking another 251 hostage, Eisenkot joined Netanyahu's war cabinet as an observer.
He quit after eight months, criticising Netanyahu's leadership.
“I want a simple thing. We defined, and I raised my hand in favor of, the destruction of Hamas's military and governmental power,” Eisenkot said in the Channel 7 interview.
“We decided to achieve this within a year. Over three years have passed, and it hasn't happened,” he said, criticizing Netanyahu for declaring a goal of “total victory”.
Israel flattened much of the Gaza Strip after the October 7 attacks, killing 74,000 people, according to Gaza health officials.
A UN inquiry determined Israel committed genocide in Gaza, a finding rejected by Israel.
A peace plan announced by US President Donald Trump a year ago led to a ceasefire and the release of the remaining hostages seized in 2023. Eisenkot said freeing the hostages was the only war goal achieved by Israel.
Trump's wider Gaza peace plans foresee Hamas disarming, new Palestinian governance for Gaza under international supervision and an Israeli withdrawal. Those goals remain unfulfilled, with Israel occupying more than half of Gaza and Hamas still armed.
Under a Trump-backed plan unveiled in July, Hamas said it had agreed to disarm in return for gradual Israeli withdrawal. But Netanyahu rejected the plan, saying Hamas must be disarmed before any withdrawal.
In the Channel 7 interview, Eisenkot restated the goal of eliminating Hamas' military power.
"This is where we need to see how it gets done, how Hamas' military wing is destroyed or dismantled. It must end with that," he said.
TWO STATES ‘IS A MISTAKE'
He is against statehood for the Palestinians, who have long sought self-determination in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip with a capital in East Jerusalem, telling Channel 7 "two states for two peoples is a mistake".
“My position is that between the Jordan River and the Sea, Israel must have overriding security responsibility. There must not be any foreign army between the Mediterranean and the Jordan if we wish to live,” he said.
While voicing support for settlements, he has opposed the Netanyahu government’s moves to build homes in what's known as the E1 bloc, a plan that has drawn particularly strong objections from Western states because it would bisect the West Bank, making a Palestinian state even harder to achieve.
Eisenkot has said he won't partner with parties representing Arab Israelis because he says none accepts his four core principles, including destroying or dismantling Israel's enemies. That could complicate Eisenkot's path to a governing majority even if Yashar emerges as the largest party.
“I will make efforts to bring in more Zionist parties because Israel needs a broad coalition with a government that will bring a broad national consensus,” he told Channel 7. REUTERS

Israeli elections and the limits of change
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
07:06:33 UTC
16:06:33 KST

Israel’s forthcoming elections on 27th October, the first since the events of 7th October three years ago and their aftermath, are taking place amid deep polarisation and fierce competition among rival political currents. Issues dividing groups of differing orientations, successive last-minute surprises and opinion poll findings all underscore the complexity of the political landscape. Although Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party have seen their standing decline, the standing of the right wing has not declined. Depending on the projected electoral outcomes, change could bring de-escalation in the occupied Palestinian territory, but it would not guarantee a fundamental shift in Israel’s occupation policies towards the Palestinians more broadly. Palestinian votes within Israel could weaken the electoral position of Netanyahu, Likud and the governing coalition. The number of seats won by Palestinian electoral lists could also improve the prospects of Netanyahu’s rivals forming a government, although those lists would still have very limited influence over its policies and plans for now.
Just one week before Israel’s elections, Israeli opinion polls remain unable to predict with certainty which party, or even which coalition, will govern, amid fluctuating and closely contested results and the pragmatism of rival parties when it comes to forming a government. This uncertainty persists despite sharp differences among the main contenders over the political leadership’s responsibility for security failures, the conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jews, the rising cost of living and settler violence in the West Bank. US President Donald Trump’s endorsement of Israel’s prime minister in the final days before the elections represents an unusual and widely criticised departure from established US practice, suggesting foreign interference at the heart of domestic affairs.
Nevertheless, it may have little influence on undecided Israeli voters, as Trump does not command much trust among Israelis. The late withdrawal of Benny Gantz, leader of the Blue and White party, from the race also benefits the anti-Netanyahu camp by helping to consolidate its vote.
In a repeat of an earlier electoral contest, the political landscape appears to be taking shape around a competition between a camp led by Netanyahu and another seeking to bring his tenure to an end. Netanyahu’s standing as prime minister has declined in opinion polls, reflecting public dissatisfaction with his government’s policies, with Gadi Eisenkot emerging as the main beneficiary, enjoying an average lead of nine percentage points. Netanyahu’s Likud and Eisenkot’s Yashar party have alternated at the top of party rankings in opinion polls, with only narrow margins separating them. The change camp led by Eisenkot, which includes, alongside Yashar, the Together list headed by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu and the Democrats led by Yair Golan, is also polling very close to Netanyahu’s right-wing camp in both support and projected seats. Under the current electoral arithmetic, however, neither camp would have enough seats to form a government. Under Israel’s established procedures, the president assigns the task of forming a government to the party best placed to do so, regardless of whether it has won the largest number of seats. This could give Eisenkot’s change camp an advantage in forming a government, given the support it receives in these elections from Palestinian parties in Israel, even if those parties do not participate in the next government.
READ: Israeli opposition leaders accuse Netanyahu of clinging to power at country’s expense
Netanyahu and his Likud party bear direct responsibility for the decline in the electoral standing of his right-wing camp. Yet opinion polls reveal that this decline does not stem from a weakening of the right’s political standing in Israeli society, and may even point to its consolidation. Likud is projected to lose around ten seats compared with the previous election results, while the religious and far-right parties have largely maintained their electoral strength. This shows that the decline in the camp’s electoral standing is attributable to Likud’s losses, with the overall reduction in seats broadly corresponding to those lost by Netanyahu’s party.
Current opinion polls indicate that the Israeli right continues to retain its electoral strength. Although the ultra-Orthodox Shas party has lost a small number of seats over its position on the conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jews, some of the younger voters it is losing are shifting their support to more extreme right-wing parties that are also its coalition partners.
The ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism party has likewise largely maintained its electoral standing. Meanwhile, Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power party is gaining seats, while the Religious Zionism–Zehut list led by Bezalel Smotrich has broadly maintained its position.
These indicators are consistent with a recent Reuters report highlighting growing support for Ben-Gvir among young voters. A Hebrew University poll found that around a third of supporters of Ben-Gvir’s party will be voting for the first time in the forthcoming elections. Current opinion polls also suggest that the left’s electoral standing is unlikely to improve. The Zionist left, represented by the Democrats, which brings together the Labour and Meretz parties, is projected to win around nine seats, compared with the four seats held by Labour in the current Knesset. However, this increase does not necessarily reflect a broader societal shift towards the left. Rather, it can be explained by the merger of the two parties, which helps to prevent Meretz votes from once again going unrepresented in parliament, as they did in 2022, when the party failed to cross the electoral threshold of 3.25 per cent, equivalent to approximately four seats.
Although Eisenkot’s camp is expected to emerge as the leading electoral bloc, with its principal figures united in their desire to replace Netanyahu, the challenges of maintaining political cohesion remain significant, given their differing political orientations and the difficulty of reaching agreement on a unified programme. Eisenkot leans towards the centre and has a military background, while Bennett comes from the nationalist right, with roots in the religious settler movement. Lapid, Bennett’s alliance partner, represents the secular liberal centre, whereas Lieberman represents the hardline secular nationalist right. Golan belongs to the liberal Zionist left. On the Palestinian question, Eisenkot and Bennett both lean to the right. Eisenkot combines opposition to the two-state solution following the 7th October attack with criticism of the E1 settlement project and settler violence; Bennett, for his part, explicitly rejects the establishment of a Palestinian state. While Lapid supports the two-state solution and Golan calls for curbing settler violence and pursuing a political solution to the Palestinian question, Lieberman advocates scrapping the Oslo Accords and dismantling the Palestinian Authority.
However, the success of this scenario would not, from a Palestinian perspective, mean a shift in Israel’s objectives regarding their cause, although it would probably curb the escalation against them that has persisted for years. Under Netanyahu’s current government, the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, has witnessed a sharp escalation in killings and settlement expansion. The annual average number of Palestinians killed by Israeli forces and settlers during its tenure has risen to around five times the level recorded in preceding years. The imposition of settlement facts on the ground, settler violence and the undermining of prospects for a geographically contiguous Palestinian state have also accelerated markedly. Gaza, meanwhile, has witnessed a genocidal war unparalleled since the 1948 war. Eisenkot’s camp may therefore be inclined to reduce this escalation without fundamentally altering the dynamics of the conflict with the Palestinians.
Eisenkot opposes the collapse of the Palestinian Authority or direct Israeli rule over millions of Palestinians, while insisting on Israel retaining overall security control in the West Bank. In Gaza, he supports the US plan, but makes the complete disarmament of Hamas a precondition for any other arrangements. He has made no commitment to a full Israeli withdrawal from Gaza, nor has he specified a timetable for one.
On settlements and annexation, he supports settlement activity that serves Israel’s security interests and does not propose withdrawing from settlements. He has criticised the decision to place the police under Ben-Gvir’s authority and to grant Smotrich powers over the administration of civil affairs, calling instead for the military establishment to regain control. Bennett explicitly rejects the establishment of a Palestinian state, proposing autonomy instead. In Gaza, his electoral list favours maintaining Israeli control up to the Yellow Line and retaining freedom of military action until Hamas is disarmed. Bennett has stated that Area C, roughly two-thirds of the West Bank, would become part of Israel, while the remaining third would be self-governing. Lieberman openly advocates preventing the establishment of a Palestinian state. In Gaza, he supports handing over its administration to a foreign authority after Hamas has been eliminated. He opposes the evacuation of settlements and insists on full Israeli control over Area C and security control over the rest of the West Bank, alongside a Jordanian role in its administration.
Nevertheless, several possible scenarios for the outcome of Israel’s elections cannot be overlooked. One involves the opposition agreeing to form a unity government bringing together Likud and Yashar, alongside additional coalition partners. Such an arrangement could offer Netanyahu a way to remain in power while allowing him to break free from his dependence on his more hardline partners. At the same time, it could give Eisenkot an opportunity to assume the premiership under a rotation agreement with Netanyahu. This would allow greater scope for de-escalation and regional understandings, without guaranteeing any fundamental shift in Israel’s approach to Palestinian rights. According to press reports, the Trump administration favours this scenario as an opportunity to advance regional understandings and normalisation with Saudi Arabia.
Under another scenario, Netanyahu’s government and its current coalition could remain in office while efforts to form a new government are stalled. Israeli law allows 28 days to form a government, with a possible extension of a further 14 days. If this period expires without a government being formed, another election becomes a serious possibility, giving Netanyahu additional time in power. This scenario could arise if neither camp emerges from the elections with a clear majority capable of forming a government, the opposition maintains its refusal to enter a coalition with Netanyahu, neither side succeeds in attracting additional partners, and Eisenkot’s camp is unable to benefit from the support of Palestinian parties.
If Netanyahu succeeds in remaining in power, he may present the outcome as a mandate to continue his policies and as encouragement to pursue more hardline measures, depending on the composition of his coalition. An opposition victory, on the other hand, would not automatically signal a shift towards recognising a Palestinian state or ending the occupation.
Nevertheless, a change of government could allow for tighter curbs on settler violence and more flexibility over arrangements for Gaza and regional understandings, opening the way for relative de-escalation compared with the current escalation.

Tanks, Mandates and Caretakers: The Story of Bulgaria’s Presidency Since 1990
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
07:05:00 UTC
16:05:00 KST

Prices Keep Bulgaria’s Public Tension High Despite Gradual Decline
Bulgaria’s Public Tension Index edged down to 6.10 points in the third quarter of 2026 from 6.22 in the previous quarter, continuing its decline at a slower pace
Bulgaria has had seven presidents since the post of head of state was created in the spring of 1990: a communist reformer who lasted three months, a dissident philosopher, a provincial lawyer, a socialist historian, a construction businessman, an air force general and a former television journalist. Only five of them won the office at the ballot box, only two were elected twice, and only one was voted out. Each of them left the presidency looking slightly different from the way they found it, and their stories explain a good deal about the choice Bulgarians face on Sunday.
Petar Mladenov, born in 1936 in a village near Vidin, spent 18 years as communist Bulgaria's foreign minister before turning on the man who had appointed him. After the mass expulsion of Bulgarian Turks in the summer of 1989, he and a small group of Politburo colleagues, reportedly with Mikhail Gorbachev's tacit approval, moved against Todor Zhivkov. Mladenov resigned as foreign minister in October, and on November 9 he persuaded Zhivkov to step down. Zhivkov's 35-year rule ended the next day, and Mladenov took over the party and the State Council.
On April 3, 1990, the outgoing National Assembly abolished the State Council and elected Mladenov as the country's first president. His tenure was short. During the campaign for the June 1990 elections, the opposition released a video of a protest outside parliament the previous December in which Mladenov could be heard saying "По-добре танковете да дойдат," roughly "Better that the tanks come." Students occupied Sofia University demanding his departure and he resigned on July 6, 1990. He died in Sofia in 2000.
Zhelyu Zhelev was the anti-communist opposition's intellectual figurehead long before he held office. A philosopher born in 1935, he published Fascism in 1982, a study of the Italian, German and Spanish dictatorships whose parallels with the Soviet-bloc states were obvious enough that the book was pulled from shops and libraries within weeks. In 1989 he helped found the Club for Support of Openness and Reform and went on to chair the Union of Democratic Forces (SDS).
The Grand National Assembly elected him president on August 1, 1990, a compromise between a communist-successor majority and the opposition it needed for legitimacy. After the 1991 constitution made the post directly elected, Zhelev and his running mate, the poet Blaga Dimitrova, won Bulgaria's first popular presidential vote in January 1992, beating Velko Valkanov in the runoff with 52.85 percent on a turnout of almost 76 percent, a level no later presidential election has approached.
His presidency set many of the conventions his successors inherited. He used the mandate to form governments as a political instrument, quickly fell out with his own camp's Filip Dimitrov government, and backed the technocratic Lyuben Berov cabinet that followed. Dimitrova resigned as vice president in 1993, leaving the post vacant for the rest of his term. In 1996 the SDS chose Petar Stoyanov over him in its primary, making Zhelev the only directly elected president who never got the chance to seek a second term from voters. He died in 2015.
Petar Stoyanov, a Plovdiv civil lawyer born in 1952, beat Zhelev in the SDS primary and then the socialist Ivan Marazov in the November 1996 runoff by almost 20 points. He took the oath in January 1997 in the middle of the worst crisis of the "transition" period. Hyperinflation had wiped out savings, banks had collapsed, and tens of thousands of protesters were in the streets after the socialist Videnov government resigned.
Stoyanov's handling of that winter defined his presidency. When the Bulgarian Socialist Party moved to form a new cabinet from the same parliament, he urged it to hand back the mandate, and after days of protest Nikolay Dobrev and Georgi Parvanov did so. Stoyanov appointed a caretaker government under Sofia mayor Stefan Sofiyanski, called early elections and watched the SDS win an outright majority under Ivan Kostov. At his initiative, Bulgaria formally applied to join NATO, and he backed the alliance during the 1999 Kosovo war despite strong public sympathy for Serbia.
In 2001 he became the first and so far only Bulgarian president to lose a re-election bid, beaten in the runoff by the same Georgi Parvanov who had returned the mandate four years earlier. He later served as a SDS MP and party leader.
Georgi Parvanov, a historian born in 1957 who wrote his doctorate on the socialist pioneer Dimitar Blagoev, had led the BSP since the collapse of December 1996. In 2001 he edged Stoyanov in the first round and won the runoff with 54.1 percent, then took the presidency with Angel Marin as his vice president. In 2006 he became the first Bulgarian president to be re-elected, crushing the nationalist Volen Siderov with 76 percent in the runoff.
His decade spanned the country's two great Western milestones, NATO membership in 2004 and EU accession in 2007, both of which he championed. He also pursued close energy ties with Moscow, and in 2008 he presided over the so-called Grand Slam: agreements with Vladimir Putin's Russia on the Belene nuclear plant, the South Stream gas pipeline and the Burgas-Alexandroupolis oil pipeline, none of which was ultimately built. In 2006 he acknowledged the existence of a communist-era State Security file under the code name "Gotse," saying he had only been consulted as a historian on Macedonian questions. He later turned ABV, a movement he launched in 2010, into a small left-wing party, which is backing Yotova in this election.
Rosen Plevneliev, born in 1964 in Gotse Delchev, was a construction entrepreneur whose company built the Sofia Business Park before Boyko Borissov made him regional development minister in 2009. As GERB's candidate in 2011, with former justice minister Margarita Popova as his running mate, he beat the socialist Ivaylo Kalfin in the runoff with 52.58 percent.
He arrived in office with little political profile and was quickly tested. When the Borissov government resigned amid mass protests over electricity bills in February 2013, he appointed Marin Raykov's caretaker cabinet, and in 2014 he appointed a second, under Georgi Bliznashki, becoming the first president to install two caretaker governments. Nationalist party "Ataka" tried to start impeachment proceedings against him in 2013 after he backed early elections, without coming close. After Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014 he became one of the most outspoken critics of the Kremlin among EU heads of state, warning repeatedly of Russian hybrid warfare against Bulgaria. He did not seek a second term in 2016 and has since remained an active voice for Bulgaria's Euro-Atlantic orientation.
Rumen Radev, born in 1963, was a fighter pilot and commander of the Bulgarian Air Force with no political record when the BSP put him forward in 2016, with Iliana Yotova as his running mate. He beat GERB's Tsetska Tsacheva with 59.4 percent in the runoff, a defeat so heavy that Borissov's government resigned. In 2021 he was re-elected with 66.7 percent against Anastas Gerdzhikov, though on a turnout of under 35 percent in the second round, the lowest in the country's history.
No president used the office as aggressively. In 2019 he refused to appoint Ivan Geshev as prosecutor general, until the constitution forced his hand. In July 2020, after prosecutors raided the offices of two of his advisers inside the presidency, he called for the Borissov government to resign and raised his fist in support of the protesters who filled Sofia's streets for months. From 2021 onward, as one parliament after another failed to produce a government, his caretaker cabinets under Stefan Yanev and Galab Donev ran the country for long stretches, prompting parliament to curb his choice of caretaker prime minister in 2023.
His foreign policy statements drew equally sharp reactions. During the 2021 campaign he described Crimea as "currently Russian," provoking a formal protest from Kyiv, and he consistently opposed sending weapons to Ukraine, criticized EU sanctions policy and pushed for a referendum on delaying euro adoption. In January 2026 he became the first directly elected Bulgarian president to resign, leaving office to found Progressive Bulgaria. Three months later the party won 131 of 240 seats, and on May 8 he was sworn in as prime minister.
Iliana Yotova, born in Sofia in 1964, worked as a journalist at Bulgarian National Television and as the BSP's spokeswoman before spending a decade in the European Parliament and nine years as Radev's vice president. On January 23, 2026, she became the first woman and the first vice president to hold the office, completing his term without a vote of her own. Within weeks she was choosing a caretaker prime minister under the restricted rules her predecessor had fought, and eventually settled on Andrey Gyurov, the man she now faces at the polls. On Sunday she will try to become the first president whose path to a full term began with an inherited presidency.
No candidate has ever won in the first round and in every direct election since 1992 the candidate who led the first round went on to win the runoff, a record that strongly favors Yotova on November 1. Turnout has fallen from almost 76 percent in 1992 to just under 35 percent in the 2021 runoff, and pollsters expect fewer than four in ten voters to take part this time.
The presidency has also swung between camps. Zhelev, Stoyanov and Plevneliev came from the center-right, while Mladenov, Parvanov, Radev and Yotova came from the left or were backed by it. Every holder has stretched the office further than its modest constitutional wording suggests and parliament pushed back only once, in 2023, after Radev had gone furthest. The next president will inherit an office shaped by all seven and the November 1 runoff will decide whether it stays in Radev's camp or passes to someone outside it.

Most November discount spending expected online
Unknown

2026-10-23

Nearly 69 percent of planned consumer spending during this year’s November discounts is expected to take place through online channels, highlighting the dominance of e-commerce during the country’s biggest annual sales campaigns, according to PwC Türkiye’s 2026 Legendary Friday Survey.
Meanwhile, the share of consumers in Türkiye using AI assistants to research purchases rose to 20 percent in 2026 from 13 percent in 2025.
About 33 percent of consumers used AI to compare products, while 29 percent used it to check discounts and 27 percent relied on it to identify products that best matched their needs.
Some 28 percent of consumers said they would like to set a spending limit for AI to make purchases on their behalf, while 24 percent said retaining the final approval before a purchase is made was important to them.
According to PwC’s survey, the share of consumers planning to shop during the November discounts period rose to 94 percent in 2026 from 87 percent in 2025.
However, the proportion of consumers expecting to spend more in real terms than last year declined to 39 percent from 47 percent, while the share of those expecting to spend less increased to 20 percent from 13 percent.
Among the product categories consumers plan to purchase during the sales period, clothing ranked first at 47 percent, followed by electronics at 32 percent and home and living products at 26 percent.

Sports technology is a significant contributor to the Swiss economy

Sports technology is a significant contributor to the Swiss economy
Technology in sport represents a significant sector of the Swiss economy, with over 400 companies generating an estimated turnover of CHF8 billion ($9.6 billion) accounting for around 17,000 full-time jobs.
The sector’s scale is comparable to that of the biotechnology industry, according to the Swiss SportsTech Report published on Friday. It was commissioned by Swiss Olympic – which is both the National Olympic Committee and the umbrella organisation for Swiss sport – and carried out in collaboration with the consultancy firms PwC and Generis.
The sector comprises companies that develop products, materials, processes, platforms and services for sport, or adapt existing technologies to the needs of athletes and sports organisations. Despite the presence of major research centres and industrial hubs, however, the sector remains relatively low-profile, according to the study’s authors. Among the study’s recommendations is the proposal to establish a national organisation dedicated specifically to “Sportstech”, with the aim of strengthening collaboration between sport and business, increasing the international visibility of companies and facilitating access to new capital for growth.
More
Switzerland remains centre of global sport – for now
The outlook appears positive: 88% of the companies in the sector surveyed expect an increase in turnover over the next two years. According to the study’s co-author Mike Kurt, the sector offers Switzerland the opportunity to open up new markets, accelerate innovation and strengthen both international competitiveness and elite sport.

US offers Russia Nord Stream restart as part of peace deal

US proposes restart of Nord Stream as part of peace deal with Russia
The United States is proposing that Russian gas supplies to Europe and the operation of the Nord Stream pipeline be resumed as an economic incentive for Moscow as part of a potential peace settlement to end Russia's war against Ukraine.
Source: The Economist
Details: The Economist describes the gas proposal as the latest concession Washington is offering Vladimir Putin. Ukrainian officials, meanwhile, do not yet know all the details of the latest US proposals.
The magazine reports that Russia would be offered commercial deals with US companies, sanctions relief and the normalisation of political relations. Ukraine would be offered an investment package and EU membership in exchange for abandoning its bid to join NATO. The proposals also envisage the creation of a demilitarised zone in Donbas.
The Economist stresses that the US cannot unilaterally decide to restore Russian gas supplies to the European market. It assesses that such a proposal would run counter to EU law.
Ukrainian negotiators fear that US representatives could strike lucrative economic deals with Russia even before the war ends.
The Economist itself questions Moscow's willingness to make peace. It assesses that Russia is likely to drag out the negotiations while securing immediate concessions on sanctions.
The renewed diplomatic push comes after US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff visited St Petersburg on 21 October, The Economist notes.
Background: On 18 October, it was reported that the Trump administration had proposed that Europe resume purchases of Russian gas. According to The New York Times, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff raised the idea during talks with Ukrainian and European officials.
