U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett issued the order during a hearing in Miami on Thursday after lawyers for the British broadcaster accused Trump of delaying his deposition. The president had canceled a previously agreed October 16 appearance, citing matters of national importance. The BBC's attorney, Charles Tobin, argued that Trump had instead attended a political campaign event in Georgia that day.
The judge ruled that Trump must appear for questioning by December 11 or risk sanctions, including possible dismissal of his lawsuit, unless the court extends the discovery period. The current deadline for exchanging evidence is December 18. The BBC's lawyers have maintained that obtaining Trump's testimony before that date is essential to preparing their defense.
According to court filings, the broadcaster first requested deposition dates in July and repeatedly sought confirmation from Trump's legal team. After the October appearance was canceled, the BBC was informed that the president would not be available before the discovery deadline and could instead testify in January 2027. Trump's lawyers have cited his presidential responsibilities in explaining the scheduling difficulties.
The hearing also addressed a dispute over access to financial information. Lett authorized the BBC to obtain records showing the number of membership applications at Trump's Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida between January 2020 and January 2026, along with membership and initiation fees. The broadcaster argues that such information could help establish whether the documentary affected Trump's reputation and financial interests. Trump's lawyers disputed the relevance of the records, arguing that the president does not personally manage the club and that its membership does not directly reflect his reputation.
Trump filed the lawsuit in Florida in December 2025, accusing the BBC of defamation and violations of the state's laws against deceptive and unfair trade practices. He is seeking at least $10 billion in damages over a documentary that included edited footage of his January 6, 2021, speech, delivered shortly before his supporters stormed the U.S. Capitol.
The documentary, titled "Trump: A Second Chance," aired as part of the BBC's Panorama program shortly before the 2024 U.S. presidential election. Trump alleges that the broadcaster combined separate portions of his speech in a way that falsely suggested he had directly encouraged the violence at the Capitol.
The BBC has acknowledged that the editing created a misleading impression and apologized to Trump, although it maintains that the broadcast did not constitute defamation. The controversy also led to the resignations of the broadcaster's director-general and its senior news executive.

Lockheed-Northrop venture lands $420M Apache radar deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
06:24:02 UTC
15:24:02 KST

- The U.S. Army awarded Longbow LLC a $419.6 million contract for Apache fire control radar systems and post-production support through Jan. 31, 2032.
- Longbow LLC, a Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman joint venture, builds the AN/APG-78 radar mounted above the AH-64 Apache’s rotor.
The U.S. Army has awarded Longbow LLC a $419.6 million contract to supply fire control radar systems and post-production support for the AH-64 Apache attack helicopter, keeping work on the Apache’s distinctive mast-mounted radar going into the next decade.
The contract, announced on Oct. 22, 2026, covers the AH-64D and AH-64E versions of the helicopter and runs through Jan. 31, 2032. It combines cost-no-fee, cost-plus-fixed-fee and firm-fixed-price terms, and work locations and funding will be set with each individual order. Army Contracting Command at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama, solicited one bid and received one.
Longbow LLC, based in Orlando, Florida, is a joint venture of Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman that builds the AN/APG-78 Longbow fire control radar. The radar sits in the rounded dome mounted above the Apache’s main rotor, which lets the helicopter scan the battlefield while staying hidden behind trees, hills or buildings.
The radar automatically searches for, detects, locates, classifies and prioritizes multiple moving or stationary targets on land and in the air, and it works in bad weather and through battlefield smoke and dust. The latest Version 6 software added a maritime mode for tracking vessels, single-target tracking, a 360-degree surveillance mode and longer detection range against land, air and sea targets.
Post-production support is a major part of the Longbow business. Such work typically covers program and logistics management, repair of radar modules, replenishment of depot spare parts, field engineering support and training for operators and maintainers, as described in Longbow’s earlier sustainment contracts. In 2020, the U.S. Army awarded Longbow a five-year contract worth up to $235.8 million to provide that support to international Apache operators, covering 12 foreign military customers in 11 nations at the time.
The radar is in service far beyond the U.S. Army. Longbow delivered its 500th fire control radar in 2020, to the Qatar Emiri Air Force, and the customer base later grew to 16 foreign militaries in 14 nations after Morocco, the Netherlands and the Indian Army joined the program alongside an upgrade for the United Arab Emirates.
The new award follows a steady run of Longbow contracts. In July 2025, the U.S. Army issued a $348.3 million modification for fire control radar systems, and in late 2024 the company received a $24.6 million order for radar electronic units and ground support spares for Australia and Kuwait.
Individual orders under the new contract will set the specific work and funding for U.S. and international Apache fleets through the January 2032 completion date.

Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia are having only a "limited" economic impact on the kingdom so far, owing to robust domestic demand, the IMF's regional director told AFP, though geopolitical uncertainty remains a threat.
The world's largest oil exporter, Saudi Arabia has had its crude shipments squeezed by Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and the Houthis' declaration of a maritime blockade.
But shipments continue to move despite the conflicts, Jihad Azour told AFP.
The Gulf kingdom also has "strong internal demand and a robust public sector, so the impact is limited, "he said of the Houthi attacks.
Nevertheless, the economy is expected to contract by 3.3 percent this year, owing to the impacts of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.
In its regional report released on Oct. 22, the IMF said that every Gulf state bar Oman had suffered reductions in its hydrocarbon production.
The economy of the region as a whole is expected to shrink 4.8 percent in 2026.
Still, the IMF expects a strong rebound of around 9.1 percent growth next year, albeit with deep uncertainty amid the ongoing geopolitical tensions and stalled diplomacy between Washington and Tehran.

'Can't drive into future looking at rearview mirror': India calls for urgent UNSC reforms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
06:17:37 UTC
15:17:37 KST

India's Permanent Representative to the UN, Ambassador Parvathaneni Harish
India has called for urgent reforms to the United Nations Security Council (UNSC), warning that its 80-year-old structure is struggling to address some of the world’s gravest conflicts. New Delhi said the Council’s composition must reflect present-day global realities, arguing that its post-Second World War framework no longer adequately represents the international community.According to news agency PTI, India’s Permanent Representative to the UN, Ambassador Harish Parvathaneni, said on Thursday that the authority inherited from the Second World War could no longer compensate for the Council’s lack of representative membership.
“The cost is already visible. Eighty years on, the Organisation is struggling to deliver peace and reconciliation in some of the gravest conflicts before the Council,” Parvathaneni said while addressing the UN General Assembly on equitable representation and an expansion of the Security Council.He added that “the authority derived from a victory eight decades ago cannot compensate for the deficit in legitimacy of an unrepresentative Security Council today.”
The Indian envoy argued that 1945, when the UN was established after the Second World War, could not remain the sole reference point for global governance.“No war, especially one that took place over 80 years ago, should determine today’s state of the world,” he said.“History can be a guide for what not to do. It cannot determine today’s choices for what needs to be done to face contemporary challenges. We cannot reasonably drive into the future by constantly looking at the rearview mirror,” he added.Parvathaneni also highlighted India’s contribution to the World Wars, arguing that the sacrifices of several nations had not received adequate recognition in the post-war international order.“An organisation crafted of the victors, for the victors and by the victors did not, obviously, care to include the concerns of the victims,” he said, calling for the Security Council to evolve “for the sake of its own relevance”.According to PTI, he noted that around 2.5 million Indians participated in the Second World War, with approximately 90,000 dying in military service. He also referred to the Bengal famine, which he attributed to colonial wartime policies.India further pointed to the under-representation of Asia-Pacific, Africa and Latin America. The Asia-Pacific region accounts for more than 60 per cent of the world’s population but has only one permanent seat on the Council, alongside a fluctuating elected representation.“Reform is not the settlement of old scores. It is an investment in a Council that all Member States can trust, and which would be stronger as a result,” Parvathaneni said.The 15-member UNSC comprises five permanent members — China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States — with veto powers, alongside 10 elected members serving two-year terms.
India supports expanding both permanent and non-permanent membership, arguing that changes limited to elected seats would leave the central imbalance intact.Criticising the pace of negotiations, Parvathaneni said, “That is not negotiation; it is merely perpetuation of status quo.”He added, “Convergences are not consensus, and the search for a lowest common denominator must not become an excuse for cosmetically tinkering with the existing structure while calling it reform.”India also maintained that any permanent membership expansion must address the veto question fairly. “A two-tier permanent membership would only institutionalise inequality,” he said.
Subhadra Srivastava is a journalist with The Times of India, covering geopolitics, international and national affairs. With over three years of experience, she focuses on national and global developments, conflict, diplomacy and their impact on India. Her work combines breaking news with in-depth analysis, offering readers context and clarity on the stories shaping the world.

le poisson volant: red-lit restaurant in paris transforms into nightclub after dark
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
06:15:47 UTC
15:15:47 KST

le poisson volant: red-lit restaurant in paris transforms into nightclub after dark
a former paris music venue becomes a moody, mirrored interior where dinner gradually gives way to late-night dancing.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
claves designs a restaurant for the late hours
At Le Poisson Volant in Paris, dinner gradually gives way to a nightclub as the evening progresses. Large illuminated ceiling panels cast a soft glow over the dining room before the lighting becomes sharper and the music takes over. The venue opened on October 2nd at 5–7 rue Marguerite-Moret.
Designed by Parisian interior architecture studio Claves, the new restaurant and club occupies the former L’International music venue in the city’s 11th arrondissement. Its interiors bring together Brutalist geometry and decorative references drawn from Chinese restaurants of the 1980s, creating an atmosphere that changes considerably between dinner and the early hours of the morning.
The project was conceived by Bertrand Chauveau and Paul Henri, the founders of nearby restaurant Le Cornichon, in collaboration with chef Yanxin Yin. The team returned to Claves founders Laure Gravier and Soizic Fougeront, who previously designed Le Cornichon, to transform the two-level space. Among their references was New York’s former China Chalet, a Chinese restaurant in the Financial District that became a well-known late-night gathering place.
brutalist structure meets decorative details
Claves has reorganized the interior of Le Poisson Volant around a new framework of columns and beams. The team takes cues from Brutalist architecture and the industrial character of the surrounding neighborhood. The structural elements establish a strong geometry across the rooms, interrupted by slender decorative lines and reflective surfaces. Large mirrors follow the architectural grid, extending views through the interior and making the spaces appear to continue beyond their physical boundaries.
On the restaurant‘s ground floor, a large oval bar in patinated steel occupies the center of the room, surrounded by built-in banquettes and dark, purple-brown walls. Patterned carpeting introduces another layer of texture, while high-backed chairs inspired by the furniture of Charles Rennie Mackintosh add an unexpectedly delicate silhouette against the heavier architecture. Silver-painted geometric motifs trace the walls and columns, recalling traditional Chinese decorative patterns alongside Art Deco ornament.
a cinematic interior inspired by wong kar-wai
The architects looked to the films of Wong Kar-wai for their saturated colors and atmospheric interiors, particularly the director’s fascination with reflections and confined spaces. Here, dark surfaces absorb the light while mirrors catch fragments of the surrounding rooms. The effect is especially striking under the reddish illumination, which gives the restaurant the slightly mysterious character of a place suspended somewhere between different cities and decades.
Claves describes the setting as an imaginary Shanghai by night, with references drawn freely from decorative arts and cinema. Even the surfaces contribute to this sense of ambiguity. Hand-painted mirrors introduce illustrated details into the architecture, while the repeating ceiling grid lends a distinctive rhythm to the rooms. The combination feels intentionally theatrical, although the architectural framework remains legible throughout.
an aquarium conceals a private room downstairs
Connecting the two floors, the staircase becomes an important part of the spatial experience. A monumental diptych by Chinese artist Shuo Hao, commissioned specifically for Le Poisson Volant, accompanies the descent toward the basement. The artwork introduces its own imagery into the interior, marking the passage between the restaurant above and the darker spaces below.
The lower level houses the DJ booth and a private room concealed behind an aquarium filled with mineral compositions. Inspired in part by the aquarium installations of artist Pierre Huyghe, the feature introduces an unusual architectural partition, its illuminated contents visible through the glass. Reflections continue across the surrounding surfaces, while the enclosed basement creates a setting increasingly removed from the street outside.
lighting and sound shape the transition into night
The lighting design, developed with Paris-based studio Matière Noire, plays a central role in the transformation. Large luminous panels are integrated into the ceiling grid, providing diffuse illumination during dinner before shifting toward more concentrated, dramatic lighting as the night progresses. Their geometric arrangement reinforces the architecture, while the changing intensity can alter the atmosphere of the room without requiring a physical reconfiguration.
Sound design by FLEiK works alongside the lighting to support the transition, as music gradually becomes the focus of the venue. From around 11 pm, Le Poisson Volant begins its shift toward club mode, continuing into the early morning on selected nights. The same columns and mirrored walls that define the dining room remain in place, but their appearance changes under the pulsing lights. It is an interesting approach to a hybrid hospitality interior, allowing the architecture to accommodate two very different rhythms within a single evening.
project info:
name: Le Poisson Volant | @lepoissonvolant.paris
interior architecture: Claves Architecture | @clavesarchitecture
location: 5–7 rue Marguerite-Moret, Paris 11th arrondissement, France
lead architects: Laure Gravier, Soizic Fougeront
opening: October 2nd, 2026
photography: © Félix Dol Maillot | @felixdolmaillot
founders: Bertrand Chauveau, Paul Henri
lighting design: Matière Noire
sound design: FLEiK
commissioned artwork: Shuo Hao
chef collaboration: Bertrand Chauveau, Yanxin Yin

2026-10-23
14:08:27 CST

MELBOURNE, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Australian authorities have charged three people over an attempt to import 120 kg of cocaine concealed in furniture.
The Australian Federal Police said on Friday that an investigation began on Oct. 9 when Australian Border Force officers detected anomalies in two cabinets that arrived in Melbourne from Greece.
Officers X-rayed the consignment, which was declared as household furniture, and located 120 packages of suspected drugs concealed within. Testing identified the substance as cocaine with a total weight of 120 kg.
The joint organized crime taskforce in the state of Victoria removed the illicit drugs and delivered the consignment to a storage facility in northwest Melbourne.
A 49-year-old woman allegedly attended the facility and coordinated the collection and movement of the cabinets. Two men, aged 31 and 40, were identified by police during the delivery.
All three were arrested after the shipment was separated and taken to addresses in west and northwest Melbourne.
They were each charged with importing a commercial quantity of a border-controlled drug and attempting to possess a commercial quantity of an unlawfully imported border-controlled drug. Both offenses carry maximum penalties of life imprisonment.
The two men were denied bail during initial court appearances on Wednesday, while the woman was granted conditional bail. They will return to court in February. ■

The area surrounding the epicenter has an average altitude of more than 4,800 meters. COLOMBO, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Sri Lanka's Hambantota International Port Group (HIPG) said Thursday that it expects the return of container shipping through the Red Sea and Suez Canal to create new commercial opportunities as the port prepares to expand annual container handling capacity to 2 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) in the first quarter of 2027.
Bindu Ranasinghe, HIPG general manager for commercial and marketing, said that disruptions in the Red Sea had accelerated Hambantota's entry into container transshipment.
The port began handling MSC container transshipment services in April 2024 and has since committed 149 million U.S. dollars to new container-handling equipment, he said.
Located about 10 nautical miles from the main East-West shipping route, Hambantota is well positioned to serve vessels returning to the Suez corridor after diversions around the Cape of Good Hope, Ranasinghe said.
HIPG also expects increased vessel traffic to raise demand for bunkering, ship supplies and other marine services.
The port is also preparing to expand into gateway container cargo for Sri Lankan imports and exports, supported by its industrial park, nearby investment zones and a planned container inspection center, he said. ■

8 inmates killed in Ecuador prison riots
China

Photo taken on Oct. 22, 2026 shows Ecuadorian military personnel deployed near El Inca prison, in northern Quito, capital of Ecuador. Eight inmates were killed Thursday in two separate riots at prisons in the Andean provinces of Cotopaxi and Pichincha in Ecuador, the National Service for Comprehensive Care for Adults Deprived of Liberty and Adolescent Offenders (SNAI) said. (Photo by Ricardo Landeta/Xinhua)
QUITO, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Eight inmates were killed Thursday in two separate riots at prisons in the Andean provinces of Cotopaxi and Pichincha in Ecuador, the National Service for Comprehensive Care for Adults Deprived of Liberty and Adolescent Offenders (SNAI) said.
According to an official statement, four inmates died at the Cotopaxi No. 1 Deprivation of Liberty Center in Latacunga, and four others at the Pichincha No. 1 Provisional Detention Center, known as El Inca prison, in Quito.
The SNAI said that 10 other people were injured and are receiving medical treatment.
The alleged participants have been identified and will be transferred to El Encuentro, a maximum-security prison in the coastal province of Santa Elena, it said.
The SNAI added that the Security Bloc, made up of the National Police and the Armed Forces, is keeping security protocols in place and conducting operations at the affected prisons to maintain order.
Ecuadorian prisons are considered one of the main hotspots of violence in the Andean country and have been the scene of massacres with dozens of deaths since 2021, the result of clashes between rival criminal gangs.
Since January 2024, Ecuador's military has been deployed to prisons under the government's declaration of an "internal armed conflict" against organized crime groups. ■

North Korea's internet outages likely caused by cyberattack, network monitor says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
06:04:05 UTC
15:04:05 KST

A cyberattack likely caused intermittent internet outages in North Korea this week, disrupting more than 40 state-managed websites, according to analysis by US network monitoring company Kentik.
North Korea’s internet experienced multiple waves of traffic from overseas, including Vietnam and Venezuela, as several websites suffered outages over a 32-hour period beginning on Tuesday, Doug Madory, Kentik’s director of internet analysis, told Reuters on Friday.
“This traffic all started at the same time and it is coming from Vietnam and Venezuela. That’s definitely a DDoS (Distributed Denial-of-Service) attack,” Madory said.
Kentik’s data showed sharp spikes in traffic beginning at around 11 am local time (0201 GMT) on Tuesday. However, the data did not identify those responsible, and Kentik analysed only part of the traffic directed at North Korea, Madory said.
The outages affected more than 40 official websites using the country’s .kp domain, including those of the foreign ministry and state news agency KCNA, according to South Korean media reports.
South Korean media also cited security experts as saying that North Korea’s unstable electricity supply could have contributed to the disruption. The outage appeared unrelated to wider internet problems linked to the disclosure of vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language later in the week.

====================================================================================================

Canada, Turkey sign 'strategic partnership' as part of Carney push to cut reliance on US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
06:03:55 UTC
15:03:55 KST

NATO allies Canada and Turkey upgraded their relations to a "strategic partnership" during the first bilateral visit by a Canadian prime minister on Thursday, as Mark Carney seeks new global trade partners to reduce reliance on the United States.
The agreement by Carney and Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan marks a significant thaw in diplomatic ties that had long been cool over Canadian concerns over human rights and a past embargo on sending weapons to Turkey.
The new partnership signed in Ankara focuses on trade and investment, defense and security, energy, and social and diplomatic ties. It aims to create jobs and opportunities for Canadian and Turkish companies to do more business together.
Carney is on a global trade blitz that he hopes will help buffer Canada from a trade war with the US, where President Donald Trump has applied sweeping tariffs and questioned the neighboring country's sovereignty.
Speaking next to Erdogan at Turkey's presidential palace, Carney said the strategic partnership would have four pillars and include a three-year action plan.
"We've planted the seeds of something new: a strategic partnership that will create new opportunities for our workers and businesses, and greater security and prosperity for both our peoples. With care and commitment, it will grow for generations to come," Carney said.
At the ceremony, Canadian and Turkish ministers signed cooperation deals on energy, defense and air transport.
'Long-standing disconnect'
Turkey, a major emerging market economy and regional military power, is seeking new investment and collaboration for its burgeoning defense industry, new nuclear power plants and mining sector.
Erdogan, who has led Turkey for 23 years, praised Carney as a leader with "common sense and acumen" on the world political stage.
"Today, we have alleviated the long-standing Turkey-Canada disconnect. Now, we are starting a new era between Turkey and Canada," Erdogan said. The two sides expect to raise their trade volume from $3 billion first to $5 billion and then to $10 billion, he said, without giving a timeframe.
Canadian and Turkish negotiators will kick off the first round of free trade talks next month in Ankara, Carney said, adding that Export Development Canada and Turkey's Eximbank would sign a new deal to boost companies' cooperation on projects in third nations.
Carney referenced the need to move forward with Turkey amid the "rupture" and "new world order," though neither he nor Erdogan mentioned the United States. Carney will meet prominent Turkish business leaders and investors in Istanbul on Friday.
In the energy sector, Canada and Turkey pledged to ramp up collaboration in areas such as nuclear energy, critical minerals, and liquefied natural gas.
Reuters first reported this week that the countries planned to sign a declaration deepening cooperation in the four areas outlined on Thursday.
Decreasing focus on rights
Although trade between Canada and Turkey is tiny, Turkey accounted for less than 0.3% of Canada’s total merchandise trade, or C$4.34 billion ($3.09 billion); bilateral trade has risen nearly 50% in the past five years.
Still, Canada sends nearly 70% of exports to the US.
"This trip is part of the geopolitical necessity of signaling to Americans that we are not sitting around waiting for them," said Bessma Momani, professor of political science at the University of Waterloo.
In the last year, Canada has signed more than 20 trade deals as part of Carney’s push to double non-US exports in the next decade. This included a trip to China to reset fractured relations, which was criticized because Canadian authorities previously said Beijing had interfered in at least two federal elections. China says it does not interfere in other countries' internal affairs.
Turkey's crackdown on the opposition since 2024 and new arrests targeting the LGBTQ+ community since September have drawn criticism from rights groups and some European officials. Ankara says the judiciary is independent, denying that investigations or court cases are politically motivated.
Carney has focused less on rights than his predecessors, analysts say.
"Carney will have to walk a very fine line in Turkey between opening new economic possibilities for Canada while trying to maintain Canada's middle power role in fighting for equality," said Anna Agathangelou, a professor of politics at York University.
Nuclear plant
At the NATO leaders' summit in July, Carney and Erdogan launched negotiations for a free-trade agreement, and Turkey also agreed to join Canada’s Defense, Security and Resilience Bank as a founding member.
Turkey has held talks with Canadian engineering firm AtkinsRealis as well as South Korea's Korea Electric Power Corporation and China's State Power Investment Corporation about potentially building its planned second and third nuclear power plants.
In 2024, Canada removed weapons-export controls on Turkey, including on optical technology used in drones that Turkey exports to dozens of nations. Canada mainly exports lentils, aircraft and electronics to Turkey, and imports medical devices, fishing vessels, aircraft engines and jewelry.

EU entering winter with lowest gas reserves on record, IEA boss warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
06:02:15 UTC
15:02:15 KST

EU entering winter with lowest gas reserves on record, IEA boss warns
Al Jazeera interviews Fatih Birol in Berlin as the Iran war disrupts global energy supplies.
Berlin, Germany – Europe is entering winter with historically low gas reserves and cannot withstand further supply shocks, Fatih Birol, head of the International Energy Agency, has warned, as the US-Israel war on Iran disrupts global supply chains.
Speaking to Al Jazeera on the sidelines of an international conference in Berlin on Wednesday, Birol said all regions are being hit by energy disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz but that Europe is particularly vulnerable and will likely face rising costs of liquefied natural gas (LNG) in the coming months – even if peace returns to the Gulf today.
“The best day for a ceasefire would have been yesterday,” the energy economist, whose agency advises wealthy member nations and coordinates emergency responses, said.
“Normally before the winter, European countries have a lot of gas stocks, but the gas stocks we have while we are entering this winter are much lower than historical averages,” he said, adding that Europe’s gas is competing with that of Asian countries, which are even more dependent on the Middle East.
“I think if we have a harsh winter, we may see higher prices of natural gas in Europe,” Birol said, adding that the increasingly political nature of energy adds to the uncertainty. “Life will not be easy for Europe this year and also next year.”
European nations have long relied on imported gas to generate electricity for industries and warm homes in the freezing winter. Nearly a 10th of the continent’s LNG transited through the Hormuz Strait before the war. However, Iran’s attacks on vessels have plummeted imports.
As the winter chill settles, the European Union’s natural gas storage is only 72 percent full, down from the usual 90 percent. The shortfall is equivalent to the energy needed to power 10 to 12 million homes, analysts say.
EU energy ministers are now mulling over whether they should ask households and businesses to ration consumption, according to news reports.
Birol said he had long thought about the dangers of relying on the Strait of Hormuz. In fact, he said, his standard question to recruits seeking to join his agency was often: What would they do if the strait shuts down today?
The fallout has hardly come as a surprise. The flare-ups in the alternative Bab al-Mandeb strait, he added, have only worsened things.
“World leaders, how do they think?” Birol, who was born in Turkiye, said in his usual measured tone.
“I am really disappointed that governments didn’t take the necessary measures. Now, everybody is in a hurry, taking measures; the Middle East countries are building new pipelines, expanding the new pipelines that are bypassing the Strait of Hormuz … but in my view, these efforts should have been done much earlier.”
Europe’s historical over-reliance to blame
The EU, whose ageing refineries have processed less crude in recent years, also faces shortages of imported refined products such as the diesel that powers the bloc’s trucking, agricultural and industrial sectors.
Birol said Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries were also behind a looming diesel scarcity. About a third of Russian deliveries have stopped coming, he said.
When the Group of Seven (G7) nations agreed to push 400 million barrels of crude and diesel from their strategic reserves in March, it was Birol who coordinated how those emergency stocks reached global markets – the third time he has had to oversee emergency stock releases since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
For years, the energy economist said, his agency warned that the bloc was too tethered to Russia’s fuel, and that it had turned away too early from nuclear-generated power, which gave countries domestic leverage.
When Russia invaded Ukraine, his warnings manifested after Moscow cut gas supplies in retaliation for sanctions. The EU plans to permanently phase out Russian gas, but amid the Gulf crisis, members like France have again stepped up orders.
Price buffers stretched
Industry experts say emergency reserves that hit the market have limited use, as some estimate only a few months will be covered.
But Birol argued that his agency recorded real impact – a $20 drop in soaring oil prices immediately after the G7 countries agreed to release 100 billion barrels of crude oil and diesel earlier this month.
Prices are, however, on the rise again. Gas has surged by 140 percent since February, and Brent crude is trading well above $100.
Whatever happens now, the war will be felt for months, Birol pointed out, adding that it has irrevocably altered how energy will travel around the world.
It is also altering Europe’s politics, Birol noted. Russia has wielded gas as a weapon. And populist parties, from France to Germany, are capturing growing public anger to frame mainstream governments as incompetent.
“I have never ever seen the dark and long shadow of geopolitics so dominant in the energy sector,” Birol mused. “The world has gone through so many difficult periods, but this is the worst in terms of the geopolitics dominating the energy game. Energy is not currently considered a business but a political leverage. As an energy man, this worries me.”
The EU still has about 80 percent of its emergency stocks, and Birol hopes he will not have to oversee a fourth release. But the world’s supply can’t take more shocks, he said.
“I really hope that both of the straits will be unconditionally opened sometime soon; otherwise, in the energy world, we don’t have much more buffer zones to still keep the prices at a certain level (as) we have today,” he concluded.

The Defence Universities Alliance was established to connect the department with universities on research, skills and careers. Universities carry statutory duties on freedom of speech under the Higher Education (Freedom of Speech) Act 2023, which apply irrespective of their research partnerships.
Encampments and occupations over university links with defence companies have taken place at institutions across Britain since 2023, and a number of universities have reviewed their investment and research arrangements.
John McDonnell, the member for Hayes and Harlington, asked about the alliance earlier this month and established that membership carries no departmental funding, which this publication reported at the time.

2,800-year-old bone flute found at Troy, the first in 160 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
05:54:29 UTC
14:54:29 KST

This photo shows the bone flute (top), the site’s first musical instrument, and a 4,500-year-old idol head.
In a historic breakthrough at the UNESCO World Heritage site of ancient Troy, archaeologists have discovered a 2,800-year-old bone flute, the site’s first musical instrument in more than 160 years of digs, together with a 4,500-year-old idol head.
Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy announced the discoveries from the 2026 excavation season, saying the flute provided direct archaeological evidence of musical culture at Troy.
Discovered in deposits dating to the Archaic Period, the bone flute is the only musical instrument ever found in over 160 years of excavations at Troy. Dating to approximately 750-480 B.C., the instrument provides evidence of music in a period when it played an important role in religious rituals as well as social and public life.
The preservation of the flute’s head section, attached to its body, will help researchers assess its structure and function. The survival of instruments made from organic materials is particularly rare, further increasing the significance of the discovery.
Wind instruments, including panpipes known as the syrinx, were used in the ancient world, with some associated with the cult of Dionysus and related rituals.
The human-shaped idol head was discovered near the city gate of Troy II and dates to around 2500 B.C. The find offers new evidence for research into Early Bronze Age culture and the symbolic traditions of western Anatolia.
Small human-shaped idols are characteristic archaeological finds from the third millennium B.C. in western Anatolia. Similar examples discovered at Troy and other regional settlements help researchers investigate production and use traditions as well as cultural interactions.

‘Harem Ballet’ continues its 28-year journey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
05:53:48 UTC
14:53:48 KST

‘Harem’ explores the mysterious world of the Ottoman palace, the lives of women in the imperial harem and the musical culture of the period.
“Harem Ballet,” staged by director and choreographer Merih Çimenciler in 1998 as part of celebrations marking the 700th anniversary of the Ottoman Empire, continues to meet audiences 28 years later, with successive generations of dancers bringing the production to life.
The ballet explores the mysterious world of the Ottoman palace, the lives of women in the imperial harem and the musical culture of the period. It has been performed on numerous stages in Türkiye and abroad.
Staged by the Ankara State Opera and Ballet, the production has played to full houses for 28 years, earning a place among Türkiye’s longest-running ballets.
Speaking to state-run Anadolu Agency, Çimenciler said he had never imagined the work would remain on stage for so long.
“I never thought, when it was first staged years ago, that it would last 28 years. Moreover, there are no empty seats at any performance, so it is certainly wonderful to see the venue packed with audiences,” he said.
Çimenciler said the public’s enduring interest in Ottoman history, the story’s realism and the use of Turkish music had helped sustain the ballet’s popularity.
He emphasized that the imperial harem should not be viewed solely as a place associated with sultans and palace life, noting that women living there underwent extensive education.
“I believe audiences have shown great interest because it was an academy. The women received training, took music lessons, read books and went on to become mothers of princes,” he said.
Çimenciler said he had conducted extensive research into the imperial harem and spent three years preparing the production, drawing on historical sources.
“What makes this work valuable is its realism. Telling Ottoman history through the performing arts has resonated with audiences, which is why it continues to attract interest every year,” he said.
Traditional Turkish music meets ballet
One of the production’s distinctive features is its combination of ballet with traditional Turkish musical instruments, including the ney, kanun, bendir and davul, alongside piano and orchestral music.
The ballet incorporates compositions by prominent Turkish composers such as İsmail Dede Efendi and Hacı Arif Bey. Çimenciler said he sought to integrate the music with the events unfolding on stage, making it part of the narrative rather than merely an accompaniment to the dancing.
The production was also staged at the Shanghai Expo in 2010, where it attracted audiences from different cultural backgrounds. It has appeared at various festivals abroad and was included in the repertoire of Germany’s Dortmund Staatsoper.
Over the past 28 years, successive generations of dancers have joined the production, making each season a renewed journey for its choreographer.
Çimenciler praised the dancers’ national and international achievements, saying their performances contributed to the production’s quality.
“I experience a different excitement at every rehearsal. They are very good because my dancers are extraordinary,” he said.
He added that some audience members had watched the ballet more than once and that the strong response motivated the team to keep improving.
“We try to live up to our audience’s expectations and do good work,” he said.
Çimenciler said the production had received new invitations from abroad and that he hoped to continue representing Turkish ballet on international stages.
‘Humility is very important’
Now in his 57th year in the arts, Çimenciler has also created a ballet adaptation of Reşat Nuri Güntekin’s novel “Çalıkuşu,” a production about the martyrs of Çanakkale and the work “Fırat.”
He said dedication to work and humility were essential to a lasting artistic career.
“I love working, but I never like becoming conceited. People should always remain humble, and that is what I try to do,” he said.
His interest in history has shaped much of his artistic work. Recalling that he played Hürrem Sultan at a young age, Çimenciler said Ottoman history had always held a special place in his life.
He added that the Ottoman palace and harem continued to fascinate audiences in different countries, with the ballet offering a glimpse into that historical world.
Çimenciler said he hoped “Harem Ballet” would continue reaching audiences in different countries and venues, stressing the importance of representing Türkiye internationally.
“Wherever our country wants us to represent it successfully, we will be ready to go,” he said.
The ballet will return to Ankara for its first performances of the new season at Atatürk Arts Center, a different venue from its previous performances.
Thanking audiences for their support over nearly three decades, Çimenciler said, “I thank our audience time and again for their interest, attention and appreciation over these 28 years, and extend my respects on behalf of the State Ballet.”

“We built a wall and wire fence along the Zap River and installed a concrete barrier system on the highway edge,” he said. Safety was the priority, he said.
The project combines riverside recreation with winter precautions in a region where snow and avalanches occur from December to March.

Global delegates gathering in Antalya for the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) will be treated to authentic local specialties, including “şiş köfte,” “piyaz” and “kabak tatlısı” as Türkiye puts its Mediterranean cuisine on the world stage.
The conference, to be held from Nov. 9 to 20, will bring thousands of participants from around 200 countries to Antalya. Preparations are underway for accommodation, catering, exhibitions and conference venues, with plans to showcase the city’s cultural and gastronomic identity alongside the climate agenda.
The 1,200-decare conference site will be divided into two sections: The Blue Zone, reserved for world leaders and high-level participants, and the Green Zone, open to civil society and other visitors.
An Antalya House will be established in the Green Zone to introduce visitors to the region’s traditional cuisine and geographically indicated products. Geographical indication status identifies products whose qualities or reputation are linked to a particular place of origin.
Yavuz Tekelioğlu, head of the Local Products and Geographical Indications Research Network, said both registered products and other regional specialties would be presented to heads of state, government officials and civil society representatives.
“Antalya’s products registered with geographical indications, as well as its unregistered local delicacies, will be introduced at the Antalya House to guests arriving from around 200 countries,” Tekelioğlu said.
He added that showcasing local products at an international event of this scale could support efforts to secure geographical indication registrations abroad, helping protect regional specialties. Companies selected to present the food are continuing preparations for the summit.
In the Blue Zone, where leaders and senior officials will gather, “şiş köfte,” grilled minced meat shaped around skewers, will be served alongside “piyaz,” a traditional bean salad often prepared with tahini in Antalya, and “kabak tatlısı,” a dessert made from sweetened pumpkin.
Cem Yıldırım, a third-generation restaurateur heading one of the participating establishments, shared that conference organizers gave high marks during a recent menu tasting, adding that the event offers an ideal platform to promote Antalya through gastronomy tourism.

Fortnite returns to Apple's Australian app stores after landmark case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
05:52:13 UTC
14:52:13 KST

Apple forced to change app store rules in a win for roughly 15 million Australian users
The Federal Court has ordered Apple to open up its devices to other app stores, as part of a landmark finding that the tech giant violated Australian competition law.
It's a fundamental shift for an estimated 15 million Australian Apple users, who will soon be able to download apps from the open web as well as rival app stores as a result.
The company has until March 2027 to make the changes, Federal Court Justice Jonathan Beach ruled on Thursday.
It's the latest chapter in a six-year anti-trust legal battle between Apple and the game developer behind Fortnite, Epic Games, spanning Europe, UK, the US and Australia.
The long-awaited judgement sets out the consequences of the Federal Court's decision in August last year in which both Apple and Google were found to have misused their market power in how their app stores were run.
Epic Games, and lawyers in a parallel class action, had long alleged Apple and Google were running illegal monopolies, by effectively banning other app stores from their devices and forcing apps to use their payment platform, where they collect between 15 and 30 per cent in fees.
The iPhone maker had cited security and intellectual property concerns in its defence throughout the case.
Now, as a result of yesterday's decision Apple will also have to permit the use of alternative payment methods, as well as allowing alternative app stores.
Consumer advocates are hopeful the changes will result in increased competition and lower prices for millions of Apple users.
In publishing his reasons, Justice Beach said Apple had contravened the Competition and Consumer Act with an "intricate web of terms and technical measures", and ordered the company to pay 85 per cent of Epic Games' legal costs from the months-long trial.
The decision signals the immediate return of one of the world's most popular games, Fortnite, to Apple's Australian app store from today, after a six-year hiatus.
Apple told Reuters it disagreed with many of the court's findings and would seek to challenge them.
"We will request a stay and appeal the outcome to seek a resolution that respects our intellectual property and protects the safe, secure experience that consumers and developers expect from the App Store," an Apple spokesperson said.

The magnitude 7 earthquake that struck Tibet in southwestern China has injured 65 people, while the death toll remains at 16, local authorities said on Friday.
The quake struck Baqen County in Nagqu City late on Thursday, according to state news agency Xinhua. The high-altitude region is sparsely populated.
Chinese President Xi Jinping ordered all-out search and rescue efforts for missing people and prompt medical treatment for the injured following the earthquake.
China raised its national earthquake emergency response from Level IV to Level III on Friday, according to the Ministry of Emergency Management, and dispatched a work team to guide and assist rescue and relief operations.
China's National Fire and Rescue Force sent 350 rescuers and 83 vehicles to the affected area. As of 6.30 am on Friday (2230 GMT on Thursday), 120 rescuers and 27 vehicles had arrived, while the remaining personnel and vehicles were on their way.
Authorities also mobilised emergency supplies, including 1,000 prefabricated housing units, 3,239 tents, 2,821 folding beds and 4,280 quilts, Xinhua reported.
More than 300 police officers, including traffic and community police personnel, were also sent to the epicentre to assist with rescue and emergency relief operations, the Nagqu police department said in a post on WeChat early on Friday.
Officers assessed damage to homes and helped residents move to safer locations. A video posted by police on Douyin, China's version of TikTok, showed officers loading supplies into a truck in the dark and inspecting a building and rubble with flashlights.
More than 12,000 people have been safely relocated, Xinhua reported. Videos released earlier by local official media showed residents leaving their homes and seeking shelter outdoors or in cars parked along the streets. One resident said the strong tremor woke them up and caused their house to creak.
Damage assessment and aftershocks
The US Geological Survey (USGS) said the earthquake struck at a depth of 10 kilometres, about 183 kilometres from Nagqu.
The agency issued a yellow alert for earthquake-related deaths, indicating that casualties were possible, and an orange alert for economic losses, warning that significant damage was likely and the impact could be widespread.
“Estimated economic losses are less than 1 percent of GDP of China. Past events with this alert level have required a regional or national level response,” the USGS said, adding that people in the region generally live in structures vulnerable to earthquake shaking.
The China Earthquake Networks Center said 413 aftershocks had been recorded.
In 2010, a magnitude 7.1 earthquake struck Yushu in neighbouring Qinghai province, killing at least 2,698 people and leaving nearly 300 missing.

Türkiye’s low debt levels strengthen its ability to withstand economic shocks and sustain growth, Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek said on Oct. 22.
Speaking at the 19th Verona Eurasian Economic Forum in Istanbul, Şimşek said the global economy was facing a difficult period marked by volatility and uncertainty.
He described the current energy supply shock as seven times as large as the one experienced in 2022.
High indebtedness posed another major challenge, he said, with total debt exceeding 300 percent of global output and the ratio in emerging markets surpassing 230 percent.
Türkiye was better placed to respond to shocks because of its relatively low debt burden, Şimşek said.
The country’s budget deficit-to-GDP ratio was approximately half the emerging-market average, while its public debt-to-GDP ratio was around one-third of the corresponding average, he added.
Şimşek said Türkiye’s economy was expected to reach approximately $1.8 trillion this year at current exchange rates, or about $4 trillion in purchasing power parity terms. He also pointed to the country’s large population and strong infrastructure.
The minister acknowledged that high inflation remained a challenge, saying the government was pursuing comprehensive policies to bring it down.
He described President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and his economic team as business-friendly and pledged support for companies operating in Türkiye.
“If you choose to conduct all or part of your business in Türkiye, we want to assist you,” he said.

Türkiye and Canada launched a strategic partnership on Oct. 22, signing agreements on defense, air transport and energy and agreeing to begin free trade negotiations before the end of the year.
President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney adopted a three-year action plan during talks at the presidential complex in Ankara.
The trip marked the first bilateral visit to Türkiye by a Canadian prime minister.
“We are now starting a new era between Türkiye and Canada,” Erdoğan told a joint press conference.
Erdoğan said the two countries aimed to raise annual bilateral trade from around $3 billion to $5 billion initially, and eventually to $10 billion.
Carney said the first round of free trade negotiations would take place in Ankara in November.
The updated air transport agreement would nearly double direct flights between the two countries, Erdoğan said.
Türkiye will also host the next meeting of their Joint Economic and Trade Committee in 2027, with private sector participation.
The leaders discussed joint investments in third countries, with Erdoğan pointing to opportunities across Africa, Latin America and Asia.
A planned agreement between Türk Eximbank and Export Development Canada would support such projects, he said.
The defense memorandum was signed by Defense Industries Presidency head Haluk Görgün and Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand.
It builds on an earlier defense cooperation agreement and aims to expand partnerships between companies in the two NATO allies.
Carney said the agreement would create jobs and export opportunities while improving security and strengthening NATO.
“Allies must be able to rely on each other for equipment and capabilities that keep us safe,” he said.
Erdoğan also said the Canada-led Defense, Security and Resilience Bank, being established to finance allied defense industries, could support bilateral cooperation.
On energy, the two countries signed a joint declaration covering cooperation in areas including liquefied natural gas, nuclear power, mining and critical minerals.
Erdoğan said the declaration reflected significant potential for joint work, particularly in nuclear energy.
Carney described Türkiye as “an exceptional partner,” citing its economy, strategic location and defense industry.
He also praised Ankara’s role in efforts to resolve conflicts involving Gaza, Ukraine and Iran.
The leaders discussed developments in Gaza, Ukraine and the Gulf. Erdoğan said they shared the view that diplomacy should open the way to lasting peace in Ukraine and the Gulf.
He also welcomed Canadian sanctions targeting Israeli settlement activity as a step toward deterring violations by the Israeli government.
Erdoğan said the strategic partnership would produce concrete results, rather than remain a symbolic commitment on paper.
Carney was due to meet business leaders and investors in Istanbul on Oct. 23.
Erdoğan said he also planned to visit Canada with business representatives.
In his remarks, Carney quoted Mustafa Kemal Atatürk’s principle, “Peace at home, peace in the world,” in Turkish.

Parliament passes law on fund repayments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
05:37:11 UTC
14:37:11 KST

Parliament approved legislation on Oct. 22 allowing interim payments of up to 1 million Turkish Liras to eligible investors in troubled funds and setting rules for recovering assets to cover losses.
The measure will take effect after presidential approval and publication in the Official Gazette.
It covers funds ordered into liquidation by the Capital Markets Board (SPK) on Sept. 17 whose liquidation remains unfinished.
An amendment adopted during the parliamentary debate also includes investors whose redemption orders were submitted on or before Sept. 17 but could not be completed because the funds defaulted or stopped publishing unit prices.
Interim payments will be based on investors’ actual cash deposits and withdrawals, without inflation adjustment, and deducted from their final settlement.
Investors with net investments below 1 million liras may receive that amount, while those above the threshold will be eligible for a maximum of 1 million liras.
If available cash is insufficient, the SPK may prioritize investors with the smallest net investments or set a common minimum interim payment.
Except for money market funds, payments also cannot exceed the value of investors’ holdings calculated for the payment date.
Where fund assets fall short of pre-liquidation valuations, net investment calculations for final settlement will include an inflation adjustment based on the average change in consumer and domestic producer price indices.
The legislation places primary responsibility for losses on the portfolio management companies that founded or managed the funds.
If recovery from those companies is insufficient or impossible, individuals and companies identified by the SPK as responsible, including those acting jointly with them, will be personally liable.
The Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (TMSF) will pursue recovery from their assets, with proceeds held in separate accounts for each fund.
Where appointed as trustee, it will be able to sell assets before court proceedings conclude.
The law also allows voluntary returns of gains exceeding an inflation-adjusted benchmark.
Those found by the SPK to have participated in market abuse, insider trading or manipulation will be excluded from payments.
The SPK may authorize alternative asset sales, including off-exchange transactions, to protect investors’ recovery values.
Meanwhile, cash payments and asset transfers have reached 49.7 billion liras across 55,755 accounts, the Communications Directorate said following an Oct. 22 meeting of the Fund Coordination Board chaired by Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz.
The number of funds still undergoing liquidation has fallen from 131 to 47. Liquidation of 18 of Hedef Portföy’s 31 funds was completed by Oct. 21, with 8.9 billion liras paid to 10,008 accounts.
Work continues on its remaining 13 funds.
In the related criminal investigation, five more suspects, including former ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) lawmaker Ertan Aydın, were detained, bringing the number taken into custody in the latest operation to 31.
A court also ordered 11 suspects remanded in custody.

Caught out in a record-breaking storm: Why we didn't see it coming
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
05:34:04 UTC
14:34:04 KST

IN BRIEF:
- Rainfall and flash floods in south-east Queensland on Thursday far exceeded forecasts.
- Experts say that while weather forecasting is always improving, climate change has complicated things.
A freak storm tore through south-east Queensland on Thursday, dumping more than 200mm of rain in three hours, leading to flash floods and hundreds of State Emergency Service calls.
Between Wednesday and Friday morning, at least eight weather stations just north of Brisbane in the catchments of the Pine and Caboolture rivers recorded huge 48-hour rainfall totals exceeding 300mm, according to weather tracking site Weatherzone.
While initial forecasts from the Bureau of Meteorology (BoM) predicted that Thursday would be the wettest day of the week in parts of Queensland, the severity of the downpour was unprecedented. Monthly rainfall records were broken in Nambour on the Sunshine Coast, where a running total of 401mm to Friday morning broke the old October record of 370.6mm, and in Beerburrum, in the same region, where the running monthly total rainfall of 354.2mm broke the old October record of 311.5mm.
Earlier this week, the BoM was questioned over false rainfall predictions later revealed to be caused by Bogong Moth migration. There were other times when its forecasts were off track, including in August, when Queensland rain outpaced forecasts, and after the 2023-2024 summer, when the El Niño weather event the bureau had predicted failed to materialise.
Senior lecturer in climate science at the University of Melbourne, Andrew King, said that while weather forecasts have improved immensely over time, "that doesn't mean they're always perfect", especially when it comes to forecasting thunderstorms and rainfall.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"Small-scale storms, which can dump a lot of rainfall and have major impacts, are still hard to predict precisely, as it's difficult to forecast exactly where they'll occur, and that can mean forecast accuracy suffers, even over short timeframes."
Smaller weather events like the thunderstorms in Queensland over the past few days are harder to represent in the models meteorologists use to simulate the atmosphere, he said.
Dr Michael Barnes from Monash University's School of Earth, Atmosphere and Environment told SBS News that while there had been vast improvements to the technology used to forecast weather, there were "limits to what is physically possible".
"Events such as thunderstorms that deliver 200 millimetres of rain within 24 hours are driven by highly localised atmospheric processes," he said.
"When weather is highly localised, even a small error can mean the storm's path or location isn't forecast particularly well.
"We often cannot know exactly where those storms will form or how intense they will become."
Weather forecasts are improving
"A seven-day forecast today is about as accurate as a two-day forecast was 40 years ago," Barnes said.
"There have been three major drivers of improved weather forecasting: better scientific understanding, greater computing power, and more observations.
"Twenty years ago, a forecast might have said that moderate rain was expected tomorrow afternoon. Today, people have weather apps that provide hourly rainfall forecasts and detailed estimates of expected precipitation."
But he said that also meant expectations of weather forecasting have become much higher.
King agreed that there were higher expectations on the BoM, which he said had "certainly" come under scrutiny in recent years.
"Part of that is because Australians are relatively knowledgeable about climate drivers such as El Niño and La Niña. However, that understanding can sometimes become oversimplified."
But he warned that general understanding can sometimes "oversimplify" complex systems.
"People often hear 'El Niño' and assume conditions will be hot and dry. In reality, El Niño merely increases the likelihood of those outcomes; it doesn't guarantee them."
Many factors influence Australia's weather, including the Indian Ocean, the Southern Ocean, Antarctica and tropical regions to the north.
"El Niño and La Niña are only part of the picture," he said.
"To be fair to the Bureau, it has tried to shift attention away from a narrow focus on those weather events and encourage people to pay more attention to seasonal outlooks, which incorporate all these influences."
SBS News has contacted the BoM for comment.
Climate change 'complicates' perceptions
When it comes to severe weather events, Barnes said, climate change "complicates things".
"Particularly in situations like the recent event in south-east Queensland, there is good evidence that daily and even sub-daily rainfall extremes are intensifying, primarily driven by thunderstorms," he said.
Produced by "the inherent chaos of the atmosphere", thunderstorms would continue to be challenging to predict.
While climate change doesn't necessarily reduce meteorologists' technical ability to forecast weather, it can affect how forecast accuracy is perceived.
Difficult-to-predict weather phenomena, such as localised severe thunderstorms, may be becoming "more consequential".
"As a result, it can appear that forecasts are becoming less reliable when, in reality, the impacts are increasing," Barnes said.
King from the University of Melbourne said climate scientists had discussed the tendency for "El Niño to become a scapegoat for everything that's happening in the climate system".
When people see severe weather during a strong El Niño, they naturally assume El Niño is the cause; however, climate change is operating in the background and is amplifying many extreme weather events.
"Climate change hasn't gone away. It's continuing to worsen as greenhouse gas emissions increase."
And climate change is "already" making extreme weather events worse, particularly heatwaves, which in Australia are more intense, more frequent and longer-lasting because of climate change.
But he said that as Australia's weather worsened, he understood the tendency to attribute severe weather to big events like El Niño and La Niña.
"There's a natural human desire to make sense of things that are difficult to understand," he said.
"Weather and climate are complicated, and reality is often more complex than it first appears."

Kazakhstan also secured the top two places in the women’s 55-kilometer road race. Anastassiya Kalaus and pilot Polina Bratchikova won gold in 2 hours, 5 minutes and 47 seconds, while Zhuldyz Kainarova and pilot Anzhela Solovyeva took silver with a time of 2 hours, 9 minutes and 43 seconds.
The results gave Kazakhstan a clean sweep of the gold and silver medals in both road races, adding four medals to the national team’s tally.
After the seventh day of competition at the 5th Asian Para Games, Kazakhstan had won 47 medals in total: 12 gold, 15 silver and 20 bronze.

Mecanoo Releases New Images of the Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen Renovation in Rotterdam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
05:30:00 UTC
14:30:00 KST

Delft-based practice Mecanoo has just released images of the renovation project for the Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen in Rotterdam, the Netherlands. The first images of the project were released in 2020, when the practice unveiled a proposal for a new wing as part of a larger renovation of the existing Museum Garden and a general reorganization of the layout to clarify circulation and connections throughout the complex. The comprehensive project includes a new building, the restoration and interior design of the existing premises, and a landscape project. The site, which has been closed since 2019 due to fire risk, water issues, overdue maintenance, and the presence of substantial amounts of asbestos, is a national monument expected to meet the updated standards and logistical requirements of an art institution of its kind.
The Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen is one of the oldest museums in the Netherlands, housing works ranging from the early Middle Ages to contemporary art. Its 25,000 m² museum complex is composed of buildings designed by architects Adriaan Van der Steur in 1935, Alexander Bodon in 1972, and Hubert-Jan Henket in 1991, all of which are listed monuments. Over the years, the complex has been partially renovated, becoming an increasingly complex environment. Among the identified problems are the difficulty of finding the entrance, visitor orientation, numerous level changes within the buildings, and the overall difficulty of safely unloading artworks. The new project by Mecanoo introduces a comprehensive vision for the premises, including a new entrance area with a museum shop, additional exhibition spaces, distinct circulation routes for people and goods, educational spaces, a café, an event space, a logistics centre, storage depots, offices, workshops, facility spaces, and a new landscape design.
The main entrance will be at the heart of the building ensemble, which comprises the three heritage buildings and the new wing designed by Mecanoo. Visitors will arrive through the original Van der Steur gate at the Buitenhof outer courtyard, framed by three façades of Van der Steur's distinctive brick building, which is primarily dedicated to the museum's permanent collection. The fourth façade will be transformed into a new transparent envelope called the "Connector," while the building's classical interior museum atmosphere will be restored and made more accessible through adjustments to the level changes. The Van der Steur wing will remain accessible through the "Hollandse Trap," the historic Dutch Staircase, which will be extended to connect with the new buildings and complemented by a new lift.
In addition to the outer Buitenhof courtyard, the Van der Steur wing has a Binnenhof inner courtyard, which will be covered with a patterned glass roof to improve energy efficiency and create a new space with an acoustic floor and varied levels for informal seating areas. The Buitenhof outer courtyard will be conceived as an adjacent open-air exhibition space. The Rotunda, a sunken circular patio at its centre, brings daylight down into the subterranean entrance hall. This new underground entrance area will house the information desk, museum shop, lockers, and toilets. The courtyard connects the Connector façade of the Van der Steur wing with the modern Bodon wing, which will primarily house temporary exhibitions. The Bodon building's large windows will be restored to reinstate the wing's original sense of space and light, while providing new views of the city.
The third heritage building, the Van Beuningen-De Vriese Pavilion by Henket, will be transformed into a restaurant designed as a garden pavilion within the redesigned sculpture garden. Distinguished by its high-tech, transparent design, it will offer views of the sculpture garden and reflecting pool. The stairs and lifts in the restaurant will be framed by a display reminiscent of a storage depot, showcasing the ceramics and household items once stored in the pavilion's basement. The restaurant will feature a new sheltered outdoor terrace accessible outside the museum's opening hours. According to Mecanoo, all three buildings will be renovated to improve their sustainability standards as much as possible. To allow for interventions in the original buildings, a 2003 addition by Robbrecht & Daem will be largely removed, with only the basement and part of the concrete structure retained, making way for a new logistical route for artwork and goods deliveries.
The area occupied by this rear addition will be repurposed for loading and unloading operations, which will be concentrated on the east side of the complex. The movement of artworks, goods, and waste will remain out of public view and follow dedicated routes through a sunken facilities centre on the south side of the Bodon wing. Above the loading dock, a new recessed volume will house the museum workshop on the first floor. A new non-climate-controlled space will be created for emerging artists. This two-storey exhibition space will feature crafted brickwork to match the original Bodon and Van der Steur buildings, reinforcing the identity of the museum complex as a cohesive whole.
The renovation of this heritage ensemble dedicated to the arts adds to Mecanoo's portfolio of recent projects. The firm recently completed the Lawson Centre for Sustainability, the first new building for the historic facilities of Trinity College in Toronto since 1979. One of the most anticipated projects of 2026, it was designed to be one of Canada's most advanced sustainability-driven academic and residential buildings. The firm also designed a museum facility in Abu Dhabi: a new Natural History Museum that opened in November 2025. Covering more than 35,000 m², the design is intended to resonate with natural rock formations. Geometry acts as the museum's unifying theme, with pentagonal shapes referencing cellular structures. Mecanoo was also a finalist in the Shift International Architecture Competition, following the company's call to establish a new standard for a purpose-driven destination that turns circular living into "something individuals, companies, and organisations can feel, experience, and act on."

Asia-Pacific Community: Chinese-built solar project supports Vietnam's green energy transition
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:11:23 CST
14:11:23 KST

GIA LAI, Vietnam, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Across a vast stretch of white sandy land once considered unsuitable for cultivation in central Vietnam's Gia Lai province, rows upon rows of solar panels shimmer under the tropical sun, turning the landscape into a source of clean electricity.
The Phu My Solar Power Plant, with a total installed capacity of 330 MWp, covers more than 323 hectares and comprises over 750,000 photovoltaic panels, making it one of Vietnam's largest solar power projects.
"Each year, the project can provide about 520 million kWh of clean electricity and reduce carbon dioxide emissions by around 400,000 tonnes," said Zhang Huibing, general manager of the Asia-Pacific headquarters of PowerChina's Jiangxi Electric Power Engineering Co., Ltd.
Power Construction Corporation of China (PowerChina) undertook the Phu My project on an engineering, procurement and construction basis, covering design, procurement of equipment and materials, and construction.
The contribution comes as Vietnam works toward its pledge, made at the 26th United Nations Climate Change Conference in 2021, to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050.
In the first half of 2026, solar power generated 14.59 billion kWh of electricity, accounting for about 8.5 percent of Vietnam's total electricity output, compared with 54.5 percent from coal-fired power and 21 percent from hydropower, according to state utility Vietnam Electricity.
Vietnam's electricity demand is also rising alongside economic growth, with the Ministry of Industry and Trade saying the country's goal of annual economic growth of at least 10 percent through the end of the decade will require more power for industrial production, industrial parks and broader economic activity.
Hoang Quoc Dung, an executive board member of the Vietnam Association for Conservation of Nature and Environment, said Vietnam has seen a surge in energy demand in recent years, while climate change is severely affecting the southern part of the country.
"Chinese companies are playing a very significant role in advancing the green transition in Vietnam and other Southeast Asian countries," Dung said, adding that their participation has helped lower equipment costs, shorten construction periods and accelerate the expansion of renewable energy capacity.
The project's impact extends beyond the electricity fed into the grid.
"The project has transformed 323.5 hectares of low-value white sandy land into land with economic value," said Huynh Tan Huy, deputy general director of Clean Energy Vision Development Joint Stock Company, the plant's operator.
The project has also created jobs and opportunities for local workers to acquire technical skills.
PowerChina said it created about 3,100 jobs during construction and provided technical training to more than 500 local personnel, helping build a Vietnamese workforce with experience in solar power construction and operation.
Tran Thanh Tung joined the plant shortly after graduating from university and has now worked there for about six years, receiving training in equipment operation and maintenance while working alongside Chinese specialists.
"The Chinese colleagues are very friendly and easygoing, and they are always willing to help the plant whenever problems occur," Tung told Xinhua.
For Tung, the project has also provided stable employment close to home.
"It gives us a stable and long-term source of income as local people who have the opportunity to work here," he added. ■

An upper-level trough that supercharged rainfall and thunderstorms across south-east Queensland is moving out to sea, having wreaked havoc with flash floods and emergency calls.
Torrential rain caused flooding, water rescues and hundreds of calls for help from emergency services on Thursday, with several schools forced to close on Friday.
Bureau of Meteorology meteorologist Robert Urbaniak told the Australian Associated Press the silver lining in the forecast was that an upper-atmosphere trough, which had given rainfall totals and thunderstorms an "additional kick", had moved out to sea.
"So while it will still be a rainy few days in south-eastern Queensland, it just won't be anywhere near the scale we got yesterday," he said.
More than 300 mm of rain fell in southeast Queensland in the past two days, according to the Bureau of Meteorology (BoM).

The wet and stormy pattern is expected to continue through the weekend and expand into southern and southeastern parts of Australia, but conditions are expected to ease.
Severe thunderstorms may still develop across central and eastern inland Queensland, bringing damaging winds, heavy rainfall and large hail, the BoM warned.
The bureau still had minor flood warnings in place and one moderate warning across the region, Urbaniak added.
540 callouts

An ABC reporter and bystander swam to save a trapped man before his car was completely submerged at Morayfield, north of Brisbane.
Many roads remain closed due to floodwaters, and the State Emergency Service has responded to more than 540 callouts.
The City of Moreton Bay has urged residents to stay alert this weekend, with more showers forecast and many creeks still running high.
"Short bursts of heavy rain have potential to cause flash flooding quickly and with little warning," it said in a statement.
Parts of the city received more than 270mm of rain in 24 hours, with intense falls on Thursday morning causing flash flooding and road closures.
