Shanghai tea shop Basao draws on "Rockbund’s historic buildings"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Shanghai tea shop Basao draws on “Rockbund’s historic buildings”
Architect Keiji Ashizawa drew on the surrounding traditional architecture, as well as British studio David Chipperfield Architects‘ restoration of the district, when designing this tea shop and cafe in central Shanghai.
The flagship store for Chinese tea brand Basao combines a retail space with a cafe section where visitors can enjoy the tea.
Located in Shanghai’s Rockbund area, it is surrounded by historic architecture but sits in an area that was part of a restoration by David Chipperfield Architects.
Ashizawa, founder of Keiji Ashizawa Design (KAD), aimed to design an “open and inviting retail space” that would have a natural connection to the street.
“When designing an interior, we place great importance on understanding the building’s location, history, and relationship with its surroundings,” he told Dezeen.
“The restoration and regeneration work led by David Chipperfield Architects has also played an important role in shaping the district’s character.”
The studio used metal structure and details to reinterpret some of the area’s traditional architecture in a more contemporary way for the interior of Basao.
“Drawing inspiration from the arches and repeated architectural details of Rockbund’s historic buildings, we introduced a series of vaulted steel ceiling elements,” Ashizawa said.
“Together with the delicate steel shelving, they bring a sense of lightness and openness, while subtly connecting the retail and seating areas, each with its own distinct atmosphere.”
In a nod to the buildings in Xiamen, Fujian, where the Basao brand originated, KAD used a “plaster-like finish” inspired by rammed earth for the shop area.
“Rather than drawing directly from the traditional tea room, we explored the use of earth, a material deeply connected to tea culture, as a defining element of the interior,” Ashizawa explained.
“The retail area is bright and open, with earthen walls inspired by the traditional rammed-earth architecture of Fujian Province,” he continued.
“In contrast, the seating area features darker tones reminiscent of smoked timber, creating a more intimate atmosphere, much like the living room of a friend’s home.”
While the main materials used in the space are timber and steel, KAD also added a brick floor in the shop part of the 108-square-metre space, which is juxtaposed with the wooden floor in the cafe area.
“We chose brick for the flooring, a material commonly found in Rockbund’s historic architecture, particularly on building facades and occasionally on floors,” Ashizawa said.
The studio aimed for the material to tie the store into the neighbourhood while grounding the interior with its gridded pattern.
“The regular pattern of the brickwork creates a sense of rhythm and order, allowing the material to feel at home in a contemporary setting,” Ashizawa said.
In the retail area, the studio used a light colour palette to create an airy atmosphere that would underline the natural light from its floor-to-ceiling windows, while the shop space has deeper wood tones.
“Rather than relying on strong colours to define the space, we focused on the natural tones of wood and brick, along with the subtle interplay of light and shadow,” Ashizawa said.
“Bronze-colored metal finishes were also introduced as a reference to the historical use of copper in traditional Chinese tea utensils, creating a subtle connection to Chinese tea culture.”
The walls of the tea room were decorated with traditional Chinese lacquer Da Qi Hua pieces.
“The artistic concepts reflect Basao’s brand identity, while their colours were carefully selected to harmonise with the overall atmosphere of the space,” Ashizawa said.
Overall, the studio hopes that it has created a peaceful space in a busy part of the city.
“In a vibrant city like Shanghai, we see value in creating a space that remains connected to its surroundings while offering a sense of calm,” Ashizawa said.
“One of the most rewarding parts of this project was the opportunity to create such an experience through the culture of tea.”
KAD has previously designed a Nagoya coffee shop clad in locally produced tiles and created a restaurant that draws on the “whiteness of tofu”.

Tile: Yinji Tile Design
Furniture: Karimoku Case
Lighting plan: Aurora Inc / Yoshiki

Board of Directors of Bank of Russia to make decision on key interest rate
Unknown

04:58:42 UTC

MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. The Board of Directors of the Bank of Russia will make a decision on the key interest rate at a meeting later in the day. All 23 experts interviewed by TASS expect the regulator to keep the rate at 14% per annum.
The scope for lowering the rate is constrained by persistently high inflation, the secondary effects of rising fuel costs, and utility tariff hikes, as well as the fiscal stimulus expected toward the end of the year, according to analysts.
At its previous meeting in September, the Bank of Russia decided for the first time since June 2025 not to lower the key interest rate, maintaining it at 14% per annum. The regulator pointed then to an acceleration in the underlying growth of prices, reaching an annualized rate of 5-6%, primarily due to the impact of a temporary reduction in production capacity across certain sectors. At the same time, the Central Bank noted that the Russian economy was growing at a moderate pace in the third quarter of 2026.
According to experts surveyed, the available data point to the interest rate to be maintained at 14%. That said, some participants do not rule out a 25-basis-point cut, though they do not consider this the base case scenario.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered the city of Hebron to be cordoned off and for the entire West Bank to be blocked from entry and exit starting on Friday morning, after five people were wounded in a terror attack in the area carried out by Hamas terrorists.
"I have instructed the IDF and security forces to immediately impose a closure on the city of Hebron and prepare for a full lockdown of all of Judea and Samaria, beginning today," Netanyahu said, adding that the IDF would be carrying out extensive waves of arrests.
"We will pursue Hamas terrorists and those who send them, wherever they are and at any time," Netanyahu said. "You have nowhere to hide."
Two soldiers were killed, and three were lightly injured in the attack, according to the IDF.
The military had announced earlier that morning that two terrorists involved in the attack had been killed. The IDF and the Shin Bet are investigating whether the two terrorists were part of a small self-contained cell or whether their vast ammunition shows that they were connected to a larger terror cell.
There were no other terrorists involved.
Netanyahu also said that the military would be applying the methods used in refugee camps, with the IDF going house-to-house and dismantling the terror infrastructure.
The prime minister explained that the model would be used in Hebron, while it could be expanded to other cities in the future if it shows that it's an effective way to fight terrorism in the area.
"We also wish to make another promise: the Defense Minister and I have overseen the planning of a very extensive IDF operation in Judea and Samaria -- on a scale not seen since the Six-Day War. The IDF is prepared to carry it out; we will determine the timing, but it is coming," he added.
What happened in the Hamas-backed attack near Hebron?
The two Palestinian terrorists were traveling in a car with an M4 machine gun and a pistol toward the Yehuda junction.
IDF sources estimated that they intended to go past the junction to carry out a larger attack on Route 35, which has many civilians.
However, when they saw how many soldiers were present at the Yehuda junction checkpoint, they realized they would not get through and decided to attack the soldiers there. There were initially around four soldiers on site.
Magen David Adom said that five people had been wounded in the attack, with two in critical condition, one moderate, and two mild. The mildly and moderately wounded people were evacuated to the hospital.
The two critically wounded people are receiving medical care, MDA said in a statement.
"We brought a man in his 20s into the ambulance. He was unconscious, suffering from gunshot wounds, and in extremely serious condition. We provided him with medical treatment," said MDA emergency medical technician Zuriel Edri.
"We evacuated additional wounded people to MDA ambulances that had arrived at the scene and immediately began transporting them to hospitals. Another person in extremely serious condition was treated by IDF medical personnel in a mobile intensive care unit."
The company commander, deputy battalion commander, a nearby deputy battalion 101 commander, and their various soldiers came to reinforce the soldiers who were initially taken by surprise.
The reinforcement forces eventually overwhelmed and killed the two terrorists, Hamouda and Firas Jua'ba. According to Army Radio, the pair were from the same family in Hebron, both aged 27, and both married with two children each.
Next, the IDF said that it had surrounded and cut off the Hebron and Chalchul areas to avoid copycat attacks and to arrest all potentially connected nearby Palestinians.
In addition, the IDF announced it would map out the houses of the two terrorists for sealing off and for eventual demolition, following the relevant legal proceedings.
The IDF also said that it would be checking all cars in the Jebin, Nablus, and Jericho areas to reduce the likelihood of copycat attackers.
"This was a serious attack," said IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir in a statement.
"The soldiers' swift actions prevented an even more serious attack and further harm to civilians and security forces. A large quantity of ammunition was found in the vehicle used by the terrorists to reach the scene of the attack, which was intended to be used to carry out an attack on a larger scale."
The soldiers who killed the two terrorists were part of the Ari Battalion from the IDF Search and Rescue Brigade.
Lt.-Col. L., the battalion's commander, commended the soldiers for their actions.
"The two terrorists were neutralized by the battalion’s combat soldiers, who acted with professionalism and were optimally deployed across the area as part of the effort to protect the residents of the State of Israel," L. said.
"Even during their very first operational deployment, the battalion’s soldiers demonstrated the importance of their mission and their operational readiness. Maintaining a high state of alert and operational vigilance, the soldiers engaged the enemy, acting with determination and speed to thwart the threat - all while ensuring no civilians were harmed - and successfully accomplished their mission."

In a video recorded at the scene, a soldier can be heard saying that the terrorists had been actively shooting for over 20 minutes.

Grenade exercise sparked deadly fire at Canada military base, army says
High winds propelled the blaze across the army base in Wainwright, killing four soldiers and injuring dozens more.
A fire that killed four soldiers at a western Canadian military base was sparked by an exercise using live grenades, a military official said.
The deadly fire broke out on a grenade launcher range during military exercises on Saturday, with high winds propelling it across the base, Brigadier-General Vanessa Hanrahan, commander of the Canadian Forces Military Police Group, told reporters on Thursday.
“A subsequent change in wind direction and velocity significantly increased the fire’s intensity,” she added, with the flames spreading to a training area at the Wainwright military base in Alberta.
Due to the blaze being in the “permanent danger area” of the range, firefighters were unable to directly combat it, Hanrahan added.
The fire spread on Saturday afternoon during high-intensity combat training involving Charlie Company of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.
The military base lies in the prairies, a landscape of wide, open grasslands, rolling plains and scattered groves of trees.
About 84 soldiers were split between a grenade range and an area where they practised attacks on simulated enemy positions. The fire swept into the second training area.
Four soldiers died and 39 were injured, with 27 requiring hospitalisation. The incident was one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada’s military.
The soldiers and reserve members were participating in exercises ahead of a planned deployment to Latvia, where Canadian forces have their largest international military operation.
The Wainwright base is one of the largest bases operated by the Canadian Armed Forces. It regularly hosts training exercises involving military personnel from NATO countries.
During the final months of World War II and for several months in 1946, the base was used as an internment centre for German prisoners of war.

Discarded acrylic nails, beer can enshrined in mosaic of Aussie drag icon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
04:37:25 UTC
13:37:25 KST

Australian drag icon Courtney Act glitteringly enshrined at National Portrait Gallery
Discarded fingernails, sequins, a pair of high heels, a beer can, and a dismembered Barbie doll have been used to capture the likeness of Australia's most celebrated drag queen.
A glittering new portrait of Courtney Act has been unveiled at the National Portrait Gallery in Canberra.
The large mosaic by artist Paul Yore is an eclectic assemblage of thousands of objects, each meticulously placed with tweezers, to pay tribute to the queer icon.
"I sent Paul a bag of my old fingernails and eyelashes and broken jewellery, and so I knew that it was going to be made of found objects and mixed media, but to see it hanging on the wall is absolutely amazing,"
Act said.
Courtney Act has spent more than two decades in the public eye and is an internationally celebrated drag performer, queer advocate and television personality.
She is the alter ego of Queensland-born Shane Janek, who never felt like he fit into masculine norms growing up.
"Imagine beaming back to 14-year-old me, listening to the Spice Girls, wearing my platform buffalo boots to school," Act said.
"In Brisbane in the 90s there was certainly nobody like me around and not anybody like me portrayed in the media.
"So when an institution like the National Portrait Gallery commissions a portrait of you, it feels very validating."
'Get that off my face'
Among the objects used in the portrait is an old Nokia phone — the same model used by a young Shane Janek to come out to his parents.
There is also a statue of Aphrodite, an array of Australian iconography, and a football — something Act admits she has never played.
Artist Paul Yore said he was initially intimidated when he was approached by the gallery to create the portrait.
"I've obviously followed Courtney's career for decades now and idolise her as an icon as so many of us in the queer community do," he said.
The process took him about a year, and Yore said he felt a great sense of responsibility to "get it right".
"It was one of the most challenging things I've ever had to make,"
he said.
"At different times, I did hear Courtney's voice in my head being like, 'Oi, what are you doing? Why are you putting that there? Get that off my face!'"
'Monument to queer culture'
Growing up queer in a Catholic household, Yore said he took inspiration from illuminated icons — including the Virgin Mary — to make the portrait.
National Portrait Gallery director Bree Pickering described the artwork as a "monument to queer culture".
"At a distance, this is a glossy likeness of Courtney, yet up close thousands of small details tell another story, about a big life lived without apology," she said.
The portrait is now the first artwork you see when you walk into the gallery.
"Well, they say that you should always open with a strong number," Act said.
"I think that when people turn in, and they see this, they're just going to have a smile on their face.
"There's a sense of joy about it.
"I'm very grateful that this portrait has been created of me and that it celebrates drag and queerness in all of its sparkle."

Keeping Madhubala alive: The fight for Karachi’s captive elephants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
04:27:55 UTC
13:27:55 KST

Keeping Madhubala alive: The fight for Karachi’s captive elephants
Karachi’s last two African elephants remain in captivity. Their sisters are already dead. Will they survive?
At Karachi Zoo, Jude Allen sang, You Are My Sunshine, to an elephant he could not save.
Noor Jehan, the 17-year-old African elephant, was suffering. Allen recalls massaging her legs, nursing her bedsores and spending her final days beside her.
She died on April 22, 2023, surrounded by a few activists. Allen, 45, had held various corporate jobs while volunteering as an animal caregiver since an early age.
But Noor Jehan changed something in him, he said. “The day this wild African elephant rested her painful forehead on mine, and I hugged her for the first time – it all made sense,” he tells Al Jazeera.
“I quit my job without a plan B.”
Now three years later, Allen has turned the grief of Noor Jehan’s loss into care for one of her sisters, Madhubala, who also faces major health challenges. He is part of a growing campaign of Pakistani and international activists and doctors trying to save Madhubala, a victim, her carers say, not just of medical conditions, but also of a system that is simply unable to give animals in captivity the attention and facilities they need.
The elephant sisters
In 2009, four elephant calves captured in Tanzania were brought to Pakistan, allegedly through an animal trader.
Two of them, Noor Jehan and Madhubala, were kept at the Karachi Zoo, while their sisters Sonia and Malika were taken to Safari Park, a larger facility also in Pakistan’s largest city that has both a zoo and other viewing spaces for visitors to watch animals up close.
Then, in 2020, Pakistan was gripped by the story of Kaavan, an Asian elephant that had spent 35 years in the capital city of Islamabad, eight of them alone after his companion Saheli died. Four Paws, an international animal welfare organisation, helped move Kaavan to an animal sanctuary in Cambodia, where he now lives with other elephants.
That episode also shone a light on the Karachi sisters. At the time, Allen was helping a friend with another animal shelter, and came to know Four Paws was in town. He reached out to them, and they led him to Noor Jehan and Madhubala.
By 2021, Noor Jehan’s tusk was infected. She suffered from malnutrition and stress, too.
Allen and the other activists couldn’t save Noor Jehan, but the campaign had turned into a wider cry, demanding care and justice for captive animals in the urban jungle of Karachi, the coastal home to 20 million people.
One animal in particular became the focus of attention.
Named after an iconic Indian film actress from the mid-20th century, Madhubala was now the only African elephant at the Karachi Metropolitan Corporation-run zoo. She was alone, banging her head against the gate of her enclosure, Allen recalls. “She didn’t have a friend.”
Allen says she needed company – she wanted a friend.
Tragic reunion, and a slow recovery
Allen, along with Four Paws, helped prepare her for a move to Safari Park, so she could join her sister elephants, Sonia and Malika.
Four Paws assessed the elephants and found that they needed better diets, enrichment and medical treatment. The organisation recommended reuniting them.
The reunion came in November 2024. Four Paws documented the meeting between the siblings at Safari Park. Sonia approached Madhubala first. Malika followed. The three touched one another with their trunks and drank together.
But days later, on December 8, Sonia died, aged about 19, after collapsing in her enclosure. The park’s director initially described an apparent heart failure. Subsequent findings, reported by Four Paws, identified a severe bacterial infection associated with an advanced abscess on her foot.
Amir Khalil, a Four Paws wildlife vet involved in the elephants’ care, told The Associated Press at the time that “such infections don’t spread in one day”. Four Paws linked her death to prolonged unsuitable living conditions and malnutrition.
Meanwhile, Madhubala and Malika were both diagnosed with tuberculosis, although recent examinations reported by her veterinarian have indicated that Madhubala is no longer testing positive.
Now Madhubala, 22, is recovering after losing more than 200kg (440 pounds) and becoming too weak to get up safely after lying down.
Khalil, who has also rescued wild animals from multiple conflict zones, is one of the carers who has taken charge of Madhubala’s recovery. He told Al Jazeera that Madhubala had recovered 85 percent of her ability to walk, and was a good patient: “She really wants to follow the standard operation procedure and to adhere to the programme that I put in,” he says. That includes a “water massage for the leg with high-pressure water”.
He says the required medication needs to be administered properly, and treating all the wounds – and they were getting better when he left Pakistan a few days ago.
Football friendship and ‘hurt’
For Allen, the work began with Noor Jehan.
While she was unwell, he says he visited the zoo daily, checking that the elephants received their food on time and in the right quantities. During Noor Jehan’s final 10 days, he was a near-permanent presence there, assisting the medical team however he could.
Her death became the beginning of the “I Am Noor Jehan” movement, which Allen leads for animals in captivity. The Pakistan Animal Welfare Society (PAWS), with I Am Noor Jehan, held a memorial for Noor Jehan with artists, filmmakers, and other animal activists.
Then came Madhubala. Preparing her to enter a transport crate required patience. Allen describes an elephant who could be aggressive and difficult to approach. Four Paws specialists helped him understand her needs.
But delays to the relocation disrupted the training, he says. Madhubala became frustrated and bored. Allen tried football.
He entered her enclosure, an approach he acknowledges Four Paws did not endorse. The caretakers warned him too: Madhubala wasn’t in a playful mood.
But within 20 minutes, he says, Madhubala wanted the ball.
She picked it up with her trunk and hid it between her legs. Then she began teasing her caretakers who were trying to retrieve it, offering the ball before concealing it again.
The sessions helped him build a relationship with her, he says. Madhubala began responding eagerly to training again.
“Earning her trust was the most significant accomplishment.”
That trust is especially important to Allen because he believes that Noor Jehan, and then Sonia, could have been saved.
When Sonia was unwell, Allen says he had raised concerns with local authorities about her weight loss and a swelling beneath her body. He says those warnings were not adequately acted upon.
“I felt I betrayed Sonia.”
‘What was meant to be a sanctuary became a zoo’
The deaths of two of the four African elephants in Karachi raise questions about the resources, expertise and accountability behind keeping wild animals in public institutions, experts say.
Karachi Municipal Corporation has not procured any animals in the last 20 years, and the elephants were brought in long before his time, Karachi Mayor Murtaza Wahab said, speaking to Al Jazeera.
“I’ve always said that animal welfare should be paramount. Anyone who wants to come join hands, to look after the animal, we would be ready and willing to work with them,” he said.
He argued that his team at KMC had done whatever it could to look after Madhubala with Khalil and other doctors.
“Madhubala was being treated, and the good thing is, now, Dr Khalil is also saying things are moving in the right direction and we’ve got a third-party perspective endorsing whatever was being done,” Wahab said.
But Allen says Safari Park, where Madhubala was moved after Noor Jehan’s death, has been a disappointment. Allen says he helped develop Madhubala’s new enclosure there, working on landscaping and the procedures that caregivers needed to use to help her.
Moving her was supposed to change the conditions of her life. But at Safari Park, he says, people come right up to the elephants, feed them, and treat the facility like a zoo.
“What was meant to be a sanctuary became a zoo,” he says.
Javed Maher, the top wildlife official in the government of Sindh, the province containing Karachi, says elephants and wildlife need to be in their own habitat, and people caring for them need to have knowledge of animals.
Currently, the Safari Park enclosure for elephants is about 14 hectares, roughly 35 acres, according to Four Paws.
Mahar says he offered hundreds of acres in the rural country for these elephants so they can live freely.
“Karachi Zoo, along with the majority of the zoos of the country, is not capable,” he says.
But the elephants have remained at Safari Park.
Former Islamabad High Court Chief Justice Athar Minallah, in a landmark 2020 judgement, declared that animals had rights. It was that ruling that enabled the transfer of Kaavan to Cambodia, and two Himalayan bears to a sanctuary in Jordan. The zoo in Islamabad was closed, and all 878 animals kept there were released or relocated.
“That judgement remains the law, as no appeal was filed against it,” says Minallah speaking to Al Jazeera.
“Under this jurisprudence, Madhubala has the right to live in an environment where her social, behavioural, and psychological needs can be met,” he says.
To be sure, the challenges that officials like those at KMC and elsewhere face are also real.
Pakistan already faces profound human hardship. A United Nations account published in March says more than 60 percent of people in the country cannot afford a healthy diet.
Acquiring animals that require specialist care creates obligations lasting decades. Once confined, they depend on people for every meal, for movement, companionship and treatment.
But that, say analysts, is even more reason to “stop keeping them in our custody”, says Allen.
He last saw Madhubala on October 8, when he was assisting the Four Paws team. When there are lots of people, he says, she gets distracted easily.
But she can also get jealous for Allen’s attention. “She will literally throw rocks if she can at anyone talking to me,” he smiled.

A recent BBC investigation has uncovered alarming evidence of the RSF's assault on numerous healthcare facilities in el-Fasher, Sudan.

The city’s population includes non-Arab communities that have faced attacks amid longstanding ethnic tensions, with Arab militias now forming the backbone of the RSF.The BBC investigation provides a detailed chronology of attacks on healthcare facilities during the prolonged siege, shedding further light on the conflict’s impact on medical services and civilians.

A work team has also been dispatched to the quake-hit area to guide and assist rescue and relief efforts.
The earthquake struck Baqen County of Nagqu City at 10:33 p.m. Thursday, leaving 16 people dead and 54 injured.
After the quake, a deputy commander of the State Council earthquake relief headquarters and relevant ministry officials have continued to coordinate and guide emergency response efforts.
The ministry has also guided Xizang's emergency management department in arranging for Wing Loong drone deployment to the quake-hit area for disaster reconnaissance.
China's national comprehensive fire and rescue force has dispatched a total of 350 rescuers and 83 vehicles for rescue operations.
As of 6:30 a.m. Friday, 120 rescuers and 27 vehicles had arrived in the quake-hit area, while the remaining 230 rescuers and 56 vehicles from the Xizang fire and rescue corps were en route as reinforcements, having all entered Nagqu's administrative area.
As of 4:30 a.m. Friday, authorities mobilized relief supplies at the central, regional, municipal and county levels and delivered them in batches to the quake-hit area.
The supplies included 1,000 prefabricated housing units, 3,239 tents, 2,821 folding beds and 4,280 quilts, among other essentials. ■

2 Election Commissioners complained against poll panel officer, but Cabinet Secretariat took no action: RTI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
04:12:24 UTC
13:12:24 KST

RTI reveals why ECs’ complaints against officer went unacted upon
NEW DELHI: The Cabinet Secretariat did not take any action on complaints filed by two election commissioners against an officer in the Election Commission, saying the letters were written in their “individual capacity” and did not represent the poll panel as a whole, according to documents released in response to an RTI application.Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had separately written to Cabinet Secretary T V Somanathan on July 29, raising concerns about the conduct of senior deputy election commissioner Maneesh Garg, an IAS officer appointed to the Commission by the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC) on September 2, 2024.
The letters were provided in an RTI response to activist Commodore Lokesh K Batra (retd).The Indian Express had reported in September that the two Election Commissioners approached the Cabinet Secretary after Garg issued a work allocation order that they believed could concentrate powers over changes to voter records at the central level, instead of allowing officials at the state level to handle them.In a statement on September 26, the Election Commission said the work allocation orders issued by Garg were never implemented following directions from the two Commissioners.The poll panel also said the complaints concerned an officer on deputation and not matters related to policy or the IT division.
What did the Election Commissioners allege
According to a Cabinet note included in the RTI response, both Commissioners alleged that Garg had issued an order changing the work allocation of officers senior or equivalent to him after taking charge as the link officer of the deputy election commissioner (Administration).
The Commissioners said the changes were made without consulting the Commission or the officers concerned. They also alleged that Garg acted despite repeated oral and written instructions against making such changes without prior discussion or approval from the Commission."Both the ECs have stated that Shri Garg, after assuming the charge as link officer of DEC (Admn), has issued an order regarding work allocation of equivalent and senior officers to him without discussing the revised work allocation with the Commission or the officers concerned. Further, the aforementioned ECs have stated that this has happened despite repeated oral and written instructions to all concerned officers against taking such actions without prior discussion/approval of the Commission," the Cabinet note said.The two Commissioners alleged that Garg's actions violated the chief election commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023.Joshi also said that when he sought the relevant file from the Administration Division, it was not provided to him.
Why did the Cabinet Secretariat refrain from taking action
A Cabinet note prepared on August 3 proposed seeking the chief election commissioner's opinion on the complaints."In this connection, we may request the chief election commissioner for his opinion on the issue. Accordingly, a draft DO is put up for approval, please."However, a subsequent note dated August 4 said taking action on complaints from individual Election Commissioners without an official communication from the Commission as a whole could be seen as interference in the functioning of the constitutional body."The Commission is a Constitutional Body and is insulated from executive interference by design to ensure that it functions independently and in a transparent manner. The working and functioning of the Commission are governed by the rules and guidelines of the Election Commission. The above communications are from the Election Commissioners in their individual capacity and, while they must be taken with due seriousness, they cannot be seen as a formal communication from the Commission as a whole," the note said.It added that although Garg had been appointed by the ACC, he was now an officer of the Election Commission, and his work and conduct were governed by the poll panel's rules and guidelines.The note also referred to Section 18 of the 2023 Act, which states that the Commission should conduct its business unanimously as far as possible, with any differences of opinion settled by a majority decision."Election Commissioners have sent these communications for appropriate action; however, in the absence of any official communication from the Commission as a whole, any action at this stage may be inappropriate. It may also be construed as interference in the functioning of the Constitutional Body. Hence, it would be appropriate to send acknowledgement to both Election Commissioners with a copy to PPS to CEC for information of CEC," the note said.
The draft note signed by Cabinet Secretary T V Somanathan was also marked to the secretary of the department of personnel and training and the establishment officer to keep the matter on record.The note said this would "enable it to be taken into account in future decision-making regarding the officer".Somanathan also signed an acknowledgement letter confirming receipt of the complaints and sent copies to both election commissioners.The letters were acknowledged on August 5, 2026, with copies marked to the department of personnel and training, the Establishment Officer and the office of the chief election commissioner.

WASHINGTON/BEIJING – US and South Korean officials see the chances fading of a meeting between President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in 2026, according to five people with knowledge of the situation.
Trump, the only US president to have met a North Korean leader, has been eager to jump-start talks with North Korea, but Pyongyang has shown little interest in diplomacy aimed at containing its nuclear programme.
The US has received no response from North Korea on holding a Trump-Kim meeting, and there is little time left before a regional summit in China in November where it might occur, said the five people – four of them briefed by senior officials from the US and South Korea, as well as a South Korean official.
North Korean state media has said Pyongyang would put tough conditions on agreeing to a bilateral summit, potentially including sanctions relief, even as Kim’s powerful sister has said the two leaders have an “excellent” relationship.
Trump ‘open’ to talks, nothing scheduled, official says
In August, the Republican President said he planned to meet Kim later in 2026 and that the North Korean leader had responded to his outreach.
South Korea’s intelligence agency told lawmakers late in September that there was a 50% chance of Trump and Kim meeting on the sidelines of the Nov 18 to 19 summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) group in Shenzhen, China.
But on Oct 19, Trump, who met Kim three times in his first term, downplayed the prospects of such a meeting happening during the APEC meeting or a regional summit in the Philippines, also in November.
“I get along with him very well, and I’m not sure that anybody’s asking for a meeting,” Trump told reporters at the White House.
Another South Korean official familiar with the matter said Pyongyang has made no move indicating it is preparing for a meeting with Trump. All of the people spoke on the condition of anonymity to relay private conversations.

Washington has occasionally sought the assistance of China, which has maintained close ties with Kim, in brokering talks with North Korea.

The attack and clampdown came amid heightened tensions across the Palestinian territory as Israeli settlers and soldiers engage in violent pogroms. Attacks on olive harvesters have been rife as aggression has been on the rise before Tuesday’s Israeli elections.
Declaring that the security forces had prevented a “major attack”, Netanyahu announced on social media that he had ordered security forces to immediately close Hebron and “prepare for a full lockdown across all of Judea and Samaria [the Israeli term for the West Bank] starting today”.
Israeli sources said earlier that two Palestinians driving a car with an Israeli licence plate began shooting towards soldiers near one of the many military checkpoints surrounding Hebron.
Israel’s ambulance service reported at least five Israeli soldiers were injured in addition to the two who died.
Witnesses in the area said the shooting lasted for 20 minutes, which complicated the process of evacuating the injured.
Images shared by the AFP news agency appeared to show a man holding a handgun during the fight and later lying on the ground surrounded by Israeli soldiers.
Following the incident, the military raided several areas across the occupied West Bank and detained two Palestinians.
Israeli forces locked down Hebron while Netanyahu cancelled election-related events ahead of next week’s poll.
Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir responded to the gun battle by calling for Israel to take full control of the West Bank, in which the Israeli government is encouraging the construction of numerous settlements.
“We have to act before it’s too late. The Palestinian Authority must be dismantled and demilitarised, and its terror infrastructure wiped out completely,” Ben-Gvir said in a statement on social media.
Ben-Gvir also said the attack would be enough reason to have Israel restrict Palestinians’ freedom of movement in the West Bank.
Hamas, Palestinian Islamic Jihad and the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP) praised the attack on the checkpoint, calling it a response to Israeli military operations, settler violence and Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza, and encouraged intensified confrontations with Israeli soldiers and settlers.
Israeli raids
Reporting from Ramallah, Al Jazeera’s Nida Ibrahim noted the precarious situation in the territory as settlers and Israeli security forces maintain pressure on the Palestinian population.
“This is coming at a time of great tension, not just before the Israeli elections, but there has been a ramp-up in attacks by settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank,” she said.
Israeli forces arrested 36 Palestinians during raids across the West Bank on Thursday as attacks on Palestinian farmers and their land during the olive harvest ramp up.
In Jenin governorate, Israeli forces raided towns and villages, arresting 10 Palestinians, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported, citing data from the Palestinian Prisoner’s Society.
The town of Tuqu in the Hebron governorate was also raided by soldiers who arrested former prisoner Shorok al-Badan along with five other people from other parts of Hebron, according to Wafa.
The Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission said Israeli forces also arrested 14 people in Khirbet Jawaya, a village in Masafer Yatta in Hebron governorate, while Wafa reported three other Palestinians were arrested across the governorate, quoting a security source.
In Nablus and Jerusalem governorates, three more Palestinians were arrested during Israeli raids in the village of Burin, the town of Awarta and the Qalandiya refugee camp.
Attack pattern
The Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission said it documented 17 pogroms by Israeli forces and settlers on Thursday against Palestinian farmers and their land during the olive harvest.
The incidents were recorded across West Bank governorates, including Hebron, Qalqilya, Nablus, Ramallah and el-Bireh, Jenin and Salfit.
According to the commission, the attacks included assaulting farmers, preventing them from reaching their land, stealing crops and farm equipment, and damaging and burning olive trees as well as arrests, threats at gunpoint and live fire.
The commission said the pattern represents an escalation in attacks targeting the olive harvest and undermines Palestinians’ ability to access and cultivate their land and maintain their livelihoods.
Israeli attacks on Palestinian farmers have garnered international attention and condemnation. US Democratic congressional candidate Brad Lander was briefly detained on Wednesday by the Israeli military while volunteering to help Palestinian farmers harvest olives in the West Bank.

iF Design Award 2027 calls for projects that "hold up beyond aesthetics"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23

iF Design Award 2027 calls for projects that “hold up beyond aesthetics”
This year’s edition of the prestigious iF Design Award is open for entries until 2 November, with 93 distinct categories across architecture and design.
Established in Germany in 1953 by the nonprofit iF Design Foundation, the annual award programme celebrates excellence in design and architecture, and receives nearly 10,000 entries from over 70 countries each year.
The iF Design Award is open to all, welcoming submissions from local studios and emerging creatives through to international firms and long-established brands.
The award spans 93 categories across nine design disciplines: product design, packaging, branding and communication design, service, system and process design, UX, UI, architecture, interior architecture and concepts.
While the award celebrates visually compelling design, its evaluation extends well beyond appearance. According to iF Design, every entry is assessed against five equally weighted criteria – idea, form, function, differentiation and sustainability – each accounting for 20 per cent of the overall score.
This approach reflects iF Design’s longstanding ambition to recognise projects that “hold up beyond aesthetics”, setting a high standard for design excellence across creative industries, it told Dezeen.
Through careful scrutiny, an independent jury of international design experts evaluates each project, selecting those whose ideas “break new ground” and whose impact merits recognition on the global stage.
“Based on [the] criteria, the jurors [score] each aspect of an entry and provide participants with meaningful feedback at every stage,” iF Design explained.
The award’s rigorous and transparent judging framework requires the 130-plus jury members to examine entries over two rounds of evaluations. According to iF Design, every entry receives a detailed feedback chart, regardless of award outcome.
The chart provides a breakdown of the jury’s scores across the five criteria, along with comparisons with other entries, offering objective insight into a project’s strengths and areas for improvement, backed by independent expert validation.
“We see the iF Design Award as one of the world’s most important design platforms where leading brands, start-ups, designers and creators can challenge themselves, be inspired and stand out from the competition,” said iF Design CEO Uwe Cremering.
For award recipients, that recognition carries particular significance, iF Design explained.
“Being part of this [award], surrounded by the very best in the industry, is both humbling and deeply inspiring,” said Christian Schluender, senior vice president, general manager of Global Design at Harman.
“We are truly honoured to be recognised among such an outstanding group of peers. This award means so much to us because of the calibre of the competition and the excellence it represents.”
The award’s international standing is evident in its illustrious list of former winners, which includes Spanish designer Patricia Urquiola, who received the iF Design Lifetime Achievement Award for 2026.
Last year, British architect Norman Foster was the recipient of the same award, following German industrial designer Dieter Rams in 2024.
A former iF jury member with longstanding ties to the organisation, Rams has also contributed to the iF Design Foundation’s research and initiatives on design education.
Winners of the iF Design Award 2026 also include The Grand Ring – a landmark wooden structure created for Expo 2025 Osaka by Japanese architect Sou Fujimoto, which received the Gold Award for architecture.
Meanwhile, the wireless Music Studio 5 speaker designed by Erwan Bouroullec for Samsung took home the Gold Award for product design. In 2025, the sculptural Haikou Gaoxingli Insun Cinema by One Plus Partnership was among the Gold Award winners for interior architecture.
Alongside the award, iF Design further advances design excellence and impact with its annual iF Design Trend Report, Trend Conference, and award-winning Future of XYZ interview series, while the recently launched iF Design Academy offers expert-led courses tailored specifically for design leaders.
“With the final deadline for the iF Design Award 2027 fast approaching, designers, studios and brands have one last opportunity to enter,” said iF Design.
“For those with exceptional projects deserving of international recognition, this is the final chance to have your work celebrated alongside some of the world’s most respected names in design.”
Entries to the iF Design Award 2027 close on 2 November 2026. To learn more and enter, visit ifdesign.com before the final deadline.

November 29 votes: flying start for Swiss fireworks initiative
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

November 29 votes: flying start for Swiss fireworks initiative
A strong early lead for the fireworks initiative, widespread indecision over the proposal on the taxation of married couples, and no clear majority for initiatives on funding the 13th state pension payment and on easing war materiel export rules. These are the key findings of the first Swiss Broadcasting Corporation (SBC) poll on the November 29 nationwide votes.
The campaign ahead of the November 29 votes is only just getting under way, according to experts at the gfs.bern research institute that conducted the survey on behalf of the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation (SBC), Swissinfo’s parent company.
Voters are still in the relatively early stages of forming their opinions overall and even more so among Swiss citizens living abroad, who are generally less exposed to political debate than residents of Switzerland.
Of the four proposals on the ballot, however, one appears to have already captured voters’ attention: the initiative to restrict the sale and use of noisy fireworks, known as the “Fireworks Restriction Initiative”. Three-quarters of respondents say they have already decided how they will vote.
If the vote had been held on October 11, the initiative would have been approved by nearly 70% of voters. With only 2% still undecided and the yes camp enjoying a 40-point lead, “the initiative is entering the main phase of the campaign from a position of strength”, according to gfs.bern.
The proposal commands majority support across all language regions and political camps. Backing is strongest among left-wing and Green voters (91% of Green Party supporters, 83% of Social Democratic Party supporters and 80% of Green Liberal Party supporters). However, a majority of Centre Party (67%), centre-right Radical-Liberal Party (59%) and right-wing Swiss People’s Party (53%) voters also favour the initiative.
Support is particularly strong among women, with 76% in favour compared with 60% of men.
More than 80% of respondents agree with the yes camp’s arguments that fireworks pollute the environment, cause distress to animals and increase the risk of accidents. Of these, safety concerns appear to be the most persuasive factor driving support.
13th pension payment funding backed by older people
At this stage, neither side has secured a majority on the proposal to increase value added tax (VAT) to fund the 13th state pension payment. Only just over half of respondents have made up their minds, leaving “considerable room for manoeuvre”, according to gfs.bern.
Age is emerging as the decisive factor. While the no vote is clearly ahead among 18-39-year-olds (56%), support for the measure reaches the same level among those aged over 65. This is the group that stands to benefit directly from the introduction of the 13th payment for the old-age and survivors’ insurance (OASI), which is due to be paid for the first time in December.
By contrast, income levels make little difference, despite the planned VAT increase. “Purchasing power does not come into play here,” notes Lukas Golder, a political scientist at gfs.bern.
Party affiliation reveals a familiar pattern. “The centre-left is cautiously positive, while the right is more critical,” Golder says. According to the poll, 60% of Social Democrat supporters back the proposal along with 58% of Green and Centre voters, and 56% of Green Liberal voters. Opposition is strongest among Radical-Liberals (54%) and People’s Party (68%) voters.
The arguments put forward by opponents are gaining traction. Nearly 70% of those surveyed believe that the shortfall in OASI funding should be addressed through structural reforms rather than higher taxes. At the same time, the claim that a VAT increase represents a “reasonable compromise” to fund the 13th pension payment is the argument most likely to persuade undecided voters.
Uncertainty over tax initiative
With around seven weeks remaining before the ballot, 55% of respondents say they would support an initiative to keep joint taxation for married couples and end marriage-related tax disadvantages, known as the “Fair Taxation Initiative”. Meanwhile, 34% would definitely vote against it. However, the relatively high share of undecided voters (11%) means voting intentions could still shift significantly, according to the institute.
Support is strongest among Centre Party voters (71%), followed by People’s Party supporters (64%). Radical-Liberal Party supporters are more evenly divided (52%). By contrast, only 40% of Green and Social Democratic Party supporters, and 45% of Green Liberal voters, are in favour.
The gfs.bern institute identifies an urban-rural divide, with support reaching 67% in rural areas compared with 51% in urban centres. But relationship status is the main fault line.
“Support is clearly strongest among those who feel personally affected,” explains political scientist Corina Schena, referring to people who are married or in a registered partnership. Within this group, 65% support the initiative, whereas only a minority of single people or unmarried couples would vote yes.
Swiss citizens living abroad appear more supportive of the Centre Party’s proposal than voters in Switzerland. However, political scientist Agnese Zucca says it remains too early to draw definite conclusions about this trend.
Familiar divisions over war materiel exports
The proposed amendment to the Federal Act on War Materiel, which aims to ease restrictions on Swiss arms exports to certain countries, currently falls short of securing majority support, attracting the backing of 49% of respondents.
Opinion could still move considerably. “Given the narrow balance of forces, mobilisation is likely to play an important role during the remainder of the campaign,” the institute notes.
Political divisions are already clearly visible. Support is concentrated on the right, led by Radical-Liberal voters (73%), followed by Centre Party supporters (65%), Green Liberals (60%) and People’s Party voters (57%). In contrast, more than 60% of Green and Social Democrat supporters oppose the amendment.
Swiss citizens living abroad are less supportive of the proposal than voters in Switzerland. “This difference is not surprising given that Swiss citizens abroad often tend to vote further to the left,” says Zucca.
Age and gender differences are also pronounced, “which is quite typical for military issues”, according to Schena. While voters aged 18-39 are clearly opposed to the amendment, 60% of those over 65 support it. Men tend to favour the proposal (57%), whereas a majority of women oppose it.
Regional differences are also evident. A majority of voters in German-speaking Switzerland support the amendment, while opinion remains mostly negative in French-speaking and Italian-speaking Switzerland.

Pavilions as Stances: 6 Unbuilt Proposals from the ArchDaily Community
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

In architecture, the word "pavilion" can describe an endless variety of structures. It might be defined as a principle and a typology, a freestanding structure, a temporary intervention, a gathering place in the city, or a space for experimentation. This last quality is what unites the six unbuilt projects featured here, all designed and submitted by ArchDaily readers. Here, the definition lies in their sculptural qualities and formal exploration, while their permanence and location vary according to each structure's purpose. The proposals also demonstrate another quality inherent to the pavilion: the intention to symbolically represent a stance. Their exploration of form and material thus also reflects a search for a sense of boundary, wonder, or a shared future.
Here, we look at project ideas in South Korea, Iran, Thailand, Peru, and Kazakhstan. Though they stand as isolated, independent structures, they connect symbolically to their cultural contexts through references to traditional architecture, a relationship with local productive activities, or a deeply rooted idea of landscape and nature. Some of the pavilions stand as a human imprint in dialogue with nature, whether as a space for pause, entry, or restoration. Others interpret architecture as a catalyst for action, facilitating activities, providing infrastructure, or bringing living beings together in a shared pursuit. Despite their differences, the structures as a whole break into the landscape as a point of contrast, appealing to our capacity for wonder.

Pentagon Bets Big on Drone-Killing APKWS Laser-Guided Rockets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
03:51:07 UTC
12:51:07 KST

The Pentagon has concluded a new agreement to buy laser-guidance kits that turn rockets into drone-killing weapons.
BAE Systems and the Defense Department announced a framework deal of up to seven years for 25,000 Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System guidance kits annually for the U.S. military.
Another 10,000 kits could be produced each year for international customers, who are increasingly interested in the system.
APKWS is a laser-guidance kit that converts 2.75-inch unguided rockets into precision munitions. It is currently fielded by the U.S. Air Force, Army, Marine Corps, and Navy, as well as U.S. allies.
APKWS has become the preferred method for U.S. warplanes to down drones fired by Iran and Iranian-backed militias in the Middle East over the past few years. But it is not just an air-to-air weapon. APKWS munitions can also be fitted to various platforms for air-to-surface, surface-to-surface, and surface-to-air use.
APKWS is an attractive capability for the Pentagon because of its low cost—roughly $35,000, according to officials. That gives the Air Force a way to shoot down drones without expending costly air-to-air missiles.
For compraison, Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missiles cost roughly $1 million each, and AIM-9s cost hundreds of thousands of dollars depending on the variant. The most capable model is the AIM-9X, which costs around $500,000. APKWS was first tested in an air-to-air role in 2019. The Air Force did not pursue the idea heavily until a few years later, before fielding it in combat in 2024.
“We were on the wrong side of the cost curve in our munitions employment,” former Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. David Allvin said in an interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine.
“The great thing about it is that there wasn’t a formal requirement set out for this. This was sort of organic. People started figuring it out without it being a big program of record,” Allvin added. “Good thing they did.”
Now, just a few years later, the Pentagon is betting big on APKWS’ future.
APKWS scored its first combat air-to-air kill in the fall of 2024 in the Middle East by F-16 from the 510th Fighter Squadron at Aviano Air Base, Italy, current and former officials told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
When the 480th Fighter Squadron from Spangdahlem Air Base, Germany, deployed to the Middle East soon after, they scored dozens more aerial kills—108 in total using all weapons during their deployment.
By the spring of 2025, the Air Force began flight testing APKWS on F-15E Strike Eagles, and fielded the capability in the Middle East within roughly a week. Around the same time, U.S. Air Forces in Europe also fielded APKWS for its air-to-air training. The system has also been on A-10s to shoot down drones.
The APKWS has its origins in the decades-old Hydra rocket system and was first used as precision air-to-ground weapon during the Global War on Terror, deploying in 2012.
It was adapted to serve in an air-to-air role when Air Forces Central, commanded by then-Lt. Gen. Alexus G. Grynkewich from 2022-2024, began looking for an alternative to using costly air-to-air missiles against drones. CENTCOM and the Air Force supported the effort.
The framework agreement is intended as a signal of what the Pentagon plans to buy, subject to specific contracts and the congressional funding needs for those deals.
BAE says the new agreement will help expand production at its facilities in Hudson, N.H., and Austin, Texas.
“This agreement highlights the importance of sustained investment in critical munitions to strengthen readiness and equip forces for evolving operational needs,” BAE Systems president and CEO Tom Arseneault said in a statement.
“By securing multiyear demand, this agreement keeps production lines running at capacity, provides our forces with interceptor inventory, and flips the cost calculus in the taxpayer’s favor,” Michael Duffey, undersecretary of defense for acquisition and sustainment, added.
APKWS can also be used in a ground-to-air role, as the modifications needed to hit aerial targets are largery limited to software and the use of a proximity fuse. It can be fitted to anti-air systems such as Sierra Nevada Corporation’s BRAWLR, which is deployed overseas by the U.S. military, and L3Harris’ VAMPIRE, which is used by Ukraine and is being supplied to the U.S. It has been fitted to other nations’ fighter platforms and has been tested on the MQ-9 Reaper as well.
“This drone problem is not going away,” retired Lt. Gen. Derek C. France, who led Air Forces Central from April 2024-August 2026, said in a recent interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine. “It’s accelerating in tactics, speed, advancements, and the numbers. That’s the direction that we’re going.”

How scientists count Kazakhstan’s snow leopards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
03:47:13 UTC
12:47:13 KST

How scientists count Kazakhstan’s snow leopards
How do you count an animal that rarely lets itself be seen? Scientists use camera traps and DNA to tell snow leopards apart. Today, October 23, marks International Day of the Snow Leopard. Qazinform News Agency explores how researchers count these elusive cats in Kazakhstan.
Built to stay out of sight
A snow leopard’s gray-white coat blends into rocky slopes. Its broad paws help it cross snow, while its long tail provides balance. Wrapped around the body, that tail also keeps the animal warm.
Snow leopards usually live alone and are most active at dawn and dusk. Their home ranges can span hundreds of square kilometers. Cubs stay with their mothers until they become independent at around two years old.
In Kazakhstan, their habitats stretch across the country’s southern, southeastern, and eastern mountains. These include the Tien Shan, Zhetysu Alatau, Altai, and Saur-Tarbagatai ranges.
Recognizing the same cat
Ten photographs do not necessarily mean ten snow leopards. The same animal may walk past several cameras or return to one spot.
Scientists tell them apart by their spots. Each snow leopard has a unique pattern. Matching those patterns across photographs helps researchers count cats without counting one twice.
In Kazakhstan, a UNDP-backed project installed 294 camera traps between 2018 and 2024. The cameras offer glimpses of lives researchers rarely witness themselves.
In March 2021, UNDP shared footage of a snow leopard family in Zhambyl Region. Three cats appeared on cameras in the Merke Forestry area.
At Kolsai Kolderi National Park, a camera recorded a snow leopard walking at night.
In Altyn-Emel, researchers found evidence in 2021 that snow leopards were raising young. According to UNDP, better protection, recovering habitats, and more prey helped the cats return.
Where do they go next?
A camera records a snow leopard passing by. A satellite collar helps scientists follow its journey beyond that spot.
Kazakhstan began using these collars in November 2021, starting with a cat in Altyn-Emel. By the end of 2023, researchers had fitted 11 animals with tracking devices. They worked in the Northern and Central Tien Shan.
The cats crossed borders, too. Tracking revealed routes into China and Kyrgyzstan. Knowing these routes helps scientists understand which areas need protection beyond individual parks.
In 2024, four parks and reserves in Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan agreed to work together. Their five-year agreement covers research and protection of the habitats these cats share.
Counting cats through DNA
A snow leopard does not have to appear on camera to leave identifying evidence. Researchers can extract DNA from hair and scat to identify animals and investigate family relationships.
A 2011 study in Nepal demonstrated this approach. Researchers tested 71 scat samples suspected to come from snow leopards. They confirmed snow leopard DNA in 19 samples. Ten yielded enough genetic information to identify nine cats.
Two samples found around four kilometers apart came from the same animal. Matching their DNA prevented a double count. Researchers identified three males and six females without capturing them.
The results established a minimum count, not the area’s entire population. Some samples belonged to other carnivores. Others contained DNA too degraded for analysis, highlighting the need for careful storage.
DNA can also reveal a species’ past. In 2025, Stanford University researchers and collaborators, including the Snow Leopard Trust, reported findings from genome research. Their work increased the number of sequenced snow leopard genomes from four to 41.
The team found exceptionally low genetic diversity. Their analysis suggested that snow leopard populations remained small for at least 900,000 years. Limited diversity could make adapting to environmental change harder.
How many live in Kazakhstan?
Kazakhstan had an estimated 80–100 snow leopards by 1995, according to UNDP’s 2024 overview. Habitat degradation, human pressure, and declining prey had reduced their numbers.
A UN publication from May 2026 cites estimates of 130 animals in 2019 and 152–189 by 2024. UNDP’s 2024 assessment placed around 70% of the country’s snow leopards within protected areas.
The species remains classified as vulnerable by the International Union for Conservation of Nature. Poaching, declining prey, habitat loss, and climate change continue to threaten its survival.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that researchers fitted a snow leopard named Altai with a satellite collar. The procedure took place at Katon-Karagay National Park, a first for Kazakhstan’s Southern Altai. The device will help scientists track its movements and identify key habitats.

40 years later, Chernobyl's nuclear fallout is not what scientists expected
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
03:35:13 UTC
12:35:13 KST

40 years later, Chernobyl's nuclear fallout is not what scientists expected
- Date:
- October 22, 2026
- Source:
- Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf
- Summary:
- Forty years after the Chornobyl disaster, tiny radioactive particles still linger in the soil, carrying a dangerous legacy. Using powerful X-rays, scientists discovered that some of these particles have remained surprisingly stable, trapping radioactive substances inside instead of releasing them into the environment.
- Share:
Four decades after the Chernobyl (known today as Chornobyl) nuclear disaster, microscopic radioactive particles remain scattered throughout the surrounding soil. The explosions that devastated the reactor released enormous quantities of debris, leaving behind contamination that continues to pose serious health risks. Even after 40 years, particles measuring just 8 to 50 micrometers remain highly radioactive, and entering affected areas still requires protective clothing.
Scientists have now taken a closer look at these tiny remnants and uncovered a surprising finding: some have preserved much of their original internal structure despite decades of exposure to the environment.
"There are three classes of these particles," explains Tobias Weissenborn, a physicist and doctoral candidate at Leibniz University Hannover. "First, there are particles that are chemically and physically still very similar to the nuclear fuel uranium dioxide. Then, there are particles that are partially or fully encased in, or completely fused with, their zirconium layer."
The second category originated during the extreme temperatures reached inside the reactor. As the nuclear fuel melted, it combined with zirconium, a highly resistant metal used in the fuel's protective outer layer.
"The third type of particle was created when the graphite-moderator caught fire," Weissenborn adds.
Under normal operating conditions, the graphite moderator slows fast neutrons, helping sustain the nuclear chain reaction. During the disaster, however, the graphite ignited and continued burning for ten days.
"In the process, the fuel oxidized into various uranium oxides" - such as U3O8.
Unlike more stable materials, this uranium oxide is mechanically fragile and can readily break apart into microscopic fragments. Wind can then carry these radioactive particles through the environment, where inhaling them presents serious health hazards.
Scientists Examine Chornobyl's Radioactive Dust in Unprecedented Detail
Despite decades of research, scientists still do not fully understand why radioactive particles from Chornobyl break down at different speeds. As these materials weather, they can produce several forms of uranium oxide, making their long term behavior difficult to predict.
Investigating these changes requires exceptionally precise equipment, including synchrotron X-ray diffraction, a technique that reveals the arrangement of atoms inside crystalline materials.
Dr. Christoph Hennig, a crystallographer at the Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf (HZDR), has now completed the first successful structural analysis of radioactive fragments of this kind at the Rossendorf Beamline in Grenoble.
Working with Weissenborn, Hennig analyzed six particles recovered from the Chornobyl region. By identifying the different crystalline phases within them, the researchers gained information that could help determine how quickly radioactive substances escape into the surrounding environment.
"The colleagues from Hanover and I used various methods to isolate the particles from Ukrainian soil samples and attach them to tungsten electrodes," Weissenborn explains.
Because the samples were highly radioactive, they had to be enclosed within several layers of containment before being transported to Grenoble. There, Hennig's research team used X-ray diffraction to examine their internal structures by measuring how X-rays scattered as they passed through the material.
"First, we had to figure out how to examine the particle structure," Christoph Hennig explains. "Ultimately, we fully rotated the particles in an X-ray beam focused down to 100 micrometers - about the thickness of a human hair. We measured each particle from 2,000 different angles to seamlessly capture all the reflections."
The measurements allowed the scientists to distinguish different uranium oxide phases within the radioactive fragments, revealing details that had previously been inaccessible.
A Surprising Discovery About 40-Year-Old Nuclear Fallout
The results revealed something unexpected. Despite spending four decades in the environment, the nuclear fuel inside the six examined particles had retained much of its original crystal structure.
This suggests that at least some of the radioactive debris produced by the Chornobyl disaster is more chemically stable than researchers previously believed.
That stability could have important environmental implications. Rather than rapidly releasing radioactive substances, the particles appear capable of retaining fission products within their structures. If this behavior occurs more widely, it could help limit the movement of radioactive contaminants into nearby soil and water.
However, the researchers emphasize that their findings should not be interpreted as evidence that Chornobyl's radioactive contamination is becoming harmless.
"However, every single particle has a different structure," warns Weissenborn, "and our experiment only studied six such particles from two different locations."
The relatively small sample means the findings cannot yet establish how radioactive particles behave throughout the entire contaminated region. To understand their stability more comprehensively, scientists would need to investigate many additional particles collected from a much broader range of locations.
Why Chornobyl's Radioactive Legacy Remains Unpredictable
Even with substantially more data, predicting the long term dangers of Chornobyl's radioactive debris would remain challenging. Individual particles can differ in composition, structure, and resistance to environmental weathering, potentially affecting when they release radioactive materials.
"And even if we obtained some averages at some point, we still wouldn't be able to make universal statements about health risks in the region," Weissenborn cautions. "Because even if the particles decay in a largely uniform patten, there will always be outliers, more persistent particles, that will release radionuclides at a later point in time."
These persistent particles could continue releasing radioactive substances long after other remnants have broken down, complicating efforts to assess future contamination and health risks.
For that reason, the new findings do not suggest that restrictions on the Chornobyl Exclusion Zone can be removed anytime soon.
Research into the disaster's enduring consequences is continuing. Weissenborn and Hennig are already conducting additional experiments focused on highly radioactive transuranic phases found in the remaining debris. Their work could provide a clearer picture of how Chornobyl's nuclear materials change over time and how long their environmental effects may persist.
Journal Reference:
- Tobias Weissenborn, Christoph Hennig, Laura Leifermann, Paul Hanemann, Eleanor Lawrence Bright, Florian Meurer, Aaron Lehnert, Kristina Kvashnina, Clemens Walther. X-ray diffraction phase analysis of single hot particles from Chornobyl. Journal of Hazardous Materials, 2026; 505: 141533 DOI: 10.1016/j.jhazmat.2026.141533

CANBERRA, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Surging solar output drove Australia's renewable energy generation to a third-quarter record high from July to September, the market operator said on Friday.
The Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) said in its energy dynamics report that renewables supplied 44.3 percent of national electricity market generation from July 1 through Sept. 30, surpassing the previous third-quarter record of 41.8 percent set in 2025.

The report noted that underlying national electricity market demand grew 1.3 percent to a new third-quarter high of 25,471 MW. It attributed the rise to ongoing electrification, higher industrial demand and increasing data center consumption. ■

KDDI said Yasuhiro Ochi, head of its Mongolian subsidiary Mobicom, and two other executives were inside the reserve when the incident occurred. The company said it took the fire's considerable impact on Mongolia's natural environment "extremely seriously."

KDDI said Mobicom executives had entered the protected area by vehicle to conduct tests on its 4G communications network and had obtained official permission to enter the area. The company has not disclosed further details about how the fire started.
However, several Mongolian media outlets have questioned whether the group had another purpose for entering the reserve, including the possibility of hunting or fishing for an endangered fish species. Government officials have pledged to pursue legal accountability and seek compensation for the damage, according to media reports.
KDDI said the company had notified the border security agency in advance and that the group's movements on the day followed a designated route, adding that it understood the visit was intended for 4G network testing but would refrain from further comment pending the results of an official investigation.
Preliminary figures released Tuesday by Mongolia's Ministry of Environment and Climate Change showed that the fire burned about 530,000 hectares, including approximately 470,000 hectares within the protected area, equivalent to 79.8 percent of the reserve's total area.
The ministry has launched a comprehensive assessment of the ecological and environmental damage caused by the blaze. ■
