In Florida, Trump vows to deal with Cuba after Iran gets settled
FORT MYERS, Florida - US President Donald Trump on Oct 23 used a campaign rally in Florida, where Cuban Americans are a potent voting bloc, to vow to address his concerns about Cuba once the Iran war is settled.
In a 90-minute speech in Fort Myers, Trump repeated more military action against Iran may lie ahead as he tries to address the causes of a spike in oil prices that has put Republicans on the defensive ahead of the Nov 3 midterm elections.
With an eye toward the senior Americans who live in Florida, Trump said he planned to spend US$250 million to hire at least 5,000 new nurses in elder care facilities all across America.
While the Iran war has no end in sight, Trump talked tough about Cuba, part of a pattern of putting pressure on the communist government there after ousting the leader of Venezuela early this year.
Trump, who won 68% of the Cuban-American vote in Florida in the 2024 election, said American naval forces from Iran will stop at Cuba on the way home.
“We’ll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They’ll raise up their hands, and then we’re going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal,” he said.
Secretary of State Rubio, a former US senator from Florida, has been handling much of the Cuba-related policy for Trump.
“To those who seek to create positive change in Cuba - now is the time,” Rubio said on X on Oct 23, urging those disappointed by Cuba’s government “to create the change you desire through a discrete partnership with the CIA”. His post did not elaborate.
Trump’s rally was intended to boost the electoral prospects of Florida Republican Representative Byron Donalds, who is running for governor against Democrat David Jolly.
His speech, the latest in a near-daily blitz of campaign rallies in largely friendly areas, rambled from topic to topic such as the size of his crowds and his White House renovations.
Trump has increased pressure on Cuba in his second term. 
In September, he labelled Cuba a “failed state” at the UN General Assembly and said, “Freedom will be coming to Cuba”, prompting a walkout by the Cuban delegation.
Trump has openly stated that his goal is to fundamentally change Cuba’s government. A US-imposed oil blockade has put the country under severe strain as it contends with fuel shortages and blackouts exacerbated by failing infrastructure.
UN human rights experts have condemned the oil blockade as a violation of international law while rights advocates say the Trump administration’s threats have echoed an imperialist approach. REUTERS

Judge puts off decision on Charlie Kirk murder trial date, media reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
16:56:51 UTC
01:56:51 KST

Judge puts off decision on Charlie Kirk murder trial date, media reports
A Utah judge on Oct 23 said he needed more time to decide when to start the trial of Tyler Robinson, the man accused of killing prominent right-wing activist Charlie Kirk more than a year ago, media reported.
At a hearing in Provo, Utah, District Court Judge Tony Graf heard arguments from defence lawyers, prosecutors and a lawyer for Kirk’s widow, Erika Kirk, before saying he needed to consider their positions. He set a new hearing for Nov 9, television station KUTV reported.
Robinson, 23, has pleaded not guilty to seven counts, including aggravated murder, for allegedly shooting Kirk as he held one of his trademark debates at Utah Valley University in Orem. Robinson’s lawyers expect a six-to-seven-month trial.
Robinson’s attorneys had asked for a late 2029 trial to give them time to challenge Utah’s request for the death penalty, gather additional evidence and seek a change of venue, among other issues, according to a scheduling memo.
Prosecutors, meanwhile, sought a date of Jan 31, 2028 to start what they expect to be a 17-week trial, according to their scheduling memo.
In a separate filing, Erika Kirk said the defence request was “grossly out of line with comparable cases” and requested the trial start no later than Oct 4, 2027.
Shortly before the Oct 23 hearing, US President Donald Trump, with whom Kirk had been allied, slammed Graf’s handling of the case in a social media post, saying it should be tried within a month and Graf was asking “questions that people already know the answer to”.
Kirk was a polarising figure in US politics. He was admired by conservatives for mobilising young voters around his Christian and right-wing views. Opponents criticised his rhetoric on immigration, race, gender and other social issues.
Prosecutors allege Robinson targeted Kirk for his opposition to gay marriage and transgender rights.
Defence attorney Richard Novak has said Kirk spoke “hatefully” about people who did not have traditional gender identities or were not heterosexual, but there was no evidence Robinson opposed those views. REUTERS
